0.title: Psalms: From Blessed Is the Man to Praise the LORD
0.overview:
The message. The Psalms are God’s word given to us as our own words. In them God teaches his people how to speak to him in every condition of life: guilty or forgiven, afraid or glad, betrayed, homesick, or full of thanks. Under all of it lies one great fact: “The LORD reigns” (Psalm 93:1), and he has set his anointed King on Zion, so that “Blessed are all who take refuge in him” (Psalm 2:12). Because his steadfast love endures for ever, his people may tell him the truth, and the book moves, slowly and not without tears, from lament to praise. Luther called it a little Bible; Calvin called it an anatomy of all the parts of the soul.

Background: the writers. The book gathers one hundred and fifty psalms from many hands. Seventy-three carry the name of David, “the sweet psalmist of Israel” (2 Samuel 23:1), who appointed Levites to lead Israel’s singing (1 Chronicles 16:7). Others are ascribed to Asaph, his chief musician (50; 73–83), the sons of Korah, a family of temple singers (eleven psalms, among them 42 and 84), Heman (88), Ethan (89), Solomon (72; 127) and Moses (90); thirty-four have no title. Some of David’s titles name the moment he wrote, such as Psalm 3, “when he fled from Absalom his son”.

Can we trust the titles? Many scholars think the titles were added later by those who collected the psalms, and note that the Hebrew behind “of David” can mean by, for, or belonging to. But the titles stand in the Hebrew text and were already there when the psalms were translated into Greek, well before Christ. Jesus said that “David himself, in the Holy Spirit” spoke Psalm 110 (Mark 12:36), and the apostles name David as the author of Psalms 16 and 32 (Acts 2:25; Romans 4:6). This commentary’s view is that the titles are trustworthy guides.

When and where. The psalms span many centuries: from Moses, through David’s reign (about 1010 to 970 BC) and Solomon’s temple, to the fall of Jerusalem in about 586 BC, when the exiles sat “by the waters of Babylon” and wept (Psalm 137:1), and on to the return. They were gathered in stages (Psalm 72:20 marks the end of an earlier collection), and the whole probably took its final shape after the exile. These were songs for the temple and the road. Pilgrims sang the Songs of Ascents (120–134) going up to Jerusalem for the pilgrim feasts, and Psalms 113–118 were sung at Passover, very likely the hymn Jesus and his disciples sang that last night (Matthew 26:30).

The kind of writing. This is poetry, meant to be sung. Hebrew poetry rhymes thoughts rather than sounds: a second line repeats, deepens or answers the first, as in “How long, O LORD? Will you forget me forever? How long will you hide your face from me?” (Psalm 13:1). It thinks in pictures (rock, shield, shepherd, refuge), so read it slowly and let it be felt. Laments are the most common kind; there are also songs of thanksgiving, hymns, royal psalms about the king, wisdom psalms, and acrostics such as Psalm 119, whose stanzas run through the Hebrew alphabet. Because the Hebrew often counts a title as verse 1, its verse numbers can run one ahead of ours.

How the book makes its case. The Psalter has a shape. It is divided into five books, perhaps echoing the five books of Moses, each of the first four closing with a blessing on God (Psalms 41:13; 72:19; 89:52; 106:48). Psalms 1 and 2 stand at the gate: the man who delights in God’s law, and the King set on Zion. Books One and Two [1–72] are mostly David’s, many of them cries of a king hunted and betrayed, yet trusting. Book Three [73–89] darkens: Asaph nearly loses his faith (73), the temple lies in ruins (74), and the book ends with David’s crown “in the dust” (Psalm 89:39). Book Four [90–106] answers with Moses, “Lord, you have been our dwelling place in all generations” (Psalm 90:1), and with psalms that cry “The LORD reigns” (93; 96–99): before Israel had a king, God was King. Book Five [107–150] gathers the people home with thanksgiving, sets the priest-king of Psalm 110 on the throne, delights in God’s word (119), climbs the Songs of Ascents, and ends in five psalms of “Praise the LORD!” The book that opens “Blessed is the man” (Psalm 1:1) closes “Let everything that has breath praise the LORD!” (Psalm 150:6).

The psalms that curse. Some psalms ask God to destroy enemies in terrible terms (35, 69, 109, 137), and readers rightly ask how a follower of Jesus can pray them. Some say Christians should not. But Jesus and the apostles quote them as Scripture (John 15:25; Acts 1:20), and they are not private revenge: they are the cries of people who suffered real injustice and handed their cause to God, as Paul commands: “never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God” (Romans 12:19). This commentary’s view is that a Christian may pray them as cries for God’s justice against unrepentant evil, while praying first for the enemy’s repentance, as Christ prayed for those who crucified him (Luke 23:34).

Where it leads: to Christ. Jesus said that “everything written about me in the Law of Moses and the Prophets and the Psalms must be fulfilled” (Luke 24:44). The Psalms lead to him first by promise. God swore that David’s son would reign for ever (89), and the royal psalms speak of a King greater than any who sat in Jerusalem. Hebrews applies Psalm 2:7 to Jesus: “You are my Son, today I have begotten you” (Hebrews 1:5). Psalm 110:1, “Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool”, is quoted and echoed in the New Testament more than any other Old Testament verse, and this commentary holds that Christ reigns there now. They lead by pattern too: David, anointed yet hunted and betrayed, prayed as the suffering king, and his prayers reach their full meaning in his greater Son. On the cross Jesus cried, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matthew 27:46, from Psalm 22:1), and died praying Psalm 31:5: “Father, into your hands I commit my spirit!” (Luke 23:46). And they expose a need: no one but Jesus is the blessed man of Psalm 1. Not every psalm is a prophecy of him, but every psalm shows the God we meet in him, and Hebrews puts Psalm 22 on his lips as he leads his people’s praise: “I will tell of your name to my brothers; in the midst of the congregation I will sing your praise” (Hebrews 2:12). So Christians pray the psalms with Christ and in him.

For us. You do not have to be strong to pray the Psalms; most were written by people who were not. They give you words when you have none, and leave to tell God the truth, because in Christ he has welcomed you. If you are guilty, begin with Psalm 51 or 130: “But with you there is forgiveness” (Psalm 130:4). If you are afraid, begin with 23 or 91; if grieving and wordless, Psalm 88 has the words. This commentary holds that the church may sing faithful hymns that name Christ, though some Reformed churches sing only psalms, but the Psalms deserve a far larger place in our singing than most churches give them. Keep going: the book is heading toward praise, and so is everyone who takes refuge in the King.

1.title: Blessed Is the Man
1.text: <sup>1</sup>Blessed is the man who walks not in the counsel of the wicked, nor stands in the way of sinners, nor sits in the seat of scoffers;<sup>2</sup>but his delight is in the law of the LORD, and on his law he meditates day and night.<sup>3</sup>He is like a tree planted by streams of water that yields its fruit in its season, and its leaf does not wither. In all that he does, he prospers.<sup>4</sup>The wicked are not so, but are like chaff that the wind drives away.<sup>5</sup>Therefore the wicked will not stand in the judgment, nor sinners in the congregation of the righteous;<sup>6</sup>for the LORD knows the way of the righteous, but the way of the wicked will perish.
1.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 1 stands at the gate of the whole Psalter, and with Psalm 2 forms its doorway (see the introduction). Before a single prayer or song, it sets two ways of life before the reader and asks which one we will walk.

The message. God declares that the happy life belongs to the one who is rooted in his word rather than in the world’s advice, and he says plainly that there are only two roads, ending in two places. The life that delights in God’s word is planted, fruitful and known by God; the life without him has no weight and will not stand in the judgment. The difference rests finally not on the man’s strength but on the LORD’s knowing.

Why it was said. Israel sang the psalms in every condition, often among people who mocked faith and seemed to prosper (see the introduction). Psalm 1 tells them, before they begin, that the scoffers’ success is chaff and that God’s word is the water a life is meant to grow by. It also teaches them to read all that follows as God’s instruction, not merely as human feeling.

How the chapter makes its case. The blessed man is described first by what he refuses, the slow slide from walking to standing to sitting in the company of the wicked (v. 1); then by what he loves, the law of the LORD, turned over day and night (v. 2); then by what he becomes, a tree planted by water that bears fruit in its season (v. 3). The wicked are set against him in one curt line: chaff, blown away, with no footing in the judgment and no place among God’s people (vv. 4–5). The last verse gives the reason under both ends: the LORD knows the way of the righteous, while the other way perishes of itself (v. 6).

Where it leads. To Christ, first by the need it exposes: no one but Jesus has ever been the man of verse 1, who could say, “I delight to do your will, O my God; your law is within my heart” (Psalm 40:8). It also leads by pattern: the righteous man was hanged on a tree and took the curse that belonged to the wicked (Galatians 3:13), so that rootless people might be planted in him and share his blessing. Psalm 2 completes the thought: “Blessed are all who take refuge in him” (Psalm 2:12).

For us. The psalm asks whose voice is in your ear when you decide, and whether God’s word is a rule book you put up with or a Father’s teaching you delight in. If you find you are not the blessed man, run to the one who is. Joined to him you are planted, and his Spirit grows the delight.
1.theology:
The psalm is a beatitude, a declaration of blessing, before it is a set of instructions. The blessed man is defined by what he loves and where he is rooted, and the tree is planted, set there by another hand (v. 3). Delight comes first and meditation follows (v. 2): this is grace at work, not willpower.

There are two ways and no third, and the end is a verdict: the wicked will not stand in the judgment (v. 5). The ground of it all is that the LORD knows his people as his own (v. 6; John 10:14). And the portrait is finally of Christ, the only man who fits verse 1, who took the curse of the wicked on himself (Gal 3:13) so that people with no root could be planted. Psalms 1 and 2 form one doorway, opening with Blessed is the man (1:1) and closing with Blessed are all who take refuge in him (2:12).
1.examples: Nobody plans to sit with scoffers; the descent from walking to standing to sitting is made by small steps. The words day and night were first said to Joshua on the eve of a war (Josh 1:8), and a life fed on God's word still bears fruit in its season, winters included.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–3 — Planted by Streams of Water
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The blessed life is defined by its roots, not its achievements. The psalm opens with a congratulation, not a command, and paints the happy man in three strokes. He refuses the gradual slide into the company of those who ignore and then mock God, from walking to standing to sitting (v. 1). He delights in the LORD’s instruction and keeps turning it over, so that it shapes him from within (v. 2). And so he is like a tree someone else has planted beside channels of water: fruitful in its season, green in drought, and reaching the end God intends (v. 3). What he refuses and what he loves come before what he becomes.
verseByVerse.theology: The blessed life is described not by what it achieves but by where it is rooted and what it loves.

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed is the man who walks not in the counsel of the wicked, nor stands in the way of sinners, nor sits in the seat of scoffers;
verseByVerse.commentary:
God calls happy the one who will not let people who ignore him set the course of his life, and he shows how gradually that course gets set.

Blessed is the man. The Psalter opens with a word of congratulation, not a command. Blessed is ashre, a plural form that works like an exclamation: O the happinesses of that man! Before Israel sings anything, she is shown a life and asked whether she wants it.

Walks not in the counsel of the wicked. He is described first by what he does not do, in three lines that walk downhill: walks, then stands, then sits; passing through, then stopping to listen, then pulling up a chair. The company worsens at the same rate, from the wicked, to sinners, to scoffers, who have got past arguing about God to laughing at him. Nobody plans the third step. It is reached by taking the first one often enough.

Happiness comes sideways. Our culture has made happiness a project, planned, measured and pursued head-on, and we are not noticeably happier for it. John Stuart Mill found this out in a breakdown as a young man, and wrote in his Autobiography, “Ask yourself whether you are happy, and you cease to be so.” The psalm agrees, and goes deeper. It opens with happiness, for the Bible is not against our joy, but it never tells this man to pursue happiness. It shows him delighting in something outside himself, the word of God, and happiness arrives while he is looking the other way. That overturns two opposite mistakes: the moralist thinks God wants duty instead of joy, and the modern seeker thinks joy is found by attending to the self. Both are still looking at themselves. The one man who lived this psalm perfectly went to the cross “for the joy that was set before him” (Hebrews 12:2), and the joy included us. Joined to him, we are given what we could never chase down: a happiness that comes from being loved, and from loving him back.

In a real week. Whose counsel actually shapes what you decide? Not whom you agree with on paper, but whose voice is in your ear at the moment of choosing: that is the counsel you walk in.

Is the blessed man Christ or every believer? Both. The psalm describes what every believer is called to be, and only one man has ever been it perfectly. Those who trust in Christ are blessed in him, and are being made like him.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “man” portrays a representative godly person.

verseByVerse.quote: but his delight is in the law of the LORD, and on his law he meditates day and night.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The blessed person loves God’s word and keeps turning it over, and the love comes before the effort.

His delight is in the law of the LORD. The engine is not willpower but delight: he is not gritting his teeth over a rule book. And meditates is hagah, a word for a low, muttering sound; Isaiah uses it of a lion growling over its prey (Isaiah 31:4). It is a man chewing over a sentence of God all day, under his breath, until it gets into his bones.

Day and night. The phrase comes from the charge given to Joshua on the edge of the conquest (Joshua 1:8): what was said to a general before a war is now said of any blessed man.

What the law of the LORD is. Say “law” to most people and they hear a list of rules, handed down from above and mostly saying no. The Hebrew word, torah, is wider and warmer. It means instruction, the teaching a father gives a child he loves, and it covers everything God has said: his story, his promises and his commands together. That is why a man can delight in it. We tend to assume that freedom means nobody telling us anything. Timothy Keller often pointed out that a fish is free only in water: set it free on the grass and it dies. God’s word is the water we were made to live in. See Law in the Theological Dictionary.

Delight first. The order is the difference between dutiful religion and living faith. The psalm does not say he meditates until he learns to delight, but that he delights, and therefore meditates. You cannot manufacture that affection any more than you can order yourself to find something beautiful. You can ask God for it, and put yourself where it is given, in front of his word: the Spirit who writes the law on the heart gives the delight (Jeremiah 31:33; Ezekiel 36:26–27).

The one who loved it without a gap. Only one man has ever loved God’s word perfectly, and the Psalms let us hear him: “I delight to do your will, O my God; your law is within my heart” (Psalm 40:8). He kept it in our place, and now his Spirit writes it on our hearts. So this week, before you open the Bible, do not ask, “What am I not allowed to do?” Ask, “What is my Father telling me?”

verseByVerse.quote: He is like a tree planted by streams of water that yields its fruit in its season, and its leaf does not wither. In all that he does, he prospers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A life rooted in God’s word is like a tree someone else has planted by water: it bears fruit in God’s time, stays green in drought, and reaches the end God intends.

Like a tree planted by streams of water. Planted (shatul) is stronger than it sounds: it is used of a tree set out deliberately, put in place by another hand. Someone dug it in beside the irrigation channels, where it cannot fail for drought. The tree does not make the water. It stands where the water is.

That yields its fruit in its season. Three results follow, and the first has a mercy in it. Fruit comes in its season, not every month and not on demand; there are winters in a fruitful life, and the psalm allows for them. The leaf does not wither, because the roots reach something that does not dry up. And in all that he does, he prospers, which is not a promise of money, for this same man is surrounded by scoffers. It is the promise that his life reaches the end God intends.

The tree through the Bible. Another psalm plants the same tree indoors: “They are planted in the house of the LORD; they flourish in the courts of our God. They still bear fruit in old age” (Psalm 92:13–14). Jeremiah took this verse up almost whole and added the drought: “He is like a tree planted by water … for its leaves remain green, and is not anxious in the year of drought” (Jeremiah 17:8). Jesus used the same logic of himself: a branch bears fruit only by abiding in the vine, “for apart from me you can do nothing” (John 15:5). And at the end of the Bible the tree is still standing by the water, “yielding its fruit each month”, its leaves for the healing of the nations (Revelation 22:2).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–6 — The LORD Knows the Way of the Righteous
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: There are only two ways, and they end in two places. Against the rooted tree the psalm sets chaff, the weightless husk that the evening wind carries off the threshing floor (v. 4). Such lives will have no footing when God gives his verdict, and no place in the assembly of his people (v. 5). Then comes the reason under the whole psalm: the LORD knows the way of the righteous, with the close, personal knowing of a covenant God who walks with his own, while the other way does not need to be struck down; it simply comes to nothing (v. 6). The difference rests on God’s knowing, not on human performance.
verseByVerse.theology: There are two ways and two ends, and beneath both lies the reason: the LORD knows the way of the righteous.

verseByVerse.quote: The wicked are not so, but are like chaff that the wind drives away. Therefore the wicked will not stand in the judgment, nor sinners in the congregation of the righteous;
verseByVerse.commentary:
A life without roots in God has no weight, and when God’s judgment comes it will have nowhere to stand.

Like chaff that the wind drives away. The first line is curt, and the abruptness is deliberate: not so. Against the tree stands chaff, and its mark is not fire or violence but weightlessness. Chaff is the dry husk beaten off the wheat on the threshing floor, and the farmer does not need to remove it. He throws the whole heap in the air on a windy evening and the chaff simply goes. A life with no root also has no weight; when the wind gets under it there is nothing there to hold.

The wicked will not stand in the judgment. This is a courtroom word: they will have no footing when the verdict is read, and no place in the assembly of God’s people. John the Baptist put the winnowing fork in the Messiah’s hand: “he will clear his threshing floor and gather his wheat into the barn, but the chaff he will burn with unquenchable fire” (Matthew 3:12). The psalm’s picture points to a real day of judgment.

No third way. We want a third category: decent, undecided, not really either. The psalm offers two.
verseByVerse.note: Threshing floors were often on open, high ground, where the evening wind could carry the chaff away.

verseByVerse.quote: for the LORD knows the way of the righteous, but the way of the wicked will perish.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The final difference between the two ways is that the LORD knows his own, while the road without him comes to nothing by itself.

The LORD knows the way of the righteous. Here is the reason under both halves of the psalm, and it is not the man’s performance. Knows is yada, knowing a person rather than a fact: the word used of a husband and wife (Genesis 4:1), of God knowing Israel (Amos 3:2), and of God knowing Jeremiah before he was formed (Jeremiah 1:5). To be known like this is to be walked with and kept company. Paul gives the church the same assurance: “The Lord knows those who are his” (2 Timothy 2:19). The good Shepherd says it most warmly: “I know my own and my own know me” (John 10:14).

The way of the wicked will perish. The other way is not said to be struck down but to perish, coming to nothing on its own, as chaff does.

The man in verse 1. Read the psalm honestly and it will not leave you comfortable, because the man in verse 1 is not you. There has been one man who never walked, stood or sat in that company, whose delight was wholly in the law of God, whose way the Father knew perfectly, and he ended under the curse that belonged to the wicked: “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us” (Galatians 3:13), for Scripture says, “Cursed is everyone who is hanged on a tree.” The blessed man took the chaff’s end so that rootless people could be planted like the tree. That is how anyone gets into verse 3, and it is why the doorway has a second half: “Blessed are all who take refuge in him” (Psalm 2:12).

keyVerse.quote: for the LORD knows the way of the righteous, but the way of the wicked will perish.
keyVerse.note: The last verse gives the reason under the whole psalm. The blessed life does not rest finally on the man’s delight or his discipline, but on the LORD’s personal, covenant knowing of his own. That is good news for people who know they are not the man of verse 1, for in Christ they are known and kept.

1.reflection:
The psalm describes a slide from walking to standing to sitting with those who ignore God (v. 1). Whose counsel actually shapes your decisions in an ordinary week, and where might the slide have begun for you?

The blessed man delights in God’s law before he meditates on it (v. 2). Does God’s word feel more like a rule book or a Father’s teaching to you, and what helps the delight to grow?

The tree bears fruit “in its season” (v. 3), not every month. How does that free you in a dry or wintry stretch of your Christian life?

Only Jesus has been the man of verse 1, and he took the curse of the wicked on the cross. How does that change the way you read this psalm, both its promise and its warning?

2.title: You Are My Son
2.text: <sup>1</sup>Why do the nations rage and the peoples plot in vain?<sup>2</sup>The kings of the earth set themselves, and the rulers take counsel together, against the LORD and against his Anointed, saying,<sup>3</sup>"Let us burst their bonds apart and cast away their cords from us."<sup>4</sup>He who sits in the heavens laughs; the Lord holds them in derision.<sup>5</sup>Then he will speak to them in his wrath, and terrify them in his fury, saying,<sup>6</sup>"As for me, I have set my King on Zion, my holy hill."<sup>7</sup>I will tell of the decree: The LORD said to me, "You are my Son; today I have begotten you.<sup>8</sup>Ask of me, and I will make the nations your heritage, and the ends of the earth your possession.<sup>9</sup>You shall break them with a rod of iron and dash them in pieces like a potter's vessel."<sup>10</sup>Now therefore, O kings, be wise; be warned, O rulers of the earth.<sup>11</sup>Serve the LORD with fear, and rejoice with trembling.<sup>12</sup>Kiss the Son, lest he be angry, and you perish in the way, for his wrath is quickly kindled. Blessed are all who take refuge in him.
2.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 2 is the second half of the Psalter’s doorway (see the introduction). Psalm 1 showed one man and his book; Psalm 2 pulls back to show the whole earth, its kings, and the King God has set on Zion, and it ends with the blessing on which Psalm 1 began.

The message. The world’s revolt against God and his anointed King is real, loud and hopeless, because God has already installed his King and promised him the ends of the earth. The only wise response is to bow to that King now. The same Son who will break all resistance is the shelter of everyone who runs to him.

Why it was said. This is a royal psalm, probably sung when a king of David’s line was crowned, the very moment when subject peoples liked to break their treaties (see the note on vv. 1–3). It rested Israel’s confidence not on the king’s armies but on God’s promise to David that his son would be God’s son (2 Samuel 7:14), a promise every crowned king carried and none fulfilled.

How the chapter makes its case. The nations plot to throw off God’s rule as if it were rope (vv. 1–3). Heaven answers with laughter, then wrath, then an announcement: the King is already set on Zion (vv. 4–6). The King himself tells the decree: he is God’s Son, heir of the nations, with a rod of iron (vv. 7–9). And the rebels are offered terms: be wise, serve with fear and joy, kiss the Son, take refuge in him (vv. 10–12).

Where it leads. To Christ by promise, and the New Testament says so plainly. The church prayed verses 1–2 over Herod and Pilate (Acts 4:25–28); the Father’s voice at Jesus’ baptism echoes verse 7 (Matthew 3:17), and the apostles tie the decree to his resurrection (Acts 13:33) and his priesthood (Hebrews 5:5). The risen Christ claims the nations first by sending his gospel to them (Matthew 28:18–19), and Revelation shows him at the end with the rod (Revelation 19:15). The King the world rejected is the King God enthroned.

For us. The news can make it seem that the powerful are in charge; this psalm shows who is seated. Do not fight the King. Kiss the Son, take refuge in him, and serve him with fear and rejoicing in whatever small corner of the world you have been given.
2.theology:
God rules the world through an appointed King, and the world's quarrel with God always lands on that King (v. 2). The church prayed these verses over Herod and Pilate (Acts 4:25-28), naming the crucifixion both as the rage of the nations and as God's own plan.

The decree of verse 7 is fulfilled in Jesus: the Father speaks it at his baptism (Matt 3:17), and the apostles tie it to his resurrection and to his supremacy and priesthood (Heb 1:5; 5:5). The nations are claimed first by preaching (Matt 28:18), before the rod of judgment falls (Rev 2:26-27; 19:15).

Judgment and refuge meet in the same person: the Son whose wrath is to be feared is the one in whom all who take refuge are blessed (v. 12). With 1:1 this closes the Psalter's two-psalm doorway.
2.examples: From inside a rebellion, God's rule feels like rope, and the world still calls it that. Heaven's laughter cures the fear that the people running the world are really running it. And the psalm ends not with a threat but an invitation: kiss the Son while the door is open.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — He Who Sits in the Heavens Laughs
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The world’s revolt is loud, and heaven’s answer settles it. The nations, their kings and their rulers plot together against the LORD and his Anointed, calling his rule a set of ropes to be thrown off (vv. 1–3). God does not rise from his throne: he laughs at the folly of it (v. 4). Then he speaks in anger, and what he says is an announcement, not a debate: he has already set his King on Zion, his holy hill (vv. 5–6). The rebellion is real, but its outcome is not in doubt, because the throne it attacks has been filled by God himself.
verseByVerse.theology: The rebellion is real and the outcome is not in doubt. God's answer to a world in revolt is a King he has already installed.

verseByVerse.quote: Why do the nations rage and the peoples plot in vain? The kings of the earth set themselves, and the rulers take counsel together, against the LORD and against his Anointed, saying, "Let us burst their bonds apart and cast away their cords from us."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The whole world, from crowds to kings, sets itself against God and his chosen King, and treats his rule as ropes to be thrown off. It is a revolt in vain, because of who they are fighting.

Why do the nations rage and the peoples plot in vain? The camera pulls back from one man and his book until the whole earth is in shot, and it is conspiring. Rage is a word for a crowd in uproar (the ESV notes it can be rendered “noisily assemble”), and the kings are in session with one item on the agenda: God. Look at what they call his rule: bonds and cords, the straps of a yoke. That is how authority feels from inside a rebellion: like rope. And the instinct is not only out there; every human heart has felt God’s commands as a yoke to be thrown off.

The setting. The scene was familiar in the ancient world: when a new king came to the throne, subject peoples often seized the moment to refuse tribute and break their treaty oaths. The psalm was probably sung at the crowning of a king in David’s line, and it answers that moment of danger.

Against the LORD and against his Anointed. The plot is against two. Anointed is mashiach, from which we get Messiah. The world’s quarrel with God always lands on the man God has appointed, which is why this psalm was the first thing the church prayed when the arrests started. Peter and John came back from custody, and the believers said these very verses aloud and then named the conspirators: “for truly in this city there were gathered together against your holy servant Jesus, whom you anointed, both Herod and Pontius Pilate, along with the Gentiles and the peoples of Israel” (Acts 4:27). The kings of the earth in verse 2 turned out to be a provincial governor, Pontius Pilate, and a client ruler, Herod Antipas, on one Friday.
verseByVerse.note: This is a royal psalm about the LORD’s “Anointed” (Messiah). Acts names David as its author (Acts 4:25).

verseByVerse.quote: He who sits in the heavens laughs; the Lord holds them in derision. Then he will speak to them in his wrath, and terrify them in his fury, saying, "As for me, I have set my King on Zion, my holy hill."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God is not threatened by the world’s revolt: he laughs at it, warns it in anger, and announces that his King is already on the throne.

He who sits in the heavens laughs. God’s first response is laughter: not cruelty, but perspective. The one enthroned does not get up, consult, or check whether their plan might work. There is a kind of fear that only this verse cures: the fear that the people running the world might actually be running it. That is not because God is careless of those the powerful crush, but because their power is never final.

He will speak to them in his wrath. Then the laughter stops. The wrath is not a mood God loses control of; it is the settled opposition of a good God to everything that is wrecking his world, and here it is aimed at deliberate rebellion, not at weakness. He speaks before he acts, and that is mercy: there is still time to be warned, and the end of the psalm gives that warning.

I have set my King on Zion. What he says is an announcement, not a threat: the coronation has already happened. Zion is a modest ridge in a small country, and God calls it his: there the temple stood and the lambs died, and just outside the city the King was lifted up on a cross. The council that thought it had got rid of him found an empty tomb, and the church saw the matter settled: God had raised him and enthroned him (Acts 2:32–36).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The King tells the decree that makes him Son and heir, and then the rebels are offered terms. God has said to his King, “You are my Son”, and promised him the nations as his inheritance, with an iron rod for every power that will not bow (vv. 7–9). So the psalm turns to the kings with an invitation, not a gloat: be wise while there is time, serve the LORD with fear and joy, and kiss the Son in loyal submission (vv. 10–12). The last line opens the door to anyone: the Son whose anger is to be feared is himself the refuge of all who run to him.
verseByVerse.theology: The Son who will break the nations is the refuge of anyone who comes to him, and the New Testament reads every line of this of Jesus.

verseByVerse.quote: I will tell of the decree: The LORD said to me, "You are my Son; today I have begotten you. Ask of me, and I will make the nations your heritage, and the ends of the earth your possession. You shall break them with a rod of iron and dash them in pieces like a potter's vessel."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God has declared his King to be his Son, promised him the nations as his inheritance, and given him power to break all who resist.

You are my Son. Every king of David’s line was God’s son by covenant promise (2 Samuel 7:14), and every one of them died and left the promise unfulfilled. The New Testament puts these words where they belong. Paul preaches that God kept the promise “by raising Jesus”, quoting this line (Acts 13:33). Hebrews uses it twice: to show that the Son is greater than any angel (Hebrews 1:5), and that he did not seize the priesthood but was appointed to it (Hebrews 5:5). And the Father spoke in his own voice at Jesus’ baptism, and again at his transfiguration: “This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3:17).

Ask of me, and I will make the nations your heritage. The inheritance is not seized but asked of a Father and given. The risen Christ speaks of it as done: “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (Matthew 28:18), and the sentence that follows is the command to make disciples of all nations. The ends of the earth are claimed by preaching before they are claimed by the rod.

A rod of iron. But the rod is there, and it should not be softened. Dash them in pieces like a potter’s vessel is what happens to power that will not bow. A pot that will not hold water is smashed, and a people that will bow is governed: the same iron rod does both, depending on what it meets. Revelation uses the picture three times (Revelation 2:27; 12:5; 19:15), once with a startling twist: the authority to rule the nations with a rod of iron is promised to the believer, “the one who conquers” and holds on (Revelation 2:26–27). Christ shares his rule with his people.

Does “begotten” mean the Son had a beginning? Arius in the fourth century, and Jehovah’s Witnesses today, have read it that way. But “today” is the day of the king’s enthronement, and Paul applies it to the resurrection (Acts 13:33), when Jesus was declared “the Son of God in power” (Romans 1:4). The verse speaks of the Son’s public installation as King, not of his origin; he is eternally the Son, who “was in the beginning with God” (John 1:2).

How Jewish readers take it. Jewish interpreters read the psalm of David or a king of his line crowned in Zion, and take my Son as the language of covenant adoption promised to David’s house (2 Samuel 7:14), much as Israel is called God’s firstborn son (Exodus 4:22). Rashi notes that the rabbis expounded the psalm of King Messiah, and the Talmud pictures God saying Ask of me to the Messiah, son of David (Sukkah 52a). So both traditions hear a coming king here. This commentary reads that king as Jesus because the apostles do, tying the decree to his resurrection (Acts 13:33; Hebrews 1:5).

Textual note. The ESV notes that with different vowels the line reads “you shall rule them” rather than “break them”. That is how the Greek Old Testament took it, and it is the form the book of Revelation uses. Break or rule, the meaning is the King’s unbreakable authority.

verseByVerse.quote: Now therefore, O kings, be wise; be warned, O rulers of the earth. Serve the LORD with fear, and rejoice with trembling. Kiss the Son, lest he be angry, and you perish in the way, for his wrath is quickly kindled. Blessed are all who take refuge in him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The psalm ends with an offer, not a gloat: bow to God’s King while there is time, for all who run to him for shelter are blessed.

Now therefore, O kings, be wise. The psalm ends by addressing the conspirators, not in triumph but with an offer. In the first psalm wisdom looked like delight in God’s law. Here wisdom is surrender while surrender is still possible.

Serve the LORD with fear, and rejoice with trembling. The command holds together two things we keep pulling apart. Joy that has no trembling in it has forgotten who God is; trembling with no joy in it has forgotten what he has done. The Christian life is both at once, and a church where only one is audible has lost half the psalm.

Kiss the Son. It is the gesture of a subject to a sovereign, the act by which a man publicly declared his loyalty: Samuel anointed Saul and kissed him (1 Samuel 10:1). The warning that follows is real: refuse, and you perish on the road, for the King’s anger flares quickly.

Blessed are all who take refuge in him. And there is the last word of the doorway. The Psalter opened with Blessed is the man (1:1), and it closes this pair with blessed are all: not the blameless or the successful, but all who run to him. “Refuge” sounds soft, but in the Psalms it is a word for running: to take refuge is to flee to shelter because staying in the open will kill you, a fugitive making for a walled town, a chick diving under its mother’s wing. It is the Psalter’s favourite picture of faith: not confidence in your own strength, but a move away from it. Everyone runs somewhere when the ground shakes, to money, to control, to being liked, and those shelters are only as strong as we are. Here the refuge is the very King whose anger the rebels should fear, and that is the gospel in a sentence. The Son bore the wrath of God against sin at the cross, so that those who run to him run into safety, not judgment; the only safe place from the Son is in his arms. Hebrews calls Christians “we who have fled for refuge” (Hebrews 6:18).

When the ground is moving. If the news makes the ground feel as if it is moving, the psalm does not ask you to pretend the rage is harmless. It asks you to notice who is seated, and whose Son already holds the title deed to the ends of the earth. The next time fear rises, notice where you run first, and then run to him by name. Then, in the strength of the Spirit the risen King has poured out (Acts 2:33), get on with verse 11, serving with fear and rejoicing with trembling, in whatever small square of the raging earth you have been given.

Uncertain wording. The word for Son here is bar, the Aramaic word, not the Hebrew ben of verse 7, and the line is hard to translate. The Greek Old Testament reads “accept correction”; some take bar as a Hebrew word for purity and translate “kiss sincerely”; and some translations rearrange the line to read “kiss his feet”. Most English Bibles keep Son, which fits verse 7 and the psalm’s last line. Whichever is right, the call is the same: bow to the King God has installed.

keyVerse.quote: Kiss the Son, lest he be angry, and you perish in the way, for his wrath is quickly kindled. Blessed are all who take refuge in him.
keyVerse.note: The whole psalm comes to a point in this offer. The Son whose rule no rebellion can overturn is also the shelter of everyone who runs to him, so the same verse that warns of his wrath opens the door to blessing. With Psalm 1:1 it frames the Psalter’s doorway: the blessed man, and blessing for all who take refuge in him.

2.reflection:
The rebels call God’s rule “bonds” and “cords” (v. 3). Where do you most feel God’s commands as a rope rather than a gift, and what does that reveal about your heart?

“He who sits in the heavens laughs” (v. 4). How does knowing who is seated change the way you take in the news, and the fear it can stir?

The apostles read verse 7 of Jesus’ resurrection and enthronement. What difference does it make to your week that Jesus already holds all authority in heaven and on earth?

To take refuge is to run from danger to shelter (v. 12). Where do you tend to run first when the ground shakes, and what would it look like to run to Christ instead?

3.title: A Shield About Me
3.text: A Psalm of David, when he fled from Absalom his son. 1O LORD, how many are my foes! Many are rising against me;2many are saying of my soul, "There is no salvation for him in God." Selah3But you, O LORD, are a shield about me, my glory, and the lifter of my head.4I cried aloud to the LORD, and he answered me from his holy hill. Selah5I lay down and slept; I woke again, for the LORD sustained me.6I will not be afraid of many thousands of people who have set themselves against me all around.7Arise, O LORD! Save me, O my God! For you strike all my enemies on the cheek; you break the teeth of the wicked.8Salvation belongs to the LORD; your blessing be on your people! Selah
3.overview:
Where we are. After the two-psalm doorway, Psalm 3 is the Psalter’s first prayer and the first psalm with a heading: David wrote it “when he fled from Absalom his son” (2 Samuel 15–17). The king of David’s line, whom Psalm 2 saw set on Zion, is now running from Zion.

The message. When everything says that God has abandoned you, faith answers not with arguments but with God himself: he is a shield all round, the one who restores honour and lifts the bowed head. Because he hears, a hunted man can sleep, leave his enemies to God rather than take revenge, and pray blessing on the very people who have turned against him. Salvation belongs to the LORD, not to numbers.

Why it was said. David’s own son had taken the kingdom, much of Israel had followed him, and men like Shimei shouted that this was God’s judgment (2 Samuel 16:8). The psalm gave David, and every believer after him, words for trouble that comes with a verdict attached (see the introduction on the titles).

How the chapter makes its case. David counts the many against him and the taunt that hurts most, that God will not save him (vv. 1–2). He answers with who God is to him and how God answered him from his holy hill (vv. 3–4). He has slept and woken under threat, so he will not fear the thousands (vv. 5–6). He asks God to rise and disarm his enemies, confesses that salvation belongs to the LORD, and blesses God’s people (vv. 7–8).

Where it leads. To Christ by pattern, not by prediction: the New Testament does not quote Psalm 3 of Jesus. But David’s flight foreshadows his greater Son. Jesus too crossed the Kidron to the Mount of Olives by night (2 Samuel 15:23; John 18:1), betrayed by a trusted friend; he too heard that God would not save him (Matthew 27:43), and he handed his cause to his Father rather than strike back (1 Peter 2:23). God lifted his head on the third day, and heaven sings the psalm’s last line to him: “Salvation belongs to our God who sits on the throne, and to the Lamb!” (Revelation 7:10).

For us. When people, or your own heart, say that there is no help for you in God, answer with God, not with your record. Hand him the watch and sleep, hand him your enemies and keep your hands clean, and pray for the good of those who have hurt you.
3.theology:
The title, an ancient heading in the Hebrew text, anchors the psalm in 2 Samuel 15-17, and the psalm answers that story: the covered head of the fleeing king is lifted by God (v. 3), and the night attack is slept through (v. 5).

Faith answers a taunt about God with God, and it is God who is asked to act on the enemy (v. 7), so the sufferer keeps his own hands clean. Sleep is an act of trust in the one who does not sleep (Ps 121:4). Salvation belongs to the LORD (v. 8) is the Psalter's confession in one line and heaven's song at the end (Rev 7:10).

Many Christians have seen David's Son in this flight. He too crossed the Kidron to the Mount of Olives by night (2 Sam 15:23; John 18:1), betrayed by a trusted friend as David was by Ahithophel, and God lifted his head on the third day. The New Testament does not quote Psalm 3 of him, so this is a pattern, not a prediction.
3.examples: When trouble comes with a commentary attached (“God has finished with you”), the commentary often wounds deeper than the trouble. This psalm answers it not with arguments but with God, and then lies down to sleep while the enemy plans a night raid.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — Many Are Rising Against Me
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Faith answers a taunt about God with God himself. David, driven from his city by his own son, counts the crowds rising against him and the cruellest thing they say: that God has given him up (vv. 1–2). He does not argue with them. He turns to the LORD and names what God is to him: a shield on every side, his honour when every other honour has been stripped away, and the one who lifts the head bowed in grief (v. 3). Cut off from the city where God was worshipped, he cried out, and God answered him from his holy hill all the same (v. 4).
verseByVerse.theology: The taunt is about God, not about David, and the answer comes from God's hill, not from David's resources.

verseByVerse.quote: O LORD, how many are my foes! Many are rising against me; many are saying of my soul, "There is no salvation for him in God." Selah
verseByVerse.commentary:
Driven out by his own son, David counts his enemies, and their worst weapon is the claim that God has given him up.

A prayer with a date on it. The heading puts us in the worst week of David’s life: his son Absalom has taken the kingdom, and the king walks out of Jerusalem barefoot. “David went up the ascent of the Mount of Olives, weeping as he went, barefoot and with his head covered” (2 Samuel 15:30). Remember that covered head; the psalm comes back to it.

Many are saying of my soul. Three times many, and the third is the one that hurts. The crowd has decided what God thinks of him. Shimei shouted it along the road: “The LORD has avenged on you all the blood of the house of Saul … See, your evil is on you” (2 Samuel 16:8). When trouble comes with a commentary attached (“this is what you deserve; God has dropped you”), the commentary wounds deeper than the trouble.

The same taunt at the cross. At the cross David’s greater Son heard it too: “He trusts in God; let God deliver him now, if he desires him” (Matthew 27:43). It was a lie both times, and because the Son was forsaken in our place and raised, no one who trusts him need believe it about themselves.

Uncertain wording. No one knows for certain what Selah means (seventy-one times in the Psalms, three in Habakkuk 3). It may be a musical direction, perhaps for an interlude. Whatever the musicians did with it, it falls here, after the worst sentence in the psalm, and the reader is made to stop where he would rather hurry on.
verseByVerse.note: In the Hebrew Bible the title is counted as verse 1, so the verse numbers there run one ahead of the ESV.

verseByVerse.quote: But you, O LORD, are a shield about me, my glory, and the lifter of my head. I cried aloud to the LORD, and he answered me from his holy hill. Selah
verseByVerse.commentary:
Against the taunt David sets God himself, his shield, his honour and the lifter of his head, who answers him even far from his house.

But you, O LORD. Two words, and the psalm turns on them. He answers the taunt not with evidence but with God, and three things God is to him.

A shield about me, my glory, and the lifter of my head. God is a shield about me, not only held in front but all around, covering the side a man cannot cover himself; it is the word God first spoke to Abram: “Fear not, Abram, I am your shield” (Genesis 15:1). He is my glory: David’s honour has been stripped by his own son, and the glory he has left is God. And he is the lifter of my head, said by the man who walked up the hill with his head covered in grief. He cannot lift it himself; Someone else puts a hand under his chin.

He answered me from his holy hill. David is on the Mount of Olives; the ark is back in the city he has just lost. Cut off from the place of worship, he is answered from there anyway. Distance from the building is not distance from God.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–8 — I Lay Down and Slept
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A hunted man sleeps, prays for rescue rather than revenge, and ends by blessing the nation that has turned on him. While his enemies planned a night attack, David lay down, slept and woke, because the LORD held him up, and so he will not fear even tens of thousands (vv. 5–6). He asks God, not his own sword, to rise and disarm the wicked, picturing an attacker struck on the cheek and his teeth broken (v. 7). Then he confesses the truth on which the whole psalm stands, that salvation belongs to the LORD, and asks God’s blessing on his people, the very people who have followed his rival (v. 8).
verseByVerse.theology: A hunted man sleeps, prays for rescue rather than revenge, and ends by blessing the nation that has turned on him.

verseByVerse.quote: I lay down and slept; I woke again, for the LORD sustained me. I will not be afraid of many thousands of people who have set themselves against me all around.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hunted by an army, David sleeps and wakes because the LORD holds him, and so he will not be ruled by fear.

I lay down and slept. This is one of the quietest miracles in the Bible. While David fled, Ahithophel was urging Absalom, “Let me choose twelve thousand men, and I will arise and pursue David tonight” (2 Samuel 17:1). While the raid was planned, the hunted king slept, woke, and was surprised enough to write it down. The night he was kept becomes the next day’s courage against many thousands (v. 6).

The LORD sustained me. Sleep is one of the plainest acts of faith there is. To sleep is to stop holding the world together and let someone else hold it, and the psalm gives the reason without embarrassment: the LORD sustained me. The Psalter says elsewhere that the one keeping you “will neither slumber nor sleep” (Psalm 121:4), which is exactly why you can. And when the disciples were bailing water in a gale, they found their Lord “in the stern, asleep on the cushion” (Mark 4:38). He slept in the storm because he trusted his Father; we sleep in the storm because we trust him.

If you are lying awake. If you are lying awake tonight doing the arithmetic of everything that could go wrong, this verse is not a rebuke. It is an invitation to hand the watch over to the one who is awake anyway. If sleeplessness goes on for weeks, seeing a doctor as well as praying is no failure of faith.

verseByVerse.quote: Arise, O LORD! Save me, O my God! For you strike all my enemies on the cheek; you break the teeth of the wicked. Salvation belongs to the LORD; your blessing be on your people! Selah
verseByVerse.commentary:
David leaves his enemies to God, confesses that rescue is God’s alone, and blesses the people who turned against him.

Arise, O LORD! … You break the teeth of the wicked. The language is violent, and it matters who holds the weapon. David does not strike anyone; he asks God to act and leaves it there. A struck cheek is an insult answered, and broken teeth are a predator disarmed: the picture is of an attacker made harmless, not of private revenge. David had Shimei within reach and refused to let him be touched (2 Samuel 16:9–12). A man who hands his grievance to God can afford to keep his hands clean (see the introduction on the psalms that curse).

Your blessing be on your people! The last line is astonishing. Your people is the nation that has just crowned his rival, and he asks God to bless them. And the first half of the line is the sentence heaven itself will sing: “Salvation belongs to our God who sits on the throne, and to the Lamb!” (Revelation 7:10). A fugitive king says it on a hillside in the dark, and an uncountable multitude will sing it in the light at the end; it was true both times.

keyVerse.quote: But you, O LORD, are a shield about me, my glory, and the lifter of my head.
keyVerse.note: This is where the psalm turns. Against the crowd’s verdict that God has abandoned him, David sets God himself: protection on every side, honour when his own is gone, and the hand that lifts the head he walked out of Jerusalem with covered. Faith answers a taunt about God with God.

3.reflection:
The cruellest thing David’s enemies said was that God would not save him (v. 2). What “commentary” tends to come with your troubles, and how does this psalm teach you to answer it?

David calls God “a shield about me, my glory, and the lifter of my head” (v. 3). Which of these three do you most need to hear today, and why?

David slept while an army was planned against him (v. 5). What keeps you awake, and what would it mean to hand the watch over to the LORD?

David asks God to deal with his enemies and then prays for blessing on the people who rejected him (vv. 7–8). How does Jesus’ way with his enemies help you to do the same?

4.title: In Peace I Will Both Lie Down and Sleep
4.text: To the choirmaster: with stringed instruments. A Psalm of David. 1Answer me when I call, O God of my righteousness! You have given me relief when I was in distress. Be gracious to me and hear my prayer!2O men, how long shall my honor be turned into shame? How long will you love vain words and seek after lies? Selah3But know that the LORD has set apart the godly for himself; the LORD hears when I call to him.4Be angry, and do not sin; ponder in your own hearts on your beds, and be silent. Selah5Offer right sacrifices, and put your trust in the LORD.6There are many who say, "Who will show us some good? Lift up the light of your face upon us, O LORD!"7You have put more joy in my heart than they have when their grain and wine abound.8In peace I will both lie down and sleep; for you alone, O LORD, make me dwell in safety.
4.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 4 is a companion to Psalm 3: the prayer of a hunted king is followed by the evening prayer of a slandered one, and both end in sleep (3:5; 4:8). It is the first psalm handed “to the choirmaster”, written to be sung by the whole congregation.

The message. The person God has set apart for himself can pray with confidence, handle anger without sinning, and find in God’s own face a joy deeper than prosperity and a peace that lets him sleep. When the crowd asks whether there is any good to be had, the answer is not better circumstances but God himself, turned toward us in favour.

Why it was said. David is under attack again, this time by men of standing who turn his honour into shame with lies, while many around him have lost heart. The psalm answers both: it warns the slanderers, and it points the discouraged to the blessing God promised Israel through its priests (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. David asks to be heard, remembering how God made room for him before (v. 1), and rebukes the men who love lies (v. 2). He tells them what they have not reckoned with: the LORD has set apart his loyal one and hears him (v. 3). He counsels them, and the angry in every age, to tremble without sinning, think it over in silence on their beds, worship rightly and trust the LORD (vv. 4–5). Then he answers the despairing crowd with the priestly blessing, asking for the light of God’s face (v. 6), testifies that God’s gift of joy outweighs a bumper harvest (v. 7), and lies down in peace (v. 8).

Where it leads. To Christ, by the promise of the priestly blessing and by God’s character revealed in him. The light of God’s face that David asks for has shone in “the face of Jesus Christ” (2 Corinthians 4:6). The godly whom God sets apart for himself are set apart in Christ, and heard for his sake. And the peace that lets a believer sleep is the peace Christ gives, “Not as the world gives” (John 14:27).

For us. Before you lie down tonight, take your anger to God rather than to the street or the screen, and remind yourself whose you are. Ask for his face, not only his gifts. In Christ it is turned toward you, and you can sleep.
4.theology:
Prayer rests on God's prior action and on belonging to him: he has set apart the godly for himself, and therefore hears (vv. 1, 3).

Anger is not itself sin, nor an excuse for sin (v. 4; quoted at Eph 4:26); the cure prescribed is reflection, silence, worship and trust.

The answer to Who will show us some good? is the face of God promised in the priestly blessing (v. 6), now shown in Jesus Christ (2 Cor 4:6). Joy in God outweighs harvest joy without despising it (v. 7), and peace that does not depend on us makes sleep possible (v. 8).
4.examples: Anger taken to bed and turned over before God does far less damage than anger taken to the street. And the psalm's claim that God's face gives more joy than grain and wine is one any believer can test.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — Know That the LORD Has Set Apart the Godly
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Prayer rests on what God has already done and on whose we are, and that steadies a man under slander. David asks the God who upholds his cause to answer him, remembering how God made room for him in a tight place before (v. 1). He turns to the men of rank who love lies and turn his honour into shame (v. 2), and tells them what they have not reckoned with: the LORD has set apart his loyal one for himself, and hears him (v. 3). Then he counsels them: let anger tremble without becoming sin, think it over silently in bed, offer honest worship and trust the LORD (vv. 4–5).
verseByVerse.theology: Prayer rests on what God has already done and on whose we are. Anger itself is not forbidden; acting on it in sin is.

verseByVerse.quote: Answer me when I call, O God of my righteousness! You have given me relief when I was in distress. Be gracious to me and hear my prayer! O men, how long shall my honor be turned into shame? How long will you love vain words and seek after lies? Selah
verseByVerse.commentary:
David asks to be heard because God has rescued him before, then confronts those ruining his name with lies.

The heading. Here is the first of fifty-five psalms handed over to the choirmaster, with the band noted: strings. These intensely personal prayers were written to be sung in public by people who did not write them. Your worst night becomes someone else’s hymn.

You have given me relief when I was in distress. He calls on the God of my righteousness, the defender of his just cause, and the middle line is the ground of his prayer. In Hebrew it is a picture: in a tight place, you made room for me. He is boxed in again, and he prays by remembering the last time the walls moved. That is not sentiment; it is evidence. Keep a record of the times God made room, because you will need it in the next narrow place.

How long shall my honor be turned into shame? My honor is literally “my glory”, the word of 3:3, where God himself is David’s glory. He does not argue with the slander; he takes it to God, then warns the slanderers. David’s greater Son walked the same road: “When he was reviled, he did not revile in return” (1 Peter 2:23), but entrusted himself to the Judge.

Uncertain wording. O men is literally “sons of man”, a phrase that can mark people of high standing (Psalm 62:9), so the ESV notes it may mean “men of rank”, people able to make a lie stick. It may simply mean “you people”. On Selah, see the note on 3:1–2.

verseByVerse.quote: But know that the LORD has set apart the godly for himself; the LORD hears when I call to him. Be angry, and do not sin; ponder in your own hearts on your beds, and be silent. Selah Offer right sacrifices, and put your trust in the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God has claimed his loyal one and hears him, so the angry should tremble without sinning, think quietly before God, worship honestly and trust him.

The LORD has set apart the godly for himself. The word for godly comes from the word for God’s own covenant love, hesed (see Steadfast love in the Theological Dictionary): the loyal one, bound to the God who has bound himself to him. He is not claiming to be impressive. He is claiming to be owned. The two halves belong together: set apart for himself, and therefore heard. Prayer is answered because of a relationship, not because of volume.

Be angry, and do not sin. Paul quotes these words in a letter about church life (Ephesians 4:26). Scripture does not tell the wronged man to feel nothing. It tells him what to do with what he feels: take it to bed rather than to the street, turn it over in God’s presence, and stop talking. Most of the damage anger does is done by the mouth in the hour before it cools. The one who has set us apart for himself also gives the Spirit whose fruit is self-control (Galatians 5:22–23), and where the mouth has already done its damage, the way back is confession and the forgiveness he has promised (1 John 1:9).

Offer right sacrifices. Right sacrifices and trust go together: the act of worship and the leaning of the heart. For the first readers right sacrifices were the offerings the law prescribed, brought honestly; the same phrase returns in Psalm 51:19. Since Christ’s one sacrifice, the offering a believer brings is “a sacrifice of praise to God”, with doing good and sharing what we have (Hebrews 13:15–16). Either one without the other is half a religion.

Outrage as a way of life. A phone can supply a fresh injustice every few minutes, and being angry about the right things has become a way of showing which side we are on, and that we are good. Anger feels like righteousness from the inside, which is why it is so hard to put down. Much in the world ought to make us angry, but the psalm moves the anger off the public stage and into the bedroom, before God, where we can see whether it is about justice or about being right. James puts it plainly: “the anger of man does not produce the righteousness of God” (James 1:20). The gospel goes to the root. If my standing depends on being on the right side, I will always need someone to be against. If it rests on Christ, who bore God’s righteous anger against my own wrongs, I no longer need to win every argument to know I am accepted, and I can be angry at evil without hating the people who do it.

Uncertain wording. Be angry translates a verb (ragaz) that means to tremble or be stirred, whether with anger or with fear; the ESV notes it can be rendered “be agitated”. The Greek Old Testament took it as anger, the wording Paul quotes; some translations render “tremble”. Either way, the stirring must not run on into sin.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–8 — More Joy Than When Their Grain and Wine Abound
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s face gives a joy greater than prosperity and a peace that lets us sleep. Many around David are asking whether there is any good to be had at all, and his answer is a prayer in the words of the priestly blessing: that the LORD would lift up the light of his face on them (v. 6). He testifies that God has given him more gladness than others have when grain and wine are plentiful (v. 7). And so, with his enemies still talking, he lies down and sleeps in peace, because the LORD alone keeps him safe (v. 8).
verseByVerse.theology: The harvest is real joy and God's face is a greater one, and the man who has the greater one can sleep.

verseByVerse.quote: There are many who say, "Who will show us some good? Lift up the light of your face upon us, O LORD!" You have put more joy in my heart than they have when their grain and wine abound. In peace I will both lie down and sleep; for you alone, O LORD, make me dwell in safety.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Asked whether any good is left, David asks for God’s face, finds in it a joy deeper than prosperity, and sleeps because God alone keeps him safe.

Who will show us some good? The question of a discouraged crowd is perfectly modern: is there any good news at all? The answer he prays is not a better year but the priestly blessing in Numbers: “the LORD make his face to shine upon you and be gracious to you; the LORD lift up his countenance upon you and give you peace” (Numbers 6:25–26). He asks for God’s face, God himself, rather than for goods. Christians know where that light now shines: God has given “the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ” (2 Corinthians 4:6).

More joy in my heart. He is not pretending harvest joy is nothing. A harvest brought in is real gladness: the bills covered, the barns full, a good year. He says he has more than that, and he has it while being slandered by men of rank. Any believer can test the claim in a plain way: which piece of news would actually change your evening more, a pay rise or an hour of the felt nearness of God?

In peace I will both lie down and sleep. Psalms 3 and 4 both take the reader to bed. There a hunted king slept because God sustained him (3:5); here a slandered man sleeps because God alone keeps him safe. You alone is what makes real rest possible. If safety depends partly on you, some part of you has to stay on watch all night. If it depends on God, you can put your head down.

What it does not mean. Not that a believer who lies awake has no faith. David’s peace rests on God’s keeping, not on feeling calm, and that holds on sleepless nights too.

keyVerse.quote: In peace I will both lie down and sleep; for you alone, O LORD, make me dwell in safety.
keyVerse.note: The psalm ends where its trust has been heading: a slandered man goes to bed in peace. The reason is in the words “you alone”: if his safety depended partly on himself, he would have to stay on watch, but because it rests on God alone he can sleep.

4.reflection:
David prays by remembering, “You have given me relief when I was in distress” (v. 1). What times can you recall when God made room for you in a tight place, and how might keeping a record of them help you pray now?

“Be angry, and do not sin” (v. 4). What tends to happen to your anger in the hour before it cools, and what would it look like to take it to bed and before God rather than to the street or the screen?

The crowd asks, “Who will show us some good?” and David asks for the light of God’s face (v. 6). How does knowing God’s face shines on us in Jesus Christ change what you most want?

David says God has given him more joy than a plentiful harvest (v. 7). Is that true for you, and what might help it become more true?

5.title: In the Morning You Hear My Voice
5.text: To the choirmaster: for the flutes. A Psalm of David. 1Give ear to my words, O LORD; consider my groaning.2Give attention to the sound of my cry, my King and my God, for to you do I pray.3O LORD, in the morning you hear my voice; in the morning I prepare a sacrifice for you and watch.4For you are not a God who delights in wickedness; evil may not dwell with you.5The boastful shall not stand before your eyes; you hate all evildoers.6You destroy those who speak lies; the LORD abhors the bloodthirsty and deceitful man.7But I, through the abundance of your steadfast love, will enter your house. I will bow down toward your holy temple in the fear of you.8Lead me, O LORD, in your righteousness because of my enemies; make your way straight before me.9For there is no truth in their mouth; their inmost self is destruction; their throat is an open grave; they flatter with their tongue.10Make them bear their guilt, O God; let them fall by their own counsels; because of the abundance of their transgressions cast them out, for they have rebelled against you.11But let all who take refuge in you rejoice; let them ever sing for joy, and spread your protection over them, that those who love your name may exult in you.12For you bless the righteous, O LORD; you cover him with favor as with a shield.
5.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 5 is the morning prayer that answers the evening prayer of Psalm 4, which closed, “In peace I will both lie down and sleep” (Psalm 4:8). Like the psalms around it, it comes from David under pressure from enemies, and here their weapon is the lie.

The message. God hears the prayer of the one who comes to him each morning on the strength of his steadfast love, and he is not neutral about evil. Because the LORD hates lies and bloodshed, the person being lied about can bring him the case, ask to be kept on a straight path, and leave the judgment of the liars with him. Everyone who takes refuge in him is covered by his favour as by a shield.

Why it was said. The heading names no occasion, but David knew courts full of flattering tongues and men who wanted his blood (see the introduction). Set “for the flutes”, the psalm became Israel’s prayer whenever God’s people woke up surrounded by smooth words and hostile intentions.

How the chapter makes its case. It begins with prayer at first light, laid out like a sacrifice and then watched (vv. 1–3). The ground of that prayer is the character of God, who cannot have evil live with him (vv. 4–6). Then David turns to himself: he enters God’s house by steadfast love, not merit, and asks to be led straight while enemies watch (vv. 7–8). He lays bare the liars’ mouth and hands their case to God instead of taking revenge (vv. 9–10). The prayer of one groaning man ends as a song for all who take refuge in God (vv. 11–12).

Where it leads. Chiefly by the need it exposes. Paul quotes verse 9 of the whole human race (Romans 3:13), so the reader who starts on David’s side of the line ends up needing verse 7 as much as the liars do. There has been only one mouth of which it could be said that “neither was deceit found in his mouth” (1 Peter 2:22), and he bore the guilt of liars so that we might enter God’s house: “we have confidence to enter the holy places by the blood of Jesus” (Hebrews 10:19). The steadfast love that lets David in has a name and a face.

For us. Begin the day with God, lay out your prayer, and watch for his answer. When you are lied about, ask first for a straight path, then leave the verdict to him. And come into his presence not on your record but on his steadfast love in Christ, which is the only door anyone has ever used.
5.theology:
God's hatred of evil (vv. 4-6) is not an embarrassment to be softened but the sufferer's hope: a God indifferent to lies would be no help to the lied-about. At the cross that hatred of evil fell on Christ rather than on us (Rom 5:8).

Entry to God's house is through the abundance of your steadfast love (v. 7), never merit. Paul applies v. 9 to the whole human race (Rom 3:13), so the reader who starts on the psalmist's side of the line ends needing v. 7 as much as the enemies do.

In the Psalter's first prayer for judgment on enemies (v. 10), the case is handed to God, not vengeance taken.
5.examples: Most of us pray and then walk away; this psalm lays its prayer out like a sacrifice and then watches for God's answer. If you are being discredited, its prayer is for a straight path, not first for your enemies' ruin.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — You Are Not a God Who Delights in Wickedness
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David prays because of who God is. He brings everything to the LORD he calls “my King and my God”: words, groaning and a cry (vv. 1–2). He does it at a set hour, laying out his prayer like a priest arranging a sacrifice, and then watching for the answer (v. 3). Then comes the ground of his confidence: this God takes no pleasure in wickedness, will not have evil stay under his roof, and stands against the boastful, the liar and the violent (vv. 4–6). For a man being lied about, God’s hatred of evil is not a threat but the very reason he can hope to be heard.
verseByVerse.theology: God's hatred of evil is the hope of a man being lied about.

verseByVerse.quote: Give ear to my words, O LORD; consider my groaning. Give attention to the sound of my cry, my King and my God, for to you do I pray. O LORD, in the morning you hear my voice; in the morning I prepare a sacrifice for you and watch.
verseByVerse.commentary:
David brings God everything, from clear words to wordless groaning, and each morning he lays out his prayer like a sacrifice and watches for the answer.

Give ear to my words, O LORD. Three words for what comes out of him: words, groaning, a cry. The middle one is a murmur, the sound a man makes when the sentence will not form, and God is asked to consider that too. If you can only groan this morning, you are still praying. And the king of Israel prays as a subject: my King and my God.

In the morning. Twice in the morning, and the verb behind prepare is used of setting things in order, including the wood and the pieces on the altar (Leviticus 1:7–8). He arranges his prayer the way a priest arranges a sacrifice. Then he does the thing most of us skip: he watches, like a lookout on the wall waiting to see what God will do about what he has just said. It is deliberate work, at a set hour, with expectation attached, and the Son of David kept the same hour (Mark 1:35).

Uncertain wording. In verse 3 the Hebrew says only “I arrange for you”, with no object. The ESV supplies a sacrifice; its note gives “I direct my prayer to you”; others think of a case set out before a judge (Job 23:4). Each reading means careful preparation followed by waiting. The heading’s for the flutes renders a word found only here, and its meaning is not certain.

verseByVerse.quote: For you are not a God who delights in wickedness; evil may not dwell with you. The boastful shall not stand before your eyes; you hate all evildoers. You destroy those who speak lies; the LORD abhors the bloodthirsty and deceitful man.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God is not neutral about evil: he will not have it live with him, and that is exactly why the person being lied about can hope in him.

You are not a God who delights in wickedness. God cannot have wickedness in the house. Dwell is the word for a guest staying under someone’s roof: evil is never welcome as his guest. You hate all evildoers is not a slip of the pen, or a crude idea the Bible later outgrew. God’s opposition to evil is personal, because evil is not a substance floating about: it is done, by someone, to someone.

Why this matters. A God who felt nothing about evil would be useless here: to someone lied about by people with power, a God who shrugs is an insult. His hatred of evil in verse 5 guarantees that the cry of verse 2 is taken seriously.

Does God hate the sinner, or only the sin? The psalm speaks of the evildoer himself, who persists in evil, and it means God’s settled opposition as Judge, not spite. Yet the same God is kind to his enemies (Matthew 5:45) and reconciled us to himself while we were enemies (Romans 5:10). Hold verse 5 beside the other sentence: “God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us” (Romans 5:8). Neither cancels the other. God’s hatred of evil went all the way to the cross, where it fell on his Son instead of on us. Weaken either half and the gospel is lost: if God hated no evil, forgiveness would mean nothing.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–12 — Lead Me, O LORD, in Your Righteousness
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The man who has just described God’s holiness does not claim to deserve his presence. He enters “through the abundance of your steadfast love” and bows in reverent fear (v. 7). Watched by enemies, he asks first to be kept on a straight path (v. 8). He lays bare the lying mouth, a throat like an open grave under a flattering tongue (v. 9), and hands the liars to God’s judgment instead of taking revenge (v. 10). The psalm ends far from where it began: not one man groaning, but all who take refuge in God singing for joy, sheltered by his favour as by a shield (vv. 11–12).
verseByVerse.theology: He enters God's house on steadfast love and not on merit, and leaves judgment with God while he sings.

verseByVerse.quote: But I, through the abundance of your steadfast love, will enter your house. I will bow down toward your holy temple in the fear of you. Lead me, O LORD, in your righteousness because of my enemies; make your way straight before me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
David comes into God’s presence not because he is better than his enemies but because God’s steadfast love lets him in, and with hostile eyes on him he asks to be kept straight.

But I. It would be easy to hear “because I am not like them”. It says the opposite. He enters through the abundance of your steadfast love, the covenant loyalty that was never earned (see Steadfast love in the Theological Dictionary). What gets him through the door is what gets anyone through it, and the New Testament names it: “we have confidence to enter the holy places by the blood of Jesus” (Hebrews 10:19). He goes in in the fear of you: welcomed, yet reverent. Temple means a palace, and was used of the LORD’s house at Shiloh before Solomon built (1 Samuel 1:9): the King’s house, where he receives his people.

Lead me, O LORD, in your righteousness. Under pressure he asks not first for his enemies’ ruin, nor for an easier road, but for a straight path, because of my enemies, literally those who watch him. He knows that the surest way to lose is to be caught crooked. When people are looking for a reason to discredit you, this is the prayer to pray.

verseByVerse.quote: For there is no truth in their mouth; their inmost self is destruction; their throat is an open grave; they flatter with their tongue. Make them bear their guilt, O God; let them fall by their own counsels; because of the abundance of their transgressions cast them out, for they have rebelled against you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The liars’ smooth words come from hearts full of death, and David hands them to God’s justice instead of taking revenge, though Paul shows that this verse describes every one of us.

Their throat is an open grave. Here is a lying mouth seen from the inside out: nothing true in it, ruin at the bottom, a throat like a dug grave breathing death, and a smooth tongue on top. The flattery is the worst of it, because flattery makes the grave look like a garden.

Make them bear their guilt, O God. In the Psalter’s first prayer against enemies, he plans nothing; he asks God to act, the opposite of revenge, which is what a man does when he will not wait for God. He asks that they fall by their own counsels, caught in the trap they built. And the last clause gives his real reason: they have rebelled against you. It is a servant asking his King to deal with treason.

Paul’s use of this verse.
