Paul puts this verse in his list of Scriptures about human sin and applies it to every person alive: “Their throat is an open grave; they use their tongues to deceive” (Romans 3:13), “so that every mouth may be stopped” (Romans 3:19). You start on David’s side of the line and end up needing the steadfast love of verse 7 as much as the men he is praying about. Only one mouth was free of it: “neither was deceit found in his mouth” (1 Peter 2:22), and at his cross God bore our treason himself.

May a Christian pray this? Jesus tells us to love our enemies, and he prayed for his executioners (Matthew 5:44; Luke 23:34); yet the New Testament also prays for God’s justice (Revelation 6:10) and quotes these psalms (Romans 11:9–10). The psalmist hands vengeance to God instead of taking it (Romans 12:19), and asks for justice against evil that will not repent. So a Christian may pray these words against evil, the powers behind it and unrepentant oppression, while praying first for the enemy’s repentance and remembering that Christ took God’s curse for every enemy who turns to him (Galatians 3:13; see the introduction on the psalms that curse).

verseByVerse.quote: But let all who take refuge in you rejoice; let them ever sing for joy, and spread your protection over them, that those who love your name may exult in you. For you bless the righteous, O LORD; you cover him with favor as with a shield.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The psalm that began with one man groaning ends with everyone who takes refuge in God singing, covered by his favour as by a shield.

Let all who take refuge in you rejoice. It is not his own rescue he sings about but all who take refuge, everyone in his position, as the Psalter’s doorway promised: “Blessed are all who take refuge in him” (Psalm 2:12). Grief that has been taken to God often comes back out as intercession for other people.

Spread your protection over them. It is the picture of a covering stretched out, like a tent over people in the open, and the shield is the large one that covered the whole body. The morning began with a man laying out his prayer and watching the horizon. It ends with him sheltered behind God’s favour as behind a shield.

keyVerse.quote: But I, through the abundance of your steadfast love, will enter your house. I will bow down toward your holy temple in the fear of you.
keyVerse.note: After describing a God who will not have evil live with him, David does not claim to be good enough to come in. He enters by God’s steadfast love alone, and with reverent fear. That is the turning point of the psalm, and the only way any of us, liars included, can come near the holy God: through the love that has now opened the way in Christ.

5.reflection:
David laid out his prayer in the morning and then watched (v. 3). What would it look like for you to pray expectantly, watching for God’s answer rather than walking away from the prayer?

Verses 4–6 say plainly that God hates evil. Why is that good news for someone who has been lied about or mistreated, and why does it also make us uncomfortable?

David enters God’s house only “through the abundance of your steadfast love” (v. 7), and Paul applies verse 9 to everyone (Romans 3:13). How should that shape the way you pray about people who have wronged you?

With hostile eyes on him, David asked first for a straight path (v. 8). Where are you tempted to answer opposition by cutting corners, and what would integrity look like there this week?

6.title: How Long, O LORD?
6.text: To the choirmaster: with stringed instruments; according to The Sheminith. A Psalm of David. 1O LORD, rebuke me not in your anger, nor discipline me in your wrath.2Be gracious to me, O LORD, for I am languishing; heal me, O LORD, for my bones are troubled.3My soul also is greatly troubled. But you, O LORD— how long?4Turn, O LORD, deliver my life; save me for the sake of your steadfast love.5For in death there is no remembrance of you; in Sheol who will give you praise?6I am weary with my moaning; every night I flood my bed with tears; I drench my couch with my weeping.7My eye wastes away because of grief; it grows weak because of all my foes.8Depart from me, all you workers of evil, for the LORD has heard the sound of my weeping.9The LORD has heard my plea; the LORD accepts my prayer.10All my enemies shall be ashamed and greatly troubled; they shall turn back and be put to shame in a moment.
6.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 6 belongs to the run of David’s prayers under pressure that fills Psalms 3 to 7, and the church has long counted it the first of seven penitential psalms. After the confident morning of Psalm 5 comes a night of tears: David is ill, troubled to the bone, aware of God’s displeasure and surrounded by foes.

The message. A believer who has come under God’s hand may plead with him for mercy rather than anger, bringing nothing but God’s own steadfast love as his argument. God hears such weeping. The turning point is not a change in the trouble but the assurance, given in the dark, that “The LORD has heard my plea” (v. 9).

Why it was said. The heading names no occasion. David knew both sickness and the discipline of sin, and Israel received his prayer as a song for the congregation, set “with stringed instruments” (see the introduction), so that the sick, the guilty and the grieving would have words to bring to God together.

How the chapter makes its case. The prayer opens with a plea against wrath, not against correction, and breaks off in “how long?” (vv. 1–3). It argues from God’s steadfast love and from the silence of the grave (vv. 4–5), then describes, without any dignity, nights of weeping (vv. 6–7). Suddenly, with nothing outside changed, David knows he has been heard, and he tells the workers of evil to leave (vv. 8–10).

Where it leads. By pattern, and by the need it exposes. The sinless Son knew this psalm’s trouble from the inside: “Now is my soul troubled” (John 12:27). In Gethsemane he “offered up prayers and supplications, with loud cries and tears … and he was heard because of his reverence” (Hebrews 5:7). He bore the anger David asks to be spared, so that God’s children receive a Father’s discipline and never a judge’s wrath. And his rising answers verse 5: the grave no longer silences those who belong to him.

For us. You may bring God your tears and your unfinished questions, out loud, without tidying them first. Plead his steadfast love, not your record. And keep praying in the dark: often the first thing God changes is not the trouble but your certainty that he has heard.
6.theology:
The prayer asks for correction without anger (v. 1) and rests on God's steadfast love rather than the sufferer's record (v. 4). Grief is bodily as well as spiritual (vv. 2-3, 6-7), and the Psalter puts an unfinished question and undignified weeping into the congregation's songbook.

In death there is no remembrance of you (v. 5) is an Old Testament voice from before the resurrection had been brought to light, answered by Christ's rising. The turn comes when he knows he is heard, not when things change (vv. 8-9), and the dismissal of the workers of evil is the sentence the Judge himself will pronounce (Matt 7:23).
6.examples: A believer under God's hand may still ask, as this one does, for a father's correction rather than a judge's anger. And when the prayer is only a broken how long?, the argument that holds is the one this psalm uses: for the sake of your steadfast love.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — I Am Weary with My Moaning
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A believer in the dark asks for mercy, not a verdict, and hides nothing about how bad it is. He asks to be corrected without anger (v. 1), describes a body and soul troubled through and through, and breaks off in the Psalter’s first “how long?” (vv. 2–3). He gives God one reason to act, his steadfast love, and adds that the dead cannot praise him (vv. 4–5). Then he describes, with no attempt at dignity, nights of weeping and eyes worn out with grief (vv. 6–7). The section teaches that honest tears, offered to God, are prayer and not unbelief.
verseByVerse.theology: A believer in the dark asks for mercy rather than a verdict, and hides nothing about how bad it is.

verseByVerse.quote: O LORD, rebuke me not in your anger, nor discipline me in your wrath. Be gracious to me, O LORD, for I am languishing; heal me, O LORD, for my bones are troubled. My soul also is greatly troubled. But you, O LORD— how long?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ill and troubled to the bone, David does not ask to escape God’s correction but to receive it from a Father’s hand rather than a judge’s anger, and his prayer breaks off in a raw “how long?”

Rebuke me not in your anger. The first line shows why the church calls this a penitential psalm. He names no particular sin, but he reads his trouble as God’s hand on him, and he does not ask to be let off. He asks that the correction not come in anger: discipline from a father’s hand, not a judge’s. The New Testament promises every child of God exactly that: “the Lord disciplines the one he loves” (Hebrews 12:6).

My bones are troubled. The same word comes again for his soul: the trouble has gone all the way through. Scripture does not divide a suffering person into spiritual and physical departments; grief gets into the bones, and God is asked to heal there too. Many hear this psalm behind Jesus’ words as the cross drew near, “Now is my soul troubled” (John 12:27), which echo the Greek of verse 3. He never prayed it as a penitent, having no sin, but he knew its trouble from the inside.

How long? The Psalter’s first how long addressed to God breaks off in the middle; how long until what, he does not say. That is exactly how the question sounds at three in the morning.

What it does not mean. Not that every sickness is punishment: of a man born blind Jesus said, “It was not that this man sinned, or his parents” (John 9:3), and Job’s friends were rebuked for reasoning that way. Where conscience is burdened, confess; where it is not, do not invent guilt.

Is guilt only a feeling? Many today would treat this man’s distress as a symptom: guilt is a feeling planted by parents, churches or culture, to be talked down until it goes quiet. Sometimes that is right, for there is false guilt. But a culture that can no longer say the word sin still feels guilty; it simply has no one to confess to and no way to be forgiven, so it numbs the feeling, punishes itself, or turns hard on others. The psalm treats guilt as real, a matter between a person and God, and for that very reason something that can be dealt with. Only a real debt can be really cancelled: “But with you there is forgiveness, that you may be feared” (Psalm 130:4). Christ did not tell us our guilt was imaginary. He carried it, so that the believer can stop both excusing and punishing himself, and rest.

Uncertain wording. The heading’s Sheminith means “the eighth”. Lyres are played “according to the Sheminith” in 1 Chronicles 15:21, so it is a musical direction, perhaps an eight-stringed instrument or a lower octave; its exact sense is lost.
verseByVerse.note: The seven penitential psalms are 6, 32, 38, 51, 102, 130 and 143.

verseByVerse.quote: Turn, O LORD, deliver my life; save me for the sake of your steadfast love. For in death there is no remembrance of you; in Sheol who will give you praise?
verseByVerse.commentary:
David’s one plea is God’s own steadfast love, and his argument, that a dead man cannot praise God, is a question the empty tomb has now answered.

Save me for the sake of your steadfast love. He gives God a reason, and it is not his own record: the covenant steadfast love God has bound himself to, the only argument any of us has. A prayer that rests on God’s character rather than our own cannot be undone by our failures.

In death there is no remembrance of you. Then a line that startles Christian readers: the dead do not praise God. Sheol is the Old Testament’s name for the realm of the dead. Hezekiah prayed the same way: “For Sheol does not thank you; death does not praise you … The living, the living, he thanks you” (Isaiah 38:18–19). The psalmist speaks from where he stood, before the resurrection had been brought into the light. He is not denying life after death; he is saying that when he dies the congregation loses a voice. It is an argument for rescue, made to a God who wants to be praised.

This side of the empty tomb. We can answer him. The one who said “I am the resurrection and the life” (John 11:25) has gone down into death and come out, and those who die in him “depart and be with Christ” (Philippians 1:23), not silenced. Psalm 6 asks its question honestly; Easter answers it.

verseByVerse.quote: I am weary with my moaning; every night I flood my bed with tears; I drench my couch with my weeping. My eye wastes away because of grief; it grows weak because of all my foes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
David weeps night after night and says so, and the Bible puts those tears into the congregation’s songbook, because grief brought to God is prayer, not unbelief.

Every night I flood my bed with tears. The detail is undignified: he is exhausted by his own crying, the bed is soaked, his eyes have gone dim, worn down further by foes who watch him suffer. The language is deliberately larger than life, as anyone knows who has cried like that: the flood is how it feels, not how much water there was.

Tears in the hymnbook. This was set to stringed instruments for a congregation to sing. Whoever decided that faith means keeping a level voice did not get it from Scripture. There is no hint that the weeping is unbelief. He weeps in God’s presence and out loud, which is the difference between grief and despair. And he is not alone: the Saviour was “a man of sorrows and acquainted with grief” (Isaiah 53:3), who wept at a friend’s grave (John 11:35), and the God who hears this psalm keeps count of every tear (Psalm 56:8).

When the nights go on. If sleeplessness and weeping last for weeks, seek help: a pastor or biblical counsellor first, and a doctor’s check-up, for body and soul are bound together; medicine, where needed, is no failure of faith. If grief turns into thoughts of ending your life, tell someone and get help the same day, calling the emergency services if you are in danger.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Without warning, the psalm turns. Nothing outside has changed, but David knows that the LORD has heard, and he says it three times (vv. 8–9). With that certainty he dismisses the workers of evil in the very words Jesus will use as Judge (Luke 13:27), and expects his enemies, not himself, to end up ashamed and troubled (v. 10). The words of his own lament now fall on them. The section shows that the first answer to prayer is often the assurance of being heard, given before the circumstances move.
verseByVerse.theology: His situation is the same; what has changed is that he knows he was heard.

verseByVerse.quote: Depart from me, all you workers of evil, for the LORD has heard the sound of my weeping. The LORD has heard my plea; the LORD accepts my prayer. All my enemies shall be ashamed and greatly troubled; they shall turn back and be put to shame in a moment.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before anything outside has changed, David knows that God has heard him, and that certainty lets him dismiss his enemies with the words the Judge himself will speak.

The LORD has heard the sound of my weeping. The psalm turns, and nothing outside the man has moved: he is still ill, and the enemies are still there. What he has is a certainty that he was heard, said three times over as if he can hardly believe it. Somewhere between verse 7 and verse 8, in a dark room, God gave him that. Often the first thing that changes is not the trouble but the knowledge that God has it in hand. The Son, too, prayed with loud cries and tears and “was heard” (Hebrews 5:7), and in him our weeping is heard.

The words turn round. The enemies will be greatly troubled, the phrase David used of his own soul (v. 3), and they will turn back, the verb of his plea, “Turn, O LORD” (v. 4). The shame and trouble that filled his night pass to those who caused it.

Depart from me, all you workers of evil. Severe words from a man in bed, but they are the words the Judge himself will speak: “Depart from me, all you workers of evil!” (Luke 13:27). He hands them the verdict of the court he has just been heard in. Every reader stands before those two outcomes: to be heard while weeping, or to be told to depart. The door to the first is still open.

keyVerse.quote: The LORD has heard my plea; the LORD accepts my prayer.
keyVerse.note: This is the hinge of the psalm. Nothing outside David has changed, yet he is sure, and says it three times over, that God has heard. For anyone praying through tears, it is the promise that weeping brought to God is never wasted, because the one who hears is the Father of those who are in Christ.

6.reflection:
David asks God not to correct him “in your anger” (v. 1). What is the difference between a father’s discipline and a judge’s wrath, and how can a believer in Christ know which one he is receiving?

Verses 2–3 and 6–7 show grief in the body as well as the soul. How does this psalm help when you, or someone you love, is worn out by sorrow or illness? What practical help might be needed as well as prayer?

David’s only argument is “for the sake of your steadfast love” (v. 4). Why is that a stronger plea than our own record, especially on days when we have failed?

The psalm turns before anything outside changes (vv. 8–9). Have you known God’s peace come before the answer? How might you pray with someone who is still waiting?

7.title: God Is a Righteous Judge
7.text: A Shiggaion of David, which he sang to the LORD concerning the words of Cush, a Benjaminite. 1O LORD my God, in you do I take refuge; save me from all my pursuers and deliver me,2lest like a lion they tear my soul apart, rending it in pieces, with none to deliver.3O LORD my God, if I have done this, if there is wrong in my hands,4if I have repaid my friend with evil or plundered my enemy without cause,5let the enemy pursue my soul and overtake it, and let him trample my life to the ground and lay my glory in the dust. Selah6Arise, O LORD, in your anger; lift yourself up against the fury of my enemies; awake for me; you have appointed a judgment.7Let the assembly of the peoples be gathered about you; over it return on high.8The LORD judges the peoples; judge me, O LORD, according to my righteousness and according to the integrity that is in me.9Oh, let the evil of the wicked come to an end, and may you establish the righteous— you who test the minds and hearts, O righteous God!10My shield is with God, who saves the upright in heart.11God is a righteous judge, and a God who feels indignation every day.12If a man does not repent, God will whet his sword; he has bent and readied his bow;13he has prepared for him his deadly weapons, making his arrows fiery shafts.14Behold, the wicked man conceives evil and is pregnant with mischief and gives birth to lies.15He makes a pit, digging it out, and falls into the hole that he has made.16His mischief returns upon his own head, and on his own skull his violence descends.17I will give to the LORD the thanks due to his righteousness, and I will sing praise to the name of the LORD, the Most High.
7.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 7 closes the run of David’s prayers under pressure that began with Psalm 3, and it is the only one whose heading names the man behind the trouble: Cush, a Benjaminite, from Saul’s own tribe. Psalm 6 was the prayer of a man who knew he deserved correction; Psalm 7 is the prayer of a man falsely accused.

The message. When you are slandered, take the charge to the one court that sees the heart. God is a righteous judge who opposes evil every day, yet gives warning so that the wicked may repent, and he has made the world so that evil comes back on the one who plans it. So the slandered believer may state his innocence to God, leave the verdict with him, and sing before it comes.

Why it was said. David was accused, probably in the years when Saul’s house was against him, of treachery towards a man at peace with him (see the introduction). The psalm gave Israel words for every time God’s people are lied about and cannot clear their own name.

How the chapter makes its case. David takes refuge in God and swears an oath of innocence on this one charge (vv. 1–5). He asks God to hold court over the nations and judge his case (vv. 6–8). Then he describes the Judge: he tests hearts, shields the upright, is indignant every day, and has his weapons ready for those who will not repent (vv. 9–13). Evil recoils on its author (vv. 14–16), and thanks rises before the verdict is in (v. 17).

Where it leads. By pattern, and by the character of God revealed in Christ. Only one man could pray “judge me, O LORD, according to my righteousness” about his whole life: Jesus, condemned on false testimony, who “continued entrusting himself to him who judges justly” (1 Peter 2:23) and was vindicated when God raised him. He is now the appointed Judge (Acts 17:31). At his cross the pit-diggers fell into their own pit, for by that death he “disarmed the rulers and authorities” (Colossians 2:15). And for all who repent, the sword of verse 12 fell on him.

For us. When you are falsely accused, you do not have to win in the court of public opinion. Tell God the truth, ask him to judge, refuse to dig a pit of your own, and pray for those who wrong you. Where some of the charge is true, go first to the cross, where there is “no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1).
7.theology:
A believer may ask to be judged in a particular matter (v. 8) without claiming to be righteous in general. God alone tests the hearts (v. 9), which is where a slandered person finally rests.

God's daily indignation (v. 11) is settled moral opposition to evil, not a mood, and his weapons are readied only against the unrepentant: if a man does not repent (v. 12). Judgment is announced before it falls, and a way out is left open.

Evil is conceived, carried and born (v. 14; Jas 1:15), and is built to recoil on its author (vv. 15-16). The righteous may therefore wait, and sing before the verdict (v. 17).
7.examples: Slander does not argue; it tears like a lion, and it leaves a man feeling there is no one to step in. This psalm takes the charge to the one court that sees the heart, and it sings before the verdict comes in.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — If There Is Wrong in My Hands
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A falsely accused man does not merely deny the charge; he swears to his innocence and asks God to hold court. He runs to God for refuge from pursuers who would tear him like a lion (vv. 1–2). He calls down on himself the penalty he would deserve if the charge were true (vv. 3–5). Then, boldly, he asks God to rise, gather the nations and take his seat as Judge, and to judge him in this matter by his integrity (vv. 6–8). The section shows a slandered believer appealing over the heads of his accusers to the only court whose verdict is final.
verseByVerse.theology: He does not merely deny the charge; he swears to it, and then asks God to convene the court.

verseByVerse.quote: O LORD my God, in you do I take refuge; save me from all my pursuers and deliver me, lest like a lion they tear my soul apart, rending it in pieces, with none to deliver. O LORD my God, if I have done this, if there is wrong in my hands, if I have repaid my friend with evil or plundered my enemy without cause, let the enemy pursue my soul and overtake it, and let him trample my life to the ground and lay my glory in the dust. Selah
verseByVerse.commentary:
Slandered and hunted, David runs to God for refuge and swears that the charge is false, calling down on himself the penalty he would deserve if it were true.

Cush, a Benjaminite. Cush appears nowhere else in the Bible. He was a Benjaminite, of Saul’s tribe, which probably places this in the years when David was hunted by a king’s men. And the psalm is about his words: someone has said something, and it has been believed.

Lest like a lion they tear my soul apart. The lion is the right picture for slander. It does not argue with you; it takes you apart. And the last phrase is the fear underneath: with none to deliver. That is what a whispering campaign does: it makes a man feel that no one is left who will step in.

If I have done this. Verses 3 to 5 are not a general claim to be a good man but an oath with a penalty attached: if I did it, let them catch me. The ESV notes that my friend is literally the one at peace with me, so the charge seems to be treachery against a man who trusted him, which is what Saul’s court said about David. He even swears he has not plundered an enemy without cause. The man who spared Saul when he had him within reach can afford this oath, and Saul himself once admitted, “you have repaid me good, whereas I have repaid you evil” (1 Samuel 24:17).

In everyday life. Most of us cannot swear it about every charge laid against us, and the psalm is not a script for pretending we can. Where the charge is false, take it to God like this. Where some of it is true, pray Psalm 6, just before it.

Uncertain wording. The heading calls the psalm a Shiggaion, a word found elsewhere only in Habakkuk 3:1, in the plural (“according to Shigionoth”). Its meaning is uncertain; it probably names a kind of song, perhaps an impassioned one.
verseByVerse.note: A Shiggaion is probably a musical or liturgical term. Cush the Benjaminite is otherwise unknown.

verseByVerse.quote: Arise, O LORD, in your anger; lift yourself up against the fury of my enemies; awake for me; you have appointed a judgment. Let the assembly of the peoples be gathered about you; over it return on high. The LORD judges the peoples; judge me, O LORD, according to my righteousness and according to the integrity that is in me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
David asks God to rise and hold court before the nations and to judge him on this charge by his integrity, appealing over his accusers’ heads to the only court whose verdict is final.

You have appointed a judgment. He asks God to hold court on the grand scale: not a private hearing but the nations assembled and God taking his seat above them. A man lied about in one small place asks for the verdict of the last day.

Awake for me. This is bold to the point of rudeness, and the Psalter will say it again: “Awake! Why are you sleeping, O Lord?” (Psalm 44:23). God is not asleep, and the psalmist knows it; he is describing how the delay feels, and asking God to act.

Judge me, O LORD, according to my righteousness. This sounds dangerous to Christian ears, and it would be, if he were asking about his standing before God in general. He is not; he is asking about this charge, the one Cush has made. A believer may say, with no arrogance at all: “Lord, in that specific matter I am innocent, and you know it.” The same man prays elsewhere, “Enter not into judgment with your servant” (Psalm 143:2), and both are true at once.

Entrusting himself to him who judges justly. Only one man could pray judge me according to my righteousness about his whole life. Jesus was slandered and condemned on false charges, and “when he was reviled, he did not revile in return … but continued entrusting himself to him who judges justly” (1 Peter 2:23). God answered by raising him. The slandered believer prays this psalm in his company.

The court that never adjourns. We live with a court David never faced: public opinion, in permanent session. A rumour like Cush’s can reach thousands before breakfast, and there is no judge, no rule of evidence and no final verdict, only a crowd that keeps on voting. So we keep pleading our case, with the careful post, the long explanation, the friends lined up to vouch for us, and it is exhausting, because a court with no judge can never acquit you. David appeals over the crowd’s head to a court that will actually sit and rule. That is not escapism; it is what lets a slandered person stop defending himself day and night. For a Christian the verdict that matters most has already been given: “There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1). Someone who has heard that can afford to be misunderstood for a while, and can even pray for the people doing the misunderstanding.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–17 — He Makes a Pit and Falls Into It
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Judge whom David has summoned is now described, and he is good news for the slandered. He tests the hidden heart, holds David’s shield, and is indignant at evil every day (vv. 9–11). His weapons are ready, but they are readied in the open, against the one who will not repent (vv. 12–13). Evil itself is pictured as a pregnancy that ends in lies and as a pit that swallows its digger (vv. 14–16). The psalm ends not with the verdict but with thanks and praise to the LORD Most High, offered while the case is still open (v. 17).
verseByVerse.theology: God's daily indignation is good news for the slandered, and evil is built so that it recoils on the head that plans it.

verseByVerse.quote: Oh, let the evil of the wicked come to an end, and may you establish the righteous— you who test the minds and hearts, O righteous God! My shield is with God, who saves the upright in heart. God is a righteous judge, and a God who feels indignation every day. If a man does not repent, God will whet his sword; he has bent and readied his bow; he has prepared for him his deadly weapons, making his arrows fiery shafts.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The God who tests the heart is a righteous judge, steadily opposed to evil, yet his weapons are readied in the open so that the wicked may still turn back.

You who test the minds and hearts. The phrase means the deepest interior, the part of a man nobody else can inspect. This is where a slandered person can finally rest. Reputation is public and can be stolen; the inside of you is known by God alone, and he will speak last.

My shield is with God. This is the third shield in five psalms: around him (3:3), over him like favour (5:12), and here simply held by God and not by David. A man under attack keeps wanting to pick his own shield up. The psalm says it is in better hands.

A God who feels indignation every day. This is not the occasional outburst of a God who loses his temper but the steady moral response of goodness to what evil is doing in his world. Take it away and you have a God who does not care what happens to you. The New Testament names the one through whom this justice will be done: God “will judge the world in righteousness by a man whom he has appointed” (Acts 17:31).

If a man does not repent. The picture is of a warrior arming himself in the open, taking his time, and everything hangs on the first clause. The sword is sharpened where it can be seen: judgment in Scripture is often announced before it falls, and the way out stays open as long as God waits. For everyone who turns, the sword has already fallen on Christ, who bore their judgment at the cross.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew of verse 12 says only “If he does not turn, he will whet his sword”, without naming either subject. The ESV, like most translations, takes it of God arming against the unrepentant man; some read it of the wicked man sharpening his own weapons, which then turn on him in verses 14–16. The first is more likely, since verse 13 says the weapons are prepared “for him”, but both readings end with evil destroyed.
verseByVerse.note: “Minds and hearts” is literally “hearts and kidneys” (ESV note), the inner person.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, the wicked man conceives evil and is pregnant with mischief and gives birth to lies. He makes a pit, digging it out, and falls into the hole that he has made. His mischief returns upon his own head, and on his own skull his violence descends. I will give to the LORD the thanks due to his righteousness, and I will sing praise to the name of the LORD, the Most High.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Evil grows in secret and is built to recoil on the one who plans it, so David leaves his case with God and sings his praise before the verdict comes.

Pregnant with mischief. Two pictures make the same point. First, evil grows like a child in the womb: conceived, carried and delivered, which is to say that the lie Cush told had a long private history before anyone heard it. James says it the same way: “desire when it has conceived gives birth to sin” (James 1:15). Nobody wakes up and destroys a reputation before breakfast; it is carried for months.

He makes a pit. Second, evil is self-defeating by design. The man digs a pit for someone else and the loose earth gives way under his own feet. Scripture tells this story again and again, most memorably of the gallows Haman built for Mordecai and was hanged on himself (Esther 7:10). God has made the world so that malice tends to come back on the one who sent it out. That is not always visible at the time, but it is one reason the righteous can wait. Its greatest instance is the cross, where the powers that dug a pit for the Son of God were undone by it: “None of the rulers of this age understood this, for if they had, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Corinthians 2:8).

What it does not mean. Not a promise that every liar will be publicly exposed in your lifetime; the psalm itself ends with the case still open. Nor permission to sit and watch for someone’s collapse. The man who wrote it twice refused to dig a pit of his own when Saul was within reach (1 Samuel 24:10–11; 26:9–11). You cannot pray verse 15 with any honesty while holding a shovel.

The LORD, the Most High. The last words give a title the Psalter has not used before. Elyon means the one above everything: above Cush, above Saul’s court, above the assembly of the peoples the psalm asked God to convene. A man slandered in a small country remembers how high above it all is the God he has told about it.

Singing before the verdict. Nothing has been settled about Cush; the last verse is a man singing anyway, thanking God for being the kind of God who judges rightly. That is what it looks like to leave a case with him: not silence, not brooding, but praise offered before the outcome is known.

keyVerse.quote: God is a righteous judge, and a God who feels indignation every day.
keyVerse.note: The whole psalm rests on this sentence. Because God is a judge who sees the heart and is never indifferent to evil, a slandered person can leave his case with him instead of fighting it alone. The next verse adds the mercy inside the warning: the weapons are readied only “if a man does not repent”.

7.reflection:
David takes a false accusation straight to God (vv. 1–5). When you have been misrepresented, where do you usually go first, and what would it look like to bring the charge to God like this?

David can say “judge me … according to my righteousness” about one specific charge (v. 8), yet elsewhere he prays, “Enter not into judgment with your servant” (Psalm 143:2). How do both prayers belong in a Christian’s life?

God’s indignation is daily, but his weapons are readied “if a man does not repent” (v. 12). How does this psalm hold together God’s justice and his patience, and how does the cross show both?

The psalm ends in praise before anything is settled (v. 17). What might it look like for you to thank God for his justice while a wrong done to you is still unresolved?

8.title: What Is Man?
8.text: To the choirmaster: according to The Gittith. A Psalm of David. 1O LORD, our Lord, how majestic is your name in all the earth! You have set your glory above the heavens.2Out of the mouth of babies and infants, you have established strength because of your foes, to still the enemy and the avenger.3When I look at your heavens, the work of your fingers, the moon and the stars, which you have set in place,4what is man that you are mindful of him, and the son of man that you care for him?5Yet you have made him a little lower than the heavenly beings and crowned him with glory and honor.6You have given him dominion over the works of your hands; you have put all things under his feet,7all sheep and oxen, and also the beasts of the field,8the birds of the heavens, and the fish of the sea, whatever passes along the paths of the seas.9O LORD, our Lord, how majestic is your name in all the earth!
8.overview:
Where we are. After five psalms of a hunted king crying out by day and night (Psalms 3 to 7), Psalm 8 lifts its eyes to the night sky. It is the Psalter’s first hymn of pure praise, and its frame, “O LORD, our Lord, how majestic is your name in all the earth!” (vv. 1, 9), sets everything in it inside God’s glory.

The message. The God whose glory is above the heavens defeats his enemies with the praise of infants, and he stoops to remember and visit frail human beings, crowning them with glory and giving them charge of his world. Human dignity is real and high, but it is given, held under God, and meant to return to him as praise.

Why it was said. Israel’s neighbours worshipped the sun, moon and stars, and spoke of their kings as the images of their gods. This psalm puts the heavens back in their place as the work of God’s fingers, and gives the crown not to an emperor but to man as such, as Genesis 1 had done.

How the chapter makes its case. It opens with praise for the LORD’s name and his surprising weapon, the praise of infants (vv. 1–2). Under the stars comes the question: what is man, that God should remember him (vv. 3–4)? The answer is a coronation: man is made a little lower than the heavenly beings and given dominion over all God’s works (vv. 5–8). Then the opening line returns, so that man’s glory is framed by God’s (v. 9).

Where it leads. By pattern and fulfilment, as Hebrews reads it. We do not yet see all things under man’s feet, “But we see him who for a little while was made lower than the angels, namely Jesus, crowned with glory and honor because of the suffering of death” (Hebrews 2:9). Adam’s race lost the crown; the last Adam won it by going lower than any of us, and shares it with those he brings to glory. Jesus also claimed verse 2 when children praised him in the temple (Matthew 21:16).

For us. Look up and feel small, then remember that the one who made the stars has you in mind. Treat every human being, unborn, disabled or old, as crowned by God, and the world as his, entrusted to us and not owned. Where you see how badly we rule, look to Jesus, who wears the crown for us.
8.theology:
God defeats the strong with the weak, and Jesus uses v. 2 that way in the temple (Matt 21:15-16).

What is man? (v. 4) is answered not with "nothing" but with a crown (v. 5) and a dominion that repeats Gen 1:26-28. Man rules the works of God's hands, which he did not make and cannot sustain: dominion, not ownership.

That dominion is plainly not yet visible, and Hebrews says so, then points to Jesus, crowned through the suffering of death (Heb 2:8-9; cf. 1 Cor 15:27). The psalm's question is answered by the incarnation: man is the creature God became.
8.examples: Under a night sky anyone can feel small. This psalm does not deny it, but asks us to notice that the God whose fingers made the stars has us in mind. And when we see how badly we rule the world we were given charge of, it points us to the one man who wears the crown.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — Out of the Mouth of Babies
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The psalm opens with the congregation praising the LORD, whose name is majestic in all the earth and whose glory is above the heavens (v. 1). His strength shows in an unlikely place: the mouths of babies, through which he silences his enemies (v. 2). Then the singer stands outside at night, sees the moon and stars as the work of God’s fingers, and asks the honest question: why would such a God remember and visit mortal man (vv. 3–4)? The section moves from God’s greatness to our smallness, so that his care for us may astonish.
verseByVerse.theology: God silences his enemies with infants, and the man who looks up at the stars is asked to notice that God looks down.

verseByVerse.quote: O LORD, our Lord, how majestic is your name in all the earth! You have set your glory above the heavens. Out of the mouth of babies and infants, you have established strength because of your foes, to still the enemy and the avenger.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD’s glory is above the heavens and his name fills the earth, yet he chooses to silence his enemies not by force but by the praise of little children.

O LORD, our Lord. Two different words open the psalm. LORD in capitals is the covenant name God gave to Moses; our Lord is the ordinary word for a master. He is the God bound to a people and the sovereign who owns them, and our makes this a congregation looking up together.

Out of the mouth of babies and infants. God’s chosen weapon against his enemies is the noise small children make. It is the Bible’s strategy in one line: God defeats what is strong with what is weak (1 Corinthians 1:27). Jesus quoted this verse, in its Greek form, on the day the temple authorities lost their tempers. Children were shouting “Hosanna to the Son of David!” in the courts, and when the priests demanded that he silence them he said: “have you never read, ‘Out of the mouth of infants and nursing babies you have prepared praise’?” (Matthew 21:15–16). Where the Hebrew says God establishes strength, the Greek says he prepares praise, and Jesus lets the verse make his defence: the strength God establishes is the children’s praise, sung to his Son.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew of the second line of verse 1 is unusually difficult and has been read in several ways; the ESV’s You have set your glory above the heavens is a reasonable reading, and every proposal puts God’s glory above or in the heavens. The heading’s according to The Gittith is probably a musical direction, perhaps a tune or an instrument named after Gath; its meaning is uncertain.

verseByVerse.quote: When I look at your heavens, the work of your fingers, the moon and the stars, which you have set in place, what is man that you are mindful of him, and the son of man that you care for him?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Under the night sky David feels how small man is, and marvels that the God who made the stars with his fingers keeps frail human beings in mind and comes to care for them.

The work of your fingers. The night sky is doing to him what it does to everyone: making him feel small. The detail that carries the verse is the work of your fingers. Not his arm, not his shoulder: his fingers. Whole galaxies are God’s needlework, done delicately and without strain.

That you are mindful of him. Then the honest question: with all that, why would you give a thought to us? The word for man here stresses frailty: mortal, breakable. Mindful means to keep someone in mind, to remember them deliberately; care for is the word for visiting, coming to see about someone. It is the visit Zechariah sang of when the Son was about to be born: “for he has visited and redeemed his people” (Luke 1:68).

Job’s bitter echo. Job took the same question and threw it back in bitterness, “What is man, that you make so much of him … visit him every morning” (Job 7:17–18), meaning, why will you not leave me alone? The same question can be asked in wonder or in agony, and Scripture prints both. Here it is wonder: the man who feels insignificant under the stars is asked to notice that their Maker has him personally in mind.

Does the size of the universe make us small? Many feel that modern astronomy has answered this verse with “not much”: billions of galaxies, one planet circling an ordinary star, a species that arrived late. But David felt his smallness without a telescope; it is where this psalm starts. Size has never been the measure of worth: a newborn is smaller than a mountain, and nobody thinks the mountain matters more. Blaise Pascal put it memorably: man is only a reed, the feeblest thing in nature, but a thinking reed, and if the universe crushed him he would still be nobler than what killed him, because he would know that he was dying and the universe would know nothing. The psalm goes further than Pascal. Our dignity is not finally that we think about the stars but that the one who made them thinks about us, and, as Hebrews will show, came down to be one of us.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–9 — Crowned with Glory and Honor
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The answer to “what is man?” is a coronation. God has made man a little lower than the heavenly beings, crowned him with glory and honour, and set him over all the works of his hands, from flocks and herds to the creatures of the sea (vv. 5–8), as Genesis 1 had said. Then the opening line returns, so that human dignity is framed on both sides by God’s majesty (v. 9). The New Testament shows that this crown, which we have not worn well, is now worn by Jesus, who shares it with his people.
verseByVerse.theology: The crown given to man in Genesis is worn in full by one man, Jesus.

verseByVerse.quote: Yet you have made him a little lower than the heavenly beings and crowned him with glory and honor. You have given him dominion over the works of your hands; you have put all things under his feet, all sheep and oxen, and also the beasts of the field, the birds of the heavens, and the fish of the sea, whatever passes along the paths of the seas.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The answer to “what is man?” is a coronation: God has set frail humanity just below the heavenly beings, crowned it with glory and honour, and given it charge of all his works.

A little lower than the heavenly beings. The frail creature of verse 4 is placed astonishingly high and crowned. Genesis said the same thing in prose: made in God’s image, told to have dominion over the fish and the birds and every living thing (Genesis 1:26–28; see Image of God in the Theological Dictionary). Every human being wears that crown, whatever his strength or usefulness: the unborn child, the disabled, the old and forgetful. That is why Scripture forbids us even to curse people “made in the likeness of God” (James 3:9).

Dominion over the works of your hands. The heavens were the work of your fingers, and this dominion is over the works of your hands. Man is given charge of things God made, not things man made: a king over a kingdom he did not create and cannot sustain. That is the difference between dominion and ownership, and forgetting it is most of what has gone wrong with the way we handle the world. Rule here means care, as the first man was put in the garden “to work it and keep it” (Genesis 2:15).

For a little while lower. Hebrews follows the Greek translation, “You made him for a little while lower than the angels” (Hebrews 2:7): Christ took that low place in his incarnation, and has been crowned with the glory the psalm promised to man.

Uncertain wording. The word behind heavenly beings is elohim, which usually means God but can mean heavenly beings. The ESV notes that the line can be read “a little lower than God”, and that the Greek Old Testament has “than the angels”, the reading Hebrews quotes. Either way the point stands: man is placed just below the heavenly world and crowned.
verseByVerse.note: “Son of man” in v. 4 is a Hebrew way of saying a human being.

verseByVerse.quote: O LORD, our Lord, how majestic is your name in all the earth!
verseByVerse.commentary:
The psalm ends where it began, with God’s majestic name, and the crown that we have not worn well is shown, in the New Testament, to be worn by Jesus.

How majestic is your name in all the earth! The psalm ends on the line it started with, which is the right shape: the middle is about us, and both ends are about him. Whatever glory man has is on loan and reflects back to him.

What we do not yet see. But a Christian cannot read verses 5–8 without the ache. All things under his feet? We cannot govern our own appetites, let alone the seas. The writer to the Hebrews quotes verses 4 to 6, then says exactly that: “At present, we do not yet see everything in subjection to him. But we see him who for a little while was made lower than the angels, namely Jesus, crowned with glory and honor because of the suffering of death, so that by the grace of God he might taste death for everyone” (Hebrews 2:8–9).

The answer to the question. There is the answer to the psalm’s question, and it is better than the question. What is man? Man is the creature God became. The crown Adam threw away is on the head of the Son of Man, and he did not seize it: he came down to where the frail and breakable are, went lower than any of us in death, and was crowned there. Paul takes the same line to its end: God “put all things under his feet and gave him as head over all things to the church” (Ephesians 1:22). Nothing in the universe is outside that rule, and the head of it loves you. Go outside and look up, and say the first line again.

Where Christians differ: is Psalm 8 a prophecy of Christ? Some read it as directly about the Messiah, hearing in son of man Jesus’ title for himself; others read it simply as a hymn about humanity, and take Hebrews 2 to speak of mankind until it reaches Jesus in verse 9. This commentary’s view: the psalm is first about man as God created him, echoing Genesis 1, and is not a prediction as Psalm 110 is; son of man here means a human being. But Hebrews shows that its crowned, ruling man is found only in Jesus, the last Adam, and through him in the “many sons” he is bringing to glory (Hebrews 2:10).

keyVerse.quote: what is man that you are mindful of him, and the son of man that you care for him?
keyVerse.note: This is the question the whole psalm turns on, asked under a sky full of stars. The answer is not that man is nothing, but that God has crowned him (v. 5), and Hebrews 2 shows the fullest answer: the God who made the stars came to visit us in his Son, who became man and now wears the crown on our behalf.

8.reflection:
The psalm begins and ends with God’s majestic name (vv. 1, 9). Why does it matter that human glory is set inside that frame, and what happens when it is not?

God silences his enemies “out of the mouth of babies and infants” (v. 2), and Jesus applied this to children praising him (Matthew 21:16). Where have you seen God use weakness to do what strength could not?

Under the stars David asks, “What is man?” (v. 4). How does this psalm answer people who feel insignificant, and how should it shape the way we treat the unborn, the disabled and the elderly?

Hebrews says, “At present, we do not yet see everything in subjection to him. But we see … Jesus” (Hebrews 2:8–9). How does looking at Jesus help when you see how badly human beings rule the world, or themselves?

9.title: A Stronghold for the Oppressed
9.text: To the choirmaster: according to Muth-labben. A Psalm of David. 1I will give thanks to the LORD with my whole heart; I will recount all of your wonderful deeds.2I will be glad and exult in you; I will sing praise to your name, O Most High.3When my enemies turn back, they stumble and perish before your presence.4For you have maintained my just cause; you have sat on the throne, giving righteous judgment.5You have rebuked the nations; you have made the wicked perish; you have blotted out their name forever and ever.6The enemy came to an end in everlasting ruins; their cities you rooted out; the very memory of them has perished.7But the LORD sits enthroned forever; he has established his throne for justice,8and he judges the world with righteousness; he judges the peoples with uprightness.9The LORD is a stronghold for the oppressed, a stronghold in times of trouble.10And those who know your name put their trust in you, for you, O LORD, have not forsaken those who seek you.11Sing praises to the LORD, who sits enthroned in Zion! Tell among the peoples his deeds!12For he who avenges blood is mindful of them; he does not forget the cry of the afflicted.13Be gracious to me, O LORD! See my affliction from those who hate me, O you who lift me up from the gates of death,14that I may recount all your praises, that in the gates of the daughter of Zion I may rejoice in your salvation.15The nations have sunk in the pit that they made; in the net that they hid, their own foot has been caught.16The LORD has made himself known; he has executed judgment; the wicked are snared in the work of their own hands. Higgaion. Selah17The wicked shall return to Sheol, all the nations that forget God.18For the needy shall not always be forgotten, and the hope of the poor shall not perish forever.19Arise, O LORD! Let not man prevail; let the nations be judged before you!20Put them in fear, O LORD! Let the nations know that they are but men! Selah
9.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 9 follows Psalm 8’s wonder at the LORD whose name is majestic in all the earth, and it opens a pair: Psalms 9 and 10 run together through the Hebrew alphabet as one acrostic poem, and the Greek Old Testament prints them as a single psalm. This is the thanksgiving half; Psalm 10 is the lament.

The message. God is not one more power that rises and falls. When the empires that frightened his people have gone so completely that no one remembers their names, he is still seated on his throne, judging the world in righteousness. So the weak have somewhere to run: the LORD is a stronghold for the oppressed, he keeps the record of the blood of the powerless, and though the needy are forgotten for now, they will not always be.

Why it was said. David had seen God scatter enemies who looked unbeatable (see the introduction), and Israel lived among nations far stronger than itself. The psalm taught a small people to praise God in public, and to pray for the day when every proud nation would learn that it is only human.

How the chapter makes its case. David resolves to thank God with his whole heart and recounts what God has done: enemies turned back, his cause upheld, nations rebuked until their very memory perished (vv. 1–6). Against all that passing away he sets the throne that does not pass: the LORD judges the world, shelters the oppressed and remembers the cry of the afflicted, so his deeds must be told among the peoples (vv. 7–12). Then thanks becomes prayer, to be lifted from the gates of death to the gates of Zion (vv. 13–14). The nations fall into their own pit, the wicked return to Sheol, and the needy will not always be forgotten (vv. 15–18). The psalm ends asking God to arise and teach the nations that they are but men (vv. 19–20).

Where it leads. To Christ by the character of God revealed in him, and by fulfilment. Paul echoed verse 8 in Athens and named the Judge: God “has fixed a day on which he will judge the world in righteousness by a man whom he has appointed” (Acts 17:31). The one enthroned for justice is the risen Jesus. He was not only brought near the gates of death but went through them and holds their keys, and the day the psalm prays for comes when “The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ” (Revelation 11:15).

For us. Praise is a decision with a memory: sit down and recount what God has done for you in Christ, and then tell someone. If you are among the oppressed, run to the stronghold and hold on to the word “always” in verse 18: your cry is on God’s record, and the risen Judge will answer it.
9.theology:
Psalms 9 and 10 are one poem in two moods: God has judged, and God seems absent. Both belong in the same book and the same believer.

God's throne outlasts every power whose memory has perished (vv. 6-7), and that permanence makes him a stronghold for the oppressed (v. 9). Trust grows from knowing his name (v. 10).

Blood cries out and is heard (v. 12; Rev 6:10), and evil is snared in its own work (vv. 15-16). The psalm admits that the needy are forgotten now and denies that they always will be (v. 18). Its last petition is that the nations learn they are only men (v. 20; cf. Rev 11:15).
9.examples: Praise in this psalm is a decision with a list attached: he sits down to recount what God has done. And for anyone who has waited long for justice, verse 18 puts a time limit on it: the needy shall not always be forgotten.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — The LORD Sits Enthroned Forever
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The throne that outlasts every empire is the refuge of people with no power at all. David begins with a decision, to thank God with his whole heart and go through the list of his wonderful deeds (vv. 1–2). The list is of enemies turned back and a just cause upheld, of nations rebuked and cities uprooted until even their memory has perished (vv. 3–6). Then comes the great “But”: when everything that looked permanent has gone, the LORD still sits enthroned, judging the world in righteousness (vv. 7–8). That makes him a stronghold for the oppressed, trusted by those who know his name (vv. 9–10), and it sends his people out to tell the nations what he has done, for he does not forget the cry of the afflicted (vv. 11–12).
verseByVerse.theology: The throne that outlasts empires is the refuge of people with no power at all.

verseByVerse.quote: I will give thanks to the LORD with my whole heart; I will recount all of your wonderful deeds. I will be glad and exult in you; I will sing praise to your name, O Most High. When my enemies turn back, they stumble and perish before your presence. For you have maintained my just cause; you have sat on the throne, giving righteous judgment. You have rebuked the nations; you have made the wicked perish; you have blotted out their name forever and ever. The enemy came to an end in everlasting ruins; their cities you rooted out; the very memory of them has perished.
verseByVerse.commentary:
David deliberately thanks God for judging in his favour and wiping out enemies so completely that even their memory has gone.

Half a poem. Psalms 9 and 10 together run through the Hebrew alphabet, stanza by stanza, and in the Greek Old Testament they are a single psalm. So this is half a poem: thanksgiving that God has judged, before the half that asks why he stands far off. Anyone who has swung between those two in a single week is holding the right book.

With my whole heart. Five verbs, all first person and all deliberate: give thanks, recount, be glad, exult, sing praise. Praise here is not a mood that arrives but a decision with a memory attached: he is going to recount, to go through the list.

Giving righteous judgment. The Judge of Psalm 7 has taken his seat and ruled, and it is his presence, not David’s sword, that turns the enemy back. Nations are rebuked and cities rooted out, and the empire that meant to be remembered forever is not remembered at all.

Uncertain wording. Muth-labben in the heading is probably the name of a tune; its meaning is uncertain.
verseByVerse.note: The acrostic is "broken": some letters are missing or out of order, especially in Psalm 10.

verseByVerse.quote: But the LORD sits enthroned forever; he has established his throne for justice, and he judges the world with righteousness; he judges the peoples with uprightness. The LORD is a stronghold for the oppressed, a stronghold in times of trouble. And those who know your name put their trust in you, for you, O LORD, have not forsaken those who seek you. Sing praises to the LORD, who sits enthroned in Zion! Tell among the peoples his deeds! For he who avenges blood is mindful of them; he does not forget the cry of the afflicted.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When every empire has gone, the LORD is still on his throne, and that makes him a fortress for the powerless, to be trusted by his people and made known to the nations.

But the LORD sits enthroned forever. Verse 7 begins with But: cities fall and their memory perishes, and God is still seated. The contrast is the argument: everything that looked permanent has gone, and the throne has not moved.

A stronghold for the oppressed. A stronghold is a fortress, out of reach of those who would drag you down, and God is that to the people with the least power in the psalm: the oppressed, those who cannot fight back. And those who know your name trust him: trust is not a leap in the dark but grows out of knowing who God is, which is why learning what he is like is never a luxury.

Tell among the peoples his deeds! Verse 11 gives two commands, and the second is the surprising one. The nations have just been rebuked (v. 5), and now God’s people are told to go and tell those same nations what he has done. Israel’s praise was never meant to stay indoors. God is enthroned in Zion, a particular hill in a particular city, and the news about him is for everyone.

He who avenges blood. The phrase goes back to the first murder, when God told Cain, “The voice of your brother’s blood is crying to me from the ground” (Genesis 4:10). Spilled blood has a voice, and God hears it. The line runs forward to the martyrs under the altar, crying, “how long before you will judge and avenge our blood” (Revelation 6:10). Every violence done to the powerless is on a record God keeps and will settle. To the person who has been hurt and never heard an apology: he does not forget the cry.

The Judge is a man. Paul echoed verse 8 when he preached in Athens: God “has fixed a day on which he will judge the world in righteousness by a man whom he has appointed”, and has given assurance of it “by raising him from the dead” (Acts 17:31). The Judge on the throne is the risen Jesus. And the command to tell the peoples runs straight to his words on a mountain in Galilee: make disciples of all nations (Matthew 28:16–19).

How do I tell his deeds? Start with what he has done. The psalm says tell his deeds, not your opinions: the cross and empty tomb, and what he has done for you. Use the openings you are given. When a colleague asks about your weekend, or a friend wonders how you coped, say plainly that God helped you, and how. Peter asks only that we be “prepared to make a defense to anyone who asks you for a reason for the hope that is in you”, and do it “with gentleness and respect” (1 Peter 3:15). Pray for names. Keep two or three people in your prayers by name, and ask for an opening with each. Invite. Bring someone where the deeds are told: to church, to your table, to read a Gospel with you. You do not carry the results. The deeds are God’s, the power is the Spirit’s, promised for exactly this (Acts 1:8), and the risen Christ goes with his witnesses: “I am with you always, to the end of the age” (Matthew 28:20).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–20 — Let the Nations Know That They Are But Men
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Thanks turns to prayer, and the psalm ends by asking God to show the nations what they really are. David asks for grace in his affliction, to be lifted from the gates of death so that he may praise God in the gates of Zion (vv. 13–14). He looks again at how God judges: the nations are caught in the pit and the net they prepared for others, and in that the LORD makes himself known (vv. 15–16). The wicked, and every nation that forgets God, return to Sheol, while the needy, forgotten now, will not be forgotten forever (vv. 17–18). So he prays: arise, O LORD, do not let mere man prevail, and let the nations know that they are but men (vv. 19–20).
verseByVerse.theology: There are two gates and two destinies, and a prayer that the nations would remember what they are.

verseByVerse.quote: Be gracious to me, O LORD! See my affliction from those who hate me, O you who lift me up from the gates of death, that I may recount all your praises, that in the gates of the daughter of Zion I may rejoice in your salvation. The nations have sunk in the pit that they made; in the net that they hid, their own foot has been caught. The LORD has made himself known; he has executed judgment; the wicked are snared in the work of their own hands. Higgaion. Selah The wicked shall return to Sheol, all the nations that forget God. For the needy shall not always be forgotten, and the hope of the poor shall not perish forever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
David asks to be lifted from death’s door to Zion’s, and sees evil caught in its own traps while the needy, forgotten now, will not be forgotten forever.

From the gates of death to the gates of Zion. Two gates stand one verse apart. He has been at the gates of death, near enough to touch the door of the grave, and he asks to stand instead in the gates of the daughter of Zion, the city gateway where people met, traded, gave evidence and sang. That is the distance salvation covers, and he wants it so that he may praise where people can hear him.

The pit that they made. The pit of Psalm 7 appears again, dug now by empires rather than by one liar, with the same result: the trap closes on the trapper. The comment on it is the important line: the LORD has made himself known. God is revealed by how history turns out, not only by what he says.

All the nations that forget God. Judgment falls not only on the nations that fight God but on those that forget him. That is how most people and most cultures leave God, not by argument but by distraction, until he simply does not come up. And return to Sheol, the realm of the dead, is a terrible phrase: a life organised without God ends where it started, in the dust.

The needy shall not always be forgotten. The word always concedes that the needy are forgotten now; the psalm is not pretending, but putting a time limit on the injustice. That concession is exactly where the next psalm begins.

Through the gates of death. That return is exactly what the gospel exists to reverse: Christ went through the gates of death and came out, and now holds “the keys of Death and Hades” (Revelation 1:18).

Uncertain wording. Higgaion (v. 16), from a verb meaning to murmur or meditate, is probably a musical direction, like Selah beside it; the exact meaning of both is unknown.

verseByVerse.quote: Arise, O LORD! Let not man prevail; let the nations be judged before you! Put them in fear, O LORD! Let the nations know that they are but men! Selah
verseByVerse.commentary:
The psalm asks God to rise and teach the proud nations the truth they have forgotten: that they are only human.

Let the nations know that they are but men! The last prayer is not that the nations be destroyed but that they be told the truth about themselves. All the damage done in this psalm was done by people who had forgotten they were people: mortal, accountable, made. To know you are but men is the beginning of sanity for a person and for a government.

The final announcement. One day it will be announced publicly: “The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ, and he shall reign forever and ever” (Revelation 11:15). Until then the church prays Psalm 9’s last line over every power that thinks it is more than dust, and prays it for herself first.

keyVerse.quote: The LORD is a stronghold for the oppressed, a stronghold in times of trouble.
keyVerse.note: The praise of the enthroned Judge (vv. 7–8) comes to rest here: the throne that outlasts every empire is a refuge for people with no power at all. The “times of trouble” it names are exactly the times Psalm 10 will describe, so this verse is the ground the next psalm stands on.

9.reflection:
David decides to “recount all of your wonderful deeds” (v. 1). What would be on your list, and how might going through it change the way you pray in a hard week?

Verses 5–7 set empires that vanish beside a throne that lasts forever. What powers or pressures seem permanent to you at the moment, and how does this psalm put them in their place?

“Those who know your name put their trust in you” (v. 10). How has learning what God is like helped you trust him? Which of his deeds in Christ could you tell a friend about this week (v. 11)?

The psalm admits that the needy are forgotten now, but “not always” (v. 18), and Paul says the Judge is the risen Jesus (Acts 17:31). How does that give hope to people who have suffered injustice, and what part can we play in remembering them?

10.title: Why Do You Stand Far Away?
10.text: <sup>1</sup>Why, O LORD, do you stand far away? Why do you hide yourself in times of trouble?<sup>2</sup>In arrogance the wicked hotly pursue the poor; let them be caught in the schemes that they have devised.<sup>3</sup>For the wicked boasts of the desires of his soul, and the one greedy for gain curses and renounces the LORD.<sup>4</sup>In the pride of his face the wicked does not seek him; all his thoughts are, "There is no God."<sup>5</sup>His ways prosper at all times; your judgments are on high, out of his sight; as for all his foes, he puffs at them.<sup>6</sup>He says in his heart, "I shall not be moved; throughout all generations I shall not meet adversity."<sup>7</sup>His mouth is filled with cursing and deceit and oppression; under his tongue are mischief and iniquity.<sup>8</sup>He sits in ambush in the villages; in hiding places he murders the innocent. His eyes stealthily watch for the helpless;<sup>9</sup>he lurks in ambush like a lion in his thicket; he lurks that he may seize the poor; he seizes the poor when he draws him into his net.<sup>10</sup>The helpless are crushed, sink down, and fall by his might.<sup>11</sup>He says in his heart, "God has forgotten, he has hidden his face, he will never see it."<sup>12</sup>Arise, O LORD; O God, lift up your hand; forget not the afflicted.<sup>13</sup>Why does the wicked renounce God and say in his heart, "You will not call to account"?<sup>14</sup>But you do see, for you note mischief and vexation, that you may take it into your hands; to you the helpless commits himself; you have been the helper of the fatherless.<sup>15</sup>Break the arm of the wicked and evildoer; call his wickedness to account till you find none.<sup>16</sup>The LORD is king forever and ever; the nations perish from his land.<sup>17</sup>O LORD, you hear the desire of the afflicted; you will strengthen their heart; you will incline your ear<sup>18</sup>to do justice to the fatherless and the oppressed, so that man who is of the earth may strike terror no more.
10.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 10 has no heading because it is the second half of the acrostic poem begun in Psalm 9. That psalm ended by insisting that the needy will not always be forgotten; this one begins by asking why they are forgotten now.

The message. When God seems far away and the wicked prosper unchecked, faith does not pretend; it takes the question to God. The predator’s creed is that no one is watching. The believer’s answer is “But you do see”: God keeps the accounts, takes up the case of the helpless as his own, and reigns as King forever, so that man who is of the earth will one day terrify no more.

Why it was said. Israel knew men of power who preyed on the poor in the villages, inside the covenant people as well as among the nations, and verse 16 sets the two side by side. The psalm gave the helpless words for the long wait between God’s promise of justice and its arrival (see the introduction on the psalms that curse).

How the chapter makes its case. It opens with the question: why do you stand far away? (v. 1). Then it lets the wicked man be seen and heard at length: proud, greedy, successful, contemptuous, sure he will never be moved, lying in ambush like a lion for the helpless, and telling himself that God has forgotten (vv. 2–11). The psalmist answers with prayer, arise and do not forget the afflicted (vv. 12–13), and with the words on which the poem turns, “But you do see” (vv. 14–15). It ends in confidence: the LORD is king forever, and he hears, strengthens and does justice for the fatherless (vv. 16–18).

Where it leads. To Christ by the need it exposes and by the character of God revealed in him. Paul quotes verse 7 among his proofs that the whole world is under sin (Romans 3:14), so the predator’s mouth is not only the other man’s. And the God who seemed far off came near in his Son, who sided with the poor, was himself ambushed by powerful men, cried “why have you forsaken me?” (Matthew 27:46), and was raised. He is the King who will do justice for the fatherless, and a high priest able “to sympathize with our weaknesses” (Hebrews 4:15).

For us. When God seems silent, do what the psalmist does: bring the question to him instead of drawing the wicked man’s conclusion. Live as someone who knows the accounts are kept, and if you are helpless, commit yourself to the one who has always been the helper of the fatherless and who, in Christ, has come near.
10.theology:
God's apparent absence is put into words rather than denied (v. 1), and the same appearance is read two ways: the believer asks why God hides, the wicked concludes that God has forgotten (v. 11).

Practical atheism, living as if there were no God, is a working assumption rather than an argument (v. 4), and Paul cites v. 7 as a description of the whole race (Rom 3:14).

The turn is the knowledge that God sees and takes the case in hand (v. 14). His first gift to the afflicted is often a strengthened heart (v. 17), and the terrifying man is only dust that has learned to frighten people (v. 18).
10.examples: Many people who would call themselves believers live as though no one is keeping accounts; the test is what we assume when nobody is looking. And predators still choose targets who cannot afford lawyers. To them, and to every helpless person, this psalm says that God sees, and has always been the helper of the fatherless.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — He Says in His Heart, God Has Forgotten
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When God seems absent, the psalm says so to his face, and then lets us hear what the predator says in his heart. It opens with two questions: why do you stand far away, why do you hide in times of trouble? (v. 1). Then comes a long portrait of the wicked man. He is proud and greedy, and lives as if there were no God (vv. 2–4). He prospers, sneers at opposition and is sure nothing will ever shake him (vv. 5–7). He hunts the helpless like a lion from its thicket (vv. 8–10). And his creed turns the psalmist’s question into a verdict: God has forgotten and will never see (v. 11). The same silence leads to two opposite conclusions.
verseByVerse.theology: The psalm lets the predator speak at length, and his creed is not atheism but the assumption that nobody is watching.

verseByVerse.quote: Why, O LORD, do you stand far away? Why do you hide yourself in times of trouble? In arrogance the wicked hotly pursue the poor; let them be caught in the schemes that they have devised. For the wicked boasts of the desires of his soul, and the one greedy for gain curses and renounces the LORD. In the pride of his face the wicked does not seek him; all his thoughts are, "There is no God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Why does God seem far away while proud men hunt the poor and live as though there were no God?

Why, O LORD, do you stand far away? This is how the join with Psalm 9 sounds: not doubt replacing faith, but faith asking its question out loud. He does not say God is absent but that he is standing far away, close enough to be seen and not close enough to help, which is somehow harder. If you have prayed that sentence, you are in the Bible.

Let them be caught. The psalm’s first petition is tucked inside the description: let them be caught in the schemes that they have devised (v. 2). It is the pit of Psalm 7 again: let the scheme close on the schemer.

There is no God. The last line of the portrait is its key. All his thoughts are, “There is no God” is not a philosophy but a working assumption. He has not sat down and disproved anything; he simply runs his life as if no one is keeping accounts, a creed held by many people who would tick the box marked believer.

Uncertain wording. Verse 3 is hard to translate. The verb rendered curses normally means “bless”, though it is sometimes used for its opposite, so older translations read it of the wicked man blessing the greedy whom the LORD renounces. Either way, greed and contempt for God go together.

verseByVerse.quote: His ways prosper at all times; your judgments are on high, out of his sight; as for all his foes, he puffs at them. He says in his heart, "I shall not be moved; throughout all generations I shall not meet adversity." His mouth is filled with cursing and deceit and oppression; under his tongue are mischief and iniquity. He sits in ambush in the villages; in hiding places he murders the innocent. His eyes stealthily watch for the helpless; he lurks in ambush like a lion in his thicket; he lurks that he may seize the poor; he seizes the poor when he draws him into his net. The helpless are crushed, sink down, and fall by his might. He says in his heart, "God has forgotten, he has hidden his face, he will never see it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The wicked man prospers, sneers and hunts the helpless, all on the assumption that God will never see.

His ways prosper at all times. Two things make him unbearable: he is successful, and he is untroubled. God’s judgments are on high, out of his sight, far above his eye level, because he never looks up. And he is sure his arrangement will never be disturbed: I shall not be moved.

He puffs at them. He blows at opposition the way you blow dust off a table. Contempt gives him away: a man frightened of nobody has usually stopped believing that anyone, God included, can call him to account.

His mouth is filled with cursing. Paul puts this verse into his catalogue of what human beings are without God: “Their mouth is full of curses and bitterness” (Romans 3:14). The psalm’s monster shows where the whole race heads when left to itself, so the portrait is a mirror before it is a window.

He sits in ambush. The hunting imagery is patient and professional: sitting, watching, lurking, netting, like a lion in his thicket. This is not a man who loses his temper but one who plans, and his victims are always the poor, the helpless, the innocent.

God has forgotten. Read verse 11 beside verse 1. The psalmist asked, why do you hide yourself? The wicked man declares, he has hidden his face. One man takes God’s hiddenness to God as a question; the other takes it as permission. What you do with God’s apparent silence is one of the truest tests of what you are.

If someone is preying on you. God’s seeing is not a reason to wait in danger. Tell someone you trust, and seek safety and help at once.

Uncertain wording. The word translated helpless (vv. 8, 10, 14) is found only in this psalm, and its exact sense is uncertain; “the hapless” or “the wretched” is close. Verse 10 is also compressed in Hebrew, though its picture is clear.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The psalm turns from describing evil to calling on God, and from appearance to truth. The psalmist asks God to arise, lift his hand and not forget the afflicted, for the wicked think he will never call them to account (vv. 12–13). Then come the words that change everything, “But you do see”: God notes every wrong in order to take it into his own hands, and the helpless commit themselves to the one who has always helped the fatherless (v. 14). So he asks God to break the arm that crushes (v. 15), and ends in confidence: the LORD is king forever; he hears the afflicted, strengthens their heart and will do them justice, until man who is of the earth strikes terror no more (vv. 16–18).
verseByVerse.theology: The God who seemed far away has been holding the fatherless all along.
