verseByVerse.quote: Arise, O LORD; O God, lift up your hand; forget not the afflicted. Why does the wicked renounce God and say in his heart, "You will not call to account"? But you do see, for you note mischief and vexation, that you may take it into your hands; to you the helpless commits himself; you have been the helper of the fatherless. Break the arm of the wicked and evildoer; call his wickedness to account till you find none.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The psalmist calls on God to rise, and remembers that God does see every wrong and takes the case of the helpless into his own hands.

Lift up your hand. Watch the hands in this psalm. The wicked man’s might crushes the helpless (v. 10); the psalmist asks God to lift up your hand (v. 12) and later to break the wicked man’s arm (v. 15). It is a plain request for one strength to overpower another, and he asks God to do it rather than hitting back himself.

But you do see. Three words turn the poem. Nothing has changed outside; no thunderbolt has fallen. The psalmist simply remembers, against appearances, that the accounts are being kept. God does not merely notice the mischief; he notes it, that you may take it into your hands, the language of a case taken up rather than filed away.

The helper of the fatherless. Two clauses carry the pastoral weight of the psalm: to you the helpless commits himself, and you have been the helper of the fatherless. Present and past, faith and evidence. Anyone with no advocate has the Judge himself.

Break the arm of the wicked. The arm is the strength that does the crushing. He asks for that power to be broken, not for the man to be tortured, and he asks God to do it (see the introduction on the psalms that curse).

The Judge has been the helpless one. The Christian can say more than the psalmist could. The God who seemed to stand far off came near in his Son, who took the side of the poor, was himself ambushed by powerful men and crushed, and was raised. The Judge who will do justice for the fatherless (v. 18) has been the helpless one himself, a high priest able “to sympathize with our weaknesses” (Hebrews 4:15).

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD is king forever and ever; the nations perish from his land. O LORD, you hear the desire of the afflicted; you will strengthen their heart; you will incline your ear to do justice to the fatherless and the oppressed, so that man who is of the earth may strike terror no more.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The psalm ends with the King who reigns forever, hears the afflicted and will do them justice, until mere earthly man frightens no one again.

The LORD is king forever and ever. The poem that began with a God standing far off ends with a King who is not going anywhere (compare Exodus 15:18), and with three verbs of nearness: he hears, he strengthens, he inclines his ear. Look at the middle one: you will strengthen their heart is often what God does first, before he changes a single circumstance. Courage given to the afflicted is already an answer, though not the whole answer.

The nations perish from his land. The word his matters. Every predator in this psalm has been operating on ground that belongs to someone else. He is a squatter with a weapon, and the owner is coming back.

Man who is of the earth. The last line puts the terrifying man in his place: he is man who is of the earth, dust that will go back to dust. That is the whole of his power. He is soil that learned to frighten people, and he will stop.

Christ’s reign. The Christian reads it knowing when: “The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ, and he shall reign forever and ever” (Revelation 11:15). Until then, the prayer of the fatherless is a prayer God has promised to hear (v. 17).

keyVerse.quote: But you do see, for you note mischief and vexation, that you may take it into your hands; to you the helpless commits himself; you have been the helper of the fatherless.
keyVerse.note: “But you do see” is the hinge of the psalm. It answers both the psalmist’s question (v. 1) and the wicked man’s creed (v. 11): nothing has changed outside, but the believer remembers that God keeps the accounts and takes up the case of those who have no one else.

10.reflection:
The psalm opens, “Why, O LORD, do you stand far away?” (v. 1). Have you ever prayed something like it? Why is it better to bring that question to God than to keep it to yourself?

The wicked man’s creed is not argued atheism but a working assumption: “There is no God” (v. 4), and no one will ever see (v. 11). Where are Christians tempted to live by that assumption? Paul applies verse 7 to us all (Romans 3:14): how does that change the way we read the portrait?

The believer and the wicked man face the same silence of God and reach opposite conclusions (vv. 1, 11). What helps you read God’s apparent silence the way the psalmist does?

God strengthens the heart of the afflicted (v. 17), often before circumstances change, and in Jesus he became the helpless one himself. Who in your community is “fatherless” or helpless, and how might your church show them the God who sees?

11.title: The LORD Is in His Holy Temple
11.text: To the choirmaster. Of David. 1In the LORD I take refuge; how can you say to my soul, Flee like a bird to your mountain,2for behold, the wicked bend the bow; they have fitted their arrow to the string to shoot in the dark at the upright in heart;3if the foundations are destroyed, what can the righteous do?4The LORD is in his holy temple; the LORD's throne is in heaven; his eyes see, his eyelids test the children of man.5The LORD tests the righteous, but his soul hates the wicked and the one who loves violence.6Let him rain coals on the wicked; fire and sulfur and a scorching wind shall be the portion of their cup.7For the LORD is righteous; he loves righteous deeds; the upright shall behold his face.
11.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 11 follows the long lament of Psalms 9 and 10, where the wicked lay in ambush for the helpless. Now the arrows are on the string, and the question is whether the righteous should run.

The message. When the structures that hold a society together are crumbling and the danger is real, the believer’s safety is not a better hiding place but the LORD himself, who is still on his throne. He sees everything, tests his people, hates violence and will judge it, and the upright will see his face. Fear must not be allowed to choose our refuge.

Why it was said. David knew years when flight was wise and moments when advisers urged it (see the introduction on the titles). The psalm does not name its occasion. It gives words to any believer in a time when justice seems to have failed and good people wonder what difference one honest life can make.

How the chapter makes its case. David opens with his confession, “In the LORD I take refuge”, and quotes the counsel he rejects: flee like a bird, for the archers are in the dark and the foundations are destroyed (vv. 1–3). He answers with where God is: in his holy temple, on his throne in heaven, his eyes examining all people, testing the righteous and hating the one who loves violence (vv. 4–5). The wicked will drink a cup of fire and sulphur, but the LORD is righteous and loves righteousness, and the upright shall behold his face (vv. 6–7).

Where it leads. To Christ by the character of God revealed in him and by promise. The cup of judgment is the cup Jesus asked might pass from him in Gethsemane and then drank at the cross, so that those who trust him are handed another cup. And the psalm’s last line becomes his promise, “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew 5:8), fulfilled when his servants “will see his face” (Revelation 22:4). The upright who see God are those made upright in him.

For us. When the news makes you want to run, do not let fear choose your refuge. Look up at the occupied throne, stay at your post where faithfulness is still possible, and live towards the day you will see his face.
11.theology:
The counsel to flee is sensible and is refused, because it lets fear choose the refuge, and in the LORD I take refuge was already true (v. 1). When the foundations shake, the answer is an occupied throne (v. 4).

God inspects closely (v. 4) and tests the righteous rather than exempting them (v. 5). What he hates is the love of violence, a settled taste, not a single failure.

Everyone drinks a cup (v. 6), and Christ drank the cup of the wicked. The upright are promised not safety but sight: the upright shall behold his face (v. 7; Matt 5:8; Rev 22:4).
11.examples: The voice urging us to run often sounds like a friend's, and is right about the facts. When decent people watch the walls of their society crack, this psalm does not tell them the cracks are imaginary; it tells them that God’s throne is not in the building, and that in the end the upright will see his face.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–3 — How Can You Say, Flee Like a Bird?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The pressure in this psalm comes from friends giving sensible advice, and the advice is to run. David begins with what is already true, “In the LORD I take refuge”, and so asks how anyone can tell him to flee like a bird to the hills (v. 1). Their reasons are real: the wicked have their arrows fitted to the string, ready to shoot from the dark at the upright (v. 2). And they end with a question that has haunted good people in every bad age: if the foundations are destroyed, what can the righteous do? (v. 3). David does not deny the danger; he refuses to let fear decide where his refuge is.
verseByVerse.theology: The pressure in this psalm comes from friends giving sensible advice, and the advice is to run.

verseByVerse.quote: In the LORD I take refuge; how can you say to my soul, Flee like a bird to your mountain, for behold, the wicked bend the bow; they have fitted their arrow to the string to shoot in the dark at the upright in heart; if the foundations are destroyed, what can the righteous do?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Friends urge David to run because the danger is real, but he already has a refuge in the LORD and will not let fear choose another.

Flee like a bird to your mountain. The voice being answered is most naturally a friend’s, not an enemy’s. People who care about him are saying: take to the hills like a bird off a branch. And their reasons are good: archers shoot from the dark (v. 2), which is how the upright usually get hit.

If the foundations are destroyed. When the structures that hold a society upright give way (courts that can be bought, laws that mean whatever power says, a king’s court run on flattery), what is the point of one honest man?

In the LORD I take refuge. David disputes not the facts but the conclusion, with the psalm’s first line: “I already have a refuge; why are you offering me a mountain?” There are times to flee, and David hid in caves from Saul for years. This is not a rule against prudence but a refusal to let fear pick the refuge.

The one who did not run. Jesus heard the same advice: “Get away from here, for Herod wants to kill you” (Luke 13:31). He went on towards Jerusalem, trusting his Father, and because he did not run, we have a refuge that cannot be destroyed.

Uncertain wording. Verse 3 can also be read as a statement rather than a question, as the ESV notes: “for the foundations will be destroyed; what has the righteous done?”

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The answer to a shaking world is not a better hiding place but an occupied throne. The LORD is in his holy temple and his throne is in heaven, beyond the reach of any collapse on earth, and his eyes examine every human being (v. 4). He tests the righteous, and he hates the wicked and the one who loves violence (v. 5). So the wicked will receive their portion, a cup of coals, fire and sulphur like the judgment on Sodom (v. 6). But the LORD is righteous and loves righteous deeds, and the psalm ends on its highest promise: the upright shall behold his face (v. 7).
verseByVerse.theology: The answer to a shaking world is not a better hiding place but an occupied throne, and a face the upright will see.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD is in his holy temple; the LORD's throne is in heaven; his eyes see, his eyelids test the children of man. The LORD tests the righteous, but his soul hates the wicked and the one who loves violence.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD is still on his throne, examining everyone closely, testing the righteous and hating those who love violence.

The LORD is in his holy temple. His whole answer is to say where God is: the foundations may be going, but God’s throne is not in the building. Habakkuk answered a collapsing nation with the same sentence: “the LORD is in his holy temple; let all the earth keep silence before him” (Habakkuk 2:20).

His eyelids test the children of man. The narrowing eyelids are the look of someone leaning in to be sure of what he sees. God is inspecting the world at close range, and the arrow fired from the dark was fired in full light as far as he is concerned.

The LORD tests the righteous. Not only the wicked: testing is not evidence that God has looked away but part of what he does with the people he loves, as gold is tested by fire (1 Peter 1:6–7). What he hates is not the tested man but the one who loves violence: a love, a settled taste, not a single act.

Does God hate people? The psalm means God’s settled opposition to those given over to evil, not a flare of temper. The same God “so loved the world, that he gave his only Son” (John 3:16) and calls the violent to repent, as Saul the persecutor became Paul; his hatred of violence is part of his love for its victims.

verseByVerse.quote: Let him rain coals on the wicked; fire and sulfur and a scorching wind shall be the portion of their cup. For the LORD is righteous; he loves righteous deeds; the upright shall behold his face.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The wicked will drink a cup of judgment, but the upright will see the face of the righteous LORD.

Let him rain coals on the wicked. The imagery is taken from Sodom, where “the LORD rained on Sodom and Gomorrah sulfur and fire” (Genesis 19:24), and the New Testament ends the devil’s story in a lake of the same two substances (Revelation 20:10). All of it, with the scorching desert wind, is the portion of their cup, the measure poured out for a man to drink, his allotted share. Every person is drinking something. And one man drank the wicked’s cup though it was not his. In Gethsemane Jesus prayed, “let this cup pass from me” (Matthew 26:39), and then drank it at the cross, so that those who trust him are handed a different cup.

The upright shall behold his face. The last line is the best thing in the psalm: what the upright receive is not safety, not a restored society, not even vindication against the archers, but his face. The psalm that began with people urging a man to run for the hills ends with him looking God in the eye.

The promise fulfilled. It is the promise Jesus made, “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew 5:8), and it is how the Bible’s last chapter describes God’s servants: “They will see his face, and his name will be on their foreheads” (Revelation 22:4). If the foundations are destroyed, the righteous can do this: stay, look up at an occupied throne, and wait to see his face.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew of verse 6 reads snares; with a small change it reads coals, which the ESV and most modern translations follow because it fits the fire and sulphur.

keyVerse.quote: The LORD is in his holy temple; the LORD’s throne is in heaven; his eyes see, his eyelids test the children of man.
keyVerse.note: This is David’s whole answer to the advice to flee. The foundations on earth may be shaking, but God’s throne is not in the building; it is in heaven, and from it he sees everything. The refuge of verse 1 rests on the throne of verse 4.

11.reflection:
The advice to “flee like a bird” (v. 1) comes from people who read the danger accurately. When is fleeing wise, and when does it mean letting fear choose our refuge?

“If the foundations are destroyed, what can the righteous do?” (v. 3). Where do you see foundations shaking today, and what does verse 4 say to that?

“The LORD tests the righteous” (v. 5). How have you experienced God’s testing, and how is it different from God looking away?

Jesus drank the cup of verse 6 for us, and promises that the pure in heart will see God (Matthew 5:8). How does the hope of seeing his face (v. 7) change the way you live now?

12.title: The Words of the LORD Are Pure Words
12.text: To the choirmaster: according to The Sheminith. A Psalm of David. 1Save, O LORD, for the godly one is gone; for the faithful have vanished from among the children of man.2Everyone utters lies to his neighbor; with flattering lips and a double heart they speak.3May the LORD cut off all flattering lips, the tongue that makes great boasts,4those who say, "With our tongue we will prevail, our lips are with us; who is master over us?"5"Because the poor are plundered, because the needy groan, I will now arise," says the LORD; "I will place him in the safety for which he longs."6The words of the LORD are pure words, like silver refined in a furnace on the ground, purified seven times.7You, O LORD, will keep them; you will guard us from this generation forever.8On every side the wicked prowl, as vileness is exalted among the children of man.
12.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 12 continues the run of David’s laments in Book One. Psalm 11 faced arrows shot in the dark; Psalm 12 faces words, a whole generation of flattery, lies and boasting.

The message. When everyone around seems to lie, flatter and boast that their tongues make them answerable to no one, God speaks, and his word is the opposite of theirs: pure, tested, with no falsehood mixed in. He rises for the plundered and the groaning, and he will keep his people safe in a generation that honours what is vile.

Why it was said. In David’s Israel, as in every age, power was won and kept by talk: flattery at court, false witness at the gate, boasts that no one could call the powerful to account. The psalm gave the godly, who felt they were the last ones left, a word to stand on (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. It begins with a cry, “Save, O LORD”, for the faithful have vanished, and describes the speech of the age: lies, flattering lips, a double heart, and the proud boast, “who is master over us?” (vv. 1–4). At the centre God himself speaks: because the poor are plundered, “I will now arise” (v. 5). The psalmist answers that the LORD’s words are pure as silver refined seven times, and trusts him to keep his people, though the wicked still prowl and vileness is exalted (vv. 6–8).

Where it leads. To Christ by the character of God revealed in him and by the need the psalm exposes. God’s pure word became flesh in Jesus, in whose mouth “neither was deceit found” (1 Peter 2:22), “the faithful and true witness” (Revelation 3:14). He stood silent while lying lips condemned him, and came, as God promised in verse 5, “to proclaim good news to the poor” (Luke 4:18).

For us. Watch your own tongue first: flattery and a double heart are not only other people’s sins, and Christ gives one heart in place of two. Then put your weight on what God has said, the one word that will not give way, and bring even your wordless groan to the God who rises for the plundered.
12.theology:
"There is no one faithful left" is a real feeling and a false measurement (v. 1; cf. 1 Kgs 19:18). The sin of the age is counterfeit speech: flattery, the double heart, and words used to claim that no one rules over us (vv. 2-4).

God's single utterance in the psalm is provoked by the groan of the plundered, and he sets the time himself (v. 5).

Against human speech, which is mixed with falsehood, the words of the LORD are refined silver, purified seven times (v. 6): the one thing a believer can stand on when nothing else said to him can be trusted. The psalm ends with the wicked still prowling (v. 8); the promise is held, not yet seen.
12.examples: In a season of spin, propaganda and flattery, when words seem to mean whatever the speaker wants, this psalm sets God's word against all of it. And it reminds anyone who can manage only a groan that God answers the groan of the plundered, not the boast of the talkers.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Words have come loose from truth, and speech itself has become a way of claiming to answer to no one. The psalm opens with a cry for help: the godly and the faithful seem to have vanished from among people (v. 1). What has gone with them is honest speech: everyone lies to his neighbour, with flattering lips and a double heart (v. 2). David asks God to cut off such lips and the boastful tongue (v. 3), and then lets the boasters speak for themselves: with our tongue we will prevail, our lips are with us, who is master over us? (v. 4). The sin of the age is counterfeit speech, and its root is a refusal to have any Lord.
verseByVerse.theology: Words have come loose from truth, and speech itself has become a way of claiming to answer to no one.

verseByVerse.quote: Save, O LORD, for the godly one is gone; for the faithful have vanished from among the children of man. Everyone utters lies to his neighbor; with flattering lips and a double heart they speak. May the LORD cut off all flattering lips, the tongue that makes great boasts, those who say, "With our tongue we will prevail, our lips are with us; who is master over us?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Faithful people, and honest speech with them, seem to have vanished, leaving flattery, double hearts and the boast that no one is master over us.

For the godly one is gone. Micah said it in almost the same words, “The godly has perished from the earth, and there is no one upright among mankind” (Micah 7:2), and Elijah said it at Horeb, “I, even I only, am left” (1 Kings 19:10), and was wrong: God had seven thousand he had never mentioned (1 Kings 19:18). Take the feeling seriously, but do not believe it absolutely: you may simply be unable to see the faithful.

With flattering lips and a double heart. A double heart is, in Hebrew, “a heart and a heart”: one for what a man says and one for what he means. And flattery is not kindness: it is saying whatever will move someone, true or not.

Who is master over us? The creed of the age, in any age: our lips are our own, and nobody is over us. It is the spirit of the kings in Psalm 2, “Let us burst their bonds apart”, now on the lips of people whose only weapon is their mouth.

When words become weapons. With our tongue we will prevail could be the motto of modern life: advertising that sells a feeling, politics run on slogans, the online reply crafted to wound. George Orwell argued in his essay “Politics and the English Language” that political speech is built to make lies sound truthful and murder respectable. Many now go further: if all speech is spin, there is no truth, only stories that win. The psalm agrees about human words but refuses that last step. One speaker’s words are not spin (v. 6), and only because of him can the flatterer be called a liar at all. Without a true word, “spin” is just our name for the other side’s story.

The true Word was silent. The true Word did not prevail with his tongue; he stood silent while lying lips condemned him (Mark 14:55–61), so that people with double hearts could be given one heart again (Ezekiel 11:19).

Not only other people. The flattering lip is also the half-truth that smooths a meeting and the compliment that wants something back. “No human being can tame the tongue” (James 3:8): we need a new heart, not merely better manners.

Uncertain wording. The heading’s Sheminith, literally “the eighth”, is probably a musical direction, perhaps an octave or an eight-stringed instrument; its meaning is uncertain.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–8 — I Will Now Arise, Says the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Against a world of counterfeit speech God sets his own word, and speaks it on behalf of the plundered. At the centre of the psalm the LORD answers: because the poor are plundered and the needy groan, he will now arise and place them in the safety they long for (v. 5). David responds by praising God’s words, pure like silver refined seven times, the one speech with no falsehood mixed in (v. 6). On that word he rests his confidence that the LORD will keep and guard his people from this generation forever (v. 7). But the psalm ends honestly, with the wicked still prowling and vileness exalted (v. 8): the promise is held, not yet seen.
verseByVerse.theology: Against a world of counterfeit speech God sets his own word, refined seven times, and speaks it on behalf of the plundered.

verseByVerse.quote: "Because the poor are plundered, because the needy groan, I will now arise," says the LORD; "I will place him in the safety for which he longs." The words of the LORD are pure words, like silver refined in a furnace on the ground, purified seven times.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God himself answers that he will rise for the plundered, and his words, unlike the flatterers’, are pure as refined silver.

I will now arise. God speaks, the only time in the psalm. He does not answer the boasters; he gives his reason first, the groan of the plundered, and sets the time himself: I will now arise. All through these psalms people have begged God to get up (7:6; 9:19; 10:12); here, unasked, he says he is getting up.

Because the needy groan. What moves him is not eloquence but the wordless noise of the robbed. If you can manage nothing but a groan, you are making the sound that gets God on his feet.

Purified seven times. Put this verse where the psalm puts it, straight after the flattering lips and double hearts. Human words have proved to be like impure metal, mixed with falsehood. God’s words are the same substance all the way through, run through the furnace until nothing else is left; seven times means completely, with nothing left to burn out. That is why a believer can build on a sentence of God when he cannot build on anything else he is told: “Every word of God proves true; he is a shield to those who take refuge in him” (Proverbs 30:5). In a season of spin, this verse is where you put your weight.

The pure word took flesh. Jesus “committed no sin, neither was deceit found in his mouth” (1 Peter 2:22). He is “the faithful and true witness” (Revelation 3:14), silver all the way through, and he came, as verse 5 promised God would, for the poor and the plundered (Luke 4:18).

Uncertain wording. The end of verse 5 is compressed: it may mean the safety for which he longs or, with the verb of 10:5, safety “from him that puffeth at him”, as older translations have it. A furnace on the ground (v. 6) is also obscure, probably a crucible set in the earth.

verseByVerse.quote: You, O LORD, will keep them; you will guard us from this generation forever. On every side the wicked prowl, as vileness is exalted among the children of man.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s pure word becomes a promise to keep his people, though the wicked still prowl.

You, O LORD, will keep them. God’s refined words become a promise for people: you will keep them, the poor and needy of verse 5, and you will guard us. The ESV notes that guard us can also be read “guard him”, the single afflicted man of God’s own speech. Either way, the word that cannot be corrupted keeps people who can be.

As vileness is exalted. Then the psalm simply stops, with the wicked prowling and what is worthless honoured in public. There is no closing hallelujah: the believer is left holding a pure word in a filthy generation, which is most of Christian life. But it has given us the two steady things: God’s promise to the plundered, and his word about everything.

The first instalment. The God who said I will now arise has not yet risen for all to see, but on the third day he raised his Son, the plundered and condemned one, and the keeping of verse 7 now rests in the hands of the one who says of his sheep, “no one will snatch them out of my hand” (John 10:28).

Where Christians differ: whom does God keep? Some, especially those who hold the King James Version alone to be the faithful English Bible, cite “You, O LORD, will keep them” as a promise to preserve the words of verse 6, even as an argument for one translation. Most read it of the poor and needy. This commentary’s view: the ones God keeps are most likely the poor and needy, since the line goes on, “you will guard us”. God does preserve his word (Isaiah 40:8), but this verse is about his people, and it requires no single translation.

keyVerse.quote: The words of the LORD are pure words, like silver refined in a furnace on the ground, purified seven times.
keyVerse.note: Set straight after a world of flattering lips and double hearts, and straight after God’s own promise in verse 5, this verse is the psalm’s answer to an age of spin. Human words are alloyed with falsehood; God’s are pure all the way through, which is why his promise to the plundered can be trusted.

12.reflection:
David feels that “the faithful have vanished” (v. 1), as Elijah did (1 Kings 19:10, 18). When have you felt alone in your faith, and how might you have been wrong about who else was faithful?

The psalm describes “flattering lips and a double heart” (v. 2). Where are you most tempted to flatter, spin, or say one thing while meaning another? What would having one heart look like there?

God rises because “the needy groan” (v. 5). What does that teach about praying when you have no words, and about whose cause God takes up?

“The words of the LORD are pure words” (v. 6). In a world of spin, how can we put our weight more fully on God’s word, and how does Jesus, the true witness, help us trust it?

13.title: How Long, O LORD?
13.text: To the choirmaster. A Psalm of David. 1How long, O LORD? Will you forget me forever? How long will you hide your face from me?2How long must I take counsel in my soul and have sorrow in my heart all the day? How long shall my enemy be exalted over me?3Consider and answer me, O LORD my God; light up my eyes, lest I sleep the sleep of death,4lest my enemy say, "I have prevailed over him," lest my foes rejoice because I am shaken.5But I have trusted in your steadfast love; my heart shall rejoice in your salvation.6I will sing to the LORD, because he has dealt bountifully with me.
13.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 13 is one of the shortest laments in the Psalter, and it comes after a run of psalms in which the wicked seem to have the upper hand (Psalms 9 to 12). Psalm 6 had asked “How long?” once and broken off; here the question is asked four times and finished.

The message. A believer may tell God plainly that he feels forgotten, and he is right to say it to God rather than about him. Faith does not wait for the feelings or the circumstances to change: it plants its feet on God’s steadfast love and sings of what he has already done, while the question “how long?” is still unanswered.

Why it was said. David spent long years hunted and opposed (see the introduction), but this psalm names no occasion, so it fits every long trouble. It gave Israel, and gives the church, words for the stretch of waiting when God seems silent and the enemy seems to be winning.

How the chapter makes its case. The psalm climbs out of the pit in three steps, each shorter than the last. First the complaint (vv. 1–2): four questions that face towards God, who seems to have forgotten, towards David himself, arguing with his own soul all day, and towards the enemy on top. Then the prayer (vv. 3–4): look, answer, light up my eyes before I die, and before my enemy boasts. Last the trust and the song (vv. 5–6): “But I have trusted in your steadfast love”, and God “has dealt bountifully with me”, said before anything visible has changed.

Where it leads. By pattern, and by an answer only the cross gives. David felt as if God had hidden his face; at Calvary God truly did, from his own Son, who cried, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matthew 27:46). Jesus also prayed in lament himself, in Gethsemane, so he knows this psalm from the inside. Because he bore the hidden face, God says to everyone who trusts him, “I will never leave you nor forsake you” (Hebrews 13:5), and the steadfast love David stood on has been shown in full.

For us. When God seems silent, do not stop speaking to him; tell him the truth, all four “how longs” if need be. Then do what David did: reach back to what God has already done, above all at the cross, and stand on his steadfast love until the feelings catch up and the song comes.
13.theology:
Lament is prayer, not grumbling: the psalmist says to God the very things the wicked man of Ps 10:11 said about him. His argument for rescue is God's reputation rather than his own comfort (v. 4).

The turn comes from what he stands on, not from what he sees (v. 5), and the final verb is past tense: God has dealt bountifully before the deliverance arrives (v. 6). The question itself goes unanswered here and is still being asked at the end of Scripture (Rev 6:10).
13.examples: Anyone who has lain awake holding the same anxious meeting with themselves at three in the morning knows the sound of these four how longs. The psalm does not hurry such a reader. It shows them a man who praises God in the past tense before the rescue has come, standing on what God has already done.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Lament is honest prayer, said to God and not about him. David asks “How long?” four times: how long will God forget him and hide his face (v. 1), how long must he argue with himself and carry sorrow all day, and how long will his enemy be on top (v. 2)? Then the questions turn into requests: look at me, answer me, light up my eyes before I sleep the sleep of death (v. 3). His argument is not only his own pain but what his enemies will say about him, and so about God, if he falls (v. 4). The section shows that a believer may say the darkest things, provided he says them to God.
verseByVerse.theology: Four complaints and one prayer, all of it said to God rather than about him.

verseByVerse.quote: How long, O LORD? Will you forget me forever? How long will you hide your face from me? How long must I take counsel in my soul and have sorrow in my heart all the day? How long shall my enemy be exalted over me?
verseByVerse.commentary:
David tells God plainly that he feels forgotten and asks how long it will last; to bring that complaint to God, instead of grumbling about him, is itself an act of faith.

How long, O LORD? Four times in two verses: the sound of a mind that has waited too long. Psalm 6 asked it once and broke off (Psalm 6:3); here it is finished, again and again.

Will you forget me forever? God does not forget; this is how his silence feels, and a hidden face is favour withdrawn. The wicked man of Psalm 10 said in his heart that God had forgotten and hidden his face, and it made him bold (Psalm 10:11). A believer says the same two things and it makes him pray. The darkness is the same, but he talks not about God but to him. That is the difference between a lament and a grumble.

Take counsel in my soul. Two questions name what makes a long trouble unbearable: the endless committee meeting in the soul at three in the morning, and sorrow “all the day”, which does not lift when the sun comes up.

A prayer Jesus prayed. The Son of God did not rise above this kind of prayer: “My soul is very sorrowful, even to death” (Matthew 26:38). To say the hard thing to God is not a lapse of faith but walking where he walked.

verseByVerse.quote: Consider and answer me, O LORD my God; light up my eyes, lest I sleep the sleep of death, lest my enemy say, "I have prevailed over him," lest my foes rejoice because I am shaken.
verseByVerse.commentary:
David asks God to look, to answer and to revive him before he dies, and he argues from God’s honour: his fall would let the enemy boast.

Consider and answer me, O LORD my God. Three short requests follow: look, answer, revive. To consider is to look closely, the reverse of a hidden face (v. 1), and he still says “my God”.

Light up my eyes. When Jonathan was faint from battle and tasted a little honey, “his eyes became bright” (1 Samuel 14:27). Dull eyes belong to a face with no strength left; light in the eye is life coming back. He is honest that he is close to going out: “lest I sleep the sleep of death”.

Lest my foes rejoice. His argument is God’s reputation: if I go under, my enemy will say he beat me, and that God could not keep his own. Grief shrinks our world to ourselves; faith keeps a wider view.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Faith turns the psalm before the circumstances do. With one word, “But”, David moves from complaint to trust and plants his feet on God’s steadfast love, the covenant loyalty that does not change with what he can see (v. 5). Then he promises to sing, because God “has dealt bountifully” with him (v. 6), a past tense spoken before any rescue has come. The section teaches the order of perseverance: trust first, then singing, with the feelings catching up along the way. The question “how long?” is left unanswered, and that too is honest.
verseByVerse.theology: The psalm turns in one word, and the last verb is past tense: he has already dealt bountifully, before anything visibly changes.

verseByVerse.quote: But I have trusted in your steadfast love; my heart shall rejoice in your salvation. I will sing to the LORD, because he has dealt bountifully with me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before anything has changed, David plants his feet on God’s steadfast love and sings of what God has already done.

But I have trusted in your steadfast love. One word, “But”, turns the psalm. Nothing outside has moved; what changes is where he stands. Steadfast love (ḥesed) is God’s covenant loyalty, which does not rise and fall with what David can see.

The three tenses. “I have trusted”: already done. “My heart shall rejoice”: a promise. “He has dealt bountifully with me”: past tense, written before any rescue shows up. He does not pretend the trouble has ended; he stands on what God has done until the answer comes. That is how most perseverance goes: not feeling, then trust, but trust, then singing, with the feeling catching up.

God did hide his face once. “How long” goes unanswered here, and the martyrs still ask it at the end of the Bible (Revelation 6:10). But the Christian has one more reason to say verse 5 in the dark. God did hide his face once, completely, from his Son on the cross (Matthew 27:46), and because Christ bore that, God’s face will never finally be turned from anyone who trusts him: “I will never leave you nor forsake you” (Hebrews 13:5).

When the sorrow lasts. If sorrow “all the day” goes on for months, it is no failure of faith, as well as praying, to tell your pastor and see a biblical counsellor, who will also ask for a medical check-up; nor is taking medicine, if it is needed. God uses his people and his gifts. And anyone whose darkness turns to thoughts of ending their life should tell someone that same day.

keyVerse.quote: But I have trusted in your steadfast love; my heart shall rejoice in your salvation.
keyVerse.note: This is the hinge of the psalm: one word, “But”, and the whole prayer turns from complaint to trust while the circumstances stay exactly as they were. David’s confidence rests not on what he can see but on God’s steadfast love, the covenant loyalty that was shown in full when God hid his face from his Son so that he need never finally hide it from us.

13.reflection:
David asks “How long?” four times and says these things to God, not about him (vv. 1–2). Why does that difference matter, and what keeps us from being as honest with God as this?

In verse 4 David argues from what his enemies will say if he falls. How can concern for God’s name widen our view when trouble has shrunk our world to ourselves?

Verse 6 says God “has dealt bountifully with me” before any rescue has come. What has God already done for you, above all in Christ, that you can stand on while you wait?

Jesus prayed in lament in Gethsemane, and on the cross God hid his face from him (Matthew 27:46). How does that change the way you pray when God seems silent, and how can we walk with someone in our church whose “how long” has lasted a long time?

14.title: There Is None Who Does Good
14.text: To the choirmaster. Of David. 1The fool says in his heart, "There is no God." They are corrupt, they do abominable deeds; there is none who does good.2The LORD looks down from heaven on the children of man, to see if there are any who understand, who seek after God.3They have all turned aside; together they have become corrupt; there is none who does good, not even one.4Have they no knowledge, all the evildoers who eat up my people as they eat bread and do not call upon the LORD?5There they are in great terror, for God is with the generation of the righteous.6You would shame the plans of the poor, but the LORD is his refuge.7Oh, that salvation for Israel would come out of Zion! When the LORD restores the fortunes of his people, let Jacob rejoice, let Israel be glad.
14.overview:
Where we are. After the lone sufferer of Psalm 13, Psalm 14 widens the view to the whole human race. It returns to the wicked of Psalms 10 and 12, who live as if God does not see, and it appears again in Book Two, with small changes, as Psalm 53.

The message. Godlessness begins in the heart, not the head, and when God himself searches mankind he finds no one who does good, not even one. Yet he is not absent: he stands with his people and is the refuge of the poor whom the wicked devour. Since no one can save himself, the only hope is salvation sent by God, out of Zion.

Why it was said. In David’s Israel, as everywhere, powerful men used the weak and lived as though no one was over them (see the introduction). The psalm warned them, comforted the poor they crushed, and taught the whole congregation, which sang it, that the verdict of verse 3 falls on every one of them.

How the chapter makes its case. It begins with the fool’s creed and its fruit: “There is no God”, and corrupt deeds to match (v. 1). Then heaven holds its own inquiry, and the finding is universal: “there is none who does good, not even one” (vv. 2–3). The scene turns to the evildoers who eat up God’s people like bread; they are seized by terror, because the God they ignored is with the righteous and shelters the poor (vv. 4–6). The psalm ends not with a human solution but with a longing for salvation out of Zion and the restoring of God’s people (v. 7).

Where it leads. By the need it exposes, and by promise. Paul quotes verses 1–3 to stop every mouth (Romans 3:10–12) and then announces, “But now the righteousness of God has been manifested apart from the law” (Romans 3:21). The salvation the psalm longs for came out of Zion in David’s Son, the one man who passed heaven’s search, who died outside Jerusalem’s wall so that people who do no good might be counted righteous through faith; and Paul still hears this hope in “The Deliverer will come from Zion” (Romans 11:26).

For us. Do not read this psalm only about other people. Practical atheism, planning, spending and treating people as if God were not watching, is a believer’s temptation too. Then look where the psalm looks, to the salvation God has sent in Christ, and stand with the poor, as God does.
14.theology:
The fool here is a matter of morals, not of intelligence (v. 1), and his creed is held in the heart and proved by a way of life.

God conducts the search himself and finds no one (vv. 2-3); Paul quotes the verdict to open his case that the whole world is accountable (Rom 3:10-12). The psalm exempts nobody, the religious reader included. God stands with the righteous by choice, not because verse 3 has exceptions (v. 5).

Because no one does good, the only hope is rescue from outside, salvation ... out of Zion (v. 7), which is what came (Rom 3:21-22). Psalm 53 repeats this psalm, and the exposition stands here.
14.examples: Most of the harm done to the poor is done casually, by people who are not plotting anything, just eating. This psalm names it, puts every reader in the same survey, and then points to the only hope it can see: salvation coming out of Zion.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–3 — The LORD Looks Down from Heaven
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: No one does good, not even one: that is heaven’s verdict on the human race. The fool says in his heart that there is no God, and his creed shows in corrupt and abominable deeds (v. 1). Then the LORD himself leans down from heaven to search all mankind for anyone who understands and seeks him (v. 2). The finding is total: all have turned aside, together they have become corrupt, there is none who does good, not even one (v. 3). Paul quotes these verses to prove that the whole world is accountable to God, so no reader, religious or not, stands outside the survey.
verseByVerse.theology: God conducts the search himself, and the result is the Bible's verdict on the whole race.

verseByVerse.quote: The fool says in his heart, "There is no God." They are corrupt, they do abominable deeds; there is none who does good. The LORD looks down from heaven on the children of man, to see if there are any who understand, who seek after God. They have all turned aside; together they have become corrupt; there is none who does good, not even one.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Denying God is first a matter of the heart and the life, and when God himself searches the human race he finds no one who does good, not even one.

The fool. The word (nābāl) is moral, not intellectual: the man who has shut God out of his thinking and lives accordingly. One man in 1 Samuel was actually called Nabal, and his wife Abigail said, “as his name is, so is he. Nabal is his name, and folly is with him” (1 Samuel 25:25): rich, drunk and churlish.

Says in his heart, “There is no God.” Spoken in the heart, where the predator of Psalm 10 said God had forgotten (Psalm 10:11), the creed is less a theory than the conclusion of a life arranged as though no one were above it, and its evidence is corrupt, abominable deeds.

The LORD looks down from heaven. God himself leans over the edge of heaven and searches all mankind for one person genuinely seeking him, as he went down to see Sodom (Genesis 18:21), where not even ten righteous were found. To understand (the ESV notes it can be read act wisely) is not cleverness but having one’s bearings.

Not even one. Paul quotes these verses to open his case that the whole world is accountable to God (Romans 3:10–12). Let it land on yourself: the comfortable religious reader and the fool of verse 1 are in the same survey.

Is the psalm exaggerating? Unbelievers do kind and brave things, but no one does good in the sense that matters: nothing a fallen person does springs from love for God or seeks his glory (Romans 3:10–12; Hebrews 11:6). God restrains sin and gives common grace to all, so people are not as bad as they could be. But no one is good enough for God, and no one seeks him until he seeks them.
verseByVerse.note: Psalm 53 is almost the same psalm.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–7 — God Is with the Generation of the Righteous
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God is not absent from the world the fool imagines. The evildoers who eat up God’s people as casually as bread, and never pray, will suddenly be in great terror, because God is with the generation of the righteous (vv. 4–5). They mock the plans of the poor, but the LORD is the poor man’s refuge (v. 6). Then the psalm lifts its eyes beyond the present: since no one does good, the only hope is salvation from God himself, coming out of Zion, when he restores his people and Jacob rejoices (v. 7). The longing is answered in Christ.
verseByVerse.theology: The psalm ends not with a solution but with a longing, and the longing is for someone to come out of Zion.

verseByVerse.quote: Have they no knowledge, all the evildoers who eat up my people as they eat bread and do not call upon the LORD? There they are in great terror, for God is with the generation of the righteous. You would shame the plans of the poor, but the LORD is his refuge.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those who devour God’s people as casually as they eat bread will be struck with sudden terror, because God stands with the righteous and shelters the poor.

Who eat up my people as they eat bread. They consume people the way a man eats his lunch, without a thought, and most harm done to the poor is done like that. The last clause gives them away: they “do not call upon the LORD”. Not praying and using people grow from one root, living as if no God were over us.

There they are in great terror. There points to a moment: suddenly men who had settled that nobody was watching are in a terror they cannot explain, because the God they had ruled out is present: he “is with the generation of the righteous”, not because they are impressive (verse 3 has said no one is), but because he has chosen to stand with them.

The plans of the poor. The poor man’s small plans are laughed at by the powerful, but the LORD is his refuge, the whole of his security, and enough. It is the sentence for anyone whose plans have been mocked by people with more power, and Jesus came anointed “to proclaim good news to the poor” (Luke 4:18).

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew of verse 6 is compressed. The ESV takes it, probably rightly, as the evildoers trying to frustrate the poor man; some read a taunt: shame his plans if you like, the LORD is his refuge. Psalm 53 has a different line here, about God scattering the bones of the besieger (Psalm 53:5).

verseByVerse.quote: Oh, that salvation for Israel would come out of Zion! When the LORD restores the fortunes of his people, let Jacob rejoice, let Israel be glad.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Since no one does good, the psalm’s only hope is salvation from outside, sent by God out of Zion, and that is exactly what came in Christ.

Oh, that salvation for Israel would come out of Zion! The psalm ends not with a fix but with a groan shaped like a wish. If there is “none who does good”, no reform will work; salvation must come from outside, out of Zion, where God had set his name.

Salvation came out of Zion. That is what happened: David’s Son, born in Bethlehem and crucified outside Jerusalem’s wall, the one exception to verse 3 and the reason anyone else escapes its verdict. Paul quotes this psalm to prove that no one is righteous, then says, “But now the righteousness of God has been manifested apart from the law … through faith in Jesus Christ for all who believe” (Romans 3:21–22). The psalm asks for it; the gospel reports it.

Let Jacob rejoice. Pray it as a prayer still partly unanswered, in a world where the poor are still devoured (v. 4). Paul hears the same hope in “The Deliverer will come from Zion, he will banish ungodliness from Jacob” (Romans 11:26). Jacob will rejoice: not yet, and certainly.

Uncertain wording. Older versions rendered “restores the fortunes” as bringing back the captivity, which would point to the exile. The phrase can mean that, but it is used of any great reversal of ruin (Job 42:10), so it fits David’s day as well as later ones.

keyVerse.quote: They have all turned aside; together they have become corrupt; there is none who does good, not even one.
keyVerse.note: This is heaven’s verdict after God’s own search, and it includes every reader. Paul builds his case that the whole world is accountable to God on it (Romans 3:10–12), and it is the reason the psalm can only end by longing for salvation from outside, which God has given in Christ, the one man who did good and the one through whom the guilty are made righteous.

14.reflection:
The fool says “There is no God” in his heart, and it shows in how he lives (v. 1). Where are you tempted to live, spend or plan as if God were not watching, even while believing in him?

Verse 3 leaves no exceptions, and Paul uses it to say that every mouth is stopped (Romans 3:19). Why do good, decent people often find this harder to accept than obvious sinners do?

The evildoers eat up God’s people “as they eat bread”, without a second thought (v. 4). What are the casual, unthinking ways the poor and weak are consumed in our society, and how can a church stand with them as the LORD does (v. 6)?

The psalm ends longing for salvation “out of Zion” (v. 7), and the gospel says it has come in Jesus (Romans 3:21–22). How does knowing that rescue comes from outside us change the way we pray for ourselves and for people far from God?

15.title: Who Shall Dwell on Your Holy Hill?
15.text: A Psalm of David. 1O LORD, who shall sojourn in your tent? Who shall dwell on your holy hill?2He who walks blamelessly and does what is right and speaks truth in his heart;3who does not slander with his tongue and does no evil to his neighbor, nor takes up a reproach against his friend;4in whose eyes a vile person is despised, but who honors those who fear the LORD; who swears to his own hurt and does not change;5who does not put out his money at interest and does not take a bribe against the innocent. He who does these things shall never be moved.
15.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 14 searched the earth and found no one who does good; Psalm 15 asks who, then, may live with God. It pictures worshippers at the gate of the sanctuary, as Psalm 24 does, and many readers have noticed that these two entrance psalms frame the psalms between them.

The message. The LORD welcomes into his presence the one whose life matches his own character: true to the heart, clean in speech, faithful to his word, honest with his money. God’s guest is known by how he treats people. Read honestly, the standard shows that we need someone to bring us in, and Christ, who kept it whole, does.

Why it was said. Israel came up to Zion to worship (see the introduction), and was always tempted to think that being at the sanctuary and bringing sacrifices was enough. The prophets said otherwise (Isaiah 1:11–17; Micah 6:8), and this psalm says it in the act of worship itself.

How the chapter makes its case. First the question, asked twice: who may stay in God’s tent as a guest, and who may live on his hill (v. 1)? The answer begins with three broad marks, a blameless walk, right deeds and truth in the heart (v. 2), then gives particulars, mostly about the neighbour: the tongue that will not slander or pass on a reproach (v. 3), judgments that honour the God-fearing, a costly promise kept (v. 4), money that does not profit from need and a hand that will not take a bribe (v. 5). It ends not with admission but with a promise: “He who does these things shall never be moved.”

Where it leads. By the need it exposes, and by fulfilment. No one but Jesus has walked blamelessly and spoken truth in his heart without a flaw, and he kept his word at a cost no one else could reckon. Christians come to God’s hill in him: “you have come to Mount Zion … and to Jesus, the mediator of a new covenant” (Hebrews 12:22–24). Welcomed for his sake, we find the list rewritten by his Spirit as the shape of our life inside.

For us. Do not treat this psalm as a ladder to climb into God’s favour, nor as a list to admire and ignore. Come in through Christ, and then let it search you: the gossip you pass on, the promise that has grown expensive, the profit made from someone else’s need.
15.theology:
The psalm is an entrance liturgy, a question and answer spoken at the sanctuary gate (cf. 24:3-4), asking both to be a guest in God's tent and to live on his hill (v. 1).

The requirements are moral, not ritual: inward truth, a guarded tongue, company chosen by the fear of God, costly promises kept, and money that does not profit from a neighbour's disaster (vv. 2-5).

Read honestly, the list bars everyone. One man keeps it whole, and believers come to the hill in him (Heb 12:22-24); after that, the list no longer bars the door; it describes the life lived inside.
15.examples: Someone hands you a damaging story about a friend; this psalm says to refuse delivery. And when a promise turns out expensive, it says keep it anyway.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–3 — The Question at the Gate
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Access to God is the question, and the first answers are about integrity and the tongue. At the sanctuary gate someone asks who may stay in the LORD’s tent as a guest and live on his holy hill as a resident (v. 1). The answer opens with three broad marks: a blameless walk, right actions, and truth spoken in the heart, where no one else can check (v. 2). Then it turns to speech and the neighbour: no slander, no harm done to a neighbour, and no damaging story about a friend picked up and passed on (v. 3). The person at home with God is first an honest person.
verseByVerse.theology: The question is about access to God, and the first answers are all about the tongue.

verseByVerse.quote: O LORD, who shall sojourn in your tent? Who shall dwell on your holy hill? He who walks blamelessly and does what is right and speaks truth in his heart; who does not slander with his tongue and does no evil to his neighbor, nor takes up a reproach against his friend;
verseByVerse.commentary:
The question is who may be God’s guest and live in his presence, and the first answer is a person of integrity: blameless in his walk, right in his deeds, true right down to the heart, and unwilling to use his tongue against his neighbour.

Who shall sojourn in your tent? Worshippers arriving at the sanctuary probably asked who may come in, and a priest answered, as in Psalm 24 (compare Isaiah 33:14–16). The tent recalls the one David pitched for the ark on Zion (2 Samuel 6:17). To sojourn is to be a guest under someone’s protection; to dwell is to live there. The psalm wants both: welcome now, and a permanent address.

He who walks blamelessly. Blameless means whole, undivided, not sinless: Noah was “blameless in his generation” (Genesis 6:9). Of the three marks, the third goes furthest in: he speaks truth “in his heart”, honest where nobody can check, so not lying to himself either. That is rarer than public honesty, and it is where public honesty comes from.

Nor takes up a reproach against his friend. Someone hands you a damaging story about a friend, and you pick it up and carry it on. The person who may live with God refuses the parcel.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–5 — He Who Swears to His Own Hurt
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Keeping a costly promise and refusing easy money are the tests, and the one who passes them is immovable. God’s guest values people as God does, unimpressed by the vile and honouring those who fear the LORD; and when his word turns out to cost him dearly, he keeps it (v. 4). He will not make money out of a poor neighbour’s need, and he will not sell justice for a bribe (v. 5a). The psalm ends with a promise: such a person “shall never be moved” (v. 5b). Read honestly, the list bars everyone, and sends us to the one who kept it whole.
verseByVerse.theology: Keeping a costly promise and refusing easy money are the tests, and the man who passes them is immovable.

verseByVerse.quote: in whose eyes a vile person is despised, but who honors those who fear the LORD; who swears to his own hurt and does not change; who does not put out his money at interest and does not take a bribe against the innocent. He who does these things shall never be moved.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s guest values people as God does, keeps his word when it costs him, and will not profit from a neighbour’s need or sell justice; such a person will never be moved.

In whose eyes a vile person is despised. His judgments run against the world’s: unimpressed by a successful scoundrel, he honours ordinary people who fear God. Whose company do you actually want?

Who swears to his own hurt and does not change. He promised something, it cost far more than he thought, and he did it anyway. When Joshua found that the Gibeonites had tricked Israel into a treaty, the leaders still kept it: “We have sworn to them by the LORD” (Joshua 9:19). Most of us keep an escape clause for when our word gets expensive; God’s guest does not. (A promise to do wrong is different: it must not be kept.)

Does not put out his money at interest. The law forbade lending at interest to a poor fellow Israelite (Exodus 22:25; Leviticus 25:36–37; Deuteronomy 23:19–20). Loans then were rarely for business but for a family that had run out of grain. So this forbids not banking but making money out of a neighbour’s disaster, and the bribe is the same sin in a courtroom: turning someone’s vulnerability into your gain.

He who does these things shall never be moved. Not that trouble never comes, but that he is not dislodged; the same verb comes in Psalm 16:8, “I shall not be shaken”. And there is not one ritual item on the list: the test at God’s gate is how we treat our neighbours.

Kept the whole list without a gap. Now ask honestly whether you are through the gate. One man, Jesus, has kept the whole list, and kept his word at a cost he alone could reckon. Hebrews tells Christians where they stand: “you have come to Mount Zion and to the city of the living God … and to Jesus, the mediator of a new covenant” (Hebrews 12:22–24). We come in not on our record but with him. Then the list stops being a barrier and describes what living there makes of us, as his Spirit writes it on the heart (Ezekiel 36:27); and where we fail at any line, the way back is confession to the host who has already taken us in (1 John 1:9).

Isn’t being a good person enough? Many people would happily sign this psalm: no ritual, no creed, just be honest, keep your promises and do not exploit the poor. It is a far better answer than cynicism. But take the psalm at its word. Its standard is not decency on average but truth spoken “in his heart” (v. 2) and promises kept “to his own hurt” (v. 4). Measured against that, the decent person stands where the religious person stands, hoping his record will be enough. The gospel does not lower the bar at the gate; it brings through someone who cleared it, and makes his welcome ours. Good people need that as much as bad ones, and often find it harder, because they must give up thinking they are owed a place.

Where Christians differ: may a Christian lend or borrow at interest? For many centuries the church, reading this verse with the law, condemned all lending at interest as usury, and some Christians still refuse it. Others, Calvin among them, argued that the law forbade exploiting the poor, not charging fair interest on a business loan. This commentary’s view: commercial interest is lawful, but exploiting the poor through it is wrong; help for a neighbour in need should be generous, often given rather than lent (Luke 6:35), and care for the poor is not optional.

keyVerse.quote: O LORD, who shall sojourn in your tent? Who shall dwell on your holy hill?
keyVerse.note: The whole psalm answers this question, which is the deepest question anyone can ask: who may live with God? The answer describes a life of truth, faithfulness and justice that only Jesus has lived without fault, and so it drives us to him, through whom we have come to Mount Zion (Hebrews 12:22) and in whom we are welcome guests for ever.

15.reflection:
The psalm asks both who may be God’s guest and who may live with him (v. 1). What would it mean for you to be not just a visitor in God’s presence on Sundays but someone at home there all week?

Almost every mark in verses 2–5 is about how we treat other people. Why do you think the test at God’s gate is so much about the tongue, our promises and our money, and so little about religious activity?

“Who swears to his own hurt and does not change” (v. 4). Can you think of a promise that has become costly to keep? What would keeping it look like, and how does Christ’s faithfulness to his word help?

If no one but Jesus keeps this list, how does Hebrews 12:22–24 change the way we read it? How can our church welcome people who think being a decent person is enough, while showing them their need of Christ?

16.title: My Chosen Portion and My Cup
16.text: A Miktam of David. 1Preserve me, O God, for in you I take refuge.2I say to the LORD, "You are my Lord; I have no good apart from you."3As for the saints in the land, they are the excellent ones, in whom is all my delight.4The sorrows of those who run after another god shall multiply; their drink offerings of blood I will not pour out or take their names on my lips.5The LORD is my chosen portion and my cup; you hold my lot.6The lines have fallen for me in pleasant places; indeed, I have a beautiful inheritance.7I bless the LORD who gives me counsel; in the night also my heart instructs me.8I have set the LORD always before me; because he is at my right hand, I shall not be shaken.9Therefore my heart is glad, and my whole being rejoices; my flesh also dwells secure.10For you will not abandon my soul to Sheol, or let your holy one see corruption.11You make known to me the path of life; in your presence there is fullness of joy; at your right hand are pleasures forevermore.
16.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 15 asked who may live with God; Psalm 16 is the voice of someone who does, and who has found that God himself is all his good. It is one of the psalms most often quoted in the New Testament, because the first Christian sermon, at Pentecost, was built on its last verses.

The message. The LORD is not one good thing among others but the source of every good, and the one who takes him as his portion has an inheritance that is beautiful now and does not end at the grave. Because God will not abandon his holy one to death, his people can rest secure, body and soul, and look ahead to fullness of joy in his presence for ever.

Why it was said. David prays for protection, so some danger lies behind the psalm, and he writes in a land still full of the gods of Canaan, whose worship tempted Israel throughout its history (see the introduction). Against both threats he sets one confession: “You are my Lord; I have no good apart from you” (v. 2).

How the chapter makes its case. It opens with refuge and confession: no good apart from God, delight in his people, no other gods (vv. 1–4). Then, in the language of the sharing out of the land, he calls the LORD his portion and his cup, and says the lines have fallen in pleasant places (vv. 5–6). He blesses God for counsel by day and night, and by setting the LORD always before him stands unshaken (vv. 7–8). Last comes the reason for his gladness: God will not abandon his holy one to Sheol, but will show him the path of life and fullness of joy (vv. 9–11).

Where it leads. By direct promise, as the apostles preached it. Peter reminded Jerusalem that David “both died and was buried, and his tomb is with us to this day”, so that David, being a prophet, “foresaw and spoke about the resurrection of the Christ” (Acts 2:29–31); Paul argued the same (Acts 13:35–37). Jesus is the holy one whose flesh did not see corruption, and his resurrection is the guarantee of the hope the psalm gives to all who take refuge in God.

For us. Ask what you are treating as your portion, the thing without which life would not be worth living, and bring it to the one who says, in effect, “I am your portion.” Practise setting the LORD before you through the day. And face death, your own and that of those you love, in the light of an empty tomb: in God’s presence there is fullness of joy.
16.theology:
Contentment begins where verse 2 begins: God is not the best of a man’s good things; he is the source of them all. The inheritance language (vv. 5-6) comes from the Levites, given God instead of land (Num 18:20), and David chooses it, against the men whose portion is in this life (17:14).

Idolatry is described by what it produces, multiplied sorrows (v. 4), and stability comes from deliberate practice, setting the LORD before oneself (v. 8).

Peter preached vv. 8-11 at Pentecost as a prophecy of Christ's resurrection (Acts 2:25-31; 13:35). The hope reaches the body (v. 9), and the psalm ends with God’s presence rather than rescue: fullness of joy and pleasures forevermore (v. 11).
16.examples: Every substitute god charges more and delivers less as time goes on, and people discover it slowly. This psalm offers the opposite discovery: that the one who has God has a portion that is enough because of who it is, and a joy coming that is full, a cup that cannot hold more.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — The Lines Have Fallen for Me in Pleasant Places
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God himself is the believer’s whole good and his beautiful inheritance. David asks to be kept and confesses that he has no good apart from the LORD (vv. 1–2). Two loves follow from that confession: delight in God’s people, and a flat refusal of other gods, whose worshippers find only multiplying sorrows (vv. 3–4). Then he borrows the language of Israel’s land settlement, portion, cup, lot and boundary lines, to say that the LORD is his share, as he was for the Levites who received no land; and he declares that the lines have fallen for him in pleasant places (vv. 5–6). Contentment is found in who God is, not in what he gives.
verseByVerse.theology: A man surveys his life as if it were land he has been allotted, and finds that his share is God himself.

verseByVerse.quote: Preserve me, O God, for in you I take refuge. I say to the LORD, "You are my Lord; I have no good apart from you." As for the saints in the land, they are the excellent ones, in whom is all my delight. The sorrows of those who run after another god shall multiply; their drink offerings of blood I will not pour out or take their names on my lips.
verseByVerse.commentary:
David takes refuge in God and confesses that he has no good apart from him; that one confession makes him love God’s people and refuse other gods.

Preserve me, O God. The psalm opens by asking to be kept alive, and it will end with a promise about the grave. Hold the two ends together: the prayer of a man who wants to survive the week is answered with something far larger than the week.

I have no good apart from you. This line holds the whole psalm. He does not mean “you are the best of my good things”; nothing is good for him apart from God. Everything he goes on to enjoy in this psalm, he enjoys as coming out of that one relationship.

The saints in the land. The second thing he loves is God’s people, and the words are strong: the excellent ones, the noble ones. Anyone who genuinely delights in God finds, usually to his surprise, that he has started to enjoy God’s people, the awkward ones included. The two loves arrive together.

The sorrows of those who run after another god. The alternative is described without heat. Idolatry is not portrayed as wicked fun but as multiplying sorrows. Every substitute god charges more and delivers less as time goes on. David will not go near the rites; he will not even say the names. The drink offerings were probably poured to the gods of Canaan, and Israel was forbidden to drink blood (Leviticus 17:10–14) or even to speak the names of other gods (Exodus 23:13). Staying away from an old idol sometimes has to mean staying away in body and in speech, not only in intention.

Uncertain wording. The heading’s Miktam is a term of uncertain meaning, used again for Psalms 56 to 60, most of them prayers from times of danger. Verses 2–4 are among the hardest Hebrew in the Psalter: verse 2 is very compressed, though the ESV’s sense is widely accepted. Some take “the saints” and “the excellent ones” of verse 3 not as God’s people but, ironically, as the “holy ones” of the land, its gods or their devotees, whom verse 4 then rejects; the ESV’s reading, delight in God’s people, is the more natural. “Drink offerings of blood” may mean offerings mixed with blood, or offerings from hands stained with it.
verseByVerse.note: A Miktam is probably a musical or liturgical term.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD is my chosen portion and my cup; you hold my lot. The lines have fallen for me in pleasant places; indeed, I have a beautiful inheritance.
verseByVerse.commentary:
David takes the LORD himself as his share in life, as the Levites received God instead of land, and he declares that share beautiful.

You hold my lot. Every word here comes from the sharing out of the land. When Israel took Canaan, each tribe received its portion, measured out with lines, the surveyor’s cord, and assigned by lot. One tribe received nothing: the Levites were given no territory, and the reason was this: “I am your portion and your inheritance among the people of Israel” (Numbers 18:20). No fields, no border, no deeds: God himself instead.

The lines have fallen for me in pleasant places. David takes that arrangement, which on paper looked like the worst deal in Israel, and chooses it. He walks the boundary of his own life and reports that the cord fell in good ground. Read the verse remembering that he wrote a good many psalms in caves.

My cup. Five psalms earlier, fire and sulphur and a scorching wind were “the portion of their cup” for the wicked (Psalm 11:6). Here the cup is God. A man in Lamentations says the same with Jerusalem in ruins around him: “‘The LORD is my portion,’ says my soul, ‘therefore I will hope in him’” (Lamentations 3:24). That is not pretending you have what you wanted. It is the discovery that what you have is enough because of who it is.

Why is enough never enough? Our economy runs on a quiet assumption: the good life lies one upgrade away. The next house, role or holiday will finally be enough, and when it arrives it becomes ordinary and the line moves again: a portion never built to carry that weight. The Puritan Jeremiah Burroughs, in The Rare Jewel of Christian Contentment, argued that the world seeks contentment by adding to what it has, while a Christian comes to it more by subtracting from his desires. That is what David has done. He does not pretend the boundary lines are wider than they are; they fell in pleasant places because of who stands inside them with him. Jesus shows that this is no consolation prize: he had nowhere to lay his head, yet said, “My food is to do the will of him who sent me” (John 4:34). A person whose portion is God can enjoy the upgrade when it comes, and live without it when it does not.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–11 — You Will Not Abandon My Soul
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The one who sets the LORD before him is unshaken in life and secure in death. David blesses God for counsel by day and night, and says that because the LORD is at his right hand he will not be shaken (vv. 7–8). So his heart, his whole being and his body rest secure, because God will not abandon him to Sheol or let his holy one see corruption (vv. 9–10). The psalm ends in God’s presence: the path of life, fullness of joy, pleasures for evermore (v. 11). Peter preached these verses at Pentecost as David’s prophecy of the resurrection of Christ, whose body did not see corruption.
verseByVerse.theology: The psalm is about a grave that could not hold God's holy one.

verseByVerse.quote: I bless the LORD who gives me counsel; in the night also my heart instructs me. I have set the LORD always before me; because he is at my right hand, I shall not be shaken.
verseByVerse.commentary:
David blesses God for guiding him day and night, and because he deliberately keeps the LORD before him, he stands unshaken.

In the night also my heart instructs me. By day God counsels him; at night his own inner self keeps teaching him, the deep interior that speaks when the house is quiet. Wakefulness at two in the morning is usually a courtroom where we prosecute ourselves; in a man who has taken God’s counsel by day, the night shift works for him instead.

I have set the LORD always before me. This is deliberate practice, not a mood: putting God in the field of vision on purpose, again and again. The result is stability. At my right hand is the supporter’s position, where an advocate stood. Not to be shaken does not mean not troubled; it means not dislodged.

How do I set the LORD before me? The verb means to place something on purpose, the way you put a photograph where you will see it. Begin the day facing him. Before the news or the messages, say a sentence to him about the day ahead and hand it over. Bring him into the decisions. At the meeting, the purchase, the reply you are about to send, ask in a breath what would please him here. Use the small hinges of the day. Let the commute, the kettle, the school run remind you that he is at your right hand. Turn the night worry towards him. When the mind wakes and starts its prosecution, name the fear to him and recall one promise. And when you notice you have gone hours without a thought of him, do not despair; simply turn again.

The Son who never looked away. Peter hears these lines on the lips of Jesus: “I saw the Lord always before me” (Acts 2:25). The Son kept the Father before him all the way to the cross and through the grave, and because he now sits at the Father’s right hand for us, we who forget are still held, and can always begin again.
verseByVerse.note: “My heart instructs me” is literally “my kidneys instruct me” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore my heart is glad, and my whole being rejoices; my flesh also dwells secure. For you will not abandon my soul to Sheol, or let your holy one see corruption. You make known to me the path of life; in your presence there is fullness of joy; at your right hand are pleasures forevermore.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because God will not abandon him to the grave, David rests secure in body and soul and looks to fullness of joy in God’s presence for ever; Peter shows that these words came true to the letter in the resurrection of Jesus.

My flesh also dwells secure. Gladness runs all the way down: heart, whole being (the ESV notes the Hebrew is my glory), and then flesh. The body is included in the confidence, and the reason is a promise about the grave: God will not leave him in Sheol, the realm of the dead, or let his loyal one rot.

Or let your holy one see corruption. About seven weeks after the crucifixion, Peter read these verses to a crowd in Jerusalem and pointed out that David “both died and was buried, and his tomb is with us to this day” (Acts 2:29). David’s body did see corruption; everyone knew where he lay. So either the psalm failed, or David was speaking as a prophet of someone else, and Peter’s conclusion was that “he foresaw and spoke about the resurrection of the Christ” (Acts 2:31). Paul preached the verse the same way in Antioch in Pisidia (Acts 13:35–37).

Out of a borrowed tomb. This was not a new idea imposed on an old poem, but an old poem waiting for the one man whose body it fitted. One man’s flesh dwelt secure in the tomb of Joseph of Arimathea, and came out.

Fullness of joy. The psalm ends not with better circumstances but with a path, a presence and a pleasure that does not run out: not a topped-up cup but one that cannot hold more. If you have wondered whether the Christian hope is rather thin, harps and clouds, this verse is the correction. What is coming is not less enjoyment than this life holds but more, unspoiled, at the right hand of the God to whom David said, “I have no good apart from you”, and he was right.

Did Christ descend into hell?
