The Apostles’ Creed says so, and readers take it differently: that Christ went to the realm of the dead to proclaim his victory (compare 1 Peter 3:19), or, as Calvin and the Heidelberg Catechism put it, that he suffered the anguish of hell on the cross. Between death and resurrection his soul was in paradise (Luke 23:43) and his body in the tomb. Peter’s point from this verse is that the body did not see corruption (Acts 2:31).

Where Christians differ: of whom does David speak in verse 10? Many Jewish interpreters hear David’s own trust: that God will keep him from an untimely death, or, as some medieval commentators took it, that the soul of the faithful does not perish with the body; Jewish faith also hopes for the resurrection of the dead. Some Christians likewise read the verse first as David’s own hope, fulfilled in a fuller sense in Christ. This commentary’s view: David’s own trust is truly here, but Peter’s argument from David’s tomb shows that, as a prophet, he spoke words that only Jesus fulfilled to the letter, so the verse is a direct promise of Christ’s resurrection (Acts 2:29–31; 13:35–37), and David’s hope, and ours, rests on it.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew word behind “corruption” usually means “the pit”, the grave, as the ESV’s note allows, though it may also mean decay. The ancient Greek translation took it as corruption, and the apostles quote that form (Acts 2:27). Either way the promise is that God’s holy one would not be left to the grave, and the argument stands: David’s body was left there; Jesus’ was not.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “holy one” may also be rendered “godly one.”

keyVerse.quote: You make known to me the path of life; in your presence there is fullness of joy; at your right hand are pleasures forevermore.
keyVerse.note: The psalm that began with a prayer to be kept alive ends here, in the presence of God, where joy is full and pleasure never runs out. It completes the confession of verse 2, “I have no good apart from you”, and because Jesus walked the path of life through death and out of the tomb (Acts 2:28), it is the sure future of everyone who takes refuge in him.

16.reflection:
David says, “I have no good apart from you” (v. 2). What is the difference between treating God as the best of your good things and treating him as the source of them all, and how would it show in your life?

The Levites received God instead of land, and David chooses the same portion (vv. 5–6). What are you tempted to treat as the thing you cannot be content without, and what helps you say, “the lines have fallen for me in pleasant places”?

“I have set the LORD always before me” (v. 8). What practical habits help you keep God in view through an ordinary day, and what usually crowds him out?

Peter preached verses 8–11 as a prophecy of Jesus’ resurrection (Acts 2:25–32). How does Christ’s empty tomb change the way you face your own death and grieve for those who have died in him?

17.title: The Apple of Your Eye
17.text: A Prayer of David. 1Hear a just cause, O LORD; attend to my cry! Give ear to my prayer from lips free of deceit!2From your presence let my vindication come! Let your eyes behold the right!3You have tried my heart, you have visited me by night, you have tested me, and you will find nothing; I have purposed that my mouth will not transgress.4With regard to the works of man, by the word of your lips I have avoided the ways of the violent.5My steps have held fast to your paths; my feet have not slipped.6I call upon you, for you will answer me, O God; incline your ear to me; hear my words.7Wondrously show your steadfast love, O Savior of those who seek refuge from their adversaries at your right hand.8Keep me as the apple of your eye; hide me in the shadow of your wings,9from the wicked who do me violence, my deadly enemies who surround me.10They close their hearts to pity; with their mouths they speak arrogantly.11They have now surrounded our steps; they set their eyes to cast us to the ground.12He is like a lion eager to tear, as a young lion lurking in ambush.13Arise, O LORD! Confront him, subdue him! Deliver my soul from the wicked by your sword,14from men by your hand, O LORD, from men of the world whose portion is in this life. You fill their womb with treasure; they are satisfied with children, and they leave their abundance to their infants.15As for me, I shall behold your face in righteousness; when I awake, I shall be satisfied with your likeness.
17.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 17 follows the confidence of Psalm 16, where David called the LORD “my chosen portion and my cup” (Psalm 16:5). Now, hunted by men whose portion is in this life, he puts that confidence to work. It is one of only five psalms headed “A Prayer”.

The message. When you are wronged and in danger, bring your case to God, for he is the Saviour of all who run to him, and he guards them as instinctively as you guard your own eye. And when the people against you seem to have everything, remember that their portion ends with this life, while those who belong to God will wake to see his face and be satisfied.

Why it was said. David was surrounded by violent, arrogant men and treated as guilty when he was not, perhaps in the years when Saul hunted him (see the introduction). The psalm gave Israel words for every time the righteous are pressed by people who prosper while they do wrong.

How the chapter makes its case. David asks God to hear a just cause and to clear him from his own presence: on this charge God’s night inspection will find nothing, because God’s word has kept his feet on God’s paths (vv. 1–5). He calls on God’s steadfast love and asks to be kept as the apple of his eye and hidden under his wings (vv. 6–9). He describes enemies who shut their hearts, close in and lie in wait like a lion, and asks God himself to confront them (vv. 10–14a). Then he sets two portions side by side: theirs, full and generous and over at the grave (v. 14b), and his, the face of God on waking (v. 15).

Where it leads. By pattern and by promise. David could claim lips free of deceit on one charge; Jesus is the one of whom it is said, “neither was deceit found in his mouth” (1 Peter 2:22), the wholly just cause, condemned by men and vindicated from the Father’s presence when God raised him. The sheltering wings of verse 8 are the picture Jesus used of himself as he wept over Jerusalem (Matthew 23:37). And the waking of verse 15 is promised in him: “we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2).

For us. You do not have to win every argument or match what others have, because the God who keeps you as the apple of his eye has given you a better portion. Bring your wrongs to him instead of avenging them, let his word keep your feet when the violent road is open, and when you envy the prosperous, ask whose satisfaction will last.
17.theology:
Vindication is sought from God's presence rather than from public opinion (v. 2), and the claim of innocence concerns one charge, not a whole life (v. 3). What kept him off the violent road was the word of your lips (v. 4).

God’s care is pictured as quick and instinctive: the pupil of the eye and a bird covering her young (vv. 8-9; Matt 23:37).

Cruelty begins by closing the heart (v. 10). The heart of the psalm is the contrast between two portions: everything one life can hold, given generously by God and stopping at the grave (v. 14), against the face of God on waking (v. 15). Both parties are satisfied; only one satisfaction survives the night.
17.examples: Ask what kept you from the last wrong thing you nearly did; this psalm says it was the word of God's lips, not temperament. And for anyone reading with a list of what they lack, it sets the full, enviable portion of this life beside the face of God, and lets the reader see which one lasts.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — You Have Visited Me by Night
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David’s first move under attack is to bring his case to God and to shelter in him. He asks God to hear a just cause and to vindicate him from his own presence, not from public opinion (vv. 1–2). He can face God’s scrutiny on this charge, for God has searched him by night and found nothing, because God’s word has kept him off the road of the violent (vv. 3–5). Then the appeal turns from his cause to God’s love: he calls on the Saviour of those who take refuge, asking to be kept as the apple of God’s eye and hidden in the shadow of his wings from the enemies who surround him (vv. 6–9).
verseByVerse.theology: A man asks God to examine him on one specific charge, and appeals to the God whose habit is to save people who run to him.

verseByVerse.quote: Hear a just cause, O LORD; attend to my cry! Give ear to my prayer from lips free of deceit! From your presence let my vindication come! Let your eyes behold the right! You have tried my heart, you have visited me by night, you have tested me, and you will find nothing; I have purposed that my mouth will not transgress. With regard to the works of man, by the word of your lips I have avoided the ways of the violent. My steps have held fast to your paths; my feet have not slipped.
verseByVerse.commentary:
David asks God to hear his case and clear his name, and he can face God’s own searching on this charge, because God’s word has kept him on God’s paths.

A Prayer of David. Only five psalms are headed a prayer, and this one earns the title: no instrument, no choirmaster, just a man in trouble, talking.

From your presence let my vindication come! He is not asking public opinion for a hearing. Vindication has to come from where God is, or it does not hold; a reputation restored by clever handling is a different thing altogether.

You have visited me by night. God’s inspection is a night visit, in the hours when a person is least guarded and most himself. And the claim is narrow: in this dispute, you will find nothing. The same man prays, “Enter not into judgment with your servant” (Psalm 143:2). A clean conscience on one charge and a clean record before God are two different claims, and only the first is made here.

By the word of your lips. Not temperament or good company but what God had said steered him away from the violent men’s road. Any Christian can test that by asking what kept him from the last wrong thing he nearly did.

The one wholly just cause. Only one man could pray these verses about his whole life: Jesus, who “committed no sin, neither was deceit found in his mouth” (1 Peter 2:22), who was tried by night and found guilty of nothing he had done, and vindicated from the Father’s presence when God raised him.

Uncertain wording. In verse 3 I have purposed can also be read “my thoughts do not go beyond my mouth”, and in verse 4 with regard to the works of man probably means “whatever others do”. Either way the sense is plain: his words were honest, and God’s word kept him from violence.

verseByVerse.quote: I call upon you, for you will answer me, O God; incline your ear to me; hear my words. Wondrously show your steadfast love, O Savior of those who seek refuge from their adversaries at your right hand. Keep me as the apple of your eye; hide me in the shadow of your wings, from the wicked who do me violence, my deadly enemies who surround me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
David calls on God with confidence, asking to be guarded as instinctively as we guard our eyes and as a bird covers her young.

For you will answer me. Said before the answer comes, this is not hoping aloud but stating the character of the one he is calling, who has a title: Saviour of those who seek refuge. This is what God does; it is his line of work.

The apple of your eye. The apple of your eye is the pupil, the part of the body we protect without thinking: you blink before you can decide to. The Hebrew is literally “the little man, the daughter of the eye”, the tiny reflection you see in another’s pupil. God used the phrase of Israel in the desert: “he kept him as the apple of his eye” (Deuteronomy 32:10), and Zechariah made it a warning: “he who touches you touches the apple of his eye” (Zechariah 2:8).

The shadow of your wings. The second picture is a bird covering her young. Boaz blessed Ruth as one who had come to the LORD, “under whose wings you have come to take refuge” (Ruth 2:12). And Jesus wept over Jerusalem in the same picture: “How often would I have gathered your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, and you were not willing!” (Matthew 23:37). The God under whose wings David hid stood in the city as a man and longed to gather its people.

What it does not mean. Not that God’s people never suffer harm: David prays this surrounded by deadly enemies, and Jesus promised both “some of you they will put to death” and “not a hair of your head will perish” (Luke 21:16, 18). To be the apple of God’s eye is to be guarded in a way no enemy can finally undo.

Uncertain wording. In verse 7 at your right hand may say where the refugees shelter, as the ESV takes it, or how God saves them, “by your right hand”. Both are true of God, and the sense is not affected.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–15 — I Shall Behold Your Face
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The psalm ends by setting two kinds of people, and two portions, side by side. The enemies have shut their hearts to pity, talk proudly, close in, and wait like a lion for the kill (vv. 10–12), so David asks God himself to rise, confront them and rescue him (vv. 13–14a). Then he describes them with surprising honesty: men whose portion is in this life, full of good things God has given, satisfied with children and leaving their wealth to their heirs (v. 14b). Against all that he sets one sentence: he will see God’s face and, when he awakes, be satisfied (v. 15). Both are satisfied; only one satisfaction lasts.
verseByVerse.theology: Two portions are set side by side: everything this life can hold, or the face of God on waking.

verseByVerse.quote: They close their hearts to pity; with their mouths they speak arrogantly. They have now surrounded our steps; they set their eyes to cast us to the ground. He is like a lion eager to tear, as a young lion lurking in ambush. Arise, O LORD! Confront him, subdue him! Deliver my soul from the wicked by your sword, from men by your hand, O LORD, from men of the world whose portion is in this life. You fill their womb with treasure; they are satisfied with children, and they leave their abundance to their infants.
verseByVerse.commentary:
David’s enemies have switched off pity and close in like a hunting lion, so he asks God himself to confront them; all they have, however full, is a portion that ends with this life.

Real danger. His enemies are “deadly” (v. 9), and they lie in wait like a lion. The tenderness of verse 8 is what a hunted man reaches for.

They close their hearts to pity. Literally, “they close up their fat”: the heart grown thick and unfeeling. In three verses the heart shuts, the mouth opens, and the body closes in, the order in which cruelty happens. Pity has to be switched off first, and they do it themselves. Nobody is born unable to feel for the person in front of him.

Arise, O LORD! He asks God to act with his sword and his hand, and does not reach for his own. Handing an enemy to God is the alternative to revenge, not a form of it (Romans 12:19).

Men of the world whose portion is in this life. Look at what their portion contains: full bellies, treasure, children they are satisfied with, an estate to leave the grandchildren. This is not a picture of misery, and that is the point. God gives them a great deal, all of it inside the span of one life, and then it stops.

Two portions. The previous psalm said, “The LORD is my chosen portion and my cup” (Psalm 16:5). Here is the other portion, set out honestly and enviably. The choice is not between a full life and an empty one, but between a full life that ends and a portion that does not.

Uncertain wording. Verse 14 is one of the hardest in the Psalter. The ESV reads it as a description of the worldly and their plenty; others as a prayer that God fill them with the judgment stored up for them; others of God’s own treasured people, whom he feeds. The ESV’s reading suits verse 15, where “satisfied” answers “satisfied”.

verseByVerse.quote: As for me, I shall behold your face in righteousness; when I awake, I shall be satisfied with your likeness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Against everything his enemies have, David sets the one thing he wants: to see God’s face, and to wake up satisfied in his presence.

I shall behold your face. As for me sets him over against the men with the treasure and the heirs. What he wants is not a larger share of what they have. It is the face of God, and he expects to see it in righteousness: not by talking his way in, but put right with God. The seeing is the reward itself; nothing else is named.

When I awake. Surrounded by men who may kill him, he speaks of waking up satisfied. Some read this of the morning after a night in danger; many, from the early church on, have heard the waking from the sleep of death (compare Daniel 12:2). Every morning God keeps him alive is a rehearsal of the last one. The men of verse 14 are satisfied too, for now. Only one of the two satisfactions survives the night.

Seeing God’s face. How can he see God’s face, when “man shall not see me and live” (Exodus 33:20)? No one sees God’s unveiled glory in this life, but believers see him in Christ (John 14:9; 2 Corinthians 4:6), and the full sight comes at the resurrection: “They will see his face” (Revelation 22:4).

Satisfied with your likeness. Seeing him is what will make us like him: “we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2). Whoever reads this psalm with a list of what they lack (the treasure, the security, the family, the vindication that never came), its last word is not a consolation prize. It is the thing everything else was a picture of.

keyVerse.quote: As for me, I shall behold your face in righteousness; when I awake, I shall be satisfied with your likeness.
keyVerse.note: The whole psalm turns on this last sentence. Against enemies who have a full portion in this life, David sets the one thing he wants, the face of God, and the satisfaction that will still be there when he wakes. It is the Old Testament hope that the New Testament fulfils in the promise that we shall see Christ as he is.

17.reflection:
David asks for vindication “from your presence” rather than from the people around him (v. 2). When you are misunderstood or wrongly blamed, whose verdict do you find yourself chasing, and what would it change to want God’s first?

David says it was “the word of your lips” that kept him from the ways of the violent (v. 4). Think of a time you were kept from doing wrong. What actually held you back, and how could God’s word play a larger part next time?

God keeps his people “as the apple of your eye” and in “the shadow of your wings” (v. 8), yet David is still surrounded by enemies. How do you hold together God’s tender protection and the real suffering believers face? How does Jesus’ lament over Jerusalem (Matthew 23:37) help?

Verses 14 and 15 set a full portion in this life beside the face of God. Where are you most tempted to envy people who seem to have everything, and how does this psalm reshape that envy?

18.title: The LORD Is My Rock
18.text: To the choirmaster. A Psalm of David, the servant of the LORD, who addressed the words of this song to the LORD on the day when the LORD delivered him from the hand of all his enemies, and from the hand of Saul. He said: 1I love you, O LORD, my strength.2The LORD is my rock and my fortress and my deliverer, my God, my rock, in whom I take refuge, my shield, and the horn of my salvation, my stronghold.3I call upon the LORD, who is worthy to be praised, and I am saved from my enemies.4The cords of death encompassed me; the torrents of destruction assailed me;5the cords of Sheol entangled me; the snares of death confronted me.6In my distress I called upon the LORD; to my God I cried for help. From his temple he heard my voice, and my cry to him reached his ears.7Then the earth reeled and rocked; the foundations also of the mountains trembled and quaked, because he was angry.8Smoke went up from his nostrils, and devouring fire from his mouth; glowing coals flamed forth from him.9He bowed the heavens and came down; thick darkness was under his feet.10He rode on a cherub and flew; he came swiftly on the wings of the wind.11He made darkness his covering, his canopy around him, thick clouds dark with water.12Out of the brightness before him hailstones and coals of fire broke through his clouds.13The LORD also thundered in the heavens, and the Most High uttered his voice, hailstones and coals of fire.14And he sent out his arrows and scattered them; he flashed forth lightnings and routed them.15Then the channels of the sea were seen, and the foundations of the world were laid bare at your rebuke, O LORD, at the blast of the breath of your nostrils.16He sent from on high, he took me; he drew me out of many waters.17He rescued me from my strong enemy and from those who hated me, for they were too mighty for me.18They confronted me in the day of my calamity, but the LORD was my support.19He brought me out into a broad place; he rescued me, because he delighted in me.20The LORD dealt with me according to my righteousness; according to the cleanness of my hands he rewarded me.21For I have kept the ways of the LORD, and have not wickedly departed from my God.22For all his rules were before me, and his statutes I did not put away from me.23I was blameless before him, and I kept myself from my guilt.24So the LORD has rewarded me according to my righteousness, according to the cleanness of my hands in his sight.25With the merciful you show yourself merciful; with the blameless man you show yourself blameless;26with the purified you show yourself pure; and with the crooked you make yourself seem tortuous.27For you save a humble people, but the haughty eyes you bring down.28For it is you who light my lamp; the LORD my God lightens my darkness.29For by you I can run against a troop, and by my God I can leap over a wall.30This God—his way is perfect; the word of the LORD proves true; he is a shield for all those who take refuge in him.31For who is God, but the LORD? And who is a rock, except our God?—32the God who equipped me with strength and made my way blameless.33He made my feet like the feet of a deer and set me secure on the heights.34He trains my hands for war, so that my arms can bend a bow of bronze.35You have given me the shield of your salvation, and your right hand supported me, and your gentleness made me great.36You gave a wide place for my steps under me, and my feet did not slip.37I pursued my enemies and overtook them, and did not turn back till they were consumed.38I thrust them through, so that they were not able to rise; they fell under my feet.39For you equipped me with strength for the battle; you made those who rise against me sink under me.40You made my enemies turn their backs to me, and those who hated me I destroyed.41They cried for help, but there was none to save; they cried to the LORD, but he did not answer them.42I beat them fine as dust before the wind; I cast them out like the mire of the streets.43You delivered me from strife with the people; you made me the head of the nations; people whom I had not known served me.44As soon as they heard of me they obeyed me; foreigners came cringing to me.45Foreigners lost heart and came trembling out of their fortresses.46The LORD lives, and blessed be my rock, and exalted be the God of my salvation—47the God who gave me vengeance and subdued peoples under me,48who rescued me from my enemies; yes, you exalted me above those who rose against me; you delivered me from the man of violence.49For this I will praise you, O LORD, among the nations, and sing to your name.50Great salvation he brings to his king, and shows steadfast love to his anointed, to David and his offspring forever.
18.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 18 is the longest psalm in Book One and the great thanksgiving after the prayers of the hunted king in Psalms 3 to 17. David looks back from safety on the years when Saul chased him, and the same song stands, with small differences, as 2 Samuel 22.

The message. The LORD answers the cry of his servant with the whole strength of heaven, and he does it because he delights in him. The God who bows the heavens to pull one man out of deep water is a rock to all who take refuge in him, and his steadfast love to his anointed king, and to that king’s offspring, has no end.

Why it was said. David wrote it on the day God had rescued him “from the hand of all his enemies, and from the hand of Saul” (see the introduction). It reminded Israel that their king’s throne rested on God’s faithfulness, not his strength.

How the chapter makes its case. David opens with love and a pile of names for God (vv. 1–3). He tells how the cords of death caught him and he cried out (vv. 4–6), and how God came down in earthquake and storm (vv. 7–15) to draw him out of many waters, because he delighted in him (vv. 16–19). He explains the rescue: on this charge his hands were clean, and God meets people as they come to him and lights a lamp in the dark (vv. 20–30). Then the king tells how God equipped him for battle, made him great by his gentleness, and set him over the nations (vv. 31–45), and he ends with praise for the living God and his steadfast love to David’s offspring for ever (vv. 46–50).

Where it leads. By covenant and promise, and by pattern. The last line looks to David’s “offspring forever”, the King God promised in 2 Samuel 7. Peter speaks of God “loosing the pangs of death” when he raised Jesus (Acts 2:24), the Son of David held by death’s cords until the third day and drawn out. Paul quotes verse 49 to show that the nations were always meant to join Israel’s praise (Romans 15:9). And only Jesus could pray verses 20 to 24 with no Psalm 51 beside them; his clean hands are counted to all who trust him.

For us. Name God from your own landscape, as David did: what has he been to you this year? Call on him in the tight place, for he still bows the heavens for one person. And rest in the reason he gives for rescuing you: not your usefulness, but his delight in you in Christ.
18.theology:
The centre of the psalm is grace on a grand scale. God answers one cry (v. 6) with an earthquake, and the reason given for the rescue is delight, not merit (v. 19). Even the clean hands David claims in verses 20-24 are credited to God in the end (v. 32), and the same author wrote Psalm 51.

God deals with people as they deal with him (vv. 25-27), and he more often lights a lamp than removes the darkness (v. 28). The battle report belongs to a king's duty, not to the church's methods: the psalm itself runs on to the nations praising God with Israel (v. 49; Rom 15:9) and to David's offspring forever (v. 50).
18.examples:
David gives God eight names in a single verse, and every one comes from the ground that kept him alive: rock, fortress, shield, the horn of a strong animal. Any reader can do the same with his own year and ask what God has actually been to him.

Heaven bows like a man ducking through a low door, and the whole storm is spent on one fugitive. That is the God who answers when a believer in trouble calls.

And in the middle of a war song stands its gentlest line: your gentleness made me great.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–19 — He Bowed the Heavens and Came Down
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: One man’s cry brings down the whole power of heaven. David begins with love and eight names for God, all drawn from the ground that kept him alive (vv. 1–3). Death had him in its ropes and floods, and he called for help, and his cry reached God’s ears (vv. 4–6). Then God came down: the earth shook, fire and smoke went out from him, he rode on a cherub, wrapped in cloud, and thundered until the sea bed lay bare (vv. 7–15). After all the noise the rescue is simple: a hand reaches down from on high and pulls David out of deep water into a broad place, because God delighted in him (vv. 16–19).
verseByVerse.theology: Heaven is emptied and the mountains shake, and the whole operation is for one hunted man.

verseByVerse.quote: I love you, O LORD, my strength. The LORD is my rock and my fortress and my deliverer, my God, my rock, in whom I take refuge, my shield, and the horn of my salvation, my stronghold. I call upon the LORD, who is worthy to be praised, and I am saved from my enemies.
verseByVerse.commentary:
David begins his song of rescue with love, and piles up names for God drawn from the ground that kept him alive: the LORD is his rock, his fortress and his deliverer.

The heading. It dates the song “on the day when the LORD delivered him from the hand of all his enemies, and from the hand of Saul”: his whole decade as a fugitive, looked back on from safety. The same song stands as 2 Samuel 22.

I love you, O LORD, my strength. The verb in I love you is a rare and tender one, from the family of words for compassion, and nowhere else in the Old Testament is it used of a person loving God (2 Samuel 22 does not have this opening line). After years of caves and close escapes, the first thing out of him is not analysis but affection.

And I am saved. “I call upon the LORD … and I am saved” is the psalm in one line. The verbs describe the habit of a lifetime, not a single event, and the fifty verses tell the story.

My rock and my fortress. Eight images in one verse, tumbling over each other, all from the years he is describing: the rock faces of Engedi, a hill fort, a shield in a skirmish, the horn of a strong animal, its strength. This is not a classroom list of God’s qualities. It is a soldier naming God after the terrain that kept him alive, and it invites the same from any reader: what has God actually been to you this year? Name it out of your own landscape.
verseByVerse.note: The heading calls David the servant of the LORD, a title given before him to Moses and Joshua.

verseByVerse.quote: The cords of death encompassed me; the torrents of destruction assailed me; the cords of Sheol entangled me; the snares of death confronted me. In my distress I called upon the LORD; to my God I cried for help. From his temple he heard my voice, and my cry to him reached his ears.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Caught in death’s ropes and swept by its floods, David cried to the LORD, and his cry reached God’s own ears.

The cords of death encompassed me. Death is a hunter: ropes, nets, snares, and a flash flood in a dry wadi. Sheol is the grave, the place of the dead. He was not merely frightened (the ESV notes that assailed can be read terrified); he was caught.

In my distress I called upon the LORD. Verse 6 is the turning point of all fifty verses. He called; God heard. And his cry “reached his ears”: not overheard in general; it arrived.

Loosing the pangs of death. The Hebrew word for cords can also mean birth pangs, and the Greek Old Testament took it so here. Peter, preaching at Pentecost, says God raised Jesus by “loosing the pangs of death” (Acts 2:24). Whether or not Peter had this line in mind, the shape is the same: the Son of David was not only caught by death’s cords but held in them until the third day, and God reached down and drew him out.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the earth reeled and rocked; the foundations also of the mountains trembled and quaked, because he was angry. Smoke went up from his nostrils, and devouring fire from his mouth; glowing coals flamed forth from him. He bowed the heavens and came down; thick darkness was under his feet. He rode on a cherub and flew; he came swiftly on the wings of the wind.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In answer to one man’s cry, God comes down in earthquake, fire and storm, angry at what has been done to his servant.

Then the earth reeled and rocked. What follows the cry is nine verses of storm, the language of Sinai, where the mountain shook and smoke went up (Exodus 19:16–18), and of the old war songs where God marched out and the earth trembled. God does not send an angel with a message; he “bowed the heavens and came down” like a man ducking through a low door, with darkness under his feet and a cherub for a chariot.

Smoke went up from his nostrils. The usual Hebrew word for anger is the word for nose or nostrils, so smoke from the nostrils is anger made visible. And it is not aimed at David but at what was done to him, at the cords of death that held God’s servant (vv. 4–5). For a man hunted for years, it is a great comfort that God is not neutral about it.

He rode on a cherub and flew. The cherubim guarded Eden (Genesis 3:24), and their golden figures spread their wings over the ark, where the LORD was “enthroned on the cherubim” (1 Samuel 4:4). Here the throne is moving. The God of the tabernacle is not tied to one tent; he comes “swiftly on the wings of the wind” to wherever his servant is (compare Psalm 104:3).

verseByVerse.quote: He made darkness his covering, his canopy around him, thick clouds dark with water. Out of the brightness before him hailstones and coals of fire broke through his clouds.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God travels hidden in thick cloud, and the darkness that looked like his absence is the very tent in which he comes.

He made darkness his covering. Earlier in this book a man asked why God hides himself (Psalm 10:1), and another how long the face would stay hidden (Psalm 13:1). Here the darkness is not absence at all: it is the tent God travels in. He had been coming all the time, wrapped in the very thing that looked like his absence.

Out of the brightness before him. Inside the darkness is light, a brightness so fierce that it breaks through as hail and burning coals: the cloud and fire that led Israel through the wilderness (Exodus 13:21). The darkness is itself a mercy, for no one can look on God’s glory unveiled and live (Exodus 33:20).

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD also thundered in the heavens, and the Most High uttered his voice, hailstones and coals of fire. And he sent out his arrows and scattered them; he flashed forth lightnings and routed them. Then the channels of the sea were seen, and the foundations of the world were laid bare at your rebuke, O LORD, at the blast of the breath of your nostrils.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s voice thunders, his arrows scatter the enemy, and at his rebuke the floor of the sea is laid bare, all to rescue one hunted man.

The LORD also thundered. Now the storm becomes a battle. Thunder is God’s voice (Psalm 29:3–9), lightning his arrows, and the enemies who had David surrounded are scattered without his lifting a hand. God is named “the Most High”, the title that sets him over every power on earth (Genesis 14:19–20): David’s pursuers had a king on their side; David had the one who rules over kings.

At your rebuke, O LORD. Rebuke is used of God driving back the waters (Psalm 104:7), and “the blast of the breath of your nostrils” recalls the Red Sea: “At the blast of your nostrils the waters piled up” (Exodus 15:8), and Israel walked through on dry ground. David tells his own rescue in the colours of the exodus: the same God, the same breath, for one man.

The foundations of the world were laid bare. Creation itself is pulled back like a sheet. And this was no national emergency. David was one man on the run, with a few hundred followers and a price on his head. Scripture is perfectly happy to spend an earthquake on an individual. When a believer in trouble calls, what answers is not a sympathetic presence but the God who bows the heavens.

verseByVerse.quote: He sent from on high, he took me; he drew me out of many waters. He rescued me from my strong enemy and from those who hated me, for they were too mighty for me. They confronted me in the day of my calamity, but the LORD was my support. He brought me out into a broad place; he rescued me, because he delighted in me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After all the thunder, the rescue is one hand reaching down to pull David out of deep water, and the reason given is simply that God delighted in him.

He drew me out of many waters. The verb is the one behind the name Moses, named for what Pharaoh’s daughter said: “I drew him out of the water” (Exodus 2:10). David is a man pulled out of the river a second time.

But the LORD was my support. Do not skip verse 18. Two things arrived on the same day: the trouble came on schedule, and so did the support, something you lean your whole weight on. God did not cancel the day; he held the man up inside it. David admits his enemies “were too mighty for me”, and the destination is not another cave but a broad place, room to stand after years of hiding in crevices.

Because he delighted in me. Then the reason, the last thing a self-made man would write. Not because David was necessary to the plan, not because he had earned it: God delighted in him. That is the engine of the whole psalm, and Scripture says the same of all God’s people, over whom he rejoices with gladness (Zephaniah 3:17).

The approval we are starving for. Much of modern life is a hunt for someone to delight in us. We curate a public self and watch the response; we judge a day by how we were seen in it. The sociologist Charles Cooley called it the looking-glass self: we come to know who we are by imagining how others see us. Every audience is fickle, and a self built in its mirror has to be rebuilt every morning. David’s line comes from outside the whole competition. The gospel makes it astonishing for us: the Father’s words over his Son, “with whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3:17), are spoken over everyone who is in Christ. Someone who knows that does not stop caring what people think. He simply stops needing it in order to live.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–30 — This God: His Way Is Perfect
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Why did God rescue him, and what kind of God is he? David says that on the charge laid against him in the Saul years his hands were clean: he kept God’s ways and kept God’s rules before his eyes (vv. 20–24). That is no boast of sinlessness, for the God who rewarded him also made his way blameless (v. 32). It shows how God deals with everyone: merciful to the merciful, pure to the pure, hard to follow for the crooked, saving the humble and bringing down the proud (vv. 25–27). And for those who trust him he lights a lamp in the dark and gives strength for the wall in front of them, for his way is perfect and his word proves true (vv. 28–30).
verseByVerse.theology: People meet God as they have dealt with him, and even a righteous man's blamelessness turns out to be God's gift.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD dealt with me according to my righteousness; according to the cleanness of my hands he rewarded me. For I have kept the ways of the LORD, and have not wickedly departed from my God. For all his rules were before me, and his statutes I did not put away from me. I was blameless before him, and I kept myself from my guilt. So the LORD has rewarded me according to my righteousness, according to the cleanness of my hands in his sight.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the charge of seizing Saul’s throne, David’s hands were clean, and God rewarded his loyalty; yet the psalm itself credits even that blamelessness to God.

According to my righteousness. Five verses of a man saying he deserved rescue make Christian readers uneasy. Two things help us read it rightly. First, the subject is the Saul years. Twice he had the king at his mercy and did not kill him; he refused to take the throne by blood. In that matter his hands were clean, and he says so.

All his rules were before me. Look at what the loyalty consisted of: “all his rules were before me, and his statutes I did not put away from me” (v. 22; the ESV notes that rules may be rendered “just decrees”). He kept God’s instructions where he could see them through a decade when nobody would have blamed him for improvising. Most moral collapse happens after the rules quietly go out of the field of vision.

I was blameless before him. The word he uses of himself is the word used of God’s way in verse 30 (ESV note), and verse 32 credits David’s own to God: “the God who equipped me with strength and made my way blameless”. Even the clean hands were God’s gift.

Beside Psalm 51. Second, the same man wrote Psalm 51 after Bathsheba, where there is not a word about clean hands and the only plea is mercy. Scripture prints both psalms, and both are true. A believer can say of a particular fight, before God, “I did not cheat”, while knowing that his standing with God rests on nothing of the kind.

No Psalm 51 beside them. Only one Son of David could pray verses 20 to 24 with no Psalm 51 beside them. Jesus kept the ways of the LORD without a single lapse, and the gospel’s news is that his clean hands are counted to everyone who trusts him (2 Corinthians 5:21; Philippians 3:9).

verseByVerse.quote: With the merciful you show yourself merciful; with the blameless man you show yourself blameless; with the purified you show yourself pure; and with the crooked you make yourself seem tortuous. For you save a humble people, but the haughty eyes you bring down.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God meets people as they come to him: the merciful find him merciful, the crooked find him hard to follow, and the humble find him a Saviour.

With the merciful you show yourself merciful. This is not God being moody; it is how he has made the moral world to work. A merciful man finds God merciful, because mercy is what he has learned to recognise. The crooked man finds God devious and hard to pin down, because to a bent ruler a straight line looks crooked.

The haughty eyes you bring down. What God actively opposes is haughty eyes, and what he saves is a humble people. Come as a beggar and you will find him generous.

What it does not mean. Not that we earn God’s kindness by being kind first: the psalm has just said he rescued David because he delighted in him (v. 19). The heart God has humbled comes to see him truly; the proud heart cannot.

verseByVerse.quote: For it is you who light my lamp; the LORD my God lightens my darkness. For by you I can run against a troop, and by my God I can leap over a wall. This God—his way is perfect; the word of the LORD proves true; he is a shield for all those who take refuge in him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God lights a lamp in David’s darkness and gives him strength for the obstacle in front of him, because God’s way is perfect and his word proves true.

It is you who light my lamp. The first mercy is the one people in the dark should hold on to: God does not always remove the darkness; he lights a lamp in it. A lamp is not daylight. It is enough to take the next step, which is all anyone actually needs.

I can leap over a wall. Then energy for exactly what is in front of him; a troop and a wall were not metaphors in David’s life. God does not lift him over the obstacles: he still has to run, and still has to jump. And the credit is given away twice in one verse: by you, by my God.

This God: his way is perfect. The summary: his way is perfect, which the ESV notes can be read blameless, the same word David used of himself. The perfection is God’s first; anything of it in a man is borrowed. And the word of the LORD proves true: it has been through the fire like refined metal and come out pure, a line Proverbs repeats almost word for word (Proverbs 30:5).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 31–50 — Your Gentleness Made Me Great
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The fugitive is now a king, and every victory is credited to God. There is no God but the LORD, and he has equipped David for battle: sure feet, trained hands, a shield, and the gentleness that made him great (vv. 31–36). David pursued and overcame his enemies, by strength God supplied (vv. 37–42). God ended the civil war and set him over nations he had never known (vv. 43–45). So the song ends in praise of the living God who gave him the victory, and with two horizons: the nations who will hear this praise, and the steadfast love God will show to his anointed, “to David and his offspring forever” (vv. 46–50).
verseByVerse.theology: The victory song credits God with the strength and the gentleness, and ends on a promise that outlives David.

verseByVerse.quote: For who is God, but the LORD? And who is a rock, except our God?— the God who equipped me with strength and made my way blameless. He made my feet like the feet of a deer and set me secure on the heights. He trains my hands for war, so that my arms can bend a bow of bronze. You have given me the shield of your salvation, and your right hand supported me, and your gentleness made me great. You gave a wide place for my steps under me, and my feet did not slip.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The only God there is has equipped David with everything his task demanded, and what made him great was not God’s power alone but his gentleness.

He made my feet like the feet of a deer. There is no God but the LORD and no other rock (v. 31), and his gifts are specific and practical: sure feet on broken ground, the strength to draw a heavy bow, high places to stand on. God’s help here is not a mood of comfort but competence for a hard job. He equips people for the work he has given them, and that is a thing to ask for by name.

Your gentleness made me great. In the middle of a war song stands the loveliest line in the psalm. Not your power, not your discipline, but your gentleness. The man who has just described an earthquake says that what made him what he is was the way God stooped and handled him carefully.

Gentle and lowly. That gentleness came in person: “I am gentle and lowly in heart”, said Jesus (Matthew 11:29). The God who stooped to lift David stooped all the way, to a manger and a cross, to make his people great.

Uncertain wording. The word rendered gentleness usually means humility, and its sense when used of God is debated. Many take it as God’s stooping down to help, and the slightly different form in 2 Samuel 22:36 has also been read as “your answering” or “your help”. The likely meaning is God’s humble, stooping care.

verseByVerse.quote: I pursued my enemies and overtook them, and did not turn back till they were consumed. I thrust them through, so that they were not able to rise; they fell under my feet. For you equipped me with strength for the battle; you made those who rise against me sink under me. You made my enemies turn their backs to me, and those who hated me I destroyed. They cried for help, but there was none to save; they cried to the LORD, but he did not answer them. I beat them fine as dust before the wind; I cast them out like the mire of the streets.
verseByVerse.commentary:
David pursued and destroyed the enemies of God’s people, but he credits every victory to the God who equipped him.

I pursued my enemies. This is a battle report, and it is bloody. David was Israel’s king, charged with defending a people from raiders who came to take their harvest and their children, and a king who lost those wars got his nation enslaved. The wars in view are probably those of 2 Samuel 8, where David subdued the Philistines, Moab, Aram and Edom. The most sobering line is verse 41: his enemies at the end cry to the LORD, and he does not answer. Fear at the end is not repentance.

For you equipped me with strength. In the middle of the battle report is the sentence that explains it. David pursued and overtook, but the strength was supplied: “you equipped me”, “you made those who rise against me sink”, “you made my enemies turn their backs”. The same verb opened this part of the psalm (v. 32), and it keeps the boasting from being David’s. The victories were real, and they were given.

verseByVerse.quote: You delivered me from strife with the people; you made me the head of the nations; people whom I had not known served me. As soon as they heard of me they obeyed me; foreigners came cringing to me. Foreigners lost heart and came trembling out of their fortresses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God ended the war within Israel and made David head over nations he had never known, though their submission came from fear, a kingdom that points beyond itself to Christ’s.

You made me the head of the nations. First God delivered him from “strife with the people”, probably the long war between the house of Saul and the house of David (2 Samuel 3:1); then he set him over peoples he had never known, who obeyed at the sound of his name, while others gave up their strongholds in fear. Submission from fear is not love, and that is exactly where David’s kingdom falls short of the one it points to.

Christ and the nations. In the kingdom this psalm points towards, the nations come in freely, and the Son who rules them was killed by them first. The line runs from David’s conquered foreigners to the day when people “from every tribe and language and people and nation” stand and sing (Revelation 5:9). Christians are not given David’s sword; they are given the promise made to him.

Uncertain wording. Two rare words close this section. Came cringing comes from a verb that usually means to deceive, so it probably means feigned, flattering submission. Came trembling in verse 45 translates a word found only here, and 2 Samuel 22:46 has a slightly different one; the general sense, enemies leaving their fortresses in fear, is clear.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD lives, and blessed be my rock, and exalted be the God of my salvation— the God who gave me vengeance and subdued peoples under me, who rescued me from my enemies; yes, you exalted me above those who rose against me; you delivered me from the man of violence. For this I will praise you, O LORD, among the nations, and sing to your name. Great salvation he brings to his king, and shows steadfast love to his anointed, to David and his offspring forever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The song ends with a shout that the LORD lives, a promise that the nations will hear his praise, and God’s steadfast love pledged to David’s offspring for ever.

The LORD lives. The final shout is not an idea about God but a fact about him, said by a man who has been kept alive by it. Vengeance is something God gave; it was never David’s to take, which is why he could leave Saul unharmed in a cave.

I will praise you, O LORD, among the nations. Paul quotes this verse to prove that God always meant the Gentiles to join in the praise: “Therefore I will praise you among the Gentiles, and sing to your name” (Romans 15:9). David sang it as a king making God’s name known among neighbouring peoples. Paul reads it as a promise that those peoples would one day be singing with him, which is what happened.

To David and his offspring forever. The last word of this very personal song is about David’s offspring, the line God promised to establish for ever (2 Samuel 7:12–16), which runs from a cave in Judah to a manger and an empty tomb. The rescue of one hunted man turns out to be part of God keeping his covenant with David’s house. The psalm ends by looking down the generations to the King who was not rescued from violent men, because he gave himself into their hands on purpose.

keyVerse.quote: He brought me out into a broad place; he rescued me, because he delighted in me.
keyVerse.note: This is the reason behind the whole storm of verses 7 to 15. God did not rescue David because he was useful or had earned it, but because he delighted in him, and the psalm’s closing promise of steadfast love to David’s offspring shows where that delight finally rests: on Christ, and on all who are in him.

18.reflection:
David names God eight times in verse 2, each name drawn from the places where God kept him alive. If you described what God has been to you this past year from your own “landscape”, what names would you use?

Verses 7 to 15 describe the whole power of heaven coming down to rescue one man. How does this picture challenge the way you think God responds when you call on him in trouble?

David says God rescued him “because he delighted in me” (v. 19), yet he also speaks of being rewarded for his clean hands (vv. 20–24). How do these fit together, and how does Jesus help us hold both?

In the middle of a war song David says, “your gentleness made me great” (v. 35). Where have you experienced God’s gentleness when you deserved otherwise, and how has it shaped who you are?

19.title: The Heavens Declare the Glory of God
19.text: To the choirmaster. A Psalm of David. 1The heavens declare the glory of God, and the sky above proclaims his handiwork.2Day to day pours out speech, and night to night reveals knowledge.3There is no speech, nor are there words, whose voice is not heard.4Their voice goes out through all the earth, and their words to the end of the world. In them he has set a tent for the sun,5which comes out like a bridegroom leaving his chamber, and, like a strong man, runs its course with joy.6Its rising is from the end of the heavens, and its circuit to the end of them, and there is nothing hidden from its heat.7The law of the LORD is perfect, reviving the soul; the testimony of the LORD is sure, making wise the simple;8the precepts of the LORD are right, rejoicing the heart; the commandment of the LORD is pure, enlightening the eyes;9the fear of the LORD is clean, enduring forever; the rules of the LORD are true, and righteous altogether.10More to be desired are they than gold, even much fine gold; sweeter also than honey and drippings of the honeycomb.11Moreover, by them is your servant warned; in keeping them there is great reward.12Who can discern his errors? Declare me innocent from hidden faults.13Keep back your servant also from presumptuous sins; let them not have dominion over me! Then I shall be blameless, and innocent of great transgression.14Let the words of my mouth and the meditation of my heart be acceptable in your sight, O LORD, my rock and my redeemer.
19.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 18 ended its praise of the God who rescues with the line “the word of the LORD proves true” (Psalm 18:30). Psalm 19 turns from the battlefield to the two great ways God makes himself known: the sky above and the Scriptures. C. S. Lewis judged it the greatest poem in the Psalter.

The message. God speaks. Through the heavens he shows his glory to everyone, everywhere, without a word; through his law he gives life, wisdom, joy and light to those who listen, and it is sweeter than honey. But the word that delights also exposes, so the psalm ends where every honest reader must: asking the Redeemer to clear him of faults he cannot see and keep him from the sins he would choose.

Why it was said. David’s Israel lived among peoples who worshipped the sun and stars and praised the sun as the all-seeing judge. The psalm answers them by making the sun a servant in a tent God pitched, and by giving Israel a word from God that no sky could give (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. The heavens speak day and night, in no language and so to all (vv. 1–4b), and the sun runs its course with joy, with nothing hidden from its heat (vv. 4c–6). Then the covenant name of God fills six lines: his word is perfect, sure, right, pure, clean and true, and it revives the soul, makes the simple wise, rejoices the heart and enlightens the eyes (vv. 7–9). It is more to be desired than gold, and it warns and rewards (vv. 10–11). And the reader turns to himself: hidden faults, presumptuous sins, and a prayer that his words and thoughts be acceptable to his rock and redeemer (vv. 12–14).

Where it leads. By promise, and by the character of God revealed in Christ. Paul hears in verse 4 the gospel going out to the ends of the world (Romans 10:18). The word this psalm praises became flesh in Jesus (John 1:14), who alone kept it without hidden fault or presumptuous sin. And the psalm’s last word, redeemer, the next of kin who pays to set a relative free, is the part Christ came to play: he took our flesh and blood and ransomed us “with the precious blood of Christ” (1 Peter 1:19).

For us. Look up and let the sky make you small and glad. Open the Bible expecting it to revive, teach and gladden you, and ask for a taste for it. And when it shows you faults you cannot see, neither excuse them nor despair: take them to your Redeemer, who has already paid.
19.theology:
Creation speaks of God's glory continually, without words, to everyone (vv. 1-4), but it cannot tell anyone how to be forgiven, which is why the psalm turns to the word. Scripture revives, makes wise, gladdens and gives light (vv. 7-9), and it is worth wanting more than gold (v. 10): a claim about desire, not only usefulness.

Read honestly, the word uncovers sins a person cannot see as well as sins he chooses (vv. 12-13). The psalm's last word is redeemer, the relative who pays to set his kinsman free (v. 14), and the New Testament gives that kinsman a name.
19.examples:
The sky's witness is handed on in shifts, day to day and night to night, and it has not missed an hour since the beginning. Because it uses no language, no one is out of its reach.

The sun comes up like a glad bridegroom and runs like an athlete, and nothing is hidden from its heat. God's word reaches into a life in the same way.

The six lines on Scripture answer a plain question: what will the Bible do to me if I read it? The last line answers another: where does someone go who has found faults he cannot even see? To a relative who pays.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Day to Day Pours Out Speech
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Creation never stops preaching God’s glory. The heavens declare it and the sky proclaims his handiwork, and the message is passed on in shifts, day to day and night to night (vv. 1–2). They use no words, yet their voice goes out to the end of the world, so that no one anywhere is beyond its reach (vv. 3–4b). The sun is the chief preacher: housed by God in a tent, it comes out each morning like a glad bridegroom and runs its course like an athlete, and nothing is hidden from its heat (vv. 4c–6). That last line opens the way to the second half, where God’s word reaches into a life the same way.
verseByVerse.theology: Creation talks constantly and says one thing: glory. Nobody is out of earshot.

verseByVerse.quote: The heavens declare the glory of God, and the sky above proclaims his handiwork. Day to day pours out speech, and night to night reveals knowledge. There is no speech, nor are there words, whose voice is not heard. Their voice goes out through all the earth, and their words to the end of the world. In them he has set a tent for the sun,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sky never stops telling everyone, everywhere, about the glory of the God who made it, though it uses no words at all.

The heavens declare the glory of God. The verbs are in the present tense and they do not stop. The sky is not evidence lying about for clever people to interpret; it is a mouth, talking now. The message is handed on in shifts: day tells the next day, night briefs the next night, so the testimony has not missed an hour since the world began. The ESV notes that the sky above is the expanse of Genesis 1: the psalm is walking through the creation account with its head tipped back.

There is no speech, nor are there words. No speech, no words, and yet a voice that carries everywhere: creation does not preach in any language, which is exactly why it preaches in all of them. There is no country where the stars need a translator.

Their voice goes out through all the earth. Paul takes this verse and uses it of the gospel: “Their voice has gone out to all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Romans 10:18). He has just said that “faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ” (Romans 10:17). The sky’s testimony is universal; the gospel’s must be carried by people, and God intends it to travel just as far.

What creation cannot do. It cannot tell you how to be forgiven: the stars leave everyone without excuse (Romans 1:20), but they give no one a Saviour. That is why the psalm turns to the word.

Does this teach that the sun moves round the earth? It speaks as we still speak of sunrise and sunset: the way the sun appears to move. The psalm is poetry about God’s glory, not astronomy.

Uncertain wording. Verse 3 can be read two ways. Most modern translations, like the ESV, make it a paradox: no speech, no words, yet their voice goes out (v. 4). Older ones read “There is no speech nor language, where their voice is not heard”: they are heard in every tongue. Either way the witness is universal.

Textual note. Where the ESV has their voice in verse 4, the standard Hebrew text (the Masoretic Text) reads their line, the reach marked out by a measuring line; the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint) reads their sound, which the ESV follows and Paul quotes. The sense is the same: the message reaches everywhere.
verseByVerse.note: “The sky” is literally “the expanse” (ESV note), as in Genesis 1.

verseByVerse.quote: which comes out like a bridegroom leaving his chamber, and, like a strong man, runs its course with joy. Its rising is from the end of the heavens, and its circuit to the end of them, and there is nothing hidden from its heat.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sun rises each day like a glad bridegroom and runs its course like an athlete, and nothing escapes its heat, a picture of how God’s word will reach into everything.

Like a bridegroom leaving his chamber. A bridegroom stepping out of his chamber: scrubbed, dressed, radiant, and not remotely embarrassed to be looked at. And an athlete at the start of a race, all energy and gladness, who will run the whole circuit without tiring. The psalm says the sun does it with joy. Nothing in creation is dragging itself round out of duty.

A tent for the sun. Israel’s neighbours worshipped the sun; in Babylon it was the god who saw everything and judged. Here it is a creature God has housed in a tent, glorious and glad, but a servant, running the course he set it.

Nothing hidden from its heat. You can shelter from the light but not from the warmth; it gets into everything. The next verse turns to the law of the LORD, and this is the link: as the sun reaches everything under the sky, so God’s word reaches everything in a person’s life.

The starry heavens and the moral law. Immanuel Kant, one of the architects of modern thought, wrote near the end of his Critique of Practical Reason that two things filled him with ever greater wonder and awe the longer he thought about them: the starry heavens above him and the moral law within him. He was no traditional believer, yet he stood where this psalm stands, between a sky that speaks and a law that binds. Many still feel both: awe under a night sky, and an “ought” they cannot argue away, that cruelty to a child is really wrong and not merely disliked. A universe of matter and chance has trouble accounting for either (see the note on Genesis 1:1). David holds them together because one God made both. But the psalm goes past Kant’s wonder. The sky makes David small; the law makes him guilty, of faults he cannot even find (v. 12). Up close the moral law leaves us needing a Redeemer, the word the psalm ends on.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–14 — The Law of the LORD Is Perfect
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The sky shows God’s glory; his word shows his will and his grace, and the psalm turns to it with delight. Six lines name the word, describe it and say what it does: it revives the soul, makes the simple wise, rejoices the heart and enlightens the eyes, and it endures and is true (vv. 7–9). It is more desirable than gold and sweeter than honey, and it both warns and rewards (vv. 10–11). Then the reader looks at himself in its light, sees errors he cannot discern and sins that would master him, and asks for a verdict of innocence and for keeping. He ends by offering his words and his heart to the LORD, “my rock and my redeemer” (vv. 12–14).
verseByVerse.theology: The sky shows God's glory; the word shows his will, and the man who has read both ends up asking to be cleared of sins he cannot even see.

verseByVerse.quote: The law of the LORD is perfect, reviving the soul; the testimony of the LORD is sure, making wise the simple; the precepts of the LORD are right, rejoicing the heart; the commandment of the LORD is pure, enlightening the eyes; the fear of the LORD is clean, enduring forever; the rules of the LORD are true, and righteous altogether.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s word is perfect, sure, right, pure, clean and true, and it does for a person what nothing else can: it revives, makes wise, gladdens and gives light.

The law of the LORD is perfect. Six lines built the same way: a name for God’s word, a quality, and in four of them what it does to a person. Read them as answers to “what will the Bible do to me?” And notice the name: the first half of the psalm spoke of “God”, the Creator; now, six times, it is “the LORD”, the covenant name. The sky shows his power; the word shows him as Israel’s own God.

Reviving the soul. It brings a life back, as you revive someone who has collapsed. It makes the simple wise: not the clever but the teachable, the person who knows he needs to be told. It is rejoicing the heart, which cuts against the assumption that God’s commands are a weight. It is enlightening the eyes, the phrase David used when he was at the end of his strength (Psalm 13:3). It is clean and stays clean, when every other teaching keeps changing. And it is true, and righteous altogether, with no bad clauses hidden in the small print.

The fear of the LORD is clean. The fifth line names the fear of the LORD as if it were one of God’s writings. The reverence the word produces belongs on the same list as the word itself.

A way of reading. Together the lines describe a way of reading, not just a book: not one of the four effects is information. A man reads and something in him comes back to life; a slow learner gets wise; a heavy heart lifts; eyes that had stopped seeing start again. That is what to expect, and what to ask for before you open it.

verseByVerse.quote: More to be desired are they than gold, even much fine gold; sweeter also than honey and drippings of the honeycomb. Moreover, by them is your servant warned; in keeping them there is great reward.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s word is worth wanting more than wealth and is sweeter than the sweetest thing we know, and it both warns and rewards those who keep it.

More to be desired are they than gold. Gold and honey: the thing people work hardest to get and the sweetest thing they knew. Not more useful than gold, but more to be desired, and sweeter. The claim is about what we want. Most of us believe it in principle and live as though gold were worth far more, and the cure is not a scolding but a fresh taste, asked of the God who opens the eyes.

By them is your servant warned. The word is a warning sign at the cliff edge as well as honey on the tongue; the sweetness and the warning are one kindness.

In keeping them there is great reward. The speaker is already your servant, so great reward is not wages that earn him a place in God’s house; it is a Father’s gift found inside the obedience itself.

verseByVerse.quote: Who can discern his errors? Declare me innocent from hidden faults. Keep back your servant also from presumptuous sins; let them not have dominion over me! Then I shall be blameless, and innocent of great transgression. Let the words of my mouth and the meditation of my heart be acceptable in your sight, O LORD, my rock and my redeemer.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Shown his faults by God’s word, David asks to be cleared of those he cannot see and kept from those he would choose, and he offers his words and thoughts to God, his rock and his redeemer.

Who can discern his errors? Read honestly, the word drives a man to his knees about sins he did not know he had. Errors nobody can discern, including himself. Hidden faults are hidden from him, not from God: the habits everyone else can see and he cannot. And presumptuous sins are done with the eyes open, and do not stay occasional: he asks that they not gain dominion, because deliberate sin always tries to become the master.

Declare me innocent from hidden faults. The prayer for the first two is declare me innocent, a courtroom word: he cannot clean what he cannot find, so he asks for a verdict. The prayer for the third is keep back your servant; he does not trust himself with an open door. Anyone serious about holiness ends up praying both halves, and the second is answered by the Spirit God puts within his people (Ezekiel 36:27).

Let the words of my mouth. He has looked at the sky and read the law, and at the end he asks that his speech and his private thinking be accepted, brought in as an offering. Acceptable is sacrificial language.

My rock and my redeemer. The last word is the one the whole psalm has been leading to. The redeemer is the family rescuer, the relative with the right and the duty to buy his kinsman out of debt or slavery (Leviticus 25:25), as Boaz did for Ruth (Ruth 4), the one Job longed for when everything had gone: “I know that my Redeemer lives” (Job 19:25). A man who has found faults he cannot even see needs not a standard but a relative who will pay. The heavens told him the glory. The law told him the trouble. The last two words tell him where to go.

That relative has a name. Christians know him: the Son of God, who took our flesh and blood so that he could be our next of kin (Hebrews 2:14–17), and who paid “not with perishable things such as silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ” (1 Peter 1:18–19). His death is how God answers the prayer declare me innocent. A tender conscience can rest here: the faults it cannot find were known and paid for by its Redeemer.

Uncertain wording. The word behind presumptuous sins in verse 13 usually means proud or insolent people, so the line may mean “keep back your servant from the arrogant”, either from their influence or from becoming one of them. The ESV takes it of the sins such people commit. Either way he asks to be kept from wilful, high-handed sin and the pride it grows from.

keyVerse.quote: Let the words of my mouth and the meditation of my heart be acceptable in your sight, O LORD, my rock and my redeemer.
keyVerse.note: After the sky has shown God’s glory and the law has shown both his goodness and David’s hidden faults, the psalm ends with this offering of words and heart. Its last word, redeemer, the next of kin who pays to set a relative free, says where a person goes when God’s word has exposed him, and points to the Redeemer who paid with his own blood.

19.reflection:
Verses 1 to 6 say “The heavens declare the glory of God” to everyone without words. When have you sensed God’s glory in creation, and why can creation alone never tell us how to be forgiven?

Verses 7 to 9 list what God’s word does: revives the soul, makes wise the simple, rejoices the heart, enlightens the eyes. Which of these have you experienced, and which would you most like to ask God for the next time you open the Bible?

David says God’s rules are “more to be desired … than gold” and “sweeter also than honey” (v. 10). Honestly, what do you desire more than God’s word, and how might that desire be changed?

David prays about “hidden faults” and “presumptuous sins” (vv. 12–13), and ends by calling God “my redeemer” (v. 14). How does knowing Christ as your Redeemer help you face the faults God’s word uncovers without excuse or despair?

20.title: Some Trust in Chariots
20.text: To the choirmaster. A Psalm of David. 1May the LORD answer you in the day of trouble! May the name of the God of Jacob protect you!2May he send you help from the sanctuary and give you support from Zion!3May he remember all your offerings and regard with favor your burnt sacrifices! Selah4May he grant you your heart's desire and fulfill all your plans!5May we shout for joy over your salvation, and in the name of our God set up our banners! May the LORD fulfill all your petitions!6Now I know that the LORD saves his anointed; he will answer him from his holy heaven with the saving might of his right hand.7Some trust in chariots and some in horses, but we trust in the name of the LORD our God.8They collapse and fall, but we rise and stand upright.9O LORD, save the king! May he answer us when we call.
20.overview:
Where we are. Psalms 20 and 21 are a pair of royal psalms. In Psalm 20 the people pray for their king as he goes out to battle; in Psalm 21 they give thanks for the victory. After the king’s own song of rescue in Psalm 18, here is the congregation standing behind him.

The message. The safety of God’s people and their king does not rest on their weapons but on the name of the LORD. So they pray hard for the one who leads them, lean on the sacrifice already offered, and are sure that the LORD saves his anointed. Those who trust in chariots collapse; those who trust in the LORD rise and stand.

Why it was said. Israel’s kings went to war against neighbours with larger armies and chariot forces, while God’s law forbade the king to pile up horses (Deuteronomy 17:16). Before battle, sacrifice was offered at the sanctuary, and this psalm was probably sung there as the king set out (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. The congregation prays for the king: that the God of Jacob would answer and protect him, send help from Zion, remember his offerings and grant his plans, and that they may shout for joy and raise banners in God’s name (vv. 1–5). A single voice answers with certainty: the LORD saves his anointed and will answer him from heaven (v. 6). The people declare where their trust lies, in the name of the LORD and not in chariots and horses, and what follows: they fall, we rise (vv. 7–8). They end with one cry for the king and for themselves (v. 9).

Where it leads. By promise and pattern. Anointed is the word behind Messiah. The people prayed that their king would be saved in the day of trouble; the true Anointed prayed “to him who was able to save him from death, and he was heard” (Hebrews 5:7), not by being spared the cross but by being raised from it. He rode into Jerusalem not on a war horse but on a donkey (Zechariah 9:9), and now the psalm is reversed: the King intercedes for his people (Hebrews 7:25).

For us. Pray hard for those who lead, in the church and in the nation. Name honestly the chariots you lean on, and ask what would be left if they were gone. And when you are knocked down, remember that the promise is not that God’s people never fall but that they rise, because the King they trust went through the day of trouble for them.
20.theology:
God is called on as the God of Jacob (v. 1), and help is sought from the sanctuary on the ground of sacrifice already offered (vv. 2-3), not from the armoury.

Verse 7 is not a case against preparation; it asks what a nation finally leans on. The promised outcome is not that God's people are never knocked down but that they rise (v. 8). The prayer for the king widens into a prayer for everyone (v. 9), and the King it finally points to was not saved from the day of trouble but carried through it.
20.examples:
Before a reader looks for himself in this psalm, he sees a congregation praying hard for the one who carries the weight. Churches can still do that for those who lead them.

Verse 7 leaves a blank to fill in honestly: some trust in chariots, and some in savings, reputation or a second passport. What would be left if those were gone?

Hosanna means save us, we pray. The crowd shouted it at a King who would not save himself, because he had come to save them.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — May the LORD Answer You
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Before the king rides out, his people pray for him, and every line asks God to be his help. May the LORD answer him in the day of trouble, and the name of the God of Jacob, the God who carried an undeserving schemer, protect him (v. 1). May help come from the sanctuary on Zion rather than the armoury, because God remembers the offerings already made (vv. 2–3). May God grant his heart’s desire and his plans, and may the people soon shout for joy over his victory and raise their banners in God’s name, not the king’s (vv. 4–5). It is a picture of a congregation carrying its leader to God.
verseByVerse.theology: A whole people praying for one man, and asking for nothing but that God would act.

verseByVerse.quote: May the LORD answer you in the day of trouble! May the name of the God of Jacob protect you! May he send you help from the sanctuary and give you support from Zion! May he remember all your offerings and regard with favor your burnt sacrifices! Selah May he grant you your heart's desire and fulfill all your plans! May we shout for joy over your salvation, and in the name of our God set up our banners! May the LORD fulfill all your petitions!
verseByVerse.commentary:
The congregation prays for its king as he goes out to battle: that the God of Jacob would answer him, help him from Zion, accept his offerings and grant his plans.

May the LORD answer you in the day of trouble! The king is going out to war, and every line is addressed to him and every request made to God about him. Before you look for yourself in this psalm, see its shape: a people who have learned to pray hard for the one who carries the weight.

The name of the God of Jacob. God’s name is God himself as he has made himself known, the theme that returns in verse 7. And they call him by an old name. Not Abraham the friend of God, not Isaac the promised son, but Jacob, the schemer who got what he had no right to and was carried anyway. It is the name to use when asking for help you cannot claim to deserve.

Help from the sanctuary. The help is asked “from the sanctuary … from Zion”: from the altar, not the armoury. The king’s standing with God on the battlefield rests on what has already been offered at the temple. Leaders in Israel offered sacrifice before battle (1 Samuel 7:9; 13:9–12), and the congregation asks God to remember it and to regard with favor the burnt sacrifices, literally to accept them as rich, fat offerings (v. 3).

Fulfill all your plans! They are praying for a man they trust: they can ask God to fulfil his heart’s desire and his plans, which is not a thing to pray for just anyone. And they are already planning the celebration: banners up, in God’s name rather than the king’s.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–9 — We Trust in the Name of the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The mood turns from asking to certainty. One voice declares, “Now I know that the LORD saves his anointed,” and that he will answer from heaven with the strength of his right hand (v. 6). Then the people confess their trust: others lean on chariots and horses, but we trust in the name of the LORD our God (v. 7). The outcome is set out plainly: the self-reliant collapse and fall, while those who trust God rise and stand upright (v. 8). The psalm ends where it began, in prayer, asking the LORD to save the king and to answer all who call (v. 9).
verseByVerse.theology: The contrast is not between weapons and prayer. The question is what a nation finally leans on.

verseByVerse.quote: Now I know that the LORD saves his anointed; he will answer him from his holy heaven with the saving might of his right hand. Some trust in chariots and some in horses, but we trust in the name of the LORD our God. They collapse and fall, but we rise and stand upright.
verseByVerse.commentary:
