One voice answers with certainty that the LORD will save his anointed king, and the people declare that their trust is in the name of the LORD, not in chariots and horses, so that when others fall, they rise.

Now I know. The tone changes from asking to certainty. Something settled it between verse 5 and verse 6, a word from a priest or the assurance God gives a praying people. Many know it: you begin praying for someone in fear and finish in confidence, with nothing new to report except that God has been asked. Anointed is the Hebrew word behind Messiah, and Christ is its Greek equivalent.

He was heard. In Gethsemane the true Anointed prayed “to him who was able to save him from death, and he was heard” (Hebrews 5:7): not spared the cross, but raised from it.

Some trust in chariots. Chariots were the tanks of the ancient world, and Israel’s kings were told, “he must not acquire many horses for himself” (Deuteronomy 17:16). The command was not against being prepared; it guarded against a strong army becoming the thing its owners lean on. Proverbs puts the balance exactly: “The horse is made ready for the day of battle, but the victory belongs to the LORD” (Proverbs 21:31). Israel still saddled the horse.

What we rest on. So the psalm is not praising unpreparedness. It asks what a nation is finally resting on, and the test is what you would still have if the chariots were gone. Put in place of chariots whatever your generation counts on, savings, reputation or a second passport, and the psalm has done its work. And when we find we have leaned on the wrong thing, the name is still the LORD our God: he was their God before they trusted him well.

We rise and stand upright. Not “we never get knocked down”, but we get up: “the righteous falls seven times and rises again” (Proverbs 24:16).

verseByVerse.quote: O LORD, save the king! May he answer us when we call.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The people end with one cry for their king and for themselves, for the God who answers him answers them.

O LORD, save the king! The congregation’s last word is a nation’s whole request: save the king. Then the door swings open: may he answer us when we call. The psalm began with prayer for one man and ends with prayer for everybody, because the king’s cause and the people’s are the same cause.

He refused to save himself. Here the psalm quietly reaches past David. Israel’s anointed rode out with horses he was told not to trust; the King this psalm points to came into his capital “humble and mounted on a donkey”, and God promised with him, “I will cut off the chariot from Ephraim and the war horse from Jerusalem” (Zechariah 9:9–10). The crowd that shouted Hosanna, “Save us, we pray” (Psalm 118:25), watched him refuse to save himself. He was not rescued from the day of trouble. He went through it, which is how he saves the people who pray this psalm.

May Christians pray this psalm for their own rulers? They should pray for those in authority (1 Timothy 2:1–2), but no modern nation is Israel and no president or army is the LORD’s anointed. The church prays this psalm first for the cause of the King it points to, then for rulers to govern justly.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew of verse 9 can be divided two ways: “O LORD, save the king! May he answer us”, as in the ESV, or “O LORD, save! May the King answer us when we call”, where the King is God himself. Both readings end in the same confidence: the LORD, the true King, hears his people.

keyVerse.quote: Some trust in chariots and some in horses, but we trust in the name of the LORD our God.
keyVerse.note: This is the confession on which the whole psalm stands. The prayers of verses 1 to 5 and the certainty of verse 6 rest not on the king’s army but on the name of the LORD, and verse 8 shows where each kind of trust ends. Every generation has its chariots, and the verse asks what we would still be standing on if they were gone.

20.reflection:
The whole first half of the psalm is a people praying for their leader (vv. 1–5). Who carries weight on your behalf, in the church, at work or in the nation, and how might you pray for them more intentionally this week?

The people call on “the God of Jacob” (v. 1) and to remember the sacrifices already offered (v. 3). Why is it encouraging to come to God on the ground of what he has already done rather than what you deserve?

“Some trust in chariots and some in horses” (v. 7). What are the chariots and horses of your life, the things you instinctively lean on? How can you prepare wisely without trusting your preparations?

Jesus, the true Anointed, was not saved from the day of trouble but through it (Hebrews 5:7). How does that change the way you pray when you are in trouble yourself?

21.title: A Crown of Fine Gold
21.text: To the choirmaster. A Psalm of David. 1O LORD, in your strength the king rejoices, and in your salvation how greatly he exults!2You have given him his heart's desire and have not withheld the request of his lips. Selah3For you meet him with rich blessings; you set a crown of fine gold upon his head.4He asked life of you; you gave it to him, length of days forever and ever.5His glory is great through your salvation; splendor and majesty you bestow on him.6For you make him most blessed forever; you make him glad with the joy of your presence.7For the king trusts in the LORD, and through the steadfast love of the Most High he shall not be moved.8Your hand will find out all your enemies; your right hand will find out those who hate you.9You will make them as a blazing oven when you appear. The LORD will swallow them up in his wrath, and fire will consume them.10You will destroy their descendants from the earth, and their offspring from among the children of man.11Though they plan evil against you, though they devise mischief, they will not succeed.12For you will put them to flight; you will aim at their faces with your bows.13Be exalted, O LORD, in your strength! We will sing and praise your power.
21.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 21 is the answering half of Psalm 20. There the people prayed for their king as he went out to battle; here, with the battle won, they thank God for what he has done for him. It is one of the royal psalms, songs about Israel’s anointed king.

The message. Everything the king has is God’s gift, and the best gift of all is God himself: “you make him glad with the joy of your presence” (v. 6). The king stands because he trusts in the LORD and is held by his steadfast love, and every enemy of God and his anointed will be found out and fail. So the last word of praise belongs not to the king but to the LORD whose strength won.

Why it was said. Israel’s king was God’s anointed, and the nation’s safety was bound up with him (see the introduction). Victory tempted king and people alike to boast in the man. This song, headed “A Psalm of David”, taught them to rejoice in God’s strength and to trust God, not the king, for the king’s future.

How the chapter makes its case. The king rejoices in God’s strength and salvation, because God has granted his heart’s desire, crowned him and given him life (vv. 1–4). God clothes him with splendour and gladdens him with his presence, and the king stands firm because he trusts (vv. 5–7). Then the people look ahead: God’s hand will find out every enemy, and their plots will fail (vv. 8–12). Last, they exalt the LORD himself (v. 13), and the word “strength” frames the whole psalm.

Where it leads. By promise and by pattern. “Length of days forever and ever” (v. 4) is more than David or any of his sons received. It rests on God’s covenant that David’s throne would be established for ever (2 Samuel 7:16), and it comes true only in the risen Jesus, “crowned with glory and honor because of the suffering of death” (Hebrews 2:9). His first crown was made of thorns. He is the King who trusted his Father perfectly, and the fire of verses 8–12 belongs to his appearing.

For us. Answered prayer should end where this psalm ends, in praise of God’s strength rather than our success. Test your desires by verse 6: is God’s company the gift you want most? And when evil seems to be winning, remember that it will not succeed, because the King has already been crowned.
21.theology:
Psalms 20 and 21 belong together: the request of 20:4 is answered in 21:2. Everything the king has is God's gift, the best of it is God's own company (v. 6), and the reason for it all is trust, not competence (v. 7).

The judgment in verses 8-12 belongs to God, whose search does not fail. Christians read it through the cross and through Jesus' command to love enemies, which does not soften the judgment but insists that it is God's, not ours. And length of days forever and ever (v. 4) is more than any king of Israel received; it waits for the King whose crown was first made of thorns.
21.examples:
Psalm 20 asked for the king's heart's desire, and Psalm 21 says he got it. Even so, his joy is aimed at the strength that won rather than at the win.

God comes out to meet him like a host, crowns him with his own hands, and lends him his own splendour and majesty. A song that celebrates a leader as warmly as this still ends by looking away from him to God.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — You Have Given Him His Heart's Desire
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Everything the king has, he was given, and the best of it is God himself. The psalm begins where Psalm 20 left off: the prayer for the king’s heart’s desire has been answered, and he rejoices in God’s strength and salvation rather than his own (vv. 1–2). God has met him with rich blessings, set a crown on his head and given him life beyond measure (vv. 3–4). He has clothed him with splendour and majesty and, best of all, made him glad with the joy of his presence (vv. 5–6). Verse 7 gives the reason for it all: the king trusts in the LORD, and the steadfast love of the Most High holds him.
verseByVerse.theology: Everything the king has, he was given, and the best of it is not the crown but God's own company.

verseByVerse.quote: O LORD, in your strength the king rejoices, and in your salvation how greatly he exults! You have given him his heart's desire and have not withheld the request of his lips. Selah For you meet him with rich blessings; you set a crown of fine gold upon his head. He asked life of you; you gave it to him, length of days forever and ever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God has answered the prayer of Psalm 20, and the king rejoices, not in his victory, but in the strength of the LORD who gave it.

You have given him his heart’s desire. Read straight after Psalm 20, this is the answer arriving: “May he grant you your heart’s desire” (20:4) has become “You have given him his heart’s desire.”

In your strength the king rejoices. The joy is aimed carefully: not “in his victory”, but in your strength, in your salvation. Knowing whose the win was is a harder discipline after a success than before one, and it is the difference between a thanksgiving and a boast.

Length of days forever and ever. God “meets” him like a host greeting a guest, and crowns him with his own hands. Then comes a line too large for David: he asked for life and was given “length of days forever and ever”. David died. Israel sang words about her king, resting on God’s promise of a throne “established forever” (2 Samuel 7:16), that would come true only of the risen Jesus.

verseByVerse.quote: His glory is great through your salvation; splendor and majesty you bestow on him. For you make him most blessed forever; you make him glad with the joy of your presence. For the king trusts in the LORD, and through the steadfast love of the Most High he shall not be moved.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God dresses the king in his own splendour, yet the king’s deepest gladness is God’s presence, and what holds him steady is not his own grip but God’s steadfast love.

Splendor and majesty you bestow on him. These are words the Psalter usually gives to God himself (Psalms 96:6; 104:1). Here he lends them to a man: dressing his servant from his own wardrobe.

The joy of your presence. The best line of the psalm is tucked in among the gifts. He has a crown, glory, splendour and long life, yet his gladness comes from God’s face. Take the rest away and that joy remains; give him the rest without it and he has everything and is miserable. Of everything you hope God will give you, how far down the list is his company?

For the king trusts in the LORD. The reason for it all is not the king’s competence: what holds him is “the steadfast love of the Most High”, not his own grip. Jesus is the King who trusted his Father all the way to the cross (Hebrews 2:13), and his people stand by the same love.

Uncertain wording. Verse 6 is literally you set him blessings for ever. It may mean richly blessed, as the ESV text has it, or, as its note allows, a source of blessing, echoing the promise to Abraham: “so that you will be a blessing” (Genesis 12:2). Both are true of the king, and above all of Christ.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The king’s future is as secure as his present, because his enemies are God’s enemies. The people turn from thanks to confidence: God’s hand will find out all who hate him, his fire will consume them when he appears, and their line will be cut off (vv. 8–10). They plan evil, but they will not succeed; they will turn and run (vv. 11–12). Then the psalm that has celebrated a king gives its last word to God: “Be exalted, O LORD, in your strength!” (v. 13). The judgment belongs to God, not to us, and so does the praise.
verseByVerse.theology: The psalm of the king's success ends by taking the congregation's eyes off the king.

verseByVerse.quote: Your hand will find out all your enemies; your right hand will find out those who hate you. You will make them as a blazing oven when you appear. The LORD will swallow them up in his wrath, and fire will consume them. You will destroy their descendants from the earth, and their offspring from among the children of man. Though they plan evil against you, though they devise mischief, they will not succeed. For you will put them to flight; you will aim at their faces with your bows.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No enemy of God and his king can hide or succeed: God’s hand will find them all out, and the fire of his judgment will end every plot against him.

Your hand will find out all your enemies. Find out pictures a search that does not fail: no hiding place holds. The oven and the fire reach beyond any border skirmish towards the final judgment (compare 2 Thessalonians 1:7–8).

You will destroy their descendants from the earth. The hardest line, verse 10, is a sentence on a dynasty rather than a man: the ending of a house that lives by evil, spoken of people who plan evil and devise mischief as a policy. The psalm does not gloat; it states that such plotting “will not succeed”, something to hold on to when you are on the receiving end of it and, for now, it seems to be succeeding.

In the light of the cross. Christians pray these verses in the light of the cross, where the plot against God’s King did succeed for one Friday and was then overturned, and with Jesus’ own command to love enemies and leave judgment to God. That is not a softening of the psalm. It insists that the fire in it belongs to God and not to us.

Uncertain wording. The psalm does not say who “you” is in these verses: the king, whose hand acts for God’s (verse 9 speaks of the LORD in the third person), or God himself, which suits the fire. It seems content to let the two blur, because the king’s war was God’s war.

verseByVerse.quote: Be exalted, O LORD, in your strength! We will sing and praise your power.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The congregation turns its eyes off the king it has celebrated and exalts the LORD, whose strength won everything.

Be exalted, O LORD, in your strength! After twelve verses on the king, the last goes to God: Be exalted, not “long live the king”, with the strength of verse 1 framing the whole psalm. Any song about a leader that cannot end like this has become worship of the man.

The crown has not finished its journey. The New Testament says of Jesus that he was “crowned with glory and honor because of the suffering of death” (Hebrews 2:9), and that the rider on the white horse wears “many diadems” (Revelation 19:12). But before either, soldiers “twisted together a crown of thorns and put it on his head” (John 19:2). The king of Psalm 21 asked life and was given length of days for ever; the King this psalm was waiting for was given death first, and rose to hold the promise for everyone who trusts him.

keyVerse.quote: For the king trusts in the LORD, and through the steadfast love of the Most High he shall not be moved.
keyVerse.note: This verse is the hinge of the psalm. It gives the reason for every gift in verses 1–6, and it is the ground of the confidence in verses 8–12: the king stands not by his strength but by trust in God and God’s steadfast love. Jesus is the King who trusted perfectly, and all who trust him are held by the same love.

21.reflection:
The king rejoices “in your strength” and “in your salvation”, not in his own victory (v. 1). Why is it harder to give God the credit after a success than to ask for his help before one? Think of a recent answer to prayer: how did you respond?

Of all the king’s gifts, the psalm puts “the joy of your presence” at the top (v. 6). If God gave you everything else you are hoping for but not his company, would you notice? What does your answer show about your heart?

Verses 8–12 speak of God’s fire against his enemies. How does the cross, and Jesus’ command to love our enemies, shape the way a Christian prays these verses without softening them?

The crown of verse 3 reaches its fulfilment in Jesus, who wore thorns before he wore glory (Hebrews 2:9). How does it help you to know that your King went through suffering to his crown?

22.title: Why Have You Forsaken Me?
22.text: To the choirmaster: according to The Doe of the Dawn. A Psalm of David. 1My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? Why are you so far from saving me, from the words of my groaning?2O my God, I cry by day, but you do not answer, and by night, but I find no rest.3Yet you are holy, enthroned on the praises of Israel.4In you our fathers trusted; they trusted, and you delivered them.5To you they cried and were rescued; in you they trusted and were not put to shame.6But I am a worm and not a man, scorned by mankind and despised by the people.7All who see me mock me; they make mouths at me; they wag their heads;8"He trusts in the LORD; let him deliver him; let him rescue him, for he delights in him!"9Yet you are he who took me from the womb; you made me trust you at my mother's breasts.10On you was I cast from my birth, and from my mother's womb you have been my God.11Be not far from me, for trouble is near, and there is none to help.12Many bulls encompass me; strong bulls of Bashan surround me;13they open wide their mouths at me, like a ravening and roaring lion.14I am poured out like water, and all my bones are out of joint; my heart is like wax; it is melted within my breast;15my strength is dried up like a potsherd, and my tongue sticks to my jaws; you lay me in the dust of death.16For dogs encompass me; a company of evildoers encircles me; they have pierced my hands and feet —17I can count all my bones— they stare and gloat over me;18they divide my garments among them, and for my clothing they cast lots.19But you, O LORD, do not be far off! O you my help, come quickly to my aid!20Deliver my soul from the sword, my precious life from the power of the dog!21Save me from the mouth of the lion! You have rescued me from the horns of the wild oxen!22I will tell of your name to my brothers; in the midst of the congregation I will praise you:23You who fear the LORD, praise him! All you offspring of Jacob, glorify him, and stand in awe of him, all you offspring of Israel!24For he has not despised or abhorred the affliction of the afflicted, and he has not hidden his face from him, but has heard, when he cried to him.25From you comes my praise in the great congregation; my vows I will perform before those who fear him.26The afflicted shall eat and be satisfied; those who seek him shall praise the LORD! May your hearts live forever!27All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the LORD, and all the families of the nations shall worship before you.28For kingship belongs to the LORD, and he rules over the nations.29All the prosperous of the earth eat and worship; before him shall bow all who go down to the dust, even the one who could not keep himself alive.30Posterity shall serve him; it shall be told of the Lord to the coming generation;31they shall come and proclaim his righteousness to a people yet unborn, that he has done it.
22.overview:
Where we are. Two psalms celebrating the king’s victory (Psalms 20–21) are followed by the king’s darkest hour. Psalm 22 is the psalm the Gospels hear most clearly at the crucifixion, and its first line is the cry of Jesus from the cross. Psalm 23 follows it.

The message. God’s anointed sufferer is forsaken, mocked, pierced and brought to the dust of death, yet he keeps calling God “my God”, and God hears him. His rescue is not a private relief but news that sends the whole world to worship: the afflicted eat, the nations turn to the LORD, and people not yet born are told “that he has done it” (v. 31).

Why it was said. The heading gives the psalm to David but names no occasion. Israel sang it as the cry of God’s afflicted king (see the introduction), and in singing it learned that complaint can be made in faith and that God does not despise the afflicted. Yet its language reaches far beyond any one man’s trouble.

How the chapter makes its case. The cry of forsakenness is met by God’s holiness and the fathers’ rescue (vv. 1–5); mocked as a worm, the sufferer remembers the God who has held him from the womb (vv. 6–11). Then enemies close in like beasts, his body fails, his hands and feet are pierced and his clothes are gambled for (vv. 12–18). He pleads once more, and in the middle of the sentence the answer comes (vv. 19–21). The rest is praise, first in the congregation (vv. 22–26), then to the ends of the earth and to generations not yet born (vv. 27–31).

Where it leads. By direct prophecy, as the New Testament reads it, carried in the pattern of David’s sufferings. Jesus prayed verse 1 on the cross (Matthew 27:46); the mockers quoted verse 8 (Matthew 27:43); soldiers did what verse 18 describes (John 19:24); Hebrews hears the risen Christ singing verse 22 among his brothers (Hebrews 2:11–12). David suffered, but no one except Jesus went down into the dust of death and rose so that the nations turned to God. The psalm’s last word, “he has done it”, answers to the last word from the cross in John: “It is finished” (John 19:30).

For us. In the dark, keep praying to “my God”: the Son prayed this psalm before you, and was forsaken so that those who trust him never will be. God does not find your affliction distasteful. And when the answer comes, join Christ’s song, and tell the next generation what he has done.
22.theology:
The loudest complaint in Scripture is made inside faith, and the psalm twice answers itself with yet: God is holy and the fathers were rescued (vv. 3-5), and God has held this man since birth (vv. 9-10).

The New Testament reads the psalm as written about Christ, and the details are not vague: the cry (Matt 27:46), the taunts (Matt 27:39-43), the thirst (John 19:28) and the gambling for his clothes (John 19:24). The case does not rest on the disputed line in verse 16. The rescue comes without explanation (v. 21), and the suffering bears fruit far beyond one man: the risen sufferer leads the church's praise (v. 22; Heb 2:11-12), the nations turn to the LORD, and a finished work is proclaimed to people not yet born (vv. 27-31).
22.examples:
When Jesus took the first line of this psalm on his lips at the cross, he had all of it in mind, from the forsakenness to the praise.

The mockers at Golgotha quoted verse 8 without knowing that they were speaking lines written for them, and soldiers threw dice for his clothes as verse 18 had described.

The psalm ends with he has done it, and the last word from the cross in John's Gospel is It is finished.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Faith argues with God out of the dark, and keeps calling him “my God”. The sufferer cries that God has forsaken him and does not answer, by day or by night (vv. 1–2), yet he holds on to God’s holiness and to the record of the fathers, who trusted and were rescued (vv. 3–5). Scorned as a worm, he hears the crowd throw his own faith at him (vv. 6–8), yet he remembers the God who has held him since he was born (vv. 9–10), and pleads with him not to stay far away when trouble is near (v. 11). Jesus made the first line his own on the cross, and the mockers at Golgotha spoke the eighth.
verseByVerse.theology: Faith argues with God out of the dark: the fathers were heard, I was made yours from birth, and yet here I am.

verseByVerse.quote: My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? Why are you so far from saving me, from the words of my groaning? O my God, I cry by day, but you do not answer, and by night, but I find no rest. Yet you are holy, enthroned on the praises of Israel. In you our fathers trusted; they trusted, and you delivered them. To you they cried and were rescued; in you they trusted and were not put to shame.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the darkest cry in Scripture the sufferer still says “my God”, holding on to God’s holiness and past rescues while heaven is silent; Jesus took these words as his own on the cross.

My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? Not simply “God”, but my God, twice: the relationship is appealed to at the very moment it seems to have failed. This is the loudest complaint in the Bible, and it is made inside faith, not outside it.

I cry by day, but you do not answer. By day, no answer; by night, no rest: the prayer has gone round the clock and met only silence.

Yet you are holy. The first yet. He does not explain how God can be silent and still be holy; he holds on to both. Then the history: three times in two verses, they trusted, and every time it worked. That makes his position worse: the fathers cried and were rescued; I cry and am not. Faith that knows the track record feels the silence more sharply, not less.

For the first readers. The heading gives the psalm to David but names no occasion, and nothing in David’s recorded life matches it closely; the years Saul hunted him come nearest. Israel sang it as the cry of God’s afflicted king, forsaken and then rescued. Yet its language outruns any one man’s trouble: no ordinary rescue brings the ends of the earth to worship (v. 27), and that overflow is part of why the apostles read it of David’s greater Son.

Words from the cross. These are the words Jesus said from the cross, in his own language, at about three in the afternoon (Matthew 27:46; Mark 15:34). He did not compose them; he reached for this psalm, which means the whole of it was in his mind while he hung there. That day darkness covered the land from noon until three, and the day itself turned to night. Read every verse that follows knowing whose lips they reached.

Why trust a God who stays out of the pain? The strongest modern objection to faith is usually not an argument but a hospital ward, a war, a child’s grave: if God is there, why does he keep his distance? The fuller answer belongs to Job (see the note on Job 1:20–22), but this psalm adds something no philosopher proposed. On the cross God does not explain suffering from a safe height; in his Son he goes into it, and prays its worst line himself. John Stott wrote in The Cross of Christ that he could never himself believe in God if it were not for the cross, because in a world of pain he could not worship a God who was immune to it. That does not answer every question, but it changes who is asking it with us. Whoever prays this psalm in the dark is not shouting at an empty sky but joining a prayer the Son prayed first, and the Father answered on the third day.

Where Christians differ: did the Father really forsake the Son? Some say Jesus only felt abandoned, as any sufferer may. This commentary’s view: the forsakenness was real. On the cross God “made him to be sin” for us (2 Corinthians 5:21), and Christ became “a curse for us” (Galatians 3:13); the darkness was God’s judgment. He bore the Father’s just wrath against sin in our place, and the fellowship he had always known was withdrawn. The Trinity was not broken: the Son still says “My God”, and the Father’s love never stopped. But the forsakenness was real, so that those who trust him never will be.

Uncertain wording. The heading’s The Doe of the Dawn is probably the name of a tune; what it refers to is unknown. In verse 3 the ESV notes that “enthroned on the praises of Israel” may be read dwelling in the praises, God at home among his people’s worship.
verseByVerse.note: Matthew and Mark give the cry in Aramaic, the everyday language of Jesus' home, and then translate it.

verseByVerse.quote: But I am a worm and not a man, scorned by mankind and despised by the people. All who see me mock me; they make mouths at me; they wag their heads; "He trusts in the LORD; let him deliver him; let him rescue him, for he delights in him!" Yet you are he who took me from the womb; you made me trust you at my mother's breasts. On you was I cast from my birth, and from my mother's womb you have been my God. Be not far from me, for trouble is near, and there is none to help.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Scorned and mocked for trusting God, the sufferer looks back to the God who has held him since birth, and begs him not to stay far away.

But I am a worm and not a man. Something you step on without noticing. That is how he describes himself, and the crowd confirms it: pulling faces, wagging their heads, and then the cruellest stroke of all, throwing his own faith at him as a joke.

Yet you are he who took me from the womb. The second yet, and it reaches back further than the fathers, to his own first minutes. The God who seems absent now acted as midwife and taught a baby to trust before it could speak. When a believer cannot see God today, this is where to look: not at the present evidence but at who has been holding him since before he can remember.

Be not far from me. This is the whole prayer in one line: trouble near, God far, nobody in between.

They wag their heads. Stand at Golgotha and listen: “those who passed by derided him, wagging their heads … He trusts in God; let God deliver him now, if he desires him” (Matthew 27:39, 43). The mockery at the cross did not merely resemble this psalm; it quoted it, from people who did not know they were reading their lines. The leaders thought they were scoring a point from Scripture; they were showing that the psalm was about him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–21 — They Have Pierced My Hands and Feet
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The sufferer goes all the way down, and God answers him there. Enemies close in like bulls, lions and dogs, and his body fails: poured out, out of joint, dried up, laid in the dust of death (vv. 12–15). They pierce his hands and feet, stare at him, and divide his clothes by lot (vv. 16–18). He makes one last plea, “do not be far off!”, and in the middle of the sentence the plea becomes thanks: “You have rescued me” (vv. 19–21). The Gospels watched these verses happen at the cross, down to the soldiers’ dice.
verseByVerse.theology: The suffering is described from inside, and the answer arrives in the middle of a sentence.

verseByVerse.quote: Many bulls encompass me; strong bulls of Bashan surround me; they open wide their mouths at me, like a ravening and roaring lion. I am poured out like water, and all my bones are out of joint; my heart is like wax; it is melted within my breast; my strength is dried up like a potsherd, and my tongue sticks to my jaws; you lay me in the dust of death. For dogs encompass me; a company of evildoers encircles me; they have pierced my hands and feet — I can count all my bones— they stare and gloat over me; they divide my garments among them, and for my clothing they cast lots.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ringed by enemies like wild beasts and wasting away, the sufferer is pierced and stripped while men gloat and gamble for his clothes, as the Gospels saw at the cross.

Strong bulls of Bashan. The enemies come as animals, and the choice of animal is precise. Bashan, east of the Jordan, was famous cattle country: prize beasts, heavy and well fed, like powerful men enjoying themselves at someone else’s expense.

I am poured out like water. Now the body, from inside: poured out and shapeless; joints pulled apart; the heart gone to wax; strength baked dry like a piece of broken pottery; the tongue stuck to the roof of the mouth. Anyone who has read how crucifixion kills will recognise the list, written centuries before Israel had seen a crucifixion. At the cross, John says, “Jesus, knowing that all was now finished, said (to fulfill the Scripture), ‘I thirst’” (John 19:28). And notice who lays him in the dust: you lay me in the dust of death. Behind the enemies stands the will of God, as Isaiah says of the Servant: “it was the will of the LORD to crush him” (Isaiah 53:10).

I can count all my bones. Verse 17 holds two horrors in one line. He is so wasted that the ribs stand out and could be counted, and there is an audience doing the counting. The psalm records not only pain but the humiliation of being looked at in pain.

They divide my garments among them. Verse 18 needs no textual defence at all. John watched soldiers do exactly that, split the clothes four ways and gamble for the seamless tunic, and wrote: “This was to fulfill the Scripture” (John 19:24). A thousand years early, a dying man described soldiers throwing dice for his shirt.

How Jewish readers take it. Jewish Bibles follow the standard Hebrew text, like a lion (see the textual note), reading the psalm as the cry of David hunted by his enemies or, with Rashi, of Israel in exile, surrounded by the nations. The Talmud puts its opening words on the lips of Queen Esther as she went in to the king (Megillah 15b), and some later rabbinic homilies borrow its language for the sufferings of the Messiah. Both traditions hear in it a righteous sufferer whom God rescues. This commentary reads it of Christ because he made its first line his own on the cross (Matthew 27:46), and John saw verse 18 happen at Calvary (John 19:24).

Textual note. Verse 16 has a textual question, and it should be stated plainly rather than smoothed over. The ESV notes that “they have pierced my hands and feet” follows some Hebrew manuscripts together with the ancient Greek, Latin and Syriac versions, while most Hebrew manuscripts read something like like a lion, my hands and feet. The reading the ESV prints is old and well attested (the Greek translation was made long before the crucifixion), but a Christian does not need to win the argument to preach the psalm. Even on the other reading, the hands and feet are the point, where the nails went (John 20:25), and the next lines stand on their own.
verseByVerse.note: Dogs (v. 16) was a common insult for outsiders and the lawless; Paul turns it on false teachers (Phil 3:2).

verseByVerse.quote: But you, O LORD, do not be far off! O you my help, come quickly to my aid! Deliver my soul from the sword, my precious life from the power of the dog! Save me from the mouth of the lion! You have rescued me from the horns of the wild oxen!
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sufferer pleads once more, and in the middle of the sentence the plea turns to thanks: God has answered.

But you, O LORD, do not be far off! For the third time he turns from his trouble to God (Yet you in verses 3 and 9, now But you). He is still asking, sword, dog, lion, and then, in the middle of the last sentence, the asking stops: “Save me from the mouth of the lion! You have rescued me.” The ESV notes the Hebrew is literally you have answered me.

You have rescued me from the horns of the wild oxen! The answer arrives inside the sentence. Nothing is narrated: no rescue is described, no enemy is driven off. One moment he is begging and the next he is thanking, and everything after verse 21 is praise. Any believer who has prayed through a long night knows the change can come like that: mid-sentence, with nothing to point to. Jesus too offered “loud cries and tears, to him who was able to save him from death, and he was heard” (Hebrews 5:7); the answer came on the third day.

For anyone praying in the dark. Because Jesus prayed this psalm first, no believer prays verse 1 alone or unheard. He went into real forsakenness, not only the feeling of it, so that the promise to everyone who is his can be “I will never leave you nor forsake you” (Hebrews 13:5). You may feel abandoned; the truth is that he was abandoned in your place.
verseByVerse.note: From here to the end the psalm asks for nothing more. Everything is thanks.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–31 — They Shall Proclaim His Righteousness
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: One man’s rescue becomes the whole world’s worship. The rescued sufferer praises God among his brothers and calls Israel to join him, for God has not despised the afflicted or hidden his face (vv. 22–24). He keeps his vows at a meal where the afflicted eat and are satisfied (vv. 25–26). Then the praise spreads: the ends of the earth turn to the LORD, rich and dying alike bow before him, and the story is told to people yet unborn, “that he has done it” (vv. 27–31). Hebrews hears the risen Christ leading this song, and “It is finished” is its echo from the cross.
verseByVerse.theology: The psalm turns from one man's agony to the whole world's worship, and ends on a finished work.

verseByVerse.quote: I will tell of your name to my brothers; in the midst of the congregation I will praise you: You who fear the LORD, praise him! All you offspring of Jacob, glorify him, and stand in awe of him, all you offspring of Israel! For he has not despised or abhorred the affliction of the afflicted, and he has not hidden his face from him, but has heard, when he cried to him. From you comes my praise in the great congregation; my vows I will perform before those who fear him. The afflicted shall eat and be satisfied; those who seek him shall praise the LORD! May your hearts live forever!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Rescued, the sufferer gathers God’s people to praise the God who has not despised the afflicted, and invites the poor to his thanksgiving meal.

I will tell of your name to my brothers. The first thing the rescued man does is gather a congregation.

He has not hidden his face from him. Here is the psalm’s verdict on its own first line. It began, “why have you forsaken me?”; now God “has not hidden his face”. The second does not cancel the first; it interprets it. What felt like abandonment was not contempt, and the cry that seemed to go nowhere had been heard the whole time.

He has not despised or abhorred the affliction of the afflicted. Take verse 24 slowly if you have ever suspected that God finds your trouble distasteful. Three negatives: he has not despised it, not abhorred it, not hidden his face from it. God is not embarrassed by the afflicted and does not look away. And the positive at the end is the whole of it: “but has heard, when he cried to him.”

My vows I will perform. “The afflicted shall eat and be satisfied” (the ESV notes the word may be the meek), and his vows are paid in public, which in Israel meant a thank offering shared as a meal with the poor. The man who was starving in verse 15 is hosting dinner.

The risen Christ leads the singing. Hebrews puts verse 22 in the mouth of Jesus, as proof that he is not ashamed of us: “he is not ashamed to call them brothers, saying, ‘I will tell of your name to my brothers; in the midst of the congregation I will sing your praise’” (Hebrews 2:11–12). On the morning he rose, his first message to the disciples used that very word: “go to my brothers” (John 20:17). The one who went through verses 1–18 stands in the middle of the church and leads the singing, as the risen Christ does in every gathering of his people.

verseByVerse.quote: All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the LORD, and all the families of the nations shall worship before you. For kingship belongs to the LORD, and he rules over the nations. All the prosperous of the earth eat and worship; before him shall bow all who go down to the dust, even the one who could not keep himself alive. Posterity shall serve him; it shall be told of the Lord to the coming generation; they shall come and proclaim his righteousness to a people yet unborn, that he has done it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This one sufferer’s rescue brings the whole world to worship, and people not yet born are told that he has done it.

All the ends of the earth shall remember. The psalm now goes as wide as the world. One man’s agony becomes the reason the nations come home to God. No ordinary sufferer’s pain could do that; the cross did. The ends of the earth remember: they had known once and forgotten. And verse 28 gives the reason: the suffering has served the reign of the LORD.

Even the one who could not keep himself alive. Three groups, and between them nobody is left out: the prosperous, the dying, and the not yet born. The one who could not keep himself alive is every human being in the end, and even he bows. In this psalm that bowing is not defeat but worship, because the singer himself has been down to the dust of death (v. 15) and is standing here alive.

He has done it. The psalm ends, “he has done it”: not “he will”, not he is working on it, but a thing completed. A man who began by asking why God had abandoned him signs off announcing that the work is complete, news to be carried to people not yet born, which includes everyone reading this.

It is finished. On the cross, at the end, Jesus “said, ‘It is finished,’ and he bowed his head and gave up his spirit” (John 19:30). He had begun with the psalm’s first line. He ended where the psalm ends.

Uncertain wording. Verse 29 is among the hardest lines of the psalm. “The prosperous” is literally the fat ones of the earth, and the Hebrew is so compressed that translations differ over whether it pictures the living, the dead, or both bowing; the last clause is also obscure. The sense is clear: no one, from the richest to the dying, stands outside this worship. In verse 31, “he has done it” is a single verb with no object: he has acted.

keyVerse.quote: My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? Why are you so far from saving me, from the words of my groaning?
keyVerse.note: Jesus took this line on his lips at the cross (Matthew 27:46), and with it the whole psalm, from forsakenness to praise. Even here the sufferer says “my God”: the cry is made inside faith. The rest of the psalm answers it, for God “has not hidden his face from him, but has heard” (v. 24), and because the Son was forsaken in our place, those who trust him never will be.

22.reflection:
The sufferer cries “why have you forsaken me?” and in the same breath calls God “my God” (v. 1). What does this teach you about bringing your honest complaints to God? How is a complaint made in faith different from one made against him?

Twice he answers his darkness with “yet”: God is holy and rescued the fathers (vv. 3–5), and God has held him since birth (vv. 9–10). When you cannot see God at work today, what parts of his record, in Scripture and in your own life, can you look back to?

Jesus prayed this psalm on the cross, and the Gospels saw its details fulfilled there (Matthew 27:39–46; John 19:24). How does it change your view of suffering to know that the Son of God went into it and was really forsaken in your place?

The psalm ends with the nations turning to God and people yet unborn hearing “that he has done it” (vv. 27–31). Who in the “coming generation” around you needs to hear what God has done, and how could you tell them?

23.title: The LORD Is My Shepherd
23.text: A Psalm of David. 1The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want.2He makes me lie down in green pastures. He leads me beside still waters.3He restores my soul. He leads me in paths of righteousness for his name's sake.4Even though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, for you are with me; your rod and your staff, they comfort me.5You prepare a table before me in the presence of my enemies; you anoint my head with oil; my cup overflows.6Surely goodness and mercy shall follow me all the days of my life, and I shall dwell in the house of the LORD forever.
23.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 23 comes straight after the agony and rescue of Psalm 22 and just before the King of glory enters his city in Psalm 24. Read together, the three move from the sufferer, to the shepherd who cares for his flock, to the King who comes in. It is the best loved psalm in the book, and one of the shortest.

The message. The LORD himself cares for his people as a shepherd cares for his flock and a host for his guest. So they lack nothing they truly need, they need fear nothing in the darkest valley because he is with them, and his goodness and steadfast love will pursue them all their lives until they are home with him for ever.

Why it was said. David had been a shepherd before he was a king, and as king he was often hunted (see the introduction). In the ancient world kings were called the shepherds of their people, and Israel’s shepherds often failed them (Ezekiel 34:1–10). This psalm taught every Israelite, king and commoner, that the LORD is the shepherd who does not fail.

How the chapter makes its case. The shepherd provides rest and water, brings back the wandering and the weary, and leads his sheep on right paths for his name’s sake (vv. 1–3). The path runs into the valley of deep darkness, and there the psalm turns from speaking about God to speaking to him: “you are with me” (v. 4). Then the field becomes a house: a table spread before the enemies, a cup running over, goodness and mercy in pursuit, and a home in the house of the LORD (vv. 5–6).

Where it leads. By promise, and by the character of God revealed in Christ. Through Ezekiel God promised, “I myself will be the shepherd of my sheep” (Ezekiel 34:15), and Jesus said, “I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep” (John 10:11). Placed after Psalm 22, this psalm’s pastures lie on the far side of a death already died for the flock, and at the end of the Bible “the Lamb in the midst of the throne will be their shepherd” (Revelation 7:17).

For us. If Christ is your shepherd, you may say “I shall not want” even when you lack much that you would like. Receive rest as his gift rather than earning it. In the valley, speak to him, for he is with you. And face death as a sheep going home, not into the dark.
23.theology: I shall not want promises what the sheep needs, not all it wants (v. 1), and the sheep’s safe arrival rests on the shepherd's name, not its own worth (v. 3). The psalm is placed straight after Psalm 22, where a sufferer goes down to death. So its pastures lie on the far side of a death already suffered for the sheep (see on vv. 5-6). The shepherd is the one who lays down his life for the sheep (John 10:11; cf. Ezek 34:11-12; Isa 40:11), and at the last the Lamb is the shepherd (Rev 7:17).
23.examples: Sheep shy away from a fast stream, so a good shepherd leads them to quiet water: he knows what they need better than they do. And many believers have found that the valley is where they first learned to speak to God rather than about him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — Even Though I Walk Through the Valley
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The LORD himself is his people’s shepherd, so they have everything they need, even in the dark. David, who had kept sheep, says that with this shepherd he will lack nothing (v. 1). The shepherd makes his flock lie down in green pasture and leads it beside quiet water; he brings back the wanderer and revives the weary, and he leads them on right paths, because his own name is at stake (vv. 2–3). Then the path runs into the valley of deep darkness, and the psalm turns from speaking about God to speaking to him: “for you are with me” (v. 4). The rod and staff that guard and rescue are a comfort, not a threat.
verseByVerse.theology: In the valley, talk about God becomes talk to him.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want. He makes me lie down in green pastures. He leads me beside still waters. He restores my soul. He leads me in paths of righteousness for his name's sake.
verseByVerse.commentary:
With the LORD himself as his shepherd, David will lack nothing he needs: rest, restoring, and right paths, for the sake of God’s own name.

The LORD is my shepherd. It may be the best known sentence in the Old Testament, written by a man who had done the job. David knew a shepherd’s day: the walking, the counting, the carrying, the nights out with the flock. He also knew that sheep are not gentle and wise but nervous, short-sighted animals that will walk off a ledge or into water they cannot get out of.

I shall not want. This does not mean he gets everything he wants. It means he will not lack what he needs, which is a different promise and a better one.

He makes me lie down in green pastures. Sheep do not lie down while they are frightened or hungry, so a flock lying down shows how well its shepherd has cared for it. And there is a quiet mercy in the verb: some of us rest only when we are made to. The shepherd knows when the flock has been driven long enough, and stops it, and that stopping is care, not waste.

The world of total work. Modern people are oddly proud of being busy; we answer “How are you?” with “Flat out,” half as a boast. The German philosopher Josef Pieper, writing just after the Second World War in Leisure: The Basis of Culture, warned of a world of “total work”, where people are valued only for what they produce and even rest is just recovery for more output. Underneath lies an old fear: if I stop, I will be found out as worth nothing. The shepherd’s verb answers that fear. Rest here is not a reward for productivity but something received from another, which is exactly why driven people find it hard; Pieper saw that true leisure is the capacity to receive. The gospel is the deepest form of that: “Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28). A sheep does not earn the pasture. It lies down in it.

He restores my soul. The verb means to bring back: the shepherd goes after the sheep that has wandered and carries it home, and he revives the one that is spent. It covers the believer who has drifted and the one simply worn out, and neither finds the way back alone.

Paths of righteousness for his name’s sake. The ESV notes that paths of righteousness can be read right paths, the tracks that actually get somewhere, rather than the ones the sheep would choose. And the reason given is not the sheep’s value but “for his name’s sake”. A shepherd who lost half his flock would be shamed in the village; God’s reputation is bound up with getting his people home, the strongest guarantee anyone could be given.

I myself will be the shepherd. God promised to do this in person: “I myself will be the shepherd of my sheep, and I myself will make them lie down” (Ezekiel 34:15). Jesus claimed that role (see the note on vv. 5–6).
verseByVerse.note: “Still waters” is literally “waters of rest” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: Even though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, for you are with me; your rod and your staff, they comfort me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the darkest valley the believer need not fear, because the shepherd is with him; here the psalm stops speaking about God and speaks to him.

Even though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death. He walks through: not camping, not settling. The valley covers more than dying: depression, disgrace, a diagnosis, the months after a bereavement. The comfort is not that the valley is short but that it has an exit, and he is not walking it alone.

For you are with me. Something easy to miss changes the whole psalm: the pronoun. For three verses God has been he: he makes, he leads, he restores. In the valley he becomes you. The psalm starts talking to God at precisely the point where the light goes. Say that to anyone in the valley now: the darkness is not where faith goes quiet; it is very often where talking about God turns into talking to him.

Your rod and your staff. The rod is the club a shepherd carried against wolves and lions; the staff is the crook for hooking a sheep out of a hole. One is for enemies, the other for the sheep’s own wandering, and both comfort an animal that is threatened from outside and prone to fall into trouble by itself. The Christian needs exactly these two.

The shepherd who walked it alone. The one who says, “I am with you always, to the end of the age” (Matthew 28:20), went through the darkest valley forsaken (Psalm 22:1), so that his sheep never go through it alone.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew behind “the shadow of death” has long been read as shadow plus death, but many scholars think it simply means deep darkness, as the ESV notes. Either way it is the darkest place a sheep can walk, and death is the darkest of all.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The shepherd is also a host, and his guest will be at home with him for ever. The scene moves from field to house: God spreads a table while the enemies look on, anoints his guest’s head with oil and keeps filling the cup past the brim (v. 5). All his life the guest has been chased by enemies; now God’s goodness and steadfast love pursue him every day of his life, and he will dwell in the house of the LORD for ever (v. 6). Placed after Psalm 22, this table is spread on the far side of a finished work.
verseByVerse.theology: The pasture becomes a house, the sheep becomes a guest, and the pursuit that follows him is kindness.

verseByVerse.quote: You prepare a table before me in the presence of my enemies; you anoint my head with oil; my cup overflows. Surely goodness and mercy shall follow me all the days of my life, and I shall dwell in the house of the LORD forever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The shepherd becomes a lavish host, and his goodness and steadfast love pursue his guest all his life, until he is home in the LORD’s house for ever.

You prepare a table before me. The picture changes from field to house. He is no longer a sheep but a guest, and the host is setting a table while the enemies watch. They are not destroyed or sent away; they are made to watch a meal.

You anoint my head with oil. Oil on the head was the ordinary courtesy of a good host, the thing Jesus noted was missing when Simon the Pharisee received him (Luke 7:46). And my cup overflows: the host keeps pouring after the cup is full, as people do when they are enjoying themselves. God is not a careful provider; he is a lavish one.

Goodness and mercy shall follow me. All his life enemies have followed him; now God’s goodness and steadfast love are on his trail (the ESV note gives steadfast love for mercy). They are not trailing at a polite distance; they are after him, and they will catch him.

All the days of my life. This includes the bad ones, for the psalm has already been through the valley. Then the last line reaches beyond those days: David meant at least a lifetime near God, but the New Testament shows how far the promise runs. Jesus told the dying thief, “today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43), and Paul would rather be “away from the body and at home with the Lord” (2 Corinthians 5:8). Death is still an enemy, and grief is still grief. But the sheep that goes through the last valley does not go into the dark. It goes home to the shepherd, to wait there for the resurrection of the body.

After Psalm 22. Psalm 22, just before this one, brought a sufferer down to “the dust of death” (22:15) and ended with the news “that he has done it” (22:31); this table is spread on the far side of that finished work. The shepherd of this psalm said, “I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep” (John 10:11), which no ordinary shepherd would do, since a shepherd is worth more than his sheep. And at the end of the Bible the shepherd turns out to be the Lamb who was slain for the flock: “the Lamb in the midst of the throne will be their shepherd” (Revelation 7:17).

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew of “I shall dwell” can be read I shall return, and the ESV notes shall return to dwell. Either way the guest ends at home in God’s house. “Surely” can also mean only: nothing but goodness and mercy will follow him.
verseByVerse.note: “Forever” is literally “for length of days” (ESV note).

keyVerse.quote: The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want.
keyVerse.note: Everything else in the psalm unfolds from this first line: because of who the shepherd is, the sheep lacks nothing it needs, in pasture, valley or house. The promise is not that we get all we want, but that we will not lack what we need. Jesus took this role as his own when he said, “I am the good shepherd” (John 10:11).

23.reflection:
“I shall not want” promises what we need, not everything we want (v. 1). What is the difference in your own life right now, and how does trusting the shepherd change the way you hold the things you lack?

“He makes me lie down in green pastures” (v. 2). Why do so many of us find it hard to rest, and what would it look like to receive rest from Christ as a gift rather than earn it as a reward?

In the valley the psalm turns from “he” to “you” (v. 4). Have you found that hard times drew you to speak to God rather than only about him? How can we help one another do that in a dark season?

Psalm 23 follows Psalm 22, and Jesus is the shepherd who “lays down his life for the sheep” (John 10:11). How does knowing the cost of his care change the way you read verses 5 and 6, and the way you think about your own death?

24.text: A Psalm of David. 1The earth is the LORD's and the fullness thereof, the world and those who dwell therein,2for he has founded it upon the seas and established it upon the rivers.3Who shall ascend the hill of the LORD? And who shall stand in his holy place?4He who has clean hands and a pure heart, who does not lift up his soul to what is false and does not swear deceitfully.5He will receive blessing from the LORD and righteousness from the God of his salvation.6Such is the generation of those who seek him, who seek the face of the God of Jacob. Selah7Lift up your heads, O gates! And be lifted up, O ancient doors, that the King of glory may come in.8Who is this King of glory? The LORD, strong and mighty, the LORD, mighty in battle!9Lift up your heads, O gates! And lift them up, O ancient doors, that the King of glory may come in.10Who is this King of glory? The LORD of hosts, he is the King of glory! Selah

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Who Shall Ascend the Hill of the LORD?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The God who owns the whole earth calls people up his hill, and supplies what he requires. The psalm begins as wide as possible: the earth, everything in it and everyone on it belong to the LORD, who founded it (vv. 1–2). Then the question at the gate: who may climb his hill and stand in his holy place (v. 3)? The answer is clean hands, a pure heart, a soul not lifted up to idols and a tongue that does not deceive (v. 4). Yet the one who comes receives blessing and righteousness from God (v. 5), and such people are named those who seek his face (v. 6).
verseByVerse.theology: The whole earth is his, and the question is who may come up the hill. Two of the four marks cannot be seen by anyone else.

verseByVerse.quote: The earth is the LORD's and the fullness thereof, the world and those who dwell therein, for he has founded it upon the seas and established it upon the rivers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The whole world and everyone in it belongs to the LORD, because he made it and holds it steady.

The earth is the LORD’s. The psalm begins as wide as it can: the planet, everything in it, and everyone on it. He owns it all by right of making it.

And the fullness thereof. Paul settled a live church argument with this verse. Christians in Corinth were worried about meat that might have been offered to idols, and he told them to eat what was set in front of them without raising questions, “For the earth is the Lord’s, and the fullness thereof” (1 Corinthians 10:26). If it is all God’s, no piece of it is the devil’s to spoil, and a conscience may be free in a world full of things with murky histories.

Founded it upon the seas. This is picture language, not plumbing: dry land set above the chaos of water, as in Genesis 1. The world is stable because he holds it there, not because the seas have agreed to behave. The New Testament names the Maker: “all things were created through him and for him” (Colossians 1:16).

Tenants, not owners. If the earth is the LORD’s, we are tenants and stewards, not owners (Genesis 2:15; Leviticus 25:23). Anyone who carelessly destroys what he made will answer to the Owner. Creation is not to be worshipped, but it is to be cared for.

verseByVerse.quote: Who shall ascend the hill of the LORD? And who shall stand in his holy place? He who has clean hands and a pure heart, who does not lift up his soul to what is false and does not swear deceitfully. He will receive blessing from the LORD and righteousness from the God of his salvation. Such is the generation of those who seek him, who seek the face of the God of Jacob. Selah
verseByVerse.commentary:
Only the clean in hands and heart may stand in God’s holy place, yet they receive their righteousness from God; Christ has gone up, and takes his people with him.

Who shall ascend the hill of the LORD? It is the question at the gate again, as in Psalm 15, and this time the answer is four marks instead of eleven. Two of them are visible and two are not. Clean hands: what he has done. A pure heart: what he has wanted, which no gatekeeper on earth can check; only God can.

Does not lift up his soul to what is false. This covers the whole of idolatry in one phrase: lifting your inner life up towards something that is not there. The word for what is false is the one the third commandment uses for taking God’s name “in vain” (Exodus 20:7): emptiness. And does not swear deceitfully is the same failure in speech: words used to create an impression rather than to tell the truth.

He will receive blessing from the LORD. Then the give-away: the righteousness is received, not produced. The man who comes up the hill with clean hands is given the very thing the list required. That is not a contradiction but the gospel already showing: what God demands, God supplies, by the Spirit who gives a new heart (Ezekiel 36:26).

The generation of those who seek him. Such people are “the generation of those who seek him”: still seeking God, not people who have arrived. Jesus made the same promise to the same people: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew 5:8).

He did not go up for himself. In the end only one man has gone up that hill with hands and heart wholly clean, and he did not go up for himself alone. Christ has entered “into heaven itself, now to appear in the presence of God on our behalf” (Hebrews 9:24), and those who trust him may draw near with him, their hearts sprinkled clean (Hebrews 10:19–22). The question at the gate is answered by a person.

Textual note. The ESV notes a textual difference in the last phrase of verse 6: most Hebrew manuscripts read who seek your face, Jacob, while the ESV follows the Greek and Syriac and two Hebrew manuscripts. Either way the seekers are those who come to the God of Jacob.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–10 — Lift Up Your Heads, O Gates
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The direction reverses: the King himself is coming in. The ancient gates are told to lift their heads for the King of glory, and twice a voice asks who he is (vv. 7–10). The first answer is the LORD, strong and mighty in battle; the second, the climax of the psalm, is the LORD of hosts. It was probably sung as the ark came up to Jerusalem, and the church has long sung it at Ascension and Advent, because the King of glory is the crucified and risen Jesus. Every reader stands at a door with the same question.
verseByVerse.theology: The second half reverses the first: not who may go up to God, but who is coming in.

verseByVerse.quote: Lift up your heads, O gates! And be lifted up, O ancient doors, that the King of glory may come in. Who is this King of glory? The LORD, strong and mighty, the LORD, mighty in battle! Lift up your heads, O gates! And lift them up, O ancient doors, that the King of glory may come in. Who is this King of glory? The LORD of hosts, he is the King of glory! Selah
verseByVerse.commentary:
The gates must open for the King of glory, the LORD mighty in battle, who comes in as victor: the crucified and risen Christ.

Lift up your heads, O gates! Now the direction reverses. The first half asked who may come up to God; the second announces that God is coming in, and the city gates are told to make themselves taller to let him through. It is the language of a procession, probably the ark coming up to Jerusalem while David danced before it (2 Samuel 6), sung antiphonally: one group outside calling, another inside challenging.

The LORD, mighty in battle! The question is asked twice and answered twice, and the answers are military: strong and mighty … mighty in battle, and then the title that closes the psalm, the LORD of hosts, the LORD of armies. He has been fighting, and he has won.

The crucified Lord of glory. The church has long sung this psalm at Advent and Ascension. The King who came into Jerusalem on a donkey came through gates that did not need raising, to be executed outside them. He went out of the city carrying a cross, died, and came back alive from the grave. Paul calls the crucified Jesus “the Lord of glory” (1 Corinthians 2:8), and the Bible’s last picture of him echoes this psalm’s warrior King: the rider called Faithful and True, who “judges and makes war” (Revelation 19:11).

Who is this King of glory? Every reader stands at a door with the same question at it. The gates of a city can be told to lift their heads; each of us has to open his own life to this King.
verseByVerse.note: Selah, which closes both halves of the psalm (vv. 6, 10), is probably a musical direction, perhaps a pause.

24.title: Who Is This King of Glory?
24.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 24 completes the three psalms that begin with the sufferer of Psalm 22 and the shepherd of Psalm 23: now the King comes in. It asks again the question of Psalm 15, who may come near to God, and then turns it round.

The message. The God who owns the whole earth invites people up to his holy hill, but only those clean in hands and heart may stand there, and those who seek him receive the righteousness they need from him. Then the movement reverses: the King of glory, the LORD mighty in battle, is coming in himself, and every gate must open to him.

Why it was said. It was probably first sung when David brought the ark up to Jerusalem (2 Samuel 6), and afterwards as worshippers went up to the temple at the feasts (see the introduction). It reminded Israel that the God of their small hill owned the whole world, and that coming before him needs clean lives, not only correct ritual.

How the chapter makes its case. It opens with ownership: the earth is the LORD’s because he founded it (vv. 1–2). Then comes the question at the gate, who may ascend the hill of the LORD, with its four marks and its surprise, that the one who comes receives righteousness from God (vv. 3–6). Last, the gates are told to lift their heads, and the challenge “Who is this King of glory?” is answered twice: the LORD mighty in battle, the LORD of hosts (vv. 7–10).

Where it leads. By the need it exposes and by pattern. No one but Jesus has gone up God’s hill with hands and heart wholly clean, and he entered “into heaven itself, now to appear in the presence of God on our behalf” (Hebrews 9:24). The King of glory is the one Paul calls “the Lord of glory”, crucified (1 Corinthians 2:8), who rose and ascended in triumph and will come again as the rider called Faithful and True (Revelation 19:11). The church has long sung this psalm at Ascension and Advent.

For us. Hold everything you have as a steward of its true Owner. Come to God not on your own record but in Christ, who supplies the righteousness the gate requires. And open the door of your own life to the King of glory, for he is coming in.
24.theology:
God owns the world by right of making it (v. 1), and that ownership frees the conscience and calls for careful stewardship.

The entrance questions (vv. 3-4; cf. Ps 15) set a standard no one can meet by checking his own heart, and then the psalm gives away its secret: the righteousness required is received from God (v. 5). What God demands, God supplies. The second half turns the movement round: the King himself is coming in, and he comes as a victor (vv. 7-10). Christians hear in it the King who entered Jerusalem to be executed and rose from the dead.
24.examples:
Paul used the opening verse to settle a dinner-table argument: if the earth is the Lord's, a Christian may eat what is set before him with a free conscience.

The gatekeeper can check clean hands, but not a pure heart. No ceremony at any door can see inside a person, and the psalm knows it.

A city's gates can be told to lift their heads for the King; each person has to open his own life to him.

keyVerse.quote: Who is this King of glory? The LORD of hosts, he is the King of glory!
keyVerse.note: The psalm builds to this question and answers it with God’s grandest title, the LORD of armies. The God who asks who may come up to him (v. 3) is himself the King who comes in, and the New Testament names him: the crucified and risen Jesus, “the Lord of glory” (1 Corinthians 2:8).

24.reflection:
“The earth is the LORD’s and the fullness thereof” (v. 1). How should knowing that you are a tenant, not an owner, change the way you use your money, possessions and the created world?

The gate asks for clean hands and a pure heart (v. 4), yet the one who comes “will receive … righteousness from the God of his salvation” (v. 5). How do these two belong together, and how does Christ answer the question of verse 3 for us?

Lifting up the soul “to what is false” is giving our inner life to something empty (v. 4). What empty things most draw your heart today, and what would it look like to seek God’s face instead (v. 6)?

The King of glory comes in as a victor (vv. 7–10), and the church sees in him the crucified and risen Jesus. In what areas of your life are the gates still shut to him, and what would it mean to open them?

25.text: Of David. 1To you, O LORD, I lift up my soul.2O my God, in you I trust; let me not be put to shame; let not my enemies exult over me.3Indeed, none who wait for you shall be put to shame; they shall be ashamed who are wantonly treacherous.4Make me to know your ways, O LORD; teach me your paths.5Lead me in your truth and teach me, for you are the God of my salvation; for you I wait all the day long.6Remember your mercy, O LORD, and your steadfast love, for they have been from of old.7Remember not the sins of my youth or my transgressions; according to your steadfast love remember me, for the sake of your goodness, O LORD!8Good and upright is the LORD; therefore he instructs sinners in the way.9He leads the humble in what is right, and teaches the humble his way.10All the paths of the LORD are steadfast love and faithfulness, for those who keep his covenant and his testimonies.11For your name's sake, O LORD, pardon my guilt, for it is great.12Who is the man who fears the LORD? Him will he instruct in the way that he should choose.13His soul shall abide in well-being, and his offspring shall inherit the land.14The friendship of the LORD is for those who fear him, and he makes known to them his covenant.15My eyes are ever toward the LORD, for he will pluck my feet out of the net.16Turn to me and be gracious to me, for I am lonely and afflicted.17The troubles of my heart are enlarged; bring me out of my distresses.18Consider my affliction and my trouble, and forgive all my sins.19Consider how many are my foes, and with what violent hatred they hate me.20Oh, guard my soul, and deliver me! Let me not be put to shame, for I take refuge in you.21May integrity and uprightness preserve me, for I wait for you.22Redeem Israel, O God, out of all his troubles.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — Make Me to Know Your Ways
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The first thing a troubled believer needs is not relief but to be taught and forgiven. David begins by lifting his soul to the LORD and trusting him, sure that none who wait for God will be put to shame (vv. 1–3). Before he asks for rescue he asks to be taught: to know God’s ways and be led in his truth, while he waits all day (vv. 4–5). Then he asks God to remember rightly: his own mercy and steadfast love, which are older than David’s sin; not the sins of David’s youth; and David himself, according to that love and for the sake of God’s goodness (vv. 6–7). The whole request rests on who God is, not on David’s record.
verseByVerse.theology: Before he asks to be rescued he asks to be taught, and his plea for pardon rests on God's memory rather than his own record.

verseByVerse.quote: To you, O LORD, I lift up my soul. O my God, in you I trust; let me not be put to shame; let not my enemies exult over me. Indeed, none who wait for you shall be put to shame; they shall be ashamed who are wantonly treacherous. Make me to know your ways, O LORD; teach me your paths. Lead me in your truth and teach me, for you are the God of my salvation; for you I wait all the day long. Remember your mercy, O LORD, and your steadfast love, for they have been from of old. Remember not the sins of my youth or my transgressions; according to your steadfast love remember me, for the sake of your goodness, O LORD!
verseByVerse.commentary:
David lifts his whole inner life to God, asks first to be taught his ways, and pleads to be remembered by God’s steadfast love rather than by the sins of his youth.

Of David. No tune, no occasion, no instrument: the psalm needs none, because its subject belongs to every ordinary day. It is an alphabet poem (each verse begins with the next Hebrew letter), made for memorising: an A to Z of what a believer needs, carried in the head.

To you, O LORD, I lift up my soul. The previous psalm let up God’s hill only the one “who does not lift up his soul to what is false” (Psalm 24:4). Here is the same motion pointed the right way: the inner life raised deliberately towards God rather than towards something that is not there.

None who wait for you shall be put to shame. Waiting runs through this psalm like a thread (vv. 3, 5, 21). It is the hardest thing faith does, and the promise is not that the wait is short but that it will not end in humiliation. Paul says the same of Christian hope: “hope does not put us to shame” (Romans 5:5).

Make me to know your ways, O LORD. Four verses in, and he has not yet asked to be rescued. He asks to be taught: know, teach, lead, teach again. A man with enemies and a guilty past wants direction more than relief, an order of priorities most of us reverse. And what he wants is not information but a path: “your ways”, “your paths”, walked rather than merely learned.

Remember not the sins of my youth. Three times he asks God to remember, and the middle request is to forget. He seems old enough that the worst things he has done are decades behind him, and still in the room. Anyone who has lain awake over something from twenty years ago knows this verse from the inside.

For the sake of your goodness, O LORD! Notice what he offers God as grounds. Not the years of service since, not that it was long ago, not that he was young, but “according to your steadfast love … for the sake of your goodness”. He asks God to consult his own character and leave the record out of it.

The internet never forgets. Our age has built what David could hardly have imagined: a permanent public record. A foolish remark at nineteen can be dug up at forty-five. We say we believe in second chances, but we have made a world in which nothing is forgotten, and so nothing is quite forgiven: plenty of ways to judge and very few to absolve. David’s prayer is startling by contrast. He asks the one being who really does remember everything not to hold it against him, and he grounds the request in God’s character, not in his own improvement.

Remembered once, at the cross. The prophets promised exactly this: “I will forgive their iniquity, and I will remember their sin no more” (Jeremiah 31:34). This is not divine amnesia. God remembers our sins no more because they were remembered once, fully, at the cross, and dealt with there. So a Christian haunted by an old screenshot or an old sin has somewhere to go that no archive can reach.
verseByVerse.note: An acrostic poem: each verse begins with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet (ESV note).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–15 — He Instructs Sinners in the Way
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s goodness is the reason he teaches sinners, not the reason he keeps them at a distance. David turns from asking to describing: because the LORD is good and upright, he instructs sinners and leads the humble (vv. 8–9), and every path he sets them on is made of steadfast love and faithfulness for those who keep his covenant (v. 10). In the middle of that confidence comes the plea for pardon, grounded on God’s name and on the greatness of the guilt (v. 11). Then the promise widens: the one who fears the LORD is taught how to choose, blessed with well-being and descendants, and taken into God’s friendship and covenant, while his eyes stay on the LORD who frees his feet from the net (vv. 12–15).
verseByVerse.theology: God teaches sinners because he is good, not because they are; and the reward for fearing him is being let into his confidence.

verseByVerse.quote: Good and upright is the LORD; therefore he instructs sinners in the way. He leads the humble in what is right, and teaches the humble his way. All the paths of the LORD are steadfast love and faithfulness, for those who keep his covenant and his testimonies. For your name's sake, O LORD, pardon my guilt, for it is great.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because the LORD is good, he does not shut sinners out but teaches them his way; so David dares to ask pardon for great guilt, pleading God’s name.

Therefore he instructs sinners in the way. The logic is not what anyone expects. You would expect: he is upright, therefore he has nothing to say to sinners. Instead: “therefore he instructs sinners”. His goodness is the reason he stoops to teach the very people who have made a mess of the way. The Pharisees grumbled the same truth about Jesus as a complaint: “This man receives sinners and eats with them” (Luke 15:2).

He leads the humble. The people he leads are named twice in one verse: “the humble”. Not the clever, not the accomplished, not those with a clean record. The one qualification for being taught by God is knowing you need telling.
