All the paths of the LORD. All of them, not some. The road God puts his people on is made of two materials the whole way: his covenant love and his faithfulness. Remember that on the stretch that feels like neither.

Pardon my guilt, for it is great. Verse 11, near the centre of the alphabet, is one of the boldest sentences in the Bible. He does not shrink the guilt to make the pardon easier; he pleads its size as the reason. Great guilt calls for a great pardon, and a great pardon makes a great name for God. Moses argued the same way on Sinai, asking pardon for Israel precisely because it was a stiff-necked people (Exodus 34:9). When what you have done feels too big to bring, bring the size of it, and ask for a pardon on that scale.

How God can pardon. The New Testament shows how a holy God can pardon great guilt for his name’s sake without pretending it is small. He put forward his Son as a sacrifice that turns away his wrath, “so that he might be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus” (Romans 3:26). At the cross God pardons the sinner, and his own just name is upheld, not stained.

verseByVerse.quote: Who is the man who fears the LORD? Him will he instruct in the way that he should choose. His soul shall abide in well-being, and his offspring shall inherit the land. The friendship of the LORD is for those who fear him, and he makes known to them his covenant. My eyes are ever toward the LORD, for he will pluck my feet out of the net.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The one who fears the LORD is taught how to choose, blessed beyond himself and taken into God’s confidence, so he keeps his eyes on the LORD even while his feet are in the net.

Who is the man who fears the LORD? The promise to him is instruction “in the way that he should choose”: not that God hands down each decision, but that he teaches him to choose well. That is a better gift than a series of answers.

His offspring shall inherit the land. The promise reaches past him: “his soul shall abide in well-being, and his offspring shall inherit the land”. A man who fears God is not building for himself alone; people who come after him are still drawing on what he received. That is the quiet answer to anyone who feels their obedience is going nowhere. The land was Israel’s covenant inheritance; in Christ the meek “shall inherit the earth” (Matthew 5:5; Romans 4:13). For families today a godly upbringing carries real blessing, but not a guarantee.

The friendship of the LORD. Here is the surprise at the heart of the psalm (v. 14). The word speaks of the circle of trusted advisers, the conversation that happens when the door is shut. God said of Abraham, “Shall I hide from Abraham what I am about to do” (Genesis 18:17), and through Amos, “the Lord GOD does nothing without revealing his secret to his servants the prophets” (Amos 3:7).

I have called you friends. To men who had followed him for three years Jesus said: “No longer do I call you servants, for the servant does not know what his master is doing; but I have called you friends, for all that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you” (John 15:15). The fear of God is not the opposite of intimacy with him; in this psalm it is the door into it.

He will pluck my feet out of the net. The net is still on his feet while he looks to the LORD. Looking up is what he does inside the trap, not after he is out of it.

Uncertain wording. The word translated “friendship” in verse 14 (Hebrew sôd) can mean a council, its confidential talk, or close intimacy; the ESV notes the rendering “the secret counsel”. Which shade is uppermost cannot be settled, but either way those who fear the LORD are admitted to his confidence.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–22 — I Am Lonely and Afflicted
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Loneliness, affliction, sin and enemies can all be brought to God in the same prayer. Now David names the trouble itself: he is lonely and afflicted, and the troubles of his heart have grown (vv. 16–17). He asks God to look at his affliction and forgive all his sins, to see how many and how violent his enemies are, and to guard him, because he has taken refuge in God and waits for him (vv. 18–21). Nothing in his circumstances has changed when the alphabet ends. Then one more line, beyond the last letter, widens the prayer from himself to the whole people: “Redeem Israel, O God, out of all his troubles” (v. 22).
verseByVerse.theology: A private prayer that ends by praying for the whole nation.

verseByVerse.quote: Turn to me and be gracious to me, for I am lonely and afflicted. The troubles of my heart are enlarged; bring me out of my distresses. Consider my affliction and my trouble, and forgive all my sins. Consider how many are my foes, and with what violent hatred they hate me. Oh, guard my soul, and deliver me! Let me not be put to shame, for I take refuge in you. May integrity and uprightness preserve me, for I wait for you. Redeem Israel, O God, out of all his troubles.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Lonely, worn down and guilty, David brings his whole trouble and all his sins to God in one breath, asks to be guarded because he takes refuge in him, and ends by praying for all God’s people.

I am lonely and afflicted. Now, at last, the trouble itself: one word for isolation and one for being worn down, an honest description of many people’s ordinary week, and rarely said aloud in church. And the troubles of his heart are “enlarged”: not more numerous but bigger, the way a worry swells overnight.

Forgive all my sins. This comes in the same breath as the request for rescue. He does not claim the affliction is deserved, and he does not claim to be innocent either; he brings both to the same God in the same sentence.

May integrity and uprightness preserve me. Is he trusting his own goodness after pleading great guilt (v. 11)? No: integrity here is wholeness of heart before God, which he asks God to keep in him, not a merit he offers. It stands beside his plea for pardon.

Let me not be put to shame. The alphabet ends where it began, waiting and asking not to be shamed (vv. 2–3). The acrostic has run from A to Z and the enemies are still there.

Redeem Israel, O God. Then one more verse, outside the alphabet, which has already finished. A man who has spent twenty-one verses on his own loneliness, guilt and enemies adds a line for the whole nation. When you have said everything about your own trouble, pray for somebody else. The psalm’s last word is not “me”.

A Redeemer who was lonely too. The lonely believer is not praying to a stranger to the condition: the Son of God was deserted by every friend on the night he was arrested (Mark 14:50), and he sympathises from the inside (Hebrews 4:15). And the prayer of verse 22 is answered in him, who “gave himself for us to redeem us from all lawlessness” (Titus 2:14).

25.title: Remember Not the Sins of My Youth
25.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 25 follows Psalm 24, where only the one “who does not lift up his soul to what is false” may climb the LORD’s hill (Psalm 24:4). Here David opens, “To you, O LORD, I lift up my soul” (v. 1), and then admits at once that he has no clean record to bring with it.

The message. A sinner with nothing to plead but God’s own character may come to him and ask for everything: guidance, pardon, friendship and rescue. Because the LORD is good, he teaches sinners instead of shutting them out, and he pardons great guilt for the sake of his own name. So the believer’s part is to lift up his soul to God and wait for him.

Why it was said. The psalm names no occasion, though David had enemies and a past he could not undo (see the introduction). The prayer is shaped as an alphabet, each verse beginning with the next Hebrew letter, so that Israel could learn it by heart and carry it into ordinary days of confusion, guilt and loneliness.

How the chapter makes its case. David asks first to be taught God’s ways, and to be remembered by God’s steadfast love rather than by the sins of his youth (vv. 1–7). Then he describes the God he prays to: good and upright, and therefore the teacher of sinners (vv. 8–10). Near the centre of the alphabet comes the boldest prayer, “pardon my guilt, for it is great” (v. 11), and then the promise that those who fear the LORD are taken into his friendship and taught his covenant (vv. 12–15). Last comes the trouble itself, loneliness, affliction, sin and violent enemies, all brought to God together (vv. 16–21), and one line more, beyond the alphabet, for all Israel (v. 22).

Where it leads. Chiefly by the need it exposes and by the character of God revealed in Christ. David asks a holy God to pardon great guilt for his name’s sake, and the psalm does not say how that can be just. The cross does, where God shows himself “just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus” (Romans 3:26). The God who “instructs sinners in the way” (v. 8) came among us as the friend of sinners, called his disciples friends and made known to them all he had heard from his Father (John 15:15), and gave himself to redeem his people (v. 22).

For us. You do not need a clean past to pray this psalm; you need only to know your need. Bring the old sins that still keep you awake, ask God to remember you by his steadfast love, and ask him to teach you his way for the decision in front of you. And when you have told him all your own trouble, pray for his people.
25.theology:
The soul lifted to God (v. 1) answers the soul lifted to what is false in 24:4. God's instruction is aimed at sinners and the humble because he is good: the only qualification is need (vv. 8-9). The plea for pardon rests on God's name and steadfast love, not the sinner's record, and he even gives the size of his guilt as a reason for pardon (vv. 6-7, 11).

Fear of God opens into friendship with him (v. 14). Rescue and forgiveness are asked for in one breath (v. 18), nothing is resolved by the end, and the last verse turns from self to the nation (v. 22).
25.examples:
Most of us ask God for rescue first and direction later, if at all. David asks four times to be taught before he asks once to be rescued.

Anyone who has lain awake over something done twenty years ago can pray verse 7 as it stands. And verse 11 gives courage to bring the biggest thing of all, and to ask for a pardon on the same scale.

keyVerse.quote: For your name’s sake, O LORD, pardon my guilt, for it is great.
keyVerse.note: Near the centre of the alphabet stands the psalm’s boldest prayer and its heart. David pleads not his record but God’s name, and not the smallness of his guilt but its greatness. Everything else he asks for, guidance, friendship and rescue, depends on this pardon, and the cross shows how a holy God can grant it and keep his name just (Romans 3:26).

25.reflection:
David asks to be taught God’s ways (vv. 4–5) long before he asks to be rescued (vv. 16–20). What do you usually ask God for first, and what would change if you prayed in David’s order?

Verse 7 asks God to remember us “according to your steadfast love” rather than by the sins of our youth. Is there an old sin that still haunts you, or someone you know? How do verse 11 and the cross answer it?

Verse 8 says God teaches sinners because he is good. How should that shape the way we come back to God after failing, and the way our church welcomes people with a past?

A lonely and afflicted man ends his prayer for himself by praying for all God’s people (vv. 16, 22). Who in your church could you pray for this week, and how might doing so help you in your own trouble?

26.text: Of David. 1Vindicate me, O LORD, for I have walked in my integrity, and I have trusted in the LORD without wavering.2Prove me, O LORD, and try me; test my heart and my mind.3For your steadfast love is before my eyes, and I walk in your faithfulness.4I do not sit with men of falsehood, nor do I consort with hypocrites.5I hate the assembly of evildoers, and I will not sit with the wicked.6I wash my hands in innocence and go around your altar, O LORD,7proclaiming thanksgiving aloud, and telling all your wondrous deeds.8O LORD, I love the habitation of your house and the place where your glory dwells.9Do not sweep my soul away with sinners, nor my life with bloodthirsty men,10in whose hands are evil devices, and whose right hands are full of bribes.11But as for me, I shall walk in my integrity; redeem me, and be gracious to me.12My foot stands on level ground; in the great assembly I will bless the LORD.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — Prove Me, O LORD, and Try Me
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A man under accusation asks God, who sees the heart, to judge him, and shows that the deepest thing about him is love for God’s presence. David asks to be vindicated, since he has walked in integrity and trusted the LORD, and he invites God to test his heart and mind (vv. 1–2). What keeps him steady is God’s steadfast love kept before his eyes, and his evidence is the company he refuses: liars, hypocrites and the assembly of evildoers (vv. 3–5). Then he comes to worship, washing his hands in innocence, going round the altar with thanksgiving and telling God’s wonders (vv. 6–7), and he names what the whole plea is about: he loves the house where God’s glory dwells (v. 8).
verseByVerse.theology: A man asks to be examined at the deepest level, and offers as evidence the company he keeps and his love for God's house.

verseByVerse.quote: Vindicate me, O LORD, for I have walked in my integrity, and I have trusted in the LORD without wavering. Prove me, O LORD, and try me; test my heart and my mind. For your steadfast love is before my eyes, and I walk in your faithfulness. I do not sit with men of falsehood, nor do I consort with hypocrites. I hate the assembly of evildoers, and I will not sit with the wicked.
verseByVerse.commentary:
David asks God to search his heart and clear him of one accusation, offering as evidence the love of God he keeps in view and the company he refuses.

Read after Psalm 25. The heading is bare (“Of David”), and the psalm will be misunderstood unless it is read straight after Psalm 25. One psalm ago the same man asked God to forget “the sins of my youth” and to pardon his guilt, “for it is great” (Psalm 25:7, 11). He has not changed his mind. This is not a claim to be sinless but a specific case, brought to a specific court, and in that matter he asks to be examined.

I have walked in my integrity. Integrity is wholeness: the undivided life, the same man in public and at home. And the examination he invites is not of his record but of his heart, in the Hebrew his “kidneys” and heart, the innermost parts no one else can see. He asks God to look there and see whether it matches.

I do not sit with men of falsehood. His evidence is not a list of achievements but a list of chairs he has refused to sit in. It is Psalm 1 in the first person: not walking, not standing, not sitting with them (Psalm 1:1). What holds him steady, and lets him leave the wrong table, comes first (v. 3): God’s steadfast love “before my eyes”, kept in view the way a walker keeps a landmark ahead of him.

Must Christians separate from unbelievers? Jesus ate with sinners to call them (Luke 15:1–2), and Paul says we cannot avoid them in this world (1 Corinthians 5:9–10). What David refuses is fellowship with deceivers in their counsels and schemes, the partnership Paul forbids (2 Corinthians 6:14). And “hate” here is a refusal to share in evil, not a will to harm; we are to love our enemies (Matthew 5:44).
verseByVerse.note: “My heart and my mind” is literally “my kidneys and my heart” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: I wash my hands in innocence and go around your altar, O LORD, proclaiming thanksgiving aloud, and telling all your wondrous deeds. O LORD, I love the habitation of your house and the place where your glory dwells.
verseByVerse.commentary:
David comes to worship with clean hands and thanksgiving, and reveals what lies under the whole plea: he loves the place where God’s glory dwells.

I wash my hands in innocence. He borrows the language of rites. Priests washed at the bronze basin before approaching the altar (Exodus 30:17–21), and the elders of a town washed their hands to declare themselves innocent of a killing (Deuteronomy 21:6–7). The gesture says: I am not bringing my mess in here. And under suspicion he does not hide at home but joins the thanksgiving round the altar (v. 7).

An empty washing. The same gesture can be a lie. Pilate “took water and washed his hands before the crowd, saying, ‘I am innocent of this man’s blood’” (Matthew 27:24), and it changed nothing: he used the rite to escape a decision, not to come before God. The difference between Psalm 26 and Pilate is not the water. It is whether a man is asking to be examined or trying to close the case.

I love the habitation of your house. Here is what the psalm is really about. Under the legal language is a man who loves being where God is, and fears to be shut out. The evidence of verses 4–5 is all about avoiding one company because he wants another. Jesus loved his Father’s house like this, so that his disciples remembered, “Zeal for your house will consume me” (John 2:17).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–12 — I Love the Habitation of Your House
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The one who loves God’s house fears above all being swept away with those who hate it, and he asks for grace as well as justice. David prays not to share the end of bloodthirsty men, whose hands hold evil schemes and bribes (vv. 9–10), in contrast to his own washed hands. He resolves to go on walking in integrity, and in the same breath asks God to redeem him and be gracious to him (v. 11), because integrity is no substitute for mercy. The psalm ends in confidence: his foot stands on level ground, and the private plea becomes public praise in the great assembly (v. 12).
verseByVerse.theology: The integrity he pleads and the redemption he asks for stand in the same breath, and the psalm ends in church.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not sweep my soul away with sinners, nor my life with bloodthirsty men, in whose hands are evil devices, and whose right hands are full of bribes. But as for me, I shall walk in my integrity; redeem me, and be gracious to me. My foot stands on level ground; in the great assembly I will bless the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Fearing to share the end of the wicked, David pleads his integrity and asks for grace in the same breath, and ends praising God in public.

Do not sweep my soul away with sinners. Now the fear comes out: to be swept away with the people he has refused to sit with. The detail is telling: their “right hands are full of bribes”, and his own hands have just been washed. The psalm is built on two pairs of hands.

Redeem me, and be gracious to me. Here is the balance the whole psalm has held: “I shall walk in my integrity”, and in the next breath, “redeem me, and be gracious to me”. To redeem is to buy someone out; grace is unearned. A man can honestly plead his integrity in a particular matter and still ask to be bought out and treated better than he deserves.

My foot stands on level ground. Level ground is what he will ask for again in the next psalm (Psalm 27:11): footing that does not slide. Here he says he already stands on it. And the last line takes this private prayer into the great assembly: what is settled alone with God gets said out loud among his people.

Nothing held back. Only one man has ever invited God’s examination with nothing held back: Jesus, who “committed no sin, neither was deceit found in his mouth” (1 Peter 2:22). Yet he is the one who was swept away with sinners, crucified between two criminals and “numbered with the transgressors” (Isaiah 53:12), so that those who trust him never will be. Every other believer who prays “vindicate me” leans on him: his integrity is counted as theirs, and his blood is the price behind “redeem me”.

26.title: I Love the Habitation of Your House
26.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 26 comes straight after Psalm 25, where David asked God to forget the sins of his youth and to pardon his guilt, “for it is great” (Psalm 25:11). Now the same man asks God to vindicate him. The two psalms must be read together: this is not a claim to be sinless but a plea in one matter.

The message. A believer who is falsely accused may ask God, the Judge who sees the heart, to examine him and clear him, because the deepest thing about him is that he loves to be where God is. Honest integrity and a plea for grace belong together: David can say “I shall walk in my integrity” and in the same breath “redeem me, and be gracious to me” (v. 11).

Why it was said. The psalm names no occasion, but it reads like a man going up to worship while an accusation hangs over him, like the slanders and intrigues that dogged David’s life (see the introduction). It taught Israel that the way to answer a false charge is to bring it into God’s court.

How the chapter makes its case. David asks to be vindicated and tested to the depths of his heart (vv. 1–2). His evidence is the love of God he keeps before his eyes and the company he refuses to keep (vv. 3–5). He washes his hands, goes round the altar giving thanks, and says what the psalm is really about: “I love the habitation of your house” (vv. 6–8). Then he names his fear, to be swept away with bloodthirsty and corrupt men (vv. 9–10), pleads both his integrity and God’s grace (v. 11), and ends standing on level ground, blessing God in the great assembly (v. 12).

Where it leads. By pattern, and by the need it exposes. Only one man has ever invited God’s examination with nothing hidden: Jesus, who “committed no sin, neither was deceit found in his mouth” (1 Peter 2:22), and whose love for his Father’s house consumed him (John 2:17). Yet he was the one swept away with sinners, crucified between criminals and “numbered with the transgressors” (Isaiah 53:12), so that those who trust him never will be. God vindicated him by raising him from the dead, and in him his people are vindicated too.

For us. When you are falsely accused, take the case to God before you take it anywhere else, and ask him to search you as well as to clear you. Let love for his presence and his people shape the company you keep. And plead your honesty only alongside the blood of Christ: “redeem me, and be gracious to me.”
26.theology:
Read beside Psalm 25, this is plainly not a claim to sinlessness but a plea in one case (v. 1). Integrity means wholeness, the same person in public and in private, and the examination invited is of the heart (v. 2). The company a person keeps and refuses is treated as evidence (vv. 4-5; cf. 1:1).

Verse 11 holds together what every believer must: an honest plea in a particular matter, and a request for mercy no one earns. The private prayer ends in the public assembly (v. 12).
26.examples:
David's evidence is made of chairs he refused to sit in. It is a fair question for any reader: whose table am I actually at, and whose approval shapes my week?

Two pairs of hands run through the psalm, one washed and one full of bribes. And Pilate shows that the same basin can be used to close a case rather than to come before God.

keyVerse.quote: O LORD, I love the habitation of your house and the place where your glory dwells.
keyVerse.note: Strip away the legal language and this is the heart of the psalm: a man who loves to be where God is. His refusal of evil company (vv. 4–5) and his fear of being swept away with sinners (v. 9) both flow from this love. Jesus loved his Father’s house with a zeal that consumed him (John 2:17), and by his death he opened the way for sinners into the presence of God’s glory.

26.reflection:
Psalm 26 comes straight after David’s plea for pardon in Psalm 25. How can a believer honestly say “I have walked in my integrity” (v. 1) and still ask for grace (v. 11)? Which of the two are you more tempted to lean on without the other?

David invites God to test his heart and mind (v. 2). What makes that prayer frightening, and what difference does it make that he prays it with God’s steadfast love before his eyes (v. 3)?

David’s evidence is the company he refuses to keep (vv. 4–5), yet Jesus ate with sinners to call them. How can we tell the difference between loving people outside the faith and joining in their schemes?

“I love the habitation of your house” (v. 8). What draws you to gathering with God’s people, and what keeps you away? How might Christ’s love for his Father’s house reshape ours?

27.text: Of David. 1The LORD is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear? The LORD is the stronghold of my life; of whom shall I be afraid?2When evildoers assail me to eat up my flesh, my adversaries and foes, it is they who stumble and fall.3Though an army encamp against me, my heart shall not fear; though war arise against me, yet I will be confident.4One thing have I asked of the LORD, that will I seek after: that I may dwell in the house of the LORD all the days of my life, to gaze upon the beauty of the LORD and to inquire in his temple.5For he will hide me in his shelter in the day of trouble; he will conceal me under the cover of his tent; he will lift me high upon a rock.6And now my head shall be lifted up above my enemies all around me, and I will offer in his tent sacrifices with shouts of joy; I will sing and make melody to the LORD.7Hear, O LORD, when I cry aloud; be gracious to me and answer me!8You have said, "Seek my face." My heart says to you, "Your face, LORD, do I seek."9Hide not your face from me. Turn not your servant away in anger, O you who have been my help. Cast me not off; forsake me not, O God of my salvation!10For my father and my mother have forsaken me, but the LORD will take me in.11Teach me your way, O LORD, and lead me on a level path because of my enemies.12Give me not up to the will of my adversaries; for false witnesses have risen against me, and they breathe out violence.13I believe that I shall look upon the goodness of the LORD in the land of the living!14Wait for the LORD; be strong, and let your heart take courage; wait for the LORD!

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — One Thing Have I Asked
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A believer whose light and stronghold is the LORD can face an army without fear, because what he wants most is God himself. David asks two questions that expect the answer “nobody”: whom shall I fear, of whom shall I be afraid (v. 1)? Attackers stumble, and even if an army camps round him his heart will stay confident (vv. 2–3). The reason is his single request: to live in God’s house all his days, gaze on the LORD’s beauty and seek him there (v. 4). That same God will hide him in the day of trouble and lift him high on a rock, so the section ends not in quiet relief but in sacrifices with shouts of joy and singing (vv. 5–6).
verseByVerse.theology: A man surrounded by an army asks for one thing, and it is not the army's defeat.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear? The LORD is the stronghold of my life; of whom shall I be afraid? When evildoers assail me to eat up my flesh, my adversaries and foes, it is they who stumble and fall. Though an army encamp against me, my heart shall not fear; though war arise against me, yet I will be confident.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because the LORD is his light, salvation and stronghold, David will not let fear get inside him, even with an army camped outside.

Whom shall I fear? Two questions, both expecting the answer “nobody”. He does not say he has no enemies: verse 3 has an army camped outside. He says they have lost their power to frighten him, a different claim and the only one most of us can make.

The LORD is my light. To call God “my light” is rare in the Old Testament, and it says more than that God gives light: a man’s ability to see anything at all comes from him. Isaiah promised a city that would not need the sun, for “the LORD will be your everlasting light” (Isaiah 60:19).

Though an army encamp against me. A whole army arranges itself around a man standing still. The confidence is about his heart: not that the walls will hold, but that fear will not get inside. There is no promise here that the siege will be lifted.

The light of the world. Jesus said the sentence in the first person: “I am the light of the world. Whoever follows me will not walk in darkness” (John 8:12). And Paul turned David’s questions into every Christian’s: “If God is for us, who can be against us?” (Romans 8:31).

verseByVerse.quote: One thing have I asked of the LORD, that will I seek after: that I may dwell in the house of the LORD all the days of my life, to gaze upon the beauty of the LORD and to inquire in his temple. For he will hide me in his shelter in the day of trouble; he will conceal me under the cover of his tent; he will lift me high upon a rock. And now my head shall be lifted up above my enemies all around me, and I will offer in his tent sacrifices with shouts of joy; I will sing and make melody to the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
With an army outside, David asks for one thing, not rescue but God’s presence, and is sure God will shelter him and lift him up to sing.

One thing have I asked of the LORD. He has asked for “one thing”, and it is not the removal of the army. Most of us in a crisis have one thing we want, and it is always the crisis ending. His single request is to be somewhere, and the somewhere is where God is.

To gaze upon the beauty of the LORD. The one request has three movements, and together they are a whole life. Dwell: to live there, not visit, and “all the days of my life”, not just the frightening ones. Gaze: to look long, the way you look at a face rather than glance at a clock; God has beauty, and a man under siege wants to look at it. Inquire: to seek, to ask direction, to keep asking. In David’s day there was no stone temple yet, but the word was already used of the sanctuary at Shiloh (1 Samuel 1:9), and the next verse calls God’s dwelling a tent.

He will hide me in his shelter. Three pictures of the same protection: hidden, covered, lifted. The tent is God’s own, and in that world a guest in someone’s tent was his host’s to defend. Then the head is lifted, as God lifted David’s head when he fled from Absalom (Psalm 3:3). His response is not quiet relief but loud praise: “sacrifices with shouts of joy; I will sing and make melody to the LORD”.

The scattered heart. A great many companies compete for our attention, and most of us feel the result: a mind pulled in twenty directions an hour, never quite present anywhere. Søren Kierkegaard gave one of his books a title that could sum up this verse: Purity of Heart Is to Will One Thing. His point was that a divided person is not free but scattered, and that only the Good, finally only God, can be willed with the whole heart without tearing it apart; money and reputation split us, because they are many and they disappoint. David’s “one thing” is not a technique for concentration but a person beautiful enough to gather the heart. So the cure for a scattered life is not first more discipline but a better sight. Jesus said as much to a distracted Martha: “one thing is necessary. Mary has chosen the good portion, which will not be taken away from her” (Luke 10:42). The good portion was sitting at his feet.

A question for us. If God granted exactly one request this year, and you had to write it now, would it be this? The psalm is not scolding; it shows what a man wants when he has learned where safety really is.

Uncertain wording. The verb translated “to inquire” (v. 4) is uncommon, and the ESV notes that it can be rendered “meditate”. It may mean seeking guidance at the sanctuary or reflecting there on God; either way it pictures an unhurried life attending to him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–14 — Your Face, LORD, Do I Seek
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Confidence in God does not stop a believer crying out to him, and the cry is for God’s face more than for rescue. Suddenly urgent, David begs to be heard, answers God’s invitation to seek his face, and pleads not to be turned away or forsaken (vv. 7–9), even if his own father and mother forsake him, for the LORD will take him in (v. 10). He asks to be taught and led on a level path, and not handed over to false witnesses who breathe out violence (vv. 11–12). He ends believing he will see the LORD’s goodness in this life, and turns to everyone listening: wait for the LORD, be strong, take courage, wait (vv. 13–14).
verseByVerse.theology: The confidence of the first half does not save him from having to pray like this, and the psalm ends waiting rather than answered.

verseByVerse.quote: Hear, O LORD, when I cry aloud; be gracious to me and answer me! You have said, "Seek my face." My heart says to you, "Your face, LORD, do I seek." Hide not your face from me. Turn not your servant away in anger, O you who have been my help. Cast me not off; forsake me not, O God of my salvation! For my father and my mother have forsaken me, but the LORD will take me in.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The confident man now cries urgently to be heard and not forsaken, seeking God’s face, sure that even if father and mother forsake him the LORD will take him in.

Hear, O LORD, when I cry aloud. The tone changes so sharply that some have thought this a second psalm. But a man can mean every word of “whom shall I fear?” and still, an hour later, beg God to answer. Anyone who has sung confidently on Sunday and panicked on Tuesday is not a hypocrite; he is in Psalm 27.

You have said, “Seek my face.” The command “seek” is plural, spoken to a congregation. God issued a general invitation to a whole people, and one man overhears it and takes it personally: “My heart says to you”. That is what should happen when the Bible is read in public.

Hide not your face from me. What he asks for is a face. Not an outcome, not an explanation: the face of God, which the priestly blessing asked to shine on Israel (Numbers 6:25) and which Moses was not allowed to see (Exodus 33:20). He wants the one thing no one can arrange for himself. The New Testament says where that face is now seen: God “has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ” (2 Corinthians 4:6). The light of verse 1 and the face of verse 8 meet in him.

My father and my mother have forsaken me. Verse 10 names the deepest abandonment a human being knows, and does not soften it: father and mother, the two people who are supposed to be incapable of it. Whether David meant his own family or the worst case imaginable, the answer is “the LORD will take me in”. The verb is the one for gathering someone up off the street and bringing him into the house. Isaiah heard God say the same: even a mother may forget her nursing child, “yet I will not forget you” (Isaiah 49:15).

But the LORD will take me in. Anyone who was not wanted by the people who should have wanted them will find that this verse was written for them. It does not say God will make up for it. It says God takes you in. He can promise it because his Son was truly forsaken, crying “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matthew 27:46), so that he could say to his own, “I will not leave you as orphans” (John 14:18).

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew of verse 8 is compressed and hard to construe, as the ESV notes. Word for word it runs roughly, “To you my heart has said, ‘Seek my face’”, and the ESV supplies “You have said”, as most translations do in some way. The sense is clear: the heart takes up God’s invitation as its own answer.

verseByVerse.quote: Teach me your way, O LORD, and lead me on a level path because of my enemies. Give me not up to the will of my adversaries; for false witnesses have risen against me, and they breathe out violence. I believe that I shall look upon the goodness of the LORD in the land of the living! Wait for the LORD; be strong, and let your heart take courage; wait for the LORD!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Under false accusation David asks to be taught and protected, trusts he will see God’s goodness in this life, and calls us to wait for the LORD with courage.

Lead me on a level path. Again, under pressure, the request is to be taught (compare Psalm 25:4; 26:1–2). A level path is ground you cannot be tripped on, and the reason given is “because of my enemies”: when people are watching for you to slip, a straight walk is the only defence. “Breathe out violence” is exact: there are people whose ordinary speech is a threat.

In the land of the living. What kept him upright was believing he would yet see God’s goodness “in the land of the living”: not only in some future world, but here, among people still breathing.

Wait for the LORD. The psalm ends by turning to whoever is listening and saying the hardest thing twice. Not “the LORD has answered”, not “the enemies have gone”, but wait. And between the two commands to wait is the only instruction for the interval: be strong, let your heart take courage. Courage is taken up on purpose while the waiting lasts, not after it is over, leaning on “the stronghold of my life” (v. 1), and for a Christian on the Spirit given to strengthen the inner being (Ephesians 3:16).

What it means to wait for the LORD. We hear “wait” as doing nothing: the queue, the waiting room, time lost until life starts again. The Hebrew word (qavah) leans forward. It means to look for someone with expectation, the way a family watches the road for a traveller they know is coming. It is aimed at a person, not only an outcome, and that is why it is hard: waiting for the LORD means wanting him more than the answer. And we do not wait alone. Christ, having offered one sacrifice for sins, “sat down at the right hand of God, waiting from that time until his enemies should be made a footstool for his feet” (Hebrews 10:12–13). The King waits too, and his waiting cannot be disappointed. So the Christian waits “for his Son from heaven” (1 Thessalonians 1:10), and strength is given in the waiting, not after it: “they who wait for the LORD shall renew their strength” (Isaiah 40:31). This week, name to God each morning the thing you are waiting for, and then do the next plain duty in front of you.

Still waiting. The man who asked for one thing (v. 4) has not been given it yet. He is still looking at an army, still hearing false witnesses, still asking God not to hide. And he tells us to wait, because he knows what he will see: goodness, in the land of the living, from the one who is his light.

Textual note. The ESV notes that other Hebrew manuscripts read “Oh! Had I not believed that I would look …”, with the sentence left hanging, as if he cannot bring himself to finish the thought of what he would have done without faith. Either way the content is the same: what holds him up is the belief that he will see the LORD’s goodness in this life.

27.title: The LORD Is My Light and My Salvation
27.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 27 follows two psalms in which David, under pressure from enemies and accusers, asked to be taught, pardoned and vindicated (Psalms 25–26). It gathers up their themes: love for God’s house (Psalm 26:8), the request to be taught and led on level ground, and waiting for the LORD.

The message. With the LORD as his light, his salvation and his stronghold, a believer need not be mastered by fear, even with an army at the door, because what he wants most is not safety but God himself. Confidence and urgent pleading belong together, and when every human support fails, even father and mother, the LORD takes his people in. So the answer to unresolved trouble is to seek God’s face and wait for him with courage.

Why it was said. The psalm names no occasion, but it speaks of armies, war and false witnesses, the troubles of a hunted and slandered king (see the introduction). It gave Israel a song for siege and slander, and for the long wait between.

How the chapter makes its case. The psalm has two movements. First comes confidence (vv. 1–6): with the LORD as his light, he will not fear an army (vv. 1–3); the one thing he asks is to dwell with God, gaze on his beauty and seek him (v. 4); and God will hide him, lift him up and fill his mouth with praise (vv. 5–6). Then, without warning, urgent prayer (vv. 7–14): he begs to be heard and answers God’s invitation to seek his face (vv. 7–8); he pleads not to be forsaken, though father and mother forsake him (vv. 9–10); he asks to be taught and kept from false witnesses (vv. 11–12); and he ends believing he will see God’s goodness in this life, telling all who hear to wait for the LORD (vv. 13–14).

Where it leads. By the character of God revealed in Christ, and by pattern. The God who is David’s light came as “the light of the world” (John 8:12), and the face David sought now shines “in the face of Jesus Christ” (2 Corinthians 4:6). David feared being cast off; on the cross the Son was forsaken by his Father, so that God will never forsake those who trust him, and Jesus promises, “I will not leave you as orphans” (John 14:18). Even the waiting is shared: the King waits at God’s right hand until his enemies are made his footstool (Hebrews 10:12–13).

For us. Ask what your one thing is, and whether it is God himself or only the end of your trouble. If those who should have loved you have let you down, hear verse 10: the LORD will take you in. And while you wait, take courage on purpose, leaning on the one who is the stronghold of your life.
27.theology:
The two halves belong together in this order: confidence first, urgent pleading second. Meaning every word of whom shall I fear? does not exempt a believer from crying aloud an hour later (vv. 1, 7). The confidence is that fear will not master his heart, not that the walls will hold (v. 3), and what a man under siege asks for is not rescue but God's presence (v. 4).

The worst human abandonment is named without softening and answered: the LORD will take me in (v. 10). The psalm ends unanswered, with courage commanded between two commands to wait (v. 14).
27.examples:
Most of us, in a crisis, ask for one thing, and it is always the crisis ending. David, with an army outside, asks to live near God and look at his beauty, the way you look at a face rather than glance at a clock.

Anyone who has sung confidently on Sunday and panicked on Tuesday will find both days in this one psalm, and will find the instruction for the days between: wait, and take courage.

keyVerse.quote: One thing have I asked of the LORD, that will I seek after: that I may dwell in the house of the LORD all the days of my life, to gaze upon the beauty of the LORD and to inquire in his temple.
keyVerse.note: With an army outside, David’s single request is not rescue but God himself, and this explains the whole psalm: why fear cannot master him (vv. 1–3), why he seeks God’s face (v. 8), and what he waits for (v. 14). The beauty he longed to gaze on is now seen “in the face of Jesus Christ” (2 Corinthians 4:6), and those who trust him will dwell in God’s house for ever.

27.reflection:
David asks God for “one thing” (v. 4), and it is not the end of his trouble. If God granted you one request this year, what would you ask for, and what does your answer show about what you want most?

The psalm moves from bold confidence (vv. 1–6) to urgent pleading (vv. 7–12). Why is it a help that both stand in the same psalm, and how does that speak to the gap between our Sunday confidence and our weekday fears?

“For my father and my mother have forsaken me, but the LORD will take me in” (v. 10). How do this verse and Christ’s being forsaken on the cross speak to people let down by those who should have loved them? How can a church show that welcome in practice?

Verse 14 sets a command to take courage between two commands to wait. What are you waiting for now, and what would it look like to wait for the LORD himself, not only for the answer?

28.text: Of David. 1To you, O LORD, I call; my rock, be not deaf to me, lest, if you be silent to me, I become like those who go down to the pit.2Hear the voice of my pleas for mercy, when I cry to you for help, when I lift up my hands toward your most holy sanctuary.3Do not drag me off with the wicked, with the workers of evil, who speak peace with their neighbors while evil is in their hearts.4Give to them according to their work and according to the evil of their deeds; give to them according to the work of their hands; render them their due reward.5Because they do not regard the works of the LORD or the work of his hands, he will tear them down and build them up no more.6Blessed be the LORD! For he has heard the voice of my pleas for mercy.7The LORD is my strength and my shield; in him my heart trusts, and I am helped; my heart exults, and with my song I give thanks to him.8The LORD is the strength of his people; he is the saving refuge of his anointed.9Oh, save your people and bless your heritage! Be their shepherd and carry them forever.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — Lest You Be Silent to Me
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The worst thing a believer can face is not opposition but God’s silence, and the right answer to deceitful enemies is to hand them to God’s justice. David calls on the LORD, his rock, not to be deaf, because unheard he would be no better than the dead (v. 1), and he lifts his hands towards the innermost sanctuary as he pleads (v. 2). He asks not to be dragged off with the wicked, who speak peace to their neighbours while planning evil (v. 3). He asks God to give them back the work of their own hands (v. 4), because they pay no attention to what God has done, and God will tear them down (v. 5).
verseByVerse.theology: The thing he cannot survive is not the enemies but God's silence.

verseByVerse.quote: To you, O LORD, I call; my rock, be not deaf to me, lest, if you be silent to me, I become like those who go down to the pit. Hear the voice of my pleas for mercy, when I cry to you for help, when I lift up my hands toward your most holy sanctuary.
verseByVerse.commentary:
David fears God’s silence more than any enemy, for unheard he would be as good as dead.

Be not deaf to me. He fears not the enemies, who do not appear until verse 3, but God’s silence. He can survive being opposed; he cannot survive being ignored, and he says so in the first sentence. Yet even now he calls God “my rock”.

Like those who go down to the pit. Unanswered, he would be not merely sad but no different from the dead. If that is where you are, the psalm itself is a mercy: it gives words for the silence, and it ends in “he has heard”. The Son of God prayed the same way, “with loud cries and tears”, and he was heard (Hebrews 5:7).

Toward your most holy sanctuary. The ESV notes that the phrase is literally “your innermost sanctuary”: the most holy place, the one room in Israel no ordinary worshipper could ever enter. He stands outside and lifts his hands towards it. The gesture is the whole Old Testament in one picture: a man reaching towards a room with a curtain across it, the very curtain that tore when Christ died (Matthew 27:51). Through him believers may now “enter the holy places” (Hebrews 10:19).

Should Christians lift their hands in prayer? It is a biblical posture (Psalm 134:2; 1 Timothy 2:8), neither required nor forbidden. What matters is the heart lifted with them: “Let us lift up our hearts and hands to God in heaven” (Lamentations 3:41).

verseByVerse.quote: Do not drag me off with the wicked, with the workers of evil, who speak peace with their neighbors while evil is in their hearts. Give to them according to their work and according to the evil of their deeds; give to them according to the work of their hands; render them their due reward. Because they do not regard the works of the LORD or the work of his hands, he will tear them down and build them up no more.
verseByVerse.commentary:
David asks not to share the fate of smooth-tongued deceivers, and hands them to God to receive back their own work.

Who speak peace with their neighbors. One line describes a particular sin precisely: pleasant to your face, arranging your ruin behind your back. Jeremiah said the same of his generation: “with his mouth each speaks peace to his neighbor, but in his heart he plans an ambush” (Jeremiah 9:8). It is how the worst betrayal in history was carried out: “Greetings, Rabbi!” and a kiss from Judas (Matthew 26:49).

Give to them according to their work. Three times he asks the same thing, and it is narrower than it looks: not more than they have earned, nor a punishment of his own devising, but that their own work come back to them. That is the principle the New Testament states: God “will render to each one according to his works” (Romans 2:6). Handing a matter to God is not asking for a heavier sentence; it is refusing to set the sentence yourself.

They do not regard the works of the LORD. The root of it all is inattention: not defiance but indifference to what God has done. It is the quiet ruin of the fool of Psalm 14, who simply leaves God out. A man who never looks at what God has made or done ends up speaking peace while planning an ambush, because there is nothing above him to stop it.

May Christians pray “render them their due reward”? They may ask God for justice against those who will not repent, leaving vengeance to him (Romans 12:19), while praying first for their repentance (Matthew 5:44; see the introduction on the psalms that curse).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–9 — Blessed Be the LORD, for He Has Heard
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Prayer can end in praise before anything outward changes, and rescue opens into prayer for all God’s people. With nothing narrated in between, David blesses the LORD for hearing his pleas (v. 6). The LORD is his strength and shield; his heart trusts and is helped, and then exults in song (v. 7). The prayer widens at once: the LORD is the strength of his people and the saving refuge of his anointed king (v. 8). So David ends by asking God to save and bless his people, his own inheritance, and to be their shepherd and carry them for ever (v. 9).
verseByVerse.theology: Nothing is narrated between the pleading and the blessing, and the answered man immediately prays for everyone else.

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed be the LORD! For he has heard the voice of my pleas for mercy. The LORD is my strength and my shield; in him my heart trusts, and I am helped; my heart exults, and with my song I give thanks to him. The LORD is the strength of his people; he is the saving refuge of his anointed. Oh, save your people and bless your heritage! Be their shepherd and carry them forever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sure that God has heard, David blesses him, and widens his prayer to ask the LORD to shepherd and carry his whole people for ever.

Blessed be the LORD! The turn comes with nothing in between. The psalm does not tell us what happened. It is the same sudden turn as in Psalm 6 and Psalm 20: often the first thing that changes is not the situation but the praying man’s certainty that he has been heard.

In him my heart trusts. Watch the heart in verse 7: “in him my heart trusts”, and then “my heart exults”. Trust comes first, and the leaping joy after.

The saving refuge of his anointed. The anointed is David, Israel’s king, but the word is the one from which “Messiah” comes, and God proved the saving refuge of his Anointed in full when he heard his Son and raised him from the dead.

Be their shepherd and carry them forever. A man who has just been rescued turns round and prays for everyone else, as Psalm 25 did in its last verse. The words he reaches for are a shepherd’s. Carrying is what a shepherd does with the lamb that cannot keep up, and he asks God to do it for a whole nation, “forever”. Isaiah pictures God doing exactly that: “he will gather the lambs in his arms; he will carry them in his bosom” (Isaiah 40:11), and he promises, “even to your old age … I will carry and will save” (Isaiah 46:4). The Gospels show that shepherd in the flesh, laying the lost sheep on his shoulders and carrying it home rejoicing (Luke 15:5).

Textual note. In verse 8 most Hebrew manuscripts read “their strength”, while a few, with the Greek and Syriac, read “the strength of his people”, as the ESV does. Either way the psalm has widened from one man to a whole people.

28.title: Be Not Deaf to Me
28.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 28 closes a run of David’s prayers under pressure from deceitful enemies (Psalms 25–28). It takes up the fear of Psalm 26, not to be swept away with the wicked (Psalm 26:9), and like Psalm 27 it turns from urgent pleading to settled trust.

The message. What a believer dreads most is not his enemies but God’s silence, and he may tell God so. He can hand the deceitful over to God’s justice instead of taking revenge, and once he has prayed he may bless God for hearing before anything outward has changed. And the one who has been helped at once prays for all God’s people, asking the LORD to shepherd them and carry them for ever.

Why it was said. The psalm names no occasion, but its enemies are smooth-tongued plotters, the kind of treachery David met in Saul’s court and in Absalom’s revolt (see the introduction). As king he also prays for “his anointed” and for the people in his care (vv. 8–9), so the psalm became a prayer for the whole nation.

How the chapter makes its case. The psalm turns on one verse. First comes the plea (vv. 1–5): he begs God not to be deaf, lest he become like the dead (v. 1), and lifts his hands towards the inner sanctuary (v. 2); he asks not to be dragged off with those who speak peace and plan evil, and asks God to give them back their own work, since they ignore all that God has done (vv. 3–5). Then, with nothing narrated in between, comes the praise (vv. 6–9): “he has heard” (v. 6); trust comes first and joy follows (v. 7); and the prayer widens to the strength of God’s people and his anointed, ending with a shepherd’s plea to carry them for ever (vv. 8–9).

Where it leads. By promise and pattern. The LORD is “the saving refuge of his anointed” (v. 8), and the Anointed One, the Christ, prayed “with loud cries and tears” and was heard (Hebrews 5:7). He was betrayed by a man who spoke peace with a kiss (Matthew 26:49), and at his death the curtain before the most holy place, towards which David could only lift his hands, was torn in two (Matthew 27:51). And he is the shepherd of verse 9, who lays the lost sheep on his shoulders and carries it home (Luke 15:5).

For us. When God seems silent, keep calling him “my rock”, and tell him that his silence is what you fear most. Leave those who wrong you to his justice, and pray first for their repentance. And when he has helped you, do not stop at your own rescue: pray for his whole church, that the Good Shepherd would carry it to the end.
28.theology:
The dread in this psalm is God's silence rather than the enemy's success (v. 1). The prayer against the wicked asks only that wrongdoers receive their own work back (v. 4), and the root of their evil is not defiance but inattention to what God has done (v. 5).

The turn comes by assurance, not by a change of circumstance (v. 6); trust comes before joy (v. 7); and the rescued man at once prays for the whole people in a shepherd's words (v. 9; cf. Ps 23).
28.examples:
Some people can bear opposition far better than silence. David is one of them, and he gives words to anyone who feels that heaven has gone quiet.

Verse 7 puts trust before joy: my heart trusts, then my heart exults. Feelings often follow the decision rather than lead it.

And the last request, carry them, is what a shepherd does with the lamb that cannot keep up.

keyVerse.quote: Blessed be the LORD! For he has heard the voice of my pleas for mercy.
keyVerse.note: This is the hinge of the psalm. It answers verses 1–2 word for word, “the voice of my pleas for mercy”, and turns dread of God’s silence into praise before anything outward is said to have changed. The God who heard David heard his greater Son “with loud cries and tears” (Hebrews 5:7), and for his sake hears all who call on him.

28.reflection:
David fears God’s silence more than his enemies (v. 1). Have you known a time when God seemed silent? What does it mean that David still called God “my rock” while he waited?

Verse 3 describes people “who speak peace with their neighbors while evil is in their hearts”. How should a Christian respond to that kind of betrayal, and what does it mean to hand it to God instead of setting the sentence yourself (vv. 4–5; Romans 12:19)?

The psalm turns from pleading to praise in verse 6 without telling us what changed. How can we bless God for hearing us before we see the answer?

Once helped, David prays for all God’s people to be shepherded and carried for ever (v. 9). Who in your church needs carrying just now, and how can you pray for them, and help to carry them, this week?

29.text: A Psalm of David. 1Ascribe to the LORD, O heavenly beings, ascribe to the LORD glory and strength.2Ascribe to the LORD the glory due his name; worship the LORD in the splendor of holiness.3The voice of the LORD is over the waters; the God of glory thunders, the LORD, over many waters.4The voice of the LORD is powerful; the voice of the LORD is full of majesty.5The voice of the LORD breaks the cedars; the LORD breaks the cedars of Lebanon.6He makes Lebanon to skip like a calf, and Sirion like a young wild ox.7The voice of the LORD flashes forth flames of fire.8The voice of the LORD shakes the wilderness; the LORD shakes the wilderness of Kadesh.9The voice of the LORD makes the deer give birth and strips the forests bare, and in his temple all cry, "Glory!"10The LORD sits enthroned over the flood; the LORD sits enthroned as king forever.11May the LORD give strength to his people! May the LORD bless his people with peace!

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–2 — Ascribe to the LORD Glory
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Worship begins with God, not with us, and even heaven is told to give him what is his. David summons the heavenly beings, the court around God’s throne, and three times commands them to ascribe to the LORD glory and strength (vv. 1–2). To ascribe is to hand over what is already owed, the glory due his name, not to add anything to him. They are to worship in the splendour of holiness, dressed for an occasion that deserves the best. Before the psalm hears a single thunderclap, it has settled who is King, so that when the storm comes the reader knows whose voice it is.
verseByVerse.theology: The summons is not addressed to us at all: the angels are told to give God what is already his.

verseByVerse.quote: Ascribe to the LORD, O heavenly beings, ascribe to the LORD glory and strength. Ascribe to the LORD the glory due his name; worship the LORD in the splendor of holiness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before a word is said about the storm, heaven itself is told to give the LORD the glory that is already his.

O heavenly beings. The ones commanded to worship are not us but the court around God’s throne. A man on earth telling the angels what to do: presumption, were it not an invitation to join worship already going on in heaven.

Ascribe to the LORD. Three times. To ascribe is to hand over: not to invent praise or work up a feeling, but to give God what is already “due his name”. Worship is bookkeeping before it is emotion, putting the glory in the column where it belongs.

What glory is. The Hebrew word for glory, kabod, comes from a root meaning heavy. Something with glory has weight: it matters, it presses on you, it cannot be shrugged off. To give the LORD “the glory due his name” is to let him be as weighty in your life as he really is. Most of us hand the weight to something else, other people’s opinion, the bank balance, our own name, and then wonder why we feel crushed. The glory Moses asked to see (Exodus 33:18) came close at last in a person: “we have seen his glory, glory as of the only Son from the Father, full of grace and truth” (John 1:14). The weightiest One in the universe stooped to carry the weight of our sin. This week, when someone’s opinion feels heavier than God’s, say verse 2 to yourself, slowly. See Glory in the Theological Dictionary.

In the splendor of holiness. And the manner: dressed for it. Something is happening here that deserves the best clothes a person owns.

Uncertain wording. “Heavenly beings” is literally “sons of God” or “sons of might” (ESV note); most take it of the angels, a few of earthly rulers. “The splendor of holiness” may mean “in holy attire” (ESV note). Either way the mightiest must bow, and worship is a holy occasion.
verseByVerse.note: “Heavenly beings” is literally “sons of God” or “sons of might” (ESV note). The psalm may deliberately claim for the LORD the storm-power the Canaanites gave to Baal.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 3–9 — The Voice of the LORD Breaks the Cedars
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Nothing in creation can stand against the voice of the LORD. Seven times the psalm names it, as a thunderstorm builds over the waters (vv. 3–4), comes ashore to snap the cedars of Lebanon and make the northern mountains skip like calves (vv. 5–6), flashes with lightning (v. 7), and rolls south to shake the wilderness of Kadesh, stripping forests and startling the deer into giving birth (vv. 8–9). The storm crosses the whole land, and every part of it is claimed for the LORD rather than Baal. In the middle of the noise one line comes from somewhere else: in his temple, all cry, “Glory!”
verseByVerse.theology: A thunderstorm crosses the whole country, and the psalm hears one thing in it: God speaking.

verseByVerse.quote: The voice of the LORD is over the waters; the God of glory thunders, the LORD, over many waters. The voice of the LORD is powerful; the voice of the LORD is full of majesty. The voice of the LORD breaks the cedars; the LORD breaks the cedars of Lebanon. He makes Lebanon to skip like a calf, and Sirion like a young wild ox. The voice of the LORD flashes forth flames of fire. The voice of the LORD shakes the wilderness; the LORD shakes the wilderness of Kadesh. The voice of the LORD makes the deer give birth and strips the forests bare, and in his temple all cry, "Glory!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The storm that crosses the whole land is the LORD’s voice, and nothing in creation can stand against it; in his temple his people see it for what it is and cry, “Glory!”

The voice of the LORD. Seven times in seven verses. Count them as they come, because the repetition is the poem. A thunderstorm is tracked across the map: it builds out at sea (v. 3), comes ashore and hits the northern mountains (vv. 5–6), and rolls south into the desert (v. 8). Israel’s Canaanite neighbours praised Baal as the storm god whose voice was the thunder; the psalm, probably on purpose, gives every thunderclap to the LORD.

The cedars of Lebanon. The cedars of Lebanon were the prized timber of the ancient world, the wood kings imported for temples and palaces, the standard picture of what lasts. The storm snaps them. Then the mountains start behaving like livestock: Lebanon and Sirion, which is Mount Hermon, skip like a calf and a young ox. The most immovable things in the landscape are jumping about.

Flashes forth flames of fire. Lightning, the desert shaking, deer dropping their young early with the shock, forests stripped bare: terror and birth in the same line.

In his temple all cry, “Glory!” In the middle of the noise, one sentence from somewhere else. Outside there is chaos; inside the sanctuary the response is a single word. Those who see clearly do not duck; they say what they are seeing.

God’s voice as thunder. When the Father answered his Son, “I have glorified it, and I will glorify it again”, the crowd “that stood there and heard it said that it had thundered” (John 12:28–29). The voice that breaks cedars has now spoken in the Son: “See that you do not refuse him who is speaking” (Hebrews 12:25).

What it does not mean. Not that God is the storm, as the nations thought of Baal, or that every storm is a coded message. The LORD rules his creation; he is not part of it. Elijah found that he was not in the wind, the earthquake or the fire, and then came “the sound of a low whisper” (1 Kings 19:11–12).

Uncertain wording. “Makes the deer give birth” may instead mean “makes the oaks to shake” (ESV note), for the Hebrew words are very close. The first fits the birth imagery, the second the forests stripped bare.
verseByVerse.note: Kadesh is probably the wilderness of Kadesh in the far south, so the storm crosses the whole land from north to south.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The God whose voice is in the storm is not shaken by it, and he uses his power for his people. After the noise comes stillness: the LORD sits enthroned over the flood, the word Scripture otherwise uses only of Noah’s flood, and he reigns as King for ever (v. 10). The storm was never a rival; the one whose voice does all this has not stood up. Then the psalm turns from heaven and storm to his people, and ends with two gifts no one would predict after nine verses of thunder: strength, for the storm is real, and peace, for its Lord is on their side (v. 11).
verseByVerse.theology: The storm ends with God seated, and the last word of the psalm is peace.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD sits enthroned over the flood; the LORD sits enthroned as king forever. May the LORD give strength to his people! May the LORD bless his people with peace!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Above every storm, even the flood that once undid the world, the LORD sits as King for ever, and he uses that strength to give his people strength and peace.

The LORD sits enthroned over the flood. After nine verses of noise, stillness: the LORD seated on his throne. The word for flood is used elsewhere in the Bible only of Noah’s flood, the moment the world came apart, and God sat enthroned over that as King. So the storm in verses 3–9 was never a rival power. The cedars break, the mountains skip, and the one whose voice does it has not stood up.

Sitting in the stern. When Jesus woke in a boat on a stormy lake and spoke to the wind and the sea, his disciples asked the question this psalm answers: “Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?” (Mark 4:41). The voice that rules the waters had taken flesh and was sitting in the stern.

May the LORD bless his people with peace! Eleven verses of thunder, and the final word is peace: shalom, wholeness, everything in its place. Strength, then peace, and in that order: strength, because the storm is real and his people are in it; peace, because the one whose voice is in the storm is on their side. Whatever is breaking your cedars this month, he is seated, and what he intends for his people at the end of it is peace.

Uncertain wording. The lines of verse 11 can be read as prayers or as promises: the LORD will give strength, the LORD will bless (ESV note). Prayer to this King rests on his promise, so the difference is small.

29.title: The Voice of the LORD
29.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 28 began with David begging the LORD not to be silent (Psalm 28:1) and ended with a prayer that God would save and bless his people. Psalm 29 answers with the loudest psalm in the book: God is not silent, his voice thunders across the whole land, and it ends with that same blessing on his people.

The message. The LORD alone is King over every power in creation, and his voice is stronger than the most fearsome things we know, so heaven and earth must give him the glory due his name. Yet this overwhelming King turns his strength towards his people: the psalm that begins with glory in heaven ends with peace on earth.

Why it was said. Israel lived in a land that depended on the rains and among peoples who praised Baal, the Canaanite storm god, as the rider of the clouds whose voice was the thunder. The pull to credit the storm, the harvest and the future to him was constant. The psalm takes every thunderclap and gives it to the LORD.

How the chapter makes its case. It begins in heaven: the heavenly beings are told three times to ascribe glory and strength to the LORD and to worship him (vv. 1–2). Then the storm: seven times “the voice of the LORD” is heard as a thunderstorm builds over the sea, breaks the cedars and shakes the mountains in the north, and rolls south into the wilderness of Kadesh, while in his temple all cry, “Glory!” (vv. 3–9). Finally stillness: the LORD sits enthroned over the flood as King for ever, and the one with all this strength gives strength and peace to his people (vv. 10–11).

Where it leads. By the character of God revealed in Christ, and by pattern. The voice that rules the waters took flesh and spoke to the wind and the sea, and they obeyed him (Mark 4:39–41). When the Father spoke over his Son, the crowd said that it had thundered (John 12:28–29), and the risen Christ’s voice is “like the roar of many waters” (Revelation 1:15). Even the psalm’s shape, glory in heaven and peace for God’s people on earth, is what the angels sang over his birth (Luke 2:14), and he gives that peace to his own: “Peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you” (John 14:27).

For us. Whatever feels strongest in your life, illness, money, an enemy or your own fear, is weaker than the voice of the LORD, and that voice speaks to us now in his Son. Give him the weight he deserves, and ask him for what this psalm promises his people: strength for the storm, and peace at the end of it.
29.theology:
Worship is ascribing, handing over to God what is already his due (vv. 1-2), and human praise joins worship already going on in heaven.

The psalm hears a storm as God speaking (vv. 3-9), and the response in the temple is not panic but one word, Glory. God was enthroned over the deluge itself (v. 10), so the storm is never a rival power, and the psalm of thunder ends in peace (v. 11), with strength given for the storm his people are actually in.
29.examples:
Worship begins as giving God what is already his, before it is a feeling. A person can do that on a flat Sunday as truly as on a bright one.

The storm snaps the cedars kings imported for their palaces and sets the mountains skipping like calves. Even so, the one whose voice it is never stands up, and his last word is peace.

keyVerse.quote: The LORD sits enthroned over the flood; the LORD sits enthroned as king forever.
keyVerse.note: After nine verses of thunder, this is the still centre of the psalm: the God whose voice breaks cedars is seated, unshaken even by the flood that once undid the world. It explains both the call to give him glory (vv. 1–2) and the closing gift of strength and peace (v. 11), since only the King over the storm can give peace in it. The disciples saw this King sitting in the stern of their boat (Mark 4:41).

29.reflection:
The psalm’s first command is not to us but to heaven: “Ascribe to the LORD, O heavenly beings” (v. 1). What does it change about our worship on Sunday to know that we are joining something already going on around God’s throne?

“Glory” in Hebrew carries the idea of weight. What in your life is tempted to carry more weight than God, and what would it look like this week to give him “the glory due his name” (v. 2)?

Israel’s neighbours gave the storm and the harvest to Baal. What powers are people tempted to credit with control over their lives today, and how does verse 10 answer them?

The psalm ends not with thunder but with peace (v. 11). How do Jesus’ stilling of the storm (Mark 4:35–41) and his words in John 14:27 help someone who is in the middle of a storm now?

30.text: A Psalm of David. A song at the dedication of the temple. 1I will extol you, O LORD, for you have drawn me up and have not let my foes rejoice over me.2O LORD my God, I cried to you for help, and you have healed me.3O LORD, you have brought up my soul from Sheol; you restored me to life from among those who go down to the pit.4Sing praises to the LORD, O you his saints, and give thanks to his holy name.5For his anger is but for a moment, and his favor is for a lifetime. Weeping may tarry for the night, but joy comes with the morning.6As for me, I said in my prosperity, "I shall never be moved."7By your favor, O LORD, you made my mountain stand strong; you hid your face; I was dismayed.8To you, O LORD, I cry, and to the Lord I plead for mercy:9"What profit is there in my death, if I go down to the pit? Will the dust praise you? Will it tell of your faithfulness?10Hear, O LORD, and be merciful to me! O LORD, be my helper!"11You have turned for me my mourning into dancing; you have loosed my sackcloth and clothed me with gladness,12that my glory may sing your praise and not be silent. O LORD my God, I will give thanks to you forever!

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — Weeping May Tarry for the Night
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God rescues his people from the edge of death, and the right response is praise that draws others in. David begins with a vow to extol the LORD, who has drawn him up like a bucket from a well and not let his enemies gloat (v. 1). He cried for help and was healed; he was brought back from Sheol, the realm of the dead (vv. 2–3). Then he turns to God’s saints and asks for a choir (v. 4), because his own story has taught him something about God’s character: his anger is for a moment and his favour for a lifetime, and weeping, however long the night, is a guest who leaves when the morning comes (v. 5).
verseByVerse.theology: A rescued man does the arithmetic of God's dealings: a moment of anger against a lifetime of favour.

verseByVerse.quote: I will extol you, O LORD, for you have drawn me up and have not let my foes rejoice over me. O LORD my God, I cried to you for help, and you have healed me. O LORD, you have brought up my soul from Sheol; you restored me to life from among those who go down to the pit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God drew David up from the edge of death and healed him, and David vows to praise him.

You have drawn me up. The word is used for drawing water: a bucket dropped into the dark and hauled back up. Three times in three verses the movement is upward: drawn up, healed, brought up from Sheol, the realm of the dead. Whatever the illness was, he had been close enough to death to use the language of the grave.

At the dedication of the temple. The heading raises a plain question: David did not live to see the temple built. The Hebrew says simply “the house”, and some think it meant the temple site David prepared (1 Chronicles 22:1) or his own palace. More likely his song of personal rescue was taken up when the house was dedicated: one man’s recovery became everybody’s hymn.

What it does not mean. Not that every believer who prays will recover. God heals in answer to prayer, but not always (2 Corinthians 12:7–9); those he does not raise from the sickbed, Christ will raise from the grave.

Textual note. The ESV notes another reading in verse 3: “to life, that I should not go down to the pit”.

verseByVerse.quote: Sing praises to the LORD, O you his saints, and give thanks to his holy name. For his anger is but for a moment, and his favor is for a lifetime. Weeping may tarry for the night, but joy comes with the morning.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s anger towards his own lasts a moment and his favour a lifetime, so all his people should sing.

Give thanks to his holy name. He wants a choir. The ESV notes the last phrase is literally “to the memorial of his holiness”, pointing back to the name God gave Moses at the bush to be remembered through all generations (Exodus 3:15). What he wants sung is not his own recovery but the character of the God who did it.

His anger is but for a moment. Two comparisons, and both are about proportion: a moment against a lifetime, a night against a morning. Neither half is denied: the anger was real and the weeping lasted all night. It measures them against each other, which nobody can do at three in the morning without help.

Weeping may tarry for the night. “Tarry” is a gentle word: weeping is a guest who stays the night, not a resident. And “joy comes with the morning” does not promise that every trouble ends by breakfast, but that in God’s dealings with his people the night has a morning attached. For the Christian that is not optimism but arithmetic: “this light momentary affliction” against “an eternal weight of glory”, as Paul does the same sum (2 Corinthians 4:17).

Their morning came early. Jesus said the same to his disciples on the night before he died: “You will be sorrowful, but your sorrow will turn into joy” (John 16:20). Their night was the Friday and the Sabbath after it; their morning came early on the first day of the week, at an empty tomb. God’s anger towards his people can last only a moment because its full weight fell on Christ.

Uncertain wording. Verse 5 is compressed in Hebrew: “a moment in his anger, life in his favour”. The ESV reads “for a lifetime”; older versions read “in his favour is life”. Either way his favour has the longest word.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–12 — You Have Turned My Mourning into Dancing
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Comfort can make a believer forget God, and God’s hidden face can bring him back. David tells the story honestly. In prosperity he had boasted that he would never be moved, forgetting that his strong mountain stood only by God’s favour (vv. 6–7a). Then God hid his face and he collapsed (v. 7b). From the edge of the pit he pleaded, arguing boldly that the dead cannot praise God or tell of his faithfulness (vv. 8–10). And God answered: mourning turned to dancing, sackcloth untied and gladness put on, so that David’s whole being would sing God’s praise and never be silent, but give thanks for ever (vv. 11–12).
verseByVerse.theology: At the centre of the psalm is an honest confession: comfort had made a believer forget where his strength came from.

verseByVerse.quote: As for me, I said in my prosperity, "I shall never be moved." By your favor, O LORD, you made my mountain stand strong; you hid your face; I was dismayed. To you, O LORD, I cry, and to the Lord I plead for mercy: "What profit is there in my death, if I go down to the pit? Will the dust praise you? Will it tell of your faithfulness? Hear, O LORD, and be merciful to me! O LORD, be my helper!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Prosperity made David forget that his security was God’s gift, until God hid his face and he pleaded from the edge of the pit.

I shall never be moved. The confession at the heart of the psalm is unusually honest. When everything was going well he said, “I shall never be moved”, almost exactly the creed of the wicked man of Psalm 10, who has decided God will never call him to account (Psalm 10:6). Comfort had quietly taught a believer to talk like a fool.

By your favor, O LORD. Even as he confesses he gives the credit: the mountain stood strong only by God’s favour. That is what he had forgotten: the stability he boasted of was a gift, and he had begun to hold it as a possession.

Why does comfort make God feel unnecessary? Sociologists have noticed a pattern across many countries: as people grow richer and safer, religious belief tends to fade. Pippa Norris and Ronald Inglehart, in Sacred and Secular, argued that a sense of security, more than any argument, is what makes faith feel optional. Moses predicted it: when you have eaten and are full and have built good houses, “take care lest you forget the LORD your God” (Deuteronomy 8:11). And this psalm confesses it from the inside. Comfort does not refute God; it hides him, the way city lights hide the stars. But security is only ever on loan, and illness, loss or old age eventually call it in.
