The mercy in this psalm is that God let David’s mountain shake so that he could find his footing in God again; and the gospel’s mercy is that Christ became poor, so that we might find our riches in him.

You hid your face; I was dismayed. Seven words explain the whole illness. God withdrew the sense of his presence, and the man who could not be moved collapsed. If God has gone quiet for you after a stretch of things going well, this psalm has been there, and it ends in dancing. The Son knew a darker hiding of the Father’s face, on the cross (Mark 15:34), so that no believer’s night is without a morning. If the darkness lasts and sleep or hope begin to fail, talk to a pastor or biblical counsellor and see a doctor too; medicine is no failure of faith.

What profit is there in my death? His argument is the one from Psalm 6:5: a dead man is one voice fewer in the choir. The ESV notes the first phrase is literally “in my blood”, and that “the pit” may be rendered “corruption”. It is a bold way to pray, and God does not rebuke it; he answers it.

Does this deny life after death? The psalmist speaks of this life: in the grave a man can no longer praise God before the congregation. Other psalms look past it to God’s presence (Psalms 16:10–11; 49:15; 73:24), and in Christ that hope is made clear (2 Timothy 1:10).

verseByVerse.quote: You have turned for me my mourning into dancing; you have loosed my sackcloth and clothed me with gladness, that my glory may sing your praise and not be silent. O LORD my God, I will give thanks to you forever!
verseByVerse.commentary:
God turned David’s mourning into dancing, so that his whole being would praise God for ever.

You have turned for me my mourning into dancing. Two physical pictures. Mourning turned to dancing: the same body, doing the opposite thing. And the sackcloth, the rough cloth of grief (see Mourning Customs), is untied and taken off him like a coat, and gladness put on instead. He did not dress himself. Isaiah promised the same change of clothes to people in ashes: “a beautiful headdress instead of ashes, the oil of gladness instead of mourning” (Isaiah 61:3), in the passage Jesus read in Nazareth and said was fulfilled that day (Luke 4:16–21).

That my glory may sing your praise. God rescued him so that he would sing. He asked in verse 9 whether dust could praise God, and the answer he has been given is a voice that will not be silenced. “Not be silent”, and then “forever”: a word a man in a sickbed has no right to use, unless the God who hauled him up out of the well intends to keep him.

Uncertain wording. “My glory” probably means the whole self, as in Psalm 16:9, where the same Hebrew lies behind “my whole being”; some take it as the soul or the tongue.

30.title: Joy Comes with the Morning
30.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 29 ended with the LORD blessing his people with peace; Psalm 30 shows what that looks like in one man’s life. David has come back from the edge of death, and he cannot keep the thanks to himself.

The message. When God disciplines his people, his anger lasts a moment and his favour a lifetime: the night of weeping has a morning attached to it. Prosperity tempts us to forget that every good thing is a gift, and God may hide his face to bring us back. When he rescues, it is so that we will praise him, and go on praising him for ever.

Why it was said. David had been gravely ill, close enough to death to speak of Sheol and the pit, after a season in which comfort had made him careless (vv. 6–7). The heading shows that his personal song was later sung by the whole people at the dedication of “the house” (see the note on vv. 1–3).

How the chapter makes its case. It begins with the rescue: David praises the God who drew him up, healed him and brought him back from Sheol (vv. 1–3). He calls all God’s saints to join him, because God’s anger is for a moment and his favour for a lifetime, and joy comes with the morning (vv. 4–5). Then he tells the story honestly: in prosperity he had said, “I shall never be moved”, until God hid his face (vv. 6–7), and he pleaded from the edge of the pit (vv. 8–10). It ends where it began, in praise: God turned his mourning into dancing so that he would never be silent (vv. 11–12).

Where it leads. By pattern, and by the need it exposes. David was drawn up from the edge of the grave; Jesus went all the way down into death and was raised, “because it was not possible for him to be held by it” (Acts 2:24). God hid his face from David for a moment; on the cross he turned it from his Son, who cried, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Mark 15:34), so that for his people the anger is only for a moment and the favour for ever. And the disciples learned the psalm’s pattern on the first Easter: a night of weeping, and joy in the morning (John 16:20).

For us. If things are going well, hold them as gifts, not possessions, and thank God for them before he has to remind you whose they are. If you are in the night, it is not the end of the story for anyone in Christ: the morning is coming, and the one who promises it has already risen.
30.theology:
The psalm measures God's dealings by proportion: a moment of anger against a lifetime of favour, one night's weeping against the morning (v. 5). Neither half is denied; they are weighed.

At its centre is a confession that prosperity had made a believer forget that his security was a gift (vv. 6-7). He argues for rescue on the ground that the dead do not praise (v. 9; cf. 6:5), and God answers rather than rebukes. The change of clothes is God's doing (v. 11), and its purpose is praise that does not fall silent (v. 12).
30.examples:
Weeping, the psalm says, is a guest who stays the night, not a resident. Nobody can weigh one night against a lifetime at three in the morning without help, which is why it is written down.

The danger in this psalm is not hardship but ease: a comfortable season in which God's gifts begin to feel like possessions. And God rescued him so that he would sing.

keyVerse.quote: For his anger is but for a moment, and his favor is for a lifetime. Weeping may tarry for the night, but joy comes with the morning.
keyVerse.note: This verse is the lesson David learned in his illness, and it is why he calls the whole congregation to sing (v. 4). It does not deny the anger or the weeping, but it sets them in proportion: a moment against a lifetime, a night against a morning. For believers the proportion is secured by Christ, who bore the full weight of God’s anger and rose early on the first day of the week.

30.reflection:
David says that in his prosperity he thought, “I shall never be moved” (v. 6). In what ways does comfort or success make God feel less necessary to you, and what helps you hold good things as gifts rather than possessions?

“You hid your face; I was dismayed” (v. 7). Have you known a time when God seemed silent? What does this psalm, and Christ’s cry on the cross, say to someone in that place now?

Verse 5 sets a moment against a lifetime and a night against a morning. How does the resurrection change the way a Christian measures present sorrow (compare 2 Corinthians 4:17)?

David wants a choir, not a private thank-you (vv. 4, 12). Whose story of God’s rescue could you tell this week, and how can your church make room for people to give thanks in public?

31.text: To the choirmaster. A Psalm of David. 1In you, O LORD, do I take refuge; let me never be put to shame; in your righteousness deliver me!2Incline your ear to me; rescue me speedily! Be a rock of refuge for me, a strong fortress to save me!3For you are my rock and my fortress; and for your name's sake you lead me and guide me;4you take me out of the net they have hidden for me, for you are my refuge.5Into your hand I commit my spirit; you have redeemed me, O LORD, faithful God.6I hate those who pay regard to worthless idols, but I trust in the LORD.7I will rejoice and be glad in your steadfast love, because you have seen my affliction; you have known the distress of my soul,8and you have not delivered me into the hand of the enemy; you have set my feet in a broad place.9Be gracious to me, O LORD, for I am in distress; my eye is wasted from grief; my soul and my body also.10For my life is spent with sorrow, and my years with sighing; my strength fails because of my iniquity, and my bones waste away.11Because of all my adversaries I have become a reproach, especially to my neighbors, and an object of dread to my acquaintances; those who see me in the street flee from me.12I have been forgotten like one who is dead; I have become like a broken vessel.13For I hear the whispering of many— terror on every side!— as they scheme together against me, as they plot to take my life.14But I trust in you, O LORD; I say, "You are my God."15My times are in your hand; rescue me from the hand of my enemies and from my persecutors!16Make your face shine on your servant; save me in your steadfast love!17O LORD, let me not be put to shame, for I call upon you; let the wicked be put to shame; let them go silently to Sheol.18Let the lying lips be mute, which speak insolently against the righteous in pride and contempt.19Oh, how abundant is your goodness, which you have stored up for those who fear you and worked for those who take refuge in you, in the sight of the children of mankind!20In the cover of your presence you hide them from the plots of men; you store them in your shelter from the strife of tongues.21Blessed be the LORD, for he has wondrously shown his steadfast love to me when I was in a besieged city.22I had said in my alarm, "I am cut off from your sight." But you heard the voice of my pleas for mercy when I cried to you for help.23Love the LORD, all you his saints! The LORD preserves the faithful but abundantly repays the one who acts in pride.24Be strong, and let your heart take courage, all you who wait for the LORD!

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — Into Your Hand I Commit My Spirit
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The safest place for a threatened life is God’s hand. David runs to the LORD as his refuge, rock and fortress, and asks for rescue quickly, appealing to God’s own righteousness and the honour of his name (vv. 1–4). Then he says the sentence Jesus would say as he died: “Into your hand I commit my spirit”, handing his life over for safekeeping to the faithful God who has redeemed him (v. 5). He turns from worthless idols to trust the LORD (v. 6), and rejoices before the trouble is over, because God has seen his affliction, known his distress and given him room to stand (vv. 7–8).
verseByVerse.theology: The verse Jesus died saying is, in its own psalm, a living man's daily act of handing himself over.

verseByVerse.quote: In you, O LORD, do I take refuge; let me never be put to shame; in your righteousness deliver me! Incline your ear to me; rescue me speedily! Be a rock of refuge for me, a strong fortress to save me! For you are my rock and my fortress; and for your name's sake you lead me and guide me; you take me out of the net they have hidden for me, for you are my refuge. Into your hand I commit my spirit; you have redeemed me, O LORD, faithful God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
David runs to God as his rock and fortress, appeals to God’s own righteousness, and puts his whole life into God’s hand for safekeeping.

Rescue me speedily! The opening is all stone: rock, refuge, fortress. And in the middle, one word that shows how bad things are: “speedily”. He is not asking for eventual help.

In your righteousness deliver me. We expect God’s righteousness to be what a guilty person fears. Yet this man, who will admit that his strength fails “because of my iniquity” (v. 10), appeals to God’s righteousness to save him. In the Psalms God’s righteousness is his being true to himself and to his word, and he has promised to rescue those who take refuge in him. Isaiah puts the two words side by side: “a righteous God and a Savior” (Isaiah 45:21). How can a just God rescue the guilty and stay just? The answer is a person. Our sin was judged in Christ, so God’s righteousness now stands on the side of everyone who trusts him: “we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous” (1 John 2:1). When your conscience accuses you, do not argue your record. Pray this line, and lean on his.

Into your hand I commit my spirit. This is the sentence the world knows, because it is the last thing Jesus said before he died: “Father, into your hands I commit my spirit!” (Luke 23:46). He prefaced it with “Father” and said the rest almost exactly as it stands here. Stephen, being stoned, prayed it to Jesus himself: “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit” (Acts 7:59).

You have redeemed me, O LORD, faithful God. But read it where it sits. In its own psalm this is not a dying man’s line: the writer goes on living for nineteen more verses, and the next thing he says is that God has redeemed him, past tense, already done. “Commit” is the word for depositing something valuable with someone you trust, handing over a purse for safekeeping. So the verse is first a living act (I put my life in your hands this morning), and only then a way to die. Peter tells suffering Christians to do exactly this: “let those who suffer according to God’s will entrust their souls to a faithful Creator while doing good” (1 Peter 4:19). Learning the sentence now is how it will be ready on our lips at the end.
verseByVerse.note: Terror on every side (v. 13) became a byword in Jeremiah, who uses it again and again (Jer 6:25; 20:3, 10; 46:5).

verseByVerse.quote: I hate those who pay regard to worthless idols, but I trust in the LORD. I will rejoice and be glad in your steadfast love, because you have seen my affliction; you have known the distress of my soul, and you have not delivered me into the hand of the enemy; you have set my feet in a broad place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Turning from idols to the LORD, David is glad before the rescue comes, because God has seen and known his distress.

I hate those who pay regard to worthless idols. This is a refusal to share in idolatry and its works, not personal spite. The idols are literally “vanities of emptiness”; Jonah uses almost the same phrase in his prayer from the fish (Jonah 2:8). The Christian loves idolaters and calls them to turn “from idols to serve the living and true God” (1 Thessalonians 1:9).

You have seen my affliction. Two verbs are the reason he can be glad in the middle of trouble: you have seen, you have known. The trouble is not yet mended, but it is seen and known. A great deal of what a suffering person actually wants is contained in those two words, and they are given before any rescue is.

You have set my feet in a broad place. The opposite of the tight place of distress (Psalm 4:1); as in Psalm 18:19, he has room to stand.

Textual note. The ESV notes a textual question in the first line: most Hebrew manuscripts have “I hate”, while one manuscript and the ancient versions read “You hate”. Either way, worthless idols stand on one side and trust in the LORD on the other.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–18 — I Have Become Like a Broken Vessel
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Faith does not need to pretend, and it can say “But I trust in you” in the middle of the worst. David describes long trouble without tidying it up: grief in eye, soul and body, years of sighing, strength failing partly through his own sin (vv. 9–10). He has become a disgrace to his neighbours, forgotten like the dead, a broken pot, while enemies whisper and plot (vv. 11–13). Then the turn: “But I trust in you, O LORD”, and the words that have carried so many: “My times are in your hand” (vv. 14–15). So he asks for rescue, for God’s face to shine, and for the lying lips to be silenced (vv. 16–18).
verseByVerse.theology: The most complete description of social shame in the Psalter, answered by six words about whose hand holds the clock.

verseByVerse.quote: Be gracious to me, O LORD, for I am in distress; my eye is wasted from grief; my soul and my body also. For my life is spent with sorrow, and my years with sighing; my strength fails because of my iniquity, and my bones waste away. Because of all my adversaries I have become a reproach, especially to my neighbors, and an object of dread to my acquaintances; those who see me in the street flee from me. I have been forgotten like one who is dead; I have become like a broken vessel. For I hear the whispering of many— terror on every side!— as they scheme together against me, as they plot to take my life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
David holds nothing back about long trouble: body and soul worn out, partly by his own sin, neighbours avoiding him, enemies plotting.

My eye is wasted from grief. This is one of the fullest descriptions in the Psalter of what long trouble does to a person, and it does not separate body from soul. The eye goes first, then the whole frame. “Years”, not days: this has been going on. And he does not tidy up the cause: “my strength fails because of my iniquity”. Some of what is crushing him is his own doing, and he says so without despairing.

Especially to my neighbors. Scripture takes social pain as seriously as physical. He has become an embarrassment, worst of all to the people closest in, whose doors he passes every day. Acquaintances cross the road. Two images finish it: “forgotten like one who is dead”, which is what it feels like when people stop asking how you are; and “like a broken vessel”, a cracked pot, no longer good for anything, swept up and thrown out.

Terror on every side! Jeremiah would use the same cry about the men waiting for him to stumble (Jeremiah 20:10). The whispering is the worst of it: not a public accusation he could answer, but a murmur he can hear and cannot address.

For anyone in long trouble. Anyone who has been through a public disgrace, a long illness, a divorce, a scandal true or false, knows these verses from the inside, and it matters that they stand in the Bible unresolved. The one who would pray this psalm’s fifth verse on the cross knew this part too: the leaders “plotted together” to kill him (Matthew 26:4), and on the night of his arrest his friends fled.

What it does not mean. Not that every illness or sorrow is caused by the sufferer’s sin; Jesus denied that of the man born blind (John 9:3). David knew his share in his trouble; many carry trouble that is not their fault. For both the way through is “But I trust in you” (v. 14).

verseByVerse.quote: But I trust in you, O LORD; I say, "You are my God." My times are in your hand; rescue me from the hand of my enemies and from my persecutors! Make your face shine on your servant; save me in your steadfast love! O LORD, let me not be put to shame, for I call upon you; let the wicked be put to shame; let them go silently to Sheol. Let the lying lips be mute, which speak insolently against the righteous in pride and contempt.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the middle of the whispering David says, “You are my God”, puts every season of his life into God’s hand, and still asks for rescue.

But I trust in you, O LORD. This is said straight after the whispering, not after it stopped. And then six words that have carried more people through more than almost any others in the book: “My times are in your hand.”

My times are in your hand. Not my life in general: my times. The plural is the point: this stretch and the next, the waiting and the ending of it, the years of sighing in verse 10 and whatever comes after. All of it is held, and by the same hand he put his spirit into in verse 5. The hand that has his spirit also has his calendar.

Anxiety: what control feels like from the inside. Modern life gives us more control than any generation has had: we schedule, insure, track, plan and optimise. And many of us are more anxious than ever. That is not a coincidence. Control promises safety, and the more we lean on it the more every unplanned thing feels like a threat. Anxiety is often what control feels like from the inside, when we notice how little of life it reaches: a diagnosis, a grown child’s choices, a phone call at night. The psalm does not tell the anxious to plan harder or stop caring. It moves the calendar into another hand. “My times are in your hand” is not resignation but relief, because the hand belongs to the “faithful God” of verse 5. And the Christian knows what that hand looks like: it was pierced, and the one it belongs to said that not a sparrow falls to the ground apart from the Father (Matthew 10:29). People who have handed over their times still make plans. They simply hold them loosely, and sleep.

Rescue me from the hand of my enemies. Trusting God with his times does not stop him asking for a change in them. The very next clause is “rescue me”. Submission and petition are not rivals.

Let the lying lips be mute. The prayer against the enemies is aimed at their mouths: the whispering campaign of verse 13 silenced, and the shame he is carrying transferred to where it belongs. He asks a just God for it rather than taking it into his own hands (Romans 12:19). The one who prayed verse 5 on the cross also prayed, “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do” (Luke 23:34). We may ask God to silence lies and judge evil, and in the same breath pray for the liars to be forgiven.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–24 — How Abundant Is Your Goodness
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s goodness to those who trust him is greater than their fears, and he hears even the prayers they thought were lost. David praises the abundant goodness God has stored up for those who fear him and shows openly, and the shelter of his presence from the strife of tongues (vv. 19–20). He tells how God showed him steadfast love when he was besieged, though in his alarm he had said, “I am cut off from your sight” (vv. 21–22). So he turns to the whole congregation: love the LORD, who preserves the faithful and repays the proud, and be strong and take courage, all who wait for him (vv. 23–24).
verseByVerse.theology: God had already heard the prayer the man thought was wasted.

verseByVerse.quote: Oh, how abundant is your goodness, which you have stored up for those who fear you and worked for those who take refuge in you, in the sight of the children of mankind! In the cover of your presence you hide them from the plots of men; you store them in your shelter from the strife of tongues. Blessed be the LORD, for he has wondrously shown his steadfast love to me when I was in a besieged city. I had said in my alarm, "I am cut off from your sight." But you heard the voice of my pleas for mercy when I cried to you for help. Love the LORD, all you his saints! The LORD preserves the faithful but abundantly repays the one who acts in pride. Be strong, and let your heart take courage, all you who wait for the LORD!
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s goodness is greater than David’s fears: he heard even the prayer David thought was lost, so all his people may take courage.

Which you have stored up. Two kinds of storing. God has stored up goodness, a reserve laid by and not all of it issued yet, and he stores his people, the same word, in a shelter. The goodness is kept safe, and so are the people.

In the sight of the children of mankind! God does not only do good to his people; at some point he does it where everyone can see. The man whose neighbours crossed the street in verse 11 is promised something just as public: God’s kindness to him, shown in daylight where those neighbours can see it.

From the strife of tongues. Not the strife of armies but of tongues, the damage done in conversations you are not present at. And the shelter from it is “the cover of your presence”: not a defence you mount but a place you are put.

I am cut off from your sight. One of the most reassuring confessions in the Psalter. In his panic he said the worst thing: God is not looking at me any more. He was wrong. “But you heard.” God was listening to the very prayer the man had decided was not being heard. Only one person has ever truly been cut off from God’s sight, the Son on the cross, “cut off out of the land of the living” (Isaiah 53:8), and he was cut off so that those who trust him never will be.

The LORD preserves the faithful. The reason given is a pair: God “preserves the faithful” and “abundantly repays the one who acts in pride”. Both halves are needed. Without the first, faithfulness looks pointless; without the second, arrogance looks as if it works.

Be strong, and let your heart take courage. The psalm ends almost as Psalm 27 ended, turning outwards. A man who has been avoided in the street tells the whole congregation to love God and take courage. The command is the one he has just obeyed himself, and it rests on what he has just been given: God “has wondrously shown his steadfast love” to him. God gives the reason for courage before he commands it.

Uncertain wording. “In a besieged city” (v. 21) may be literal, as when David was nearly trapped in the walled town of Keilah (1 Samuel 23:7–13), or a picture of being hemmed in on every side. “In my alarm” (v. 22) may also be rendered “in my haste” (ESV note): either the panic of fear or a rash conclusion. Both fit what he confesses.

31.title: My Times Are in Your Hand
31.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 30 gave thanks after the rescue; Psalm 31 prays from inside the trouble, swinging between pleading and trust more than once. It ends almost as Psalm 27 ended, telling everyone who waits for the LORD to be strong and take courage.

The message. When everything is against you, enemies, neighbours, your own body and your own past, you may put your life, and every season of it, into God’s hand, because he is the faithful God who sees, hears and redeems. Fear says, “I am cut off from your sight”; faith says, “You are my God”, and God hears even the prayer we thought he had ignored.

Why it was said. David writes as a hunted and slandered man, plotted against, avoided in the street, worn down in body and aware that some of it is his own fault (vv. 10–13), and at one point hemmed in “in a besieged city” (v. 21). The psalm gave Israel words for every long trouble, and Jeremiah later made its cry, “terror on every side”, his own (Jeremiah 20:10).

How the chapter makes its case. First, refuge: David runs to God as rock and fortress, commits his spirit into his hand, and rejoices that God has seen his affliction (vv. 1–8). Then the full account of the trouble: grief in body and soul, disgrace among neighbours, the whispering of enemies (vv. 9–13). Against it he sets the turning point: “But I trust in you, O LORD… My times are in your hand”, with a plea that the lying lips be silenced (vv. 14–18). Last comes praise: God’s goodness is stored up for those who fear him, he heard the prayer David had given up on, so let all his saints love him and take courage (vv. 19–24).

Where it leads. By pattern fulfilled in Christ, who made this psalm his own. His last words on the cross were verse 5, with one word added: “Father, into your hands I commit my spirit!” (Luke 23:46). He lived verses 11–13, plotted against by the leaders and deserted by his friends, and he was truly cut off, “cut off out of the land of the living” (Isaiah 53:8), so that no one who trusts him will ever be. Because he entrusted himself to his Father and was raised, his people can say verse 5 and verse 15 with full confidence, as Stephen did (Acts 7:59).

For us. Learn verse 5 as a morning prayer, so that it is ready on your lips at the end. When you are anxious, say verse 15 and mean it: your times, this stretch and the next, are held by a pierced hand. And if you have said in your alarm that God has stopped listening, read verse 22 again.
31.theology:
Verse 5 is a living man's daily act of trust before it is a dying man's last word, and the New Testament uses it both ways. God's seeing and knowing (v. 7) are given before any rescue.

Social shame is treated as seriously as bodily pain (vv. 9-13), and the part caused by his own sin is admitted without despair (v. 10). My times are in your hand (v. 15) does not stop him asking for those times to change: submission and petition are not rivals. And God heard the prayer the man had written off (v. 22).
31.examples:
Commit is the word for handing a purse to someone you trust. Learning to say verse 5 each morning is how it will be ready on our lips at the end.

Anyone who has been avoided after a disgrace or a long illness will find themselves in verses 9-13: forgotten like the dead, a cracked pot, the subject of whispers they cannot answer.

And anyone who has prayed while sure it was pointless has verse 22 for company. Being sure you are unheard is not evidence that you are.

keyVerse.quote: My times are in your hand; rescue me from the hand of my enemies and from my persecutors!
keyVerse.note: Spoken straight after the whispering and the plots (v. 13), this verse is the hinge of the psalm, where lament turns to trust. Every season of David’s life is held by the same hand into which he committed his spirit (v. 5), the hand into which Jesus committed his own spirit as he died (Luke 23:46). Trust does not stop the prayer for rescue; it gives it somewhere to go.

31.reflection:
Jesus died with verse 5 on his lips, yet in the psalm it is first a prayer for living (“you have redeemed me”). What would it look like to say “Into your hand I commit my spirit” at the start of an ordinary day?

Verses 9–13 describe grief, shame and isolation without resolving them. Why is it a help that such words are in the Bible? How could you or your church be a neighbour to someone who feels “forgotten like one who is dead” (v. 12)?

“My times are in your hand” (v. 15). What are you anxious about at the moment, and how does handing your times to God differ from simply giving up planning or caring?

David admits he said, “I am cut off from your sight”, and was wrong (v. 22). When have you concluded that God was not listening? How does Christ being cut off for us (Isaiah 53:8) answer that fear?

32.text: A Maskil of David. 1Blessed is the one whose transgression is forgiven, whose sin is covered.2Blessed is the man against whom the LORD counts no iniquity, and in whose spirit there is no deceit.3For when I kept silent, my bones wasted away through my groaning all day long.4For day and night your hand was heavy upon me; my strength was dried up as by the heat of summer. Selah5I acknowledged my sin to you, and I did not cover my iniquity; I said, "I will confess my transgressions to the LORD," and you forgave the iniquity of my sin. Selah6Therefore let everyone who is godly offer prayer to you at a time when you may be found; surely in the rush of great waters, they shall not reach him.7You are a hiding place for me; you preserve me from trouble; you surround me with shouts of deliverance. Selah8I will instruct you and teach you in the way you should go; I will counsel you with my eye upon you.9Be not like a horse or a mule, without understanding, which must be curbed with bit and bridle, or it will not stay near you.10Many are the sorrows of the wicked, but steadfast love surrounds the one who trusts in the LORD.11Be glad in the LORD, and rejoice, O righteous, and shout for joy, all you upright in heart!

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Forgiveness is the deepest happiness there is, and it comes only by confession. The psalm opens with two beatitudes for the forgiven, using three words for sin and three for its removal: forgiven, covered, not counted, for the person who no longer pretends (vv. 1–2). Then David tells how he learned it. While he kept silent his body wasted away and God’s hand lay heavy on him day and night, drying him up like summer heat (vv. 3–4). When at last he acknowledged his sin and stopped covering it, saying, “I will confess”, God forgave the iniquity of his sin (v. 5). What he stopped covering, God covered.
verseByVerse.theology: There are two ways to deal with sin, covering it yourself or letting God cover it, and the psalm has tried both.

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed is the one whose transgression is forgiven, whose sin is covered. Blessed is the man against whom the LORD counts no iniquity, and in whose spirit there is no deceit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The truly blessed person is not the one who has never sinned but the one whose sin God has forgiven, covered and does not count.

Blessed is the one whose transgression is forgiven. The Psalter’s first word was “blessed”, of the man who delights in God’s law (Psalm 1:1). Here is the other blessedness, the one most of us need first: not the happiness of the man who has kept the rules but of the man who has broken them and been forgiven.

Three words for sin. They cover the ground between them. Transgression is rebellion, crossing a line on purpose. Sin is missing the mark, falling short of what you were made for. Iniquity is the crookedness in a man, the bend in the timber.

Whose sin is covered. And three words for the remedy, which are better still. Forgiven: the weight lifted off. Covered: put out of sight, and watch who does the covering, because verse 5 will say what happens when a man covers his own. And “counts no iniquity” is an accountant’s word: the debt is not entered in the column.

Paul’s use of these verses. Paul builds an argument on these two verses. Having said that God “justifies the ungodly” (Romans 4:5), he calls David as his witness: “Blessed are those whose lawless deeds are forgiven, and whose sins are covered; blessed is the man against whom the Lord will not count his sin” (Romans 4:7–8). What he draws out is the silence in the verses: nothing at all is said about what the man did to deserve it. Justification by faith (being counted righteous by God through trusting him, not by earning it) is not a doctrine the church invented late; it is what the Old Testament sings. And Paul ends the argument by saying why God can leave the sin out of the column: Christ “was delivered up for our trespasses and raised for our justification” (Romans 4:25). The debt was entered against him.

In whose spirit there is no deceit. The last clause adds the one thing required: not sinlessness (there is none of that in this psalm), but the end of pretending.
verseByVerse.note: Maskil, in the heading, is probably a musical or liturgical term; it may mean a psalm that teaches, which suits verse 8.

verseByVerse.quote: For when I kept silent, my bones wasted away through my groaning all day long. For day and night your hand was heavy upon me; my strength was dried up as by the heat of summer. Selah I acknowledged my sin to you, and I did not cover my iniquity; I said, "I will confess my transgressions to the LORD," and you forgave the iniquity of my sin. Selah
verseByVerse.commentary:
While David hid his sin, God’s hand pressed on him until his strength dried up; the moment he resolved to confess, God forgave.

His own story. This is autobiography: he knows what unconfessed sin costs because he paid it. The psalm does not name the sin; if, as many think, it belongs to the months after Bathsheba, the silence may have lasted the best part of a year.

For when I kept silent. The silence was not peaceful. “Groaning all day long”: he was making plenty of noise, just not the one sentence that would have helped. The body took it: bones wasting, strength dried out like a puddle in August. And the pressure is named without flinching: “your hand was heavy upon me”. That weight was mercy in disguise, and he only calls it God’s hand after it lifted. This does not mean every illness or depression is a sign of hidden sin: Job’s suffering was not, nor was the blindness of the man in John 9:3. But where a conscience knows what it is hiding, the body often carries the cost.

I will confess my transgressions to the LORD. Watch where the pardon arrives. “I said, I will confess”, and the sentence does not even finish before the forgiveness comes. God does not wait for the full account, adequate remorse or demonstrated improvement; he meets him the moment he turns.

I did not cover my iniquity. The psalm is built on a contrast. He had been covering his own iniquity; he stopped, and discovered that God had covered it (v. 1). Those are the only two options with sin: what you cover, God exposes; what you uncover, God covers. “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:9).

Guilt will not be managed away. Our culture has many ways of handling guilt and few of removing it: we explain it, shrink it, outweigh it with good deeds, or stay too busy to hear it. Silence was David’s method for months, and his body kept the score anyway. Shakespeare saw the same thing in Lady Macbeth, walking in her sleep and scrubbing hands that would not come clean: “Out, damned spot!” Her husband asks the doctor whether he cannot minister to a mind diseased and pluck from the memory a rooted sorrow, and the doctor answers that in such cases the patient must minister to himself. That is much of the modern answer too, and it does not work. The psalm’s answer is uncovering, before the one person who can cover truly because he has already paid. Guilt is not only a feeling to be soothed; it is a debt, and debts are settled by payment. That is why confession, which looks like the most painful option, is the only one that ends in singing.

Was David unforgiven while he kept silent? A believer’s justification is not lost when he sins, but his joy, peace and clear conscience are, and the Father disciplines the children he loves (Hebrews 12:5–11). David asks not for salvation again but “Restore to me the joy of your salvation” (Psalm 51:12). Delay in confessing costs dearly; confession brings the joy back.

Uncertain wording. “My strength was dried up” renders a rare word; the ESV notes that the Hebrew is “my vitality was changed”. It probably means his sap or life-force, drying out like a plant in drought.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–11 — You Are a Hiding Place for Me
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The forgiven are invited to live close to God, guided by him and glad in him. David urges everyone godly to pray while God may be found, because the floodwaters will not reach the one who does (v. 6), and he names God as the hiding place he once ran from (v. 7). Then God himself speaks: he will instruct and counsel the forgiven with his eye upon them, so they should not be like a horse or mule that must be dragged by bit and bridle (vv. 8–9). The wicked have many sorrows, but steadfast love surrounds whoever trusts the LORD, so the psalm ends calling the righteous to rejoice and shout for joy (vv. 10–11).
verseByVerse.theology: The forgiven man is taught by a glance rather than a bridle, and the psalm ends in shouting.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore let everyone who is godly offer prayer to you at a time when you may be found; surely in the rush of great waters, they shall not reach him. You are a hiding place for me; you preserve me from trouble; you surround me with shouts of deliverance. Selah
verseByVerse.commentary:
Having learned the cost of delay, David urges everyone to pray while God may be found, for the God he hid from is now his hiding place.

Therefore let everyone who is godly offer prayer. “Therefore”: this is what the testimony is for. He tells everyone else to do the thing he delayed, and with urgency: “at a time when you may be found”. Confession has a season. Not because God tires of waiting, but because a man who puts it off learns to live with the weight, and the longer the silence the more natural it feels.

How do I confess? Confession is not a mood to wait for; it is something a person does, and it can be done today. Name it plainly. Tell God what you did in the words you would use if someone else had done it: not “I was a bit short with her” but “I lied to protect myself.” Do not wait to feel sorry enough. David’s pardon came at “I said, I will confess” (v. 5), before any proof of remorse. Put it right where you can. Return what was taken, apologise to the person you wronged, and give up the habit that fed it: “he who confesses and forsakes them will obtain mercy” (Proverbs 28:13). Tell someone you trust when a sin keeps its grip in secret: “confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, that you may be healed” (James 5:16). And confess looking at the cross, not at your record. You are not talking God into covering your sin. In Christ the covering already exists: “He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree” (1 Peter 2:24). Confession is simply coming out from behind your own cover into his.

You are a hiding place for me. He had been hiding from God; now God is his hiding place. That is the whole movement of the psalm in one sentence. And what surrounds him is noise: “shouts of deliverance”, the sound of people celebrating a rescue, all round him where the guilt used to be.

verseByVerse.quote: I will instruct you and teach you in the way you should go; I will counsel you with my eye upon you. Be not like a horse or a mule, without understanding, which must be curbed with bit and bridle, or it will not stay near you. Many are the sorrows of the wicked, but steadfast love surrounds the one who trusts in the LORD. Be glad in the LORD, and rejoice, O righteous, and shout for joy, all you upright in heart!
verseByVerse.commentary:
God promises to guide the forgiven by a look rather than a bridle, and surrounds them with steadfast love, so the psalm ends in a shout of joy.

With my eye upon you. The voice changes, and God now speaks to the forgiven man. Three verbs of teaching, and then a picture to sit with: guidance by a look. That is how you direct someone close and paying attention: a glance across a room is enough. For a Christian that guiding presence is the Spirit: “all who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God” (Romans 8:14).

Be not like a horse or a mule. The alternative is an animal that has to be hauled about by the mouth. The difference is not obedience (the horse ends up going the right way too) but understanding. God can guide a responsive man with a look and a stubborn one with a bit, and it matters a great deal which of the two we make necessary. The heavy hand of verse 4 was the bridle. The eye in verse 8 is the better way, and it is offered to a man who has stopped pretending.

Steadfast love surrounds the one who trusts. Two things surround a man in this psalm, shouts of deliverance (v. 7) and steadfast love (v. 10), and both replaced a year of groaning. A psalm about confession ends not in a whisper of relief but in the noise of people who have been pardoned. The blessedness announced in verse 1 turns out to sound like a crowd cheering.

Where Christians differ. Who speaks in verses 8–9? Some hear David, keeping the vow of Psalm 51:13, “Then I will teach transgressors your ways”. Most hear the LORD answering the forgiven man.

This commentary’s view. The LORD is the speaker: the guiding eye and the promise to counsel fit God best. David’s own teaching is still there, in verses 6 and 10–11.

Uncertain wording. “Maskil”, in the heading, is of uncertain meaning, probably a psalm of instruction or a skilful song; “instruct” in verse 8 comes from the same Hebrew root. The last clause of verse 9 is also compressed: it probably means the animal will not come near you unless it is curbed, though some take it as “so that it does not come near and harm you”. Either way, God wants a willing nearness.

32.title: Blessed Is the One Whose Transgression Is Forgiven
32.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 31 ended by calling the faithful to take courage; Psalm 32 shows how a guilty person comes to be counted among the “righteous” and “upright in heart” at all (v. 11). It is one of the psalms the church has long called penitential, and the one Paul chose to prove that God justifies the ungodly (Romans 4:6–8).

The message. The happiest person in the world is not the one who has never sinned but the one God has forgiven. Hiding sin crushes us, because God’s hand presses on a conscience that keeps silent; confessing it brings pardon at once, because God is eager to forgive. And the forgiven are not left to themselves: God himself undertakes to guide them, close enough to lead by a look.

Why it was said. David tells his own story: a long silence over a sin, a body that paid for it, and the relief of confession. The psalm does not name the sin, but many connect it with the months after Bathsheba (2 Samuel 11–12; compare Psalm 51). The heading calls it a Maskil, probably a psalm for teaching, and David turns his experience into instruction for all God’s people (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. It opens with the conclusion: blessed is the one whose sin is forgiven, covered and not counted (vv. 1–2). Then the proof from David’s life: while he kept silent, God’s hand was heavy and his strength dried up; when he confessed, God forgave (vv. 3–5). So he urges everyone godly to pray while God may be found, for God is a hiding place (vv. 6–7). God then speaks, promising to instruct the forgiven with his eye on them, and warning against being a mule that needs a bridle (vv. 8–9). The psalm ends with steadfast love surrounding those who trust, and a shout of joy (vv. 10–11).

Where it leads. By promise and covenant, and here the Old Testament speaks the gospel almost in so many words. Paul reads verses 1–2 as David’s description of “the blessing of the one to whom God counts righteousness apart from works” (Romans 4:6), and he shows why God can leave sin out of the account: Christ “was delivered up for our trespasses and raised for our justification” (Romans 4:25). The covering David received rests on Christ, who “bore our sins in his body on the tree” (1 Peter 2:24).

For us. If there is something you are keeping silent about before God, this psalm is his invitation to stop: say it plainly to him today, for the forgiveness is already waiting in Christ. And then live as forgiven people do, close enough to God to be guided by a look, and loud enough in gladness that others want to know why.
32.theology:
Three words for sin are met by three for pardon (vv. 1-2), and Paul quotes both verses to show that God credits righteousness apart from works (Rom 4:7-8). The cost of unconfessed sin is described honestly (vv. 3-4), and pardon comes as soon as the man turns to confess (v. 5).

The psalm is built on the contrast between two coverings: what a man covers, God exposes; what he uncovers, God covers. The forgiven are guided by a look rather than a bridle (vv. 8-9), and repentance ends in shouting (v. 11).
32.examples:
The Psalter's first blessing was for those who keep God's way. This one is for people who have broken it, which is all of us.

David groaned all day and never said the one sentence that would have helped. When he finally said it, God did not wait for him to finish.

He had been hiding from God, and he ends up hiding in him.

keyVerse.quote: Blessed is the one whose transgression is forgiven, whose sin is covered.
keyVerse.note: The psalm’s opening is its conclusion: everything after it, the misery of silence, the relief of confession and the joy of the forgiven, is David’s proof of this sentence. Paul quotes it as Old Testament witness that God counts sinners righteous apart from works (Romans 4:6–8). The covering it celebrates rests on Christ, who bore our sins in his body on the tree (1 Peter 2:24).

32.reflection:
The psalm’s first word is “Blessed”, not of someone who has never sinned but of someone forgiven (vv. 1–2). Why is that good news, and how does Paul’s use of these verses in Romans 4 deepen it?

David describes what silence about sin did to him in body and spirit (vv. 3–4). What are the ways people today try to manage guilt without confessing it, and why do they not work?

God forgave as soon as David said, “I will confess” (v. 5). What keeps Christians from confessing quickly, and what practical steps from this psalm and James 5:16 might help?

God says he will guide with his eye rather than with bit and bridle (vv. 8–9). In what areas of life do you respond to God more like the mule than like someone close enough to follow a look?

33.text: <sup>1</sup>Shout for joy in the LORD, O you righteous! Praise befits the upright.<sup>2</sup>Give thanks to the LORD with the lyre; make melody to him with the harp of ten strings!<sup>3</sup>Sing to him a new song; play skillfully on the strings, with loud shouts.<sup>4</sup>For the word of the LORD is upright, and all his work is done in faithfulness.<sup>5</sup>He loves righteousness and justice; the earth is full of the steadfast love of the LORD.<sup>6</sup>By the word of the LORD the heavens were made, and by the breath of his mouth all their host.<sup>7</sup>He gathers the waters of the sea as a heap; he puts the deeps in storehouses.<sup>8</sup>Let all the earth fear the LORD; let all the inhabitants of the world stand in awe of him!<sup>9</sup>For he spoke, and it came to be; he commanded, and it stood firm.<sup>10</sup>The LORD brings the counsel of the nations to nothing; he frustrates the plans of the peoples.<sup>11</sup>The counsel of the LORD stands forever, the plans of his heart to all generations.<sup>12</sup>Blessed is the nation whose God is the LORD, the people whom he has chosen as his heritage!<sup>13</sup>The LORD looks down from heaven; he sees all the children of man;<sup>14</sup>from where he sits enthroned he looks out on all the inhabitants of the earth,<sup>15</sup>he who fashions the hearts of them all and observes all their deeds.<sup>16</sup>The king is not saved by his great army; a warrior is not delivered by his great strength.<sup>17</sup>The war horse is a false hope for salvation, and by its great might it cannot rescue.<sup>18</sup>Behold, the eye of the LORD is on those who fear him, on those who hope in his steadfast love,<sup>19</sup>that he may deliver their soul from death and keep them alive in famine.<sup>20</sup>Our soul waits for the LORD; he is our help and our shield.<sup>21</sup>For our heart is glad in him, because we trust in his holy name.<sup>22</sup>Let your steadfast love, O LORD, be upon us, even as we hope in you.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — For He Spoke, and It Came to Be
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s word deserves the best praise his people can give, because that word is upright and all-powerful. The righteous are called to shout, to play skilfully and to sing a new song (vv. 1–3), and the reason is God’s character: what he says is straight, what he does is faithful, and the earth is already full of his steadfast love (vv. 4–5). Then the same word is shown at work in creation. With a breath he spoke the heavens and their stars into being, and he handled the untameable sea like grain put into storehouses (vv. 6–7). The right response to a universe made by a word is awe, for there is no gap between his command and the fact (vv. 8–9).
verseByVerse.theology: The praise is skilled and loud, and its reason is that the universe came out of a sentence.

verseByVerse.quote: Shout for joy in the LORD, O you righteous! Praise befits the upright. Give thanks to the LORD with the lyre; make melody to him with the harp of ten strings! Sing to him a new song; play skillfully on the strings, with loud shouts. For the word of the LORD is upright, and all his work is done in faithfulness. He loves righteousness and justice; the earth is full of the steadfast love of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s people should praise him with joy, skill and fresh song, because his word is true, his work is faithful, and his steadfast love already fills the earth.

Shout for joy in the LORD. This psalm has no heading, and it begins where Psalm 32 ended, with a shout for joy (Psalm 32:11). Read together, the forgiven man of Psalm 32 leads the congregation into the praise of Psalm 33. Praise “befits the upright”: it suits them and looks right on them.

Sing to him a new song. Three things are asked of the musicians. The song is to be new: fresh composition, not only the old repertoire. It is to be skilful: God is not honoured by slapdash playing, and rehearsal is a spiritual activity. And it is to be loud, “with loud shouts”.

For the word of the LORD is upright. The reason for the noise is God’s character: what he says is straight, what he does is reliable, what he loves is right. Then comes a line to lift your head: “the earth is full of the steadfast love of the LORD”. Not will be full, but is. The world that is full of trouble in the rest of this book is full of covenant love now, and the psalm assumes a person could look out of a window and see it.

verseByVerse.quote: By the word of the LORD the heavens were made, and by the breath of his mouth all their host. He gathers the waters of the sea as a heap; he puts the deeps in storehouses. Let all the earth fear the LORD; let all the inhabitants of the world stand in awe of him! For he spoke, and it came to be; he commanded, and it stood firm.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God made the whole universe simply by speaking, so all the earth should stand in awe of him, and nothing we ask of him can strain him.

By the word of the LORD the heavens were made. Genesis in one line: God did not assemble the universe or wrestle it out of something; he said it. The stars were made “by the breath of his mouth”: what it costs him to make a galaxy is a breath.

He gathers the waters of the sea as a heap. The sea, which every ancient people feared as the great untameable thing, is handled like a farmer’s produce: gathered up and put away in storehouses, as you would store grain. The heap recalls the Red Sea, where “the floods stood up in a heap” (Exodus 15:8).

Let all the earth fear the LORD. The proper response to a spoken universe is fear: not fright, but the awe of a creature who has understood what he is standing on. “He spoke, and it came to be”: there is no gap between God’s word and the fact. We know this by faith, not by having watched it: “By faith we understand that the universe was created by the word of God” (Hebrews 11:3). So the God who called light out of nothing, asked in psalm after psalm for bread and rescue, is not stretched by either.

He spoke a dead man out of a tomb. John opens his Gospel on this truth and gives the Word a name: “All things were made through him”, and “the Word became flesh” (John 1:3, 14). The one by whom the heavens were made later stood at a tomb and spoke a dead man out of it (John 11:43). There is no gap between his word and the fact either.

Uncertain wording. Read with different vowels, the Hebrew for “heap” (v. 7) becomes “wineskin”, and some ancient translations take it so. Either way, God holds the sea like something stored.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–19 — The Counsel of the LORD Stands Forever
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The God who made the world by his word also rules its history, so only he can be trusted to save. Nations hold their councils and lay their plans, but he brings them to nothing, while his own counsel stands to all generations; the people he has chosen are therefore the truly blessed (vv. 10–12). He is no distant spectator: from his throne he sees every person, having shaped each heart himself (vv. 13–15). So the strongest things a king can count on, a great army, a champion, a war horse, are a false hope (vv. 16–17). Real security is the eye of the LORD resting on those who fear him and hope in his love, keeping them alive even in famine (vv. 18–19).
verseByVerse.theology: Two kinds of plan and two kinds of security, with the world's best version of each dismissed in a line.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD brings the counsel of the nations to nothing; he frustrates the plans of the peoples. The counsel of the LORD stands forever, the plans of his heart to all generations. Blessed is the nation whose God is the LORD, the people whom he has chosen as his heritage! The LORD looks down from heaven; he sees all the children of man; from where he sits enthroned he looks out on all the inhabitants of the earth, he who fashions the hearts of them all and observes all their deeds.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No human plan can outlast God’s purpose, so the people whose God is the LORD are truly blessed, and every heart lies open to the one who shaped it.

The counsel of the LORD stands forever. Two councils are in session, the nations’ and God’s. One is brought to nothing; the other stands. That is not a claim that human planning is worthless (Scripture is full of good planning), but that no plan can outrank his. Isaiah gives it as God’s own claim: “My counsel shall stand, and I will accomplish all my purpose” (Isaiah 46:10).

The plans of his heart. God’s purposes are not cold policy; they are what he has set his heart on, and they last “to all generations”: what he intended for your grandmother and intends for your grandchildren is one continuous purpose. There is comfort here when your own plan has come to nothing: underneath it lies a counsel that does not collapse, and the rule that frustrates the nations protects God’s people.

Blessed is the nation whose God is the LORD. Many countries have claimed this line, but it belongs first to the people God chose, and now to the church gathered “from every tribe and language” (Revelation 5:9), “a holy nation” marked on no map (1 Peter 2:9).

He who fashions the hearts of them all. In Psalm 14 God looked down and found no one who sought him. Here he looks down as the one who “fashions the hearts of them all”. The verb is a potter’s, used of forming clay. He is not scanning a crowd. He made every heart in it and knows what is in it, which is the most comforting and the most exposing fact a human being can know.

verseByVerse.quote: The king is not saved by his great army; a warrior is not delivered by his great strength. The war horse is a false hope for salvation, and by its great might it cannot rescue. Behold, the eye of the LORD is on those who fear him, on those who hope in his steadfast love, that he may deliver their soul from death and keep them alive in famine.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The strongest things a nation can trust cannot save, but the LORD watches over those who fear him and keeps them through the worst.

The king is not saved by his great army. Psalm 20 shouted this before a battle (Psalm 20:7); here it is stated calmly as doctrine. Three of the strongest things in that world, a standing army, a champion and a war horse, are dismissed with one verdict. The word is exact: not a weak hope but a “false” one. The horse does not help a little while God helps more; it cannot save at all. Every generation keeps its own horses, usually things we are proud of and would be ashamed to name in a prayer.

Behold, the eye of the LORD. Against the armies and the horses, an eye. That is the whole security offered, and it rests on those who fear him and hope in his love. What is promised is deliverance from death and life kept “in famine”, not out of it. God’s people are not exempted from the hungry year; they are kept through it.

What it does not mean. Not that armies, doctors or savings are wrong to have: “The horse is made ready for the day of battle, but the victory belongs to the LORD” (Proverbs 21:31). Use the horse; do not call it your saviour.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–22 — Our Soul Waits for the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The fitting answer to such a God is to wait for him gladly. The congregation speaks together: we wait for the LORD, for he is our help and our shield (v. 20). Their hearts are glad already, not because the waiting is over but because they trust his holy name, all that he has shown himself to be (v. 21). The last line is a prayer that asks for his steadfast love in the measure of their hope in him (v. 22). So even the poorest believer, with nothing to offer but expectation, may ask for the full measure, and the psalm that began with a shout ends in quiet, confident hope.
verseByVerse.theology: The psalm of the spoken universe ends with a congregation waiting.

verseByVerse.quote: Our soul waits for the LORD; he is our help and our shield. For our heart is glad in him, because we trust in his holy name. Let your steadfast love, O LORD, be upon us, even as we hope in you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Knowing how great God is, his people wait for him with glad hearts, trusting his name and asking for his love in the measure of their hope.

Our soul waits for the LORD. After a universe made by a word, nations frustrated and armies dismissed, the psalm ends with a congregation standing still. “Our soul waits”: the note on which Psalm 31 ended, and Psalm 27 before it. It is the posture of people who know exactly how strong God is and are still in the middle of their own story.

Because we trust in his holy name. The gladness does not wait for the waiting to end. The heart is glad in the middle of it, and what makes it glad is a name: all that God has revealed himself to be, which does not change while they wait.

Even as we hope in you. The last line is a beautiful piece of logic. He does not ask for love in proportion to their obedience, their gifts or their record, but to their hope. So the poorest believer in the room, with nothing to bring but expectation, is asking for the full measure.

33.title: He Spoke, and It Came to Be
33.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 33 is one of the few psalms in Book One with no heading, and it takes up the last words of Psalm 32: “shout for joy, all you upright in heart!” (Psalm 32:11). The forgiven man now leads the congregation in a hymn to the God who made the world and rules it.

The message. God deserves glad, skilful, fresh praise, because his word is utterly reliable: by it he made the heavens in an instant, and by it he governs history, so that no nation’s plan can outlast his and no army can save a king. The only safe place in such a world is under his eye, among those who fear him and hope in his steadfast love, and so his people wait for him with glad hearts.

Why it was said. Israel lived among empires with great armies and war horses (see the introduction), and was always tempted to trust what could be counted. This psalm taught each generation that a nation is blessed not for its strength but because the LORD is its God.

How the chapter makes its case. A call to praise (vv. 1–3) is followed by its reasons. God’s word is upright and his love fills the earth (vv. 4–5); by that word he made the heavens and stored up the sea, so all the earth should fear him (vv. 6–9). The same word rules history: the nations’ counsel fails, his stands, and the people he has chosen are blessed (vv. 10–12). He sees every person and has shaped every heart (vv. 13–15), so armies and war horses are a false hope, while his eye rests on those who fear him (vv. 16–19). The congregation answers by waiting gladly in hope (vv. 20–22).

Where it leads. By the character of God revealed in Christ. The word by which the heavens were made became flesh: John opens his Gospel on this psalm’s truth, “All things were made through him” (John 1:3), and he healed and raised the dead by a word. The counsel of the LORD that stands for ever reached its centre at the cross, where the plotting nations did only what “your hand and your plan had predestined to take place” (Acts 4:28). And the new song finds its fullest words in heaven, sung to the Lamb: “for you were slain, and by your blood you ransomed people for God” (Revelation 5:9).

For us. Ask what you are really leaning on: savings, health, a career, a plan; every generation has its war horse. Then put your weight on the God whose word made the stars and whose eye is on you, and wait for him gladly, asking for his love by your hope, not your record.
33.theology:
Worship here is grounded in God's character rather than the worshippers' mood (vv. 4-5). Creation is by speech (vv. 6, 9; Gen 1): there is no gap between God's word and the fact.

Two councils sit, and only God's stands (vv. 10-11). He fashions each heart himself (v. 15). The war horse is not a weak hope but a false one (v. 17), and what is promised instead is God's watchful eye and life kept through famine (vv. 18-19). The closing prayer asks for love in proportion to hope, not merit (v. 22).
33.examples:
What it costs God to make a galaxy is a breath, and the sea every ancient people feared he stores away like grain. A God like that is not stretched by a request for bread.

Everyone keeps a war horse of some kind: savings, qualifications, contacts, a plan B. The psalm does not tell anyone to sell it, only what it cannot do.

keyVerse.quote: For he spoke, and it came to be; he commanded, and it stood firm.
keyVerse.note: Everything in the psalm rests on this: there is no gap between God’s word and the fact. Because his word made the world, it also rules history (vv. 10–11) and is more to be trusted than any army (vv. 16–17). The Word through whom all things were made became flesh, and he still speaks with the same power.

33.reflection:
The psalm calls for praise that is joyful, skilful and new (vv. 1–3). What would each of these look like in our church’s worship, and in our own private praise?

“The earth is full of the steadfast love of the LORD” (v. 5). Where have you seen God’s love in the ordinary world this week, and why do we so often fail to notice it?

Verses 10–11 set the nations’ plans against God’s counsel, and Acts 4:27–28 shows that even the plot to crucify Jesus served God’s purpose. How does that change the way you face plans of your own that have collapsed?

Every generation has its “war horse” (v. 17). What are the false hopes people trust most where you live, and how can we use good things without leaning our weight on them?

34.text: Of David, when he changed his behavior before Abimelech, so that he drove him out, and he went away. 1I will bless the LORD at all times; his praise shall continually be in my mouth.2My soul makes its boast in the LORD; let the humble hear and be glad.3Oh, magnify the LORD with me, and let us exalt his name together!4I sought the LORD, and he answered me and delivered me from all my fears.5Those who look to him are radiant, and their faces shall never be ashamed.6This poor man cried, and the LORD heard him and saved him out of all his troubles.7The angel of the LORD encamps around those who fear him, and delivers them.8Oh, taste and see that the LORD is good! Blessed is the man who takes refuge in him!9Oh, fear the LORD, you his saints, for those who fear him have no lack!10The young lions suffer want and hunger; but those who seek the LORD lack no good thing.11Come, O children, listen to me; I will teach you the fear of the LORD.12What man is there who desires life and loves many days, that he may see good?13Keep your tongue from evil and your lips from speaking deceit.14Turn away from evil and do good; seek peace and pursue it.15The eyes of the LORD are toward the righteous and his ears toward their cry.16The face of the LORD is against those who do evil, to cut off the memory of them from the earth.17When the righteous cry for help, the LORD hears and delivers them out of all their troubles.18The LORD is near to the brokenhearted and saves the crushed in spirit.19Many are the afflictions of the righteous, but the LORD delivers him out of them all.20He keeps all his bones; not one of them is broken.21Affliction will slay the wicked, and those who hate the righteous will be condemned.22The LORD redeems the life of his servants; none of those who take refuge in him will be condemned.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Praise grows out of rescue, and a rescued man wants company in it. David vows to bless the LORD at all times and calls the humble to magnify his name with him (vv. 1–3). Then he tells his story: he sought the LORD and was delivered from his fears; those who look to God are radiant, not ashamed; this poor man cried and was saved; the angel of the LORD camps round those who fear him (vv. 4–7). So he turns to his hearers with an invitation: taste and see that the LORD is good (v. 8). Those who fear and seek him, unlike the hungry young lions, lack no good thing (vv. 9–10).
verseByVerse.theology: A psalm written after a humiliating escape, inviting everyone to try God for themselves.

verseByVerse.quote: I will bless the LORD at all times; his praise shall continually be in my mouth. My soul makes its boast in the LORD; let the humble hear and be glad. Oh, magnify the LORD with me, and let us exalt his name together!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Freshly rescued from a humiliating mess, David vows to praise God at all times and calls the humble to join him.

The story behind the psalm. The heading sends us to one of the least dignified pages in David’s life. On the run from Saul, he fled to Gath, a Philistine city, and was recognised as the man who had killed their champion. So he saved himself by pretending to be mad, making marks on the doors of the gate and letting spittle run down his beard (1 Samuel 21:13). The heading calls the king Abimelech; 1 Samuel names him Achish, and Abimelech was probably a royal title, as Pharaoh was in Egypt (compare Genesis 26:1). That is the occasion of “taste and see that the LORD is good”: not a coronation but an escape by humiliation, from a mess he had walked into himself.

I will bless the LORD at all times. “At all times” and “continually” are large words from a man who has just been scrabbling at a gate. And he names who will enjoy his testimony: “let the humble hear and be glad”. A story about God rescuing a man who had made a fool of himself is no use to the self-assured, and food and drink to everyone else.

Oh, magnify the LORD with me. To magnify does not mean to make God bigger; nothing can. It means to show him as big as he is, as a telescope shows a star, not to exaggerate. And he will not do it alone: “with me … together”.
verseByVerse.note: The heading names the king Abimelech; 1 Samuel calls him Achish, and Abimelech was probably a royal title. The psalm is an acrostic (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: I sought the LORD, and he answered me and delivered me from all my fears. Those who look to him are radiant, and their faces shall never be ashamed. This poor man cried, and the LORD heard him and saved him out of all his troubles. The angel of the LORD encamps around those who fear him, and delivers them. Oh, taste and see that the LORD is good! Blessed is the man who takes refuge in him! Oh, fear the LORD, you his saints, for those who fear him have no lack! The young lions suffer want and hunger; but those who seek the LORD lack no good thing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God answered David’s cry, so David invites everyone to find out for themselves that the LORD is good.

Those who look to him are radiant. Of three testimonies (vv. 4–6), the middle one is about faces. A face turned towards God catches the light, and the psalm sets that against the shame of the man dribbling at the gate of Gath. He was ashamed there; he says here that those who look to God “shall never be ashamed”.

This poor man cried. This is how he now describes himself: not the giant-killer, not the anointed king, but “this poor man”. It is the right way to remember your own rescue.

The angel of the LORD encamps. One angel, and the verb is an army’s: he “encamps”. Elisha’s servant would one day have his eyes opened to see what that looks like: “the mountain was full of horses and chariots of fire all around Elisha” (2 Kings 6:17).

Oh, taste and see that the LORD is good! “Taste” is the invitation of a man handing you a spoon: you cannot know a thing by being told; you have to try it. Peter quotes the line to young Christians and treats it as already happening to them: “if indeed you have tasted that the Lord is good” (1 Peter 2:3). And he goes on, “As you come to him, a living stone” (1 Peter 2:4): to taste the Lord is to come to Jesus.

The young lions suffer want and hunger. The strongest hunters in the land go hungry, while those who seek God “lack no good thing”. Not nothing they want, but no good thing, which leaves God to judge what is good for us. A man who has just escaped a city by drooling knows that strength is not provision.

Where Christians differ: who is the angel of the LORD? Elsewhere he speaks as God himself, and many see in him the Son before his incarnation; others take him as the chief of God’s angels. This commentary’s view: where he speaks and acts as God, he is best read as the Son before his incarnation. Either way, God sends his angels “to serve for the sake of those who are to inherit salvation” (Hebrews 1:14). Scripture does not say that each believer has one guardian angel, though Jesus speaks of the little ones’ angels before the Father (Matthew 18:10).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–22 — The LORD Is Near to the Brokenhearted
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The fear of the LORD is learned as a way of life, and it rests on a God who is near and who rescues. David becomes a teacher of children: whoever wants a long and good life must guard his tongue, turn from evil, do good and go after peace (vv. 11–14). The LORD’s eyes and ears are open to the righteous, while his face is against evildoers (vv. 15–17). He is near the brokenhearted and saves the crushed (v. 18). The righteous have many afflictions, but he brings them out of every one and keeps all their bones (vv. 19–20). The psalm ends with two verdicts: the wicked condemned, and none condemned who take refuge in him (vv. 21–22).
verseByVerse.theology: The fear of the LORD is taught as a set of habits, and the promise is not exemption from affliction but rescue through it.

verseByVerse.quote: Come, O children, listen to me; I will teach you the fear of the LORD. What man is there who desires life and loves many days, that he may see good? Keep your tongue from evil and your lips from speaking deceit. Turn away from evil and do good; seek peace and pursue it. The eyes of the LORD are toward the righteous and his ears toward their cry. The face of the LORD is against those who do evil, to cut off the memory of them from the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The fear of the LORD is learned as ordinary habits of tongue and life, above all the pursuit of peace, under the eyes of a God who is not neutral.

I will teach you the fear of the LORD. Now he turns teacher, and the fear of the LORD, which sounds abstract, is handed over as ordinary habits. Control your tongue. Stop lying. Leave off evil. Do good. And then one that will not sit still: “seek peace and pursue it”. Peace does not stay where you put it; you have to go after it.

Keep your tongue from evil. Peter hands these verses, almost word for word, to Christians facing hostility: “Whoever desires to love life and see good days, let him keep his tongue from evil and his lips from speaking deceit; let him turn away from evil and do good; let him seek peace and pursue it” (1 Peter 3:10–11). A man who escaped by a trick wrote them; Peter quotes them to people who must suffer without deceit.

The face of the LORD is against those who do evil. Eyes, ears, face: God attends with all three, and the third is the frightening one. The same face that shines on the righteous is set “against” the evildoer. God is not neutral, and the psalm is not embarrassed to say so.

The habits of the rescued. The teacher has just been rescued by grace. These are the habits of people who have tasted that the LORD is good (v. 8), the fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22), not a fee for God’s favour. When the tongue slips, the way back is the one David took: “This poor man cried” (v. 6).

How do I pursue peace? “Pursue” is a hunter’s word: peace is not waited for but gone after, and usually that means taking the first step. Go first. If a friendship has gone cold or a family is not speaking, do not wait for the other person to ring. Jesus tells the worshipper to leave his gift at the altar: “First be reconciled to your brother” (Matthew 5:24). Own your part, without the “but”. Begin the hard conversation with what you did wrong, not with what they did. Guard the tongue on the way. Peace is usually lost by the remark, the exaggeration, the story passed on. Do not say about someone what you would not say to him. Know where it stops. “If possible, so far as it depends on you, live peaceably with all” (Romans 12:18). You cannot make another person reconcile, and peace is never bought with a lie. Nor does it mean putting yourself back within reach of someone who is harming you.

Gone after first. The strength to go first comes from having been gone after. While we were still enemies, God came to us, and Christ “himself is our peace” (Ephesians 2:14), “making peace by the blood of his cross” (Colossians 1:20). Peacemakers are people who have been on the receiving end of that.

verseByVerse.quote: When the righteous cry for help, the LORD hears and delivers them out of all their troubles. The LORD is near to the brokenhearted and saves the crushed in spirit. Many are the afflictions of the righteous, but the LORD delivers him out of them all. He keeps all his bones; not one of them is broken. Affliction will slay the wicked, and those who hate the righteous will be condemned. The LORD redeems the life of his servants; none of those who take refuge in him will be condemned.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD stays near the brokenhearted, brings the righteous out of all their many troubles, and condemns none who take refuge in him.

The LORD is near to the brokenhearted. One of the great sentences of the Bible. God is not near only to the cheerful, nor does he wait until you have pulled yourself together. The second half goes further: “the crushed in spirit”, ground down as grain is crushed. If you are reading this from inside that condition, the psalm does not explain it or ask you to feel better. It tells you where God is standing.

Many are the afflictions of the righteous. Hold both halves. “Many”: the psalm does not pretend that faith reduces the number of afflictions. And “out of them all”: not round them, but through them and out. Every affliction the righteous have had has been one they were brought out of; the last will be no different, though it will take a resurrection.

Not one of them is broken. Said of an ordinary righteous man, this is a promise not that believers never break a bone but that nothing of theirs slips past God’s care. Then once it happened literally. When the soldiers came to break the legs of the crucified men to hasten their deaths, “when they came to Jesus and saw that he was already dead, they did not break his legs”, and John writes, “For these things took place that the Scripture might be fulfilled: ‘Not one of his bones will be broken’” (John 19:33, 36). John’s words echo both this verse and the Passover rule that no bone of the lamb was to be broken (Exodus 12:46), and he probably meant both: the righteous sufferer and the Lamb are one person. God’s care for the bones of his righteous one was exact on the day it mattered most.

None of those who take refuge in him will be condemned. The alphabet poem ends on “condemned”, used twice: the haters will be, and those who take refuge will not. The man who escaped a king by feigning madness ends by saying that the only refuge that ever really worked was God, and that the verdict on all who run there is settled. In Christ that verdict has been given in full (Romans 8:1).

When the crushing lasts. If it goes on for months, it is no failure of faith to see a biblical counsellor, have a medical check-up, or take medicine if needed. If the darkness turns to thoughts of ending your life, tell someone that same day.

34.title: Taste and See That the LORD Is Good
