34.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 33 ended with God’s eye on those who fear him (Psalm 33:18); Psalm 34 tells one man’s story of that eye at work. Its heading takes us back to David’s flight from Saul, when he escaped the Philistine king of Gath by pretending to be mad (1 Samuel 21:10–15). It is an acrostic, its verses running through the Hebrew alphabet.

The message. God hears and rescues the humble who cry to him, even when the trouble is partly of their own making, and anyone may find out for himself that the LORD is good. The fear of the LORD that grows from that discovery is learned as ordinary habits of tongue and life. The God who rescues stays near the brokenhearted and brings the righteous out of all their troubles, and none who take refuge in him will be condemned.

Why it was said. David wrote it after one of the least dignified escapes of his life (on the headings, see the introduction), and turned his own humiliation into teaching for others. Its alphabet form made it easy to learn by heart.

How the chapter makes its case. First comes testimony (vv. 1–10). David vows to bless the LORD at all times and calls the humble to magnify him together (vv. 1–3); he tells how the LORD answered him and how his angel encamps round those who fear him (vv. 4–7); then he invites everyone to taste and see that the LORD is good, for those who seek him lack no good thing (vv. 8–10). Then comes teaching (vv. 11–22). Like a father he teaches the fear of the LORD as plain habits: a guarded tongue, turning from evil, pursuing peace (vv. 11–14). God’s eyes are on the righteous and his face against evildoers (vv. 15–16); he stays near the brokenhearted, delivers the righteous out of many afflictions and redeems his servants (vv. 17–22).

Where it leads. By pattern, and by a fulfilment John saw. The righteous sufferer whose bones the LORD keeps (v. 20) is fulfilled in Jesus: when the soldiers did not break his legs, John wrote, “For these things took place that the Scripture might be fulfilled: ‘Not one of his bones will be broken’” (John 19:36). Peter heard the invitation of verse 8 as an invitation to come to Christ (1 Peter 2:3–4), and the last line, that none who take refuge in the LORD will be condemned, becomes Paul’s promise: “There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1).

For us. If you have made a fool of yourself, or walked into trouble by your own choices, this psalm was written by someone who did the same and was still heard. Taste for yourself that the Lord is good: come to Christ himself, not only to the idea of him. If you are brokenhearted now, it tells you where God is standing.
34.theology:
The invitation to taste and see (v. 8) comes from a man whose latest experience of God was a humiliating escape, which is why the humble are the ones told to listen (v. 2). The fear of the LORD is taught as habits, not a mood (vv. 11-14), and grown by grace.

God's nearness is located precisely, with the brokenhearted (v. 18). The promise to the righteous is not fewer afflictions but rescue out of all of them (v. 19), which for the last one will take a resurrection. Not one of them is broken (v. 20) came true to the letter at the cross (John 19:36), and the psalm closes on the verdict: those who take refuge in him are not condemned (v. 22).
34.examples:
The psalm of taste and see was written after an escape that left David's dignity at the gate of Gath. He remembers himself afterwards not as a giant-killer but as this poor man, which is the right way to remember any rescue.

We tend to picture God at the top of the ladder. Verse 18 puts him at the bottom of the stairs, close to the person who cannot get up.

keyVerse.quote: Oh, taste and see that the LORD is good! Blessed is the man who takes refuge in him!
keyVerse.note: Spoken by a man just rescued from a humiliation of his own making, this invitation is the heart of the psalm: God’s goodness is to be tried, not only heard about, and the one who takes refuge in him is blessed. Peter applies it to coming to Christ (1 Peter 2:3–4), and the psalm’s last word shows where taking refuge ends: in no condemnation (v. 22).

34.reflection:
The psalm comes out of one of David’s most embarrassing moments (see the heading and 1 Samuel 21:10–15). Why is it a help that “taste and see that the LORD is good” was first said by a man who had just made a fool of himself?

“Taste and see” (v. 8) is an invitation to experience, not only to information. What is the difference between knowing about the Lord’s goodness and tasting it, and how might we invite a friend to taste?

Verses 12–14 turn the fear of the LORD into habits of the tongue and the pursuit of peace. Which of these is hardest for you, and is there a relationship where you need to “go first” this week?

“The LORD is near to the brokenhearted” (v. 18). How can we hold this together with “Many are the afflictions of the righteous” (v. 19), and how can a church show that nearness to those who are crushed in spirit?

35.text: Of David. 1Contend, O LORD, with those who contend with me; fight against those who fight against me!2Take hold of shield and buckler and rise for my help!3Draw the spear and javelin against my pursuers! Say to my soul, "I am your salvation!"4Let them be put to shame and dishonor who seek after my life! Let them be turned back and disappointed who devise evil against me!5Let them be like chaff before the wind, with the angel of the LORD driving them away!6Let their way be dark and slippery, with the angel of the LORD pursuing them!7For without cause they hid their net for me; without cause they dug a pit for my life.8Let destruction come upon him when he does not know it! And let the net that he hid ensnare him; let him fall into it—to his destruction!9Then my soul will rejoice in the LORD, exulting in his salvation.10All my bones shall say, "O LORD, who is like you, delivering the poor from him who is too strong for him, the poor and needy from him who robs him?"11Malicious witnesses rise up; they ask me of things that I do not know.12They repay me evil for good; my soul is bereft.13But I, when they were sick— I wore sackcloth; I afflicted myself with fasting; I prayed with head bowed on my chest.14I went about as though I grieved for my friend or my brother; as one who laments his mother, I bowed down in mourning.15But at my stumbling they rejoiced and gathered; they gathered together against me; wretches whom I did not know tore at me without ceasing;16like profane mockers at a feast, they gnash at me with their teeth.17How long, O Lord, will you look on? Rescue me from their destruction, my precious life from the lions!18I will thank you in the great congregation; in the mighty throng I will praise you.19Let not those rejoice over me who are wrongfully my foes, and let not those wink the eye who hate me without cause.20For they do not speak peace, but against those who are quiet in the land they devise words of deceit.21They open wide their mouths against me; they say, "Aha, Aha! Our eyes have seen it!"22You have seen, O LORD; be not silent! O Lord, be not far from me!23Awake and rouse yourself for my vindication, for my cause, my God and my Lord!24Vindicate me, O LORD, my God, according to your righteousness, and let them not rejoice over me!25Let them not say in their hearts, "Aha, our heart's desire!" Let them not say, "We have swallowed him up."26Let them be put to shame and disappointed altogether who rejoice at my calamity! Let them be clothed with shame and dishonor who magnify themselves against me!27Let those who delight in my righteousness shout for joy and be glad and say evermore, "Great is the LORD, who delights in the welfare of his servant!"28Then my tongue shall tell of your righteousness and of your praise all the day long.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — Say to My Soul, I Am Your Salvation
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A believer attacked without cause may ask God to fight for him, and leave the fighting to God. Every verb in the opening is God’s: contend, fight, take up shield and buckler, draw the spear (vv. 1–3). The one thing David asks for himself is a word: “Say to my soul, ‘I am your salvation!’” (v. 3). Then he asks that his pursuers be shamed and turned back, blown away like chaff and chased down a dark, slippery road by the angel of the LORD (vv. 4–6). Because they hid a net and dug a pit for him for no reason, he asks for the oldest justice of all: let the trap catch the man who set it (vv. 7–8).
verseByVerse.theology: Every request is handed to God, and the one thing he asks for himself is a word.

verseByVerse.quote: Contend, O LORD, with those who contend with me; fight against those who fight against me! Take hold of shield and buckler and rise for my help! Draw the spear and javelin against my pursuers! Say to my soul, "I am your salvation!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
David asks God to fight for him, and for himself asks only to hear God say, “I am your salvation!”

Contend, O LORD. There is no softening this prayer against enemies, but read what it actually asks. Every verb is God’s: you contend, you fight, you take the shield, you draw the spear. David has a sword and does not mention it. The whole psalm is a man handing over a case he could have prosecuted himself, which is just what the New Testament tells Christians to do: “Beloved, never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God” (Romans 12:19). A psalm calling on God to judge enemies (an imprecatory psalm) is not the opposite of loving them. Handing the case to God is what keeps you from taking revenge yourself.

Say to my soul, “I am your salvation!” Everything else concerns his opponents; his one personal request is for God’s voice, spoken inwardly to steady a frightened man. Christians hear that word in the name Jesus, given “for he will save his people from their sins” (Matthew 1:21).

verseByVerse.quote: Let them be put to shame and dishonor who seek after my life! Let them be turned back and disappointed who devise evil against me! Let them be like chaff before the wind, with the angel of the LORD driving them away! Let their way be dark and slippery, with the angel of the LORD pursuing them!
verseByVerse.commentary:
David asks that his hunters fail in plain view, driven off by the angel of the LORD.

Let them be put to shame. The first request is not for their death but for their defeat: shame, dishonour, being “turned back and disappointed”. In the Psalms shame means public failure: he asks that what they “devise” should be seen by all to come to nothing, and so show whose side God is on.

Like chaff before the wind. The pictures come from earlier psalms, turned round. The wicked were chaff in Psalm 1; the angel of the LORD camped round the godly in Psalm 34, and here the same angel does the chasing. A dark, slippery road is the exact reverse of the “level path” asked for in Psalm 27:11.

verseByVerse.quote: For without cause they hid their net for me; without cause they dug a pit for my life. Let destruction come upon him when he does not know it! And let the net that he hid ensnare him; let him fall into it—to his destruction!
verseByVerse.commentary:
His enemies set traps “without cause”, twice over, so David asks that their own trap catch them. Jesus took that phrase onto his own lips (v. 19).

Let destruction come upon him when he does not know it! From “them” to “him”: probably the ringleader, or each enemy in turn. The net was hidden; let the ruin come just as unseen, the surprise he planned for another falling on himself.

Let the net that he hid ensnare him. This is the oldest justice in the Psalter: let the trap work as designed, on the man who set it (Psalms 7:15; 9:15). He is not inventing a punishment.

Uncertain wording. The ESV notes that it has moved the word “pit” from the first line of verse 7 to the second, to make sense of compressed Hebrew. The meaning is clear: a hidden trap.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–16 — They Repay Me Evil for Good
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The deepest wound is kindness repaid with cruelty, and even here David looks ahead to praise. He promises that when God acts his whole frame will say, “O LORD, who is like you”, the rescuer of the weak from the strong (vv. 9–10). Then he tells what has happened. Malicious witnesses accuse him of things he knows nothing about, repaying evil for good until he grieves as if bereaved (vv. 11–12). Yet when these same people were ill he fasted, wore sackcloth and mourned as for a brother or a mother (vv. 13–14). Now that he has stumbled, they gather in glee, strangers join in, and they mock like profane men at a feast (vv. 15–16).
verseByVerse.theology: The injury is not from strangers: he had nursed these people, and they gathered when he fell.

verseByVerse.quote: Then my soul will rejoice in the LORD, exulting in his salvation. All my bones shall say, "O LORD, who is like you, delivering the poor from him who is too strong for him, the poor and needy from him who robs him?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Rescued, David’s whole being will praise the God who defends the weak against the strong.

Then my soul will rejoice. “Then”, when God has answered verses 1–8. The joy is “in the LORD” and “in his salvation”, not in the enemies’ fall, and it answers the one personal request of verse 3.

All my bones shall say. The purpose of the rescue is worship, and the worship is physical: the frame that has ached with fear will do the praising. The title he gives God is the one this psalm exists for: the deliverer of the poor “from him who is too strong for him”. Mary sang of the same God, who “has brought down the mighty from their thrones” (Luke 1:52).

verseByVerse.quote: Malicious witnesses rise up; they ask me of things that I do not know. They repay me evil for good; my soul is bereft.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Falsely accused by people he has treated well, David grieves as for a death.

Malicious witnesses rise up. Now the setting is a court. False witnesses stand up and question him about things he knows nothing of. The law said that a false witness should suffer the penalty he had planned for his neighbour (Deuteronomy 19:16–19). The same was done to Jesus, when “many bore false witness against him” (Mark 14:56).

My soul is bereft. Literally “it is bereavement to my soul” (ESV note): he grieves as for a death. Now the psalm turns from the general to the wound underneath, which is not that he is opposed but that he is betrayed.

verseByVerse.quote: But I, when they were sick— I wore sackcloth; I afflicted myself with fasting; I prayed with head bowed on my chest. I went about as though I grieved for my friend or my brother; as one who laments his mother, I bowed down in mourning.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When these same people were ill, David fasted and mourned for them like family.

But I, when they were sick. When these people were ill, he fasted for them. He put on sackcloth, prayed with his head bowed on his chest, and went about as if the sick man were his own brother or his own mother. Love that prayed is not wasted when its object turns: God saw (v. 22).

Uncertain wording. The ESV notes that verse 13 may end “my prayer shall turn back”: unanswered, some think, or its blessing returning on himself (compare Matthew 10:13).

verseByVerse.quote: But at my stumbling they rejoiced and gathered; they gathered together against me; wretches whom I did not know tore at me without ceasing; like profane mockers at a feast, they gnash at me with their teeth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When David stumbled, those he had prayed for gathered in glee, and strangers joined in.

At my stumbling they rejoiced. When he stumbled, they held a party. The word for their gathering is used twice, as a crowd forms round an accident; people he had never met joined in. The crowd at the cross did the same to the Son of David (Matthew 27:39–44).

In everyday life. Anyone who has prayed for someone who later led the campaign against them knows what this psalm is for. The bitterness in it is not petty. It is the ache of kindness repaid with pleasure at your fall.

Uncertain wording. The ESV notes that the meaning of the Hebrew phrase in verse 16, “like profane mockers at a feast”, is uncertain. The picture is clear: mockery as entertainment.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–28 — You Have Seen, O LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God sees what the gloaters see, so David asks him not to stay silent but to judge rightly, and to make the end praise. He cries, “How long, O Lord, will you look on?”, asks to be rescued from the lions, and promises thanks in the great congregation (vv. 17–18). His enemies hate him without cause, plot against the quiet in the land and jeer, “Aha, Aha!” (vv. 19–21). But God has seen too, so David asks him to wake, speak and vindicate him by his righteousness, and to clothe the gloaters with shame (vv. 22–26). The psalm ends with the righteous shouting, “Great is the LORD”, and David telling of God’s righteousness all day long (vv. 27–28).
verseByVerse.theology: Their eyes have seen; God's eyes have seen; the psalm asks the one who sees to speak.

verseByVerse.quote: How long, O Lord, will you look on? Rescue me from their destruction, my precious life from the lions! I will thank you in the great congregation; in the mighty throng I will praise you. Let not those rejoice over me who are wrongfully my foes, and let not those wink the eye who hate me without cause. For they do not speak peace, but against those who are quiet in the land they devise words of deceit. They open wide their mouths against me; they say, "Aha, Aha! Our eyes have seen it!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
David asks how long God will only watch, vows public praise, and describes enemies who hate him without cause.

How long, O Lord, will you look on? A hard and honest thing to say: you are watching this. It is the complaint of Psalms 10:1 and 13:1, and the psalm will answer it in verse 22 with the same verb turned into comfort.

I will thank you in the great congregation. In the middle of the fear comes a vow about the future: he plans the testimony before the rescue. Decide in advance where the story will be told.

Who hate me without cause. This is the phrase Jesus quoted from this psalm and Psalm 69 about the world’s hatred of himself: “But the word that is written in their Law must be fulfilled: ‘They hated me without a cause’” (John 15:25). He said it to prepare his followers. When hostility has no rational cause, it is not a sign that something has gone wrong with your discipleship.

Those who are quiet in the land. A lovely phrase for the targets: not fighters, but people going about their business. To “wink the eye” was a sign of malice shared (Proverbs 10:10), and “Aha, Aha! Our eyes have seen it!” is the sound of someone enjoying your disgrace, which the psalm records because God is not squeamish about how ugly this is.

verseByVerse.quote: You have seen, O LORD; be not silent! O Lord, be not far from me! Awake and rouse yourself for my vindication, for my cause, my God and my Lord! Vindicate me, O LORD, my God, according to your righteousness, and let them not rejoice over me! Let them not say in their hearts, "Aha, our heart's desire!" Let them not say, "We have swallowed him up." Let them be put to shame and disappointed altogether who rejoice at my calamity! Let them be clothed with shame and dishonor who magnify themselves against me! Let those who delight in my righteousness shout for joy and be glad and say evermore, "Great is the LORD, who delights in the welfare of his servant!" Then my tongue shall tell of your righteousness and of your praise all the day long.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God has seen it all, so David asks him to speak and judge rightly, and wants the outcome to be a shout that the LORD is great.

You have seen, O LORD. They said “our eyes have seen it”; the psalmist says to God, “You have seen”. The same seeing from a different height: their eyes saw a chance to gloat, God’s eyes see a case to be judged. The complaint of verse 17, that God only looks on, has become the ground of the appeal: because you have seen, do not stay silent. Faith does not always resolve the tension between God’s watching and God’s acting. It leans on the first while asking for the second.

We have swallowed him up. He cannot bear their triumph made final, as if God agreed. So he asks for vindication “according to your righteousness”: judge it properly, not in my favour merely because I am the one praying.

Great is the LORD. The psalm ends with a sentence to be shouted, and it is not about David: “Great is the LORD, who delights in the welfare of his servant!” That is what he wants the outcome to prove: not that he was right, but that God takes pleasure in the good of those who belong to him. The word for welfare is shalom, peace: the enemies “do not speak peace” (v. 20), but God delights in his servant’s.

Praying this psalm today. Pray it as it is written: hand the case over, ask God to act and not yourself, ask that the verdict be righteous, and want the result to be praise for God rather than a triumph for you, while praying first for the enemy’s repentance (see the introduction). The cross is where hatred without cause did its worst, and where the one who was hated without cause prayed, “Father, forgive them” (Luke 23:34).

What it does not mean. Handing the case to God does not mean keeping silent while you are harmed: tell those who can protect you, and report crimes to the authorities, through whom God’s justice often comes (Romans 13:4).

35.title: Contend with Those Who Contend with Me
35.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 35 follows David’s calm testimony in Psalm 34 and turns it into a battle cry: the angel of the LORD who camped round the godly (Psalm 34:7) is now asked to drive the wicked away (vv. 5–6). It is one of the psalms that call on God to judge enemies (see the introduction).

The message. When you are attacked and betrayed without cause, you may hand the whole case to God and ask him to fight for you, instead of taking revenge yourself. What a wronged believer needs most is God’s own word to his soul, “I am your salvation”, and the outcome he should long for is not his own triumph but a righteous verdict that shows how great the LORD is.

Why it was said. The psalm names no occasion, but it fits David’s years when men he had treated kindly turned on him, under Saul and later in his own court (see the introduction). It gave Israel words for false accusation, betrayal by friends, and the wait while mockers seemed to win.

How the chapter makes its case. The psalm pleads three times, and each plea ends in a vow of praise (vv. 9–10, 18, 27–28). First, a call to battle (vv. 1–10): let God take up shield and spear, speak salvation to David’s soul and catch his hunters in their own nets (vv. 1–8), and his bones will praise him (vv. 9–10). Second, the wound (vv. 11–18): false witnesses accuse him, and those he fasted for when they were sick tear at him when he stumbles (vv. 11–16); “How long, O Lord, will you look on?” he asks, and vows public thanks (vv. 17–18). Third, the verdict (vv. 19–28): those who hate him without cause gloat, “Aha, Aha!” (vv. 19–21); but “You have seen, O LORD”, so let God wake and judge by his righteousness (vv. 22–26), and let all who love the right shout that the LORD is great (vv. 27–28).

Where it leads. By pattern, and by Jesus’ own words. He took the phrase of verse 19 on his lips: “They hated me without a cause” (John 15:25). False witnesses stood up again at his trial (Mark 14:56). Like David he handed his case to God, “entrusting himself to him who judges justly” (1 Peter 2:23), but he went further than David and prayed for those who did it: “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do” (Luke 23:34). God vindicated him by raising him, and because he bore judgment for sinners, those who hated him can be made his friends.

For us. If you have been falsely accused or betrayed by people you helped, this psalm lets you say so to God in strong words and hand him the case, instead of taking it into your own hands. Ask him first to speak to your soul, pray for your enemies’ repentance as Christ prayed for his, and want the last word to be praise of God, not your own triumph.
35.theology:
Every petition here asks God to act, and the psalmist never lifts a hand (vv. 1-8, 22-26). That is the handover the New Testament commands (Rom 12:19), which makes such a psalm the opposite of private revenge. The first thing he asks for himself is a word from God (v. 3).

The injury is betrayal by people he had cared for (vv. 13-14), and the hatred is without cause (v. 19), a phrase Jesus took for himself. The complaint that God is only looking on (v. 17) becomes the ground of the appeal (v. 22), and the outcome he wants is God's glory, not his own: Great is the LORD, who delights in the welfare of his servant (v. 27).
35.examples:
David has a sword and never mentions it. Every verb in the opening belongs to God, and the only thing David asks for himself is a word spoken to his soul.

He had fasted for the people who later gathered to watch him fall. Anyone who has been repaid for kindness with pleasure at their downfall will find the ache named here, and handed to God.

keyVerse.quote: Draw the spear and javelin against my pursuers! Say to my soul, “I am your salvation!”
keyVerse.note: In a psalm full of requests about his enemies, David’s one request for himself is to hear God speak salvation to his soul. That shows the heart of the psalm: he is handing the fight to God, and what he needs most is God himself. The word he longed for is spoken to us in Jesus, whose very name means that he saves his people.

35.reflection:
Every verb in verses 1–3 asks God to act, not David. Why is handing a case to God (Romans 12:19) different from pretending not to be hurt, and different from taking revenge?

David had fasted and prayed for the very people who now mocked him (vv. 13–16). Have you known the pain of kindness repaid with cruelty? How does this psalm help you speak to God about it honestly?

Jesus applied “They hated me without a cause” to himself (John 15:25), and on the cross prayed for those who hated him (Luke 23:34). How should his example shape the way Christians pray a psalm like this one?

The psalm ends with a shout that the LORD is great and delights in his servant’s welfare (v. 27). In a conflict you are facing, what would it look like to want God’s praise more than your own vindication?

36.text: To the choirmaster. Of David, the servant of the LORD. 1Transgression speaks to the wicked deep in his heart; there is no fear of God before his eyes.2For he flatters himself in his own eyes that his iniquity cannot be found out and hated.3The words of his mouth are trouble and deceit; he has ceased to act wisely and do good.4He plots trouble while on his bed; he sets himself in a way that is not good; he does not reject evil.5Your steadfast love, O LORD, extends to the heavens, your faithfulness to the clouds.6Your righteousness is like the mountains of God; your judgments are like the great deep; man and beast you save, O LORD.7How precious is your steadfast love, O God! The children of mankind take refuge in the shadow of your wings.8They feast on the abundance of your house, and you give them drink from the river of your delights.9For with you is the fountain of life; in your light do we see light.10Oh, continue your steadfast love to those who know you, and your righteousness to the upright of heart!11Let not the foot of arrogance come upon me, nor the hand of the wicked drive me away.12There the evildoers lie fallen; they are thrust down, unable to rise.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — No Fear of God Before His Eyes
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Wickedness grows from one root: a heart that has stopped reckoning with God. David pictures sin as a voice speaking deep inside a man, and the man listening, because there is no fear of God before his eyes (v. 1). He flatters himself so thoroughly that he cannot see his own iniquity clearly enough to hate it (v. 2). Then the decline shows outwardly, step by step: his words turn to trouble and deceit, he gives up doing good, he lies awake planning harm, and at last he settles into a way that is not good and no longer says no to evil (vv. 3–4). The portrait is drawn so that we may recognise the road, not admire it.
verseByVerse.theology: Four verses inside a man who has stopped fearing God, ending with him lying awake planning.

verseByVerse.quote: Transgression speaks to the wicked deep in his heart; there is no fear of God before his eyes. For he flatters himself in his own eyes that his iniquity cannot be found out and hated. The words of his mouth are trouble and deceit; he has ceased to act wisely and do good. He plots trouble while on his bed; he sets himself in a way that is not good; he does not reject evil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wickedness grows from a heart that has stopped reckoning with God: sin speaks within, self-flattery hides it, and step by step a man stops refusing evil.

Transgression speaks to the wicked. Sin is given a voice here, and a listener. It speaks deep down, where no one else can hear the conversation, and the man has learned to take its advice.

There is no fear of God before his eyes. The diagnosis, and Paul thought it the last word on the human race. He ends his long chain of Old Testament quotations about sin (throats like open graves, feet swift to shed blood) with this verse: “There is no fear of God before their eyes” (Romans 3:18). Everything else in the list grows out of that one absence. It is not hatred of God but no fear of him: he never reckons with God, and looks no higher than himself.

He flatters himself in his own eyes. In the story he tells himself about himself, he always comes out well, and so he cannot see his iniquity clearly enough to hate it. That is the real damage of self-flattery: not that it makes a man vain, but that it blinds him at exactly the point where he would need to see in order to repent.

He has ceased to act wisely and do good. Watch the progression, for it describes a road travelled step by step, not a fixed character. First his words go bad. Then he stops doing good: he does not become a monster; he stops doing what he used to do. Then the planning, on his bed in the dark, where a man is alone with his own mind. And finally the settled position: he “does not reject evil”. Not that he loves it; he has simply stopped saying no to it.

Isn’t thinking well of myself healthy? We are often told that our deepest problem is low self-esteem, and some people truly need to hear that they are not worthless. But psychologists also find the opposite tendency almost everywhere: most of us rate ourselves above average at nearly everything, and remember our stories so as to stay the hero. The psalm calls this self-flattery and names its cost: it keeps a man’s iniquity from being “found out and hated”. That is why a better self-image never brings rest. Whether I flatter myself or despise myself, I am still the judge in my own court, and still on trial. The gospel takes the case out of my hands. At the cross God tells the truth about me that flattery hid, and in the same place tells me I am wanted. Someone who no longer needs to flatter himself can at last look straight at his sin and hate it, because looking at it no longer means losing himself.

Uncertain wording. The word translated “speaks” (v. 1) is the one the prophets used in “declares the LORD”, so the line reads literally “an oracle of transgression”: sin has become the wicked man’s prophet. Verse 2 is compressed Hebrew that translations render differently, but its picture of self-regard hiding sin is clear.

Textual note. The ESV notes that most Hebrew manuscripts read “in my heart”, which would make it the psalmist reporting an oracle he has received about the wicked. Either way the picture of the wicked heart is the same.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Against the cramped heart of the wicked stands the boundless love of God, the true source of life and light. David measures God’s steadfast love, faithfulness, righteousness and judgments against the heavens, the clouds, the mountains and the deep, and marvels that his saving care reaches man and beast (vv. 5–6). People of every nation take refuge under his wings, feast on the plenty of his house and drink from the river of his delights, because with him is the fountain of life and in his light we see light (vv. 7–9). So David prays that God would keep his love coming and keep the proud from driving him away, and he sees the evildoers already fallen (vv. 10–12).
verseByVerse.theology: Against four verses of a closed heart, five verses of a God whose love has no ceiling.

verseByVerse.quote: Your steadfast love, O LORD, extends to the heavens, your faithfulness to the clouds. Your righteousness is like the mountains of God; your judgments are like the great deep; man and beast you save, O LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Against the cramped heart of the wicked, David sets God’s immeasurable love, faithfulness, righteousness and judgments, and a saving care that reaches even the animals.

Extends to the heavens. The psalm turns without warning, deliberately: four verses of a man’s cramped interior, and then the sky. Four of God’s attributes are measured against the biggest things there are. His steadfast love reaches the heavens and his faithfulness the clouds. His righteousness is like the great mountains: immovable, visible from far off, older than anyone looking at them. His judgments are like “the great deep”: unfathomable, and not always comfortable to sail over.

Steadfast love. The Hebrew is ḥesed, and about half its uses in the Old Testament are in the Psalms: it is this book’s favourite word for God. It is love that has bound itself by promise and does not let go. What this psalm adds is its size. The man of verses 1–4 has made himself the measure of everything; David measures God’s love against the sky, and the sky runs out first. We usually measure God’s love by our circumstances, and it shrinks whenever life does. Paul measured it at the cross and prayed that believers might grasp “the breadth and length and height and depth” of a love that surpasses knowledge (Ephesians 3:18–19). Tonight, look up, and let the sky correct your arithmetic. See Steadfast love in the Theological Dictionary.

Your righteousness is like the mountains of God. “Mountains of God” is a Hebrew way of saying the mightiest mountains. The pairing matters: righteousness you can see and climb, judgments you cannot see the bottom of. Both are God. A believer who knows only God’s plain righteousness will be shaken when his dealings cannot be understood; one who knows only the mystery will think God acts without reason.

Man and beast you save, O LORD. Then the line nobody expects. In the middle of a psalm about human wickedness, God’s care takes in the animals. He saves creatures who cannot sin, cannot praise him in words, and will never read this psalm. That clause shows the reach of his kindness as the grand comparisons cannot. Jesus said the same of sparrows: “not one of them is forgotten before God” (Luke 12:6).

verseByVerse.quote: How precious is your steadfast love, O God! The children of mankind take refuge in the shadow of your wings. They feast on the abundance of your house, and you give them drink from the river of your delights. For with you is the fountain of life; in your light do we see light.
verseByVerse.commentary:
People of every nation may shelter in God’s precious love, feast and drink from it, for he is the source of life and the light by which we see.

The shadow of your wings. This is the picture of Psalm 17:8, and here the whole human race is invited under the wings: “the children of mankind”, not only Israel. Once there they are not merely safe but fed. “Abundance” is a strong word, the word for the fat portion of a sacrifice: God’s hospitality is not rationing.

The river of your delights. The word for “delights” comes from the same root as Eden, the garden of delight, where a river flowed (Genesis 2:10). There is a river at the end of the Bible too, “the river of the water of life, bright as crystal, flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb” (Revelation 22:1). The psalm puts believers drinking from it now.

For with you is the fountain of life. God is the source, not merely a supplier. He does not keep a stock of life; he is its fountain, the spring where it comes out of the ground. John writes of the Word, “In him was life, and the life was the light of men” (John 1:4), and Jesus says, “I am the light of the world” (John 8:12).

In your light do we see light. The Bible’s whole account of how we know anything, in seven words. You do not examine God by some other light and reach a verdict; you see everything else, yourself included, by his. That is exactly what the man of verses 1–4 has lost. He flatters himself in his own eyes because he is looking by his own light, and in that light his iniquity cannot be found. Bring him into God’s light and he would see it at once.

verseByVerse.quote: Oh, continue your steadfast love to those who know you, and your righteousness to the upright of heart! Let not the foot of arrogance come upon me, nor the hand of the wicked drive me away. There the evildoers lie fallen; they are thrust down, unable to rise.
verseByVerse.commentary:
David asks God to keep his love flowing and to keep the proud from driving him away, and he sees the end already: the evildoers fallen for good.

Oh, continue your steadfast love. After the mountains and the deep, a small and very human request: keep it coming. He is not asking for a new experience but for the same one tomorrow. And the fear is concrete: a foot on him, a hand shoving him out.

There the evildoers lie fallen. The psalm ends abruptly, in the past tense, as though the psalmist has been shown the end of the story and is pointing at it: “there”. Look, over there: it is done. That is the answer to the first four verses, not an argument but an outcome. So the middle of the psalm matters most: the difference between the two men is not intelligence or luck but which light they see by, and whose wings they are under.

Unable to rise. The evildoers fall and stay down. One man was thrust down into death who had done no evil, and he rose; those who take refuge in him will rise with him (1 Corinthians 15:20–22).

36.title: In Your Light Do We See Light
36.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 36 follows David’s long plea against unjust enemies in Psalm 35 and steps back to look at evil from the inside: what goes on in the heart of a man who has no fear of God. Its heading calls David “the servant of the LORD”, a title found in the headings only here and in Psalm 18.

The message. Evil begins inside, when a man stops reckoning with God and flatters himself until he can no longer see his own sin. Over against that cramped heart stands the vast, faithful love of God, which shelters, feeds and gives life to all who take refuge in him, so that only in his light do we see truly. Those who know him may ask him to keep that love coming, sure that evil will fall.

Why it was said. The psalm names no occasion, but David knew both the arrogant men who plotted against him and the temptations of his own heart (see the introduction). It taught Israel to see wickedness for what it is, and to look up to the God who outlasts it.

How the chapter makes its case. The psalm moves from the heart of the wicked to the heart of God, then to prayer. First comes a portrait of the godless (vv. 1–4): sin speaks within, there is no fear of God before his eyes, he flatters himself, his words go bad, he stops doing good, plots on his bed and no longer refuses evil. Then the sky opens (vv. 5–9). God’s love, faithfulness, righteousness and judgments are measured against heavens, clouds, mountains and the deep, and his care takes in man and beast (vv. 5–6). People of every nation shelter under his wings, feast and drink, for with him is the fountain of life (vv. 7–9). Last come prayer and a glimpse of the end (vv. 10–12): continue your love; do not let the proud trample me; there the evildoers lie fallen.

Where it leads. By the character of God revealed in Christ, and by the need the psalm exposes. Paul quotes verse 1 to sum up the whole human race, “There is no fear of God before their eyes” (Romans 3:18), and then announces “the righteousness of God through faith in Jesus Christ for all who believe” (Romans 3:22). The fountain of life and the light are given a name in John’s Gospel: “In him was life, and the life was the light of men” (John 1:4). And at the end the river of God’s delights flows “from the throne of God and of the Lamb” (Revelation 22:1).

For us. Self-flattery is the most comfortable sin and the most blinding, so ask God to show you yourself in his light, and do not be afraid of what you will see, for the same light shows a love higher than the sky. Then come under his wings and drink: the life you need is not in yourself but in him, freely given in Christ.
36.theology:
The root of human wickedness is the absence of the fear of God (v. 1; Rom 3:18), and it works by self-flattery, which blinds a man to the very sin he would need to see (v. 2).

Against that closed heart stands a God whose love has no ceiling and whose righteousness and judgments are as great as mountains and sea (vv. 5-6). He is the fountain of life, not merely its supplier, and in your light do we see light (v. 9) answers verse 2: a man who looks by his own light can never find his own sin.
36.examples:
Two men lie awake at night in the early psalms. One ponders on his bed and is silent before God (4:4); the other plots (36:4). The night makes no difference; what is already in the heart does.

In a psalm about human evil, God's care still takes in the animals: man and beast you save, O LORD.

And the whole of how we come to know anything is in seven words: in your light do we see light.

keyVerse.quote: For with you is the fountain of life; in your light do we see light.
keyVerse.note: This verse is the answer to the wicked man of verses 1–4, who lives by his own light and so cannot see his sin. God is not only the giver of life but its spring, and only in his light do we see ourselves and everything else truly. John gives that life and light a name: “In him was life, and the life was the light of men” (John 1:4).

36.reflection:
Verses 1–4 trace a man’s decline step by step, ending with “he does not reject evil”. Which step on that road do you think is most dangerous, and why does the decline so often go unnoticed by the one travelling it?

The psalm calls self-flattery the thing that keeps sin from being “found out and hated” (v. 2). How does the gospel free us both from flattering ourselves and from despising ourselves?

David measures God’s love against the heavens, the mountains and the deep (vv. 5–6). What do we tend to measure God’s love by instead, and what difference would it make to measure it by the cross?

“In your light do we see light” (v. 9). What does it mean in practice to see yourself, your work and the world in God’s light, and where do you most need that light now?

37.text: Of David. 1Fret not yourself because of evildoers; be not envious of wrongdoers!2For they will soon fade like the grass and wither like the green herb.3Trust in the LORD, and do good; dwell in the land and befriend faithfulness.4Delight yourself in the LORD, and he will give you the desires of your heart.5Commit your way to the LORD; trust in him, and he will act.6He will bring forth your righteousness as the light, and your justice as the noonday.7Be still before the LORD and wait patiently for him; fret not yourself over the one who prospers in his way, over the man who carries out evil devices!8Refrain from anger, and forsake wrath! Fret not yourself; it tends only to evil.9For the evildoers shall be cut off, but those who wait for the LORD shall inherit the land.10In just a little while, the wicked will be no more; though you look carefully at his place, he will not be there.11But the meek shall inherit the land and delight themselves in abundant peace.12The wicked plots against the righteous and gnashes his teeth at him,13but the Lord laughs at the wicked, for he sees that his day is coming.14The wicked draw the sword and bend their bows to bring down the poor and needy, to slay those whose way is upright;15their sword shall enter their own heart, and their bows shall be broken.16Better is the little that the righteous has than the abundance of many wicked.17For the arms of the wicked shall be broken, but the LORD upholds the righteous.18The LORD knows the days of the blameless, and their heritage will remain forever;19they are not put to shame in evil times; in the days of famine they have abundance.20But the wicked will perish; the enemies of the LORD are like the glory of the pastures; they vanish—like smoke they vanish away.21The wicked borrows but does not pay back, but the righteous is generous and gives;22for those blessed by the LORD shall inherit the land, but those cursed by him shall be cut off.23The steps of a man are established by the LORD, when he delights in his way;24though he fall, he shall not be cast headlong, for the LORD upholds his hand.25I have been young, and now am old, yet I have not seen the righteous forsaken or his children begging for bread.26He is ever lending generously, and his children become a blessing.27Turn away from evil and do good; so shall you dwell forever.28For the LORD loves justice; he will not forsake his saints. They are preserved forever, but the children of the wicked shall be cut off.29The righteous shall inherit the land and dwell upon it forever.30The mouth of the righteous utters wisdom, and his tongue speaks justice.31The law of his God is in his heart; his steps do not slip.32The wicked watches for the righteous and seeks to put him to death.33The LORD will not abandon him to his power or let him be condemned when he is brought to trial.34Wait for the LORD and keep his way, and he will exalt you to inherit the land; you will look on when the wicked are cut off.35I have seen a wicked, ruthless man, spreading himself like a green laurel tree.36But he passed away, and behold, he was no more; though I sought him, he could not be found.37Mark the blameless and behold the upright, for there is a future for the man of peace.38But transgressors shall be altogether destroyed; the future of the wicked shall be cut off.39The salvation of the righteous is from the LORD; he is their stronghold in the time of trouble.40The LORD helps them and delivers them; he delivers them from the wicked and saves them, because they take refuge in him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — Delight Yourself in the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Do not let the success of the wicked make you burn; put your attention on the LORD instead. The psalm opens with the problem, envy of evildoers, and the reason it need not rule us: they fade like grass (vv. 1–2). Then come the positive commands, all pointed away from the wicked and towards God: trust and do good, delight in the LORD, commit your way to him, and he will act and bring your cause into the light (vv. 3–6). Be still and wait, refrain from anger, because fretting leads only to evil (vv. 7–8). In a little while the wicked will be gone, and the meek will inherit the land and delight in abundant peace (vv. 9–11).
verseByVerse.theology: Five commands for a believer watching the wrong people win, and every one of them is about where he puts his attention.

verseByVerse.quote: Fret not yourself because of evildoers; be not envious of wrongdoers! For they will soon fade like the grass and wither like the green herb. Trust in the LORD, and do good; dwell in the land and befriend faithfulness. Delight yourself in the LORD, and he will give you the desires of your heart. Commit your way to the LORD; trust in him, and he will act. He will bring forth your righteousness as the light, and your justice as the noonday.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When dishonest people prosper, do not burn with envy: trust the LORD, delight in him and roll your way onto him, and he will act.

Fret not yourself because of evildoers. The psalm names the feeling exactly, and it is envy before it is anger. Watching people who cut corners do well produces a particular heat in a decent person, and the Hebrew word for “fret” means just that: to grow hot, a slow burn. Proverbs gives the same instruction in almost the same words (Proverbs 24:19), a sign of how universal the problem is. And the first reason is time: they “will soon fade like the grass”.

An alphabet poem. Its stanzas run through the Hebrew alphabet (see the note), a form made for memorising, because this problem does not go away after one reading.

Trust in the LORD, and do good. Four commands, all pointed away from the problem: trust, do good, stay where God has put you, befriend faithfulness. Graze where it is safe rather than chewing over what the wicked are getting.

Delight yourself in the LORD. One of the most misquoted verses in the Bible: not a promise that God will hand over whatever you want if you ask religiously enough. The delight comes first, and it changes the desires: a man who delights in God starts wanting different things, and those are what he is given. That is why the promise is safe to make.

How do I delight myself in the LORD? Delight cannot be ordered up, but it can be fed, as an appetite grows by eating. Look where he shows himself. Read a Gospel slowly and watch Jesus with the leper, the widow, the thief beside him; delight answers beauty, and Jesus said, “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father” (John 14:9). Trace the gifts back. When the meal is good or the friend rings, thank the Giver by name; joy in the gift is meant to lead to joy in him. Sing. Praise is how delight is practised, and it often comes before the feeling. Notice the rival delights. What does your mind run to when it is free, and what would you most hate to lose? That is the desire verse 4 promises to reshape. And delight begins on God’s side. The Father says of his Son, “with whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3:17), and in Christ he takes pleasure in us before we take any in him: “he will rejoice over you with gladness” (Zephaniah 3:17). Our delight in him is the echo of his in us.

Commit your way to the LORD. To commit your way is literally to roll it onto him, the way a load is rolled off your own back onto someone stronger. Peter says the same: “casting all your anxieties on him, because he cares for you” (1 Peter 5:7). Then three words for anyone trying to arrange his own vindication: “he will act”.

Your justice as the noonday. Not a whispered verdict but daylight. The man who has been misrepresented does not have to publish his own defence; God does the publishing, and he does it at noon.

Uncertain wording. “Befriend faithfulness” (v. 3) renders a compressed phrase, and the ESV notes two other readings: “feed on faithfulness” or “find safe pasture”. The verb can mean to graze or to keep company with, so the line either calls the believer to cultivate faithfulness or promises him safe grazing in the land. Either way it pictures settled life with God, set against restless envy.

verseByVerse.quote: Be still before the LORD and wait patiently for him; fret not yourself over the one who prospers in his way, over the man who carries out evil devices! Refrain from anger, and forsake wrath! Fret not yourself; it tends only to evil. For the evildoers shall be cut off, but those who wait for the LORD shall inherit the land. In just a little while, the wicked will be no more; though you look carefully at his place, he will not be there. But the meek shall inherit the land and delight themselves in abundant peace.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Be still and wait for God instead of seething, for fretting leads to evil, the wicked will soon be gone, and the meek will inherit the land.

Be still before the LORD. Two of the hardest things asked of anyone in Scripture, and neither is passive. Staying still while someone else is rewarded for dishonesty takes more strength than acting, and God supplies it: in a Christian it is the Spirit’s fruit of patience and self-control (Galatians 5:22–23).

Fret not yourself; it tends only to evil. “Fret not” a second and third time, and now with a diagnosis attached. Fretting does not stay a private discomfort. It sours a man, and then it recruits him: the person most likely to adopt the methods of the wicked is the one who has spent a year seething about how well they work.

In just a little while. The psalm’s whole answer is time: not immediately, and not never. Verse 10 is exact and slightly eerie: you will look carefully at the place where he was, and he will not be there. Everyone who lives long enough sees this happen to someone.

But the meek shall inherit the land. The meek are not the spineless but people who have stopped grabbing, precisely the ones who in the world’s accounting inherit nothing. For the first readers “the land” was each family’s God-given share of Canaan, which powerful men could swallow up by debt and fraud (Isaiah 5:8; Micah 2:2); the psalm promises that in the end the shares will rest with the meek. Jesus lifted this verse into the Beatitudes, widening the land to the whole earth: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth” (Matthew 5:5). The land promise points beyond Canaan to the whole new earth (Romans 4:13).

Because the Meek One did. Jesus did not only teach it; he lived it. He called himself “gentle and lowly in heart” (Matthew 11:29), would not grab, and for a little while was cut off in death. Now he is “the heir of all things” (Hebrews 1:2), and those who belong to him are “fellow heirs with Christ” (Romans 8:17). The meek inherit because the Meek One did.

How do I stop fretting? It usually starts with a comparison: the colleague who fiddled the figures and was promoted. Catch the heat early. When you find yourself rehearsing their success at 2 a.m., call it what the psalm calls it, before it hardens into bitterness. Starve it. Stop checking their news and steering every conversation back to them. Hand the case over. Tell God plainly what is unjust, and leave the verdict with him: “Beloved, never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God” (Romans 12:19). Do the next good thing. Fretting is cured more by getting on with your own task (v. 3) than by winning the argument in your head. Christ was still in exactly this way: “When he was reviled, he did not revile in return; when he suffered, he did not threaten, but continued entrusting himself to him who judges justly” (1 Peter 2:23). He bore the worst injustice ever done, for us; and because the Judge has ruled in his favour, and ours in him, we can afford to be still.
verseByVerse.note: An acrostic poem in stanzas (ESV note).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–26 — Better Is the Little That the Righteous Has
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A little with God is better than plenty without him, because the two are headed for different futures. The wicked plot and snarl, but the Lord laughs, seeing their day coming (vv. 12–13); their swords, drawn against the poor, turn back on them (vv. 14–15). The righteous have little, but the LORD upholds them, knows their days and keeps their inheritance, even in famine, while his enemies vanish like smoke (vv. 16–20). The wicked take and do not repay; the righteous give. Their steps are established by the LORD, and though they fall they are not thrown down, for he holds their hand. An old man testifies that he has watched God sustain such people (vv. 21–26).
verseByVerse.theology: The comparison is not between two amounts but between two futures.

verseByVerse.quote: The wicked plots against the righteous and gnashes his teeth at him, but the Lord laughs at the wicked, for he sees that his day is coming.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The wicked plot in earnest, but the Lord laughs, because he sees their day of judgment coming.

The wicked plots against the righteous. The wicked man is not careless: he plots, and he hates. Gnashing the teeth is the snarl of an animal about to attack (compare 35:16). The psalm takes the threat seriously before it puts it in proportion.

But the Lord laughs at the wicked. God laughed the same way at the plotting kings of Psalm 2:4, and it is not cruelty. God laughs because he can see the calendar. The plotter works hard on a scheme whose expiry date is already fixed, which from a great enough height is absurd.

verseByVerse.quote: The wicked draw the sword and bend their bows to bring down the poor and needy, to slay those whose way is upright; their sword shall enter their own heart, and their bows shall be broken.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The violence the wicked aim at the poor and upright will turn back on themselves.

To bring down the poor and needy. The wicked man who dug a pit in Psalm 7 appears again, armed this time. Note who the targets are: the poor and needy. That is almost always who suffers when the unscrupulous do well: not their rivals, but the people with the least protection.

Their sword shall enter their own heart. Verse 15 answers verse 14 weapon for weapon: the sword drawn against the upright turns into their own heart, and the bent bows are broken. It is the recoil of 7:15–16 stated as a rule of God’s world. It does not always happen on the day; it does happen in the end, which is the whole argument of the psalm (v. 10).

verseByVerse.quote: Better is the little that the righteous has than the abundance of many wicked. For the arms of the wicked shall be broken, but the LORD upholds the righteous.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A little held by God is better than plenty held by those whose strength he will break.

Better is the little that the righteous has. The comparison is not between two bank balances but between two futures. That is the only honest way the sum works, and the psalm knows that today the abundance looks better.

The LORD upholds the righteous. Verse 17 gives the reason for verse 16. The arms of the wicked, the strength they work and fight with, will be broken; the righteous are held up by an arm that is not their own. Proverbs says it in its own words: “Better is a little with the fear of the LORD than great treasure and trouble with it” (Proverbs 15:16).

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD knows the days of the blameless, and their heritage will remain forever; they are not put to shame in evil times; in the days of famine they have abundance. But the wicked will perish; the enemies of the LORD are like the glory of the pastures; they vanish—like smoke they vanish away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God watches over every day of his people, so their inheritance lasts and he provides in hard times, while his enemies vanish like smoke.

The LORD knows the days of the blameless. “Knows” is more than awareness: it is watchful care, as in “the LORD knows the way of the righteous” (1:6). Every one of their days is on a list he keeps, and what he watches over cannot be lost, so their heritage, the land promised in verses 9 and 11, outlasts the wicked.

In the days of famine they have abundance. Provision in the famine, not exemption from it (as at 33:19). The enemies of God, by contrast, are like the bloom of the pastures, bright for a season, and like smoke: rising, filling the sky, gone with the first wind.

Uncertain wording. The word rendered “pastures” (v. 20) can also mean “lambs”. The King James Version took it so (“as the fat of lambs”), picturing sacrificial fat burning into smoke, which fits the next line; the ESV pictures field flowers that fade. Either way the wicked vanish.

verseByVerse.quote: The wicked borrows but does not pay back, but the righteous is generous and gives; for those blessed by the LORD shall inherit the land, but those cursed by him shall be cut off. The steps of a man are established by the LORD, when he delights in his way; though he fall, he shall not be cast headlong, for the LORD upholds his hand. I have been young, and now am old, yet I have not seen the righteous forsaken or his children begging for bread. He is ever lending generously, and his children become a blessing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The righteous give rather than grasp, and God holds them so that when they stumble they are not thrown down; an old man testifies that he has watched God sustain such people.

The righteous is generous and gives. The contrast is not rich against poor but the man who takes and does not return against the man who gives unasked. Generosity is evidence of which side of the psalm you are on.

Though he fall. A promise for people not managing very well. “Though he fall” (it is assumed he will), “he shall not be cast headlong”: he stumbles while a stronger hand keeps hold of his, so he goes down, but not face first, because he was never holding himself up. Peter fell as badly as anyone and was not cast off, for Jesus had said, “I have prayed for you that your faith may not fail” (Luke 22:32).

I have not seen the righteous forsaken. Verse 25 must be handled honestly or it will wound someone. It is an old man’s testimony, not a universal law, and the Bible itself supplies the exceptions: Job on his ash heap, and the believers of Hebrews 11 who were destitute and sawn in two. Scripture does not promise that a godly family never goes hungry, or that faith brings wealth or health; it promises that God will not abandon his people.

A lifetime’s pattern. David reports the pattern he has watched: God does not abandon his people, and generous households tend to be sustained in ways hard to explain from the accounts. Taken as a guarantee, the verse is cruel to the faithful poor. Taken as a witness statement from a man with grey hair, it is worth a great deal.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 27–40 — There Is a Future for the Man of Peace
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: There is a future for the person of peace, because his salvation comes from the LORD. The old man urges a life of turning from evil and doing good, for the LORD loves justice and will not forsake his saints (vv. 27–29). Such a person carries God’s law in his heart, so his mouth speaks wisdom and his steps hold; when the wicked try to destroy him, God will not let him be condemned (vv. 30–33). So wait for the LORD and keep his way. The old man has seen a ruthless man spreading like a green tree, and then gone without trace (vv. 34–36). The ending sets two futures side by side and rests everything on one ground: the LORD saves them, because they take refuge in him (vv. 37–40).
verseByVerse.theology: An old man reports what he has watched happen, twice: the tree that vanished and the righteous who were never abandoned.

verseByVerse.quote: Turn away from evil and do good; so shall you dwell forever. For the LORD loves justice; he will not forsake his saints. They are preserved forever, but the children of the wicked shall be cut off. The righteous shall inherit the land and dwell upon it forever. The mouth of the righteous utters wisdom, and his tongue speaks justice. The law of his God is in his heart; his steps do not slip. The wicked watches for the righteous and seeks to put him to death. The LORD will not abandon him to his power or let him be condemned when he is brought to trial.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Turn from evil and do good, for the LORD loves justice and will not forsake his people, who carry his law in their hearts and whom no human court can finally condemn.

For the LORD loves justice. The command is the one Psalm 34 gave (34:14), and the reason offered is God’s own taste: “the LORD loves justice”. He is not merely committed to it as a policy; he likes it. That is why injustice will not be allowed to stand, and why his saints, who practise it, are not forsaken.

The law of his God is in his heart. The order runs from inward to outward: the law in the heart, and therefore wisdom in the mouth, and therefore steps that hold. The first psalm said the blessed man meditates on God’s law day and night; here is what that produces after some years. What a man says under pressure comes out of what he has been storing. God promised to write his law on his people’s hearts in the new covenant (Jeremiah 31:33), and Hebrews puts Psalm 40, “your law is within my heart” (40:8), on the lips of Christ (Hebrews 10:5–7): the one man in whom the law was perfectly at home.

When he is brought to trial. The wicked man watches the righteous patiently and means to kill him (v. 32), and the psalm does not pretend the trial will not happen. It says the verdict is not theirs to give. “When he is brought to trial” (so he will be), God will not let the court’s word be the last one. Paul asks the same question in a sharper form: “Who shall bring any charge against God’s elect? It is God who justifies” (Romans 8:33).

verseByVerse.quote: Wait for the LORD and keep his way, and he will exalt you to inherit the land; you will look on when the wicked are cut off. I have seen a wicked, ruthless man, spreading himself like a green laurel tree. But he passed away, and behold, he was no more; though I sought him, he could not be found. Mark the blameless and behold the upright, for there is a future for the man of peace. But transgressors shall be altogether destroyed; the future of the wicked shall be cut off. The salvation of the righteous is from the LORD; he is their stronghold in the time of trouble. The LORD helps them and delivers them; he delivers them from the wicked and saves them, because they take refuge in him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wait for the LORD and keep his way: the wicked have no future, but the person of peace has one, because the LORD saves those who take refuge in him.

Wait for the LORD and keep his way. Waiting again, and paired with activity. The waiting is never idleness in this psalm; it is doing the next right thing while the outcome is delayed.

Like a green laurel tree. The second thing the old man has watched: a tree in its own soil, leafy, spreading, everywhere. Then the psalm in miniature: he was no more, and though the old man went looking, he could not be found.

There is a future for the man of peace. The word that carries the ending is “future”. It is not that the righteous man has a better present; the psalm has admitted all along that he often does not. He has an after. And what the wicked man lacks is not comfort or success but a tomorrow that belongs to him.

Because they take refuge in him. The last verse gives the only qualification in forty verses of instruction: “because they take refuge in him”. Not because they managed not to fret, or waited well, or never envied anyone. The psalm’s commands are real, and none of them is the ground of the rescue. Refuge is. And Christ, who waited without fretting and did good when it was repaid with evil, did it in their place: “by the one man’s obedience the many will be made righteous” (Romans 5:19). So a believer who has fretted all week starts again from the same refuge, not from a clean record.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew behind “a green laurel tree” (v. 35) seems to mean a native tree flourishing in its own soil; no species is named (the King James Version has “bay tree”). In verse 36, “he passed away” is literally “he passed”, which could mean someone passed by his place; either way, he was gone.

37.title: Fret Not Yourself
37.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 36 set the wicked man, with “no fear of God before his eyes”, beside the steadfast love of God that reaches to the heavens. Psalm 37 takes up the question that contrast raises for every believer: then why do the wicked do so well? It is a wisdom psalm of David, an acrostic spoken not to God but to us, like an old man to the young.

The message. Do not fret when evil people prosper. Their success is as brief as spring grass, while God’s care for those who trust him lasts for ever. So trust him, delight in him, roll your way onto him, be still and wait, and keep doing good. The future belongs to the meek, because the LORD himself is their salvation and their refuge.

Why it was said. David writes in old age (v. 25) for people who watched the ruthless grow rich, sometimes by preying on the poor and swallowing their land (vv. 14, 21), and who were tempted either to envy them or to copy them. Israel’s land was held in family shares as a gift under God’s covenant, so “inherit the land” was a promise they could feel. Proverbs meets the same temptation in the same words (Proverbs 24:19–20).

How the chapter makes its case. First come the commands: do not fret but trust, delight, commit and wait, for in a little while the wicked will be gone and the meek shall inherit the land (vv. 1–11). Then contrasts: the Lord laughs at the plotting wicked, whose weapons turn on themselves; the little of the righteous outlasts the abundance of the wicked; and the righteous who stumble are never thrown down (vv. 12–26). Last, the old man’s testimony: turn from evil and do good; he has seen the spreading tree of the wicked vanish, and there is a future for the man of peace, whose salvation is from the LORD (vv. 27–40).

Where it leads. By promise and by pattern. Jesus took verse 11 into the Beatitudes and widened it: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth” (Matthew 5:5), so the land promise reaches its goal in the new earth, inherited with Christ, “the heir of all things” (Hebrews 1:2). And Christ is the psalm lived out. He did not fret or retaliate but “continued entrusting himself to him who judges justly” (1 Peter 2:23); he was cut off, and then God brought forth his righteousness as the noonday by raising him from the dead.

For us. When you watch someone prosper by cutting corners, this psalm tells you where to look instead: at the LORD who loves justice and has already vindicated his meek Son. Your future is secure in him, so you can afford to be still, hand the case over, and get on with doing good.
37.theology:
The answer to prospering wickedness is time: in just a little while (v. 10), and there is a future for the man of peace (v. 37). The righteous are not promised a better present but an after. Fretting is dangerous, not merely unpleasant, because envy of the wicked ends in joining them (v. 8).

Delight in God reshapes the desires he then satisfies (v. 4), and Jesus took the meek shall inherit the land into the Beatitudes (v. 11). Verse 25 is an old man's testimony, not a universal law (Heb 11:37 stands beside it), and the psalm's last word gives the ground of rescue: because they take refuge in him (v. 40).
37.examples:
The Hebrew word for fret means to get hot: the slow burn of watching cheats win. The psalm's cure is to look away from them, and to the LORD.

An old man tells of a green tree that filled the landscape; he passed by again, and it could not be found. And he tells of righteous people who fell many times and never fell face first, because a stronger hand was holding theirs.

keyVerse.quote: Be still before the LORD and wait patiently for him; fret not yourself over the one who prospers in his way, over the man who carries out evil devices!
keyVerse.note: The verse holds the whole psalm in one breath: the temptation (watching the wicked prosper), the forbidden response (fretting) and the commanded one (stillness and patient waiting before the LORD). Everything else in the psalm gives reasons why that stillness is wise rather than naive: the wicked fade, the meek inherit, and the LORD is the refuge of those who trust him.

37.reflection:
Who are the people whose success is most likely to make you “fret” (vv. 1, 7–8)? Why does the psalm say fretting “tends only to evil”, and where have you seen that happen?

Verse 4 is often read as a promise to get what we want. How does delighting in the LORD change our desires, and what practical habits help that delight to grow?

Verse 25 is an old man’s testimony, not a guarantee. How would you use it to encourage a struggling believer without wounding someone whose family is going without?

Jesus took verse 11 into the Beatitudes (Matthew 5:5) and lived it to the cross (1 Peter 2:23). What would it look like this week to be “meek” in a situation where you are tempted to grab or retaliate?

38.text: A Psalm of David, for the memorial offering. 1O LORD, rebuke me not in your anger, nor discipline me in your wrath!2For your arrows have sunk into me, and your hand has come down on me.3There is no soundness in my flesh because of your indignation; there is no health in my bones because of my sin.4For my iniquities have gone over my head; like a heavy burden, they are too heavy for me.5My wounds stink and fester because of my foolishness,6I am utterly bowed down and prostrate; all the day I go about mourning.7For my sides are filled with burning, and there is no soundness in my flesh.8I am feeble and crushed; I groan because of the tumult of my heart.9O Lord, all my longing is before you; my sighing is not hidden from you.10My heart throbs; my strength fails me, and the light of my eyes—it also has gone from me.11My friends and companions stand aloof from my plague, and my nearest kin stand far off.12Those who seek my life lay their snares; those who seek my hurt speak of ruin and meditate treachery all day long.13But I am like a deaf man; I do not hear, like a mute man who does not open his mouth.14I have become like a man who does not hear, and in whose mouth are no rebukes.15But for you, O LORD, do I wait; it is you, O Lord my God, who will answer.16For I said, "Only let them not rejoice over me, who boast against me when my foot slips!"17For I am ready to fall, and my pain is ever before me.18I confess my iniquity; I am sorry for my sin.19But my foes are vigorous, they are mighty, and many are those who hate me wrongfully.20Those who render me evil for good accuse me because I follow after good.21Do not forsake me, O LORD! O my God, be not far from me!22Make haste to help me, O Lord, my salvation!

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — No Soundness in My Flesh
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Under God’s discipline, David tells the truth about where his trouble comes from and how deep it goes. He asks not to escape correction but to be spared God’s anger, and he names the source plainly: God’s arrows and God’s hand (vv. 1–2). Then he lays out the damage without dressing it up: no soundness in his flesh, iniquities gone over his head like a flood and too heavy to carry, festering wounds he traces to his own folly, a body bowed and burning, and a heart in uproar (vv. 3–8). Nothing is softened, because the God he is speaking to already knows.
verseByVerse.theology: Sickness, guilt and grief are described together; nothing is tidied up and nothing is hidden from God.

verseByVerse.quote: O LORD, rebuke me not in your anger, nor discipline me in your wrath! For your arrows have sunk into me, and your hand has come down on me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
David asks God to correct him without anger, and admits that the blows come from God’s own hand.

For the memorial offering. Probably a rite: a handful of the grain offering was burned as a “memorial portion” (Leviticus 2:2), bringing the worshipper to God’s remembrance. This psalm is that handful put into words.

Rebuke me not in your anger. Almost word for word the opening of Psalm 6. He does not ask to be let off the correction, only that it not come in anger, and he does not pretend about the source: God’s arrows, God’s hand. That is braver than blaming circumstances, and more hopeful: the hand that strikes is the hand he can appeal to.

Uncertain wording. “For the memorial offering” (also over Psalm 70) is one Hebrew word, “to bring to remembrance”, as the King James Version renders it. It may tie the psalm to the memorial portion, or simply mark it as a prayer that calls a sufferer to God’s remembrance.

verseByVerse.quote: There is no soundness in my flesh because of your indignation; there is no health in my bones because of my sin. For my iniquities have gone over my head; like a heavy burden, they are too heavy for me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
David’s body and soul are broken, and he says plainly that his own sin lies behind it.

Because of my sin. A connection modern readers flinch at, to be handled carefully. It does not teach that every illness punishes a particular sin: Job settles that, and so does Jesus at John 9:3. But it insists that this man’s sin and this man’s state are connected, and he is the one saying so. Some suffering we bring on ourselves, and pretending otherwise helps nobody.

My iniquities have gone over my head. Guilt is water closing over a man who cannot touch the bottom, and “a heavy burden… too heavy for me”: anyone who has carried something unconfessed knows both. That load was, in the end, carried by another: “the LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all” (Isaiah 53:6).

What it does not mean. Not that a sick believer must hunt for a hidden sin behind every symptom, or that seeing a doctor shows a lack of faith. When Hezekiah was ill, God promised healing and the prophet prescribed a poultice of figs (Isaiah 38:21). Bring your soul to God and your body to a doctor.

verseByVerse.quote: My wounds stink and fester because of my foolishness, I am utterly bowed down and prostrate; all the day I go about mourning. For my sides are filled with burning, and there is no soundness in my flesh. I am feeble and crushed; I groan because of the tumult of my heart.
verseByVerse.commentary:
David describes his wrecked body without dressing it up, and calls the sin behind it his own foolishness.

My wounds stink and fester. One of the most unsparing descriptions of a body in the Psalter: infected wounds, fever, exhaustion. Scripture is not squeamish, and it does not require a sufferer to be presentable before praying.

Because of my foolishness. In the Old Testament folly is not low intelligence but moral failure, a life lived as though God did not matter (14:1). He calls his sin by that name: not an accident or bad luck, but foolishness, and his own.

The tumult of my heart. Verse 8 ends where the trouble goes deepest: the heart in uproar, and under the symptoms a groan, the sighing that verse 9 says is “not hidden” from God.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–22 — But for You, O LORD, Do I Wait
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Deserted by friends and surrounded by enemies, David waits for God, confesses his sin and holds on to God as his salvation. All his longing lies open before the Lord (vv. 9–10). Friends keep their distance and enemies plot, yet he answers them nothing, like a man who cannot hear, because he is waiting for God to answer (vv. 11–16). He admits he is ready to fall, confesses his iniquity and grieves over his sin (vv. 17–18), while maintaining that his foes hate him without cause and repay good with evil (vv. 19–20). The psalm ends unresolved, with a plea for haste and the confidence of the words “my salvation” (vv. 21–22).
verseByVerse.theology: He will not defend himself, he confesses what is true, and he ends still waiting.

verseByVerse.quote: O Lord, all my longing is before you; my sighing is not hidden from you. My heart throbs; my strength fails me, and the light of my eyes—it also has gone from me. My friends and companions stand aloof from my plague, and my nearest kin stand far off. Those who seek my life lay their snares; those who seek my hurt speak of ruin and meditate treachery all day long.
