But I am like a deaf man; I do not hear, like a mute man who does not open his mouth. I have become like a man who does not hear, and in whose mouth are no rebukes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God sees every longing David cannot put into words, and when friends desert him and enemies plot, he leaves his case with God.

All my longing is before you. One restful sentence. He cannot explain himself, and need not: the wanting he cannot shape into a request already lies in God’s sight, and the sighing that is not even words has been heard. For anyone too ill or too low to pray properly, this verse is all the permission needed.

My friends and companions stand aloof. Two circles, and both fail him. Those who love him keep their distance “from my plague”, and the phrase is honest about why: illness frightens people, and the visibly sick are left alone in every century. Those who hate him move closer, because a man who is down is easier to finish.

But I am like a deaf man. His response to the whispering is nothing: no defence, no returned rebukes. Silence under accusation is not weakness; it is what a man can afford when he has handed the case to someone else.

The silent Lamb. Isaiah’s Servant “opened not his mouth” (Isaiah 53:7); questioned at length by Herod, Jesus gave no reply (Luke 23:9), and his friends “stood at a distance” at the cross (Luke 23:49). “When he was reviled, he did not revile in return” (1 Peter 2:23). But David was silent with sin on his conscience; Jesus was silent with none, bearing the sins of others.

verseByVerse.quote: But for you, O LORD, do I wait; it is you, O Lord my God, who will answer. For I said, "Only let them not rejoice over me, who boast against me when my foot slips!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
David is silent before men because he is waiting for God to answer, and he asks only that his enemies not gloat over his fall.

But for you, O LORD, do I wait. The reason for the silence: he is waiting for God to answer, and is sure he will. Until God speaks, he has nothing to add.

Only let them not rejoice over me. Verse 16 gives the content of his waiting prayer. He dreads not only falling but being gloated over by men who “boast” the moment his foot slips, because a believer’s stumble is made into mockery of the God he trusts.

verseByVerse.quote: For I am ready to fall, and my pain is ever before me. I confess my iniquity; I am sorry for my sin.
verseByVerse.commentary:
David admits he is close to falling, and confesses his sin plainly and with real grief.

I am ready to fall. A candid thing for a king to write. He is not steady, he knows it, and his pain never leaves the front of his mind.

I confess my iniquity. No excuses, no circumstances, no comparison with anyone worse. This is the sentence Psalm 32 describes David avoiding for so long. Everything else in the psalm is description; this is the turn, and it is the way back God has always kept open, for “he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins” (1 John 1:9).

I am sorry for my sin. The second half of verse 18 adds the heart to the admission. The word means troubled or anxious: he is not reciting a form but grieved by what he has done, the “godly grief” that “produces a repentance that leads to salvation” (2 Corinthians 7:10).

verseByVerse.quote: But my foes are vigorous, they are mighty, and many are those who hate me wrongfully. Those who render me evil for good accuse me because I follow after good.
verseByVerse.commentary:
David is truly guilty before God and truly wronged by his enemies, and the psalm holds both truths without blending them.

My foes are vigorous. His enemies are strong and many, and they hate him “wrongfully”, literally “with a lie”. Verse 20 names their method: they “accuse” him, using the verb from which the name Satan, the accuser, comes. They repay his good with evil, and his very goodness becomes the charge (compare 35:12).

Guilty and wronged. He is genuinely guilty before God (v. 18) and genuinely wronged by men (vv. 19–20). Confession does not oblige a man to accept every accusation, and being sinned against does not cancel his own sin. Most real situations are exactly this mixed.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not forsake me, O LORD! O my God, be not far from me! Make haste to help me, O Lord, my salvation!
verseByVerse.commentary:
The psalm ends with no rescue yet, only a plea for God to come quickly, and the certainty that he is “my salvation”.

Make haste to help me. No rescue is reported, no health returns, the friends are still at a distance. The last lines are pure asking: do not leave, do not stay far off, hurry. And the final word is the one thing he is sure of: “my salvation”. Some prayers end without answers, and are still prayed by people who know they belong to God. The believer who prays it now has a firmer reason still: in Christ God has promised, “I will never leave you nor forsake you” (Hebrews 13:5).

38.title: I Confess My Iniquity
38.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 37 promised that the LORD upholds the righteous even when they fall. Psalm 38 shows what such a fall can look like from the inside: a man sick in body, crushed by guilt, deserted by friends and hunted by enemies. It is one of the seven psalms the church has long called penitential (with 6, 32, 51, 102, 130 and 143), and it opens almost exactly as Psalm 6 does.

The message. When you are under God’s discipline for your own sin, the way out is not to hide, excuse or defend yourself, but to go straight to the God whose hand is on you. He already sees all your longing and hears your sighing. Confess your sin plainly, leave your accusers to him, and hold on to him as your salvation even before the answer comes.

Why it was said. David wrote it “for the memorial offering”, probably for use when a sufferer brought himself to God’s remembrance in worship. It names no occasion, but describes a king laid low by illness he connects with his own sin, while friends keep away and enemies seize their chance: words for when guilt and suffering arrive together.

How the chapter makes its case. It begins with God’s hand: arrows sunk in, a body with no soundness, and iniquities gone over his head like floodwater (vv. 1–8). At the centre he turns to God, whose sight already holds all his longing; friends stand aloof and enemies plot, but he answers them nothing, because he is waiting for the LORD to answer (vv. 9–16). He confesses his iniquity, insists that his foes hate him wrongfully, and ends with no rescue yet, only “my salvation” (vv. 17–22).

Where it leads. By pattern and by the need it exposes. Christ walked much of this psalm’s road: his acquaintances “stood at a distance” at the cross (Luke 23:49), and before his accusers he was silent like a man who does not hear. But he could never pray verse 18, for he had no sin of his own. The arrows that sank into David for his sin fell on Christ for ours: “the LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all” (Isaiah 53:6). That is why a guilty believer may pray this psalm and still call God “my salvation”.

For us. If guilt and trouble have come together in your life, do not run from God, and do not waste strength defending yourself to people. Tell him the truth, confess what is yours to confess, and wait for him. Because Christ bore the wrath, his discipline of you is a Father’s, and he will not forsake you.
38.theology:
The psalm ties this man's illness to his own sin (vv. 3, 5, 18), and he is the one who makes the connection. It does not turn that into a rule for every sickness, and it does not let him pretend that suffering he has brought on himself is anything else.

Real guilt before God and real injury from men stand side by side without cancelling each other (vv. 18-20). His silence before his accusers, like the Servant's (Isa 53:7), comes from having handed the case to God, and the psalm closes unanswered but still holding on to my salvation (v. 22).
38.examples: The psalm supplies its own pictures. A handful of grain was burned to bring the worshipper to God's remembrance, and this prayer is that handful put into words. Guilt is water closing over the head, and a load too heavy to carry. Friends keep their distance because illness frightens them, while the sighing that never becomes words is already heard. And the prayer ends without an answer, as many faithful prayers do.

keyVerse.quote: But for you, O LORD, do I wait; it is you, O Lord my God, who will answer.
keyVerse.note: This is the hinge of the psalm. David is sick, guilty, deserted and accused, yet he refuses to answer his enemies, because he has put his whole case in God’s hands and trusts God to speak. That waiting turns into confession (v. 18) and ends in the confidence of “my salvation” (v. 22).

38.reflection:
David says plainly that his suffering is connected with his own sin (vv. 3–5), while Job and John 9:3 show that this is not true of all suffering. How can we tell the difference, and how should we speak to a friend who is ill without adding wrongly to their burden?

Verse 9 says that all our longing is before God even when we cannot put it into words. When have you found it hard to pray, and how does this verse help?

David does not answer his accusers but waits for God (vv. 13–15), as Jesus did before his (1 Peter 2:23). When is silence the right response to criticism, and when should we speak?

The psalm ends with no answer yet, only “my salvation” (v. 22). How does Christ’s bearing of our sin (Isaiah 53:6) give us a firmer hold on that word than David had?

39.text: To the choirmaster: to Jeduthun. A Psalm of David. 1I said, "I will guard my ways, that I may not sin with my tongue; I will guard my mouth with a muzzle, so long as the wicked are in my presence."2I was mute and silent; I held my peace to no avail, and my distress grew worse.3My heart became hot within me. As I mused, the fire burned; then I spoke with my tongue:4"O LORD, make me know my end and what is the measure of my days; let me know how fleeting I am!5Behold, you have made my days a few handbreadths, and my lifetime is as nothing before you. Surely all mankind stands as a mere breath! Selah6Surely a man goes about as a shadow! Surely for nothing they are in turmoil; man heaps up wealth and does not know who will gather!7"And now, O Lord, for what do I wait? My hope is in you.8Deliver me from all my transgressions. Do not make me the scorn of the fool!9I am mute; I do not open my mouth, for it is you who have done it.10Remove your stroke from me; I am spent by the hostility of your hand.11When you discipline a man with rebukes for sin, you consume like a moth what is dear to him; surely all mankind is a mere breath! Selah12"Hear my prayer, O LORD, and give ear to my cry; hold not your peace at my tears! For I am a sojourner with you, a guest, like all my fathers.13Look away from me, that I may smile again, before I depart and am no more!"

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Let Me Know How Fleeting I Am
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Silence alone cannot carry grief; it has to become prayer, and the first thing prayer learns is how short life is. David resolves to muzzle his mouth while the wicked are watching, a wise instinct, but holding the feeling down only makes the distress grow until it burns and bursts out (vv. 1–3). When he finally speaks, he speaks to God, and asks to be shown his end: his days are a few handbreadths, every person a mere breath, a shadow busy for nothing, piling up wealth for hands he will never know (vv. 4–6). Knowing that frees a person from the frantic heaping up.
verseByVerse.theology: He muzzles himself until he boils over, and when he finally speaks, his first request is to be told how short his life is.

verseByVerse.quote: I said, "I will guard my ways, that I may not sin with my tongue; I will guard my mouth with a muzzle, so long as the wicked are in my presence." I was mute and silent; I held my peace to no avail, and my distress grew worse. My heart became hot within me. As I mused, the fire burned; then I spoke with my tongue:
verseByVerse.commentary:
David tries to keep his grief bottled up in front of the wicked, but the silence only makes it burn hotter, until he speaks, and rightly speaks to God.

I will guard my ways. A good resolution, and it fails. He decided not to complain in front of people who would use it against him, a wise instinct many believers have adopted in a hostile workplace or family. He put a “muzzle” on his mouth, the word for the strap over an animal’s jaws. The heading hands this very private struggle to Jeduthun, one of the Levite musicians David appointed to give thanks at the sanctuary (1 Chronicles 16:41–42; 25:1).

My distress grew worse. What came was not peace. The heat built up with nowhere to go until it caught fire, and then he spoke anyway. The psalm is honest about something religious people rarely admit: bottling it up is not the same as trusting God, and silence that only holds the feeling down eventually bursts.

Then I spoke with my tongue. What matters is whom he finally speaks to. He does not turn on the wicked; he turns to God, which is what he should have done in verse 1.

verseByVerse.quote: "O LORD, make me know my end and what is the measure of my days; let me know how fleeting I am! Behold, you have made my days a few handbreadths, and my lifetime is as nothing before you. Surely all mankind stands as a mere breath! Selah Surely a man goes about as a shadow! Surely for nothing they are in turmoil; man heaps up wealth and does not know who will gather!
verseByVerse.commentary:
David asks God to show him how short his life is, because a person who knows he is only a breath stops trusting in what he heaps up.

Make me know my end. After months of pent-up frustration, not the obvious request. He asks, as a favour, to be shown how short his life is, the thing most of us work hard not to think about, because a man who knows the length of his life stops taking certain things so seriously, including the prosperity of the wicked that had him fuming in verse 1.

A few handbreadths. A handbreadth is the width of four fingers, the shortest measure they had. And “a mere breath” is a puff of vapour on a cold morning, there and gone. James says the same to people planning next year’s business: “What is your life? For you are a mist that appears for a little time and then vanishes” (James 4:14).

Man heaps up wealth. Two pictures of futility, and the second has teeth: a man spends decades accumulating and has no idea whose hands it will end up in. Jesus told of the barn-builder whose soul was required that night: “the things you have prepared, whose will they be?” (Luke 12:20). The psalm is not saying work is pointless, but that turmoil over possessions is, when the possessor lasts a handbreadth.

Everyone dies, except me. In Tolstoy’s story The Death of Ivan Ilyich, a successful judge falls ill and realises that the syllogism he learned at school (Caius is a man, men are mortal, therefore Caius is mortal) had always seemed right for Caius but never for him. That is the modern posture: we know about death in general and arrange life so as not to meet it in particular: the old in homes, the dying in hospitals, the ageing face retouched. Ivan’s worst agony was not dying but discovering that the life he had built, correct, comfortable and admired, had been arranged to keep the question away. David asks for the opposite: to know his end while there is still time to live differently. The prayer is not morbid: a man who knows he is a breath stops expecting his possessions to make him last.

The one who numbers our days. A Christian can pray it without despair, because the one who numbers our days went into death himself and came out the other side. The end David asked to know is no longer the end.
verseByVerse.note: “For nothing” in v. 6 is literally “as a breath” (ESV note), the same word as “a mere breath” in v. 5: the word Ecclesiastes uses for vanity.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–13 — For What Do I Wait?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: If life is a breath, the only hope left is God himself, and David holds on to him even under his discipline. “My hope is in you” is the turn of the psalm (v. 7). He asks to be delivered from his sins and spared the scorn of fools, then falls silent again, but now in submission, because he sees God’s hand at work (vv. 8–9). He asks God to lift the blow, which eats away what a man values like a moth (vv. 10–11). He ends as a sojourner pleading with his host: hear my tears, and look away from me, that I may smile again before I go (vv. 12–13).
verseByVerse.theology: The second silence is yielding to God, not bottling things up, and the psalm ends by asking God to look somewhere else.

verseByVerse.quote: "And now, O Lord, for what do I wait? My hope is in you. Deliver me from all my transgressions. Do not make me the scorn of the fool! I am mute; I do not open my mouth, for it is you who have done it. Remove your stroke from me; I am spent by the hostility of your hand. When you discipline a man with rebukes for sin, you consume like a moth what is dear to him; surely all mankind is a mere breath! Selah
verseByVerse.commentary:
If life is that short, the only hope left is God, so David turns to him, confesses his sin, accepts God’s hand in silence and asks him to lift it.

For what do I wait? Asked and answered in the same breath, this is the turning point. If life is that short and wealth that uncertain, what is left to hope in? Nothing that can be heaped up. “My hope is in you” is not a pious add-on here; it is the only surviving option after verses 4–6.

Deliver me from all my transgressions. He takes his own transgressions to God before his circumstances, and then admits an ordinary fear: being laughed at by people whose opinion he does not even respect.

For it is you who have done it. He is silent again, and it is a different silence. In verse 2 he was muzzled and boiling; here he is quiet because he has seen God’s hand in what has happened. The first silence only held his anger down, and it failed; the second yields to God, and it holds. That is the difference between not saying something because you dare not and not saying it because you have understood who is at work.

Like a moth. Submission does not stop him asking for the discipline to end. And the moth is dreadfully exact: not a fire that destroys everything at once, but something small working quietly in the dark on what a man values, until he takes the coat out of the cupboard and finds it ruined.

Uncertain wording. The word translated “hostility” in verse 10 (“the hostility of your hand”) appears only here in the Old Testament. From its root and the context it seems to mean a blow or an attack: God’s disciplining hand felt as an opponent he cannot withstand.

verseByVerse.quote: "Hear my prayer, O LORD, and give ear to my cry; hold not your peace at my tears! For I am a sojourner with you, a guest, like all my fathers. Look away from me, that I may smile again, before I depart and am no more!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
David pleads as God’s guest, dependent on his host, and ends asking God to ease his gaze so that he may smile again before he dies.

I am a sojourner with you, a guest. Having just been silent himself, he asks God not to be silent, and gives a reason. Jacob spoke to Pharaoh of “the days of the years of my sojourning” (Genesis 47:9), and Hebrews says the patriarchs “acknowledged that they were strangers and exiles on the earth” (Hebrews 11:13). In that world a sojourner, a foreigner living in another people’s land, owned no land, had no standing, and depended entirely on a host’s protection. That is his argument: a guest is the host’s responsibility. A man whose life is a few handbreadths claims the one standing that gives him a claim on the everlasting God.

No longer strangers. The gospel goes one step further. Through Christ, Paul tells Gentile believers, “you are no longer strangers and aliens, but you are fellow citizens with the saints and members of the household of God” (Ephesians 2:19). The guest is made family, though still a pilgrim on the earth until he goes home (1 Peter 2:11).

Look away from me, that I may smile again. One of the strangest requests in the Psalter. Everyone else asks God to turn his face towards them; this man asks him to look away, because at present God’s gaze is the pressure crushing him. Job said it twice in the same mood (Job 7:19; 14:6).

An honest prayer. Scripture prints it without comment, which is itself a mercy. There are seasons when a believer’s honest prayer is not “draw near” but “ease off”, and the Bible does not edit them out or scold the man who prays that way. He is still praying, still calling God his host, still hoping in him (v. 7). And the heavy gaze he asked God to lift fell, at the cross, on God’s own Son, so that for those who are his, God’s face now shines rather than crushes.

Before I depart and am no more! This means gone from this life and this world, not ceasing to exist. Other psalms look to God’s presence after death (49:15; 73:24), and in Christ that hope is clear.

If you are in that place. If this psalm voices your own wish to be gone, do not carry it alone: tell a pastor or a trusted friend, see a biblical counsellor, and have a medical check-up, for the body can weigh down the soul and medicine is no failure of faith. If you are thinking of ending your life, call the emergency services or a crisis line today.

39.title: A Sojourner with You
39.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 38 ended with a sufferer silent before his enemies and waiting for God. Psalm 39 begins with the same silence, and shows it failing. It is one of the darkest psalms in Book One, close in mood to Job and Ecclesiastes, and it ends with no resolution but a prayer.

The message. Human life is a breath, and everything we heap up in it slips out of our hands. Seeing that clearly is not despair but the beginning of wisdom, because it leaves only one place for hope: “My hope is in you.” Even under God’s discipline, a believer may bring the rawest feelings to him, plead as his guest, and keep praying when he has no answer yet.

Why it was said. David writes under some discipline for sin (vv. 8–11) and in the presence of the wicked, whom he will not give the satisfaction of hearing him complain (v. 1). The heading hands the psalm to Jeduthun, one of the Levite musicians, so this very private struggle was given to Israel to sing.

How the chapter makes its case. First, the failed silence: he muzzles his mouth before the wicked, but the distress grows until the fire burns and he speaks (vv. 1–3). He speaks to God, asking to know how fleeting he is: his days a few handbreadths, mankind a breath, wealth heaped up for someone else (vv. 4–6). Then the turn: if that is life, what is left to wait for? “My hope is in you” (v. 7). He asks for deliverance from his sins, falls silent again in submission, and asks God to lift his hand (vv. 8–11). He ends pleading as a sojourner and guest, asking God to look away so that he may smile again before he dies (vv. 12–13).

Where it leads. By the need it exposes and by God’s character revealed in Christ. The psalm asks for an answer it does not receive: what hope is there for a creature who is a breath, under God’s just rebuke? In Christ the Son of God became a man whose days were cut short, and the gaze David asked God to turn away fell in full on him at the cross. He rose, so that for his people the end David feared is not the end, and the guest becomes one of “the household of God” (Ephesians 2:19).

For us. Number your days honestly; it will loosen your grip on what you heap up. When you cannot hold your feelings in, take them to God rather than pouring them out on others. And when your prayer is no more than “ease off”, pray it anyway: you are his guest, and in Christ his face is turned towards you in favour.
39.theology:
Two silences frame the psalm. The first, a muzzle over his grievance, only made the distress worse (vv. 1-3). The second, before a hand he has recognised as God's, is submission, and it holds (v. 9); yet submission does not stop him asking for the discipline to end (v. 10).

Knowing how short life is comes as a mercy he asks for (v. 4; cf. 90:12), and it cures his fretting over the prosperity of others. His only claim on God is a guest's claim on his host (v. 12), and Scripture prints even his last request, to be left alone for a while, without rebuke (v. 13).
39.examples: Hold up your hand: four fingers wide is how the psalm measures a life. Think of a man heaping up savings that a stranger will spend, or of a moth working unseen in a wardrobe until a good coat is found ruined. Beside these stand the guest whose safety rests on his host, and the prayer that dares, for a season, to ask God to ease off.

keyVerse.quote: And now, O Lord, for what do I wait? My hope is in you.
keyVerse.note: This is the turning point of the psalm. Having seen that his days are a few handbreadths and that all he could heap up will pass to others, David asks what is left to hope in, and answers in the same breath: God himself. Everything before leads to this verse, and everything after is prayed in its light.

39.reflection:
David tried to stay silent but found that “my distress grew worse” (vv. 1–3). What is the difference between the silence of verse 2 and the silence of verse 9, and which do you tend towards?

Why would anyone pray, “make me know my end” (v. 4)? How might facing the shortness of life change what you spend your time and money on (v. 6; Luke 12:20)?

David pleads as “a sojourner with you, a guest” (v. 12). How does Ephesians 2:19 change the standing of a believer, and why are we still called pilgrims (1 Peter 2:11)?

The psalm ends with “look away from me, that I may smile again” and no answer. How does it help to know that Scripture includes prayers like this, and how does the cross give hope to someone praying it?

40.text: To the choirmaster. A Psalm of David. 1I waited patiently for the LORD; he inclined to me and heard my cry.2He drew me up from the pit of destruction, out of the miry bog, and set my feet upon a rock, making my steps secure.3He put a new song in my mouth, a song of praise to our God. Many will see and fear, and put their trust in the LORD.4Blessed is the man who makes the LORD his trust, who does not turn to the proud, to those who go astray after a lie!5You have multiplied, O LORD my God, your wondrous deeds and your thoughts toward us; none can compare with you! I will proclaim and tell of them, yet they are more than can be told.6In sacrifice and offering you have not delighted, but you have given me an open ear. Burnt offering and sin offering you have not required.7Then I said, "Behold, I have come; in the scroll of the book it is written of me:8I delight to do your will, O my God; your law is within my heart."9I have told the glad news of deliverance in the great congregation; behold, I have not restrained my lips, as you know, O LORD.10I have not hidden your deliverance within my heart; I have spoken of your faithfulness and your salvation; I have not concealed your steadfast love and your faithfulness from the great congregation.11As for you, O LORD, you will not restrain your mercy from me; your steadfast love and your faithfulness will ever preserve me!12For evils have encompassed me beyond number; my iniquities have overtaken me, and I cannot see; they are more than the hairs of my head; my heart fails me.13Be pleased, O LORD, to deliver me! O LORD, make haste to help me!14Let those be put to shame and disappointed altogether who seek to snatch away my life; let those be turned back and brought to dishonor who delight in my hurt!15Let those be appalled because of their shame who say to me, "Aha, Aha!"16But may all who seek you rejoice and be glad in you; may those who love your salvation say continually, "Great is the LORD!"17As for me, I am poor and needy, but the Lord takes thought for me. You are my help and my deliverer; do not delay, O my God!

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — He Drew Me Up from the Pit
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God rescued David when he could do nothing but wait, and the rescue has become a song for others. He waited, and God inclined, heard, drew him up from the pit and the sucking mud, set his feet on rock and made his steps secure (vv. 1–2). Then God put a new song in his mouth, and its purpose reaches beyond him: many will see, fear and trust the LORD (v. 3). So he pronounces a blessing on whoever trusts the LORD rather than the proud and their lies (v. 4), and confesses that God’s wondrous deeds and his thoughts toward us are more than he can ever count or tell (v. 5).
verseByVerse.theology: A man hauled out of mud onto rock is given a song, and it turns out to be for other people.

verseByVerse.quote: I waited patiently for the LORD; he inclined to me and heard my cry. He drew me up from the pit of destruction, out of the miry bog, and set my feet upon a rock, making my steps secure. He put a new song in my mouth, a song of praise to our God. Many will see and fear, and put their trust in the LORD. Blessed is the man who makes the LORD his trust, who does not turn to the proud, to those who go astray after a lie! You have multiplied, O LORD my God, your wondrous deeds and your thoughts toward us; none can compare with you! I will proclaim and tell of them, yet they are more than can be told.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When David could only wait, God lifted him from the pit onto rock and gave him a new song, so that many will trust the LORD.

Out of the miry bog. The mud explains everything: not a prison or a battle but a bog, and the horror of mud is that there is nothing to push against: a man who struggles in it goes down faster. That is why the psalm opens with waiting: not because waiting is noble, but because it was the only thing left to do.

He drew me up from the pit. The rescue is entirely God’s: he inclined, he heard, he drew up, he set, he made secure. Five verbs, none of them the psalmist’s. He moves from mud that gives way to rock that does not, and then God is “making my steps secure”: not carried, but walking.

He put a new song in my mouth. A new rescue calls for new words; the old repertoire will not carry what he now knows. And the song has a purpose. “Many will see”: they watch a man who was in the bog standing on rock and singing, and they trust God. Your testimony is not only yours.

Your wondrous deeds and your thoughts toward us. God has multiplied two things: his deeds, and his thoughts toward us. The first is history; the second is attention. And the man who has just been given a song admits he cannot finish it: there is more material than he can get through, which is the happiest defeat in the Psalter.

Uncertain wording. “The pit of destruction” (v. 2) renders a phrase that is literally something like “pit of tumult” or “pit of roaring”, perhaps of rushing water. Either way it is a place of death from which only God can lift a man.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: What God wants in return for rescue is not more sacrifice but the person himself, given gladly to his will. David sees that God never delighted in offerings for their own sake; instead he has dug open David’s ears to hear and obey (v. 6). So David presents himself: “Behold, I have come”, with God’s will his delight and God’s law within his heart (vv. 7–8). Hebrews hears these words on the lips of Christ entering the world, and shows that his perfect obedience, offered once in his body, ended the old sacrifices and made his people holy (Hebrews 10:5–10).
verseByVerse.theology: Hebrews puts these verses in the mouth of Christ as he comes into the world.

verseByVerse.quote: In sacrifice and offering you have not delighted, but you have given me an open ear. Burnt offering and sin offering you have not required. Then I said, "Behold, I have come; in the scroll of the book it is written of me: I delight to do your will, O my God; your law is within my heart."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God never wanted sacrifices for their own sake but the worshipper himself, delighting in his will; Hebrews hears these words spoken by Christ, whose obedience ended the old sacrifices.

In sacrifice and offering you have not delighted. Not an attack on the sacrificial system God himself commanded, but the prophets’ point: God never wanted the animals for their own sake. “To obey is better than sacrifice,” Samuel told Saul (1 Samuel 15:22). What he wants is the worshipper himself.

You have given me an open ear. The Hebrew is “ears you have dug for me”: hollowed out, opened, the way you would dig a channel. God does not merely ask for obedience; he himself opens the ears that make obedience possible.

A body have you prepared for me. Hebrews puts these words into the mouth of Christ at the incarnation, when the Son of God became man: “when Christ came into the world, he said, ‘Sacrifices and offerings you have not desired, but a body have you prepared for me’” (Hebrews 10:5), and “Behold, I have come to do your will, O God” (10:7). And it draws the conclusion: “He does away with the first in order to establish the second. And by that will we have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all” (Hebrews 10:9–10).

I delight to do your will, O my God. So the psalm’s “I delight to do your will”, true in part of David and wholly true only of Christ, becomes the sentence that ends the animal sacrifices. The body prepared was offered once, and what all those sacrifices pointed at arrived; and in those who are his, the Spirit now writes that same law on the heart (Jeremiah 31:33; Ezekiel 36:27). “In the scroll of the book it is written of me”: Jesus told his disciples that everything written about him in the Law, the Prophets and the Psalms must be fulfilled (Luke 24:44).

Uncertain wording. We do not know exactly what David meant by “the scroll of the book” (v. 7). It may be the law of Moses, which the king was to copy and read all his days (Deuteronomy 17:18–19), or a written record of his own commitment. Either way, what God has written, David comes to do.

Textual note. When this verse was translated into Greek, probably in the two centuries before Christ, “an open ear” came out as “a body have you prepared for me”. Probably an interpretation rather than a word-for-word rendering (some think the change arose in copying), taking the part for the whole: the opened ear stands for the whole person prepared for obedience. Hebrews quotes the Greek.
verseByVerse.note: Hebrews 10:5 follows the Greek Old Testament, “a body have you prepared for me,” where the Hebrew has the opened ear.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–17 — I Am Poor and Needy
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The rescued man still needs rescuing, and he prays as one who has told God’s faithfulness and counts on it. He has proclaimed God’s deliverance, faithfulness and steadfast love openly in the great congregation (vv. 9–10), and trusts that God will not hold back his mercy (v. 11). Yet evils surround him, and his own iniquities, more than the hairs of his head, overtake him (v. 12). So he cries for quick help, asks that those who seek his life be turned back and those who seek God rejoice and say, “Great is the LORD!” (vv. 13–16), and rests on the Lord who takes thought for the poor and needy (v. 17).
verseByVerse.theology: The psalm of the new song ends in the mud again, but its last word is that God is thinking about him.

verseByVerse.quote: I have told the glad news of deliverance in the great congregation; behold, I have not restrained my lips, as you know, O LORD. I have not hidden your deliverance within my heart; I have spoken of your faithfulness and your salvation; I have not concealed your steadfast love and your faithfulness from the great congregation. As for you, O LORD, you will not restrain your mercy from me; your steadfast love and your faithfulness will ever preserve me! For evils have encompassed me beyond number; my iniquities have overtaken me, and I cannot see; they are more than the hairs of my head; my heart fails me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
David has told God’s faithfulness openly and trusts God’s mercy, yet even after rescue his troubles and sins overtake him again.

I have not restrained my lips. Three times he says what he has not done: not restrained, not hidden, not concealed. His temptation was to keep it in, and he names the refusal three ways. The ESV notes that “deliverance” here is literally “righteousness”: what he has been publishing is not merely that he got out of the bog but that God is right.

You will not restrain your mercy from me. He has not restrained his lips; God will not restrain his mercy (v. 11). The same verb, turned round.

For evils have encompassed me beyond number. In the middle of a thanksgiving psalm, the ground opens again. Not a different psalm badly joined on, but what actually happens: a man can be genuinely rescued, genuinely singing the new song in public, and find his sins catching up with him so that he cannot see straight.

My iniquities have overtaken me. They ran after him and caught him, and they outnumber the hairs on his head. Whoever thought that being rescued once settles the question of sin has not read verse 12.

Whose are these iniquities? If Hebrews hears Christ in verses 6–8, whose are the iniquities of verse 12? The psalm is David’s, and David’s sins are his own. Christ fulfils the psalm’s obedience; and the sins that overtook David are among those Christ bore on the cross as though they were his own (Isaiah 53:6; 2 Corinthians 5:21).

verseByVerse.quote: Be pleased, O LORD, to deliver me! O LORD, make haste to help me! Let those be put to shame and disappointed altogether who seek to snatch away my life; let those be turned back and brought to dishonor who delight in my hurt! Let those be appalled because of their shame who say to me, "Aha, Aha!" But may all who seek you rejoice and be glad in you; may those who love your salvation say continually, "Great is the LORD!" As for me, I am poor and needy, but the Lord takes thought for me. You are my help and my deliverer; do not delay, O my God!
verseByVerse.commentary:
David cries for quick help, asks that his hunters be shamed and God’s seekers rejoice, and rests on the Lord who thinks about the poor and needy.

The same prayer twice. These five verses appear again, almost word for word, as Psalm 70. Here it is the last movement of a thanksgiving, there an emergency call on its own. A prayer God has answered once deserves to be known by heart.

May all who seek you rejoice. The request is even-handed: shame for those hunting him, gladness for everyone seeking God. He is not asking for a private rescue but for the right outcome all round, and what he wants people saying is not his name but “Great is the LORD!”

As for me, I am poor and needy. The psalm that began with a man hauled out of a bog ends with him poor and needy and still asking, and the middle of it holds the words Christ said when he came into the world. That is the shape of the Christian life: a rescue behind you, a Saviour who delighted to do God’s will in your place, and a present condition that still needs the words “do not delay”.

The Lord takes thought for me. The best words in the psalm are the quietest. He does not only act for him; he thinks about him. The God whose thoughts toward us were multiplied beyond counting in verse 5 is, at this moment, thinking about a poor and needy man.
verseByVerse.note: Psalm 70 repeats these verses.

40.title: I Delight to Do Your Will
40.overview:
Where we are. After the unresolved laments of Psalms 38 and 39, Psalm 40 opens with an answered prayer: “I waited patiently for the LORD; he inclined to me and heard my cry.” Yet it does not stay there. Thanksgiving turns back into lament, and the closing verses reappear on their own as Psalm 70.

The message. God rescues the helpless who wait for him, and the right response is not more sacrifices but a whole life given to him: an opened ear, a heart that delights in his will, and lips that will not stop telling of his faithfulness. Yet the rescued still need rescuing. Those who have sung the new song still find their sins overtaking them, and they go on praying, “the Lord takes thought for me.”

Why it was said. David looks back on a deliverance he had waited for and celebrates it publicly in “the great congregation”, while he faces fresh trouble from enemies and from his own iniquities. In a worship centred on the altar he states what the prophets would repeat: God wants not the animals but the worshipper himself.

How the chapter makes its case. First, the rescue and the new song: drawn from the miry bog onto rock, he sings, and many see and trust the LORD; God’s deeds and thoughts toward us are too many to tell (vv. 1–5). Then the response: not sacrifice but an open ear and the words, “Behold, I have come… I delight to do your will, O my God” (vv. 6–8). He has told God’s faithfulness without holding back, and trusts God not to hold back his mercy, just as evils and iniquities overtake him again (vv. 9–12). He ends pleading for haste, asking that God’s seekers rejoice, and resting on this: “I am poor and needy, but the Lord takes thought for me” (vv. 13–17).

Where it leads. Here the New Testament itself shows the way. Hebrews hears verses 6–8 spoken by Christ as he came into the world: “a body have you prepared for me… Behold, I have come to do your will, O God” (Hebrews 10:5–7). What David could say only in part, Jesus said wholly, and the body prepared for him was offered on the cross, so that “we have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all” (Hebrews 10:10). He also bore the iniquities that overtake David and us.

For us. If you are in the bog, wait for the LORD; the rescue is his work, not yours. If he has drawn you out, tell it, because others will see and trust him. And answer his salvation not with occasional religious offerings but with an opened ear and a delighted will, leaning still on the Lord who thinks about the poor and needy.
40.theology:
The rescue is wholly God's (vv. 1-2), and the song it produces is meant for others: they see and trust (v. 3).

Hebrews hears verses 6-8 as the words of Christ entering the world. His delight to do God's will is what ends the animal sacrifices, because his own prepared body was the offering they pointed to.

Being rescued does not end the struggle with sin (v. 12), and the psalm closes poor, needy and still asking, comforted that God is thinking of him (v. 17).
40.examples: Mud is worse than a pit because it gives nothing to push against, and struggling only sinks a man faster; that is why the psalm begins with waiting. The ears God dug are like a channel cut so that water can flow: he makes the very hearing that obedience needs. And a man rescued once may still find his sins running after him and catching him, so the new song and the cry for help belong in the same life.

keyVerse.quote: I delight to do your will, O my God; your law is within my heart.
keyVerse.note: This is the answer the psalm gives to God’s rescue: not more sacrifices but a will that delights in God’s will. Hebrews hears these words spoken by Christ as he came into the world (Hebrews 10:5–7); he alone lived them perfectly, and by his once-for-all offering the people whose hearts he now writes them on are made holy.

40.reflection:
David “waited patiently for the LORD” in a bog where struggling only made things worse (vv. 1–2). What situations in your life feel like that, and what does it mean to wait for God in them?

The new song was meant to be seen: “Many will see and fear” (v. 3). Who has heard from you what God has done for you, and what holds you back from telling it (vv. 9–10)?

Read Hebrews 10:5–10 alongside verses 6–8. What does it mean that Christ said, “I delight to do your will”, and how does his obedience change what God asks of us?

The rescued man still finds his iniquities overtaking him (v. 12) and still calls himself poor and needy (v. 17). How does this psalm help a Christian who feels that he should be past such struggles by now?

41.text: To the choirmaster. A Psalm of David. 1Blessed is the one who considers the poor! In the day of trouble the LORD delivers him;2the LORD protects him and keeps him alive; he is called blessed in the land; you do not give him up to the will of his enemies.3The LORD sustains him on his sickbed; in his illness you restore him to full health.4As for me, I said, "O LORD, be gracious to me; heal me, for I have sinned against you!"5My enemies say of me in malice, "When will he die, and his name perish?"6And when one comes to see me, he utters empty words, while his heart gathers iniquity; when he goes out, he tells it abroad.7All who hate me whisper together about me; they imagine the worst for me.8They say, "A deadly thing is poured out on him; he will not rise again from where he lies."9Even my close friend in whom I trusted, who ate my bread, has lifted his heel against me.10But you, O LORD, be gracious to me, and raise me up, that I may repay them!11By this I know that you delight in me: my enemy will not shout in triumph over me.12But you have upheld me because of my integrity, and set me in your presence forever.13Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, from everlasting to everlasting! Amen and Amen.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — The LORD Sustains Him on His Sickbed
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God takes thought for the one who takes thought for the weak, and that includes the day he is weak himself. The psalm opens with a blessing (v. 1) that recalls the first word of Book One (1:1), and then unfolds it: deliverance in trouble, protection, life, a good name and rescue from enemies (vv. 1–2), and God himself at the sickbed, restoring the patient (v. 3). Then David turns from the general truth to his own case. He is ill, and he asks God for grace, for healing and for forgiveness in one breath (v. 4), resting not on his kindness to the poor but on God’s kindness to a sinner.
verseByVerse.theology: The man who has thought carefully about the poor is the man God thinks carefully about when he is ill.

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed is the one who considers the poor! In the day of trouble the LORD delivers him; the LORD protects him and keeps him alive; he is called blessed in the land; you do not give him up to the will of his enemies. The LORD sustains him on his sickbed; in his illness you restore him to full health. As for me, I said, "O LORD, be gracious to me; heal me, for I have sinned against you!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
God takes thought for the one who takes thought for the weak, and when that man falls ill, conscious of his own sin, he may ask God for healing and forgiveness together.

Blessed is the one who considers the poor! Considers is not the word for giving but for giving thought: weighing a situation, working out what would actually help. (The ESV notes that “the poor” may be rendered “the weak”.) Anyone can drop a coin in a tin without considering anybody; this blessing is on the person who has thought carefully about someone with nothing.

In the day of trouble the LORD delivers him. The promise matches the deed: the one who gives attention to the helpless receives attention when he is helpless. This is not a wage earned. The merciful are people who have first received mercy, and God cares for them as a Father for his own: “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall receive mercy” (Matthew 5:7).

The LORD sustains him on his sickbed. The ESV notes that the second line is literally “you turn all his bed”: a nurse straightening the sheets and turning a patient who cannot turn himself. That is God at the bedside, doing the intimate, undignified work of care, and anyone who has done it for a parent knows what kind of love is meant.

Heal me, for I have sinned against you! He asks for healing and confesses sin in the same breath, without making one the price of the other. He does not say his illness is punishment; he does say that a sick man before God is still a sinner before God, and he wants both dealt with. His only plea is “be gracious”, not his kindness to the poor. Jesus forgave the paralysed man first and then healed him (Mark 2:5, 11). This line is David’s alone: the Son of David, who quoted verse 9, had no sin to confess.

What it does not mean. Not that every illness comes from a particular sin (John 9:3), nor that kindness guarantees health; the psalm’s last hope lies beyond the sickbed (v. 12). And praying for healing does not rule out the doctor: medicine is no failure of faith.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: While David lies ill, the people around him are waiting for him to die. His enemies ask aloud when his name will perish (v. 5); a visitor says the right things at the bedside and then spreads his own diagnosis outside (v. 6); the whisperers agree that he is finished and will not rise again (vv. 7–8). Last and worst comes the close friend who ate at his table and has turned against him (v. 9). The section names every kind of sickroom cruelty without softening it, and its last line became the words Jesus used of Judas on the night he was betrayed.
verseByVerse.theology: The sickroom becomes a place to collect gossip, and last on the list comes the friend who shared his table.

verseByVerse.quote: My enemies say of me in malice, "When will he die, and his name perish?" And when one comes to see me, he utters empty words, while his heart gathers iniquity; when he goes out, he tells it abroad. All who hate me whisper together about me; they imagine the worst for me. They say, "A deadly thing is poured out on him; he will not rise again from where he lies." Even my close friend in whom I trusted, who ate my bread, has lifted his heel against me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
While David lies ill, his enemies long for his death, his visitors gather gossip, and his closest friend turns on him, the betrayal Jesus would claim as his own.

When will he die, and his name perish? They are not merely waiting for him to go; they want the memory of him gone too.

He utters empty words. The scene is ugly and instantly recognisable. Someone visits the sickbed and says the right things, while his real business is collecting things to repeat; outside he tells everyone how bad it looked. The whisperers have decided he is finished, and they are pleased. (Go to a sickbed to bring comfort, not to collect news.)

Even my close friend in whom I trusted. The worst is kept for last: not an enemy but the friend who ate at his table. In that world sharing bread was a bond of loyalty; you did not eat a man’s food and then move against him. Many have thought of Ahithophel, David’s counsellor, who joined Absalom’s revolt (2 Samuel 15:12, 31) and later hanged himself (2 Samuel 17:23), as Judas would; but the psalm names no one.

Jesus and Judas. On the last night of his life, with Judas at the table, Jesus said: “I know whom I have chosen. But the Scripture will be fulfilled, ‘He who ate my bread has lifted his heel against me’” (John 13:18). He left out “in whom I trusted”, for he had known from the beginning who would betray him (John 6:64), yet he washed that man’s feet and handed him the morsel (John 13:26). Every betrayed believer since has this verse, and the knowledge that the Lord used it first about himself.

Uncertain wording. The ESV notes other possible readings in verses 7 and 8: “they devise evil against me”, and that the deadly thing “has fastened” on him. The “deadly thing” is literally a thing of belial, worthlessness, perhaps a fatal disease, perhaps a curse. Either way the whisperers think he is finished.
verseByVerse.note: To lift the heel against someone is to turn on him, like a kick from behind.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David answers his enemies’ verdict with a prayer and a confidence. He asks again for grace, and to be raised up so that the treachery can be dealt with (v. 10). He takes the enemy’s failure to triumph as the sign that God delights in him (v. 11), and looks beyond the sickbed to being set in God’s presence for ever (v. 12). Then a doxology closes not only the psalm but the whole of Book One (v. 13): the blessing on God is said, and sealed with a double Amen, while the trouble is still unresolved.
verseByVerse.theology: Book One is sealed with a blessing on God, said while the trouble is still unresolved.

verseByVerse.quote: But you, O LORD, be gracious to me, and raise me up, that I may repay them! By this I know that you delight in me: my enemy will not shout in triumph over me. But you have upheld me because of my integrity, and set me in your presence forever. Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, from everlasting to everlasting! Amen and Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
David asks God to raise him up, takes his enemy’s failure as a sign of God’s favour, and looks beyond the sickbed to God’s presence for ever; then a doxology seals Book One.

That I may repay them! David wants to get up off the bed where they said he would never rise (v. 8), in order to settle accounts, and the psalm does not hide it. He is a king, and judging treachery was part of a king’s duty, so this is probably a ruler asking to be restored so that justice can be done, rather than a private grudge. But when a greater Son of David quoted this psalm, he took verse 9 and stopped. He did not pray verse 10. He was raised up, and he did not repay; he prayed for those who crucified him (Luke 23:34) and sent his apostles to preach forgiveness “beginning from Jerusalem” (Luke 24:47), the city that killed him.

By this I know that you delight in me. His evidence is not his recovery (the psalm never says he got better) but that the enemy does not get the last word.

Because of my integrity. How can a man who confessed sin in verse 4 plead his integrity here? Integrity means wholeheartedness, not sinlessness: he has not been the false friend or the gossiping visitor, and his own sin he has already brought to God. Even so, it is God who has “upheld” him.

Set me in your presence forever. A man written off as finished says he has been placed in God’s presence permanently, a hope no diagnosis can revise. The one betrayed at the table has gone ahead to secure it, “now to appear in the presence of God on our behalf” (Hebrews 9:24).

Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel. This verse closes not just Psalm 41 but Book One: each of the first four books ends with a doxology like this (72:18–19; 89:52; 106:48), and Psalm 150 closes the fifth (see the introduction). Forty-one psalms began with a man delighting in God’s law and a King installed on Zion, and went through caves, sickbeds, betrayal, guilt, slander and the cry of a man forsaken by God. The book closes not with everything resolved but with a blessing “from everlasting to everlasting”, doubled: “Amen and Amen.” Praise does not wait until the story is tidy.
verseByVerse.note: Verse 13 is the doxology that closes Book I of the Psalms.

41.title: Blessed Is the One Who Considers the Poor
41.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 41 closes Book One of the Psalter, almost all of it carrying David’s name. Psalm 40 ended with David “poor and needy” and sure that “the Lord takes thought for me” (Psalm 40:17); Psalm 41 opens with a blessing on the one who takes thought for the poor, and its last verse seals Book One.

The message. God takes thought for those who take thought for the weak, and he does not abandon his servant when he is weak himself. Laid low by illness, written off by enemies, gossiped about by visitors and betrayed by his closest friend, David throws himself on God’s grace for healing and forgiveness together, and is sure that God will raise him up and keep him in his presence for ever.

Why it was said. The title names David but no occasion. Many have connected it with the years of Absalom’s revolt, when David’s trusted counsellor Ahithophel went over to his son (2 Samuel 15:12, 31), but the psalm does not say so. Given “To the choirmaster”, it became Israel’s song for every sickroom and every betrayal (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. A general truth: God blesses and nurses the one who considers the weak (vv. 1–3). David’s own case: he asks for grace, healing and forgiveness in one breath (v. 4). The sickroom around him: enemies longing for his death, a false visitor, whisperers, and last the friend who ate his bread (vv. 5–9). He asks again for grace, and to be raised up, and rests in the God who upholds him and sets him in his presence for ever (vv. 10–12). A doxology seals Book One (v. 13).

Where it leads. By pattern, and Jesus himself says so. On the night he was betrayed he quoted verse 9 of Judas (John 13:18): David, the anointed king betrayed by a friend at his table, foreshadows the Son of David betrayed by a friend at his. Yet where the pattern breaks, Christ is greater: he had no sin to confess (v. 4). He considered the poor as no one else has, for “though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor” (2 Corinthians 8:9). And when God raised him up, he did not repay his betrayers but sent forgiveness to the city that killed him.

For us. Give careful thought to the weak, the sick and the forgotten, as God has given thought to you. When you are the one on the sickbed, or the one betrayed, bring God your body and your sin together, and rest on his grace rather than your record. The one betrayed at the table still keeps his table open for those who come back to him.
41.theology:
The blessing of v. 1 rests on careful thought for the helpless, and the man who attends to others is attended to, not as a wage but as a Father's kindness to the merciful (cf. Matt 5:7). Healing and forgiveness are asked for together, without making the illness a punishment (v. 4).

Jesus quoted v. 9 of Judas and stopped there; he did not pray v. 10's that I may repay them. And the hope of the psalm reaches past the sickbed: set me in your presence forever (v. 12).
41.examples: Anyone can drop a coin into a tin; considers means sitting down to work out what would actually help. The God of verse 3 is like a nurse turning the sheets of a patient who cannot turn himself. The visitor who says the right things at the bedside and then tells everyone outside how bad it looked is someone most sick people have met. And the doxology that ends Book One is sung while the trouble is still there.

keyVerse.quote: Blessed is the one who considers the poor!
keyVerse.note: The opening blessing sets the terms of the whole psalm, and echoes the first word of Book One (1:1). The God who “takes thought” for the needy (40:17) blesses those who do the same, and the rest of the psalm shows David, now weak himself, finding God as good as his word. Its fullest meaning is in Christ, who became poor for our sake and considers the weak still.

41.reflection:
Verse 1 blesses the one who “considers” the poor, giving careful thought and not only money. Who are the weak, sick or forgotten people near you, and what would it look like to think carefully about what would actually help them?

In verse 4 David asks for healing and forgiveness together, without saying that his illness is a punishment. How does that help us pray when we are ill, and how does it guard us both against ignoring sin and against inventing guilt?

Verses 5–9 describe enemies, a false visitor and a friend who turned. Have you known the pain of betrayal? How does it help to know that Jesus applied verse 9 to himself (John 13:18)?

Jesus quoted verse 9 but not verse 10, and when he was raised up he sent forgiveness instead of repayment. What would it mean for you to hand a betrayal over to God rather than settle it yourself?

42.text: To the choirmaster. A Maskil of the Sons of Korah. 1As a deer pants for flowing streams, so pants my soul for you, O God.2My soul thirsts for God, for the living God. When shall I come and appear before God?3My tears have been my food day and night, while they say to me all the day long, "Where is your God?"4These things I remember, as I pour out my soul: how I would go with the throng and lead them in procession to the house of God with glad shouts and songs of praise, a multitude keeping festival.5Why are you cast down, O my soul, and why are you in turmoil within me? Hope in God; for I shall again praise him, my salvation6and my God. My soul is cast down within me; therefore I remember you from the land of Jordan and of Hermon, from Mount Mizar.7Deep calls to deep at the roar of your waterfalls; all your breakers and your waves have gone over me.8By day the LORD commands his steadfast love, and at night his song is with me, a prayer to the God of my life.9I say to God, my rock: "Why have you forgotten me? Why do I go mourning because of the oppression of the enemy?"10As with a deadly wound in my bones, my adversaries taunt me, while they say to me all the day long, "Where is your God?"11Why are you cast down, O my soul, and why are you in turmoil within me? Hope in God; for I shall again praise him, my salvation and my God.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A believer far from God’s house thirsts for God himself, and then speaks to his own soul. His longing is as urgent as a deer’s need for water, and its object is the living God and the joy of appearing before him (vv. 1–2). Instead he has tears for food and a taunt in his ears: “Where is your God?” (v. 3). Memory makes it worse, for he used to lead the festival crowds to the house of God (v. 4). Then he turns, questions his own soul and gives it an order: “Hope in God” (v. 5). The section shows that faith in the dark is not the absence of sorrow but what you say to it.
verseByVerse.theology: Thirst, tears and a taunt meet a man who turns round and speaks to his own soul instead of listening to it.

verseByVerse.quote: As a deer pants for flowing streams, so pants my soul for you, O God. My soul thirsts for God, for the living God. When shall I come and appear before God? My tears have been my food day and night, while they say to me all the day long, "Where is your God?" These things I remember, as I pour out my soul: how I would go with the throng and lead them in procession to the house of God with glad shouts and songs of praise, a multitude keeping festival.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Far from God’s house, the singer longs for the living God as urgently as a deer for water, while tears replace his meals, the taunt goes on and the memory of festival days hurts most of all.

As a deer pants for flowing streams. A deer panting for water is not in a spiritual mood; it is in trouble, and will die without what it is looking for. That is the level at which this man wants God.

For the living God. What he wants is specific: the living God, and to appear before him. That was the law’s phrase for the pilgrim feasts, when every Israelite man was to come to the sanctuary three times a year (Exodus 23:17; Deuteronomy 16:16), so what he misses is the festival journey he used to make (v. 4). Anyone cut off from church by illness, distance or disgrace knows this particular thirst.

My tears have been my food. The tears have replaced his meals, and the taunt comes all the day long. “Where is your God?” is the cruellest thing anyone can ask a believer in trouble, and the psalm does not pretend it has an easy answer; the taunt comes back at verse 10.

These things I remember. The memory that hurts most is that he used to lead the singing: the crowd, the shouting, the festival, and he at the front of it. Remembering good days in a bad season can be medicine or poison, and here it is both; he pours his soul out over it.

The sons of Korah. Book Two begins with a family whose name is a warning. Korah led a rebellion against Moses in the wilderness, and the ground opened and swallowed him (Numbers 16). Yet his sons did not die (Numbers 26:11), and centuries later the sons of Korah are the temple singers. The family of the great rebellion became the family of the choir. Whoever thinks their ancestry disqualifies them can look at whose name stands at the top of this psalm.

The thirst we keep renaming. Modern people still feel this thirst; we have simply stopped calling it thirst for God. We call it restlessness or burnout, and treat it with whatever is to hand: the next trip, the next relationship, a weekend of streaming. Each helps for an evening. Pascal argued that our endless craving is the empty print of a happiness we were made for, a gap so deep that only an infinite object, God himself, can fill it. The religious can do the same, chasing a feeling at church instead of God. This man knows exactly what he is missing: the living God, not an experience of him. And the one he thirsted for came looking for the thirsty. On the last day of a feast in the temple Jesus stood up and cried out, “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink” (John 7:37).

Uncertain wording. Maskil in the title is probably a skilful or instructive song, but its exact sense is unknown. In verse 2 the ESV notes that a different vocalisation of the Hebrew gives “and see the face of God”; either way, he longs to stand before God himself.
verseByVerse.note: Book II begins. Psalms 42 and 43 share a refrain and were probably once one psalm; many Hebrew manuscripts copy them as one. A Maskil is probably a skilful or instructive song; the exact sense is uncertain. The sons of Korah were a family of temple singers.

verseByVerse.quote: Why are you cast down, O my soul, and why are you in turmoil within me? Hope in God; for I shall again praise him, my salvation
verseByVerse.commentary:
The singer stops listening to his downcast soul and starts speaking to it, telling it to hope in God because a day of praise is coming.

Why are you cast down, O my soul? This refrain comes three times (42:5, 11; 43:5), and what happens in it is the most practical thing in the psalm: he is talking to himself. Most of us listen to ourselves instead. The soul reports that everything is hopeless, and we take the report as news. Here a man interrupts, asks his soul two questions and then gives it an order: hope in God. Faith is not the absence of the downcast feeling; it is what you say to the feeling, and “the Spirit helps us in our weakness” (Romans 8:26) as we say it.

I shall again praise him. He does not tell himself the trouble is small or that things will soon improve. The reason he gives his soul lies in the future: a day is coming when this same mouth will be singing, so hold on. My salvation is literally “the salvation of my face”: the face that is fallen now will be lifted by God himself.

The Saviour of the downcast. In Gethsemane Jesus said, “My soul is very sorrowful, even to death” (Matthew 26:38), words that echo this refrain as it reads in the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint). He has been downcast himself; he does not stand over you but beside you. And when you cannot find the words at all, he “always lives to make intercession” for his people (Hebrews 7:25). You do not preach to your soul to hold yourself up; you preach to it because you are already held.

How do I talk to my own soul? The psalm gives the pattern for an ordinary bad morning. Ask the question. Name what the heaviness is actually saying: that you have failed, that nothing will change, that God has forgotten you. Answer with what is true. Set against each claim something God has said, and say it to yourself as you would to a friend: “The steadfast love of the LORD never ceases; his mercies never come to an end” (Lamentations 3:22). Remember on purpose. He does this in verse 6. Write down particular times God has helped you, and read the list when the dark comes. Look ahead. Tell your soul that this is not the last chapter. Then do the next small thing: eat, sleep, ring a friend, go to church on Sunday.

Is the downcast believer sinning? The psalm never scolds him. Some darkness of soul is grief, some is spiritual, and some has causes in the body. A pastor and a biblical counsellor can help, and a good counsellor will ask for a medical check-up so that any bodily cause is found and treated; seeking that help, and taking medicine where it is needed, is no failure of faith. If the darkness ever brings thoughts of ending your life, tell someone and get help the same day.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew of verse 5 reads slightly differently from verse 11, “the salvation of his face” (so the King James Version, “the help of his countenance”), with “my God” beginning the next line. The ESV, like most modern versions, makes it match verse 11 and 43:5. The sense is the same: God himself is the help he waits for.
verseByVerse.note: “My salvation” is literally “the salvation of my face” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The second stanza goes deeper into the darkness and finds God there. Cast down in the far north, by the sources of the Jordan, the singer makes his very sorrow a reason to remember God (v. 6). The roaring waters around him become God’s own waves breaking over his head (v. 7), yet the same God commands his steadfast love by day and gives him a song at night (v. 8). Then the questions return: why has God, his rock, forgotten him (v. 9)? The taunt cuts like a wound in the bones (v. 10), and the refrain comes again, word for word (v. 11). Nothing is tidied up, but faith keeps speaking.
verseByVerse.theology: The waves are called God's own, and the song in the night is given by the one who sent them.

verseByVerse.quote: and my God. My soul is cast down within me; therefore I remember you from the land of Jordan and of Hermon, from Mount Mizar. Deep calls to deep at the roar of your waterfalls; all your breakers and your waves have gone over me. By day the LORD commands his steadfast love, and at night his song is with me, a prayer to the God of my life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
His very sorrow becomes the reason to remember God, and the waters that seem to drown him are God’s own waves, sent by the same God who commands his steadfast love by day and gives a song at night.

From the land of Jordan and of Hermon. He tells us where he is: the far north, the headwaters of the Jordan under Mount Hermon, a long way from Jerusalem. The therefore shows the habit this psalm teaches: because I am cast down, I remember you. The downcast feeling becomes the reason to turn towards God rather than away.

Deep calls to deep. He is probably standing where the streams come crashing off Hermon, and the noise of the water becomes the sound of his own trouble: one depth shouting to another, wave after wave going over his head. Jonah used the same line from the depths: “all your breakers and your waves passed over me” (Jonah 2:3).

Your breakers and your waves. The pronoun matters: your waterfalls, your breakers, your waves. He does not say the trouble is random or that it came from his enemies. He says it is God’s, which is either the worst thing about it or the only comfort in it, depending on what you believe about God.

By day the LORD commands his steadfast love. This is the one place in the psalm where the covenant name, the LORD, appears, and it appears in the dark. God commands his steadfast love, sending it out on orders, and at night there is a song. The one whose breakers went over him in verse 7 is the one who gives the song in verse 8. Both are his, on the same day. And the waves that went over this singer went over the Son of God in full at the cross, so that for those in him they can only be the waves of a Father’s hand.

Uncertain wording. Mount Mizar (“little mountain”) is otherwise unknown, probably a small peak in the Hermon range.
verseByVerse.note: Mount Hermon and the Jordan’s sources lie in the far north.

verseByVerse.quote: I say to God, my rock: "Why have you forgotten me? Why do I go mourning because of the oppression of the enemy?" As with a deadly wound in my bones, my adversaries taunt me, while they say to me all the day long, "Where is your God?" Why are you cast down, O my soul, and why are you in turmoil within me? Hope in God; for I shall again praise him, my salvation and my God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The questions and the taunt return, and so does the refrain, word for word: in a long darkness faith keeps saying the same true thing, even when it does not feel like progress.

I say to God, my rock. He calls God my rock in the same breath as asking why he has been forgotten, and both are honest. The taunt returns word for word from verse 3, because that is how taunts work: they do not arrive once and leave. He feels it like a wound in the bones, where something hurts that will not stop.

The refrain again. Nothing has changed between verse 5 and verse 11: the trouble is the same, and so is the sorrow. That is the honest pattern of a long darkness: the same sermon preached to the same soul more than once, without feeling like progress. God’s people have always sung this in the dry season, and the thirst it began with is answered on the last pages of the Bible: “To the thirsty I will give from the spring of the water of life without payment” (Revelation 21:6).

42.title: As a Deer Pants for Flowing Streams
42.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 42 opens Book Two of the Psalter (Psalms 42–72) and a run of psalms by the sons of Korah, the temple singers (42–49). It belongs with Psalm 43: the two share one refrain and were probably once a single poem. After David’s sickbed in Psalm 41 comes a worshipper far from the house of God.

The message. A believer can be desperate for God, mocked for trusting him and overwhelmed by sorrow, and still turn and speak to his own soul: “Hope in God”. Longing for God when he seems absent is not the opposite of faith but one of its truest forms, and the God who sends the waves also commands his steadfast love by day and gives a song in the night (v. 8).

Why it was said. The singer is cut off from the temple, in the far north by the sources of the Jordan (v. 6), perhaps on the road into captivity; the psalm does not say. Around him people taunt, “Where is your God?” (v. 3). Israel kept the song so that every worshipper kept from God’s house, by distance, illness or disgrace, would have words for that thirst (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. Two stanzas, each ending in the refrain. In the first (vv. 1–5) he thirsts for God, eats tears, hears the taunt and remembers leading the festival crowds; then he turns on his own soul and tells it to hope. In the second (vv. 6–11) his sorrow becomes the reason to remember God; the roaring waters become God’s waves over him (v. 7), yet God gives steadfast love by day and a song at night (v. 8). The questions, the taunt and the refrain return (vv. 9–11). Psalm 43 adds the third stanza.

Where it leads. By the need it exposes, and by pattern. The thirst for the living God is answered in Jesus, who stood up at the feast and cried, “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink” (John 7:37). And the downcast soul of the refrain was once his: in Gethsemane he said, “My soul is very sorrowful, even to death” (Matthew 26:38), echoing this refrain in its Greek wording, and on the cross he heard the same taunt in other words (Matthew 27:43). He went under the waves so “that he might bring us to God” (1 Peter 3:18).

For us. When you are downcast, do not only listen to your soul; speak to it, and tell it what is true about God. When you are kept from God’s people, let the thirst drive you to God himself, and to the Saviour who gives living water. And do not be ashamed if you must preach the same sermon to yourself again tomorrow.
42.theology:
Psalms 42 and 43 are probably one poem with one refrain (42:5, 11; 43:5). Across Psalms 42-83 the word God largely replaces the LORD, the covenant name, which makes the single LORD of v. 8 stand out.

Desire for God is pictured as bodily need, and the loss he feels most is the shared worship of God's people (vv. 1-4). The refrain does not deny the darkness; it answers it with future praise (v. 5). The waves are God's, and so is the song in the night (vv. 7-8), and nothing is tidied up by the end (v. 11).
42.examples: The choir that sang this psalm descended from the man the ground swallowed in the wilderness, which is good news for anyone who thinks their family history disqualifies them. A panting deer is in trouble, not in a mood. A former leader of the festival singing, now too far away to join it, finds his memories both medicine and poison. And many believers know what it is to preach the same sermon to their own soul a second and a third time.

keyVerse.quote: Why are you cast down, O my soul, and why are you in turmoil within me? Hope in God; for I shall again praise him, my salvation and my God.
keyVerse.note: The refrain is the heart of the poem, sung three times across Psalms 42 and 43. It shows faith not as the absence of sorrow but as what a believer says to his sorrow: he questions his own soul, commands it to hope, and gives it a reason in the future. Christ, who knew this sorrow in Gethsemane, is the one in whom that future praise is sure.

42.reflection:
The psalmist thirsts for “the living God” (v. 2), not merely for an experience of him. What do people around you thirst for, and with what lesser things do we try to satisfy that thirst? What would it mean to bring it to Jesus (John 7:37)?

“Where is your God?” (vv. 3, 10). Have you heard that question, from others or from inside yourself? How does the psalm answer it, and what does it leave unanswered?

In verse 5 he speaks to his own soul instead of only listening to it. What does your soul tend to tell you on a bad day, and which truths from God would you say back?

Verse 7 calls the waves “your” waves, and verse 8 says the same God gives a song in the night. Why can it be a comfort that even our troubles are in God’s hands, and how would you say this gently to someone who is grieving?

43.text: <sup>1</sup>Vindicate me, O God, and defend my cause against an ungodly people, from the deceitful and unjust man deliver me!<sup>2</sup>For you are the God in whom I take refuge; why have you rejected me? Why do I go about mourning because of the oppression of the enemy?<sup>3</sup>Send out your light and your truth; let them lead me; let them bring me to your holy hill and to your dwelling!<sup>4</sup>Then I will go to the altar of God, to God my exceeding joy, and I will praise you with the lyre, O God, my God.<sup>5</sup>Why are you cast down, O my soul, and why are you in turmoil within me? Hope in God; for I shall again praise him, my salvation and my God.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — To God My Exceeding Joy
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The last stanza of the poem that began in Psalm 42 turns longing into requests and names the true goal of the journey. The singer asks God to defend his cause against a deceitful enemy, even while asking why God has rejected him (vv. 1–2). He asks God to send out his light and his truth as guides to bring him back to the holy hill (v. 3). There he will go to the altar, and past the altar to “God my exceeding joy”, and praise him with the lyre (v. 4). The refrain sounds a third time (v. 5): nothing outside has changed, but hope has a destination.
verseByVerse.theology: The thirst of Psalm 42 becomes a request for guides, and the destination is not a place but a person.

verseByVerse.quote: Vindicate me, O God, and defend my cause against an ungodly people, from the deceitful and unjust man deliver me! For you are the God in whom I take refuge; why have you rejected me? Why do I go about mourning because of the oppression of the enemy?
verseByVerse.commentary:
