Slandered and far from God’s house, the singer asks God to take up his case, and holds two things in one breath: God is his refuge, and God seems to have rejected him.

One psalm in two. This psalm has no heading because it is the last stanza of the one before. Its refrain (v. 5) is the refrain of 42:5 and 42:11, and verse 2 repeats 42:9 almost word for word. Many Hebrew manuscripts copy the two as one.

Vindicate me, O God, and defend my cause. Law-court language: he asks God to judge in his favour and plead his case, as an advocate takes up a client’s cause. He does not defend himself; he hands the case to God. So did Christ: “when he was reviled, he did not revile in return … but continued entrusting himself to him who judges justly” (1 Peter 2:23).

Why have you rejected me? Here is the hardest question a believer ever has to hold: you are the God in whom I take refuge, and why have you rejected me? Both in one sentence, neither cancelling the other. That is what faith sounds like when everything seems to say that God has gone.

verseByVerse.quote: Send out your light and your truth; let them lead me; let them bring me to your holy hill and to your dwelling! Then I will go to the altar of God, to God my exceeding joy, and I will praise you with the lyre, O God, my God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He asks God to send out his light and truth as guides to bring him home, and the home he means is not the altar but God himself, his exceeding joy.

Send out your light and your truth. He does not ask for the destruction of the ungodly, or an explanation. He asks God to send out two servants, light and truth, to fetch a man who cannot find his own way back, as the pillar of cloud and fire once went ahead of Israel (Exodus 13:21). They are exactly what a person in his condition has lost: he is in the dark and he is being lied about, so he wants light to see by and truth to stand on.

What God sent. A Christian hears the words of Jesus: “I am the light of the world” (John 8:12), and “I am the way, and the truth, and the life” (John 14:6). What the psalmist asked God to send out, God sent.

To God my exceeding joy. The destination is named twice, and the second naming is the real one. He wants to reach the altar, and then he goes further: to God my exceeding joy, literally “the gladness of my joy”. Not the building, the music or the crowd he used to lead: the person at the end of the journey. Anyone kept from church may ask what exactly they miss. This man wants the altar because God is there, and he says so in case anybody mistook his homesickness for nostalgia.

verseByVerse.quote: Why are you cast down, O my soul, and why are you in turmoil within me? Hope in God; for I shall again praise him, my salvation and my God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The refrain comes a third time, word for word, with nothing resolved: in a long darkness the faithful thing is to say the true thing again.

Hope in God. He is still far from the sanctuary; the ungodly people are still there; the taunt of 42:3 has not been answered. What he has is a refrain, and the discipline to say it again.

In a long darkness. Take that as the psalm’s gift rather than its failure. Christians often expect the right insight to lift a darkness once and for all, and are ashamed to be back at the same sentence a week later. Preach it to yourself again. I shall again praise him was true the first time, and it is still true now, because the one who will be praised does not change.
verseByVerse.note: The same refrain as Psalm 42.

43.title: Send Out Your Light and Your Truth
43.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 43 has no title because it is the closing stanza of Psalm 42. It has the same refrain (v. 5; 42:5, 11), the same complaint about “the oppression of the enemy” (v. 2; 42:9) and the same longing for God’s house. The singer is still far from the sanctuary, still slandered, still downcast.

The message. The thirst of Psalm 42 becomes prayer. He asks God to take up his case and to send out his light and his truth to lead him home, not finally to a building but “to God my exceeding joy” (v. 4). The God who seems to have rejected him is still the God in whom he takes refuge, and still the goal of all his longing.

Why it was said. As in Psalm 42, a worshipper is cut off from the temple and surrounded by “an ungodly people” and a “deceitful and unjust man” (v. 1). The song gave Israel, and gives the church, words for every exile from God’s house and every time of being lied about (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. He asks God to vindicate him, while asking in the same breath why God has rejected him (vv. 1–2). He asks for guides, God’s light and truth, to bring him back to the holy hill (v. 3). He promises to go to the altar, and past the altar to God himself, and to praise him with the lyre (v. 4). The refrain closes the poem a third time (v. 5), with nothing outside changed but hope now given a destination.

Where it leads. The psalm is a prayer, not a prediction, but God has answered it in his Son, and in that answer his character is revealed. The light and truth the singer asked God to send came in person: “I am the light of the world” (John 8:12); “I am the way, and the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me” (John 14:6). The altar he longed to reach gives way to Christ’s once-for-all sacrifice, by which believers “enter the holy places by the blood of Jesus” (Hebrews 10:19): not a hill in Jerusalem but the presence of God himself, our exceeding joy.

For us. When you are confused or lied about, ask God for light and truth, and look for them in Christ and his word. When you are kept from church, ask what you really miss, and let your joy be God himself. And when the darkness lasts, say the refrain again.
43.theology:
Faith can hold refuge and rejection in one sentence without either cancelling the other (v. 2). What he asks for is escort rather than rescue: light and truth sent out to fetch a man who cannot find his way back, and the New Testament names both in one person.

The goal is not the altar for its own sake but God my exceeding joy (v. 4), and the unchanged refrain (v. 5) shows that in a long darkness, repetition is not failure.
43.examples: Picture a traveller lost at night who is met by two servants sent from the house with a lamp and the true road: that is verse 3. Someone kept from church by illness or distance may find that what they miss most is not the building, the music or the crowd but God himself. And a believer back at the same sentence a week later has not gone backwards; the psalmist got there three times.

keyVerse.quote: Send out your light and your truth; let them lead me; let them bring me to your holy hill and to your dwelling!
keyVerse.note: Here the long lament of Psalms 42 and 43 turns into a request, and a surprising one: not for rescue or an explanation, but for guides to bring a lost worshipper home. The next verse names the true destination, “God my exceeding joy”. God answered the prayer by sending his Son, the light of the world and the truth, who brings us to the Father.

43.reflection:
In verse 2 the singer calls God his refuge and asks why God has rejected him, in one breath. Why does it matter that Scripture lets faith speak like this? Have you ever prayed both at once?

He asks God to send out his “light” and “truth” to lead him (v. 3). Where do you most need light and truth just now, and how has God sent them to us in Jesus (John 8:12; 14:6) and in his word?

The goal is not the altar for its own sake but “God my exceeding joy” (v. 4). When you are kept away from church, or when you are there, what do you really long for?

The refrain comes a third time with nothing outside changed (v. 5). How can we help one another keep saying “Hope in God” through a long darkness?

44.text: To the choirmaster. A Maskil of the Sons of Korah. 1O God, we have heard with our ears, our fathers have told us, what deeds you performed in their days, in the days of old:2you with your own hand drove out the nations, but them you planted; you afflicted the peoples, but them you set free;3for not by their own sword did they win the land, nor did their own arm save them, but your right hand and your arm, and the light of your face, for you delighted in them.4You are my King, O God; ordain salvation for Jacob!5Through you we push down our foes; through your name we tread down those who rise up against us.6For not in my bow do I trust, nor can my sword save me.7But you have saved us from our foes and have put to shame those who hate us.8In God we have boasted continually, and we will give thanks to your name forever. Selah9But you have rejected us and disgraced us and have not gone out with our armies.10You have made us turn back from the foe, and those who hate us have gotten spoil.11You have made us like sheep for slaughter and have scattered us among the nations.12You have sold your people for a trifle, demanding no high price for them.13You have made us the taunt of our neighbors, the derision and scorn of those around us.14You have made us a byword among the nations, a laughingstock among the peoples.15All day long my disgrace is before me, and shame has covered my face16at the sound of the taunter and reviler, at the sight of the enemy and the avenger.17All this has come upon us, though we have not forgotten you, and we have not been false to your covenant.18Our heart has not turned back, nor have our steps departed from your way;19yet you have broken us in the place of jackals and covered us with the shadow of death.20If we had forgotten the name of our God or spread out our hands to a foreign god,21would not God discover this? For he knows the secrets of the heart.22Yet for your sake we are killed all the day long; we are regarded as sheep to be slaughtered.23Awake! Why are you sleeping, O Lord? Rouse yourself! Do not reject us forever!24Why do you hide your face? Why do you forget our affliction and oppression?25For our soul is bowed down to the dust; our belly clings to the ground.26Rise up; come to our help! Redeem us for the sake of your steadfast love!

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — Not by Their Own Sword
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel begins by remembering, and everything it remembers is God’s doing. The fathers handed down the story of the conquest: God drove out the nations and planted his people, not by their sword but by his right hand and the light of his face, because he delighted in them (vv. 1–3). The present generation makes the same confession its own. God is their King, their victories come through his name, and they do not trust in bow or sword (vv. 4–7). Their boast has been in God continually (v. 8). The section establishes that this is a people trusting God, which makes what follows so hard to bear.
verseByVerse.theology: The nation's whole history is told as something God did, with the army as a bystander.

verseByVerse.quote: O God, we have heard with our ears, our fathers have told us, what deeds you performed in their days, in the days of old: you with your own hand drove out the nations, but them you planted; you afflicted the peoples, but them you set free; for not by their own sword did they win the land, nor did their own arm save them, but your right hand and your arm, and the light of your face, for you delighted in them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel’s founding story is told entirely as God’s gift: he won the land and planted his people, not by their sword but by his power and his favour, because he delighted in them.

Our fathers have told us. Another Maskil of the sons of Korah, this one sung by a whole nation. It opens as a history lesson passed down at the table, and the whole conquest of Canaan under Joshua is told as something Israel received, not something it achieved: you drove out, you planted, and explicitly not their sword, not their arm. Even the reason is on God’s side: for you delighted in them.

The light of your face. Verse 3 names what won the land: God’s right hand and arm, his power, and the light of your face, his favour turned towards them, the blessing the priests spoke over Israel: “the LORD make his face to shine upon you” (Numbers 6:25). Victory came from God’s strength and God’s smile, not from Israel’s merit.

Why do nations need a heroic past? Almost every people tells its founding story as achievement: we fought, we built, we earned this place. That is why arguments about statues and textbooks grow so bitter: if our worth rests on our story, every honest look at its dark chapters feels like an attack. Israel sang something different. A people whose story is grace has nothing to protect, so it can tell the truth, even the ugly parts, as the Old Testament does on almost every page. The church has the same freedom at its centre. Its founding event is a cross, where its sins were exposed and forgiven, so its only boast is the one Paul allows: “Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord” (1 Corinthians 1:31).

Was it just for God to drive out the nations? It was his unique judgment on peoples whose sin had reached its full measure (Genesis 15:16; Deuteronomy 9:4–5), carried out through Israel at his command. It is no pattern or licence for any nation or church today.

verseByVerse.quote: You are my King, O God; ordain salvation for Jacob! Through you we push down our foes; through your name we tread down those who rise up against us. For not in my bow do I trust, nor can my sword save me. But you have saved us from our foes and have put to shame those who hate us. In God we have boasted continually, and we will give thanks to your name forever. Selah
verseByVerse.commentary:
The present generation makes the fathers’ confession its own: God is their King, their victories are his, and they trust in him, not in their weapons.

You are my King, O God; ordain salvation for Jacob! The history becomes a present confession, and the plural we narrows for a moment to my King: perhaps the king or the leader of the singing speaking for all. (Jacob is the nation.) To ordain salvation is to command it, as a king gives an order and it is carried out. The God who won the land with a word is asked to speak the word again.

Through you we push down our foes. The verb pictures an ox goring with its horns (as in Deuteronomy 33:17). Israel’s army does fight, but through you and through your name: the strength is borrowed, and they know it.

For not in my bow do I trust. The present generation says of itself what the fathers said, and makes Psalm 20’s “Some trust in chariots” (Psalm 20:7) the nation’s own confession. That matters enormously for what follows: these are not people presuming on their own strength. They have boasted in God … continually. Keep that in mind, because the next verse begins But you.

Uncertain wording. On Selah, see the note on Psalm 3:1–2. Here it falls between the confident praise and the sudden turn.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–22 — You Have Made Us Like Sheep for Slaughter
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Suddenly the song turns: “But you have rejected us.” God is the subject of every verb. He has not gone out with their armies; he has made them retreat, given them up like sheep for slaughter, scattered them and sold them cheap (vv. 9–12), and made them a laughingstock among the nations (vv. 13–16). Then comes the claim that makes the psalm stand out: all this has happened though they have kept the covenant, and God, who knows the secrets of the heart, can test it (vv. 17–21). Their suffering is not punishment but “for your sake” (v. 22), the line Paul takes up for Christians in Romans 8:36.
verseByVerse.theology: A whole people insists that it has not deserved this, and names God as the one who did it.

verseByVerse.quote: But you have rejected us and disgraced us and have not gone out with our armies. You have made us turn back from the foe, and those who hate us have gotten spoil. You have made us like sheep for slaughter and have scattered us among the nations. You have sold your people for a trifle, demanding no high price for them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Suddenly the song turns: God, not circumstance, is named as the one who has rejected his people, deserted their armies, given them up to slaughter and sold them cheap.

But you have rejected us and disgraced us. Count the accusations: you rejected, you disgraced, you stayed home from the battle, you made us retreat, you made us sheep for the knife, you scattered us. God is the subject of every verb. Nobody in this psalm blames circumstances.

Have not gone out with our armies. This is the sharpest loss of all. In Israel’s wars God was the commander who “goes with you to fight for you” (Deuteronomy 20:4), and the ark went out at the head of the army (Numbers 10:35). Now, as far as anyone can see, the army marched out alone.

Like sheep for slaughter. Sheep kept for eating, led off without a struggle. Scattered us among the nations means captives taken and sold abroad, one of the covenant curses (Deuteronomy 28:64), yet this generation insists it has kept the covenant (vv. 17–18).

You have sold your people for a trifle. The most bitter line in the psalm. God is pictured as a man selling his own household, and not even driving a hard bargain: he let them go cheap. When a believer feels that God has not merely allowed a loss but seems to have valued him at nothing, this verse has been there first. And the psalm’s last word answers it: “Redeem us” (v. 26), buy us back.

Which defeat is this? The psalm does not say. Suggestions range from a setback in David’s wars with Edom (compare Psalm 60) to the Assyrian invasions around 700 BC; none can be proved, and the psalm’s very openness has let every later generation of sufferers sing it.

verseByVerse.quote: You have made us the taunt of our neighbors, the derision and scorn of those around us. You have made us a byword among the nations, a laughingstock among the peoples. All day long my disgrace is before me, and shame has covered my face at the sound of the taunter and reviler, at the sight of the enemy and the avenger.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The wound is public: God’s people have become a joke among the nations, and every jeer at them is really a jeer at their God.

A byword among the nations. The ESV notes that byword is literally “a shaking of the head”: the gesture strangers make as they pass. It is the taunt of Psalm 42, now aimed at a whole nation, and it goes on all day long.

At the sound of the taunter and reviler. Shame has covered my face: the speaker can no longer look anyone in the eye. What keeps the wound open is the voice of the taunter and the sight of the enemy and the avenger, the one who pays back old scores (the same pair as in 8:2). For a people whose boast was in God (v. 8), every jeer was really aimed at him: where is your God now?

The head-shaking at the cross. The same gesture met the Son of God: “those who passed by derided him, wagging their heads” (Matthew 27:39). He bore that scorn so that his people’s disgrace would not be the last word about them.

verseByVerse.quote: All this has come upon us, though we have not forgotten you, and we have not been false to your covenant. Our heart has not turned back, nor have our steps departed from your way; yet you have broken us in the place of jackals and covered us with the shadow of death. If we had forgotten the name of our God or spread out our hands to a foreign god, would not God discover this? For he knows the secrets of the heart. Yet for your sake we are killed all the day long; we are regarded as sheep to be slaughtered.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The people insist that they have not betrayed God’s covenant, and that their suffering is not punishment but comes because they belong to him: “for your sake we are killed all the day long”.

Though we have not forgotten you. Here is what makes this psalm so difficult, and so necessary. The usual explanation for national disaster in the Old Testament is national sin, and this psalm refuses it. They have not forgotten God, not gone after other gods, not turned back. It is Job’s question, why the faithful suffer, asked by a whole people.

Would not God discover this? To spread out our hands is to pray; to spread them to a foreign god is idolatry. If we had, they say, you would know (vv. 20–21). They invite the examination rather than avoiding it. That is not arrogance; it is the honest thing to say when the usual explanation does not fit, and a relief to anyone told that their suffering must be the result of some hidden sin.

Yet for your sake we are killed all the day long. Their suffering is not merely undeserved; it is for your sake, because they belong to him. Paul reaches for this verse at the climax of his great passage on God’s love, having asked whether tribulation or sword can separate us from Christ: “As it is written, ‘For your sake we are being killed all the day long; we are regarded as sheep to be slaughtered’” (Romans 8:36). And then: “No, in all these things we are more than conquerors through him who loved us” (Romans 8:37). Paul does not soften the verse. He grants the whole of it (this happens to God’s own people, all day long) and denies the conclusion people draw from it, that God has stopped loving them. The slaughter is real; the separation is not.

Are they claiming to be sinless? No. They mean that they have not turned to idols, the sin that brought the covenant curses (Deuteronomy 28). No one is righteous before God (143:2), but this suffering was not punishment for unfaithfulness.

Uncertain wording. The shadow of death (v. 19) translates a Hebrew word traditionally read as “shadow of death” but which many scholars take to mean simply deep darkness, as the ESV notes at 23:4. Either way it is a darkness as thick as death’s.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–26 — Awake! Why Are You Sleeping?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The psalm ends not with an answer but with the boldest prayer in the Psalter. God seems asleep, his face hidden and their affliction forgotten, so they cry to him to wake and rouse himself (vv. 23–24). They lie flat in the dust, unable to rise (v. 25). And their final appeal is not to the faithfulness they have just protested but to his: “Redeem us for the sake of your steadfast love!” (v. 26). No rescue is reported. The section teaches God’s people to keep praying when heaven is silent, and to rest their case on the one ground that never depended on them.
verseByVerse.theology: The boldest prayer in the Psalter ends by appealing to God’s steadfast love, the one thing that never depended on them.

verseByVerse.quote: Awake! Why are you sleeping, O Lord? Rouse yourself! Do not reject us forever! Why do you hide your face? Why do you forget our affliction and oppression? For our soul is bowed down to the dust; our belly clings to the ground. Rise up; come to our help! Redeem us for the sake of your steadfast love!
verseByVerse.commentary:
With no answer in sight, the people cry to God to wake and rise, and they rest their final plea not on their faithfulness but on his steadfast love.

Awake! Why are you sleeping, O Lord? The boldest thing anybody says to God in the Psalter, and it is in the hymnbook, for the congregation to sing: God put these words in his people’s mouths. They do not believe God is asleep; they have just said that he knows the secrets of the heart (v. 21), and Israel knew that “he who keeps Israel will neither slumber nor sleep” (Psalm 121:4). They are describing how it looks, and asking him to stop looking like that.

Our soul is bowed down to the dust. Face down in the dust, unable to get up: the posture of defeat, and of prayer. They are flat on the ground either way, and they have decided to speak from there.

For the sake of your steadfast love! After all their insistence on their innocence, look at the ground they finally stand on. Not “for the sake of our faithfulness”, but for the sake of your steadfast love. They were right that they had not deserved this, but they know better than to claim rescue as something earned. And redeem answers verse 12: the God who seemed to sell them cheap is asked to buy them back.

Christ asleep in the storm. There is one place in the Gospels where God incarnate really was asleep in a crisis, and his friends woke him with almost this cry: “Teacher, do you not care that we are perishing?” (Mark 4:38). He did not rebuke the waking. He rebuked the wind.

The God who seemed asleep rose up. The psalm ends unanswered, with a battered people still asking for the right reason. Its protest finally found the one sufferer who was wholly innocent. Of Jesus it was written, “Like a sheep he was led to the slaughter” (Acts 8:32, quoting Isaiah 53:7). He was killed for no sin of his own, and on the third day God raised him. We were redeemed not for a trifle but “with the precious blood of Christ, like that of a lamb without blemish or spot” (1 Peter 1:19). That is why Paul can tell sufferers that nothing will separate them from the love of God in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:39).

44.title: Sheep to Be Slaughtered
44.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 44 is the second psalm of the sons of Korah in Book Two, and the first of the Psalter’s great laments sung by the whole nation. After the lonely worshipper of Psalms 42 and 43, a whole people now asks why God seems to have rejected them.

The message. God’s people may suffer defeat and disgrace not because they have abandoned him but because they belong to him. When they do, they may say so to God plainly, and ask him to rise up and redeem them, not on the ground of their own faithfulness but “for the sake of your steadfast love” (v. 26). Faith can hold together the God of the glorious past and a present that makes no sense.

Why it was said. Israel had been beaten, its people killed or sold, its neighbours jeering (vv. 9–16), at a time when, as far as the nation knew, it had not turned to idols (vv. 17–18). The psalm does not say which defeat this was (see the note on vv. 9–12). The usual explanation, that disaster follows unfaithfulness (Deuteronomy 28), did not seem to fit, and the psalm gave the faithful words for that bewilderment.

How the chapter makes its case. History: God, not their sword, won the land (vv. 1–3), and the present generation still trusts him, not its bow (vv. 4–8). Then comes the shock, “But you have rejected us”: defeat, slaughter, scattering and public shame, all laid at God’s door (vv. 9–16). They protest their loyalty to the covenant and invite God to examine their hearts, concluding, “for your sake we are killed all the day long” (vv. 17–22). The psalm ends by crying to God to wake, and pleading his steadfast love (vv. 23–26).

Where it leads. By its use in the New Testament, and by pattern. Paul quotes verse 22 of Christians who suffer for Christ, and answers it: “No, in all these things we are more than conquerors through him who loved us” (Romans 8:37). And the psalm’s cry of innocent suffering finds its one wholly innocent sufferer in Jesus, led “like a sheep … to the slaughter” (Acts 8:32), not for his own sake but for ours. The cry “Rise up” (v. 26) was answered on Easter morning, and that is why nothing “will be able to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Romans 8:39).

For us. When suffering comes, do not assume it must be punishment, and do not let others assume it for you. Tell God the truth, even the hard parts; Scripture gives you the words. Then rest your plea where this psalm finally rests it: on his steadfast love, which in Christ has proved that it will not let you go.
44.theology:
The founding story gives God all the credit, and this generation disowns its own bow (v. 6), so this is not a psalm of presumption. It then refuses the usual explanation of disaster: these sufferers have not turned to idols, and the psalm lets them say so (vv. 17-21).

Paul grants v. 22 in full and denies the conclusion people draw from it (Rom 8:36-37). And after all its protested innocence, the psalm asks for rescue not on the ground of faithfulness but for the sake of your steadfast love (v. 26).
44.examples: Imagine a family history told at the dinner table in which the family itself never once does the winning. Or a man selling his own household cheaply, without even haggling: that is how verse 12 feels. Many believers have been told that their suffering must hide some secret sin; this psalm lets them say plainly that it does not, and still teaches them to ask for help on the ground of God's love rather than their record.

keyVerse.quote: Yet for your sake we are killed all the day long; we are regarded as sheep to be slaughtered.
keyVerse.note: This is the climax of the psalm’s protest: the people suffer not for unfaithfulness but because they belong to God. Paul quotes it in Romans 8:36, granting it in full and denying the conclusion people draw from it, that God has stopped loving them. It finds its deepest meaning in the Lamb led to the slaughter, whose love holds his suffering people fast.

44.reflection:
The psalm begins by remembering what God did “not by their own sword” (v. 3). Why is it important for a church or a family to tell its story as God’s doing rather than its own achievement?

Verses 9–16 lay every defeat at God’s door, and verses 17–21 insist that it was not deserved. Is it right to speak to God so boldly? How does this psalm help people who have been told that their suffering must be caused by some hidden sin?

Paul quotes verse 22 in Romans 8:36 and answers, “No, in all these things we are more than conquerors through him who loved us.” How does the love of Christ change the way we read our own suffering?

After protesting their faithfulness, they finally plead “for the sake of your steadfast love” (v. 26). Why is that the safest ground for any prayer, and what difference would it make to pray that way this week?

45.text: To the choirmaster: according to Lilies. A Maskil of the Sons of Korah; a love song. 1My heart overflows with a pleasing theme; I address my verses to the king; my tongue is like the pen of a ready scribe.2You are the most handsome of the sons of men; grace is poured upon your lips; therefore God has blessed you forever.3Gird your sword on your thigh, O mighty one, in your splendor and majesty!4In your majesty ride out victoriously for the cause of truth and meekness and righteousness; let your right hand teach you awesome deeds!5Your arrows are sharp in the heart of the king's enemies; the peoples fall under you.6Your throne, O God, is forever and ever. The scepter of your kingdom is a scepter of uprightness;7you have loved righteousness and hated wickedness. Therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness beyond your companions;8your robes are all fragrant with myrrh and aloes and cassia. From ivory palaces stringed instruments make you glad;9daughters of kings are among your ladies of honor; at your right hand stands the queen in gold of Ophir.10Hear, O daughter, and consider, and incline your ear: forget your people and your father's house,11and the king will desire your beauty. Since he is your lord, bow to him.12The people of Tyre will seek your favor with gifts, the richest of the people.13All glorious is the princess in her chamber, with robes interwoven with gold.14In many-colored robes she is led to the king, with her virgin companions following behind her.15With joy and gladness they are led along as they enter the palace of the king.16In place of your fathers shall be your sons; you will make them princes in all the earth.17I will cause your name to be remembered in all generations; therefore nations will praise you forever and ever.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — Gird Your Sword on Your Thigh
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The King God gives his people is beautiful, righteous and, astonishingly, addressed as God. The poet, overflowing, describes the groom: handsome, gracious in speech, and blessed by God for ever (vv. 1–2). He arms him and sends him out to win, not for plunder but for truth, meekness and righteousness, with arrows that find the hearts of his enemies (vv. 3–5). Then the song soars: the king is addressed as God, with a throne that lasts for ever and a sceptre of uprightness, and yet God, his God, has anointed him with the oil of gladness above all others (vv. 6–7). The wedding is full of fragrance, music and royal company, with the queen in gold at his right hand (vv. 8–9). Hebrews hears the Father speaking to the Son.
verseByVerse.theology: A wedding song that calls the bridegroom God says more than any ordinary royal wedding could bear.

verseByVerse.quote: My heart overflows with a pleasing theme; I address my verses to the king; my tongue is like the pen of a ready scribe. You are the most handsome of the sons of men; grace is poured upon your lips; therefore God has blessed you forever. Gird your sword on your thigh, O mighty one, in your splendor and majesty! In your majesty ride out victoriously for the cause of truth and meekness and righteousness; let your right hand teach you awesome deeds! Your arrows are sharp in the heart of the king's enemies; the peoples fall under you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The poet’s heart overflows as he praises the king: beautiful, gracious in speech, and riding out to win for truth, meekness and righteousness.

My heart overflows with a pleasing theme. The only psalm titled “a love song”, written for a royal wedding: the poet’s heart is bubbling over, and his tongue can barely keep up. Scripture is not embarrassed by a love song; it puts one in the middle of its prayer book.

Grace is poured upon your lips. First the groom’s face, then his speech. When Jesus preached in Nazareth, the crowd “marveled at the gracious words that were coming from his mouth” (Luke 4:22), and a Christian can hardly miss the echo.

Gird your sword on your thigh. A sword at a wedding: the bridegroom is a warrior, and his cause is “truth and meekness and righteousness”. No nation writes meekness on its banners, yet it is one of the three things this King fights for. John saw the same rider at the end: “in righteousness he judges and makes war” (Revelation 19:11). His arrows find “the heart of the king’s enemies” (v. 5), and Christ’s first conquests were exactly that: hearers “cut to the heart” by the gospel (Acts 2:37).
verseByVerse.note: A royal wedding song.

verseByVerse.quote: Your throne, O God, is forever and ever. The scepter of your kingdom is a scepter of uprightness; you have loved righteousness and hated wickedness. Therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness beyond your companions; your robes are all fragrant with myrrh and aloes and cassia. From ivory palaces stringed instruments make you glad; daughters of kings are among your ladies of honor; at your right hand stands the queen in gold of Ophir.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The king is addressed as God, with an everlasting throne and a righteous sceptre, yet God has anointed him with joy above all others: words that only Christ, God the Son made man, can fully bear.

Your throne, O God, is forever and ever. Here the Old Testament does something it almost never does. The king being married is addressed as God, and in the next line has a God of his own who anoints him: language too great for any merely human king. His sceptre is one of uprightness, for he has “loved righteousness and hated wickedness”, as Christ did every day of his life, hating wickedness enough to die to destroy it.

How Hebrews reads it. Hebrews takes the matter as settled. Arguing that the Son is greater than any angel, it quotes these verses from the Greek Old Testament as the Father speaking to the Son (Hebrews 1:8–9). The Father calls the Son God. And “God, your God” then makes sense: the Son is God, and as the anointed man and King he also has God as his God (John 20:17). A wedding song becomes a witness to the deity of Christ.

The oil of gladness. The verb anointed is the root of the word Messiah, “the anointed one”, and the anointing gives not merely office but “the oil of gladness beyond your companions”. Isaiah promised “the oil of gladness instead of mourning” to those who mourn in Zion (Isaiah 61:3); this King has more of it than anyone. Joy is part of the job.

Myrrh and aloes and cassia. Perfume, music, the queen in the finest gold: the psalm is enjoying the wedding, and Revelation pictures the end of everything the same way (Revelation 19:7–9). But there is a hint of the price: myrrh and aloes were also what Nicodemus brought to bind the body of Jesus (John 19:39). The King came to his wedding by way of the tomb.

How Jewish readers take it. Jewish interpreters read it as a song for a Davidic king’s wedding, and usually take verse 6 so that the king is not himself called God (see below). Yet the Aramaic Targum at verse 2 addresses the bridegroom as King Messiah, fairer than the sons of men. So both traditions find the Messiah here. This commentary follows Hebrews 1:8–9, where the Father speaks these words to the Son.

Uncertain wording. Can a king be called God? The Hebrew of verse 6 can also be construed “Your throne is God”, “Your divine throne”, or “Your throne is like God’s throne”, and some take “God” as a title for the king as God’s representative (compare 82:6). But the most natural reading addresses the king as God, and the Greek translation and Hebrews 1:8 read it so.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The bride who leaves everything for the king is desired, honoured and brought in with joy, and the king’s line and name will fill the earth. The poet speaks to the bride like a father: listen, forget your people and your father’s house, for the king desires your beauty, so honour him as your lord (vv. 10–11). The richest of the nations will court her favour (v. 12). She is dressed in gold-woven, many-coloured robes and led to the king with her companions, amid joy and gladness (vv. 13–15). Then the poet turns back to the king: his sons will be princes through all the earth, and his name will be remembered and praised by the nations for ever (vv. 16–17).
verseByVerse.theology: The bride leaves everything to belong to him, and what she receives is his desire and his house.

verseByVerse.quote: Hear, O daughter, and consider, and incline your ear: forget your people and your father's house, and the king will desire your beauty. Since he is your lord, bow to him. The people of Tyre will seek your favor with gifts, the richest of the people. All glorious is the princess in her chamber, with robes interwoven with gold. In many-colored robes she is led to the king, with her virgin companions following behind her. With joy and gladness they are led along as they enter the palace of the king.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The bride is called to leave her old loyalties and give herself to the king, and she finds that she is desired, honoured and led to him with joy: the story of every believer’s coming to Christ.

Forget your people. What the poem asks of the bride is total. A royal marriage usually meant a foreign princess, and she is told not merely to travel but to forget her nation and home. Genesis says that “a man shall leave his father and his mother and hold fast to his wife” (Genesis 2:24); here it is the bride who leaves everything.

The king will desire your beauty. The promise is not security or status: she is not being acquired; she is wanted. For Christ’s people that is the order of every conversion: a leaving, and then the discovery that the one you came to has been desiring you. Honour follows at once: “the people of Tyre”, the wealthy Phoenician port whose merchants traded across the Mediterranean, court her favour with gifts (v. 12).

In many-colored robes she is led to the king. She is dressed by others and led in with joy. Paul saw the church this way and said who does the dressing: Christ gave himself for her “so that he might present the church to himself in splendor, without spot or wrinkle or any such thing” (Ephesians 5:27). She does not supply the glorious robes; he does.

Who makes us beautiful? Few anxieties are as modern, or as old, as the fear of being looked at and found wanting; a whole economy of filters and procedures lives on it. Our culture says either that beauty must be earned, so work harder on yourself, or that it is self-declared, so tell yourself you are enough. The first exhausts us, and the second rarely convinces at three in the morning, because nobody can confer beauty on himself. It has to come from the eyes of someone whose look counts. That is what this song gives the bride. Augustine, preaching on John’s first letter, observed that Christ loved us when we were unlovely in order to make us lovely: his love did not find us beautiful, it made us so. We are not trying to become beautiful enough to be loved. We are loved, by the one look that finally matters, and the beauty follows.

What it does not mean. “Since he is your lord, bow to him” does not mean a wife must grovel before her husband. This is a subject before her king, and this King rides out for meekness. Scripture’s pattern for marriage is a husband who loves his wife “as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her” (Ephesians 5:25); abuse is never to be tolerated, and anyone suffering it should seek safety at once.

Uncertain wording. “In her chamber” (v. 13) renders a single Hebrew word meaning “within” or “inside”. It probably means inside the palace, before the procession of verse 14. The King James Version attached it to her (the king’s daughter is all glorious within), and many preachers applied that to the church’s inner beauty, a point true elsewhere (1 Peter 3:4).

verseByVerse.quote: In place of your fathers shall be your sons; you will make them princes in all the earth. I will cause your name to be remembered in all generations; therefore nations will praise you forever and ever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The poet promises the king sons who will rule the whole earth and a name the nations will praise for ever, a promise only Christ’s kingdom has kept.

In place of your fathers shall be your sons. The poet promises the king a future and a name: a line that goes on, which for a dynasty is everything, and a memory his song will keep alive.

I will cause your name to be remembered. A large promise about a monarch whose name we no longer know, and it came true in a way the poet did not expect. The wedding this psalm celebrated is forgotten; the psalm is read every week somewhere in the world, because the King it turned out to be about has a throne for ever and ever.

Princes in all the earth. Christ’s “sons” are the people he is “bringing many sons to glory” (Hebrews 2:10), and he has made them “a kingdom and priests to our God, and they shall reign on the earth” (Revelation 5:10). So the last line can be taken at its full meaning: “nations will praise you forever and ever”. That is not wedding flattery. It is what is happening now, wherever the gospel goes.

45.title: Your Throne, O God, Is Forever
45.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 45 follows the bewildered lament of Psalm 44, where a faithful nation asked why God seemed asleep while it was crushed. Into that darkness the sons of Korah set a wedding song for the king, the only psalm its title calls “a love song”, and Psalms 46 to 48 go on to celebrate God as King in his city.

The message. God’s King is lovely, gracious and righteous, and his throne lasts for ever, for the king this song addresses is called God. He rides out for truth, meekness and righteousness, and he takes a bride who leaves everything to belong to him and finds that she is wanted. A royal wedding in Jerusalem becomes a window onto the marriage at the centre of history.

Why it was said. The song was written for the wedding of a king of David’s line, probably to a foreign princess; which king is unknown, though Solomon is often suggested. Every such wedding mattered, because God had promised David, “Your throne shall be established forever” (2 Samuel 7:16), and a royal marriage carried the hope of the next heir (see the introduction on the royal psalms).

How the chapter makes its case. The poet’s heart overflows (v. 1). He praises the groom’s beauty and gracious speech, then arms him and sends him out to win for truth, meekness and righteousness (vv. 2–5). Then the song soars: the king is addressed as God, with an everlasting throne, yet God, his God, has anointed him with gladness, and perfume, music and the queen in gold fill the scene (vv. 6–9). The poet turns to the bride: forget your people, for the king desires your beauty, and she is led to him in joy (vv. 10–15). He ends with promises to the king: sons who will be princes in all the earth, and a name the nations will praise for ever (vv. 16–17).

Where it leads. To Christ by promise, and the New Testament says so in so many words. Hebrews quotes verses 6–7 as the Father speaking to the Son (Hebrews 1:8–9). No son of David could bear the name God or a throne that lasts for ever; Jesus does, God the Son and the anointed man. His bride is the church, whom he washes and dresses in splendour (Ephesians 5:25–27), and the song looks on to “the marriage supper of the Lamb” (Revelation 19:9).

For us. Christ is not only to be obeyed but admired: look at him until your heart overflows too. Coming to him means leaving old loyalties behind, but you come to a King who desires you, dresses you in robes you did not weave, and leads you in with joy.
45.theology:
The king is addressed as God and also has a God who anoints him (vv. 6-7), language too large for any merely human king, which Hebrews hears as the Father speaking to the Son. His cause includes meekness, and his anointing is the oil of gladness beyond his companions: joy is part of the office.

The bride leaves everything in order to belong, and the promise is that she is wanted (vv. 10-11); Paul sees in her the church that Christ dresses and presents to himself (Eph 5:27). The promise of a remembered name (vv. 16-17) outran the king it was first written for.
45.examples: Scripture's prayer book makes room for a love song, and Christian readers need not hurry past the perfume and music to reach the theology. A sword at a wedding is strange enough; stranger still is a banner with meekness on it. The bride's robes are ones she did not weave, which is how every Christian comes to Christ. And a court poet's promise to keep a now-forgotten king's name alive came true in a way he never imagined.

keyVerse.quote: Your throne, O God, is forever and ever.
keyVerse.note: This is the line that lifts the psalm beyond any king in Jerusalem. The king is addressed as God and given a throne that never ends, and Hebrews hears the Father saying it to the Son (Hebrews 1:8). Everything else in the song, the beauty, the righteous cause, the joyful bride, belongs to this King.

45.reflection:
The poet’s heart “overflows” as he describes the king (vv. 1–2). When did you last think about Christ simply to admire him, and what would help you do it more?

The king rides out “for the cause of truth and meekness and righteousness” (v. 4). Why is meekness so surprising on a warrior’s banner, and where does Christ’s meekness challenge the way you fight for what matters to you?

The bride must “forget your people and your father’s house” (v. 10). What old loyalties does following Christ ask you to loosen, and how does the promise that “the king will desire your beauty” change the cost?

The bride is dressed and led in by others (vv. 13–15). How does it free you to know that Christ makes his people beautiful rather than waiting for them to make themselves so?

46.text: To the choirmaster. Of the Sons of Korah. According to Alamoth. A Song. 1God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble.2Therefore we will not fear though the earth give way, though the mountains be moved into the heart of the sea,3though its waters roar and foam, though the mountains tremble at its swelling. Selah4There is a river whose streams make glad the city of God, the holy habitation of the Most High.5God is in the midst of her; she shall not be moved; God will help her when morning dawns.6The nations rage, the kingdoms totter; he utters his voice, the earth melts.7The LORD of hosts is with us; the God of Jacob is our fortress. Selah8Come, behold the works of the LORD, how he has brought desolations on the earth.9He makes wars cease to the end of the earth; he breaks the bow and shatters the spear; he burns the chariots with fire.10"Be still, and know that I am God. I will be exalted among the nations, I will be exalted in the earth!"11The LORD of hosts is with us; the God of Jacob is our fortress. Selah

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — Though the Earth Give Way
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Because God himself is present with his people, nothing in creation or history can finally shake them. The psalm begins with the worst imaginable, the earth giving way and the mountains toppling into a roaring sea, and answers it before describing it: God is refuge, strength and help already on hand (vv. 1–3). Then the scene moves to the city, which has no great river yet is gladdened by God’s own provision; with God in her midst she cannot be moved, and he helps her at daybreak (vv. 4–5). The nations rage, but one word from him melts the earth (v. 6). The refrain gathers it up: the LORD of hosts is with us (v. 7).
verseByVerse.theology: The psalm names the end of the world in its second verse, and then mentions a quiet river.

verseByVerse.quote: God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble. Therefore we will not fear though the earth give way, though the mountains be moved into the heart of the sea, though its waters roar and foam, though the mountains tremble at its swelling. Selah
verseByVerse.commentary:
God himself is his people’s safety and is already with them in trouble, so they need not fear even if the whole created world collapses.

God is our refuge and strength. Verse 1 gives three words for God: refuge, strength, help. The third does the work. A very present help means help already on site: not summoned, not dispatched, not on its way. When trouble arrives, the help is already there.

Though the earth give way. Most comfort begins small and works up. This psalm begins with the worst. If the ground itself failed, if the mountains, the standing symbol of permanence, slid into the sea and the sea went wild, we would still not be afraid. It is the end of the world in two verses, and the answer is already in verse 1. That is the right order for a frightened person: you do not calm someone by telling them the worst will not happen, but by telling them who is with them if it does.

The end of the world, every morning. Every generation has had its fears, but ours receives them hourly: the phone brings a fresh way for the world to end with breakfast. Some dangers are real and call for wise action. But some people look away and keep shopping, and others sink into a low, permanent dread. Both assume that if the world is going to be held together, we will have to hold it, and that is a weight no generation can carry. The psalm does not deny the catastrophe; it simply refuses to let the catastrophe have the last word, because God is “in the midst of her” (v. 5). The New Testament goes further. The worst thing that could happen to the world has already happened once: its Maker was put to death. And on the third day he came out of the grave, the first piece of a new creation. So Jesus could tell frightened friends, “In the world you will have tribulation. But take heart; I have overcome the world” (John 16:33).

Uncertain wording. “A very present help” renders a compressed phrase, literally something like “a help in troubles, found exceedingly”, and the ESV notes that it may be rendered “well proved”: God has been found, again and again, to be the help his people need. Either way the help is real and near. The title’s “according to Alamoth” is also uncertain; the word means “young women”, and may point to high voices or instruments (compare 1 Chronicles 15:20).
verseByVerse.note: The basis of Luther’s hymn “A Mighty Fortress Is Our God.”

verseByVerse.quote: There is a river whose streams make glad the city of God, the holy habitation of the Most High. God is in the midst of her; she shall not be moved; God will help her when morning dawns. The nations rage, the kingdoms totter; he utters his voice, the earth melts. The LORD of hosts is with us; the God of Jacob is our fortress. Selah
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s presence is his city’s quiet, unfailing supply and its unbreakable defence: however the nations rage, one word from him settles it, for the LORD of hosts is with us.

There is a river. After the roaring sea, a river; yet Jerusalem had no river. The great cities of the ancient world sat on one: Babylon on the Euphrates, Thebes on the Nile, Nineveh on the Tigris. The city of God had a spring, the Gihon, whose water Hezekiah brought inside the walls by a tunnel (2 Chronicles 32:30). So the river here is a picture of God’s own provision, not a real stream.

Whose streams make glad. Set it against verse 3: the sea roars and shakes the mountains; these streams make glad. Isaiah drew the same contrast in the same crisis: Judah had refused “the waters of Shiloah that flow gently” and would face “the waters of the River, mighty and many, the king of Assyria and all his glory” (Isaiah 8:6–7). The world’s power is loud and destructive; God’s provision is quiet, gladdening and unfailing. Ezekiel saw the river flowing from the temple (Ezekiel 47:1–12); John saw it at the end, “bright as crystal, flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb” (Revelation 22:1); and Jesus promised rivers of living water to whoever believes in him (John 7:38).

God is in the midst of her. The mountains were “moved” in verse 2 and the city is “not moved” in verse 5: the same word, and the difference is the clause between: “God is in the midst of her.” Her safety is not in her walls.

When morning dawns. The help comes at daybreak, which means there was a night. Once in Jerusalem’s history the Assyrian army camped outside her walls, and in the morning the city woke to find them dead (2 Kings 19:35). Many think this psalm was first sung after that night, about 701 BC, though it does not say so. God’s people are not spared the night; they are met at the end of it.

He utters his voice, the earth melts. The nations rage as in Psalm 2, and God simply speaks; he does not raise an army. What the roaring waters of verse 3 could not do to the city, God’s voice does to the world.

The LORD of hosts is with us. Then the refrain, the whole psalm in one line. LORD of hosts means LORD of armies; “the God of Jacob” is the God who bound himself to a schemer and kept his word. In the same Assyrian crisis Isaiah told Judah that the flood would not have the last word, “for God is with us” (Isaiah 8:10), and named the land Immanuel (Isaiah 8:8). Matthew gives that name to Jesus (Matthew 1:23): the presence the psalm sings came and lived among us.
verseByVerse.note: Jerusalem had no great river; this one is God’s own provision.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–11 — Be Still, and Know That I Am God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God will end war on his own terms, and the whole earth will know that he is God. The psalm invites us to come and look at a battlefield after he has finished with it: desolation for his enemies, their bows and spears broken and their chariots burned (vv. 8–9). Then God himself speaks, ordering the raging nations to stop, let go and acknowledge him, for he will be exalted among them all (v. 10). His people overhear that command and find rest in it, and the refrain closes the psalm on the one fixed point that remains: the LORD of hosts is with us (v. 11).
verseByVerse.theology: The famous command is spoken to the armies, not to the anxious: stop fighting and look at who this is.

verseByVerse.quote: Come, behold the works of the LORD, how he has brought desolations on the earth. He makes wars cease to the end of the earth; he breaks the bow and shatters the spear; he burns the chariots with fire. "Be still, and know that I am God. I will be exalted among the nations, I will be exalted in the earth!" The LORD of hosts is with us; the God of Jacob is our fortress. Selah
verseByVerse.commentary:
God will end war by disarming his enemies, and he commands the raging nations to stop and acknowledge him; his people, overhearing, can let go and rest in his presence.

He breaks the bow and shatters the spear. We are invited to look at a battlefield after God has finished with it. What has been destroyed is not armies but weapons: bows snapped, spears shattered, chariots burning. God’s way of ending war is to ruin the equipment.

Be still, and know that I am God. This verse is usually quoted to an anxious Christian over a cup of tea. But it comes amid smashed weapons and raging nations, and God is speaking to them. It is not first “calm down”; it is closer to “stop, drop it, and look at who I am”. The word means to let go, to cease striving.

I will be exalted among the nations. The reason God gives is not peace for its own sake: “I will be exalted among the nations, I will be exalted in the earth!” That is the settled end of history, stated in the future tense with no conditions attached.

The God of Jacob is our fortress. The refrain a second time, and it is where the psalm leaves us. Not “the earth is stable”: it may give way. Not “the nations are calm”: they are raging. The one fixed point is a presence: he is with us, and our fortress is not a wall but God himself.

The comfort still stands. Hearing verse 10 as a command to the nations grounds its comfort. The believer overhears God telling the nations to stand down, and stands down himself: the God who can silence the armies of the earth can handle what is on his mind at 2 a.m. And the disciples once heard this voice at close quarters. On a sea that was swamping their boat, Jesus “rebuked the wind” and said to the sea, “Peace! Be still!” “And the wind ceased, and there was a great calm” (Mark 4:39). The God who silences the nations came and sat in the boat with his people, so our stillness rests on his word and presence, not on our effort to calm ourselves.

What this looks like. Being still is not emptying the mind; it is loosening the grip. Stop. When the worry starts its loop over the scan result, the redundancy letter, the grown child who will not answer the phone, put down the phone and the planning for a few minutes. Let go. Name to God the thing you have been trying to control, and say aloud that it is his. Know. Fill the space with something true about him: read this psalm slowly and say its refrain. Then pick up the next duty. Stillness is not idleness; it is going back to work without the grip.

What it does not mean. It is not a promise that calm will always be felt, nor a rebuke to the believer whose anxiety will not lift. Persistent anxiety is worth bringing to a wise biblical counsellor and to a doctor, and treatment is no failure of faith.

46.title: A Very Present Help in Trouble
46.overview:
Where we are. After the royal wedding of Psalm 45, Psalms 46 to 48 form a small group of songs about God as King in Zion, his city. Psalm 46 comes first and is the best loved of them: Martin Luther built “A Mighty Fortress Is Our God” on it.

The message. God himself is his people’s safety, and he is already with them, so they need not fear even if the created world collapses or the nations rage. He will end every war on his own terms, and the whole earth will be made to stop and know that he is God. The refrain says it all: “The LORD of hosts is with us.”

Why it was said. The psalm names no event, but its picture of nations raging against the city and God rescuing it at daybreak fits Jerusalem’s deliverance from the Assyrian army in 701 BC (2 Kings 19:35), and many link it there. It gave a small, threatened people a confidence that rested not on walls or armies but on God in their midst (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. Three stanzas, the last two closed by the same refrain. Creation in chaos (vv. 1–3): though the earth give way and the sea roars, God is a help already present. The city under siege (vv. 4–7): God’s quiet river gladdens his city; the nations rage, but he speaks and the earth melts, for the LORD of hosts is with us. The war ended (vv. 8–11): come and see the battlefield where he has broken the weapons, and hear him command the nations, “Be still, and know that I am God,” before the refrain sounds again.

Where it leads. Not by direct prophecy but by the character of God, fully revealed in Christ. “The LORD of hosts is with us” is the promise Isaiah gave the same threatened city under the name Immanuel (Isaiah 8:8–10), and Matthew gives that name to Jesus, “God with us” (Matthew 1:23), who promises his people, “I am with you always” (Matthew 28:20). The river reappears in his offer of living water (John 7:38) and flows at last “from the throne of God and of the Lamb” (Revelation 22:1). And the voice that silences the nations spoke on a stormy lake: “Peace! Be still!” (Mark 4:39).

For us. Fear says the worst might happen; this psalm says that even if it does, God is with you. So be still: stop grasping for control and look at who he is, the God who in Christ has already overcome the world. Then go back to the day’s duties with your grip loosened.
46.theology:
The psalm names the worst case first and answers it with a presence: help that is already there (vv. 1-3). God's provision for his city is quiet and gladdening where the world's power is loud (vv. 3-4; cf. Ezek 47; John 7:38), and help comes in the morning, so the night is not skipped (v. 5).

Be still (v. 10) is first a command to the raging nations, and the believer's calm rests on it. The refrain (vv. 7, 11) puts all the security in one fact: the LORD of hosts is with us.
46.examples: Most comfort starts small and works up; this psalm starts with the end of the world and has already answered it in the first verse. A city with no river is given one anyway, and its streams gladden where the sea only roars. God ends wars by ruining the equipment. And the famous Be still, spoken to armies, is overheard by the anxious believer, who finds that it holds for him too.

keyVerse.quote: God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble.
keyVerse.note: The whole psalm unfolds this opening line. It answers the worst before the worst is even described, and it puts all our safety in a person rather than in circumstances: God himself, already present. The refrain (vv. 7, 11) and the command to be still (v. 10) are this verse sung again.

46.reflection:
The psalm imagines the worst first, the earth giving way and the mountains falling into the sea (vv. 2–3), and has already answered it. What “worst case” do you most often rehearse, and how does verse 1 speak to it?

Jerusalem had no great river, yet “there is a river whose streams make glad the city of God” (v. 4). Where have you seen God’s quiet provision sustain you or your church when the world’s power was loud?

“Be still, and know that I am God” (v. 10) is first spoken to raging nations. How does it change the verse to hear it that way, and what would it look like this week to stop, let go and know?

“The LORD of hosts is with us” (vv. 7, 11). How does Jesus, Immanuel, make that refrain more certain and more personal for a Christian than it was even for the first singers?

47.text: To the choirmaster. A Psalm of the Sons of Korah. 1Clap your hands, all peoples! Shout to God with loud songs of joy!2For the LORD, the Most High, is to be feared, a great king over all the earth.3He subdued peoples under us, and nations under our feet.4He chose our heritage for us, the pride of Jacob whom he loves. Selah5God has gone up with a shout, the LORD with the sound of a trumpet.6Sing praises to God, sing praises! Sing praises to our King, sing praises!7For God is the King of all the earth; sing praises with a psalm!8God reigns over the nations; God sits on his holy throne.9The princes of the peoples gather as the people of the God of Abraham. For the shields of the earth belong to God; he is highly exalted!

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — Clap Your Hands, All Peoples
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The God of Israel is King of all the earth, so every people is called to praise him. The psalm opens with a command to the whole world: clap your hands and shout to God with joy (v. 1). The reason is who he is: the Most High, to be feared, a great King over all the earth (v. 2). He showed it in Israel’s history, subduing peoples under them and choosing their inheritance, the land that was the pride of Jacob, because he loves them (vv. 3–4). Strangely, the nations are told to rejoice in the victories of a God who defeated them, and the end of the psalm will show why.
verseByVerse.theology: The command to worship is addressed to every nation, and the reason given is that God is king of all of them.

verseByVerse.quote: Clap your hands, all peoples! Shout to God with loud songs of joy! For the LORD, the Most High, is to be feared, a great king over all the earth. He subdued peoples under us, and nations under our feet. He chose our heritage for us, the pride of Jacob whom he loves. Selah
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every people is commanded to celebrate the LORD with joy and awe, for he is King of all the earth, who gave his people victory and land because he loves them.

Clap your hands, all peoples! Not “Israel, clap” but “all peoples”: the psalm is missionary from its first line, and it commands the nations rather than inviting them, which only makes sense if the LORD is “a great king over all the earth”, not a small country’s local deity.

Shout to God with loud songs of joy! Worship in the Psalter is often noisy, and in the same breath God is “to be feared”. Loud joy and awe are not alternatives.

He subdued peoples under us. An odd reason for the nations to rejoice: God gave Israel victories over them. Yet by verse 9 they are standing in the assembly as family. The conquest is not the end of the story.

He chose our heritage for us. Even the land was his gift, not their choice, and the one thing said about Jacob is that God “loves” him (compare Deuteronomy 7:7–8).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–9 — Sing Praises with a Psalm
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God has taken his throne over the nations, so sing his praise with joy and understanding, for his people now include the nations. God has gone up with shouting and the sound of the horn, like a king carried to his throne (v. 5). Five times the singers are told to sing praises to their King, and to do it with skill and understanding (vv. 6–7), because he reigns over the nations now, seated on his holy throne (v. 8). The psalm ends with its goal: the princes of the peoples gathered as the people of the God of Abraham, every defence of the earth belonging to him (v. 9).
verseByVerse.theology: God goes up with a shout, and the last verse has foreign rulers counted as Abraham's family.

verseByVerse.quote: God has gone up with a shout, the LORD with the sound of a trumpet. Sing praises to God, sing praises! Sing praises to our King, sing praises! For God is the King of all the earth; sing praises with a psalm! God reigns over the nations; God sits on his holy throne.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God has gone up to his throne with shouting, so sing his praise again and again, with understanding, for he reigns over the nations now.

God has gone up with a shout. The picture is most likely the ark, the gold-covered chest that marked God’s throne among his people, carried up to Zion: “David and all the house of Israel brought up the ark of the LORD with shouting and with the sound of the horn” (2 Samuel 6:15). The shout and the horn were also how Israel acclaimed a new king (1 Kings 1:39–40; 2 Kings 9:13), so the scene is an enthronement: the God who is “a great king over all the earth” (v. 2) taking his seat.

Sing praises to God, sing praises! Five times in two verses: the psalm has one idea and cannot leave it alone, which is what happens to people who are actually glad. And “with a psalm” (v. 7) keeps the noise from being empty.

God reigns over the nations. “Reigns” is present tense: not “will reign” but reigns, now, over nations that do not know it and would not agree.

A cloud took him out of their sight. The church has long read this psalm on Ascension Day, and the instinct is right, though it is a pattern, not a quotation. Jesus went up with his disciples watching, “and a cloud took him out of their sight” (Acts 1:9), and Paul applies another psalm of going up to him (Ephesians 4:8, from 68:18). The ark carried to its throne rehearses the greater going-up, when Christ sat down at God’s right hand (Hebrews 1:3), and the trumpet will sound again when he returns (1 Thessalonians 4:16).

Uncertain wording. “With a psalm” (v. 7) translates maskil (ESV note), a word found in some psalm titles (32; 45) whose exact meaning is unknown. Its root means insight or skill, so it probably means a skilful or thoughtful song: praise understood as well as loud.
verseByVerse.note: “A psalm” in v. 7 translates maskil (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: The princes of the peoples gather as the people of the God of Abraham. For the shields of the earth belong to God; he is highly exalted!
verseByVerse.commentary:
The psalm ends with its goal: the rulers of conquered nations gathered not as captives but as Abraham’s family, every power on earth belonging to God.

The princes of the peoples gather. The last verse is the biggest thing in the psalm. The princes of the very peoples subdued in verse 3 are counted not as prisoners but “as the people of the God of Abraham”.

The promise to Abraham. That promise goes back to the beginning: God told Abraham that “in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed” (Genesis 12:3), which Paul calls the gospel preached beforehand (Galatians 3:8): Abraham was to be “the father of all who believe without being circumcised” (Romans 4:11). Here is the whole mission to the Gentiles, the non-Jewish nations, in one line.

The shields of the earth belong to God. “Shields” names the rulers themselves, the protectors of their nations, as in “our shield belongs to the LORD, our king to the Holy One of Israel” (Psalm 89:18). Every defence the world has is God’s.

He is highly exalted! The psalm that ordered the nations to clap ends with their leaders inside the congregation, and Paul says it of Jesus: “God has highly exalted him” (Philippians 2:9). Every Gentile Christian is standing in verse 9, and every prayer for the nations asks that it be filled up.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew has no word for “as”; the ESV rightly supplies it, since the princes now belong to Abraham’s people. The ancient Greek translation read the same letters as “with the God of Abraham”. Either way, the rulers are gathered in to Abraham’s God.

47.title: God Has Gone Up with a Shout
47.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 47 stands between two psalms about God’s city: Psalm 46, where God silences the raging nations, and Psalm 48, where the kings who attack Zion flee. Here the nations are not silenced but summoned, to clap and shout for their King.

The message. The LORD is not a local god but the great King of all the earth, and he has taken his throne. So every people on earth is called to praise him with joy and understanding, and the psalm ends with the rulers of the nations gathered in as members of Abraham’s family.

Why it was said. The psalm names no occasion. It may have been sung when the ark was carried up to Zion, or at a festival celebrating the LORD’s kingship, or after a victory; some link it with the day of 2 Chronicles 20, when the Korahite singers praised God “with a very loud voice” (2 Chronicles 20:19). Whatever the setting, it taught a small nation that its God ruled the empires around it (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. Two stanzas, each a call to praise followed by its reason. Clap and shout, all peoples, for the LORD is a great King over all the earth, who gave his people victory and their inheritance because he loves them (vv. 1–4). God has gone up with a shout; so sing praises again and again, with understanding, to the King who reigns over the nations from his holy throne (vv. 5–8). The last verse is the goal: the princes of the peoples gathered as the people of the God of Abraham, their shields handed over to him (v. 9).

Where it leads. By pattern and by promise. The New Testament does not quote this psalm, but the church has long read it on Ascension Day, and rightly: the King going up with a shout to his throne is a small picture of Jesus ascending to the right hand of God (Acts 1:9; Hebrews 1:3). And verse 9 is God’s promise to Abraham coming true, the promise Paul calls the gospel preached beforehand: “In you shall all the nations be blessed” (Galatians 3:8). Every Gentile believer is standing in that verse.

For us. The King of all the earth is our King, and he reigns now. Praise him loudly and thoughtfully, bow to him with joy, and pray and work for the gathering of the nations, since the psalm’s last verse is still being fulfilled wherever the gospel goes.
47.theology:
The psalm is missionary from its first line, commanding every nation to worship because God is king of all of them (vv. 1-2). The church has long heard the going up of verse 5 as a picture of Christ's ascension.

Its last verse is the promise to Abraham coming true: rulers of the nations counted among God's people, their defences handed over to him (v. 9).
47.examples: Picture a herald in a foreign capital ordering the crowd to cheer for a king whose armies have just beaten them, and then picture those same people welcomed into the king's household. That is the movement of this psalm. Clapping and holy fear belong together, and loud praise is meant to be sung with understanding, the mind as engaged as the voice.

keyVerse.quote: The princes of the peoples gather as the people of the God of Abraham. For the shields of the earth belong to God; he is highly exalted!
keyVerse.note: The psalm’s call to all peoples (v. 1) reaches its goal here. The rulers of nations once subdued are gathered not as captives but as family, members of Abraham’s people, as God promised that in Abraham all the families of the earth would be blessed (Genesis 12:3). It is the mission to the nations in a single verse, and it is fulfilled in Christ.

47.reflection:
The psalm commands “all peoples” to clap and shout to God (v. 1). What does it say about God that he can command, and not merely invite, the whole world to worship him?

Loud joy and holy fear stand side by side (vv. 1–2), and praise is to be sung “with a psalm”, that is, with understanding (v. 7). Which of these is weakest in your own worship, and how could you grow in it?

The church has long heard verse 5 as a picture of Christ’s ascension. What difference does it make to you today that Jesus has gone up and is reigning now?

Verse 9 shows the rulers of the nations gathered as Abraham’s people. How does this verse shape the way you pray for people of other nations and backgrounds, near you and far away?

48.text: A Song. A Psalm of the Sons of Korah. 1Great is the LORD and greatly to be praised in the city of our God! His holy mountain,2beautiful in elevation, is the joy of all the earth, Mount Zion, in the far north, the city of the great King.3Within her citadels God has made himself known as a fortress.4For behold, the kings assembled; they came on together.5As soon as they saw it, they were astounded; they were in panic; they took to flight.6Trembling took hold of them there, anguish as of a woman in labor.7By the east wind you shattered the ships of Tarshish.8As we have heard, so have we seen in the city of the LORD of hosts, in the city of our God, which God will establish forever. Selah9We have thought on your steadfast love, O God, in the midst of your temple.10As your name, O God, so your praise reaches to the ends of the earth. Your right hand is filled with righteousness.11Let Mount Zion be glad! Let the daughters of Judah rejoice because of your judgments!12Walk about Zion, go around her, number her towers,13consider well her ramparts, go through her citadels, that you may tell the next generation14that this is God, our God forever and ever. He will guide us forever.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — The Kings Assembled, and Fled
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God himself is the glory and the defence of his city, and kings who come against it flee without a fight. The LORD is great in Zion, a low ridge the psalm crowns with the titles the nations gave the mountain of their gods, because God lives there and has shown himself its fortress (vv. 1–3). The kings assemble and advance, and the moment they see the city they panic and run, gripped like a woman in labour, shattered like ships in a storm (vv. 4–7). Israel lifts no weapon. So the people confess that what they had heard from their fathers they have now seen, in the city God will establish for ever (v. 8).
verseByVerse.theology: An army arrives, looks and runs, and no battle is described at all.

verseByVerse.quote: Great is the LORD and greatly to be praised in the city of our God! His holy mountain, beautiful in elevation, is the joy of all the earth, Mount Zion, in the far north, the city of the great King. Within her citadels God has made himself known as a fortress.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD is great in his city: he has made a low hill the true mountain of God and the joy of the earth, because he lives there as its fortress.

Beautiful in elevation. Two things in verse 2 would puzzle a geographer. Zion is a modest ridge, overlooked by the Mount of Olives; and it is not “in the far north” but in the south of the country. The poet is borrowing. The nations around Israel spoke of a great mountain in the far north, Zaphon, where the gods held court, and this psalm pins that language on a low hill in Judah. The real mountain of God is the one he chose, and Isaiah promised it would be “established as the highest of the mountains” (Isaiah 2:2). Paul says the same about people: “God chose what is low and despised in the world” (1 Corinthians 1:28).

The joy of all the earth. An extravagant claim, remembered when it seemed to collapse: after Jerusalem fell, passers-by jeered, “Is this the city that was called the perfection of beauty, the joy of all the earth?” (Lamentations 2:15). Jesus called it “the city of the great King” (Matthew 5:35), and he is that King. Hebrews tells Christians that they “have come to Mount Zion” (Hebrews 12:22), where the psalm’s language finally fits.

God has made himself known as a fortress. Not the walls but God, inside them, is the city’s defence.
verseByVerse.note: Zaphon was the sacred mountain of Canaanite myth in the far north; the psalm claims that title for Zion.

verseByVerse.quote: For behold, the kings assembled; they came on together. As soon as they saw it, they were astounded; they were in panic; they took to flight. Trembling took hold of them there, anguish as of a woman in labor. By the east wind you shattered the ships of Tarshish. As we have heard, so have we seen in the city of the LORD of hosts, in the city of our God, which God will establish forever. Selah
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hostile kings fled in panic at the sight of God’s city, without a battle, so his people have now seen for themselves what they had heard of God.
