As soon as they saw it, they were astounded. A strange battle report, because there is no battle. The kings gather and advance, and then everything happens to them: astounded, panicked, fled, seized with trembling. No defender is mentioned.

Anguish as of a woman in labor. A deliberately undignified picture for an army: pain that cannot be fought off, arriving in waves. And the great ships of Tarshish are broken by a wind.

In Israel’s history. Israel saw something like this more than once: in Hezekiah’s day Sennacherib’s army went home without taking Jerusalem (2 Kings 19), and Jehoshaphat’s choir went out ahead of the soldiers and found the enemy destroyed (2 Chronicles 20:20–24). The psalm does not say which, if either, it remembers.

As we have heard, so have we seen. Verse 8 answers Psalm 44, which began, “O God, we have heard with our ears, our fathers have told us”, and complained that its singers had seen nothing like it. This generation has seen. Both psalms are true, and a believer will live through both kinds of season. The greatest “seeing” came later: “we have seen his glory” (John 1:14), in the Son who entered the city, was crucified outside it and rose again.

Uncertain wording. Where Tarshish was is not known for certain (many think of southern Spain), and “ships of Tarshish” came to mean any great seagoing ship (compare 1 Kings 10:22). Either way, the mightiest ships of the age are shattered by God’s wind.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: After the rescue God’s people ponder his steadfast love, and then gather the evidence to tell their children who he is. In the temple they think carefully about his covenant love, and they praise the God whose name and fame reach the ends of the earth and whose right hand is full of righteousness (vv. 9–10). Zion and the towns of Judah rejoice in his judgments, his decisions carried out (v. 11). Then they walk the walls, counting the towers and examining the ramparts still standing, so that they may tell the next generation that this is their God for ever, who will guide them for ever (vv. 12–14).
verseByVerse.theology: Count the towers, and then tell the children, not about the towers but about God.

verseByVerse.quote: We have thought on your steadfast love, O God, in the midst of your temple. As your name, O God, so your praise reaches to the ends of the earth. Your right hand is filled with righteousness. Let Mount Zion be glad! Let the daughters of Judah rejoice because of your judgments!
verseByVerse.commentary:
After the rescue the people think deeply in the temple about God’s steadfast love, and praise his righteous judgments, which gladden the whole land.

We have thought on your steadfast love. After the deliverance, they go inside and think: careful, deliberate thought, like the meditating of Psalm 1. Something happened outside the walls; its meaning is worked out inside the temple. That is the right order after any rescue, and most of us skip it.

As your name, O God, so your praise. God’s fame and his praise reach equally far, to the ends of the earth: a rescue in one small city is news for the world.

Let the daughters of Judah rejoice. The towns and villages of Judah celebrate too. God’s judgments, his decisions carried out, are a reason for ordinary people in ordinary towns to be glad.

verseByVerse.quote: Walk about Zion, go around her, number her towers, consider well her ramparts, go through her citadels, that you may tell the next generation that this is God, our God forever and ever. He will guide us forever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The people walk round the rescued city to gather evidence for their children, and what they pass on is not the walls but God himself, their God and guide for ever.

Walk about Zion. Five commands, all physical: walk, go round, count, consider, go through. A tour of the walls the morning after the siege lifted: every tower still standing, not a stone gone.

That you may tell the next generation. The point of the whole psalm. The survey is not nostalgia or civic pride but evidence-gathering for children who will need to know that this happened, on a day their parents saw.

This is God, our God forever and ever. Look at what they are to report: not “these are our towers”, but God. The towers are the visual aid; God is the message. Which is just as well, because in about 586 BC every one of those towers came down, and the psalm was still true: it had always been about the one inside the walls, not the walls.

He will guide us forever. A promise no survey of masonry can give. It reaches past the generation doing the counting, and past their city, to the Zion that is above (Hebrews 12:22) and the city “coming down out of heaven from God” (Revelation 21:2), whose walls will never need surveying again.

Uncertain wording. “Forever” (v. 14) renders a difficult phrase. The ESV notes the reading “beyond death”; the Hebrew is literally “over death” (King James Version, even unto death). Some think the words are a musical note belonging to the next psalm’s title (compare Psalm 9, “according to Muth-labben”). Either way, the God who guides his people does not let go of them at the grave.

48.title: Walk About Zion
48.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 48 closes the group of Korahite songs about God as King in his city (46–48). Psalm 46 sang of God’s help in the city when the nations raged; Psalm 47 called the nations to praise; now the singers walk the walls of Zion after a deliverance and praise the God who lives there.

The message. The glory of God’s city is God himself. Kings came against it and fled without a battle, so his people have seen with their own eyes what they had only heard, and they ponder his steadfast love and tell their children. The towers are only the visual aid; the message is “this is God, our God forever and ever.”

Why it was said. The psalm names no event. It may remember Jehoshaphat’s day, when the Korahite singers praised God and the invading kings destroyed one another (2 Chronicles 20:19–24), or Sennacherib’s army leaving Jerusalem untaken in 701 BC (2 Kings 19). Either way, its singers had seen the old stories of God’s rescue come true in their own day (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. Outside the walls (vv. 1–8): the LORD is great in his city, a low ridge given the titles of the mountain of the gods, where he is known as a fortress (vv. 1–3); kings assembled, saw, panicked and fled, broken like ships in an east wind (vv. 4–7); and what we heard, we have now seen (v. 8). Inside the walls (vv. 9–14): the people think on God’s steadfast love in the temple and rejoice in his judgments (vv. 9–11), then walk round the city, counting its towers, so that they may tell the next generation that this is their God for ever, who will guide them (vv. 12–14).

Where it leads. By pattern, and the New Testament draws it out. Jesus called Jerusalem “the city of the great King” (Matthew 5:35), and he is that King. He called his own body the temple where God dwells (John 2:19–21), and Hebrews tells believers, “you have come to Mount Zion and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem” (Hebrews 12:22). The earthly towers fell in about 586 BC, but the promise that God “will establish forever” his city (v. 8) is kept in the church gathered to Christ now and in the new Jerusalem to come (Revelation 21:2).

For us. When God rescues you, do not hurry past it: think on his steadfast love, and then tell your children and anyone younger in the faith what he has done. And keep the message on God, not on the walls; buildings, churches and institutions fall, but he will guide his people for ever.
48.theology:
The psalm gives a modest ridge the language the nations used for the mountain of their gods, because the true mountain of God is the one he chose (v. 2). The deliverance is told without a battle: everything happens to the attackers (vv. 4-7).

After the rescue comes meditation (v. 9), and the tour of the walls gathers testimony for the children whose subject is God, not the towers (vv. 12-14). Those towers fell in about 586 BC, and the last line held.
48.examples: Think of a family walking round their town the morning after a storm, counting the houses still standing, so that the children will remember who kept them: that is the tour of verses 12-13. Many believers know both the decade of Psalm 44, when the old stories seem not to come true, and the decade of this psalm, when they see for themselves what they had only heard.

keyVerse.quote: that this is God, our God forever and ever. He will guide us forever.
keyVerse.note: The whole tour of Zion ends here. The walls and towers were only the evidence; what the children are to be told is not “this is our city” but “this is our God”. When the towers later fell, this line still stood, because it had always been about the God inside the walls.

48.reflection:
Zion was a modest ridge, yet the psalm calls it “the joy of all the earth” (v. 2), because God chose it and lived there. What does this say about the places and people God chooses, including you and your church?

“As we have heard, so have we seen” (v. 8). Can you name a time when you saw for yourself what you had only heard about God? If you are in a season more like Psalm 44, what helps you keep trusting?

After the rescue the people “thought on your steadfast love” in the temple (v. 9). What would it look like for you to stop and reflect on God’s love after he has helped you, instead of moving straight on?

The tour of the walls was so that they could “tell the next generation” (v. 13). Who in the next generation could you tell about God, and what would you tell them?

49.text: To the choirmaster. A Psalm of the Sons of Korah. 1Hear this, all peoples! Give ear, all inhabitants of the world,2both low and high, rich and poor together!3My mouth shall speak wisdom; the meditation of my heart shall be understanding.4I will incline my ear to a proverb; I will solve my riddle to the music of the lyre.5Why should I fear in times of trouble, when the iniquity of those who cheat me surrounds me,6those who trust in their wealth and boast of the abundance of their riches?7Truly no man can ransom another, or give to God the price of his life,8for the ransom of their life is costly and can never suffice,9that he should live on forever and never see the pit.10For he sees that even the wise die; the fool and the stupid alike must perish and leave their wealth to others.11Their graves are their homes forever, their dwelling places to all generations, though they called lands by their own names.12Man in his pomp will not remain; he is like the beasts that perish.13This is the path of those who have foolish confidence; yet after them people approve of their boasts. Selah14Like sheep they are appointed for Sheol; death shall be their shepherd, and the upright shall rule over them in the morning. Their form shall be consumed in Sheol, with no place to dwell.15But God will ransom my soul from the power of Sheol, for he will receive me. Selah16Be not afraid when a man becomes rich, when the glory of his house increases.17For when he dies he will carry nothing away; his glory will not go down after him.18For though, while he lives, he counts himself blessed— and though you get praise when you do well for yourself—19his soul will go to the generation of his fathers, who will never again see light.20Man in his pomp yet without understanding is like the beasts that perish.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — The Ransom of Their Life Is Costly
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Death is the great leveller, and no fortune can buy a life back from it. The psalmist summons the whole world, rich and poor together, to hear wisdom he has first listened to himself and now sets to music as a riddle (vv. 1–4). His question is honest: why should he be afraid when dishonest, wealthy men surround him (vv. 5–6)? The first answer is that the one purchase everyone needs is the one no money can make, for no man can ransom another from death (vv. 7–9). The wise and the foolish die alike and leave their wealth behind, and men who named estates after themselves end in the grave (vv. 10–11). The refrain sums it up: man in his pomp will not remain (v. 12).
verseByVerse.theology: Wealth cannot buy the one thing every person needs: a life ransomed from death.

verseByVerse.quote: Hear this, all peoples! Give ear, all inhabitants of the world, both low and high, rich and poor together! My mouth shall speak wisdom; the meditation of my heart shall be understanding. I will incline my ear to a proverb; I will solve my riddle to the music of the lyre. Why should I fear in times of trouble, when the iniquity of those who cheat me surrounds me, those who trust in their wealth and boast of the abundance of their riches?
verseByVerse.commentary:
The whole world, rich and poor alike, is called to learn why the wealthy who wrong us are nothing to fear.

Hear this, all peoples! This psalm of the Sons of Korah is not addressed to God. It is a lecture, and the lecture hall is the world, low and high summoned to the same seat. Death is the one subject on which the classes cannot be separated.

I will incline my ear to a proverb. The poet first takes his place among the learners: he listens before he speaks. Then he calls what follows a riddle, a saying whose meaning stays hidden until it is solved, and he will solve it to music. Some truths are so hard that they have to be sung before they can be borne.

Why should I fear in times of trouble? As in Psalms 37 and 73, dishonest people have money and a believer is losing to them. His question is not why they prosper but why he should fear them, and the answer is not that their fortunes will be reversed. It has to do with their funeral.

Uncertain wording. “Those who cheat me” (v. 5) can also be read “my heels” (older versions: “the iniquity of my heels”). The root is that of the name Jacob, the heel-grabber who cheated Esau (Genesis 27:36). Either way, wrongdoers hem him in.

verseByVerse.quote: Truly no man can ransom another, or give to God the price of his life, for the ransom of their life is costly and can never suffice, that he should live on forever and never see the pit. For he sees that even the wise die; the fool and the stupid alike must perish and leave their wealth to others. Their graves are their homes forever, their dwelling places to all generations, though they called lands by their own names. Man in his pomp will not remain; he is like the beasts that perish.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No money can buy a life back from death: wise and foolish alike die and leave everything behind.

Truly no man can ransom another. The riddle is solved on the rich man’s own ground. A ransom bought a man out of slavery or off a death sentence, and the one purchase everybody needs is the one no fortune can make. It is costly and can never suffice: not rarely, not only for the very rich. Never.

Even the wise die. The wise, the fool and the stupid all die and leave their wealth to others. The detail that stings is that they “called lands by their own names”, and their permanent address turned out to be a grave. Every country has estates and streets named after men nobody can now identify.

Man in his pomp will not remain. Pomp is splendour and display, everything a life looks like from outside. Will not remain is literally “will not lodge overnight”: the grandest man is a guest who does not even stay the night.

The question Jesus asked. Jesus put the same riddle to a crowd: “For what can a man give in return for his soul?” (Mark 8:37). The answer is nothing, which is why the New Testament describes salvation as a purchase made by someone else: “you were ransomed … not with perishable things such as silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ” (1 Peter 1:18–19). Peter names the wealth this psalm says cannot ransom, and then the price that did.

If no man can ransom another, how could Jesus? Because he is not only a man. He who came “to give his life as a ransom for many” (Mark 10:45) is God the Son made man, and his life outweighed all the lives it bought.

The last taboo. Our culture talks about almost everything except death. We move it to the hospital and soften it to “passed”, while some of the richest people alive fund research to reverse ageing. Medicine is a good gift, but money buys a better room to die in, not one day past the appointment. The psalm’s strange kindness is to make us look: facing death does not make life gloomy but honest, and shows what we have really been trusting. And Christ went down into death to “deliver all those who through fear of death were subject to lifelong slavery” (Hebrews 2:15).

Does “like the beasts that perish” mean the wicked simply cease to exist? No. The point is death’s certainty, which takes rich and poor as it takes animals. Verse 15 shows that death is not the end: God redeems the believer from Sheol, and the wicked face judgment (Daniel 12:2).

Textual note. “Their graves are their homes forever” (v. 11) follows some ancient translations; the Hebrew text reads “their inward thought is that their homes are forever” (the words differ by two transposed letters). Either way, the only permanent house was the grave.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–20 — But God Will Ransom My Soul
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Everyone is being led by someone, and the psalm turns on who: death shepherds the self-confident into Sheol, but God will ransom and receive the one who trusts him. The proud are admired after they die, yet death herds them like sheep, and a morning is coming when the upright will rule (vv. 13–14). Then the great “but”: what no man can pay, God will pay (v. 15). So the psalm returns to its opening question and answers it plainly: do not be afraid when a man grows rich, for he carries nothing away and his glory stays at the graveside (vv. 16–19). The refrain closes it with one phrase added: it is splendour without understanding that makes a man like the beasts (v. 20).
verseByVerse.theology: Everyone in the psalm dies; the difference is whether death is their shepherd or God ransoms them.

verseByVerse.quote: This is the path of those who have foolish confidence; yet after them people approve of their boasts. Selah Like sheep they are appointed for Sheol; death shall be their shepherd, and the upright shall rule over them in the morning. Their form shall be consumed in Sheol, with no place to dwell. But God will ransom my soul from the power of Sheol, for he will receive me. Selah
verseByVerse.commentary:
Death herds the self-confident like sheep into the grave, but God will pay the ransom no one else can pay and take the believer to himself.

After them people approve of their boasts. The saddest half-line in the psalm. Once they are dead, the next generation quotes them admiringly, and young men set out to copy a life that has plainly ended in the grave.

Death shall be their shepherd. Psalm 23 turned upside down. There the LORD is my shepherd; here death herds a flock down into Sheol, the realm of the dead. Everyone is being led by someone; the question is by whom.

The upright shall rule over them in the morning. The night of death has a daybreak in it, and those who were losing to the rich all through this psalm are on top when the light comes.

But God will ransom my soul. After insisting that no man can pay the ransom, the psalm says who can: the same word, now with God as the purchaser. The whole poem turns here. Verse 7 never said that God could not pay; it said that no man could.

For he will receive me. The verb is the one used of Enoch, whom God “took” (Genesis 5:24), and Asaph uses it with the same hope: “afterward you will receive me to glory” (Psalm 73:24). Hosea speaks of ransoming from the power of Sheol (Hosea 13:14; the ESV reads it as a question, older versions as a promise), and Paul takes up its next words in his resurrection chapter: “O death, where is your sting?” (1 Corinthians 15:55). Before the resurrection was clearly revealed, this believer says the one thing that makes the psalm bearable.

Where Christians differ. Many scholars read verse 15 as hope only of rescue from an early death. Most of the church’s interpreters hear hope beyond death: God will take the believer out of Sheol’s power to himself.

This commentary’s view. The second reading fits the psalm. Its argument is that everyone dies (v. 10), so a mere postponement would answer nothing; the contrast is between two ends, not two dates. The hope is dim here; Christ “brought life and immortality to light through the gospel” (2 Timothy 1:10).

Uncertain wording. The end of verse 14 is among the hardest lines in the Psalter, and translations differ widely; the sense is that their splendour wastes away in the grave, far from their grand houses. The end of verse 13 is also uncertain: later admirers (ESV), or followers on the same path.

verseByVerse.quote: Be not afraid when a man becomes rich, when the glory of his house increases. For when he dies he will carry nothing away; his glory will not go down after him. For though, while he lives, he counts himself blessed— and though you get praise when you do well for yourself— his soul will go to the generation of his fathers, who will never again see light. Man in his pomp yet without understanding is like the beasts that perish.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not be intimidated by the rich, who take nothing with them; what divides people is whether they understand.

Be not afraid when a man becomes rich. The command is not “do not envy” but “do not be afraid”, which is more honest about what wealth in other hands does to us: it intimidates. The cure is a single fact: he will carry nothing away. As Paul says, “we brought nothing into the world, and we cannot take anything out of the world” (1 Timothy 6:7). The glory stays at the graveside with the mourners.

You get praise when you do well for yourself. A sharp aside. The world congratulates self-interest; that is simply how applause works. Verse 19 sets it beside where the man is going: to those “who will never again see light.”

Yet without understanding. The refrain returns from verse 12 with one change, and everything turns on it; in Hebrew the verbs “remain” and “understand” differ by a single letter (yalin, yabin). The psalm has not attacked wealth. The man like the beasts is the one who lives in splendour and never thinks about its end.

A different dividing line. So the psalm that summoned rich and poor to the same lecture divides them along another line: not what a man owns, but whether he has understood who pays the ransom. Jesus told it as a story, of a farmer planning bigger barns who heard God say, “Fool! This night your soul is required of you”, and he warned against laying up treasure for oneself and not being “rich toward God” (Luke 12:20–21).

49.title: No Man Can Ransom Another
49.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 49 closes the first collection of psalms of the Sons of Korah in Book Two (42–49). After three songs celebrating God as King in Zion (46–48), it turns from the nations to the individual and from the city to the grave. It is a wisdom psalm: a lecture addressed not to God but to the whole world.

The message. Do not be afraid of people who are rich and powerful, because death strips every one of them, and no fortune can buy a single life back from it. The ransom every person needs is one no man can pay, but God himself will pay it for those who trust him, and take them to himself. So the real dividing line among people is not wealth but understanding: knowing who pays the ransom.

Why it was said. A faithful believer was surrounded by dishonest, wealthy people who cheated him and boasted of their riches (vv. 5–6), and he was tempted not merely to envy them but to fear them. Israel’s wise men often wrestled with this (compare Psalms 37 and 73; see the introduction), and this psalm answers it by looking at the end of the story.

How the chapter makes its case. A summons to everyone, rich and poor, to hear a riddle set to music (vv. 1–4), and the question: why fear the wealthy (vv. 5–6)? The first answer: no man can ransom another; wise and fool die alike and leave their wealth, and men who named estates after themselves end in the grave, for man in his pomp does not last (vv. 7–12). The second: death herds the self-confident into Sheol, but God will ransom my soul and receive me (vv. 13–15). So do not fear the rich man, who carries nothing away; and the refrain returns with one telling phrase added, “without understanding” (vv. 16–20).

Where it leads. Chiefly by the need it exposes, and by the hope it voices. The psalm insists that no human price can ransom a life, and then says that God will. The New Testament names the price: the Son of Man came “to give his life as a ransom for many” (Mark 10:45), and believers were ransomed “not with perishable things such as silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ” (1 Peter 1:18–19). And the dim hope of verse 15, to be taken by God out of the grave’s power, became daylight when Christ rose as “the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep” (1 Corinthians 15:20).

For us. Look honestly at death and you will see what you really trust. No savings, success or reputation will go down into the grave with you, but Christ has already paid what you never could. So do not fear the wealthy or envy them; hold money loosely, and rest your life on the one who ransoms.
49.theology:
Death levels every class, and the psalm's centre is a statement about money: the ransom for a life can never suffice (vv. 7-9). The New Testament agrees, and names the price that did suffice, the blood of Christ.

Everyone is shepherded by someone (v. 14), and what no man can do, God does: God will ransom my soul (v. 15). The refrain's one added phrase (v. 20) shows that the danger is not wealth itself but splendour without understanding.
49.examples: Walk through any old town and read the street names: many honour men nobody can now identify, who called lands by their own names. The psalm sets two shepherds side by side, the LORD of Psalm 23 and death leading a flock to Sheol. And it names honestly what other people's wealth does to us: not only envy, but fear.

keyVerse.quote: But God will ransom my soul from the power of Sheol, for he will receive me.
keyVerse.note: This is the riddle’s answer and the turning point of the psalm. After insisting that no man can pay the price of a life (vv. 7–9), the psalmist says who can, and uses the same word with God as the one who pays. The New Testament names the price, the precious blood of Christ, and his resurrection turns this hope into certainty.

49.reflection:
The psalm admits that other people’s wealth can make us afraid, not only envious (vv. 5, 16). Where do you feel small or intimidated beside people with more money, status or power, and how does the fact that “he will carry nothing away” (v. 17) change that?

“No man can ransom another” (v. 7). What do people around you, or you yourself, trust to secure your future? Why is it so hard to talk honestly about death, and what does facing it reveal?

Verse 14 pictures death as a shepherd and Psalm 23 pictures the LORD as one. Who is shepherding your life in practice, and what difference does verse 15 make when read alongside Mark 10:45 and 1 Peter 1:18–19?

The refrain changes from verse 12 to verse 20 by adding “without understanding”. What would it look like for you to be rich toward God (Luke 12:21) in how you earn, spend and give this year?

50.text: A Psalm of Asaph. 1The Mighty One, God the LORD, speaks and summons the earth from the rising of the sun to its setting.2Out of Zion, the perfection of beauty, God shines forth.3Our God comes; he does not keep silence; before him is a devouring fire, around him a mighty tempest.4He calls to the heavens above and to the earth, that he may judge his people:5"Gather to me my faithful ones, who made a covenant with me by sacrifice!"6The heavens declare his righteousness, for God himself is judge! Selah7"Hear, O my people, and I will speak; O Israel, I will testify against you. I am God, your God.8Not for your sacrifices do I rebuke you; your burnt offerings are continually before me.9I will not accept a bull from your house or goats from your folds.10For every beast of the forest is mine, the cattle on a thousand hills.11I know all the birds of the hills, and all that moves in the field is mine.12"If I were hungry, I would not tell you, for the world and its fullness are mine.13Do I eat the flesh of bulls or drink the blood of goats?14Offer to God a sacrifice of thanksgiving, and perform your vows to the Most High,15and call upon me in the day of trouble; I will deliver you, and you shall glorify me."16But to the wicked God says: "What right have you to recite my statutes or take my covenant on your lips?17For you hate discipline, and you cast my words behind you.18If you see a thief, you are pleased with him, and you keep company with adulterers.19"You give your mouth free rein for evil, and your tongue frames deceit.20You sit and speak against your brother; you slander your own mother's son.21These things you have done, and I have been silent; you thought that I was one like yourself. But now I rebuke you and lay the charge before you.22"Mark this, then, you who forget God, lest I tear you apart, and there be none to deliver!23The one who offers thanksgiving as his sacrifice glorifies me; to one who orders his way rightly I will show the salvation of God!"

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Our God Comes; He Does Not Keep Silence
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God is coming to judge, and the people summoned are his own. Three names for God stack up, the Mighty One, God, the LORD, and he calls the whole earth from east to west (v. 1). He shines out of Zion, not keeping silence, with fire before him and storm around him, as at Sinai (vv. 2–3). Heaven and earth are called as witnesses, as Moses called them when the covenant was made (v. 4). Then the shock: the defendants are “my faithful ones, who made a covenant with me by sacrifice” (v. 5). The heavens declare that the judge is righteous, for he is God himself (v. 6).
verseByVerse.theology: The court is convened, the witnesses are the sky and the ground, and the defendants are his own people.

verseByVerse.quote: The Mighty One, God the LORD, speaks and summons the earth from the rising of the sun to its setting. Out of Zion, the perfection of beauty, God shines forth. Our God comes; he does not keep silence; before him is a devouring fire, around him a mighty tempest. He calls to the heavens above and to the earth, that he may judge his people: "Gather to me my faithful ones, who made a covenant with me by sacrifice!" The heavens declare his righteousness, for God himself is judge! Selah
verseByVerse.commentary:
God comes as judge, with heaven and earth as witnesses, and the people he summons to the bar are his own covenant worshippers.

The Mighty One, God the LORD, speaks. This is the first psalm of Asaph, one of David’s chief musicians (1 Chronicles 16:4–5). It opens like a courtroom. The first line stacks three names for God, and a summons goes out to the whole earth, east to west. The ESV notes that verse 3 can be read as a prayer, “May our God come, and not keep silence”, but either way the silence is ending. The fire and tempest recall Sinai, where God first gave the covenant he now enforces.

He calls to the heavens above and to the earth. Heaven and earth are called as witnesses, as Moses called them when the covenant was made (Deuteronomy 32:1). This is a covenant lawsuit: God charges his people with breaking their covenant with him. The shock is who stands accused. Not the nations: “that he may judge his people”, his “faithful ones, who made a covenant with me by sacrifice.” That is how the covenant began at Sinai: it was sealed with burnt offerings, and the blood of the covenant was thrown on the people (Exodus 24:5–8). These are the committed, the churchgoing, the sacrificing. That is who this psalm is for.

For God himself is judge! Judgment begins with the household of God (1 Peter 4:17), and the judge is not one of them but God himself. In Christ the same judge has taken the judgment of his people on himself, so they may hear his charges and live.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–15 — If I Were Hungry, I Would Not Tell You
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God needs nothing from his people; he wants them to need him. He begins by clearing their attendance: their sacrifices are continually before him (vv. 7–8). But he will not take their bulls as if they supplied him, for every animal in forest and field is already his, and he knows each bird by name (vv. 9–11). If he were hungry he would not tell them; he does not eat flesh or drink blood (vv. 12–13). What he asks instead flows the other way: give thanks, keep your vows, and call on him in trouble, so that he may deliver you and you may glorify him (vv. 14–15).
verseByVerse.theology: The offerings were faultless; the belief behind them was that God needed feeding.

verseByVerse.quote: "Hear, O my people, and I will speak; O Israel, I will testify against you. I am God, your God. Not for your sacrifices do I rebuke you; your burnt offerings are continually before me. I will not accept a bull from your house or goats from your folds. For every beast of the forest is mine, the cattle on a thousand hills. I know all the birds of the hills, and all that moves in the field is mine. "If I were hungry, I would not tell you, for the world and its fullness are mine. Do I eat the flesh of bulls or drink the blood of goats?
verseByVerse.commentary:
God has no complaint about their attendance; his complaint is that they treat him as if he needed what they bring, when everything already belongs to him.

Not for your sacrifices do I rebuke you. God first clears away the obvious charge. Their sacrifices are “continually” before him: the rota is kept, the animals arrive, nobody has skipped a feast. Whatever is wrong is wrong underneath a faultless religious practice, which is the most frightening kind of thing to be told.

The cattle on a thousand hills. Here is the problem: they had come to think their sacrifices supplied something God needed. God answers that the animal on the altar was his before they bought it. “The cattle on a thousand hills” has become a proverb, and the line beside it is just as good: “I know all the birds of the hills.” He does not merely own them; he knows them one by one.

Do I eat the flesh of bulls? The sarcasm is deliberate, aimed at a religion the surrounding nations practised in earnest: feeding the gods, who were thought to need it. Paul told Athens the same: God is not “served by human hands, as though he needed anything” (Acts 17:25).

A God who needs nothing. Any religion that treats God as needy (needing our attendance, our money, our defence) has become this psalm’s target, however correct its beliefs. He does not need you, so what he asks of you is never to meet his needs.

Isn’t a God who wants praise rather vain? It is a fair question. We dislike people who need to be told how wonderful they are, and a God who asks to be praised can sound like the worst of them. C. S. Lewis admitted that the Psalms’ calls to praise once troubled him in just this way. What changed his mind, as he explained in Reflections on the Psalms, was noticing that people spontaneously praise what they enjoy: a walk, a book, a game, a face. And, he wrote, “I think we delight to praise what we enjoy because the praise not merely expresses but completes the enjoyment; it is its appointed consummation.” This psalm makes the point from God’s side. He needs nothing, not even our praise. When he calls for thanks, he is not feeding a hunger in himself but inviting us into a joy that stays unfinished until we say it aloud. So the old catechism could say that our chief end is “to glorify God, and to enjoy him for ever”: the two turn out to be one. And the God who needs nothing gave everything, his own Son, so that we would have something worth praising.

verseByVerse.quote: Offer to God a sacrifice of thanksgiving, and perform your vows to the Most High, and call upon me in the day of trouble; I will deliver you, and you shall glorify me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
What God wants is a grateful, dependent people: thanks, kept promises and prayer in trouble, so that he delivers and they glorify him.

Offer to God a sacrifice of thanksgiving. He asks three things instead, and none of them feeds God. The first is thanksgiving (the ESV notes the line may be “Make thanksgiving your sacrifice to God”), which by definition admits that everything came from him. The second, “perform your vows”: keep the promises you made when you were desperate, which most people do not.

Call upon me in the day of trouble. The third is astonishing in a lawsuit. In the middle of testifying against them, God tells them to ask him for help. The worship he wants from his people is that they should need him and say so.

I will deliver you, and you shall glorify me. That is the whole relationship, and the giving runs from him to us. He delivers; we glorify. A man who has been rescued and says so has given God exactly what the bulls could not.

A sacrifice of praise. The animals were never what God was after, and Hebrews says why: the blood of bulls and goats could not take away sins, and God prepared a body for his Son, whose single offering did (Hebrews 10:4–10). Since then the Christian’s offering is the one this psalm asks for: “let us continually offer up a sacrifice of praise to God, that is, the fruit of lips that acknowledge his name” (Hebrews 13:15).

How do I offer thanksgiving? A sacrifice cost something and was brought on purpose, and thanksgiving is meant to be the same, not a passing glow. Be specific. At the end of the day name three things God gave you: the conversation that went better than you feared, the bill that could be paid, the friend who noticed. Come back after the answer. Most of us ask loudly in trouble and forget to thank; of ten lepers healed, only one turned back to give thanks (Luke 17:15–18). Keep your vows. If you promised God something when you were desperate, do it now that the crisis has passed. Say it where others can hear. Tell your household or your church what God has done; that is how he is glorified (v. 15). And give thanks in the hard seasons too, for what does not change: “give thanks in all circumstances; for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus for you” (1 Thessalonians 5:18). At the bottom of every list is the gift that covers all the rest: “Thanks be to God for his inexpressible gift!” (2 Corinthians 9:15).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–23 — You Thought That I Was One Like Yourself
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s patience is not his approval, and those who recite his word while living against it will be called to account. The second charge falls on people who quote the statutes yet throw his words over their shoulder, enjoy thieves and adulterers, and use their tongues to slander their own brother (vv. 16–20). Because God was silent, they assumed he was like them (v. 21). Now he speaks: a warning given before the blow falls, to those who forget God (v. 22). And the trial ends in promise: the one who offers thanksgiving glorifies God, and the one who orders his way will see the salvation of God (v. 23).
verseByVerse.theology: They had taken God's silence for agreement, and now he corrects them.

verseByVerse.quote: But to the wicked God says: "What right have you to recite my statutes or take my covenant on your lips? For you hate discipline, and you cast my words behind you. If you see a thief, you are pleased with him, and you keep company with adulterers. "You give your mouth free rein for evil, and your tongue frames deceit. You sit and speak against your brother; you slander your own mother's son. These things you have done, and I have been silent; you thought that I was one like yourself. But now I rebuke you and lay the charge before you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those who recite God’s word while stealing, sleeping around and slandering their own brother have mistaken his silence for agreement; now he speaks.

What right have you to recite my statutes? The second charge is against people who can quote Scripture. They “recite my statutes”, knowing the texts and saying the words in the service, and they “cast my words behind” them: the gesture of tossing something over your shoulder to get it out of sight while walking on.

You sit and speak against your brother. The list runs from theft and adultery to false witness (the eighth, seventh and ninth commandments), and it ends closest to home. “You sit”, comfortably and at length, and take apart your own brother. The psalm has moved from the cattle on a thousand hills to a man being unpleasant about his family at a dinner table, and treats the second as the more serious evidence. Paul presses the same charge on the teacher of the law: “While you preach against stealing, do you steal?” (Romans 2:21).

I have been silent. Here is the sentence the whole psalm has been building to. God’s silence had been read as agreement. Because nothing happened, they concluded that nothing was wrong: that God shared their standards, kept the same company, found the same jokes funny. “You thought that I was one like yourself.”

Patience is not approval. It is one of the commonest errors about God, committed not by atheists but by people in the congregation with the statutes on their lips. God’s patience is meant to lead us to repentance (Romans 2:4), and one day he says so.

verseByVerse.quote: "Mark this, then, you who forget God, lest I tear you apart, and there be none to deliver! The one who offers thanksgiving as his sacrifice glorifies me; to one who orders his way rightly I will show the salvation of God!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The trial ends with a warning given in time and a promise: the thankful, who put their lives in order, will see God’s salvation.

You who forget God. The warning is violent, and it is a mercy: it is given before anything happens. “You who forget God” is the psalm’s final description of them: not deniers but forgetters. And the last words of verse 22, “none to deliver”, remove the assumption everyone in this psalm has been living on, that there will always be a way out.

To one who orders his way rightly. The psalm ends by restating its case positively. Thanksgiving, again, is what glorifies God; and the one who orders his way, putting his daily conduct in order and not only his worship, is promised a sight of “the salvation of God.”

How the trial ends. The defendants are not told to bring more animals or try harder at the festivals. They are told to be grateful, keep their word, call for help and mend their behaviour, as people he has already called “my people” (v. 7). And the God who needs nothing from them has salvation to show them. None of us orders his way perfectly; Christ did, in our place, and his obedience is counted as ours (Romans 5:19). So the one who has failed comes back the way verse 15 says, by calling on God, and the Spirit God gives is the power to walk in his ways (Ezekiel 36:27).

Does salvation depend on right conduct? The psalm began with grace: “call upon me in the day of trouble; I will deliver you” (v. 15). Ordering one’s way rightly is the fruit and evidence of belonging to God, not the price of it (Ephesians 2:8–10).

Uncertain wording. “Orders his way rightly” renders a compressed phrase, literally “sets a way”. It may mean one who prepares or keeps to the right road, and some scholars suggest a one-letter change giving “blameless in his way”. Either way the contrast is with the forgetters of verse 22: one who lives in step with the God he thanks.

50.title: The Cattle on a Thousand Hills
50.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 50 follows the Korahite psalms of Book Two and is the first psalm of Asaph, the only one outside Book Three (73–83). Psalm 49 called the whole world to hear wisdom about death; Psalm 50 calls heaven and earth to witness a trial, and Psalm 51, David’s great confession, follows as if in answer to it.

The message. God comes to judge, and the people in the dock are not the pagan nations but his own worshippers. He has no complaint about their attendance; his complaint is that they treat him as if he needed their offerings, and that they recite his word while living against it. What he wants is a grateful, dependent people who call on him in trouble, keep their promises and live as he speaks: “I will deliver you, and you shall glorify me.”

Why it was said. Israel’s worship was busy and correct: sacrifices arrived “continually” (v. 8). But it was easy to slide into the thinking of the surrounding nations, who fed their gods, and to take God’s patience for approval (v. 21). The prophets brought the same charge again and again (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. The court is convened: God comes from Zion in fire, summons heaven and earth as witnesses and calls his covenant people to the bar (vv. 1–6). The first charge, against formal worshippers: he does not fault their sacrifices, but he owns every animal and eats nothing; he wants thanksgiving, kept vows and prayer in trouble (vv. 7–15). The second, against the hypocrite who quotes Scripture yet steals, commits adultery and slanders his brother, mistaking God’s silence for agreement (vv. 16–21). The verdict is a warning given in time, and a promise: the thankful who order their way will see the salvation of God (vv. 22–23).

Where it leads. By pattern and by the character of God revealed in Christ. The psalm says the blood of bulls and goats was never what God was after, and Hebrews explains why: such blood could not take away sins, so the Son came to do God’s will and offered his own body once for all (Hebrews 10:4–10). Since then the sacrifice this psalm asks for is the Christian’s daily offering: “a sacrifice of praise to God” (Hebrews 13:15). And the God who comes in fire to judge has given all judgment to the Son (John 5:22), who bore our condemnation so that we could call on him and be delivered.

For us. Regular churchgoing can hide the very faults this psalm exposes: treating God as if he were better off for our service, and reading his patience as permission. The cure is not more effort but the gospel’s order: he delivers, we glorify. Thank him specifically, keep the promises you made in trouble, and let the brother you criticise at dinner be safe in your mouth.
50.theology:
This is a covenant lawsuit, and the defendants are God's own worshipping people, whose religious practice is not at fault (vv. 4-8). Their error is to treat God as needy (vv. 9-13; cf. Acts 17:25); what he asks instead runs the other way: I will deliver you, and you shall glorify me (v. 15).

The second charge reaches people who can quote Scripture and ends at the family table (vv. 16-20). Its verdict, you thought that I was one like yourself (v. 21), names an error of the religious rather than of unbelievers.
50.examples: A churchgoer can keep every rota and still imagine that God is somehow better off for the attendance; this psalm aims straight at that. Picture a man walking on while tossing a letter over his shoulder: that is you cast my words behind you. And notice where the evidence lands at the last: not in the temple but at a dinner table where a brother is being taken apart.

keyVerse.quote: and call upon me in the day of trouble; I will deliver you, and you shall glorify me.
keyVerse.note: In the middle of a lawsuit against his own people, God tells them to ask him for help. The verse turns the false religion of the psalm upside down: God does not need what we give him; he gives, and we glorify him by needing him and saying so. It is the order of the gospel, which the closing verse repeats as promise.

50.reflection:
God puts his own faithful, sacrificing people on trial (vv. 4–5), and he does not fault their attendance (v. 8). Why is it possible to do all the right religious things and still have something wrong underneath? What would that look like in a church like ours?

“If I were hungry, I would not tell you” (v. 12). In what ways are we tempted to think God is better off for our service, our money or our defence of him? How does a God who needs nothing make his invitation to thanks and prayer more generous, not less?

Verses 14–15 ask for thanksgiving, kept vows and prayer in trouble. Which comes hardest to you? Name one specific thing to thank God for this week, and one promise you made to him in a hard time that you have not yet kept.

“You thought that I was one like yourself” (v. 21). Where might God’s patience have been read as approval, in our own lives or in our speech about others (v. 20)? How does Christ, who bore God’s judgment, change the way we hear this warning?

51.text: To the choirmaster. A Psalm of David, when Nathan the prophet went to him, after he had gone in to Bathsheba. 1Have mercy on me, O God, according to your steadfast love; according to your abundant mercy blot out my transgressions.2Wash me thoroughly from my iniquity, and cleanse me from my sin!3For I know my transgressions, and my sin is ever before me.4Against you, you only, have I sinned and done what is evil in your sight, so that you may be justified in your words and blameless in your judgment.5Behold, I was brought forth in iniquity, and in sin did my mother conceive me.6Behold, you delight in truth in the inward being, and you teach me wisdom in the secret heart.7Purge me with hyssop, and I shall be clean; wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow.8Let me hear joy and gladness; let the bones that you have broken rejoice.9Hide your face from my sins, and blot out all my iniquities.10Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me.11Cast me not away from your presence, and take not your Holy Spirit from me.12Restore to me the joy of your salvation, and uphold me with a willing spirit.13Then I will teach transgressors your ways, and sinners will return to you.14Deliver me from bloodguiltiness, O God, O God of my salvation, and my tongue will sing aloud of your righteousness.15O Lord, open my lips, and my mouth will declare your praise.16For you will not delight in sacrifice, or I would give it; you will not be pleased with a burnt offering.17The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit; a broken and contrite heart, O God, you will not despise.18Do good to Zion in your good pleasure; build up the walls of Jerusalem;19then will you delight in right sacrifices, in burnt offerings and whole burnt offerings; then bulls will be offered on your altar.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Against You, You Only, Have I Sinned
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Forgiveness begins with mercy asked on the scale of God’s love and with sin owned without excuse. David pleads on the ground of God’s steadfast love and abundant mercy, and asks him to blot out, wash and cleanse (vv. 1–2). He does not explain or bargain: his sin is always before him (v. 3). Every wrong he did to others was finally done against God, and he concedes in advance that God is right to judge (v. 4). Then he goes beneath the act to its root, a nature sinful from his very beginning (v. 5), and sets beside it what God wants: truth and wisdom in the hidden heart (v. 6).
verseByVerse.theology: Three words for sin, three for pardon, and an admission that the trouble began at his birth, not at the crime.

verseByVerse.quote: Have mercy on me, O God, according to your steadfast love; according to your abundant mercy blot out my transgressions. Wash me thoroughly from my iniquity, and cleanse me from my sin! For I know my transgressions, and my sin is ever before me. Against you, you only, have I sinned and done what is evil in your sight, so that you may be justified in your words and blameless in your judgment.
verseByVerse.commentary:
David asks mercy on the scale of God’s love, owns his sin as against God, and concedes that God is right to judge him.

The heading. The heading does not spare him. It names the woman and the prophet, dates the psalm to the day his sin was exposed, and hands it to the choirmaster: Israel’s king made his confession a national hymn. It lays the guilt where Nathan laid it, on David (2 Samuel 12:7–9), the king who sent for another man’s wife; many rightly see an abuse of power in it as well as adultery.

Have mercy on me, O God. He does not open with an explanation. The first words are a plea for mercy, and the measure asked for is not the size of the sin but the size of God: “according to your steadfast love; according to your abundant mercy.”

Blot out my transgressions. There are three words for what he has done (transgression, iniquity, sin) and three for what he wants done about it. Blot out is to erase writing from a record. Wash is the word for laundering cloth until the stain comes out. Cleanse is the priest’s word for declaring someone ritually clean. The record, the stain, the status: all three.

Against you, you only, have I sinned. He had plainly sinned against Uriah, against Bathsheba, and against his army and people, and he is not denying it. He is saying who the offended party ultimately is: every wrong done to a person is a wrong done to the God who made them, and God alone can pardon it. A man can apologise to his neighbour and still be unforgiven by God.

So that you may be justified. The last clause concedes the verdict before it is passed. Paul quotes it to show that God is in the right when he judges (Romans 3:4). Real confession does not negotiate over the sentence; it is the prodigal’s “I have sinned against heaven and before you” (Luke 15:18).
verseByVerse.note: The title links this psalm to Nathan’s rebuke after David’s sin with Bathsheba. Paul quotes v. 4.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, I was brought forth in iniquity, and in sin did my mother conceive me. Behold, you delight in truth in the inward being, and you teach me wisdom in the secret heart.
verseByVerse.commentary:
David traces his act to its root, a nature sinful from the start, and sets beside it what God wants: truth in the hidden heart.

I was brought forth in iniquity. Verse 5 is not an excuse. Having confessed the act, he goes underneath it to a nature bent towards sin from his very beginning. Had he confessed only the adultery, he would be treating himself as a good man who did a bad thing. Every serious repentance reaches this point, what I am and not only what I did, which is why verse 10 asks for something no effort can produce.

You delight in truth in the inward being. Two “beholds” stand side by side: here is what I am, and here is what you want, truth in the very part David had been managing for months while the affair was covered up.

Original sin. This is what the church calls original sin: the fallen nature inherited from Adam, so that we are “by nature children of wrath” (Ephesians 2:3; Romans 5:12). It is not a slur on David’s mother or on conception, which God blesses. It speaks of a nature, not of deeds done in the womb; on the infants who die, compare 2 Samuel 12:23, where David says, “I shall go to him.”

Uncertain wording. The words for “inward being” and “secret heart” are rare (the first appears elsewhere only in Job 38:36), but both clearly mean a person’s hidden depths. “You teach me” may also be read as a prayer, “teach me”. Either way, God wants truth exactly where sin has its root.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–12 — Create in Me a Clean Heart
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Only God can clean a sinner and give him a heart worth having. David asks for the treatment of the unclean, to be purged with hyssop and washed whiter than snow (v. 7), and for the bones God has broken under conviction to rejoice again (v. 8). He asks God to hide his face from his sins and blot them out (v. 9). Then he asks for something only the Creator can do, a clean heart and a steadfast spirit (v. 10). He begs not to be cast away or to lose the Holy Spirit as Saul did (v. 11), and asks for the joy of salvation and a willing spirit to uphold him (v. 12).
verseByVerse.theology: He does not ask for his heart to be repaired; he asks for a new creation.

verseByVerse.quote: Purge me with hyssop, and I shall be clean; wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow. Let me hear joy and gladness; let the bones that you have broken rejoice. Hide your face from my sins, and blot out all my iniquities. Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me. Cast me not away from your presence, and take not your Holy Spirit from me. Restore to me the joy of your salvation, and uphold me with a willing spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Only God can make a defiled sinner clean and give him a new heart, so David asks for both, and begs not to lose God’s Spirit.

Purge me with hyssop. Hyssop is a small bushy plant used as a brush. It daubed the lamb’s blood on the doorposts at Passover, sprinkled a cleansed leper, and applied the water of purification to one who had touched a corpse (Numbers 19:18). David asks to be treated as an unclean man with blood on his hands, and made clean.

I shall be whiter than snow. This is the promise Isaiah would put in God’s own mouth: “though your sins are like scarlet, they shall be as white as snow” (Isaiah 1:18). Not less scarlet. White.

Let the bones that you have broken rejoice. He says God broke his bones, and asks that they be made to rejoice: the honest account of what conviction of sin feels like: an injury, inflicted by God, and survivable only if the same hand heals it.

Create in me a clean heart, O God. Create is bara, the verb of Genesis 1:1, used in the Old Testament only of work God does and nobody else can. He does not ask for his heart to be mended, for verse 5 has said there is nothing good in him to build on. This is the Old Testament asking for the new birth, which God promised through Ezekiel: “a new heart, and a new spirit I will put within you” (Ezekiel 36:26).

The best version of yourself. Our culture believes in self-improvement with religious fervour: habit apps, morning coaches, books promising the best version of ourselves. Much of the advice is sensible, but it assumes what verse 5 denies, a good self underneath waiting to be developed. The moralist says, try harder; the sceptic says, you are fine as you are. David says neither. He has seen what came out of him with Bathsheba and Uriah, and knows the problem is not a weak habit but a heart, so he asks God to create a new one. That is what the gospel promises: “if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation” (2 Corinthians 5:17). Grace is not self-improvement with God’s help but something more like resurrection, and then, because the heart has changed, the habits finally can.

Take not your Holy Spirit from me. David had watched this happen: the Spirit of the LORD departed from Saul just after he came upon David (1 Samuel 16:13–14), and he is terrified of becoming another Saul. Christians under the new covenant are given a better promise: the Spirit is a seal “for the day of redemption” (Ephesians 4:30). But feel the horror of the request before hurrying to the comfort. And if you fear you have sinned the Spirit away, the grief itself is his work in you: hard hearts do not lie awake over this.

Restore to me the joy of your salvation. What he asks to have restored is precise: not his salvation, but the joy of it. And he asks for a willing spirit: not merely to be forgiven but to want to obey, which is the thing sin destroys first and quietest.

Where Christians differ. Some read verse 11 as showing that a true believer can lose the Spirit and fall away. Others note that the Spirit came on Saul and David with their anointing as king, so David may be asking not to be set aside as Saul was.

This commentary’s view. The prayer covers both his office and his life with God, and it is a real prayer. But those God has truly saved are sealed by the Spirit and kept by his power (Ephesians 1:13–14; John 10:28), and prayers like this are among the means by which he keeps them.
verseByVerse.note: Hyssop was used to sprinkle cleansing blood or water.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–19 — A Broken and Contrite Heart
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A forgiven sinner brings God the only offering he wants, a broken heart, and then turns outward in praise and prayer for others. Restored, David will teach transgressors God’s ways and sinners will return (v. 13). He names his bloodguilt plainly and asks God even to open his lips for praise (vv. 14–15). No sacrifice in the law fitted his sin, but a broken and contrite heart God will not despise (vv. 16–17). His private repentance ends by praying for Zion and its walls, and for a day when right sacrifices offered by cleansed hearts will please God (vv. 18–19).
verseByVerse.theology: A forgiven man immediately becomes a teacher, and the only offering he has is his own broken heart.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I will teach transgressors your ways, and sinners will return to you. Deliver me from bloodguiltiness, O God, O God of my salvation, and my tongue will sing aloud of your righteousness. O Lord, open my lips, and my mouth will declare your praise. For you will not delight in sacrifice, or I would give it; you will not be pleased with a burnt offering. The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit; a broken and contrite heart, O God, you will not despise.
verseByVerse.commentary:
With no sacrifice that fitted his sin, David brings the one offering God never despises, a broken heart, and the forgiven man becomes a singer and a teacher of sinners.

Then I will teach transgressors your ways. Then means after the clean heart, not before. A forgiven man teaches the people he now belongs to, transgressors and sinners, as this very psalm does: he knows the way back because he has walked it.

Deliver me from bloodguiltiness. He names the crime unsoftened: a man is dead because of him. And he cannot even begin praise on his own: “open my lips”, because guilt had shut them. Churches have long opened worship with this verse: nobody starts it under their own power.

You will not delight in sacrifice. Verse 16 is not false piety. The law provided sacrifices for many sins, even deliberate fraud (Leviticus 6:1–7), but none for sins done “with a high hand”, in open defiance (Numbers 15:30), and adultery and murder carried the death penalty. David has nothing to bring, and says so: “I would give it” if it would work. He stands with empty hands.

How was David forgiven? Yet God forgave him: “The LORD also has put away your sin” (2 Samuel 12:13). How, when no sacrifice fitted? Paul answers that God in his forbearance passed over former sins, looking ahead to the cross, where Christ was put forward as the sacrifice that covers them (Romans 3:25–26). The consequences did not all vanish (2 Samuel 12:14), but the guilt did, and the blood of Jesus “cleanses us from all sin” (1 John 1:7), adultery and murder included. Whatever you have done, this mercy reaches you.

A broken and contrite heart. So his only offering is his broken heart. Contrite is the word used of the broken bones in verse 8: crushed small. The promise is gentle: God “will not despise” it, will not look at a man in pieces and turn away.

The tax collector’s prayer. That is the mercy the tax collector was relying on when he stood at a distance and beat his breast, and Jesus said he went home justified (Luke 18:13–14). It is the only entry requirement this psalm knows.

verseByVerse.quote: Do good to Zion in your good pleasure; build up the walls of Jerusalem; then will you delight in right sacrifices, in burnt offerings and whole burnt offerings; then bulls will be offered on your altar.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Real repentance widens: the king’s confession ends in prayer for the whole city and its worship.

Then will you delight in right sacrifices. Verse 19 does not contradict verse 16. God rejects sacrifice offered instead of a broken heart and delights in sacrifice from hearts broken and cleansed. The same altar, with a different man standing at it.

Build up the walls of Jerusalem. The king’s private repentance ends by praying for the city. His sin did not stay private: a nation is affected by what its leaders do in the dark. Real repentance always widens; it starts with “have mercy on me” and ends asking God to do good to everybody else.

Where Christians differ. Some think these verses were added in the exile, when the walls were down, so that the exiles could make David’s confession their own. Others read them as David’s prayer for the city in his own day.

This commentary’s view. Nothing requires a later date: building Jerusalem’s walls was work of David’s and Solomon’s reigns (2 Samuel 5:9; 1 Kings 3:1). The exiles were right to make the prayer theirs.

51.title: Create in Me a Clean Heart
51.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 51 opens a run of psalms of David in Book Two (51–65), and it stands straight after Psalm 50, where God put his worshippers on trial and asked for a sacrifice of thanksgiving rather than bulls. Here a guilty man answers that trial in the only way that works. It is the best known of the church’s penitential psalms.

The message. There is mercy for the worst of sinners, but it comes only on God’s terms and from God’s hand. David brings nothing but an honest confession and a broken heart, asks God to wipe the record, wash the stain and declare him clean, and asks for what only God can do: a new heart. God does not despise such a heart, and a sinner forgiven like this becomes a singer and a teacher of others.

Why it was said. The heading names the occasion: Nathan had confronted King David after his adultery with Bathsheba and the murder of her husband Uriah (2 Samuel 11–12). The law offered no sacrifice for sins done in such open defiance, so David had nowhere to go but to God himself, and he made his confession a hymn for the whole nation.

How the chapter makes its case. A plea and a confession (vv. 1–6): mercy is asked on the scale of God’s steadfast love; the sin is owned as against God, his verdict conceded, and traced beneath the act to a nature sinful from birth. A prayer for cleansing and renewal (vv. 7–12): purge me with hyssop, wash me whiter than snow, create in me a clean heart, do not take your Holy Spirit from me, restore the joy of salvation. A forgiven man’s response (vv. 13–17): he will teach sinners the way back and sing, for the sacrifice God wants is a broken and contrite heart. And repentance widens into prayer for the city and its worship (vv. 18–19).

Where it leads. By the need it exposes and by promise. David had no sacrifice that fitted his sin, yet God put it away (2 Samuel 12:13); Paul explains that God passed over former sins in view of the cross, where Christ was put forward as the sacrifice that covers them (Romans 3:25–26). The clean heart David asked for is what God promised in the new covenant, “a new heart, and a new spirit” (Ezekiel 36:26), and gives through the Spirit Christ sends. David’s greater Son never needed this psalm for himself, yet he bore the guilt it confesses so that its prayer could be answered for us.

For us. No sin is too great for this mercy, and no religious performance can substitute for it. Come to God as David did: without excuses, owning what you have done and what you are, asking him for a new heart. Then let the joy of being forgiven make you gentle with other sinners and eager to show them the way back.
51.theology:
Pardon is asked for on the scale of God's mercy, not of the sin (v. 1). Against you, you only (v. 4) does not deny the human victims; it names the one who alone can pardon, and concedes his verdict in advance.

Repentance goes beneath the act to the nature (v. 5), so it asks for what only God can do: a heart created new (v. 10). With no sacrifice that fitted his sin, David brings only a broken heart, which God will not despise (vv. 16-17), and he was forgiven through the sacrifice the old ones looked forward to. Repentance then widens into prayer for the whole city (v. 18).
51.examples: The heading itself is a lesson: a king let his worst sin be named in the nation's hymnbook. Picture a record erased, a stained garment scrubbed clean, a priest declaring someone fit to come back in: those are the three pictures of pardon in verses 1-2. And anyone who fears they have sinned beyond reach can stand where the tax collector stood, with nothing to bring but a broken heart, and go home forgiven.

keyVerse.quote: Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me.
keyVerse.note: Here the psalm goes from pardon to renewal. David uses the verb of Genesis 1:1, which only God does: he does not ask for his old heart to be improved but for a new one to be made. It is the Old Testament asking for what the new covenant promises and Christ gives by his Spirit, a new creation.

51.reflection:
David asks for mercy “according to your steadfast love” (v. 1), not according to the size of his sin. Why is it so hard to come to God like this, without explanations or bargaining? What excuses do we most often reach for?

“Against you, you only, have I sinned” (v. 4), and “in sin did my mother conceive me” (v. 5). How does seeing sin as against God, and as rooted in the heart, change the way we confess it, both to God and to people we have wronged?

Verse 10 asks God to create a clean heart rather than help us improve the old one. Where have you been relying on self-improvement instead of asking God for change? What would asking him look like this week?

David’s forgiven heart turns outward: he will teach sinners the way back (v. 13) and pray for the whole city (v. 18). How could the experience of being forgiven make us gentler and more useful to others who have failed?

52.text: To the choirmaster. A Maskil of David, when Doeg, the Edomite, came and told Saul, "David has come to the house of Ahimelech." 1Why do you boast of evil, O mighty man? The steadfast love of God endures all the day.2Your tongue plots destruction, like a sharp razor, you worker of deceit.3You love evil more than good, and lying more than speaking what is right. Selah4You love all words that devour, O deceitful tongue.5But God will break you down forever; he will snatch and tear you from your tent; he will uproot you from the land of the living. Selah6The righteous shall see and fear, and shall laugh at him, saying,7"See the man who would not make God his refuge, but trusted in the abundance of his riches and sought refuge in his own destruction!"8But I am like a green olive tree in the house of God. I trust in the steadfast love of God forever and ever.9I will thank you forever, because you have done it. I will wait for your name, for it is good, in the presence of the godly.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The man who destroys with his tongue and trusts in himself will be uprooted by God. David addresses the “mighty man” with sarcasm: why boast of evil, when God’s steadfast love outlasts every boast (v. 1)? His tongue is a sharp razor, and he loves evil, lying and words that devour as a settled taste, not a slip (vv. 2–4). God will break him down for ever, tear him from his tent and uproot him from the land of the living (v. 5). The righteous will watch with awe and then laugh at the collapse of his boast, seeing a man who trusted riches and would not make God his refuge (vv. 6–7).
verseByVerse.theology: The hero's great exploit was informing, and his tongue did the work of a razor.

verseByVerse.quote: Why do you boast of evil, O mighty man? The steadfast love of God endures all the day. Your tongue plots destruction, like a sharp razor, you worker of deceit. You love evil more than good, and lying more than speaking what is right. Selah You love all words that devour, O deceitful tongue.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The man who destroys with his tongue boasts in vain, for God’s steadfast love outlasts him.

Doeg the Edomite. The heading takes us to one of the darkest pages in Samuel. David, on the run, came to the priests at Nob and was given bread and Goliath’s sword. One of Saul’s men saw it: Doeg the Edomite. He told the king, and when Saul’s soldiers refused to touch the priests, Doeg killed eighty-five of them himself and then destroyed their town (1 Samuel 22:9–10, 18–19).

An accurate report. Why then does the psalm call him a liar (vv. 3–4)? Because he told the truth in order to destroy: he made innocent priests, who knew nothing of David’s flight, look like traitors (1 Samuel 22:14–15). A true sentence can do a liar’s work.

Why do you boast of evil, O mighty man? This is sarcasm, and it stings: the title belongs to a champion, and this champion’s great exploit was carrying a report. Against his boasting the psalm sets not David’s strength but God’s steadfast love, which “endures all the day”, outlasting whatever the man is enjoying now.

Like a sharp razor. A razor is a small blade, useful, ordinary, kept close to the face, and capable of opening a throat. James makes the same point with a spark and a forest (James 3:5–6). What Doeg did required no army; it required a sentence.

You love evil more than good. Twice the psalm says he loves it: evil over good, lying over truth, as a settled taste. And “words that devour” is exact: some speech eats people alive. A staff meeting or a group chat can still serve it.

Uncertain wording. The meaning of Maskil in the heading is unknown. It comes from a word for insight, so it may mean a skilful or instructive psalm; it is probably a musical or liturgical term.
verseByVerse.note: The title links this psalm to Doeg the Edomite, who betrayed the priests of Nob.

verseByVerse.quote: But God will break you down forever; he will snatch and tear you from your tent; he will uproot you from the land of the living. Selah The righteous shall see and fear, and shall laugh at him, saying, "See the man who would not make God his refuge, but trusted in the abundance of his riches and sought refuge in his own destruction!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
God will uproot the destroyer, and the righteous will see the end of a man who trusted riches instead of God.

But God will break you down forever. Four verbs, all God’s, and all violent: break down, snatch, tear away, uproot. The tent is his settled place, and he is pulled out of it like a peg. A man who made his living by loyalty to a king will be thrown out by God, the King he never reckoned with.

The righteous shall see and fear. The laughter in verse 6 needs care. It is not amusement at another man’s pain; it follows “fear” in the same sentence, and what it laughs at is the collapse of a boast. Here was a man with money and access who declined the one refuge that holds.

Uncertain wording. The ESV notes that “his own destruction” (v. 7) may be read “his work of destruction”. Either way the irony stands: he took shelter in the very thing that ruined him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–9 — But I Am Like a Green Olive Tree
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The one who trusts God’s steadfast love is rooted and fruitful, whatever his circumstances. Against the uprooted man stands David, like a green olive tree flourishing in the house of God, though he writes as a fugitive far from it (v. 8). He trusts God’s love for ever, thanks God for a rescue he speaks of as already done, and waits for God’s good name to be shown, keeping company with the godly while he waits (v. 9).
verseByVerse.theology: One man is torn out of his tent; the other is planted indoors, and gives thanks before anything has visibly changed.

verseByVerse.quote: But I am like a green olive tree in the house of God. I trust in the steadfast love of God forever and ever. I will thank you forever, because you have done it. I will wait for your name, for it is good, in the presence of the godly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever trusts God’s steadfast love is rooted and fruitful in his presence, even when hunted, and can thank him now for a rescue still awaited.

Like a green olive tree in the house of God. Set the two pictures side by side, as the psalm means you to. One man is torn from his tent and uprooted; the other is a tree “in the house of God”, planted in the courts, where trees do not normally grow. An olive tree is slow, long-lived and productive for centuries; Jeremiah used the same image of Israel, “a green olive tree, beautiful with good fruit” (Jeremiah 11:16).

Written as a fugitive. David writes this living in caves and forests (1 Samuel 22:1, 5). He has no tent to tear down and no access to the house of God. The claim is not about his circumstances; it is about where his roots are.

What no informer can uproot. The Christian has a firmer reason to say it. David’s greater Son was also hunted by the powerful and handed over by Judas, who knew where to find him. In him believers are “rooted and built up” (Colossians 2:7) and are themselves being built into a dwelling place for God (Ephesians 2:22). What is planted there no informer can uproot.

Because you have done it. This is in the past tense, about a rescue that has not yet occurred, and in the same breath, “I will wait.” Thanking God for a finished work while still waiting for it is not a contradiction; it is how faith ordinarily lives, as every Christian at the Lord’s Table does, thankful for the cross and waiting for Christ’s return.

In the presence of the godly. Doeg had the king’s ear and favour, and no one in the record stands with him. David, hunted, names the company he intends to keep.

52.title: A Green Olive Tree in the House of God
52.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 52 follows David’s confession in Psalm 51 and begins a group of psalms called Maskil (52–55). Its heading takes us back to David’s years as a fugitive from King Saul, and to one of the darkest episodes of that time.

The message. The powerful man who uses his tongue to destroy may look secure, but God will pull him up by the roots, because he refused to make God his refuge. The one who trusts in God’s steadfast love, even while hunted and homeless, is like a flourishing tree planted in God’s own house. So God’s love, not the wicked man’s power, has the last word.

Why it was said. David, on the run, had been fed and armed by the priests at Nob. Doeg the Edomite, one of Saul’s men, saw it, reported it to the king, and then killed the priests and destroyed their town himself (1 Samuel 21–22). David wrote with innocent blood on the ground and his own life in danger.

How the chapter makes its case. The charge (vv. 1–4): the “mighty man” boasts of evil while God’s steadfast love outlasts him; his tongue is a razor, and he loves lying and words that devour. The sentence (vv. 5–7): God will break him down, tear him from his tent and uproot him, and the righteous, awed, will see the end of a man who trusted riches instead of God. The contrast (vv. 8–9): but I, like a green olive tree in the house of God, trust God’s love for ever, give thanks for what he has done, and wait among the godly.

Where it leads. By pattern. David, the anointed king hunted by the powerful and betrayed by an informer, foreshadows his greater Son, who was handed over by Judas, a man who knew where to find him, and condemned by false and twisted words (Mark 14:55–58). God vindicated him by raising him, and all who are rooted in him are planted where no accuser can reach (Romans 8:33–34).

For us. Watch your tongue: a true sentence told to wound does a liar’s work, and gossip often wears the clothes of accuracy.
