When you are on the receiving end, do not envy the powerful or answer like with like. Put your roots down in God’s steadfast love in Christ, and stay close to his people while you wait.
52.theology:
Doeg's report was accurate, yet the psalm calls it lying, because a true sentence told in order to destroy does a liar's work (vv. 2-4; cf. Jas 3:5-6). His sin is a settled taste, not a lapse: twice he is said to love it.

The righteous fear before they laugh (v. 6), and the pictures of uprooting and planting (vv. 5, 8) are set side by side. David writes as a fugitive, so his claim is about roots, not circumstances, and he gives thanks for a rescue he is still waiting for (v. 9).
52.examples: A razor is small and ordinary, kept close to the face every morning, and it can open a throat; so can a sentence. Think of the colleague who passes on something true about you for the purpose of ruining you. Against that, picture an olive tree growing inside a house of worship: slow, rooted, fruitful for centuries, and out of reach of any informer.

keyVerse.quote: But I am like a green olive tree in the house of God. I trust in the steadfast love of God forever and ever.
keyVerse.note: This is the psalm’s great “but”, set against the uprooted man of verse 5. Written by a fugitive far from the sanctuary, it locates security not in circumstances but in roots: the steadfast love of God, which the first verse said endures all the day. In Christ, believers are planted where no accuser can tear them out.

52.reflection:
Doeg’s report was accurate, yet the psalm calls it lying (vv. 3–4). How can true words do a liar’s work? Where are we most tempted to pass on something true in order to hurt, and what would loving speech look like instead?

The righteous “see and fear” before they laugh (v. 6). How should we respond when a powerful person who has done harm finally falls? What keeps that response from becoming gloating?

David calls himself “a green olive tree in the house of God” while living as a fugitive (v. 8). What difference does it make to locate your security in your roots rather than your circumstances? Where are your roots in practice?

David thanks God “because you have done it” and in the same breath says “I will wait” (v. 9). What are you waiting for God to do, and how can the finished work of Christ help you give thanks while you wait?

53.text: To the choirmaster: according to Mahalath. A Maskil of David. 1The fool says in his heart, "There is no God." They are corrupt, doing abominable iniquity; there is none who does good.2God looks down from heaven on the children of man to see if there are any who understand, who seek after God.3They have all fallen away; together they have become corrupt; there is none who does good, not even one.4Have those who work evil no knowledge, who eat up my people as they eat bread, and do not call upon God?5There they are, in great terror, where there is no terror! For God scatters the bones of him who encamps against you; you put them to shame, for God has rejected them.6Oh, that salvation for Israel would come out of Zion! When God restores the fortunes of his people, let Jacob rejoice, let Israel be glad.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — The Same Verdict, Sung Again
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s verdict on mankind has not changed, but the evidence of his rescue has grown, and salvation can still only come from him. The psalm repeats Psalm 14 almost word for word: the fool says in his heart that there is no God, and God, searching from heaven, finds none who does good, not even one, while the evildoers devour his people and never pray (vv. 1–4). One verse is rewritten: the besiegers fall into terror where there is no terror, and God scatters their bones (v. 5). The ending is the same longing: oh, that salvation for Israel would come out of Zion (v. 6).
verseByVerse.theology: This is Psalm 14 printed a second time, with the divine name changed throughout and one verse rewritten after a deliverance.

verseByVerse.quote: The fool says in his heart, "There is no God." They are corrupt, doing abominable iniquity; there is none who does good. God looks down from heaven on the children of man to see if there are any who understand, who seek after God. They have all fallen away; together they have become corrupt; there is none who does good, not even one. Have those who work evil no knowledge, who eat up my people as they eat bread, and do not call upon God?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Psalm 14 is sung again almost word for word, and its verdict stands: before God, simply as God, no one does good. The fool and God’s search are explained at Psalm 14; here the differences are what to study.

The fool says in his heart. The fool is not first a man with intellectual doubts but one who lives as if God will never call him to account. “None who does good” means none in God’s sight, from faith and for his glory (Romans 3:10–12); unbelievers still do kind and useful things by God’s common grace.

The name of God. In Psalm 14 the covenant name, the LORD, appears four times; here every occurrence has become God. Psalm 53 sits in Book Two, where the general name for God largely replaces the covenant name, and the effect is to widen the verdict. Psalm 14 said this of human beings before the God of Israel; Psalm 53 says it before God simply as God, so no one can plead that he serves a different god.

Abominable iniquity. The small verbal changes run the same way: abominable deeds has become abominable iniquity, and turned aside has become fallen away. Nothing in the diagnosis has softened with the years.

Uncertain wording. The heading has changed too: Psalm 14 was simply “To the choirmaster. Of David.”; this one is set “according to Mahalath” and called a Maskil, musical or liturgical terms whose exact meaning is no longer known. Maskil comes from the verb behind “any who understand” in verse 2, so it probably marks a psalm meant to make its singers wise: fitting, in a psalm about the man who will not understand.
verseByVerse.note: Almost the same as Psalm 14.

verseByVerse.quote: There they are, in great terror, where there is no terror! For God scatters the bones of him who encamps against you; you put them to shame, for God has rejected them. Oh, that salvation for Israel would come out of Zion! When God restores the fortunes of his people, let Jacob rejoice, let Israel be glad.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The one rewritten verse tells of a besieging army struck with panic and left as scattered bones: the old verdict now carries fresh evidence that God rescues his people.

There they are, in great terror. Set the two versions side by side. Psalm 14 said: “There they are in great terror, for God is with the generation of the righteous. You would shame the plans of the poor, but the LORD is his refuge.” This version is sharper: their terror came where there is no terror, panic with no visible cause, the kind that empties a camp overnight, and God scatters the bones of him who encamps against you.

God scatters the bones. Perhaps something happened between the two editions: an army had encamped, and in the morning all that was left of it was unburied bones, the last disgrace in the ancient world. The psalm names no event, but the most famous such morning is the night the Assyrian camp outside Jerusalem was struck down (2 Kings 19:35). The verdict had not changed, but the evidence that God rescues his people had grown. That is how a congregation sings an old song after something has happened to them: same words, one verse updated.

Oh, that salvation for Israel would come out of Zion! The longing is unchanged, except that here it is God who restores rather than the LORD. If there is none who does good, no reform will do; salvation has to come from outside, out of Zion.

It came. The wish at the end of both psalms was answered by Jesus, David’s Son, the one man who passed heaven’s search, who walked out of that city to die for those who failed it. At his cross the real enemies of God’s people were routed and shamed like the besiegers: God “disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame, by triumphing over them in him” (Colossians 2:15). Whatever is encamped against a believer now is a defeated army.

Uncertain wording. Where there is no terror is compressed: it may mean panic with no cause, or terror such as they had never known. The Hebrew of him who encamps against you is unusual and has been rendered in other ways, but the ESV fits the picture of a routed siege. On restores the fortunes, see the note on Psalm 14:7.

53.title: There Is None Who Does Good: A Second Time
53.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 53 stands in Book Two of the Psalter, after the double-tongued man of Psalm 52, and it is a song we have already heard: Psalm 14, sung again with the name of God changed throughout and one verse rewritten. The Psalter does not print a poem twice by accident, so the differences are worth noticing.

The message. When God searches mankind he finds that no one does good, not even one, and the verdict has not softened with the years. Yet the God the fool denies is real: he has shattered the enemies of his people, leaving their bones on the field. Since no one can save himself, the only hope is the salvation God sends out of Zion.

Why it was said. Like Psalm 14, it was written by David for a people living among powerful men who used the weak and ignored God (see the introduction). Its rewritten verse suggests that it was sung again after a deliverance, when an army that had camped against God’s people was routed.

How the chapter makes its case. The verdict (vv. 1–4): the fool denies God in his heart, God looks down from heaven, and all have fallen away; the evildoers eat up God’s people like bread and never pray. The evidence (v. 5): the besiegers are seized by a terror with no cause, and God scatters their bones, for he has rejected them. The longing (v. 6): salvation must come out of Zion, and when God restores his people, Jacob will rejoice.

Where it leads. By the need it exposes, and by promise. Paul quotes the verdict to stop every mouth (Romans 3:10–12), and then announces, “But now the righteousness of God has been manifested apart from the law” (Romans 3:21). The salvation the psalm longs for came out of Zion in David’s Son, the one man who passed heaven’s search, who went out of Jerusalem to die for people who do no good. At the cross God routed the true enemies of his people: he “put them to open shame, by triumphing over them in him” (Colossians 2:15).

For us. Do not hear the verdict as if it were about other people: it includes the reader, religious or not. Then look where the psalm looks, away from ourselves to the salvation God has sent in Christ, and take heart that the enemies of God’s people never have the last word.
53.theology: Changing the LORD to God widens the verdict to every human being before God, and the one rewritten verse adds evidence of God's answer: an attacking army gone (v. 5). Since none does good, salvation must still come from outside, out of Zion (v. 6).
53.examples: Imagine a hymn reprinted in a later hymnbook with one verse rewritten after a remarkable answer to prayer: that is a fair picture of this psalm. The verdict on the human heart is the same as before; only the evidence of God's rescue has grown.

keyVerse.quote: Oh, that salvation for Israel would come out of Zion! When God restores the fortunes of his people, let Jacob rejoice, let Israel be glad.
keyVerse.note: After a verdict that leaves no one standing, this is the only way out the psalm can see: salvation that comes from God, not from us. It is the line both versions of the psalm end on, and the gospel answers it, for salvation came out of Zion in Jesus, through whom people who do no good are made right with God.

53.reflection:
Psalm 53 repeats Psalm 14 almost word for word. Why do you think God gave his people the same verdict on the human heart twice? What truths do you most need to hear again and again?

The fool says “There is no God” in his heart, not necessarily with his lips (v. 1). How can people who believe in God still live as practical atheists? Where are you tempted to do so?

Verse 5 seems to record a real deliverance, sung into an old song. What deliverances has God given you or your church that you could “write into” the way you pray and praise?

Verse 6 longs for salvation from outside ourselves, and Paul says it has come (Romans 3:21–22). How does knowing that rescue comes from God, not from our own goodness, change the way we treat people who seem far from him?

54.text: To the choirmaster: with stringed instruments. A Maskil of David, when the Ziphites went and told Saul, "Is not David hiding among us?" 1O God, save me by your name, and vindicate me by your might.2O God, hear my prayer; give ear to the words of my mouth.3For strangers have risen against me; ruthless men seek my life; they do not set God before themselves. Selah4Behold, God is my helper; the Lord is the upholder of my life.5He will return the evil to my enemies; in your faithfulness put an end to them.6With a freewill offering I will sacrifice to you; I will give thanks to your name, O LORD, for it is good.7For he has delivered me from every trouble, and my eye has looked in triumph on my enemies.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — Save Me by Your Name
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God himself is the helper of the betrayed, even before anything has changed. David, sold out by men of his own tribe, appeals to God’s name and might, because ruthless men who have put God out of sight are hunting him (vv. 1–3). Then, with Saul still searching, he points to a fact: God is my helper, the upholder of my life, and he will turn their evil back on them (vv. 4–5). So David promises the one offering nobody owed, a freewill offering, and gives thanks in the past tense for a deliverance he cannot yet see (vv. 6–7).
verseByVerse.theology: In seven verses he moves from betrayal by his own tribe to thanksgiving in the past tense, with nothing in between but God.

verseByVerse.quote: O God, save me by your name, and vindicate me by your might. O God, hear my prayer; give ear to the words of my mouth. For strangers have risen against me; ruthless men seek my life; they do not set God before themselves. Selah
verseByVerse.commentary:
Betrayed by his own people, David appeals to God himself, to all God has shown himself to be, because men who have put God out of sight will stop at nothing.

The Ziphites. The heading names the occasion (1 Samuel 23:19). The Ziphites were men of Judah, David’s own tribe; he was hiding in their hills, and they sent word to the king who wanted him dead, and did it twice (1 Samuel 26:1).

O God, save me by your name. Not by an army or an angel, but by all that God has revealed himself to be. Learning God’s character is not only for scholars: it is what you reach for when your neighbours have sold you. Vindicate me asks God to take up his case as judge and declare him in the right.

For strangers have risen against me. The word is bitter: these men were not foreigners but his own kin, and he can no longer tell the difference. Betrayal turns family into strangers.

They do not set God before themselves. The diagnosis explains everything. Once God is out of view, a man reckons only what will profit him, and handing a fugitive to a murderous king is simply good politics.

His own did not receive him. The pattern runs on to David’s greater Son, who “came to his own, and his own people did not receive him” (John 1:11), and was handed over by one of the Twelve. The name David appealed to is now fully known in him: there is “no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved” (Acts 4:12).

Textual note. The ESV notes that some manuscripts read insolent men, as in the similar line of Psalm 86:14. Either way the men are ruthless and godless.
verseByVerse.note: The title links this psalm to the Ziphites betraying David’s hiding place to Saul.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, God is my helper; the Lord is the upholder of my life. He will return the evil to my enemies; in your faithfulness put an end to them. With a freewill offering I will sacrifice to you; I will give thanks to your name, O LORD, for it is good. For he has delivered me from every trouble, and my eye has looked in triumph on my enemies.
verseByVerse.commentary:
With nothing yet changed, David looks at God and calls him his helper; so he leaves the repaying to God and gives thanks for a rescue he cannot yet see.

Behold, God is my helper. The behold is the turning point, and it comes with nothing changed: Saul is still coming, the Ziphites have still informed. David looks away from the situation to a fact and points to it as if it were in the room. Hebrews teaches Christians to say the same in the same tone: “So we can confidently say, ‘The Lord is my helper; I will not fear; what can man do to me?’” (Hebrews 13:6).

He will return the evil to my enemies. The evil comes back on those who planned it, and God returns it, in your faithfulness to his promises. Twice David was close enough to kill Saul and twice he walked away (1 Samuel 24; 26). A man who believes verse 5 does not need to take revenge (Romans 12:19).

With a freewill offering. The one sacrifice nobody owed: not required by the calendar, not demanded for a sin, not the payment of a vow, but brought because a man wanted to. It is the fitting answer to a rescue nobody earned.

He has delivered me from every trouble. Past tense, from a man still in the wilderness with the search parties out, about a deliverance not yet visible. That is not self-deception; it is how faith speaks about a God who does not lose.

Uncertain wording. The upholder of my life may also be read among those who uphold my life; either way God holds him up. In verse 7 in triumph is supplied: the Hebrew says simply that his eye has looked on his enemies, seeing them defeated. It is the relief of the rescued, not gloating.

54.title: God Is My Helper
54.overview:
Where we are. After the universal verdict of Psalm 53, Book Two returns to the years when David was hunted by Saul. Psalms 52 to 59 belong largely to that time, and several headings name the moment: Doeg the informer (52), the Philistines in Gath (56), the cave (57). Psalm 54 is the shortest of them: seven verses written when his own neighbours gave him away.

The message. When the people who should have sheltered you betray you, you can still appeal to God himself, to everything he has shown himself to be. He is your helper before anything changes, so you can leave the repaying to him and thank him in advance for a rescue you cannot yet see.

Why it was said. The Ziphites were men of Judah, David’s own tribe. He was hiding in their hill country, and they sent word to Saul and offered to hand him over (1 Samuel 23:19–20); later they did it again (1 Samuel 26:1). David was the anointed king-to-be, hunted by the reigning king, and now sold out by his kin (see the introduction on the titles).

How the chapter makes its case. The plea (vv. 1–3): save me by your name, for ruthless men seek my life, men who do not set God before them; then a Selah, a pause. The turn (vv. 4–5): with nothing changed, “Behold, God is my helper”, and the evil they planned will come back on them, in God’s faithfulness, not by David’s hand. The thanks (vv. 6–7): a freewill offering promised, and thanksgiving in the past tense for a deliverance still on its way.

Where it leads. By pattern. David, the anointed king betrayed by his own people, foreshadows his greater Son, who “came to his own, and his own people did not receive him” (John 1:11) and was sold to his enemies by a man of his own company. Yet where David was rescued from Saul, Jesus was not rescued from his betrayers; he gave himself up, freely, as the offering nobody could demand: “No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of my own accord” (John 10:18). The name David appealed to is now fully known in him: there is “no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved” (Acts 4:12).

For us. Betrayal by family, friends or church is a particular wound, and this psalm was written inside it. Take it to God by name, refuse to settle the score yourself, and give thanks for what he has already done in Christ, who was betrayed so that you would never be abandoned.
54.theology:
David appeals to God's revealed character (v. 1) and names the root of the betrayal: they do not set God before themselves (v. 3). The turn comes in v. 4 with nothing changed, and he leaves the repaying to God (v. 5).

He promises the one offering nobody owed and gives thanks in the past tense for a deliverance not yet visible (vv. 6-7).
54.examples: Being betrayed by your own family or church is a particular wound, and this psalm was written in it. David had two chances to kill Saul and walked away both times, leaving the repaying to God. And a freewill offering, the gift nobody required, is the fitting answer to a rescue nobody earned.

keyVerse.quote: Behold, God is my helper; the Lord is the upholder of my life.
keyVerse.note: This is the hinge of the psalm. Nothing outside David has changed, yet everything turns on this one look at God, and from here he can leave the repaying to God and give thanks in advance. Hebrews puts the same confidence on every Christian’s lips (Hebrews 13:6), because in Christ God has shown that he will never leave his people.

54.reflection:
The Ziphites were David’s own tribe, and their betrayal turned family into “strangers” (v. 3). Why is betrayal by those close to us so much harder to bear than hostility from outsiders? How does Jesus, betrayed by one of his own, meet us there?

David asks to be saved “by your name”, by all God has shown himself to be (v. 1). Which truths about God’s character do you reach for in a crisis, and how could you come to know them better before the crisis comes?

Twice David could have killed Saul and walked away, leaving the repaying to God (v. 5). What does it look like to leave justice to God in a real conflict, without pretending the wrong did not happen?

David gives thanks in the past tense for a deliverance not yet visible (v. 7). What has God already done for you in Christ that you could thank him for, even while your present trouble continues?

55.text: To the choirmaster: with stringed instruments. A Maskil of David. 1Give ear to my prayer, O God, and hide not yourself from my plea for mercy!2Attend to me, and answer me; I am restless in my complaint and I moan,3because of the noise of the enemy, because of the oppression of the wicked. For they drop trouble upon me, and in anger they bear a grudge against me.4My heart is in anguish within me; the terrors of death have fallen upon me.5Fear and trembling come upon me, and horror overwhelms me.6And I say, "Oh, that I had wings like a dove! I would fly away and be at rest;7yes, I would wander far away; I would lodge in the wilderness; Selah8I would hurry to find a shelter from the raging wind and tempest."9Destroy, O Lord, divide their tongues; for I see violence and strife in the city.10Day and night they go around it on its walls, and iniquity and trouble are within it;11ruin is in its midst; oppression and fraud do not depart from its marketplace.12For it is not an enemy who taunts me— then I could bear it; it is not an adversary who deals insolently with me— then I could hide from him.13But it is you, a man, my equal, my companion, my familiar friend.14We used to take sweet counsel together; within God's house we walked in the throng.15Let death steal over them; let them go down to Sheol alive; for evil is in their dwelling place and in their heart.16But I call to God, and the LORD will save me.17Evening and morning and at noon I utter my complaint and moan, and he hears my voice.18He redeems my soul in safety from the battle that I wage, for many are arrayed against me.19God will give ear and humble them, he who is enthroned from of old, Selah because they do not change and do not fear God.20My companion stretched out his hand against his friends; he violated his covenant.21His speech was smooth as butter, yet war was in his heart; his words were softer than oil, yet they were drawn swords.22Cast your burden on the LORD, and he will sustain you; he will never permit the righteous to be moved.23But you, O God, will cast them down into the pit of destruction; men of blood and treachery shall not live out half their days. But I will trust in you.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — Oh, That I Had Wings Like a Dove
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A believer overwhelmed by fear may tell God everything, even that he wants to run away. David begs God not to hide from his plea, for the noise and grudges of his enemies have brought him to anguish, the terrors of death, trembling and horror (vv. 1–5). Then comes one of the most human wishes in Scripture: wings like a dove, to fly far off and find shelter in the wilderness from the storm (vv. 6–8). The wish is not rebuked; it is said to God, and the rest of the psalm will find the shelter he longs for not in a place but in God himself.
verseByVerse.theology: He lives in a violent city and would rather be a bird, and he says so to God.

verseByVerse.quote: Give ear to my prayer, O God, and hide not yourself from my plea for mercy! Attend to me, and answer me; I am restless in my complaint and I moan, because of the noise of the enemy, because of the oppression of the wicked. For they drop trouble upon me, and in anger they bear a grudge against me. My heart is in anguish within me; the terrors of death have fallen upon me. Fear and trembling come upon me, and horror overwhelms me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
David pours out to God a fear that has overwhelmed him, and asks above all that God would not look away.

Hide not yourself from my plea for mercy! The verb is the law’s word for walking past a neighbour’s strayed ox and pretending not to see it (Deuteronomy 22:1–4), and Isaiah’s for turning from one’s own flesh in need (Isaiah 58:7). David asks God not to do what he forbids his people to do.

Because of the noise of the enemy. The trouble is loud: shouting, threats, rumour. They drop trouble upon me pictures something tipped down from above, and bear a grudge is the verb for Esau’s settled hatred of Jacob (Genesis 27:41): hostility nursed over time. Who the enemy is, the psalm reveals later (see the note on vv. 9–15).

The terrors of death have fallen upon me. Five words for his state: restless, moaning, anguish, fear and trembling, horror. This is not a man being brave about it, and Scripture does not ask him to be. In Gethsemane the Lord Jesus said, “My soul is very sorrowful, even to death” (Mark 14:34): the Saviour is no stranger to this verse.

When the anguish does not lift. If fear like this has become your daily state, do not carry it alone. Talk to a pastor or biblical counsellor, and see a doctor, since the body is often involved; medicine, where it helps, is no failure of faith.

verseByVerse.quote: And I say, "Oh, that I had wings like a dove! I would fly away and be at rest; yes, I would wander far away; I would lodge in the wilderness; Selah I would hurry to find a shelter from the raging wind and tempest."
verseByVerse.commentary:
David longs simply to escape, and Scripture lets him say so to God; the shelter he wants will be found not in the wilderness but in God.

Oh, that I had wings like a dove! One of the most human wishes in the Bible, and God had it sung in worship. He does not want to fight, or win, or even be vindicated; he wants to leave. And a dove, of all birds: not an eagle to fight, but a dove to slip away quietly.

I would lodge in the wilderness. Where David had once hidden from Saul, and where Jeremiah wished to go: “Oh that I had in the desert a travelers’ lodging place, that I might leave my people” (Jeremiah 9:2). The psalm will find his shelter from the raging wind and tempest not in a place but in God (vv. 16–17, 22), and in the one who did not fly away but “set his face to go to Jerusalem” (Luke 9:51), staying in the storm to become his people’s shelter.

Without a word of rebuke. The wish is not treated as unbelief, and anyone who has longed to be out of it all is in good company. What matters is what he does with it: he tells God, and keeps talking.

When leaving is wisdom. David himself fled Jerusalem when his son rose against him (2 Samuel 15:14). If the danger is in your own home, Scripture does not ask you to stay and be harmed: abuse is never to be tolerated, and the abused should seek safety at once and tell someone who can help.

When the wish becomes darker. If the longing to be at rest has become a wish not to be alive, tell someone you trust today; if you are in danger of harming yourself, call the emergency services now.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–21 — It Is You, My Familiar Friend
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The worst wound is betrayal by a friend, and even that can be brought to God in prayer. The city is patrolled by violence and fraud, and David asks God to confuse the plotters (vv. 9–11). But the enemy is no stranger: it is his equal, his companion, the friend he walked with to God’s house, and David hands his fierce cry for justice to God (vv. 12–15). He prays evening, morning and noon, and is heard; God, enthroned from of old, will humble men who never change (vv. 16–19). The friend broke his covenant, his words smooth as butter and his heart at war (vv. 20–21).
verseByVerse.theology: What makes it unbearable is not the hatred but who it comes from: it is you, a friend he used to worship beside.

verseByVerse.quote: Destroy, O Lord, divide their tongues; for I see violence and strife in the city. Day and night they go around it on its walls, and iniquity and trouble are within it; ruin is in its midst; oppression and fraud do not depart from its marketplace. For it is not an enemy who taunts me— then I could bear it; it is not an adversary who deals insolently with me— then I could hide from him. But it is you, a man, my equal, my companion, my familiar friend. We used to take sweet counsel together; within God's house we walked in the throng. Let death steal over them; let them go down to Sheol alive; for evil is in their dwelling place and in their heart.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The city is rotten with violence and fraud, but the wound David cannot bear is that his enemy is a close friend and fellow worshipper; and he hands his fierce cry for justice to God.

Divide their tongues. This asks for Babel again: God confused the builders’ language so the project stopped (Genesis 11:7). Shrewdly, he asks first not that the plotters be destroyed but that they stop understanding each other.

Violence and strife in the city. The city is patrolled by the wrong things: violence and strife walk the walls where the watchmen should be, and fraud keeps regular hours in the market. It is somewhere respectable and rotten, most likely Jerusalem.

It is not an enemy who taunts me. Everything has been leading to verses 12–14. An enemy he could bear. What cannot be borne is who this is: you, a man, my equal, my companion, my familiar friend, each description closer than the last. Then the detail that makes it unbearable: within God’s house we walked in the throng. They went up to worship together, in sweet counsel about the things they both believed.

Betrayal by a fellow worshipper. A wound of its own kind, and Scripture has a psalm for it. David’s counsellor Ahithophel went over to Absalom (2 Samuel 15:31) and later hanged himself (2 Samuel 17:23), as Judas did after betraying Jesus (Matthew 27:5). Jesus said at the table, “He who has dipped his hand in the dish with me will betray me” (Matthew 26:23). The man who wrote this verse and the Lord who was betrayed both know what it costs.

Let them go down to Sheol alive. The prayer of verse 15 is savage, and it is a prayer, addressed to God, not a plan. Go down to Sheol (the realm of the dead) alive recalls Korah’s rebellion, when the ground swallowed the conspirators (Numbers 16:33). David does not reach for a knife; he hands the wish to the only one with the right to grant it (on praying such prayers, see the introduction, The psalms that curse).

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew behind Let death steal over them is unusual and can be read in more than one way (some take it as desolation be upon them), but the ESV is likely, and the sense of a sudden end is clear.

verseByVerse.quote: But I call to God, and the LORD will save me. Evening and morning and at noon I utter my complaint and moan, and he hears my voice. He redeems my soul in safety from the battle that I wage, for many are arrayed against me. God will give ear and humble them, he who is enthroned from of old, Selah because they do not change and do not fear God. My companion stretched out his hand against his friends; he violated his covenant. His speech was smooth as butter, yet war was in his heart; his words were softer than oil, yet they were drawn swords.
verseByVerse.commentary:
David keeps praying at set times, sure that God hears him and will humble men who never change, while he names the friend whose smooth words hid a sword.

But I call to God, and the LORD will save me. The covenant name returns: the LORD keeps covenant when friends break it (v. 20).

Evening and morning and at noon. Three times a day, at set hours, the same moaning as verse 2. And the verse ends, without fuss, he hears my voice. That is ordinary prayer in a long trouble: fixed times, repeated content, and a God who does not tire of the subject. Daniel prayed three times a day in Babylon (Daniel 6:10), and the hours held him steady.

They do not change and do not fear God. The first follows from the second: a man who answers to no one above him has no reason to change. Against them stands he who is enthroned from of old: their schemes are recent; his throne is not.

His speech was smooth as butter. Butter and oil, smooth and soft, and underneath, war and drawn swords. Not rudeness, but one of the most dangerous kinds of speech, the kind that sounds like friendship. Anyone undone by someone unfailingly pleasant knows the taste of butter in this verse. It reached its worst in a garden: “Judas, would you betray the Son of Man with a kiss?” (Luke 22:48).

Uncertain wording. They do not change is literally they have no changes: no change of heart, or no reversals, life always going their way so that they never learn to fear God. In verse 20 the ESV supplies My companion; the Hebrew says only “he”, but the friend of verses 13–14 is plainly meant.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–23 — Cast Your Burden on the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Throw your load onto the LORD, and he will hold you up. After twenty-one verses of honest anguish, David turns to whoever is listening: cast your burden on the LORD, for he will sustain you and never let the righteous be moved (v. 22). The treacherous will be cast down by God, not by David, and they will not outlive their days; and the psalm ends, with nothing outwardly resolved, on a decision spoken aloud: but I will trust in you (v. 23).
verseByVerse.theology: The burden is thrown onto God, and the treacherous are thrown down by him.

verseByVerse.quote: Cast your burden on the LORD, and he will sustain you; he will never permit the righteous to be moved. But you, O God, will cast them down into the pit of destruction; men of blood and treachery shall not live out half their days. But I will trust in you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Throw your load onto the LORD: he may not remove it at once, but he will hold you up and deal with the treacherous, so the betrayed can end, with nothing yet resolved, by trusting him.

Cast your burden on the LORD. The psalm turns to whoever is listening. Cast is decisive: throw it, get it off you. The promise is not that the load will be removed but that he will sustain you: God holds the man rather than lifting the weight.

How Peter applies it. Peter tells a church under pressure the same, with the reason: “casting all your anxieties on him, because he cares for you” (1 Peter 5:7). The psalmist has spent twenty-one verses doing exactly this, so he is not giving advice from a comfortable chair.

How do I cast my burden on the LORD? By telling God exactly what it is and leaving it with him. Name it. The friend who turned on you, the diagnosis, the overdraft, the child who has stopped speaking to you: vague dread is hard to hand over. Hand it over in words. “In everything by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known to God” (Philippians 4:6). Do the next duty, and leave the rest. Casting a burden is not neglecting it: write the email, make the appointment, then refuse to carry tomorrow’s share tonight. Cast it again. At 2 a.m. the load will climb back on. That is not failure; throw it again, as often as it returns.

He carried the heaviest load. Christ has already carried the heaviest load of all, our sin, to the cross, and he still says, “Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28). The one who bore that will not refuse the smaller weights.

Cast them down into the pit. The same verb twice: we cast our burden onto God, and God casts the treacherous down. The burden and the judgment both end in his hands, not ours.

But I will trust in you. The psalm’s real ending. Nothing is resolved: the friend is still a traitor, the city still violent, the wings not given. What he has is a decision, said aloud, in the present tense.

Do the wicked always die young? No; Psalm 73 says they often prosper. This is the general pattern, not a law without exceptions: the wicked are never finally secure, and the psalmist’s hope rests on God, not on their timetable.

Uncertain wording. The word for burden occurs only here. It seems to mean what has been given you, your lot or load; the old Greek translation rendered it care, the word Peter uses for anxieties in 1 Peter 5:7.

55.title: Cast Your Burden on the LORD
55.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 55 is another Maskil of David among the Book Two psalms of a king under attack. In Psalm 54 he was betrayed by neighbours; here the traitor is a close friend, a man he once worshipped beside.

The message. The deepest wounds often come from those closest to us, and God lets his people tell him all of it: the terror, the wish to run away, the cry for justice. The answer the psalm finds is not wings to escape but God himself: “Cast your burden on the LORD, and he will sustain you.” He may not lift the weight at once, but he will hold up the one who carries it.

Why it was said. The heading names no occasion. Many link the psalm with Absalom’s revolt, when David’s trusted counsellor Ahithophel joined the conspiracy and Jerusalem became a city of plotting (2 Samuel 15:12, 31). That fits well, but it cannot be proved, and the psalm was left open so that every betrayed believer could pray it (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. Anguish (vv. 1–8): the terrors of death have fallen on him, and he longs for wings like a dove to fly away and be at rest. Betrayal (vv. 9–21): the city is full of violence and fraud, but the unbearable thing is that the enemy is “my companion, my familiar friend”; David hands his fierce prayer to God, keeps praying evening, morning and noon, and is heard, while the friend’s words, smooth as butter, hide drawn swords. Trust (vv. 22–23): cast your burden on the LORD; God will deal with the treacherous; “But I will trust in you.”

Where it leads. By pattern. Ahithophel, the counsellor who betrayed David, went home and hanged himself (2 Samuel 17:23), and so did Judas, the friend who betrayed David’s greater Son (Matthew 27:5). Jesus applied a psalm of betrayal to Judas (John 13:18), and Judas came with a kiss, speech smooth as butter. But unlike David, Jesus did not wish to fly away: in Gethsemane he said, “My soul is very sorrowful, even to death” (Mark 14:34), and stayed, to carry the heaviest burden of all. Because he bore it, Peter can tell the church to cast all its anxieties on God, “because he cares for you” (1 Peter 5:7).

For us. If someone close has turned on you, this psalm gives you words, and permission to be honest with God about the hurt and the wish to escape. Do not take revenge; hand the case to God. Then throw your load on him, again and again, trusting the one who was himself betrayed and never betrays his own.
55.theology:
The wish to escape is printed without rebuke, provided it is said to God (vv. 6-8), and the savage prayer of v. 15 is handed to God rather than acted on. The deepest wound is betrayal by a companion in worship (vv. 12-14), and smooth speech with war underneath is named as especially dangerous (v. 21).

Prayer in a long trouble keeps fixed hours and repeats itself, and it is heard (v. 17). Cast your burden promises that God will hold the man, not that the weight will vanish (v. 22), and the psalm ends unresolved, on a decision to trust.
55.examples: Many people have wished, in an office or a hospital corridor, that they could simply fly away; the psalm lets them say it to God. The friend who sat beside you in church and then turned on you is a wound Scripture names directly. And butter and oil are a fair picture of the unfailingly pleasant voice that hides a drawn sword.

keyVerse.quote: Cast your burden on the LORD, and he will sustain you; he will never permit the righteous to be moved.
keyVerse.note: Everything in the psalm has been building to this. David has done it himself for twenty-one verses, telling God the fear, the wish to escape and the betrayal, and now he urges us to do the same. The promise is not that the load will vanish but that God will hold us up, and Peter grounds it in God’s care for us (1 Peter 5:7), shown most fully in Christ, who carried our heaviest burden.

55.reflection:
David wishes he had wings like a dove to fly away (vv. 6–8), and Scripture records it without rebuke. When have you felt that way? What is the difference between running away from God and telling God you want to run away?

The deepest wound in the psalm is betrayal by a close friend and fellow worshipper (vv. 12–14, 20–21). Why does betrayal within the church hurt so much? How does Jesus, betrayed by Judas with a kiss, help those who have been hurt in this way?

David prays “evening and morning and at noon”, with the same complaint, and is heard (v. 17). What might regular, repeated prayer look like for you in a long trouble?

“Cast your burden on the LORD, and he will sustain you” (v. 22). What burden are you carrying now, and what would it mean to name it, hand it to God, do the next duty, and cast it again when it returns?

56.text: To the choirmaster: according to The Dove on Far-off Terebinths. A Miktam of David, when the Philistines seized him in Gath. 1Be gracious to me, O God, for man tramples on me; all day long an attacker oppresses me;2my enemies trample on me all day long, for many attack me proudly.3When I am afraid, I put my trust in you.4In God, whose word I praise, in God I trust; I shall not be afraid. What can flesh do to me?5All day long they injure my cause; all their thoughts are against me for evil.6They stir up strife, they lurk; they watch my steps, as they have waited for my life.7For their crime will they escape? In wrath cast down the peoples, O God!8You have kept count of my tossings; put my tears in your bottle. Are they not in your book?9Then my enemies will turn back in the day when I call. This I know, that God is for me.10In God, whose word I praise, in the LORD, whose word I praise,11in God I trust; I shall not be afraid. What can man do to me?12I must perform my vows to you, O God; I will render thank offerings to you.13For you have delivered my soul from death, yes, my feet from falling, that I may walk before God in the light of life.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Faith does not wait for fear to go before it trusts God. David is trampled by attackers all day long, and he says so (vv. 1–2). Then he sets fear and trust side by side: when I am afraid, I put my trust in you, and from that trust, resting on God’s word, comes the refrain: in God I trust, I shall not be afraid; what can flesh do to me? (vv. 3–4). The pressure goes on, with words twisted, steps watched and life hunted, and David hands the question every wronged person asks, will they escape?, to God (vv. 5–7).
verseByVerse.theology: Fear and trust in the same sentence, and the trust is the thing he does about the fear.

verseByVerse.quote: Be gracious to me, O God, for man tramples on me; all day long an attacker oppresses me; my enemies trample on me all day long, for many attack me proudly. When I am afraid, I put my trust in you. In God, whose word I praise, in God I trust; I shall not be afraid. What can flesh do to me? All day long they injure my cause; all their thoughts are against me for evil. They stir up strife, they lurk; they watch my steps, as they have waited for my life. For their crime will they escape? In wrath cast down the peoples, O God!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hounded all day long, David admits that he is afraid and trusts God anyway, resting on God’s word, so that what men can do to him loses its final power.

The setting. The heading puts this in Gath, the Philistine city where David escaped by pretending to be insane (1 Samuel 21:10–15). It was Goliath’s city, and David arrived carrying Goliath’s sword (1 Samuel 21:9). Psalm 34 belongs to the same episode and reads as the relief after the escape; this one is written from inside the fear, and the difference in tone shows.

Man tramples on me. Trample twice, all day long twice. The repetition is the point: it is the relentlessness that wears a person down, not any single blow.

When I am afraid, I put my trust in you. This has carried frightened Christians through many nights. It does not say “I am never afraid”, or “if I trusted properly I would not be afraid”. The fear is assumed and given a time (when, not if), and trust is what he does inside it. Faith here is not a feeling that replaces fear; it is an action taken while afraid.

I shall not be afraid. The next verse says he will not be afraid, one line after admitting that he is. Both are true: the fear is what he feels, and the fearlessness is the conclusion his trust reaches.

In God, whose word I praise. The ground of his trust is not his circumstances or his record but a word God has given, praised while the danger is still in the room. And what can flesh do to me? is a real question with a real answer: flesh can do a great deal, including kill him. The psalm means: nothing that finally counts.

What this looks like. Trusting while afraid is a set of small acts, not a mood. Admit the fear to God. The test results, the redundancy meeting, the noise downstairs at night: tell him plainly. Take hold of a word. Fix on one promise and say it over, such as This I know, that God is for me (v. 9). Ask the psalm’s question. What can flesh do to me? Name the worst that could happen, and then what it cannot touch. Do the duty in front of you, still afraid. Make the call, walk into the room; courage is often trust with shaking hands.

Because of Christ. Hebrews puts these words in every believer’s mouth: “The Lord is my helper; I will not fear; what can man do to me?” (Hebrews 13:6). Jesus knew fear in Gethsemane, greatly distressed and troubled (Mark 14:33), and still entrusted himself to his Father. So the fear that remains in us does not cancel our trust; he holds us through it.

All day long they injure my cause. The surveillance is patient: stirring up strife, lurking, watching his steps, waiting. Then the question a wronged person always asks, will they escape?, handed to God rather than answered by his own hand.

Uncertain wording. The ESV notes that verse 5 may be read they twist my words, exactly what people do to a man they have already decided about. Verse 7 is compressed, and some render it as a prayer (do not let them escape) rather than a question; either way the verdict is left to God. The tune name in the heading may also be read the silent dove of distant places, and the meaning of Miktam is unknown.
verseByVerse.note: The title links this psalm to the Philistines seizing David in Gath.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–13 — Put My Tears in Your Bottle
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God keeps a record of his people’s sorrows, and he is for them. David pictures God counting his sleepless tossings, storing his tears in a bottle and writing them in his book (v. 8). From that comes the one certainty he claims: this I know, that God is for me (v. 9). The refrain returns, fuller than before, with the covenant name added: in God I trust; I shall not be afraid (vv. 10–11). Then he promises thank offerings for a rescue already sure, and names its purpose: not mere survival, but to walk before God in the light of life (vv. 12–13).
verseByVerse.theology: Every sleepless turn is counted and every tear kept, and the rescue is for walking, not just surviving.

verseByVerse.quote: You have kept count of my tossings; put my tears in your bottle. Are they not in your book? Then my enemies will turn back in the day when I call. This I know, that God is for me. In God, whose word I praise, in the LORD, whose word I praise, in God I trust; I shall not be afraid. What can man do to me? I must perform my vows to you, O God; I will render thank offerings to you. For you have delivered my soul from death, yes, my feet from falling, that I may walk before God in the light of life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God keeps count of every sleepless night and every tear, and he is for his people; so David can say his confidence again and look forward to walking before God in the light of life.

God’s records. Three pictures say one thing: God records what nobody else notices.

You have kept count of my tossings. Either the turning of a man who cannot sleep, or the miles of a fugitive’s aimless travel; and God has kept count. Someone has been keeping a tally of the nights.

Put my tears in your bottle. Tears are the least durable thing a person produces; they dry in minutes and nobody sees most of them. He asks God to collect them in a flask, a leather bottle like the wineskins of the day, and keep them. It is one of the tenderest requests in Scripture, and it assumes a God who would want to. The last book of the Bible shows him doing more than keeping them: “He will wipe away every tear from their eyes” (Revelation 21:4).

Are they not in your book? The question expects yes. What is happening to you is written down. Nobody else is keeping this record. God is.

Does anyone keep count? The modern picture of the universe can make this verse sound naïve. The physicist Steven Weinberg wrote that the more the universe seems comprehensible, the more it also seems pointless, and many feel something like that without putting it so starkly. We are brief accidents on a small planet; our private griefs are noticed by a few friends, and then by nobody. If that is true, most tears are simply lost, and the hardest suffering is the suffering nobody saw. The psalm makes the opposite claim, a bigger one than it looks: the God who made the galaxies counts the nights a fugitive could not sleep. That is not sentiment but what Jesus taught: “even the hairs of your head are all numbered” (Matthew 10:30). And the God who keeps the record did not watch from a distance. In Christ he wept at a friend’s grave and cried out on a cross, so that no tear of his people is wasted, and one day there will be none left to cry.

This I know, that God is for me. The one certainty he claims, and it is not about the outcome. Paul puts it as a question no one can answer, “If God is for us, who can be against us?” (Romans 8:31), and gives the proof: God “did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all” (Romans 8:32). Both know how many are against them; the point is who is on their side.

What can man do to me? Verses 10 and 11 repeat the refrain of verse 4, expanded, with the covenant name, the LORD, added in the middle, rare in this part of the Psalter. Flesh has become man: the question is asked twice, because a frightened man has to say it more than once.

I must perform my vows to you. Promises made in danger are kept in safety, and he pledges thank offerings, sacrifices of gratitude, while still in the enemy city.

For you have delivered my soul from death. Past tense again: you have delivered. And the purpose is the best thing in the psalm. He was rescued not merely to stay alive but that I may walk before God in the light of life: to live in the open, in daylight, in God’s presence, after so long spent hiding and pretending to be mad. That is what God saves people for.

The light of life. David’s Son also prayed with tears to the one able to save him from death, and was heard (Hebrews 5:7): not spared death, but raised through it. Now he offers what David longed for: “Whoever follows me will not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life” (John 8:12).

Uncertain wording. My tossings may also be read my wanderings (ESV note). The Hebrew words for “wandering” and “bottle” sound alike, a play on words: the God who counts my wanderings keeps my tears in his flask.

56.title: When I Am Afraid, I Put My Trust in You
56.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 56 opens a run of psalms called Miktam (56–60), and like Psalm 54 its heading names the moment: “when the Philistines seized him in Gath.” David, fleeing Saul, had taken refuge in the home town of Goliath, was recognised, and escaped only by pretending to be mad (1 Samuel 21:10–15). Psalm 34 gives thanks after the escape; this psalm prays from inside the fear.

The message. Faith is not the absence of fear but trust in God while afraid. God keeps count of every sleepless night and stores every tear, and the one thing his people can be sure of is that he is for them. So what men can do loses its final power, and the rescued can look forward to walking before God in the light of life.

Why it was said. With Saul behind and Philistines around, David was alone in an enemy city, watched, misrepresented and in danger of his life (see the introduction on the titles). The psalm turns that fear into prayer.

How the chapter makes its case. Twice the psalm moves from danger to a refrain of trust. Trampled all day (vv. 1–2), he says, “When I am afraid, I put my trust in you”, and then the refrain: “in God I trust; I shall not be afraid. What can flesh do to me?” (vv. 3–4). Watched and misrepresented (vv. 5–7), he hands his enemies to God. Then God’s records: tossings counted, tears kept, “This I know, that God is for me” (vv. 8–9), and the refrain again, fuller (vv. 10–11). He ends paying vows for a deliverance that lets him walk before God in the light of life (vv. 12–13).

Where it leads. By pattern, and by the character of God revealed in Christ. Paul turns verse 9 into the triumphant question, “If God is for us, who can be against us?” (Romans 8:31), and proves it by the cross. David’s Son also prayed in fear and tears: he “offered up prayers and supplications, with loud cries and tears, to him who was able to save him from death, and he was heard” (Hebrews 5:7). The God who stores tears will at last “wipe away every tear” (Revelation 21:4), and Jesus calls himself the source of what David longed for: “Whoever follows me will not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life” (John 8:12).

For us. You do not have to stop being afraid before you can trust God; trust is what you do with the fear. Tell him plainly, hold on to his word, and remember that in Christ God is for you and no tear of yours is lost.
56.theology:
Verse 3 grants the fear and trusts anyway: faith here is not a feeling that replaces fear but a decision taken while afraid, grounded in God's word (v. 4). God keeps the records nobody else keeps (v. 8), and the one certainty claimed is not the outcome but that God is on his side (v. 9).

Deliverance has a purpose beyond survival: a life lived openly before God (v. 13).
56.examples: A soldier on night watch, or a parent beside a hospital bed, can pray verse 3 without pretending to be calm. Tears dry in minutes and most are never seen, yet the psalm pictures God collecting them in a flask. And a man who had spent weeks hiding and pretending to be mad looks forward to walking in daylight again, which is what God rescues people for.

keyVerse.quote: When I am afraid, I put my trust in you.
keyVerse.note: This short line holds the whole psalm. It does not deny the fear; it says what to do with it, and the refrains of verses 4 and 11 grow from it. Because in Christ God is for us (Romans 8:31), believers may pray it in any danger without pretending to be calm.

56.reflection:
“When I am afraid, I put my trust in you” (v. 3). Why is it important that the psalm assumes fear rather than forbidding it? What does it look like for you to trust God while you are still afraid?

David’s trust rests on “God, whose word I praise” (vv. 4, 10). Which promise of God would you take hold of in your present fears, and how could you keep it before you?

God counts our tossings and keeps our tears (v. 8). How does it change your experience of hidden suffering to know that God notices and records it? How could we as a church notice what others are quietly carrying?

David was rescued “that I may walk before God in the light of life” (v. 13). What has God rescued you for, and how does Jesus as “the light of life” (John 8:12) shape the way you live now?

57.text: To the choirmaster: according to Do Not Destroy. A Miktam of David, when he fled from Saul, in the cave. 1Be merciful to me, O God, be merciful to me, for in you my soul takes refuge; in the shadow of your wings I will take refuge, till the storms of destruction pass by.2I cry out to God Most High, to God who fulfills his purpose for me.3He will send from heaven and save me; he will put to shame him who tramples on me. Selah God will send out his steadfast love and his faithfulness!4My soul is in the midst of lions; I lie down amid fiery beasts— the children of man, whose teeth are spears and arrows, whose tongues are sharp swords.5Be exalted, O God, above the heavens! Let your glory be over all the earth!6They set a net for my steps; my soul was bowed down. They dug a pit in my way, but they have fallen into it themselves. Selah7My heart is steadfast, O God, my heart is steadfast! I will sing and make melody!8Awake, my glory! Awake, O harp and lyre! I will awake the dawn!9I will give thanks to you, O Lord, among the peoples; I will sing praises to you among the nations.10For your steadfast love is great to the heavens, your faithfulness to the clouds.11Be exalted, O God, above the heavens! Let your glory be over all the earth!

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — In the Shadow of Your Wings
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The hunted man’s refuge is God himself, and his first desire is God’s glory. Hiding in a cave from Saul, David asks for mercy and shelters under God’s wings until the storm passes, sure that God Most High is fulfilling his purpose and will send his steadfast love and faithfulness from heaven (vv. 1–3). He lies among men as fierce as lions, whose words are weapons (v. 4), yet his central request is that God be exalted above the heavens (v. 5). He admits that his soul was bowed down, and sees his hunters fall into the pit they dug (v. 6).
verseByVerse.theology: A man hiding in a cave says he is sheltering under wings, and asks first for God's glory.

verseByVerse.quote: Be merciful to me, O God, be merciful to me, for in you my soul takes refuge; in the shadow of your wings I will take refuge, till the storms of destruction pass by. I cry out to God Most High, to God who fulfills his purpose for me. He will send from heaven and save me; he will put to shame him who tramples on me. Selah God will send out his steadfast love and his faithfulness!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hiding from Saul in a cave, David takes refuge in God himself, sure that God is still carrying out his purpose for him.

In the cave. The heading places him in the cave, fleeing from Saul: either Adullam (1 Samuel 22:1) or En-gedi, where Saul came in unaware and David cut off the corner of his robe but refused to harm him (1 Samuel 24). Its tune, Do Not Destroy, is what David later said over the sleeping Saul (1 Samuel 26:9).

In the shadow of your wings. He is in a refuge made of rock, and describes it as feathers: the bird covering her young, the image of Psalm 17:8 and of Ruth coming under God’s wings (Ruth 2:12). The stone keeps the rain off; God is keeping him. And he asks only to be covered till the storms of destruction pass by, not for the storm to stop. That is often the whole of what can be prayed. That is often the whole of what can be prayed.

God who fulfills his purpose for me. Anointed king and living in a hole in the ground, he says this in the present tense, still in the cave. The purpose is not suspended while circumstances are bad; the cave is part of it.

God will send out his steadfast love and his faithfulness! God’s loyal covenant love and his faithfulness to his word are dispatched like messengers (compare Psalm 43:3), sent on errands to particular people in particular caves.

Anointed, hunted, then exalted. That is the road David’s greater Son walked: anointed, hunted, despised, and only then exalted (Philippians 2:8–9). God’s purpose for him was fulfilled through the suffering, not in spite of it, and his people are told the same of their trials (Romans 8:28–29). The wings David hid under were spread wide in Jesus (Matthew 23:37).

Uncertain wording. The meaning of Miktam (Psalms 16 and 56 to 60) is lost; guesses include “inscription” and “golden poem”.
verseByVerse.note: The title links this psalm to David hiding from Saul in the cave.

verseByVerse.quote: My soul is in the midst of lions; I lie down amid fiery beasts— the children of man, whose teeth are spears and arrows, whose tongues are sharp swords. Be exalted, O God, above the heavens! Let your glory be over all the earth! They set a net for my steps; my soul was bowed down. They dug a pit in my way, but they have fallen into it themselves. Selah
verseByVerse.commentary:
Among men as savage as lions, David asks first not for escape but for God’s glory, and sees their trap close on themselves.

My soul is in the midst of lions. The lions turn out to be men, the children of man, and their weapons are their mouths: teeth like spears and arrows, tongues like sharp swords. Speech is a weapon for the third time in six psalms (52:2; 55:21), and Saul’s court ran on slander (1 Samuel 24:9). And I lie down: the lions are his neighbours.

Be exalted, O God, above the heavens! In the middle of the lions comes the psalm’s central request, and it is not “get me out”. It is that God’s glory fill the earth, which will not shorten his danger by a day. A hunted man’s top priority is God’s reputation in places he will never visit: the order Jesus taught, hallowed be your name before daily bread (Matthew 6:9–11).

They dug a pit in my way. The pit comes again (7:15; 9:15): his hunters dug it and fell in. The middle clause is the honest one: my soul was bowed down. The trap weighed on him before it caught them. Faith in these psalms is rarely unhurt; it is bowed down and still speaking.

Uncertain wording. The word behind fiery beasts means something like “blazing” or “devouring”; some versions have “ravenous beasts”.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A heart fixed on God can sing while the danger is unchanged. Nothing outside the cave has altered, but David’s heart is steadfast and he resolves to sing (v. 7). He wakes himself and his harp, meaning to be singing before the sun comes up (v. 8). His audience is the nations, because God’s steadfast love and faithfulness are as high as the heavens (vv. 9–10). The refrain returns (v. 11): the man who began by asking to be covered ends by asking nothing for himself, only that God’s glory fill the earth. These verses were later joined to part of Psalm 60 to make Psalm 108.
verseByVerse.theology: The refrain returns, and the fugitive announces that he intends to wake the sunrise.

verseByVerse.quote: My heart is steadfast, O God, my heart is steadfast! I will sing and make melody! Awake, my glory! Awake, O harp and lyre! I will awake the dawn! I will give thanks to you, O Lord, among the peoples; I will sing praises to you among the nations. For your steadfast love is great to the heavens, your faithfulness to the clouds. Be exalted, O God, above the heavens! Let your glory be over all the earth!
verseByVerse.commentary:
With nothing outside changed, David’s heart is fixed on God, and he resolves to wake the dawn with praise meant for the nations.

My heart is steadfast, O God. He says it twice, telling himself as much as God. Steadfast is fixed, settled, prepared, the opposite of the bowed-down soul of verse 6, yet the lions are still there and the cave is still a cave. A steadfast heart is not a mood waiting for good news; it is a decision about God made before the news comes.

I will awake the dawn! He wakes himself first (my glory), then the harp and lyre he may have had with him in the cave, and then the sunrise. Normally the dawn wakes the singer; David means to be up before it, so that the sun rises to find the music already going: a fugitive with soldiers outside decides to be the first thing awake in the country.

I will sing praises to you among the nations. His audience is not the cave. He expects this song to travel, because the love behind it is great to the heavens. Paul quotes the matching vow of Psalm 18:49 to show that God always meant the Gentiles to praise him with his people (Romans 15:9). The song written underground travelled further than its singer could have guessed.

Let your glory be over all the earth! The refrain closes the psalm. The man who asked to be covered until the storm passed ends asking nothing for himself, only that God be high and his glory wide.

The song of the risen King. David vowed to sing among the nations; Christ does it, leading his people’s praise (Hebrews 2:12). The Son of David came out of a rock tomb at dawn, and the praise of the nations has been rising ever since.

Uncertain wording. The ESV notes that my glory may mean my whole being, as Psalm 108:1 reads.
verseByVerse.note: Verses 7–11 reappear in Psalm 108.

57.title: I Will Awake the Dawn
57.overview:
Where we are. Psalms 52 to 59 come largely from the years when David was hunted by Saul, and Psalm 57 follows straight on from 56. There David was among the Philistines in Gath; from Gath he escaped to the cave of Adullam (1 Samuel 22:1), and both psalms open with the same cry for mercy. This is the first of three psalms set to the tune Do Not Destroy (57 to 59).

The message. The man God has promised to make king is hiding in a hole in the rock, surrounded by men like lions, and he says he is sheltering under God’s wings. Danger does not cancel God’s purpose; the cave is where it is being carried out. So the deepest prayer of a hunted believer can be, not first “get me out”, but “be exalted, O God”, and a heart fixed on that can sing before the dawn.

Why it was said. David had been anointed but not crowned. Saul wanted him dead, and he lived as an outlaw in caves and wilderness (1 Samuel 22 to 24; see the introduction on the titles). He needed to know whether God’s promise still stood when everything visible denied it.

How the chapter makes its case. Two halves, each closing with the refrain. The refuge (vv. 1–3): mercy, the shadow of God’s wings, God Most High who fulfils his purpose, and steadfast love and faithfulness sent from heaven. The danger (vv. 4–6): lions whose tongues are swords, the refrain asking only for God’s glory (v. 5), and the pit that catches its diggers. The song (vv. 7–11): a steadfast heart, a harp to wake the dawn, praise among the nations for a love as high as the heavens, and the refrain again (v. 11).

Where it leads. By pattern. David, anointed but hunted, whose road to the throne ran through a cave, foreshadows his greater Son: anointed by the Spirit, hunted from his birth, laid in a tomb cut in the rock, and only then highly exalted (Philippians 2:9). Jesus used the picture of verse 1 himself, longing to gather Jerusalem “as a hen gathers her brood under her wings” (Matthew 23:37); the wings David hid under were spread out in him. And the song David meant for the nations is now sung by them, as Paul says, so “that the Gentiles might glorify God for his mercy” (Romans 15:9).

For us. You may be in a cave of your own, waiting on a promise of God while everything says the opposite. His purpose for you is not suspended there; in Christ it is being carried out. Shelter in him, ask first for his glory, and let your heart be fixed enough to sing before the morning comes.
57.theology:
A refuge of rock is described as a refuge of feathers, and what is asked is covering while the storm passes, not the cancelling of the storm (v. 1). The cave is not an interruption of God's purpose but part of it (v. 2), and God's steadfast love and faithfulness are sent out like messengers to a man in a cave (v. 3).

The psalm's own petition asks nothing for the psalmist: Be exalted, O God (vv. 5, 11). Faith here is bowed down and still speaking (v. 6), and steadfastness is declared with nothing outside changed (v. 7).
57.examples: Picture a man under a rock ledge in the dark who insists that he is sheltering under feathers. Or a fugitive with soldiers outside who resolves to be singing before the sun is up, so that the dawn rises to find the music already going. And among the lions, his first request is that God's glory should fill places he will never visit.

keyVerse.quote: Be exalted, O God, above the heavens! Let your glory be over all the earth!
keyVerse.note: The refrain stands at the centre and at the end of the psalm (vv. 5, 11), and it asks nothing for David. A hunted man in a cave makes God’s glory his first request, and that is what steadies his heart and turns his lament into song. It is the first petition Jesus taught his disciples: hallowed be your name.

57.reflection:
David describes a cave of rock as the shadow of God’s wings (v. 1). What would it mean for you to see God, rather than your circumstances or your own resources, as your real shelter in a present difficulty?

He calls God the one “who fulfills his purpose for me” while he is still hiding (v. 2). How does Jesus’ path from suffering to glory help you believe that God’s purpose is not suspended in your hard seasons?

Surrounded by lions, David’s central request is that God be exalted (v. 5). What would change in your prayers if God’s glory came first, before your own requests?

Nothing outside has changed, yet David says “My heart is steadfast” and plans to wake the dawn with song (vv. 7–8). What helps you to praise God before the trouble is over, and how could you practise that this week?

58.text: To the choirmaster: according to Do Not Destroy. A Miktam of David. 1Do you indeed decree what is right, you gods? Do you judge the children of man uprightly?2No, in your hearts you devise wrongs; your hands deal out violence on earth.3The wicked are estranged from the womb; they go astray from birth, speaking lies.4They have venom like the venom of a serpent, like the deaf adder that stops its ear,5so that it does not hear the voice of charmers or of the cunning enchanter.6O God, break the teeth in their mouths; tear out the fangs of the young lions, O LORD!7Let them vanish like water that runs away; when he aims his arrows, let them be blunted.8Let them be like the snail that dissolves into slime, like the stillborn child who never sees the sun.9Sooner than your pots can feel the heat of thorns, whether green or ablaze, may he sweep them away!10The righteous will rejoice when he sees the vengeance; he will bathe his feet in the blood of the wicked.11Mankind will say, "Surely there is a reward for the righteous; surely there is a God who judges on earth."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — Do You Indeed Decree What Is Right?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The rulers appointed to give God’s justice have become its enemies, and they will not listen. David puts the judges themselves on trial: do they decree what is right? No; they plan wrongs in their hearts and deal out violence with their hands (vv. 1–2). Their corruption is no accident of circumstance but runs back to birth, and their words are lies (v. 3). Like a snake that will not hear the charmer, they have closed their ears to every appeal (vv. 4–5), which is why the psalm stops arguing with them and turns to God.
verseByVerse.theology: The psalm opens by cross-examining the judges, and finds that the judges’ bench is where the violence is being planned.

verseByVerse.quote: Do you indeed decree what is right, you gods? Do you judge the children of man uprightly? No, in your hearts you devise wrongs; your hands deal out violence on earth. The wicked are estranged from the womb; they go astray from birth, speaking lies. They have venom like the venom of a serpent, like the deaf adder that stops its ear, so that it does not hear the voice of charmers or of the cunning enchanter.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The judges who should give God’s justice have become the source of violence: liars from birth, and as deaf to appeal as a snake that stops its ear.

Do you indeed decree what is right, you gods? The tune is Psalm 57’s, Do Not Destroy, and this time the psalm asks God to do a great deal of destroying. Those addressed are judges, whom Scripture can call gods because they do God’s own work of deciding between right and wrong for others (Psalm 82:1, 6; compare Exodus 22:8–9, where the KJV reads the judges). The questions are accusations, and the answer comes at once: No. The violence on the streets was devised in their hearts. When justice is for sale, the men in robes are not bystanders to the violence; they are its source.

The wicked are estranged from the womb. The teaching of 51:5, that we are sinful from birth, applied to others. It is not a comment on any individual baby; it means this corruption is no accident of training or circumstance, but began long before these men were judges.

Like the deaf adder that stops its ear. A snake charmer can handle a snake that listens. This one has stopped its ear, deliberately, the picture suggests, so that the music cannot reach it. There is a deafness that is chosen, and no reasonable appeal gets through it. That is why the psalm turns to God in the next verse: it has already tried talking.

Before a bought court. Jesus stood before such a bench and “continued entrusting himself to him who judges justly” (1 Peter 2:23).

Where Christians differ. Most take the gods of verse 1 to be human rulers, as in Psalm 82, which Jesus applied to those “to whom the word of God came” (John 10:35). Some see heavenly powers behind unjust human rule.

This commentary’s view. Human judges: they deal out violence on earth and have gone astray from birth. Either way they are creatures under God’s judgment.

Uncertain wording. As the Hebrew stands, the word rendered you gods seems to mean “in silence”; a small change of vowels gives “gods” or “mighty ones” (the ESV notes “you mighty lords”), and the KJV has “O congregation”.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–11 — Surely There Is a God Who Judges
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Justice is handed wholly to God, and its goal is that the world should know he judges. David asks God to break the teeth of these predators, so that their power to harm is gone, and to make them vanish like water into sand, like a snail melting away, like a child who never sees the sun, swept off before a cooking pot can heat (vv. 6–9). Then the righteous will rejoice, not in cruelty but in justice done at last, and everyone will say that righteousness is rewarded and there is a God who judges on earth (vv. 10–11).
verseByVerse.theology: Every request is handed to God, and what the psalm finally wants is for the world to know that justice exists.

verseByVerse.quote: O God, break the teeth in their mouths; tear out the fangs of the young lions, O LORD! Let them vanish like water that runs away; when he aims his arrows, let them be blunted. Let them be like the snail that dissolves into slime, like the stillborn child who never sees the sun. Sooner than your pots can feel the heat of thorns, whether green or ablaze, may he sweep them away!
verseByVerse.commentary:
David hands the corrupt judges wholly to God, asking him to break their power to harm and make them pass away quickly, and he takes no vengeance himself.

A hard passage. This is the hardest passage in this stretch of the Psalter, and there is no honest way to make it comfortable. Its pictures are of things that come to nothing: water running into the ground, a snail leaving only slime, a fire of thorns swept off before the pot is warm. The wicked look permanent; God can end them quickly.

Like the stillborn child. A picture of plans that come to nothing; it is no judgment on any child who died before birth. Parents who have lost a child this way may hold to what Scripture says elsewhere: God knits a child together in the womb (139:13), and David, bereaved of an infant, said I shall go to him (2 Samuel 12:23).

Three limits on the prayer. First, every verb is addressed to God. O God, break … tear out … let them vanish. The psalmist asks for nothing he intends to do himself, which is the difference between imprecation (asking God to judge) and revenge, and exactly what Paul commands: never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God (Romans 12:19). A man praying this way has disarmed himself. Second, the images are of disabling, not torture. The prayer is that the teeth, fangs and arrows stop working, and a judge’s weapon is his mouth. Third, the psalm is not personal. It is about a legal system devouring the helpless, which God hates. A person who feels nothing when the courts are bought has a defective conscience, not a superior one.

Through the cross. The Christian prays this psalm through the cross, where God’s judgment fell on his own Son, so that people who deserve verse 6 may find mercy. That does not cancel the prayer: Revelation has the martyrs praying it still (Revelation 6:10).

May a Christian pray this? Jesus commands us to love our enemies (Matthew 5:44; compare Romans 12:14), but David hands vengeance to God, and his cry is against unjust rulers who will not repent. A Christian may pray for God to break the power of such evil while praying for the persons to repent, as Jesus prayed for his executioners (Luke 23:34). Christ bore the curse for every enemy who turns (Galatians 3:13).

Uncertain wording. In verse 7 it is unclear who he is who aims the arrows, the wicked or God; either way the arrows are to fail. The word for snail is rare, and verse 9, as the ESV notes, is obscure, though it seems to picture thorns under a pot swept away before the pot feels the heat. The overall sense is clear.

verseByVerse.quote: The righteous will rejoice when he sees the vengeance; he will bathe his feet in the blood of the wicked. Mankind will say, "Surely there is a reward for the righteous; surely there is a God who judges on earth."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When God acts at last, his people will rejoice that justice is done, and the world will confess that God really does judge.
