He will bathe his feet in the blood of the wicked. The picture is a battlefield after God has acted, the ground so wet that a man’s feet are washed as he walks through. The killing is not the righteous man’s. The rejoicing is not glee but the relief of people who had begun to believe that nothing would ever be put right, when it finally is.

Surely there is a God who judges on earth. This is what the whole psalm has been after: that everyone should see again that justice exists. The two surelys answer the two questions of verse 1. Anyone who has watched the guilty walk free with a smile knows how much they want verse 11 to be true, and this is God’s word saying it is, on earth and not only in eternity.

The judge God has appointed. The nearest New Testament image to verse 10 is the rider whose own robe is dipped in blood, who will tread the winepress of the fury of the wrath of God the Almighty (Revelation 19:13, 15), while the armies following him wear white and carry nothing. God has named the judge (Acts 17:31): the one who was unjustly judged and died for the unjust.

For the wronged. This psalm lets you bring outrage at injustice to God in strong words. Leaving vengeance to him never means staying silent or unprotected: where there is abuse or danger, tell the authorities and get to safety the same day.

58.title: A God Who Judges on Earth
58.overview:
Where we are. This is the second of the three psalms set to Do Not Destroy (57 to 59), another Miktam of David. The heading names no occasion. After two psalms about David’s own danger, this one turns to a public evil: rulers who use the courts to do violence.

The message. When those appointed to judge on God’s behalf become the source of injustice and will not listen to any appeal, God’s people need neither give up on justice nor take it into their own hands. They may cry to God to disarm the wicked, sure that he will act, until the whole world says, “Surely there is a God who judges on earth.”

Why it was said. Israel’s judges, elders and kings were meant to give God’s own justice to the weak (Deuteronomy 16:18–20), and Scripture can call them “gods” because they judged in his place (Psalm 82:6). When they took bribes and planned violence, their victims had nowhere left to appeal but heaven (see the introduction on the psalms that curse).

How the chapter makes its case. The accusation (vv. 1–5): the judges are questioned and found guilty; they devise wrongs and deal out violence, are liars from birth, and like a deaf snake refuse every appeal. The petition (vv. 6–9): every request is handed to God, to break their teeth and make them drain away, wither and be swept off before the pot can heat. The outcome (vv. 10–11): the righteous rejoice when God acts, and mankind confesses that righteousness is rewarded and God judges.

Where it leads. By the character of God revealed in Christ. The God this psalm longs to see judging has named the judge: “he will judge the world in righteousness by a man whom he has appointed” (Acts 17:31), and that man is Jesus. When he stood before corrupt courts himself, he did not curse them but “continued entrusting himself to him who judges justly” (1 Peter 2:23), the very stance this psalm teaches. And at the cross the judgment the wicked deserve fell on him, so that even unjust judges and liars may be forgiven before the day of verse 11.

For us. Do not grow numb to injustice; a conscience that feels nothing when the courts are bought is defective, not superior. Bring the outrage to God rather than to revenge, pray for wrongdoers to repent, and work for honest justice where you can, knowing that the last word belongs to Christ.
58.theology:
The judges are called gods because they do God's work of judging (v. 1), and the violence of the streets is devised on their bench (v. 2). Their deafness is chosen, so the psalm turns from argument to prayer.

The prayer is not softened, but it is handed wholly to God, aimed at disabling the weapons of the unjust, and free of personal grudge. Its goal is that the world should know again that there is a God who judges on earth (v. 11).
58.examples: Imagine a courtroom where the verdict was bought before the hearing: this psalm is written from the public gallery. The snake that presses its ear down so that the charmer's music cannot reach it is a picture of a conscience that has chosen not to hear. And the closing cry is what every victim of a bought court longs to hear said aloud: someone does judge.

keyVerse.quote: Mankind will say, “Surely there is a reward for the righteous; surely there is a God who judges on earth.”
keyVerse.note: This is what the whole psalm has been after: not revenge, but the open vindication of justice. Its two “surelys” answer the two questions put to the corrupt judges in verse 1. The New Testament names the judge: God “will judge the world in righteousness by a man whom he has appointed” (Acts 17:31).

58.reflection:
The psalm accuses judges whose violence is planned “in your hearts” before it is dealt out by their hands (v. 2). Where in our own society, or in our own small share of authority at home, work or church, is that temptation real?

The deaf adder “stops its ear” so that no appeal can reach it (vv. 4–5). What are the signs that a heart is becoming deaf to correction, and how does the gospel keep our ears open?

Every request in verses 6 to 9 is handed to God, and none is something David will do himself. How does this prayer differ from revenge? How can we pray it alongside Jesus’ command to love our enemies?

Verse 11 longs for all to see “a God who judges on earth”. How does knowing that Jesus, who was unjustly condemned, will judge the world help you to bear injustice now and to work for justice?

59.text: To the choirmaster: according to Do Not Destroy. A Miktam of David, when Saul sent men to watch his house in order to kill him. 1Deliver me from my enemies, O my God; protect me from those who rise up against me;2deliver me from those who work evil, and save me from bloodthirsty men.3For behold, they lie in wait for my life; fierce men stir up strife against me. For no transgression or sin of mine, O LORD,4for no fault of mine, they run and make ready. Awake, come to meet me, and see!5You, LORD God of hosts, are God of Israel. Rouse yourself to punish all the nations; spare none of those who treacherously plot evil. Selah6Each evening they come back, howling like dogs and prowling about the city.7There they are, bellowing with their mouths with swords in their lips— for "Who," they think, "will hear us?"8But you, O LORD, laugh at them; you hold all the nations in derision.9O my Strength, I will watch for you, for you, O God, are my fortress.10My God in his steadfast love will meet me; God will let me look in triumph on my enemies.11Kill them not, lest my people forget; make them totter by your power and bring them down, O Lord, our shield!12For the sin of their mouths, the words of their lips, let them be trapped in their pride. For the cursing and lies that they utter,13consume them in wrath; consume them till they are no more, that they may know that God rules over Jacob to the ends of the earth. Selah14Each evening they come back, howling like dogs and prowling about the city.15They wander about for food and growl if they do not get their fill.16But I will sing of your strength; I will sing aloud of your steadfast love in the morning. For you have been to me a fortress and a refuge in the day of my distress.17O my Strength, I will sing praises to you, for you, O God, are my fortress, the God who shows me steadfast love.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — For No Fault of Mine
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The innocent man surrounded by enemies cries to God, and God laughs at those who think nobody hears. With assassins outside his house, David asks four times to be rescued from bloodthirsty men (vv. 1–2), and insists that he has done nothing to deserve it (vv. 3–4). He calls on the LORD God of hosts, Israel’s God, to wake and judge all who plot treachery (vv. 4–5). Each evening his enemies prowl like scavenging dogs, boasting as if no one could hear (vv. 6–7). But someone does: the LORD laughs at them and holds all the nations in derision (v. 8).
verseByVerse.theology: Watchers surround a man who has done nothing, and God laughs at them.

verseByVerse.quote: Deliver me from my enemies, O my God; protect me from those who rise up against me; deliver me from those who work evil, and save me from bloodthirsty men. For behold, they lie in wait for my life; fierce men stir up strife against me. For no transgression or sin of mine, O LORD, for no fault of mine, they run and make ready. Awake, come to meet me, and see! You, LORD God of hosts, are God of Israel. Rouse yourself to punish all the nations; spare none of those who treacherously plot evil. Selah Each evening they come back, howling like dogs and prowling about the city. There they are, bellowing with their mouths with swords in their lips— for "Who," they think, "will hear us?" But you, O LORD, laugh at them; you hold all the nations in derision.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Surrounded by men sent to kill him, though he has done them no wrong, David cries to God to wake and act, and God laughs at those who think no one hears.

When Saul sent men to watch his house. The heading fixes the night (1 Samuel 19:11). David is inside; the assassins wait outside in the dark for morning. His wife Michal let him down through a window and put an idol in the bed to buy him time. Four requests in two verses: he asks the same thing four ways because the men are outside.

For no fault of mine. Twice he says it. He is not claiming to be sinless (the psalms of this same author say the opposite), but that in this matter he has done nothing to deserve a death squad, and Scripture lets an innocent man say so plainly. Awake is the bold speech of faith, not a belief that God sleeps.

Rouse yourself to punish all the nations. Why all the nations, when the enemies are Saul’s men? Perhaps because those who hunt God’s anointed have joined his enemies, whatever their nationality; many also think the psalm was later sung by all Israel against foreign foes.

Howling like dogs. Not wolves in the wild but dogs, the scavenging packs that came into ancient towns after dark, circling, howling, looking for anything left out. Saul’s men are reduced to a nuisance that comes with nightfall, and their creed is that of Psalms 10 and 50: nobody is listening.

But you, O LORD, laugh at them. Somebody is listening. The laugh is the one from Psalms 2 and 37, and it lands on a besieged house in a small town: the men outside think they are unobserved, and heaven finds them absurd.

Hated without a cause. In Psalm 2 that laughter falls on rulers plotting against the LORD’s Anointed, and the apostles prayed that psalm about the plot against Jesus (Acts 4:25–27). The anointed man hunted for no fault of mine is a pattern fulfilled in Jesus, David’s greater Son, of whom even Pilate said, I find no guilt in him (John 18:38). David slipped out through a window; Jesus let the dogs close in (Psalm 22:16), for those who hunted him.

In everyday life. If, like David, you are in danger from someone in your own home, get to safety and get help, as he did.

Uncertain wording. The ESV notes that the Hebrew lacks they think in verse 7, so Who will hear us? may be a shout as much as a thought.
verseByVerse.note: The title links this psalm to Saul’s men watching David’s house.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–17 — Kill Them Not, Lest My People Forget
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God is the fortress and the faithful lover of his servant, so the servant can leave the enemy to him and sing. David watches for God, his strength and fortress, sure that God’s steadfast love will meet him (vv. 9–10). He asks that the enemies be humbled rather than simply killed, so that God’s people will not forget, and brought down for their lies, so that all may know God rules (vv. 11–13). The dogs come back (vv. 14–15), but he plans to sing of God’s strength and love in the morning, to the God who shows him steadfast love (vv. 16–17).
verseByVerse.theology: He asks God not to kill them, so that the lesson lasts, and schedules his singing for dawn.

verseByVerse.quote: O my Strength, I will watch for you, for you, O God, are my fortress. My God in his steadfast love will meet me; God will let me look in triumph on my enemies. Kill them not, lest my people forget; make them totter by your power and bring them down, O Lord, our shield! For the sin of their mouths, the words of their lips, let them be trapped in their pride. For the cursing and lies that they utter, consume them in wrath; consume them till they are no more, that they may know that God rules over Jacob to the ends of the earth. Selah
verseByVerse.commentary:
David waits for God, his fortress, and asks that his enemies be humbled rather than simply killed, so that God’s people will learn that God rules.

O my Strength, I will watch for you. They are watching the house; he will watch for God: the same verb, turned into worship. And inside a surrounded house he calls God his fortress, which is exactly what a house is not, tonight.

Kill them not, lest my people forget. He asks for the men to be left alive and humbled, and gives his reason. A dead enemy is forgotten by the next generation. A humbled one, still walking the city with everyone knowing what he tried and what became of him, is a standing lesson. The psalm wants the teaching to outlast the incident, and is prepared to let the men live to get it. That is a long way from bloodlust.

Consume them in wrath. The two petitions sit oddly together (do not kill them, and consume them), and the psalm does not tidy it up; that is what praying under threat sounds like. But both aim at the same end: that they may know that God rules to the ends of the earth.

Brought down to know. In Christ God went further than David asked. Saul of Tarsus, who hunted the church, was brought down on the road and made to know who rules (Acts 9:4–5), and lived as a standing lesson of mercy (1 Timothy 1:16).

Textual note. In verse 9 most Hebrew manuscripts read his strength (so the KJV); the ESV follows some manuscripts and ancient translations in reading O my Strength, matching verse 17.

verseByVerse.quote: Each evening they come back, howling like dogs and prowling about the city. They wander about for food and growl if they do not get their fill. But I will sing of your strength; I will sing aloud of your steadfast love in the morning. For you have been to me a fortress and a refuge in the day of my distress. O my Strength, I will sing praises to you, for you, O God, are my fortress, the God who shows me steadfast love.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The danger is unchanged, but David plans to sing in the morning, because the God who has been his fortress loves him.

Each evening they come back. The refrain returns unchanged, which is the psalm’s honesty: after all that prayer, the dogs are still doing their rounds. They growl when they go unfed, and they go unfed every night that David survives.

But I will sing of your strength. The dogs come at evening; he schedules his singing for the morning. Psalm 57 had him waking the dawn with a harp in a cave; here he sets the alarm from inside a besieged house. And the tense has turned: you have been to me a fortress, written at night, about a siege that is not over.

The God who shows me steadfast love. The psalm ends on my Strength and adds the words that make the difference between a fortress and a friend. Any strong God can be a wall. This one loves him, and that is what gets a hunted man through a night of howling.

A morning appointed. The longest night ended with a morning: an empty tomb on the first day of the week. Because of it, every night of his people has a dawn appointed. If fear steals your sleep for weeks, talk to a pastor or biblical counsellor and see your doctor; that is no failure of faith.

59.title: Howling Like Dogs
59.overview:
Where we are. The third of the Do Not Destroy psalms (57 to 59) goes back to the first night of the hunted years. Its heading names the night Saul sent men to watch David’s house to kill him, when Michal let him down through a window (1 Samuel 19:11–17), long before the cave of Psalm 57.

The message. When enemies surround you for no fault of your own, God is neither asleep nor impressed: he laughs at those who think nobody hears. He is your fortress and, more than that, the God who loves you. So you can ask him to deal with evil in the way that best teaches his people, and plan to sing in the morning while the howling still goes on.

Why it was said. David was Saul’s son-in-law and his most successful captain, and had done him nothing but good, yet Saul’s jealousy had turned to murder (1 Samuel 18 to 19; see the introduction on the titles). The psalm was later sung by all Israel, which may be why it widens to all the nations (v. 5).

How the chapter makes its case. Two halves, each with the refrain of the howling dogs and each ending with God as fortress. The siege (vv. 1–8): a cry for rescue from bloodthirsty men, a plea of innocence, a call for God to wake, the dogs prowling at evening, and God’s laughter. The answer (vv. 9–17): God awaited as strength and fortress, a plea that the enemies be humbled rather than simply killed so that God’s people learn, the dogs again, and the morning song to the God who shows steadfast love.

Where it leads. By pattern. David, the anointed one hunted for no fault of mine, foreshadows his greater Son, who took the psalms’ words as fulfilled in himself: “They hated me without a cause” (John 15:25). The laughter of verse 8 is the laughter of Psalm 2 at rulers plotting against the LORD’s Anointed, a psalm the apostles prayed about the plot against Jesus (Acts 4:25–27). But David escaped through a window in the night; Jesus did not escape. He let the dogs close in (Psalm 22:16), and on the third morning he rose, so that his people can sing of God’s strength and steadfast love whatever is prowling outside.

For us. When you are wronged without cause, you may say so plainly to God. Hand the enemy to him, ask that evil be dealt with in a way that teaches rather than merely satisfies, and plan your morning praise while the night is still loud. In Christ the strong God is also the God who loves you.
59.theology:
Scripture lets an innocent man say plainly that he has done nothing to deserve this (vv. 3-4), and answers the watchers' creed that nobody hears with heaven's laughter (vv. 7-8).

Verse 11 asks that the enemies be humbled rather than killed, so that the lesson outlasts the incident, and even the fiercest petition aims at knowledge of God's rule (v. 13). The singing is planned for morning while the howling still goes on, and the last word is not power but affection: the God who shows me steadfast love (v. 17).
59.examples: Picture a house at night with men waiting outside, a wife letting her husband down from a window, and an idol in the bed to buy time. Then picture the stray dogs that roamed every ancient town after dark, howling at the edges. The psalm's answer to both is a man inside who books his singing for the morning, because the God he trusts is not only strong but fond of him.

keyVerse.quote: But I will sing of your strength; I will sing aloud of your steadfast love in the morning. For you have been to me a fortress and a refuge in the day of my distress.
keyVerse.note: This verse answers the howling refrain that comes just before it. While the dogs still prowl, David plans the morning’s praise and speaks of God’s protection in the past tense. Strength and steadfast love belong together: the God who guards him also loves him, and that is what carries him through the night.

59.reflection:
David says twice that he is hunted “for no fault of mine” (vv. 3–4). How is honesty about our innocence in a particular wrong different from self-righteousness? How does Jesus, hated without a cause, help us here?

The enemies ask who will hear them, and God laughs (vv. 7–8). When evil seems to go unseen, what difference does it make to know that God hears and holds the proud in derision?

David asks God not simply to kill his enemies, “lest my people forget” (v. 11). What does this reveal about his concern for others? How does the story of Saul of Tarsus show God’s purpose in humbling his enemies?

The dogs howl at evening, but David plans to sing “in the morning” (vv. 14–16). What “nights” are you facing, and what would it look like to plan your morning praise now?

60.text: To the choirmaster: according to Shushan Eduth. A Miktam of David; for instruction; when he strove with Aram-naharaim and with Aram-zobah, and when Joab on his return struck down twelve thousand of Edom in the Valley of Salt. 1O God, you have rejected us, broken our defenses; you have been angry; oh, restore us.2You have made the land to quake; you have torn it open; repair its breaches, for it totters.3You have made your people see hard things; you have given us wine to drink that made us stagger.4You have set up a banner for those who fear you, that they may flee to it from the bow. Selah5That your beloved ones may be delivered, give salvation by your right hand and answer us!6God has spoken in his holiness: "With exultation I will divide up Shechem and portion out the Vale of Succoth.7Gilead is mine; Manasseh is mine; Ephraim is my helmet; Judah is my scepter.8Moab is my washbasin; upon Edom I cast my shoe; over Philistia I shout in triumph."9Who will bring me to the fortified city? Who will lead me to Edom?10Have you not rejected us, O God? You do not go forth, O God, with our armies.11Oh, grant us help against the foe, for vain is the salvation of man!12With God we shall do valiantly; it is he who will tread down our foes.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — You Have Made Your People See Hard Things
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A defeat comes from God’s hand, and only God’s hand can mend it. The psalm traces every part of the disaster to God: he has rejected his people, broken their defences, shaken and split the land like an earthquake, and made them drink a cup that leaves them reeling (vv. 1–3). Yet the same God has raised a banner for those who fear him, a rallying point out of bowshot (v. 4), and the people pray that his right hand would save his beloved ones (v. 5). They take the blow to the one who struck it.
verseByVerse.theology: A defeat is described as God's own work, and prayed about in exactly those terms.

verseByVerse.quote: O God, you have rejected us, broken our defenses; you have been angry; oh, restore us. You have made the land to quake; you have torn it open; repair its breaches, for it totters. You have made your people see hard things; you have given us wine to drink that made us stagger. You have set up a banner for those who fear you, that they may flee to it from the bow. Selah That your beloved ones may be delivered, give salvation by your right hand and answer us!
verseByVerse.commentary:
The psalm traces a national defeat to God himself, and for that very reason asks God alone to heal it.

The heading. One of the longest in the Psalter, it names real campaigns against Aram and Edom under Joab. (The histories give eighteen thousand Edomites, 2 Samuel 8:13 and 1 Chronicles 18:12, and Chronicles credits Abishai; the heading counts differently, and the psalm is not written to settle it.) In the middle come two words that change how the psalm is read: for instruction. Israel put her worst days on the syllabus.

O God, you have rejected us. Every verb belongs to God. Not “we were outnumbered” or “the alliance failed”, but you rejected, you broke, you made the land quake, you tore it open. The psalm goes straight past the immediate causes to God, who stands behind them, and asks the same God to mend it: oh, restore us. The hand that tore is the only hand that can stitch.

You have made your people see hard things. Sights you cannot forget, and a cup of wine that leaves a people reeling: God’s anger poured out, a cup the prophets would use again and again (Isaiah 51:17; Jeremiah 25:15).

You have set up a banner. A banner was a rallying point planted on high ground so scattered soldiers could find each other. This one is not to march behind but to flee to, out of range of the bow: a place to regroup rather than a slogan. And they are still your beloved ones: under discipline, still loved.

The cup and the banner. The cup ends up in Gethsemane, where Jesus, David’s greater Son, asked whether it could pass and then drank it (Matthew 26:39). And Isaiah uses the word for banner of the root of Jesse, standing “as a signal for the peoples” (Isaiah 11:10): Christ crucified and risen is the banner God has raised for scattered people to run to.

What it does not mean. Not that every hardship punishes a particular sin; the psalm names none. It means nothing reaches God’s people outside his hand, so every defeat is taken to him.

Uncertain wording. Shushan Eduth is probably a tune name. In verse 4 the ESV notes the possible reading “because of truth”, since the Hebrew words for bow and truth look alike.
verseByVerse.note: The title refers to David’s wars with Aram and Edom.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–12 — Vain Is the Salvation of Man
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God still owns everything, so his beaten people can go out again with him. God speaks in his holiness as owner of the whole land: Shechem and Succoth, Gilead and Manasseh are his, Ephraim is his helmet and Judah his scepter, while the hostile nations are his washbasin and the place he throws his shoe (vv. 6–8). But the fortified city still stands, and God has not gone out with the armies (vv. 9–10). So the people pray for his help, renounce human rescue, and confess that with God they shall do valiantly (vv. 11–12).
verseByVerse.theology: God surveys the map, and a beaten army states its two-line creed.

verseByVerse.quote: God has spoken in his holiness: "With exultation I will divide up Shechem and portion out the Vale of Succoth. Gilead is mine; Manasseh is mine; Ephraim is my helmet; Judah is my scepter. Moab is my washbasin; upon Edom I cast my shoe; over Philistia I shout in triumph."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God answers his beaten people as owner of the land and master of every nation around it, showing their enemies at their true size.

God has spoken in his holiness. The tone is of a landowner walking his property with obvious pleasure, naming places on both sides of the Jordan as a man might name fields. Shechem and Succoth were where Jacob settled on his return to the land (Genesis 33:17–18): God begins with the places of the old promise.

Ephraim is my helmet; Judah is my scepter. Two tribes get jobs: the largest northern tribe is God’s headgear in battle, and Judah is the staff in his hand, where the kings come from and eventually the King (Genesis 49:10). The army that has just been beaten is told that it is God’s own equipment.

Moab is my washbasin. Now the neighbours, in deliberately humiliating language. Moab is the bowl God washes his feet in; Edom is where he tosses his sandal. The point is not contempt for those peoples but their true size: Israel, just mauled by them, cannot see over the top of them, and God describes them as household items.

The nations claimed. God has since claimed these nations in mercy: Ruth of Moab was David’s great-grandmother (Ruth 4:17), and the gospel goes to every people.

Uncertain wording. In his holiness may be in his sanctuary (ESV note). Casting the shoe may be a master tossing his sandals to a servant, or a sign of claiming land (compare Ruth 4:7); either way Edom is under God’s feet.
verseByVerse.note: Verses 5–12 reappear in Psalm 108.

verseByVerse.quote: Who will bring me to the fortified city? Who will lead me to Edom? Have you not rejected us, O God? You do not go forth, O God, with our armies. Oh, grant us help against the foe, for vain is the salvation of man! With God we shall do valiantly; it is he who will tread down our foes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
With the enemy city still standing and God seemingly absent, the people renounce human help and confess that only with God will they fight bravely and win.

Who will bring me to the fortified city? After that magnificent speech the psalm returns to the facts on the ground: a fortified city nobody has taken, and the honest sentence, You do not go forth, O God, with our armies. God’s ownership of the world (vv. 6–8) and his apparent absence from this campaign (v. 10) are put in the same poem, and neither is used to silence the other. That is faith in a bad season.

Vain is the salvation of man! The creed of a defeated army, and first the negative, brutal about what they have just tried: everything human (the alliances, the generals, the numbers) has been weighed and found empty.

With God we shall do valiantly. Then the positive, and it is not passive. They are going back out; the question is who goes with them. And the last clause hands over the outcome: it is he who will tread down our foes.

The one who comes from Edom. Isaiah answers verse 9 with a conqueror “who comes from Edom, in crimsoned garments” (Isaiah 63:1), a picture Revelation gives to the returning Christ (Revelation 19:13–15). No human army could lead God’s people to final victory; God came to do it himself.

In any hard task. Together the two halves give the Christian’s stance in any hard task: nothing you can do will save you, and with God you will act bravely and leave the result to him. These verses reappear in Psalm 108, because a beaten people needs this sentence more than once.

60.title: With God We Shall Do Valiantly
60.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 60 closes the run of Miktams (56 to 60) and moves from David the fugitive to David the king at war. The heading sets it in the wars of 2 Samuel 8, when David fought the Arameans and Joab returned to win a great victory over Edom in the Valley of Salt. The psalm itself, though, is written out of a defeat.

The message. Even God’s own people, under his anointed king, can suffer defeats that God himself sends. The answer is to go back to God, not to human help: the one who tore can heal, he still owns the land and every enemy around it, and with him his people will act bravely and win, for “vain is the salvation of man”.

Why it was said. In the middle of a victorious reign the army had been beaten, the land felt split by an earthquake, and God seemed not to have gone out with them. The heading adds for instruction: this defeat was written up so that later generations would learn how to pray in theirs (see the introduction on the titles).

How the chapter makes its case. The lament (vv. 1–5): God has rejected and broken his people and made them drink a staggering cup, yet he has raised a banner for them to flee to; so save us by your right hand. The oracle (vv. 6–8): God speaks in his holiness as owner of the land on both sides of the Jordan, with his tribes as his armour and the hostile nations around as his household things. The prayer (vv. 9–12): who will lead us to Edom? Not man, whose help is vain, but God, with whom we shall do valiantly.

Where it leads. By promise, and by the need it exposes. Judah is my scepter (v. 7) recalls the promise that the scepter would not depart from Judah (Genesis 49:10), kept in Jesus, “the Lion of the tribe of Judah” (Revelation 5:5). The question “Who will lead me to Edom?” is answered in Isaiah’s vision of the one “who comes from Edom”, who has “trodden the winepress alone” (Isaiah 63:1, 3): the conqueror no human army could supply. And the staggering cup of God’s anger (v. 3) was drunk by Christ in Gethsemane and on the cross, so that his people, beaten as they often are, are “more than conquerors through him who loved us” (Romans 8:37).

For us. Churches and Christians have defeats too, and some are God’s fatherly discipline. Do not explain them away or trust clever schemes. Go back to the God who wounded and can heal, rally to the banner he has raised in Christ, and go out again with him.
60.theology:
The disaster is attributed to God in every verb, and the God who tore is the only one asked to mend (vv. 1-3). His speech then reduces the nations that have just mauled Israel to household items, a statement of scale rather than contempt (vv. 6-8).

The psalm refuses to resolve the tension between God's ownership of everything and his absence from this campaign (vv. 9-10). Its closing creed is not retirement from the field but a different companion: human help is empty, and with God we shall do valiantly (vv. 11-12).
60.examples: Most nations write up their victories; Israel put this defeat on the syllabus. A banner on a hill, where a scattered army could find each other again, is a picture of what God gives a beaten people. And the closing two lines suit any hard enterprise, from a struggling church to a family crisis: our own strength is empty, and we go back out with God.

keyVerse.quote: With God we shall do valiantly; it is he who will tread down our foes.
keyVerse.note: The psalm’s last line is the creed of a beaten army. Having confessed that human help is vain (v. 11), the people do not retire from the field but go out again with God, leaving the victory to him. Christians stand in the same place: “more than conquerors through him who loved us” (Romans 8:37).

60.reflection:
The psalm attributes Israel’s defeat to God in every verb, and asks him alone to heal it (vv. 1–3). Why is it a comfort, and not only a hard truth, that nothing reaches us outside God’s hand?

God gave his beaten people “a banner” to flee to (v. 4). In what sense is Christ that banner for you? Where do you tend to run instead when you have failed or been defeated?

God speaks of the nations that had just beaten Israel as his washbasin and the place for his shoe (v. 8). What problems or opponents look enormous to you right now, and how does seeing their true size before God change the way you face them?

“Vain is the salvation of man! With God we shall do valiantly” (vv. 11–12). How do you hold together real effort and complete dependence on God in a hard task you face, whether in church, work or family?

61.text: To the choirmaster: with stringed instruments. Of David. 1Hear my cry, O God, listen to my prayer;2from the end of the earth I call to you when my heart is faint. Lead me to the rock that is higher than I,3for you have been my refuge, a strong tower against the enemy.4Let me dwell in your tent forever! Let me take refuge under the shelter of your wings! Selah5For you, O God, have heard my vows; you have given me the heritage of those who fear your name.6Prolong the life of the king; may his years endure to all generations!7May he be enthroned forever before God; appoint steadfast love and faithfulness to watch over him!8So will I ever sing praises to your name, as I perform my vows day after day.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — Lead Me to the Rock
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When the heart is faint and far away, God is the refuge above us, and those he hears answer with lifelong praise. David cries from the end of the earth, asking to be led to the rock higher than he is, because God has been his refuge and strong tower before (vv. 1–3). He longs to live as God’s guest in his tent and to shelter under his wings (v. 4). Then assurance arrives: God has heard and given him the heritage of those who fear him (v. 5). So he prays for the king to reign for ever under the guard of steadfast love and faithfulness, a prayer only the Messiah fulfils (vv. 6–7), and ends with a promise of daily praise (v. 8).
verseByVerse.theology: A faint man at the far edge of things asks to be taken up to a rock he cannot climb.

verseByVerse.quote: Hear my cry, O God, listen to my prayer; from the end of the earth I call to you when my heart is faint. Lead me to the rock that is higher than I, for you have been my refuge, a strong tower against the enemy. Let me dwell in your tent forever! Let me take refuge under the shelter of your wings! Selah
verseByVerse.commentary:
Far from home and too weak to climb, David asks God to bring him to a refuge higher than himself, and to let him live under God’s roof and wings.

From the end of the earth. He is far away, in geography or in feeling, and exhausted: “when my heart is faint”, like a man about to pass out.

Lead me to the rock that is higher than I. The point of this great phrase is in the last two words. A rock at his own level would be no use: the water rises to that. He needs the high ledge, the one out of reach, so being shown it is not enough. He asks to be led there: what he lacks is strength, not information.

A strong tower against the enemy. He can ask because of what God has already been to him, his refuge and strong tower. Proverbs says the same: “The name of the LORD is a strong tower; the righteous man runs into it and is safe” (Proverbs 18:10).

Let me dwell in your tent forever! Verse 4 names two shelters, and the first is an odd choice. A tent is the most temporary building there is, and he asks to live in one for ever. What makes it permanent is not the canvas but the owner. Under the tent comes a softer covering, the wings of a bird, as in Psalms 17:8, 57:1 and 63:7. He wants to be God’s guest and God’s chick at once.

The Rock above us. “The Rock was Christ” (1 Corinthians 10:4): the refuge higher than we are came down to where we are, to lift us up to where he is. And “Lead me” needs no eloquence or strength, only the admission that you cannot get there yourself.

verseByVerse.quote: For you, O God, have heard my vows; you have given me the heritage of those who fear your name. Prolong the life of the king; may his years endure to all generations! May he be enthroned forever before God; appoint steadfast love and faithfulness to watch over him! So will I ever sing praises to your name, as I perform my vows day after day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Assured that God has heard him, David prays for the king to reign for ever under God’s steadfast love and faithfulness, and promises to praise God and keep his vows every day.

You, O God, have heard my vows. Between verse 4 and verse 5 something has settled. He asked to be led to the rock; now he reports that God has heard and given him the inheritance of those who fear his name. His circumstances have not changed; he has been given the certainty that he is heard.

Prolong the life of the king. If David is the author, he prays for himself in the third person, thinking of the office rather than of himself. Yet the request is for years “to all generations” and a throne “forever”, and no king of Judah got that. They all died, many of them badly.

May he be enthroned forever before God. The prayer reaches past every king who sat on that throne to God’s promise to David’s house, “your throne shall be established forever” (2 Samuel 7:16). It was answered when an angel said of a child, “he will reign over the house of Jacob forever, and of his kingdom there will be no end” (Luke 1:33). A prayer sung for centuries was granted to Jesus, enthroned before God now, who does not die.

Appoint steadfast love and faithfulness to watch over him! The two attendants set to guard the king like a bodyguard are the ones this book keeps sending on errands: God’s covenant love and his reliability (compare 57:3).

As I perform my vows day after day. The psalm ends with two things that belong together and are often separated: singing, and doing what he promised. Vows are kept “day after day”, not in one grand gesture but a little at a time, which is how promises are actually kept.

What it does not mean. The vows are not the price of a hearing. He has already been heard (v. 5); the daily faithfulness is the grateful answer of a man already given the heritage. He began at the end of the earth with a fainting heart and finishes with a daily routine and a song.

61.title: The Rock That Is Higher Than I
61.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 61 opens a short run of David’s prayers of trust (61–64) that follows the hunted cries of Psalms 54–60. The tone is quieter now: no enemy is described, only distance, weariness and longing for God’s presence.

The message. When you are far away and too worn out to climb, God himself is the refuge above you, and you may ask him to take you there. He hears before anything changes, and the one who is heard answers with a lifetime of kept promises and praise. Behind the praying man stands the king, and behind the king stands God’s promise that David’s throne would last for ever.

Why it was said. The heading names David, and the prayer for “the king” in verses 6–7 suggests he prays as king, perhaps during the flight from Absalom, when he was driven across the Jordan and far from the tent of worship (2 Samuel 15–17). It was then given to the choirmaster, so that Israel could pray it for its king (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. First the cry: from the end of the earth, with a fainting heart, he asks to be led to the rock that is higher than he is, because God has been his refuge before (vv. 1–3). He asks to live in God’s tent and shelter under his wings (v. 4). Then the turn: God has heard his vows and given him the heritage of those who fear him (v. 5). So he prays for the king’s life to last to all generations, guarded by steadfast love and faithfulness (vv. 6–7), and ends with a vow of daily praise (v. 8).

Where it leads. Chiefly by promise. A prayer that a king may be “enthroned forever before God” was never granted to any son of David who died; it reaches for the covenant of 2 Samuel 7, and it is answered in Jesus, of whose kingdom “there will be no end” (Luke 1:33). He is also the higher Rock David could not reach by himself (1 Corinthians 10:4), and the King who lives for ever to pray for those who shelter in him.

For us. When you are too tired to pray well, you can still pray “lead me”: it needs no strength, only somewhere to be taken. Christ the King is enthroned for ever, so the shelter you run to will not fall with you. And the answer to being heard is not one grand gesture but faithfulness day after day.
61.theology: The prayer moves from need to certainty. Help that is out of reach is asked for by being led there (v. 2), and the answer comes first in assurance rather than in changed circumstances (v. 5). The petition for the king (vv. 6-7) reaches past every occupant to the promise of 2 Sam 7:16, granted at last in Christ (Luke 1:33). Vows kept day after day (v. 8) are the response of a man already heard and given the heritage (v. 5), not the price of a hearing.
61.examples: Those who feel far from God, or too tired to pray well, can still ask to be led: the prayer of verse 2 needs no strength, only somewhere to be taken. The higher rock matters because a refuge at our own level goes under with us. And promises to God, like promises made to a husband, a wife or a friend, are kept in instalments, day after day, not in one grand gesture.

keyVerse.quote: from the end of the earth I call to you when my heart is faint. Lead me to the rock that is higher than I
keyVerse.note: This is the heart of the psalm’s prayer and one of the best-loved lines in the Psalter. David asks not for information but to be led, because the refuge he needs is above his own strength. It teaches the weary how to pray, and it points to Christ, the Rock who came down to lift us up.

61.reflection:
David prays “Lead me to the rock that is higher than I” (v. 2). Why does it matter that the refuge is higher than we are? What refuges at our own level do we tend to run to instead?

In verse 5 David is sure he has been heard before anything has changed. How can we know God has heard us when our circumstances stay the same?

The prayer for a king “enthroned forever” (vv. 6–7) was answered in Jesus (Luke 1:33). How does Christ’s endless reign comfort you when you feel far from God?

David ends by keeping his vows “day after day” (v. 8). What promises to God or to others do you need to keep in small daily instalments this week?

62.text: To the choirmaster: according to Jeduthun. A Psalm of David. 1For God alone my soul waits in silence; from him comes my salvation.2He alone is my rock and my salvation, my fortress; I shall not be greatly shaken.3How long will all of you attack a man to batter him, like a leaning wall, a tottering fence?4They only plan to thrust him down from his high position. They take pleasure in falsehood. They bless with their mouths, but inwardly they curse. Selah5For God alone, O my soul, wait in silence, for my hope is from him.6He only is my rock and my salvation, my fortress; I shall not be shaken.7On God rests my salvation and my glory; my mighty rock, my refuge is God.8Trust in him at all times, O people; pour out your heart before him; God is a refuge for us. Selah9Those of low estate are but a breath; those of high estate are a delusion; in the balances they go up; they are together lighter than a breath.10Put no trust in extortion; set no vain hopes on robbery; if riches increase, set not your heart on them.11Once God has spoken; twice have I heard this: that power belongs to God,12and that to you, O Lord, belongs steadfast love. For you will render to a man according to his work.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — He Alone Is My Rock
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God alone can bear the full weight of trust, so faith rules out every other support and preaches to itself until it stands firm. David confesses that God only is his rock and salvation, so he will not be greatly shaken (vv. 1–2). His enemies treat him as a leaning wall and a tottering fence, one shove from collapse, and they work by smiling lies (vv. 3–4). Then he turns and commands his own soul to wait for God alone, repeating his confession with a change: no longer “not greatly shaken” but “I shall not be shaken” (vv. 5–7). Between the two he has preached to himself.
verseByVerse.theology: The same confession twice, first as a report and then as an order he gives himself.

verseByVerse.quote: For God alone my soul waits in silence; from him comes my salvation. He alone is my rock and my salvation, my fortress; I shall not be greatly shaken. How long will all of you attack a man to batter him, like a leaning wall, a tottering fence? They only plan to thrust him down from his high position. They take pleasure in falsehood. They bless with their mouths, but inwardly they curse. Selah For God alone, O my soul, wait in silence, for my hope is from him. He only is my rock and my salvation, my fortress; I shall not be shaken. On God rests my salvation and my glory; my mighty rock, my refuge is God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God alone is David’s rock, so while enemies push at him like a leaning wall, he waits quietly for God and commands his soul to do the same, until he can say he will not be shaken at all.

One small word. One small Hebrew word opens six verses of this psalm, and the English has to spread it about: “alone”, “only”, “but”. It is used of God (vv. 1–2, 5–6), of the enemies’ only plan (v. 4), and of how much a human being weighs (v. 9). The effect is of a man ruling out every other support until only God is left.

For God alone my soul waits in silence. Not sulking, but the stillness of someone who has stopped arguing his case and casting about for alternatives. And there is an honest limit at the end of verse 2: “not greatly shaken”. He may be shaken, but not overthrown.

Like a leaning wall, a tottering fence. They see him as a wall already leaning: one good shove and it comes down. It is how a group treats someone it has decided is finished. Their aim is to thrust him “down from his high position”, and their method is words: “They bless with their mouths, but inwardly they curse”, the two-faced speech of 55:21, where the words were smooth and the heart was war.

For God alone, O my soul, wait in silence. Verse 1 was a statement: my soul waits. Verse 5 is a command: “O my soul, wait”. He commands himself to do what he has just claimed to be doing. That is not hypocrisy but how faith works under pressure, and Psalm 42 does the same with its refrain (42:5).

I shall not be shaken. Verse 2 said “not greatly shaken”; verse 6 drops the word “greatly”. Between the two, he has preached to himself.

The silent King. David’s greater Son stood where David stood, battered by false accusers, and was silent before them: “When he was reviled, he did not revile in return; when he suffered, he did not threaten, but continued entrusting himself to him who judges justly” (1 Peter 2:23). His silence was not defeat but trust, and his Father raised him.

God as one holding in the portfolio. The modern instinct is to spread our trust around. Financial advisers tell us never to put everything in one place, and we live the same way: a little career, a little family, a little savings, and a little God, so that if one fails the others will hold. It feels prudent. But the psalm’s small word “alone” exposes it. A God who is one holding among several is not really God to us but a hedge, and whatever we lean on most is what actually rules us. Those supports give way just when we need them (v. 9). David is not despising family or provision; he is refusing to let any of them be his rock. And putting our whole weight on God does not shrink life. It frees us to enjoy everything else without needing it to save us. The God who asks to be our only rock is the God who gave his only Son, so that the weight would be safe with him.

Uncertain wording. The verb translated “attack” in verse 3 occurs only here in the Old Testament, and its sense (“rush at”, “assail” or perhaps “shout at”) is worked out from related words and the context. The next words, “to batter him”, can also be read differently: older translations such as the King James Version take them to mean that the attackers themselves will be slain and become the leaning wall. The ESV’s reading fits the flow of verses 3–4 best, and on either reading the picture is of a man under a sustained assault.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–12 — Pour Out Your Heart Before Him
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Because God is a refuge, everyone can trust him and tell him everything, and nothing else deserves that trust. David turns to the whole people: trust him at all times and pour out your hearts before him (v. 8). Put every human being on the scales, the lowly and the great together, and the pan goes up: they weigh less than a breath (v. 9). Wealth gained by extortion is empty, and even wealth that grows honestly must not hold the heart (v. 10). He closes with what God has spoken, heard twice over: power belongs to God, and so does steadfast love, and he will repay each person according to his work (vv. 11–12).
verseByVerse.theology: One utterance of God, two things heard in it, and neither of them is what a frightened man expects.

verseByVerse.quote: Trust in him at all times, O people; pour out your heart before him; God is a refuge for us. Selah Those of low estate are but a breath; those of high estate are a delusion; in the balances they go up; they are together lighter than a breath. Put no trust in extortion; set no vain hopes on robbery; if riches increase, set not your heart on them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
David calls everyone to trust God at all times and pour out their hearts to him, because every human being weighs less than a breath and riches, however gained, are no place to rest the heart.

Pour out your heart before him. He turns from his own soul to everyone else’s with one of the kindest commands in Scripture: tip the whole thing up, as Hannah said of her own praying, “I have been pouring out my soul before the LORD” (1 Samuel 1:15).

Silence and pouring out. This does not contradict “wait in silence”. The silence of verses 1 and 5 is towards other people and other sources of help; the pouring out is towards God. A believer may be quite silent in public about his trouble and entirely unrestrained in private.

How do I pour out my heart? Many believers pray politely, telling God what they think he wants to hear; the psalm asks for the whole contents, “at all times”. Say what is really there. The anger at the colleague who lied about you, the fear about money, the disappointment with God himself: he knows it already, and he would rather hear it from you than have you hide it. Borrow the psalms’ words. When you have none, pray a lament such as Psalm 13 aloud, and linger on the lines that are yours. Write it down. A page of honest prayer at the kitchen table can do what an hour of brooding cannot. End where the psalm ends. After pouring out, say back to God what is true of him: “God is a refuge for us.”

A High Priest who prayed this way. We can be this open because we come through one who prayed like this himself: “In the days of his flesh, Jesus offered up prayers and supplications, with loud cries and tears” (Hebrews 5:7). He is not embarrassed by ours; through him we may “with confidence draw near to the throne of grace” (Hebrews 4:16).

In the balances they go up. Put every human being on the scales, the nobodies and the somebodies together, and the pan goes up: together they weigh less than a breath. This is Psalm 39’s “mere breath” again, said to a man battered by people who seemed to have all the power. It cuts his terror of them down to size, and his hope in them too.

If riches increase, set not your heart on them. Extortion and robbery are obvious false hopes, but the last clause is for people who never robbed anyone. Wealth can arrive honestly; the danger is the heart quietly coming to rest on it. The command is not to give it all away but to watch where the heart goes when the balance grows, for, as verse 8 said: “God is a refuge for us”, so the heart has somewhere better to rest.

verseByVerse.quote: Once God has spoken; twice have I heard this: that power belongs to God, and that to you, O Lord, belongs steadfast love. For you will render to a man according to his work.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God has made two things unmistakably clear: all power belongs to him, and so does steadfast love, so he will deal with every person justly according to what they have done.

Once God has spoken; twice have I heard this. A formula for something said with great weight, as Elihu says, “For God speaks in one way, and in two” (Job 33:14). God said one thing, and the listener heard two.

That power belongs to God. Exactly what a battered man needs, in that order. Power belongs to God, so the men pushing at him in verse 3 do not have the last word. Steadfast love belongs to him too, so that power is not neutral, and not against him.

Power and love together. Either half alone would be unbearable. Power without love is a tyrant; love without power is a sympathetic bystander. The Christian faith holds the two together at a cross, where God’s power looked like weakness and his love did the costliest thing it could, and Christ crucified is “the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1:24).

You will render to a man according to his work. The last line puts both to use. The men who bless with their mouths and curse inwardly will be repaid for what they did, not what they said. Paul quotes this line as a principle of God’s judgment: “He will render to each one according to his works” (Romans 2:6; compare Matthew 16:27). The psalm that began by narrowing everything to God alone ends by leaving the accounts with him.

Does “according to his work” deny salvation by grace? No. The believer is accepted for Christ’s work, not his own (Ephesians 2:8–9). But works show what a heart truly trusts, and at the judgment they are the evidence of faith or unbelief (Romans 2:6–7; James 2:18). Believers will not be condemned, but their lives will be revealed and their works rewarded by grace.

62.title: For God Alone My Soul Waits in Silence
62.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 62 follows Psalm 61’s quiet prayer for the king with a psalm of pure trust. There is no request to God in it at all: David speaks to his own soul, to his enemies and to the people, and only at the very end to God himself.

The message. God alone is a safe place to rest your whole weight, so be still before people and pour out everything before him. Everyone else, high or low, weighs less than a breath, and riches cannot hold you up. Power belongs to God and so does steadfast love, and he will settle every account justly.

Why it was said. David is under attack from people who smile to his face and curse him inwardly, scheming to push him from his high position (vv. 3–4), perhaps in the years of Absalom’s plotting. The heading gives it to Jeduthun, one of the Levite musicians, for Israel to sing (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. First his confession: God alone is his rock, so he will not be greatly shaken (vv. 1–2). Then the enemies, treating him as a leaning wall ready to be pushed over, blessing with their mouths and cursing inwardly (vv. 3–4). He turns and commands his soul to do what he has just claimed, and now says he will not be shaken at all (vv. 5–7). He calls the people to trust God and pour out their hearts, because all humanity is lighter than a breath on the scales and wealth is no hope (vv. 8–10). He ends with what God has said: power and steadfast love both belong to him, and he will render to each according to his work (vv. 11–12).

Where it leads. By pattern and by God’s character revealed in Christ. The Son of David was battered by false friends and lying witnesses, and “continued entrusting himself to him who judges justly” (1 Peter 2:23). At the cross God’s power and steadfast love, the two things this psalm hears, meet in one act, for Christ crucified is “the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1:24). And the judge who renders to each according to his work is the one who bore the penalty for his people’s works.

For us. Do not spread your trust across many supports with God as one of them; rest your whole weight on him. Be quiet before your accusers and completely honest before God. And when money grows, watch where your heart goes.
62.theology: The psalm narrows every option to God alone, and one small Hebrew word (vv. 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 9) carries the argument. Faith under pressure does not only report its trust; it orders the soul to trust (v. 5; cf. 42:5), until the honest limit of v. 2 becomes the plain claim of v. 6. God's power and his steadfast love (v. 11) meet at the cross, and his judgment follows deeds, not speech (v. 12).
62.examples: When people treat you as finished, a wall already leaning, the psalm does not tell you to argue back. It tells you to be still before others and to pour out everything before God, and to keep preaching to yourself until not greatly shaken becomes I shall not be shaken. For anyone whose savings are growing honestly, verse 10 asks a quiet question: where is the heart resting as the balance rises?

keyVerse.quote: For God alone my soul waits in silence; from him comes my salvation.
keyVerse.note: The psalm’s first line sets out its whole argument. The small word “alone” rules out every other support, and the silence is the stillness of a soul that has stopped looking elsewhere. Everything that follows, from the leaning wall to the empty scales, explains why God is the only safe place to rest.

62.reflection:
Psalm 62 uses the word “alone” or “only” again and again. What other supports do you tend to lean on alongside God, and what would it look like to make him your only rock?

David tells his own soul to wait for God (v. 5). Why do we need to preach to ourselves, and how might you do that this week?

Verse 8 calls us to “pour out your heart before him”. What stops you being fully honest with God in prayer, and how does Hebrews 4:16 help?

Power and steadfast love both belong to God (vv. 11–12). How does the cross show them together, and why do we need both?

63.text: A Psalm of David, when he was in the wilderness of Judah. 1O God, you are my God; earnestly I seek you; my soul thirsts for you; my flesh faints for you, as in a dry and weary land where there is no water.2So I have looked upon you in the sanctuary, beholding your power and glory.3Because your steadfast love is better than life, my lips will praise you.4So I will bless you as long as I live; in your name I will lift up my hands.5My soul will be satisfied as with fat and rich food, and my mouth will praise you with joyful lips,6when I remember you upon my bed, and meditate on you in the watches of the night;7for you have been my help, and in the shadow of your wings I will sing for joy.8My soul clings to you; your right hand upholds me.9But those who seek to destroy my life shall go down into the depths of the earth;10they shall be given over to the power of the sword; they shall be a portion for jackals.11But the king shall rejoice in God; all who swear by him shall exult, for the mouths of liars will be stopped.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — My Soul Thirsts for You
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God himself is the deepest thirst and the richest feast of the human soul, and his love is worth more than life. David, parched in the wilderness, says his soul and body long for God like dry ground for water, and he lives on the memory of God’s power and glory in the sanctuary (vv. 1–2). Because God’s steadfast love is better than life, he will bless him as long as he lives (vv. 3–4). Far from going hungry, he is satisfied as with the richest food, even in the night watches, singing under God’s wings (vv. 5–7). His soul clings to God, and God’s right hand holds him up (v. 8).
verseByVerse.theology: A man with no water calls God better than life, and describes a feast in a desert.

verseByVerse.quote: O God, you are my God; earnestly I seek you; my soul thirsts for you; my flesh faints for you, as in a dry and weary land where there is no water. So I have looked upon you in the sanctuary, beholding your power and glory. Because your steadfast love is better than life, my lips will praise you. So I will bless you as long as I live; in your name I will lift up my hands.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Parched in the desert and far from the sanctuary, David longs for God more than his body longs for water, lives on what he has seen of God, and declares that God’s steadfast love is better than life itself.

In the wilderness of Judah. The heading places him in the dry hills west of the Dead Sea, either during the Saul years (1 Samuel 23:14) or the flight from Absalom (2 Samuel 15:23). Verse 11 calls him “the king”, which fits the Absalom years best.

O God, you are my God. The first five words are the whole relationship. Not “the God” or “a God” but mine: the difference between knowing about God and trusting him.

My soul thirsts for you. Not a figure of speech laid over a comfortable life: he is actually parched, and he says that what his body is doing for water his soul is doing for God. “My flesh faints for you”: even the physical craving has been drawn into the longing.

I have looked upon you in the sanctuary. He is remembering. Cut off from the place of worship, he goes back over what he saw of God’s power and glory there. That is what a believer in a dry season lives on: not new experiences but stored ones, gone over carefully.

Your steadfast love is better than life. Perhaps the boldest statement of worth in the Psalter, and the circumstances give it its force. A man in a place that could kill him within days says that God’s covenant love is better than life: not better than comfort, wealth or reputation, but than the thing everybody else is trying to hold on to. Test it by the alternative: if life is the highest good, anyone who can threaten your life owns you. This man’s enemies have no hold over him, and that is not bravado; it follows from what he values most. Paul reasons the same way: “to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (Philippians 1:21).

The King who thirsted. David’s greater Son was tested in the wilderness and cried from the cross, “I thirst” (John 19:28). He went without so that he could call out, “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink” (John 7:37). The longing of verse 1 is answered in him.

Uncertain wording. The “So” linking verses 1 and 2 is compressed: he may mean that he once looked on God in the sanctuary with this same longing, or that he now seeks God in the wilderness as he did there. Either way, his thirst is fed by what he has already seen of God in worship.
verseByVerse.note: The title places David in the wilderness of Judah — the dry hills west of the Dead Sea.

verseByVerse.quote: My soul will be satisfied as with fat and rich food, and my mouth will praise you with joyful lips, when I remember you upon my bed, and meditate on you in the watches of the night; for you have been my help, and in the shadow of your wings I will sing for joy. My soul clings to you; your right hand upholds me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even in the desert and through sleepless nights, David is satisfied with God as with a feast, and he clings to God while God’s own hand holds him fast.

As with fat and rich food. In a desert he reaches for a banquet: the best cuts at a feast. Whatever he is living on, it is not rations. This is one of Scripture’s plainest statements that God himself is enjoyable, not merely necessary.

In the watches of the night. The feast happens at night, awake, in the hours when the mind normally works against a man. The watches of the night were the sentry shifts, and while somebody stood guard he lay meditating on God (compare 4:4; 16:7). Scripture keeps turning sleepless hours into a meeting with God.

My soul clings to you; your right hand upholds me. Verse 8 holds two grips. “My soul clings to you” uses the word Genesis uses when a man holds fast to his wife (Genesis 2:24). And at once: “your right hand upholds me”. He is holding on, and underneath his grip is a hand doing the real holding. The clinging is real; the security is in the upholding.

Held twice over. Jesus put the same double grip into words for his sheep: “no one will snatch them out of my hand”, and “no one is able to snatch them out of the Father’s hand” (John 10:28–29). The believer who fears his hold is slipping is held twice over.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–11 — The King Shall Rejoice in God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Those who set themselves against God’s king will fall, and the king and all who trust God will rejoice. The men who hunt David’s life will go down to the depths, die by the sword and lie unburied for the jackals (vv. 9–10). This is stated as their end at God’s hand, not as David’s plan. Meanwhile the king will rejoice in God, everyone who swears by him will exult, and the lying mouths that have pursued him will be stopped (v. 11). The psalm that began in a dry land ends in joy, because the last word belongs to God, not to the liars.
verseByVerse.theology: The psalm ends with the liars silenced: not answered, but stopped.

verseByVerse.quote: But those who seek to destroy my life shall go down into the depths of the earth; they shall be given over to the power of the sword; they shall be a portion for jackals. But the king shall rejoice in God; all who swear by him shall exult, for the mouths of liars will be stopped.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The men hunting David will die and be disgraced, but the king will rejoice in God with all who trust him, and every lying mouth will be silenced.

A portion for jackals. A body left unburied for scavengers was the ancient world’s picture of total disgrace, and the men who hunted him through the wilderness will end there. He is not planning any of this; it is stated as their end at God’s hand, not as something he will do (on prayers like this, see the introduction on the psalms that curse).

The mouths of liars will be stopped. David calls himself “the king”, as in Psalm 61, and his joy is “in God”, not in his enemies’ fall. As for the liars, the psalm does not say they will be refuted, or that the truth will come out and everyone will apologise: their mouths will be stopped. That is a realistic comfort to anyone being lied about. Slander is often never answered in this life; the correction does not catch up with the rumour. But a day is coming when the talking simply ends.

The King’s joy. Christ too was hunted and lied about, and the false witnesses seemed to have the last word. But he rose, and every tongue will confess him as Lord (Philippians 2:11).

Uncertain wording. “All who swear by him” could refer to God or to the king. Most take it of God, since swearing by his name marked those who belonged to him (Deuteronomy 6:13); if it means the king, it describes his loyal people. Either way, they share the king’s joy.

63.title: Better Than Life
63.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 63 continues the run of trusting prayers after Psalms 61 and 62, and like Psalm 61 it ends with “the king”. Its heading puts it in the wilderness of Judah, and it is one of the most loved expressions of longing for God in the Bible.

The message. God himself is what the soul thirsts for, and his steadfast love is better than life itself. Even in a dry and dangerous place, cut off from public worship, a believer can feast on God by remembering him, cling to him, and know that God’s right hand is holding him. Those who hunt and slander God’s king will come to nothing, and the liars will be silenced.

Why it was said. David is in the dry hills of Judah, hunted, thirsty and far from the sanctuary. Because he calls himself “the king” (v. 11), the flight from Absalom fits best, when he crossed the brook Kidron toward the wilderness (2 Samuel 15:23), though some place it in the years he hid from Saul (see the introduction on the headings).

How the chapter makes its case. First the longing: his soul thirsts for God as his body thirsts in a land without water, and he remembers the power and glory he saw in the sanctuary (vv. 1–2). Then the valuation that drives the psalm: God’s steadfast love is better than life, so he will praise him as long as he lives (vv. 3–4). He is satisfied as at a feast, even through sleepless nights, singing under God’s wings, his soul clinging while God’s right hand holds him (vv. 5–8). Finally the outcome: his hunters will go down to the grave, but the king will rejoice in God and the mouths of liars will be stopped (vv. 9–11).

Where it leads. By pattern and by promise. David, the king driven into the wilderness by his own people, foreshadows the Son of David, who was tested in the wilderness, was rejected by his own, and cried on the cross, “I thirst” (John 19:28). He thirsted so that he could say to us, “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink” (John 7:37). He is the King who rejoices in God, and the one in whose hand his people are held.

For us. If God’s love is better than life, nothing that threatens your life can own you. In a dry season, live on what you have already seen of God, and turn sleepless hours into meeting him. And when your grip feels weak, remember whose hand is underneath it.
63.theology: The psalm is an argument from scarcity. A man with nothing to drink, cut off from the sanctuary, lives on remembered worship (v. 2) and finds God not only necessary but enjoyable (vv. 3-6). His valuation in v. 3 carries weight because it is made in real danger. His security rests less on his own clinging than on the right hand that upholds him (v. 8), and his comfort against slander is that lying mouths will one day be stopped (v. 11).
63.examples: Anyone in a dry season, kept from church by illness, work or distance, can do what David did: go back over what they have seen of God and live on it. Anyone who lies awake can turn the night watches into an appointment. And anyone being lied about, whose rumour has outrun every correction, may take the realistic comfort of verse 11: the talking will end, and God will have the last word.

keyVerse.quote: Because your steadfast love is better than life, my lips will praise you.
keyVerse.note: This is the valuation that drives the whole psalm. David says it in a desert, with his life in danger, so it is no figure of speech: God’s covenant love is worth more to him than staying alive. Anyone who believes it is freed from the power of whoever threatens his life.

63.reflection:
David says to God, “O God, you are my God” (v. 1). What is the difference between knowing about God and being able to say “my God”?

Cut off from the sanctuary, David lives on what he has already seen of God (v. 2). What have you seen of God in the past that you can “go back over” in a dry season?

What would change in your fears and priorities if you really believed God’s steadfast love is “better than life” (v. 3; Philippians 1:21)?

Verse 8 speaks of our clinging and God’s upholding. How do John 10:28–29 and this verse help someone who fears their faith is too weak?

64.text: To the choirmaster. A Psalm of David. 1Hear my voice, O God, in my complaint; preserve my life from dread of the enemy.2Hide me from the secret plots of the wicked, from the throng of evildoers,3who whet their tongues like swords, who aim bitter words like arrows,4shooting from ambush at the blameless, shooting at him suddenly and without fear.5They hold fast to their evil purpose; they talk of laying snares secretly, thinking, "Who can see them?"6They search out injustice, saying, "We have accomplished a diligent search." For the inward mind and heart of a man are deep.7But God shoots his arrow at them; they are wounded suddenly.8They are brought to ruin, with their own tongues turned against them; all who see them will wag their heads.9Then all mankind fears; they tell what God has brought about and ponder what he has done.10Let the righteous one rejoice in the LORD and take refuge in him! Let all the upright in heart exult!

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Shooting from Ambush at the Blameless
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Words can be weapons, and their users think they are hidden, so David asks God to hide him and to free him from fear. He prays first to be kept from dread of the enemy, not only from the enemy, and to be hidden from a crowd of plotters (vv. 1–2). They prepare their words like a swordsman at the whetstone and shoot them like arrows from ambush at the blameless, suddenly and without fear (vv. 3–4). They are committed to their schemes, sure that no one sees their traps, and they work hard at injustice; the human heart is deep beyond anyone’s seeing, except God’s (vv. 5–6).
verseByVerse.theology: Sharpened tongues, arrows fired from cover, and a great deal of hard work put into malice.

verseByVerse.quote: Hear my voice, O God, in my complaint; preserve my life from dread of the enemy. Hide me from the secret plots of the wicked, from the throng of evildoers, who whet their tongues like swords, who aim bitter words like arrows, shooting from ambush at the blameless, shooting at him suddenly and without fear. They hold fast to their evil purpose; they talk of laying snares secretly, thinking, "Who can see them?" They search out injustice, saying, "We have accomplished a diligent search." For the inward mind and heart of a man are deep.
verseByVerse.commentary:
David asks God to keep him from fear and to hide him from people who sharpen their words like weapons and fire them in secret, confident that no one sees what they are doing.

Preserve my life from dread of the enemy. He does not ask first to be preserved from the enemy but from dread of him. The fear is treated as a separate danger, and it is: a man can be worn down by the anticipation of an attack that never comes. Someone lying awake rehearsing what another might do needs more than the trouble removed.

Who whet their tongues like swords. Once again the weapon is a mouth, and here it is the whole subject. Two military images: a sword put to the whetstone (deliberate, unhurried preparation, a man sitting down to make his words sharper) and arrows shot from cover.

Shooting from ambush at the blameless. The ambush is what makes it unbearable. The victim has no warning, cannot see who fired, and often does not know he has been hit until the damage is done. That is how a reputation is taken apart. And “without fear”: they are not nervous about it, because ambushers are never identified.

Who can see them? Verse 5 gives their creed once more. The predator of Psalm 10 and the prowling dogs of Psalm 59 said the same. The whole psalm answers it: God can.

They search out injustice. Verse 6 prompts two sobering observations. The first is how hard malice works: they search, call it a “diligent search”, and congratulate each other on the thoroughness. Some people work harder at damaging someone than they ever worked at their job.

The inward mind and heart of a man are deep. The second is the line that ends the verse. There is more in a human being than anyone can see down into, which is why the plotting stays hidden, and why only God can reach the bottom of it (Jeremiah 17:9–10).

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew of verse 6 is notoriously difficult, and translations differ. The words behind “We have accomplished a diligent search” are compressed, and some translations render them as a boast of a perfect plan. The general sense is clear: the plotters work thoroughly and are proud of it, and their hearts are too deep for anyone but God to see.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–10 — But God Shoots His Arrow
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God answers the ambushers in kind, and the result is a world that fears him and righteous people who rejoice in him. God shoots his own arrow and they are wounded suddenly, as suddenly as they shot (vv. 4, 7). Their own tongues bring them down, and onlookers shake their heads (v. 8). Everyone then fears God, tells what he has done and thinks about it (v. 9). The righteous are told where to put their gladness: not in the enemy’s fall, but in the LORD, their refuge (v. 10).
verseByVerse.theology: The ambush is answered in kind, by an archer they never saw, and the outcome is a world that has learned something.

verseByVerse.quote: But God shoots his arrow at them; they are wounded suddenly. They are brought to ruin, with their own tongues turned against them; all who see them will wag their heads. Then all mankind fears; they tell what God has brought about and ponder what he has done. Let the righteous one rejoice in the LORD and take refuge in him! Let all the upright in heart exult!
verseByVerse.commentary:
God answers the hidden archers with his own sudden arrow, their own words bring them down, and the result is that everyone fears God and the righteous rejoice in him.

But God shoots his arrow at them. The reply is in kind. They fired arrows from cover; God fires one. They shot “suddenly” (v. 4); they are wounded “suddenly” (v. 7), the same word. The ambushers are ambushed, by an archer they never saw taking aim. And this is not the psalmist’s revenge: he has not touched a bow, and asked in verse 2 only to be hidden. The answer comes from God, far above their hiding place.

Their own tongues turned against them. The ruin is exact: not a thunderbolt but their own words coming back. The thing they sharpened cut them. Paul states the principle: “whatever one sows, that will he also reap” (Galatians 6:7).

All who see them will wag their heads. The mockery the righteous suffered elsewhere (22:7; 44:14) now falls on the mockers.

Then all mankind fears. The outcome is not the righteous man gloating. Everybody now takes God seriously: they fear, they tell, they ponder. A public act of God becomes a public conversation, and people go away thinking.
