Cut to the heart. The clearest case of this pattern is the trial of Jesus, the one wholly blameless man, against whom testimony was hunted out and false witnesses found (Mark 14:55–59). God’s answer was the resurrection, and when Peter told the crowd that God had made “this Jesus whom you crucified” both Lord and Christ, “they were cut to the heart” (Acts 2:36–37): the fear, the telling and the pondering of verse 9, ending in repentance rather than ruin.

Let the righteous one rejoice in the LORD. The last verse tells the righteous where to put their gladness: “in the LORD”, not in the outcome. It sends the victim back to the refuge he asked for in verse 2, not to enjoy the downfall but to enjoy God.

Uncertain wording. Verse 8 is compressed in Hebrew, roughly “they make him stumble, their tongue against them”: it may mean that God makes them stumble or that their own tongues trip them. The ESV’s “with their own tongues turned against them” gives the likely sense: their words are the means of their fall.

64.title: They Whet Their Tongues Like Swords
64.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 64 closes the run of David’s prayers of trust (61–64) before the great songs of praise in Psalms 65–68. Psalm 63 ended with the mouths of liars stopped; Psalm 64 is entirely about those mouths, and about the God who stops them.

The message. Words can be weapons, sharpened in secret and fired from cover, and those who use them think no one sees. But God sees, and he answers in kind: suddenly, from where they cannot see him, and with their own tongues turned against them. The result is not the victim’s gloating but a world that learns to fear God, and righteous people who find their joy and refuge in him.

Why it was said. David faces a group of plotters who work by slander and secret schemes, and he is afraid. No particular occasion is named, which made the psalm easy for Israel to sing whenever the righteous were under attack by words (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. First the prayer: hear me, keep me from dread of the enemy, and hide me from their plots (vv. 1–2). Then the enemy described: they sharpen their tongues like swords and shoot bitter words like arrows from ambush, sure that no one can see their snares, and work hard at their wrongdoing, for the human heart is deep (vv. 3–6). Then the turn, in one word, “But”: God shoots his arrow, and they are wounded suddenly, ruined by their own tongues (vv. 7–8). Last, the outcome: all mankind fears and ponders what God has done, and the righteous rejoice in the LORD and take refuge in him (vv. 9–10).

Where it leads. By pattern. The one wholly blameless man was the target of exactly this: plotters searching for testimony and false witnesses shooting from cover (Mark 14:55–59). God’s answer was the resurrection, and when it was preached, the hearers were “cut to the heart” (Acts 2:37). The fear and pondering of verse 9 became repentance, and the plotters were offered refuge in the very one they had attacked.

For us. When you lie awake dreading what someone may say or do, ask God to spare you the dread, not only the danger. Leave the reply to him rather than sharpening your own words. And let the psalm search you too: if you have sat at the whetstone, the refuge of verse 10 is open to the sorry as well as the wronged.
64.theology: The psalm treats words as weapons and fear as a danger of its own (vv. 1, 3-4). God answers the ambushers in their own currency, suddenly for suddenly (vv. 4, 7), and their own tongues bring them down (v. 8). The point of the reversal is not the victim's revenge but a world that learns to fear God, and a righteous man who rejoices in the LORD rather than in anyone's fall (vv. 9-10).
64.examples: Someone who lies awake rehearsing what a colleague or relative might say or do can pray verse 1: spare me the dread, not only the danger. The psalm is also a mirror. Malice can be hard work (v. 6), and it is worth asking whether we ever sit at the whetstone ourselves, sharpening a remark for later. If we have, the refuge of verse 10 is open to the sorry as well as to the wronged.

keyVerse.quote: But God shoots his arrow at them; they are wounded suddenly.
keyVerse.note: This is the turning point, and it hangs on one word, “But”. The archers who shot suddenly from cover are themselves wounded suddenly by an archer they never saw. It assures everyone attacked by hidden words that God sees, and that the last shot is his.

64.reflection:
David asks to be preserved from “dread of the enemy” (v. 1), not only from the enemy. Why can fear itself be a danger, and how can we pray about it?

The plotters ask, “Who can see them?” (v. 5). How does knowing that God sees the heart (v. 6) both comfort the slandered and warn the slanderer?

God turns their own tongues against them (v. 8). How should this shape the way we speak about people who are not in the room?

At Pentecost the fear and pondering of verse 9 led to repentance (Acts 2:36–37). How does the gospel offer refuge even to those who attacked Jesus, and to us?

65.text: To the choirmaster. A Psalm of David. A Song. 1Praise is due to you, O God, in Zion, and to you shall vows be performed.2O you who hear prayer, to you shall all flesh come.3When iniquities prevail against me, you atone for our transgressions.4Blessed is the one you choose and bring near, to dwell in your courts! We shall be satisfied with the goodness of your house, the holiness of your temple!5By awesome deeds you answer us with righteousness, O God of our salvation, the hope of all the ends of the earth and of the farthest seas;6the one who by his strength established the mountains, being girded with might;7who stills the roaring of the seas, the roaring of their waves, the tumult of the peoples,8so that those who dwell at the ends of the earth are in awe at your signs. You make the going out of the morning and the evening to shout for joy.9You visit the earth and water it; you greatly enrich it; the river of God is full of water; you provide their grain, for so you have prepared it.10You water its furrows abundantly, settling its ridges, softening it with showers, and blessing its growth.11You crown the year with your bounty; your wagon tracks overflow with abundance.12The pastures of the wilderness overflow, the hills gird themselves with joy,13the meadows clothe themselves with flocks, the valleys deck themselves with grain, they shout and sing together for joy.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — O You Who Hear Prayer
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God is to be praised in Zion because he hears prayer, deals with sin himself and rules the whole world. Praise and vows wait for him in his house (v. 1), and his very name is that he hears prayer, so that all flesh will come to him (v. 2). When iniquities overwhelm, he atones, and the one he chooses he brings near to be satisfied in his courts (vv. 3–4). His answers are awesome deeds: he set the mountains in place, stills the roaring seas and the tumult of the nations, and is the hope of the ends of the earth, so that from sunrise to sunset the world shouts for joy (vv. 5–8).
verseByVerse.theology: A God whose title is that he hears, who deals with sin and stills both oceans and nations.

verseByVerse.quote: Praise is due to you, O God, in Zion, and to you shall vows be performed. O you who hear prayer, to you shall all flesh come. When iniquities prevail against me, you atone for our transgressions. Blessed is the one you choose and bring near, to dwell in your courts! We shall be satisfied with the goodness of your house, the holiness of your temple!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Praise belongs to the God who hears prayer, who himself covers the sins that overwhelm his people and brings near those he chooses to enjoy him in his house.

O you who hear prayer. Praise stands ready in Zion like a servant in an anteroom, with the vows made in days of need (compare 66:13–14). And God is given a name made out of what he always does. Not “you who answered once”; this is what he is. The promise is as wide as the world, “to you shall all flesh come”, startling in a psalm sung at the temple of a small country. “All flesh” does not mean that everyone will be saved or that all religions reach God. It means people of every nation coming to the one God who hears prayer, as verse 4 says: “Blessed is the one you choose and bring near”.

When iniquities prevail against me, you atone. Watch the pronouns: iniquities prevail against me, and God atones for our transgressions. One man’s experience of being overwhelmed by his own sin turns at once into the congregation’s forgiveness. And the verb is the great one: atone, the Hebrew kaphar, to cover sin and make it right, the word of the Day of Atonement, when the blood was taken behind the curtain (Leviticus 16). Here it is God who does it: sin prevails against the sinner, and God covers it.

Blessed is the one you choose and bring near. Two verbs, and both are God’s. Nobody in this psalm arrives under his own steam, and what they find in his courts is not merely safety but satisfaction, the word Psalm 63:5 used of a feast.

The atonement God provides. The New Testament says how God covers sin: he put Christ forward “as a propitiation by his blood, to be received by faith” (Romans 3:25), so that those once far off “have been brought near by the blood of Christ” (Ephesians 2:13).

Uncertain wording. The ESV reads “Praise is due to you” and notes the alternative “Praise waits for you in silence”; the rare Hebrew word can mean stillness or silence (compare 62:1). Either way, praise belongs to God and waits ready for him in Zion.

verseByVerse.quote: By awesome deeds you answer us with righteousness, O God of our salvation, the hope of all the ends of the earth and of the farthest seas; the one who by his strength established the mountains, being girded with might; who stills the roaring of the seas, the roaring of their waves, the tumult of the peoples, so that those who dwell at the ends of the earth are in awe at your signs. You make the going out of the morning and the evening to shout for joy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God answers his people with awesome deeds, and his rule over seas and nations makes him the hope of the whole world.

The hope of all the ends of the earth. The God who hears prayer answers “with righteousness”, faithful to his promises. And the horizon keeps widening. In verse 2 all flesh comes; here God is the hope of people this congregation had never met and of sailors beyond the known map.

Who stills the roaring of the seas. The roaring sea and the roaring nations are named in the same breath (as in Psalm 46): the God who fixed the mountains stills both.

The going out of the morning and the evening. A lovely line, easy to hurry past: sunrise and sunset are two gates the day goes out of, and both are shouting. Every dawn and every dusk, somewhere on the planet, is a noise of gladness.

The one who stills the seas is God. Verse 7 has an echo that would have stopped any Jewish reader. One night on a lake a man stood up in a boat, “rebuked the wind and said to the sea, ‘Peace! Be still!’”, and the men with him asked, “Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?” (Mark 4:39–41). This psalm answers their question: the one who stills the seas is God.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–13 — The Valleys Deck Themselves with Grain
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The God who forgives in Zion goes out in person to the fields, and the harvest is his gift. He visits the earth, fills the river of God and prepares the grain (v. 9); he waters the furrows, settles the ridges and softens the soil with showers (v. 10). He crowns the year with his bounty, and his wagon tracks overflow (v. 11). The whole landscape answers him: the pastures overflow, the hills put on joy, the meadows are clothed with flocks and the valleys with grain, and all of it shouts and sings (vv. 12–13). The psalm that began with atonement ends in a field, because forgiveness and harvest come from the same hand.
verseByVerse.theology: God goes round the fields himself, and the countryside dresses up and sings.

verseByVerse.quote: You visit the earth and water it; you greatly enrich it; the river of God is full of water; you provide their grain, for so you have prepared it. You water its furrows abundantly, settling its ridges, softening it with showers, and blessing its growth. You crown the year with your bounty; your wagon tracks overflow with abundance. The pastures of the wilderness overflow, the hills gird themselves with joy, the meadows clothe themselves with flocks, the valleys deck themselves with grain, they shout and sing together for joy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God goes round the land in person like a farmer, and crowns the year with a harvest so rich that the countryside seems to dress up and sing.

You visit the earth and water it. Now God becomes a farmer, and the psalm follows him round the fields. You visit: he comes in person, the verb used of God visiting his people to help them. (The ESV notes “make it overflow” as an alternative.) “The river of God” is probably the rain stored above, a channel that never runs dry.

You water its furrows abundantly. Four verbs, the work of one who knows soil: furrows watered, ridges settled, the crust softened so the seed can get up through it, the growth blessed. It is what a farmer prays for, in order, and the psalm says God does each step himself.

Your wagon tracks overflow with abundance. God drives a loaded cart round the countryside, and so much spills off the back that the ruts overflow: not careful measures, but generosity spilling over.

The hills gird themselves with joy. The land gets dressed. The hills belt themselves with gladness, the meadows put on sheep like a coat, the valleys wrap themselves in wheat, and the whole landscape sings. Scripture has no embarrassment about God’s pleasure in ordinary fertility.

Why harvest belongs with forgiveness. The psalm was probably sung at one of Israel’s harvest festivals (Deuteronomy 16:9–15), when the people came up to Zion to give thanks and pay their vows (v. 1). That is why forgiveness in the temple and rain on the fields belong in one song.

God’s witness to the nations. Paul preached this to a crowd of pagans in Lystra: God “did not leave himself without witness, for he did good by giving you rains from heaven and fruitful seasons, satisfying your hearts with food and gladness” (Acts 14:17). The rain that fell on people who did not know his name was already his sermon, and Jesus pointed to the same Father who “sends rain on the just and on the unjust” (Matthew 5:45). The psalm that began with atonement in Zion ends in a field, because the God who forgives sin is the same one who softens soil.

65.title: You Crown the Year with Your Bounty
65.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 65 opens a run of four songs of praise (65–68) that follow the hunted king’s prayers of Psalms 61–64. Here the Psalter breaks into thanksgiving, and this psalm of David looks out from the temple in Zion across the fields to the ends of the earth.

The message. The God who forgives sin in his house is the same God who waters the fields. He hears prayer, covers the transgressions that overwhelm his people, and brings the one he chooses near to be satisfied in him. He rules seas and nations, and goes round the land in person, crowning the year with harvest.

Why it was said. The psalm was very likely sung at one of Israel’s harvest festivals, when worshippers came up to Zion to give thanks and pay the vows they had made (v. 1; see the introduction on the pilgrim feasts). In a land that lived or starved by the rain, they needed to see that crops and forgiveness came from the same hand.

How the chapter makes its case. Praise waits in Zion for the God who hears prayer; when iniquities prevail he atones, and blessed is the one he chooses and brings near to be satisfied in his house (vv. 1–4). His deeds reach far beyond Israel: he stills the seas and the tumult of the peoples and is the hope of the ends of the earth (vv. 5–8). Then the psalm follows him round the fields as he visits, waters, softens and blesses the land and crowns the year, until pastures, hills, meadows and valleys dress themselves and sing (vv. 9–13).

Where it leads. To Christ by the character of God revealed in him, and by promise. The atonement that God himself provides (v. 3) is shown in full at the cross, where God put Christ forward “as a propitiation by his blood, to be received by faith” (Romans 3:25), and those once far off “have been brought near by the blood of Christ” (Ephesians 2:13). The God who stills the roaring seas (v. 7) stood up in a boat on Galilee and said to the sea, “Peace! Be still!” (Mark 4:39). And “to you shall all flesh come” (v. 2) is being kept as the gospel goes to every nation.

For us. When your sins feel stronger than you, pray to the God whose name is “you who hear prayer” and who atones for “our transgressions”: in Christ you have been chosen and brought near. And let every meal, every shower and every harvest send you back to the same God in thanks, because the hand that forgives you is the hand that feeds you.
65.theology: The psalm holds together what are often kept apart: the God who forgives sin in Zion (vv. 3-4) and the God who softens soil in the fields (vv. 9-13). Both are his own work, done in person. Forgiveness and access come by his choosing and bringing near; the harvest comes by his visiting the land. His reach is the whole world, seas, nations and the ends of the earth (vv. 2, 5-8), and the kindness of rain is his witness even to those who do not yet know his name (Acts 14:17).
65.examples: Grace said at a meal, a walk past a ploughed field, a good harvest: the psalm teaches us to see each of these as God going round the fields in person. It also gives a name to pray to on the days prayer feels useless: you who hear prayer, a God whose habit is to listen. And a believer weighed down by sin can notice the pronouns of verse 3: me overwhelmed, our transgressions atoned for. No one is forgiven alone, and no one has to arrive under his own power.

keyVerse.quote: When iniquities prevail against me, you atone for our transgressions.
keyVerse.note: A harvest song could have thanked God for grain alone, but this one begins with the deepest gift: sin covered by God himself when it is too strong for us. The psalm holds forgiveness in Zion and rain on the fields together, and this verse explains why it can: the God who supplies the crops has first dealt with the guilt of those who eat them, as he has now done in Christ.

65.reflection:
God is named “you who hear prayer” (v. 2). How might it change your prayers on a day when prayer feels useless to remember that hearing is what God is like, not something he did once?

Verse 3 moves from “me” to “our”. Why does it matter that forgiveness is received in a congregation and not alone, and how does Romans 3:25 tell us how God atones?

Verses 9–13 picture God going round the fields in person. What everyday gifts do you tend to treat as automatic, and what would it look like to receive them as his visits?

Paul told pagans in Lystra that rain and harvest were God’s witness to them (Acts 14:17). How could the ordinary goodness of life become a starting point for speaking about God to friends who do not yet know him?

66.text: To the choirmaster. A Song. A Psalm. 1Shout for joy to God, all the earth;2sing the glory of his name; give to him glorious praise!3Say to God, "How awesome are your deeds! So great is your power that your enemies come cringing to you.4All the earth worships you and sings praises to you; they sing praises to your name." Selah5Come and see what God has done: he is awesome in his deeds toward the children of man.6He turned the sea into dry land; they passed through the river on foot. There did we rejoice in him,7who rules by his might forever, whose eyes keep watch on the nations— let not the rebellious exalt themselves. Selah8Bless our God, O peoples; let the sound of his praise be heard,9who has kept our soul among the living and has not let our feet slip.10For you, O God, have tested us; you have tried us as silver is tried.11You brought us into the net; you laid a crushing burden on our backs;12you let men ride over our heads; we went through fire and through water; yet you have brought us out to a place of abundance.13I will come into your house with burnt offerings; I will perform my vows to you,14that which my lips uttered and my mouth promised when I was in trouble.15I will offer to you burnt offerings of fattened animals, with the smoke of the sacrifice of rams; I will make an offering of bulls and goats. Selah16Come and hear, all you who fear God, and I will tell what he has done for my soul.17I cried to him with my mouth, and high praise was on my tongue.18If I had cherished iniquity in my heart, the Lord would not have listened.19But truly God has listened; he has attended to the voice of my prayer.20Blessed be God, because he has not rejected my prayer or removed his steadfast love from me!

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — Come and See What God Has Done
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The whole earth is summoned to praise God and to look at what he has done for his people. All the earth is to shout for joy, sing the glory of his name, and tell God how awesome his deeds are, so great that even his enemies come cringing (vv. 1–4). Then the invitation: come and see. He turned the sea into dry land and brought his people through the river on foot, and the singers, centuries later, say “There did we rejoice in him” (vv. 5–6). The God who did it still rules by his might, and his eyes keep watch on the nations, a warning to the rebellious (v. 7).
verseByVerse.theology: The whole earth is called to look at one nation's history, and the singers say we about a crossing centuries before they were born.

verseByVerse.quote: Shout for joy to God, all the earth; sing the glory of his name; give to him glorious praise! Say to God, "How awesome are your deeds! So great is your power that your enemies come cringing to you. All the earth worships you and sings praises to you; they sing praises to your name." Selah Come and see what God has done: he is awesome in his deeds toward the children of man. He turned the sea into dry land; they passed through the river on foot. There did we rejoice in him, who rules by his might forever, whose eyes keep watch on the nations— let not the rebellious exalt themselves. Selah
verseByVerse.commentary:
The whole earth is summoned to come and see what God did for his people at the sea and the river, a rescue every later generation could call its own.

Shout for joy to God, all the earth. The psalm opens as widely as it can and then narrows: the world here, the congregation from verse 8, a single man from verse 13, who ends by telling a small group what happened to him.

He turned the sea into dry land. Verse 6 puts two crossings in one line: the Red Sea, where the water stood up and Israel walked out of Egypt (Exodus 14), and the Jordan, where it happened again on the way in (Joshua 3). Two generations, forty years apart, one God.

There did we rejoice in him. The singer was born centuries later, yet he says we, because what God did for his people then was done for him. Scripture teaches a congregation to hold its history as family memory. And the God of the exodus has not retired: his eyes still “keep watch on the nations”.

Our exodus. Christians say the same we about a cross they did not stand at, and Paul tells Gentile believers that “our fathers” passed through the sea (1 Corinthians 10:1–2). Jesus called his coming death at Jerusalem his “departure” (Luke 9:31), in Greek his exodus: the greater rescue every believer can say we about.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–15 — Tried as Silver Is Tried
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God kept his people alive through an ordeal that he himself sent, and brought them out into abundance, and the rescued man pays what he vowed. The peoples are called to bless the God who has not let Israel’s feet slip (vv. 8–9). He tested them as silver is refined, brought them into the net, laid burdens on them and let men ride over their heads; they went through fire and water, yet he brought them out to a place of abundance (vv. 10–12). Now the voice becomes one man’s, coming to the temple with costly burnt offerings to keep the promises he made when he was in trouble (vv. 13–15).
verseByVerse.theology: Every verb of the ordeal belongs to God, including the net, and so does the way out.

verseByVerse.quote: Bless our God, O peoples; let the sound of his praise be heard, who has kept our soul among the living and has not let our feet slip. For you, O God, have tested us; you have tried us as silver is tried. You brought us into the net; you laid a crushing burden on our backs; you let men ride over our heads; we went through fire and through water; yet you have brought us out to a place of abundance.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The nations are to bless the God who kept his people alive through an ordeal he himself sent to refine them, and then brought them out into abundance.

Who has kept our soul among the living. Two modest mercies most people never count: still alive, and not fallen.

For you, O God, have tested us. Read the verbs: you tested, you tried, you brought us into the net, you laid the burden. Scripture does not offer the comfort that the trouble came from somewhere else. The net was God’s.

You have tried us as silver is tried. The image is a refinery. Silver is not purified by being left alone; it is melted, and the dross rises so that it can be lifted off. Peter says the same of Christians, that the tested genuineness of their faith is “more precious than gold that perishes though it is tested by fire” (1 Peter 1:7).

You let men ride over our heads. A defeated army ridden across, bodies used as ground. Then fire and water, the two ways the ancient world knew a person could be destroyed. Isaiah promised both by name: “When you pass through the waters, I will be with you … when you walk through fire you shall not be burned” (Isaiah 43:2). Not round: through.

Yet you have brought us out to a place of abundance. The psalm turns on yet: the hand that held them in the net has set them down somewhere wide and well supplied. Where they ended up explains the way he took them; it does not deny how bad that way was.

What it does not mean. God’s hand in the ordeal does not make him the author of the riders’ cruelty, which was their own (compare Genesis 50:20), nor does it make every hardship a punishment. Here the purpose is refining, and the end is abundance.

verseByVerse.quote: I will come into your house with burnt offerings; I will perform my vows to you, that which my lips uttered and my mouth promised when I was in trouble. I will offer to you burnt offerings of fattened animals, with the smoke of the sacrifice of rams; I will make an offering of bulls and goats. Selah
verseByVerse.commentary:
The rescued worshipper keeps the costly promises he made to God in trouble.

I will perform my vows to you. The plural becomes I, and the first thing the rescued man does is pay what he promised in the crisis, “when I was in trouble”. Vows made in a hospital corridor are real vows, and Scripture says plainly, “When you vow a vow to God, do not delay paying it” (Ecclesiastes 5:4).

Burnt offerings of fattened animals. The list is expensive: fattened animals, rams, bulls, goats. Most people’s gratitude shrinks as the memory of the danger fades. This man’s has kept its size.

Our offering now. Since Christ has made the one sacrifice, believers bring praise: “Through him then let us continually offer up a sacrifice of praise to God” (Hebrews 13:15).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–20 — Come and Hear What He Has Done for My Soul
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The psalm ends with one man’s testimony to those who fear God: God heard him and did not withdraw his love. He invites them to come and hear what God did for his soul: he cried out, and praise was already on his tongue (vv. 16–17). He knows that if he had cherished iniquity in his heart, the Lord would not have listened (v. 18). But God has listened (v. 19), and the psalm closes by blessing God for two things he did not do: he did not reject the prayer, and he did not remove his steadfast love (v. 20).
verseByVerse.theology: The psalm narrows from the whole earth to one man's testimony, and ends on two things God did not do.

verseByVerse.quote: Come and hear, all you who fear God, and I will tell what he has done for my soul. I cried to him with my mouth, and high praise was on my tongue. If I had cherished iniquity in my heart, the Lord would not have listened. But truly God has listened; he has attended to the voice of my prayer. Blessed be God, because he has not rejected my prayer or removed his steadfast love from me!
verseByVerse.commentary:
One man tells those who fear God that God heard his cry and did not withdraw his steadfast love, though cherished sin would have shut God’s ear.

Come and hear, all you who fear God. Verse 5 said “come and see” what God did for the nation; this says “come and hear” what he has done for one soul. Both are needed. A church with only the big story becomes a history lecture; a church with only personal testimony becomes a series of anecdotes. This psalm has the Red Sea and one man’s answered prayer in the same song.

If I had cherished iniquity in my heart. Everything depends on cherished. He does not say “if I had any sin in my heart”; that would end all prayer. He means: if I had kept it, been fond of it, and meant to keep it. Proverbs puts it sharply: “If one turns away his ear from hearing the law, even his prayer is an abomination” (Proverbs 28:9). The remedy is not to pray louder but to bring the sin into the light and confess it, the way back God has always kept open (Psalm 32:5), and the Spirit he gives his people is the one who loosens the grip. A tender conscience that fears it has done this is usually evidence that it has not; cherished sin does not worry about itself.

The one who was heard. Only one man ever prayed with no iniquity in his heart, and of him it is written that “he was heard because of his reverence” (Hebrews 5:7). Believers pray in his name, and are heard for his sake.

Blessed be God. The psalm ends by blessing God for two things that did not happen: the prayer was not turned away, and the love was not withdrawn. It is an honest way to finish, by a man who had feared both, as the nation had in the net and under the horses. The God who put them in the fire did not withdraw his steadfast love, and the man who came out the other side is standing in the congregation with a bull, telling everybody.

66.title: We Went Through Fire and Through Water
66.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 66 is the second of the four songs of praise (65–68), and like Psalm 65 it opens out to “all the earth”. It carries no author’s name.

The message. What God has done for his people is a public invitation: come and see. He brought Israel through the sea, and he has brought his people through testing, fire and water into abundance; the hard road was his doing, and so was the way out. And the God who acts on the scale of nations also listens to one person’s prayer and does not take away his steadfast love.

Why it was said. The occasion is not given. Some link it with a deliverance such as Jerusalem’s rescue from the Assyrians in Hezekiah’s day (2 Kings 19), but its words fit many. What is clear is that a worshipper made vows in trouble and has come to the temple to pay them (vv. 13–14).

How the chapter makes its case. The psalm narrows like a funnel. All the earth is called to sing and to come and see what God did at the sea and the river (vv. 1–7). The peoples are called to bless the God who kept Israel alive, tried them as silver is tried, and brought them through fire and water to a place of abundance (vv. 8–12). Then one man speaks: he brings costly offerings to pay the vows he made in trouble (vv. 13–15), and invites those who fear God to come and hear how God listened to him when cherished sin would have closed God’s ear (vv. 16–20).

Where it leads. To Christ by pattern, and by the need verse 18 exposes. The crossing of the sea is the pattern of a greater rescue: Jesus spoke of the death he would accomplish at Jerusalem as his “departure” (Luke 9:31), using the word exodus, and he passed through the fire and water of God’s judgment for his people and came out to life. And only one man ever prayed with no iniquity cherished in his heart; of him it is written that “he was heard because of his reverence” (Hebrews 5:7). Believers are heard in his name.

For us. Christian testimony needs both halves of this psalm: what God has done for his people in Christ, and what he has done for my soul. Hard seasons are not outside his hand, and he means them to refine, not destroy. Keep the promises you made to God in trouble, and if you fear that some sin has shut his ear, confess it and come back: his steadfast love has not been removed.
66.theology: The psalm funnels from all the earth to the congregation to one man, and it needs both the big story and the personal one (vv. 5, 16). It does not pretend the ordeal came from somewhere else: every verb of the testing is God's (vv. 10-12), and the hinge is yet, the same hand bringing them out to abundance. What closes the line of prayer is sin cherished rather than sin committed (v. 18), and the remedy is confession. The last word is God's steadfast love, not withdrawn (v. 20).
66.examples: A congregation that has come through hard years together, or a believer who has come out of a long illness, can borrow both halves of this psalm: come and see what God has done for his people, and come and hear what he has done for me. Vows made in a hospital corridor deserve to be kept when the corridor is far behind. And anyone afraid that some sin has shut God's ear can read verse 18 beside verse 20: confession reopens the line.

keyVerse.quote: we went through fire and through water; yet you have brought us out to a place of abundance.
keyVerse.note: The whole psalm turns on the word “yet”. It does not pretend the ordeal was mild or that it came from somewhere other than God’s hand, but it insists that the same hand brought his people out into a wide and well-supplied place. That is the shape of every Christian’s story in Christ, who went through the deepest waters for us.

66.reflection:
The singers say “There did we rejoice in him” (v. 6) about a crossing centuries before they were born. How does the gospel make Christ’s death and resurrection part of your own story, not just something that happened to someone else (1 Corinthians 10:1–2)?

Verses 10–12 say that God himself tested and tried his people. Is that a comfort or a difficulty to you? How does the picture of silver being refined, and 1 Peter 1:6–7, help?

What promises have you made to God in a time of trouble? Why do they tend to fade once the danger passes, and what would keeping them look like now (vv. 13–14)?

Verse 18 speaks of “cherished” sin. What is the difference between having sin and cherishing it, and what does verse 20 offer to someone afraid that God has stopped listening?

67.text: To the choirmaster: with stringed instruments. A Psalm. A Song. 1May God be gracious to us and bless us and make his face to shine upon us, Selah2that your way may be known on earth, your saving power among all nations.3Let the peoples praise you, O God; let all the peoples praise you!4Let the nations be glad and sing for joy, for you judge the peoples with equity and guide the nations upon earth. Selah5Let the peoples praise you, O God; let all the peoples praise you!6The earth has yielded its increase; God, our God, shall bless us.7God shall bless us; let all the ends of the earth fear him!

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — That Your Way May Be Known on Earth
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God blesses his people so that all the nations may know him and be glad in him. The congregation asks for the priestly blessing, God’s grace and the shining of his face, so that his way and his saving power may be known on earth (vv. 1–2). A refrain calls every people to praise him (vv. 3, 5), and at the centre stands the reason for their joy: he judges the peoples with equity and guides the nations of the earth (v. 4). The harvest already gathered is a pledge that God will go on blessing, and the psalm ends where it has been aiming, with all the ends of the earth fearing him (vv. 6–7).
verseByVerse.theology: Israel asks for the priestly blessing and gives God a reason: so that the nations will find out what he is like.

verseByVerse.quote: May God be gracious to us and bless us and make his face to shine upon us, Selah that your way may be known on earth, your saving power among all nations.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel asks for the priestly blessing so that the whole earth may come to know God’s saving power.

May God be gracious to us and bless us. Every Israelite knew this: the blessing Aaron and his sons were told to say over the people, “The LORD bless you and keep you; the LORD make his face to shine upon you and be gracious to you” (Numbers 6:24–25). The priest said it to them; here the congregation says it back to God as a request. The best material for prayer is what God has already said he wants to give.

That your way may be known on earth. The blessing has a purpose beyond Israel’s comfort: bless us, so that they may know you. It is the promise to Abraham turned into prayer: “I will bless you … so that you will be a blessing … and in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed” (Genesis 12:2–3). Israel is asking to be blessed in the way a lamp asks to be lit: for the sake of the room.

The blessing of Abraham in Christ. Paul says where the promise is fulfilled: Christ redeemed us “so that in Christ Jesus the blessing of Abraham might come to the Gentiles” (Galatians 3:14).

When we pray for God’s favour. Ask for it; the psalm does. But the psalm gives a reason, and the reason is other people. A church praying only for its own health has dropped half of this prayer.

verseByVerse.quote: Let the peoples praise you, O God; let all the peoples praise you! Let the nations be glad and sing for joy, for you judge the peoples with equity and guide the nations upon earth. Selah Let the peoples praise you, O God; let all the peoples praise you!
verseByVerse.commentary:
The nations are called not to submit to Israel but to praise God gladly, because he judges every people fairly and guides their history.

Let the peoples praise you, O God. The refrain returns unchanged in verse 5, framing the middle verse. The request is not that the nations be conquered, but that they praise: that they end up enjoying God.

You judge the peoples with equity. At the centre, the reason given for the nations’ gladness is startling: God’s judgment. We hear judgment as bad news, but to people governed by the strong and the corrupt, a judge who cannot be bought is very good news. Equity means fairness, every case heard on its merits; and “guide the nations upon earth” means their history is not drifting. For nations that have been someone else’s plaything, that is a reason to sing.

The Judge who saves. God “has fixed a day on which he will judge the world in righteousness by a man whom he has appointed” (Acts 17:31). For the wronged he is justice at last; for sinners he is good news because he first bore judgment in their place.

verseByVerse.quote: The earth has yielded its increase; God, our God, shall bless us. God shall bless us; let all the ends of the earth fear him!
verseByVerse.commentary:
The gathered harvest is a sign that God will go on blessing, until all the ends of the earth fear him.

The earth has yielded its increase. The tense changes and a fact appears: the barns are filling, and the congregation takes that as evidence for everybody, not merely themselves.

The witness of the harvest. Paul preached the logic of Psalm 65 to pagans in Lystra: God gave “rains from heaven and fruitful seasons” as his witness to people who had never heard his name (Acts 14:17). This psalm wants that evidence shown to the ends of the earth.

Let all the ends of the earth fear him! The psalm’s whole aim: not admire, not acknowledge, but fear, in the sense this book has taught throughout: the reverence that is the beginning of wisdom and the door into friendship with God (25:14).

A missionary prayer. Peoples or nations appear in four of seven verses. It is a missionary prayer written centuries before there was a mission, and its answer is a scene John was shown at the end: “a great multitude that no one could number, from every nation, from all tribes and peoples and languages, standing before the throne” (Revelation 7:9). They are doing exactly what verse 3 asked for.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew verbs of verses 6–7 can be read either as statements (“God shall bless us”, as the ESV has it) or as prayers (“may God bless us”), and translations differ. Either way, the gathered harvest grounds confidence that God’s blessing will continue and reach the nations.

67.title: Let All the Peoples Praise You
67.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 67 is the third of the four songs of praise (65–68), a short song “with stringed instruments”. Like Psalm 65 it is a harvest psalm (v. 6), and like Psalm 66 it calls the nations; in Psalm 68 they will be seen coming.

The message. God blesses his people so that the whole world may come to know him. Israel asks for God’s gracious favour, but asks for it with a purpose beyond itself: that his way and his saving power may be known among all nations, and that every people may be glad in him under his just rule. Blessing is meant to overflow.

Why it was said. The harvest has been gathered (v. 6), and the congregation, probably at a harvest feast, turns the blessing the priests spoke over them (Numbers 6:24–26) into a prayer. Israel was a small nation among great empires, but it had been told from the beginning that through Abraham “all the families of the earth shall be blessed” (Genesis 12:3), and this psalm remembers why it had been blessed at all.

How the chapter makes its case. The psalm is built like a mirror around its centre. It opens with the priestly blessing and its purpose, that God’s way may be known on earth (vv. 1–2). A refrain calls all the peoples to praise (vv. 3, 5), and between the two refrains stands the reason the nations should be glad: God judges the peoples with equity and guides the nations (v. 4). It closes with the harvest as a sign that God will go on blessing, until all the ends of the earth fear him (vv. 6–7).

Where it leads. By promise. The blessing promised to Abraham for all nations comes through Christ, who redeemed us “so that in Christ Jesus the blessing of Abraham might come to the Gentiles” (Galatians 3:14). When the old man Simeon held the infant Jesus, he called him God’s salvation, “a light for revelation to the Gentiles” (Luke 2:32), and the face God makes to shine on us is seen “in the face of Jesus Christ” (2 Corinthians 4:6). The psalm’s answer is the multitude from every nation standing before the throne (Revelation 7:9).

For us. Ask God boldly for his blessing on your life and your church, but ask with this psalm’s purpose attached: so that neighbours, colleagues and the nations may come to know him. A church that prays only for its own comfort has dropped half of verse 1. And every harvest, every good gift, is a reason to tell others how good he is.
67.theology: The psalm turns God's own promised blessing into prayer (v. 1) and gives it a purpose beyond Israel (v. 2): the nations are to know him, praise him and fear him. What is wanted for them is gladness, not conquest, and the reason is a just Judge who guides them (v. 4). Every good harvest becomes evidence offered to the ends of the earth (vv. 6-7).
67.examples: When a church prays for its own growth, health or funds, this psalm adds a question: what is the blessing for? Ask for it, but ask with the second half of verse 1 attached, so that neighbours, colleagues and the nations may come to know God. Praying Scripture back to God, as this psalm does with the priest's blessing, is a good way to start: we are asking for what he has already said he loves to give.

keyVerse.quote: that your way may be known on earth, your saving power among all nations.
keyVerse.note: Verse 2 gives the blessing of verse 1 its purpose, and that purpose is the key to the whole psalm. Israel asks to be blessed in the way a lamp asks to be lit: for the sake of the room. It is the promise to Abraham turned into prayer, and it is answered as the gospel of Christ goes to every nation.

67.reflection:
Verse 1 turns the priestly blessing of Numbers 6:24–26 into a prayer. Which promises of God could you pray back to him this week, and why is that a good way to pray?

The psalm asks for blessing “that your way may be known on earth” (v. 2). When you pray for your own family, church or work, how often is the purpose other people? What would change if it were?

Verse 4 gives God’s just judgment as a reason for the nations to be glad. Why would a fair Judge be good news to people who have been oppressed, and what makes judgment good news for sinners (Acts 17:31)?

Revelation 7:9 shows the answer to this psalm. How does that picture shape the way you pray for and support the spread of the gospel among other peoples?

68.text: To the choirmaster. A Psalm of David. A Song. 1God shall arise, his enemies shall be scattered; and those who hate him shall flee before him!2As smoke is driven away, so you shall drive them away; as wax melts before fire, so the wicked shall perish before God!3But the righteous shall be glad; they shall exult before God; they shall be jubilant with joy!4Sing to God, sing praises to his name; lift up a song to him who rides through the deserts; his name is the LORD; exult before him!5Father of the fatherless and protector of widows is God in his holy habitation.6God settles the solitary in a home; he leads out the prisoners to prosperity, but the rebellious dwell in a parched land.7O God, when you went out before your people, when you marched through the wilderness, Selah8the earth quaked, the heavens poured down rain, before God, the One of Sinai, before God, the God of Israel.9Rain in abundance, O God, you shed abroad; you restored your inheritance as it languished;10your flock found a dwelling in it; in your goodness, O God, you provided for the needy.11The Lord gives the word; the women who announce the news are a great host:12"The kings of the armies—they flee, they flee!" The women at home divide the spoil—13though you men lie among the sheepfolds— the wings of a dove covered with silver, its pinions with shimmering gold.14When the Almighty scatters kings there, let snow fall on Zalmon.15O mountain of God, mountain of Bashan; O many-peaked mountain, mountain of Bashan!16Why do you look with hatred, O many-peaked mountain, at the mount that God desired for his abode, yes, where the LORD will dwell forever?17The chariots of God are twice ten thousand, thousands upon thousands; the Lord is among them; Sinai is now in the sanctuary.18You ascended on high, leading a host of captives in your train and receiving gifts among men, even among the rebellious, that the LORD God may dwell there.19Blessed be the Lord, who daily bears us up; God is our salvation. Selah20Our God is a God of salvation, and to GOD, the Lord, belong deliverances from death.21But God will strike the heads of his enemies, the hairy crown of him who walks in his guilty ways.22The Lord said, "I will bring them back from Bashan, I will bring them back from the depths of the sea,23that you may strike your feet in their blood, that the tongues of your dogs may have their portion from the foe."24Your procession is seen, O God, the procession of my God, my King, into the sanctuary—25the singers in front, the musicians last, between them virgins playing tambourines:26"Bless God in the great congregation, the LORD, O you who are of Israel's fountain!"27There is Benjamin, the least of them, in the lead, the princes of Judah in their throng, the princes of Zebulun, the princes of Naphtali.28Summon your power, O God, the power, O God, by which you have worked for us.29Because of your temple at Jerusalem kings shall bear gifts to you.30Rebuke the beasts that dwell among the reeds, the herd of bulls with the calves of the peoples. Trample underfoot those who lust after tribute; scatter the peoples who delight in war.31Nobles shall come from Egypt; Cush shall hasten to stretch out her hands to God.32O kingdoms of the earth, sing to God; sing praises to the Lord, Selah33to him who rides in the heavens, the ancient heavens; behold, he sends out his voice, his mighty voice.34Ascribe power to God, whose majesty is over Israel, and whose power is in the skies.35Awesome is God from his sanctuary; the God of Israel—he is the one who gives power and strength to his people. Blessed be God!

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — God Settles the Solitary in a Home
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The God who rises to scatter his enemies is, at home, a father to those who have no one. The psalm opens with the ark’s war-cry: God arises, and his enemies vanish like smoke and melt like wax, while the righteous are jubilant before him (vv. 1–3). Sing to the one who rides through the deserts, whose name is the LORD (v. 4). Then comes the heart of the psalm: in his holy habitation he is father of the fatherless and protector of widows; he settles the solitary in a home and leads prisoners out to prosperity, though the rebellious stay in the parched land (vv. 5–6).
verseByVerse.theology: The war-cry of the ark is followed at once by a description of God as a father to orphans.

verseByVerse.quote: God shall arise, his enemies shall be scattered; and those who hate him shall flee before him! As smoke is driven away, so you shall drive them away; as wax melts before fire, so the wicked shall perish before God! But the righteous shall be glad; they shall exult before God; they shall be jubilant with joy! Sing to God, sing praises to his name; lift up a song to him who rides through the deserts; his name is the LORD; exult before him! Father of the fatherless and protector of widows is God in his holy habitation. God settles the solitary in a home; he leads out the prisoners to prosperity, but the rebellious dwell in a parched land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When God rises his enemies vanish like smoke, yet at home this conquering God is a father to orphans and a refuge for widows, the lonely and prisoners.

God shall arise, his enemies shall be scattered. It is what Moses said every time the ark was lifted to lead the next stage of the march: “Arise, O LORD, and let your enemies be scattered” (Numbers 10:35). So the psalm begins as a procession song, and verses 24–27 will show the parade arriving.

As smoke is driven away. Smoke in wind, wax near flame: neither has to be fought; they simply cannot last. Yet the same coming makes the righteous “jubilant with joy” (v. 3): the difference lies in those he comes to.

Him who rides through the deserts. A rider crossing open country: the God of a people on the move, not fixed to one shrine. “His name is the LORD” uses the short form Yah, as in “Hallelujah”.

Father of the fatherless and protector of widows. Four verses into a war song comes its heart: the God of twenty thousand chariots (v. 17) describes himself by his care for four kinds of people with nothing. He is father to the fatherless: not a patron, a father. He is the widow’s protector, a judge who takes up her case when nobody else would. He “settles the solitary in a home”: not merely visited but given a household to belong to, as God does when he puts lonely people into a church. He leads prisoners out, while the rebellious stay in the parched land.

In his holy habitation. Caring for them is no sideline; it is what he is like at home. And Jesus promised: “I will not leave you as orphans; I will come to you” (John 14:18). In Christ the fatherless are adopted and taught to cry “Abba! Father!” (Galatians 4:4–6).

What if the word “father” hurts? For many people “father” calls up not protection but an empty chair, or a temper, or worse, and God as Father can feel like a door closing. Freud argued that belief in God is a projection of the father we wished we had (see the note on Luke 15:20). The psychologist Paul Vitz, in Faith of the Fatherless, turned it round, noting how many well-known modern atheists had lost their fathers early or been badly failed by them. Neither argument settles whether God is there, but both show how deeply our fathers shape the face we expect God to have. This psalm works the other way: God defines fatherhood by what he does for those who have none. Every family in heaven and on earth is named from the Father (Ephesians 3:14–15), so he is the original and every earthly father a copy, good or bad. And Jesus, who could say “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father” (John 14:9), shows us the Father the fatherless have been looking for all along.

Uncertain wording. The verb behind “lift up a song” usually means to build up a road (as in Isaiah 62:10), so some translate cast up a highway for the rider. And “deserts” is close to a word for clouds: the KJV reads him that rideth upon the heavens, and many think the line deliberately takes a title of the Canaanite storm-god Baal, “rider of the clouds”, and gives it to the LORD (compare v. 33).
verseByVerse.note: Compare Num 10:35.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s power, shown from Sinai to Zion, is power that carries his people and defeats their enemies. He marched before Israel through the wilderness while the earth quaked, then rained on his weary land and provided for the needy (vv. 7–10). He spoke the word, kings fled, and the women at home spread the news and shared the spoil (vv. 11–14). The great mountains of Bashan look with envy at the hill God chose, where he has ascended with captives in his train, receiving gifts even among the rebellious, so that he may dwell there (vv. 15–18). He daily bears his people up, holds the ways out of death, and will strike his enemies wherever they hide (vv. 19–23).
verseByVerse.theology: The verse Paul quotes of Christ's ascension sits next to the verse about God carrying his people every day.

verseByVerse.quote: O God, when you went out before your people, when you marched through the wilderness, Selah the earth quaked, the heavens poured down rain, before God, the One of Sinai, before God, the God of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God marched at the head of his people, and at Sinai the earth shook before him.

When you went out before your people. God is pictured at the head of the column, as he went before Israel in the pillar of cloud and fire (Exodus 13:21) and as the ark set out with the cry of verse 1. “The earth quaked” recalls Sinai, where “the whole mountain trembled greatly” (Exodus 19:18).

Before God, the One of Sinai. The psalm remembers the march in the words of Deborah’s old victory song (Judges 5:4–5). And if “the One of Sinai” is a title, as the ESV takes it, the mountain got its reputation from him, not the other way round.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew behind “the One of Sinai” is two words, literally this Sinai. Many take it as a title of God; others read that even Sinai itself quaked, as in Deborah’s song.

verseByVerse.quote: Rain in abundance, O God, you shed abroad; you restored your inheritance as it languished; your flock found a dwelling in it; in your goodness, O God, you provided for the needy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God watered his weary land and settled his flock in it, providing for the needy.

Rain in abundance, O God, you shed abroad. The storm of verse 8 becomes rain for the crops. The weather that terrifies at Sinai waters a field in Canaan, and verse 10 names who benefits: “the needy”. Verse 5’s orphans and widows are being fed.

Your flock found a dwelling in it. It is the land, God’s inheritance: his own estate, which he restored when it “languished” and then gave his flock to live in. It is verse 6 on a national scale: the God who “settles the solitary in a home” settled a whole people (see the note on vv. 1–6). Israel’s land was a gift kept by God’s goodness, not a prize held by Israel’s strength.

verseByVerse.quote: The Lord gives the word; the women who announce the news are a great host: "The kings of the armies—they flee, they flee!" The women at home divide the spoil— though you men lie among the sheepfolds— the wings of a dove covered with silver, its pinions with shimmering gold. When the Almighty scatters kings there, let snow fall on Zalmon.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God speaks, enemy kings flee, and a host of women spreads the news of victory.

The Lord gives the word. The victory starts with God speaking. Nothing happens on the field until he has spoken, and then the outcome is settled before the first blow.

The women who announce the news are a great host. A lovely detail: the heralds are women, a great many of them, carrying the news home, as Miriam and the women sang after the Red Sea, and Deborah after Sisera’s defeat. Their report repeats itself for delight: “The kings of the armies, they flee, they flee!” Fittingly, women were the first to run with the news of the empty tomb (Matthew 28:8).

Though you men lie among the sheepfolds. This probably echoes Deborah’s song again, which rebuked the tribe of Reuben for sitting at home among the flocks while others fought (Judges 5:16).

Uncertain wording. Verses 12–14 are among the most obscure in the Psalter: spoil divided at home, a dove covered with silver, snow falling on Zalmon. The shape is clear: an army routed, treasure carried home, something beautiful glinting after a night of fear. The silvered dove may be fine spoil brought home, or Israel itself, whom another psalm calls God’s “dove” (74:19), shining with the wealth of the defeated. Zalmon is probably the wooded hill near Shechem (Judges 9:48). Some take the snow as the weapons and bodies of the routed kings strewn white over its slopes; others as a real snowstorm in the rout, as the storm once fought against Sisera (Judges 5:20–21). Either way the scene is God’s victory and his people’s joy in it.

verseByVerse.quote: O mountain of God, mountain of Bashan; O many-peaked mountain, mountain of Bashan! Why do you look with hatred, O many-peaked mountain, at the mount that God desired for his abode, yes, where the LORD will dwell forever? The chariots of God are twice ten thousand, thousands upon thousands; the Lord is among them; Sinai is now in the sanctuary. You ascended on high, leading a host of captives in your train and receiving gifts among men, even among the rebellious, that the LORD God may dwell there.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God chose little Zion over the towering mountains, and has gone up to it in triumph to dwell even among rebels.

O mountain of God, mountain of Bashan. The psalm teases the mountains. Bashan’s range in the north is high, rugged and spectacular (the ESV notes that “many-peaked” may mean hunch-backed), and Zion is a low ridge in the south. Why the jealous stare? Because God chose the small one. That is the Bible’s pattern with mountains, nations and people: God passes over the impressive and makes his home with the unimpressive, as his Son would be born in Bethlehem, “too little to be among the clans of Judah” (Micah 5:2).

You ascended on high. Twenty thousand chariots (v. 17), and then an ascent: God goes up Zion’s hill with defeated enemies in his train and tribute handed over, as a victorious king came home. The tribute is received “even among the rebellious”, so “that the LORD God may dwell there”. The conquest ends in God moving in among the people who fought him.

How Paul quotes it. Paul quotes this verse of Jesus with one startling difference, a wording also found in the ancient Aramaic paraphrase (the Targum): “When he ascended on high he led a host of captives, and he gave gifts to men” (Ephesians 4:8). The psalm says the conqueror received gifts; Paul says he gave them. Both are true: a victor receives tribute to share it out when he gets home, and what the ascended Christ shared out was apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors and teachers for his church. The captives are the powers he defeated, for he “disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame, by triumphing over them” (Colossians 2:15).

Uncertain wording. “Sinai is now in the sanctuary” renders a very compressed Hebrew line, literally the Lord among them, Sinai, in holiness. The likely sense is that the God of Sinai, with all the glory and terror of that mountain, has now come to dwell in his holy place on Zion.
verseByVerse.note: On Paul's wording, see Eph 4:8 and the comment above.

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed be the Lord, who daily bears us up; God is our salvation. Selah Our God is a God of salvation, and to GOD, the Lord, belong deliverances from death. But God will strike the heads of his enemies, the hairy crown of him who walks in his guilty ways. The Lord said, "I will bring them back from Bashan, I will bring them back from the depths of the sea, that you may strike your feet in their blood, that the tongues of your dogs may have their portion from the foe."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God carries his people daily, holds the ways out of death, and will defeat his enemies wherever they hide.

Who daily bears us up. One verse after the great ascent, the God of twenty thousand chariots daily bears us up (or “bears our burden”). The word is used of loading a pack animal: he carries us every day, as a load he has taken on, doing the daily work of carrying people who cannot manage.

Deliverances from death. The plural is striking: deliverances, more than one, and the Hebrew speaks of escapes that belong to God. Every escape from death there has ever been was his to give, and the risen Christ says, “I have the keys of Death and Hades” (Revelation 1:18).

God will strike the heads of his enemies. The battlefield language returns, grim. The hairy crown is the long hair a warrior wore with pride; no enemy escapes, on Bashan’s heights or in the sea’s depths; and the victors walk through the blood of the fallen. As at Psalm 58, the killing is God’s and the war is already decided (see the introduction on the psalms that curse). Christians pray it with the cross in view, and many hear in it the old promise that the serpent’s head would be crushed by one whose own heel was bruised (Genesis 3:15): “The God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet” (Romans 16:20). It is the language of God’s own victory, not a licence for ours.

Uncertain wording. Verse 22 does not say whom the Lord will bring back from Bashan and the depths of the sea. Most take it of his enemies, fetched back from wherever they flee to face judgment (compare Amos 9:2–3), which suits verses 21 and 23; some take it of his own people brought home.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 24–35 — Cush Shall Hasten to Stretch Out Her Hands
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The victory procession arrives, and the nations are drawn into the praise of the God who gives strength. The procession of God the King enters the sanctuary with singers, musicians and girls playing tambourines, and the tribes march together, little Benjamin in the lead (vv. 24–27). The psalm asks God to summon his power again, and foresees kings bringing gifts to his temple, the war-loving powers rebuked, and even Egypt and Cush stretching out their hands to God (vv. 28–31). All the kingdoms of the earth are called to sing to the one who rides the ancient heavens and speaks with a mighty voice, and who gives power and strength to his people (vv. 32–35).
verseByVerse.theology: The parade ends with the nations invited in and the last word given to the strength God hands out.

verseByVerse.quote: Your procession is seen, O God, the procession of my God, my King, into the sanctuary— the singers in front, the musicians last, between them virgins playing tambourines: "Bless God in the great congregation, the LORD, O you who are of Israel's fountain!" There is Benjamin, the least of them, in the lead, the princes of Judah in their throng, the princes of Zebulun, the princes of Naphtali.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God the King enters his sanctuary in procession, with music and with the tribes, small and great, together.

Your procession is seen, O God. The parade the psalm began with arrives, and the order of march is telling: singers at the front, players at the back, girls with tambourines in the middle. No soldiers are mentioned.

O you who are of Israel’s fountain! Every descendant of Israel is called to bless God. Israel, that is Jacob, is pictured as the spring from which the whole people flowed, as Isaiah speaks of those “who came from the waters of Judah” (Isaiah 48:1). All of them, from the head of the stream to the last trickle, owe him praise.

There is Benjamin, the least of them, in the lead. Benjamin, the smallest tribe, nearly wiped out in Judges 20, walks at the head. Two southern tribes and two northern ones are named together, and since north and south were so often divided, that was itself a small miracle.

verseByVerse.quote: Summon your power, O God, the power, O God, by which you have worked for us. Because of your temple at Jerusalem kings shall bear gifts to you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The psalm asks God to act in power again, and foresees kings bringing him gifts.

Summon your power, O God. Praise turns to prayer: the power God showed in the past (vv. 7–23) is asked for again. Remembering what God has done should lead to asking him to act now.

Kings shall bear gifts to you. The word for temple can mean any house of God, and was used of the tabernacle at Shiloh (1 Samuel 1:9); later readers sang it of Solomon’s temple. Foreign rulers did bring gifts there: the queen of Sheba and the kings who sought Solomon’s wisdom (1 Kings 10:10, 24–25), and after Sennacherib’s defeat many brought gifts to the LORD in Jerusalem (2 Chronicles 32:23). The wise men’s gifts to the child Jesus (Matthew 2:11) were a first instalment, and the picture looks further, to the city into which “the kings of the earth will bring their glory” (Revelation 21:24).

verseByVerse.quote: Rebuke the beasts that dwell among the reeds, the herd of bulls with the calves of the peoples. Trample underfoot those who lust after tribute; scatter the peoples who delight in war. Nobles shall come from Egypt; Cush shall hasten to stretch out her hands to God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God is asked to rebuke the war-loving powers, and even Egypt and distant Cush will reach out to him.

Scatter the peoples who delight in war. The beasts among the reeds are usually taken as Egypt, whose emblem was the crocodile or the hippopotamus of the Nile marshes, and the bulls as proud rulers with their peoples. What is clear is the last line, a prayer for the end of a particular kind of nation: those who “delight in war”. Not merely those who fight, but those who enjoy it.

Nobles shall come from Egypt. Egypt is the house of slavery, and Cush is the land beyond Egypt’s southern border, in today’s Sudan, at the edge of the known world; the New Testament calls it Ethiopia. Both are pictured coming to God with hands stretched out in prayer. Centuries later Philip met a man from Cush on a desert road, reading Isaiah in a chariot, and baptised him (Acts 8:27–39). On that road this verse began to come true.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew of verse 30 is uncertain at several points (the ESV notes it), especially “trample underfoot those who lust after tribute”. The general sense, that God would humble proud and violent powers, is clear.

verseByVerse.quote: O kingdoms of the earth, sing to God; sing praises to the Lord, Selah to him who rides in the heavens, the ancient heavens; behold, he sends out his voice, his mighty voice. Ascribe power to God, whose majesty is over Israel, and whose power is in the skies. Awesome is God from his sanctuary; the God of Israel—he is the one who gives power and strength to his people. Blessed be God!
verseByVerse.commentary:
All kingdoms are to sing to the God of the heavens, whose power is given as strength to his people.

He sends out his voice. The rider of verse 4 crossed deserts; here he rides the sky, and a psalm full of chariots ends with the only weapon God needs: “he sends out his voice, his mighty voice”. In these last days that voice has spoken by his Son (Hebrews 1:2).

The one who gives power and strength. After all that power, the final clause is about giving: “he is the one who gives power and strength to his people”. It is the same movement as verse 18 read through Paul: the conqueror comes home and hands out what he has won, and the ascended Christ promised, “you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you” (Acts 1:8).

One God throughout. And it is the same God as verse 5, the father of the fatherless: not two Gods but one. The God whose strength fills the skies is the God who is kind to the widow, and both go to the same people: his people.

68.title: Father of the Fatherless
68.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 68 is the last and grandest of the four songs of praise (65–68). Psalm 67 prayed that the nations would come to know God; here they are seen coming with gifts. This psalm of David is one of the hardest in the Psalter to translate.

The message. The God who marched from Sinai at the head of his people has come up to his chosen home on Zion as conquering King, and all his power is for the weak. He scatters his enemies like smoke, yet calls himself father of the fatherless; he carries his people daily and gives them strength, until the kingdoms of the earth sing to him.

Why it was said. The opening words are the cry Moses raised whenever the ark set out (Numbers 10:35), and verses 24–27 describe a procession entering the sanctuary. Many therefore link it with David bringing the ark up to Jerusalem (2 Samuel 6), though the occasion is not stated (see the introduction on the titles).

How the chapter makes its case. God arises and his enemies scatter, and the God who rides through the deserts is father of the fatherless (vv. 1–6). He marched through the wilderness, watered his land and routed kings (vv. 7–14). The great mountains of Bashan envy little Zion, which God chose; he has ascended it with captives in his train (vv. 15–18). He bears his people up daily, delivers from death and crushes his enemies (vv. 19–23). The procession enters the sanctuary, tribes great and small together (vv. 24–27). Finally it sees kings, Egypt and Cush coming to God, and calls all kingdoms to sing to him (vv. 28–35).

Where it leads. By promise and by pattern, with the New Testament’s own warrant. Paul quotes verse 18 of Christ: “When he ascended on high he led a host of captives, and he gave gifts to men” (Ephesians 4:8). Having triumphed at the cross, Christ ascended and shared out his victory as gifts to his church. In him the fatherless are adopted (John 14:18), the keys of death are in his hand (Revelation 1:18), and the Cushite reading Isaiah on the desert road (Acts 8:27) was the first of the nations of verse 31 to stretch out his hands.

For us. No one is too small for this God: he chose the low hill, and he describes himself by his care for orphans, widows, the lonely and prisoners, so his church should be a home for such people. When you cannot face another day, remember that he “daily bears us up”. And when you feel weak, look to the ascended Christ, who gives strength to his people.
68.theology: The psalm is a procession song, beginning with the ark's war-cry (v. 1) and arriving at the sanctuary (vv. 24-27). Its centre is that the God of twenty thousand chariots defines himself, at home in his holy habitation, by his care for orphans, widows, the lonely and prisoners (vv. 5-6). He chooses the low hill over the spectacular ranges (vv. 15-16), and his power always ends in giving: the ascended conqueror distributes what he has won (v. 18; Eph 4:8), carries his people daily (v. 19), and gives power and strength to his people (v. 35).
68.examples: The orphan, the widow, the lonely flat-dweller and the released prisoner are not at the edge of God’s concern: he describes himself by his care for them. That makes verse 6 a job description for a church: a place where the solitary are given a household to belong to, not merely a visit. Anyone who feels too small or too ordinary for God to notice can take heart from the little hill he chose over the mountains, and anyone who cannot manage another day can rest on verse 19: he carries us daily, as a load he has chosen to take on.

keyVerse.quote: Father of the fatherless and protector of widows is God in his holy habitation.
keyVerse.note: In a psalm full of chariots, armies and earthquakes, this is how God chooses to be known. The conqueror who scatters kings is, at home in his holy place, a father to orphans and the champion of widows, and all his power in the rest of the psalm serves that kindness. In Christ the fatherless are adopted and learn to call him Father.

68.reflection:
Verses 5–6 describe God by his care for orphans, widows, the lonely and prisoners. Who are such people in your community and church, and what would it mean to give them a home to belong to, rather than only visit them?

God chose little Zion over the towering mountains of Bashan (vv. 15–16). Where do you see this pattern in the rest of the Bible and in Christ, and how does it encourage someone who feels unimpressive?

Paul reads verse 18 as Christ ascending and giving gifts (Ephesians 4:8–12). What gifts has the ascended Christ given your church, and how are you using what he has given you?

The God of twenty thousand chariots “daily bears us up” (v. 19). What burden do you need to let him carry today?

69.text: To the choirmaster: according to Lilies. Of David. 1Save me, O God! For the waters have come up to my neck.2I sink in deep mire, where there is no foothold; I have come into deep waters, and the flood sweeps over me.3I am weary with my crying out; my throat is parched. My eyes grow dim with waiting for my God.4More in number than the hairs of my head are those who hate me without cause; mighty are those who would destroy me, those who attack me with lies. What I did not steal must I now restore?5O God, you know my folly; the wrongs I have done are not hidden from you.6Let not those who hope in you be put to shame through me, O Lord GOD of hosts; let not those who seek you be brought to dishonor through me, O God of Israel.7For it is for your sake that I have borne reproach, that dishonor has covered my face.8I have become a stranger to my brothers, an alien to my mother's sons.9For zeal for your house has consumed me, and the reproaches of those who reproach you have fallen on me.10When I wept and humbled my soul with fasting, it became my reproach.11When I made sackcloth my clothing, I became a byword to them.12I am the talk of those who sit in the gate, and the drunkards make songs about me.13But as for me, my prayer is to you, O LORD. At an acceptable time, O God, in the abundance of your steadfast love answer me in your saving faithfulness.14Deliver me from sinking in the mire; let me be delivered from my enemies and from the deep waters.15Let not the flood sweep over me, or the deep swallow me up, or the pit close its mouth over me.16Answer me, O LORD, for your steadfast love is good; according to your abundant mercy, turn to me.17Hide not your face from your servant, for I am in distress; make haste to answer me.18Draw near to my soul, redeem me; ransom me because of my enemies!19You know my reproach, and my shame and my dishonor; my foes are all known to you.20Reproaches have broken my heart, so that I am in despair. I looked for pity, but there was none, and for comforters, but I found none.21They gave me poison for food, and for my thirst they gave me sour wine to drink.22Let their own table before them become a snare; and when they are at peace, let it become a trap.23Let their eyes be darkened, so that they cannot see, and make their loins tremble continually.24Pour out your indignation upon them, and let your burning anger overtake them.25May their camp be a desolation; let no one dwell in their tents.26For they persecute him whom you have struck down, and they recount the pain of those you have wounded.27Add to them punishment upon punishment; may they have no acquittal from you.28Let them be blotted out of the book of the living; let them not be enrolled among the righteous.29But I am afflicted and in pain; let your salvation, O God, set me on high!30I will praise the name of God with a song; I will magnify him with thanksgiving.31This will please the LORD more than an ox or a bull with horns and hoofs.32When the humble see it they will be glad; you who seek God, let your hearts revive.33For the LORD hears the needy and does not despise his own people who are prisoners.34Let heaven and earth praise him, the seas and everything that moves in them.35For God will save Zion and build up the cities of Judah, and people shall dwell there and possess it;36the offspring of his servants shall inherit it, and those who love his name shall dwell in it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — The Waters Have Come Up to My Neck
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Suffering for God’s sake can feel like drowning, and faith says so honestly. David is up to his neck in water with no foothold, hoarse from praying, and hated without cause by more enemies than he has hairs (vv. 1–4). He owns his own folly before God, and his deepest fear is that his disgrace will shame others who hope in God (vv. 5–6). Then he gives the reason for his trouble: it is for God’s sake. Zeal for God’s house has cost him his own brothers, and his fasting and sackcloth have made him the talk of the elders at the gate and the drunkards’ songs (vv. 7–12). The New Testament hears Jesus in these verses: hated without a cause, consumed by zeal, bearing the reproaches aimed at God.
verseByVerse.theology: A man drowning, who admits his own folly and whose chief fear is that his shame will hurt other believers.

verseByVerse.quote: Save me, O God! For the waters have come up to my neck. I sink in deep mire, where there is no foothold; I have come into deep waters, and the flood sweeps over me. I am weary with my crying out; my throat is parched. My eyes grow dim with waiting for my God. More in number than the hairs of my head are those who hate me without cause; mighty are those who would destroy me, those who attack me with lies. What I did not steal must I now restore? O God, you know my folly; the wrongs I have done are not hidden from you. Let not those who hope in you be put to shame through me, O Lord GOD of hosts; let not those who seek you be brought to dishonor through me, O God of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sinking in deep water and hated without cause, David cries to God, owns his own folly, and asks above all that his disgrace will not make other believers ashamed of their God.

According to Lilies. The heading gives the tune (see the note at the end), the same one Psalm 45 used for a royal wedding song; now it carries a man drowning.
