I sink in deep mire, where there is no foothold. Psalm 40 described a man hauled out of a miry bog; this one is still in it, with the water at his chin. “No foothold” is the horror of the picture: nothing to stand on, and the more he struggles the deeper he goes.

I am weary with my crying out. He has prayed himself hoarse, and his eyes have given out from scanning the horizon. Anyone who has waited that long knows that waiting is its own labour.

Those who hate me without cause. The last line of verse 4 is what being wrongly accused feels like: “What I did not steal must I now restore?” He is made to pay back what he never took.

O God, you know my folly. Verse 5 must be handled honestly. The man praying is a sinner and says so. He does not claim that every charge against him is false, only that the hatred is undeserved.

Let not those who hope in you be put to shame through me. A surprising request: that his public disgrace will not make other believers ashamed of their God. At the end of his strength he is still thinking about what his trouble is doing to the faith of people watching.

How the New Testament uses it. Jesus took the phrase of verse 4 (found also in Psalm 35) and applied it to the world’s hatred of himself: “They hated me without a cause” (John 15:25). And many Christians have heard in verse 4’s last line a picture of the gospel: Christ, who took nothing, paid back what we had stolen, “the righteous for the unrighteous” (1 Peter 3:18). The New Testament quotes the psalm’s sufferings of Christ, never its confession in verse 5: here is a righteous sufferer who is still a sinner, and in him the pattern of one who would suffer the same way with no folly to confess.

Uncertain wording. “According to Lilies” is probably the name of a tune or a way of singing; what it refers to is not known. In verse 1 the ESV notes that “the waters have come up to my neck” may also be read “the waters threaten my life”: the Hebrew word can mean throat or neck, and also life or soul.

verseByVerse.quote: For it is for your sake that I have borne reproach, that dishonor has covered my face. I have become a stranger to my brothers, an alien to my mother's sons. For zeal for your house has consumed me, and the reproaches of those who reproach you have fallen on me. When I wept and humbled my soul with fasting, it became my reproach. When I made sackcloth my clothing, I became a byword to them. I am the talk of those who sit in the gate, and the drunkards make songs about me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
His trouble comes from his loyalty to God: zeal for God’s house has cost him his family and made him a joke to the whole town, and the insults aimed at God have landed on him.

For it is for your sake. The reproach comes because he belongs to God. And it has cost him his family, not distant relatives but “my mother’s sons”, the boys he grew up with. John says the same of Jesus in one flat sentence: “For not even his brothers believed in him” (John 7:5).

Zeal for your house has consumed me. Both halves of verse 9 are quoted in the New Testament, of two different moments. When Jesus drove the traders out of the temple, “His disciples remembered that it was written, ‘Zeal for your house will consume me’” (John 2:17). John puts the verb in the future, probably because the disciples had just watched the kind of act that would get him killed.

The reproaches of those who reproach you have fallen on me. Paul quotes the second half to teach Christians to bear with the weak: “For Christ did not please himself, but as it is written, ‘The reproaches of those who reproached you fell on me’” (Romans 15:3). The insults aimed at God landed on him. That happens to anyone who stands close enough to God to be in the line of fire, and it happened to Christ most fully of all.

I became a byword to them. His devotion is what they laugh at. He fasted and it was held against him; he wore sackcloth and became a byword, a standing joke. The two audiences are the top and bottom of society: “those who sit in the gate” are the elders and men of business who ran the town at its gate, and the drunkards are making songs about him in the tavern. The respectable and the rowdy agree in finding him ridiculous.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–21 — I Looked for Pity, but There Was None
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In the deepest water he turns to God’s steadfast love and leaves the timing with him. He asks for an answer “at an acceptable time” and pleads to be pulled out before the flood, the deep and the pit close over him (vv. 13–15). Seven urgent requests follow, ending with the buying words redeem and ransom (vv. 16–18). Then he tells God what he has suffered: God knows his shame; reproach has broken his heart; he looked for one person to pity him and found none, and for his thirst they gave him sour wine (vv. 19–21). These are some of the loneliest lines in Scripture, and the Gospels saw the last of them fulfilled at the cross.
verseByVerse.theology: The loneliest verses in the Psalter, and the Gospels record the last of them happening.

verseByVerse.quote: But as for me, my prayer is to you, O LORD. At an acceptable time, O God, in the abundance of your steadfast love answer me in your saving faithfulness. Deliver me from sinking in the mire; let me be delivered from my enemies and from the deep waters. Let not the flood sweep over me, or the deep swallow me up, or the pit close its mouth over me. Answer me, O LORD, for your steadfast love is good; according to your abundant mercy, turn to me. Hide not your face from your servant, for I am in distress; make haste to answer me. Draw near to my soul, redeem me; ransom me because of my enemies! You know my reproach, and my shame and my dishonor; my foes are all known to you. Reproaches have broken my heart, so that I am in despair. I looked for pity, but there was none, and for comforters, but I found none. They gave me poison for food, and for my thirst they gave me sour wine to drink.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He pleads with God to answer in his own good time and pull him out before the deep closes over him, and he tells God of a grief so lonely that no one pitied him and they gave him sour wine for his thirst.

At an acceptable time. A drowning man asks for an answer and leaves the timing with God, not because he is calm, but because he believes there is such a thing as God’s right moment.

Or the pit close its mouth over me. Three mouths are open to swallow him: the flood, the deep and the pit. The last is a grave closing over him.

Draw near to my soul, redeem me. Verses 16–18 make seven urgent requests: answer, turn, do not hide, make haste, draw near, redeem, ransom. The last two come from buying and selling: buy me back, pay whatever it costs to get me out.

Reproaches have broken my heart. Verses 20–21 are among the loneliest lines in the Psalter. He looked round for one person to feel something for him, and for anyone at all to sit with him, and there was nobody. Whoever reads this psalm from inside that experience should know that it is here in Scripture without correction or rebuke. And Jesus knew it: in Gethsemane he came back three times to find his friends asleep. “So, could you not watch with me one hour?” (Matthew 26:40).

For my thirst they gave me sour wine. At the cross they offered Jesus “wine to drink, mixed with gall”, and he would not drink it (Matthew 27:34); later, when he said “I thirst”, they held a sponge of sour wine to his mouth (John 19:28–29). The Gospel writers plainly have this verse in view: the last kindness offered to a dying man was a mouthful of vinegar, written down about a thousand years before.

How Jewish readers take it. Jewish readers hear the lament of David, or of any faithful Israelite (some say the nation in exile) bearing shame for God’s sake, and they note that the speaker confesses his own folly and wrongs (v. 5) and calls down judgment on his enemies (vv. 22–28), which does not suit a sinless Messiah. Christians agree that the psalm is first David’s prayer. This commentary reads it of Christ as the greater David: the New Testament quotes it of his zeal, of the hatred he met and of the reproaches he bore (John 2:17; 15:25; Romans 15:3), and the Gospels see verse 21 at the cross.

Uncertain wording. The word translated “poison” in verse 21 names a bitter plant, perhaps a poisonous one; which plant is not known. The ancient Greek translation rendered it “gall”, the word Matthew uses for what was mixed with the wine offered to Jesus (Matthew 27:34).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–36 — Let Their Own Table Become a Snare
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The wronged man hands his enemies to God’s justice and then sings, because God hears the needy. The curse is long and fierce: their table a trap, their eyes darkened, their camp empty, their names struck from the book of the living (vv. 22–28). Its charge is that they hunted a man God had already struck down. Yet the curse changes nothing for him; what he needs is God’s salvation (v. 29). So he vows a song of thanks that pleases God more than the finest bull (vv. 30–31). The humble will see it and take heart (vv. 32–33), and the psalm ends with heaven, earth and sea praising the God who will rebuild Zion for the children of his servants (vv. 34–36).
verseByVerse.theology: One of the Psalter's longest curses, and then a song that costs nothing and pleases God more than cattle.

verseByVerse.quote: Let their own table before them become a snare; and when they are at peace, let it become a trap. Let their eyes be darkened, so that they cannot see, and make their loins tremble continually. Pour out your indignation upon them, and let your burning anger overtake them. May their camp be a desolation; let no one dwell in their tents. For they persecute him whom you have struck down, and they recount the pain of those you have wounded. Add to them punishment upon punishment; may they have no acquittal from you. Let them be blotted out of the book of the living; let them not be enrolled among the righteous.
verseByVerse.commentary:
David asks God to judge his persecutors in the fiercest terms, because they hunted a man God had already struck down, and he leaves the judgment entirely in God’s hands.

Let their own table before them become a snare. Here begins one of the longest curses in the Psalter, and it is not gentle: the table, the place of safety and fellowship, is to become a trap.

How to read the curse. First, it is prayer: he asks God to act, and does not act himself. Second, and more startling, Paul quotes these very verses about Israel’s hardening against the gospel (Romans 11:9–10), in the same letter where he writes, “my heart’s desire and prayer to God for them is that they may be saved” (Romans 10:1). Paul can pray this psalm and weep over the people it describes at the same time, because carrying out judgment belongs to God, and pleading for sinners belongs to us.

May their camp be a desolation. In the upper room Peter applied verse 25 to one man: “May his camp become desolate, and let there be no one to dwell in it” (Acts 1:20), of Judas, whose place had to be filled. The psalm of the betrayed one supplied the words for what happened to the betrayer.

They persecute him whom you have struck down. Verse 26 is the charge beneath the curse. Their sin is not that they attacked a strong man, but that they went after someone God had already brought low, and then talked about his pain for entertainment.

Blotted out of the book of the living. The book of the living is the register of God’s people, and the last request is that these names be struck off it, the most terrible thing asked for in the Psalter. The risen Christ says the opposite to a faithful church: “I will never blot his name out of the book of life” (Revelation 3:5). Both sentences are about the same register. Those whom God has truly written there are never erased, and that is the difference the gospel makes.

Why is such a prayer in Scripture at all? Because God does not ask the wronged to pretend that evil is small. These curses hand the case to the Judge instead of taking revenge (Romans 12:19). And at the cross the two halves of this psalm meet. The one hated without cause bore the curse himself, for “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us” (Galatians 3:13), and he prayed for those who crucified him (Luke 23:34).

Where Christians differ: may a Christian pray these curses? Some hold that they belong to a harsher stage of revelation, or to David’s own anger, and should not be on the lips of those told to love their enemies (Matthew 5:44). This commentary’s view: the apostles quote this very psalm as Scripture (Acts 1:20; Romans 11:9–10), so a Christian may pray it as a cry for God’s justice against unrepentant evil, handing vengeance to God, while praying first for the enemy’s repentance, as Christ did (see the introduction).

verseByVerse.quote: But I am afflicted and in pain; let your salvation, O God, set me on high! I will praise the name of God with a song; I will magnify him with thanksgiving. This will please the LORD more than an ox or a bull with horns and hoofs.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Still in pain, he asks God to lift him up, and vows a song of thanks that will please God more than the most costly sacrifice.

But I am afflicted and in pain. After all that, he is still in the water. The curse has changed nothing about his condition. What he needs is in the next line, God’s salvation setting him “on high”, out of the mire and onto safe ground.

I will magnify him with thanksgiving. To magnify God is not to make him bigger, which no one can do, but to make his greatness seen, as a telescope makes a distant star look as great as it really is. Thanksgiving does that: it tells others what God has done.

This will please the LORD more than an ox. Here the psalm turns. He cannot bring a bull; he is drowning, disgraced, abandoned, mocked. What he has is a voice, and God prefers it. “Horns and hoofs” describes a fully grown, perfect animal, the most expensive thing a man could offer, and a song of thanks outranks it (as at 50:14 and 51:17). Hebrews draws the same line for Christians, who offer through Christ “a sacrifice of praise to God, that is, the fruit of lips that acknowledge his name” (Hebrews 13:15).

verseByVerse.quote: When the humble see it they will be glad; you who seek God, let your hearts revive. For the LORD hears the needy and does not despise his own people who are prisoners.
verseByVerse.commentary:
His rescue will give heart to every humble believer who sees it, because the LORD hears the needy and never despises his own people in chains.

When the humble see it they will be glad. His rescue will do other people good. The humble will see it and take heart, which answers his fear in verse 6 that his disgrace would damage their faith. And the reason is a plain statement of how God always acts: he “hears the needy” and does not despise his people “who are prisoners”, wherever they are being held.

verseByVerse.quote: Let heaven and earth praise him, the seas and everything that moves in them. For God will save Zion and build up the cities of Judah, and people shall dwell there and possess it; the offspring of his servants shall inherit it, and those who love his name shall dwell in it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The psalm ends with all creation praising the God who will save Zion and rebuild Judah, so that the children of his servants will live there in safety.

God will save Zion and build up the cities of Judah. The psalm ends with the whole people, not the singer alone. Judah’s towns were often left ruined by war, and these lines were probably sung with special longing in and after the exile, when God promised of the cities of Judah, “I will raise up their ruins” (Isaiah 44:26). “The offspring of his servants shall inherit it”: the promise reaches the children, and it belongs to “those who love his name”.

Let heaven and earth praise him. The psalm that began with one man up to his neck in water ends with the sea itself praising and children living safely in rebuilt cities. That is the true shape of Christian hope: the personal rescue is real, and it is the smallest part of what God is doing. The sufferer the Gospels saw drinking the sour wine is the one through whom God saves his Zion, and the children of his servants dwell there because of him.

69.title: Zeal for Your House Has Consumed Me
69.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 69 comes near the end of Book Two, straight after the triumphant procession of Psalm 68, and drops from the heights into deep water. After Psalm 22, no psalm is quoted more often in the New Testament of the sufferings of Christ.

The message. A servant of God is sinking, hated without cause and disowned by his family, because of his loyalty to God. He does not pretend to be sinless, and he does not take revenge: he hands everything to God, his own rescue and his enemies’ judgment alike. Then, still in pain, he sings, sure that “the LORD hears the needy” (v. 33) and will save Zion for generations to come.

Why it was said. The heading gives the psalm to David, and Paul quotes it as David’s words (Romans 11:9), though no occasion is named. Israel sang it as the prayer of the righteous sufferer (see the introduction), and the closing promise to rebuild the cities of Judah (v. 35) may have been sung with special longing in and after the exile.

How the chapter makes its case. First the flood: water at his neck, enemies past counting, his own folly confessed, and his fear that his disgrace will shame others (vv. 1–6). The cause is zeal for God’s house, which has made him the joke of the gate and the tavern (vv. 7–12). He prays for God’s acceptable time, and tells of finding no comforters and being given sour wine (vv. 13–21). Then one of the Psalter’s longest curses, handed to God rather than carried out (vv. 22–28). Last, a song that pleases God more than a prize bull, and all creation praising the God who will rebuild Zion (vv. 29–36).

Where it leads. By pattern, as the New Testament itself reads it: the hatred without cause (John 15:25), the zeal and the reproaches (John 2:17; Romans 15:3), the sour wine (John 19:28–29) and Judas’ empty place (Acts 1:20). Yet the New Testament never quotes verse 5: David was a sinner suffering for God, and Jesus suffered the same way with no folly to confess. And the curse this psalm calls down on the guilty, Christ bore for all who turn to him (Galatians 3:13).

For us. If you are in deep water, this prayer is yours, without correction or rebuke. You can still care how your trouble looks to weaker believers, leave the timing with God, and bring the offering left to you, a song of thanks. If you are mocked for your faith, you stand where Christ stood; leave the reckoning to God, and pray for those who wrong you.
69.theology: The heading names David, and Paul cites verses 22–23 as David’s words (Romans 11:9); the promise to rebuild Judah’s cities (v. 35) has led some to think the psalm was also sung, perhaps extended, in the exile. The speaker is a sinner and says so (v. 5), yet the New Testament applies the psalm’s suffering to Christ, never its confession: the hatred without cause, the zeal, the reproaches and the sour wine. David is a pattern of one who would suffer the same way with no folly to confess. The curse is handed to God, not carried out (Paul could quote it and still pray for the people it describes, Rom 10:1), and it changes nothing for the sufferer; what lifts him is God's salvation (v. 29), and his song, the offering of a man with nothing, pleases God more than the costliest animal (vv. 30-31; cf. 50:14; 51:17).
69.examples: Anyone praying from deep water, hoarse from asking, will find their experience here without correction or rebuke, including the search for one person to sit with them (v. 20). The psalm also shows what can still be done there. Like this man, we can care how our trouble looks to weaker believers (v. 6), leave the timing with God (v. 13), and bring the one offering left to us, a song of thanks, which God prefers to a prize bull. Those mocked for their faith, by the respectable or the rowdy, stand where Christ stood (v. 9).

keyVerse.quote: For zeal for your house has consumed me, and the reproaches of those who reproach you have fallen on me.
keyVerse.note: This verse gives the reason for all the suffering in the psalm: he is hated because he belongs to God. The New Testament quotes both halves of it of Jesus, of his zeal in cleansing the temple (John 2:17) and of the insults aimed at God that fell on him (Romans 15:3). It shows why the psalm leads so clearly to Christ, who bore the reproach for God’s sake with no folly of his own to confess.

69.reflection:
David is drowning, yet his first concern is that his disgrace will not shame others who hope in God (v. 6). How does your own trouble affect the faith of people who are watching you? What would it look like to care about that without pretending to be fine?

He confesses his own folly (v. 5), yet the New Testament applies the psalm’s sufferings to Jesus, who had none. What does this teach you about the difference between David and David’s greater Son, and about how to read the psalms of suffering?

The long curse of verses 22–28 hands the enemies to God instead of taking revenge. Is there someone who has wronged you whose case you need to hand over to God? How can you do that and still pray for their repentance, as Paul did (Romans 10:1) and as Jesus did on the cross?

A song of thanks from a man with nothing pleases God more than the finest bull (vv. 30–31). What “sacrifice of praise” (Hebrews 13:15) could you offer this week, even in a hard season?

70.text: To the choirmaster. Of David, for the memorial offering. 1Make haste, O God, to deliver me! O LORD, make haste to help me!2Let them be put to shame and confusion who seek my life! Let them be turned back and brought to dishonor who delight in my hurt!3Let them turn back because of their shame who say, "Aha, Aha!"4May all who seek you rejoice and be glad in you! May those who love your salvation say evermore, "God is great!"5But I am poor and needy; hasten to me, O God! You are my help and my deliverer; O LORD, do not delay!

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In an emergency, faith may simply cry “Hurry!”, and God has given words for it. The psalm is Psalm 40:13–17 issued on its own, with every unhurried word removed. It begins at a run, “make haste” twice (v. 1), asks that those who seek his life and gloat “Aha, Aha!” be turned back in shame (vv. 2–3), and then, even in his danger, prays that all who seek God will rejoice and say “God is great!” (v. 4). Where Psalm 40 paused to reflect that the Lord takes thought for him, this version adds one more plea: “hasten to me, O God! … do not delay!” (v. 5). The content of faith is unchanged; only the pace has changed.
verseByVerse.theology: Psalm 40's closing prayer, reissued on its own with every unhurried word removed.

verseByVerse.quote: Make haste, O God, to deliver me! O LORD, make haste to help me! Let them be put to shame and confusion who seek my life! Let them be turned back and brought to dishonor who delight in my hurt! Let them turn back because of their shame who say, "Aha, Aha!" May all who seek you rejoice and be glad in you! May those who love your salvation say evermore, "God is great!" But I am poor and needy; hasten to me, O God! You are my help and my deliverer; O LORD, do not delay!
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is the end of Psalm 40 made into a prayer for emergencies: with no time for anything else, the needy believer begs God to hurry, and still asks that all who seek God will be glad. It is explained at Psalm 40:13–17; here we note the differences.

For the memorial offering. One thing has been added: the heading, the same as Psalm 38’s (see the note at the end). The emergency prayer has been given a place in Israel’s regular worship.

Make haste, O God, to deliver me! The original reads “Be pleased, O LORD, to deliver me!” (40:13). The courteous “be pleased” has gone; what is left begins at a run. The twelve verses of testimony that led up to the prayer in Psalm 40 (the pit, the new song, the scroll, the great congregation) have gone too. This psalm opens in the emergency.

Days for the short prayer. There are days for the long version, rehearsing all God has done before asking anything. And there are days when the house is on fire, and Scripture provides a prayer for those too: five verses, no preamble, twice “make haste” and once “do not delay”.

Aha, Aha! The petitions against the enemies stand almost as in Psalm 40; “Aha, Aha!” is the same noise of delighted malice heard at 35:21.

God is great! The first real change is one word. Psalm 40:16 has “Great is the LORD!”, using the covenant name; this has “God is great!” That is the pattern of Psalms 42–83 (the “Elohistic Psalter”), where Elohim (God) mostly stands in place of Yahweh (printed LORD), as when Psalm 53 repeated Psalm 14. The change is not mechanical: the last line has “O LORD, do not delay!” where Psalm 40 had “do not delay, O my God!”

May all who seek you rejoice. Even with his life in danger, he asks that everyone who seeks God should be glad. Panic has not made him selfish.

Hasten to me, O God! The second change is the most telling. Psalm 40:17 reads: “As for me, I am poor and needy, but the Lord takes thought for me.” That was a man pausing in trouble to remember that God is thinking of him; this version puts another plea in its place. It is the same prayer, kept for the moment when a believer cannot manage reflection but can still manage hurry. The faith is unchanged; the pace has changed, and God’s word makes room for both.

With loud cries and tears. These verses first ended Psalm 40, which Hebrews puts in Christ’s mouth: “Behold, I have come to do your will, O God” (Hebrews 10:7). The Christian who can manage only “make haste” prays through a high priest who prayed “with loud cries and tears” and was heard (Hebrews 5:7), and who bids the poor and needy “with confidence draw near to the throne of grace” for help in time of need (Hebrews 4:16).

Uncertain wording. “For the memorial offering” translates a Hebrew word meaning “to bring to remembrance”. It probably refers to the memorial portion of the grain offering, the handful burned on the altar (Leviticus 2:2), so that the psalm was sung when it was offered; it may simply mark the psalm as a prayer asking God to remember the one who prays.
verseByVerse.note: Almost identical to Psalm 40:13–17.

70.title: Make Haste, O God
70.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 70 follows the long lament of Psalm 69 with a short cry of five verses. It is not new: it is the closing prayer of Psalm 40 (40:13–17), taken out and given a life of its own. Psalm 71, which has no heading and may once have been joined to it, carries on in the same voice.

The message. When there is no time for anything else, it is enough to cry “Make haste” to God. God’s word keeps a prayer for the emergency, stripped of every unhurried word, and it is still a prayer of faith: the one who prays is “poor and needy”, God is “my help and my deliverer”, and even in panic he asks that all who seek God will be glad.

Why it was said. The heading gives it to David and adds “for the memorial offering”, as with Psalm 38, which suggests that this emergency prayer was given a regular place in Israel’s worship (see the introduction on how the psalms were gathered). The small changes from Psalm 40 also match the habit of Psalms 42–83, which mostly call on “God” rather than the covenant name, the LORD.

How the chapter makes its case. It opens at a run, “make haste” twice (v. 1). It asks that those who hunt him and jeer “Aha, Aha!” be turned back in shame (vv. 2–3). It prays, generously, that everyone who seeks God will rejoice and say “God is great!” (v. 4). And it ends where Psalm 40 paused to reflect that the Lord thinks of him, with one more plea: “hasten to me, O God! … do not delay!” (v. 5).

Where it leads. By pattern, and by the character of God revealed in Christ. Hebrews puts Psalm 40, the psalm these verses first closed, on the lips of Christ: “Behold, I have come to do your will, O God” (Hebrews 10:7). The Son of David also prayed in urgent need, “with loud cries and tears”, and was heard (Hebrews 5:7). So the believer who can manage only “make haste” prays through a high priest who knows that prayer from the inside, and who bids the needy come boldly for help in time of need (Hebrews 4:16).

For us. Some prayers are said in an ambulance, a waiting room or the middle of the night. This psalm is God’s permission to pray like that, with no preamble. Hurry is not unbelief, and the short prayer is as welcome as the long one.
70.theology: The Psalter keeps both editions of this prayer on purpose: the long one for days when a believer can rehearse God's history of rescues, and this one for days when all that is left is make haste. The content of faith is unchanged; only the pace differs. Even in the emergency he still asks that all who seek God be glad (v. 4), and the Christian prays the hurried prayer through Christ, who was heard in his own anguish.
70.examples: Some prayers are said in an ambulance, a waiting room or the middle of the night, with no time for preamble. This psalm is God's permission to pray like that: make haste, twice, and do not delay. The longer prayers of praise can wait for calmer days, and God hears both.

keyVerse.quote: But I am poor and needy; hasten to me, O God! You are my help and my deliverer; O LORD, do not delay!
keyVerse.note: This last verse holds the whole psalm: a needy believer, a God who is his help, and a plea to hurry. It is where the psalm differs most from Psalm 40, which paused here to reflect that the Lord takes thought for him; this version can manage only one more cry for help. God’s word makes room for that prayer, and the believer prays it through Christ, who was heard in his own anguish.

70.reflection:
Psalm 70 keeps Psalm 40’s closing prayer but removes its long testimony and its calm reflection. When have you needed a prayer like this, with no time or strength for more? What does it mean to you that God has given words for such moments?

Even in his emergency, David asks that all who seek God will rejoice and say “God is great!” (v. 4). Why do you think trouble so often turns us inward, and how can praying for others guard us against that?

Hebrews says Jesus prayed “with loud cries and tears” and was heard (Hebrews 5:7). How does knowing that he prayed in anguish change the way you come to God when you are desperate?

The Psalter keeps both a long and a short version of this prayer. How might you use each in your own prayer life, and in praying with someone in crisis?

My praise is continually of you.<sup>7</sup>I have been as a portent to many, but you are my strong refuge.<sup>8</sup>My mouth is filled with your praise, and with your glory all the day.<sup>9</sup>Do not cast me off in the time of old age; forsake me not when my strength is spent.<sup>10</sup>For my enemies speak concerning me; those who watch for my life consult together<sup>11</sup>and say, "God has forsaken him; pursue and seize him, for there is none to deliver him."<sup>12</sup>O God, be not far from me; O my God, make haste to help me!<sup>13</sup>May my accusers be put to shame and consumed; with scorn and disgrace may they be covered who seek my hurt.<sup>14</sup>But I will hope continually and will praise you yet more and more.<sup>15</sup>My mouth will tell of your righteous acts, of your deeds of salvation all the day, for their number is past my knowledge.<sup>16</sup>With the mighty deeds of the Lord GOD I will come; I will remind them of your righteousness, yours alone.<sup>17</sup>O God, from my youth you have taught me, and I still proclaim your wondrous deeds.<sup>18</sup>So even to old age and gray hairs, O God, do not forsake me, until I proclaim your might to another generation, your power to all those to come.<sup>19</sup>Your righteousness, O God, reaches the high heavens. You who have done great things, O God, who is like you?<sup>20</sup>You who have made me see many troubles and calamities will revive me again; from the depths of the earth you will bring me up again.<sup>21</sup>You will increase my greatness and comfort me again.<sup>22</sup>I will also praise you with the harp for your faithfulness, O my God; I will sing praises to you with the lyre, O Holy One of Israel.<sup>23</sup>My lips will shout for joy, when I sing praises to you; my soul also, which you have redeemed.<sup>24</sup>And my tongue will talk of your righteous help all the day long, for they have been put to shame and disappointed who sought to do me hurt.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The God who has held you from before your birth will not cast you off when your strength is spent. An old man takes refuge in God in words borrowed from Psalm 31, prayed all his life (vv. 1–3). He has trusted God from his youth, and leaned on him before he was born (vv. 4–6). His long life has been a sign that people watch, and he wants them to see God as his refuge and hear his praise all day (vv. 7–8). Then comes the heart of the psalm: “Do not cast me off in the time of old age” (v. 9), for his enemies take his weakness as proof that God has left him (vv. 10–11). He asks God to hurry (vv. 12–13).
verseByVerse.theology: A man who has leaned on God since before he could speak, asking not to be dropped now that he is weak.

verseByVerse.quote: In you, O LORD, do I take refuge; let me never be put to shame! In your righteousness deliver me and rescue me; incline your ear to me, and save me! Be to me a rock of refuge, to which I may continually come; you have given the command to save me, for you are my rock and my fortress.
verseByVerse.commentary:
An old believer takes refuge in God with the prayers of a lifetime, asking him to be the rock he can keep coming back to.

An old man’s psalm. The psalm has no heading in the Hebrew (the ancient Greek translation, the Septuagint, gives it to David, and many think it continues Psalm 70). The man who prays it is unmistakable all the same: he is old, and he prays in words he has used all his life.

Borrowed prayers. Verses 1–3 are nearly identical to Psalm 31:1–3. Verse 6 echoes Psalm 22:9–10; verse 12 is Psalm 22:11 and 40:13; verse 13 comes out of Psalm 35. The phrases learned young are the ones that come to hand when strength is gone, as anyone who has sat with a dying believer singing old hymns knows.

In your righteousness deliver me. God’s righteousness is a ground for hope here: his faithfulness to do right by his own, and so to save them. The word runs through the psalm (vv. 15, 16, 19, 24). “You have given the command to save me”: the order has already gone out, and the old man asks only that it be carried out.

To which I may continually come. “Continually” is one of this psalm’s key words, here and again in verses 6 and 14. He is describing a lifetime’s habit, not a crisis visit.
verseByVerse.note: Compare Psalm 31:1–3.

verseByVerse.quote: Rescue me, O my God, from the hand of the wicked, from the grasp of the unjust and cruel man. For you, O Lord, are my hope, my trust, O LORD, from my youth. Upon you I have leaned from before my birth; you are he who took me from my mother's womb. My praise is continually of you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He asks to be rescued from cruel men, because God has been his hope from his youth and has carried him since before he was born.

From the grasp of the unjust and cruel man. Old age makes a man easy prey, and there are people who take advantage of it. What they say comes out in verses 10–11.

Upon you I have leaned from before my birth. He measures the relationship in decades, and further back: “from my youth”, and behind that, “from before my birth”, with God pictured as the midwife who delivered him. What an old man wants to tell you is not how long he has believed, but how long he has been held.

verseByVerse.quote: I have been as a portent to many, but you are my strong refuge. My mouth is filled with your praise, and with your glory all the day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
People have watched his life as a sign, and he wants what they see to be God as his strong refuge and what they hear to be praise all day long.

I have been as a portent to many. A portent is a sign people point at, a wonder or a warning (see the note at the end): people watch his life and draw conclusions.

My mouth is filled with your praise. If people are watching, he wants them to see what verse 7 ends with, “you are my strong refuge”, and to hear praise from him “all the day”, not only on good days. The same “all the day” returns in the psalm’s last verse (v. 24).

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew word for “portent” is used both of wonders and of warning signs. Some think people read his many troubles as a sign that God was against him (as in v. 11); others, that his survival made him a wonder. Either way, the answer is the same: “but you are my strong refuge.”

verseByVerse.quote: Do not cast me off in the time of old age; forsake me not when my strength is spent. For my enemies speak concerning me; those who watch for my life consult together and say, "God has forsaken him; pursue and seize him, for there is none to deliver him." O God, be not far from me; O my God, make haste to help me! May my accusers be put to shame and consumed; with scorn and disgrace may they be covered who seek my hurt.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He begs God not to discard him now that he is old and weak, while his enemies say that God has forsaken him.

Do not cast me off in the time of old age. Here is the request this psalm exists for. “Cast me off” is the word for discarding something, and the fear is specific: that God’s interest was in his usefulness, and that when the usefulness runs out the relationship will quietly end.

Forsake me not when my strength is spent. Anyone who has watched a capable person become dependent knows the fear from inside: the shrinking of attention, the sense of being stored somewhere rather than wanted. This psalm brings it to God directly, and God had already answered it through Isaiah: “even to your old age I am he, and to gray hairs I will carry you. I have made, and I will bear; I will carry and will save” (Isaiah 46:4).

God has forsaken him. His enemies take his weakness as proof that God has left him. It is the taunt thrown at the sufferers of Psalm 22 and Psalm 42, and it was thrown at Jesus on the cross: “He trusts in God; let God deliver him now” (Matthew 27:43). It was wrong every time, though the weak, watching their strength go, are tempted to agree.

If the mind fails. And if the decline is of the mind, if memory is failing and the old prayers no longer come, verse 6 still holds: he was held before he could pray at all. God does not let go of those who can no longer hold on.

O God, be not far from me. The closing petitions are two more borrowed lines (22:11; 40:13): an old man in a hurry.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–24 — Until I Proclaim Your Might to Another Generation
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The old believer will not fade into silence: he will praise more and more, and he asks to live until he has told the next generation what God is like. While everything else in him declines, his hope and praise are to increase (v. 14). He has lost count of God’s rescues (vv. 15–16). Taught by God from his youth, he asks not to be forsaken in grey hairs until he has proclaimed God’s might to those to come (vv. 17–18). Then he praises the God who has no rival: the same God who made him see many troubles will revive him and bring him up from the depths of the earth (vv. 19–21). He ends with harp and lyre, still talking of God’s help (vv. 22–24).
verseByVerse.theology: The one thing he asks to live for is to tell the next generation what God is like.

verseByVerse.quote: But I will hope continually and will praise you yet more and more. My mouth will tell of your righteous acts, of your deeds of salvation all the day, for their number is past my knowledge. With the mighty deeds of the Lord GOD I will come; I will remind them of your righteousness, yours alone. O God, from my youth you have taught me, and I still proclaim your wondrous deeds. So even to old age and gray hairs, O God, do not forsake me, until I proclaim your might to another generation, your power to all those to come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
While everything else in him declines, his praise will increase, and he asks God to keep him going until he has told the next generation what God has done.

Yet more and more. Everything else about him is diminishing; the praise is to increase. Paul says the same: “Though our outer self is wasting away, our inner self is being renewed day by day” (2 Corinthians 4:16).

Their number is past my knowledge. After a long life with God he has lost count of the rescues (see the note at the end), and that is the best possible reason for not keeping quiet about them.

Until I proclaim your might to another generation. The request of verse 9 comes back, now with a purpose attached, and the purpose is not himself. He does not ask for more years to enjoy his grandchildren, but to hand on what God has done.

The use of old age. That is the great use of old age in Scripture, to be said plainly to people who think their usefulness has ended. The old know what God has done over fifty years; nobody else in the room does. The young have energy, but not that memory. This psalm makes handing it on a reason for staying alive.

Uncertain wording. In verse 15 the Hebrew reads literally “for I do not know numbers”; most take it, as the ESV does, to mean that God’s deeds are past counting. In verse 16, “I will come” with God’s mighty deeds may mean coming into the temple to tell of them, or going on in their strength. The sense is clear either way: he will keep telling of them.

verseByVerse.quote: Your righteousness, O God, reaches the high heavens. You who have done great things, O God, who is like you? You who have made me see many troubles and calamities will revive me again; from the depths of the earth you will bring me up again. You will increase my greatness and comfort me again. I will also praise you with the harp for your faithfulness, O my God; I will sing praises to you with the lyre, O Holy One of Israel. My lips will shout for joy, when I sing praises to you; my soul also, which you have redeemed. And my tongue will talk of your righteous help all the day long, for they have been put to shame and disappointed who sought to do me hurt.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one is like God, who sent him many troubles and will bring him up again, even from the depths of the earth, so he ends singing.

Who is like you? The question is asked by a man who has had his whole life to look for a rival to God and has not found one.

You who have made me see many troubles. Verse 20 sums up a long life with God, and both halves are addressed to the same God. He does not pretend the troubles came from somewhere else. The same God “will revive me again”: three times “again” in two verses. He has been revived before; he expects it once more.

From the depths of the earth you will bring me up again. This says more than any recovery of health could mean. For an old man near the end, being brought up from the depths of the earth means resurrection, and here the Old Testament’s hope of it shows through. For the Christian that hope rests on an event and a person: Christ has been raised, “the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep” (1 Corinthians 15:20), and the old believer is joined to him.

O Holy One of Israel. He reaches for Isaiah’s favourite title, rare in the Psalter: the God whose holiness terrified the prophets, addressed as “my God” by a man with grey hair and a harp.

All the day long. The last verse answers verse 11. They said God had forsaken him; they were wrong, and the psalm ends with the old man still talking, “all the day long”, which is exactly what he asked for in verse 18.

71.title: Even to Old Age and Gray Hairs
71.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 71 has no heading and follows straight on from the emergency prayer of Psalm 70, which it may once have continued. Just before Psalm 72 closes Book Two, the voice here is old: a believer looking back over a lifetime with God.

The message. The God who held you before you were born does not drop you when your strength is gone. Old age does not end a believer’s usefulness to God; it gives him something only the old can give, the memory of decades of God’s faithfulness to hand on to the next generation. And the God who has let him see many troubles will bring him up again, even “from the depths of the earth” (v. 20).

Why it was said. The man who prays is old and weak, and enemies take his weakness as proof that God has left him (vv. 9–11). He prays in borrowed words, lines from Psalms 22, 31, 35 and 40, the prayers he has used all his life. It is the Psalter’s fullest prayer for old age.

How the chapter makes its case. He takes refuge in the God who has held him since before his birth (vv. 1–8). Then the request the psalm exists for: “Do not cast me off in the time of old age” (v. 9), for his enemies say “God has forsaken him” (vv. 10–13). The answer is not retirement but more praise, “yet more and more”, and a request to live until he has told another generation of God’s might (vv. 14–18). He ends sure that the God who sent him troubles will bring him up again, and takes up harp and lyre (vv. 19–24).

Where it leads. By the character of God revealed in Christ, and by the hope of resurrection. The faithfulness that held this man from the womb to grey hairs is the faithfulness of the God who “will never leave you nor forsake you” (Hebrews 13:5). The taunt “God has forsaken him” was flung at Jesus too as he hung on the cross (Matthew 27:43), and it was as wrong there: God raised him. Christ has been raised as “the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep” (1 Corinthians 15:20), so the old believer’s hope of being brought up from the depths of the earth rests on an event and a person.

For us. If you are old, God has not finished with you, and the church needs your memory of his faithfulness. If you are young, ask the old what God has done. And if strength or mind is failing, rest on the God who held you before you could pray at all.
71.theology: This is the Psalter's longest treatment of old age, and it meets the fear that God's interest in us ends when our usefulness does (v. 9). The answer is God's own long faithfulness, from before birth (v. 6) to grey hairs (Isa 46:4). Praise increases as the body declines (v. 14), more life is asked for so that what God has done can be handed on (v. 18), and the hope of being brought up from the depths (v. 20) reaches towards resurrection (1 Corinthians 15:20).
71.examples: Older believers who feel stored rather than wanted can pray verse 9 as it stands, and then take up verse 18: the church needs their memory of decades of God's faithfulness, which nobody else in the room has. Younger believers can make room for that handover by asking the old what God has done. And those who sit with someone whose mind is failing can rest on verse 6: he was held before he could pray at all, and he is held still.

keyVerse.quote: So even to old age and gray hairs, O God, do not forsake me, until I proclaim your might to another generation, your power to all those to come.
keyVerse.note: This verse joins the psalm’s two great themes: the fear of being forsaken in old age (v. 9) and the purpose that old age still has. The old man asks for more life not for himself but so that he can hand on what God has done. It answers the lie that a believer’s usefulness ends with his strength.

71.reflection:
The old man prays in words he learned long ago, borrowed from other psalms (compare vv. 1–3 with Psalm 31:1–3). Which words of Scripture or hymns do you want to have ready when your strength is gone? How could you begin storing them now?

He fears that God will cast him off now that he is weak (v. 9), and his enemies say God has forsaken him (v. 11). Why is it so easy to believe that our worth to God depends on our usefulness? How does the gospel answer that fear?

He asks to live “until I proclaim your might to another generation” (v. 18). What has God done in your life that the next generation needs to hear? Who could you tell, or who older in your church could you ask?

He expects God to bring him up again “from the depths of the earth” (v. 20). How does the resurrection of Jesus shape the way you think about growing old and dying?

72.text: Of Solomon. 1Give the king your justice, O God, and your righteousness to the royal son!2May he judge your people with righteousness, and your poor with justice!3Let the mountains bear prosperity for the people, and the hills, in righteousness!4May he defend the cause of the poor of the people, give deliverance to the children of the needy, and crush the oppressor!5May they fear you while the sun endures, and as long as the moon, throughout all generations!6May he be like rain that falls on the mown grass, like showers that water the earth!7In his days may the righteous flourish, and peace abound, till the moon be no more!8May he have dominion from sea to sea, and from the River to the ends of the earth!9May desert tribes bow down before him, and his enemies lick the dust!10May the kings of Tarshish and of the coastlands render him tribute; may the kings of Sheba and Seba bring gifts!11May all kings fall down before him, all nations serve him!12For he delivers the needy when he calls, the poor and him who has no helper.13He has pity on the weak and the needy, and saves the lives of the needy.14From oppression and violence he redeems their life, and precious is their blood in his sight.15Long may he live; may gold of Sheba be given to him! May prayer be made for him continually, and blessings invoked for him all the day!16May there be abundance of grain in the land; on the tops of the mountains may it wave; may its fruit be like Lebanon; and may people blossom in the cities like the grass of the field!17May his name endure forever, his fame continue as long as the sun! May people be blessed in him, all nations call him blessed!18Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, who alone does wondrous things.19Blessed be his glorious name forever; may the whole earth be filled with his glory! Amen and Amen!20The prayers of David, the son of Jesse, are ended.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — Like Rain on the Mown Grass
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The king’s justice must come from God, and its test is what it does for the poor. Israel prays that God will give the royal son his own justice and righteousness, so that he judges God’s people rightly and God’s poor fairly (vv. 1–2). Under such a king even the land flourishes (v. 3), the cause of the poor is defended, and the oppressor is crushed, since the two go together (v. 4). The prayer reaches beyond any human reign, asking for a rule as lasting as sun and moon (v. 5), as life-giving as rain on mown grass (v. 6), and as long as the moon endures (v. 7). No son of David came close, and Israel went on praying it.
verseByVerse.theology: A prayer for a government measured entirely by what it does for people with no power.

verseByVerse.quote: Give the king your justice, O God, and your righteousness to the royal son! May he judge your people with righteousness, and your poor with justice! Let the mountains bear prosperity for the people, and the hills, in righteousness! May he defend the cause of the poor of the people, give deliverance to the children of the needy, and crush the oppressor! May they fear you while the sun endures, and as long as the moon, throughout all generations! May he be like rain that falls on the mown grass, like showers that water the earth! In his days may the righteous flourish, and peace abound, till the moon be no more!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel prays that God will give the king his own justice, so that he defends the poor and crushes their oppressors, and that his reign will bring life like rain and last as long as the moon.

Of Solomon. The psalm echoes what Solomon asked for when God offered him anything he wished: “Give your servant therefore an understanding mind to govern your people, that I may discern between good and evil” (1 Kings 3:9). Here that request becomes a prayer for the king: the justice a king administers has to be given to him first, because it is “your” justice and “your” righteousness before it is his.

Your people, your poor. The king is a steward of what is God’s, not an owner, which every government has needed to hear and few have believed.

May he defend the cause of the poor. This is the test the psalm applies to a reign, four times (vv. 2, 4, 12, 13). Not the borders or the buildings, but what happens to people with no power. And the two halves of verse 4 belong together: no king can defend the cause of the poor unless he will also “crush the oppressor”, because someone is doing the oppressing.

Like rain that falls on the mown grass. One of the loveliest pictures of government in the Bible: rain on a field just cut, which looks finished until the rain brings it back. A good reign is like weather that makes things grow, quiet, reaching everyone, and mostly noticed only when it is gone.

As long as the moon. The time asked for outruns any human reign: “throughout all generations”, “till the moon be no more”. Solomon reigned forty years, and then his kingdom split in two. Israel prayed this for every king she had, and no king came close.

The ruler we keep hoping for. Read this psalm and you hear the hopes of every modern election. We still pray Psalm 72; we simply address it to candidates. We load a leader with hopes no human being can carry, and when he turns out ordinary, or worse, we turn on him with something close to contempt and look for the next one (see the note on Acts 17:7). Israel did the same with son after son of David. The psalm’s honesty breaks the cycle: it asks for a justice God must give (v. 1) and a reign that outlasts the moon, which no Solomon could deliver. That frees us to expect rulers to do a real but limited job, and to hold them to it without making them saviours. The King this psalm describes has come. He does not need our votes; he was crushed for the poor rather than crushing them; and “of the increase of his government and of peace there will be no end” (Isaiah 9:7).

Uncertain wording. The heading “Of Solomon” can also mean “for Solomon”, and verse 20 has led many to think David prayed it for his son. In verse 5 the Hebrew reads “May they fear you”; the ancient Greek translation reads “May he endure”, which some modern translations follow.
verseByVerse.note: A royal psalm “of Solomon” — a prayer for the ideal king, fulfilled only in Christ.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–20 — Precious Is Their Blood in His Sight
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The king’s worldwide rule rests on his mercy to those who have no one, and in the end all the glory belongs to God. The prayer opens out to the whole map: from sea to sea, with desert tribes bowing and kings from far west and south bringing gifts (vv. 8–11). The reason is introduced by “for”: he rescues the needy, the weak and the one with no helper, and their blood is precious in his sight (vv. 12–14). So his people pray for him gladly, the land is fruitful even on the hilltops, and the promise to Abraham is fulfilled as all nations are blessed in him (vv. 15–17). The doxology closing Book Two gives the glory to God alone, and David’s prayers are ended (vv. 18–20).
verseByVerse.theology: The reason for the king's worldwide dominion is that he rescues people nobody else will help.

verseByVerse.quote: May he have dominion from sea to sea, and from the River to the ends of the earth! May desert tribes bow down before him, and his enemies lick the dust! May the kings of Tarshish and of the coastlands render him tribute; may the kings of Sheba and Seba bring gifts! May all kings fall down before him, all nations serve him! For he delivers the needy when he calls, the poor and him who has no helper. He has pity on the weak and the needy, and saves the lives of the needy. From oppression and violence he redeems their life, and precious is their blood in his sight.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The psalm prays for a king whose rule reaches the ends of the earth, and gives the reason: he rescues the needy who have no one to help them, and their lives are precious to him.

From sea to sea. The map opens out. The ESV notes that “the River” is the Euphrates; Tarshish lay far west across the Mediterranean, and Sheba far south in Arabia. Kings arrive from both directions with gifts, and Matthew, without quoting the psalm, tells of wise men from the east who opened their treasures and offered gold, frankincense and myrrh to a child in Bethlehem (Matthew 2:11).

Beyond Solomon. No king of Israel came anywhere near this. The queen of Sheba did come with gifts (1 Kings 10:1–2), but Solomon ruled one region. “All kings … all nations” is a prayer that outgrew every man it was prayed for.

For he delivers the needy when he calls. Now the reason for the worldwide dominion: what he does for “him who has no helper”. That phrase is the psalm’s definition of the poor: not merely those without money, but those with no one.

Precious is their blood in his sight. The last clause of verse 14 is the test of any society: the lives of people who can do nothing for him are of great worth to him, not to be thrown away. Most ancient kings used up the poor; to this one each life is precious.

Where Christians differ: when is this worldwide reign fulfilled? Premillennial readers expect a literal earthly reign of Christ after his return; postmillennial readers expect the gospel to bring a golden age, with most nations converted, before he returns. This commentary’s view: with the New Testament, the King’s worldwide rule is being fulfilled now in Christ’s reign from heaven and the gospel going to every nation, and will be completed in the new creation, when the whole earth is filled with his glory (v. 19).

Uncertain wording. The word translated “desert tribes” in verse 9 is used elsewhere of desert creatures; most take it here of desert nomads.
verseByVerse.note: Seba, named with Sheba in v. 10, also lay in the far south.

verseByVerse.quote: Long may he live; may gold of Sheba be given to him! May prayer be made for him continually, and blessings invoked for him all the day! May there be abundance of grain in the land; on the tops of the mountains may it wave; may its fruit be like Lebanon; and may people blossom in the cities like the grass of the field! May his name endure forever, his fame continue as long as the sun! May people be blessed in him, all nations call him blessed!
verseByVerse.commentary:
A people governed with such mercy will pray for their king and flourish under him, and through him the promise to Abraham will come true as all nations are blessed in him.

May prayer be made for him continually. A people governed like this will pray for their king, continually, and mean it. That is the natural result of verses 12–14, not a duty added to them.

On the tops of the mountains may it wave. Grain waving on the mountain tops is a deliberately extravagant picture: the hilltops are the last place a farmer would sow. Even the poor ground is heavy with wheat, and fruit is like the forests of Lebanon. And then the cities: “may people blossom in the cities like the grass of the field”.

May people be blessed in him. Here the prayer reaches back to Abraham, “in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed” (Genesis 12:3), and asks that the promise be fulfilled through the king. Paul calls that promise the gospel preached beforehand (Galatians 3:8).

The King to come. No ordinary son of David could bring that about, but God had promised, so Israel went on praying it. Isaiah saw him coming, a shoot from the stump of Jesse: “with righteousness he shall judge the poor, and decide with equity for the meek of the earth” (Isaiah 11:4), which is this psalm’s own test. The wise men who came with gifts came to a child whose kingdom would have no end.

He shed his own for them. That child grew up to announce “good news to the poor” (Luke 4:18), and he passes the psalm’s test of a king. The King who counts the blood of the poor precious shed his own for them, and the day is set when “at the name of Jesus every knee should bow” (Philippians 2:10). Isaac Watts built his hymn “Jesus Shall Reign” on this psalm.

Uncertain wording. Verse 15 is compressed in Hebrew. The ESV takes the king as the subject throughout; others take it to be the poor man just rescued, who will live, give the king gold and pray for him. In verse 16 the Hebrew behind “may its fruit be like Lebanon” may mean the crops wave or rustle in the wind like Lebanon’s forests.

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, who alone does wondrous things. Blessed be his glorious name forever; may the whole earth be filled with his glory! Amen and Amen! The prayers of David, the son of Jesse, are ended.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Book Two closes by blessing the LORD, who alone does wonders, and longing for the whole earth to be filled with his glory; with that, the prayers of David are ended.

The end of Book Two. Verses 18–19 are not part of Solomon’s prayer. They are the doxology (a burst of praise) that closes Book Two of the Psalter, like those at 41:13, 89:52 and 106:48. It also guards the psalm: after seventeen verses asking enormous things for a king, it says God “alone does wondrous things”.

May the whole earth be filled with his glory! The horizon is bigger than the psalm’s. The prayer wanted the king’s fame to last; the doxology wants “the whole earth” filled with God’s glory. Habakkuk and Isaiah both foresaw that day (Habakkuk 2:14; Isaiah 11:9), and John saw a city where it had come, for “the glory of God gives it light, and its lamp is the Lamb” (Revelation 21:23).

The prayers of David, the son of Jesse, are ended. Verse 20 is an editor’s note, and a moving one. The collection that began “Blessed is the man” ends with an old king’s prayers running out, and, if David prayed this psalm, the last thing he prays for is his son, and a reign that will treat the poor as precious.

Not the end of the Psalter. Three more books follow, with more psalms of David. But this collection closes where the whole Bible is heading, with the earth full of God’s glory and all nations calling one King blessed.
verseByVerse.note: The doxology that closes Book II.

72.title: May All Kings Fall Down Before Him
72.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 72 closes Book Two of the Psalter. After the old man’s prayer of Psalm 71, it turns to the king’s son, and it ends with the doxology of Book Two and an editor’s note: “The prayers of David, the son of Jesse, are ended” (v. 20).

The message. Israel prays for a king who rules with God’s own justice, and the test of his reign is what happens to the poor, the needy and “him who has no helper” (v. 12). Such a king would be like rain on a mown field, his rule would reach the ends of the earth, and in him all nations would be blessed. The prayer asks for more than any son of David could give, and so it became a promise waiting for its King.

Why it was said. The heading reads “Of Solomon”, and the psalm echoes the wisdom Solomon asked for to govern God’s people (1 Kings 3:9); verse 20 has led many to think David prayed it for his son. It kept God’s promise to David’s line (2 Samuel 7) before Israel through every reign that fell short (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. It asks God to give the king his justice, to defend the poor and crush the oppressor, and a reign like rain on mown grass, lasting as the moon (vv. 1–7). It asks that his rule run from sea to sea, with kings bringing gifts (vv. 8–11), and gives the reason: he delivers the needy, and their blood is precious in his sight (vv. 12–14). It prays for his long life, for grain on the mountain tops, and for all nations to be blessed in him (vv. 15–17). Then the doxology gives all the glory to God (vv. 18–20).

Where it leads. By promise. No king of Israel came near this prayer; Solomon’s kingdom split after him. Isaiah saw a King coming who would judge the poor with righteousness (Isaiah 11:4), and the prayer that all nations be blessed in him carries God’s promise to Abraham (Genesis 12:3; Galatians 3:8). Jesus came announcing “good news to the poor” (Luke 4:18), and the King who counts the blood of the poor precious shed his own for them. He now reigns, and every knee will bow to him (Philippians 2:10).

For us. Pray for those who govern, and measure them by how they treat the people with no helper, without expecting them to be saviours. Ask whether the powerless are precious in your sight. And pray with confidence: the King this psalm longs for has come, and his reign will fill the earth.
72.theology: The psalm measures a reign by one test, applied four times: what happens to those with no power (vv. 2, 4, 12, 13). The king's justice is God's gift, his people are God's people, and his worldwide dominion rests on mercy to the one who has no helper. The prayer outgrew every king it was prayed for, carrying the promise to Abraham (v. 17) until it reached Jesus, and the closing doxology gives the glory where it belongs: God alone does wondrous things, and the horizon is the whole earth filled with his glory (vv. 18-19; cf. 41:13; 89:52; 106:48).
72.examples: The psalm gives Christians a way to pray for those who govern, from parliament to parish council: give them your justice, and let it be measured by what happens to people with no one to speak for them. It also asks something of anyone with a little power, at work or at home: are the people who can do nothing for us precious in our sight? And it lets us pray with confidence, because the king it describes has come, and his reign will cover the earth.

keyVerse.quote: For he delivers the needy when he calls, the poor and him who has no helper.
keyVerse.note: This verse gives the reason for the king’s worldwide rule: not his armies or his wealth, but his mercy to those with no one to help them. It is the psalm’s test of a reign, applied again and again, and no son of David passed it until Jesus came with good news to the poor. The King who rules the nations is the one who stoops to the helpless.

72.reflection:
The psalm measures a king by what he does for the poor, the needy and “him who has no helper” (vv. 2, 4, 12–14). How would it change the way you pray for those who govern if you measured them by this test? How can you do that without expecting them to be saviours?

“Precious is their blood in his sight” (v. 14). Who in your community, church or workplace is easily overlooked because they can do nothing for anyone? What would it look like to treat them as precious?

No king of Israel came close to this prayer, yet Israel kept praying it. How do you see Jesus fulfilling it, in his first coming, his present reign and his return?

The doxology says that God “alone does wondrous things” and longs for “the whole earth” to be filled with his glory (vv. 18–19). How does that hope shape the way you pray for the nations and take part in the gospel going out to them?

73.text: A Psalm of Asaph. 1Truly God is good to Israel, to those who are pure in heart.2But as for me, my feet had almost stumbled, my steps had nearly slipped.3For I was envious of the arrogant when I saw the prosperity of the wicked.4For they have no pangs until death; their bodies are fat and sleek.5They are not in trouble as others are; they are not stricken like the rest of mankind.6Therefore pride is their necklace; violence covers them as a garment.7Their eyes swell out through fatness; their hearts overflow with follies.8They scoff and speak with malice; loftily they threaten oppression.9They set their mouths against the heavens, and their tongue struts through the earth.10Therefore his people turn back to them, and find no fault in them.11And they say, "How can God know? Is there knowledge in the Most High?"12Behold, these are the wicked; always at ease, they increase in riches.13All in vain have I kept my heart clean and washed my hands in innocence.14For all the day long I have been stricken and rebuked every morning.15If I had said, "I will speak thus," I would have betrayed the generation of your children.16But when I thought how to understand this, it seemed to me a wearisome task,17until I went into the sanctuary of God; then I discerned their end.18Truly you set them in slippery places; you make them fall to ruin.19How they are destroyed in a moment, swept away utterly by terrors!20Like a dream when one awakes, O Lord, when you rouse yourself, you despise them as phantoms.21When my soul was embittered, when I was pricked in heart,22I was brutish and ignorant; I was like a beast toward you.23Nevertheless, I am continually with you; you hold my right hand.24You guide me with your counsel, and afterward you will receive me to glory.25Whom have I in heaven but you? And there is nothing on earth that I desire besides you.26My flesh and my heart may fail, but God is the strength of my heart and my portion forever.27For behold, those who are far from you shall perish; you put an end to everyone who is unfaithful to you.28But for me it is good to be near God; I have made the Lord GOD my refuge, that I may tell of all your works.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — My Feet Had Almost Stumbled
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A believer can come within a step of abandoning God simply by watching the godless do well. Asaph states his conclusion first, that God is good to the pure in heart, and then confesses how nearly he lost it (vv. 1–3). The cause was envy. He paints the prosperous wicked as they looked to him: untroubled and healthy to the end (vv. 4–5), wearing pride like jewellery and violence like a coat, their talk strutting across heaven and earth (vv. 6–9). Worse, God’s own people were drawn after them, while they shrugged at the idea that God notices anything (vv. 10–11). He closes the evidence like a lawyer: always at ease, always richer (v. 12).
verseByVerse.theology: A believer watching dishonest people thrive, and drawing the obvious conclusion.

verseByVerse.quote: Truly God is good to Israel, to those who are pure in heart. But as for me, my feet had almost stumbled, my steps had nearly slipped. For I was envious of the arrogant when I saw the prosperity of the wicked.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Asaph begins with the conclusion he nearly lost: God really is good to his people, though envy of the prosperous wicked almost made him walk away.

Truly God is good to Israel. The psalm opens with its conclusion, as testimony does, because the next twelve verses are very dark. The small Hebrew word behind Truly returns at the two hinges of the psalm, “All in vain” (v. 13) and “Truly you set them in slippery places” (v. 18).

My feet had almost stumbled. Two words carry the whole psalm: almost, and nearly. He came within an inch of walking away from God, and he is going to tell the congregation exactly what nearly did it.

I was envious of the arrogant. Not persecution, not bereavement, not doubt about God’s existence: envy. Life was going well for people who had no time for God, and it nearly finished his faith. Psalm 37, Job (Job 21:7) and Jeremiah (Jeremiah 12:1) all wrestle with it, because it keeps happening.

A worship leader. Asaph was one of the Levites David appointed to lead the singing before the ark (1 Chronicles 16:4–5). The man who nearly lost his faith was leading the songs: such struggles do not disqualify a believer.
verseByVerse.note: Book III begins (73–89). Asaph was one of David’s chief musicians; twelve psalms bear his name (50, 73–83).

verseByVerse.quote: For they have no pangs until death; their bodies are fat and sleek. They are not in trouble as others are; they are not stricken like the rest of mankind.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To the envious eye, the wicked seemed to have been excused from the troubles everyone else must bear, even in dying.

They have no pangs until death. So the wicked looked to him: healthy, well fed, dying comfortably, spared the troubles others have. That last point hurt most.

Not stricken like the rest of mankind. “Stricken” is a word for blows that fall on a man, the word Isaiah uses of the servant, “stricken, smitten by God” (Isaiah 53:4), and the word Asaph will use of himself in verse 14. Trouble is the common lot in a fallen world; what galls him is that these men seem excused from it (compare Job 21:7–13).

Uncertain wording. The ESV’s “they have no pangs until death” means a painless life to the end. Dividing the same Hebrew letters differently, some translations read “they have no pangs; their bodies are sound and sleek”. The picture is the same: an untroubled life.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore pride is their necklace; violence covers them as a garment. Their eyes swell out through fatness; their hearts overflow with follies. They scoff and speak with malice; loftily they threaten oppression. They set their mouths against the heavens, and their tongue struts through the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Prosperity has made them not humble but proud and violent, and their talk struts about as if they owned heaven and earth.

Pride is their necklace. Pride is worn like jewellery, and violence put on like a coat. Success did not make them decent; it made them worse.

Their hearts overflow with follies. Verse 7 shows them from the inside: faces bloated with good living, and hearts overflowing not with wisdom but with folly, imaginings with nothing to check them. Verse 8 says where it comes out: in scoffing, malice and threats spoken “loftily”, the talk of people who look down on everyone and expect to be obeyed.

Their tongue struts through the earth. A wonderful line for a certain kind of public talk: language walking about as if it owns the place. And they aim it upward, against the heavens, with no consequence that anyone can see.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore his people turn back to them, and find no fault in them. And they say, "How can God know? Is there knowledge in the Most High?" Behold, these are the wicked; always at ease, they increase in riches.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Worst of all, God’s own people are drawn after the prosperous wicked, who shrug at the thought that God notices anything.

His people turn back to them. This is the worst part: God’s own people drift after them and find nothing to criticise. Success persuades without needing an argument, and a congregation watching it long enough begins to want it.

How can God know? The creed of the arrogant is the creed of Psalm 10 again, in a politer form. They do not deny God. They shrug at the idea that he is paying attention.

Always at ease, they increase in riches. In verse 12 he sums up the evidence like a man laying a file on a table, and so far the case looks strong.

Uncertain wording. The ESV notes that verse 10 is difficult in Hebrew; its second line seems literally to speak of “waters of fullness” being drained. Many take it of people drinking in the words of the wicked like water. The details are unclear, but the drift is not: even God’s people are drawn to the prosperous and swallow what they say.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–22 — Until I Went into the Sanctuary
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The turning point is not an argument but a place. Asaph draws the bitter conclusion that his clean life has been wasted, a daily round of being stricken while the careless thrive (vv. 13–14). Two things hold him back from the edge. He refuses to say it aloud, knowing it would betray the younger generation of God’s children (v. 15). And when thinking only wore him out, he went into God’s sanctuary and saw the end of the road the wicked are on: slippery ground, sudden ruin, a dream that vanishes on waking (vv. 16–20). In that light he sees himself too, embittered and as unthinking as an animal before God (vv. 21–22).
verseByVerse.theology: He kept his doubts to himself, and then went to church, and the perspective changed.

verseByVerse.quote: All in vain have I kept my heart clean and washed my hands in innocence. For all the day long I have been stricken and rebuked every morning. If I had said, "I will speak thus," I would have betrayed the generation of your children. But when I thought how to understand this, it seemed to me a wearisome task, until I went into the sanctuary of God; then I discerned their end.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He nearly concluded that his godliness had been wasted, but he kept the thought from the young, and in God’s sanctuary he finally saw where the prosperous were heading.

All in vain have I kept my heart clean. Here is the conclusion he nearly drew: they are at ease and growing richer; he keeps clean and is stricken daily. To wash the hands in innocence was a known way of declaring oneself clear of guilt (Deuteronomy 21:6–7; Psalm 26:6), so both his inner life and his outward conduct have been kept clean. And every morning is the detail that hurts: not one great calamity but a daily, grinding correction.

The bargain beneath the goodness. All in vain gives something away. If the clean heart was in vain, it was meant to buy something, namely what the arrogant already had: ease, money, the untroubled life. Asaph and the men he envies wanted the same prize. They took the short road and he took the long, religious one, and he is furious that the short road arrived first. That is the hidden kinship between the moralist and the libertine: one breaks the rules to get what he wants and the other keeps them for the same reason; neither wants God. The cure in this psalm is not better wages for goodness but a different treasure: there is nothing on earth that I desire besides you (v. 25). Jesus told of a dutiful elder son who was angry in just this way, and the father’s answer is the gospel to every disappointed moralist: “Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours” (Luke 15:31).

I would have betrayed the generation of your children. Verse 15 is the sentence that saved him. He did not stop feeling it. He stopped short of saying it publicly, because he could see what it would do to younger believers if a man like him stood up and announced that serving God was a waste of time.

Where doubt belongs. There is a place to say all in vain: this psalm, addressed to God. There is a place not to say it: in front of the young, as a verdict. This is no rule against telling a pastor or a mature friend; it is the difference between bringing doubt to God and broadcasting it to people who are not carrying it.

It seemed to me a wearisome task. He tried to think his way out, and it exhausted him, as it exhausts anyone lying awake trying to reason themselves back into contentment.

Until I went into the sanctuary of God. What changed everything was a place. He received no new information and no explanation of the general problem; he stood where God is worshipped and saw the same facts in the light of where they lead: their end.

A sanctuary Asaph never saw. For the Christian that sanctuary is open in a way Asaph never knew: we enter the holy places by the blood of Jesus (Hebrews 10:19). At the cross both things Asaph saw are seen at once: the end of sin, judged in full, and a God who will not let his own slip.
