There hangs the one man whose heart truly was clean, “stricken, smitten by God” (Isaiah 53:4) for the sins of others, yet he never called his obedience vain (Hebrews 12:2).

If this is where you are. If you are in the middle of this psalm now, envious, sore, half-convinced it has all been for nothing, the psalm does not scold you for verses 2 to 14. It lets you say them to God, then takes you where you can see how things end. Do not settle your verdict on God in the middle of the psalm. When life does not add up, do not work at the sum alone: go where God is worshipped, where he is at the centre and eternity is in view.

verseByVerse.quote: Truly you set them in slippery places; you make them fall to ruin. How they are destroyed in a moment, swept away utterly by terrors! Like a dream when one awakes, O Lord, when you rouse yourself, you despise them as phantoms. When my soul was embittered, when I was pricked in heart, I was brutish and ignorant; I was like a beast toward you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In God’s presence the picture turns over: it is the wicked who stand on slippery ground and vanish like a dream, and the envious believer sees that he had been thinking like an animal.

Truly you set them in slippery places. Truly comes back from verse 1, and the whole picture turns upside down. He thought they were standing and his own feet were slipping (v. 2). It is the other way round: they are the ones on the slippery ground.

Destroyed in a moment. The timing changes everything: not a slow decline but a sudden collapse. Like a dream when one awakes: vivid, absorbing, and then you open your eyes and there is nothing there.

When my soul was embittered. He calls it being embittered and pricked in heart: nursed envy brings no clearer thinking, only a sore heart. And he looks back at himself with real shame: brutish, ignorant, like a beast. Envy had reduced him to an animal that sees the food and nothing else: no past, no future, no God.

What it does not mean. Seeing the end of the wicked is not gloating. God has “no pleasure in the death of the wicked” (Ezekiel 33:11), and a believer who has seen their end is moved to pity and warning.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–28 — Whom Have I in Heaven but You?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Envy is cured not by wanting nothing but by wanting God. One word carries the psalm, “Nevertheless”: while Asaph was bitter and brutish, God was holding his right hand (v. 23). God guides him now and will afterward receive him to glory (v. 24). So he can say what he could not say before: there is no one in heaven and nothing on earth he wants beside God, who remains his strength and portion when body and heart give way (vv. 25–26). Those far from God perish; for him it is good to be near God, and the man who once kept silent now has God’s works to tell (vv. 27–28).
verseByVerse.theology: The man who nearly walked away ends up saying one of the boldest sentences in the Psalter.

verseByVerse.quote: Nevertheless, I am continually with you; you hold my right hand. You guide me with your counsel, and afterward you will receive me to glory. Whom have I in heaven but you? And there is nothing on earth that I desire besides you. My flesh and my heart may fail, but God is the strength of my heart and my portion forever. For behold, those who are far from you shall perish; you put an end to everyone who is unfaithful to you. But for me it is good to be near God; I have made the Lord GOD my refuge, that I may tell of all your works.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even while he was bitter and brutish, God was holding him; God guides him now, will take him to glory, and is himself the treasure that makes envy unnecessary.

Nevertheless, I am continually with you. The greatest word in the psalm is nevertheless. He has just called himself a beast, and the next sentence begins: and yet. Not that God cast him off, nor that he pulled himself together: while he was brutish, ignorant and bitter, he was continually with God, and the hand-holding is God’s doing: you hold my right hand, the way you take the hand of a child who is not paying attention near a road. Jesus says the same of his sheep: “no one will snatch them out of my hand” (John 10:28).

Afterward you will receive me to glory. Verse 24 has two tenses: guidance now, glory afterwards. The verb receive is the one in Psalm 49:15, “for he will receive me”, and the one used of Enoch, whom God took (Genesis 5:24). Before the resurrection had been clearly revealed, an Old Testament believer says that God himself will take him home, as Jesus later promised plainly: “I will come again and will take you to myself” (John 14:3). That is what the sanctuary gave him: not fewer troubles, but a longer view. Verses 4 to 12 were true, but measured against this life only.

Whom have I in heaven but you? One of the boldest sentences in the Psalter, from the man who twenty verses ago was eaten up with wanting what others had. Heaven would not interest him without God in it, and earth has nothing he would swap for him. That is the cure for envy: not being told to stop wanting, but wanting something else so much that the old cravings lose their grip. Nobody argues themselves out of envy; they are drawn out, by the God who goes on holding their hand.

My flesh and my heart may fail. In verse 26 he grants the worst case: body and courage both giving out. Even then God is his heart’s rock (ESV note) and portion: the Levites were given no land, for the LORD himself was their share, as David sang: “The LORD is my chosen portion and my cup” (Psalm 16:5).

It is good to be near God. The psalm ends by redefining wealth. The question was never who has more but who is near God, and that is enough. The last clause turns him outward: that I may tell of all your works. The man who kept quiet in verse 15 to protect the young now has something to say to them; the doubt he refused to broadcast became a testimony worth publishing, which is why this psalm exists.

What it does not mean. Verse 25 does not despise God’s gifts; he “richly provides us with everything to enjoy” (1 Timothy 6:17). It is a ranking, not a renunciation: nothing could take God’s place, so the gifts can be enjoyed without being worshipped, and lost without being the end of you.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew of verse 24 is very compressed, roughly “and after, glory, you will take me”. Some read it of being restored to honour in this life. The ESV’s “receive me to glory” is more likely: the verb is the one used of Enoch and of Psalm 49:15, and verse 26 looks beyond the failing of flesh and heart.
verseByVerse.note: “Strength” is literally “rock” (ESV note).

73.title: Until I Went into the Sanctuary
73.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 73 opens Book Three of the Psalter, the darkest of its five books, and a run of eleven psalms of Asaph (73–83) (see the introduction). Book Two has just closed with a prayer for a king whose reign would bring prosperity to God’s people (Psalm 72); Psalm 73 asks what faith does when prosperity goes to the wicked instead.

The message. God really is good to his people, even when faithfulness seems to earn nothing and the godless seem to have everything. The psalm lets a believer say the worst he felt, then shows how God brought him back: not with an explanation, but by showing him where the wicked are heading, and that God had been holding his hand all along. The treasure worth having is not what the arrogant have, but God himself: “for me it is good to be near God”.

Why it was said. The Psalter opens by promising that the LORD blesses the righteous (Psalm 1), but life in Israel often looked like the opposite. A Levite who led the nation’s worship nearly lost his faith over it, and wrote this psalm so that the congregation would know the road back.

How the chapter makes its case. The conclusion comes first, then the confession of a near fall (vv. 1–3). The case against God is set out honestly: the wicked, healthy, proud, scornful of heaven and admired even by God’s people (vv. 4–12), and the believer’s bitter sum, “All in vain” (vv. 13–14). Two things stopped the fall: he would not betray the young by saying it aloud (v. 15), and he went into the sanctuary, where he saw their end (vv. 16–20) and his own brutishness (vv. 21–22). Then comes the great “Nevertheless”: God holds him, guides him and will receive him to glory, and God himself is his portion for ever (vv. 23–28).

Where it leads. To Christ, first by the character of God that he reveals: the God who will not let go of a bitter believer’s hand is the Good Shepherd who says of his sheep, “no one will snatch them out of my hand” (John 10:28). It leads by pattern too: the truly innocent man was “stricken” (Isaiah 53:4), never called his obedience vain, and went through death into the glory Asaph glimpsed (Luke 24:26). By his blood the sanctuary where Asaph’s eyes were opened stands open to us (Hebrews 10:19).

For us. When envy or disappointment tells you that your faithfulness has been wasted, do not settle your verdict on God in the middle of the psalm. Bring the complaint to him, among his people, and ask what you hoped your goodness would buy. Then let the hand that has held you all along teach you to say, “Whom have I in heaven but you?”
73.theology: The psalm's crisis is envy, and it is honest that envy nearly ended his faith (v. 2). Two things held him: he would not unload his doubt on younger believers (v. 15), and he went into the sanctuary, where the same facts looked different once he saw their end (v. 17). Then comes the word the psalm turns on, a word of grace, nevertheless (v. 23): while he was brutish, God was holding his hand. Envy is cured not by wanting nothing but by wanting God more (v. 25), and the doubt he refused to broadcast became the testimony this psalm is.
73.examples: Anyone watching dishonest colleagues promoted, or careless neighbours prosper, while their own faithfulness seems to earn only trouble, is in the middle of this psalm, and may say verses 13-14 to God without being scolded. The psalm's counsel is practical: do not settle your verdict on God in the middle; take the doubt to him rather than to people who are not carrying it; and go where God is worshipped and is at the centre of the room. There the hand that holds yours turns out to have been holding it all along.

keyVerse.quote: Whom have I in heaven but you? And there is nothing on earth that I desire besides you.
keyVerse.note: The man who nearly lost his faith through envy of what others had ends by wanting God more than anything in heaven or on earth. This is the psalm’s cure for envy: not wanting nothing, but wanting God, the treasure the prosperous wicked never had. In Christ that treasure is given to everyone he holds by the hand.

73.reflection:
Asaph nearly walked away from God simply by watching godless people do well (vv. 2–3). Where are you most tempted to envy, and what does that envy tell you about what you were hoping God would give you?

He kept his bitter conclusion from the young (v. 15) but said it honestly to God in this psalm. How do we tell the difference between bringing doubts to God and to wise friends, and broadcasting them as a verdict?

Nothing changed in his circumstances; he went into the sanctuary and saw the end (v. 17). How does gathering with God’s people for worship change the way you see your life, and what keeps you from it when you are struggling?

“Nevertheless … you hold my right hand” (v. 23). What difference does it make that God was holding Asaph while he was bitter and brutish, and how does Jesus’ promise in John 10:28 make this more certain for us?

74.text: A Maskil of Asaph. 1O God, why do you cast us off forever? Why does your anger smoke against the sheep of your pasture?2Remember your congregation, which you have purchased of old, which you have redeemed to be the tribe of your heritage! Remember Mount Zion, where you have dwelt.3Direct your steps to the perpetual ruins; the enemy has destroyed everything in the sanctuary!4Your foes have roared in the midst of your meeting place; they set up their own signs for signs.5They were like those who swing axes in a forest of trees.6And all its carved wood they broke down with hatchets and hammers.7They set your sanctuary on fire; they profaned the dwelling place of your name, bringing it down to the ground.8They said to themselves, "We will utterly subdue them"; they burned all the meeting places of God in the land.9We do not see our signs; there is no longer any prophet, and there is none among us who knows how long.10How long, O God, is the foe to scoff? Is the enemy to revile your name forever?11Why do you hold back your hand, your right hand? Take it from the fold of your garment and destroy them!12Yet God my King is from of old, working salvation in the midst of the earth.13You divided the sea by your might; you broke the heads of the sea monsters on the waters.14You crushed the heads of Leviathan; you gave him as food for the creatures of the wilderness.15You split open springs and brooks; you dried up ever-flowing streams.16Yours is the day, yours also the night; you have established the heavenly lights and the sun.17You have fixed all the boundaries of the earth; you have made summer and winter.18Remember this, O LORD, how the enemy scoffs, and a foolish people reviles your name.19Do not deliver the soul of your dove to the wild beasts; do not forget the life of your poor forever.20Have regard for the covenant, for the dark places of the land are full of the habitations of violence.21Let not the downtrodden turn back in shame; let the poor and needy praise your name.22Arise, O God, defend your cause; remember how the foolish scoff at you all the day!23Do not forget the clamor of your foes, the uproar of those who rise against you, which goes up continually!

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — There Is No Longer Any Prophet
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s people may bring him their ruin and ask him why. The psalm begins with a cry that God’s anger seems endless, and pleads with him to remember the people he redeemed and the mountain where he lived, and to walk through the rubble (vv. 1–3). An eyewitness describes the destruction: enemy soldiers roaring in the holy place, their emblems planted where God’s signs had been, axes hacking the carved woodwork, and fire bringing the house to the ground, along with every meeting place of God in the land (vv. 4–8). Worst of all is the silence: no signs, no prophet, no one who knows how long, and God’s hand still held back (vv. 9–11).
verseByVerse.theology: The building is ashes, the prophets have stopped, and nobody can say how long it will last.

verseByVerse.quote: O God, why do you cast us off forever? Why does your anger smoke against the sheep of your pasture? Remember your congregation, which you have purchased of old, which you have redeemed to be the tribe of your heritage! Remember Mount Zion, where you have dwelt. Direct your steps to the perpetual ruins; the enemy has destroyed everything in the sanctuary!
verseByVerse.commentary:
From the ruins of the temple, God’s people ask why his anger seems endless, and plead with him to remember that they are his own.

Why do you cast us off forever? The psalm opens with “why” and “forever”, and both words matter. “Why” is not a demand for an explanation God owes, but the question of people who believe he has reasons they cannot see. “Forever” is how a long disaster feels from inside. The anger “smokes”, like a fire still smouldering, as the sanctuary will (v. 7).

The sheep of your pasture. The arguments are all about ownership: the sheep of your pasture, your congregation, which you purchased and redeemed, and Zion where you have dwelt. “Purchased” and “redeemed” are words from the song Israel sang beside the Red Sea (Exodus 15:13, 16). They are not claiming to deserve rescue; they are pointing out whose property has been damaged. The church can plead ownership more strongly still, as “the church of God, which he obtained with his own blood” (Acts 20:28).

Direct your steps to the perpetual ruins. This psalm is prayed in a ruin. The congregation asks God to come and walk through the rubble, as you would ask someone to come and see what has happened to a house.

The title. A Maskil is probably a psalm that teaches: someone thought the congregation needed teaching how to pray in the worst year of its history.

How can an Asaph psalm describe the temple’s destruction centuries after David’s Asaph? “Of Asaph” covers the guild of singers descended from him, who served for generations (2 Chronicles 35:15; Ezra 2:41).
verseByVerse.note: Probably written after the Babylonians destroyed the temple in about 587/586 BC.

verseByVerse.quote: Your foes have roared in the midst of your meeting place; they set up their own signs for signs. They were like those who swing axes in a forest of trees. And all its carved wood they broke down with hatchets and hammers. They set your sanctuary on fire; they profaned the dwelling place of your name, bringing it down to the ground. They said to themselves, "We will utterly subdue them"; they burned all the meeting places of God in the land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Like an eyewitness, the psalmist describes enemy soldiers shouting in God’s house, hacking its carved woodwork and burning every place where God was worshipped.

Your foes have roared in the midst of your meeting place. Soldiers shouting in the holy place; then the carved cedar of Solomon’s temple, “in the form of gourds and open flowers” (1 Kings 6:18), centuries-old craftsmanship, hacked with axes as though they were clearing woodland.

They set up their own signs for signs. The enemy’s “signs” were probably military standards and the emblems of their gods, planted where the signs of God’s presence had stood. The same word comes back in verse 9: “We do not see our signs”. The invaders’ signs are everywhere, and God’s are gone.

They burned all the meeting places of God in the land. “We will utterly subdue them” shows that the aim was not only to win a war but to finish a people. Whatever these meeting places were, every place in the land where God was sought had been burned.

What the history records. The history books record it flatly: “he burned the house of the LORD” (2 Kings 25:9). That was Nebuchadnezzar’s army, in about 586 BC, which also broke down Jerusalem’s walls and carried the people into exile (2 Kings 25:8–11). This psalm is what it sounded like from inside. (Some link it instead to the Greek king Antiochus IV in 167 BC, but he profaned the temple rather than burning it to the ground.)

Uncertain wording. The ESV notes that verse 5 is obscure in Hebrew: the picture of axes in a forest is clear, how the sentence runs is not. The plural “meeting places of God” in verse 8 are also uncertain: perhaps local places where people gathered to pray and be taught, though synagogues in the later sense are not clearly known this early.

verseByVerse.quote: We do not see our signs; there is no longer any prophet, and there is none among us who knows how long. How long, O God, is the foe to scoff? Is the enemy to revile your name forever? Why do you hold back your hand, your right hand? Take it from the fold of your garment and destroy them!
verseByVerse.commentary:
The worst loss is not the building but God’s silence: no signs, no prophet, no one who can say how long, so they beg God to stop holding back his hand.

There is no longer any prophet. Three losses in one line: the visible signs of God’s presence, any prophet through whom God is speaking, and anyone who can say how long. That last loss removes the final comfort of people in trouble, knowing when it will end.

Why do you hold back your hand, your right hand? The ESV notes that “the fold of your garment” is literally “your bosom”: God is pictured with his right hand tucked inside his robe, like a man standing with his hands in his pockets while his house burns. Take it out, they say. It is bold, and it is still prayer: not a description of God as he is, but of how his inaction looks.

But were Jeremiah and Ezekiel not alive? Yes, but Ezekiel was among the exiles in Babylon and Jeremiah was soon taken to Egypt (Jeremiah 43:6–7). The psalm speaks for those left among the ruins. Lamentations says the same: “her prophets find no vision from the LORD” (Lamentations 2:9).

The silence of the prophets ended. The church reads this verse from the far side of an answer: “in these last days he has spoken to us by his Son” (Hebrews 1:2). In a season when God seems silent, the believer still has that word, and the word is a person, Jesus Christ.

Disaster plus silence. A congregation can survive a disaster if God is still talking. Any believer who has lived through a season when God seemed to have stopped speaking will recognise this one. The psalm’s answer is not to pretend otherwise, but to keep talking to him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–17 — Yet God My King Is from of Old
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When there is nothing to point to in the present, faith points to what God has already done. The single word “Yet” turns the psalm: God is the psalmist’s King from of old, still working salvation on earth (v. 12). He divided the sea at the exodus and broke the heads of the sea monsters and Leviathan, the pagan pictures of chaos, leaving them for scavengers (vv. 13–14). He opened springs and dried up rivers (v. 15). And day and night, sun and seasons, and the boundaries of the earth are his (vv. 16–17). The temple is ash, but the sun rose this morning, and it rose because God reigns.
verseByVerse.theology: With nothing left to point at in the present, he points backwards: to the Red Sea, and to the sun and seasons.

verseByVerse.quote: Yet God my King is from of old, working salvation in the midst of the earth. You divided the sea by your might; you broke the heads of the sea monsters on the waters. You crushed the heads of Leviathan; you gave him as food for the creatures of the wilderness. You split open springs and brooks; you dried up ever-flowing streams. Yours is the day, yours also the night; you have established the heavenly lights and the sun. You have fixed all the boundaries of the earth; you have made summer and winter.
verseByVerse.commentary:
With nothing to point to in the present, faith points back: God is the King who has always worked salvation, who split the sea and crushed the monsters of chaos, and who still rules day and night and the seasons.

Yet God my King is from of old. Yet, and the psalm turns, not to a new promise or prophecy: with nothing in the present to point at, he points backwards, and calls God my King with the throne room in ashes.

You divided the sea by your might. The sea divided is the exodus. The sea monsters and Leviathan, the sea dragon of Job 41 and Isaiah 27, were Canaanite pictures of the wild sea they feared; the psalm borrows them to say that God has already beaten whatever the pagans feared. Leviathan, left for scavengers, perhaps stands for Egypt too, crushed at the Red Sea.

Yours is the day, yours also the night. Verse 15 probably recalls water from the rock and the Jordan dried up; then come day and night, sun and stars, coastlines and seasons. With the sanctuary a burnt-out shell, the sun still comes up and summer still follows spring, and he takes that as evidence that God still reigns.

The heads crushed. Scripture carries the picture forward: the woman’s offspring “shall bruise your head” (Genesis 3:15), and the LORD will punish “Leviathan the fleeing serpent” (Isaiah 27:1). At the cross Christ struck the head of “that ancient serpent, who is the devil and Satan” (Revelation 20:2).

Faith with nothing in view. Faith with nothing in front of it reaches for what God has done and is still visibly doing. Anyone praying in a ruin can still say verse 16.

Uncertain wording. The ESV notes that the “sea monsters” (v. 13) may be simply “the great sea creatures”. In verse 14 the Hebrew behind “the creatures of the wilderness” is compressed, roughly “a people, desert-dwellers”; most take it of wild animals, a few of desert tribes.
verseByVerse.note: Leviathan, the sea monster, pictures the chaos God rules — and perhaps Egypt at the Red Sea.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–23 — Do Not Forget the Life of Your Poor
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When nothing else can be pleaded, God’s people plead his covenant and his name. The final prayers keep returning to two words, “remember” and “do not forget”. Remember the enemy’s scoffing at your name (v. 18). Do not hand your defenceless dove to the wild beasts, nor forget your poor (v. 19). Have regard for the covenant, for violence fills the dark places (v. 20). Let the downtrodden praise you, not turn back in shame (v. 21). Rise and defend your own cause (v. 22). And the psalm stops with the enemy’s uproar still going up (v. 23): no answer yet, only a prayer that refuses to let go.
verseByVerse.theology: The last claim they have is the covenant, and the psalm ends with the noise still going on.

verseByVerse.quote: Remember this, O LORD, how the enemy scoffs, and a foolish people reviles your name. Do not deliver the soul of your dove to the wild beasts; do not forget the life of your poor forever. Have regard for the covenant, for the dark places of the land are full of the habitations of violence. Let not the downtrodden turn back in shame; let the poor and needy praise your name. Arise, O God, defend your cause; remember how the foolish scoff at you all the day! Do not forget the clamor of your foes, the uproar of those who rise against you, which goes up continually!
verseByVerse.commentary:
They end by pleading God’s covenant and God’s own name: let him not forget his defenceless people, but rise and defend his cause.

Remember this, O LORD. The closing prayers keep returning to remember (vv. 18, 22) and do not forget (vv. 19, 23): God does not forget, but they ask him to act as one who remembers.

Do not deliver the soul of your dove. Your dove is the tenderest thing said about Israel in this psalm: not an army, not a nation, but a bird with no defence at all against wild animals. And the request is touchingly small: not victory, only that God should not forget.

Have regard for the covenant. Here is the one claim they have left, and it is the right one. They cannot plead their record: the burned temple is a judgment on that. They plead the covenant God made and bound himself to. When a believer has nothing else to plead, God has still given his word, and Christians plead it with more in hand: “This cup that is poured out for you is the new covenant in my blood” (Luke 22:20), and “all the promises of God find their Yes in him” (2 Corinthians 1:20).

The dark places of the land. The second half of the verse is a phrase for any age: the dark corners of a country fill up with violence when the light goes out. Where God is not feared, violence always finds somewhere to settle.

Arise, O God, defend your cause. Having appealed to his ownership of the sheep, the city and the covenant, they end by handing God his own reputation as the reason to act.

An unresolved ending. And the psalm stops there. No answer comes, no fire falls, no promise is given. The last word is the noise of the enemies, still going up continually. Scripture leaves it unresolved because that is where the people who first sang it were living, and a congregation that has only psalms with happy endings has nothing to sing in a year like theirs.

74.title: Have Regard for the Covenant
74.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 73 was one believer’s crisis of faith; Psalm 74 is a whole nation’s. The temple lies in ashes, and this Maskil, a psalm meant to teach, gives the congregation words for the worst year in its history. It belongs to the dark Book Three of the Psalter (see the introduction), and Psalm 79 mourns the same ruin.

The message. When everything visible of God’s presence has been burned and God himself is silent, his people may still pray, and should. They do not plead their own record. They plead that they are his, that he has saved before and still rules every sunrise and season, and above all that he has bound himself by covenant. Faith can hold God to his word before any answer comes.

Why it was said. Most likely after the Babylonian army burned Solomon’s temple in about 586 BC (2 Kings 25:9). The worship, the prophets and the signs of God’s presence were gone, the enemy was mocking God’s name, and no one could say how long the judgment would last (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. It opens with “why” and a plea to remember the people God redeemed and the mountain where he lived (vv. 1–3). An eyewitness then describes the destruction: soldiers roaring in the holy place, axes on the carved panelling, fire (vv. 4–8). Worse is the silence: no signs, no prophet, no end date, and God’s hand held back (vv. 9–11). Then the psalm turns on “Yet”: God is King from of old, who divided the sea, crushed Leviathan and rules day, night and seasons (vv. 12–17). It ends with pleas to remember, not to forget the defenceless dove, to regard the covenant and to rise, and the enemy’s uproar still rising (vv. 18–23).

Where it leads. To Christ by covenant and by pattern. The covenant they pleaded was not abandoned but renewed in a better form, “the new covenant in my blood” (Luke 22:20). The burned temple was not God’s last dwelling: Jesus said, “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up”, speaking “about the temple of his body” (John 2:19, 21). The prophetic silence ended when God “has spoken to us by his Son” (Hebrews 1:2). And the God who crushed the heads of Leviathan has, in Christ, struck the ancient serpent the fatal blow (Genesis 3:15; Revelation 20:2).

For us. When a church is scattered, or God seems to have stopped speaking, this psalm gives words that neither pretend nor despair. Point back to what God has done, above all at the cross and the empty tomb; plead what he has promised; and keep praying, even when the prayer ends before the answer comes.
74.theology: Every argument in this lament rests on God's ownership and his covenant, not on Israel's record (vv. 1-8, 20). Its worst loss is silence without an end date (v. 9), a silence God has since broken by his Son. Its great lesson is the turn at v. 12: with nothing to point at in the present, faith reaches for what God has done and is still visibly doing. Nor is a burned temple the end of God's dwelling with his people: Jesus said of his body, Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up (John 2:19). And the psalm ends unanswered, so that a church in such a year still has something to sing.
74.examples: Churches have burned, congregations have been scattered, and believers have lived through seasons when God seemed to have stopped speaking. This psalm gives them words that neither pretend nor despair. When there is nothing to point to in the present, point back: to the exodus, to the cross and the empty tomb, to the sun that still rose this morning. And when nothing else can be pleaded, plead what God has promised.

keyVerse.quote: Yet God my King is from of old, working salvation in the midst of the earth.
keyVerse.note: This is the hinge of the psalm. With the temple in ashes and no prophet to speak, faith does not wait for new evidence but turns to what God has always been: King, and Saviour. The God who worked salvation at the Red Sea worked it supremely at the cross, in the midst of the earth, outside Jerusalem’s walls.

74.reflection:
The psalm’s arguments rest on God’s ownership of his people (“your congregation, which you have purchased”, v. 2), not on their record. How does it change your prayers to plead what God has done and promised rather than what you have done?

The worst loss in verse 9 is God’s silence and not knowing how long. Have you known a season like that? What helped, and what does Hebrews 1:2 add for a Christian in such a time?

With nothing to point to in the present, the psalmist points to the exodus and to the sun and the seasons (vv. 12–17). What has God already done, in Scripture and in your life, that you can point back to when things are dark?

The psalm ends without an answer (v. 23). Why might it be good for a church to sing laments that end unresolved, and how might that help someone in your church now?

75.text: To the choirmaster: according to Do Not Destroy. A Psalm of Asaph. A Song. 1We give thanks to you, O God; we give thanks, for your name is near. We recount your wondrous deeds.2"At the set time that I appoint I will judge with equity.3When the earth totters, and all its inhabitants, it is I who keep steady its pillars. Selah4I say to the boastful, 'Do not boast,' and to the wicked, 'Do not lift up your horn;5do not lift up your horn on high, or speak with haughty neck.'"6For not from the east or from the west and not from the wilderness comes lifting up,7but it is God who executes judgment, putting down one and lifting up another.8For in the hand of the LORD there is a cup with foaming wine, well mixed, and he pours out from it, and all the wicked of the earth shall drain it down to the dregs.9But I will declare it forever; I will sing praises to the God of Jacob.10All the horns of the wicked I will cut off, but the horns of the righteous shall be lifted up.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — At the Set Time That I Appoint
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s judgment is not late; it has a set time, and meanwhile he holds the world steady. The congregation begins with thanks, not because the trouble is over but because God’s name is near and his deeds can be told (v. 1). Then God himself speaks. He will judge with equity at the time he appoints (v. 2). When the earth and all its people totter, it is he who keeps its pillars steady (v. 3). And his first word to the arrogant is a warning, not yet a sentence: do not boast, do not toss your horn like a bull, do not speak with your neck stiff with pride (vv. 4–5).
verseByVerse.theology: God's first word about judgment is about its timing, and his second is to the people currently getting away with it.

verseByVerse.quote: We give thanks to you, O God; we give thanks, for your name is near. We recount your wondrous deeds. "At the set time that I appoint I will judge with equity. When the earth totters, and all its inhabitants, it is I who keep steady its pillars. Selah I say to the boastful, 'Do not boast,' and to the wicked, 'Do not lift up your horn; do not lift up your horn on high, or speak with haughty neck.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s people give thanks because he is near, and God himself answers: he has fixed the time of judgment, holds the shaking world steady, and warns the proud while there is still time.

Your name is near. The reason for the thanks is unusual: not that the trouble has ended, but that God himself is close.

At the set time that I appoint. From verse 2 God speaks, and his first sentence is about timing. The delay everyone complains about in these psalms is not neglect: he has already fixed the day, the day when he “will judge the world in righteousness by a man whom he has appointed” (Acts 17:31).

It is I who keep steady its pillars. The world really does totter, and God really does hold it up (1 Samuel 2:8). He is not merely going to judge the world at the end; he keeps it standing in the meantime, through the Son in whom “all things hold together” (Colossians 1:17).

Do not lift up your horn. The horn is the ancient image of strength, what a bull has and uses. To lift up the horn is to throw your weight around; the haughty neck is the posture of a man who has stopped looking up because he has decided there is nothing above him. What God says to such people is a warning, not yet a sentence: even now they may repent.

Uncertain wording. The title’s “Do Not Destroy” is probably the name of a tune, as in the titles of Psalms 57 to 59. Selah (seventy-one times in the Psalms) is of uncertain meaning, most likely a musical or liturgical marker. The Hebrew does not mark where God’s speech ends; the ESV ends it at verse 5.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–10 — The Cup in the Hand of the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Rising and falling are in God’s hand alone. The psalmist draws out what God has said. Promotion does not come from east or west or the southern wilderness, from anywhere on the map, for it is God who judges, bringing one down and raising another up (vv. 6–7). In the LORD’s hand stands a cup of foaming, spiced wine, the cup of his judgment, and the wicked of the earth will drink it to the bottom (v. 8). So the psalmist vows to go on praising the God of Jacob (v. 9), and the psalm ends with the great reversal: the proud horns cut off, and the righteous lifted up (v. 10).
verseByVerse.theology: Promotion comes from no direction on the compass, and there is a cup being kept for those who rose without him.

verseByVerse.quote: For not from the east or from the west and not from the wilderness comes lifting up, but it is God who executes judgment, putting down one and lifting up another. For in the hand of the LORD there is a cup with foaming wine, well mixed, and he pours out from it, and all the wicked of the earth shall drain it down to the dregs. But I will declare it forever; I will sing praises to the God of Jacob. All the horns of the wicked I will cut off, but the horns of the righteous shall be lifted up.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Promotion comes from no direction on the map but from God alone, who holds a cup of judgment the wicked must drain, and who will cut down the proud and lift up the righteous.

Not from the east or from the west. The psalm rules out east, west and the wilderness to the south: promotion does not come from anywhere on the map. It comes from God (v. 7).

Putting down one and lifting up another. Scripture keeps saying it. Hannah sang, “The LORD makes poor and makes rich; he brings low and he exalts” (1 Samuel 2:7). Mary sang, “he has brought down the mighty from their thrones and exalted those of humble estate” (Luke 1:52). Every career, dynasty and collapse is the work of one hand.

A cup with foaming wine, well mixed. The cup has been standing ready, well mixed with spices to make it stronger. Judgment here is not an outburst; it is poured from a vessel that has been in God’s hand the whole time. Jeremiah was told to take this cup round the nations (Jeremiah 25:15), and John saw it at the end (Revelation 14:10).

The cup drained by another. In Gethsemane Jesus, who had never lifted his horn in pride, asked whether that cup could pass from him, and then drank it (Matthew 26:39). The wicked drain it down to the dregs in this psalm; at Golgotha Christ drained it instead, for people who deserved to drink it, and no one who takes refuge in him will be handed that cup. He is also the supreme case of verse 7: humbled to the cross, and “highly exalted” (Philippians 2:8–9).

The horns of the righteous shall be lifted up. The psalm ends by reversing the horn picture: the horns lifted in pride are cut off, and the horns of the righteous, who never raised their own, are lifted by God, the only way anyone in this psalm rises at all. The I who cuts off the horns in verse 10 is probably the king, or the psalmist speaking for him as God’s agent; some hear God himself speaking again, as in verses 2 to 5. Either way, the cutting off is God’s judgment carried out.

In everyday life. If lifting up comes from God, you can work hard without scheming, and be passed over without despair.

Uncertain wording. The last Hebrew word of verse 6, which the ESV takes as “lifting up”, can also mean “mountains”: “not from the east or west or from the desert of the mountains”, with verse 7 finishing the sentence. Either way, help comes from no direction but God.

75.title: It Is God Who Executes Judgment
75.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 74 ended with the enemy’s uproar still rising and no answer from heaven. Psalm 75 reads like a reply: this time God himself speaks. It is the third of Asaph’s psalms in the dark Book Three of the Psalter (see the introduction), and with Psalm 76 it lifts the gloom for a moment.

The message. Judgment is not late; God has fixed its time. Until then he holds the tottering world steady, and he alone decides who rises and who falls. So the proud are warned while there is still time, a cup of judgment stands ready in the LORD’s hand, and God’s people give thanks before the day has come, because his name is near.

Why it was said. Israel lived among boastful powers and kept asking, “How long, O God, is the foe to scoff?” (Psalm 74:10). This psalm answers the question of timing and the deeper fear behind it: that the arrogant were in control and God was absent.

How the chapter makes its case. The congregation gives thanks, because God’s name is near (v. 1). Then God speaks: at the time he appoints he will judge rightly; when the earth shakes he keeps its pillars steady; and he warns the boastful not to lift up their horn (vv. 2–5). The psalmist draws the lesson: lifting up comes from no point on the compass but from God, who puts down one and lifts up another (vv. 6–7), and the wicked will drain the cup in his hand to the dregs (v. 8). He ends by vowing endless praise, and with the promise that the horns of the wicked will be cut off and those of the righteous lifted up (vv. 9–10).

Where it leads. To Christ by the character of God and by pattern. The God who appoints the set time “has fixed a day on which he will judge the world in righteousness by a man whom he has appointed” (Acts 17:31). The God who holds the pillars steady does it through the Son, in whom “all things hold together” (Colossians 1:17). The pattern of “putting down one and lifting up another” is seen fully in Jesus, who “humbled himself” to the cross, and whom God “highly exalted” (Philippians 2:8–9). And the cup the wicked must drain he drank himself in their place (Matthew 26:39).

For us. When the proud seem to be winning, remember that the date is already fixed and the world is in steady hands. Look for your lifting up to God, not to the next contact or lucky break. And if you have been lifting your own horn, hear the warning while the door is open, and run to the one who drank the cup for you.
75.theology: The psalm answers the complaint that God is slow: judgment is appointed, not late (v. 2), and meanwhile he holds the tottering world steady (v. 3). Every rise and fall is the work of one hand (vv. 6-7), so the boastful are warned while there is still time (vv. 4-5). The cup of wrath stands ready in God's hand (v. 8), and for all who take refuge in Christ it has already been drunk.
75.examples: When someone at work or in public life seems to be rising without God and getting away with it, verse 2 says God has already fixed the day. When we are tempted to look for advancement over some horizon, a contact, a move, a lucky break, verse 6 reminds us where lifting up comes from. And when we have lifted our own horn, the warning of verse 4 is spoken while the door is still open.

keyVerse.quote: but it is God who executes judgment, putting down one and lifting up another.
keyVerse.note: This is the centre of the psalm’s answer to the boastful. Rising and falling do not come from any point on the compass but from God, who has fixed the time of judgment. It is fulfilled supremely in Christ, brought down to the cross for us and lifted up by God to the highest place.

75.reflection:
The congregation gives thanks “for your name is near” (v. 1), before anything has changed. What would it look like to thank God for his nearness in a situation that has not yet been put right?

God says the time of judgment is set and that he holds the world’s pillars steady (vv. 2–3). How does that answer the feeling that God is late, or that the world is out of control?

“Not from the east or from the west … comes lifting up” (v. 6). Where do you tend to look for advancement or security, and how would trusting God for it change the way you work and compete?

The cup of verse 8 was drunk by Jesus in Gethsemane and on the cross. How does that change the way you hear this psalm’s warnings, both for yourself and for people who are still lifting up their horn?

76.text: To the choirmaster: with stringed instruments. A Psalm of Asaph. A Song. 1In Judah God is known; his name is great in Israel.2His abode has been established in Salem, his dwelling place in Zion.3There he broke the flashing arrows, the shield, the sword, and the weapons of war. Selah4Glorious are you, more majestic than the mountains full of prey.5The stouthearted were stripped of their spoil; they sank into sleep; all the men of war were unable to use their hands.6At your rebuke, O God of Jacob, both rider and horse lay stunned.7But you, you are to be feared! Who can stand before you when once your anger is roused?8From the heavens you uttered judgment; the earth feared and was still,9when God arose to establish judgment, to save all the humble of the earth. Selah10Surely the wrath of man shall praise you; the remnant of wrath you will put on like a belt.11Make your vows to the LORD your God and perform them; let all around him bring gifts to him who is to be feared,12who cuts off the spirit of princes, who is to be feared by the kings of the earth.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — There He Broke the Flashing Arrows
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The God who lives among his people breaks the weapons of those who come against them. He has made himself known in Judah, and his dwelling is in Salem, the old name of Jerusalem, the city whose name sounds like peace (vv. 1–2). There he snapped the flashing arrows, the shield, the sword and every weapon of war (v. 3). He is more glorious than the mountains where the plunderers lurk (v. 4). The psalm then shows the morning after: the enemy’s bravest men robbed of the spoil they came for, sunk into the sleep of death, unable to lift a hand, and horse and rider lying stunned at one rebuke from the God of Jacob (vv. 5–6).
verseByVerse.theology: The city whose name means peace is where God snaps the weapons, and the enemy’s soldiers sleep in death.

verseByVerse.quote: In Judah God is known; his name is great in Israel. His abode has been established in Salem, his dwelling place in Zion. There he broke the flashing arrows, the shield, the sword, and the weapons of war. Selah Glorious are you, more majestic than the mountains full of prey. The stouthearted were stripped of their spoil; they sank into sleep; all the men of war were unable to use their hands. At your rebuke, O God of Jacob, both rider and horse lay stunned.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God has made himself known among his people and lives in Jerusalem, the city of peace, and there he broke the weapons of war, leaving the enemy’s best soldiers asleep in death without Israel lifting a hand.

His abode has been established in Salem. Salem is an old name for Jerusalem, most think the city of Melchizedek (Genesis 14:18), and it sounds like the Hebrew word for peace, shalom. The psalm uses the ancient name deliberately, because of what happens in the next verse: the city called Peace is where God destroys the weapons.

There he broke the flashing arrows. Every item is broken rather than captured. This is Psalm 46’s God, who “breaks the bow and shatters the spear” (Psalm 46:9). He does not take his enemies’ equipment for his own use; he ends its usefulness.

The stouthearted were stripped of their spoil. The morning after: the stouthearted, the enemy’s best soldiers, have been robbed of the plunder they came for. And nobody on Israel’s side has done anything. They sank into sleep, the sleep of death, unable to lift a hand, and both rider and horse lay stunned, as at the Red Sea, where “the horse and his rider he has thrown into the sea” (Exodus 15:1).

The night the army died. Jerusalem saw this at least once, when an Assyrian army camped outside her walls and the city woke to find it dead (2 Kings 19:35). Hezekiah had only prayed (2 Kings 19:14–19).

The king of peace. Hebrews reads the name Salem the same way, calling Melchizedek “king of Salem, that is, king of peace” (Hebrews 7:2), a picture of Christ, the priest-king who made peace not by our weapons but “by the blood of his cross” (Colossians 1:20).

Uncertain wording. “Mountains full of prey” (v. 4) is literally “mountains of prey”, perhaps the hills where the enemy lurked like beasts of prey; the ancient Greek translation reads it differently. The word for God’s abode (v. 2) can mean a lion’s lair (Jeremiah 25:38), and some see God pictured as a lion going out from his den.
verseByVerse.note: Salem is Jerusalem. Many link this psalm to the defeat of Sennacherib’s army; the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint) adds concerning the Assyrian to its heading.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–12 — Surely the Wrath of Man Shall Praise You
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s judgment is terrible to the proud and the rescue of the humble. No one can stand before him when his anger is roused (v. 7). He spoke judgment from heaven and the earth fell silent, because he rose to save all the humble of the earth (vv. 8–9). Even the rage of human beings will add to his praise, and whatever fury remains he binds on himself like a belt (v. 10). So the psalm calls everyone to respond: make vows to the LORD and keep them, bring gifts to the God who is to be feared, for he breaks the spirit of princes and the kings of the earth should tremble before him (vv. 11–12).
verseByVerse.theology: God rises to judge, and the sentence says what that is for: to save the humble.

verseByVerse.quote: But you, you are to be feared! Who can stand before you when once your anger is roused? From the heavens you uttered judgment; the earth feared and was still, when God arose to establish judgment, to save all the humble of the earth. Selah Surely the wrath of man shall praise you; the remnant of wrath you will put on like a belt. Make your vows to the LORD your God and perform them; let all around him bring gifts to him who is to be feared, who cuts off the spirit of princes, who is to be feared by the kings of the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one can stand before God when he rises to judge, yet he rises to save the humble; even human rage will end up praising him, so everyone, kings included, should fear him and keep their vows.

Who can stand before you? The question is meant literally: everyone in the psalm who tried to stand is lying down. Revelation asks it again of the last day (Revelation 6:17), and answers with a multitude “standing before the throne and before the Lamb”, washed in his blood (Revelation 7:9, 14): the only people left standing stand in Christ.

To save all the humble of the earth. The weapons were broken by a word from heaven, and the earth went quiet the way a room does when someone in authority speaks. Then comes the purpose. Judgment and salvation are not two separate works of God; they are the same act seen from two sides. The stopping of the violent is the rescue of the people underneath them. Anyone who wishes God were less severe should ask what that would mean for the humble of the earth, who are relying on exactly this.

Surely the wrath of man shall praise you. One of the boldest claims in Scripture: human rage, intending nothing but destruction, will end up adding to God’s praise. Not that God approves of it, or that it becomes harmless; but when it has done its worst, the result will be his glory. Whatever rage is left over, God fastens round himself like a belt: it too is under his control.

The greatest example. It is the cross. Peter preached it this way: Jesus was “delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God”, and also crucified and killed “by the hands of lawless men” (Acts 2:23). The wrath of man did its very worst and produced the salvation of the world.

Make your vows to the LORD your God and perform them. The response asked of the rescued is practical: keep your promises to him, and bring him something, as thanks for a victory they slept through, not payment for it. And the psalm names the kings of the earth: the God who cuts off the spirit of princes, breaking their pride and courage, is the one every government should fear, and most do not.

Uncertain wording. Verse 10 is difficult in Hebrew. The ESV pictures God girding himself with what is left of human rage; the King James Version reads “the remainder of wrath shalt thou restrain”; some modern versions take the first line of God’s wrath against mankind. Every reading keeps the main claim: no fury escapes God’s purpose or his praise.

76.title: The Wrath of Man Shall Praise You
76.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 75 promised that God would cut off the horns of the wicked; Psalm 76 celebrates a day when he did. It is the fourth of Asaph’s psalms in Book Three (see the introduction), and like Psalms 46 and 48 it is a song of Zion, glad that God dwells in Jerusalem and defends it.

The message. God has made himself known and lives among his people, and when he rises, the weapons of the mightiest army break and its soldiers fall asleep for ever. He judges in order to save the humble, and even human rage ends up adding to his praise. So he is to be feared, thanked and obeyed by everyone, kings included.

Why it was said. The psalm very likely remembers the night in 701 BC when the Assyrian army of Sennacherib, camped against Jerusalem in the days of Hezekiah, was struck down without a battle (2 Kings 19:35). Judah had done nothing but pray; this song teaches it to give God the glory and to keep its promises to him.

How the chapter makes its case. God is known in Judah and dwells in Salem, and there he broke the weapons of war (vv. 1–3). The morning after shows the enemy’s best soldiers stripped of their plunder, asleep in death, horse and rider stunned at his rebuke (vv. 4–6). Then the psalm asks who can stand before him, and answers that he rose to judge in order to save all the humble of the earth (vv. 7–9). Even the wrath of man will praise him (v. 10). So keep your vows and bring him gifts, for he humbles princes and is to be feared by the kings of the earth (vv. 11–12).

Where it leads. To Christ by pattern and by the character of God. Salem recalls Melchizedek, “king of Salem, that is, king of peace” (Hebrews 7:2), a picture of Christ the priest-king, who made peace “by the blood of his cross” (Colossians 1:20). The wrath of man did its worst at the cross and only served God’s plan of salvation (Acts 2:23). And the question “Who can stand?” is asked again at the end of the Bible (Revelation 6:17), and answered by a multitude standing before the Lamb, washed in his blood (Revelation 7:9, 14).

For us. When the news is full of armies and threats, pray with a steady heart: the God of the city of peace breaks weapons, and no rage is outside his reach. When someone’s anger has harmed you, the harm will not have the last word. And if God has rescued you in a battle you slept through, keep your promises to him.
76.theology: The psalm makes two great claims. Judgment and salvation are one act seen from two sides: God rises to judge in order to save all the humble of the earth (v. 9), and stopping the violent is rescuing those underneath them. And human rage, intending only destruction, ends up adding to God's praise (v. 10), as it did supremely at the cross. The fitting response is kept vows and grateful gifts (v. 11), and the kings of the earth are put on notice (v. 12).
76.examples: When the news is full of armies and threats, this psalm lets believers pray with steady hearts: the God of the city of peace breaks weapons, and no rage is outside his reach. When someone's anger has done us real harm, verse 10 does not call the harm good, but it promises that the harm will not have the last word. And those rescued by a victory they slept through can at least keep their promises to the one who won it.

keyVerse.quote: Surely the wrath of man shall praise you; the remnant of wrath you will put on like a belt.
keyVerse.note: This is the psalm’s boldest claim: human rage, intending only destruction, will end up serving God’s glory. The defeat of the army outside Jerusalem showed it once; the cross showed it supremely, where the worst that human hatred could do became the salvation of the world.

76.reflection:
The enemy’s army fell while Jerusalem slept (vv. 5–6). What does this psalm teach about where real security comes from, for a nation, a church or a family?

God rose to judge “to save all the humble of the earth” (v. 9). How does seeing judgment as the rescue of the oppressed change the way you think about God’s justice?

“Surely the wrath of man shall praise you” (v. 10). How does the cross show this most clearly, and how might it help you when someone else’s anger has harmed you?

The psalm ends with a call to make vows and keep them (v. 11). What promises have you made to God, perhaps in a time of rescue, that you need to keep?

77.text: To the choirmaster: according to Jeduthun. A Psalm of Asaph. 1I cry aloud to God, aloud to God, and he will hear me.2In the day of my trouble I seek the Lord; in the night my hand is stretched out without wearying; my soul refuses to be comforted.3When I remember God, I moan; when I meditate, my spirit faints. Selah4You hold my eyelids open; I am so troubled that I cannot speak.5I consider the days of old, the years long ago.6I said, "Let me remember my song in the night; let me meditate in my heart." Then my spirit made a diligent search:7"Will the Lord spurn forever, and never again be favorable?8Has his steadfast love forever ceased? Are his promises at an end for all time?9Has God forgotten to be gracious? Has he in anger shut up his compassion?" Selah10Then I said, "I will appeal to this, to the years of the right hand of the Most High."11I will remember the deeds of the LORD; yes, I will remember your wonders of old.12I will ponder all your work, and meditate on your mighty deeds.13Your way, O God, is holy. What god is great like our God?14You are the God who works wonders; you have made known your might among the peoples.15You with your arm redeemed your people, the children of Jacob and Joseph. Selah16When the waters saw you, O God, when the waters saw you, they were afraid; indeed, the deep trembled.17The clouds poured out water; the skies gave forth thunder; your arrows flashed on every side.18The crash of your thunder was in the whirlwind; your lightnings lighted up the world; the earth trembled and shook.19Your way was through the sea, your path through the great waters; yet your footprints were unseen.20You led your people like a flock by the hand of Moses and Aaron.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — My Soul Refuses to Be Comforted
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When you cannot pray your way out of the dark, keep praying, and say the hardest questions to God himself. He cries aloud to God through the night, hands stretched out, yet his soul refuses comfort, and the thought of God makes him groan (vv. 1–3). God holds his eyes open; he cannot sleep or speak (v. 4). He searches the past for a song he once sang in such nights (vv. 5–6), and the search turns up the questions most believers are afraid to ask: will the Lord spurn for ever? Has his steadfast love ceased? Has God forgotten to be gracious (vv. 7–9)? The section ends with the questions hanging, unanswered.
verseByVerse.theology: Five questions a believer is allowed to ask out loud, in a night God is keeping him awake through.

verseByVerse.quote: I cry aloud to God, aloud to God, and he will hear me. In the day of my trouble I seek the Lord; in the night my hand is stretched out without wearying; my soul refuses to be comforted. When I remember God, I moan; when I meditate, my spirit faints. Selah
verseByVerse.commentary:
He spends the whole sleepless night crying out to God, sure God will hear, yet his soul refuses comfort and even the thought of God makes him groan.

Aloud to God, and he will hear me. The psalm opens with a cry, twice addressed “to God”, and a confidence the next eight verses seem to lose. It may be the faith he began with, or the place the psalm finally reached, set at the top; either way the long night that follows is spent talking to God, not walking away from him.

In the night my hand is stretched out. He prays with his body as well as his voice, hands lifted all night. The trouble lies deeper: “my soul refuses to be comforted.” He knows consolation is offered and that something in him will not take it; anyone who has been there knows how accurate refuses is.

When I remember God, I moan. The things that normally help are making it worse: thinking about God produces a groan, meditating leaves him fainting. The medicine has stopped working.

Uncertain wording. The heading’s “according to Jeduthun” names one of David’s Levite musicians (1 Chronicles 16:41), but whether it means his choir, a tune or a style of performance is not known (compare Psalm 62). “Selah” (v. 3) is a musical term whose meaning is lost; it probably marks a pause.

verseByVerse.quote: You hold my eyelids open; I am so troubled that I cannot speak. I consider the days of old, the years long ago. I said, "Let me remember my song in the night; let me meditate in my heart." Then my spirit made a diligent search:
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sleepless and speechless, he turns to the past, looking for a song he once sang in nights like this, and the search becomes an interrogation.

You hold my eyelids open. He names God as the cause of his sleeplessness: not the enemy, not anxiety, but you. The man crying aloud in verse 1 has lost his words altogether.

I consider the days of old. Verse 5 is the first move towards recovery, though it does not feel like one yet. He turns from the present to “the years long ago”. For now the past only sharpens the pain, because it shows how different things once were; but from verse 10 the same remembering, aimed at what God did, becomes the way out (see the note on vv. 10–15).

Let me remember my song in the night. He goes looking for a song he used to sing in such nights (the ESV notes that the Hebrew lacks “I said”). What the diligent search turns up is not comfort but a string of terrible questions.

verseByVerse.quote: "Will the Lord spurn forever, and never again be favorable? Has his steadfast love forever ceased? Are his promises at an end for all time? Has God forgotten to be gracious? Has he in anger shut up his compassion?" Selah
verseByVerse.commentary:
A believer asks God to his face whether his love has run out and his promises expired, and God has kept these questions in his hymnbook.

Has God forgotten to be gracious? Each question takes something God said about himself, his steadfast love, his promises, his grace (Exodus 34:6), and asks whether it has failed. Has God forgotten to be gracious, not refused but forgotten, as a man forgets a habit? Has compassion been locked away out of reach? God later answers the same fear through Isaiah: “Even these may forget, yet I will not forget you” (Isaiah 49:15).

Questions God preserves. These are the questions people are ashamed to say aloud in church, and here they are, set to music and handed to the choirmaster. God is not injured by them; he has preserved them, so that the next believer awake at four in the morning knows he is not the first.

When the night goes on. Sleepless nights and a soul that will not be comforted can also mark depression or grief that need a pastor’s and a biblical counsellor’s help as well as prayer, with the medical check-up a good counsellor will ask for; seeking help, or medicine, is no failure of faith. If the darkness turns to thoughts of ending your life, get help that same day.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–15 — I Will Remember the Deeds of the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The way out of the dark is not a feeling but a decision to remember what God has done. He resolves to appeal to “the years of the right hand of the Most High” (v. 10), and four verbs follow: remember, remember, ponder, meditate (vv. 11–12). He is doing what made him groan in verse 3, remembering, but now he remembers deeds, not abstractions. What he finds is a holy God beyond compare (v. 13), the God who works wonders before the nations (v. 14), and the arm that redeemed the whole people, “the children of Jacob and Joseph” (v. 15).
verseByVerse.theology: Four deliberate verbs, applied by a sleepless man to himself.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I said, "I will appeal to this, to the years of the right hand of the Most High." I will remember the deeds of the LORD; yes, I will remember your wonders of old. I will ponder all your work, and meditate on your mighty deeds. Your way, O God, is holy. What god is great like our God? You are the God who works wonders; you have made known your might among the peoples. You with your arm redeemed your people, the children of Jacob and Joseph. Selah
verseByVerse.commentary:
He decides to take his stand on what God has done, and turns from God in the abstract to God’s particular deeds of redemption.

I will appeal to this. Here is the turn: he will take his stand on the years when God’s right hand was at work for his people. Four deliberate verbs follow (remember, remember, ponder, meditate), each a resolve: a man in the dark using the means God gives, going back over what God has actually done.

What he remembers now. He was remembering in verse 3 too, and it made him moan. The difference is what he remembers. There he remembered God in the abstract and it hurt; here he remembers deeds, wonders, work, mighty deeds: specific things God did on particular days. Vague thoughts about God will not hold a man up at night. Facts will. The questions of verses 7–9 are not answered one by one; they are left behind, because the man asking them has started looking at something else.

Your way, O God, is holy. Verse 13 echoes the song Israel sang on the far shore of the sea: “Who is like you, majestic in holiness” (Exodus 15:11).

The children of Jacob and Joseph. The redeemed are named the children of Jacob and Joseph: Joseph stands for the northern tribes descended from his sons Ephraim and Manasseh, so the whole people, north as well as south, is in view.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew of verse 10 can be read two ways. The ESV’s footnote gives the alternative: “This is my grief: that the right hand of the Most High has changed”, which makes verse 10 the bottom of the pit rather than the turn. This commentary follows the ESV’s main reading, but on either reading he turns at once to remembering what that hand has done.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–20 — Your Way Was Through the Sea
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s hiddenness is not his absence: he made a way where no way was, and left no footprints. The exodus is retold as a thunderstorm: the waters see God and tremble, clouds pour, lightning flashes like arrows, the earth shakes (vv. 16–18). Then the climax, quiet after the storm: God’s path lay through the great waters, “yet your footprints were unseen” (v. 19). The psalm ends abruptly on a homely picture: a flock, led by the hands of Moses and Aaron (v. 20). Nothing is said of the psalmist’s own trouble; he has simply stopped looking at himself.
verseByVerse.theology: The great rescue left no tracks — and the psalm ends there, with the flock and the shepherds.

verseByVerse.quote: When the waters saw you, O God, when the waters saw you, they were afraid; indeed, the deep trembled. The clouds poured out water; the skies gave forth thunder; your arrows flashed on every side. The crash of your thunder was in the whirlwind; your lightnings lighted up the world; the earth trembled and shook. Your way was through the sea, your path through the great waters; yet your footprints were unseen. You led your people like a flock by the hand of Moses and Aaron.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The exodus answers his questions: God went through the deep water and left no footprints, yet his people got across, led by ordinary human hands.

When the waters saw you, O God. This is the exodus, told as a thunderstorm. Exodus 14 says a strong east wind drove the sea back; this psalm hears the thunder, sees lightning like arrows, and the sea itself frightened at the sight of God. The man who could not speak in verse 4 now describes at length the greatest thing that ever happened to his people: that is what remembering produced.

Yet your footprints were unseen. The whole psalm has been walking towards verse 19: God went through the sea and left no tracks (the ESV notes that “unseen” is literally “unknown”). Hold that against verses 7–9. He could not see what God was doing and asked whether God had stopped caring; yet the greatest rescue in his nation’s history was carried out by a God who leaves no footprints. That is the answer to his questions, and it is not an explanation. It is a fact about how God works: invisibly, in deep water, and afterwards you find that a nation got across.

Why doesn’t God make himself plainer? This psalm puts a serious modern objection in God’s own hymnbook. If God is there and wants to be known, why not write his name across the sky? Bertrand Russell, asked what he would say if he met God after death, is reported to have said that he would complain that God had not given enough evidence. Pascal saw the question coming three centuries earlier. He argued that God has given light enough for those who want to see him and shadow enough for those who would rather not, because a God who overwhelmed us would have our surrender but never our love. The psalm adds that hiddenness is not absence: the footprints were unseen, yet the sea was crossed. And when God finally came out of hiding, he came in the most easily refused form there is: a baby, a carpenter, a man on a cross. “No one has ever seen God; God the only Son, who is at the Father’s side, he has made him known” (John 1:18). He hides his power so that he can be met by faith, not forced.

The deepest water of all. The God whose way was through the sea came walking on it in person (Matthew 14:25). The deepest water he ever passed through unseen was the cross, where he seemed most absent and was working his greatest redemption, the “departure” (literally exodus) that Jesus accomplished at Jerusalem (Luke 9:31).

By the hand of Moses and Aaron. After all that thunder the psalm ends on a quiet, homely picture: no footprints, but two men walking in front, and the psalm calls that God’s leading. He guides by ordinary hands, two brothers then, a pastor or a friend now, and the flock gets home. Moses and Aaron were prophet and priest, and Hebrews tells Christians to “consider Jesus, the apostle and high priest of our confession” (Hebrews 3:1), who is both, and greater than either: the shepherd who leads his flock himself (John 10:11).

The abrupt ending. Nothing is said of the psalmist’s own trouble or of any change in it. He simply stops talking about himself and finishes looking at the sea. That is often how God heals a sleepless believer: not by answering every question, but by giving him something greater to look at.
verseByVerse.note: “Unseen” is literally “unknown” (ESV note).

77.title: Your Footprints Were Unseen
77.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 77 belongs to the Asaph collection (Psalms 73–83) that opens Book Three, a book written in the shadow of national disaster. Psalm 74 lamented a temple in ruins; here the trouble is closer in, a single believer lying awake, unable to pray his way out.

The message. When you cannot see God at work and every thought of him hurts, take your stand on what he has actually done. God does not answer the sleepless man’s questions one by one; he turns his eyes from God in the abstract to God’s deeds, above all the exodus, where God made a way through the sea and left no footprints. God’s hiddenness is not his absence: you may not see his tracks, but his people get across.

Why it was said. The psalm names no event, and it may come from any of Israel’s dark seasons (see the introduction). Its first hearers knew what it was to pray and find heaven silent, and to ask whether the covenant love sworn to their fathers had run out.

How the chapter makes its case. First the night: he cries aloud, stretches out his hands, refuses comfort, and finds that even remembering God makes him groan (vv. 1–3). Sleepless and speechless, he searches the past, and the search throws up terrible questions: has the Lord spurned for ever, has his steadfast love ceased, has God forgotten to be gracious (vv. 4–9)? Then the turn: he resolves to appeal to “the years of the right hand of the Most High” and to remember God’s deeds, his holy way and his arm that redeemed his people (vv. 10–15). Finally the exodus, told as a thunderstorm, ending in quiet: a path through the great waters, footprints unseen, and a flock led by Moses and Aaron (vv. 16–20).

Where it leads. By pattern and by the character of God revealed in Christ. The exodus was the great redemption of the Old Testament, and on the mountain Jesus spoke with Moses and Elijah of “his departure” (Luke 9:31), literally his exodus, which he would accomplish at Jerusalem. The God whose way was through the sea came walking on the sea in person (Matthew 14:25), and the deepest water he ever passed through unseen was the cross, where he seemed most absent and was doing his greatest work. The prophet and priest who led the flock give way to the one who is both, “the apostle and high priest of our confession” (Hebrews 3:1).

For us. You are allowed to bring God your worst questions; this psalm puts them in your mouth. But do not stay with vague thoughts of him at four in the morning: go back to what he has done, above all at the cross and the empty tomb. The God who left no footprints in the Red Sea is still leading his flock through deep water by ordinary hands.
77.theology: The psalm lets believers say the worst questions aloud to God (vv. 7-9), and preserves them so that no sleepless believer thinks he is the first. It does not answer them one by one. It turns the sufferer from God in the abstract to God's deeds (vv. 11-12), and lets the exodus answer with a fact: God's footprints were unseen, yet a nation got across (v. 19). He leads that hidden way by ordinary hands (v. 20), and the deepest such water was the cross.
77.examples: Some readers will come to this psalm in the middle of a long night, unable to take comfort and ashamed of the questions they are asking. The psalm does not hurry them. It shows a believer who said those questions to God and was not cast off, and who slowly turned to remember particular things God had done. In grief or depression that turning may take weeks or months, and it is often helped by a friend, a pastor or a biblical counsellor walking in front, as Moses and Aaron did, with a medical check-up so that nothing bodily is missed. God's footprints are not always visible, but his leading does not stop.

keyVerse.quote: Your way was through the sea, your path through the great waters; yet your footprints were unseen.
keyVerse.note: The whole psalm walks towards this verse. It answers the questions of verses 7–9 not with an explanation but with a fact: the greatest rescue in Israel’s history was carried out by a God who left no visible tracks. That we cannot see what God is doing has never meant that he is not there.

77.reflection:
The psalmist says his “soul refuses to be comforted” (v. 2), and that even remembering God made him moan (v. 3). Have you known a time when the things that usually help made it worse? What helped you in the end?

The questions of verses 7–9 stand in Israel’s hymnbook, handed to the choirmaster. What difference does it make to know that God has given us words like these? Why are we often ashamed to say them aloud in church?

The turn comes when he stops thinking about God in general and starts remembering specific deeds (vv. 11–12). Which of God’s deeds, in Scripture and in your own life, could you go back to on a sleepless night?

God’s “footprints were unseen” (v. 19), yet he led his people “by the hand of Moses and Aaron” (v. 20). Where have you seen God lead through ordinary people? How might he use you to lead someone else through deep water?

78.text: A Maskil of Asaph. 1Give ear, O my people, to my teaching; incline your ears to the words of my mouth!2I will open my mouth in a parable; I will utter dark sayings from of old,3things that we have heard and known, that our fathers have told us.4We will not hide them from their children, but tell to the coming generation the glorious deeds of the LORD, and his might, and the wonders that he has done.5He established a testimony in Jacob and appointed a law in Israel, which he commanded our fathers to teach to their children,6that the next generation might know them, the children yet unborn, and arise and tell them to their children,7so that they should set their hope in God and not forget the works of God, but keep his commandments;8and that they should not be like their fathers, a stubborn and rebellious generation, a generation whose heart was not steadfast, whose spirit was not faithful to God.9The Ephraimites, armed with the bow, turned back on the day of battle.10They did not keep God's covenant, but refused to walk according to his law.11They forgot his works and the wonders that he had shown them.12In the sight of their fathers he performed wonders in the land of Egypt, in the fields of Zoan.13He divided the sea and let them pass through it, and made the waters stand like a heap.14In the daytime he led them with a cloud, and all the night with a fiery light.15He split rocks in the wilderness and gave them drink abundantly as from the deep.16He made streams come out of the rock and caused waters to flow down like rivers.17Yet they sinned still more against him, rebelling against the Most High in the desert.18They tested God in their heart by demanding the food they craved.19They spoke against God, saying, "Can God spread a table in the wilderness?20He struck the rock so that water gushed out and streams overflowed. Can he also give bread or provide meat for his people?"21Therefore, when the LORD heard, he was full of wrath; a fire was kindled against Jacob; his anger rose against Israel,22because they did not believe in God and did not trust his saving power.23Yet he commanded the skies above and opened the doors of heaven,24and he rained down on them manna to eat and gave them the grain of heaven.25Man ate of the bread of the angels; he sent them food in abundance.26He caused the east wind to blow in the heavens, and by his power he led out the south wind;27he rained meat on them like dust, winged birds like the sand of the seas;28he let them fall in the midst of their camp, all around their dwellings.29And they ate and were well filled, for he gave them what they craved.30But before they had satisfied their craving, while the food was still in their mouths,31the anger of God rose against them, and he killed the strongest of them and laid low the young men of Israel.32In spite of all this, they still sinned; despite his wonders, they did not believe.33So he made their days vanish like a breath, and their years in terror.34When he killed them, they sought him; they repented and sought God earnestly.35They remembered that God was their rock, the Most High God their redeemer.36But they flattered him with their mouths; they lied to him with their tongues.37Their heart was not steadfast toward him; they were not faithful to his covenant.38Yet he, being compassionate, atoned for their iniquity and did not destroy them;
