he restrained his anger often and did not stir up all his wrath.39He remembered that they were but flesh, a wind that passes and comes not again.40How often they rebelled against him in the wilderness and grieved him in the desert!41They tested God again and again and provoked the Holy One of Israel.42They did not remember his power or the day when he redeemed them from the foe,43when he performed his signs in Egypt and his marvels in the fields of Zoan.44He turned their rivers to blood, so that they could not drink of their streams.45He sent among them swarms of flies, which devoured them, and frogs, which destroyed them.46He gave their crops to the destroying locust and the fruit of their labor to the locust.47He destroyed their vines with hail and their sycamores with frost.48He gave over their cattle to the hail and their flocks to thunderbolts.49He let loose on them his burning anger, wrath, indignation, and distress, a company of destroying angels.50He made a path for his anger; he did not spare them from death, but gave their lives over to the plague.51He struck down every firstborn in Egypt, the firstfruits of their strength in the tents of Ham.52Then he led out his people like sheep and guided them in the wilderness like a flock.53He led them in safety, so that they were not afraid, but the sea overwhelmed their enemies.54And he brought them to his holy land, to the mountain which his right hand had won.55He drove out nations before them; he apportioned them for a possession and settled the tribes of Israel in their tents.56Yet they tested and rebelled against the Most High God and did not keep his testimonies,57but turned away and acted treacherously like their fathers; they twisted like a deceitful bow.58For they provoked him to anger with their high places; they moved him to jealousy with their idols.59When God heard, he was full of wrath, and he utterly rejected Israel.60He forsook his dwelling at Shiloh, the tent where he dwelt among mankind,61and delivered his power to captivity, his glory to the hand of the foe.62He gave his people over to the sword and vented his wrath on his heritage.63Fire devoured their young men, and their young women had no marriage song.64Their priests fell by the sword, and their widows made no lamentation.65Then the Lord awoke as from sleep, like a strong man shouting because of wine.66And he put his adversaries to rout; he put them to everlasting shame.67He rejected the tent of Joseph; he did not choose the tribe of Ephraim,68but he chose the tribe of Judah, Mount Zion, which he loves.69He built his sanctuary like the high heavens, like the earth, which he has founded forever.70He chose David his servant and took him from the sheepfolds;71from following the nursing ewes he brought him to shepherd Jacob his people, Israel his inheritance.72With upright heart he shepherded them and guided them with his skillful hand.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — That the Next Generation Might Know
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Teach the children what God has done, so that they will hope in him and not repeat their fathers’ sins. Asaph calls the whole people to listen to a “parable” and “dark sayings”, the meaning of a history they already know (vv. 1–3). The fathers told it; we will not hide it from our children (v. 4); God commanded it, so that generations yet unborn would hear and pass it on (vv. 5–6). The purpose is stated plainly: that they would set their hope in God, remember his works and keep his commandments (v. 7), and not be a stubborn, unsteady generation like their fathers (v. 8).
verseByVerse.theology: Seventy-two verses of national history, and the stated reason is the children.

verseByVerse.quote: Give ear, O my people, to my teaching; incline your ears to the words of my mouth! I will open my mouth in a parable; I will utter dark sayings from of old, things that we have heard and known, that our fathers have told us. We will not hide them from their children, but tell to the coming generation the glorious deeds of the LORD, and his might, and the wonders that he has done. He established a testimony in Jacob and appointed a law in Israel, which he commanded our fathers to teach to their children, that the next generation might know them, the children yet unborn, and arise and tell them to their children, so that they should set their hope in God and not forget the works of God, but keep his commandments; and that they should not be like their fathers, a stubborn and rebellious generation, a generation whose heart was not steadfast, whose spirit was not faithful to God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Asaph will tell the next generation what God has done, so that they will set their hope in God and not repeat their fathers’ unfaithfulness.

Give ear, O my people. Asaph is teaching (the heading calls it a Maskil), and the classroom is the whole congregation with its children in it.

I will open my mouth in a parable. Matthew quotes verse 2 of Jesus’ parables: “I will open my mouth in parables; I will utter what has been hidden since the foundation of the world” (Matthew 13:35). He calls it a word of “the prophet” (Asaph is called a seer in 2 Chronicles 29:30), and Jesus’ parables did what this verse promised, opening hidden things to those with ears to hear. A “dark saying” is a truth that has to be worked at, and history is exactly that: the facts are public, the meaning has to be taught.

We will not hide them from their children. The fathers told us, and we will tell their children; verses 5–6 stretch the chain to four generations, and the teaching is commanded. Each generation is the link that could break.

So that they should set their hope in God. Verse 7 states the whole reason this long psalm exists: that children would set their hope in God, not forget, and keep his commandments. Hope, memory, obedience, in that order.

That they should not be like their fathers. So this is no proud parade of national heroes but an account of Israel’s own failures, taught to her children on purpose: a rare and healthy thing in a national story, and a model for a church honest about its own past. Yet the hope the children are taught is not in doing better than their fathers but in the God who atoned for their fathers’ iniquity (v. 38).

What this looks like. The chain is kept by ordinary means, and Moses named the settings long before Asaph: “when you sit in your house, and when you walk by the way, and when you lie down, and when you rise” (Deuteronomy 6:7). Tell the stories, the exodus and the cross above all, and what God has done in your own family. Answer the questions: a child’s “Why did Jesus have to die?” at bedtime is the opening the psalm means; answer simply, and say “I don’t know; let’s find out” when you must. Be honest about failure: let children hear that you sin too, say sorry to them, and show them where you go for forgiveness. Bring them among God’s people, where many voices sing and preach it. Those without children can still be a link: Timothy’s faith “dwelt first in your grandmother Lois and your mother Eunice” (2 Timothy 1:5). No parent can make a child believe, but the story we hand on ends at a cross where Christ bore his people’s sins, and that is the hope we are asked to pass down.

Shouldn’t children be left to choose for themselves? A fair-minded home, we think, would stay neutral until children are old enough to decide. The poet Samuel Taylor Coleridge once had a guest who argued exactly that. Coleridge took him into the garden, which was full of weeds, and explained that he had not wanted to prejudice the soil in favour of roses and strawberries. There is no neutral garden. If parents say nothing, the advertisers, the screen and the playground will not be so shy; every child is being taught what to love by somebody. The psalm does not ask parents to force anything, and they cannot: faith is not inherited like eye colour. It asks them to tell the truth, and the story is not rules to keep children in line but news of a God who keeps his promises to sinners: not an imposition but an inheritance, and Peter said it was meant for them: “the promise is for you and for your children” (Acts 2:39).

Uncertain wording. The meaning of Maskil in the heading is not certain. It comes from a root meaning insight, so it probably means a teaching psalm; some think it is a musical term.
verseByVerse.note: Matthew quotes v. 2 of Jesus’ teaching in parables.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–39 — Can God Spread a Table in the Wilderness?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Forgetting God’s works breeds unbelief, yet God’s compassion outlasts it. Ephraim turns back in battle because it forgot what God had done (vv. 9–11): the wonders in Egypt, the sea, the pillar, water from the rock (vv. 12–16). Israel answers with a demand: “Can God spread a table in the wilderness?” (vv. 17–20). God is angry, and feeds them anyway with manna (vv. 21–25), then sends quails, and the craving granted becomes a judgment (vv. 26–31). Under further judgment they seek him, but only with their lips (vv. 32–37). Then the turning point: God, being compassionate, atoned for their iniquity, remembering that they were but flesh (vv. 38–39).
verseByVerse.theology: Wonder, forgetting, rebellion, judgment — and then the verse the whole psalm turns on.

verseByVerse.quote: The Ephraimites, armed with the bow, turned back on the day of battle. They did not keep God's covenant, but refused to walk according to his law. They forgot his works and the wonders that he had shown them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ephraim, well armed, ran from battle, and the reason lay deeper than cowardice: they had broken the covenant and forgotten what God had done.

The Ephraimites, armed with the bow. Joseph’s son Ephraim gave his name to the leading northern tribe, named first here and last in verse 67. They were armed and they ran anyway; the equipment was not the problem.

They did not keep God’s covenant. Verse 10 gives the inside of the retreat: before Ephraim turned back in battle, it had “refused to walk according to his law”. In this psalm failure in war and failure to keep the covenant are one story, and the forgetting of verse 11 lies under both.

They forgot his works. Forgetting is the sin this psalm is written against, and it is not a lapse of memory but a failure to keep rehearsing what God has done, which is why the remedy in verses 4–6 is telling the story.

Uncertain wording. The ESV notes that the Hebrew of verse 9 is literally “armed and shooting” the bow, an unusual phrase. Which battle is meant is not known: no retreat of Ephraim is recorded that fits exactly, and it may stand for the northern tribes’ long unfaithfulness rather than a single day.

verseByVerse.quote: In the sight of their fathers he performed wonders in the land of Egypt, in the fields of Zoan. He divided the sea and let them pass through it, and made the waters stand like a heap. In the daytime he led them with a cloud, and all the night with a fiery light. He split rocks in the wilderness and gave them drink abundantly as from the deep. He made streams come out of the rock and caused waters to flow down like rivers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The fathers had seen God’s wonders with their own eyes, which is what made their forgetting so serious.

In the sight of their fathers. These wonders were not rumours handed down; the fathers saw them in Egypt, “in the fields of Zoan”, the region of a city in the Nile delta (see v. 43). The waters stood “like a heap”, the picture in the song Israel sang on the far shore (Exodus 15:8). They had been eyewitnesses.

He split rocks in the wilderness. Four wonders in four verses: the plagues, the sea, the pillar, the rock. Paul says of the rock that “they drank from the spiritual Rock that followed them, and the Rock was Christ” (1 Corinthians 10:4), and then warns the Corinthians, using this very history, not to repeat it.

verseByVerse.quote: Yet they sinned still more against him, rebelling against the Most High in the desert. They tested God in their heart by demanding the food they craved. They spoke against God, saying, "Can God spread a table in the wilderness? He struck the rock so that water gushed out and streams overflowed. Can he also give bread or provide meat for his people?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
With the water from the rock still running, Israel tested God by demanding food, doubting he could provide the next mercy.

Yet they sinned still more. The question of verse 19 was not honest perplexity but a test: they “tested God in their heart by demanding the food they craved”. To test God in this sense is to set him conditions, as if he must prove himself again on our terms before we will trust him. Jesus refused to do it when the devil quoted Scripture at him: “You shall not put the Lord your God to the test” (Matthew 4:7, quoting Deuteronomy 6:16).

Can God spread a table in the wilderness? They ask it while the water from the rock is still running. That is how unbelief works: it does not deny the last mercy; it simply cannot see how the next one could possibly arrive. Every Christian who has thanked God for one answered prayer on Sunday and panicked about the next thing on Monday has asked verse 19.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, when the LORD heard, he was full of wrath; a fire was kindled against Jacob; his anger rose against Israel, because they did not believe in God and did not trust his saving power. Yet he commanded the skies above and opened the doors of heaven, and he rained down on them manna to eat and gave them the grain of heaven. Man ate of the bread of the angels; he sent them food in abundance.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God was angry at their unbelief, and fed them anyway, raining down manna from heaven.

Because they did not believe in God. The grumbling about food was the symptom; the disease was unbelief: they “did not trust his saving power”. Hebrews draws the same lesson from the same years: “they were unable to enter because of unbelief” (Hebrews 3:19).

He rained down on them manna to eat. Watch the sequence: anger, and then bread. He was “full of wrath”, and he opened the doors of heaven and fed them anyway. Jesus took up this very verse in Capernaum: their fathers ate manna and died, and he is the true bread that came down from heaven (John 6:31–35).

Uncertain wording. “The bread of the angels” (v. 25) is literally “bread of the mighty ones”. The ancient Greek translation took the mighty ones to be angels, as the ESV does; others take it more generally as food fit for the mighty. Either way, it is food from heaven, not from the earth.

verseByVerse.quote: He caused the east wind to blow in the heavens, and by his power he led out the south wind; he rained meat on them like dust, winged birds like the sand of the seas; he let them fall in the midst of their camp, all around their dwellings. And they ate and were well filled, for he gave them what they craved. But before they had satisfied their craving, while the food was still in their mouths, the anger of God rose against them, and he killed the strongest of them and laid low the young men of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God gave them the meat they craved, and it became their judgment: sometimes God’s yes is the punishment.

He rained meat on them like dust. Verses 26–28 retell the quails of Numbers 11, brought by wind in such numbers that they fell all round the camp. He “rained down” manna (v. 24) and he “rained” meat (v. 27): the same generosity, but this time given in answer to a demand, and with a sting in it.

He gave them what they craved. Among the most sobering verses in the Old Testament: they got exactly what they asked for, and it killed them. Sometimes God gives people what they demand, to their hurt.

When God says yes. Our culture assumes that the good life is the satisfied want, and whole industries compete to get us what we crave faster. This verse is a quiet bomb under that. Oscar Wilde gave one of his characters a line that says the same thing with a smile: “When the gods wish to punish us they answer our prayers.” The problem is not wanting; God made us to want. The problem is a heart that has decided it knows what it needs better than God does, and the moralist and the pleasure-seeker can share that heart, one demanding blessings as wages and the other as rights. Jesus did the opposite. In Gethsemane he wanted something with all his being and said, “Nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done” (Luke 22:42). Because he took the refusal, we can trust a Father who sometimes says no, and who never gives his children a stone when they ask for bread (Matthew 7:9).

verseByVerse.quote: In spite of all this, they still sinned; despite his wonders, they did not believe. So he made their days vanish like a breath, and their years in terror. When he killed them, they sought him; they repented and sought God earnestly. They remembered that God was their rock, the Most High God their redeemer. But they flattered him with their mouths; they lied to him with their tongues. Their heart was not steadfast toward him; they were not faithful to his covenant.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Under judgment they turned to God, but only with their lips, and the psalm calls their repentance flattery.

So he made their days vanish like a breath. Verses 32–33 compress forty years. After the spies’ report Israel again refused to believe, and God swore that the whole generation would die in the wilderness (Numbers 14:22–23, 29–35). Their days went by “like a breath” and their years “in terror”, a long procession of funerals with no promised land at the end. Moses’ own psalm mourns the same years: “we are brought to an end by your anger” (Psalm 90:7).

They flattered him with their mouths. This is shallow repentance: under judgment they sought God “earnestly”, saying the right things because they were frightened, and the psalm, which sees the heart, calls it lying. Anyone can produce religion in a crisis; the question is what happens when the pressure lifts.

Their heart was not steadfast toward him. Verse 37 echoes verse 8: the children are shown exactly what the psalm warned them against, words of return without a heart that stays.

verseByVerse.quote: Yet he, being compassionate, atoned for their iniquity and did not destroy them; he restrained his anger often and did not stir up all his wrath. He remembered that they were but flesh, a wind that passes and comes not again.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The whole psalm turns here: God, being compassionate, covered their sin himself and held back his anger, remembering how weak and brief they were.

Yet he, being compassionate, atoned for their iniquity. After the craving, the lying and the flattery comes this “yet”. The verb is the law’s word for atonement, the covering of sin by sacrifice, as on the Day of Atonement; here God covered their sin himself. John names where that covering was finally made: Christ “is the propitiation for our sins” (1 John 2:2), the sacrifice that turns away God’s anger. The children taught this psalm could not keep the covenant either; the one who kept it in their place gives his Spirit, so that the hope of verse 7 becomes a new obedience (Ezekiel 36:27).

He restrained his anger often. Often, because they needed it often. The reason is not anything in them but a fact about them: “he remembered that they were but flesh.” He knows what he is dealing with. Nobody in this psalm gets away with anything, and nobody is treated as though he were stronger than he is.

A wind that passes and comes not again. Man is not only weak flesh but brief, a breath of wind that blows once and is gone. Another psalm says the same of God’s pity: “he knows our frame; he remembers that we are dust” (Psalm 103:14). Their days had vanished “like a breath” as a judgment (v. 33); here their brevity is the very thing that moves God to mercy.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 40–55 — He Made a Path for His Anger
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The story steps back to Egypt because Israel had forgotten even the day of its redemption. They grieved God in the wilderness and tested him again and again, because they did not remember his power (vv. 40–42). So the plagues are retold, not as a chronicle but as a sermon: rivers of blood, flies and frogs, locusts, hail and frost, a company of destroying angels, and finally the firstborn of Egypt (vv. 43–51). Then the tone changes: the same hand led his people out like sheep, kept them safe while the sea covered their enemies, and brought them to his holy mountain and their inheritance (vv. 52–55).
verseByVerse.theology: The same God made a path for his anger in Egypt and led his people out like a flock.

verseByVerse.quote: How often they rebelled against him in the wilderness and grieved him in the desert! They tested God again and again and provoked the Holy One of Israel. They did not remember his power or the day when he redeemed them from the foe,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Their rebellion pained God, and its root was that they did not remember the day he redeemed them.

Grieved him in the desert. Grieved is the striking word: God is not merely offended but pained (compare Ephesians 4:30). And the root is named again: they did not remember.

Provoked the Holy One of Israel. “They tested God again and again” recalls Numbers 14:22, where God says Israel had “put me to the test these ten times”. “The Holy One of Israel”, Isaiah’s favourite name for God and rare in the Psalms, says who it was they kept provoking: not a tribal god to be bargained with, but the holy God who had bound himself to them and redeemed them “from the foe” (v. 42).

verseByVerse.quote: when he performed his signs in Egypt and his marvels in the fields of Zoan. He turned their rivers to blood, so that they could not drink of their streams. He sent among them swarms of flies, which devoured them, and frogs, which destroyed them. He gave their crops to the destroying locust and the fruit of their labor to the locust. He destroyed their vines with hail and their sycamores with frost. He gave over their cattle to the hail and their flocks to thunderbolts. He let loose on them his burning anger, wrath, indignation, and distress, a company of destroying angels. He made a path for his anger; he did not spare them from death, but gave their lives over to the plague. He struck down every firstborn in Egypt, the firstfruits of their strength in the tents of Ham.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The plagues on Egypt are retold to rebuild a forgotten memory: God himself struck Egypt, down to the firstborn, to set his people free.

He turned their rivers to blood. The plagues are retold because they had been forgotten (v. 42), and a generation that cannot remember what God did to Egypt will ask whether he can manage a table in the wilderness.

Not a chronicle. Anyone comparing this with Exodus will notice that the psalm names only some of the plagues (six or seven, depending on how they are counted) and puts the flies before the frogs. It is not a chronicle but a sermon on a well-known story, bringing out the point, as verse 2 promised (“in a parable”). Zoan was a city in the Nile delta.

A company of destroying angels. Verse 49 piles up four words for God’s anger and then calls them “a company of destroying angels”, messengers of disaster sent by him. Exodus speaks of “the destroyer” whom the LORD would not allow into the houses marked with blood (Exodus 12:23). The plagues were not accidents of nature but God’s own acts, and “he made a path for his anger” (v. 50): nothing stood in its way.

He struck down every firstborn in Egypt. The list ends on the firstborn, “the firstfruits of their strength in the tents of Ham” (Ham being the ancestor of Egypt, Genesis 10:6), the night Israel walked out under the blood of the Passover lamb. Every household in Egypt lost its eldest son; and centuries later God “did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all” (Romans 8:32).
verseByVerse.note: Zoan was a city in the Nile delta.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he led out his people like sheep and guided them in the wilderness like a flock. He led them in safety, so that they were not afraid, but the sea overwhelmed their enemies. And he brought them to his holy land, to the mountain which his right hand had won. He drove out nations before them; he apportioned them for a possession and settled the tribes of Israel in their tents.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The same hand that struck Egypt led Israel out like a shepherd and brought them safely to the land he had won for them.

He led out his people like sheep. After the destroying angels and the firstborn, the picture is a shepherd moving sheep. The same hand did both, on the same night, and the psalm sets them side by side without apology.

To the mountain which his right hand had won. He led them “in safety, so that they were not afraid”, while the sea closed over their enemies (Exodus 14:28), and then brought them to his holy land and the mountain his own hand had won, which in this psalm points ahead to Zion (v. 68). The land was a gift taken by God’s power, not theirs (Psalm 44:3), and the people who received it went on to test him there too (v. 56).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 56–72 — He Chose David His Servant
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s people failed again, but God did not abandon his purpose; he chose Zion and gave them a shepherd-king. In the land they tested him with high places and idols, twisting like a deceitful bow (vv. 56–58). So God forsook his dwelling at Shiloh, let the ark go into captivity and gave his people to the sword (vv. 59–64). Then the Lord awoke like a strong man and routed his enemies (vv. 65–66). He set aside Ephraim, chose Judah and Mount Zion and built his sanctuary there, and took David from following the ewes to shepherd Israel with an upright heart and a skilful hand (vv. 67–72).
verseByVerse.theology: Even the sanctuary was no guarantee — and the psalm ends with a shepherd taken out of a field.

verseByVerse.quote: Yet they tested and rebelled against the Most High God and did not keep his testimonies, but turned away and acted treacherously like their fathers; they twisted like a deceitful bow. For they provoked him to anger with their high places; they moved him to jealousy with their idols.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Settled in the land, Israel repeated their fathers’ unfaithfulness, keeping the forms of faith while giving their hearts to idols.

They twisted like a deceitful bow. A warped bow looks like a weapon but will not shoot where it is aimed: the psalm’s picture of a people who keep the outward forms of faith without the faithfulness. And “like their fathers” is the very thing verse 8 was trying to prevent.

Their high places … their idols. Verse 58 names what the treachery looked like: “high places”, local hilltop shrines where worship drifted into the ways of Canaan, and idols. God’s answer is called jealousy, not petty envy but the rightful zeal of a husband whose wife has gone after others (Exodus 20:5; 34:14). The covenant is a marriage, and idolatry is unfaithfulness to it.

verseByVerse.quote: When God heard, he was full of wrath, and he utterly rejected Israel. He forsook his dwelling at Shiloh, the tent where he dwelt among mankind, and delivered his power to captivity, his glory to the hand of the foe.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God abandoned his own sanctuary at Shiloh and let the ark be captured: no holy place is a guarantee against judgment.

He utterly rejected Israel. “Israel” here probably means above all the northern tribes led by Ephraim, as verse 67 makes plain (see the note on vv. 67–72). It was not the end of God’s people, for the psalm goes on to Judah and David; but it was the end of Shiloh.

He forsook his dwelling at Shiloh. Shiloh is the psalm’s most frightening word. The tabernacle stood there for generations, until the ark was captured and the place was finished (1 Samuel 4). Jeremiah would later stand in the temple gate and tell people to go and look at what was left of it (Jeremiah 7:12). “His power” and “his glory” in verse 61 are the ark itself, carried off by the Philistines; the dying wife of the priest Phinehas named her son Ichabod, saying, “The glory has departed from Israel!” (1 Samuel 4:21).

No building is a guarantee. God abandoned his own sanctuary. It was a privilege, never a guarantee, and it could be withdrawn. Any congregation that assumes God is obliged to stay because of its building or its history should read verse 60.

verseByVerse.quote: He gave his people over to the sword and vented his wrath on his heritage. Fire devoured their young men, and their young women had no marriage song. Their priests fell by the sword, and their widows made no lamentation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Four flat sentences show what a national catastrophe actually is: young men dead, no weddings, no proper funerals.

Their young women had no marriage song. A generation of young men was gone, so there were no weddings. The detail about the widows not lamenting is the worst: there was no one left to do it, or no time. The priests were Eli’s sons Hophni and Phinehas, killed on the day the ark was taken, and Phinehas’s wife died in childbirth when the news came (1 Samuel 4:11, 19–20).

verseByVerse.quote: Then the Lord awoke as from sleep, like a strong man shouting because of wine. And he put his adversaries to rout; he put them to everlasting shame.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After long silence God rose up suddenly like a warrior and routed his enemies.

Then the Lord awoke as from sleep. The image is meant to startle. God has long looked like a man asleep; then he is suddenly up and roaring like a soldier who has had a drink. It answers Psalm 44’s “Awake! Why are you sleeping, O Lord?” (Psalm 44:23), not by rebuking the question but by picturing what the waking looks like when it comes. The rout probably looks back to the plague that struck the Philistines while they held the ark, so that they sent it home (1 Samuel 5:6–12), and to the victories over them that followed under Samuel and David.

Uncertain wording. The verb behind “shouting because of wine” is rare, and it can be read either as a warrior shouting, flushed with wine, or as one who wakes from the sleep that wine brings. The picture is the same either way: sudden, overwhelming strength after apparent inactivity.

verseByVerse.quote: He rejected the tent of Joseph; he did not choose the tribe of Ephraim, but he chose the tribe of Judah, Mount Zion, which he loves. He built his sanctuary like the high heavens, like the earth, which he has founded forever. He chose David his servant and took him from the sheepfolds; from following the nursing ewes he brought him to shepherd Jacob his people, Israel his inheritance. With upright heart he shepherded them and guided them with his skillful hand.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God set Ephraim aside and chose Judah, Zion and David, taking a young shepherd from the sheepfolds to shepherd his people with integrity and skill.

He rejected the tent of Joseph. The psalm began with Ephraim running away (v. 9) and ends with Ephraim set aside: Shiloh was in Ephraim’s territory, Zion in Judah’s. God moved house, and the move was a judgment on one tribe and a mercy to the whole nation.

He chose David his servant. Seventy-two verses of rebellion end with a young man being fetched out of a field (1 Samuel 16:11–13). The detail is deliberate: “from following the nursing ewes”, the slowest and most demanding animals in the flock, which a shepherd walks behind at their pace (see shepherds and sheepfolds). That is the training God chose for a king.

With upright heart he shepherded them. Upright heart and skillful hand: integrity and skill together. Neither is enough alone, and both were needed to lead the people this psalm has just described.

The shepherd still to come. The psalm stops here, but David is not the end of the story. The shepherd taken from the sheepfolds is a picture waiting for the one who would call himself the good shepherd and lay down his life for the sheep (John 10:11). David’s heart was not always upright; his Son’s always was. The children taught this psalm were being prepared for him.

78.title: Tell to the Coming Generation
78.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 78 follows straight on from Psalm 77, which ended with God leading his flock through the sea by the hand of Moses and Aaron. Asaph now tells the rest of that story at length, from Egypt to the choice of David: at seventy-two verses it is the second longest psalm in the Psalter, and the longest of the history psalms.

The message. Tell your children what God has done, so that they will hope in him and not be like their fathers. Israel’s history is a long record of forgetting: wonder after wonder answered with unbelief, testing and shallow repentance. Yet through it all God kept his people, atoning for their iniquity again and again, and in the end he gave them a shepherd-king after his own heart. The lesson is both warning and hope: forgetting God breeds unbelief, and God’s mercy is greater than his people’s failure.

Why it was said. The psalm was written for teaching (a Maskil), sung in Jerusalem after Shiloh had fallen and Zion had been chosen. It explains why God’s house and king now stood in Judah rather than in the northern tribe of Ephraim, and it calls every generation to break the chain of unfaithfulness (see the introduction on Asaph’s psalms).

How the chapter makes its case. The opening sets the purpose: what the fathers told us we will tell our children, so that they set their hope in God (vv. 1–8). Then the wilderness: Ephraim forgets, God splits rocks and sends water, Israel demands food, God gives manna and quails, and the craving granted becomes a judgment; they repent with their lips only, “yet he, being compassionate, atoned for their iniquity” (vv. 9–39). The story steps back to Egypt, since they had forgotten even that: the plagues, the firstborn, and the shepherd leading his flock to the holy land (vv. 40–55). In the land they test him again with idols, and God abandons Shiloh to the Philistines; then the Lord awakes, routs his enemies, chooses Judah, Zion and David, the shepherd taken from the sheepfolds (vv. 56–72).

Where it leads. By promise, pattern and the need it exposes. Matthew hears verse 2 fulfilled in Jesus’ parables (Matthew 13:35). Paul says the rock that followed Israel “was Christ” (1 Corinthians 10:4), and Jesus calls himself the true bread from heaven, of which the manna was only a sign (John 6:31–35). The psalm shows a people who could not keep the covenant, and a God who covered their sin himself (v. 38); that covering was finally made at the cross, where Christ became “the propitiation for our sins” (1 John 2:2). And the shepherd-king taken from the sheepfolds points to David’s greater Son, the good shepherd who lays down his life for the sheep (John 10:11).

For us. Every Christian is a link in the chain of verses 4–6: tell the next generation what God has done, honestly, failures included. Watch for the forgetting that breeds unbelief, and be wary of demanding what you crave from God. Above all, set your hope not in doing better than your fathers but in the God who atones for iniquity and has given us his Shepherd.
78.theology: The psalm teaches history as both warning and hope. The warning is that forgetting God's works breeds unbelief (vv. 11, 19, 42), that a granted craving can be a judgment (vv. 29-31), and that even a sanctuary can be withdrawn (v. 60). The hope is verse 38: God himself atoned for their iniquity and restrained his anger often, remembering that they were flesh. The story ends with a shepherd-king (vv. 70-72), a picture waiting for the Good Shepherd.
78.examples: Parents, Sunday school teachers and grandparents are given their task here: tell the next generation what God has done, including the honest story of how his people failed, so that the children set their hope on God rather than on doing better than their fathers. The psalm also searches the one telling it. Most of us have thanked God for one answered prayer and then doubted he could meet the next need, and verse 38 is for us too.

keyVerse.quote: Yet he, being compassionate, atoned for their iniquity and did not destroy them; he restrained his anger often and did not stir up all his wrath.
keyVerse.note: The whole long story of forgetting and rebellion turns on this “yet”. Israel’s repentance had just been exposed as flattery, and God covered their sin himself. It is the hope the children are taught to set in God (v. 7), and it was fulfilled when Christ became the propitiation for our sins.

78.reflection:
The psalm’s purpose is that children “should set their hope in God and not forget the works of God” (v. 7). Who handed the faith on to you? Who is the next link in the chain that you could tell about what God has done?

Israel asked, “Can God spread a table in the wilderness?” while the water from the rock was still running (vv. 19–20). Why is it so easy to thank God for one mercy and doubt him about the next? Where are you doing that now?

“He gave them what they craved” (v. 29), and it became a judgment. Have you ever been glad, looking back, that God did not give you what you demanded? How does Jesus’ prayer in Gethsemane help us to pray about our wants?

Verse 38 says God “atoned for their iniquity” when their repentance was only words (vv. 36–37). How does the cross show us both how serious our sin is and how great God’s compassion is?

79.text: A Psalm of Asaph. 1O God, the nations have come into your inheritance; they have defiled your holy temple; they have laid Jerusalem in ruins.2They have given the bodies of your servants to the birds of the heavens for food, the flesh of your faithful to the beasts of the earth.3They have poured out their blood like water all around Jerusalem, and there was no one to bury them.4We have become a taunt to our neighbors, mocked and derided by those around us.5How long, O LORD? Will you be angry forever? Will your jealousy burn like fire?6Pour out your anger on the nations that do not know you, and on the kingdoms that do not call upon your name!7For they have devoured Jacob and laid waste his habitation.8Do not remember against us our former iniquities; let your compassion come speedily to meet us, for we are brought very low.9Help us, O God of our salvation, for the glory of your name; deliver us, and atone for our sins, for your name's sake!10Why should the nations say, "Where is their God?" Let the avenging of the outpoured blood of your servants be known among the nations before our eyes!11Let the groans of the prisoners come before you; according to your great power, preserve those doomed to die!12Return sevenfold into the lap of our neighbors the taunts with which they have taunted you, O Lord!13But we your people, the sheep of your pasture, will give thanks to you forever; from generation to generation we will recount your praise.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — They Have Laid Jerusalem in Ruins
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The disaster is told first as an outrage against God, then as a question about his anger. The nations have entered God’s inheritance, defiled his temple and ruined Jerusalem (v. 1). His servants lie dead and unburied, their blood poured out like water (vv. 2–3). The neighbours mock (v. 4). So the people ask “How long, O LORD?” (v. 5): they know whose hand is behind this, and that his jealous love burns like fire. They ask him to turn his anger on the nations that do not know him and have devoured Jacob (vv. 6–7), for an instrument of judgment is not excused by being used.
verseByVerse.theology: The same catastrophe as Psalm 74, seen from the street: unburied dead, and neighbours enjoying it.

verseByVerse.quote: O God, the nations have come into your inheritance; they have defiled your holy temple; they have laid Jerusalem in ruins. They have given the bodies of your servants to the birds of the heavens for food, the flesh of your faithful to the beasts of the earth. They have poured out their blood like water all around Jerusalem, and there was no one to bury them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The psalm reports the destruction of Jerusalem as trespass against God’s own property, and counts the unburied dead as God’s own loss.

The nations have come into your inheritance. Two things in the first sentence are called God’s own: “your inheritance” and “your holy temple”. The land was God’s own property, the building the place he had put his name, so the opening line is not “look what they did to us” but a report of trespass filed with the owner. That is how a believer laments: the first move is not to catalogue the damage to oneself but to say what has been done to God.

There was no one to bury them. This is Psalm 74’s disaster seen from outside the building, probably the Babylonian destruction of 586 BC (2 Kings 25:8–10). Jeremiah had warned that it would come to this: “the dead bodies of this people will be food for the birds of the air, and for the beasts of the earth” (Jeremiah 7:33). In a culture where burial was the last duty owed to anyone (see burial customs), “there was no one to bury them” is a sentence about total collapse.

The flesh of your faithful. Whose bodies? “Your servants … your faithful.” The psalm does not claim the dead were innocent (v. 8), but people who belonged to God died badly and were left unburied, and it counts that as God’s own loss. “Blood like water” is something spilled and not collected, and verse 10 will ask about it again: God does not forget it. That is comfort for anyone whose loved one died badly, unseen or uncared for: “Precious in the sight of the LORD is the death of his saints” (Psalm 116:15).

verseByVerse.quote: We have become a taunt to our neighbors, mocked and derided by those around us. How long, O LORD? Will you be angry forever? Will your jealousy burn like fire? Pour out your anger on the nations that do not know you, and on the kingdoms that do not call upon your name! For they have devoured Jacob and laid waste his habitation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Mocked by their neighbours, the people ask God how long his anger will last, and plead that it fall instead on the nations who devoured them.

We have become a taunt to our neighbors. On top of the deaths, the jeering. The neighbouring peoples, Edom, Moab and Ammon, are enjoying it (compare Psalm 137:7). The shame is a separate wound from the loss, and it is felt for longer.

How long, O LORD? The question is aimed at God: they know whose hand is behind this. They are not asking why such things happen, but how long God will remain angry.

Will your jealousy burn like fire? Jealousy is the covenant word, taken from marriage. It is not petty; it is what love does when it has been betrayed and still refuses to let go. A God who watched his people go after other gods with mild interest would not be worth praying to. But the fire is hard to live in, and the honest prayer is “how long”, which quietly assumes that it will not be for ever.

They have devoured Jacob. Verses 6–7 ask that the anger be redirected, and Jeremiah prayed them almost word for word (Jeremiah 10:25), a prayer the faithful shared in those years. The charge is specific: the nations did not merely defeat Israel, they devoured her. God may use a nation as a rod and still judge the rod for the way it swung. Isaiah says exactly that of Assyria: when the Lord has finished his work on Zion, “he will punish the speech of the arrogant heart of the king of Assyria” (Isaiah 10:12). Being an instrument of judgment is not a defence.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–13 — For the Glory of Your Name
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The people plead nothing of their own, only God’s compassion and his name. They ask that their iniquities not be remembered against them, for they are brought very low (v. 8), and that God, for the glory of his name, would deliver them and atone for their sins himself (v. 9). Then they set out their case: the nations ask “Where is their God?”, the blood of his servants cries out (v. 10), prisoners groan under sentence of death (v. 11), and the taunts are aimed at God himself (v. 12). The psalm ends quietly: the sheep of his pasture will praise him for ever (v. 13).
verseByVerse.theology: They do not claim innocence. They ask for atonement, and the only reason they give is God's own name.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not remember against us our former iniquities; let your compassion come speedily to meet us, for we are brought very low. Help us, O God of our salvation, for the glory of your name; deliver us, and atone for our sins, for your name's sake!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Claiming no innocence, the people ask God to forgive and to atone for their sins himself, resting their whole case on his name.

Do not remember against us our former iniquities. Unlike Psalm 44, where a nation protested that it had done nothing to deserve the catastrophe, there is no protest here. They ask only that the iniquities not be remembered against them. “We are brought very low” is the whole of their case. When a man has stopped arguing his record and started describing his condition, he has begun to pray properly.

For your name’s sake! Twice in one verse the same ground: “for the glory of your name … for your name’s sake”. Not their usefulness, not their record, not even the sincerity of their repentance: God’s own reputation is the entire argument, as it is in Daniel’s prayer for the same ruined city (Daniel 9:17–19). That is no trick for getting round a reluctant God; it is the deepest reason anything is ever done, and the only ground that never depends on the state of the person pleading.

Atone for our sins. In the middle comes the request that carries the most weight. The altar is rubble and the sacrifices God appointed have stopped, so they ask God himself to provide the atonement. The answer, when it came, was that God put forward his Son “as a propitiation by his blood”, a sacrifice that turns away wrath, and did it to show his own righteousness (Romans 3:25–26). For his name’s sake, exactly as they asked. Christians pray “for Jesus’ sake” on the same ground.

Uncertain wording. “Our former iniquities” can also be translated “the iniquities of former generations”, as the ESV notes. On that reading they are carrying an account their fathers ran up (compare Lamentations 5:7). Both readings are honest, and neither claims to deserve anything.

verseByVerse.quote: Why should the nations say, "Where is their God?" Let the avenging of the outpoured blood of your servants be known among the nations before our eyes! Let the groans of the prisoners come before you; according to your great power, preserve those doomed to die! Return sevenfold into the lap of our neighbors the taunts with which they have taunted you, O Lord! But we your people, the sheep of your pasture, will give thanks to you forever; from generation to generation we will recount your praise.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They ask God to vindicate his name, hear the prisoners and repay the insults against him, and they promise that his flock will praise him for generations.

Where is their God? It is the taunt from Psalm 42:3, where one man heard it all day long; now whole nations say it, and the psalm uses it as an argument (compare Joel 2:17). God’s reputation is genuinely bound up with what happens to his people, and the believer is allowed to say so in prayer.

The outpoured blood of your servants. The blood of verse 3 comes back, and they ask that its avenging be public and in their lifetime. John heard the same prayer at the far end of the Bible, from martyrs under the altar: “O Sovereign Lord, holy and true, how long before you will judge and avenge our blood on those who dwell on the earth?” (Revelation 6:10). They were told to rest a little longer: the wait is longer than anyone wants, but the answer will come.

Let the groans of the prisoners come before you. A groan is what is left when speech has gone, and the psalm asks for it to be admitted as evidence. “Those doomed to die” are, in the Hebrew idiom, the sons of death: men already assigned to execution. The prayer for them is not comfort but preservation, and the measure asked is “your great power”. Nothing smaller will reach into that cell.

Return sevenfold into the lap of our neighbors. Two things keep this from being simple spite. The repayment is asked of God, not taken by the person praying; and the insult is not described as theirs. The taunts were shouted at the survivors, and the psalm says they taunted you. What is said about a believer’s God, in his hearing, while he is down, is registered in heaven as an insult to God himself.

The sheep of your pasture will give thanks. The ending is quiet and stubborn. Nothing has been restored, and the last word is thanks and a promise that the children will be told. They call themselves “the sheep of your pasture”, as in Psalm 74:1: not a strong name, and not one they gave themselves. A flock has nothing but its shepherd, which is precisely their position. To “recount your praise” from generation to generation is the task Psalm 78 gave to every generation; a congregation in the wreckage, with no altar and no city, decides that the telling will go on anyway. It is the only thing they have left to give, and they give it.

How can a Christian pray this? It asks God to vindicate his own name and to judge unrepentant evil, as the martyrs pray in Revelation 6:10. We pray it leaving vengeance to God (Romans 12:19), while loving and praying for our enemies (Matthew 5:44), knowing that the judgment we deserved fell on Christ.

79.title: Where Is Their God?
79.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 78 ended with God choosing Zion and building his sanctuary there; Psalm 79 stands in its ruins. Like Psalm 74, it is a lament for the destruction of Jerusalem and the temple, most likely by the Babylonians in 586 BC, sung by the temple singers who carried Asaph’s name.

The message. When everything is lost, God’s people may still pray, and the ground of their prayer is God’s own name. They do not claim innocence; they ask God to forgive, to atone for their sins himself, and to act so that the nations stop asking “Where is their God?” Even with nothing restored, the flock promises to go on praising its shepherd for generations.

Why it was said. The city lay in ruins, the dead unburied, prisoners waiting for execution, and the neighbouring peoples jeering (see the introduction on Book Three). With the altar destroyed, the sacrifices that covered sin could no longer be offered.

How the chapter makes its case. First the facts, reported as trespass on God’s property: the nations have entered his inheritance, defiled his temple and left his servants’ bodies to the birds (vv. 1–3). Then the shame and the question, “How long, O LORD?”, with a plea that his anger fall instead on the nations that devoured Jacob (vv. 4–7). At the centre, a confession and a plea: do not remember our iniquities, atone for our sins, “for your name’s sake” (vv. 8–9). Then the arguments: the nations’ taunt, the outpoured blood, the groans of the prisoners, the insults against God himself (vv. 10–12). It ends quietly with the sheep of his pasture promising thanks for ever (v. 13).

Where it leads. By promise and by the need it exposes. With the altar in rubble, the psalm asks God himself to “atone for our sins, for your name’s sake” (v. 9). The answer came when God “put forward” his Son “as a propitiation by his blood” to show his own righteousness (Romans 3:25–26): atonement provided by God, for his name. Jesus wept over Jerusalem and foretold that it would again “be trampled underfoot by the Gentiles” (Luke 21:24), and he himself was the temple destroyed and raised (John 2:19–21). The cry for God to avenge his servants’ blood is taken up by the martyrs in Revelation 6:10 and answered at his return.

For us. In your worst losses, you may bring God not your record but your need and his name. Ask him to forgive you for Christ’s sake, leave vengeance to him, and keep telling the next generation of his praise, even in the rubble.
79.theology: This lament reports the catastrophe as trespass against God's own property (v. 1), makes no claim of innocence (v. 8), and rests its whole appeal on God's name (v. 9). Its central request, that God himself atone for sin when the altar lies in ruins, was answered at the cross for his name's sake. Vengeance is asked of God, not taken (v. 12), and even with nothing restored the people promise to go on praising him from generation to generation (v. 13).
79.examples: Christians who see churches attacked, believers killed and their faith mocked, or who have lost someone in a death that seemed uncared for, may pray this psalm as it stands: report it to the owner, ask how long, and leave the avenging to God. It also shows how to pray after our own failures: not by arguing a record, but by saying we are brought very low and asking for help for the sake of his name. And it ends with a pledge any of us can keep in the hardest year: to tell our children of God's praise.

keyVerse.quote: Help us, O God of our salvation, for the glory of your name; deliver us, and atone for our sins, for your name’s sake!
keyVerse.note: This is the heart of the psalm. With the temple destroyed and no sacrifice possible, the people plead nothing of their own, only God’s name, and ask God himself to atone for their sins. That prayer was answered at the cross, where God provided the sacrifice to show his own righteousness.

79.reflection:
The psalm opens by describing the disaster as an attack on what belongs to God: “your inheritance … your holy temple” (v. 1). How might it change the way you pray about your troubles to begin with God’s honour rather than your own loss?

The people make no claim to innocence (v. 8); their whole appeal is to God’s compassion and his name (v. 9). Why is God’s name a stronger ground for prayer than our record? What does it mean to pray “for Jesus’ sake”?

Verses 10–12 ask God to avenge his servants and repay their enemies. How can Christians pray for justice against evil while also obeying Jesus’ command to love our enemies?

With nothing restored, they promise to “recount your praise” from generation to generation (v. 13). What would it look like for your church or family to keep praising God and telling his story in a season of loss?

80.text: To the choirmaster: according to Lilies. A Testimony. Of Asaph, a Psalm. 1Give ear, O Shepherd of Israel, you who lead Joseph like a flock. You who are enthroned upon the cherubim, shine forth.2Before Ephraim and Benjamin and Manasseh, stir up your might and come to save us!3Restore us, O God; let your face shine, that we may be saved!4O LORD God of hosts, how long will you be angry with your people's prayers?5You have fed them with the bread of tears and given them tears to drink in full measure.6You make us an object of contention for our neighbors, and our enemies laugh among themselves.7Restore us, O God of hosts; let your face shine, that we may be saved!8You brought a vine out of Egypt; you drove out the nations and planted it.9You cleared the ground for it; it took deep root and filled the land.10The mountains were covered with its shade, the mighty cedars with its branches.11It sent out its branches to the sea and its shoots to the River.12Why then have you broken down its walls, so that all who pass along the way pluck its fruit?13The boar from the forest ravages it, and all that move in the field feed on it.14Turn again, O God of hosts! Look down from heaven, and see; have regard for this vine,15the stock that your right hand planted, and for the son whom you made strong for yourself.16They have burned it with fire; they have cut it down; may they perish at the rebuke of your face!17But let your hand be on the man of your right hand, the son of man whom you have made strong for yourself!18Then we shall not turn back from you; give us life, and we will call upon your name!19Restore us, O LORD God of hosts! Let your face shine, that we may be saved!

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — Shepherd of Israel, Shine Forth
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The people’s only hope is that the Shepherd of Israel will turn them back and turn his shining face towards them. They call on him as the one who leads Joseph like a flock and sits enthroned above the cherubim, asking him to go before the northern tribes as he once did in the wilderness (vv. 1–2). The refrain asks the priestly blessing back: “let your face shine” (v. 3). Then the complaint: God seems angry even with their prayers, feeds them tears, and leaves them a laughing-stock (vv. 4–6). The refrain returns with a fuller name, “O God of hosts” (v. 7).
verseByVerse.theology: A shepherd who seems to have stopped listening is asked, twice, simply to turn his face towards his flock.

verseByVerse.quote: Give ear, O Shepherd of Israel, you who lead Joseph like a flock. You who are enthroned upon the cherubim, shine forth. Before Ephraim and Benjamin and Manasseh, stir up your might and come to save us! Restore us, O God; let your face shine, that we may be saved!
verseByVerse.commentary:
The northern tribes ask the Shepherd enthroned above the ark to lead them again as in the wilderness, and to turn his shining face towards them.

Give ear, O Shepherd of Israel. The names show where the psalm comes from: Joseph, Ephraim and Manasseh are northern tribes, with Benjamin on the border. It is a prayer for the north, probably in the long collapse that ended when “the king of Assyria captured Samaria” (2 Kings 17:6), though the psalm never says so. “You who lead Joseph like a flock” takes up the endings of Psalms 77 and 78.

Before Ephraim and Benjamin and Manasseh. In the wilderness these three tribes camped together west of the tabernacle (Numbers 2:18–24) and marched directly behind the Kohathites carrying the holy things (Numbers 10:21–24). So the ark’s God, “enthroned upon the cherubim”, is asked to go before them as he once did. The prayer reaches for the oldest memory the people have of God leading them.

Let your face shine. This is the refrain, three times in the psalm, and it is the priestly blessing Aaron and his sons spoke over Israel: “the LORD make his face to shine upon you and be gracious to you” (Numbers 6:25).

Restore us, O God. The ESV notes that “restore us” may be rendered “turn us again”, and the order matters. They do not ask first for the Assyrians to go home, but for God to turn them and to turn his face. Everything else follows from the face.

Uncertain wording. The heading’s “according to Lilies” (as in Psalms 45 and 69) probably names a tune, and “A Testimony” may refer to God’s covenant; the meaning of both is not known.

verseByVerse.quote: O LORD God of hosts, how long will you be angry with your people's prayers? You have fed them with the bread of tears and given them tears to drink in full measure. You make us an object of contention for our neighbors, and our enemies laugh among themselves. Restore us, O God of hosts; let your face shine, that we may be saved!
verseByVerse.commentary:
God seems angry even with his people’s prayers and has fed them on tears, yet they keep calling on him by an ever larger name.

How long will you be angry with your people’s prayers? A startling complaint: God is angry even with their prayers; the Hebrew verb pictures his anger as smoke, fuming against them while they pray. Anyone who has prayed long unheard knows the feeling, and the psalm lets it be said.

The bread of tears. Grief has become their daily food and drink, served “in full measure” as by a host, and the host is God: you have fed them. Meanwhile the neighbours quarrel over what is left of Israel and laugh among themselves.

Restore us, O God of hosts. The refrain has grown: first “O God”, now “O God of hosts”, at the end “O LORD God of hosts”. The circumstances do not improve, but the name they call on grows. That is how lament climbs: not by the situation changing, but by the God addressed coming more fully into view.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–13 — You Brought a Vine out of Egypt
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel is God’s vine, planted by his hand alone, and now he has let it be ravaged. He brought it out of Egypt, drove out the nations and cleared the ground (vv. 8–9). It took root and filled the land, covering the hills and the cedars, and reaching from the sea to the Euphrates (vv. 10–11). So why has he broken down its walls, leaving it to every passer-by and to the wild boar (vv. 12–13)? The psalm asks why without claiming innocence; Isaiah had already given God’s answer. It brings the ruin to the gardener and asks him to look.
verseByVerse.theology: The vine was God's own planting, and the question is why the gardener has pulled down his own wall.

verseByVerse.quote: You brought a vine out of Egypt; you drove out the nations and planted it. You cleared the ground for it; it took deep root and filled the land. The mountains were covered with its shade, the mighty cedars with its branches. It sent out its branches to the sea and its shoots to the River.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel’s whole history is told as a vine God brought out of Egypt and planted by his own hand until it filled the land.

You brought a vine out of Egypt. The exodus was a transplanting. Every verb is God’s: brought, drove out, planted, cleared. The vine did nothing except take root (see vine and vineyard).

The vine in the prophets. Isaiah sang of a vineyard God “dug it and cleared it of stones, and planted it with choice vines” (Isaiah 5:2), and Jeremiah heard God say, “I planted you a choice vine, wholly of pure seed” (Jeremiah 2:21). In both, the vine went wrong. This psalm does not yet say so; it is remembering the planting.

It sent out its branches to the sea. The vine shaded the hill country and climbed the cedars, and its reach ran from the Mediterranean to “the River”, the Euphrates. That was the boundary God had promised Abraham (Genesis 15:18), and under David and Solomon it was reached (1 Kings 4:21). It was a vine that had outgrown its garden.
verseByVerse.note: Compare the vineyard song of Isa 5:1-7.

verseByVerse.quote: Why then have you broken down its walls, so that all who pass along the way pluck its fruit? The boar from the forest ravages it, and all that move in the field feed on it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God has broken down the vineyard’s walls and left his vine to be plundered, and the psalm asks him why.

Why then have you broken down its walls? If you did all that, why this? The stone wall or hedge that kept out passers-by and animals is gone. Every traveller helps himself, and the wild boar, the most destructive animal in the country, is rooting through the vines.

Isaiah’s answer. The psalm asks why; Isaiah had already given the answer from God’s side: “I will break down its wall, and it shall be trampled down” (Isaiah 5:5), because “he looked for justice, but behold, bloodshed” (Isaiah 5:7). The broken wall was not an accident of history but God’s judgment.

Bringing the ruin to the gardener. This psalm neither mentions that reason nor claims innocence; it brings the ruin to the gardener and asks him to look. A believer may know why the wall came down, and still the right prayer is an appeal: this was yours; see what has become of it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–19 — The Man of Your Right Hand
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The hope for the burned vine rests on one man at God’s right hand, through whom God will give his people life. They ask God to turn again and look on the vine his right hand planted, the son he made strong for himself (vv. 14–15). It has been burned and cut down (v. 16). Then the plea: let God’s hand be on the man of his right hand, described in the same words as the vine (v. 17). Then his people will not turn back; given life, they will call on his name (v. 18). The last refrain names God in full: “O LORD God of hosts” (v. 19).
verseByVerse.theology: The ruined vine and the man at God's right hand are described in the same words: the hope for the one rests on the other.

verseByVerse.quote: Turn again, O God of hosts! Look down from heaven, and see; have regard for this vine, the stock that your right hand planted, and for the son whom you made strong for yourself. They have burned it with fire; they have cut it down; may they perish at the rebuke of your face!
verseByVerse.commentary:
They ask God to turn and look on the vine he planted, the son he made strong, now burned and cut down.

Turn again, O God of hosts! The refrain asked God to turn us; here they ask God himself to turn again. Both are needed: a people will not turn back unless God turns them, and it does them no good unless his face is turned towards them.

The son whom you made strong for yourself. The vine, “the stock that your right hand planted”, suddenly becomes a person: “the son whom you made strong for yourself”. The vine is Israel, God’s son (Exodus 4:22 calls Israel God’s firstborn son), and the picture merges with the people it stands for. A later Jewish Aramaic paraphrase of the Psalms (the Targum) renders this son as “King Messiah”.

They have burned it with fire. The vine has not merely been raided but cut down and burned. The face they asked to shine on them is the same face they ask to rebuke the destroyers. The whole psalm turns on which way the face is turned.

Uncertain wording. “Stock” (v. 15) renders a word found only here (root, stock or shoot). “Son” can also mean a branch of a plant (compare Genesis 49:22), which is why vine and son blend so easily.

verseByVerse.quote: But let your hand be on the man of your right hand, the son of man whom you have made strong for yourself! Then we shall not turn back from you; give us life, and we will call upon your name! Restore us, O LORD God of hosts! Let your face shine, that we may be saved!
verseByVerse.commentary:
The hope for the ruined vine rests on one man at God’s right hand, through whom God will give his people life so that they never turn back.

The man of your right hand. Verse 15 spoke of “the son whom you made strong for yourself”; verse 17 speaks of “the son of man whom you have made strong for yourself”, “the man of your right hand”. Vine and man are described in the same words, and the hope for the ruined vine is placed on one figure at God’s right hand.

Who the man is. In its first setting this meant the king, in whom the nation stood or fell. But the psalm asks for more than any king of Israel delivered, and later Scripture shows who the man is. God said to David’s Lord, “Sit at my right hand” (Psalm 110:1), and Jesus, the Son of Man, said he would be seen “seated at the right hand of Power” (Mark 14:62). He told a parable of a vineyard whose owner “had still one other, a beloved son”, and sent him (Mark 12:6). And on the night before he died he said, “I am the true vine, and my Father is the vinedresser” (John 15:1).

A vine that cannot fail. That is the answer to this psalm: the burned vine is replaced by one that cannot fail, because the vine is now the Son himself and his people are branches in him. He too was cut down, at the cross, and he rose again.

Then we shall not turn back from you. The whole history of the vine was turning back; the man at God’s right hand produces a people who will not. What they could not do in their own strength they will do when God’s hand is on his man, and the Christian knows how: for the Son exalted to God’s right hand has poured out the promised Holy Spirit (Acts 2:33). The request “give us life” is exactly right: a cut-down, burned vine does not need improvement. It needs to live.

Restore us, O LORD God of hosts! The third refrain gives the name in full: the covenant name and the title of the commander of heaven’s armies together. Nothing in the vineyard has been repaired since verse 3, but the one they speak to has grown in their sight, and the man of his right hand has come into view. The shining face of God, which Aaron could only pronounce over the people, is now seen “in the face of Jesus Christ” (2 Corinthians 4:6), and in that face the prayer is answered for every branch in the true vine.

Where Christians differ. Some read “the man of your right hand” as a direct prophecy of the Messiah; others take it first of Israel’s king, or of Israel as God’s son, fulfilled in Christ.

This commentary’s view. The psalmist prayed for the king who stood for the nation, but his words reach beyond any king Israel had and are fulfilled in Jesus, the true Israel and David’s Son.

80.title: Let Your Face Shine
80.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 79 ended with God’s people calling themselves “the sheep of your pasture”; Psalm 80 begins by calling on the “Shepherd of Israel”. This time the ruin is in the north: the tribes named are Joseph, Ephraim, Benjamin and Manasseh, and the vine God planted has been cut down and burned.

The message. When God’s people are ruined, their one hope is that God will turn them back and turn his face towards them. Nothing in their circumstances improves through the psalm, but the God they call on grows larger in their sight, and their hope narrows to one man at God’s right hand, through whom God will give his people life so that they never turn back again.

Why it was said. It is probably a prayer from the long collapse of the northern kingdom under Assyria, which ended with the fall of Samaria in 722 BC (see the introduction on Book Three), though the psalm names no enemy. The people had prayed and God seemed angry with their very prayers.

How the chapter makes its case. The refrain “Restore us … let your face shine, that we may be saved!” comes three times (vv. 3, 7, 19), and each time the name of God grows: “O God”, “O God of hosts”, “O LORD God of hosts”. First the appeal to the Shepherd enthroned on the cherubim to lead the tribes as he did in the wilderness (vv. 1–3). Then the complaint: tears for bread, neighbours laughing (vv. 4–7). Then the parable of the vine, brought out of Egypt and planted until it filled the land, now with its walls broken down (vv. 8–13). Finally the plea that God would look on the burned vine and set his hand on “the man of your right hand”, so that his people will live and not turn back (vv. 14–19).

Where it leads. By promise and pattern. The vine and the man are described in the same words (vv. 15, 17), and the hope for the vine rests on one figure at God’s right hand. Israel’s kings could not bear that weight; Jesus can. He is seated at God’s right hand (Psalm 110:1; Mark 14:62), he is the beloved son sent to the vineyard (Mark 12:6), and he is “the true vine” in whom his people live and bear fruit (John 15:1). He was cut down at the cross and rose again, and the shining face of God the psalm longs for is seen “in the face of Jesus Christ” (2 Corinthians 4:6).

For us. When your life or your church looks like a broken vineyard, pray this refrain. Ask God to turn you and to turn his face towards you, and look to the Man at his right hand, in whom you are a branch and cannot finally be cut off.
80.theology: The psalm climbs. Its circumstances never improve, but each refrain names God more fully (vv. 3, 7, 19), and its hope narrows to one figure: the vine (v. 15) and the man at God's right hand (v. 17) are described in the same words. What Israel's kings could not be, the Son is: seated at God's right hand (Ps 110:1), sent as the beloved son to the vineyard, the true vine in whom his people live and do not turn back (v. 18). The shining face of God the psalm longs for is seen at last in the face of Jesus Christ.
80.examples: Believers who pray long and find heaven silent, or who live on the bread of tears, are given the refrain to pray: turn us, and let your face shine. A church that has seen its walls broken down, whether by its own sin or by hostile times, may bring the ruin to the gardener and ask him to look. And all who are branches in Christ can pray verse 18 with confidence: what we could not do in our own strength, his Spirit does in us.

keyVerse.quote: But let your hand be on the man of your right hand, the son of man whom you have made strong for yourself!
keyVerse.note: Here the psalm’s hope for the ruined vine settles on a single person at God’s right hand, described in the same words as the vine itself (v. 15). In its first setting he was Israel’s king, but no king of Israel could bear this weight. It is fulfilled in Jesus, the Son of Man seated at God’s right hand and the true vine.

80.reflection:
The refrain asks God to “restore us” and to “let your face shine” (vv. 3, 7, 19). What is the difference between asking God to change your circumstances and asking him to turn you and turn his face towards you? Which do you usually pray for first?

The people feel that God is “angry with your people’s prayers” (v. 4). Have you known a season when your prayers seemed to be met with silence? How does this psalm help you keep praying?

Every verb in verses 8–11 is God’s: he brought, drove out, planted, cleared. What has God planted and built in your life or your church that you could thank him for, even in a hard season?

Jesus calls himself “the true vine” (John 15:1). How does knowing that you are a branch in him, rather than a vine on your own, change the way you face weakness and failure?

81.text: To the choirmaster: according to The Gittith. Of Asaph. 1Sing aloud to God our strength; shout for joy to the God of Jacob!2Raise a song; sound the tambourine, the sweet lyre with the harp.3Blow the trumpet at the new moon, at the full moon, on our feast day.4For it is a statute for Israel, a rule of the God of Jacob.5He made it a decree in Joseph when he went out over the land of Egypt. I hear a language I had not known:6"I relieved your shoulder of the burden; your hands were freed from the basket.7In distress you called, and I delivered you; I answered you in the secret place of thunder; I tested you at the waters of Meribah. Selah8Hear, O my people, while I admonish you! O Israel, if you would but listen to me!9There shall be no strange god among you; you shall not bow down to a foreign god.10I am the LORD your God, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt. Open your mouth wide, and I will fill it.11"But my people did not listen to my voice; Israel would not submit to me.12So I gave them over to their stubborn hearts, to follow their own counsels.13Oh, that my people would listen to me, that Israel would walk in my ways!14I would soon subdue their enemies and turn my hand against their foes.15Those who hate the LORD would cringe toward him, and their fate would last forever.16But he would feed you with the finest of the wheat, and with honey from the rock I would satisfy you."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — I Hear a Language I Had Not Known
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In the middle of Israel’s loudest feast God himself begins to speak, and he begins with rescue. The psalm calls for shouting, tambourine, lyre and harp, and the ram’s horn at new moon and full moon, because the festival is God’s own decree, given when he went out over Egypt (vv. 1–5). Then the music gives way to a voice the singer had not known (v. 5). God reminds his people that he lifted the brick basket from their shoulders, answered their cry from the thunder-cloud of Sinai, and tested them at Meribah, where they quarrelled with him (vv. 6–7). Rescue and rebellion stand side by side, and the rest of the psalm shows why.
verseByVerse.theology: In the middle of the festival the music stops and a voice speaks that the singer did not expect to hear.

verseByVerse.quote: Sing aloud to God our strength; shout for joy to the God of Jacob! Raise a song; sound the tambourine, the sweet lyre with the harp. Blow the trumpet at the new moon, at the full moon, on our feast day. For it is a statute for Israel, a rule of the God of Jacob. He made it a decree in Joseph when he went out over the land of Egypt. I hear a language I had not known:
verseByVerse.commentary:
God commanded this festival joy to bring his people back to the rescue behind it, and at the height of the music he speaks.

Blow the trumpet at the new moon. The psalm opens loud, with the ram’s horn sounding over the band at the new moon and again at the full moon. The law told Israel to blow the trumpets “at your appointed feasts and at the beginnings of your months” (Numbers 10:10), and the likeliest occasion for this psalm is the autumn, when the new moon of the seventh month opened the season and the full moon brought the Feast of Booths.

It is a statute for Israel. The joy is commanded. That sounds odd until you see why: the festival was a decree from the exodus, given to make Israel remember what God did when he “went out over the land of Egypt” (the ESV notes “against” as a possible rendering). “Joseph” here stands for the whole people, as in Psalm 80:1. Worship ordered by God is not the enemy of joy; it keeps a forgetful people coming back to the reason for it.

I hear a language I had not known. Then the music stops. Someone in the choir, perhaps a Levite or a prophet, hears a voice he was not expecting, and from here on God is the speaker. That is what the festival was for, and what God says is less comfortable than their songs.

Must Christians keep the new moon and feasts? No. These were shadows fulfilled in Christ (Colossians 2:16–17), and no festival day binds the Christian. What carries over is the loud, glad praise of verses 1–2.

Uncertain wording. “The Gittith” in the heading (also Psalms 8 and 84) is not understood: perhaps a tune, an instrument from Gath, or a harvest song (the word resembles the Hebrew for winepress). “I hear a language I had not known” is also compressed: most take it as God’s voice breaking into the festival, some as Israel hearing a foreign tongue in Egypt.
verseByVerse.note: The new moon began each month; the full moon marked the great feasts of Passover and Booths.

verseByVerse.quote: "I relieved your shoulder of the burden; your hands were freed from the basket. In distress you called, and I delivered you; I answered you in the secret place of thunder; I tested you at the waters of Meribah. Selah
verseByVerse.commentary:
God opens not with rebuke but with rescue: he lifted the slave’s load, answered his people’s cry, and tested them at Meribah.

I relieved your shoulder of the burden. God’s first words recall something they had felt in their bodies. In Egypt the Israelites carried bricks and clay in baskets on their shoulders, and God had promised, “I will bring you out from under the burdens of the Egyptians” (Exodus 6:6). Here he remembers doing it: the weight lifted off the shoulder, the hands let go of the basket. (The ESV notes that the Hebrew says “his” shoulder: Israel spoken of as one man.)

Kindness before rebuke. Whatever God is about to say against his people, he begins not with their sin but with the moment he took the load off them.

In distress you called, and I delivered you. Three memories in order. They cried out in Egypt, and he delivered. He answered them at Sinai from “the secret place of thunder”, the cloud on the mountain, where “the people saw the thunder and the flashes of lightning” and begged Moses, “do not let God speak to us, lest we die” (Exodus 20:18–19). And he tested them at Meribah.

I tested you at the waters of Meribah. At Meribah, whose name means quarrelling, the people asked, “Is the LORD among us or not?” (Exodus 17:7), and God gave them water from a rock. The rescue and the rebellion sit in the same sentence, which is exactly where the rest of the psalm is going.
