verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–16 — Oh, That My People Would Listen
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God pleads with his people to listen, because everything he longs to give them waits on it. He echoes “Hear, O Israel”, repeats the first commandment with its preface of rescue, and adds a promise as wide as their need: open your mouth wide and I will fill it (vv. 8–10). But they would not listen, and his judgment was to give them over to the stubbornness they chose (vv. 11–12). Even so, the psalm ends on longing rather than judgment. If only they would walk in his ways, he would soon subdue their enemies and feed them with the finest wheat and honey from the rock (vv. 13–16). The invitation is left open for every generation that sings it.
verseByVerse.theology: God offers to fill any mouth opened to him, and the saddest judgment in the psalm is that he let his people have what they preferred.

verseByVerse.quote: Hear, O my people, while I admonish you! O Israel, if you would but listen to me! There shall be no strange god among you; you shall not bow down to a foreign god. I am the LORD your God, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt. Open your mouth wide, and I will fill it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The God who rescued his people asks only that they have no other god, and promises to fill every mouth opened wide to him.

Hear, O my people. “Hear, O Israel” was the first line of the confession every Israelite knew (Deuteronomy 6:4), and here God speaks it himself. The tone is a parent’s more than a lawgiver’s: “if you would but listen to me!” is the voice of someone who has said it many times and is still saying it.

There shall be no strange god among you. This is the first commandment heard again at the festival, with the preface that came before it at Sinai: “I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt” (Exodus 20:2). Rescue first, then the command. God does not say, “Keep my law and I will save you”, but, “I saved you, so have no other god.” In God’s covenant grace always comes before obedience.

Open your mouth wide, and I will fill it. Straight after the command comes the most generous sentence in the psalm. The picture is a nest of young birds with their beaks stretched open: the only thing required is the open mouth, the posture of need that expects to be fed. That is what having no other god looks like from the inside: not a narrowing of life but a refusal to feed anywhere else, because this God has promised to fill whatever you open to him. Most of our spiritual poverty is not that God gives too little, but that we open our mouths too little, or open them towards someone else.

Is “open your mouth wide” a promise of whatever we ask? It is a promise to a people who will have no other god (v. 9), and verse 16 shows what God fills them with: the finest wheat and honey from the rock. It is a call to look to him for everything, not a blank cheque.

verseByVerse.quote: "But my people did not listen to my voice; Israel would not submit to me. So I gave them over to their stubborn hearts, to follow their own counsels.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel would not listen, and God’s judgment was to give them what they insisted on: their own stubborn way.

Israel would not submit to me. After the offer, the history. They “would not” submit: they heard the voice and preferred not to.

So I gave them over to their stubborn hearts. The judgment is terrible because it is so quiet. God does not strike them; he lets them have what they insisted on. The worst thing God can do to someone who will not listen is to stop contending with him and let him walk his own way to the end of it.

The same judgment in the New Testament. Paul describes this judgment falling on the whole human race: “God gave them up in the lusts of their hearts” (Romans 1:24). Stephen said it of Israel in the wilderness: “God turned away and gave them over to worship the host of heaven” (Acts 7:42).

Has it begun to happen to me? If you can now do without distress what once troubled your conscience, the honest question is whether this verse has begun to happen. But a tender conscience that fears it has happened is itself a sign that God is still speaking, and the next verse is his longing to be heard (v. 13).

verseByVerse.quote: Oh, that my people would listen to me, that Israel would walk in my ways! I would soon subdue their enemies and turn my hand against their foes. Those who hate the LORD would cringe toward him, and their fate would last forever. But he would feed you with the finest of the wheat, and with honey from the rock I would satisfy you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even after giving them over, God longs for his people to listen, so that he could defeat their enemies and feed them with the best.

Oh, that my people would listen to me. Having handed them over, God grieves. This is God’s own longing, and it is the same voice that wept over Jerusalem: “How often would I have gathered your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, and you were not willing!” (Matthew 23:37); “Would that you, even you, had known on this day the things that make for peace!” (Luke 19:42).

I would soon subdue their enemies. The enemies they were struggling against would “soon” be subdued. The fighting they were losing was never the real problem. The listening was.

The finest of the wheat. The psalm ends not on the judgment but on the table that was set and refused: the best flour and richest bread, the gift later praised in Psalm 147:14, and “honey from the rock”, the phrase from Moses’ song: “he suckled him with honey out of the rock” (Deuteronomy 32:13). At Meribah (v. 7) the rock gave water to a quarrelling people. God says he would have made it give honey.

The Rock and the bread. Of the rock that gave Israel water in the wilderness Paul says, “the Rock was Christ” (1 Corinthians 10:4), and Jesus said, “I am the bread of life; whoever comes to me shall not hunger” (John 6:35). The finest wheat and the honey are given in him. We have not listened as we should either, but Christ heard and did his Father’s will perfectly in our place, and the Spirit he gives softens stubborn hearts to hear (Ezekiel 36:26–27).

The invitation still stands. In the last verse the Hebrew speaks of feeding “him”, Israel as one person again, and moves between “he” and “I”. The psalm does not say how Israel answered, which is why it could be sung at every festival: the invitation still stood. Psalm 95 ends the same way, and Hebrews preaches it to Christians: “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts” (Hebrews 3:7–8). The mouth can still be opened; the table is still set.

Uncertain wording. In verse 15 “their fate” is literally “their time”, and whose time is meant is unclear: the lasting doom of the LORD’s enemies, as the ESV takes it, or Israel’s lasting blessing. Either way, it is what listening would have brought.

81.title: Open Your Mouth Wide
81.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 81 is one of the psalms of Asaph in Book Three (see the introduction). Psalm 80 begged God three times to hear and restore his people; in Psalm 81 God speaks, at one of Israel’s great festivals, and pleads with his people to hear him.

The message. God has rescued his people and longs to give them everything, and the only thing standing between them and his fullness is that they will not listen. He speaks into their worship not to spoil the feast but to call them back from other gods to himself, with a promise as wide as their need: “Open your mouth wide, and I will fill it” (v. 10).

Why it was said. Israel kept its feasts with trumpets and harps, yet again and again turned to other gods and hardened its heart, as Psalm 78 had just told at length (see the introduction). Sung at a feast, probably in the autumn, the psalm made every new generation hear God’s plea while the trumpets were still sounding.

How the chapter makes its case. First the call to loud festival praise, commanded since the exodus (vv. 1–5). Then a voice the singer did not expect: God recalls taking the brick basket off their shoulders, answering them from the thunder of Sinai, and testing them at Meribah (vv. 5–7). He pleads with them to hear, repeats the first commandment with its preface of rescue, and promises to fill any mouth opened wide to him (vv. 8–10). Then the history: they would not listen, so he gave them over to their own stubborn counsels (vv. 11–12). Yet the psalm ends in longing, not judgment: if only they would listen, he would soon subdue their enemies and feed them with the finest wheat and honey from the rock (vv. 13–16).

Where it leads. By the need it exposes, and by pattern. Israel never became the listening son God longed for; Jesus did, the servant who could say, “he awakens my ear to hear as those who are taught” (Isaiah 50:4). The rock that gave water at Meribah, Paul says, was a picture of him: “the Rock was Christ” (1 Corinthians 10:4). The finest wheat is given in the one who said, “I am the bread of life” (John 6:35). And the longing voice of verse 13 is heard again when Jesus wept over Jerusalem (Luke 19:41–42).

For us. Christians can gather to sing and go home without having listened. Hear his voice “today” (Hebrews 3:7), turn from whatever else you have been feeding on, and open your mouth wide to Christ. The table is still set.
81.theology:
The festival exists so that God can speak into it (v. 5); the music is not the point.

God's address begins with rescue, not rebuke (vv. 6-7), and the commandment comes only after the reminder of rescue (v. 10; Exod 20:2), so in God’s covenant grace comes before obedience. The first commandment is paired with the widest promise: open your mouth wide, and I will fill it.

Judgment can take the form of God handing people over to what they insist on (v. 12; Rom 1:24; Acts 7:42). Yet God grieves over the refusal (v. 13), and the psalm remains an open invitation: Today, if you hear his voice (Heb 3:7).
81.examples:
Picture the whole band playing, and then a voice no one expected breaking in. Picture a labourer's shoulder freed from the brick-basket, and young birds with their beaks wide open waiting to be fed. God puts grace first and the commandment second.

The quietest judgment is getting what you insisted on. And the rock that once gave water to a quarrelling people is the rock God says he would have made flow with honey.

keyVerse.quote: I am the LORD your God, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt. Open your mouth wide, and I will fill it.
keyVerse.note: The whole psalm meets in this verse: rescue first (“who brought you up”), then the call to have God alone, then a promise as wide as our need. Everything Israel lost in verses 11–12 it lost by keeping its mouth shut to this offer, and in Christ, the bread of life, the offer is still open.

81.reflection:
The psalm calls for loud festival praise, and then God speaks into it (vv. 1–5). When your church gathers, do you come expecting mainly to sing, or also to hear God speak? What helps you listen?

God begins with what he has done for his people before he says what he requires (vv. 6–10). Why does that order matter, and how does it change the way you think about obeying him?

“Open your mouth wide, and I will fill it” (v. 10). Where are you tempted to look to something other than God for comfort, security or joy? What would opening your mouth to him look like this week?

God’s judgment in verse 12 is to give people what they insist on, yet in verse 13 he still longs for them. How should both truths shape the way we pray for people who have drifted from God, and for ourselves?

82.text: A Psalm of Asaph. 1God has taken his place in the divine council; in the midst of the gods he holds judgment:2"How long will you judge unjustly and show partiality to the wicked? Selah3Give justice to the weak and the fatherless; maintain the right of the afflicted and the destitute.4Rescue the weak and the needy; deliver them from the hand of the wicked."5They have neither knowledge nor understanding, they walk about in darkness; all the foundations of the earth are shaken.6I said, "You are gods, sons of the Most High, all of you;7nevertheless, like men you shall die, and fall like any prince."8Arise, O God, judge the earth; for you shall inherit all the nations!

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — God Stands Up in the Council
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God holds every judge answerable, and the charge is that they have favoured the wicked and abandoned those who cannot pay. The scene is a courtroom with an unexpected defendant: God takes his place in the council, not to hear a case the judges have brought, but to judge them (v. 1). His question is a weary “How long?”: how long will they judge unjustly and favour the wicked (v. 2)? Then he restates their commission, and every name on it belongs to someone without money or power: the weak, the fatherless, the afflicted, the destitute, the needy. Justice, he says, is not merely keeping your own hands clean but actively rescuing them from the hand of the wicked (vv. 3–4).
verseByVerse.theology: The judges are put on trial, and the charge is what they did for people who could not pay them.

verseByVerse.quote: God has taken his place in the divine council; in the midst of the gods he holds judgment: "How long will you judge unjustly and show partiality to the wicked? Selah
verseByVerse.commentary:
God stands up among those who judge in his name and puts them on trial for favouring the wicked.

God has taken his place in the divine council. The scene is a courtroom, and the surprise is who is in the dock. God stands up among “the gods”, not to preside over a case they have brought, but to judge them.

In the midst of the gods. Rulers and judges could be called “gods” because they sat in God’s place when they decided cases, and Jesus spoke of them as those “to whom the word of God came” (John 10:35). Whatever their title, they are creatures under God’s judgment, not rival gods.

Show partiality to the wicked. The charge is partiality. A court that favours the man with money, connections or a loud voice is not simply a bad court; because it judges in God’s name, it tells a lie about him. The law had said it plainly: “You shall not be partial in judgment … for the judgment is God’s” (Deuteronomy 1:17). And “How long?” is usually the cry of the weak to God (Psalm 13:1); here God raises it against the powerful.

Where Christians differ. Who are “the gods”? One reading takes them to be human rulers and judges, as above. The other takes them to be heavenly powers to whom the nations were entrusted: Moses spoke of God fixing the borders of the peoples “according to the number of the sons of God” (Deuteronomy 32:8), and Paul of “the cosmic powers over this present darkness” (Ephesians 6:12), who stand behind unjust human rule.

This commentary’s view. The best reading is that they are human judges and rulers, called “gods” because they judge in God’s name (compare Exodus 22:28). That is how Jesus uses verse 6 (John 10:34–35), and “like men you shall die” (v. 7) fits them best. Either way, every power behind an unjust court answers to God.

Uncertain wording. “The divine council” is literally “the assembly of God” (or “of El”), an unusual phrase. It may mean God’s heavenly court (compare Psalm 89:7) or his gathered people with their judges (the KJV has “the congregation of the mighty”). Either way, God presides over whoever judges.

Textual note. At Deuteronomy 32:8 the ESV follows the Dead Sea Scrolls and the Greek Old Testament; the standard Hebrew text, the Masoretic Text, followed by the KJV, reads “the children of Israel”.
verseByVerse.note: “The gods” here are best taken as human judges who acted in God’s name; some think of heavenly powers.

verseByVerse.quote: Give justice to the weak and the fatherless; maintain the right of the afflicted and the destitute. Rescue the weak and the needy; deliver them from the hand of the wicked."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s job description for every judge is made up of people who cannot pay, and it is summed up in one word: rescue. No one on the list can offer a bribe or a favour, and the test of any authority is what it does for them.

Rescue the weak and the needy. The verbs are give, maintain, rescue, deliver. Justice is not merely refraining from harming the poor; it is actively pulling them out of “the hand of the wicked”. A judge who keeps his own hands clean while the powerful strip the weak has not done what God appointed him for.

The one who used all authority for the least. None of us has used power this way without fault. Christ, who holds all authority, used it for the least and gave himself for us, and his Spirit now makes us that kind of people in whatever small place we hold power.

Every small share of authority. When Jehoshaphat appointed judges he told them, “Consider what you do, for you judge not for man but for the LORD” (2 Chronicles 19:6). Every parent, employer, elder and manager holds some small share of this authority, and the psalm asks what it has done for the person in the room with least power.

Does this mean the poor are always in the right? No. The same law forbids favouring either side: “You shall not be partial to the poor or defer to the great” (Leviticus 19:15). Justice puts no thumb on the scale; it makes sure the weak get the hearing the powerful get without asking.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–8 — Like Men You Shall Die
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Corrupt judges shake the world, cannot escape death, and leave only one hope: that God himself will judge. The rulers are blind, walking about in darkness, and because justice is one of the things the world stands on, their failure shakes the foundations of the earth (v. 5). God gave them a high title, “gods” and “sons of the Most High”, but it was lent, and they will die like any other man and fall like any prince (vv. 6–7). So the psalmist turns from the failed judges to the true one: “Arise, O God, judge the earth”, for the nations are his inheritance (v. 8). Jesus later took up verse 6 in defence of his own claim to be the Son of God.
verseByVerse.theology: Whatever authority God lends is lent to mortals, and the psalm ends by asking the only true Judge to take the bench himself.

verseByVerse.quote: They have neither knowledge nor understanding, they walk about in darkness; all the foundations of the earth are shaken.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The rulers are blind, and because justice is one of the things the world stands on, their corruption shakes everything.

They walk about in darkness. God turns from addressing the judges to describing them, and the verdict is blindness in the very people appointed to bring things to light.

All the foundations of the earth are shaken. When those at the top judge corruptly, it is not just a few cases that go wrong; the ground under everyone shifts. Another psalm asks, “if the foundations are destroyed, what can the righteous do?” (Psalm 11:3).

Is justice only what the strong decide? In the first book of Plato’s Republic, a sharp-tongued teacher named Thrasymachus argues that justice is nothing but the advantage of the stronger: those in power write the rules to suit themselves and call the result justice. History seems to back him, and Psalm 82 agrees with the evidence and denies the conclusion. Yes, rulers bend judgment towards the rich and well connected; God says so first, and more bluntly than any sceptic. But if Thrasymachus were right, there would be nothing to complain about, because there would be no justice above the powerful to measure them by. Our very outrage at a corrupt court assumes the courtroom of this psalm, where the judges are themselves judged.

The Judge who was judged. The Judge who sits in that courtroom did not prove his justice by crushing the weak. He was condemned by a corrupt court himself: “By oppression and judgment he was taken away” (Isaiah 53:8). The one with all the power used it to be wronged in our place, which is why the weak can trust him and the strong must fear him.

verseByVerse.quote: I said, "You are gods, sons of the Most High, all of you; nevertheless, like men you shall die, and fall like any prince."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God gave the judges a high title, but it was lent, and it will not save them from dying like any other man.

You are gods, sons of the Most High. God does not withdraw the title he gave. The dignity of the office was real; they did sit in his place. But the title was lent, and those who held it would still die.

Jesus quotes this verse. When a crowd took up stones to stone him for blasphemy, Jesus answered: “Is it not written in your Law, ‘I said, you are gods’? If he called them gods to whom the word of God came (and Scripture cannot be broken), do you say of him whom the Father consecrated and sent into the world, ‘You are blaspheming,’ because I said, ‘I am the Son of God’?” (John 10:34–36).

From the lesser to the greater. If Scripture, which cannot be set aside, gives the name “gods” to unjust men who merely received God’s word, how can it be blasphemy for the one the Father consecrated and sent to call himself God’s Son? They were called gods and died like men. He was the Son and died for men, and did not stay dead.

What it does not mean. “You are gods” is not a promise that believers may become gods, as some teachers claim; it is an accusation followed by a death sentence. The gospel promises something better: adoption as God’s children (see the note on John 10:34–35).

Uncertain wording. The ESV notes that “fall like any prince” may also be read “fall as one man, O princes”. Either way, those who judged as if answerable to no one will fall, and fall together.
verseByVerse.note: Jesus quotes v. 6 in answer to the charge of blasphemy.

verseByVerse.quote: Arise, O God, judge the earth; for you shall inherit all the nations!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Since the lesser judges have failed, the psalmist asks God himself to stand up and judge, because the nations belong to him.

Arise, O God, judge the earth. The reason given is ownership: the nations are God’s, not the property of the powers that mismanaged them.

For you shall inherit all the nations! Elsewhere in the Psalter the Father says to his Son, “Ask of me, and I will make the nations your heritage” (Psalm 2:8). At the cross Christ “disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame” (Colossians 2:15). And the Judge the psalm calls for has been named: the Father “has given all judgment to the Son” (John 5:22), and God “has fixed a day on which he will judge the world in righteousness by a man whom he has appointed” (Acts 17:31).

Comfort for the wronged. That is the comfort of this psalm for anyone on the wrong end of a corrupt decision: a court, a tribunal, an office that looked the other way. There is a council above that one, and its Judge has already stood up. “Arise, O God” is not a cry into the void. It is a request for something he has promised to do, and has begun.

What it does not mean. Praying for God’s judgment is no reason to do nothing meanwhile. Seek justice through proper means where you can, as Paul appealed to Caesar (Acts 25:11), and use any power you hold for the wronged (vv. 3–4).

82.title: Arise, O God, Judge the Earth
82.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 82 is another psalm of Asaph in Book Three (see the introduction). In Psalm 81 God spoke into Israel’s worship; here he stands up in his council and speaks to those who rule and judge in his name.

The message. Every authority on earth is borrowed from God and answerable to him, and he measures it by one test: what it does for those who cannot defend themselves. Rulers who favour the wicked and abandon the weak will fall, however grand their title, and God himself will judge the earth, because the nations belong to him.

Why it was said. Israel’s judges and kings were appointed to do justice in God’s name (Deuteronomy 1:17; 16:18–20), yet the prophets again and again accuse them of taking bribes and ignoring the widow and the fatherless (Isaiah 1:23; Amos 5:12). For the weak, who had no one to plead their case, this psalm declared that the corrupt court is not the last court.

How the chapter makes its case. God takes his place among “the gods” and charges them with partiality (vv. 1–2). He restates their commission: give justice to the weak, the fatherless, the afflicted and the needy, and rescue them from the wicked (vv. 3–4). But they are blind, and their corruption shakes the foundations of the earth (v. 5). So he passes sentence: the title “gods” was his to give, and it will not stop them dying like men (vv. 6–7). The psalmist then prays the only prayer left: “Arise, O God, judge the earth” (v. 8).

Where it leads. By promise, and by the need it exposes. The psalm ends asking God himself to come and judge, and the New Testament names the Judge: the Father “has given all judgment to the Son” (John 5:22) and will judge the world “by a man whom he has appointed” (Acts 17:31). Jesus took up verse 6 to show that his claim to be the Son of God was no blasphemy (John 10:34–36). Unlike the judges who died like men, he was condemned by a corrupt court and died for the weak, and the nations are his inheritance (Psalm 2:8).

For us. Whatever authority you hold, as parent, employer, elder or official, is God’s on loan, and he asks what it has done for the weakest person in your care. And if you have been failed by a court or an office that looked away, there is a higher court, and its Judge has already stood up.
82.theology:
Authority is held from God and answerable to him in person, whether the gods are human judges (John 10:35) or the powers behind them (Eph 6:12). Partiality is a lie told in God's name (Deut 1:17); justice is the active rescue of those who cannot pay, and its corruption shakes the world's foundations (vv. 2-5).

The dignity of the office was real but lent, with mortality attached (vv. 6-7), and Jesus argued from verse 6 for his own claim to be the Son of God (John 10:34-36). The nations are God's inheritance (v. 8), given to the Son (Ps 2:8), whose cross disarmed the powers (Col 2:15) and to whom all judgment is given (John 5:22).
82.examples:
The psalm puts the judges in the dock, and their job description is made entirely of people who cannot pay. When the courts rot, the ground shifts under everyone.

Jesus turns the psalm into an argument: if they were called gods, what of the one the Father sent? And for anyone failed by a court or an office that looked away, there is a council above the one that failed you.

keyVerse.quote: Arise, O God, judge the earth; for you shall inherit all the nations!
keyVerse.note: The whole psalm turns on this last line. The judges God appointed have failed the weak, so the psalmist appeals past them to the Judge above them, on the ground that the nations are his. The New Testament answers the prayer: all judgment has been given to the Son, who now holds the nations as his inheritance and will judge the world in righteousness.

82.reflection:
God’s job description for judges is made up entirely of people who cannot pay: the weak, the fatherless, the afflicted, the needy (vv. 3–4). Who are the people with least power in the places where you have some authority, at home, at work or in church, and what has your authority done for them?

Verse 5 says that injustice at the top shakes “all the foundations of the earth”. Where have you seen corrupt or careless authority damage far more than the cases it decided?

The rulers had a grand title, “gods”, yet they died like men (vv. 6–7). Jesus used this verse to defend his claim to be the Son of God (John 10:34–36). How is he different from every judge this psalm describes?

The psalm ends with a prayer, “Arise, O God, judge the earth” (v. 8). How can that prayer comfort someone who has been wronged by people in power, and how should it shape the way we wait and act?

83.text: A Song. A Psalm of Asaph. 1O God, do not keep silence; do not hold your peace or be still, O God!2For behold, your enemies make an uproar; those who hate you have raised their heads.3They lay crafty plans against your people; they consult together against your treasured ones.4They say, "Come, let us wipe them out as a nation; let the name of Israel be remembered no more!"5For they conspire with one accord; against you they make a covenant—6the tents of Edom and the Ishmaelites, Moab and the Hagrites,7Gebal and Ammon and Amalek, Philistia with the inhabitants of Tyre;8Asshur also has joined them; they are the strong arm of the children of Lot. Selah9Do to them as you did to Midian, as to Sisera and Jabin at the river Kishon,10who were destroyed at En-dor, who became dung for the ground.11Make their nobles like Oreb and Zeeb, all their princes like Zebah and Zalmunna,12who said, "Let us take possession for ourselves of the pastures of God."13O my God, make them like whirling dust, like chaff before the wind.14As fire consumes the forest, as the flame sets the mountains ablaze,15so may you pursue them with your tempest and terrify them with your hurricane!16Fill their faces with shame, that they may seek your name, O LORD.17Let them be put to shame and dismayed forever; let them perish in disgrace,18that they may know that you alone, whose name is the LORD, are the Most High over all the earth.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — Against You They Make a Covenant
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When God’s people are threatened with destruction, they may plead with God not to stay silent, because the threat is aimed at him. The psalm opens with a cry for God to speak while his enemies roar and raise their heads (vv. 1–2). Their plans are crafty and their aim is total: to wipe Israel out so that even its name is forgotten (vv. 3–4). They have made a covenant, and the psalm names its true target: “against you” (v. 5). Then comes the roll call: ten peoples from south, east, west and north, several of them Israel’s own relatives, with Assyria behind them (vv. 6–8).
verseByVerse.theology: A plot against the people God treasures is, in the psalm's eyes, a plot against God himself.

verseByVerse.quote: O God, do not keep silence; do not hold your peace or be still, O God! For behold, your enemies make an uproar; those who hate you have raised their heads. They lay crafty plans against your people; they consult together against your treasured ones. They say, "Come, let us wipe them out as a nation; let the name of Israel be remembered no more!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
With the enemy loud and God silent, the psalmist asks God to speak, because a plot to erase his treasured people is a plot against him.

O God, do not keep silence. It is the prayer of someone who can hear the enemy clearly and cannot hear God at all. God’s silence while opposition grows louder is one of the hardest things a believer endures, and the psalm does not dress it up. It simply asks him to speak.

Your enemies make an uproar. “Make an uproar” is the roar of a crowd, and “raised their heads” the posture of defiance, chin up and no longer bowed. It is Psalm 2 again: “Why do the nations rage … and the rulers take counsel together, against the LORD and against his Anointed” (Psalm 2:1–2). The crafty planning is the same, and so is heaven’s answer: “He who sits in the heavens laughs” (Psalm 2:4).

Against your treasured ones. The pronouns tell the story: “your” enemies, “your” people. The psalm refuses to describe this as a border dispute. Israel is God’s treasure, stored away as precious, and a plot against her is a plot against the one who treasures her. Jesus said the same to the man hunting his church: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (Acts 9:4).

Let us wipe them out as a nation. The goal is not conquest but erasure: that there should be no Israel left even to remember. It has been tried many times since, by empires ancient and modern, and it has never succeeded, because the survival of God’s people rests not on their strength but on his promise: “him who dishonors you I will curse”, God had told Abraham (Genesis 12:3).

Where Christians differ. How far does that promise still attach to the Jewish people as a nation? Some read Romans 11:26 as a future turning of ethnic Israel to Christ, others as the whole people of God, Jew and Gentile, gathered in. Faithful believers hold both views, and all agree that hatred of the Jewish people is sin and that the gospel is “to the Jew first” (Romans 1:16).

This commentary’s view. The promise to bless those who bless Abraham is fulfilled in Christ, in whom “all the nations” are blessed (Galatians 3:8), and the modern state of Israel is not itself the fulfilment of the land promises. Yet the Jewish people remain “beloved for the sake of their forefathers” (Romans 11:28), and Romans 11 most naturally looks for a future turning of many of them to Christ. So Christians should love them, pray for their salvation, and judge every nation, Israel included, by God’s justice.

verseByVerse.quote: For they conspire with one accord; against you they make a covenant— the tents of Edom and the Ishmaelites, Moab and the Hagrites, Gebal and Ammon and Amalek, Philistia with the inhabitants of Tyre; Asshur also has joined them; they are the strong arm of the children of Lot. Selah
verseByVerse.commentary:
A ring of peoples, some of them Israel’s own relatives, has made a treaty to destroy Israel, and the psalm sees it for what it is: a covenant against God.

Against you they make a covenant. Israel was the people bound to God by covenant, and the nations answer with a covenant of their own, signed against him. Every united front against God’s people is a rival treaty, and its real target is God.

The tents of Edom and the Ishmaelites. The ten peoples come from every direction: desert tribes to the south and east, Philistia on the coast, Tyre and Gebal to the north, and Assyria backing them all. Several were relatives. Edom was the line of Esau, the Ishmaelites descended from Abraham’s other son Ishmael, and “the children of Lot” were Moab and Ammon (Genesis 19:37–38). The family had gathered against the family.

Which war? No recorded battle matches the whole list. The alliance of Moab, Ammon and Edom that came against Jehoshaphat is a partial fit (2 Chronicles 20:1–2), and on that occasion a Levite “of the sons of Asaph” stood up and prophesied (2 Chronicles 20:14). The list may describe that crisis, or picture the whole ring of hostility that surrounded Israel at one time or another.

Uncertain wording. Two names are hard to place. Gebal is probably Byblos, the port north of Tyre, though some think of a district near Edom. The Hagrites were a people living east of Gilead, beyond the Jordan (1 Chronicles 5:10), about whom little else is known.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–18 — That They May Seek Your Name
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God has beaten bigger armies before, and the psalm asks him to do it again, for the sake of his name. It recalls the days of the Judges, when Sisera and Jabin were swept away at the Kishon and Gideon’s small band routed the princes of Midian, who wanted to seize “the pastures of God” (vv. 9–12). It asks God to scatter this alliance like dust and chaff, to drive it like fire and storm (vv. 13–15). Then it states its aim: shame that leads the enemies to seek the LORD’s name, or else their perishing, so that all the earth may know that he alone is Most High (vv. 16–18).
verseByVerse.theology: The fiercest prayer in the psalm has a surprising goal: that the enemies should come looking for God.

verseByVerse.quote: Do to them as you did to Midian, as to Sisera and Jabin at the river Kishon, who were destroyed at En-dor, who became dung for the ground. Make their nobles like Oreb and Zeeb, all their princes like Zebah and Zalmunna, who said, "Let us take possession for ourselves of the pastures of God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The psalm asks God to do again what he did in the days of the Judges, when he destroyed great armies that wanted to seize his land. Against ten nations, it reaches for two victories Israel could never have won by her own strength.

As to Sisera and Jabin at the river Kishon. Jabin, king of Canaan, had “900 chariots of iron” and oppressed Israel for twenty years (Judges 4:3). His commander Sisera’s army was destroyed when the Kishon rose: “The torrent Kishon swept them away” (Judges 5:21), and the song of Deborah says the stars themselves fought against him.

Do to them as you did to Midian. Midian came “like locusts in number”, with camels that “could not be counted” (Judges 6:5), and God cut Gideon’s army down to “the 300 men who lapped” before he would give the victory (Judges 7:7). Amalek was in that host too (Judges 7:12), and Amalek is on this psalm’s list (v. 7): the same enemy, and the same God.

Who became dung for the ground. A grim detail, chosen on purpose. Four psalms earlier the complaint was that Israel’s dead lay unburied around Jerusalem (Psalm 79:2–3). Here the psalm remembers that same end falling on those who once came against Israel, and asks for the harm to come back on the heads that were raised (v. 2).

The pastures of God. Oreb and Zeeb were the princes of Midian killed at a rock and a winepress that kept their names (Judges 7:25); Zebah and Zalmunna were the kings Gideon killed himself (Judges 8:21). What they wanted was “the pastures of God”. The land was never Israel’s to lose or Midian’s to take. It was God’s grazing ground, and he had put his flock on it. The point of the memory is that the size of an alliance does not settle the outcome. It never did.

Uncertain wording. En-dor is not named in Judges. It lay near Mount Tabor, where Barak gathered his army (Judges 4:6), so the psalm probably preserves a local detail of Sisera’s defeat; some refer it instead to Midian, camped in the same valley.

verseByVerse.quote: O my God, make them like whirling dust, like chaff before the wind. As fire consumes the forest, as the flame sets the mountains ablaze, so may you pursue them with your tempest and terrify them with your hurricane!
verseByVerse.commentary:
The psalm asks God himself to scatter the alliance like dust and chaff, and to drive it off like fire and storm.

Make them like whirling dust. The images grow in violence: whirling dust, chaff, a forest fire, a hillside in flames, a storm. That is the end of an alliance that seemed invincible: ten nations, a treaty, a plan, all blown away like chaff across a threshing floor. The psalm does not ask God to strengthen Israel’s army. It asks him to scatter them himself, as a storm does.

How can a Christian pray this? It is not private revenge but an appeal for God’s justice against those set on destroying his people, left in his hands (see the introduction), and it leads straight to its deepest aim: that the enemies may seek God’s name (v. 16).

Uncertain wording. The ESV notes that “whirling dust” may be rendered “like a tumbleweed”, the dried thistle-head that breaks off in the autumn wind and rolls away with nothing to hold it. The Hebrew word is related to “wheel”: something light and spinning.

verseByVerse.quote: Fill their faces with shame, that they may seek your name, O LORD. Let them be put to shame and dismayed forever; let them perish in disgrace, that they may know that you alone, whose name is the LORD, are the Most High over all the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The shame the psalm asks for has a goal: that the enemies seek the LORD, or else perish, so that all the earth knows he alone is Most High.

That they may seek your name, O LORD. Here is the turn that changes how the whole psalm should be read. The humiliation is aimed at conversion. The psalmist wants his enemies beaten so thoroughly that they stop trusting their gods and their treaty and come looking for the LORD. There is a shame that crushes and a shame that sends a person searching, and the psalm asks for the second.

Let them perish in disgrace. Verse 17 is the other possibility: those who will not seek will perish. Both outcomes end in the same place, “that they may know”: the LORD will be known as the only Most High, over “all the earth”, including Edom, Tyre and Assyria.

Whose name is the LORD. Follow the word “name”. The enemies wanted Israel’s name “remembered no more” (v. 4), and the psalm ends with the God “whose name is the LORD” (v. 18). The plot was to erase a name; the answer is that a greater name is made known.

Not wiped out but widened. A Christian prays this psalm with the cross in view, and so prays verse 16 hardest. One of the fiercest enemies of the first church, Saul of Tarsus, was “still breathing threats and murder against the disciples of the Lord” (Acts 9:1), and his face was filled with shame on the Damascus road until he sought the name he had been trying to erase. The ten nations of this psalm are, in the end, invited. The name of Israel was not wiped out. It was widened to include anyone from Edom to Tyre who seeks the LORD, and all who seek are given a place under that name.

What it means that his name is the LORD. To us a name is a label; in the Bible it tells you who someone is. When Moses asked God his name at the burning bush, God answered, “I AM WHO I AM” (Exodus 3:14), and the name the ESV prints as LORD comes from that verb “to be”. God simply is. He depends on nothing and does not change, while ten nations and their treaty blow away like tumbleweed. Everything else we lean on, health, money, a career, has its being on loan. Yet this self-existent God gave his name to slaves in Egypt, as the God who had heard their groaning and remembered his covenant: the One who needs nothing bound himself to people who had nothing. And Jesus took the name on his own lips, “before Abraham was, I am” (John 8:58), and the crowd reached for stones. The name this psalm wants every nation to know now has a face. So when everything around you is shifting, the steadiest sentence you can say is not “I will be all right” but “He is”, and then call on him, for “everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved” (Romans 10:13).

83.title: Do Not Keep Silence
83.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 83 is the last of the twelve psalms of Asaph (73–83) in Book Three (see the introduction). Psalm 82 ended by calling on God to judge the earth; this psalm faces a ring of nations that have joined together to wipe Israel off the map, and asks God to act.

The message. When God’s people are surrounded and God seems silent, they may ask him to speak and act, because those who plot against his people are plotting against him. His victories in the past show that no alliance, however large, can overturn his purposes, and the end he is working towards is that his name be known over all the earth, best of all by enemies who come to seek it.

Why it was said. Israel was a small nation, and hostile neighbours often closed in on her. No recorded war matches the whole list of ten peoples; the attack on Jehoshaphat by Moab, Ammon and Edom (2 Chronicles 20) is a partial fit, and the psalm may gather the whole ring of hostility into one picture.

How the chapter makes its case. A cry for God to break his silence, because his enemies plot to erase his people (vv. 1–4). The roll call of the conspirators: ten peoples from every side, bound in a covenant against God himself (vv. 5–8). The memory of the Judges, when God destroyed Sisera, Jabin and the princes of Midian (vv. 9–12). A prayer that God scatter them like dust and chaff, fire and storm (vv. 13–15). Then the purpose: shame that leads them to seek the LORD, or else their perishing, so that all may know he alone is Most High (vv. 16–18).

Where it leads. By the character of God revealed in Christ, and by promise. The rage of the nations reached its height at the cross, where rulers and peoples “were gathered together against your holy servant Jesus” (Acts 4:27), and God turned their plot into the salvation of the world. The prayer that enemies would “seek your name” (v. 16) is answered as the gospel goes out to the nations, as when the persecutor Saul was humbled on the Damascus road. And the people whose name was to be “remembered no more” (v. 4) now belong to the one God has given “the name that is above every name” (Philippians 2:9).

For us. When the church is opposed and God seems silent, we may pray honestly for him to act, and leave the vengeance to him. And we pray hardest for verse 16: that those who oppose Christ will be brought low enough to seek him, as we once were.
83.theology:
Opposition to God's people is read as opposition to God, and the alliance is a rival covenant made against him (vv. 2-5). The appeal to the Judges (vv. 9-12) makes the point that the size of a coalition has never settled the outcome; the land was the pastures of God.

The curses on the enemies have a stated goal: shame that leads the enemies to seek the LORD's name (v. 16), or, failing that, their perishing (v. 17). In both cases the end is the knowledge that the LORD alone is Most High over all the earth (v. 18).
83.examples: The psalm sees a treaty signed against heaven, ten nations closing in with relatives among them, and pictures the whole coalition as a dead thistle-head rolling across the field. It knows a shame that sends a man searching, like the persecutor on the Damascus road.

keyVerse.quote: that they may know that you alone, whose name is the LORD, are the Most High over all the earth.
keyVerse.note: The psalm ends by stating the purpose of everything it has asked for. The enemies wanted Israel’s name forgotten (v. 4); God answers by making his own name known over all the earth. Even the fiercest prayers of the psalm serve this one aim, which the gospel fulfils as people from every nation come to know and call on the name of the Lord.

83.reflection:
The psalm begins, “O God, do not keep silence” (v. 1). When have you felt that God was silent while opposition grew louder? What does it teach you that Scripture gives us words to say exactly that to him?

The psalm treats a plot against God’s people as a covenant “against you”, against God himself (v. 5). How does Jesus’ question to Saul, “why are you persecuting me?” (Acts 9:4), confirm this, and how might it change the way we face hostility as Christians?

To encourage itself, the psalm remembers what God did in the days of Gideon and Deborah (vv. 9–12). What past acts of God, in Scripture or in your own life, help you trust him when you feel surrounded?

The psalmist asks for his enemies to be shamed “that they may seek your name” (v. 16). How can we pray for God’s justice and, at the same time, for our opponents to be saved? Whom should you be praying for in this way?

84.text: To the choirmaster: according to The Gittith. A Psalm of the Sons of Korah. 1How lovely is your dwelling place, O LORD of hosts!2My soul longs, yes, faints for the courts of the LORD; my heart and flesh sing for joy to the living God.3Even the sparrow finds a home, and the swallow a nest for herself, where she may lay her young, at your altars, O LORD of hosts, my King and my God.4Blessed are those who dwell in your house, ever singing your praise! Selah5Blessed are those whose strength is in you, in whose heart are the highways to Zion.6As they go through the Valley of Baca they make it a place of springs; the early rain also covers it with pools.7They go from strength to strength; each one appears before God in Zion.8O LORD God of hosts, hear my prayer; give ear, O God of Jacob! Selah9Behold our shield, O God; look on the face of your anointed!10For a day in your courts is better than a thousand elsewhere. I would rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God than dwell in the tents of wickedness.11For the LORD God is a sun and shield; the LORD bestows favor and honor. No good thing does he withhold from those who walk uprightly.12O LORD of hosts, blessed is the one who trusts in you!

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — Even the Sparrow Finds a Home
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Nearness to the living God is the best thing there is, and the singer, far from God’s house, aches for it. He calls God’s dwelling lovely, and his whole self, soul, heart and flesh, longs for the courts of the LORD and sings for joy to the living God (vv. 1–2). Then he notices the birds: sparrows and swallows nest at the altars, small creatures with a settled home where he has none, and he turns to the King they live beside (v. 3). So the first blessing falls on those who live in God’s house, whose whole occupation is his praise (v. 4).
verseByVerse.theology: A worshipper who cannot be there envies the birds that nest in the temple walls.

verseByVerse.quote: How lovely is your dwelling place, O LORD of hosts! My soul longs, yes, faints for the courts of the LORD; my heart and flesh sing for joy to the living God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The singer loves God’s house and longs for it with his whole being, because the living God is there.

How lovely is your dwelling place. Lovely is a word for what is loved. The psalm opens with affection, the way someone speaks of home when a long way from it.

My heart and flesh sing for joy. The longing is total: soul, heart and flesh. Yet it sings for joy, because the ache for God is itself a kind of gladness when the one longed for is real and alive.

To the living God. This is the heart of it. It was the same cry in Psalm 42, also from the sons of Korah: “My soul thirsts for God, for the living God” (Psalm 42:2). The courts are lovely because of who lives in them. No one faints with longing for a building; the singer is homesick for a person.

The title. The heading names the Sons of Korah, and the name carries a story. Korah led a rebellion against Moses in the wilderness and the ground swallowed him, “But the sons of Korah did not die” (Numbers 26:11). Generations later their descendants served at the sanctuary as “keepers of the thresholds of the tent” (1 Chronicles 9:19). A family whose ancestor tried to seize the holy place spent its history guarding the door of it, and wrote this song about how lovely it is. That is grace, in a family tree. (On “The Gittith” in the heading, see the note on Psalm 81:1–5.)

The dwelling place has a face. The God the psalmist longed to be near came nearer still: “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14), and Jesus called his own body the temple (John 2:21). The longing of this psalm is answered not by a building but by a person, in whom God has made his home with us.

If you do not feel this. If you have never felt anything like this, the psalm is not a rebuke; it is an invitation to ask for it. And if you have felt it and lost it, the psalm is proof that the desire is meant to be there, and can be asked for again.

verseByVerse.quote: Even the sparrow finds a home, and the swallow a nest for herself, where she may lay her young, at your altars, O LORD of hosts, my King and my God. Blessed are those who dwell in your house, ever singing your praise! Selah
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even the sparrows have a home at God’s altars, and the singer, far away, envies them and all who live in God’s house to praise him.

Even the sparrow finds a home. The singer is somewhere else, and he is jealous of the birds. Sparrows and swallows nested in the eaves and crevices of the temple, flying in and out over the altars, raising their chicks in the busiest holy place in the country. Nobody drove them away. The smallest and least valued creatures in Israel had a settled home in God’s house, and he did not.

My King and my God. See the title at the end of the verse. The birds have a nest; he wants the King.

Blessed are those who dwell in your house. Those who live at the temple are called happy, not for their security or income but for their occupation: “ever singing your praise”. Luke describes a woman like that, the widow Anna, who “did not depart from the temple, worshiping with fasting and prayer night and day” (Luke 2:37). She was eighty-four, or had been a widow that long (Luke’s words can be read either way), and she was among the first on earth to recognise the child Jesus.

Room for the small. Jesus pointed to sparrows too, sold cheaply in the market and not one forgotten by the Father (Matthew 10:29–31). If God makes room at his altar for a sparrow’s nest, the believer who feels too small or too far away to be wanted in his house has misjudged the God whose house it is.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Those who cannot live near God but are on their way to him are blessed too, because their strength is in him. The second blessing is for pilgrims who carry the road to Zion in their hearts (v. 5). Their way leads through the dry Valley of Baca, yet they turn it into a place of springs, and God sends the early rain to fill the pools (v. 6). Against all the rules of a long walk, they grow stronger as they go, and every one of them arrives to appear before God in Zion (v. 7).
verseByVerse.theology: Pilgrims on the road to God turn a dry valley into a spring and arrive stronger than they set out.

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed are those whose strength is in you, in whose heart are the highways to Zion. As they go through the Valley of Baca they make it a place of springs; the early rain also covers it with pools. They go from strength to strength; each one appears before God in Zion.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those whose strength is in God carry the road to him in their hearts, turn dry valleys into springs on the way, and grow stronger until every one arrives.

In whose heart are the highways to Zion. The psalm’s second blessing is for people who cannot live at the temple but are on their way to it, and they carry the road inside them. The pilgrim routes have been worn into their affections; their hearts are set on the way to God. Every Israelite man was to “appear before the LORD” three times a year at the pilgrim feasts (Deuteronomy 16:16), and verse 7 uses that language of arrival: “each one appears before God in Zion”.

A searching test. Everyone’s heart has a well-worn road in it: the direction the mind drifts when it is not being directed. Where the road in your heart runs is where your treasure is (Matthew 6:21), and it is the Spirit who wears a road to God into hearts that had none.

They make it a place of springs. The Valley of Baca was a dry stretch on the pilgrim road. The pilgrims do not merely get through it; “they make it a place of springs”. People whose strength is in God leave the dry places they pass through wetter than they found them. Then God adds his part: “the early rain also covers it with pools”. The traveller digs; heaven fills.

In everyday life. Paul described that kind of life: “as sorrowful, yet always rejoicing; as poor, yet making many rich” (2 Corinthians 6:10). Some of the most refreshing believers you will ever meet are walking through their own dry valley, and have turned it into a well others drink from.

They go from strength to strength. A long walk normally goes from strength to weakness. The pilgrims go the other way: the nearer they get to God, the stronger they grow, and the journey ends with “each one”, none lost on the road, standing before God. That is the Christian life as pilgrimage: strangers who “desire a better country, that is, a heavenly one” (Hebrews 11:16), and who will arrive.

Uncertain wording. No one knows where the Valley of Baca was, and its name may mean “weeping” or refer to balsam trees. In verse 5 the ESV notes that the Hebrew does not actually say “to Zion”: it simply says the highways are in their heart. And in verse 6 the word for “pools” is very like the word for “blessings”, which some translations follow; either way, God fills the valley.
verseByVerse.note: The Valley of Baca may mean “valley of weeping” or of balsam trees — a dry stage on the pilgrim road.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–12 — A Day in Your Courts
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God is worth more than anything else, and he gives his people every good thing. The pilgrim prays for the king, God’s anointed, asking God to look on his face (vv. 8–9). Then comes the choice of a life: one day in God’s courts is better than a thousand elsewhere, and the doorway of his house better than a home among the wicked (v. 10). The reason is God himself. He is sun and shield, gives favour and honour, and withholds no good thing from the upright, so the last blessing rests on anyone who trusts him, wherever they are (vv. 11–12).
verseByVerse.theology: A doorkeeper's family sings that the threshold of God's house is better than the best room anywhere else.

verseByVerse.quote: O LORD God of hosts, hear my prayer; give ear, O God of Jacob! Selah Behold our shield, O God; look on the face of your anointed!
verseByVerse.commentary:
The pilgrim prays for the king, asking God to look with favour on the face of his anointed, on whom the people’s welfare depends.

O LORD God of hosts, hear my prayer. The psalm calls God the LORD “of hosts” for the fourth time (vv. 1, 3, 8, 12), and pairs it with “God of Jacob”, the patriarch who limped and schemed and was loved anyway (see Jacob). The sovereign of the universe and the God of one flawed man are the same God, and the pilgrim can ask both to listen.

Look on the face of your anointed! Then the pilgrim prays for the king. “Your anointed” is the king in Jerusalem, whose welfare and the people’s were bound together.

God looks at the face of Christ. “Anointed” is the word Messiah, in Greek Christ. He is the one on whose face God looks for his people’s sake. A believer’s standing before God rests not on what God sees in the believer, but on God looking at the face of Christ and accepting all who are his. That is why the Christian comes into the courts of God with confidence.

Uncertain wording. “Behold our shield, O God” can be read two ways. “Our shield” may be the king, the people’s protector, set in parallel with “your anointed”, as the ESV wording suggests; or it may be God himself, “Behold, O God our shield”, as verse 11 calls him a shield. Either way, the prayer is that God would look with favour on his king.

verseByVerse.quote: For a day in your courts is better than a thousand elsewhere. I would rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God than dwell in the tents of wickedness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
One day near God is worth more than a thousand anywhere else, and the lowest place in his house is better than the best among the wicked.

A day in your courts is better than a thousand elsewhere. The arithmetic is deliberate: one day against a thousand, nearly three years of days. Twenty-four hours in God’s presence outweighs a thousand days anywhere else, however those days are filled.

I would rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God. Then the job comparison, from a family of doorkeepers (see the note on vv. 1–2). A doorkeeper stood at the entrance, not in the inner courts or at the altar, but at the edge of the holy place where he could see in. The singer would rather have that least of the temple posts than live comfortably inside the tents of the wicked.

The idol of status. Few things gnaw at modern people more quietly than rank: where we stand compared with our classmates, our colleagues, our siblings. The writer Alain de Botton argued in Status Anxiety that a society which tells everyone they can rise to the top also implies that those who stay low deserve to be there, so we are more anxious about our position than our ancestors ever were. A title, a postcode or a follower count becomes a verdict on our worth. The doorkeeper has stepped off that ladder, not because he is lazy but because he has found something better than position: nearness. The point of the house is the one who lives in it.

The King in the doorkeeper’s place. The gospel goes further. The Son of God took the lowest place there is, kneeling to wash feet and then dying a slave’s death, and he said, “whoever would be great among you must be your servant” (Mark 10:43). If the King has taken the doorkeeper’s place, nobody in his house needs to fight for status again.

For unnoticed servants. This is a verse for anyone who serves in an unnoticed corner of God’s house: the person who sets up the chairs, runs the door, washes the cups, or simply sits at the back. The threshold of God’s house is better than the best room in any other.

The tents of wickedness. And it is a question for anyone weighing a comfortable life that requires living among “the tents of wickedness” against a smaller one at the edge of God’s people. The psalm has already done the sums.

verseByVerse.quote: For the LORD God is a sun and shield; the LORD bestows favor and honor. No good thing does he withhold from those who walk uprightly. O LORD of hosts, blessed is the one who trusts in you!
verseByVerse.commentary:
God gives his people all they need, light, protection, favour and honour, and withholds nothing good, so the one who trusts him is blessed wherever he is.

The LORD God is a sun and shield. Two images of what God gives: a sun, light, warmth and life, the thing that makes growth possible; and a shield, protection. Nowhere else in the Psalms is God called a sun. Isaiah later promised that “the LORD will be your everlasting light” (Isaiah 60:19), and Malachi that “the sun of righteousness shall rise with healing in its wings” (Malachi 4:2), and the pilgrim in the dark valley needs exactly that.

Blessed is the one who trusts in you! The third blessing is different from the first two. Verse 4 blessed those in the temple and verse 5 those on the road; verse 12 blesses “the one who trusts”, with no location at all. The psalm that began with homesickness for a building ends with a blessing that can be had anywhere.

The gift not withheld. The proof that God withholds no good thing is the gift he did not withhold: “He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all, how will he not also with him graciously give us all things?” (Romans 8:32). A God who gave that is not being stingy with the rest. And since none of us walks uprightly without fault, the promise rests on the upright one who walked in our place, the anointed on whose face God looks (v. 9).

The believer today. This is how the psalm reaches the believer today. Jesus said the hour was coming when people would worship the Father neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem, but “in spirit and truth” (John 4:21–23). Christians “have come to Mount Zion and to the city of the living God” (Hebrews 12:22), and in the city to come there is no temple, “for its temple is the Lord God the Almighty and the Lamb” (Revelation 21:22). The dwelling place is lovely because he is in it, and the one who trusts him is already home.

But I can name good things he has withheld. Believers sometimes find this promise hard, because they can name things they asked for and did not get. The promise is not that God gives everything we want, but that he withholds nothing that is truly good for those who walk with him. If he has held something back, the promise says that from where he sees, it was not good for you, or not yet.

84.title: How Lovely Is Your Dwelling Place
84.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 84 opens a small group of psalms of the sons of Korah (84–85, 87–88) near the end of Book Three (see the introduction). After the cries of Psalms 79–83 over a ruined temple and a threatened nation, it turns to longing and joy: the beauty of God’s house and the happiness of those who are near him.

The message. The deepest desire of the human heart is to be near the living God, and he is worth more than anything else life can offer. Those who live near him, those on the road to him, and those who simply trust him are all blessed, because he is their sun and shield and withholds no good thing from them.

Why it was said. Israelites went up to Jerusalem for the pilgrim feasts (see the introduction), and this psalm was probably sung on the road, or by a temple servant far from home. Its writers, the sons of Korah, were a family of temple singers and doorkeepers descended from a man who rebelled against God (Numbers 16; 26:11), which gives verse 10 its edge.

How the chapter makes its case. The singer longs for God’s courts and envies the sparrows that nest there, and the first blessing falls on those who dwell in God’s house (vv. 1–4). The second is for pilgrims whose strength is in God, who turn the dry valley into springs and grow stronger until each appears before him (vv. 5–7). A prayer for the king, God’s anointed (vv. 8–9), leads to the doorkeeper’s choice: one day in God’s courts over a thousand elsewhere (v. 10). And the reason is God himself, sun and shield, so the third blessing rests on anyone who trusts him (vv. 11–12).

Where it leads. By pattern and by promise. The temple the psalmist loved was where God lived among his people, and in Jesus “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14): he is the true temple, and in him we come near to God. The anointed on whose face God looks (v. 9) is the Messiah, for whose sake his people are accepted. And the God who “did not spare his own Son” (Romans 8:32) has proved that he withholds no good thing.

For us. Ask where the road in your heart runs, and whether you love God’s presence more than comfort or status. Christians need not travel to Jerusalem to find him: in Christ the one who trusts God is already home, and the dry valleys on the way can become springs.
84.theology:
The longing is for a person, not a place: the living God (v. 2). God makes room at his altars for the smallest creatures (v. 3), and pilgrims whose strength is in him grow stronger on the road (vv. 5-7).

The people's welfare is bound to God's regard for the face of his anointed (v. 9), fulfilled in Christ. God is sun and shield and withholds no good thing (v. 11), a promise sealed by the gift of his Son. The final blessing is on trust, with no place named (v. 12), and so reaches every believer who worships in spirit and truth (John 4:23).
84.examples: A rebel's descendants spend their history guarding the door he tried to force, and one of them is jealous of the sparrows in the temple eaves. The pilgrim's heart is shaped like the road to God, and he leaves the dry valley wetter than he found it. The psalm ends with a blessing that has no address attached.

keyVerse.quote: For a day in your courts is better than a thousand elsewhere. I would rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God than dwell in the tents of wickedness.
keyVerse.note: This verse puts the psalm’s longing into a choice. Nearness to God outweighs any quantity of time, comfort or rank elsewhere, and from a family of doorkeepers descended from a rebel it is a testimony of grace. It asks every reader what they would trade to be near God, and in Christ, who took the lowest place, that nearness is freely given.

84.reflection:
The psalmist’s whole being, “my heart and flesh”, longs for “the living God” (v. 2). Is that longing something you recognise? What tends to dull it, and what helps to rekindle it?

“In whose heart are the highways to Zion” (v. 5). Where does your mind drift when it is not being directed? What does that show about where your heart’s road runs?

The pilgrims turn the dry Valley of Baca into a place of springs (v. 6). Have you known someone who refreshed others while going through their own hard season? How might God use your present dry valley for others?

“I would rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God” (v. 10). Where are you tempted to chase status, comfort or recognition, and how does the Son of God taking the lowest place free us from that race?

85.text: To the choirmaster. A Psalm of the Sons of Korah. 1LORD, you were favorable to your land; you restored the fortunes of Jacob.2You forgave the iniquity of your people; you covered all their sin. Selah3You withdrew all your wrath; you turned from your hot anger.4Restore us again, O God of our salvation, and put away your indignation toward us!5Will you be angry with us forever? Will you prolong your anger to all generations?6Will you not revive us again, that your people may rejoice in you?7Show us your steadfast love, O LORD, and grant us your salvation.8Let me hear what God the LORD will speak, for he will speak peace to his people, to his saints; but let them not turn back to folly.9Surely his salvation is near to those who fear him, that glory may dwell in our land.10Steadfast love and faithfulness meet; righteousness and peace kiss each other.11Faithfulness springs up from the ground, and righteousness looks down from the sky.12Yes, the LORD will give what is good, and our land will yield its increase.13Righteousness will go before him and make his footsteps a way.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A people already restored ask God to restore them again, and they build the request on what he has done. The first three verses are all memory: God was favourable to his land, restored the fortunes of Jacob, forgave the iniquity of his people, covered all their sin and turned from his anger. Then the tense changes abruptly. The same people pray “Restore us again” and ask whether God will be angry for ever (vv. 4–5). They are not doubting the first mercy; they are leaning on it. The section ends with the heart of the request: revival, so that God’s people may rejoice in him, and a fresh sight of his steadfast love and salvation (vv. 6–7).
verseByVerse.theology: A people who have already been brought back ask to be brought back again — which is how the life of grace actually feels.

verseByVerse.quote: LORD, you were favorable to your land; you restored the fortunes of Jacob. You forgave the iniquity of your people; you covered all their sin. Selah You withdrew all your wrath; you turned from your hot anger.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The psalm begins by remembering that God once forgave all his people’s sin and turned his anger away.

LORD, you were favorable to your land. Every verb is past tense. The psalm opens with a memory of a great turning, very probably the return from exile, when “the LORD stirred up the spirit of Cyrus king of Persia” to send the captives home (Ezra 1:1), though the psalm does not name the occasion. “You restored the fortunes of Jacob” calls the nation by its ancestor’s name: the whole family had been brought back.

You covered all their sin. The heart of that restoration is not the journey home or the land, but forgiveness. The exile had been the punishment for sin, so the return meant the sin had been dealt with. All their sin: not part of the debt, but the whole of it was covered.

You withdrew all your wrath. The wrath withdrawn (v. 3) is the believer’s past too: whatever else is uncertain, it has been turned away, because the sin has been covered. The rest of the psalm is prayed from there.

verseByVerse.quote: Restore us again, O God of our salvation, and put away your indignation toward us! Will you be angry with us forever? Will you prolong your anger to all generations? Will you not revive us again, that your people may rejoice in you? Show us your steadfast love, O LORD, and grant us your salvation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
People already restored ask God to revive them again, so that they may be glad in him.

Restore us again, O God of our salvation. Abruptly, a present-tense plea from people already restored. If the setting is the return from Babylon, the disappointment is easy to picture: the people came home to ruins, poor harvests and a half-built temple. Haggai described those years: “You have sown much, and harvested little. You eat, but you never have enough” (Haggai 1:6).

Will you not revive us again? To revive means to give life again. Habakkuk prayed the same thing: “in the midst of the years revive it… in wrath remember mercy” (Habakkuk 3:2). Its purpose is gladness “in you”: not in better harvests, though those would come, but in God. Revival, in the biblical sense, is not excitement; it is a people made glad in God again.

Show us your steadfast love, O LORD. Underneath all the other requests is this one: “show us”, let us see again, the covenant love that was never actually withdrawn.

In the Christian life. The same happens to a believer. A person is converted, forgiven and brought home to God, and some years later finds the joy thin and the harvest small, and needs to be restored again. The psalm does not treat that as a contradiction of the first restoration. It builds the second prayer on the first mercy: you did it then; do it again.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–13 — Let Me Hear What God Will Speak
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Having prayed, the psalmist listens, and what he hears is a promise that God will make his attributes meet and his glory dwell among his people. God will speak peace to his saints, with a warning not to return to the folly that brought judgment, and his salvation is near to those who fear him (vv. 8–9). Then comes the vision: steadfast love and faithfulness meet; righteousness and peace kiss each other; faithfulness springs up from the earth and righteousness looks down from heaven (vv. 10–11). The fruit is a harvest in the land, and the last picture is of God walking through it with righteousness going before him to prepare the way (vv. 12–13).
verseByVerse.theology: The psalm stops asking and listens, and hears four of God’s qualities embrace, which happened at the cross.

verseByVerse.quote: Let me hear what God the LORD will speak, for he will speak peace to his people, to his saints; but let them not turn back to folly. Surely his salvation is near to those who fear him, that glory may dwell in our land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The psalmist stops asking and listens, and hears that God will speak peace and bring his glory back among his people, if they do not return to folly.

Let me hear what God the LORD will speak. Here the psalm does something prayer often forgets to do: it stops talking and listens. After seven verses of memory and asking, the singer waits for an answer, and he knows what kind of answer is coming: “he will speak peace”.

What it means that God speaks peace. We usually mean by peace a quiet afternoon, or the absence of a quarrel. The Hebrew word, shalom, is much fuller: everything as it ought to be, whole and flourishing, with God, with one another, and even in the land, which is why this psalm ends with a harvest (v. 12). Timothy Keller often pointed out that shalom means complete reconciliation and flourishing in every part of life. Notice that God speaks it. These people could not produce it. Shalom is not something we build by getting our circumstances in order. It is a gift, and it was bought: “upon him was the chastisement that brought us peace” (Isaiah 53:5). This week, before you try to make your life feel whole, let God say his word of peace over you in the gospel, and then go and carry that peace into the one relationship where it is most missing. See also Peace in the Theological Dictionary.

Let them not turn back to folly. A warning comes with the promise. The peace God speaks is not permission to return to whatever caused the exile in the first place, and a restored person who goes straight back to the old folly has misheard the word of peace. Yet the Spirit who speaks that peace also holds us to it, and the one who has turned back may return the way this psalm began, to the God who forgave all their sin (v. 2).

Surely his salvation is near. Salvation is “near”, at hand for those who fear him. And its goal is “that glory may dwell in our land”: God’s own glorious presence, which had left the temple before the exile (Ezekiel 10:18), settling back among his people.

Glory came back in a person. John chose the language of dwelling for the moment that prayer was answered beyond anything the returning exiles imagined: “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory” (John 1:14). The glory came back to the land in a person.

verseByVerse.quote: Steadfast love and faithfulness meet; righteousness and peace kiss each other. Faithfulness springs up from the ground, and righteousness looks down from the sky. Yes, the LORD will give what is good, and our land will yield its increase. Righteousness will go before him and make his footsteps a way.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When God comes to save, his love and faithfulness, his righteousness and peace meet and embrace, and his people are given a fruitful land and a road to walk on.

Steadfast love and faithfulness meet. Four of God’s qualities are pictured as people who meet on a road and embrace. The first pair is the one God announced to Moses on the mountain, “abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness” (Exodus 34:6): his loyal love, and his reliability.

Righteousness and peace kiss each other. The harder pair is righteousness and peace. Righteousness demands that sin be judged; peace means the sinner is reconciled. How can both be satisfied at once? A just judge cannot simply make peace with the guilty. Isaiah had said “the effect of righteousness will be peace” (Isaiah 32:17), but no one could see how.

Where they kissed. The cross is where they kissed. God put Christ forward as a propitiation, a sacrifice that turns away wrath, “so that he might be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus” (Romans 3:26). Righteousness was fully satisfied, and so peace became possible: “since we have been justified by faith, we have peace with God” (Romans 5:1). “He himself is our peace” (Ephesians 2:14).

Faithfulness springs up from the ground. Faithfulness grows up out of the soil like a plant; righteousness leans down from above like the sun. Isaiah used the same image: “Shower, O heavens, from above, and let the clouds rain down righteousness; let the earth open, that salvation and righteousness may bear fruit” (Isaiah 45:8). Heaven and earth meet, which is what the angels announced over Bethlehem: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace” (Luke 2:14).

Our land will yield its increase. The meagre harvests of the restoration years, sown much and harvested little, are answered. And the last image is of God walking through his land with righteousness going ahead of him like a herald, marking out the path. His people can walk in his footsteps, because righteousness has made them a road. The psalm that began with a forgiven people needing to be restored again ends with a way to walk on.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew of verse 13’s second line is compressed, and translations differ: the ESV has righteousness “make his footsteps a way”; others read it as preparing a way for his steps, or, as the King James Version did, setting us in the way of his steps. The general sense is clear: righteousness goes ahead of God as he comes, and his coming leaves a path for his people.

85.title: Righteousness and Peace Kiss Each Other
85.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 84 longed for the courts of the LORD; Psalm 85, another song of the sons of Korah, is sung by a people who have been brought home and still need God to come home to them. It looks back on a great forgiveness and asks for it to be made real again.

The message. The God who once forgave all his people’s sin can be asked to revive them again, and he will speak peace. His past mercy is the ground for present prayer. And when he comes, his love and his faithfulness, his righteousness and his peace, will not pull against each other but meet and embrace, and his glory will live among his people.

Why it was said. The psalm names no occasion, but it fits the years after the return from Babylon (see the introduction): the exile was over and the sin behind it forgiven, yet the people came home to ruins, thin harvests and a half-built temple, and the joy they had expected did not come.
