How the chapter makes its case. It begins with memory, every verb in the past tense: God was favourable, forgave, covered all their sin and withdrew his wrath (vv. 1–3). On that ground it prays, with the honesty of disappointment: “Restore us again… Will you not revive us again?” (vv. 4–7). Then it stops and listens, and hears that God will speak peace to his people, with a warning not to turn back to folly, and that his salvation is near so that glory may dwell in the land (vv. 8–9). It ends with a vision: steadfast love and faithfulness meet, righteousness and peace kiss, heaven and earth answer each other, the land yields its harvest, and righteousness prepares God’s way (vv. 10–13).

Where it leads. By promise, and by the character of God revealed in Christ. The prayer that glory would dwell in the land was answered beyond the singers’ hopes when “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory” (John 1:14). And the meeting of righteousness and peace, which no one could explain, happened at the cross, where God was shown to be “just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus” (Romans 3:26).

For us. A forgiven Christian can find the joy thin and the harvest small, and may pray this psalm without shame: you forgave me then; revive me again. Then listen for the word of peace God speaks in the gospel, refuse to go back to the folly he forgave, and rest on the cross, where his justice and his mercy embraced for you.
85.theology:
Past forgiveness is the basis of present prayer (vv. 1-4), and a restored people can need restoring again (v. 6). Prayer includes listening (v. 8), and God's word of peace carries a call not to return to folly.

The glory that dwells in the land (v. 9) came in person when the Word dwelt among us. Righteousness and peace, which seem to pull apart, meet at the cross, where God is both just and the one who declares sinners righteous (v. 10; Rom 3:26), and heaven and earth are joined (v. 11).
85.examples: Everything was forgiven, and all means all; yet the exiles came home to ruins and a thin harvest. So they pray, you did it then; do it again. The psalm ends with God’s righteousness and his peace, which seemed unable to meet, embracing at the cross.

keyVerse.quote: Steadfast love and faithfulness meet; righteousness and peace kiss each other.
keyVerse.note: This is the vision the whole prayer reaches for: the qualities of God that seemed bound to pull apart, his justice against sin and his peace with sinners, meeting and embracing. The psalm could only see that it must happen. The gospel shows where it did, at the cross, where God is both just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus.

85.reflection:
The psalm prays “Restore us again” (v. 4) on the ground of what God has already done (vv. 1–3). What has God done for you in the past that you can bring to him as a reason to ask again?

Verse 8 stops asking and listens: “Let me hear what God the LORD will speak”. What helps you listen to God in his word, and what crowds it out?

“Let them not turn back to folly” (v. 8). What folly that God has forgiven are you most tempted to return to, and how does the word of peace help you resist it?

How does the cross show that “righteousness and peace kiss each other” (v. 10)? Why does it matter for your assurance that God’s peace with you is also just?

86.text: A Prayer of David. 1Incline your ear, O LORD, and answer me, for I am poor and needy.2Preserve my life, for I am godly; save your servant, who trusts in you—you are my God.3Be gracious to me, O Lord, for to you do I cry all the day.4Gladden the soul of your servant, for to you, O Lord, do I lift up my soul.5For you, O Lord, are good and forgiving, abounding in steadfast love to all who call upon you.6Give ear, O LORD, to my prayer; listen to my plea for grace.7In the day of my trouble I call upon you, for you answer me.8There is none like you among the gods, O Lord, nor are there any works like yours.9All the nations you have made shall come and worship before you, O Lord, and shall glorify your name.10For you are great and do wondrous things; you alone are God.11Teach me your way, O LORD, that I may walk in your truth; unite my heart to fear your name.12I give thanks to you, O Lord my God, with my whole heart, and I will glorify your name forever.13For great is your steadfast love toward me; you have delivered my soul from the depths of Sheol.14O God, insolent men have risen up against me; a band of ruthless men seeks my life, and they do not set you before them.15But you, O Lord, are a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness.16Turn to me and be gracious to me; give your strength to your servant, and save the son of your maidservant.17Show me a sign of your favor, that those who hate me may see and be put to shame because you, LORD, have helped me and comforted me.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — For I Am Poor and Needy
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A believer in trouble pleads his own need and trust, and above all God’s goodness to all who call. David asks God to incline his ear because he is “poor and needy”, loyal to God’s covenant and trusting him (vv. 1–2). He asks for grace and for gladness, lifting his soul to the only one who can give it (vv. 3–4). Then the reasons move from his condition to God’s character, which is the stronger ground: God is “good and forgiving, abounding in steadfast love to all who call upon you” (v. 5). So David calls in the day of trouble, confident that God is the kind who answers (vv. 6–7).
verseByVerse.theology: Every request comes with a reason, and the reasons are his need and God's character.

verseByVerse.quote: Incline your ear, O LORD, and answer me, for I am poor and needy. Preserve my life, for I am godly; save your servant, who trusts in you—you are my God. Be gracious to me, O Lord, for to you do I cry all the day. Gladden the soul of your servant, for to you, O Lord, do I lift up my soul.
verseByVerse.commentary:
David comes to God with nothing to commend him but his need and his trust, and asks to be heard, kept and made glad.

A prayer of borrowed words. This is the only psalm in Book Three that bears David’s name, and it is a prayer made almost entirely of phrases that appear in other psalms and in the law, woven into one plea. When a man is in trouble he reaches for the words he already knows, and the psalm shows a mind so stocked with Scripture that its own prayers come out in Scripture’s language.

For I am poor and needy. The first reason he gives God for listening is his condition: “poor and needy”, the words of Psalm 40:17. It is the reason God responds to. Nobody gets God’s ear by being impressive.

For I am godly. It sounds like boasting until you read on. It is a claim to be loyal to God and his covenant, not to be sinless, and the next clause says what the loyalty consists of: “who trusts in you”. His claim is not that he deserves saving but that he belongs to God and has put his weight on him.

Gladden the soul of your servant. This is a request for joy, not merely rescue. He wants to be made glad again, and he knows where gladness comes from, because that is where he has lifted his soul.

Prayer that argues. Count the word “for” through this psalm: in verses 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 10 and 13. David does not simply ask; he argues, backing every request with a reason. It is prayer that thinks, and a believer is invited to pray that way.

verseByVerse.quote: For you, O Lord, are good and forgiving, abounding in steadfast love to all who call upon you. Give ear, O LORD, to my prayer; listen to my plea for grace. In the day of my trouble I call upon you, for you answer me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The strongest reason for God to hear is not David’s condition but God’s own character: he is good and forgiving to everyone who calls on him.

Good and forgiving. Now the reasons move from David’s condition to God’s character. “Good and forgiving, abounding in steadfast love” echoes what God proclaimed about himself to Moses, and the psalm will quote that proclamation in full at verse 15.

To all who call upon you. The scope is wide, with no qualifying test beyond the calling. Paul says the same of Christ, who is “Lord of all, bestowing his riches on all who call on him” (Romans 10:12). A person who wonders whether God’s steadfast love extends to him has only to ask whether he has called.

For you answer me. This is a settled expectation. The trouble is still on and he has not yet been answered this time, but his history with God has taught him that God is the kind who answers, and he calls on that basis.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–13 — There Is None Like You
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Because God alone is God, his servant asks not only to be rescued but to be taught and given an undivided heart. In the middle of his crisis David lifts his eyes to the whole world: there is none like the LORD among the gods, the nations he made will one day worship him, and he alone does wonders (vv. 8–10). From that wide view comes the psalm’s deepest request: “Teach me your way… unite my heart to fear your name” (v. 11). The answer is already sounding in the next line, a vow to give thanks with his whole heart, because God’s steadfast love has delivered him from the depths of Sheol (vv. 12–13).
verseByVerse.theology: Remembering how great God is shrinks the trouble back to size and makes room to ask for a whole heart.

verseByVerse.quote: There is none like you among the gods, O Lord, nor are there any works like yours. All the nations you have made shall come and worship before you, O Lord, and shall glorify your name. For you are great and do wondrous things; you alone are God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In his trouble David lifts his eyes to the whole world: there is no god like the LORD, the nations he made will come and worship him, and he alone is God.

There is none like you among the gods. Trouble shrinks our horizon to the size of the problem, and the cure is to remember how big God is: no other god compares, and no other works are like his.

All the nations you have made shall come. The logic is careful. God “made” the nations, so they belong to him, and one day they “shall come”. A poor and needy man in a corner of Israel prays with the whole world’s future in view. John heard the redeemed at the end of history singing exactly this, in “the song of Moses, the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb”: “All nations will come and worship you, for your righteous acts have been revealed” (Revelation 15:3–4). The nations come because the Lamb was slain.

You alone are God. That is the confession that makes a man’s private trouble manageable. If God alone is God, then the insolent men of verse 14 are not.

Do other gods exist? They are not rivals of the LORD’s kind. They are the gods the nations worshipped, which are idols (Psalm 96:5), and the demonic powers behind them (Deuteronomy 32:17; 1 Corinthians 10:20). “There is no God but one” (1 Corinthians 8:4).

verseByVerse.quote: Teach me your way, O LORD, that I may walk in your truth; unite my heart to fear your name. I give thanks to you, O Lord my God, with my whole heart, and I will glorify your name forever. For great is your steadfast love toward me; you have delivered my soul from the depths of Sheol.
verseByVerse.commentary:
With enemies after his life, David’s deepest request is to be taught God’s way and given an undivided heart, and he promises to use that whole heart in thanks.

Unite my heart to fear your name. He asks first for teaching, then for a heart made one. He knows his heart is split: part of it fearing God, part fearing men; part trusting, part scheming. James calls that man “a double-minded man, unstable in all his ways” (James 1:8). And a divided heart cannot fear God properly, because the fear of God is the whole heart bowed in one direction.

A request, not a resolution. Only God can do this. God later promised it as a gift of the new covenant: “I will give them one heart and one way, that they may fear me forever” (Jeremiah 32:39). Anyone who has tried to love God with a heart that keeps going elsewhere can pray this verse every morning, and the Spirit who gives the new heart (Ezekiel 36:26–27) is how God answers it.

With my whole heart. The answer is in the next line: “with my whole heart”. The united heart is a thankful one. The reason for thanks is a rescue from “the depths of Sheol”, the realm of the dead, whether a past deliverance or one so certain he speaks of it as done. Either way, the man who asked for a whole heart ends up using it to give thanks.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Against men who leave God out of account, David sets God’s own name and asks for help that his enemies can see. The threat is named at last: insolent, ruthless men seeking his life, who “do not set you before them” (v. 14). David answers not with a plan but with a confession, quoting almost word for word the name God proclaimed to Moses at Sinai: merciful, gracious, slow to anger, abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness (v. 15). On that ground he asks God to turn to him, give strength to his servant and save the son of his maidservant, and to show a sign of favour that will shame his enemies, because the LORD has helped and comforted him (vv. 16–17).
verseByVerse.theology: The difference between the godly and the ruthless is what each keeps before his eyes.

verseByVerse.quote: O God, insolent men have risen up against me; a band of ruthless men seeks my life, and they do not set you before them. But you, O Lord, are a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness. Turn to me and be gracious to me; give your strength to your servant, and save the son of your maidservant. Show me a sign of your favor, that those who hate me may see and be put to shame because you, LORD, have helped me and comforted me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Against ruthless men who leave God out of account, David sets the name God proclaimed at Sinai, and asks for strength and a visible sign that God is on his side.

They do not set you before them. The trouble is named at last: arrogant men, a gang, ruthless, after his life. And the diagnosis is exact. It is the reverse of Psalm 16, where David said, “I have set the LORD always before me” (Psalm 16:8). The difference between the godly man and the ruthless one is not that one is stronger, but what each keeps in front of his eyes. People who leave God out of their reckoning will do anything.

A God merciful and gracious. Against the gang who leave God out, David sets God’s own name, almost word for word the proclamation from Sinai: “The LORD, the LORD, a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness” (Exodus 34:6). He answers the threat by stating who God is. When men are ruthless, the believer’s refuge is that God is not.

That name took flesh. John says the Word who dwelt among us was “full of grace and truth” (John 1:14), his words for the steadfast love and faithfulness proclaimed at Sinai. The God David pleaded with is the God we see in Jesus.

The son of your maidservant. This is a household term. A servant born to a servant in the house was not bought from outside; he belonged to the household from birth and had a claim on its master’s protection. David says he was born into God’s house. Psalm 116 uses the same words: “I am your servant, the son of your maidservant” (Psalm 116:16).

Show me a sign of your favor. The last request is modest: a sign, something visible, enough that his enemies can see God is on his side. The final words are the two things God does for the poor and needy man of verse 1: he has “helped me and comforted me”. Help for the trouble outside; comfort for the soul inside. He asks for both, and the psalm speaks of both as already given.

86.title: Unite My Heart to Fear Your Name
86.overview:
Where we are. In the middle of the Korahite psalms of Book Three stands the only psalm in that book bearing the name of David. After Psalm 85’s prayer for the nation, this is one man’s prayer in trouble, made almost entirely of phrases found elsewhere in Scripture.

The message. A needy believer under threat may come to God with nothing to recommend him but his need and his trust, and plead God’s own character: good and forgiving, merciful and gracious, abounding in steadfast love to all who call. Because God alone is God, his servant can ask not only for rescue but for an undivided heart that fears him and thanks him with all of itself.

Why it was said. David is in danger: insolent and ruthless men are after his life, men who “do not set you before them” (v. 14). The psalm does not name the occasion; it was kept and sung because every believer meets such days.

How the chapter makes its case. Nearly every request comes with a reason, the little word “for” recurring through the psalm. First David pleads his need and his trust, and then, more strongly, God’s goodness to all who call (vv. 1–7). Then he lifts his eyes: there is none like God; all the nations he made will come and worship him; he alone is God (vv. 8–10). From there comes the central prayer, “unite my heart to fear your name”, and a vow of whole-hearted thanks for deliverance from Sheol (vv. 11–13). Finally he names the ruthless men and sets against them the name God proclaimed on Sinai, asking for strength and a sign of favour (vv. 14–17).

Where it leads. Chiefly by the character of God revealed in Christ. The name David pleads, “merciful and gracious… abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness” (v. 15), took flesh in the Word who was “full of grace and truth” (John 1:14). The nations David saw coming to worship are seen in Revelation singing “the song of the Lamb” (Revelation 15:3). And by pattern: the poor and needy servant who cried to God against ruthless men and was heard is filled out in Jesus, the true Servant, who “offered up prayers and supplications” and “was heard because of his reverence” (Hebrews 5:7).

For us. You do not need to be impressive to get God’s ear; you need only to call. Pray with reasons drawn from who God is, ask him daily to unite your divided heart, and when others leave God out of their reckoning, set him before you and rest on his name.
86.theology:
Prayer is argued with reasons: the need and trust of the one praying (vv. 1-4), and above all God's character (v. 5), open to all who call. Personal trouble is set within God's universal reign: the nations he made will come and worship him (vv. 8-10).

The deepest request is for an undivided heart (v. 11), which only God can give (Jer 32:39) and which leads to whole-hearted thanks (v. 12). Against those who do not set God before them (v. 14), David sets the name God proclaimed on Sinai (v. 15; Exod 34:6), the name that took flesh full of grace and truth.
86.examples: This is a prayer made of borrowed Scripture, from a man who knows nobody gets God's ear by being impressive. Trouble shrinks his horizon and the nations widen it again. His heart is pulled in several directions and he asks for it to be made one, and he takes his stand as a servant born in God's house.

keyVerse.quote: Teach me your way, O LORD, that I may walk in your truth; unite my heart to fear your name.
keyVerse.note: With his life under threat, David’s deepest request is not for rescue but for teaching and an undivided heart. It sits at the centre of the psalm, between the confession that God alone is God and the vow to thank him with the whole heart. Only God can make a divided heart one, and he promised to do it in the new covenant.

86.reflection:
David backs nearly every request with a reason, the word “for” recurring through the psalm. What reasons drawn from God’s character could you bring to him in what you are praying about now?

“For you, O Lord, are good and forgiving, abounding in steadfast love to all who call upon you” (v. 5). Why is it good news that the only qualification is calling? Who do you know who needs to hear that?

Where is your heart most divided between fearing God and fearing people, or between trusting and scheming? What would it mean to pray “unite my heart to fear your name” (v. 11) each morning?

The ruthless men “do not set you before them” (v. 14). What practical habits help you keep God before your eyes through an ordinary day?

87.text: A Psalm of the Sons of Korah. A Song. 1On the holy mount stands the city he founded;2the LORD loves the gates of Zion more than all the dwelling places of Jacob.3Glorious things of you are spoken, O city of God. Selah4Among those who know me I mention Rahab and Babylon; behold, Philistia and Tyre, with Cush — "This one was born there," they say.5And of Zion it shall be said, "This one and that one were born in her"; for the Most High himself will establish her.6The LORD records as he registers the peoples, "This one was born there." Selah7Singers and dancers alike say, "All my springs are in you."

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Zion stands because God founded her, and he loves her as the place he chose to meet his people. The psalm begins, without naming him, with “the city he founded” on the holy mountain (v. 1): in Israel only one founder could be meant. The LORD loves her gates, where his people came in to worship, more than every other dwelling place of Jacob (v. 2). And glorious things are spoken of her (v. 3). The section raises the question the rest of the psalm answers: what is the most glorious thing said about the city of God? Not her walls or her temple, as it turns out, but the people who are counted as born in her.
verseByVerse.theology: The city is glorious not for its walls but because God founded it and loves it.

verseByVerse.quote: On the holy mount stands the city he founded; the LORD loves the gates of Zion more than all the dwelling places of Jacob. Glorious things of you are spoken, O city of God. Selah
verseByVerse.commentary:
Zion stands because God founded her and loves her as the place where he meets his people, and glorious things are said of her.

The city he founded. Its founder is not named in the first line, just “he”, because in Israel there was only one person who could be meant. Zion was not chosen because it was strong or beautiful; it stands because God founded it.

The LORD loves the gates of Zion. The gates of Zion, where people came in to worship and where the city met, are loved more than every other town in Israel. God’s love for a place is really his love for what happens there: it is where he chose to put his name and meet his people.

Glorious things of you are spoken. The most glorious thing spoken of the city is not the temple, the palace or the walls, but the list of who lives there, which the psalm now reads out.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–7 — This One Was Born There
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God registers people from Israel’s old enemies as citizens born in Zion, and they sing that every spring of their life is in her. The list in verse 4 is a shock: Rahab, a poetic name for Egypt, Babylon, Philistia, Tyre and far-off Cush, all named “among those who know me”, with the verdict, “This one was born there”. Verse 5 presses it home person by person, “This one and that one”, and grounds the city’s future in the Most High himself. Verse 6 pictures God keeping the census, writing each name in. Verse 7 gives the new citizens’ song: “All my springs are in you.”
verseByVerse.theology: Israel's worst enemies are enrolled as native citizens of the city of God.

verseByVerse.quote: Among those who know me I mention Rahab and Babylon; behold, Philistia and Tyre, with Cush — "This one was born there," they say.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God names Israel’s old oppressors and enemies, from Egypt to the far south, among those who know him, and counts each of them as born in Zion.

I mention Rahab and Babylon. God now reads out a list of nations, and every one is a shock. “Rahab” here is not the woman of Jericho but a poetic name for Egypt (Isaiah calls Egypt “Rahab who sits still”, Isaiah 30:7), the house of slavery, the first oppressor. Babylon is the empire that burned the temple and carried the people away. Philistia was the old enemy on the coast, Goliath’s people. Tyre was the wealthy, proud trading city. And Cush, which the ESV notes is probably Nubia, lay at the far southern edge of the known world.

Among those who know me. To know God is how Scripture speaks of belonging to him by covenant; it was said of Israel. And each of these is a native of Zion, not a visitor, resident alien or tolerated guest.

Enemies become God’s people. Isaiah heard God say, “Blessed be Egypt my people, and Assyria the work of my hands, and Israel my inheritance” (Isaiah 19:25). The enemies of God’s people become God’s people.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew of this psalm is unusually terse, and it is not always clear who speaks. The ESV takes “I mention” as God’s words, which suits verse 6, where the LORD keeps the register; the “they say” of verse 4 may be what others say of each new citizen, or the register’s own entry. The meaning is not in doubt: these nations are counted as Zion’s own.
verseByVerse.note: Rahab here is a poetic name for Egypt, not the woman of Jericho.

verseByVerse.quote: And of Zion it shall be said, "This one and that one were born in her"; for the Most High himself will establish her. The LORD records as he registers the peoples, "This one was born there." Selah Singers and dancers alike say, "All my springs are in you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God counts each person one by one and writes their name into Zion’s register as native-born, and the new citizens find every source of life in the city of God.

This one and that one were born in her. Person by person. Membership of the city of God is not granted to whole nations at once; each person is counted. And the city’s security rests where it did in verse 1: “the Most High himself will establish her”.

The LORD records as he registers the peoples. The picture is a census. God himself keeps the register and writes each name in, with the entry: born in Zion. It is the register Jesus told his disciples to rejoice in: “rejoice that your names are written in heaven” (Luke 10:20). Hebrews calls the church “the assembly of the firstborn who are enrolled in heaven” (Hebrews 12:23).

The Jerusalem above. Paul spoke of this city: “the Jerusalem above is free, and she is our mother” (Galatians 4:26). A Gentile Christian from Galatia or Rome or Ethiopia has a birthplace in the city of God: “you are no longer strangers and aliens, but you are fellow citizens with the saints and members of the household of God” (Ephesians 2:19).

For anyone who feels an outsider. That is the answer for anyone who feels like an outsider to God’s people, from the wrong background, the wrong nation, with the wrong past. Citizenship of this city is not by ancestry but by God’s registration, and his entry is “born there”. Jesus called it being born again (John 3:3). Luke tells of an Ethiopian official, from that same far southern land, who “had come to Jerusalem to worship” (Acts 8:27) and went home with his name in the register.

Who decides who you are? Modern people are told that identity is something we create: look inside, decide who you are, and insist that the world recognise it. There is a real freedom in that, and also a crushing weight: if I make myself, I must keep making myself, and every rejection is a verdict on my own handiwork. Older cultures did the reverse and fixed your identity by birth, family and nation, which gave security but shut out whoever was born in the wrong place. Psalm 87 overturns both. Your identity here is neither self-made nor inherited. It is written in by God, and he writes Egyptians and Babylonians into Zion’s register as natives. You cannot achieve that entry, and you cannot lose it by being born in the wrong place. That is what the New Testament means by adoption: “See what kind of love the Father has given to us, that we should be called children of God; and so we are” (1 John 3:1). A name written by God does not need to be defended or performed. It can simply be lived in.

All my springs are in you. Former enemies from every nation sing and dance together, and their song is short. Every source of life and refreshment they have, they find in the city of God, which is to say, in the God of the city. In a dry land, a spring is the reason a town exists. John saw the end of it: a multitude “from every nation, from all tribes and peoples and languages, standing before the throne and before the Lamb” (Revelation 7:9). Egypt and Babylon among them.

Uncertain wording. Verse 7 is very brief in Hebrew, literally something like and singers as well as dancers, with no verb, so “say” is supplied. The word the ESV renders “dancers” may instead mean players on pipes, as the King James Version took it. Either way the picture is of the city’s new citizens making music, and the words of their song, “All my springs are in you”, are clear.

87.title: Glorious Things of You Are Spoken
87.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 87 is a short song of the sons of Korah, set in the dark third book of the Psalter between David’s prayer in trouble (86) and the bleakest lament of all (88). Like Psalms 46 and 48, it sings of Zion, the city of God, but it says something about her no other psalm says.

The message. The city God founded and loves will be filled with people from the nations that were once her enemies, and each will be registered by God himself as born there. Belonging to God’s people is not by ancestry or achievement but by God’s own entry in his register, and those he writes in find every spring of their life in him.

Why it was said. The occasion is not given. Israel had suffered at the hands of Egypt, Babylon, Philistia and Tyre, and to a small, often threatened people these names meant oppression and contempt. The psalm takes the most hostile names on the map and reads them out as citizens of Zion.

How the chapter makes its case. It begins with the city itself: founded by God on the holy mountain, loved by him above every other town of Jacob, the subject of glorious words (vv. 1–3). Then God speaks, listing Rahab (Egypt), Babylon, Philistia, Tyre and Cush among “those who know me”, and of each the verdict is, “This one was born there” (v. 4). The point is pressed home: each person is counted, the Most High establishes the city, and the LORD himself writes the entry in the register of the peoples (vv. 5–6). The psalm ends with the new citizens singing and dancing: “All my springs are in you” (v. 7).

Where it leads. By promise. God had told Abraham that in him “all the families of the earth shall be blessed” (Genesis 12:3), and this psalm sees it happening in Zion. The New Testament announces its fulfilment in Christ: “the Jerusalem above is free, and she is our mother” (Galatians 4:26), and believing Gentiles “are fellow citizens with the saints and members of the household of God” (Ephesians 2:19). The register is the one Jesus told his disciples to rejoice in, “your names are written in heaven” (Luke 10:20), and the birth is the new birth he spoke of (John 3:3).

For us. If you feel like an outsider to God’s people because of your background or your past, this psalm is for you: in Christ, God writes you in as a native. Your identity is neither self-made nor inherited but given, so you need not perform it or defend it; and every spring of your life can be found in him.
87.theology:
The city's glory lies in God's founding and love (vv. 1-3), and its most glorious feature is its citizens. Israel's oppressors and distant nations are enrolled as native-born (v. 4), as Isaiah foresaw (Isa 19:24-25), each one individually and by God's own hand (vv. 5-6).

The New Testament names the city as the Jerusalem above, mother of believers (Gal 4:26), where Gentiles are fellow citizens with names written in heaven. Every source of life is found there (v. 7), and the end is a multitude from every nation before the throne.
87.examples: The city stands because God founded it, and Egypt and Babylon are on its list of those who know him. They are counted one by one, this one and that one, like the Ethiopian official who went home with his name in the book. The psalm ends with a festival of former enemies singing about springs.

keyVerse.quote: And of Zion it shall be said, “This one and that one were born in her”; for the Most High himself will establish her.
keyVerse.note: The psalm’s great surprise is that people from Israel’s enemies are counted not as guests but as natives of Zion, one by one. Their place rests not on their ancestry but on the Most High himself, who establishes the city and writes them in. It looks forward to the church of every nation, whose names are written in heaven.

87.reflection:
Read the list in verse 4. Which nations or kinds of people would be the most surprising names on such a list today? What does it tell you about God that he writes such people into Zion’s register?

The verdict on each is “This one was born there” (vv. 4, 6), not merely that each was allowed to visit. How does knowing that you belong to God’s people as a native, not a guest, change the way you come to church or to prayer?

Our culture says identity is something you create; older cultures said it is something you inherit. How does the psalm’s answer, an identity written in by God, free you from both?

“All my springs are in you” (v. 7). Where do you actually go for refreshment and life when you are dry? What would it look like to find your springs in God this week?

88.text: A Song. A Psalm of the Sons of Korah. To the choirmaster: according to Mahalath Leannoth. A Maskil of Heman the Ezrahite. 1O LORD, God of my salvation, I cry out day and night before you.2Let my prayer come before you; incline your ear to my cry!3For my soul is full of troubles, and my life draws near to Sheol.4I am counted among those who go down to the pit; I am a man who has no strength,5like one set loose among the dead, like the slain that lie in the grave, like those whom you remember no more, for they are cut off from your hand.6You have put me in the depths of the pit, in the regions dark and deep.7Your wrath lies heavy upon me, and you overwhelm me with all your waves. Selah8You have caused my companions to shun me; you have made me a horror to them. I am shut in so that I cannot escape;9my eye grows dim through sorrow. Every day I call upon you, O LORD; I spread out my hands to you.10Do you work wonders for the dead? Do the departed rise up to praise you? Selah11Is your steadfast love declared in the grave, or your faithfulness in Abaddon?12Are your wonders known in the darkness, or your righteousness in the land of forgetfulness?13But I, O LORD, cry to you; in the morning my prayer comes before you.14O LORD, why do you cast my soul away? Why do you hide your face from me?15Afflicted and close to death from my youth up, I suffer your terrors; I am helpless.16Your wrath has swept over me; your dreadful assaults destroy me.17They surround me like a flood all day long; they close in on me together.18You have caused my beloved and my friend to shun me; my companions have become darkness.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — I Cry Out Day and Night
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Near death, shunned by his friends and feeling God’s wrath, Heman keeps calling on the God of his salvation every day. He begins with the only words of hope in the psalm and a plea to be heard (vv. 1–2). Then he describes his state: his soul full of troubles, his strength gone, counted among those who go down to the pit, like the dead whom God remembers no more (vv. 3–5). He does not blame chance or enemies: God has laid him in the depths, his wrath lies heavy, his waves overwhelm (vv. 6–7). His companions shun him, he is shut in, his eyes grow dim, and still he spreads out his hands to God every day (vv. 8–9).
verseByVerse.theology: A man near death keeps praying to the God he believes has put him there.

verseByVerse.quote: O LORD, God of my salvation, I cry out day and night before you. Let my prayer come before you; incline your ear to my cry!
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the darkest psalm in the Bible, Heman still calls the LORD “God of my salvation” before he says anything else, and he keeps crying to him day and night.

The darkest psalm. Almost every other lament in the Psalter turns somewhere: to trust, to a vow of praise, to a remembered mercy. This one begins in trouble and ends in darkness, and nothing in between lifts.

O LORD, God of my salvation. These words are the only statement of hope in the psalm, and they are spoken before a word of complaint. The man still calls God the God who saves him. He cannot see it, he does not feel it, and nothing that follows will confirm it, but he says it, and he says it first.

I cry out day and night before you. That is itself the faith of this psalm: not a feeling of confidence, but a refusal to stop speaking to God. Heman was a name associated with wisdom (1 Kings 4:31, where Solomon is said to be wiser still) and with the temple singers (1 Chronicles 6:33); whether these were one man is uncertain, and the heading names both Heman and the sons of Korah, perhaps the singer and his guild. This is what a wise man’s prayer sounds like when there is no light at all.

Uncertain wording. The heading’s “Mahalath Leannoth” is not understood. It probably names a tune or a manner of performance; some connect the words with sickness and affliction, which would suit the psalm, but that is a guess. “Maskil” is also uncertain, probably a musical or teaching term.
verseByVerse.note: Heman the Ezrahite was a famous wise man and musician.

verseByVerse.quote: For my soul is full of troubles, and my life draws near to Sheol. I am counted among those who go down to the pit; I am a man who has no strength, like one set loose among the dead, like the slain that lie in the grave, like those whom you remember no more, for they are cut off from your hand. You have put me in the depths of the pit, in the regions dark and deep. Your wrath lies heavy upon me, and you overwhelm me with all your waves. Selah
verseByVerse.commentary:
Heman is near death and already treated as one of the dead, and he says plainly that it is God who has laid him in the pit and overwhelmed him with his waves.

My soul is full of troubles. His soul is full of troubles, with no room left. He is near death and people already treat him as good as dead: “counted among those who go down to the pit”. A man who has no strength is a man whom others have stopped expecting anything from. Anyone who has been seriously ill for a long time knows how it feels to be written off while still alive.

Like those whom you remember no more. The fear goes deeper than death. It is being remembered no more by God, “cut off from your hand”. The Old Testament believer had only a dim view of what lay beyond the grave, and the horror here is not pain but abandonment: being set loose, like a discharged soldier, into a place God does not visit.

You have put me in the depths of the pit. God is the subject of every verb. Heman does not blame chance, enemies or himself: God did it. That is terrible, and it is also, strangely, a kind of faith: he refuses to believe his suffering is outside God’s hand. Jonah, in the belly of the fish, used the same image: “all your waves and your billows passed over me” (Jonah 2:3).

Does that mean God is angry with a suffering believer? Heman describes how it felt, and Scripture lets him. But for anyone in Christ the wrath itself has been carried: “There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1). What feels like wrath may be a long darkness; it is not God’s sentence.

Uncertain wording. “Set loose” (v. 5) translates a word usually meaning “free”, used of a released slave. Its sense among the dead is not certain: perhaps released from life’s duties, perhaps abandoned and left to himself. Either way it pictures a man cut adrift from God’s care.

verseByVerse.quote: You have caused my companions to shun me; you have made me a horror to them. I am shut in so that I cannot escape; my eye grows dim through sorrow. Every day I call upon you, O LORD; I spread out my hands to you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
His illness has cut him off from his friends, and with nothing coming back from heaven he still spreads out his hands to God every day.

You have caused my companions to shun me. The illness, whatever it was, has isolated him. His friends avoid him. He has become “a horror” to them (the ESV notes “an abomination” as a possible rendering), perhaps because the disease made him unclean, perhaps simply because long suffering is unbearable to watch and people stay away. Job said the same: “He has put my brothers far from me, and those who knew me are wholly estranged from me” (Job 19:13).

I spread out my hands to you. This is the posture of a beggar or a drowning man, empty and reaching. Nothing comes back. He does it the next day.

If you are praying like this. If you are praying every day, for a long time, with no answer, this psalm is in the Bible for you. God has put into his own book the prayer of a man for whom nothing got better, and has called it a song.

The God who is not a therapist. A great deal of modern religion, in and out of church, quietly assumes that God exists to make us feel better: faith is worth having if it lowers stress and lifts mood, and a prayer that does not help is a technique that has failed. Psalm 88 could not survive in that religion, and its presence in the Bible is a standing rebuke to it. Here is a man for whom faith produced no relief at all, and he went on praying anyway, because God was not his coping mechanism but his God. Nor does wishful thinking write Psalm 88; nobody invents a God in order to complain to him for eighteen verses. This is what it looks like to deal with someone real. The God of the Bible does not promise that the darkness will lift on schedule. He promises himself: “Let him who walks in darkness and has no light trust in the name of the LORD and rely on his God” (Isaiah 50:10). The Son who prayed in the dark of Gethsemane and the cross was not given a better mood. He was given a resurrection.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–12 — Do the Departed Rise Up to Praise You?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Heman argues with God by questions: if he dies, who will praise God in the grave? Each of his questions expects the answer no. Does God work wonders for the dead? Do the departed rise up to praise him (v. 10)? Is his steadfast love declared in the grave, his faithfulness in Abaddon, the place of destruction (v. 11)? Are his wonders known in the darkness, or his righteousness in “the land of forgetfulness” (v. 12)? The argument is that God’s praise needs living worshippers, so he should keep this one alive. In Heman’s day that was as far as the light reached; the resurrection of Christ has since given an answer he could not imagine.
verseByVerse.theology: He argues with God: if I die, you lose a worshipper.

verseByVerse.quote: Do you work wonders for the dead? Do the departed rise up to praise you? Selah Is your steadfast love declared in the grave, or your faithfulness in Abaddon? Are your wonders known in the darkness, or your righteousness in the land of forgetfulness?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Heman argues with God by questions that expect the answer no: the dead do not praise God, so let him live; and the resurrection of Christ has since answered yes.

Do you work wonders for the dead? The argument is simple: if I die, who gains? The dead do not sing in the temple. If God wants to be praised by this man, he had better keep him alive.

Your faithfulness in Abaddon. “Abaddon” means destruction, and “the land of forgetfulness” is a haunting name for the grave, the place where the dead forget and are forgotten. The questions expect the answer no.

Answered on the third day. In Heman’s day that was as far as the light reached. But the questions have since been answered in a way he could not have imagined. “Do the departed rise up to praise you?” The answer given on the third day, when Christ rose, was yes. And now nothing, not even death, can separate a believer from God’s steadfast love: “neither death nor life… nor height nor depth, nor anything else in all creation, will be able to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Romans 8:38–39). The land of forgetfulness is not beyond God’s memory after all.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–18 — Why Do You Hide Your Face?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Heman prays again in the morning to a God who hides his face, and the psalm ends in darkness. After the questions he does not give up but brings his prayer before God first thing (v. 13). He asks the hardest question of all: why do you cast my soul away and hide your face (v. 14)? Then he describes a lifetime of affliction: close to death from his youth, suffering God’s terrors, helpless (v. 15). God’s wrath sweeps over him and surrounds him like a flood all day (vv. 16–17). The last line returns to the lost friends: “my companions have become darkness” (v. 18). No resolution is given, and Scripture lets it stand.
verseByVerse.theology: The psalm ends without a resolution, and its last word is darkness.

verseByVerse.quote: But I, O LORD, cry to you; in the morning my prayer comes before you. O LORD, why do you cast my soul away? Why do you hide your face from me?
verseByVerse.commentary:
After the questions Heman keeps praying, first thing in the morning, and asks the hardest question of all: why does God hide his face?

In the morning my prayer comes before you. After questions that seem to leave no room for hope, he goes back to praying, first thing, before anything else. Day and night (v. 1), every day (v. 9), in the morning (v. 13). The psalm has no answer from God in it, but it has a man who keeps turning up.

Why do you hide your face from me? The worst of it is not the illness or the loneliness. It is God’s hidden face. The man who has lost his friends could perhaps bear it if God’s face were turned towards him. It is not.

The hidden face, borne by the Son. Someone has prayed these words more completely than Heman. On the cross Jesus cried, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matthew 27:46). The Son experienced the hidden face of the Father fully, so that no one who belongs to him ever will, whatever it feels like in the dark.

verseByVerse.quote: Afflicted and close to death from my youth up, I suffer your terrors; I am helpless. Your wrath has swept over me; your dreadful assaults destroy me. They surround me like a flood all day long; they close in on me together. You have caused my beloved and my friend to shun me; my companions have become darkness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Heman has suffered all his life, God’s terrors close over him like a flood, and the psalm ends with no resolution and the word “darkness”; yet Christ has entered that darkness for his people.

Close to death from my youth up. The affliction has lasted his whole life. Some people carry a sickness, a darkness of mind, or a sorrow from childhood that never lifts, and this verse is theirs.

They surround me like a flood all day long. The flood rises again from every side. It is the language of drowning: not one wave, but water that closes over the head.

My companions have become darkness. The last word of the psalm is “darkness”, with no resolution. God’s people have always needed a psalm that does not resolve, because life does not always resolve on schedule, and Heman’s prayer is in Scripture without the happy last verse he could not write.

Not alone in the dark. But he is not alone in the dark. Jesus said, “My soul is very sorrowful, even to death” (Matthew 26:38). He was “a man of sorrows and acquainted with grief” (Isaiah 53:3); at the cross “all his acquaintances… stood at a distance” (Luke 23:49). He “offered up prayers and supplications, with loud cries and tears, to him who was able to save him from death, and he was heard” (Hebrews 5:7). The God of Heman’s salvation went down into this psalm himself, and came out the other side, and the darkness is not the last companion of anyone who is his.

If darkness is your companion. Long darkness of mind is not proof of failed faith; Heman wrote this, and it is Scripture. Those who live in such darkness should pray, and also seek help from pastors and friends and a biblical counsellor, who will ask for a medical check-up too (1 Thessalonians 5:14); if a doctor prescribes medicine, taking it is no failure of faith. If the darkness has brought thoughts of ending your life, tell someone today, a pastor, a friend, a doctor or an emergency line, and do not wait until you can pray well.

Uncertain wording. The ESV notes that the meaning of the Hebrew word rendered “helpless” (v. 15) is uncertain; some states of the soul have no clear word. In verse 18 it gives another rendering of the last line: “darkness has become my only companion”. Either way the psalm ends in the dark.

88.title: My Companions Have Become Darkness
88.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 87 sang of the nations born in Zion; Psalm 88 is the darkest psalm in the Bible. Book Three of the Psalter has been growing darker, and here a single sufferer, Heman, cries to God from the edge of the grave, and nothing lifts.

The message. A believer may be in darkness for a long time, feel God’s hand against him, lose every friend, and still go on calling the LORD “God of my salvation” and praying to him day after day. Faith here is not a feeling of confidence but a refusal to stop speaking to God, and God has put this prayer, unresolved, in his own book.

Why it was said. Heman has been “afflicted and close to death from my youth up” (v. 15): a long illness or affliction has left him near death, shunned by his friends and feeling the weight of God’s wrath. The psalm gives no other occasion. It was kept for everyone whose suffering does not resolve on schedule.

How the chapter makes its case. It begins with the one statement of hope, “O LORD, God of my salvation”, and the plea to be heard (vv. 1–2). Then the descent: his soul is full of troubles, he is counted among the dead, God has laid him in the pit and overwhelmed him with waves, and his friends shun him; yet every day he spreads out his hands (vv. 3–9). He argues with God in questions: do the dead praise you? is your steadfast love declared in the grave? (vv. 10–12). He prays again in the morning and asks why God hides his face (vv. 13–14). And he ends with lifelong affliction, waves closing in, and the last word “darkness” (vv. 15–18).

Where it leads. By pattern, and by the need it exposes. Heman’s questions, “Do the departed rise up to praise you?”, had no answer in his day; on the third day after the cross the answer was yes. And someone has prayed this psalm more completely than Heman. Jesus was “a man of sorrows” (Isaiah 53:3), his friends stood at a distance, and on the cross he cried, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matthew 27:46). He bore the hidden face and the wrath so that no one who is his ever will, and he came out the other side.

For us. If you are in the dark, this psalm gives you leave to say so to God and to keep saying it; your faith has not failed because you feel no relief. Keep turning up in prayer, let others help you, and hold on to the risen Christ, who has been in the darkness and will not let it be your last companion.
88.theology:
Unlike almost every other lament, this psalm ends with no turn to trust or praise. Its faith lies in its first words, God of my salvation (v. 1), and in prayer that does not stop (vv. 1, 9, 13). Suffering is attributed to God's own hand (vv. 6-8, 16-18), which is anguish and also a refusal to place it outside his control.

The questions of vv. 10-12 reflect how little the Old Testament had yet revealed about the grave; they are answered by the resurrection and by the promise that nothing in death separates believers from God's love (Rom 8:38-39).

Christ bore the hiding of God’s face in full (Matt 27:46), the man of sorrows abandoned by his friends, who was heard (Heb 5:7). The Bible includes an unresolved prayer so that believers in lasting darkness are not told their faith has failed.
88.examples: The only light in the psalm is its first line, and every verb after it has God as its subject. Hands are spread out every day and nothing comes back. Yet the land of forgetfulness is not beyond God's memory, and a psalm whose last word is darkness is still Scripture.

keyVerse.quote: O LORD, God of my salvation, I cry out day and night before you.
keyVerse.note: These are the only words of hope in the darkest psalm, and Heman says them first, before any complaint. Everything that follows contradicts his feelings, yet he keeps calling the LORD the God who saves him and keeps praying day and night. That is what faith looks like when there is no light: not a feeling of confidence, but a refusal to stop speaking to God.

88.reflection:
Heman calls God “God of my salvation” (v. 1) though nothing in the psalm seems to confirm it. What does it mean to keep speaking to God when you feel no answer?

Why do you think God put a psalm with no happy ending in his book? How might it help someone you know who is in a long darkness?

Heman’s friends shun him (vv. 8, 18). What keeps us away from people whose suffering goes on for a long time, and how could your group stay close to such a person?

Jesus prayed in the dark of Gethsemane and the cross, and rose again. How does his resurrection answer Heman’s questions in verses 10–12, and how does it change the way you face your own darkness?

89.text: A Maskil of Ethan the Ezrahite. 1I will sing of the steadfast love of the LORD forever; with my mouth I will make known your faithfulness to all generations.2For I said, "Steadfast love will be built up forever; in the heavens you will establish your faithfulness."3You have said, "I have made a covenant with my chosen one; I have sworn to David my servant:4'I will establish your offspring forever, and build your throne for all generations.'" Selah5Let the heavens praise your wonders, O LORD, your faithfulness in the assembly of the holy ones!6For who in the skies can be compared to the LORD? Who among the heavenly beings is like the LORD,7a God greatly to be feared in the council of the holy ones, and awesome above all who are around him?8O LORD God of hosts, who is mighty as you are, O LORD, with your faithfulness all around you?9You rule the raging of the sea; when its waves rise, you still them.10You crushed Rahab like a carcass; you scattered your enemies with your mighty arm.11The heavens are yours; the earth also is yours; the world and all that is in it, you have founded them.12The north and the south, you have created them; Tabor and Hermon joyously praise your name.13You have a mighty arm; strong is your hand, high your right hand.14Righteousness and justice are the foundation of your throne; steadfast love and faithfulness go before you.15Blessed are the people who know the festal shout, who walk, O LORD, in the light of your face,16who exult in your name all the day and in your righteousness are exalted.17For you are the glory of their strength; by your favor our horn is exalted.18For our shield belongs to the LORD, our king to the Holy One of Israel.19Of old you spoke in a vision to your godly one, and said: "I have granted help to one who is mighty; I have exalted one chosen from the people.20I have found David, my servant; with my holy oil I have anointed him,21so that my hand shall be established with him; my arm also shall strengthen him.22The enemy shall not outwit him; the wicked shall not humble him.23I will crush his foes before him and strike down those who hate him.24My faithfulness and my steadfast love shall be with him, and in my name shall his horn be exalted.25I will set his hand on the sea and his right hand on the rivers.26He shall cry to me, 'You are my Father, my God, and the Rock of my salvation.'27And I will make him the firstborn, the highest of the kings of the earth.28My steadfast love I will keep for him forever, and my covenant will stand firm for him.29I will establish his offspring forever and his throne as the days of the heavens.30If his children forsake my law and do not walk according to my rules,31if they violate my statutes and do not keep my commandments,32then I will punish their transgression with the rod and their iniquity with stripes,33but I will not remove from him my steadfast love or be false to my faithfulness.34I will not violate my covenant or alter the word that went forth from my lips.35Once for all I have sworn by my holiness; I will not lie to David.36His offspring shall endure forever, his throne as long as the sun before me.37Like the moon it shall be established forever, a faithful witness in the skies." Selah38But now you have cast off and rejected; you are full of wrath against your anointed.39You have renounced the covenant with your servant; you have defiled his crown in the dust.40You have breached all his walls; you have laid his strongholds in ruins.41All who pass by plunder him; he has become the scorn of his neighbors.42You have exalted the right hand of his foes; you have made all his enemies rejoice.43You have also turned back the edge of his sword, and you have not made him stand in battle.44You have made his splendor to cease and cast his throne to the ground.45You have cut short the days of his youth; you have covered him with shame. Selah46How long, O LORD? Will you hide yourself forever? How long will your wrath burn like fire?47Remember how short my time is! For what vanity you have created all the children of man!48What man can live and never see death? Who can deliver his soul from the power of Sheol? Selah49Lord, where is your steadfast love of old, which by your faithfulness you swore to David?50Remember, O Lord, how your servants are mocked, and how I bear in my heart the insults of all the many nations,51with which your enemies mock, O LORD, with which they mock the footsteps of your anointed.52Blessed be the LORD forever! Amen and Amen.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–18 — I Will Sing of the Steadfast Love of the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Before Ethan raises his complaint, he establishes who made the promise. He vows to sing for ever of the LORD’s steadfast love and faithfulness, the psalm’s two great words, and recalls the covenant sworn to David (vv. 1–4). No heavenly being compares with this God; he rules the raging sea and crushed Rahab, the monster of chaos (vv. 5–10). Heaven and earth are his, and his arm is mighty (vv. 11–13). His throne stands on righteousness and justice, and the people who know the festal shout walk in the light of his face (vv. 14–16). And their king, their shield, belongs to him (vv. 17–18), which is the ground of everything that follows.
verseByVerse.theology: Before the crisis is named, Ethan builds the case: this is the God who made an oath, and nothing in heaven or sea can stop him keeping it.

verseByVerse.quote: I will sing of the steadfast love of the LORD forever; with my mouth I will make known your faithfulness to all generations. For I said, "Steadfast love will be built up forever; in the heavens you will establish your faithfulness." You have said, "I have made a covenant with my chosen one; I have sworn to David my servant: 'I will establish your offspring forever, and build your throne for all generations.'" Selah
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ethan vows to sing for ever of God’s steadfast love and faithfulness, and grounds his song in the covenant God swore to David. The whole psalm is an argument about these two words: praised, then promised, then questioned.

I will sing of the steadfast love of the LORD forever. Steadfast love is God’s loyal love, which keeps its promises; faithfulness is his being true to his word. Each word comes seven times. They are praised in the first part, promised in the middle, and questioned at the end: “Lord, where is your steadfast love of old, which by your faithfulness you swore to David?” (v. 49). Ethan is going to sing of God’s faithfulness while looking at evidence that seems to contradict it, and that is why the psalm is so valuable.

What faithfulness means. We praise faithfulness in a dog or an old friend: they stuck around. In Scripture it is more than staying. The Hebrew word (emunah) shares its root with “amen”: it means being solid, true to your word, the same tomorrow as on the day you promised. Most of us trust God’s promises about as far as our circumstances seem to confirm them. But a promise that holds only while things go well is hardly a promise, and God’s faithfulness does not depend on ours: “if we are faithless, he remains faithful” (2 Timothy 2:13). See also Faithfulness in the Theological Dictionary.

Steadfast love will be built up forever. The picture is construction: God’s love is being built up like a house, course by course, and his faithfulness is fixed in the heavens where nothing on earth can reach it.

I have made a covenant with my chosen one. And here is what God built: a covenant with David. Through Nathan God had promised, “I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever” (2 Samuel 7:13). The same verb, build, links God’s love in verse 2 to David’s throne in verse 4. The throne is how the love will be seen on earth, which is what makes the end of the psalm so painful.

The oath kept. God kept this oath in a Son of David who was faithful where every king failed, and who went through the grave and out the other side. So when your feelings tell you this week that God has forgotten you, do what Ethan does: take his promise and say it back to him.

Uncertain wording. The heading names Ethan the Ezrahite, a byword for wisdom (1 Kings 4:31); a singer named Ethan led the temple music with Heman and Asaph (1 Chronicles 15:17, 19), but whether they were one man is uncertain. “Maskil” is also not certainly understood: probably a musical or teaching term, perhaps “a skilful song” or “a song for instruction”.
verseByVerse.note: Ethan the Ezrahite was another famous wise man of Solomon’s day.

verseByVerse.quote: Let the heavens praise your wonders, O LORD, your faithfulness in the assembly of the holy ones! For who in the skies can be compared to the LORD? Who among the heavenly beings is like the LORD, a God greatly to be feared in the council of the holy ones, and awesome above all who are around him? O LORD God of hosts, who is mighty as you are, O LORD, with your faithfulness all around you? You rule the raging of the sea; when its waves rise, you still them. You crushed Rahab like a carcass; you scattered your enemies with your mighty arm.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before he mentions the crisis, Ethan shows how great the God is who made the promise: no heavenly being compares with him, and he rules the chaos of the sea.

Let the heavens praise your wonders, O LORD. The scene moves to heaven, where the holy ones are gathered. These “holy ones” and “heavenly beings” are the angels, God’s created host (103:20–21), and the question “who in the skies can be compared to the LORD?” declares that none can (the ESV notes that heavenly beings is literally “the sons of God”, or “the sons of might”).

With your faithfulness all around you. Even the angels fear him, and the closing detail is beautiful: God’s faithfulness surrounds him like a robe, or like attendants standing round a king. It is not one quality among others; it surrounds everything he is and does.

You rule the raging of the sea. To an ancient Israelite the sea was the image of chaos, and Rahab the monster of the deep, a name also used for Egypt (Isaiah 30:7). Job said, “By his power he stilled the sea; by his understanding he shattered Rahab” (Job 26:12). God does not merely hold the chaos back; he has already crushed it.

Asleep on a cushion in the stern. The disciples saw this with their own eyes on Galilee, when Jesus “rebuked the wind and said to the sea, ‘Peace! Be still!’” (Mark 4:39). The God who stills the waves in verse 9 was the man asleep on a cushion in the stern of that boat.
verseByVerse.note: Rahab is a poetic name for the sea monster, and also for Egypt.

verseByVerse.quote: The heavens are yours; the earth also is yours; the world and all that is in it, you have founded them. The north and the south, you have created them; Tabor and Hermon joyously praise your name. You have a mighty arm; strong is your hand, high your right hand.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everything belongs to God because he made it, and his arm is mighty to act.

The heavens are yours; the earth also is yours. Heaven, earth, north and south: all are his. Tabor and Hermon are two of Israel’s great mountains, the rounded hill in Galilee and the snow-capped peak in the far north, and they are pictured singing. The creation God founded cannot be taken from him.

You have a mighty arm. Arm, hand, right hand: three pictures of power at work. It looks back to the arm that scattered God’s enemies (v. 10), and the next section promises that same arm to David (v. 21). The God who owns everything is not an absent owner; he acts.

verseByVerse.quote: Righteousness and justice are the foundation of your throne; steadfast love and faithfulness go before you. Blessed are the people who know the festal shout, who walk, O LORD, in the light of your face, who exult in your name all the day and in your righteousness are exalted.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s throne stands on righteousness and justice, and the people who live in the light of his face are truly happy.

Righteousness and justice are the foundation of your throne. Here is the throne behind David’s throne, and its foundations do not shift. The psalm’s two great words walk ahead of God like heralds in a royal procession: wherever he goes, steadfast love and faithfulness arrive first.

Blessed are the people who know the festal shout. Happy are those who recognise the trumpet call and the cry of praise at the festival, and who live in the light of God’s face. Their joy is not in themselves but in his name, and their standing is not their own righteousness but his: “in your righteousness are exalted”.

verseByVerse.quote: For you are the glory of their strength; by your favor our horn is exalted. For our shield belongs to the LORD, our king to the Holy One of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The people’s strength comes from God alone, and their king belongs to him, which is the whole ground of the psalm’s hope.

You are the glory of their strength. It is “by your favor” that “our horn is exalted”, their strength lifted high in victory (on the horn, see the note on vv. 19–29). Notice the change from “their” to “our”: the psalmist joins the blessed people he has just described.

Our shield belongs to the LORD. The hymn ends on the king. “Our shield”, the king who protects the people, “belongs to the LORD”. The king in Jerusalem is not an independent ruler whose fortunes rise and fall on his own; he is God’s property. So whatever happens to the king happens to something that belongs to the Holy One of Israel.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–37 — I Will Not Lie to David
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s promise to David is recited in full, and its heart is that God will never withdraw his love or lie. God chose David from the people, anointed him and promised him his own arm, his faithfulness and his steadfast love (vv. 19–24). He set the king’s hand on the sea, gave him the right to call God Father, and made him firstborn, highest of the kings of the earth (vv. 25–29). If David’s sons sin, they will feel the rod, but God will not remove his steadfast love: he has sworn by his holiness, and the throne will last like the sun and the moon (vv. 30–37).
verseByVerse.theology: God's promise to David is repeated at length, with its one condition (David’s sons will be disciplined if they sin) and its unconditional core: the love will not be withdrawn.

verseByVerse.quote: Of old you spoke in a vision to your godly one, and said: "I have granted help to one who is mighty; I have exalted one chosen from the people. I have found David, my servant; with my holy oil I have anointed him, so that my hand shall be established with him; my arm also shall strengthen him. The enemy shall not outwit him; the wicked shall not humble him. I will crush his foes before him and strike down those who hate him. My faithfulness and my steadfast love shall be with him, and in my name shall his horn be exalted. I will set his hand on the sea and his right hand on the rivers. He shall cry to me, 'You are my Father, my God, and the Rock of my salvation.' And I will make him the firstborn, the highest of the kings of the earth. My steadfast love I will keep for him forever, and my covenant will stand firm for him. I will establish his offspring forever and his throne as the days of the heavens.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God chose David, anointed him, and promised him his own strength, his love, and a place as his firstborn son and highest of kings, promises that only Jesus fully fills.

I have found David, my servant. Ethan repeats God’s promise at length, almost reading it back to God. It came “in a vision”, to Nathan, and begins with God’s choosing. Paul quoted the same testimony at Antioch: “I have found in David the son of Jesse a man after my heart” (Acts 13:22).

One chosen from the people. A pointed phrase. David was no prince but the youngest son of Jesse of Bethlehem, out with the sheep when Samuel arrived. God’s king is taken from among the people he will rule, and the last Son of David was born in the same small town, into a carpenter’s household.

My arm also shall strengthen him. The arm that scattered God’s enemies (v. 10) will strengthen David, and the two great words are promised to him personally: “My faithfulness and my steadfast love shall be with him”.

In my name shall his horn be exalted. The horn is the strength of a wild ox, and verse 17 used it of the whole people. The king’s strength is raised in God’s name, not in his army or alliances. Whatever power David’s line held, it held because God had put his name to it, which is why its loss later in the psalm feels like God’s own name being put to shame.

I will set his hand on the sea. A remarkable line. In verse 9 God ruled “the raging of the sea”; now God puts the king’s hand on it. The king is given a share in God’s own rule over chaos. No king of Israel ever exercised it, until one Son of David stilled the storm on Galilee.

You are my Father. God promised David’s line, “I will be to him a father, and he shall be to me a son” (2 Samuel 7:14), and Hebrews applies those words to Christ (Hebrews 1:5). The firstborn is the heir of highest rank, and “the highest of the kings of the earth” is a claim over every throne in the world. John opens Revelation with Jesus Christ, “the firstborn of the dead, and the ruler of kings on earth” (Revelation 1:5).

My covenant will stand firm for him. Forever, and again forever (the ESV notes stand firm may be rendered “remain faithful”): the throne will last as long as the sky does.

Textual note. In verse 19 the ESV notes that some manuscripts read “godly ones” for “godly one”. Either way the vision is the word God gave through his prophet.

verseByVerse.quote: If his children forsake my law and do not walk according to my rules, if they violate my statutes and do not keep my commandments, then I will punish their transgression with the rod and their iniquity with stripes, but I will not remove from him my steadfast love or be false to my faithfulness. I will not violate my covenant or alter the word that went forth from my lips. Once for all I have sworn by my holiness; I will not lie to David. His offspring shall endure forever, his throne as long as the sun before me. Like the moon it shall be established forever, a faithful witness in the skies." Selah
verseByVerse.commentary:
If David’s sons sin, God will discipline them with the rod, but he has sworn by his holiness never to withdraw his steadfast love or lie to David. Discipline is one of the covenant’s terms, not a sign that it has failed.

If his children forsake my law. God foresaw that David’s sons would not all be faithful (the ESV notes rules may be “just decrees”). If they sin, they will feel “the rod” and “stripes”, the very words God spoke through Nathan: “I will discipline him with the rod of men, with the stripes of the sons of men” (2 Samuel 7:14). “The Lord disciplines the one he loves” (Hebrews 12:6).

I will not remove from him my steadfast love. Here is the unconditional core. The rod may fall, but the love will not be removed: God had told Nathan, “my steadfast love will not depart from him” (2 Samuel 7:15). That is the Christian’s footing too. Our sins bring a Father’s discipline, not the loss of his love, because the Son of David kept the covenant perfectly in our place; and the way back after sin is still to confess and be forgiven.

Once for all I have sworn by my holiness. There is nothing higher to swear by. “I will not lie to David.” Hebrews says God confirmed his promise with an oath “so that by two unchangeable things, in which it is impossible for God to lie, we who have fled for refuge might have strong encouragement” (Hebrews 6:18).

A faithful witness in the skies. The throne is compared to the sun and the moon. Every night the moon rises, and every night it testifies that God keeps his word. Revelation calls Jesus Christ “the faithful witness” (Revelation 1:5) in the same breath as “the firstborn”. The two titles of this promise, firstborn (v. 27) and faithful witness (v. 37), meet in one person.

Where Christians differ: how is the throne “as long as the sun” fulfilled? Dispensationalists look for a future earthly reign of Christ from Jerusalem over Israel, reading passages such as Revelation 20 that way; brothers who hold this honour the same King. Others hold that the oath is fulfilled in Christ’s present reign. This commentary’s view: Peter is the key, because there an apostle says how the oath was kept. He says God swore to seat a descendant of David on his throne and fulfilled it in raising Christ to his right hand (Acts 2:30–36). The throne is Christ’s now, and it will last for ever.

Uncertain wording. The last line of verse 37 is compressed: literally “and a witness in the sky is faithful”. Most take the witness to be the moon, as the ESV does; some take it to be God himself, the faithful witness to his own oath, and a few think of the rainbow, the sign of God’s covenant with Noah. The sense is the same either way: the oath is as sure as the heavens.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 38–52 — But Now You Have Cast Off
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: “But now” everything God promised seems reversed, and Ethan asks God where his sworn love has gone. God has cast off his anointed, thrown his crown in the dust, breached his walls, strengthened his enemies, and cut short his youth (vv. 38–45). How long will God hide? Life is short, and no one escapes the grave (vv. 46–48). Where is the steadfast love sworn to David, while the nations mock the footsteps of the anointed (vv. 49–51)? The answer is not given here, but the book ends with blessing and a double Amen (v. 52), and the answer came in the Son of David.
verseByVerse.theology: The promise said forever. The facts say the crown is in the dust. Ethan holds God to his word, and the book closes with Amen.

verseByVerse.quote: But now you have cast off and rejected; you are full of wrath against your anointed. You have renounced the covenant with your servant; you have defiled his crown in the dust. You have breached all his walls; you have laid his strongholds in ruins. All who pass by plunder him; he has become the scorn of his neighbors. You have exalted the right hand of his foes; you have made all his enemies rejoice. You have also turned back the edge of his sword, and you have not made him stand in battle. You have made his splendor to cease and cast his throne to the ground. You have cut short the days of his youth; you have covered him with shame. Selah
verseByVerse.commentary:
“But now” God seems to have done the opposite of everything he promised: the anointed king is defeated, his crown in the dust, and Ethan lays the promise beside the facts, line against line.

But now you have cast off and rejected. Thirty-seven verses of praise and promise, and then everything turns. The accusation is breathtakingly direct: “You have renounced the covenant”. The word God said he would never violate (v. 34), Ethan says God has renounced. The crown that was to last as long as the sun is lying in the dirt.

You have exalted the right hand of his foes. Every promise of verses 19 to 37 is reversed, one by one. God had said “I will crush his foes” (v. 23); now he has “exalted the right hand of his foes”. God had said “The enemy shall not outwit him” (v. 22); now “All who pass by plunder him”. The arm that was to strengthen him has turned back the edge of his sword, and the splendour God gave has been made to cease.

You have breached all his walls. These words have been heard before in Book Three. Psalm 80 asked about the vine, “Why then have you broken down its walls, so that all who pass along the way pluck its fruit?” (80:12), and Psalm 79 complained, “We have become a taunt to our neighbors” (79:4). The king suffers exactly what the city and the vine suffered. The anointed is not above his people’s ruin; he goes down into it with them.

What happened? The psalm does not say, and the setting is disputed. Ethan’s name in the heading could point to an earlier humiliation of David’s line, such as Shishak’s invasion (1 Kings 14:25–26); many read it against the later fall to Babylon, and this commentary thinks a crushing defeat of that kind the likeliest setting, the psalm perhaps written by a singer of Ethan’s guild. The fall of Jerusalem shows what such a collapse looked like. Lamentations mourns: “The breath of our nostrils, the LORD’s anointed, was captured in their pits” (Lamentations 4:20). Zedekiah’s sons were killed before his eyes, and then his eyes were put out (2 Kings 25:7).

You have cut short the days of his youth. On the Babylonian reading, think of Jehoiachin, who “was eighteen years old when he became king”, reigned three months, and was taken to Babylon (2 Kings 24:8, 12). Chronicles gives his age as eight (2 Chronicles 36:9), almost certainly a copying slip, since some Hebrew copies and the Greek there read eighteen. With a young king in chains and the throne on the ground, it looked like the end of God’s promise.

Has God broken his promise? Ethan speaks with the honesty of grief, and God lets him. But God had said he would discipline David’s sons with the rod while never removing his steadfast love (vv. 30–33). The throne was humbled, not abolished, and it was restored in the Son of David.

verseByVerse.quote: How long, O LORD? Will you hide yourself forever? How long will your wrath burn like fire? Remember how short my time is! For what vanity you have created all the children of man! What man can live and never see death? Who can deliver his soul from the power of Sheol? Selah
verseByVerse.commentary:
Life is short and no king escapes death, so Ethan asks how long God will hide; only a Son of David raised from the dead answers him.

Will you hide yourself forever? “Forever” has been the psalm’s word for God’s promise. Now Ethan turns it around. He cannot make the promise and the silence fit, and he does not pretend to.
