Remember how short my time is! The argument becomes personal. God’s promise is for all generations, but Ethan has one short lifetime, and if the promise is to be kept, he would like to see it.

For what vanity you have created all the children of man! If every life is short and ends in Sheol (the grave, the place of the dead), and even the promised king is cut down young, what was the point of making human beings at all? It is a real question, and the Psalter answers it in the very next psalm, where Moses asks God to “establish the work of our hands” (90:17). Short lives are not vanity when God establishes what is done in them.

Who can deliver his soul from the power of Sheol? No king, not even David’s son, has escaped death; the throne that was to last for ever keeps passing to men who die. The question has only one answer that satisfies it. A Son of David who died and was raised, “no more to return to corruption” (Acts 13:34), is the only king whose throne can last as long as the sun.

verseByVerse.quote: Lord, where is your steadfast love of old, which by your faithfulness you swore to David? Remember, O Lord, how your servants are mocked, and how I bear in my heart the insults of all the many nations, with which your enemies mock, O LORD, with which they mock the footsteps of your anointed. Blessed be the LORD forever! Amen and Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ethan asks where God’s sworn love has gone while the nations mock his anointed, and then the book blesses God anyway, with a double Amen, leaving the answer to come in Christ.

Lord, where is your steadfast love of old? Both great words are in the psalm’s great question. Not “did it ever exist?”: Ethan has spent the psalm insisting it did. But where is it now? Only someone who believes the promise can ask this. An unbeliever looking at the ruins would conclude there never was a promise; Ethan holds God to it. That is robust faith. Paul faced the same tension: “Does their faithlessness nullify the faithfulness of God? By no means! Let God be true though every one were a liar” (Romans 3:3–4).

They mock the footsteps of your anointed. The nations jeer at the fallen king, following him along the road and laughing at where he has ended up. When the true Anointed walked to his execution, “those who passed by derided him, wagging their heads” (Matthew 27:39). This psalm was being fulfilled at that moment in a way no one watching understood.

I bear in my heart the insults. The one praying carries the nations’ contempt inside himself, as though the insults aimed at God and his king had landed on him. Paul saw Christ in exactly that place: “For Christ did not please himself, but as it is written, ‘The reproaches of those who reproached you fell on me’” (Romans 15:3). The true Anointed bore in his heart, and in his body, the insults aimed at God.

Blessed be the LORD forever! Amen and Amen. Verse 52 closes not only Psalm 89 but the whole of Book Three, as similar blessings close Books One and Two (41:13; 72:19), and it may have been added by those who arranged the collection. But look where they put it: directly after “where is your steadfast love?”, with the throne in the dust and the anointed mocked. They wrote “Blessed be the LORD forever!” and added Amen twice.

Blessing God with the question open. That is the right response to a promise that seems broken: not to stop believing it, but to bless God while the question is still open. And the answer came. The angel told Mary that God would give her son “the throne of his father David, and he will reign over the house of Jacob forever, and of his kingdom there will be no end” (Luke 1:32–33). “For all the promises of God find their Yes in him. That is why it is through him that we utter our Amen to God for his glory” (2 Corinthians 1:20). Amen and Amen.

Uncertain wording. In verse 50 the ESV notes that the Hebrew lacks the word “insults”, though it is implied by the sentence.
verseByVerse.note: Verse 52 is the doxology that closes Book III.

89.title: Where Is Your Steadfast Love of Old?
89.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 89 closes Book Three of the Psalter, the darkest part of the book (see the introduction). Now Ethan turns to the greatest promise Israel had, God’s oath to David, and finds the crown lying in the dust.

The message. God swore to David that his throne would last for ever, and God does not lie. When everything you can see seems to contradict his promise, faith does not let go of it: it holds the promise up to God, asks him honestly where his steadfast love has gone, and still blesses him with the question open.

Why it was said. A king of David’s line has been crushingly defeated, his walls breached and his crown thrown down, and the nations are jeering. The psalm does not name the disaster; the fall of Jerusalem to Babylon (see the introduction) fits it well. Israel needed to know whether God’s sworn word had failed.

How the chapter makes its case. Ethan builds the case for God’s faithfulness before he questions it. He vows to sing of God’s steadfast love and faithfulness and recalls the oath to David (vv. 1–4). He praises the incomparable God who rules the sea, owns the world, and sits on a throne of righteousness (vv. 5–18). He recites the promise in full: David chosen, anointed, made firstborn; his sons disciplined if they sin, but God’s love never removed, sworn by God’s holiness (vv. 19–37). Then “But now”: every promise seems reversed, line by line (vv. 38–45). Life is short and no one escapes death (vv. 46–48). Where is the love you swore to David (vv. 49–51)? The book closes, astonishingly, with blessing and a double Amen (v. 52).

Where it leads. By promise and covenant, directly. The angel told Mary that God would give her son “the throne of his father David” and that “of his kingdom there will be no end” (Luke 1:32–33). The titles of verses 27 and 37, firstborn and faithful witness, are given together to Jesus Christ (Revelation 1:5). The king no one could deliver from Sheol (v. 48) is the Son of David raised “no more to return to corruption” (Acts 13:34). In him every promise of God finds its Yes.

For us. When God’s promises and your circumstances do not match, do what Ethan does: tell God the promise, tell him the facts, and ask him where his love is. Your sins may bring a Father’s rod, but never the loss of his love, because Christ kept the covenant for you. And you can say Amen before you see the answer.
89.theology:
The psalm is an argument about steadfast love and faithfulness: praised (vv. 1-18), promised (vv. 19-37), and questioned (vv. 38-51).

The Davidic covenant, God’s sworn promise to David (2 Sam 7:12-16), carries discipline as one of its terms (vv. 30-32), while the steadfast love at its core is unconditional and sworn by God's holiness (vv. 33-35). The king is given a share in God's own rule over the sea (v. 25), called the firstborn and highest of kings (v. 27), and compared to the moon as a faithful witness (v. 37), titles that meet in Jesus Christ.

Ethan lays the promise beside its apparent reversal (vv. 38-45) and asks where the steadfast love has gone (v. 49), a question that only someone who believes the promise would ask. No king escapes Sheol (v. 48) until the Son of David is raised, never to see corruption, whose kingdom has no end (Luke 1:32-33). The doxology blesses God with the question still open (v. 52); in Christ every promise finds its Yes and Amen.
89.examples:
Steadfast love and faithfulness are sung seven times each, and then questioned. The God who stills the sea is found, in Jesus, asleep in the stern of a boat. The rod is written into the covenant from the start, and the moon rises every night as a faithful witness.

Ethan lays the promise beside the facts, line against line, and still says, Blessed be the LORD, with the question open.

keyVerse.quote: Lord, where is your steadfast love of old, which by your faithfulness you swore to David?
keyVerse.note: Both of the psalm’s great words, steadfast love and faithfulness, meet in its great question. Only someone who believes God’s promise could ask it: Ethan does not doubt that the oath was sworn, he holds God to it while the crown lies in the dust. The answer came in Jesus, the Son of David whose kingdom has no end.

89.reflection:
Ethan spends thirty-seven verses praising God and reciting his promise before he raises his complaint. Why might that order matter when we bring our own disappointments to God?

God promised to discipline David’s sons with the rod but never to remove his steadfast love (vv. 30–33). How does that distinction help a Christian who has sinned, or who is suffering and wonders whether God has turned against them?

“Lord, where is your steadfast love of old?” (v. 49). Is it faith or unbelief to ask God a question like this? When have you asked it, and what kept you holding on?

The book blesses God with the question still open (v. 52). How do Jesus’ kingship and resurrection give us reasons to say Amen before we see how God will answer?

90.text: A Prayer of Moses, the man of God. 1Lord, you have been our dwelling place in all generations.2Before the mountains were brought forth, or ever you had formed the earth and the world, from everlasting to everlasting you are God.3You return man to dust and say, "Return, O children of man!"4For a thousand years in your sight are but as yesterday when it is past, or as a watch in the night.5You sweep them away as with a flood; they are like a dream, like grass that is renewed in the morning:6in the morning it flourishes and is renewed; in the evening it fades and withers.7For we are brought to an end by your anger; by your wrath we are dismayed.8You have set our iniquities before you, our secret sins in the light of your presence.9For all our days pass away under your wrath; we bring our years to an end like a sigh.10The years of our life are seventy, or even by reason of strength eighty; yet their span is but toil and trouble; they are soon gone, and we fly away.11Who considers the power of your anger, and your wrath according to the fear of you?12So teach us to number our days that we may get a heart of wisdom.13Return, O LORD! How long? Have pity on your servants!14Satisfy us in the morning with your steadfast love, that we may rejoice and be glad all our days.15Make us glad for as many days as you have afflicted us, and for as many years as we have seen evil.16Let your work be shown to your servants, and your glorious power to their children.17Let the favor of the Lord our God be upon us, and establish the work of our hands upon us; yes, establish the work of our hands!

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The eternal God is his people’s home, and they are dust, a dream and grass. Moses begins not with man but with God: the Lord has been the dwelling place of his people in every generation, and before the mountains were born he was God, from everlasting to everlasting (vv. 1–2). Against that eternity Moses sets human frailty. God returns man to dust with a word; a thousand years are to him like yesterday or a few hours of the night (vv. 3–4). Lives are swept away like a flash flood, vanish like a dream, and wither like grass that springs up in the morning and is scorched by evening (vv. 5–6).
verseByVerse.theology: The eternal God is his people's home, and the people themselves are grass.

verseByVerse.quote: Lord, you have been our dwelling place in all generations. Before the mountains were brought forth, or ever you had formed the earth and the world, from everlasting to everlasting you are God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When everything else has fallen, God himself remains the home of his people, as he has been in every generation, because he was God before the mountains and will be God for ever.

The opening of Book Four. The placement is deliberate. Book Three ended with David’s crown in the dust (89:39, 49). Book Four opens with the only psalm bearing the name of Moses, “the man of God”, as Deuteronomy calls him (Deuteronomy 33:1). Before there was a king, a temple or a Jerusalem, Moses led a people with no land and no throne through the wilderness. When the throne has fallen, the Psalter takes us back to him. Many think the titles were added later and some doubt that Moses wrote this psalm; its themes fit his life closely, and this commentary reads it as the title presents it, as his prayer (see the introduction).

You have been our dwelling place in all generations. His first sentence answers the loss of everything. Moses spent forty years in tents, and the people he led had no home: their home was God. A believer who has lost house, country, security or a way of life has not lost his dwelling place, because it was never those things.

Before the mountains were brought forth. The mountains are the oldest things a person can see, and God was there before them. Brought forth is birth language, as though the mountains were born. From everlasting to everlasting means not merely that he lasts a very long time, but that he has no beginning and no end.

Before Abraham was, I am. John began his Gospel in the same place: “In the beginning was the Word” (John 1:1). And Jesus spoke of himself in the present tense, as only the eternal God can: “before Abraham was, I am” (John 8:58). The God who was before the mountains walked among the hills of Galilee.

Textual note. The ESV notes that some manuscripts read “our refuge” for “our dwelling place”. The meaning is much the same: God is where his people live and are safe.
verseByVerse.note: Book IV begins (90–106). The only psalm credited to Moses — perhaps the oldest in the collection.

verseByVerse.quote: You return man to dust and say, "Return, O children of man!" For a thousand years in your sight are but as yesterday when it is past, or as a watch in the night. You sweep them away as with a flood; they are like a dream, like grass that is renewed in the morning: in the morning it flourishes and is renewed; in the evening it fades and withers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Against God’s eternity, human life is brief: God speaks and we return to dust, and our lives pass like a flood, a dream, or grass that withers by evening.

You return man to dust. The psalm turns abruptly from God’s eternity to man’s frailty, echoing the sentence spoken in Eden: “for you are dust, and to dust you shall return” (Genesis 3:19). The ESV notes that children of man may be rendered “of Adam”: every death is Adam’s sentence carried out again. God speaks one word, Return, and a generation goes back to the ground.

A thousand years in your sight. To God a thousand years is like yesterday, which once past seems short, or like a watch in the night, a few hours a sleeping man does not notice. Peter used this verse to explain why Christ’s return seems slow: “with the Lord one day is as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day” (2 Peter 3:8). God is not late; he simply does not measure time as we do.

Like grass that is renewed in the morning. Three images of how quickly lives go: a flash flood in a dry valley, sweeping everything away; a dream, vivid at night and gone by breakfast; and grass, which in that climate sprang up green after the morning dew and was scorched brown by the afternoon sun.

What outlasts the grass. Isaiah heard the same message: “All flesh is grass… The grass withers, the flower fades, but the word of our God will stand forever” (Isaiah 40:6, 8). That word, and those who trust it, are the only things that outlast the grass (1 Peter 1:24–25).

Where Christians differ: does “a thousand years… as yesterday” mean the creation days were long ages? Not by itself. The verse speaks of God’s relation to time, not of how to count the days of Genesis. Faithful Christians who read those days as long ages or as a literary framework are brothers, and they rightly see that God is not bound by our clocks. This commentary’s view: the days of Genesis 1 are ordinary days: each is numbered and closed with evening and morning, and Exodus 20:11 grounds Israel’s week in God’s six days. But this verse does not decide the question either way. What it settles is that God is never hurried and never late.

Uncertain wording. Verse 5 is hard Hebrew. “You sweep them away as with a flood” renders a rare verb, and “they are like a dream” is literally “they are sleep”. The general sense is clear, that God carries lives off suddenly and they vanish like sleep or a dream, but the exact picture is uncertain, and translations differ.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–12 — Teach Us to Number Our Days
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Life is short because it is lived under God’s anger at sin, so Moses asks God to teach his people to count their days. Death is not merely natural: we are brought to an end by God’s wrath, and even our secret sins lie open in the light of his face (vv. 7–8). A life ends like a sigh, seventy or eighty years of toil and trouble, and then we fly away (vv. 9–10). Hardly anyone considers the power of God’s anger (v. 11). So the practical centre of the psalm is a prayer: teach us to number our days, that we may get a heart of wisdom (v. 12).
verseByVerse.theology: Life is short because of sin, and the wise response is to learn to count our days.

verseByVerse.quote: For we are brought to an end by your anger; by your wrath we are dismayed. You have set our iniquities before you, our secret sins in the light of your presence. For all our days pass away under your wrath; we bring our years to an end like a sigh. The years of our life are seventy, or even by reason of strength eighty; yet their span is but toil and trouble; they are soon gone, and we fly away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Life is short because it is lived under God’s anger at sin; even our secret sins lie open before him, and our seventy or eighty years end like a sigh.

We are brought to an end by your anger. Moses gives the reason life is so short, and it is not merely biology. Death is not natural; it is the judgment on sin. Moses had seen that more clearly than almost anyone: he watched God’s anger consume a generation in the wilderness.

Our secret sins in the light of your presence. The most searching line. The sins no one else knows are set out on the table before God, lit by the brightness of his face. “And no creature is hidden from his sight, but all are naked and exposed to the eyes of him to whom we must give account” (Hebrews 4:13). Anyone with a secret sin should read this verse slowly, and then the promise beside it: “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins” (1 John 1:9). The light that exposes sin is also the light in which it is forgiven.

We bring our years to an end like a sigh. Seen from outside, a whole life ends like a breath let out, a small sound, and then nothing.

The years of our life are seventy. Who wrote this matters. “Moses was 120 years old when he died” (Deuteronomy 34:7), so seventy or eighty years are not his own span. He was describing the generation he led: every Israelite over twenty who left Egypt, except Caleb and Joshua, died in the wilderness (Numbers 14:30). God had said, “your dead bodies shall fall in this wilderness” (Numbers 14:29), and for forty years Moses attended their funerals.

Soon gone, and we fly away. Even the extra years, by reason of strength (the ESV notes “pride” as another rendering), are toil and trouble. Then we fly away, like a bird off a branch.

Is death still God’s anger for the believer? Death entered with sin and remains its wages. But for those in Christ the wrath has been borne (Romans 8:1); death is no longer punishment but the door to being with Christ (Philippians 1:21–23), and its sting is gone (1 Corinthians 15:55–57).

verseByVerse.quote: Who considers the power of your anger, and your wrath according to the fear of you? So teach us to number our days that we may get a heart of wisdom.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Few people think seriously about God’s anger behind death, so Moses asks God to teach his people to count their days, that they may live wisely.

Who considers the power of your anger? Almost nobody, and that is Moses’ point. People know they will die, but very few think about why. The second line means that God’s wrath is as great as the fear he is due. We live as if life were long, sin small and God mild.

So teach us to number our days. The practical centre of the psalm: a request to be taught to count, and to count days rather than years. Someone who reaches seventy has lived about twenty-five thousand days; most people have fewer left than they imagine. Numbering them means knowing that they are limited, that each is gone when spent, and that there will be a last one. Moses asks God for this rather than resolving to do it himself, because God teaches us to count, by his word and his Spirit.

That we may get a heart of wisdom. The fool in Jesus’ parable planned for years, and God said to him, “Fool! This night your soul is required of you” (Luke 12:20). James asks, “What is your life? For you are a mist that appears for a little time and then vanishes” (James 4:14). Paul says, “Look carefully then how you walk, not as unwise but as wise, making the best use of the time” (Ephesians 5:15–16). This wisdom is not morbid; it is the clarity of someone who has stopped pretending there is always tomorrow. What would you stop doing if you knew your days were numbered, and what would you start? They are.

How do I number my days? Not by brooding on death, but by letting the fact of a last day sort the days you have. Count one day at a time. In the morning ask God for this one day and give him its first minutes; it is the one you actually have, and “tomorrow will be anxious for itself” (Matthew 6:34). Weigh the calendar. When the job offer, the extra committee or the new subscription asks for your hours, ask how it will look from your last day, and say no to some good things for the sake of better ones. Do not postpone love. Ring your mother, make up with your brother, tell your children what you think of them, this week rather than “some day”. Look past the last day. Moses could pray this without despair because the LORD was his dwelling place in all generations, and Christians count their days in the light of the one who said, “I am the resurrection and the life. Whoever believes in me, though he die, yet shall he live” (John 11:25). Because Christ has drawn the sting of death, a short life is not a lost one.

Uncertain wording. The second line of verse 11, “and your wrath according to the fear of you”, is compressed in Hebrew. It most likely means that God’s wrath is as great as the reverence he deserves; some take it to mean that only those who fear God grasp how great his wrath is. Either way, the point is that we take God’s anger far too lightly.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–17 — Satisfy Us in the Morning
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moses asks God to return in mercy, to satisfy short lives with his love, and to make their work last. He turns God’s word “Return” (v. 3) back to him: return to us and have pity (v. 13). He asks for steadfast love every morning, which unlike the grass does not wither, so that a short life may be glad all its days (v. 14), and for gladness as long as the affliction has been (v. 15). Knowing his own generation will not enter the land, he prays for the children to see God’s work (v. 16), and asks twice that God establish the work of their hands (v. 17).
verseByVerse.theology: Moses asks that short lives be filled with God's love, and that the work done in them should last.

verseByVerse.quote: Return, O LORD! How long? Have pity on your servants! Satisfy us in the morning with your steadfast love, that we may rejoice and be glad all our days. Make us glad for as many days as you have afflicted us, and for as many years as we have seen evil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses asks God to come back in mercy and to satisfy his people every morning with his steadfast love, so that even a short life can be glad all its days.

Return, O LORD! The prayer uses God’s own word. In verse 3 God said to man, “Return”, go back to dust. Now Moses says to God, “Return”, come back to us. It is bold, and it is the only hope a dying people has.

Satisfy us in the morning with your steadfast love. The grass flourished “in the morning” and withered by evening (v. 6). Now Moses asks for something else in the morning: God’s steadfast love, which does not wither. The day will still end and the life will still be short, but a life satisfied with God’s love every morning is glad “all our days”. The answer to the fear of a short life is not a longer one but a fuller one. Jeremiah found it in the ruins of Jerusalem: “The steadfast love of the LORD never ceases; his mercies never come to an end; they are new every morning” (Lamentations 3:22–23).

What it means to be satisfied. Everyone is trying to be satisfied by something. We say we want a little more security, a better job, someone who finally appreciates us, but underneath most restlessness is a hunger we keep asking the wrong things to fill. Jeremiah called them “broken cisterns that can hold no water” (Jeremiah 2:13): good things asked to do what only God can do, and so always leaking. Moses asks to be satisfied not with a long life, which he knows he will not get, but with being loved by God. Jesus offers himself as exactly that: “I am the bread of life; whoever comes to me shall not hunger, and whoever believes in me shall never thirst” (John 6:35). A heart fed there stops demanding that work, marriage or reputation fill it, and can enjoy them as gifts. Tomorrow, before the phone, the news and the inbox get their turn, let the first thing you take in be a word of his love for you.

Make us glad for as many days as you have afflicted us. A daring request: joy measured to match the sorrow. After forty years in the wilderness, give us forty years of gladness. God will do more than that. For those who belong to him, the joy to come is not matched to the affliction but beyond all comparison: “He will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death shall be no more” (Revelation 21:4).

verseByVerse.quote: Let your work be shown to your servants, and your glorious power to their children. Let the favor of the Lord our God be upon us, and establish the work of our hands upon us; yes, establish the work of our hands!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses prays that the next generation will see God’s work, and that God will make the work of their brief lives last.

Your glorious power to their children. Moses knew his generation would not enter the land, so he prays for the next: let us see your work, and let our children see your glory. A dying generation can still pray for its children, and should.

Establish the work of our hands. The last request is for the favor of the Lord (the ESV notes it can be rendered “beauty”) to rest on them, and then, twice, that God establish the work of their hands: make it last. Everything in the psalm has spoken of how quickly lives pass: dust, dreams, grass, a sigh. Moses does not ask that he himself should last. He asks that the work God gave him to do should.

A prayer answered. For believers it is answered. Their days are still few and the grass still withers, but work done in the Lord is not lost with them: “be steadfast, immovable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, knowing that in the Lord your labor is not in vain” (1 Corinthians 15:58). The Lord Jesus, who said “I glorified you on earth, having accomplished the work that you gave me to do” (John 17:4), had his work established for ever when God raised him; and those united to him share that risen life. Numbering your days does not make them meaningless. It makes you ask him to make them count.

90.title: Teach Us to Number Our Days
90.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 90 opens Book Four of the Psalter. Book Three ended with David’s crown in the dust and the question “where is your steadfast love of old?” (89:49). Now the Psalter reaches back past David to Moses, the man who led a people with no land, no king and no temple, and who found that God himself was their home.

The message. God is eternal and we are not. Our lives are short, and death is not merely natural but the mark of God’s anger at our sin. So the wise do not pretend there is always tomorrow: they ask God to teach them to count their days, to satisfy them every morning with his steadfast love, and to make their brief work last.

Why it was said. Moses prays as the leader of a generation that died in the wilderness under God’s judgment, forty years of funerals after the rebellion at Kadesh (Numbers 14). Placed here, the prayer also speaks to Israel after the fall of David’s throne (see the introduction): when everything earthly has gone, the eternal God remains his people’s dwelling place.

How the chapter makes its case. Moses begins with God, everlasting and before the mountains, his people’s home in every generation (vv. 1–2). Against that he sets human frailty: dust, a thousand years like yesterday, lives swept away like a flood, a dream, grass (vv. 3–6). He names the cause: we are consumed by God’s anger, our secret sins in the light of his face, our lives ending like a sigh after seventy or eighty years (vv. 7–11). So he prays, “teach us to number our days” (v. 12). Then he asks God to return, with steadfast love every morning, gladness to match the years of sorrow, God’s work shown to the children, and the work of their hands established (vv. 13–17).

Where it leads. By the character of God revealed in Christ, and by the need the psalm exposes. The eternal God before the mountains is the Word who “was in the beginning with God” (John 1:2) and who said, “before Abraham was, I am” (John 8:58). And the need is plain: Moses can describe death under wrath but cannot cure it. Christ bore that wrath and rose, so that a believer’s days, though few, are lived under the favour of God and his labour “in the Lord” is “not in vain” (1 Corinthians 15:58).

For us. Count your days: they are fewer than you think, and each one, once spent, is gone. Begin each morning by receiving God’s steadfast love before anything else feeds you. And ask him to make what you do for him last, because in Christ it will.
90.theology:
After Book Three closed on the fallen throne, Book Four begins with Moses and a God who was Israel's home before any king (vv. 1-2). His eternity is set against how briefly humans live: dust, dream and grass (vv. 3-6; Gen 3:19; Isa 40:6-8).

Death comes from God's anger at sin, including secret sin exposed before him (vv. 7-9), and wisdom begins with numbering our days (v. 12). God's steadfast love, new each morning, satisfies short lives (v. 14), the joy to come outweighs affliction (v. 15), and the eternal God establishes the work of mortal hands (v. 17).
90.examples: When the throne falls, the Psalter goes back to a man who lived in tents and found that home is a person, not a place. He saw grass green at dawn and brown by afternoon, and attended forty years of funerals in the wilderness. He knew secret sins are laid out in God's light, and still he asked, twice, that God would establish the work of our hands.

keyVerse.quote: So teach us to number our days that we may get a heart of wisdom.
keyVerse.note: This is the practical centre of the psalm. Having set the eternal God beside our short, sin-shadowed lives, Moses does not despair but asks to be taught to count: to know that our days are limited and to spend each one wisely. Because Christ has drawn the sting of death, counting our days is not morbid but the beginning of a life that counts.

90.reflection:
Moses begins, “Lord, you have been our dwelling place in all generations” (v. 1). What earthly things are you tempted to treat as your home and security, and what would it mean to find your home in God instead?

The psalm says our lives end under God’s anger and that our secret sins lie open before him (vv. 7–8). Why do so few people “consider the power of your anger” (v. 11), and how does the cross change the way a Christian faces death?

What would it look like this week to “number our days” (v. 12)? Is there a conversation, a reconciliation or a priority you have been postponing?

Moses asks God to “satisfy us in the morning with your steadfast love” (v. 14). What do you usually reach for first in the morning, and how might you let God’s love be the first thing that feeds you?

91.text: <sup>1</sup>He who dwells in the shelter of the Most High will abide in the shadow of the Almighty.<sup>2</sup>I will say to the LORD, "My refuge and my fortress, my God, in whom I trust."<sup>3</sup>For he will deliver you from the snare of the fowler and from the deadly pestilence.<sup>4</sup>He will cover you with his pinions, and under his wings you will find refuge; his faithfulness is a shield and buckler.<sup>5</sup>You will not fear the terror of the night, nor the arrow that flies by day,<sup>6</sup>nor the pestilence that stalks in darkness, nor the destruction that wastes at noonday.<sup>7</sup>A thousand may fall at your side, ten thousand at your right hand, but it will not come near you.<sup>8</sup>You will only look with your eyes and see the recompense of the wicked.<sup>9</sup>Because you have made the LORD your dwelling place— the Most High, who is my refuge —<sup>10</sup>no evil shall be allowed to befall you, no plague come near your tent.<sup>11</sup>For he will command his angels concerning you to guard you in all your ways.<sup>12</sup>On their hands they will bear you up, lest you strike your foot against a stone.<sup>13</sup>You will tread on the lion and the adder; the young lion and the serpent you will trample underfoot.<sup>14</sup>"Because he holds fast to me in love, I will deliver him; I will protect him, because he knows my name.<sup>15</sup>When he calls to me, I will answer him; I will be with him in trouble; I will rescue him and honor him.<sup>16</sup>With long life I will satisfy him and show him my salvation."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — The Shelter of the Most High
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The one who lives with God lives under his wings, round the clock and against every danger. The psalm begins with the person who dwells in the shelter of the Most High, and the speaker says aloud that the LORD is his refuge and fortress (vv. 1–2). Then another voice promises what God will do: rescue from the hidden trap and the deadly plague, cover like a bird’s wings, and faithfulness as a shield (vv. 3–4). There is no need to fear the terror by night or the arrow by day, the plague in darkness or destruction at noon; though thousands fall nearby, it will not come near (vv. 5–8). The promise is not that dangers are unreal, but that they no longer own the one God shelters.
verseByVerse.theology: The promise is for those who live with God, and it is first a promise about fear.

verseByVerse.quote: He who dwells in the shelter of the Most High will abide in the shadow of the Almighty. I will say to the LORD, "My refuge and my fortress, my God, in whom I trust."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The person who lives close to God, not just visiting in emergencies, is sheltered by him, and faith says so to God out loud: “My refuge and my fortress, my God, in whom I trust.”

He who dwells in the shelter of the Most High. Dwells and abide are words for staying, not visiting.

In the shadow of the Almighty. Shelter is a hiding place, and shadow the shade a traveller finds from the sun, or the shadow of wings, as verse 4 will make clear. In that climate shade was not a luxury; without it, people died.

Four names for God. In two verses: the Most High, the Almighty, the LORD, my God. The highest, the all-powerful, the covenant name, and then the personal one. The psalm moves from God’s greatness to his nearness, and the last name makes the others useful. A fortress is only a refuge to the person who goes into it.

I will say to the LORD. Faith here is not a private feeling but a confession made to God’s face. There is strength in saying to God, in words, “you are my refuge”, especially on a day when it does not feel true.

The shelter is Christ. We can live there because Christ has opened the door and is himself the shelter. He longed to gather Jerusalem “as a hen gathers her brood under her wings” (Matthew 23:37), and he says to us, “Abide in me, and I in you” (John 15:4).

How do I make the LORD my dwelling place? A dwelling is where you go back to by habit, not only in a storm. Begin and end the day there. Before the phone, and again before sleep, say to him what verse 2 says: “My refuge and my fortress, my God, in whom I trust.” Go in when the news comes. When the test result, the redundancy letter or the late-night noise arrives, make him the first place you run, before you ring round or search the internet, and tell him plainly what you fear. Stay on the good days. Keep praying and reading when life is calm, so that his house is home and not an emergency shelter you visit twice a year. Stay with his people. Sunday by Sunday, the church is where you hear the promise said back to you when you cannot say it yourself.

Textual note. The ESV notes that the Greek translation reads “He will say” in verse 2.
verseByVerse.note: “Most High” and “Almighty” (Shaddai) are among the oldest names for God.

verseByVerse.quote: For he will deliver you from the snare of the fowler and from the deadly pestilence. He will cover you with his pinions, and under his wings you will find refuge; his faithfulness is a shield and buckler.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God rescues his people from both hidden malice and deadly sickness, covering them like a bird covers its young, and his faithfulness is their armour.

The snare of the fowler. Another voice now speaks to the believer, promising what God will do about two dangers: the hidden trap set by someone who wants to catch you, and the deadly pestilence, which no one sets but which kills anyway. One comes from malice, the other simply from a fallen world. God delivers from both.

He will cover you with his pinions. The most tender picture in the psalm: God as a bird covering its young. Moses sang of God “like an eagle that stirs up its nest, that flutters over its young, spreading out its wings” (Deuteronomy 32:11). Boaz blessed Ruth, a foreigner, as one who had come to take refuge under the wings of the God of Israel (Ruth 2:12). And Jesus used the image of himself over Jerusalem: “as a hen gathers her brood under her wings” (Matthew 23:37).

Under his wings you will find refuge. Warmth and closeness as much as protection: a chick under the wing does not see the danger; it sees feathers. And the wings are backed by armour: his faithfulness, his keeping of his word, is what stands between the believer and what is coming.

Should a Christian refuse medicine or precautions and rely on this psalm? No. God’s protection normally works through ordinary means. Paul told the soldiers that unless the sailors stayed in the ship they could not be saved (Acts 27:31), and Luke was “the beloved physician” (Colossians 4:14). Refusing the means God provides is the very testing of God that Jesus refused (see the note on vv. 11–13).

Uncertain wording. “Buckler” renders a Hebrew word found only here. It is probably some kind of shield or protective wall; the exact object is unknown. Paired with “shield”, the sense is clear: God’s faithfulness protects completely.

verseByVerse.quote: You will not fear the terror of the night, nor the arrow that flies by day, nor the pestilence that stalks in darkness, nor the destruction that wastes at noonday. A thousand may fall at your side, ten thousand at your right hand, but it will not come near you. You will only look with your eyes and see the recompense of the wicked.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The believer need not be ruled by fear at any hour, for though dangers are real and many fall, nothing touches him outside God’s keeping.

The terror of the night. The dangers go round the clock: night, day, darkness, noon. There is no hour when the believer is outside the shelter.

You will not fear. The promise is first about fear. The dangers are named as real; what changes is that they no longer own the person who lives under God’s wings.

A thousand may fall at your side. The picture is of a plague or a battle in which people fall all around. Israel had seen something like it on the night of the Passover, when God struck Egypt but promised that he “will not allow the destroyer to enter your houses to strike you” (Exodus 12:23). On the same night, in the same land, death passed over the houses marked with the lamb’s blood.

Reading it honestly. Faithful believers have died in plagues and wars. Hebrews lists men and women of faith who “were stoned, they were sawn in two, they were killed with the sword” (Hebrews 11:37). The psalm does not promise that no Christian will ever catch an infection. It promises that nothing reaches the one who dwells in God except by God’s permission, and that nothing which reaches him can separate him from God’s shelter. Even death cannot take him out of it (Romans 8:38–39).

Uncertain wording. “The destruction that wastes at noonday” renders a rare word, perhaps a plague or a deadly sickness that strikes in the heat of the day. Whatever it was, no danger at any hour is beyond God.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–13 — He Will Command His Angels
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Because the believer has made the LORD his dwelling place, no evil will be allowed to reach him, and God’s angels guard him on his way. The speaker breaks in with his own “my refuge” (v. 9), and the promise follows: no evil, no plague near the tent, unless God permits it (v. 10). God will command his angels to guard him in all his ways and carry him over rough ground (vv. 11–12), and he will walk over lion and serpent (v. 13). These are the verses the devil quoted to Jesus in the wilderness, and Jesus’ answer shows how they must be read: as promises for the path of obedience, never as a dare to test God.
verseByVerse.theology: The verses the devil quoted to Jesus — and the way Jesus refused to use them.

verseByVerse.quote: Because you have made the LORD your dwelling place— the Most High, who is my refuge — no evil shall be allowed to befall you, no plague come near your tent.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because the believer has made the LORD his home, no evil will be allowed to reach him: evil is real, but it is not permitted.

Because you have made the LORD your dwelling place. The condition comes again. It does not earn the promise like a wage; a shelter simply protects only those who are inside it. The speaker breaks in with his own testimony, “the Most High, who is my refuge”, as if he cannot hear the promise without saying amen to it.

No evil shall be allowed to befall you. The word allowed matters. Evil exists, and it wants to reach the believer; it is not permitted to. The question is always who does the permitting, and the answer is the one whose wings cover the tent.

Uncertain wording. The ESV notes the verse may be read differently: “For you, O LORD, are my refuge! You have made the Most High your dwelling place”. The change of speaker in mid-verse is abrupt in Hebrew, and it is not certain who says what; either way, the LORD is the refuge and the believer lives in him.

verseByVerse.quote: For he will command his angels concerning you to guard you in all your ways. On their hands they will bear you up, lest you strike your foot against a stone. You will tread on the lion and the adder; the young lion and the serpent you will trample underfoot.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s angels guard his people on the path of obedience and they will tread down every enemy, but the promise is never a licence to test God, as Jesus showed when the devil quoted it.

He will command his angels concerning you. These are the verses the devil quoted. He set Jesus on the pinnacle of the temple and said, “If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down, for it is written, ‘He will command his angels concerning you’” (Matthew 4:6). It was a nearly exact quotation, though he dropped “in all your ways”, and he used it to push God’s Son into testing God.

To guard you in all your ways. Jesus did not deny the promise. He answered with another Scripture: “You shall not put the Lord your God to the test” (Matthew 4:7). The promise is for someone walking in his ways, the ordinary path of obedience, not for someone who jumps off a building to see whether God will catch him. A believer who takes reckless risks and calls it faith has not trusted Psalm 91; he has done what the devil suggested.

Prayer under the microscope. In 1872 the scientist Francis Galton published a paper asking whether prayer works. If it did, he reasoned, the monarchs of Europe, prayed for publicly in every church every Sunday, should live longer than other people, and he found that they did not. Oddly, the sceptic and the health-and-wealth preacher share the same picture: God as a mechanism to be tested by results, broken for one, needing more faith for the other. Both treat God as something to be used, exactly what the devil urged on Jesus with this psalm. Jesus refused to make God perform, not because he doubted his Father but because he trusted him. That is the trust Psalm 91 describes: not a lever to pull, but a person to live with. And the one who refused to test God was not spared. Men stood beneath his cross and said, “He saved others; he cannot save himself” (Matthew 27:42). He stayed there, and on the third day the promise of this psalm was kept in a way no experiment could measure.

On their hands they will bear you up. The angels are real: “ministering spirits sent out to serve for the sake of those who are to inherit salvation” (Hebrews 1:14). Most of what they do we will never see. The picture is almost playful: angels carrying a child over rough ground so he does not stub his toe.

You will tread on the lion and the adder. The lion attacks openly and the snake strikes from hiding, and the believer does not merely escape them; he walks over them. The serpent under the foot recalls the first promise of rescue in the Bible, that the woman’s offspring “shall bruise your head” (Genesis 3:15). Jesus gave his disciples “authority to tread on serpents and scorpions” (Luke 10:19); a viper hung from Paul’s hand on Malta and he “shook off the creature into the fire and suffered no harm” (Acts 28:5); and “The God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet” (Romans 16:20).

Where Christians differ: does treading on serpents authorise snake-handling, and do such signs continue? A few groups handle snakes as a test of faith, and faithful Christians differ more widely on whether miraculous gifts continue. This commentary’s view: the passage about picking up serpents (Mark 16:18) is in a section missing from the earliest manuscripts, and such signs belonged to the apostolic era, when they confirmed the apostles’ message (Hebrews 2:3–4). Paul was bitten by accident and unharmed (Acts 28:3–5); he did not stage it, and Jesus refused to throw himself down to test God (Matthew 4:7). No view of the gifts turns this verse into a command to handle snakes.

Uncertain wording. The animals in verse 13 are not certainly identified. “Adder” is a venomous snake, perhaps a cobra; the word rendered “serpent” can also mean a sea monster or dragon. Either way they stand for every deadly enemy.
verseByVerse.note: Satan quoted vv. 11–12 to Jesus in the wilderness, leaving out “in all your ways.”

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–16 — I Will Be with Him in Trouble
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God himself has the last word: he will be with his child in trouble and rescue him out of it. The voice changes from “you” to “him”, as God speaks of the believer the way a father speaks of a child he loves. He gives two marks of the one he protects: he holds fast to God in love and knows God’s name (v. 14). Then come eight promises in the first person: deliver, protect, answer, be with him in trouble, rescue, honour, satisfy with long life, and show him salvation (vv. 14–16). The heart of them is not that trouble will never come, but that God will be in it with him.
verseByVerse.theology: God himself speaks the last word: not a promise of no trouble, but of his presence in it.

verseByVerse.quote: "Because he holds fast to me in love, I will deliver him; I will protect him, because he knows my name. When he calls to me, I will answer him; I will be with him in trouble; I will rescue him and honor him. With long life I will satisfy him and show him my salvation."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God himself promises to answer, rescue and honour the one who loves him, and the heart of it is not “I will keep him out of trouble” but “I will be with him in trouble”, a promise kept perfectly in Christ.

I will deliver him. Now God himself speaks, and the voice changes from you to him: God talks about the believer the way a father talks about a child he loves.

Because he holds fast to me in love. God gives two reasons. “He holds fast to me in love”: the word means clinging, attached with desire. And “he knows my name”: he knows who God is and has called on him. Neither is a work that earns anything; both describe a person who belongs to God.

I will be with him in trouble. Deliver, protect, answer, be with him, rescue, honour, satisfy, show him salvation: eight promises in three verses, all in the first person. Look at the fourth. Not “I will keep him out of trouble”. The psalm that seemed to promise that nothing bad would happen ends by admitting that trouble will come, and promising something better than its absence: God’s presence inside it, and rescue out of it.

Not kept out of trouble. One person fulfilled this psalm perfectly. Jesus dwelt in the shelter of the Most High more completely than anyone, refused to test God, trod on the serpent, and was not spared the cross. God did not keep him out of trouble. He was with him in it, rescued him from death, honoured him, and showed him his salvation on the third day. “With long life I will satisfy him” is finally true of Christ’s risen life, which does not end, and it is true of everyone united to him by faith. If you are in trouble now, the promise of this psalm is not broken. It is being kept in the way it said it would be: “I will be with him in trouble”.

91.title: Under His Wings
91.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 90 set the eternal God, “our dwelling place in all generations” (90:1), against short lives lived under his anger. Psalm 91 takes up the same word: here is what it is like to make the LORD your dwelling place (v. 9).

The message. The one who lives with God lives under his wings. Dangers are real, by night and by day, but nothing reaches him except by God’s permission, and nothing that reaches him can take him out of God’s keeping. God does not promise to keep his people out of all trouble; he promises, “I will be with him in trouble”, and rescue out of it.

Why it was said. Israel lived with snares set by enemies, plagues that swept through towns, war, and wild animals on the road. The psalm has no title and names no occasion; it was given for every believer who faces dangers he cannot control (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. It opens with the one who dwells in God’s shelter, and the speaker confesses aloud, “My refuge and my fortress” (vv. 1–2). Another voice then promises God’s care: rescue from trap and pestilence, wings to hide under, faithfulness as armour (vv. 3–4); no need to fear by night or day, though thousands fall (vv. 5–8). Because the believer has made the LORD his dwelling, evil is not allowed near; angels guard him in all his ways, and he treads on lion and serpent (vv. 9–13). Finally God himself speaks, with eight promises in the first person, the heart of which is “I will be with him in trouble” (vv. 14–16).

Where it leads. By pattern, and in the most striking way. The devil quoted this psalm to Jesus, urging him to throw himself from the temple and make God prove it (Matthew 4:6). Jesus refused to test his Father, and trusted him instead, all the way to a cross where men mocked, “He saved others; he cannot save himself” (Matthew 27:42). God did not keep him out of trouble; he was with him in it and rescued him on the third day, and the serpent was crushed under his feet (Genesis 3:15). The psalm’s promises are kept fully in Christ, and in all who are hidden in him.

For us. Make the LORD your home, not an emergency shelter: say to him in words, “my refuge and my fortress”, on calm days and dark ones. Use the ordinary means he provides and never put him to the test. And when trouble comes, as it will, the promise has not failed: he is with you in it, and nothing can take you out from under his wings.
91.theology:
The promises belong to those who dwell with God, not those who visit him (vv. 1, 9), and his care is pictured as a bird's wings (v. 4). The psalm does not guarantee that believers never suffer (Heb 11:36-38); it promises that nothing is allowed to reach them outside God's permission or beyond his shelter (vv. 7, 10).

The devil used vv. 11-12 to tempt Christ to test God, and Christ refused (Matt 4:6-7). Treading on the serpent (v. 13) echoes Gen 3:15 and is fulfilled in Christ and shared with his people. God's closing words promise presence in trouble, then rescue and honour (v. 15): Christ was not spared the cross but was delivered from death, and the promise of satisfying life is kept in him (v. 16).
91.examples: The psalm is for those who live with God, not those who visit. A chick under the wing sees feathers, not danger, and the destroyer is not allowed into the house. Jumping off the temple is not faith. Of God's eight closing promises, the fourth is to be with him in trouble, not to keep him out of it.

keyVerse.quote: When he calls to me, I will answer him; I will be with him in trouble; I will rescue him and honor him.
keyVerse.note: Here God himself speaks, and the heart of his promise is not that his people will never meet trouble, but that he will be with them in it and bring them out of it. This is how the psalm’s great promises are to be read, and it is exactly how God kept them for Jesus, who was not spared the cross but was rescued from death and honoured.

91.reflection:
The psalm speaks of those who “dwell” and “abide” with God (v. 1), not just visit in emergencies. What helps you make God your home on ordinary days, and what tends to make him only an emergency shelter?

Faithful Christians have died in plagues and wars. How would you explain to a friend what Psalm 91 does promise and what it does not?

The devil quoted verses 11–12 to Jesus, and Jesus refused to put God to the test (Matthew 4:5–7). Where are we tempted to “test” God, or to treat a promise as a lever to make him perform?

God says, “I will be with him in trouble” (v. 15). How did God keep that promise for Jesus, and how have you known his presence in trouble rather than escape from it?

92.text: A Psalm. A Song for the Sabbath. 1It is good to give thanks to the LORD, to sing praises to your name, O Most High;2to declare your steadfast love in the morning, and your faithfulness by night,3to the music of the lute and the harp, to the melody of the lyre.4For you, O LORD, have made me glad by your work; at the works of your hands I sing for joy.5How great are your works, O LORD! Your thoughts are very deep!6The stupid man cannot know; the fool cannot understand this:7that though the wicked sprout like grass and all evildoers flourish, they are doomed to destruction forever;8but you, O LORD, are on high forever.9For behold, your enemies, O LORD, for behold, your enemies shall perish; all evildoers shall be scattered.10But you have exalted my horn like that of the wild ox; you have poured over me fresh oil.11My eyes have seen the downfall of my enemies; my ears have heard the doom of my evil assailants.12The righteous flourish like the palm tree and grow like a cedar in Lebanon.13They are planted in the house of the LORD; they flourish in the courts of our God.14They still bear fruit in old age; they are ever full of sap and green,15to declare that the LORD is upright; he is my rock, and there is no unrighteousness in him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — It Is Good to Give Thanks
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: It is good to thank God, and the psalm gives thanks a timetable and a melody. On the Sabbath, when work stops, thanksgiving fills the space (v. 1). God’s steadfast love is declared in the morning, before the day’s troubles can argue against it, and his faithfulness at night, looking back on a day in which he kept his word (v. 2). Lute, harp and lyre make the thanks beautiful (v. 3). And the reason is God’s work: the singer rests from his own labour and looks at what God has made and done, and finds himself glad (v. 4).
verseByVerse.theology: A Sabbath song begins where the Sabbath began: with gladness in what God has made and done.

verseByVerse.quote: It is good to give thanks to the LORD, to sing praises to your name, O Most High; to declare your steadfast love in the morning, and your faithfulness by night, to the music of the lute and the harp, to the melody of the lyre. For you, O LORD, have made me glad by your work; at the works of your hands I sing for joy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
It is good to thank God morning and night, with music, for his unfailing love and faithfulness and for the works of his hands.

It is good to give thanks to the LORD. The title calls this “A Song for the Sabbath”, and it begins with a statement that sounds simple. Thanks is good towards God, who deserves it, and good for the one who gives it, because it puts a person back in the right relation to everything. On the day of rest, it fills the space that work leaves.

In the morning, and your faithfulness by night. Thanks has a timetable. Begin the day with the love that never fails, before the day’s troubles have a chance to argue against it; end it by looking back and seeing that God kept his word through another day. Psalm 90 asked God to “satisfy us in the morning with your steadfast love” (90:14); this psalm says what to do when he has.

To the music of the lute and the harp. With lute, harp and lyre, thanks is meant to be beautiful, not merely correct.

The Sabbath thread. The Sabbath was God’s own day of rest after the work of creation, and the psalm picks up that thread. The worshipper rests from his work and looks at God’s, in creation, providence and rescue, and finds himself glad. The Christian’s rest goes further: “There remains a Sabbath rest for the people of God, for whoever has entered God’s rest has also rested from his works as God did from his” (Hebrews 4:9–10). The deepest Sabbath is resting from trying to earn God’s favour, and singing for joy at the work Christ has already done.

Where Christians differ: must Christians keep a Sabbath? Many godly Christians, with the Westminster Confession and the 1689 London Baptist Confession, hold that the Lord’s Day is the Christian Sabbath, binding by the fourth commandment. This commentary’s view: the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ (Colossians 2:16–17), the true rest it pointed to, and the Lord’s Day is a gift. Christians gladly set Sunday apart for worship, fellowship and rest, out of joy and wisdom rather than as a law with rules about work, and no one may bind another’s conscience over days (Romans 14:5). Faithful believers differ here, and both honour the day.

Where Christians differ: are instruments proper in worship (v. 3)? Some churches holding the regulative principle (that public worship should include only what God commands) sing unaccompanied, since the temple instruments belonged to its worship. This commentary’s view: the New Testament does not forbid them, and instruments may rightly serve the singing, provided all is done “decently and in order” (1 Corinthians 14:40).

Uncertain wording. The exact instruments of verse 3 are not certainly known. The word rendered “lute” is literally “ten”, probably a ten-stringed instrument, and the shapes of harp and lyre are debated.
verseByVerse.note: The title calls it a song for the Sabbath.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–11 — But You, O LORD, Are on High Forever
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The wicked flourish only like grass, but the LORD is on high for ever. God’s works are great and his thoughts too deep for the fool, who lives only by what he can see (vv. 5–6). What he sees is evildoers sprouting and flourishing; what he cannot see is that they are doomed (v. 7). At the centre of the psalm stands one short line: “but you, O LORD, are on high forever” (v. 8). God’s enemies will perish and be scattered (v. 9), while the singer has been made strong like a wild ox, refreshed with fresh oil, and has lived to see his enemies fall (vv. 10–11).
verseByVerse.theology: The fool sees only the morning of the wicked; the singer looks up to the God who is on high forever.

verseByVerse.quote: How great are your works, O LORD! Your thoughts are very deep! The stupid man cannot know; the fool cannot understand this: that though the wicked sprout like grass and all evildoers flourish, they are doomed to destruction forever; but you, O LORD, are on high forever. For behold, your enemies, O LORD, for behold, your enemies shall perish; all evildoers shall be scattered.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The fool sees only that the wicked flourish; he cannot see that, like grass, they are doomed, while at the centre of everything the LORD is on high for ever.

Your thoughts are very deep! From gladness the psalm moves to wonder. Behind God’s great works are purposes too deep for us to see the bottom, above all on the question the psalm is about to raise: why the wicked do so well.

The stupid man cannot know. He is not unintelligent; he lives like an animal, only by what he can see, and what he sees is that the wicked flourish. But they “sprout like grass”: quick, green, everywhere, and gone. Psalm 90 had just described grass that flourishes in the morning and “fades and withers” by evening (90:6). The fool sees the morning. He cannot see the evening.

But you, O LORD, are on high forever. This is verse 8 of fifteen. Seven verses stand before it and seven after, and it is the shortest line in the psalm. At the exact centre of a song about the wicked flourishing and the righteous growing old there is one sentence about God, and everything else is measured by it. The grass is temporary; the LORD is not. The New Testament shows where that throne now is: God raised Christ and “seated him at his right hand in the heavenly places, far above all rule and authority” (Ephesians 1:20–21).

Behold, your enemies shall perish. “Your enemies”, twice, with a “behold” each time, as though the singer is pointing. They are God’s enemies before they are the singer’s, and so their end is certain.

verseByVerse.quote: But you have exalted my horn like that of the wild ox; you have poured over me fresh oil. My eyes have seen the downfall of my enemies; my ears have heard the doom of my evil assailants.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God has made the singer strong and refreshed him, and he has lived long enough to see his enemies fall.

You have exalted my horn like that of the wild ox. The singer turns to his own experience. The horn of the wild ox is raw strength held high, and God has given him that. Fresh oil poured over the head was the sign of refreshment, honour and gladness, the oil a host poured on a welcome guest (23:5; Luke 7:46).

My eyes have seen the downfall of my enemies. The grass that was so green has withered in front of him. That is one of the gifts of a long life with God: a person begins to see the evening of things he once only saw in the morning.

Uncertain wording. The ESV notes that the meaning of the Hebrew in the second line of verse 10 is uncertain, and its rendering “you have poured over me fresh oil” follows the Syriac translation.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–15 — Still Bearing Fruit in Old Age
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The righteous are not grass but trees, planted in God’s house and still bearing fruit when they are old. Like the date palm with its deep roots and the long-lived cedar of Lebanon, they grow slowly and last (v. 12). The secret is the soil: they have been planted in the house of the LORD and flourish in his courts (v. 13). Even in old age they bear fruit and stay green (v. 14). And the point of the fruit is not the tree’s glory but God’s: their lives declare that the LORD is upright, their rock, with no unrighteousness in him (v. 15).
verseByVerse.theology: The wicked spring up like grass; the righteous grow like trees that are still bearing fruit when they are old.

verseByVerse.quote: The righteous flourish like the palm tree and grow like a cedar in Lebanon. They are planted in the house of the LORD; they flourish in the courts of our God. They still bear fruit in old age; they are ever full of sap and green, to declare that the LORD is upright; he is my rock, and there is no unrighteousness in him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The righteous are like long-lived trees planted in God’s house: they bear fruit into old age, and their lives declare that God is upright.

The righteous flourish like the palm tree. The wicked flourish for a season like grass (v. 7); the righteous flourish too, but like trees. The date palm grows in the desert, sends its roots down to hidden water, and bears fruit year after year. The cedar of Lebanon is the image of height, strength and long life. Grass is quick and shallow; these are slow and deep. Jeremiah drew the same contrast: the one who trusts in the LORD “is like a tree planted by water, that sends out its roots by the stream, and does not fear when heat comes, for its leaves remain green” (Jeremiah 17:8). And the whole Psalter began there: “He is like a tree planted by streams of water” (1:3).

Planted in the house of the LORD. The secret is the soil. These trees are planted, put there by someone else, in God’s house. A believer does not flourish by effort alone but by where he has been rooted: in the worship, the word and the people of God, where the Spirit keeps him green week after week.

They still bear fruit in old age. A promise for the elderly. The world treats old age as decline; God promises fruit. “Though our outer self is wasting away, our inner self is being renewed day by day” (2 Corinthians 4:16), and “Gray hair is a crown of glory; it is gained in a righteous life” (Proverbs 16:31).

Simeon and Anna. Think of the two old people in the temple when Mary and Joseph brought the baby: Simeon, “righteous and devout, waiting for the consolation of Israel” (Luke 2:25), and Anna, a widow in her eighties who “did not depart from the temple” (Luke 2:37). Planted in the house of the LORD, still full of sap, they were among the first to recognise the Christ. If you are old, your fruit-bearing years are not behind you.

To declare that the LORD is upright. The purpose of the fruit is not the tree’s glory but God’s. An old believer still green after decades of trouble is a living argument that God is faithful. “He is my rock”, says someone who has leaned on him for a lifetime, “and there is no unrighteousness in him”. The long life that has seen the wicked flourish and fade ends its song not with a complaint but with a verdict: God has never once done wrong. The cross is where that verdict was proved beyond question, for there God punished sin in full and pardoned sinners freely, “so that he might be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus” (Romans 3:26).

92.title: Planted in the House of the LORD
92.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 90 lamented lives that wither like grass, and Psalm 91 promised shelter under God’s wings. Psalm 92, “A Song for the Sabbath”, answers with thanksgiving: the wicked may sprout like grass, but the righteous grow like trees in God’s house and are still bearing fruit when they are old.

The message. It is good to thank God, morning and night, for his steadfast love and faithfulness. The success of the wicked is short-lived, like grass, because the LORD is on high for ever; and those he has planted in his house grow slowly, deeply and fruitfully into old age, their lives declaring that he is upright and has never done wrong.

Why it was said. The title sets it for the Sabbath, the day Israel stopped its own work to rest and remember God’s. It also answers a lasting trouble for believers: why do evildoers flourish while the faithful struggle? (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. It begins with why thanks is good: declaring God’s love in the morning and his faithfulness at night, with music, glad at the works of his hands (vv. 1–4). It marvels at God’s deep thoughts, which the fool cannot grasp: the wicked sprout like grass only to be destroyed (vv. 5–7). At the exact centre stands the shortest line, “but you, O LORD, are on high forever” (v. 8). God’s enemies perish, while the singer is made strong and refreshed and has lived to see his enemies fall (vv. 9–11). The righteous flourish like palm and cedar, planted in God’s house, bearing fruit in old age, to declare that the LORD is upright (vv. 12–15).

Where it leads. By pattern, and by the character of God revealed in Christ. The Sabbath this psalm celebrates pointed to the rest Christ gives: “There remains a Sabbath rest for the people of God” (Hebrews 4:9), rest from trying to earn God’s favour. The God who is “on high forever” is seen in the risen Christ, exalted above every enemy. And the claim of verse 15, that there is no unrighteousness in God, is proved at the cross, where God showed himself both just and the justifier of those who believe (Romans 3:26).

For us. Begin the day with his love and end it with his faithfulness. Do not envy those whose success springs up overnight. Stay planted among God’s people, where the Spirit keeps you green; and if you are old, your fruit-bearing years are not behind you.
92.theology:
Thanksgiving is good, and it frames the day: love in the morning, faithfulness at night (vv. 1-2). Sabbath rest is gladness in God's works (v. 4), fulfilled when we stop trying to earn God’s favour by our works and rest in Christ (Heb 4:9-10).

The prosperity of the wicked is real but grass-like (v. 7), and the centre verse, you, O LORD, are on high forever (v. 8), is the fixed point by which all else is measured. The righteous are trees planted in God's house (vv. 12-13), and their fruitfulness in old age exists to declare his uprightness (vv. 14-15).
92.examples: The singer gives thanks for love at the start of the day and faithfulness at the end of it, and finds the deepest Sabbath in resting from trying to earn God’s favour. The fool sees the wicked flourish like morning grass and cannot see them wither by evening, while the palm sends its roots down to hidden water. A long life ends with its verdict on God: there is no unrighteousness in him.

keyVerse.quote: but you, O LORD, are on high forever.
keyVerse.note: This short line stands at the exact centre of the psalm, with seven verses before it and seven after. Everything else, the wicked sprouting like grass and the righteous growing like trees, is measured against this one fixed point. Because the LORD reigns for ever, now seen in the risen Christ at his right hand, the success of evil is brief and the faithful can give thanks.

92.reflection:
The psalm calls us to declare God’s steadfast love “in the morning” and his faithfulness “by night” (v. 2). What would it look like to build thanksgiving into the beginning and end of your day?

Why does the success of the wicked trouble believers so much? How does verse 8, “but you, O LORD, are on high forever”, change the way we see it?

The righteous flourish because they are “planted in the house of the LORD” (v. 13). How has belonging to a church kept you spiritually green, and what tends to uproot people?

“They still bear fruit in old age” (v. 14). Who are the older believers who have borne fruit in your life, and how could your group honour and learn from them?

93.text: <sup>1</sup>The LORD reigns; he is robed in majesty; the LORD is robed; he has put on strength as his belt. Yes, the world is established; it shall never be moved.<sup>2</sup>Your throne is established from of old; you are from everlasting.<sup>3</sup>The floods have lifted up, O LORD, the floods have lifted up their voice; the floods lift up their roaring.<sup>4</sup>Mightier than the thunders of many waters, mightier than the waves of the sea, the LORD on high is mighty!<sup>5</sup>Your decrees are very trustworthy; holiness befits your house, O LORD, forevermore.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The LORD is King, dressed and ready, and because he reigns the world stands firm. The psalm opens with a report, not a wish: “The LORD reigns”. The King is robed in majesty and has put on strength as his belt, like a man ready for work or battle (v. 1). Because he reigns, the world is established and cannot be moved. His throne did not begin at some moment in history; it is from of old, and he himself is from everlasting (v. 2). Everything else in the psalm, the roaring floods and the trustworthy word, rests on this opening fact.
verseByVerse.theology: Five short verses begin with three words that settle everything else.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD reigns; he is robed in majesty; the LORD is robed; he has put on strength as his belt. Yes, the world is established; it shall never be moved. Your throne is established from of old; you are from everlasting.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD is already King, dressed and ready for action, and because his eternal throne stands, the world he holds stands too.

The LORD reigns. Three words open the psalm and carry it. The same words open Psalms 97 and 99, and Psalm 96 tells Israel to say them among the nations (96:10). They are a report, not a wish: the throne is not vacant, waiting to be filled.

He is robed in majesty. The King is described getting dressed: robed twice over, as if the singer cannot take his eyes off the robe, with strength as his belt, the belt a man tightened before work or battle.

Yes, the world is established. Because he reigns, the world stands. The same words were sung when the ark came into Jerusalem (1 Chronicles 16:30). When everything in a life seems to be shifting, what holds firm is not the circumstances but God’s reign.

Your throne is established from of old. The throne did not begin at some point, and the King is from everlasting, as Moses prayed three psalms earlier (90:2). He was not elected, did not inherit and will not be succeeded.

The throne of the Son. Hebrews gives this eternal throne to Christ: “Your throne, O God, is forever and ever” (Hebrews 1:8). The risen Jesus said, “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (Matthew 28:18), and the end of history is already announced: “The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ, and he shall reign forever and ever” (Revelation 11:15). He rules for his people, not against them.

Handing back the crown. A reigning God can sound like a threat to our freedom. But someone is always reigning. If God is not on the throne of a life, something else climbs onto it: our plans, our need for control, the opinion of the people we most want to impress. They make hard masters, because none of them can hold back a single wave. Much of our anxiety is the strain of trying to run a world we were never made to run. The news of this psalm is that the throne is already occupied, and by someone good. So the next time you lie awake rehearsing what you cannot control, say these three words to yourself, and hand back the crown you were never meant to wear. See also Sovereignty in the Theological Dictionary.

Does this teach a motionless earth? No. Never be moved means never shaken from its foundation: it is poetry about the stability God gives his world, not astronomy.
verseByVerse.note: The first of a cluster of psalms celebrating the LORD as King (93; 95–99); Psalm 47 sounds the same note earlier.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 3–5 — Mightier Than the Waves of the Sea
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The floods of chaos rise and roar, but the King above them is mightier, and his word holds. Three times the floods lift up their voice, like a tide coming in wave after wave (v. 3), and the sea stands for every power that threatens to swallow God’s ordered world. The answer is not that the flood is small but that the LORD on high is mighty, mightier than the thunder of many waters (v. 4). Then the psalm closes quietly: the King who rules the flood also speaks, his decrees are very trustworthy, and holiness befits his house for ever (v. 5).
verseByVerse.theology: The flood keeps rising, and the King above it does not move.

verseByVerse.quote: The floods have lifted up, O LORD, the floods have lifted up their voice; the floods lift up their roaring. Mightier than the thunders of many waters, mightier than the waves of the sea, the LORD on high is mighty!
verseByVerse.commentary:
The powers of chaos are loud and rising, but the LORD is mightier than all of them, as Jesus showed when he stilled the storm and walked on the sea.

The floods have lifted up, O LORD. Now the danger. The floods comes three times, and you hear the water rising, wave after wave.

The sea as chaos. To Israel the sea was the image of chaos, everything that threatens to swallow the ordered world. Israel’s neighbours told of a storm god who won his kingship by defeating the Sea; this psalm needs no battle, because the LORD reigns already. The prophets used the same picture for hostile nations: “Ah, the roar of nations; they roar like the roaring of mighty waters!” (Isaiah 17:12). Whatever the floods are in a believer’s life, hostile powers, overwhelming grief, a culture rising against God, they are loud and rising.

The LORD on high is mighty! The answer is not that the flood is small, but that the LORD is mightier.

He came to them, walking on the sea. The disciples found this out in a boat. After Jesus stilled the storm, “they were filled with great fear and said to one another, ‘Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?’” (Mark 4:41). On another night “he came to them, walking on the sea” (Matthew 14:25): on top of the thing that terrified them.

The roar changed. At the end John heard the roar of many waters again, changed. It was “the voice of a great multitude, like the roar of many waters”, crying, “Hallelujah! For the Lord our God the Almighty reigns” (Revelation 19:6). The noise that once threatened now sings Psalm 93. And in the new creation “the sea was no more” (Revelation 21:1).

verseByVerse.quote: Your decrees are very trustworthy; holiness befits your house, O LORD, forevermore.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The King who rules the flood also speaks, and because his word can be trusted completely, his power is his people’s safety; and the fitting response is holiness.

Your decrees are very trustworthy. After the robes, the throne and the roaring sea, the psalm ends not with a display of power but with God’s word and God’s holiness. What the King says can be relied on completely. His power would be terrifying if his word were not trustworthy. Because it is, his power is the believer’s safety.

Holiness befits your house. The fitting thing in the palace of such a King is holiness (the seraphim cry “Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of hosts”, Isaiah 6:3), and those who live in his house are called to share it: “You shall be holy, for I am holy” (1 Peter 1:16).
