Christ has already given us this holiness (1 Corinthians 1:30), and his Spirit makes us holy in the way we live.

When the floods are rising. So believe his decrees, and live as members of a holy house. The kingdom you belong to “cannot be shaken” (Hebrews 12:28), because the LORD reigns, and he will, forevermore.

Uncertain wording. The verb rendered “befits” is a rare form: it may mean that holiness is fitting for God’s house, or that it adorns it. Either way, in the King’s house holiness belongs.

93.title: The LORD Reigns
93.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 93 is the first of the psalms that cry “The LORD reigns” (93; 96–99), set in Book Four just after Moses’ prayer (90) and the psalms of shelter and Sabbath praise (91–92). Book Three ended with David’s crown “in the dust” (89:39). This short psalm answers: before Israel had a king, and after its kings had fallen, God was King.

The message. The LORD is King, always has been and always will be, so the world he holds is secure. The floods of chaos are loud and rising, but he is mightier than all of them. And the last word is not power but trust and holiness: his word can be relied on completely, and his house is to be holy for ever.

Why it was said. The psalm has no title or occasion. Israel lived among nations that roared like the sea, and those who gathered these psalms had seen throne and temple fall (see the introduction). The psalm tells them where the real throne is: it has never been empty.

How the chapter makes its case. First the King himself: robed in majesty, belted with strength, so that the world stands firm, his throne older than time and he himself from everlasting (vv. 1–2). Then the threat: the floods lift up their voice, three times over, louder and higher; but the LORD on high is mightier than the thunder of many waters (vv. 3–4). Then, unexpectedly quiet, the ending: the King also speaks, his decrees are very trustworthy, and holiness fits his house for ever (v. 5).

Where it leads. To Christ, by the character of God revealed in him. In a boat on a stormy lake the disciples watched a man rebuke the wind and the waves, and asked, “Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?” (Mark 4:41). Hebrews gives the eternal throne of verse 2 to the Son: “Your throne, O God, is forever and ever” (Hebrews 1:8). The risen Jesus claims “all authority in heaven and on earth” (Matthew 28:18), and at the end the roar of many waters becomes the voice of a great multitude crying, “Hallelujah! For the Lord our God the Almighty reigns” (Revelation 19:6).

For us. Someone is always on the throne of a life, and much of our anxiety is the strain of trying to rule a world we were never made to run. The throne is already occupied, by a King who is good, who holds back the waves and keeps his word. Say the psalm’s first three words when the floods are rising, trust his promises, and live as members of his holy house.
93.theology:
God's reign is stated as fact (v. 1). Because he reigns, the world is established, and his throne and being are without beginning (v. 2; 90:2).

The rising floods represent chaos and hostile nations (v. 3); God is mightier (v. 4), as Christ showed on the sea, and in Revelation the roar of many waters becomes the praise of the redeemed (Rev 19:6), before the sea is no more. The psalm closes on the trustworthiness of God's word and the holiness fitting his house (v. 5), and on a kingdom that cannot be shaken.
93.examples: The psalm's first three words are a report, not a wish, and they tell us that what holds life steady is God’s reign, not our circumstances. Christ walks on top of the thing that terrified his disciples, and in the end the roar of the waters is turned into Hallelujah. Because his word can be trusted, his power is our safety and not our terror.

keyVerse.quote: The LORD reigns; he is robed in majesty; the LORD is robed; he has put on strength as his belt.
keyVerse.note: The psalm’s first three words are the foundation of everything that follows, and of the whole group of “The LORD reigns” psalms. They are a report, not a wish: the King is already dressed and ready, so the floods of verse 3 rise against a throne that cannot be moved. In Christ, who stilled the sea, we see who sits on it.

93.reflection:
The psalm opens with a report, not a wish: “The LORD reigns.” When you lie awake over things you cannot control, what tends to climb onto the throne of your life instead?

What are the “floods” rising in your life, your church or your culture just now? How does the psalm answer them without pretending they are small?

Read Mark 4:35–41. What did the disciples learn about Jesus in the storm, and how does Psalm 93 help explain their question, “Who then is this?”

The psalm ends not with power but with God’s trustworthy word and the holiness of his house (v. 5). Why do you think it ends there, and what would it look like to live as a member of his holy house this week?

94.text: <sup>1</sup>O LORD, God of vengeance, O God of vengeance, shine forth!<sup>2</sup>Rise up, O judge of the earth; repay to the proud what they deserve!<sup>3</sup>O LORD, how long shall the wicked, how long shall the wicked exult?<sup>4</sup>They pour out their arrogant words; all the evildoers boast.<sup>5</sup>They crush your people, O LORD, and afflict your heritage.<sup>6</sup>They kill the widow and the sojourner, and murder the fatherless;<sup>7</sup>and they say, "The LORD does not see; the God of Jacob does not perceive."<sup>8</sup>Understand, O dullest of the people! Fools, when will you be wise?<sup>9</sup>He who planted the ear, does he not hear? He who formed the eye, does he not see?<sup>10</sup>He who disciplines the nations, does he not rebuke? He who teaches man knowledge—<sup>11</sup>the LORD—knows the thoughts of man, that they are but a breath.<sup>12</sup>Blessed is the man whom you discipline, O LORD, and whom you teach out of your law,<sup>13</sup>to give him rest from days of trouble, until a pit is dug for the wicked.<sup>14</sup>For the LORD will not forsake his people; he will not abandon his heritage;<sup>15</sup>for justice will return to the righteous, and all the upright in heart will follow it.<sup>16</sup>Who rises up for me against the wicked? Who stands up for me against evildoers?<sup>17</sup>If the LORD had not been my help, my soul would soon have lived in the land of silence.<sup>18</sup>When I thought, "My foot slips," your steadfast love, O LORD, held me up.<sup>19</sup>When the cares of my heart are many, your consolations cheer my soul.<sup>20</sup>Can wicked rulers be allied with you, those who frame injustice by statute?<sup>21</sup>They band together against the life of the righteous and condemn the innocent to death.<sup>22</sup>But the LORD has become my stronghold, and my God the rock of my refuge.<sup>23</sup>He will bring back on them their iniquity and wipe them out for their wickedness; the LORD our God will wipe them out.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — O God of Vengeance, Shine Forth
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The psalm begins with a cry for justice from people who have watched the powerful kill the powerless and assume no one is looking. It calls on the LORD as the God of vengeance and judge of the earth to step out of hiding and repay the proud (vv. 1–2), and asks twice how long the wicked will be allowed to gloat (v. 3). Then it lays out the charges: boasting words, God’s people crushed, and the widow, the foreigner and the orphan killed (vv. 4–6). Beneath it all lies one belief, that the LORD does not see (v. 7).
verseByVerse.theology: A prayer for justice from people who have watched the powerful kill the powerless and assume no one is looking.

verseByVerse.quote: O LORD, God of vengeance, O God of vengeance, shine forth! Rise up, O judge of the earth; repay to the proud what they deserve! O LORD, how long shall the wicked, how long shall the wicked exult?
verseByVerse.commentary:
The psalmist asks the Judge of the earth to step out and set right the wrongs of the proud: not spite, but the wronged handing their cause to God instead of taking revenge.

O LORD, God of vengeance. God of vengeance, twice, makes modern readers flinch. But the word does not mean spite. It means just retribution, the setting right of wrongs by the one who has the authority to do it (Deuteronomy 32:35). The psalm asks not that God lose his temper, but that the judge of the earth act like one.

Shine forth! A plea for God to step out of hiddenness into the light, where the wicked must see him.

How long shall the wicked exult? How long, twice: the cry of the martyrs under the altar, “how long before you will judge and avenge our blood” (Revelation 6:10). Jesus answered it in a parable: “will not God give justice to his elect, who cry to him day and night? Will he delay long over them?” (Luke 18:7). But he added a harder question: “when the Son of Man comes, will he find faith on earth?” (Luke 18:8). The danger in the waiting is not that God will fail to act, but that we will stop praying.

Where the wronged are sent. This is where the New Testament sends the wronged: “Beloved, never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God, for it is written, ‘Vengeance is mine, I will repay, says the Lord’” (Romans 12:19). Praying Psalm 94 is not the opposite of forgiving your enemy; it makes forgiveness possible, because the wrong has been handed to someone who will deal with it justly, and you no longer have to carry it.

What it does not mean. Leaving vengeance to God is not keeping silent about crime or abuse. God has given governing authorities to punish wrongdoers (Romans 13:4); reporting harm to them, and getting to safety, is not revenge.

verseByVerse.quote: They pour out their arrogant words; all the evildoers boast. They crush your people, O LORD, and afflict your heritage. They kill the widow and the sojourner, and murder the fatherless; and they say, "The LORD does not see; the God of Jacob does not perceive."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The powerful are crushing the very people God promised to protect, because they believe God does not see.

They crush your people, O LORD. The wicked here are not foreign invaders but powerful people inside the nation, who talk a great deal. What they crush is your people, your heritage: the psalm insists the victims belong to God.

They kill the widow and the sojourner. The three victims named are the three the law of Moses singled out for protection (Exodus 22:21–24): the widow with no husband, the foreigner with no family, the orphan with no father. A corrupt ruler could destroy them without consequence, and God had said he would defend them. Jesus kept the same watch, condemning religious leaders “who devour widows’ houses and for a pretense make long prayers” (Mark 12:40).

The LORD does not see. Here is the root of it (compare 10:11). These men do not deny that God exists; they are Israelites, and they use his names. They simply live as if he were not watching: practical atheism, far more common than the other kind. Anyone who does in private what he would never do if God were visibly in the room has, for that moment, said this verse. Yet the God who sees is also the God who forgives what he sees when it is confessed (32:5).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–15 — He Who Planted the Ear
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The God who made ears is not deaf, and the God who disciplines his people has not abandoned them. The psalmist turns to the oppressors and calls them fools: the one who planted the ear hears, the one who formed the eye sees, and the one who teaches all knowledge knows their thoughts are a mere breath (vv. 8–11). Then he turns back to God. The believer who suffers is not forgotten but trained: blessed is the one God disciplines and teaches from his law, for that brings rest while judgment is prepared for the wicked (vv. 12–13). God will never forsake his people, and justice will return (vv. 14–15).
verseByVerse.theology: The God who made ears is not deaf, and the God who disciplines his people has not abandoned them.

verseByVerse.quote: Understand, O dullest of the people! Fools, when will you be wise? He who planted the ear, does he not hear? He who formed the eye, does he not see? He who disciplines the nations, does he not rebuke? He who teaches man knowledge— the LORD—knows the thoughts of man, that they are but a breath.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those who think God does not see are the real fools: the Maker of ear and eye hears and sees, and knows how flimsy their clever thoughts are.

Understand, O dullest of the people! Now the psalmist turns on the oppressors: they are the dullest of the people, because they have built their whole way of life on a mistake about God.

He who planted the ear, does he not hear? Someone planted the ear and formed the eye; is he supposed to be deaf and blind? The one who invented hearing hears everything. Every whispered cruelty has been heard by the designer of the ear.

Can a mind made by accident trust itself? The argument reaches further than it looks. If the eye, ear and mind were planted by someone, it makes sense to trust them; if they were thrown up by a blind process that cared only for survival, it is harder to say why. Charles Darwin felt this himself. In a letter of 1881 he wrote, “With me the horrid doubt always arises whether the convictions of man’s mind, which has been developed from the mind of the lower animals, are of any value or at all trustworthy.” C. S. Lewis pressed the point: a mind with no Maker has no guarantee that its reasoning tracks the truth. This does not settle questions of biology (see the note on Genesis 1:1), but the believer is not the one sawing off the branch he sits on. The God who teaches man knowledge came as the Word himself, “The true light, which gives light to everyone” (John 1:9), so that our thinking could at last be both humbled and trusted.

That they are but a breath. God disciplines whole nations; he will not overlook a few corrupt men. His verdict on human thinking is short: but a breath. The Greek translation reads “futile”, and Paul quotes it that way to puncture intellectual pride: “The Lord knows the thoughts of the wise, that they are futile” (1 Corinthians 3:20). The cleverest schemes of the powerful weigh about as much as an exhaled breath.

Uncertain wording. Verses 10–11 are compressed in Hebrew. “He who teaches man knowledge” seems to begin one more question (does he not know?), but the sentence breaks off and the next line finishes it, as the ESV’s dashes show. The sense is clear: the teacher of all knowledge knows every thought.
verseByVerse.note: Paul quotes v. 11.

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed is the man whom you discipline, O LORD, and whom you teach out of your law, to give him rest from days of trouble, until a pit is dug for the wicked. For the LORD will not forsake his people; he will not abandon his heritage; for justice will return to the righteous, and all the upright in heart will follow it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For God’s people, hardship under his hand is training, not rejection, and it comes with a sure promise: he will never abandon them, and justice will come home.

Blessed is the man whom you discipline, O LORD. The word discipline, used of the nations (v. 10), is used of God’s own people too, and the person under it is called blessed.

Whom you teach out of your law. This is how a believer reads his own suffering while the wicked flourish: not punishment from an enemy but training from a Father. Hebrews says the same: God “disciplines us for our good, that we may share his holiness”, and though it “seems painful rather than pleasant”, later “it yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness” (Hebrews 12:10–11).

To give him rest from days of trouble. The discipline has an end in view: rest from days of trouble. Meanwhile, out of sight, a pit is dug for the wicked. The righteous man learns and rests; the wicked walks confidently towards a hole he cannot see.

The LORD will not forsake his people. Here is the certainty the whole psalm rests on. Paul leaned on the same assurance: “God has not rejected his people whom he foreknew” (Romans 11:2). In verse 5 the wicked afflict your heritage; here he will not abandon his heritage. The oppressors thought the people had no owner; but they are God’s inheritance, and he does not abandon it to vandals.

For justice will return to the righteous. Justice, gone missing from the courts, will return like an exile coming home, and the upright will fall in behind it.

Uncertain wording. Verse 15 reads literally “judgment will return to righteousness”: probably the courts will again give righteous verdicts. The ESV takes it of the righteous people who receive justice. Either way, what has gone missing will come back.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–23 — When I Thought, My Foot Slips
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When no one rose up for him, God did, and the psalm ends in confidence against even legalised injustice. The psalmist looks for a defender and finds none on earth; without the LORD he would already be in the grave (vv. 16–17). But at the moment he felt his foot slip, God’s steadfast love held him, and for each of his many anxious thoughts God gave comfort (vv. 18–19). Then he names the worst evil, rulers who frame injustice by statute and condemn the innocent (vv. 20–21). Against them the LORD is his stronghold, and he will bring their wickedness back on them (vv. 22–23).
verseByVerse.theology: Against legalised injustice, a man finds that God's love caught him the moment he felt himself slip.

verseByVerse.quote: Who rises up for me against the wicked? Who stands up for me against evildoers? If the LORD had not been my help, my soul would soon have lived in the land of silence. When I thought, "My foot slips," your steadfast love, O LORD, held me up. When the cares of my heart are many, your consolations cheer my soul.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When no one on earth stood up for him, the LORD did: his steadfast love caught him as his foot began to slip, and his comforts met each anxious thought.

Who rises up for me against the wicked? The psalm becomes personal. He looks for a defender, and there is no one. In verse 2 he prayed, Rise up, O judge of the earth. Now he asks, Who rises up for me? Nobody on earth rose up for him; the Judge of the earth did.

The land of silence. The grave. He was that close.

When I thought, “My foot slips.” Not after he fell, but at the instant he felt his footing go, as on loose stones at a cliff edge, God’s steadfast love caught him. Many believers know that moment: the diagnosis, the phone call, the sense that faith itself is giving way. The psalm does not say he never slipped, but that the love of God was quicker than the fall.

When the cares of my heart are many. Anxious thoughts multiply at night, crowding and tangling. Against them God sets his consolations, plural, one for each. Paul knew the “God of all comfort, who comforts us in all our affliction” (2 Corinthians 1:3–4). The comfort does not remove every care; it cheers the soul in the middle of them.

The one no one stood up for. Paul lived this verse in a Roman court: “At my first defense no one came to stand by me … But the Lord stood by me and strengthened me” (2 Timothy 4:16–17). Christ had gone further alone: on the night of his arrest “they all left him and fled” (Mark 14:50). Now his people are never without someone to stand up for them: he “is at the right hand of God”, and “is interceding for us” (Romans 8:34).

What it does not mean. It does not promise that anxious thoughts vanish at once. Where anxiety or despair persists, talk to a pastor or biblical counsellor and see a doctor; medicine is no failure of faith. If you are thinking of ending your life, tell someone and get help today.

verseByVerse.quote: Can wicked rulers be allied with you, those who frame injustice by statute? They band together against the life of the righteous and condemn the innocent to death. But the LORD has become my stronghold, and my God the rock of my refuge. He will bring back on them their iniquity and wipe them out for their wickedness; the LORD our God will wipe them out.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Rulers who write injustice into law cannot claim God as their ally; he is his people’s refuge against them, and will turn their wickedness back on their own heads.

Those who frame injustice by statute. Now the worst kind of wickedness: injustice written into law. These rulers do not break the law; they frame (the ESV notes “fashion”) injustice by statute. Their cruelty is legal. Can a government like that claim God as its ally?

And condemn the innocent to death. The ESV notes that the Hebrew says they “condemn innocent blood”. A court, following procedure, sentences an innocent man to die. It happened often in Israel, and once in Jerusalem in a way that changed the world, when the high priest’s council and Pontius Pilate lawfully condemned the only wholly innocent man who ever lived. There the God of vengeance did what no one expected. The judgment sin deserves fell on the innocent one, “the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring us to God” (1 Peter 3:18), so that even oppressors who turn to him can be forgiven.

But the LORD has become my stronghold. Against law turned into a weapon, the psalmist has a stronghold no statute can reach. The psalm ends where it began, with the God of vengeance. The psalmist has handed the wrong over to God, and has found meanwhile that the God who will judge them is also the God who caught him when he slipped.

The LORD our God. Listen to the last pronouns. Verse 22 is personal: my stronghold, my God. Verse 23 ends the LORD our God. The man who stood alone finishes among a people: what God did for one sufferer becomes the confidence of the whole congregation.

Must Christians still obey unjust rulers? We obey authority (Romans 13:1–7; 1 Peter 2:13–17) unless it commands what God forbids; then “We must obey God rather than men” (Acts 5:29). The psalmist’s own answer to injustice is prayer and refuge in God (v. 22), not revenge.

Uncertain wording. “Wicked rulers” in verse 20 is literally “a throne of destruction”, a seat of power that brings ruin, and “be allied with” may also be rendered “be joined to”. The question is plain all the same: can such power claim God as its partner?

94.title: Your Consolations Cheer My Soul
94.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 94 stands among the psalms that cry “The LORD reigns” (93; 95–99). After the King above the floods (93), it asks the hard question his reign raises: if the LORD reigns, why do the wicked flourish and the innocent die?

The message. God sees, and the Judge of the earth will act. Those who crush the helpless while saying “The LORD does not see” are fools, for the one who made the ear can hear. Meanwhile God trains his own people through hardship, will never abandon them, and holds them up the moment their foot slips. So the wronged can hand their cause to him instead of carrying or avenging it themselves.

Why it was said. The oppressors here are not foreign armies but powerful people inside Israel: rulers and courts who kill the widow, the foreigner and the orphan, and write injustice into law (vv. 6, 20). It gives their victims words to pray, as one of the psalms that call on God for justice against unrepentant evil (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. It opens with a cry to the God of vengeance to shine forth and judge, and the question “how long?”, followed by the charge sheet: arrogant words, the defenceless killed, and the creed behind it all, “The LORD does not see” (vv. 1–7). Then the psalmist turns on the oppressors: the maker of the ear and eye hears and sees, and knows their thoughts are a breath (vv. 8–11). He turns back to God: blessed is the one God disciplines, for he will not forsake his people, and justice will come home (vv. 12–15). Then it turns personal: no one stood up for him, but when his foot slipped God’s steadfast love held him (vv. 16–19). Last, the worst evil, injustice by statute, and the last word, the LORD is his stronghold and will repay (vv. 20–23).

Where it leads. To Christ, by the need it exposes and by pattern. A council and a governor once lawfully condemned the only wholly innocent man, and no one stood up for him. There the God of vengeance did the unexpected: the judgment sin deserves fell on the innocent one, so that even oppressors who turn to him can be forgiven. And the Judge the psalm longs for has a name: God “will judge the world in righteousness by a man whom he has appointed” (Acts 17:31).

For us. Bring your wrongs to God and leave them with him: that is what sets you free to forgive. Live as one who is seen, because you are. And when your foot slips, his steadfast love is quicker than the fall.
94.theology:
Vengeance belongs to God as the just judge of the earth (vv. 1-2); because we can hand it to him, we need not avenge ourselves. The prayer how long (v. 3) is answered by the promise that God will give justice to his elect (Luke 18:7-8).

Oppression of the defenceless flows from practical atheism, the assumption that God does not see (vv. 6-7), but the Creator of ear and eye hears and sees (vv. 9-11). God's discipline of his people is a blessing, and he will not forsake them (vv. 12-14). His steadfast love catches the believer as the foot begins to slip, and his consolations meet each anxious care (vv. 18-19). Injustice framed by law cannot claim God as its ally (v. 20).
94.examples: Vengeance handed over to God no longer has to be carried. Many believe in God and live as if he were not looking, but the inventor of the ear is not deaf. The psalmist was caught at the instant his footing went, and found one consolation for each anxious thought.

keyVerse.quote: When I thought, “My foot slips,” your steadfast love, O LORD, held me up. When the cares of my heart are many, your consolations cheer my soul.
keyVerse.note: These verses give the psalm its heart and its title. Amid injustice that no earthly court would correct, the psalmist found that God’s steadfast love caught him at the very moment his footing went, and met each anxious thought with comfort. It is the personal proof of the psalm’s great promise that the LORD will not forsake his people (v. 14).

94.reflection:
The psalm calls God “God of vengeance” (v. 1) and leaves the wrong with him. How does handing a wrong to God make it possible to forgive, and where might you need to do that?

The oppressors say, “The LORD does not see” (v. 7), yet they still use his name. Where are we most tempted to live as if God were not watching?

Verses 12–13 call the one God disciplines “blessed”. How can a hard season be training from a Father rather than punishment from an enemy, and how would you say that gently to a suffering friend?

No one stood up for the psalmist, but God’s love held him as his foot slipped (vv. 16–18). How does Jesus, deserted and lawfully condemned, make this promise sure for us?

95.text: <sup>1</sup>Oh come, let us sing to the LORD; let us make a joyful noise to the rock of our salvation!<sup>2</sup>Let us come into his presence with thanksgiving; let us make a joyful noise to him with songs of praise!<sup>3</sup>For the LORD is a great God, and a great King above all gods.<sup>4</sup>In his hand are the depths of the earth; the heights of the mountains are his also.<sup>5</sup>The sea is his, for he made it, and his hands formed the dry land.<sup>6</sup>Oh come, let us worship and bow down; let us kneel before the LORD, our Maker!<sup>7</sup>For he is our God, and we are the people of his pasture, and the sheep of his hand. Today, if you hear his voice,<sup>8</sup>do not harden your hearts, as at Meribah, as on the day at Massah in the wilderness,<sup>9</sup>when your fathers put me to the test and put me to the proof, though they had seen my work.<sup>10</sup>For forty years I loathed that generation and said, "They are a people who go astray in their heart, and they have not known my ways."<sup>11</sup>Therefore I swore in my wrath, "They shall not enter my rest."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — Oh Come, Let Us Sing to the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The people God has saved are invited to be loud about it, because their King made and owns everything. A worshipper calls the congregation together: come, sing, shout for joy to the Rock of our salvation, and enter his presence with thanksgiving (vv. 1–2). Then come the reasons. The LORD is a great King above all the gods the nations worship (v. 3). The deepest places and the highest peaks are in his hand, and the sea and the dry land are his, for his own hands made them (vv. 4–5). Every territory other gods were thought to rule belongs to him.
verseByVerse.theology: The people God has saved are invited to be loud about it, because their King made and owns everything.

verseByVerse.quote: Oh come, let us sing to the LORD; let us make a joyful noise to the rock of our salvation! Let us come into his presence with thanksgiving; let us make a joyful noise to him with songs of praise!
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s people call one another to come and worship him with loud joy and thanksgiving, because he is the Rock who saved them.

Oh come, let us sing to the LORD. For many centuries this psalm has opened the church’s morning worship, and it begins as an invitation spoken by one worshipper to the rest. It is a congregation calling itself together.

Let us make a joyful noise. That is a shout, the sound a crowd makes when its king rides in. People who have been saved are allowed to be loud about it.

The rock of our salvation! Look at the title they shout to. At Massah and Meribah (v. 8) the fathers stood before a rock in the wilderness, quarrelling with God, and water came out of it (Exodus 17:6–7). Paul says “the Rock was Christ” (1 Corinthians 10:4). Every generation of God’s people sings to the same Rock their fathers complained at.

Let us come into his presence with thanksgiving. The way in is thanksgiving. Nobody enters God’s presence by complaint, entitlement or indifference, only by remembering what he has done and saying thank you for it.
verseByVerse.note: Used for centuries as the call to worship (the Venite) in morning prayer.

verseByVerse.quote: For the LORD is a great God, and a great King above all gods. In his hand are the depths of the earth; the heights of the mountains are his also. The sea is his, for he made it, and his hands formed the dry land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD is the great King above every so-called god, because everything, from the depths of the earth to the sea and the mountains, is his: he made it.

A great King above all gods. Now the reasons, beginning with size. Israel’s neighbours had gods of the sea, the mountains, the underworld, the harvest. The LORD is a great King above all of them. Whatever else people worship, then or now, sits below him.

The heights of the mountains are his also. The psalm surveys the world from bottom to top, the deepest places to the highest peaks, and from wet to dry, the sea and the land. Every territory pagan gods were thought to rule belongs to him, for a simple reason: he made it. All things were made through the Son (John 1:3).

His hands formed the dry land. The picture is of hands. The depths are in his hand; his hands formed the land, as a potter shapes clay. The same hands will appear in verse 7, holding sheep.

Do other gods exist? Not as rivals of the LORD’s kind. They are the gods the nations worshipped, which are idols (96:5), and the demonic powers behind them (Deuteronomy 32:17; 1 Corinthians 10:20). “There is no God but one” (1 Corinthians 8:4).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–7 — Let Us Kneel Before the LORD, Our Maker
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Joy and reverence belong together: the King to be cheered is also the Maker to be knelt to, and the Shepherd to be heard. The invitation comes a second time, but now the posture changes from shouting to kneeling, because the great King is our Maker (v. 6). And he is closer than a King: he is our God, and we are the people of his pasture and the sheep of his hand (v. 7). Then, in the middle of the verse, the singing gives way to God’s own voice, and the word that matters is “Today”.
verseByVerse.theology: Joy and reverence belong together: the King to be cheered is also the Maker to be knelt to, and the Shepherd to be heard.

verseByVerse.quote: Oh come, let us worship and bow down; let us kneel before the LORD, our Maker! For he is our God, and we are the people of his pasture, and the sheep of his hand. Today, if you hear his voice,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The King who is cheered must also be knelt to, because he is our Maker and our Shepherd, and his sheep listen when he speaks, today.

Let us worship and bow down. The invitation comes again, but now the posture goes down: bow down, kneel. The King who owns the mountains is not only to be cheered but knelt to. Joy and reverence belong together, and a church that has only one of them has lost something.

The LORD, our Maker! The reason is personal: not only the maker of the sea, but the maker of us. The day will come when “at the name of Jesus every knee should bow” (Philippians 2:10). The psalm invites us to kneel willingly now.

The sheep of his hand. From King and Maker, the psalm comes to Shepherd. The sheep of his hand is a tender phrase: the hands that formed the dry land now lead, lift and carry the flock (see Shepherds and Sheepfolds). The God of verse 3 is enormous; the God of verse 7 is close enough to touch.

Today, if you hear his voice. Then, mid-verse, the singing stops and God’s voice begins. After seven verses of invitation to come near and praise, it warns of what can happen to worshippers who come near and do not listen. Today is the key word: not someday, not when life is less busy, but today, while the voice is speaking. Jesus said, “My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me” (John 10:27).

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew can be read as a condition, “if you hear his voice”, or as a longing wish, “Oh, that today you would listen to his voice!” Hebrews quotes the Greek translation, which reads it as a condition (Hebrews 3:7). Either way, the stress falls on Today.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–11 — They Shall Not Enter My Rest
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The worship song ends with a warning from God about a generation that sang and saw and still would not listen. God speaks directly: do not harden your hearts as at Meribah and Massah, where your fathers tested him even though they had seen his work (vv. 8–9). For forty years he was grieved with a generation whose feet followed him while their hearts wandered, and they never knew his ways (v. 10). So he swore that they would not enter his rest (v. 11). Hebrews preaches this warning to Christians, and shows that the rest is still open today.
verseByVerse.theology: The worship song ends with a warning from God about a generation that sang and saw and still would not listen.

verseByVerse.quote: do not harden your hearts, as at Meribah, as on the day at Massah in the wilderness, when your fathers put me to the test and put me to the proof, though they had seen my work.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not let your heart harden against God as Israel’s did in the wilderness, when they demanded that he prove himself again although they had seen all he had done.

As at Meribah. The warning points back to a specific day. Shortly after the Red Sea, Israel ran out of water and turned on Moses, and the place was named Massah (testing) and Meribah (quarrelling), “because they tested the LORD by saying, ‘Is the LORD among us or not?’” (Exodus 17:7). A similar quarrel at Meribah came near the end of the journey (Numbers 20:1–13).

Do not harden your hearts. A hard heart does not begin as open rebellion. It begins with that question, is God really here?, asked in a moment of need and answered with a complaint rather than with trust. And it hardens a little more each time.

Though they had seen my work. They had watched the plagues, walked through the sea and eaten manna. They had seen more of God’s work than almost anyone in history, and they still demanded that he prove himself again. Experience of God does not protect a heart from hardening. A person can sit in worship every week, sing every song and remember many answered prayers, and still be hardening. When something goes wrong this week, will your first question be whether God is with you, or will you trust that he is and ask what he is doing?

How do I keep my heart from hardening? Hearts harden slowly and quietly, so the remedy is daily and ordinary. Listen while it is today. When a sermon or a passage presses on something, the grudge, the habit, the unkind way you speak at home, act on it this week rather than filing it away; every postponed word makes the next one easier to ignore. Turn the complaint into a prayer. When the money runs short or the plan collapses, say to God what you would have said about him, and then name one thing he has already done for you. Let someone ask you hard questions. Hardening is hidden from the one it happens to, which is why Hebrews makes the cure a shared one (Hebrews 3:12–13); give a friend permission to ask how you really are with God. Go back to the cross. Hearts soften not under threats but under kindness. The God who promised to remove “the heart of stone” and give “a heart of flesh” (Ezekiel 36:26) did it by sending his Son, who endured the whole wilderness test without hardening, and offers us the rest Israel missed.
verseByVerse.note: Meribah (“quarreling”) and Massah (“testing”) recall Israel testing God for water.

verseByVerse.quote: For forty years I loathed that generation and said, "They are a people who go astray in their heart, and they have not known my ways." Therefore I swore in my wrath, "They shall not enter my rest."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A generation that walked with God for forty years without giving him their hearts was shut out of his rest; that rest is still offered today, in Christ, to all who believe.

They are a people who go astray in their heart. It went on for forty years. God had told Moses that these people had “put me to the test these ten times and have not obeyed my voice” (Numbers 14:22). The diagnosis is in the heart. Their feet followed the cloud through the wilderness; their hearts wandered somewhere else. They walked with God for forty years and have not known my ways.

For forty years I loathed that generation. Loathed is a strong word, and the psalm means it to be. God is not indifferent to a people who take his gifts and refuse his voice.

They shall not enter my rest. And the psalm stops. A worship song that began Oh come, let us sing ends with a door being shut. The rest was the land of promise, and a whole generation died outside it.

Hebrews preaches this psalm. Hebrews takes this psalm and preaches it to Christians at length (Hebrews 3:7–4:11). It quotes the Greek translation, so the wording differs a little, “Therefore I was provoked with that generation” (Hebrews 3:10), but the point is the same. And it draws out what Today means for us: “exhort one another every day, as long as it is called ‘today,’ that none of you may be hardened by the deceitfulness of sin” (Hebrews 3:13).

The rest still open. Long after Israel had settled in Canaan, God was still offering his rest, “saying through David so long afterward” (Hebrews 4:7). So the rest was never only Canaan. “There remains a Sabbath rest for the people of God” (Hebrews 4:9), and “we who have believed enter that rest” (Hebrews 4:3). The rest is Christ himself, and every time this psalm is read it is still today. If you hear his voice in it, do not harden your heart but come. It is the Holy Spirit who speaks this Today (Hebrews 3:7) and who softens hard hearts, and where we have hardened, Christ, who heard and obeyed his Father perfectly in our place, is still the open door.

Where Christians differ: is the Lord’s Day the Christian Sabbath? Many godly brothers, with the Westminster Confession and the 1689 London Baptist Confession, hold that it is, under the fourth commandment. This commentary’s view: the weekly Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ, whose rest is entered by faith (Hebrews 4:3, 10). The Lord’s Day remains a gift, gladly kept for worship, fellowship and rest out of joy rather than under rules, and no one may bind another’s conscience (Romans 14:5; Colossians 2:16–17). Faithful Christians differ here.

Where Christians differ: can a true believer fall short of God’s rest? Hebrews warns Christians with this psalm (Hebrews 3:7–4:11). Arminian Christians say yes: the warning would be empty if the danger were not real. This commentary’s view: Hebrews also says “we have come to share in Christ, if indeed we hold our original confidence firm to the end” (Hebrews 3:14): holding firm shows that we truly belong. The warnings are real, aimed at all who profess faith, and they are among the means by which God keeps his own (John 10:28–29; Philippians 1:6). The one who falls away shows that he never truly entered. A believer frightened by these warnings may take the fear itself as a sign of a heart still soft: hard hearts do not tremble at God’s voice.

95.title: Today, If You Hear His Voice
95.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 95 follows the cry for justice of Psalm 94 and leads into the great “The LORD reigns” psalms (96–99). For centuries the church has used it to open morning worship, and it is the psalm Hebrews chooses to preach to Christians at length (Hebrews 3–4).

The message. Come and worship the great King who made everything and shepherds you, with loud joy and on your knees. But worship is not only singing; it is listening. The God we praise speaks, and the danger for worshippers is a heart that hardens against his voice, as Israel’s did in the wilderness and missed his rest. So hear him today, while it is still today.

Why it was said. The psalm has no title in Hebrew (the Greek translation credits it to David, and Hebrews speaks of God “saying through David”, Hebrews 4:7). It calls a congregation that sang God’s praises to remember that their fathers had seen his works too, and still hardened their hearts (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. It opens with a shout: come, sing to the Rock of our salvation, enter his presence with thanks (vv. 1–2), for he is the great King above all gods, owner and maker of the depths, the heights, the sea and the land (vv. 3–5). The invitation comes again, but now to kneel before the LORD our Maker, whose sheep we are (vv. 6–7). Then, mid-verse, God himself speaks: today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts as at Meribah and Massah, where your fathers tested me though they had seen my work (vv. 7–9). For forty years they went astray in heart, and God swore they would not enter his rest (vv. 10–11).

Where it leads. To Christ, by pattern and promise. The Rock the fathers quarrelled at was, Paul says, Christ (1 Corinthians 10:4); the Shepherd whose voice must be heard is the good Shepherd whose sheep hear his voice (John 10:27). Jesus went into the wilderness for forty days and, where Israel tested God, refused to. And Hebrews shows that the rest Israel missed was never only Canaan: “There remains a Sabbath rest for the people of God” (Hebrews 4:9), and “we who have believed enter that rest” (Hebrews 4:3). The rest is found in Christ himself.

For us. Come to worship gladly and humbly, and come ready to listen. When God’s word presses on something in your life, act on it this week, because hearts harden slowly and quietly. And if your heart has grown hard, the door has not closed: it is still today, and Christ still calls.
95.theology:
Worship is both joyful noise to the Rock of salvation (vv. 1-2) and kneeling before the Maker (v. 6), grounded in God's ownership of all creation (vv. 3-5) and his shepherding of his people (v. 7).

Worship must include hearing God's voice. A heart hardens through testing God despite having seen his work (vv. 8-9), and a heart can wander from God while the feet still follow him outwardly (v. 10). The psalm ends on exclusion from God's rest (v. 11), but Hebrews preaches it to Christians: today remains open, a Sabbath rest remains, and those who believe enter it (Heb 4:3).
95.examples: A congregation calls itself together and sings to the Rock its fathers quarrelled at. Then the song stops mid-sentence and God speaks about a generation that had seen more than almost anyone and still hardened. The worship song ends with a generation shut out of God’s rest, yet for us the way in is still open today.

keyVerse.quote: Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts
keyVerse.note: This is the hinge of the psalm, where the singing stops and God himself speaks. It shows that true worship includes listening, and that the danger for worshippers is a heart that slowly hardens. Hebrews takes up these words for Christians, and the word “Today” means the invitation into God’s rest, found in Christ, is still open.

95.reflection:
The psalm calls us both to shout for joy (vv. 1–2) and to kneel in reverence (v. 6). Which comes more naturally to you, and to your church? What is lost when one is missing?

Israel hardened their hearts “though they had seen my work” (v. 9). Why does experience of God not by itself protect a heart from hardening?

Read Hebrews 3:12–13. What would it look like for us to “exhort one another every day” so that none of us is hardened? Who has permission to ask you how you really are with God?

Hebrews says the rest Israel missed is still open “today” (Hebrews 4:7–9). How does Christ give the rest this psalm speaks of, and how would you explain it to someone who feels too far gone?

96.text: <sup>1</sup>Oh sing to the LORD a new song; sing to the LORD, all the earth!<sup>2</sup>Sing to the LORD, bless his name; tell of his salvation from day to day.<sup>3</sup>Declare his glory among the nations, his marvelous works among all the peoples!<sup>4</sup>For great is the LORD, and greatly to be praised; he is to be feared above all gods.<sup>5</sup>For all the gods of the peoples are worthless idols, but the LORD made the heavens.<sup>6</sup>Splendor and majesty are before him; strength and beauty are in his sanctuary.<sup>7</sup>Ascribe to the LORD, O families of the peoples, ascribe to the LORD glory and strength!<sup>8</sup>Ascribe to the LORD the glory due his name; bring an offering, and come into his courts!<sup>9</sup>Worship the LORD in the splendor of holiness; tremble before him, all the earth!<sup>10</sup>Say among the nations, "The LORD reigns! Yes, the world is established; it shall never be moved; he will judge the peoples with equity."<sup>11</sup>Let the heavens be glad, and let the earth rejoice; let the sea roar, and all that fills it;<sup>12</sup>let the field exult, and everything in it! Then shall all the trees of the forest sing for joy<sup>13</sup>before the LORD, for he comes, for he comes to judge the earth. He will judge the world in righteousness, and the peoples in his faithfulness.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Declare His Glory Among the Nations
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A new rescue calls for a new song, and the song is meant for every nation to hear. Three times Israel calls on all the earth to sing to the LORD, to bless his name and to tell of his salvation day after day (vv. 1–2). God’s glory and marvellous works are not to be kept at home but declared among all peoples (v. 3). The reason is the greatness of God himself: he is to be feared above all gods, because the gods of the peoples are worthless idols, while he made the heavens (vv. 4–5). Splendour, majesty, strength and beauty surround him in his sanctuary (v. 6).
verseByVerse.theology: A new rescue calls for a new song, and the song is meant for every nation to hear.

verseByVerse.quote: Oh sing to the LORD a new song; sing to the LORD, all the earth! Sing to the LORD, bless his name; tell of his salvation from day to day. Declare his glory among the nations, his marvelous works among all the peoples!
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s great salvation calls for a new song, and the song is not for Israel alone: his people are to tell every nation, every day, what he has done.

Oh sing to the LORD a new song. A new song is what people sing when God has done something new, a fresh rescue the old songs cannot quite contain. Most of this psalm appears again in 1 Chronicles 16 (vv. 23–33), in the thanks sung before the ark.

Sing to the LORD, all the earth! The call to sing to the LORD comes three times, and the choir is enormous: all the earth. It is Israel inviting every nation to join in.

Tell of his salvation from day to day. His salvation is to be told from day to day, as a daily report rather than an occasional one. The news does not go stale.

Declare his glory among the nations. This is a missionary verse, written centuries before the Great Commission. The marvelous works God has done for his people are news that belongs to all the peoples, and the Spirit given to the church is the power to tell it (Acts 1:8).

The new song of the Lamb. The greatest new song of all is sung in heaven to Christ: “Worthy are you … for you were slain, and by your blood you ransomed people for God from every tribe and language and people and nation” (Revelation 5:9). The all the earth of this psalm is finally a choir of the redeemed from every nation (compare Revelation 14:3).
verseByVerse.note: Psalm 96 also appears in David’s psalm in 1 Chronicles 16.

verseByVerse.quote: For great is the LORD, and greatly to be praised; he is to be feared above all gods. For all the gods of the peoples are worthless idols, but the LORD made the heavens. Splendor and majesty are before him; strength and beauty are in his sanctuary.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The nations should listen because the LORD alone is great: their gods are nothings, while he made the heavens, and strength and beauty fill his presence.

Great is the LORD, and greatly to be praised. Why should the nations listen? Because he is great, and his praise should match his size: greatly. Whatever the nations worship, he is higher and more to be reckoned with.

All the gods of the peoples are worthless idols. Having said the LORD is above all gods, the psalm at once clarifies: the other gods are worthless idols, nothings. The Hebrew word for idols sounds like the word for gods, a scornful pun: godlets, nobodies. Paul says the same: “an idol has no real existence” (1 Corinthians 8:4).

But the LORD made the heavens. The proof is the sky. The idols were made by men; the LORD made the heavens those men stood under. Every modern substitute for God, money, career, pleasure, the self, is equally a thing that was made, and cannot bear the weight of worship.

Splendor and majesty are before him. Four qualities attend him like courtiers: splendor, majesty, strength, beauty. Strength without beauty would be merely frightening; beauty without strength would be fragile. In God they are together, and they fill his sanctuary.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–9 — Ascribe to the LORD, O Families of the Peoples
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Worship is glory owed, not a favour done, and the nations are welcome to pay it. As Psalm 29 called the heavenly beings to ascribe glory to the LORD, this psalm calls the families of the peoples to do the same, three times over (vv. 7–8). They are to give him the glory due his name, bring an offering and come into his courts, the very courts that belonged to Israel (v. 8). They come in the splendour of holiness, and they come trembling, because the God who welcomes them is holy (v. 9).
verseByVerse.theology: Worship is glory owed, not a favour done, and the nations are welcome to pay it.

verseByVerse.quote: Ascribe to the LORD, O families of the peoples, ascribe to the LORD glory and strength! Ascribe to the LORD the glory due his name; bring an offering, and come into his courts! Worship the LORD in the splendor of holiness; tremble before him, all the earth!
verseByVerse.commentary:
The nations are summoned to give the LORD the glory he is owed and to come into his courts with offerings, welcome but trembling before his holiness.

Ascribe to the LORD, O families of the peoples. Three times the nations are told to ascribe: to acknowledge publicly what is true. In Psalm 29 the same threefold call went to the heavenly beings (29:1). Here it goes to the families of the peoples, every clan and nation on earth. What the angels do in heaven, the nations are summoned to do on earth.

The glory due his name. Not glory added to him, but glory owed. Worship is not a favour we do God; it is paying a debt.

Come into his courts! The courts of the temple were Israel’s. But the psalm invites the nations to come in with an offering in their hands, a picture of the day when Christ would break down “the dividing wall of hostility” that kept the Gentiles out (Ephesians 2:14). John saw an angel “with an eternal gospel to proclaim … to every nation and tribe and language and people”, calling, “Fear God and give him glory … and worship him who made heaven and earth” (Revelation 14:6–7).

Tremble before him, all the earth! The nations are welcome, and they are to come trembling, because the God they approach is holy.

Uncertain wording. The splendor of holiness may also be rendered “in holy attire” (as the ESV notes): either God’s holy splendour or worshippers dressed for a holy occasion. Either way, those who come must come fitly.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–13 — For He Comes to Judge the Earth
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: For a world full of injustice, the coming of a righteous Judge is the best news there is. The message the nations are to hear is simple: the LORD reigns, the world he holds is secure, and he will judge the peoples fairly (v. 10). Then the invitation widens beyond people. The heavens, the earth, the roaring sea, the fields and the trees of the forest are all told to rejoice (vv. 11–12), because he is coming, coming to judge the earth in righteousness and the peoples in his faithfulness (v. 13). Creation sings because the Judge is on his way.
verseByVerse.theology: For a world full of injustice, the coming of a righteous Judge is the best news there is.

verseByVerse.quote: Say among the nations, "The LORD reigns! Yes, the world is established; it shall never be moved; he will judge the peoples with equity."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The message for every nation is that the LORD is King: his reign holds the world steady, and he will judge all peoples fairly.

The LORD reigns! Here is the message the nations are to hear, three words long, the same words that opened Psalm 93. This is what evangelism is at its root: not first an offer of a better life, but an announcement of who is King.

He will judge the peoples with equity. Because he reigns, the world is established and creation holds together. And he will judge the peoples with equity: fairly, evenly, without favourites. For the oppressed of the earth, that is the best news there is.

Textual note. Some early Christian copies, especially in Latin, add “from the tree” after “The LORD reigns”, and early writers loved it as a prophecy of the cross. The words are not in the Hebrew and are not original, though the instinct was sound: the King announced to the nations reigns through his cross.

verseByVerse.quote: Let the heavens be glad, and let the earth rejoice; let the sea roar, and all that fills it; let the field exult, and everything in it! Then shall all the trees of the forest sing for joy before the LORD, for he comes, for he comes to judge the earth. He will judge the world in righteousness, and the peoples in his faithfulness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
All creation is called to sing for joy because the LORD is coming to judge the world in righteousness, and that Judge is the risen Jesus.

Let the sea roar. Now the invitation widens beyond people. The sea that roared in Psalm 93 as a threat now roars for joy, and the trees sing.

Then shall all the trees of the forest sing for joy. Isaiah heard the same music: “the mountains and the hills before you shall break forth into singing, and all the trees of the field shall clap their hands” (Isaiah 55:12). Paul explains why creation would be glad: it “was subjected to futility”, and “waits with eager longing” to “be set free from its bondage to corruption” (Romans 8:19–21). The creation has been groaning under the curse. It will sing when it is set free.

For he comes, for he comes to judge the earth. He comes, twice, as though the singer can already hear him approaching. That is the surprise of this psalm: judgment is the cause of celebration. We tend to hear “judgment” as only bad news, but for a world where the widow is crushed and the innocent condemned (94:6, 21), the coming of a righteous Judge is the moment everything is finally set right.

He will judge the world in righteousness. Paul told the philosophers of Athens who that Judge is: God “has fixed a day on which he will judge the world in righteousness by a man whom he has appointed; and of this he has given assurance to all by raising him from the dead” (Acts 17:31). The same words, and now we know the Judge: the risen Jesus. For everyone who belongs to him, his coming is not a terror but the day the whole creation has been singing towards. For those not yet his, the same sermon carried an invitation: God “commands all people everywhere to repent” (Acts 17:30), and the Judge who is coming can be met first as Saviour. For he comes.

96.title: Sing to the LORD a New Song
96.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 96 takes up the cry of Psalm 93, “The LORD reigns”, and sends it out to the whole world (v. 10). It is the first of a run of “new song” psalms about the King (96–99). Much of it was sung when David brought the ark to Jerusalem (1 Chronicles 16:23–33).

The message. The God who saved Israel is the King of all the earth, so his praise cannot stay at home. Every nation is to hear of his salvation, turn from idols that are nothing, and come to worship the Maker of the heavens. And all creation is called to sing, because the Judge is coming to set the world right.

Why it was said. Israel lived among nations who worshipped other gods, tempted either to fear them or to copy them. The psalm tells God’s people that those gods are nothings, and that their own calling is to tell the nations about the true King (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. Three times it calls for a new song from all the earth, and tells Israel to declare God’s glory among the nations (vv. 1–3). The reason is who he is: great beyond all gods, who are worthless idols, for he made the heavens, and splendour, majesty, strength and beauty fill his sanctuary (vv. 4–6). Then three times the families of the peoples are told to ascribe glory to him, bring an offering into his courts and worship him in holiness (vv. 7–9). The message to carry is “The LORD reigns”, and he will judge with equity (v. 10). Last, the heavens, earth, sea, fields and trees are called to rejoice, for he comes to judge the world in righteousness (vv. 11–13).

Where it leads. To Christ, by promise. The psalm looks for a day when the nations would worship Israel’s God; that day began when the risen Jesus sent his disciples to “make disciples of all nations” (Matthew 28:19), and its climax is the new song sung to the Lamb by people “from every tribe and language and people and nation” (Revelation 5:9). And the Judge whose coming makes the trees sing has a name: God “will judge the world in righteousness by a man whom he has appointed”, the one he raised from the dead (Acts 17:31).

For us. The good news of Jesus is not a private hobby but a royal announcement for every people, and we are among its messengers. Let it make your worship larger and your idols smaller. And let the coming of the Judge be, for you, not dread but the hope of a world finally set right, because you have first met him as Saviour.
96.theology:
The psalm is missionary: Israel is to declare God's glory among all nations (vv. 1-3), a new song finally sung by the redeemed of every nation (Rev 5:9). The LORD is the Creator; the gods of the nations are nothings (v. 5), and the families of the peoples are summoned into his courts (vv. 7-9).

The core announcement is The LORD reigns (v. 10). Creation rejoices at the coming of the Judge because his judgment sets the world right (vv. 11-13), and the Judge is the man God has appointed and raised from the dead (Acts 17:31).
96.examples: A new rescue calls for a new song. The psalm mocks the idols as godlets, mere nobodies, and says worship gives God the glory we owe him; it adds nothing to him. It invites Gentiles into the courts with offerings, and it hears the trees sing because the Judge is coming.

keyVerse.quote: Say among the nations, “The LORD reigns! Yes, the world is established; it shall never be moved; he will judge the peoples with equity.”
keyVerse.note: This is the message the whole psalm exists to spread. It takes the cry of Psalm 93 and puts it into the mouths of God’s people as news for every nation, joining the two great themes of the psalm: God’s reign over all peoples and his coming to judge them fairly. The gospel announces the same King, Jesus, who reigns now and will come to judge.

96.reflection:
The psalm says God’s salvation is to be told “from day to day” and “among the nations” (vv. 2–3). What would it look like for you to speak of what God has done as everyday news?

The psalm calls the gods of the nations “worthless idols” (v. 5). What modern things are treated as gods, and how does remembering that “the LORD made the heavens” cut them down to size?

“Ascribe to the LORD the glory due his name” (v. 8). How does seeing worship as glory owed, rather than a favour we do God, change the way we come to church?

Creation sings because the Judge is coming (vv. 11–13). Why is God’s judgment good news for a broken world, and how can the coming Judge be met first as Saviour (Acts 17:30–31)?

97.text: <sup>1</sup>The LORD reigns, let the earth rejoice; let the many coastlands be glad!<sup>2</sup>Clouds and thick darkness are all around him; righteousness and justice are the foundation of his throne.<sup>3</sup>Fire goes before him and burns up his adversaries all around.<sup>4</sup>His lightnings light up the world; the earth sees and trembles.<sup>5</sup>The mountains melt like wax before the LORD, before the Lord of all the earth.<sup>6</sup>The heavens proclaim his righteousness, and all the peoples see his glory.<sup>7</sup>All worshipers of images are put to shame, who make their boast in worthless idols; worship him, all you gods!<sup>8</sup>Zion hears and is glad, and the daughters of Judah rejoice, because of your judgments, O LORD.<sup>9</sup>For you, O LORD, are most high over all the earth; you are exalted far above all gods.<sup>10</sup>O you who love the LORD, hate evil! He preserves the lives of his saints; he delivers them from the hand of the wicked.<sup>11</sup>Light is sown for the righteous, and joy for the upright in heart.<sup>12</sup>Rejoice in the LORD, O you righteous, and give thanks to his holy name!

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — Clouds and Thick Darkness Are All Around Him
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The King has come, and he comes as he came to Sinai: hidden, holy and just. The psalm opens with the cry “The LORD reigns” and calls the whole earth, as far as the farthest coastlands, to rejoice (v. 1). Yet the King is wrapped in cloud and thick darkness, so that he cannot be seen, examined or managed, while his throne stands on righteousness and justice (v. 2). Fire goes before him, lightning lights up the world, and the mountains, the very image of permanence, melt like wax before the Lord of all the earth (vv. 3–5). We may not see what he is doing; we can know that he is just.
verseByVerse.theology: We may not see what God is doing inside the cloud; we can know that he is just.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD reigns, let the earth rejoice; let the many coastlands be glad! Clouds and thick darkness are all around him; righteousness and justice are the foundation of his throne.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD is King, hidden from our sight but just in everything he does, and that is good news to the ends of the earth.

The LORD reigns. The same three words that opened Psalm 93 open this one, but here they lead straight to joy. Psalms 93 and 95 to 99 celebrate the LORD as King, probably in the temple’s worship. Even after the exile, when no son of David sat on a throne, these songs taught the people that the true throne had never been empty. “The coastlands” are the islands and far shores of the Mediterranean, the edges of the known world: God’s reign is good news as far away as anyone lives.

Clouds and thick darkness. The picture is Sinai. When God came down on the mountain there were “thunders and lightnings and a thick cloud on the mountain”, and “the LORD had descended on it in fire” (Exodus 19:16, 18). The King who reigns is surrounded by darkness: he cannot be seen, examined or managed.

The foundation of his throne. Yet inside the cloud the throne stands on “righteousness and justice”, almost the words of Psalm 89:14. That is the comfort for anyone who cannot understand what God is doing: his ways are often wrapped in cloud, but his throne is never built on anything but justice.

The God we would rather manage. Modern spirituality prefers a God who is near, warm and above all understandable, who fits our experience and agrees with our sense of what is fair; a God wrapped in “clouds and thick darkness” sounds like a relic of a more fearful age. But a God we could see all round would be no bigger than our minds, and such a God can never surprise us, correct us or rescue us; he can only echo us. The moralist shrinks God into a rule book he can keep, the sceptic into an idea he can dismiss, and the comfortable believer into a counsellor who always agrees. Each is a way of staying in charge. The psalm will not allow it, and yet it does not leave us in the dark. The cloud hides his ways; the throne shows his character. And on another mountain the cloud came down again, and the disciples saw the King’s face shining like the sun (Matthew 17:2, 5). The God we cannot manage turned out to have a human face, and it was set towards a cross.

verseByVerse.quote: Fire goes before him and burns up his adversaries all around. His lightnings light up the world; the earth sees and trembles. The mountains melt like wax before the LORD, before the Lord of all the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the King comes, nothing can stand against him; even the mountains melt.

Fire goes before him. Now the storm breaks. Fire goes ahead of the King like an advance guard and consumes whatever stands against him; lightning flashes across the world, and for an instant every hidden thing is exposed.

The mountains melt like wax. Mountains are the image of permanence, the things that do not move. Before this King they soften and run like candle wax near a flame. John saw the end of it: “From his presence earth and sky fled away, and no place was found for them” (Revelation 20:11).

The Lord of all the earth. The title matters: not the god of one hill or one nation. Everything people rely on as solid, institutions, wealth, the ground itself, is wax before him. Only he stands firm, and Paul names him: the day comes “when the Lord Jesus is revealed from heaven with his mighty angels in flaming fire” (2 Thessalonians 1:7–8).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–9 — Worship Him, All You Gods
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When the King appears, every rival is exposed and his people are glad. The heavens announce his righteousness and all peoples see his glory (v. 6). In that light the worshippers of images are put to shame, because they boasted in nothing, and every power they trusted is commanded to worship him (v. 7), words Hebrews hears fulfilled when the Son comes into the world. The same judgments that shame the idolaters make Zion and the towns of Judah rejoice (v. 8), for the LORD is not merely higher than other gods but exalted far above them all (v. 9).
verseByVerse.theology: When God appears, the idols are exposed as nothing and everything that was worshipped bows.

verseByVerse.quote: The heavens proclaim his righteousness, and all the peoples see his glory. All worshipers of images are put to shame, who make their boast in worthless idols; worship him, all you gods!
verseByVerse.commentary:
When God’s glory is seen, every idol-worshipper is put to shame and every power that was worshipped is commanded to bow to him.

The heavens proclaim his righteousness. The sky itself becomes a herald announcing that God is righteous, and “all the peoples” see it: his glory will not be a private experience for a few.

All worshipers of images are put to shame. In that light the idols are exposed. Isaiah said the same: “They are turned back and utterly put to shame, who trust in carved idols” (Isaiah 42:17). The shame is not merely that the idol fails to help but that the worshipper boasted in it, staked his pride on something that turns out to be nothing. Whatever we boast in apart from God, career, looks or money, will one day look as foolish as a carved block.

Worship him, all you gods! Then a command addressed past the idol-worshippers to the powers they thought stood behind their idols: every rival power in heaven or earth is told to bow.

The gods and the angels. The Greek Old Testament reads “angels” here, and Hebrews applies words very like it (they also stand in the Greek of Deuteronomy 32:43) to the Son as he enters the world: “Let all God’s angels worship him” (Hebrews 1:6). The worship this psalm demands for the LORD, Hebrews gives to Jesus.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew word for “gods” (elohim) can mean God, the gods of the nations, angels or even human rulers, so who exactly is addressed is not certain. Most likely it is every power, real or imagined, that people worshipped in God’s place, not rival deities with a real claim; the Greek translators understood angels, and Hebrews follows them.
verseByVerse.note: Hebrews 1:6 echoes v. 7 in its Greek form.

verseByVerse.quote: Zion hears and is glad, and the daughters of Judah rejoice, because of your judgments, O LORD. For you, O LORD, are most high over all the earth; you are exalted far above all gods.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The judgments that shame the idolaters make God’s people glad, because the LORD is exalted infinitely above everything else that is worshipped.

Zion hears and is glad. Almost the same words appear in Psalm 48:11. “The daughters of Judah” are the towns and villages of the country around Jerusalem. The judgments that terrify idol-worshippers make God’s people glad, because they are the rescue of those who belong to him.

Most high over all the earth. The psalm turns to God directly. Not just high, but “most high”; not just above the gods, but “far above”. The distance between the LORD and anything else that is worshipped is not a margin; it is infinite.

What it does not mean. Not that God’s people gloat over the ruin of others. God himself says, “I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked” (Ezekiel 33:11). Zion is glad that wrong is put right and the oppressed set free, and can be glad without fear because the judgment its own sins deserved fell on Christ (Romans 8:1).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–12 — O You Who Love the LORD, Hate Evil
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Those who love the King must hate evil, and he will keep them and give them light. Loving the LORD is not a feeling that sits comfortably beside sin; it hates what he hates (v. 10a). To those who take his side he promises protection: he preserves the lives of his saints and rescues them from the wicked (v. 10b). Light is scattered for the righteous like seed in a furrow, unseen at first but sure to come up, and joy with it (v. 11). So the psalm ends where it began, in gladness: rejoice in the LORD and give thanks to his holy name (v. 12).
verseByVerse.theology: Loving the King means hating what he hates, and the reward is light scattered like seed.

verseByVerse.quote: O you who love the LORD, hate evil! He preserves the lives of his saints; he delivers them from the hand of the wicked. Light is sown for the righteous, and joy for the upright in heart. Rejoice in the LORD, O you righteous, and give thanks to his holy name!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Love for the LORD shows itself in hating evil, and he keeps those who love him and has sown light and joy along their path.

O you who love the LORD, hate evil! The psalm gives those who love God one command. Love of God is not a warm feeling that sits comfortably alongside sin. If you love a person, you hate what he hates and what destroys him. Paul put it just as bluntly: “Let love be genuine. Abhor what is evil; hold fast to what is good” (Romans 12:9).

He preserves the lives of his saints. The promise attached is protection. Those who side with God against evil will find evil siding against them, and God siding with them.

Light is sown for the righteous. Light is “sown”, like seed scattered along a furrow. Little shows at sowing time; the harvest comes later. The righteous may walk in shadow now, but light has been planted along their path, and it will come up.

Christ the light. Malachi promised that “for you who fear my name, the sun of righteousness shall rise with healing in its wings” (Malachi 4:2), and Jesus said, “I am the light of the world. Whoever follows me will not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life” (John 8:12). John tells us what the light is: “God is light, and in him is no darkness at all” (1 John 1:5). The God surrounded by cloud (v. 2) sows light for his people, and for those who love him the right response to the King who comes in fire is gladness and thanks (v. 12).

A searching test. What evil do you find merely regrettable, or even entertaining, that God hates? Loving the LORD will slowly teach you to hate it too. That is the Spirit’s work, not willpower: he makes us want what God wants (Galatians 5:16–17). And where we still cherish what God hates, Christ’s perfect love for his Father is counted as ours, and the way back is confession (1 John 1:9).

What this looks like. Hating evil is not disapproval aimed at other people; it begins at home. Stop laughing at it. Notice what you watch or repeat for entertainment that God calls evil, the cruelty, the sneer, the casual adultery of the plot, and turn it off. Name it in yourself first. Call the old resentment, the half-truth on the expenses form, the gossip waiting to be passed on, what God calls it, before you find excuses. Hate it on behalf of its victims. Let it move you to act for the bullied colleague, the exploited neighbour, the unborn and the trafficked. Love what is good with the same energy. Paul’s command has two halves, abhor and hold fast (Romans 12:9). None of this is a ladder to God’s favour: Christ loved righteousness and hated wickedness perfectly (Hebrews 1:9), and bore the evil we loved. “The grace of God has appeared”, says Paul, “training us to renounce ungodliness and worldly passions” (Titus 2:11–12). Grace, not fear, teaches the heart to hate what is killing it.

What does “preserves the lives of his saints” mean? Saints are martyred, yet God keeps his people’s souls and their final life secure (Matthew 10:28; Romans 8:35–39); he does not promise them escape from every harm in this life.

Textual note. The ESV notes that some ancient witnesses read “Light dawns” instead of “Light is sown”: the same promise from another angle.

97.title: Light Is Sown for the Righteous
97.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 97 belongs to the cluster of psalms in Book Four that proclaim “The LORD reigns” (93; 96–99), Israel’s answer to the crown lying in the dust at the end of Psalm 89 (see the introduction). Psalm 96 announced that the King is coming; Psalm 97 describes him arriving.

The message. The LORD is King, and when he comes he comes as he came at Sinai, in cloud and fire, with a throne built on justice. His appearing shames everyone who trusted anything else and gladdens everyone who loves him. So love him by hating evil, and trust that he guards his people and has sown light along their path.

Why it was said. Israel lived among nations whose gods were carved and carried, and was often tempted to trust them; and once David’s throne had fallen, it needed to know that heaven’s throne had never been empty (see the introduction). The psalm gathers language from Sinai, Isaiah and earlier psalms to tell a small people that their God is “most high over all the earth”.

How the chapter makes its case. It opens with the announcement and the King’s appearing: cloud and darkness hide him, justice upholds his throne, fire and lightning go before him, and the mountains melt (vv. 1–5). Then come the effects: the heavens declare his righteousness, idol-worshippers are put to shame, every so-called god is told to bow, and Zion rejoices at his judgments, because he is exalted far above all gods (vv. 6–9). Last comes the call to his people: those who love him must hate evil, and he will preserve them, sow light for them and fill them with joy and thanks (vv. 10–12).

Where it leads. Directly, because the New Testament reads this psalm of Christ. Hebrews hears in the summons to every heavenly power to worship him the Father’s command at the Son’s coming into the world: “Let all God’s angels worship him” (Hebrews 1:6). Paul describes the Lord Jesus revealed from heaven “in flaming fire” (2 Thessalonians 1:7–8), the very coming this psalm pictures. And the God hidden in thick darkness has shown his face in Jesus, the light sown for the righteous come up in a person: “I am the light of the world” (John 8:12).

For us. No idol survives the King’s appearing: not money, not reputation, not the approval we boast in. Bring your trust home to the one who reigns, let love for him teach you to hate what he hates, and when your path is dark, remember that light has already been sown along it, and in Christ it will come up.
97.theology:
God's reign is hidden in cloud yet founded on justice (v. 2), revealed as at Sinai in fire before which all that seems permanent melts (vv. 3-5). His appearing exposes idolatry as shameful boasting in nothing, and all powers are summoned to worship him (v. 7), words Hebrews applies to the Son.

Loving God means hating evil (v. 10). God preserves his saints, and light is sown for the righteous (v. 11) by the God who is light (1 John 1:5).
97.examples: God's reign is good news as far as the farthest coastline. The idol-worshipper's shame is that the thing he boasted in turns out to be nothing. Loving a person means hating what destroys him, and the light God sows lies planted in a furrow, waiting to come up.

keyVerse.quote: The LORD reigns, let the earth rejoice; let the many coastlands be glad!
keyVerse.note: The whole psalm unfolds these opening words. The King’s coming in cloud and fire is terrible to those who trust idols, yet the first and last note is joy, because his reign is good news for everyone who loves him, as far as the farthest shore. That reign is now exercised by the risen Christ, whom every power is commanded to worship.

97.reflection:
Verse 2 says that “clouds and thick darkness” surround God, yet “righteousness and justice are the foundation of his throne”. Where are you finding God’s ways hard to see just now, and how does this verse help you trust his character?
