The idol-worshippers are shamed because they “make their boast” in what is worthless (v. 7). What do people around us boast in, and what are you tempted to rely on for your sense of worth?

“O you who love the LORD, hate evil!” (v. 10). Why are love for God and hatred of evil inseparable? What evil do we tend to find entertaining or merely regrettable?

“Light is sown for the righteous” (v. 11). How does the picture of seed waiting in the ground encourage someone walking through a dark season, and how has Christ been light to you?

98.text: A Psalm. 1Oh sing to the LORD a new song, for he has done marvelous things! His right hand and his holy arm have worked salvation for him.2The LORD has made known his salvation; he has revealed his righteousness in the sight of the nations.3He has remembered his steadfast love and faithfulness to the house of Israel. All the ends of the earth have seen the salvation of our God.4Make a joyful noise to the LORD, all the earth; break forth into joyous song and sing praises!5Sing praises to the LORD with the lyre, with the lyre and the sound of melody!6With trumpets and the sound of the horn make a joyful noise before the King, the LORD!7Let the sea roar, and all that fills it; the world and those who dwell in it!8Let the rivers clap their hands; let the hills sing for joy together9before the LORD, for he comes to judge the earth. He will judge the world with righteousness, and the peoples with equity.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–3 — He Has Done Marvelous Things
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The new song is for a finished rescue that God carried out alone and in public. After the opening call, everything is in the past tense: he “has done marvelous things” (v. 1). No one helped; his own right hand and holy arm won the victory. He did it openly, revealing his righteousness before the nations (v. 2), and he did it because he remembered the steadfast love and faithfulness he had promised to Israel (v. 3a). The result is what Isaiah foresaw: the ends of the earth have seen the salvation of our God (v. 3b). Faith sings God’s promises as already done.
verseByVerse.theology: God has saved his people with his own arm, and the whole world has watched.

verseByVerse.quote: Oh sing to the LORD a new song, for he has done marvelous things! His right hand and his holy arm have worked salvation for him. The LORD has made known his salvation; he has revealed his righteousness in the sight of the nations. He has remembered his steadfast love and faithfulness to the house of Israel. All the ends of the earth have seen the salvation of our God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God has saved his people single-handed, before the nations and true to his promises, and that calls for a new song.

Oh sing to the LORD a new song. Psalm 96 began the same way and gave as its reason who God is; this psalm gives what God “has done”. After the opening call, everything in verses 1 to 3 is in the past tense: something has happened, and it needs a new song.

His right hand and his holy arm. The salvation was done single-handed: no army helped, no one contributed. Isaiah saw God look for someone to intervene and find no one: “then his own arm brought him salvation” (Isaiah 59:16). That is the shape of every true rescue in Scripture, above all the cross, where God did alone what no one else could do.

In the sight of the nations. The rescue was not done in a corner but “made known”, “revealed”, before the nations. God’s salvation of his people is also a display of his righteousness to the world, proof that he keeps his word.

He has remembered his steadfast love. Not that he had forgotten, but that he acted on his promises. When Mary sang about the child she was carrying, she used this language: “He has helped his servant Israel, in remembrance of his mercy” (Luke 1:54). And old Simeon, holding the baby in the temple, said, “my eyes have seen your salvation that you have prepared in the presence of all peoples” (Luke 2:30–31).

All the ends of the earth have seen. Isaiah had promised that “all the ends of the earth shall see the salvation of our God” (Isaiah 52:10). The psalm sings it as already done. Faith sings future promises in the past tense, because God’s word is as good as his deed.

A song that starts with God. This psalm starts not with how we feel but with what God has done, and the feelings follow. When joy runs thin, go back to the facts (1 Corinthians 15:3–4).
verseByVerse.note: The basis of Isaac Watts’s hymn “Joy to the World.”

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–6 — Before the King, the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The whole earth is called to celebrate as at a coronation. The response to God’s salvation is not quiet appreciation but joy that bursts out (v. 4). Strings give the melody (v. 5); trumpets and the ram’s horn, which were blown in Israel when a king was proclaimed, give the volume (v. 6a). The psalm keeps its title for him to the end of the section: all this noise is made “before the King, the LORD” (v. 6b). The question in worship is not first which instruments are played, but whether the noise is made before him.
verseByVerse.theology: The whole earth is handed instruments and told to play for its King.

verseByVerse.quote: Make a joyful noise to the LORD, all the earth; break forth into joyous song and sing praises! Sing praises to the LORD with the lyre, with the lyre and the sound of melody! With trumpets and the sound of the horn make a joyful noise before the King, the LORD!
verseByVerse.commentary:
The whole earth is to greet God’s salvation with loud, glad music, like a crowd hailing a new king.

Break forth into joyous song. The whole earth is summoned to “break forth”, like something that cannot be held in: the response to God’s salvation is not quiet appreciation.

Sing praises to the LORD with the lyre. The strings come first, then the brass: the lyre gives melody, and the trumpets and the ram’s horn give volume, the sounds of a coronation. In Israel the trumpet or horn was blown when a new king was proclaimed (1 Kings 1:39; 2 Kings 9:13), so the whole earth is asked to do for the LORD what Jerusalem did for Solomon.

Before the King, the LORD! The one being hailed is named at the end: “the King, the LORD”. Everything here is played in front of him. That is the thing to remember in any church arguing about music: the first question is not the instrument but whether the noise is being made before the King.

The last trumpet. The final coronation is still to come. At the seventh trumpet, loud voices in heaven say, “The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ, and he shall reign forever and ever” (Revelation 11:15). Our praise now rehearses for that day.

Where Christians differ: should churches use instruments? The temple used them by God’s command (2 Chronicles 29:25). Some Reformed churches sing without them, holding that worship must use only what the New Testament commands and that the instruments belonged to the temple. This commentary’s view: the New Testament does not forbid them, and they may serve the singing, provided the words come first and all is done in order (Colossians 3:16; 1 Corinthians 14:40).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–9 — Let the Rivers Clap Their Hands
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: All creation joins in, because the Judge is coming. The sea roars, the world and its people add their voices (v. 7), the rivers clap their hands and the hills sing together (v. 8), all before the LORD. The reason is surprising: he comes to judge the earth (v. 9). For a world full of injustice that is good news, because he will judge with righteousness and with equity, one standard for every people. And a world that has seen his salvation (v. 3) need not fear his judgment: the one who rescued with his own arm is the one who comes.
verseByVerse.theology: A world that has seen God's salvation need not fear his coming to judge.

verseByVerse.quote: Let the sea roar, and all that fills it; the world and those who dwell in it! Let the rivers clap their hands; let the hills sing for joy together before the LORD, for he comes to judge the earth. He will judge the world with righteousness, and the peoples with equity.
verseByVerse.commentary:
All creation is to rejoice that the LORD is coming to judge, because his judgment will be perfectly fair and those he has saved need not fear it.

Let the rivers clap their hands. These verses echo the ending of Psalm 96 with changes: there the fields and trees sang; here the rivers “clap their hands” and the hills “sing for joy together”. The whole landscape is applauding. It is right that “Joy to the World”, based on this psalm, is sung at Christmas, because the King the psalm expects is the one who came.

The peoples with equity. Psalm 96 said “for he comes, for he comes”; this psalm says it once. Psalm 96 said he will judge the peoples “in his faithfulness”; this one says “with equity”: fairly, evenly, with the same standard for every nation.

For he comes to judge the earth. Again, surprisingly, creation is glad about judgment, as if waiting to be set free (Romans 8:19–21). A world that has seen God’s salvation (v. 3) is not afraid of his coming to judge. John heard the redeemed singing by the sea of glass: “Great and amazing are your deeds, O Lord God the Almighty! Just and true are your ways, O King of the nations!” (Revelation 15:3). The one who worked salvation with his own arm is the one who comes to judge, “a man whom he has appointed” (Acts 17:31), which is why those he saved can clap along with the rivers.

We want a judge, for other people. Our age is supposed to be uneasy with judgment: “Who are you to judge?” Yet look at how we live: the outrage at the corrupt official who walks free, the documentaries about crimes never punished. We have not stopped wanting judgment; we want it for other people. What we resist is a Judge who would look at us with the same eyes. The psalm is more honest and more hopeful. It assumes that a world without a final reckoning would be one where the bully and the trafficker simply win, and that is why the rivers clap: for the oppressed, judgment is the best news there is. But it sings of salvation first (vv. 1–3), because no one could clap at that judgment unless the Judge had already rescued them. At the cross the Judge took the verdict on himself, so that those who trust him can long for his coming without dread. Only people who have been forgiven can want justice all the way down.

98.title: His Holy Arm Has Worked Salvation
98.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 98 stands among the psalms that proclaim the LORD as King (93; 96–99; see the introduction). It begins like Psalm 96, “Oh sing to the LORD a new song”, and ends almost as Psalm 96 does; but where Psalm 96 sang chiefly of who God is, this psalm sings of what he has done.

The message. God has rescued his people by his own power, in full view of the world, keeping every promise of love he made to Israel. Such a salvation deserves a new song from the whole earth, played as at a coronation before the King. And because the one who saved is the one who is coming to judge, even the sea and the hills can greet his coming with joy.

Why it was said. Israel sang this after God had acted for it, remembering rescues such as the exodus and the return from exile, which Isaiah had promised in almost these words (Isaiah 52:10; see the introduction). A small, often defeated people needed to know that its rescue was a sign to the nations that the LORD keeps faith and will one day put the world right.

How the chapter makes its case. The psalm moves outward in widening circles. First Israel sings of the salvation itself: worked by God’s own arm, made known before the nations, rooted in his remembered love, and seen by the ends of the earth (vv. 1–3). Then all the earth is summoned to make music with lyre, trumpet and horn before “the King, the LORD” (vv. 4–6). Last, the sea, the world, the rivers and the hills join in, because he comes to judge the world with righteousness and equity (vv. 7–9). Salvation comes first, so that judgment can be welcomed.

Where it leads. By promise. The “holy arm” that worked salvation is the arm Isaiah saw revealed in the suffering servant (Isaiah 53:1), and John says it was revealed in Jesus (John 12:37–38). When he was born, Mary sang that God had remembered his mercy to Israel, and Simeon, holding the child, said, “my eyes have seen your salvation” (Luke 2:30), the language of verses 2 and 3. And the Judge whose coming the rivers applaud is the same Jesus, for God “will judge the world in righteousness by a man whom he has appointed” (Acts 17:31).

For us. Our songs begin with what God has done, not with what we feel or have achieved: he saved us single-handed at the cross. People who know that can sing loudly, welcome the coming of the Judge without dread, and long with the whole groaning creation for the day he puts the world right.
98.theology:
Salvation is God's own work, done by his arm alone (v. 1), publicly revealed to the nations (v. 2), and rooted in his remembering the love he promised to Israel (v. 3), language taken up by Mary and Simeon at Christ's birth (Luke 1:54-55). Isaiah’s promise that the ends of the earth shall see God’s salvation is sung as already done.

Worship is noise made before the King (v. 6). Creation joins in at the coming of the Judge, whose judgment is righteous and even-handed (vv. 7-9), as the redeemed sing in Revelation (Rev 15:3-4).
98.examples: The psalm sings a new song because something has happened: God has rescued single-handed, and Simeon held that salvation in his arms as a baby. Faith sings the promise in the past tense, and the rivers applaud.

keyVerse.quote: Oh sing to the LORD a new song, for he has done marvelous things! His right hand and his holy arm have worked salvation for him.
keyVerse.note: The new song is for a finished rescue, done by God alone. Everything else in the psalm follows from it: the nations see it, the earth plays for its King, and creation can welcome the coming Judge because the Judge is the Saviour. The holy arm was finally bared at the cross, where God did single-handed what no one else could do.

98.reflection:
Psalm 98 calls for “a new song” because God “has done marvelous things” (v. 1). What has God done, in Christ and in your own life, that deserves a new song from you?

God’s “right hand and his holy arm have worked salvation for him” (v. 1), with no one’s help. Why does it matter that salvation is God’s work alone, and how should that shape the way we worship?

Verses 4 to 6 picture the whole earth celebrating as at a coronation. What would it look like for our church’s worship to be made truly “before the King, the LORD”?

The sea, rivers and hills rejoice, “for he comes to judge the earth” (v. 9). Why is God’s judgment good news for the oppressed, and why can only forgiven people long for it without fear?

99.text: <sup>1</sup>The LORD reigns; let the peoples tremble! He sits enthroned upon the cherubim; let the earth quake!<sup>2</sup>The LORD is great in Zion; he is exalted over all the peoples.<sup>3</sup>Let them praise your great and awesome name! Holy is he!<sup>4</sup>The King in his might loves justice. You have established equity; you have executed justice and righteousness in Jacob.<sup>5</sup>Exalt the LORD our God; worship at his footstool! Holy is he!<sup>6</sup>Moses and Aaron were among his priests, Samuel also was among those who called upon his name. They called to the LORD, and he answered them.<sup>7</sup>In the pillar of the cloud he spoke to them; they kept his testimonies and the statute that he gave them.<sup>8</sup>O LORD our God, you answered them; you were a forgiving God to them, but an avenger of their wrongdoings.<sup>9</sup>Exalt the LORD our God, and worship at his holy mountain; for the LORD our God is holy!

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — The King in His Might Loves Justice
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The King who reigns from above the mercy seat is holy, and his holiness shows itself as justice. He sits enthroned upon the cherubim, so the peoples tremble and the earth quakes (v. 1). He is great in Zion, the one place on earth he chose, and yet exalted over every people (v. 2), so all should praise his great and awesome name: “Holy is he!” (v. 3). His might is not raw power but power in love with justice, and he has done justice in Israel’s actual history (v. 4). So his people are to exalt him and bow at his footstool, the ark where his feet rest among them (v. 5).
verseByVerse.theology: The King enthroned above the mercy seat is holy, and his holiness shows itself as justice.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD reigns; let the peoples tremble! He sits enthroned upon the cherubim; let the earth quake! The LORD is great in Zion; he is exalted over all the peoples. Let them praise your great and awesome name! Holy is he!
verseByVerse.commentary:
The holy King, enthroned above the mercy seat, reigns over all peoples, and the whole earth should tremble and praise him.

Let the peoples tremble! Psalm 97 opened with the earth rejoicing; this one with the peoples trembling. Both are right. God’s reign is joy and terror, depending on where you stand, and a believer who has only ever felt one of them has not yet seen the King clearly.

He sits enthroned upon the cherubim. This is the ark in the Most Holy Place. Two gold cherubim, winged heavenly creatures, spread their wings over its lid, and God said, “from above the mercy seat, from between the two cherubim … I will speak with you” (Exodus 25:22). The throne of the King of the universe on earth was the mercy seat, where the blood of atonement was sprinkled on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:14–15). His throne and his mercy are in the same place.

Holy is he! The refrain comes three times (vv. 3, 5, 9), as the seraphim cried three times, “Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of hosts” (Isaiah 6:3). Holiness means God is utterly other, set apart from everything created and from everything sinful.

The mercy seat is now a person. The Greek word for that lid (Hebrews 9:5) is the one Paul uses when he says God put Christ forward “as a propitiation by his blood” (Romans 3:25): the place where wrath is turned away and mercy shown is now a person.

verseByVerse.quote: The King in his might loves justice. You have established equity; you have executed justice and righteousness in Jacob. Exalt the LORD our God; worship at his footstool! Holy is he!
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s holiness in action is justice, done among his people, so they should bow at his feet.

The King in his might loves justice. What does holiness look like when it acts? Justice. His strength is not raw power but power in love with what is right, which is rarely true of mighty human kings.

You have established equity. He has not only loved justice in theory; he has established it and “executed justice and righteousness in Jacob”, in his people’s actual history.

Worship at his footstool! His footstool is where the King of heaven, so to speak, rests his feet on earth: the ark and the temple (1 Chronicles 28:2). The picture is humbling in both directions. God is so great that the holiest place on earth is only where his feet rest, and so gracious that he rests them among his people. The right response is to go down on your face at the foot of the throne.

Uncertain wording. The opening of verse 4 is compressed in the Hebrew, and the ESV notes another possible reading: “The might of the King loves justice.” Either way the sense is the same: the King’s power is wedded to justice.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–9 — A Forgiving God, but an Avenger
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s holiness is seen in how he dealt with the greatest of his servants. Moses, Aaron and Samuel called on him, and he answered them (v. 6); he spoke to them from the pillar of cloud, and they kept what he commanded (v. 7). Yet they were sinners too, and he was both a forgiving God to them and an avenger of their wrongdoings: forgiven, and still disciplined, as Moses and Aaron were at Meribah (v. 8). The psalm ends with its longest refrain: exalt him and worship, for the LORD our God is holy (v. 9). The holy one is ours.
verseByVerse.theology: The greatest intercessors in Israel's history were heard and forgiven — and still disciplined, because God is holy.

verseByVerse.quote: Moses and Aaron were among his priests, Samuel also was among those who called upon his name. They called to the LORD, and he answered them. In the pillar of the cloud he spoke to them; they kept his testimonies and the statute that he gave them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel’s greatest intercessors called on the holy God and were answered; he spoke to them, and they obeyed.

They called to the LORD, and he answered them. Three men who prayed for the people “called upon his name”, and “he answered”. His holiness does not make him deaf to prayer.

Moses and Aaron were among his priests. Moses was not a priest by office, but he did a priest’s work, consecrating Aaron and his sons and offering the first sacrifices at the tabernacle (Leviticus 8); Samuel, a Levite not of Aaron’s line (1 Chronicles 6:28), also offered sacrifices (1 Samuel 7:9). All three stood between God and the people in prayer.

How they prayed. After the golden calf, Moses went back up the mountain and prayed, “if you will forgive their sin”, and “if not, please blot me out of your book” (Exodus 32:32). With the Philistines at hand, “Samuel cried out to the LORD for Israel, and the LORD answered him” (1 Samuel 7:9). Centuries later God named Moses and Samuel together as Israel’s great intercessors (Jeremiah 15:1).

In the pillar of the cloud he spoke to them. And he spoke back: “When Moses entered the tent, the pillar of cloud would descend and stand at the entrance of the tent, and the LORD would speak with Moses” (Exodus 33:9). Prayer was a conversation, and it bore obedience: “they kept his testimonies”.

A greater intercessor. Moses offered to be blotted out in the people’s place, and God refused (Exodus 32:33). What Moses could only offer, Christ did (Galatians 3:13), and he always lives to intercede for us (Hebrews 7:25). You are heard, not because you are a Moses, but because of him.

verseByVerse.quote: O LORD our God, you answered them; you were a forgiving God to them, but an avenger of their wrongdoings. Exalt the LORD our God, and worship at his holy mountain; for the LORD our God is holy!
verseByVerse.commentary:
God forgave these men and still disciplined their sins, because he is holy; and this holy God is “our God”.

You were a forgiving God to them. Here is the line that makes this psalm unforgettable: God was “a forgiving God” to these men and at the same time “an avenger of their wrongdoings”. Both, to the same people.

Moses and Aaron at Meribah. They struck the rock in anger, and God said, “you shall not bring this assembly into the land”, because they had not upheld him as holy (Numbers 20:12). They were not cast off; Moses remained God’s friend and servant to the end of his life. But he died on the wrong side of the Jordan. Forgiven, and disciplined.

The LORD our God is holy! The third refrain is the longest. The first two said “Holy is he”; the last says he is holy and ours, “our God”. The holy one enthroned above the mercy seat belongs to his people.

Forgiveness and consequences. Forgiveness does not always remove consequences. A holy God can forgive a sin completely and still let its consequences be felt, not as punishment to pay the debt, which Christ has paid, but as a Father’s discipline. “Our God is a consuming fire” (Hebrews 12:29), and he is the God who forgives. Any view of God that keeps only one of those has lost the God of this psalm.

What it does not mean. Not that every hardship is a penalty for a particular sin (John 9:2–3), nor that discipline means rejection: “the Lord disciplines the one he loves” (Hebrews 12:6). Nor must those a believer has wronged act as if nothing happened; consequences, including legal ones, may rightly remain.

99.title: Holy Is He
99.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 99 is the last of the psalms that open with “The LORD reigns” (93; 97; 99), and it closes the group celebrating the LORD as King (see the introduction). Psalm 97 began with the earth rejoicing and Psalm 98 with a new song; this one begins with the peoples trembling, because its theme is the King’s holiness.

The message. The LORD who reigns is holy, utterly above us and utterly pure, and his holiness is not cold distance: it loves justice, answers prayer, forgives sinners and disciplines those it forgives. The wonder is that this holy God calls himself “our God”, and lets his people come and worship at his feet.

Why it was said. Israel was always in danger of two errors: treating God as too high to care, or as too familiar to fear. Gathered at the temple, where the ark stood beneath the cherubim, the worshippers were reminded that the King of the whole earth had chosen to be enthroned among them, and that his nearness was a holy nearness (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. A threefold refrain, “Holy is he!”, divides the psalm. First the King reigns from above the cherubim in Zion, so the peoples should tremble and praise his awesome name (vv. 1–3). Then his holiness is seen in action, a mighty King who loves justice and has done it in Jacob, so his people should worship at his footstool (vv. 4–5). Last comes history: Moses, Aaron and Samuel called and were answered, heard his voice from the cloud, and found him a God who forgave them yet punished their wrongdoing, so his people should worship at his holy mountain, for “the LORD our God is holy!” (vv. 6–9).

Where it leads. By pattern, and by the character of God revealed in Christ. The King’s throne on earth was the mercy seat, where atoning blood was sprinkled, and Paul uses the word for that lid when he says God put Christ forward “as a propitiation by his blood” (Romans 3:25). At the cross the two sides of verse 8 meet: God remains the avenger of wrongdoing and is a forgiving God, because the punishment fell on his Son. And the intercessors Moses and Samuel point to a greater one, who “always lives to make intercession” for those who draw near to God through him (Hebrews 7:25).

For us. Do not shrink God to someone safe and manageable, and do not imagine him too holy to hear you. Come to him through Christ, trembling and glad; bring your sins to the one who forgives, and accept his discipline as the work of a Father who is making you holy.
99.theology: God's holiness is proclaimed three times (vv. 3, 5, 9; Isa 6:3) and shows itself as love of justice (v. 4). The holy God hears prayer (vv. 6-7), forgives, and disciplines those he forgives (v. 8). The last refrain says that the holy God belongs to his people: he is our God (v. 9), and Christ is the greater intercessor, the one who prays for us (Heb 7:25).
99.examples: Moses, who offered to be blotted out of God's book for his people, was forgiven and still died on the wrong side of the Jordan. The psalm holds both together: the King who is a consuming fire is the King whose throne is a mercy seat, and he is ours.

keyVerse.quote: Exalt the LORD our God, and worship at his holy mountain; for the LORD our God is holy!
keyVerse.note: The refrain “Holy is he!” reaches its fullest form here, and adds one word: the holy God is “our God”. The psalm has shown his holiness as justice, as answered prayer, and as forgiveness that still disciplines (v. 8); now it ends in wonder that such a God belongs to his people. In Christ, the mercy seat made flesh, sinners may draw near to him without being consumed.

99.reflection:
Psalm 97 begins with the earth rejoicing, Psalm 99 with the peoples trembling (v. 1). Why does our worship need both joy and fear, and which do you tend to lack?

God is enthroned “upon the cherubim”, above the mercy seat where atoning blood was sprinkled. What does it mean for you that God’s throne and his mercy are in the same place, and that Christ is now that place?

Moses, Aaron and Samuel “called to the LORD, and he answered them” (v. 6). What do their prayers teach us about praying for others, and how does Christ’s intercession encourage you to pray?

God was “a forgiving God to them, but an avenger of their wrongdoings” (v. 8). How can forgiveness be complete and yet consequences remain? How should this shape the way we handle our own failures, and the wrongs others have done to us?

100.text: A Psalm for giving thanks. 1Make a joyful noise to the LORD, all the earth!2Serve the LORD with gladness! Come into his presence with singing!3Know that the LORD, he is God! It is he who made us, and we are his; we are his people, and the sheep of his pasture.4Enter his gates with thanksgiving, and his courts with praise! Give thanks to him; bless his name!5For the LORD is good; his steadfast love endures forever, and his faithfulness to all generations.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–3 — Know That the LORD, He Is God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Glad worship rests on knowing whose we are. The psalm calls all the earth, not only Israel, to make a joyful noise to the LORD (v. 1), to serve him with gladness and to come before him singing (v. 2). Then, in the middle of the singing, comes a command to know: the LORD, Israel’s covenant God, is God and there is no other; he made us, so we belong to him; and he is not a distant maker but a shepherd, and we are the sheep of his pasture (v. 3). Service becomes glad when we remember who owns us and how he cares for us.
verseByVerse.theology: The whole earth is called to glad worship, and the reason is simple: he made us, and we belong to him.

verseByVerse.quote: Make a joyful noise to the LORD, all the earth! Serve the LORD with gladness! Come into his presence with singing!
verseByVerse.commentary:
The whole earth is invited to worship the LORD gladly, serving him with joy and coming before him with songs.

Make a joyful noise to the LORD, all the earth! Count the commands in these five verses: make a joyful noise, serve, come, know, enter, give thanks, bless. Seven. And the first is addressed to “all the earth”. This is Israel’s worship, but the invitation has no border. A “joyful noise” is the shout of homage given to a king.

Serve the LORD with gladness! “Serve” is a servant’s word: the work of a slave for a master, or a priest in the temple. The psalm joins it to gladness. Service without gladness turns into drudgery and resentment; gladness without service turns into self-indulgence. Glad service is the whole Christian life in two words, and the psalm will not let them be separated.

Come into his presence with singing! We come the way a crowd arrives at a festival, not the way a defendant enters a court. Christian worship should be glad and full-hearted, and also ordered, so that all are built up (1 Corinthians 14:26, 40).

A psalm for giving thanks. The title uses the word for the thank offering (Leviticus 7:12), so the psalm was probably sung as worshippers came up to the temple to give thanks, perhaps bringing that offering.

In everyday life. If the work you do for God, at home, in church or at your job, has become grim duty, the problem may not be the work but that you have forgotten verse 3: he made us, and we are his. Gladness is not squeezed out by effort; it is the fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22), who keeps reminding us whose we are.

What it does not mean. Not that believers must put on a smile or hide their grief. The same Psalter is full of laments, and God welcomes those who come in tears; this gladness is the settled joy of belonging to him, which can sit beside sorrow (2 Corinthians 6:10). If a heaviness will not lift for weeks, talk to your pastor or a biblical counsellor, and see a doctor too: medical help is no failure of faith.
verseByVerse.note: This psalm is the basis of the hymn “All People That on Earth Do Dwell.”

verseByVerse.quote: Know that the LORD, he is God! It is he who made us, and we are his; we are his people, and the sheep of his pasture.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Worship rests on knowing that the LORD alone is God, who made us, owns us and shepherds us.

Know that the LORD, he is God! Amid the singing comes a command to know. Worship is not only feeling; it rests on something known: the LORD, the covenant God of Israel, is God, and there is no other. Israel had shouted the same words on Mount Carmel, when Elijah prayed, the fire fell, and the people saw that Baal was nothing: “The LORD, he is God” (1 Kings 18:39).

It is he who made us, and we are his. Two facts ground everything: he made us, and therefore we belong to him. We did not make ourselves, which cuts off every kind of pride; and we are his, which is the deepest comfort there is. Paul says believers are God’s twice over: “we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus” (Ephesians 2:10). He made us once in creation, and again in Christ.

The sheep of his pasture. The one who made us is not a distant manufacturer but a shepherd, and we are “the sheep of his pasture”, close to Psalm 95’s “the people of his pasture, and the sheep of his hand” (Psalm 95:7). Sheep are not impressive animals. They wander, they panic, they cannot defend themselves; their whole safety is the shepherd. Isaiah saw what kind of shepherd this is: he “will gather the lambs in his arms; he will carry them in his bosom” (Isaiah 40:11).

Christ the good shepherd. Jesus said, “I am the good shepherd. I know my own and my own know me” (John 10:14), and “no one will snatch them out of my hand” (John 10:28). Peter wrote to believers, “you were straying like sheep, but have now returned to the Shepherd and Overseer of your souls” (1 Peter 2:25).

Why service can be glad. You serve a Shepherd who owns you, and nothing can take you out of his hand.

Textual note. The ESV notes another way of reading the Hebrew: “It is he who made us, and not we ourselves.” The Hebrew words for “not” and “his” sound alike and differ by one letter: the written Hebrew text has “not”, which the KJV follows, and the scribes’ marginal reading has “his”, which the ESV follows. Both are true.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–5 — For the LORD Is Good
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Thanks is the way into God’s presence, and the reasons for thanks will never run out. The worshippers pass through the temple gates and into its courts, and at each threshold they bring the same thing: thanksgiving and praise (v. 4). No one comes in on the strength of what they have achieved. The last verse gives the reason in three statements, each larger than the last: the LORD is good; his steadfast love endures forever; his faithfulness reaches to all generations (v. 5). The God who kept faith with the first singers keeps it with us and with our children.
verseByVerse.theology: The way into God's house is thanks, and the reason for thanks will never run out.

verseByVerse.quote: Enter his gates with thanksgiving, and his courts with praise! Give thanks to him; bless his name!
verseByVerse.commentary:
The way into God’s presence is thanksgiving: we come in thanking him, not presenting our achievements.

Enter his gates with thanksgiving. The picture is a procession approaching the temple, first through the outer gates, then into the courts. The entry fee at each stage is the same: thanks and praise. No one walks in on the strength of their achievements.

Why gratitude matters. Ingratitude is where human ruin began. Paul traces the whole downward slide of mankind to this: “although they knew God, they did not honor him as God or give thanks to him” (Romans 1:21). A thankful heart is a heart turned back towards God.

The way in is a person. For Christians the way in is no longer a temple gate but a person, Jesus Christ. “Through him then let us continually offer up a sacrifice of praise to God, that is, the fruit of lips that acknowledge his name” (Hebrews 13:15). Thanks is now the sacrifice we bring, and it is meant to be continual: “give thanks in all circumstances; for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus for you” (1 Thessalonians 5:18). That means thanks in every trouble, not for every evil.

In everyday life. Try it at the door of the next service you attend, or the next time you begin to pray. Before asking anything, name three things God has done for you this week. That is how the psalm says to go in.

verseByVerse.quote: For the LORD is good; his steadfast love endures forever, and his faithfulness to all generations.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The final reason for thanks is God himself: he is good, his covenant love never ends, and his faithfulness reaches every generation.

The LORD is good. Verse 3 said whose we are; verse 5 says what he is like, in three statements, each larger than the last. First, not merely that he does good things, but that goodness is what he is. Everything he does flows out of it.

His steadfast love endures forever. His covenant love never runs out and never expires: “The steadfast love of the LORD never ceases; his mercies never come to an end; they are new every morning” (Lamentations 3:22–23).

His faithfulness to all generations. The pair, steadfast love and faithfulness, is the name God proclaimed to Moses (Exodus 34:6). And “to all generations” means that the God who kept faith with the Israelites who first sang this psalm is keeping faith with you, and will keep it with your children and grandchildren.

What it means that the LORD is good. Most of us agree that God is good in general; the trouble comes in the particular: the prayer that went unanswered, the door that closed. The first temptation in the Bible was not an invitation to do something wicked but a question about God: “Did God actually say, ‘You shall not eat of any tree in the garden’?” (Genesis 3:1). The suggestion was that God was holding out on them, and every sin since has carried a little of that suspicion: if God were really good, he would have given me this. The answer is not an argument but a cross. “He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all, how will he not also with him graciously give us all things?” (Romans 8:32). A God who gave that is not holding out on you. So when he withholds something you long for, you can say what the singer of Psalm 119 learned to say in affliction, “You are good and do good” (Psalm 119:68), and trust that the “no” comes from the same heart as the cross.

Why the whole earth should sing. That is why the whole earth should make a joyful noise: not because life is easy, but because the God we serve is good, his love has no end, and his faithfulness will outlast every generation that sings about it.

100.title: Enter His Gates with Thanksgiving
100.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 100 closes the run of psalms that celebrate the LORD as King (93–99; see the introduction). After all their calls to the nations, it gathers everything into one short invitation headed “A Psalm for giving thanks”, which the church has sung for centuries as “All People That on Earth Do Dwell”.

The message. Come gladly into God’s presence, everyone on earth, and come thanking him. The reasons are two: he made us and we belong to him, as sheep belong to their shepherd; and he is good, with a love that never ends and a faithfulness that reaches every generation.

Why it was said. The title links the psalm with the thank offering (Leviticus 7:12), so it was probably sung as worshippers came up through the temple gates to give thanks. Israel’s worship was meant to be glad, and its invitation was meant to reach the nations, for God had promised Abraham that in him all the families of the earth would be blessed (Genesis 12:3; see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. Seven commands in five verses, in two rounds, each resting on a reason. Make a joyful noise, serve with gladness, come with singing (vv. 1–2), and know whose you are: the LORD is God, our Maker and our Shepherd (v. 3). Then enter his gates and courts with thanks and praise, give thanks and bless his name (v. 4), for the LORD is good, and his steadfast love and faithfulness never end (v. 5). Both times, glad worship rests on knowing who God is.

Where it leads. By covenant, and by the character of God revealed in Christ. The Shepherd who owns his flock has come in person: “I am the good shepherd. I know my own and my own know me” (John 10:14); and he has “other sheep that are not of this fold” (John 10:16), the nations this psalm invites. In him believers are God’s twice over, made in creation and “created in Christ Jesus” (Ephesians 2:10). And the way into God’s house is now a person: through Jesus we continually offer “a sacrifice of praise to God” (Hebrews 13:15).

For us. Worship is not a duty we drag ourselves to but a homecoming we are invited to, bringing nothing but thanks. When service turns grim, remember whose you are; when life turns hard, remember that he is good, and that his faithfulness will outlast you and reach your children.
100.theology: Seven commands to glad worship rest on two grounds: God owns us as our Maker and Shepherd (v. 3), and in Christ he has made us anew and shepherds us himself (Eph 2:10; John 10:14), and he is good, his love and faithfulness lasting to every generation (v. 5). Thanksgiving is the way into his presence (v. 4), the opposite of mankind's root sin of not thanking God (Rom 1:21), and now the continual sacrifice offered through Christ (Heb 13:15).
100.examples: Sheep are not impressive animals, and they do not need to be: their whole safety is the shepherd. That is why the psalm can call the whole earth to come in singing, bringing nothing to the gate but thanks, to a God who kept faith with the first singers and will keep it with their grandchildren.

keyVerse.quote: Know that the LORD, he is God! It is he who made us, and we are his; we are his people, and the sheep of his pasture.
keyVerse.note: At the centre of the psalm’s seven commands stands the one that grounds the rest: know. Glad service and thankful worship spring from knowing that the LORD is God, that he made us and owns us, and that he shepherds us. In Christ the good shepherd has come in person, and knows his own sheep by name.

100.reflection:
The psalm commands, “Serve the LORD with gladness!” (v. 2). Where has your service for God become grim duty, and how does verse 3 help restore the gladness?

“It is he who made us, and we are his” (v. 3). How does belonging to God, as Maker and as Shepherd, both humble us and comfort us?

Thanksgiving is the way into God’s presence (v. 4), and ingratitude is where human ruin began (Romans 1:21). What helps you to be thankful, and what tends to choke your thanks?

God’s faithfulness reaches “to all generations” (v. 5). Where have you seen his faithfulness passed down in families or churches, and how can we help the next generation to know it?

101.text: A Psalm of David. 1I will sing of steadfast love and justice; to you, O LORD, I will make music.2I will ponder the way that is blameless. Oh when will you come to me? I will walk with integrity of heart within my house;3I will not set before my eyes anything that is worthless. I hate the work of those who fall away; it shall not cling to me.4A perverse heart shall be far from me; I will know nothing of evil.5Whoever slanders his neighbor secretly I will destroy. Whoever has a haughty look and an arrogant heart I will not endure.6I will look with favor on the faithful in the land, that they may dwell with me; he who walks in the way that is blameless shall minister to me.7No one who practices deceit shall dwell in my house; no one who utters lies shall continue before my eyes.8Morning by morning I will destroy all the wicked in the land, cutting off all the evildoers from the city of the LORD.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — I Will Ponder the Way That Is Blameless
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The king’s integrity has to begin where no one is watching, and it depends on God coming to him. David opens with worship: he will sing of steadfast love and justice, the two things a ruler most needs (v. 1). He resolves to think hard about the blameless way, and then breaks off with a cry, “Oh when will you come to me?” (v. 2), admitting that his resolutions need God. Then he turns to the private places: his own house, what he sets before his eyes, what he allows to cling to him, and the heart from which all of it flows (vv. 2–4).
verseByVerse.theology: A king makes promises about his own heart, his home and his eyes, and in the middle cries out for God to come.

verseByVerse.quote: I will sing of steadfast love and justice; to you, O LORD, I will make music. I will ponder the way that is blameless. Oh when will you come to me? I will walk with integrity of heart within my house;
verseByVerse.commentary:
David vows to rule by the steadfast love and justice he sings about, beginning in his own home, and in the middle of his vows admits that he cannot keep them unless God comes to him.

I will sing of steadfast love and justice. “I will” comes again and again in these eight verses as David sets out how he intends to rule, and he begins not with policy but with worship. He sings of the two things a ruler most needs. Love without justice becomes favouritism; justice without love becomes cruelty. God holds both perfectly, and a king who has sung about them will try to rule by both.

I will ponder the way that is blameless. To “ponder” it is to think about it and study it. Integrity does not happen by accident; it is thought through.

Oh when will you come to me? Then, right in the middle of the resolutions, a cry. David knows that good intentions are not enough: unless God comes to him, every “I will” in the psalm will collapse. It is the most honest line in the psalm, and the one to pray first. The cry may also have a setting. Some link it with the day David was afraid to bring the ark to Jerusalem and asked, “How can the ark of the LORD come to me?” (2 Samuel 6:9). If so, these vows describe the house and court he meant to make fit for God’s presence.

I will walk with integrity of heart within my house. Before he says anything about the kingdom, he speaks about his home. David resolves that the man inside the house will be the same man as the king who sits in public at the city gate. A leader’s integrity is tested first where there is no audience: with his wife, his children and his servants, behind the door.

Does a leader’s private life matter? Many now say it does not: we want leaders competent, not saintly, and what they do at home is their own business so long as the economy grows. There is something fair in this, for a leader’s family deserves privacy. But underneath lies the assumption that a person can be divided, one self for the office and another for the kitchen, that never leak into each other. David’s own life disproved it: the desire indulged on his roof became a cover-up in his house and then a murder ordered through his army (2 Samuel 11:14–15). Character is the person who holds the power when no one is checking. And every one of us has a house where the audience goes home. The gospel answers both our cynicism and our pretending. It does not ask us to manage an image; it gives us a King who was the same man in the carpenter’s shop as on the cross, and his Spirit to make us whole: one person, in public and at home.

verseByVerse.quote: I will not set before my eyes anything that is worthless. I hate the work of those who fall away; it shall not cling to me. A perverse heart shall be far from me; I will know nothing of evil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The king guards his eyes and his heart, refusing to look at what is worthless or to let evil cling to him.

I will not set before my eyes. The eyes are the gateway, and he guards them. “Anything that is worthless”, anything vile, useless or corrupting, will not be “set before” his eyes, placed there to be looked at. He cannot prevent every sight from reaching him. He can decide what he sits and looks at.

It shall not cling to me. Sin “clings” like mud. The work of those who fall away is not merely something to disapprove of at a distance; it attaches itself to whoever handles it.

I will know nothing of evil. He will have no intimate acquaintance with it. There are things it is better not to be an expert in.

The vow David broke. David wrote this vow, and later, from the roof of his palace late one afternoon, he looked at a woman bathing and did not look away (2 Samuel 11:2). The vow was right. He broke it, and it cost Uriah his life and Bathsheba her child. But the roof is not the end of David’s story: Psalm 51 is the prayer of the same man, confessing and forgiven, and that mercy is open to anyone who has looked where he should not.

What this looks like. For a generation that carries a screen everywhere, the question is practical: what do you set before your eyes in the evening? Paul puts the vow positively: “whatever is true, whatever is honorable, whatever is just, whatever is pure … think about these things” (Philippians 4:8). Decide before the evening. Choose what you will watch before you sit down, not when the next autoplay starts. Change the setting, not only the resolve. Keep the phone out of the bedroom, put a filter on the family devices, and give a trusted friend leave to ask what you have been looking at. Look away quickly. You cannot stop every image reaching you; you can refuse to sit and stare, as Job did when he “made a covenant with” his “eyes” (Job 31:1). Give your eyes something better. We become like what we behold, and “beholding the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into the same image” (2 Corinthians 3:18). When you fail, go straight back to the King who kept this vow perfectly and was never ashamed of what he looked at: his blood cleanses the eyes as well as the hands.

Uncertain wording. “Those who fall away” translates a rare word for those who swerve or turn aside, whether apostates or simply the crooked. And “I will know nothing of evil” could also mean “I will not know an evil person”, which fits the court of verses 5–8. Either way, evil and evil company are kept at a distance.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–8 — No One Who Practices Deceit Shall Dwell in My House
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A good ruler chooses his company, and keeps the city of the LORD clean. The king now looks outward to the people around him. Whisperers who slander in secret and proud men with a haughty look will not be tolerated (v. 5), but the faithful in the land will be drawn near to live with him and serve him (v. 6). Liars will not stay in his house (v. 7), and every morning he will do justice, clearing evildoers out, because Jerusalem is not his city but the LORD’s (v. 8).
verseByVerse.theology: The king chooses his company and guards his court, so that the city of God is clean.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever slanders his neighbor secretly I will destroy. Whoever has a haughty look and an arrogant heart I will not endure. I will look with favor on the faithful in the land, that they may dwell with me; he who walks in the way that is blameless shall minister to me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The king will not let secret slanderers or proud men near him, but will draw the faithful close to live with him and serve him.

Whoever slanders his neighbor secretly. Two kinds of person will not come near the king. The first is the secret slanderer, who whispers against others in private and poisons the king’s mind. Every court has them, and so does every office, family and church. The second is the proud man with “a haughty look”, who looks down on everyone else. These are not spectacular sins, but they quietly rot a community from the inside, and a wise leader deals with them early.

The faithful in the land. Instead he brings close “the faithful”: not the impressive, the flattering or the useful, but the trustworthy.

The court of a better King. Christ chose his court the same way, calling fishermen and tax collectors, not the proud; and still “God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble” (James 4:6).

Who is in your court? Every person has a court: the friends they listen to, the voices they let near. The psalm asks who is in yours. The company we choose shapes who we become.

verseByVerse.quote: No one who practices deceit shall dwell in my house; no one who utters lies shall continue before my eyes. Morning by morning I will destroy all the wicked in the land, cutting off all the evildoers from the city of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No liar will stay in the king’s house, and every morning he will do justice, because Jerusalem is the city of the LORD and evil does not belong there.

No one who practices deceit. A ruler surrounded by liars can never know the truth about his own kingdom.

Morning by morning. Kings in Israel heard cases in the morning, and the picture is of a king who does justice every day, not occasionally: “A king who sits on the throne of judgment winnows all evil with his eyes” (Proverbs 20:8). And the reason is the name of the city: it is “the city of the LORD”. Evil does not belong there.

The King who kept it. No king of Israel kept this psalm. David wrote it and failed it: he looked at Bathsheba, took her into his house, lied to cover it and had her husband killed. His sons failed it too. The vow stood unkept until a King came who could say every line and mean it: whose heart had integrity inside his house, who set nothing worthless before his eyes, in whose mouth no deceit was found (1 Peter 2:22). His obedience is counted to all who trust him (Romans 5:19), and the city he is preparing will at last be clean (Revelation 21:27).

The same call for us. That King now asks the same of those who follow him: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew 5:8). Leaders in his church are to be “above reproach” (1 Timothy 3:2). No Christian can keep this psalm by resolution alone. But everyone can begin where David did, with the cry “Oh when will you come to me?”, and find that the King who kept it perfectly has come and has given his Spirit, so that his people walk in his ways (Romans 8:4).

Does this apply to Christians? It is a king’s vow as judge in Israel. The magistrate still bears the sword against evildoers (Romans 13:4); the church’s version is discipline, not execution (1 Corinthians 5:13); and personal revenge is never ours (Romans 12:19).

101.title: Integrity of Heart Within My House
101.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 101 comes straight after the psalms that cry “The LORD reigns” (93; 96–99) and the summons of Psalm 100 to serve him with gladness. Having heard who the true King is, we now hear a human king, David, vow how he will rule under him.

The message. A ruler who sings of God’s steadfast love and justice must rule by them, beginning in his own heart and home and reaching out to the whole court and city. Yet in the middle of the vows stands a cry, “Oh when will you come to me?” (v. 2): no one keeps such promises unless God comes to him.

Why it was said. Israel’s king was to rule under God’s law, not above it (Deuteronomy 17:18–20), and this psalm sets out what that means in practice. Placed in Book Four, after the crown had fallen into the dust (see the introduction), it also held up a portrait of the king Israel was still waiting for.

How the chapter makes its case. It begins with worship and with the honest cry for God’s help (vv. 1–2a). Then the king turns inward: integrity at home, guarded eyes, a heart kept far from evil (vv. 2b–4). Then he turns outward to his court: no secret slanderer, proud man or liar will stay near him, but the faithful will serve him, and every morning he will clear evil out of the city of the LORD (vv. 5–8).

Where it leads. To Christ by pattern and by the need it exposes. David wrote this vow and broke it, and his sons broke it too. Only one King has ever been able to pray every line: he “committed no sin, neither was deceit found in his mouth” (1 Peter 2:22). His perfect obedience is counted to all who trust him, and the city he is preparing will be what David longed for: “nothing unclean will ever enter it, nor anyone who does what is detestable or false” (Revelation 21:27).

For us. Every one of us has a house where the audience goes home, eyes that choose what they look at, and a circle of voices we let near. Begin where David began, with the cry for God to come, and bring your failures to the King who kept this vow for you and now gives his Spirit to make you whole.
101.theology: Rule is to be shaped by steadfast love and justice (v. 1). Its private roots are integrity at home, guarded eyes and a heart kept from evil (vv. 2-4); its public fruit is a court of faithful people and justice done daily (vv. 5-8). All of it depends on God coming to help (v. 2). David failed the vow; Christ the King kept it, and its standard remains for his people and their leaders (Matt 5:8; 1 Tim 3:2).
101.examples: The psalm is a string of good resolutions with a cry for help in the middle, and that is its wisdom: a man can be the same behind his front door as in public only if God comes to him. No king kept this vow until Christ did, and he now keeps his people.

keyVerse.quote: I will ponder the way that is blameless. Oh when will you come to me? I will walk with integrity of heart within my house;
keyVerse.note: This verse holds the whole psalm: a resolve to live blamelessly, beginning at home, with a cry for God’s help at its centre. David could not keep the vow by willpower, and neither can we. The answer to his question is Christ, the King who came, kept every line of it, and now comes to his people by his Spirit.

101.reflection:
David begins his vows with worship: “I will sing of steadfast love and justice” (v. 1). Why do love and justice need each other, in a ruler, a parent, a manager or a church leader? Which do you tend to lean on at the expense of the other?

“I will walk with integrity of heart within my house” (v. 2). Why is home the hardest place to be the same person we are in public? What would integrity look like in your home this week?

Verse 3 is a vow about the eyes. What practical steps help you decide what you set before your eyes, and how can we help one another without becoming either lax or harsh?

David asks, “Oh when will you come to me?”, and then breaks the vow he wrote. How does it change the way you read this psalm to know that Christ kept it perfectly for us?

102.text: A Prayer of one afflicted, when he is faint and pours out his complaint before the LORD. 1Hear my prayer, O LORD; let my cry come to you!2Do not hide your face from me in the day of my distress! Incline your ear to me; answer me speedily in the day when I call!3For my days pass away like smoke, and my bones burn like a furnace.4My heart is struck down like grass and has withered; I forget to eat my bread.5Because of my loud groaning my bones cling to my flesh.6I am like a desert owl of the wilderness, like an owl of the waste places;7I lie awake; I am like a lonely sparrow on the housetop.8All the day my enemies taunt me; those who deride me use my name for a curse.9For I eat ashes like bread and mingle tears with my drink,10because of your indignation and anger; for you have taken me up and thrown me down.11My days are like an evening shadow; I wither away like grass.12But you, O LORD, are enthroned forever; you are remembered throughout all generations.13You will arise and have pity on Zion; it is the time to favor her; the appointed time has come.14For your servants hold her stones dear and have pity on her dust.15Nations will fear the name of the LORD, and all the kings of the earth will fear your glory.16For the LORD builds up Zion; he appears in his glory;17he regards the prayer of the destitute and does not despise their prayer.18Let this be recorded for a generation to come, so that a people yet to be created may praise the LORD:19that he looked down from his holy height; from heaven the LORD looked at the earth,20to hear the groans of the prisoners, to set free those who were doomed to die,21that they may declare in Zion the name of the LORD, and in Jerusalem his praise,22when peoples gather together, and kingdoms, to worship the LORD.23He has broken my strength in midcourse; he has shortened my days.24"O my God," I say, "take me not away in the midst of my days— you whose years endure throughout all generations!"25Of old you laid the foundation of the earth, and the heavens are the work of your hands.26They will perish, but you will remain; they will all wear out like a garment. You will change them like a robe, and they will pass away,27but you are the same, and your years have no end.28The children of your servants shall dwell secure; their offspring shall be established before you.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — My Days Pass Away Like Smoke
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The afflicted may pour out everything before God, without tidying it first. The sufferer begins by begging God to hear, to turn his face towards him and to answer quickly (vv. 1–2). Then the complaint comes in a flood of images: days vanishing like smoke, bones burning, a heart withered like grass, meals forgotten, a body wasted by groaning (vv. 3–5). He is as lonely as a bird in a ruin and as sleepless as a sparrow on a roof (vv. 6–7), mocked by enemies, eating ashes and tears, convinced that God’s hand has thrown him down (vv. 8–10). It ends where it began, with grass withering in the evening (v. 11).
verseByVerse.theology: A man with no name, sleepless and wasting, pours out everything to God.

verseByVerse.quote: Hear my prayer, O LORD; let my cry come to you! Do not hide your face from me in the day of my distress! Incline your ear to me; answer me speedily in the day when I call!
verseByVerse.commentary:
An afflicted, exhausted man begs God to listen, to turn his face towards him, and to answer quickly.

The title. It does not name an author but a condition: “A Prayer of one afflicted, when he is faint and pours out his complaint before the LORD.” That makes it a prayer for anyone: if you are afflicted and faint, this psalm has your name on it. And it is a “complaint”, poured out. God has put in his book a prayer that empties everything out before him, without tidying it first.

Incline your ear to me. The first requests are for God’s face, ear and speed: do not hide, lean down, answer quickly. When you are faint, you have no strength for long prayers or patience for delay.

He prayed like this too. “In the days of his flesh, Jesus offered up prayers and supplications, with loud cries and tears, to him who was able to save him from death, and he was heard because of his reverence” (Hebrews 5:7). Those who pour out their complaint come to a high priest who has done the same.
verseByVerse.note: Since early times the church has counted this among the seven penitential psalms, though it is more a lament than a confession.

verseByVerse.quote: For my days pass away like smoke, and my bones burn like a furnace. My heart is struck down like grass and has withered; I forget to eat my bread. Because of my loud groaning my bones cling to my flesh. I am like a desert owl of the wilderness, like an owl of the waste places; I lie awake; I am like a lonely sparrow on the housetop.
verseByVerse.commentary:
His life is vanishing and his body wasting, and he lies awake, alone as a bird in a ruin.

My days pass away like smoke. The complaint comes in a flood of images. His days vanish like smoke, visible for a moment, then gone. His bones burn like a furnace: fever, or the burning ache of long illness or grief. His heart withers like cut grass, and his groaning has left him skin and bone (v. 5).

I forget to eat my bread. A small, true detail, which anyone who has been through deep grief or depression recognises. Food loses its point; meals are missed without noticing. If that is you, this psalm gives you leave to say so to God, and wisdom says it also to someone near you: a pastor, a friend, a biblical counsellor, who will also ask you to have a medical check-up. If medicine is needed, taking it is no failure of faith, and if your thoughts have turned to ending your life, tell someone the same day.

A lonely sparrow on the housetop. The birds picture loneliness: a bird of ruins and deserts, calling in the dark; a single sparrow on a flat roof, awake when every other bird has gone to roost. “I lie awake.” The sleepless nights of the sufferer are in the Bible.

The lonely century. Few lines in Scripture sound more modern. We are the most connected people who have ever lived, and many of us have never been lonelier. The political scientist Robert Putnam, in Bowling Alone, traced how Americans drifted out of the clubs, congregations and neighbourhood ties that once held them; since then the screens that promised friendship have often given us an audience instead. A sparrow on the housetop can watch the whole street and belong to none of it. Our remedies fail in opposite directions: network harder, or learn to be enough on your own. But Augustine saw that the heart was made for God and stays restless until it rests in him, so even the best friends cannot fill the deepest place. That is why this man turns his loneliness into prayer, and so is no longer talking to no one. And the One he prayed to entered this loneliness himself: in Gethsemane his friends slept, and on the cross he was forsaken, so that no one who trusts him will finally be left alone.

Uncertain wording. The birds of verse 6 cannot be identified with certainty (older English versions made the first “a pelican of the wilderness”), and the “sparrow” may be any small bird. The point is clear whatever the species.

verseByVerse.quote: All the day my enemies taunt me; those who deride me use my name for a curse. For I eat ashes like bread and mingle tears with my drink, because of your indignation and anger; for you have taken me up and thrown me down. My days are like an evening shadow; I wither away like grass.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Mocked and grieving, he believes God’s anger lies behind his suffering, and feels his life fading like an evening shadow.

Those who deride me use my name for a curse. His suffering has made him a byword. People use his name as an example of misfortune: “may you end up like him”.

I eat ashes like bread. Ashes were the sign of mourning, and he eats them; tears fall into his cup. Then the hardest line: “because of your indignation and anger”. He believes God’s hand is in it. “You have taken me up and thrown me down”, like someone lifted high and then dashed to the ground. The height he once had makes the fall worse.

My days are like an evening shadow. An evening shadow grows longer and fainter as the sun goes down, until it disappears into the dark. That is how he feels his life is ending: stretched thin, and fading.

I wither away like grass. The complaint is framed by grass. It began with “my heart is struck down like grass and has withered” (v. 4) and ends with “I wither away like grass” (v. 11). That is why the turn in verse 12 is so striking.

Is suffering a sign that God is angry? This man feels God’s anger without naming a sin, but suffering is not always punishment (John 9:3), and for the believer in Christ there is “no condemnation” (Romans 8:1), because the anger our sins deserved fell on him. What feels like wrath may be a Father’s discipline (Hebrews 12:6), or no judgment at all.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–22 — But You, O LORD, Are Enthroned Forever
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The sufferer looks away from his shadow to the eternal King, and finds hope for his city and for people not yet born. Nothing in his condition has changed, but the psalm turns on “But you, O LORD” (v. 12). God reigns for ever, and the appointed time has come for him to pity ruined Zion, whose very stones his servants love (vv. 13–14). When he rebuilds it, nations and kings will fear him, yet his glory is that he hears the prayer of the destitute (vv. 15–17). So the rescue is to be written down for a people yet to be created: he looked down, heard the prisoners and freed the condemned, so that the nations might gather to worship (vv. 18–22).
verseByVerse.theology: From his own ruin the sufferer looks up to the eternal King, and writes for readers not yet born.

verseByVerse.quote: But you, O LORD, are enthroned forever; you are remembered throughout all generations. You will arise and have pity on Zion; it is the time to favor her; the appointed time has come. For your servants hold her stones dear and have pity on her dust. Nations will fear the name of the LORD, and all the kings of the earth will fear your glory. For the LORD builds up Zion; he appears in his glory; he regards the prayer of the destitute and does not despise their prayer.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Looking from his fading life to the LORD enthroned for ever, he is sure God will now pity ruined Zion, for the God whose glory makes kings afraid hears the prayer of the destitute.

But you, O LORD, are enthroned forever. Here the psalm turns. Nothing about his condition has changed, but he looks away from his shadow to God’s throne. His days are smoke; God is “enthroned forever”. He is forgotten and cursed; God is “remembered throughout all generations”. Psalm 92 put the same sentence at its centre: “but you, O LORD, are on high forever” (Psalm 92:8). That is the way out of the pit that suffering digs: not denial, for he has told the truth about his pain, but a second look, upwards.

Your servants hold her stones dear. His personal ruin is tied to Zion’s. The city lies in ruins, and God’s servants love even its rubble, “her stones” and “her dust”. And he is sure that “the appointed time has come” for God to act. If, as many think, the psalm comes from the end of the exile, this probably recalls Jeremiah’s promise that after seventy years in Babylon God would bring his people home (Jeremiah 29:10), the promise Daniel saw was nearly due (Daniel 9:2).

He appears in his glory. The rebuilding of Zion will make nations and kings fear the LORD. And “he appears in his glory” stands right beside “the LORD builds up Zion”: God’s glory is seen not only in thunder on a mountain but in the patient rebuilding of what was ruined, as in every broken life and church that is his. Yet the heart of it is the last line. The God who makes kings afraid “regards the prayer of the destitute and does not despise their prayer”, and the afflicted man of the title is one of them.

The Zion being built. The exiles returned and rebuilt, but the nations came to fear the LORD’s name only through Christ. Now, says Hebrews, “you have come to Mount Zion and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem” (Hebrews 12:22), built of living stones from every nation.

verseByVerse.quote: Let this be recorded for a generation to come, so that a people yet to be created may praise the LORD: that he looked down from his holy height; from heaven the LORD looked at the earth, to hear the groans of the prisoners, to set free those who were doomed to die, that they may declare in Zion the name of the LORD, and in Jerusalem his praise, when peoples gather together, and kingdoms, to worship the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s rescue is to be written down for people not yet born: he looked down, heard the prisoners and freed the condemned, so that the nations would gather to worship.

Let this be recorded for a generation to come. The sufferer asks that his experience be written down for people not yet born. You are one of them: “a people yet to be created” includes every believer who has ever opened this psalm. A man in affliction, whose name we do not know, prayed that God would use his suffering for someone else’s praise, and God did it. No affliction handed to God is wasted.

He looked down from his holy height. This is what is to be recorded: God looked down. “The groans of the prisoners” and “doomed to die” are the words of Psalm 79:11, where they were a desperate request. Here they are recorded as something God did. The prayer of one psalm is the praise of another.

To set free those who were doomed to die. Jesus opened his ministry in Nazareth by announcing that he had been sent “to proclaim liberty to the captives” (Luke 4:18). The prisoners of this psalm picture every sinner under sentence of death, and in Christ God looked down from heaven and set them free.

To worship the LORD. The end of rescue is worship, and not only Israel’s: “peoples” and “kingdoms” gather together. The freed prisoners join the nations in praise.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A man whose life is being cut short takes refuge in the God whose years never end. His strength is broken halfway through his life, and he pleads not to be taken in the midst of his days (vv. 23–24). Then he sets his few days against God’s endless years: God laid the foundations of the earth, and earth and heavens will wear out like clothing and be changed like a robe, but God remains the same (vv. 25–27). So the psalm ends not with the man’s own recovery but with the security of his children before God (v. 28). Hebrews hears verses 25–27 spoken to the Son.
verseByVerse.theology: A man whose life is being cut short takes refuge in the one whose years never end — words Hebrews says are spoken to the Son.

verseByVerse.quote: He has broken my strength in midcourse; he has shortened my days. "O my God," I say, "take me not away in the midst of my days— you whose years endure throughout all generations!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Broken halfway through life, he pleads with the everlasting God not to take him in the middle of his days.

He has broken my strength in midcourse. The vision of Zion has not removed his own suffering. His strength is broken “in midcourse”, halfway through the journey. He is not old; his life is being cut off in the middle.

Take me not away in the midst of my days. His plea sets two lengths of time against each other: “the midst of my days”, and God’s years that “endure throughout all generations”. You have endless years; do not take my few.

Cut off in the midst of his days. There was one man whose strength was broken in midcourse more starkly than this, cut off in his thirties, in the middle of his days. And the next verses, astonishingly, the New Testament says are spoken to him.

verseByVerse.quote: Of old you laid the foundation of the earth, and the heavens are the work of your hands. They will perish, but you will remain; they will all wear out like a garment. You will change them like a robe, and they will pass away, but you are the same, and your years have no end. The children of your servants shall dwell secure; their offspring shall be established before you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Heaven and earth will wear out like old clothes, but God remains the same for ever, so his servants’ children are secure; and Hebrews hears these words spoken to the Son.

They will all wear out like a garment. The heavens and the earth feel permanent. They are not. God made them, and they will wear out like an old coat that thins and frays, and God will change them as a man changes clothes. The universe is his wardrobe. Everything wears out except him: “you are the same.”

The Son in this psalm. The letter to the Hebrews quotes these verses as addressed to the Son (Hebrews 1:10–12). The God to whom the afflicted man prays, whose years have no end, is the Son of God.

The eternal one cut off. Put that beside verse 23. The Son, whose years have no end, took on a human life and let his strength be broken in midcourse: the eternal one was cut off in the midst of his days. He knows both halves of this psalm from the inside, the sufferer’s and the eternal King’s. Hebrews ends with the same confidence: “Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever” (Hebrews 13:8). The one this psalm calls the same is not a changeless idea but a changeless person, and the believer who is wearing out like the old coat of verse 26 is held by him.

The universe is running down. Modern physics agrees with verse 26 more than the psalmist could have guessed: the useful energy in a closed system steadily runs down, and many cosmologists expect the universe, left to itself, to end cold, dark and still, a coat worn through. Most people find the thought quietly chilling and get on with their day. The instinct is to hold on to something permanent inside the world: a nation, a family name, a body of work, the human race itself. But all of these are threads in the same coat. The psalm points to the only one outside the wardrobe: “you are the same, and your years have no end”. That is not escapism but the one ground on which a fading life can still mean something. And the New Testament adds what no physics could predict: the Son who made the garment will not throw it away but change it, and his people are “waiting for new heavens and a new earth” (2 Peter 3:13).

The children of your servants shall dwell secure. The psalm ends not with the man’s recovery (we are never told whether he got better) but with the security of the next generation. His days may be short; God’s are not. Paul says that “the whole creation has been groaning together in the pains of childbirth until now” (Romans 8:22), and when it is changed like a robe, the children of God’s servants will still be standing before him.

Why does Hebrews hear these words as spoken to the Son? Partly because in the Greek Old Testament, which Hebrews quotes, verses 23–24 read as God answering the sufferer, so that verse 25 becomes God himself addressing someone as Lord. More deeply, the psalm calls the LORD the Creator, and the New Testament names the Son as the one through whom all things were made (John 1:3; Hebrews 1:2).
verseByVerse.note: Compare Isa 51:6, where the heavens vanish like smoke and the earth wears out like a garment, but God's salvation is forever.

102.title: Your Years Have No End
102.overview:
Where we are. After a king’s vow in Psalm 101, Book Four gives us a sufferer with no name. The title names not an author but a condition: “A Prayer of one afflicted, when he is faint and pours out his complaint before the LORD.” His own ruin is bound up with the ruin of Zion, which lies in stones and dust (v. 14).

The message. When your life is vanishing like smoke and withering like grass, tell God the truth, and then look up: the LORD is enthroned for ever, he hears the prayer of the destitute, and his years have no end. A short, broken life is held by the God who will rebuild what is ruined and outlast the universe, and his people’s future rests on him, not on their strength.

Why it was said. The psalm most likely comes from the end of the exile, when Jerusalem was still rubble, its exiles still loved its dust, and the time God had promised to restore it seemed near (vv. 13–14; see the introduction). Its title opens it to every afflicted person who would ever pray it.

How the chapter makes its case. It opens with a cry to be heard (vv. 1–2) and a complaint poured out: wasting, sleepless, lonely and taunted, under God’s anger, a life framed by withering grass (vv. 3–11). Then comes the turn, “But you, O LORD, are enthroned forever” (v. 12): God will pity Zion, the nations will fear him, and he hears the destitute (vv. 13–17), and this rescue is to be written down for a people not yet born (vv. 18–22). Finally the sufferer, cut off in midcourse, sets his few days against the God who made the heavens and will outlast them, and rests his children’s future on him (vv. 23–28).

Where it leads. Directly, because the New Testament hears this psalm speaking of Christ.
