Hebrews quotes verses 25–27 as words addressed to the Son: he laid the foundation of the earth, and “you are the same, and your years will have no end” (Hebrews 1:10–12). And by pattern: the eternal Son took a human life and was cut off in the midst of his days, entering the sufferer’s half of the psalm as well as the Creator’s. The prisoners set free and the nations gathering to worship are the fruit of his work.

For us. This psalm gives the afflicted permission to pour out everything before God, and then lifts their eyes from their fading days to his endless years. In Christ your short life is held by one who does not change, and no suffering handed to him is wasted.
102.theology: God gives every sufferer permission to pour out a complaint before him without tidying it first (vv. 1-11). The turn comes not from changed circumstances but from looking up from one's own fading days to God's eternal throne (v. 12), where the King whose glory makes nations afraid regards the prayer of the destitute (v. 17). Creation wears out; God alone is the same (vv. 25-27), and Hebrews hears these words spoken to the Son (Heb 1:10-12), the eternal one who was cut off in the midst of his days.
102.examples: The psalm has no author's name, only a condition, so it belongs to anyone who has forgotten to eat, or lain awake like a single sparrow on a roof. Its writer never learned what his prayer would become: words for readers not yet born, and words the Father speaks to the Son.

keyVerse.quote: but you are the same, and your years have no end.
keyVerse.note: The whole psalm turns on the contrast between a life vanishing like smoke and a God whose years never end. The sufferer’s hope, and his children’s security, rest not on his own strength but on God’s changelessness. Hebrews hears these words addressed to the Son, who is “the same yesterday and today and forever”.

102.reflection:
The title calls this psalm the prayer of one who “pours out his complaint before the LORD”. Why do you think God included such raw prayers in Scripture? What keeps us from praying this honestly?

Verses 3–11 describe sleeplessness, forgotten meals and loneliness. How can we as a church notice and come alongside people going through this, and when should we encourage them to seek other help too?

The turn comes with “But you, O LORD, are enthroned forever” (v. 12), though nothing in the man’s situation has changed. How does looking up at who God is help when circumstances stay the same?

Hebrews says verses 25–27 are spoken to the Son, who was himself cut off “in the midst of” his days. How does it help you to know that the unchanging Lord has also suffered?

103.text: Of David. 1Bless the LORD, O my soul, and all that is within me, bless his holy name!2Bless the LORD, O my soul, and forget not all his benefits,3who forgives all your iniquity, who heals all your diseases,4who redeems your life from the pit, who crowns you with steadfast love and mercy,5who satisfies you with good so that your youth is renewed like the eagle's.6The LORD works righteousness and justice for all who are oppressed.7He made known his ways to Moses, his acts to the people of Israel.8The LORD is merciful and gracious, slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love.9He will not always chide, nor will he keep his anger forever.10He does not deal with us according to our sins, nor repay us according to our iniquities.11For as high as the heavens are above the earth, so great is his steadfast love toward those who fear him;12as far as the east is from the west, so far does he remove our transgressions from us.13As a father shows compassion to his children, so the LORD shows compassion to those who fear him.14For he knows our frame; he remembers that we are dust.15As for man, his days are like grass; he flourishes like a flower of the field;16for the wind passes over it, and it is gone, and its place knows it no more.17But the steadfast love of the LORD is from everlasting to everlasting on those who fear him, and his righteousness to children's children,18to those who keep his covenant and remember to do his commandments.19The LORD has established his throne in the heavens, and his kingdom rules over all.20Bless the LORD, O you his angels, you mighty ones who do his word, obeying the voice of his word!21Bless the LORD, all his hosts, his ministers, who do his will!22Bless the LORD, all his works, in all places of his dominion. Bless the LORD, O my soul!

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — Bless the LORD, O My Soul
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The soul must be told to bless the LORD, and given the list of what he has done. David speaks not first to God or to the congregation but to himself, summoning everything within him to praise God’s holy name (v. 1). The enemy he names is forgetting, so he commands his soul to remember (v. 2). Then comes the list, five benefits in a deliberate order: forgiveness first, as the root of the rest, then healing, rescue from the pit, a crown of steadfast love and mercy, and a life satisfied with good and renewed in strength (vv. 3–5).
verseByVerse.theology: David preaches to his own soul, and the first benefit on the list is forgiveness.

verseByVerse.quote: Bless the LORD, O my soul, and all that is within me, bless his holy name! Bless the LORD, O my soul, and forget not all his benefits,
verseByVerse.commentary:
David commands his own soul to bless the LORD with everything in him and not to forget what God has done.

Bless the LORD, O my soul. David is talking not first to God or the congregation, but to his own soul. There are times when the soul does not feel like praising, and the right thing to do is not to wait for the feeling but to address the soul and give it orders.

All that is within me. The order is total: mind, affections, memory and will, the whole person, bend towards “his holy name”.

Forget not all his benefits. The command is repeated, and its enemy is named: forgetting. The soul seldom stops praising because it has decided God is not good; it stops because it has forgotten what he has done. Ingratitude is mostly a failure of memory.

The cure for forgetting. So the cure is a list, not a vague sense of blessing. For the Christian the list begins at the cross: “Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us in Christ with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places” (Ephesians 1:3). Try it: before you go to sleep tonight, name what God has done for you, one thing at a time.

verseByVerse.quote: who forgives all your iniquity, who heals all your diseases, who redeems your life from the pit, who crowns you with steadfast love and mercy, who satisfies you with good so that your youth is renewed like the eagle's.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s benefits begin with forgiveness, the root of them all, and run to a life rescued, crowned with love and filled with good.

Who forgives all your iniquity. Five benefits follow, and the order matters. Before health, before rescue, before anything else, the greatest thing God does for a person is to forgive “all” his iniquity. A healthy man with unforgiven sin is far worse off than a sick man who is forgiven.

Who heals all your diseases. This true promise must be read honestly. God does heal, and every recovery is his gift. But believers still get ill and die. The promise is not that every disease is cured in this life; it is that the God who forgives all iniquity will finally heal every disease, when “death shall be no more, neither shall there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain anymore” (Revelation 21:4). Forgiveness comes first because it is the root; healing follows because it is the fruit.

Who redeems your life from the pit. He “redeems”, buys back, your life from the pit of death, and “crowns” you: the one pulled out of the pit is not merely rescued but honoured with steadfast love and mercy. And he “satisfies you with good”, until your strength comes back like an eagle’s. Isaiah promised the same: “they who wait for the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings like eagles” (Isaiah 40:31).

Five verbs. Forgiven, healed, redeemed, crowned, satisfied: from the pit to a crown to a full table, the story of every believer’s life.

The same order in Jesus. To a paralysed man lowered through a roof, Jesus said first, “Son, your sins are forgiven” (Mark 2:5), and only then, “rise, pick up your bed” (Mark 2:11).

Uncertain wording. In verse 5 the Hebrew word behind “you” in “satisfies you with good” is obscure (elsewhere it usually means “ornament”), and translators have guessed “your mouth”, “your years” or “your desire”. The sense, a life filled with good, is clear.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–14 — As Far as the East Is from the West
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God is merciful and gracious, and he does not treat us as our sins deserve. David moves from what God has done to what God is like. He acts for the oppressed and has told his people his ways, above all in the name he proclaimed to Moses: merciful, gracious, slow to anger, abounding in steadfast love (vv. 6–8). His anger has an end, and he does not repay us as our iniquities deserve (vv. 9–10). His love is as high as the sky, he removes our sins as far as east is from west (vv. 11–12), and he pities those who fear him as a father pities his children, because he remembers that we are dust (vv. 13–14).
verseByVerse.theology: God's love is measured by the height of the sky, and our sins are removed as far as east from west.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD works righteousness and justice for all who are oppressed. He made known his ways to Moses, his acts to the people of Israel. The LORD is merciful and gracious, slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD acts for the oppressed, and has told us plainly what he is like: merciful, gracious, slow to anger and rich in steadfast love.

The LORD works righteousness and justice. The psalm moves from what God has done for one soul to what God is like. He is on the side of all who are oppressed. An Israelite would think first of his own people as slaves in Egypt, where God saw their affliction and came down to rescue them (Exodus 3:7–8), and that is why Moses is named next.

He made known his ways to Moses. God has not left people guessing about his character. Notice verse 7: to Moses he made known his “ways”; to the people, his “acts”. The people saw what God did, the plagues, the sea, the manna; Moses was shown why, and what kind of God does such things. It is possible to see God’s acts all your life and never ask to know his ways. Moses asked, and was answered with verse 8.

The LORD is merciful and gracious. After the golden calf, God passed before Moses and proclaimed his own name: “The LORD, the LORD, a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness” (Exodus 34:6). David quotes it almost exactly. It was first spoken to a people who had just broken the covenant: God revealed his mercy when it was least deserved.

The name with a face. John says that in Jesus the Word became flesh, “full of grace and truth” (John 1:14), the very words of that name. What Moses heard proclaimed, the disciples saw walking among them.

verseByVerse.quote: He will not always chide, nor will he keep his anger forever. He does not deal with us according to our sins, nor repay us according to our iniquities.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s anger at sin is real but not endless, and he does not repay us as our sins deserve.

He will not always chide. God does rebuke and grow angry at sin, but not “always”, nor “forever”. A believer under God’s discipline can know that it has an end.

He does not deal with us according to our sins. The most astonishing sentence in the psalm: if God dealt with us according to our sins, no one would survive.

How can a just God do that? Not by pretending the sins do not matter. The New Testament gives the answer David could only glimpse: “God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us” (Romans 5:8). God does not deal with us according to our sins, because he dealt with his Son according to them. The repayment we deserved was not cancelled; it was paid.

verseByVerse.quote: For as high as the heavens are above the earth, so great is his steadfast love toward those who fear him; as far as the east is from the west, so far does he remove our transgressions from us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s steadfast love is as high as the sky, and he removes the sins of those who fear him further than anyone could travel.

As high as the heavens are above the earth. How big is God’s love? Look up. David had no telescope, but he knew the sky had no measurable top, and that is the point: his steadfast love cannot be measured.

As far as the east is from the west. And how far away are our sins? Walk east, and however far you go, you never arrive at the west. That is the distance God puts between a forgiven person and his sins. He does not put them on a shelf where they can be taken down again.

The same picture in the prophets. The prophets reach for it too: “You will cast all our sins into the depths of the sea” (Micah 7:19); “you have cast all my sins behind your back” (Isaiah 38:17). And the new covenant, sealed in Christ’s blood, promises: “I will remember their sins no more” (Hebrews 8:12). If you are in Christ and your conscience keeps digging up a sin you have confessed, this verse is your answer. God has moved it further away than your memory can travel.

verseByVerse.quote: As a father shows compassion to his children, so the LORD shows compassion to those who fear him. For he knows our frame; he remembers that we are dust.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD pities those who fear him as a father pities his children, because he knows exactly how frail we are.

As a father shows compassion to his children. Now the image becomes a family. A good father’s compassion for his children is not earned by them; it comes from being their father. Jesus told of a son who came home in disgrace, and “while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and felt compassion, and ran and embraced him and kissed him” (Luke 15:20). That is the compassion of this verse.

He knows our frame. The reason for his compassion is that he knows exactly what we are made of. “Our frame” (the ESV notes it can be read “how we are formed”) is dust, as Moses said (Psalm 90:3). God does not expect dust to behave like steel. That is a verse for anyone exhausted by their own weakness, or afraid that God is disappointed in how little they can manage: he made the dust, and “remembers” it with compassion.

Permission to be finite. Our culture tells us from the nursery that we can be anything we want to be. It sounds generous, and it is exhausting. If there are no limits, every limit we meet feels like failure: the body that tires, the career that stalls, the parent who cannot be everywhere. So we are driven, and religion often makes it worse, moving the endless to-do list into the spiritual realm: pray more, serve more, never be tired. The psalm says something more radical. You are dust, and God knows it, and he is not disappointed, because he never expected you to be anything else. Being finite is not a sin; it is the shape of a creature. The first sin was the wish to be like God, without limit (Genesis 3:5). And the Son of God took a frame of dust himself. He grew weary at a well (John 4:6) and fell asleep in a boat. He did not despise our limits; he lived inside them, and died for the sins they never excused. So the gospel gives the exhausted what no self-help can: permission to be a creature, and loved.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–22 — His Kingdom Rules over All
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Our lives are brief as grass, but God’s steadfast love is everlasting, and the whole universe is summoned to bless him. A human life flourishes like a wildflower and is gone when the hot wind passes over it (vv. 15–16). Against that stands a love from everlasting to everlasting, reaching to children’s children among those who keep his covenant (vv. 17–18). Then the psalm widens to the throne: the LORD’s kingdom rules over all (v. 19), so angels, hosts and all his works are called to bless him, and the last voice in the choir is David’s own soul (vv. 20–22).
verseByVerse.theology: Short human lives rest on everlasting love, and the whole universe is summoned into one man's song.

verseByVerse.quote: As for man, his days are like grass; he flourishes like a flower of the field; for the wind passes over it, and it is gone, and its place knows it no more. But the steadfast love of the LORD is from everlasting to everlasting on those who fear him, and his righteousness to children's children, to those who keep his covenant and remember to do his commandments.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A human life is as brief as a wildflower, but the LORD’s love on those who fear him is everlasting and reaches their children’s children.

His days are like grass. From dust to grass. A human life flourishes like a wildflower, bright and brief. A hot wind passes over it and it is gone. “Its place knows it no more”: the patch of ground where it grew does not remember it.

But the steadfast love of the LORD. Against the brevity of grass stands a love that is “from everlasting to everlasting”: it had no beginning and will have no end. The flower fades; the love that rests on it does not, but reaches “children’s children”.

Remember to do his commandments. “Remember” comes again: God remembers that we are dust (v. 14), and his people are to remember him and his commandments, as David began by telling his soul not to forget (v. 2).

The love that came. Mary echoed verse 17 when she was carrying Christ: “his mercy is for those who fear him from generation to generation” (Luke 1:50). The everlasting love had come in person.

Is God’s love conditional? It is everlasting, and it rests on those who fear him and keep his covenant by faith, not by earning it. Children share the covenant blessing as they themselves come to fear him.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD has established his throne in the heavens, and his kingdom rules over all. Bless the LORD, O you his angels, you mighty ones who do his word, obeying the voice of his word! Bless the LORD, all his hosts, his ministers, who do his will! Bless the LORD, all his works, in all places of his dominion. Bless the LORD, O my soul!
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD reigns over everything, so every angel and creature is called to bless him, and David will not be the one voice missing.

His kingdom rules over all. The love that forgives, heals and remembers our frame belongs to the King of everything. There is nothing outside his rule. And the New Testament shows who now sits on that throne: the risen Christ says, “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (Matthew 28:18).

Bless the LORD, all his works. Then the circle widens. The psalm began with one soul; now it summons the angels, then all the hosts of heaven, then “all his works, in all places of his dominion”: every star, sea and creature. The whole universe is called into the song.

You mighty ones who do his word. The angels bless him by doing his word and his will. The highest praise in heaven is not only singing; it is obedience. So Jesus taught us to pray that God’s will be done on earth as it is in heaven, and gives his Spirit to make that obedience ours.

Bless the LORD, O my soul! Having gathered all creation, the psalm comes back to where it began. The last voice in the universal choir is David’s own. The angels are singing, the stars are singing, and he will not be silent. The next psalm opens with the same words (Psalm 104:1) and moves from redemption to creation.

In everyday life. If your soul is silent today, talk to it. Remind it of the list, of a love as high as the heavens, and of a Father who remembers you are dust.

103.title: Forget Not All His Benefits
103.overview:
Where we are. After the lament of Psalm 102 comes one of the Bible’s best-loved songs of praise. Psalms 103 and 104 are twins: both begin and end “Bless the LORD, O my soul”, and where 104 praises God as Creator, 103 praises him as Redeemer. The title gives it to David.

The message. Do not forget what God has done for you. He forgives all your sin; he does not treat you as your sins deserve; he removes them as far as east is from west; and he pities you as a father pities his children, because he knows you are dust. Your life is as brief as grass, but his steadfast love is everlasting, and the King of everything deserves the praise of every creature, beginning with you.

Why it was said. God’s people were always prone to forget his goodness, and Moses had warned them against it (Deuteronomy 8:11–14). The psalm builds on the name God proclaimed to Moses after the golden calf (Exodus 34:6). Placed in Book Four, it answers the frailty Moses lamented in Psalm 90, where man is dust and grass, with a love that outlasts the grass (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. David first commands his own soul to bless the LORD and lists his benefits, beginning with forgiveness (vv. 1–5). He then turns to what God is like: revealed to Moses as merciful and gracious, he does not repay us as our sins deserve, and pities us as a father who knows our frame (vv. 6–14). Our days are grass, but his love is from everlasting to everlasting (vv. 15–18). Finally, the King whose kingdom rules over all is blessed by angels, hosts and all his works, and last of all by David’s own soul (vv. 19–22).

Where it leads. To Christ by the character of God revealed in him, and by the question the psalm raises. How can a just God not deal with us according to our sins? The cross answers: God put forward his Son as a propitiation, “so that he might be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus” (Romans 3:26). The Father who runs to embrace his returning son (Luke 15:20) is the Father of this psalm, and the Son who “became flesh” (John 1:14) took on our frame of dust, knowing our weakness from the inside.

For us. Preach to your own soul, as David did, and give it the list: forgiven, healed, redeemed, crowned, satisfied. When conscience digs up a confessed sin, remember how far east is from west; when you are exhausted by your weakness, remember that your Father knows you are dust.
103.theology: Praise is commanded of one's own soul and hindered chiefly by forgetting (vv. 1-2). God's benefits begin with forgiveness, the root from which final healing grows (vv. 3-5). His character is the name he proclaimed to Moses (v. 8; Exod 34:6): he does not deal with us according to our sins because Christ died for sinners (Rom 5:8), and he pities us as a father who knows we are dust (vv. 13-14). Brief lives rest on everlasting love, and the King of all summons all creation to bless him (vv. 15-22).
103.examples: The psalm teaches a believer to give his own soul orders when it will not sing, because ingratitude is mostly forgetting. The cure is to list his benefits. At the heart of the psalm is a Father who runs down the road to a son still a long way off, and who does not expect dust to behave like steel.

keyVerse.quote: He does not deal with us according to our sins, nor repay us according to our iniquities.
keyVerse.note: This is the heart of the benefits David tells his soul not to forget, and the reason for every other one. It rests on the name God proclaimed to Moses, and it raises a question only the cross answers: God does not deal with us according to our sins because he dealt with his Son according to them.

103.reflection:
David speaks to his own soul: “Bless the LORD, O my soul, … and forget not all his benefits” (vv. 1–2). Why do we forget God’s goodness so easily? What helps you remember it?

Forgiveness comes first in the list of benefits (v. 3). Why does the order matter, and how should we understand the promise that God “heals all your diseases” when believers still get ill?

“As far as the east is from the west, so far does he remove our transgressions from us” (v. 12). Is there a sin you have confessed but keep digging up? How does this verse speak to it?

“He knows our frame; he remembers that we are dust” (v. 14). How does this change the way you treat your own weakness and limits, and the weaknesses of others?

104.text: <sup>1</sup>Bless the LORD, O my soul! O LORD my God, you are very great! You are clothed with splendor and majesty,<sup>2</sup>covering yourself with light as with a garment, stretching out the heavens like a tent.<sup>3</sup>He lays the beams of his chambers on the waters; he makes the clouds his chariot; he rides on the wings of the wind;<sup>4</sup>he makes his messengers winds, his ministers a flaming fire.<sup>5</sup>He set the earth on its foundations, so that it should never be moved.<sup>6</sup>You covered it with the deep as with a garment; the waters stood above the mountains.<sup>7</sup>At your rebuke they fled; at the sound of your thunder they took to flight.<sup>8</sup>The mountains rose, the valleys sank down to the place that you appointed for them.<sup>9</sup>You set a boundary that they may not pass, so that they might not again cover the earth.<sup>10</sup>You make springs gush forth in the valleys; they flow between the hills;<sup>11</sup>they give drink to every beast of the field; the wild donkeys quench their thirst.<sup>12</sup>Beside them the birds of the heavens dwell; they sing among the branches.<sup>13</sup>From your lofty abode you water the mountains; the earth is satisfied with the fruit of your work.<sup>14</sup>You cause the grass to grow for the livestock and plants for man to cultivate, that he may bring forth food from the earth<sup>15</sup>and wine to gladden the heart of man, oil to make his face shine and bread to strengthen man's heart.<sup>16</sup>The trees of the LORD are watered abundantly, the cedars of Lebanon that he planted.<sup>17</sup>In them the birds build their nests; the stork has her home in the fir trees.<sup>18</sup>The high mountains are for the wild goats; the rocks are a refuge for the rock badgers.<sup>19</sup>He made the moon to mark the seasons; the sun knows its time for setting.<sup>20</sup>You make darkness, and it is night, when all the beasts of the forest creep about.<sup>21</sup>The young lions roar for their prey, seeking their food from God.<sup>22</sup>When the sun rises, they steal away and lie down in their dens.<sup>23</sup>Man goes out to his work and to his labor until the evening.<sup>24</sup>O LORD, how manifold are your works! In wisdom have you made them all; the earth is full of your creatures.<sup>25</sup>Here is the sea, great and wide, which teems with creatures innumerable, living things both small and great.<sup>26</sup>There go the ships, and Leviathan, which you formed to play in it.<sup>27</sup>These all look to you, to give them their food in due season.<sup>28</sup>When you give it to them, they gather it up; when you open your hand, they are filled with good things.<sup>29</sup>When you hide your face, they are dismayed; when you take away their breath, they die and return to their dust.<sup>30</sup>When you send forth your Spirit, they are created, and you renew the face of the ground.<sup>31</sup>May the glory of the LORD endure forever; may the LORD rejoice in his works,<sup>32</sup>who looks on the earth and it trembles, who touches the mountains and they smoke!<sup>33</sup>I will sing to the LORD as long as I live; I will sing praise to my God while I have being.<sup>34</sup>May my meditation be pleasing to him, for I rejoice in the LORD.<sup>35</sup>Let sinners be consumed from the earth, and let the wicked be no more! Bless the LORD, O my soul! Praise the LORD!

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — Clothed with Splendor and Majesty
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Creator is greater than everything he made, and every force of nature is his servant. The psalm opens in the heavens: God dresses in light, stretches out the sky like a tent, builds his house above the waters, rides the clouds as his chariot and sends wind and fire as his messengers (vv. 1–4). Then it comes down to earth. He set the earth on its foundations (v. 5); the waters once covered the mountains, but at his rebuke they fled (vv. 6–7); mountains and valleys went to their appointed places (v. 8), and he drew a boundary the sea may not pass (v. 9). What people feared and worshipped, he commands.
verseByVerse.theology: The Creator dresses in light, pitches the sky like a tent, and tells the sea where to stop.

verseByVerse.quote: Bless the LORD, O my soul! O LORD my God, you are very great! You are clothed with splendor and majesty, covering yourself with light as with a garment, stretching out the heavens like a tent. He lays the beams of his chambers on the waters; he makes the clouds his chariot; he rides on the wings of the wind; he makes his messengers winds, his ministers a flaming fire.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD is greater than the world he made: he wears light, pitches the sky like a tent, and rides the storm, with wind and fire as his servants.

Bless the LORD, O my soul! Psalm 103 opened and closed with these words to praise God for redemption; this psalm uses them (vv. 1, 35) to praise him for creation. The God who forgives our sins is the God who made the world.

Covering yourself with light as with a garment. The picture is of God dressing. He puts on light like a coat: the first thing created in Genesis is his clothing. Then he stretches out the sky as easily as a bedouin pitches a tent.

He makes the clouds his chariot. His house is built above the waters of the sky; the clouds are his chariot; the wind carries him. The forces of nature that people have always feared or worshipped are his vehicles and servants. Canaanite poems praised Baal, the storm god, as the rider of the clouds; the psalm gives that picture to the LORD alone.

His ministers a flaming fire. Hebrews applies verse 4 to the angels, “He makes his angels winds, and his ministers a flame of fire” (Hebrews 1:7), and then contrasts them with the Son, who is not a servant of creation but its Lord (Hebrews 1:8–10).

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew of verse 4 can be read either “he makes his messengers winds” or “he makes the winds his messengers”; the Greek translation, which Hebrews quotes, has “angels”. Either way, wind, fire and angels alike are God’s servants.
verseByVerse.note: A creation psalm that broadly follows the order of Genesis 1.

verseByVerse.quote: He set the earth on its foundations, so that it should never be moved. You covered it with the deep as with a garment; the waters stood above the mountains. At your rebuke they fled; at the sound of your thunder they took to flight. The mountains rose, the valleys sank down to the place that you appointed for them. You set a boundary that they may not pass, so that they might not again cover the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God set the earth firm, drove back the waters that once covered it, and drew a line the sea cannot cross.

He set the earth on its foundations. The ground under your feet is stable because God set it. Psalm 93 said the same: “the world is established; it shall never be moved” (Psalm 93:1). Earthquakes are real, and verse 32 will mention the earth trembling, but they happen inside his rule, not outside it.

At your rebuke they fled. In the beginning the earth was wrapped in water (“darkness was over the face of the deep”, Genesis 1:2), the waters higher than the mountains. And God rebuked them, and they ran. The ocean flees like a scolded animal at the sound of God’s voice.

You set a boundary that they may not pass. Mountains rise, valleys sink, and every one goes to “the place that you appointed”. The sea is given a line it cannot cross. Anyone who has stood on a beach and watched the tide stop at its mark has seen this verse. The chaos is on a leash, and the leash is God’s word.

Who then is this? On the Sea of Galilee Jesus “rebuked the wind and said to the sea, ‘Peace! Be still!’” (Mark 4:39), and it obeyed. The disciples asked, “Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?” (Mark 4:41). This psalm gives the answer: only the Creator rebukes the waters.

Creation or the flood? Verses 6–9 most naturally describe the third day of creation (Genesis 1:9–10), when the waters were gathered and the dry land appeared; verse 9 echoes the promise after the flood that the waters will not again cover the earth (compare Genesis 9:11). Every shoreline is a line he drew and a promise he is keeping.

Uncertain wording. Verse 8 can also be read with the waters as the subject, flowing up the mountains and down the valleys to the place God appointed for them. Either way, God sends land and water each to its place.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–23 — Wine to Gladden the Heart of Man
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s world is a household where every creature is housed and fed, and people are given gladness as well as food. The waters he rebuked now run as springs, giving drink to wild donkeys and birds that sing in the branches, and rain from his house satisfies the earth (vv. 10–13). He grows grass for cattle and crops for people to cultivate, with bread to strengthen, wine to gladden and oil to make faces shine (vv. 14–15). The cedars, storks, goats and rock badgers each have their home (vv. 16–18). Even time is ordered: the moon marks the seasons, the night belongs to the hunting lion, and the day to human work (vv. 19–23).
verseByVerse.theology: Every creature has its home and its food, and God gives people not only enough but gladness.

verseByVerse.quote: You make springs gush forth in the valleys; they flow between the hills; they give drink to every beast of the field; the wild donkeys quench their thirst. Beside them the birds of the heavens dwell; they sing among the branches. From your lofty abode you water the mountains; the earth is satisfied with the fruit of your work.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God puts the waters to work, giving drink to every animal and watering the hills until the earth is full.

You make springs gush forth in the valleys. The waters that were rebuked are now put to work. The same water that once covered the mountains runs in springs through the valleys, and every animal drinks, even the wild donkeys, creatures of the desert that no one feeds. God does.

They sing among the branches. Where there is water there are trees; where there are trees there are birds; and the birds sing. God did not only make a world that works. He made one with music in it.

The earth is satisfied. Rain falls from God’s house onto the hills, and the earth is “satisfied”: full and content, like a guest who has eaten well. Jesus said the Father “sends rain on the just and on the unjust” (Matthew 5:45), and calls us to be as generous.

verseByVerse.quote: You cause the grass to grow for the livestock and plants for man to cultivate, that he may bring forth food from the earth and wine to gladden the heart of man, oil to make his face shine and bread to strengthen man's heart. The trees of the LORD are watered abundantly, the cedars of Lebanon that he planted. In them the birds build their nests; the stork has her home in the fir trees. The high mountains are for the wild goats; the rocks are a refuge for the rock badgers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God feeds animals and people, gives man a share in the work, provides gladness as well as bread, and gives every creature a home.

Plants for man to cultivate. Grass for cattle, crops for people, and man is given a part to play: God grows, and man farms. Then the list of what comes out of the earth goes beyond survival. Bread to strengthen is necessity. But there is also wine “to gladden the heart” and oil “to make his face shine”. God did not make a world that merely keeps us alive; he made one that makes us glad.

A witness in every meal. Paul told a pagan crowd in Lystra that God “did not leave himself without witness, for he did good by giving you rains from heaven and fruitful seasons, satisfying your hearts with food and gladness” (Acts 14:17). Every good meal is a sermon from the Creator, and the Christian who receives God’s gifts with thanks is not less spiritual than the one who refuses them.

The trees of the LORD. The great cedars of Lebanon are “the trees of the LORD”: he planted them. And every creature has an address: the stork in the fir, the wild goat on the peaks, the small rock badger hiding in the cliffs. Nothing in God’s world is homeless by design.

Neither a goddess nor a warehouse. Most of the time we treat the natural world as a warehouse: raw material to be extracted, packaged and thrown away. Troubled by the damage, some swing to the other pole and treat it as sacred in itself; the scientist James Lovelock named his picture of the earth as one self-regulating whole after Gaia, the Greek goddess of the earth. The psalm refuses both. The cedars are not gods; they are “the trees of the LORD”, which he planted. Nor are they mere stock, for he waters them, houses the storks in them and rejoices in his works (v. 31). Creation is a gift with the Giver’s name on it, and man is given his place inside it, like a gardener tending someone else’s garden. That frees Christians both from the greed that strips the earth and from the despair that worships it. And it points ahead: the one through whom all things were made came to restore the whole creation, and “the creation waits with eager longing” for that day (Romans 8:19).

May Christians drink wine? It is God’s good gift “to gladden the heart of man”, and Jesus made it (John 2:1–11). Drunkenness is forbidden (Ephesians 5:18), and abstaining for the sake of conscience or a weaker brother is right (Romans 14:21).

verseByVerse.quote: He made the moon to mark the seasons; the sun knows its time for setting. You make darkness, and it is night, when all the beasts of the forest creep about. The young lions roar for their prey, seeking their food from God. When the sun rises, they steal away and lie down in their dens. Man goes out to his work and to his labor until the evening.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God made moon and sun to keep time, giving the night to the hunting beasts and the day to human work, and feeding even the lion.

He made the moon to mark the seasons. The moon marks “the seasons”; the ESV notes it may mean “the appointed times”, the calendar of Israel’s feasts, as in Genesis 1:14. And the sun “knows” when to set, like an obedient servant. The bodies the nations worshipped are God’s timekeepers.

Seeking their food from God. Even the night is God’s making, and the predators that hunt in it are, the psalm says, “seeking their food from God”. The lion’s roar is, in its way, a prayer. The whole food chain, fierceness and all, is under his provision.

Man goes out to his work. Then a beautifully ordinary verse: the lions go to bed; people go to work. The night belongs to the beasts, the day to human labour, and both are part of God’s order. Your commute, your shift, your ordinary day’s work “until the evening” is in this psalm, among the wonders of creation.

Where Christians differ. Was predation part of the original creation? Christians who hold that the earth is very old often read this psalm as showing that God made and fed predators from the start. Others note that it describes the world as it is now, after the fall, and does not say it was made so; Genesis gives every creature plants for food (Genesis 1:30), and the prophets look for a day when “the lion shall eat straw like the ox” (Isaiah 11:7). They are brothers, and the psalm’s praise is true on either reading.

This commentary’s view. Holding to six ordinary days and a young creation (see on Genesis 1:5), this commentary reads the hunt as part of the world after the fall. Either way, the God who feeds the lion now has promised a world where nothing will hurt or destroy (Isaiah 11:9).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 24–35 — When You Send Forth Your Spirit
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Every living thing depends on God’s open hand and his Spirit, so the only fitting response is lifelong praise. The singer breaks into wonder at the variety and wisdom of God’s works, and at the teeming sea where ships pass and Leviathan plays (vv. 24–26). All creatures look to God for food; when he opens his hand they are filled, when he takes away their breath they die, and when he sends his Spirit, life is renewed (vv. 27–30). So the psalm ends in prayer that God may rejoice in his works, a vow to sing all life long, and a longing that sin be removed from his world (vv. 31–35).
verseByVerse.theology: Every living thing depends moment by moment on God's open hand and his breath, and the singer resolves to praise him for life.

verseByVerse.quote: O LORD, how manifold are your works! In wisdom have you made them all; the earth is full of your creatures. Here is the sea, great and wide, which teems with creatures innumerable, living things both small and great. There go the ships, and Leviathan, which you formed to play in it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everything God made displays his wisdom, and even the vast sea, with Leviathan in it, is his playground.

O LORD, how manifold are your works! The singer stops listing and simply exclaims. “Manifold” means countless, varied, overflowing, and all of it was made “in wisdom”. That wisdom has a name: all things were created “through him and for him”, the Son, and “in him all things hold together” (Colossians 1:16–17).

Leviathan, which you formed to play in it. Now the sea, no longer a threat but a teeming aquarium of “creatures innumerable”, from plankton to whales. Ships go by. And Leviathan, a symbol of terror elsewhere in the Bible, is here God’s creature, formed “to play in it”. What terrifies sailors is, to God, something that frolics in a bath he made: a creature, not a rival.

Uncertain wording. What Leviathan is cannot be settled. Some think of a whale or a crocodile; Job describes a fearsome beast (Job 41); other texts use the name for the sea-dragon of ancient myth, crushed by God (Psalm 74:14; Isaiah 27:1); some young-earth readers see a sea reptile now extinct. The ESV also notes that “to play in it” may mean “to play with”, as though the monster were God’s pet.

verseByVerse.quote: These all look to you, to give them their food in due season. When you give it to them, they gather it up; when you open your hand, they are filled with good things. When you hide your face, they are dismayed; when you take away their breath, they die and return to their dust. When you send forth your Spirit, they are created, and you renew the face of the ground.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every creature lives from God’s open hand: when he takes their breath they die, and when he sends his Spirit, life is renewed.

These all look to you. Every creature in the psalm “looks to” God, waiting at his hand without knowing it. Jesus pointed at the same birds: “they neither sow nor reap nor gather into barns, and yet your heavenly Father feeds them. Are you not of more value than they?” (Matthew 6:26).

When you open your hand. When he opens his hand, they are filled; if he turns his face away, they panic. Their life depends on him moment by moment, and no creature, including the strongest human being, is self-sustaining. The Son “upholds the universe by the word of his power” (Hebrews 1:3), and if he stopped, everything would fall back into dust.

They die and return to their dust. This is the sentence from Eden: “to dust you shall return” (Genesis 3:19). Death is not merely a biological event in this psalm. It is God withdrawing the breath he lent.

When you send forth your Spirit. But he does not stop giving life. He sends out his Spirit (the ESV notes the word can mean “breath”; in Hebrew it is the same word), and new life appears. Every spring is a small new creation. The same Spirit who “was hovering over the face of the waters” at the beginning (Genesis 1:2) is still breathing life into the world. He raised Jesus from the dead (Romans 8:11), and he will one day renew creation entirely.

verseByVerse.quote: May the glory of the LORD endure forever; may the LORD rejoice in his works, who looks on the earth and it trembles, who touches the mountains and they smoke! I will sing to the LORD as long as I live; I will sing praise to my God while I have being. May my meditation be pleasing to him, for I rejoice in the LORD. Let sinners be consumed from the earth, and let the wicked be no more! Bless the LORD, O my soul! Praise the LORD!
verseByVerse.commentary:
The singer prays that God may delight in his works, vows lifelong praise, and longs for sin to be gone from the world.

May the LORD rejoice in his works. The psalm wishes God joy in what he has made, as at the beginning, when “God saw everything that he had made, and behold, it was very good” (Genesis 1:31). And yet this gentle Creator has only to glance at the earth to make it shake, and touch a mountain to make it smoke. That is Sinai again, “wrapped in smoke” while “the whole mountain trembled greatly” (Exodus 19:18). The God who waters the wild donkeys is the God who shook the mountain. His gentleness is never weakness.

I will sing to the LORD as long as I live. After surveying the whole creation, the singer makes a lifelong vow. The breath God gives (v. 29) will be spent praising him. And he hopes his “meditation”, this long, careful look at the world, will please God, echoing the end of Psalm 19, which also moved from the heavens to the heart: “Let the words of my mouth and the meditation of my heart be acceptable in your sight” (Psalm 19:14). Looking thoughtfully at creation, and seeing God in it, is itself worship.

Let sinners be consumed from the earth. The prayer can seem jarring at the end of such a gentle psalm. But it is right: in all this beauty there is one thing that does not belong, sin and those who persist in it. It is the one blot on the good world, and “the whole creation has been groaning together” under it (Romans 8:22). A person who loves the world God made will long for the day when nothing spoils it.

Praise the LORD! The psalm ends where it began, with one more line added: “Praise the LORD!” In Hebrew it is Hallelujah, the first time the Psalter says it. The soul that has looked carefully at springs, storks, lions and workmen has one thing left to say: “Worthy are you, our Lord and God, to receive glory and honor and power, for you created all things” (Revelation 4:11).

What it does not mean. Not a wish to see our neighbours destroyed. The Christian prays first that sinners be forgiven, as Christ prayed for those who crucified him (Luke 23:34), and longs for sin itself to be gone (see the introduction on the psalms that curse).

104.title: How Manifold Are Your Works
104.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 104 is the twin of Psalm 103. Both begin and end “Bless the LORD, O my soul”, but where 103 praised God for redemption, 104 praises him for creation. It walks broadly through the order of Genesis 1.

The message. The world is God’s workmanship and his household. He made it in wisdom, keeps it in being moment by moment, feeds every creature from his open hand, and gives people not only bread to live but wine and oil for gladness. Everything that lives depends on his breath, so the right response is lifelong, joyful praise, and longing for the day when sin no longer spoils his world.

Why it was said. Israel’s neighbours worshipped sun and moon, feared the sea as chaos, and praised the storm god Baal as rider of the clouds. The psalm puts each in its place: light is God’s garment, the clouds his chariot, the sea his creature, the sun his servant (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. The psalm begins in the heavens, where the LORD wears light and rides the storm (vv. 1–4), and comes down to the earth, set firm, with the waters driven back behind a boundary (vv. 5–9). It then tours God’s household: springs for the animals, food and gladness for man, a home for every creature (vv. 10–18), and time itself, night for the lion and day for human work (vv. 19–23). Wonder breaks out at its wisdom and the teeming sea (vv. 24–26), and at every creature’s dependence on God’s hand and Spirit (vv. 27–30). It ends in a vow of lifelong praise and a prayer that sinners be no more (vv. 31–35).

Where it leads. To Christ through the New Testament’s revelation of the Creator. Hebrews quotes verse 4 to show that angels are servants while the Son is Lord (Hebrews 1:7–8). The New Testament reveals that all things were made through the Son and that “in him all things hold together” (Colossians 1:17). When Jesus rebuked the wind and sea and they obeyed him (Mark 4:39–41), the disciples saw the God of verse 7 in a boat with them. And the Spirit by whom God renews “the face of the ground” (v. 30) raised Jesus from the dead and will one day set the whole groaning creation free (Romans 8:11, 19–21).

For us. Every meal, every spring and every ordinary working day is a gift from the Creator’s hand, and receiving them with thanks is worship. Depend on him for each breath, tend his world as a gardener tends someone else’s garden, and let your looking at creation become praise of the Son through whom it was made.
104.theology: This psalm praises God for creation with the same opening call that Psalm 103 used for redemption. God is utterly above nature, whose forces are his clothing and servants (vv. 1-4); he restrains chaos (vv. 5-9) and gives his creatures not only food but gladness (vv. 14-15). All things were made in wisdom through the Son (Col 1:16-17) and live moment by moment by God's open hand and Spirit (vv. 27-30). He delights in his works, and sin is the one thing that does not belong in them (vv. 31-35).
104.examples: Wild donkeys that no one feeds are fed by God; the ocean that drowned the mountains runs from his voice like a scolded animal. A walk on a spring morning, a good meal, the walk to work, all are in this psalm, and the believer who notices them is learning to worship.

keyVerse.quote: O LORD, how manifold are your works! In wisdom have you made them all; the earth is full of your creatures.
keyVerse.note: Here the long tour of creation breaks into wonder, and the whole psalm is summed up: variety, wisdom and fullness, all from one Maker. The New Testament gives that wisdom a name: all things were made through the Son, and in him they hold together.

104.reflection:
The psalm sees God at work in springs, birds, crops and sunsets. What in the natural world most moves you to praise, and how can we train ourselves to see the Creator in ordinary things?

Verse 15 says God gives “wine to gladden the heart of man, oil to make his face shine and bread to strengthen man’s heart”. Why do you think God gives gladness and not only what we need? How should this shape the way we eat, drink and celebrate?

Verses 27–30 say every creature depends on God moment by moment for food and breath. Where do you live as if you were self-sufficient, and what would daily dependence on God look like for you?

The psalm ends with a prayer that sinners be “consumed” and the wicked “be no more” (v. 35). How can a Christian pray this rightly, alongside Christ’s prayer for his enemies?

they did not rebel against his words.<sup>29</sup>He turned their waters into blood and caused their fish to die.<sup>30</sup>Their land swarmed with frogs, even in the chambers of their kings.<sup>31</sup>He spoke, and there came swarms of flies, and gnats throughout their country.<sup>32</sup>He gave them hail for rain, and fiery lightning bolts through their land.<sup>33</sup>He struck down their vines and fig trees, and shattered the trees of their country.<sup>34</sup>He spoke, and the locusts came, young locusts without number,<sup>35</sup>which devoured all the vegetation in their land and ate up the fruit of their ground.<sup>36</sup>He struck down all the firstborn in their land, the firstfruits of all their strength.<sup>37</sup>Then he brought out Israel with silver and gold, and there was none among his tribes who stumbled.<sup>38</sup>Egypt was glad when they departed, for dread of them had fallen upon it.<sup>39</sup>He spread a cloud for a covering, and fire to give light by night.<sup>40</sup>They asked, and he brought quail, and gave them bread from heaven in abundance.<sup>41</sup>He opened the rock, and water gushed out; it flowed through the desert like a river.<sup>42</sup>For he remembered his holy promise, and Abraham, his servant.<sup>43</sup>So he brought his people out with joy, his chosen ones with singing.<sup>44</sup>And he gave them the lands of the nations, and they took possession of the fruit of the peoples' toil,<sup>45</sup>that they might keep his statutes and observe his laws. Praise the LORD!

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Praise begins in remembering, and remembering rests on a God who remembers. The psalm piles up commands to Abraham’s offspring: give thanks, call on his name, make his deeds known among the peoples, sing, glory in his name, seek him and his presence continually, and above all remember his wondrous works (vv. 1–6). Then comes the ground of it all. The LORD is our God and the judge of all the earth, and he remembers his covenant forever, the sworn promise made to Abraham and confirmed to Isaac and Jacob, to give them the land of Canaan (vv. 7–11). Israel is told to remember because God never forgets.
verseByVerse.theology: Israel is told to remember, because God remembers, and the history that follows is all his doing.

verseByVerse.quote: Oh give thanks to the LORD; call upon his name; make known his deeds among the peoples! Sing to him, sing praises to him; tell of all his wondrous works! Glory in his holy name; let the hearts of those who seek the LORD rejoice! Seek the LORD and his strength; seek his presence continually! Remember the wondrous works that he has done, his miracles, and the judgments he uttered, O offspring of Abraham, his servant, children of Jacob, his chosen ones!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Abraham’s children are called to give thanks, sing, seek the LORD continually and, above all, remember what he has done, and to make it known to the nations.

Three histories. Three psalms tell Israel’s history at length. Psalm 78 tells it as a warning, Psalm 106 as a confession of sin, Psalm 105 as praise. Here every event is a reason to give thanks.

Make known his deeds among the peoples! The psalm opens with a pile of commands: give thanks, call, make known, sing, tell. The audience is wider than Israel: “among the peoples”. God’s history with his people is news for the nations.

Seek his presence continually! “Seek”, three times in two verses (vv. 3–4). God seeks and keeps his people; they answer by seeking him “continually”, not in emergencies only.

Remember the wondrous works. The psalm’s key verb. Faith that forgets what God has done withers, and the whole psalm is an exercise in remembering on purpose.

How do I seek his presence continually? Christ has opened “the new and living way” into God’s presence (Hebrews 10:20), so you come as a welcome child, not a stranger at the door. Begin the day with him. Before the phone, a few minutes in his word and a short prayer for what is already in the diary. Turn to him in the middle of things. In the queue, before the hard conversation: one sentence of prayer is seeking his face. Remember on purpose. Keep a list of prayers answered and narrow escapes, and read it when he seems far away. Seek him with his people. He has promised, “where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I among them” (Matthew 18:20). Start again when you drift. You will forget him by lunchtime. He does not forget you: Christ “always lives to make intercession” for his people (Hebrews 7:25), so turn back without despair.
verseByVerse.note: Isaiah 12:4 echoes the opening call: Give thanks to the LORD, call upon his name, make known his deeds among the peoples.

verseByVerse.quote: He is the LORD our God; his judgments are in all the earth. He remembers his covenant forever, the word that he commanded, for a thousand generations, the covenant that he made with Abraham, his sworn promise to Isaac, which he confirmed to Jacob as a statute, to Israel as an everlasting covenant, saying, "To you I will give the land of Canaan as your portion for an inheritance."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel is to remember because God remembers: he keeps for ever the sworn covenant he made with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, to give their children the land.

He remembers his covenant forever. Israel is told to remember (v. 5) because God remembers (v. 8). His memory is not a vague recollection but faithfulness to his sworn promise, and it runs “for a thousand generations”, a way of saying for ever.

The covenant that he made with Abraham. One promise, made to three generations in turn, Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and never withdrawn. Everything that follows is God keeping that one word. A believer’s life is the same: not a string of random events, but one promise being kept through many chapters.

The oath kept in Christ. At the birth of John the Baptist, Zechariah used this psalm’s words: God had come “to remember his holy covenant, the oath that he swore to our father Abraham” (Luke 1:72–73). The promise was heading for one offspring, Christ (Galatians 3:16), and “all the promises of God find their Yes in him” (2 Corinthians 1:20).

Where Christians differ. Does the land still belong to ethnic Israel? Dispensationalists hold that the land promise remains literal and future for the Jewish people. Many faithful Christians who are not dispensationalists also expect a future turning of Jewish people to Christ (Romans 11:25–26), and believers differ in good faith on what, if anything, that means for the land.

This commentary’s view. The land promise was fulfilled in Joshua’s day: “Not one word of all the good promises that the LORD had made to the house of Israel had failed” (Joshua 21:45). The New Testament widens it to the whole new earth: Abraham was to be “heir of the world” (Romans 4:13). The everlasting covenant is fulfilled in Christ and his people.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–25 — He Had Sent a Man Ahead of Them
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In the years when the promise looked weakest, God was quietly keeping it. The patriarchs were a handful of homeless wanderers, yet God let no king harm them, calling them his anointed ones and his prophets (vv. 12–15). When he summoned a famine, he had already sent Joseph ahead: sold as a slave, tested in fetters by a word that seemed false, then raised to rule Egypt (vv. 16–22). In Egypt God made Israel fruitful, and even turned Egypt’s hatred to serve his plan (vv. 23–25). Weakness, betrayal and hostility all lay inside his hand.
verseByVerse.theology: Behind famine, slavery and a prison cell, God had already placed the man who would save his people.

verseByVerse.quote: When they were few in number, of little account, and sojourners in it, wandering from nation to nation, from one kingdom to another people, he allowed no one to oppress them; he rebuked kings on their account, saying, "Touch not my anointed ones, do my prophets no harm!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the family of promise was tiny and homeless, God guarded it, rebuking kings for their sake.

When they were few in number. A handful of homeless tent-dwellers moving between kingdoms: nothing about them looked like the founders of a nation.

Touch not my anointed ones. Yet God rebuked Pharaoh and Abimelech when they took the patriarchs’ wives (Genesis 12:17; 20:3), and he calls these vulnerable wanderers “my anointed ones” and “my prophets”. The weakness of God’s people is never the measure of their safety. Kings who touch them answer to God.

Safe in the Anointed One. “Anointed” is the word behind “Messiah”. Those joined to the Anointed One share his anointing (1 John 2:20), and he counts a blow against them as a blow against himself: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (Acts 9:4).

Does “touch not my anointed” forbid criticising pastors? No. The anointed here are the patriarchs, protected from kings (Genesis 12; 20; 26). The verse forbids persecuting God’s people. It does not exempt any teacher from being tested by Scripture (Acts 17:11; 1 John 4:1).

verseByVerse.quote: When he summoned a famine on the land and broke all supply of bread, he had sent a man ahead of them, Joseph, who was sold as a slave. His feet were hurt with fetters; his neck was put in a collar of iron; until what he had said came to pass, the word of the LORD tested him. The king sent and released him; the ruler of the peoples set him free; he made him lord of his house and ruler of all his possessions, to bind his princes at his pleasure and to teach his elders wisdom.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before the famine struck, God had already sent Joseph ahead; through slavery, iron and a long-delayed promise, he raised him to rule and to save his family.

When he summoned a famine on the land. The famine did not simply happen. God “summoned” it, like a servant, and “broke all supply of bread” (the ESV notes the Hebrew is “staff”, the staff of bread that people lean on).

He had sent a man ahead of them. Before the famine came, God had sent a man ahead. From Joseph’s side it looked like betrayal: his brothers sold him. Stephen told it the same way: “the patriarchs, jealous of Joseph, sold him into Egypt; but God was with him” (Acts 7:9). The worst thing that ever happened to Joseph was God sending him ahead to save his family.

The word of the LORD tested him. Genesis does not mention the fetters; the psalm fills in how prison felt (Genesis 39:20). The real test was not the iron but “the word of the LORD”: the dreams God had given him that his family would bow to him, which seemed ridiculous from a cell. Many believers are in that cell now, holding a promise that looks false, and the God who sent Joseph ahead has not forgotten his word to them.

The king sent and released him. From the collar to the palace: Pharaoh said, “You shall be over my house” (Genesis 41:40). The slave became the teacher of Egypt’s rulers.

Sold, bound and raised to save. Stephen told Joseph’s story, then Moses’, as the story of deliverers their own brothers rejected, and ended with the Righteous One his hearers had betrayed (Acts 7:9–14, 35, 52). Christians have gladly seen in Joseph an advance picture of Christ: sold for silver, bound, and raised to rule in order to save the people who had rejected him.

Is my life a story, or just one thing after another? We are told the universe has no plot, so each of us must write our own. Then something will not fit, a betrayal, a diagnosis, years in a kind of cell, and the self-authored life has no chapter for it. Joseph’s brothers were writing their own story, and so was Potiphar’s wife; none of them was writing the real one. The psalm reads Joseph’s worst years as part of a plot whose Author had sent him ahead. J. R. R. Tolkien coined a word for the sudden joyful turn in a good fairy story, when ruin is reversed beyond hope: eucatastrophe. And he wrote that the resurrection is the eucatastrophe of the story of the Incarnation. So Christians can live through chapters they do not understand. We are not the authors. But the Author has written himself into the story, sold for silver like Joseph, and his last chapter ends on a throne, not in a pit.

Uncertain wording. In verse 18, “his neck was put in a collar of iron” is literally “his soul came into iron”. The word can mean throat or neck, as the ESV takes it, or the self, as older versions did, hence the old Prayer Book line “the iron entered into his soul”. Either way, real iron, felt to the core.

Textual note. In verse 22 the ESV notes that ancient translations read “instruct” his princes rather than “bind” them.
verseByVerse.note: Joseph himself put it this way to his brothers: As for you, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good (Gen 50:20).

verseByVerse.quote: Then Israel came to Egypt; Jacob sojourned in the land of Ham. And the LORD made his people very fruitful and made them stronger than their foes. He turned their hearts to hate his people, to deal craftily with his servants.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God made Israel fruitful in Egypt, and even Egypt’s hatred of his people lay within his control and served his purpose.

Jacob sojourned in the land of Ham. “The land of Ham” is Egypt; Ham was the Egyptians’ ancestor (Genesis 10:6; see Shem, Ham and Japheth).

He turned their hearts to hate his people. The psalm does not flinch: even Egypt’s hostility lay within God’s control. It drove Israel to cry out and set the stage for the exodus.

The same hand at the cross. At the cross, those who gathered against Jesus did only “whatever your hand and your plan had predestined to take place” (Acts 4:28): human hatred never more guilty, God’s purpose of rescue never more sure.

What it does not mean. Not that God forced the Egyptians to sin or is the author of evil. Their hatred was their own, but it served his purpose.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 26–45 — He Brought His People Out with Joy
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The exodus is told as one long act of God keeping his word. He sent Moses and Aaron, and at his word darkness, blood, frogs, flies, gnats, hail, locusts and the death of the firstborn fell on Egypt (vv. 26–36). He brought Israel out with silver and gold, sheltered them with cloud and fire, and fed them with quail, bread from heaven and water from the rock, without a word about their grumbling (vv. 37–41). The reason is given plainly: “he remembered his holy promise” (v. 42). So he brought them out with joy, gave them the land, and named the goal of it all: that they might keep his laws (vv. 43–45).
verseByVerse.theology: The exodus told without a single failure of Israel's — because this telling is about God's faithfulness.

verseByVerse.quote: He sent Moses, his servant, and Aaron, whom he had chosen. They performed his signs among them and miracles in the land of Ham. He sent darkness, and made the land dark; they did not rebel against his words. He turned their waters into blood and caused their fish to die. Their land swarmed with frogs, even in the chambers of their kings. He spoke, and there came swarms of flies, and gnats throughout their country. He gave them hail for rain, and fiery lightning bolts through their land. He struck down their vines and fig trees, and shattered the trees of their country. He spoke, and the locusts came, young locusts without number, which devoured all the vegetation in their land and ate up the fruit of their ground. He struck down all the firstborn in their land, the firstfruits of all their strength.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God sent Moses and Aaron, and at his word plague after plague fell on Egypt, ending with the death of the firstborn.

He sent Moses, his servant. As he sent Joseph ahead, he sent Moses and Aaron. The history is a history of God sending the right servant at the right time.

He sent darkness. Exodus lists ten plagues; the psalm names eight, leaving out the disease on the livestock and the boils. And it begins with darkness, which in Exodus came ninth, perhaps because darkness was a direct strike at Egypt’s sun-god, and so sums up what all the plagues were: “on all the gods of Egypt I will execute judgments” (Exodus 12:12).

Even in the chambers of their kings. Frogs even in the palace bedrooms: no wall kept God out. (Exodus has the gnats before the flies.)

He spoke. Twice (vv. 31, 34). The plagues were not natural disasters God happened to use; they came at his word.

He struck down all the firstborn. The last plague broke Pharaoh. Israel’s firstborn were spared that night only under the blood of the Passover lamb, and “Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed” (1 Corinthians 5:7): judgment passes over all who shelter under his death.

Uncertain wording. “They did not rebel against his words” (v. 28) is hard to place. It probably means that Moses and Aaron obeyed God’s word; some take “they” as the Egyptians, cowed by the darkness. The ESV notes that some ancient translations omit the “not”, making it Egypt’s rebellion. The likeliest sense: God’s servants carried out every word he gave.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he brought out Israel with silver and gold, and there was none among his tribes who stumbled. Egypt was glad when they departed, for dread of them had fallen upon it. He spread a cloud for a covering, and fire to give light by night. They asked, and he brought quail, and gave them bread from heaven in abundance. He opened the rock, and water gushed out; it flowed through the desert like a river.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God brought Israel out enriched and unharmed, then sheltered and fed them in the desert, and the psalm tells it all without a word about their grumbling.

He brought out Israel with silver and gold. God had told Abraham centuries before that his descendants would “come out with great possessions” (Genesis 15:14), and they did: “Thus they plundered the Egyptians” (Exodus 12:36). Slaves walked out with their masters’ gold.

Egypt was glad when they departed. The empire that would not let them go was relieved to see the back of them. When God is finished with a people’s oppressors, the oppressors are glad to be rid of the oppressed.

They asked, and he brought quail. Notice what is missing. Psalm 78 told these events as stories of rebellion, and Psalm 106 will do the same. Here there is not a word about grumbling. “They asked”, and God gave. Even the cloud, which in Exodus led the way, is here “a covering”, a canopy against the desert sun. The psalmist has not forgotten the sins; he is letting one strand, what God did, shine on its own. There is a time to confess our failures, and a time to look only at God’s faithfulness.

Bread from heaven, water from the rock. Jesus said the manna pointed to him: “my Father gives you the true bread from heaven” (John 6:32). And Paul says of the rock that gushed in the desert, “the Rock was Christ” (1 Corinthians 10:4).

verseByVerse.quote: For he remembered his holy promise, and Abraham, his servant. So he brought his people out with joy, his chosen ones with singing. And he gave them the lands of the nations, and they took possession of the fruit of the peoples' toil, that they might keep his statutes and observe his laws. Praise the LORD!
verseByVerse.commentary:
The whole history happened because God remembered his promise to Abraham: he brought his people out with joy and gave them the land, so that they might live as his obedient people.

He remembered his holy promise. The psalm opened with God remembering his covenant (v. 8) and closes the same way. Everything between was God keeping one promise to one man. The result was not grim survival but “joy” and “singing”.

That they might keep his statutes. God did not save Israel because they kept his law; he saved them so that they would. Grace comes first, and obedience is its goal. The Christian life has the same order: rescued in order to obey, as free people in a land we did not earn, and the Spirit he gives is the power for it (Ezekiel 36:27).

Praise the LORD! The history ends not with a moral but with a shout. When you can trace through your own life the one strand of God remembering his promise, that is the right thing to say.

Was it just to give Israel the lands of the nations? This was God’s judgment on peoples whose sin had long ripened (Genesis 15:16; Deuteronomy 9:4–5), delayed for centuries and carried out once through Israel. It is no pattern for any later war, nation or church.

105.title: He Remembers His Covenant Forever
105.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 105 stands near the close of Book Four (90–106; see the introduction), the first of a pair of history psalms. Its opening fifteen verses were sung when David brought the ark up to Jerusalem (1 Chronicles 16:8–22), and Psalm 106, which follows, tells the same story again as a confession of sin.

The message. God never forgets his promise. The wandering, the famine, Joseph’s prison, the slavery in Egypt, the plagues and the desert were all God keeping one sworn word: “He remembers his covenant forever” (v. 8). So his people are to remember what he has done, give thanks, seek him continually, and live as the free people his faithfulness has made them.

Why it was said. Israel was always in danger of forgetting (see the introduction). To a people who felt small, landless or ruled by others, as Israel often did and above all after the exile, the psalm says: you were small before, “few in number, of little account” (v. 12), and the promise carried you then.

How the chapter makes its case. A call to thank, sing, seek and remember (vv. 1–6) rests on the covenant God remembers (vv. 7–11). Then the history: God guards the wandering patriarchs (vv. 12–15), sends Joseph ahead through slavery and prison to rule (vv. 16–22), and multiplies Israel in Egypt (vv. 23–25). He sends Moses and Aaron and strikes Egypt with plagues (vv. 26–36), then brings his people out laden, sheltered and fed (vv. 37–41), all because “he remembered his holy promise” (vv. 42–45). Not one of Israel’s sins is mentioned: this telling lets God’s faithfulness shine alone. The goal comes last: “that they might keep his statutes” (v. 45).

Where it leads. By promise and by pattern. The promise to Abraham was heading for one offspring, Christ (Galatians 3:16), and when Zechariah sang at the birth of the forerunner he borrowed this psalm’s words: God had come “to remember his holy covenant, the oath that he swore to our father Abraham” (Luke 1:72–73). And the pattern of God sending a deliverer, Joseph sold and raised to save his brothers, Moses sent to bring his people out, reaches its height when “God sent forth his Son” (Galatians 4:4), the true bread from heaven (John 6:32).

For us. Your life is not a string of accidents but one promise being kept through many chapters, some of them in a cell. Remember on purpose what God has done; when his word seems slow, remember Joseph; and live the obedience that grace makes possible, not the obedience that tries to earn it.
105.theology: God remembers his covenant (vv. 8, 42), so his people must remember his works (v. 5). He protects the weak people who carried his promise (vv. 12-15), rules famine and even the hatred of enemies (vv. 16, 25), and sends deliverers ahead of the need (vv. 17, 26). Grace comes first, and obedience is its goal (v. 45).
105.examples: Joseph was sold by his brothers and sent by God, and from a prison cell the promise looked false for years. Slaves walked out of Egypt with their masters' gold, singing. Looking back over a life with this psalm in hand means learning to trace the one strand that runs through it: God keeping his word.

keyVerse.quote: He remembers his covenant forever, the word that he commanded, for a thousand generations,
keyVerse.note: Every event in the psalm, from the patriarchs’ wanderings to Joseph’s prison and the exodus, is God keeping this one sworn word, and the psalm ends where it began, with God remembering (v. 42). Israel is told to remember because God never forgets. In Christ, the offspring of Abraham, that promise has found its Yes.

105.reflection:
The psalm tells Israel’s history only as praise, without mentioning their sins (compare Psalm 106). Why is it good sometimes to look only at God’s faithfulness? What would you put in your own “remember” list (v. 5)?

“He had sent a man ahead of them” (v. 17). Joseph’s worst years turned out to be God sending him ahead. How does this help you live through chapters of your life you do not understand?

“The word of the LORD tested him” (v. 19). What promise of God have you had to hold on to while circumstances seemed to contradict it?

God saved Israel “that they might keep his statutes” (v. 45). How does knowing that grace comes before obedience change the way you think about obeying God?
