verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The confession that follows begins in praise. God is good, his steadfast love endures forever, and no one can tell all his mighty deeds (vv. 1–2). The blessing on those who do righteousness “at all times” (v. 3) sets the standard against which the coming history will be measured, and Israel will fall far short of it. Then the singer prays for himself: remember me, help me when you save your people, let me share their gladness (vv. 4–5). He wants no private blessing apart from God’s people, and he asks it as one about to confess that he deserves nothing.
verseByVerse.theology: Before confessing the nation's sins, the psalmist asks to be included in God's mercy to his people.

verseByVerse.quote: Praise the LORD! Oh give thanks to the LORD, for he is good, for his steadfast love endures forever! Who can utter the mighty deeds of the LORD, or declare all his praise? Blessed are they who observe justice, who do righteousness at all times! Remember me, O LORD, when you show favor to your people; help me when you save them, that I may look upon the prosperity of your chosen ones, that I may rejoice in the gladness of your nation, that I may glory with your inheritance.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The long confession opens in praise for God’s endless love, and a plea to share in his goodness to his people.

Praise the LORD! Psalm 105 told only what God did; Psalm 106 tells what Israel did, a long record of sin. Yet it opens, like 105, with praise, and that is the key to reading it. Confession is not the opposite of praise. A people who can tell the whole truth about their failures and still say “his steadfast love endures forever” have understood grace.

Blessed are they who observe justice. Verse 3 blesses those who do righteousness “at all times”. The blessing is stated first so that Israel’s failure can be measured against it.

Remember me, O LORD. Before the confession, a personal plea: when you bless your people, do not leave me out. He wants no private blessing; he wants to rejoice with God’s people.

The thief’s prayer. It is the prayer of the thief on the cross, a man who deserved nothing: “Jesus, remember me when you come into your kingdom” (Luke 23:42). Jesus answered at once: “today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43).

Uncertain wording. The ESV notes that verse 4 may read “with the favor you show to your people”. Either way the plea is: count me in.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–33 — They Forgot God, Their Savior
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel’s sin was not one lapse but a pattern, and it is ours too. “Both we and our fathers have sinned” (v. 6) heads six scenes. At the Red Sea they rebelled, yet God saved them for his name’s sake, and for a moment they believed and sang (vv. 7–12). Then they soon forgot: craving in the desert, they got what they asked and wasted away; envying Moses, they were swallowed by the earth (vv. 13–18). They exchanged God’s glory for a calf, and only Moses standing in the breach saved them (vv. 19–23). They despised the land (vv. 24–27), joined the Baal of Peor until Phinehas intervened (vv. 28–31), and at Meribah even Moses fell (vv. 32–33).
verseByVerse.theology: Israel's wilderness history, told as a list of sins and a list of rescues God kept making anyway.

verseByVerse.quote: Both we and our fathers have sinned; we have committed iniquity; we have done wickedness. Our fathers, when they were in Egypt, did not consider your wondrous works; they did not remember the abundance of your steadfast love, but rebelled by the sea, at the Red Sea. Yet he saved them for his name's sake, that he might make known his mighty power. He rebuked the Red Sea, and it became dry, and he led them through the deep as through a desert. So he saved them from the hand of the foe and redeemed them from the power of the enemy. And the waters covered their adversaries; not one of them was left. Then they believed his words; they sang his praise.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel rebelled at the very edge of the Red Sea, yet God saved them for his name’s sake, and the singer confesses that his generation is no better.

Both we and our fathers have sinned. The heading of the whole history: three words for sin, and the crucial word “we”. The singer does not stand outside Israel’s past and judge it. The sins of the wilderness generation are the sins his own generation commits. Honest confession never says “they” when it means “we”.

Rebelled by the sea. The rebellion started at once. They had just watched the plagues, and at the edge of the sea they panicked and complained (Exodus 14:11–12). The root is named: they “did not consider” and “did not remember”. Sin in this psalm begins as forgetting.

Yet he saved them for his name’s sake. Rebellion, and yet rescue. The reason is not their repentance but God’s own name, “that he might make known his mighty power”. He saved people who were complaining at him while he saved them.

Then they believed his words. After the rescue came faith and song, the song of Moses on the far shore (Exodus 15). For a moment, everything was right.

We would not have done that. Every generation assumes it would have behaved better than the slave trader, the mob at the witch trial, the crowd that cheered a tyrant. The historian Christopher Browning studied a battalion of middle-aged German policemen who carried out mass shootings in occupied Poland, and called his book Ordinary Men: most were not fanatics, but men who went along rather than stand apart from their comrades. The psalm cuts through our self-congratulation with one word: “we”. Not the moralist, who looks down on the past, nor the cynic, who shrugs that everyone is the same, but a forgiven man, who can afford to tell the truth about himself because his standing does not depend on being better than his ancestors. Christ did not die for the people who would have done better. He died for the people who did exactly this, and that includes us.

verseByVerse.quote: But they soon forgot his works; they did not wait for his counsel. But they had a wanton craving in the wilderness, and put God to the test in the desert; he gave them what they asked, but sent a wasting disease among them. When men in the camp were jealous of Moses and Aaron, the holy one of the LORD, the earth opened and swallowed up Dathan, and covered the company of Abiram. Fire also broke out in their company; the flame burned up the wicked.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The singing soon gave way to forgetting: Israel got what they craved and were emptied by it, and some rose in envy against God’s leaders.

But they soon forgot his works. Within three days of the singing they were complaining (Exodus 15:22–24), and would not wait for God’s counsel. That kind of faith is very familiar.

He gave them what they asked. They demanded meat, and God gave them exactly that, and with it “a wasting disease” (Numbers 11:31–34). There is a kind of answered prayer that is judgment: God lets people have what they insist on, and it empties them.

The curse of getting what you want. Our culture promises that you deserve what you want and will be happy when you get it, and much modern spirituality treats God as the supplier of our desires. The ancient Greeks knew better. They told of King Midas, who asked that everything he touched would turn to gold, and was given exactly that, until his bread turned to metal in his mouth. This verse is the true story behind the myth. The deepest judgment is not always that God says no. Sometimes he says yes, and lets us discover that what we demanded cannot bear the weight we put on it. The religious do it too, demanding the comfortable life they think their goodness has earned. The gospel turns it round. In Gethsemane Jesus prayed, “not as I will, but as you will” (Matthew 26:39), and the cup was not taken away, so that we could be given what we never thought to ask for: God himself.

Jealous of Moses and Aaron. Next, envy. Dathan and Abiram joined Korah’s rebellion against Moses and Aaron, “the holy one of the LORD”, and “the earth opened its mouth and swallowed them up” (Numbers 16:32). Jealousy of those God has placed over his people is not a small sin in this list.

Uncertain wording. “A wasting disease” translates a word meaning leanness or emaciation, and the Hebrew sends it “into their soul” (or “their life”). The ESV takes it as physical sickness (Numbers 11:33); the KJV has “sent leanness into their soul”, often read as spiritual emptiness too. Both fit the story.

verseByVerse.quote: They made a calf in Horeb and worshiped a metal image. They exchanged the glory of God for the image of an ox that eats grass. They forgot God, their Savior, who had done great things in Egypt, wondrous works in the land of Ham, and awesome deeds by the Red Sea. Therefore he said he would destroy them— had not Moses, his chosen one, stood in the breach before him, to turn away his wrath from destroying them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the mountain where God had spoken, Israel traded his glory for a calf, and survived only because Moses stood in the breach.

They made a calf in Horeb. At Horeb, another name for Sinai, the very mountain where God had spoken, they made a calf. The verdict is withering: they “exchanged the glory of God for the image of an ox that eats grass” (the ESV notes the Hebrew is “their glory”, the glory that was theirs because God was theirs). The living God, for a statue of a farm animal. Paul described the whole human race doing the same: they “exchanged the glory of the immortal God for images” (Romans 1:23). Every idol is a bad trade.

They forgot God. Forgetting again, the same word as verse 13.

Stood in the breach before him. God said to Moses, “let me alone, that my wrath may burn hot against them and I may consume them”. “But Moses implored the LORD his God” (Exodus 32:10–11). He stood “in the breach”, the gap in a broken city wall where the enemy pours in, and put himself between God’s wrath and the people. The nation survived because one man stood in the gap.

A greater Mediator. Moses offered to be blotted out of God’s book for them (Exodus 32:32), and God would not take it. Jesus did more than plead: he took the wrath himself, “a propitiation by his blood, to be received by faith” (Romans 3:25).
verseByVerse.note: Compare Jer 2:11: But my people have changed their glory for that which does not profit.

verseByVerse.quote: Then they despised the pleasant land, having no faith in his promise. They murmured in their tents, and did not obey the voice of the LORD. Therefore he raised his hand and swore to them that he would make them fall in the wilderness, and would make their offspring fall among the nations, scattering them among the lands.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the border Israel despised the land because they did not believe God’s promise, so that generation fell in the wilderness.

They despised the pleasant land. After the spies’ report (Numbers 13–14) they refused the gift promised for centuries. The reason: “having no faith in his promise”. Unbelief does not only doubt God’s power; it despises his gifts. And it grumbles privately, “in their tents”.

Scattering them among the lands. The wilderness generation died outside the land. And the psalm reaches forward to the exile, as though the refusal at the border held the seed of the later catastrophe.

A rest still offered. Hebrews makes this scene a warning to Christians: they “were unable to enter because of unbelief”, so “let us therefore strive to enter that rest” (Hebrews 3:19; 4:11).

verseByVerse.quote: Then they yoked themselves to the Baal of Peor, and ate sacrifices offered to the dead; they provoked the LORD to anger with their deeds, and a plague broke out among them. Then Phinehas stood up and intervened, and the plague was stayed. And that was counted to him as righteousness from generation to generation forever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel joined the worship of the Baal of Peor and plague broke out, until Phinehas stood up for God’s honour and stopped it.

They yoked themselves to the Baal of Peor. At Peor, on the edge of the promised land, Israelite men joined Moabite women in the worship of Baal. They “yoked themselves”, bound themselves like oxen in a team, to a false god.

Ate sacrifices offered to the dead. Numbers says the Moabite women “invited the people to the sacrifices of their gods, and the people ate” (Numbers 25:2). To eat at that table was to share in the worship, which is why Paul forbids believers “the table of demons” (1 Corinthians 10:21).

Then Phinehas stood up and intervened. Phinehas, Aaron’s grandson, killed an Israelite man and a Midianite woman in the act, and the plague stopped; Numbers says he “made atonement for the people of Israel” (Numbers 25:13). And the psalm says it “was counted to him as righteousness”, the phrase used of Abraham: “he believed the LORD, and he counted it to him as righteousness” (Genesis 15:6), which Paul uses to explain justification by faith (Romans 4:3).

Was Phinehas justified by a deed rather than by faith? No. Abraham’s faith was reckoned as the righteousness that put him right with God. Phinehas’s act was reckoned as righteous, true covenant faithfulness, because, as God said, “he was jealous with my jealousy” (Numbers 25:11). His zeal was the fruit of faith. One text is about how a sinner is accepted; the other is about God publicly honouring what a believer did.

Does Phinehas’s act license killing sinners? No. It was a priest’s act of judgment at a moment of plague, under Israel’s law (Numbers 25). The church fights with other weapons (2 Corinthians 10:3–5), and vengeance belongs to God (Romans 12:19).

Uncertain wording. “Sacrifices offered to the dead” is literally “sacrifices of the dead”. It probably calls the gods of Peor “dead” because they were lifeless beside the living God; some think instead of meals held in honour of the dead. Either way it was worship at an idol’s table.

verseByVerse.quote: They angered him at the waters of Meribah, and it went ill with Moses on their account, for they made his spirit bitter, and he spoke rashly with his lips.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At Meribah the people provoked even Moses into rash words, and he too was barred from the land.

It went ill with Moses on their account. Even Moses fell. The people provoked him until he spoke rashly and struck the rock, and he was barred from the land (Numbers 20:10–12). The man who stood in the breach for them (v. 23) was worn down by them. Leaders are not immune, and constant complaining can make even a faithful man sin.

Uncertain wording. Whose spirit was made bitter? The ESV reads Moses’ spirit, and notes that the phrase may mean “they rebelled against God’s Spirit”, as Isaiah says of the wilderness generation, “they rebelled and grieved his Holy Spirit” (Isaiah 63:10). Both are true of Meribah.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 34–48 — Nevertheless, He Looked upon Their Distress
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In the land the slide reached its bottom, yet God’s mercy reached lower still. Israel failed to drive out the nations, mixed with them, learned their ways, served their idols and sacrificed their own children (vv. 34–39). God handed them over to their enemies, rescued them many times, and watched them rebel again (vv. 40–43). Nevertheless he looked upon their distress, heard their cry, remembered his covenant and relented (vv. 44–46). So the psalm ends with a prayer to be gathered from the nations and the blessing that closes Book Four: “Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, from everlasting to everlasting!” (vv. 47–48).
verseByVerse.theology: Centuries of unfaithfulness end in exile, and in a prayer to be gathered home by the God who never stopped remembering.

verseByVerse.quote: They did not destroy the peoples, as the LORD commanded them, but they mixed with the nations and learned to do as they did. They served their idols, which became a snare to them. They sacrificed their sons and their daughters to the demons; they poured out innocent blood, the blood of their sons and daughters, whom they sacrificed to the idols of Canaan, and the land was polluted with blood. Thus they became unclean by their acts, and played the whore in their deeds.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the land Israel slid step by step from compromise to idolatry, until they sacrificed their own children to the idols of Canaan.

They mixed with the nations. The decline is gradual: they did not obey, then they “mixed”, then they “learned”, then they “served”. No one wakes up an idolater. They arrive there one small compromise at a time.

They sacrificed their sons and their daughters. This is where it ends: the idols of Canaan demanded children, and Israel gave them. The psalm calls the idols “demons”, and Paul said the same of pagan worship: “what pagans sacrifice they offer to demons and not to God” (1 Corinthians 10:20). Idolatry is never harmless. It always ends by consuming what is most precious.

Played the whore in their deeds. Verse 39 uses the language of adultery: Israel was God’s bride, and went after other lovers.

Why is Israel blamed for not destroying the peoples? The command was God’s judgment on Canaan, given so that Israel would not learn their gods and their child sacrifice (Deuteronomy 7:1–5; 20:16–18). The psalm blames the compromise that followed: verses 35–38 show exactly what Moses had warned. It is no pattern for violence now.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the anger of the LORD was kindled against his people, and he abhorred his heritage; he gave them into the hand of the nations, so that those who hated them ruled over them. Their enemies oppressed them, and they were brought into subjection under their power. Many times he delivered them, but they were rebellious in their purposes and were brought low through their iniquity. Nevertheless, he looked upon their distress, when he heard their cry. For their sake he remembered his covenant, and relented according to the abundance of his steadfast love. He caused them to be pitied by all those who held them captive.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God handed his rebellious people over again and again, yet, though they did not change, he heard their cry and remembered his covenant.

He gave them into the hand of the nations. These verses are the book of Judges in a few lines. God handed them over, and enemies ruled them.

Many times he delivered them. The cycle repeated: rescue, rebellion, oppression, rescue. “Whenever the judge died, they turned back and were more corrupt than their fathers” (Judges 2:19).

Nevertheless, he looked upon their distress. “Nevertheless” is the most important word in the psalm. After almost forty verses of sin, he looked; he heard; he “remembered his covenant”, the same thing Psalm 105 said he did (Psalm 105:8, 42). Both psalms end in the same place: God’s memory is better than his people’s. Even their captors were made to pity them.

The gospel in the Old Testament. Not that the people improved, but that God’s steadfast love was more abundant than their sin: “where sin increased, grace abounded all the more” (Romans 5:20).

Does God change his mind? His purposes do not change (Numbers 23:19; Malachi 3:6), but he truly responds to repentance and prayer (Jeremiah 18:7–10). “Relented” describes that response in human terms; the change is in the people, and in what God has always purposed to do for them.

verseByVerse.quote: Save us, O LORD our God, and gather us from among the nations, that we may give thanks to your holy name and glory in your praise. Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, from everlasting to everlasting! And let all the people say, "Amen!" Praise the LORD!
verseByVerse.commentary:
The confession ends with a scattered people praying to be gathered home to thank God, and with the blessing that closes Book Four.

Gather us from among the nations. The confession ends in exile, as verse 27 warned, and the prayer is simple: bring us home, so that we can thank you. The very next psalm, which opens Book Five, begins with God’s people “gathered in from the lands, from the east and from the west” (Psalm 107:3). The final answer is Christ, who died, John says, “to gather into one the children of God who are scattered abroad” (John 11:52).

Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel. Verse 48 closes Book Four of the Psalms. When it was sung before the ark in David’s day, “all the people said, ‘Amen!’ and praised the LORD” (1 Chronicles 16:36). Because that song includes verses 1 and 47–48, some think the prayer fits any scattering of Israel; many think the psalm took its final form in or after the exile.

The church’s mirror. Paul wrote that Israel’s wilderness history “happened to them as an example, but they were written down for our instruction” (1 Corinthians 10:11). Every sin in this psalm, forgetting, craving, envy, idolatry, unbelief and compromise, is a Christian temptation. And every “yet” and “nevertheless” in it is a Christian hope. Honest confession, ending in Amen.
verseByVerse.note: Each of the first four books of the Psalms ends with a blessing of this kind (41:13; 72:18-19; 89:52), and Psalm 150 closes the whole.

106.title: Both We and Our Fathers Have Sinned
106.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 106 closes Book Four of the Psalter (see the introduction) and is the twin of Psalm 105. That psalm told Israel’s history as a record of what God did; this one tells the same history again as a record of what Israel did.

The message. God’s steadfast love is greater than his people’s persistent sin. From the Red Sea to the idols of Canaan, Israel forgot, craved, envied, rebelled and compromised, and God judged them; “nevertheless” he heard their cry and remembered his covenant (vv. 44–45). So the right response to our own history is honest confession that says “we”, held inside praise that says “his steadfast love endures forever”.

Why it was said. The psalm ends with a people scattered among the nations, praying to be gathered (v. 47; see the introduction). To Israel in or after exile it answered two questions: why did this happen, and is there any hope? It happened because of our sins and our fathers’; there is hope because God’s memory is better than ours.

How the chapter makes its case. Praise, and a personal plea to share God’s favour (vv. 1–5). Then the confession, “Both we and our fathers have sinned” (v. 6), and six scenes: rebellion at the Red Sea, yet rescue (vv. 6–12); craving in the desert and envy of Moses (vv. 13–18); the golden calf, and Moses in the breach (vv. 19–23); the land despised (vv. 24–27); the Baal of Peor, and Phinehas (vv. 28–31); Meribah, where even Moses fell (vv. 32–33). In the land the slide went on to child sacrifice (vv. 34–39), and God handed them over again and again (vv. 40–43); nevertheless he looked upon their distress (vv. 44–46). A prayer to be gathered and the blessing that closes Book Four end it (vv. 47–48).

Where it leads. By the need it exposes, and by the pattern of a mediator. A rescued people left to themselves will forget, every time; they need more than rescue, they need new hearts and someone to stand between them and judgment. Twice in this psalm one man does that, Moses in the breach (v. 23) and Phinehas (v. 30), and both point to the one Mediator who did not only plead or turn wrath aside but bore it himself. And the prayer “gather us” is answered by Christ, who died “to gather into one the children of God who are scattered abroad” (John 11:52).

For us. This history was “written down for our instruction” (1 Corinthians 10:11): every sin in it is a Christian temptation, and every “nevertheless” a Christian hope. Confess with “we”, not “they”, and finish where the psalm finishes, with Amen and praise.
106.theology: True confession says we (v. 6). Sin begins in forgetting God's works (vv. 7, 13, 21); idolatry grows by small compromises and ends by devouring what is most precious (vv. 34-38). A mediator, one who stands between God and the people, turns wrath aside (v. 23), and God's steadfast love outlasts centuries of rebellion (vv. 44-45).
106.examples: Israel sang on the shore and complained three days later; they traded the glory of God for a statue of a farm animal. Most believers recognise themselves. The psalm does not leave them there: after almost forty verses of sin comes nevertheless, and a prayer at the end of one book is answered at the start of the next.

keyVerse.quote: For their sake he remembered his covenant, and relented according to the abundance of his steadfast love.
keyVerse.note: After almost forty verses of rebellion, this is the turn of the psalm. God’s mercy is not a response to Israel’s improvement, for they did not improve, but to his own covenant and the abundance of his steadfast love. That same love has come to its fullest in Christ, where sin increased and grace abounded all the more.

106.reflection:
Psalm 106 confesses, “Both we and our fathers have sinned” (v. 6). Why is it so tempting to say “they” about the failures of the past, and what changes when we say “we”?

“He gave them what they asked, but sent a wasting disease among them” (v. 15). Have you ever got something you insisted on and found it could not satisfy? How does Jesus’ prayer in Gethsemane reshape our praying?

The slide in verses 34–39 is gradual: they mixed, learned, served and sacrificed. Where are the small compromises in our lives or churches that could lead somewhere we never meant to go?

Moses stood in the breach (v. 23), and God, “nevertheless”, remembered his covenant (vv. 44–45). How does Christ, the greater Mediator, give us hope when we are ashamed of our repeated failures?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–3 — Gathered In from the Lands
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Those God has rescued must say so. The psalm opens with the great refrain of Israel’s worship, “Oh give thanks to the LORD, for he is good”, and then calls on “the redeemed of the LORD” to speak up (vv. 1–2). They are a people redeemed from trouble and gathered in from every point of the compass, east and west, north and south (v. 3). After the exile and the prayer of Psalm 106:47, “gather us”, this is the answer: God has brought his scattered people home. And the rescued are not to keep quiet about it.
verseByVerse.theology: The redeemed are to say so: God has gathered his scattered people home.

verseByVerse.quote: Oh give thanks to the LORD, for he is good, for his steadfast love endures forever! Let the redeemed of the LORD say so, whom he has redeemed from trouble and gathered in from the lands, from the east and from the west, from the north and from the south.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God has gathered his redeemed people home from every direction, and those he has rescued are to give thanks and say so.

Book Five begins. Book Five opens with almost the same words as Psalm 106, but Psalm 106 ended in exile, praying, “gather us from among the nations” (Psalm 106:47).

Gathered in from the lands. Here is the answer, from every point of the compass: the prayer at the end of one book is answered in the first sentence of the next.

Let the redeemed of the LORD say so. The command to the redeemed is short: say so. If God has rescued you, do not keep it quiet.

Still being gathered. Paul describes the gathering in its fullest form: “you who once were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ” (Ephesians 2:13). John saw its end, “from every nation, from all tribes and peoples and languages” (Revelation 7:9).

Uncertain wording. The ESV notes that “from trouble” (v. 2) may be read “from the hand of the foe”. In verse 3, “from the south” is literally “from the sea”. Since the sea usually means the west, which is already named, most translations take it here as the south; the point is plain either way: from everywhere.
verseByVerse.note: Psalm 107 opens Book Five, the last book of the Psalms (Psalms 107–150).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–32 — Then They Cried to the LORD in Their Trouble
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In four very different troubles the way out is the same: cry to the LORD, and thank him when he answers. Some wandered lost and starving in the desert, and he led them to a city (vv. 4–9). Some sat in darkness and irons because they had rebelled, and he broke their chains (vv. 10–16). Some were fools made sick by their sin, and he sent his word and healed them (vv. 17–22). Some went to sea and were caught in a storm beyond all their skill, and he stilled it and brought them to harbour (vv. 23–32). Each time they cried and he delivered (vv. 6, 13, 19, 28), and each time they are called to thank him (vv. 8, 15, 21, 31).
verseByVerse.theology: Four kinds of trouble, one cry, one rescuer, and the same thanks each time.

verseByVerse.quote: Some wandered in desert wastes, finding no way to a city to dwell in; hungry and thirsty, their soul fainted within them. Then they cried to the LORD in their trouble, and he delivered them from their distress. He led them by a straight way till they reached a city to dwell in. Let them thank the LORD for his steadfast love, for his wondrous works to the children of man! For he satisfies the longing soul, and the hungry soul he fills with good things.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The first story: people lost and starving in the desert cried to the LORD, and he led them straight to a city and satisfied their hunger.

Some wandered in desert wastes. Four stories follow, all with one shape: a trouble, a cry, a rescue, a call to thanks, and a reason. The first is the lost, wandering in the desert, fainting from hunger and thirst.

The lost today. A picture of the person without direction or home, lost not through wickedness, just lost. Many today recognise it: wandering from one thing to the next, never arriving anywhere, spiritually starving.

Then they cried to the LORD in their trouble. The first refrain. The rescue fits the trouble exactly: lost people are given “a straight way” and “a city to dwell in”.

He satisfies the longing soul. The second refrain is thanks, with its reason: “he satisfies the longing soul, and the hungry soul he fills with good things”. Every restless heart is looking for this. Jesus said, “whoever comes to me shall not hunger, and whoever believes in me shall never thirst” (John 6:35).

verseByVerse.quote: Some sat in darkness and in the shadow of death, prisoners in affliction and in irons, for they had rebelled against the words of God, and spurned the counsel of the Most High. So he bowed their hearts down with hard labor; they fell down, with none to help. Then they cried to the LORD in their trouble, and he delivered them from their distress. He brought them out of darkness and the shadow of death, and burst their bonds apart. Let them thank the LORD for his steadfast love, for his wondrous works to the children of man! For he shatters the doors of bronze and cuts in two the bars of iron.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The second story: rebels sitting in chains through their own fault cried to the LORD, and he broke their bonds and brought them out of darkness.

They had rebelled against the words of God. These prisoners are in chains because of their own choices. The psalm is honest: some trouble is simply suffering, and some is the consequence of rebellion.

He bowed their hearts down with hard labor. God himself brought them low, until there was no one to help. Sometimes God lets a person reach the end of every other resource so that the cry of verse 13 becomes possible.

He brought them out of darkness. Even rebels in chains through their own fault can cry and be heard. That is grace. Zechariah sang of the dawn from on high coming “to give light to those who sit in darkness and in the shadow of death” (Luke 1:79), and Jesus announced that he had come “to proclaim liberty to the captives” (Luke 4:18). When an angel came for Peter in prison, “the chains fell off his hands” (Acts 12:7).

He shatters the doors of bronze. No prison built by sin is stronger than the God who breaks “doors of bronze”. Whatever habit, addiction or guilt has you in irons, this verse is written over the door.

verseByVerse.quote: Some were fools through their sinful ways, and because of their iniquities suffered affliction; they loathed any kind of food, and they drew near to the gates of death. Then they cried to the LORD in their trouble, and he delivered them from their distress. He sent out his word and healed them, and delivered them from their destruction. Let them thank the LORD for his steadfast love, for his wondrous works to the children of man! And let them offer sacrifices of thanksgiving, and tell of his deeds in songs of joy!
verseByVerse.commentary:
The third story: fools made sick by their own sin cried to the LORD at death’s door, and he sent his word and healed them.

Some were fools through their sinful ways. The third story is the sick, called fools: not unintelligent, but morally foolish. Their sin has made them ill, until they cannot eat and are at “the gates of death”. Not every illness is caused by sin, as Jesus made clear (John 9:3); but some self-destruction is.

He sent out his word and healed them. God’s word is pictured as a messenger sent on an errand of healing. A Roman centurion understood that: “say the word, and let my servant be healed” (Luke 7:7). And in the end the Word God sent out was his own Son, who “became flesh” (John 1:14).

Whatever became of sin? In 1973 the psychiatrist Karl Menninger, no preacher, published a book with that title. He noticed that what earlier ages called sin was now called sickness, crime or the product of upbringing, and wondered whether something true had been lost. Our therapeutic vocabulary has done real good: it has made us gentler with the depressed and the abused, and this psalm itself knows that much suffering is nobody’s fault. But a world with no sin also has no forgiveness. If all my wrongdoing is a symptom, I can be treated but never pardoned, and the guilt that wakes me at night has nowhere to go. The psalm is more realistic and more hopeful. It calls these sufferers fools, afflicted “because of their iniquities”, and then shows God sending his word to heal them anyway. Only a faith that names sin can offer grace. The gospel names it plainly because it has already dealt with it: Christ bore it, so it can be confessed instead of explained away.

Let them offer sacrifices of thanksgiving. The healed are to give thanks and tell the story; recovery not followed by gratitude has missed the point. The thank offering was a sacrifice whose meat was eaten at the sanctuary the same day (Leviticus 7:11–15), a meal usually shared with others, so the healed man’s gratitude became a feast where his story was told.

verseByVerse.quote: Some went down to the sea in ships, doing business on the great waters; they saw the deeds of the LORD, his wondrous works in the deep.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The fourth story begins with merchants at sea, who out on the deep saw the works of the LORD.

Some went down to the sea in ships. The fourth and longest story is of sailors. Israel was no seafaring nation, and the sea terrified them. These are merchants about ordinary business, and at sea they “saw the deeds of the LORD”.

His wondrous works in the deep. They went out for trade, and met God. For Israel the deep was the picture of untamed chaos that only the LORD masters (Genesis 1:2; Psalm 104:25–26). People taken out of their depth see what those who stay safe on dry land never see.

verseByVerse.quote: For he commanded and raised the stormy wind, which lifted up the waves of the sea. They mounted up to heaven; they went down to the depths; their courage melted away in their evil plight; they reeled and staggered like drunken men and were at their wits' end.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God raised the storm, and the sailors, tossed between sky and depths, were brought to the end of all their skill and courage.

He commanded and raised the stormy wind. The storm is God’s: “he commanded”. The ship climbs to the sky and drops into the troughs; men stagger like drunks. “At their wits’ end” is, as the ESV notes, literally “all their wisdom was swallowed up”: all their seamanship, all their skill, gone under. Some troubles are beyond every human competence.

Their courage melted away in their evil plight. Nothing is said of these sailors’ sin, unlike the rebels of verses 10–11 and the fools of verse 17. Jonah’s shipmates met such a storm because of one runaway prophet (Jonah 1:4); these meet one in the course of honest work. Either way the storm is God’s, and either way it does what courage and skill cannot: it brings them to the end of themselves.

verseByVerse.quote: Then they cried to the LORD in their trouble, and he delivered them from their distress. He made the storm be still, and the waves of the sea were hushed. Then they were glad that the waters were quiet, and he brought them to their desired haven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When their skill was gone the sailors cried to the LORD, and he stilled the storm and brought them safe to the harbour they longed for.

Then they cried to the LORD in their trouble. Then: when all their seamanship had been swallowed up (v. 27). Men who trusted their ships have nothing left but prayer, and prayer is enough.

He made the storm be still. Here the psalm walks into the Gospels. Terrified disciples in a boat on the Sea of Galilee cried out, and Jesus “rebuked the wind and said to the sea, ‘Peace! Be still!’” (Mark 4:39), “and there was a great calm” (Matthew 8:26). They asked, “Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?” (Mark 4:41). Anyone who knew Psalm 107 knew the answer. Only the LORD makes the storm be still.

He brought them to their desired haven. The rescue ends not mid-ocean but in harbour, where they wanted to be. God does not merely stop the storm; he finishes the voyage.

Four stories, one pattern. The two refrains come four times each (vv. 6, 13, 19, 28; vv. 8, 15, 21, 31). Very different troubles, some innocent and some self-inflicted, and in every case the same thing happens: “they cried to the LORD”. Whatever your trouble, the psalm has only one instruction for you before the rescue. Cry to him.

verseByVerse.quote: Let them thank the LORD for his steadfast love, for his wondrous works to the children of man! Let them extol him in the congregation of the people, and praise him in the assembly of the elders.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The rescued sailors are to thank the LORD for his steadfast love, and to do it publicly among his people.

Let them thank the LORD for his steadfast love. The second refrain closes the story, as it closed the other three (vv. 8, 15, 21). The rescue is credited not to luck or skill but to God’s steadfast love, his covenant faithfulness, the note on which the psalm opened (v. 1) and will close (v. 43).

In the congregation of the people. Look where the sailors’ thanks is to be given: “in the congregation of the people” and “in the assembly of the elders”. They were rescued alone on the sea; they are to give thanks in public. A private rescue owes a public song.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 33–43 — Consider the Steadfast Love of the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Behind the four rescues lies one God who overturns human fortunes, and the wise will learn to see his love in it. He turns rivers into desert and fruitful land into salt because of human evil, and turns desert into pools where the hungry settle, sow and flourish (vv. 33–38). When people are brought low by oppression, he pours contempt on the princes and raises the needy (vv. 39–41). The upright rejoice and wickedness falls silent (v. 42). The psalm ends as wisdom does: whoever is wise, consider these things, and see in them “the steadfast love of the LORD” (v. 43).
verseByVerse.theology: God overturns the fortunes of the proud and the poor, and the wise are told to watch it happen.

verseByVerse.quote: He turns rivers into a desert, springs of water into thirsty ground, a fruitful land into a salty waste, because of the evil of its inhabitants. He turns a desert into pools of water, a parched land into springs of water. And there he lets the hungry dwell, and they establish a city to live in; they sow fields and plant vineyards and get a fruitful yield. By his blessing they multiply greatly, and he does not let their livestock diminish.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The God of the four rescues rules the land itself, turning fruitful places to desert for human evil, and deserts into homes for the hungry.

He turns rivers into a desert. The psalm widens from four stories to how God rules. He can dry up rivers and turn farmland to salt “because of the evil of its inhabitants”. Prosperity is not guaranteed to the wicked.

He turns a desert into pools of water. And the reverse: deserts become pools, and the hungry, like the wanderers of verse 5, are settled there, build a city and plant vineyards. God reverses fortunes in both directions.

Are disasters God’s judgment? God does judge nations, and the right response to any disaster is repentance (Luke 13:1–5). But Jesus warns against assuming that those it strikes are worse sinners than others (Luke 13:4–5).

verseByVerse.quote: When they are diminished and brought low through oppression, evil, and sorrow, he pours contempt on princes and makes them wander in trackless wastes; but he raises up the needy out of affliction and makes their families like flocks. The upright see it and are glad, and all wickedness shuts its mouth. Whoever is wise, let him attend to these things; let them consider the steadfast love of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God brings down oppressive princes and lifts up the needy, and the wise will learn to see his steadfast love in it.

He pours contempt on princes. The reversals continue. These are the words of Job (Job 12:21, 24), who saw the same God humble rulers. Princes who oppressed are made to wander in trackless wastes, becoming the lost people of the first story.

He raises up the needy out of affliction. And the needy are lifted up. It is the same overturning Mary sang about: the mighty brought down, the humble exalted (Luke 1:52).

The upright see it and are glad. When God acts like this, the righteous rejoice, and the wicked have nothing left to say.

Whoever is wise, let him attend to these things. The psalm ends like wisdom literature. Consider these stories. Watch how God rescues the lost, the imprisoned, the sick and the storm-tossed; how he humbles princes and raises the poor. The wise person is not the one who has never been in trouble, but the one who has learned, from trouble, to see “the steadfast love of the LORD”, and to say so.

Uncertain wording. Verses 39–40 are compressed, and the subject shifts without warning. “They” in verse 39 are probably the settled people of verses 36–38, whose fortunes can fall again under oppression; God then humbles the oppressing princes and raises the needy. The sense is clear even where the links are not.

107.title: Let the Redeemed of the LORD Say So
107.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 107 opens Book Five of the Psalter (see the introduction). Psalm 106 ended with exiles praying, “gather us from among the nations” (Psalm 106:47); this psalm begins with the redeemed “gathered in from the lands” (v. 3). The prayer at the end of one book is answered in the first lines of the next.

The message. When people in any kind of trouble cry to the LORD, he hears and rescues them, and those he rescues should say so. Lost, imprisoned, sick or storm-tossed, innocent or guilty, the way out is the same: “they cried to the LORD in their trouble, and he delivered them from their distress”. The wise learn to see in every rescue “the steadfast love of the LORD” (v. 43).

Why it was said. For a people brought back from exile (see the introduction), the psalm turned their own story into praise and taught them that their return was God’s redemption, not good fortune. It also gave every later sufferer a pattern to pray by.

How the chapter makes its case. A call to the redeemed to give thanks and say so (vv. 1–3). Then four stories with one shape, trouble, cry, rescue and thanks: wanderers lost in the desert are led to a city (vv. 4–9); rebels in chains are set free (vv. 10–16); fools sick to death are healed by his word (vv. 17–22); sailors at their wits’ end are brought to harbour (vv. 23–32). Two refrains, each sung four times, bind the stories together: “Then they cried to the LORD in their trouble” and “Let them thank the LORD for his steadfast love”. Then the psalm widens: God turns rivers into desert and desert into pools, humbles princes and raises the needy (vv. 33–42), and the wise are told to consider it (v. 43).

Where it leads. By the character of God revealed in Christ. When Jesus rebuked the wind and the waves, his disciples asked, “Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?” (Mark 4:41). Anyone who knew this psalm knew the answer: only the LORD makes the storm be still (v. 29). Jesus came “to proclaim liberty to the captives” (Luke 4:18), healed with a word, and is himself the Word God sent (John 1:14); and the gathering from east and west is completed in him (Revelation 7:9).

For us. Whatever your trouble, whether you walked into it or it fell on you, the psalm gives one instruction before the rescue: cry to him. And one instruction after it: say so, among God’s people.
107.theology: Book Five opens with the gathering prayed for at the close of Book Four (v. 3; 106:47), and the redeemed must testify (v. 2). Trouble may be innocent or self-inflicted (vv. 11, 17), but in every case the cry to the LORD is heard. The God who stills the storm (v. 29) did it in person in Christ (Mark 4:39-41).
107.examples: Some readers will find themselves among the wanderers, never arriving anywhere; others in chains that were their own fault. The psalm offers all of them the same thing: cry to him, and when he answers, say so. When the disciples asked of Jesus, Who then is this?, anyone who knew Psalm 107 knew the answer.

keyVerse.quote: Then they cried to the LORD in their trouble, and he delivered them from their distress.
keyVerse.note: This refrain comes four times (vv. 6, 13, 19, 28), once in each story, and it holds the psalm together. Whether people were lost, guilty, sick or caught in a storm beyond their skill, the way out was the same: they cried, and the LORD delivered. In Christ, who stilled the storm with a word, the same Lord still hears.

107.reflection:
“Let the redeemed of the LORD say so” (v. 2). What has God rescued you from, and who needs to hear you say so?

Some of the troubles in this psalm are innocent and some are self-inflicted (vv. 10–11, 17). Why does it matter that God hears the cry of those who are in trouble through their own fault?

The disciples asked of Jesus, “Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?” (Mark 4:41). How does Psalm 107:29 answer them, and what storm do you need to bring to him now?

The sailors were rescued alone but told to give thanks “in the congregation of the people” (v. 32). How could our church make more room for people to tell what God has done?

108.text: A Song. A Psalm of David. 1My heart is steadfast, O God! I will sing and make melody with all my being!2Awake, O harp and lyre! I will awake the dawn!3I will give thanks to you, O LORD, among the peoples; I will sing praises to you among the nations.4For your steadfast love is great above the heavens; your faithfulness reaches to the clouds.5Be exalted, O God, above the heavens! Let your glory be over all the earth!6That your beloved ones may be delivered, give salvation by your right hand and answer me!7God has promised in his holiness: "With exultation I will divide up Shechem and portion out the Valley of Succoth.8Gilead is mine; Manasseh is mine; Ephraim is my helmet, Judah my scepter.9Moab is my washbasin; upon Edom I cast my shoe; over Philistia I shout in triumph."10Who will bring me to the fortified city? Who will lead me to Edom?11Have you not rejected us, O God? You do not go out, O God, with our armies.12Oh grant us help against the foe, for vain is the salvation of man!13With God we shall do valiantly; it is he who will tread down our foes.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — I Will Awake the Dawn
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A heart fixed on God wakes the morning with praise that reaches the nations. These verses are the closing praise of Psalm 57, sung once in a cave while David fled from Saul, but here the cave and its lions are left out. The singer’s heart is steadfast; he will sing with his whole being, rouse harp and lyre, and wake the dawn (vv. 1–2). His thanks goes out among the peoples and the nations (v. 3), because God’s steadfast love is great above the heavens and his faithfulness reaches the clouds (v. 4). He ends by asking God to be exalted over heaven and earth (v. 5).
verseByVerse.theology: The closing praise of Psalm 57, sung again without the cave that came before it.

verseByVerse.quote: My heart is steadfast, O God! I will sing and make melody with all my being! Awake, O harp and lyre! I will awake the dawn! I will give thanks to you, O LORD, among the peoples; I will sing praises to you among the nations. For your steadfast love is great above the heavens; your faithfulness reaches to the clouds. Be exalted, O God, above the heavens! Let your glory be over all the earth!
verseByVerse.commentary:
With a steadfast heart the singer wakes the dawn with praise for the nations to hear, because God’s love is greater than the heavens.

Two older psalms. Verses 1–5 are the end of Psalm 57, the song David wrote “when he fled from Saul, in the cave” (Psalm 57, title). Verses 6–13 are the second half of Psalm 60, written after a defeat. What matters is what has been left out, and what changed. The title still reads “A Psalm of David”: David may have reworked his own songs for a new day, or they were reworked later as his.

The laments left out. Psalm 57 began in the cave: “My soul is in the midst of lions”. Psalm 60 began, “O God, you have rejected us, broken our defenses”. Psalm 108 starts where those psalms ended, at the praise and the promise. The distress is set aside; the confidence that grew from it is kept.

Old songs, new occasions. A hymn written in grief is sung years later at a celebration: the faith forged in the cave becomes the song of people who were never in it.

My heart is steadfast, O God! The small changes point the same way. Psalm 57 said, “My heart is steadfast, O God, my heart is steadfast!” and then “Awake, my glory!” Here the repetition is gone, and “my glory” has moved into the first line as “with all my being”. The whole self is engaged from the start. He will not wait for morning; he will wake the dawn with his music.

Your steadfast love is great above the heavens. Psalm 57 said God’s steadfast love is great “to the heavens” (Psalm 57:10). Psalm 108 says “above the heavens”. Looking back, the singer finds the love even larger than it seemed in the cave. Paul prayed that believers would grasp it in Christ: “the breadth and length and height and depth” of a love “that surpasses knowledge” (Ephesians 3:18–19).

Uncertain wording. “With all my being” (v. 1) is literally “with my glory”, as the ESV notes. It probably means the inner self, the noblest part of a person (compare Psalm 16:9); some take it as the singer’s voice. Either way: praise with everything he is.
verseByVerse.note: Psalm 108 combines Psalm 57:7–11 and 60:5–12; both are expounded fully in their place.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–13 — Vain Is the Salvation of Man
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s promise and an honest question stand side by side, and the victory belongs to God alone. Taken from Psalm 60, these verses open with a plea for God’s beloved to be rescued (v. 6). God answers with a holy promise: the land, west and east of the Jordan, is his, Israel’s tribes are his armour and sceptre, and the hostile nations around are his to command (vv. 7–9). Then comes the question: who will lead us to Edom, and have you not rejected us? (vv. 10–11). The answer is a confession, not a strategy: human help is vain; with God we shall do valiantly, for he will tread down our foes (vv. 12–13).
verseByVerse.theology: The promise and hope of Psalm 60, sung again without its opening defeat, but with its hard question kept.

verseByVerse.quote: That your beloved ones may be delivered, give salvation by your right hand and answer me! God has promised in his holiness: "With exultation I will divide up Shechem and portion out the Valley of Succoth. Gilead is mine; Manasseh is mine; Ephraim is my helmet, Judah my scepter. Moab is my washbasin; upon Edom I cast my shoe; over Philistia I shout in triumph."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The singer asks God to rescue his beloved people, and God answers with a holy promise: the whole land and the hostile nations around it are his.

Give salvation by your right hand and answer me! Now the psalm switches to Psalm 60, with one word changed. In Psalm 60 the ESV reads “answer us” (the Hebrew there can also be read “me”); here it is plainly “answer me”. A nation’s plea is taken up by one person as his own.

God has promised in his holiness. Psalm 60 introduced this oracle with “God has spoken”; here the ESV renders the same Hebrew word “God has promised”: a word from God is a promise to hold on to.

Gilead is mine; Manasseh is mine. God claims the whole land and the nations around it. The places cover the land: Shechem lies west of the Jordan and the Valley of Succoth east of it, both places where Jacob settled on coming home (Genesis 33:17–18), and Gilead and Manasseh stretch the claim across the river. Israel’s tribes are his armour and sceptre: Ephraim, the strongest tribe, his helmet; Judah, the royal tribe, his sceptre (Genesis 49:10). Moab is his washbasin, a servant’s vessel.

Claimed by the gospel. In the end God makes good his claim on the nations by the gospel, not the sword. At the council in Jerusalem, James quoted Amos’s promise about Edom and the nations and said it was being fulfilled as Gentiles came to Christ (Acts 15:14–17; Amos 9:11–12).

Uncertain wording. The meaning of “upon Edom I cast my shoe” is not certain. Most take it as a claim of ownership, as a shoe marked a transfer of property (Ruth 4:7); others see contempt, a master tossing his sandals to a servant. Either way Edom, Israel’s bitter enemy, is under God’s feet.

verseByVerse.quote: Who will bring me to the fortified city? Who will lead me to Edom? Have you not rejected us, O God? You do not go out, O God, with our armies. Oh grant us help against the foe, for vain is the salvation of man! With God we shall do valiantly; it is he who will tread down our foes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The singer honestly asks why God has not gone with his armies, then confesses that human help is useless and that with God his people will win.

Have you not rejected us, O God? The laments were removed from both psalms, but this question was kept, beside the question of who could lead them against Edom’s fortified city (v. 10). Even a confident psalm does not pretend that God’s people never feel abandoned. The promise of verses 7–9 and the question of verse 11 stand side by side. That is honest faith: God’s word in one hand and an unanswered question in the other.

Forsaken for us. One man was truly rejected by God: the Son of David who cried, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matthew 27:46). Because he bore that, his people can feel abandoned without being abandoned: “I will never leave you nor forsake you” (Hebrews 13:5).

With God we shall do valiantly. The answer is a confession, not a strategy. “Vain is the salvation of man”: human help is empty. With God, and only with him, “we shall do valiantly”. Not that they will sit still; they will fight, and bravely. But “it is he who will tread down our foes”.

How Scripture feeds faith. Old songs of distress become new songs of confidence, and the victory still belongs entirely to God. Believers now sing these words in the light of a greater victory, won by the Son of David, who “must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet” (1 Corinthians 15:25).

108.title: My Heart Is Steadfast, O God
108.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 108 begins a short group of psalms headed “of David” early in Book Five (108–110; see the introduction). It is built from two earlier psalms of David: verses 1–5 are the closing praise of Psalm 57, and verses 6–13 the second half of Psalm 60.

The message. Faith forged in distress becomes confidence for a new day. The laments with which both older psalms began are left out. This psalm starts with a steadfast heart, sings of God’s love “great above the heavens” (v. 4), holds on to his promise, and confesses that victory is his alone: “vain is the salvation of man! With God we shall do valiantly” (vv. 12–13). Yet one honest question is kept: “Have you not rejected us, O God?” (v. 11).

Why it was said. God’s people, facing a new threat with Edom named as the enemy (v. 10), took up words that had already proved true in David’s darkest hours and found that they still spoke. This is how the Psalms were meant to be used (see the introduction): old songs given to new occasions.

How the chapter makes its case. Praise that wakes the dawn and goes out to the nations, because God’s love and faithfulness fill the heavens (vv. 1–5). A plea for rescue (v. 6), and God’s holy promise claiming the land and the nations around it (vv. 7–9). A hard question about the fortified city and God’s absence from the armies (vv. 10–11). And a final confession: human help is empty; with God his people will fight bravely, and he will tread down the foes (vv. 12–13).

Where it leads. By promise, and by the need it exposes. God’s claim on Moab, Edom and Philistia is made good in the end not by the sword but by the gospel: James heard Amos’s promise about Edom and the nations being fulfilled as Gentiles came to Christ (Acts 15:14–17). The Son of David treads down every enemy, for “he must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet” (1 Corinthians 15:25). And the question “Have you not rejected us?” finds its answer at the cross, where the Son was forsaken so that God can say to his people, “I will never leave you nor forsake you” (Hebrews 13:5).

For us. Words of Scripture that carried others through their darkest hours are given to you for yours. Sing them with your whole self, keep your honest questions, and fight your battles bravely, knowing that the victory is God’s.
108.theology: Faith forged in distress (Psalms 57, 60) becomes the confident song of later worshippers, and God's word is held as a promise (v. 7). Yet confident faith still admits the experience of seeming rejection (v. 11), and the victory is God's alone (vv. 12-13).
108.examples: A church that sings, at a wedding, a hymn first written in grief is doing what Psalm 108 does. The singer looks back on David's cave and finds the love was above the heavens, not just up to them, and he still holds God's word in one hand and an unanswered question in the other.

keyVerse.quote: With God we shall do valiantly; it is he who will tread down our foes.
keyVerse.note: The psalm ends on its answer to the hard question of verse 11. Human help is vain, yet God’s people are not passive: with God they fight bravely, while the victory remains his. In Christ, who must reign until every enemy is under his feet, that confidence has its firmest ground.

108.reflection:
Psalm 108 takes the praise from two older psalms and leaves the laments behind. What old words of Scripture, or hymns, have carried you from distress to confidence?

“Your steadfast love is great above the heavens” (v. 4), where Psalm 57 said “to the heavens”. How has your sense of God’s love grown as you have looked back on your life?

The psalm keeps the question “Have you not rejected us, O God?” (v. 11) beside God’s promise. Why is it right for faith to hold both, and how does the cross answer that question?

“Vain is the salvation of man! With God we shall do valiantly” (vv. 12–13). Where are you tempted to rely on human help, and what would it look like to act bravely while trusting God for the outcome?

109.text: To the choirmaster. A Psalm of David. 1Be not silent, O God of my praise!2For wicked and deceitful mouths are opened against me, speaking against me with lying tongues.3They encircle me with words of hate, and attack me without cause.4In return for my love they accuse me, but I give myself to prayer.5So they reward me evil for good, and hatred for my love.6Appoint a wicked man against him; let an accuser stand at his right hand.7When he is tried, let him come forth guilty; let his prayer be counted as sin!8May his days be few; may another take his office!9May his children be fatherless and his wife a widow!10May his children wander about and beg, seeking food far from the ruins they inhabit!11May the creditor seize all that he has; may strangers plunder the fruits of his toil!12Let there be none to extend kindness to him, nor any to pity his fatherless children!13May his posterity be cut off; may his name be blotted out in the second generation!14May the iniquity of his fathers be remembered before the LORD, and let not the sin of his mother be blotted out!15Let them be before the LORD continually, that he may cut off the memory of them from the earth!16For he did not remember to show kindness, but pursued the poor and needy and the brokenhearted, to put them to death.17He loved to curse; let curses come upon him! He did not delight in blessing; may it be far from him!18He clothed himself with cursing as his coat; may it soak into his body like water, like oil into his bones!19May it be like a garment that he wraps around him, like a belt that he puts on every day!20May this be the reward of my accusers from the LORD, of those who speak evil against my life!21But you, O GOD my Lord, deal on my behalf for your name's sake; because your steadfast love is good, deliver me!22For I am poor and needy, and my heart is stricken within me.23I am gone like a shadow at evening; I am shaken off like a locust.24My knees are weak through fasting; my body has become gaunt, with no fat.25I am an object of scorn to my accusers; when they see me, they wag their heads.26Help me, O LORD my God! Save me according to your steadfast love!27Let them know that this is your hand; you, O LORD, have done it!28Let them curse, but you will bless! They arise and are put to shame, but your servant will be glad!29May my accusers be clothed with dishonor; may they be wrapped in their own shame as in a cloak!30With my mouth I will give great thanks to the LORD; I will praise him in the midst of the throng.31For he stands at the right hand of the needy one, to save him from those who condemn his soul to death.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — In Return for My Love They Accuse Me
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A man repaid with hatred for his love answers not with a counter-attack but with prayer. The attack is all words: deceitful mouths, lying tongues, words of hate, all of them false and without cause (vv. 1–3). Worse, they come from people he had loved and treated well (vv. 4–5). Against the noise David asks only that God not be silent, and his own answer is two words in Hebrew, “I, prayer” (v. 4). They are all accusation; he is all prayer. He takes the case out of the court of human opinion and lays it before the only Judge whose verdict is final.
verseByVerse.theology: A man repaid with hatred for his love answers not with a counter-attack but with prayer.

verseByVerse.quote: Be not silent, O God of my praise! For wicked and deceitful mouths are opened against me, speaking against me with lying tongues. They encircle me with words of hate, and attack me without cause. In return for my love they accuse me, but I give myself to prayer. So they reward me evil for good, and hatred for my love.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Lied about and repaid with hatred for his love, David does not answer in kind: he asks God not to stay silent and gives himself to prayer.

Be not silent, O God of my praise! The man is surrounded by talk: mouths, tongues, words, and all of it false. Against the noise he asks one thing, that God not be silent. He calls God the God of my praise, the one he has always praised, even while everyone else is speaking against him.

In return for my love. They attack him without cause, and worse, in return for my love. He had loved these people. Betrayal by those you have been kind to is a wound of its own.

But I give myself to prayer. One of the most beautiful lines in the Psalter. The Hebrew has only two words, “and I, prayer”: they are all accusation, he is all prayer. Prayer is the only answer to slander that does not turn the believer into a slanderer himself.

He who ate my bread. Jesus quoted a similar psalm (41:9) about his betrayer: “He who ate my bread has lifted his heel against me” (John 13:18). Of those who hated him he said, in the words of Psalms 35 and 69, “They hated me without a cause” (John 15:25). Love repaid with hatred reaches its lowest point in the upper room.

When the crowd turns on you. David’s enemies needed a rumour and a mob; ours need only a screenshot. It has never been easier to accuse someone in front of thousands, or harder to answer, and when the facts come out a week later no one is listening. Two responses come naturally: to gather your own crowd and return the accusation with interest, or to be crushed, letting the verdict of strangers become your verdict on yourself. David does neither. He takes the case to the only Judge whose verdict is final, and that frees him from having to win the argument. The Christian has firmer ground still, because that Judge has already spoken: “There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1). Someone who has heard that verdict can be misjudged by the whole internet and still sleep at night, and can even pray for those who are shouting.
verseByVerse.note: Compare Psalm 35:12-13, where David also prayed and fasted for those who repaid him evil for good.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–20 — May Another Take His Office
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The fiercest curses in the Psalter are handed to God, not carried out, and they have a reason. The target narrows to one man, perhaps the leader of David’s enemies: let him be condemned in court with an accuser at his side, lose his office, and leave his family destitute (vv. 6–10); let him receive no pity and be forgotten, while his sins stay before the LORD (vv. 11–15). Why? Because he “pursued the poor and needy and the brokenhearted, to put them to death”, and he loved to curse (vv. 16–17). Let the curses he wore like a coat soak into him (vv. 18–19), and let the LORD give this reward to all David’s accusers (v. 20).
verseByVerse.theology: The fiercest curses in the Psalter, spoken against a man who loved cursing and hunted the poor.

verseByVerse.quote: Appoint a wicked man against him; let an accuser stand at his right hand. When he is tried, let him come forth guilty; let his prayer be counted as sin! May his days be few; may another take his office! May his children be fatherless and his wife a widow! May his children wander about and beg, seeking food far from the ruins they inhabit!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now come the fiercest curses in the Psalter, against one man: let him be condemned in court, lose his office and leave his family destitute. They are among the most shocking words in the Bible, and they are handed to God, not carried out by the man who prays them.

A change of grammar. In verses 2 to 5 the enemies are they. In verses 6 to 19 the target is him, one man. In verse 20 it is plural again: my accusers.

Let an accuser stand at his right hand. The picture is a trial. An accuser (the Hebrew word is satan) stands at the defendant’s right hand, the place of the prosecutor. Hold that detail; the psalm returns to the right hand at the end (v. 31).

Let his prayer be counted as sin! The most frightening line of all. In verse 4 David said, in effect, I am prayer. Here the enemy’s prayer is asked to count against him. Prayer from a man who hunts the poor and has no intention of turning is not neutral; it is hypocrisy, and God is not fooled by it.

May his children be fatherless. The curse spreads to his family. These words are hard to read, and they should be. They are the language of a man utterly wronged, praying in the way of his time, when a man’s whole household rose or fell with him. The law forbade courts to put children to death for a father’s sin (Deuteronomy 24:16); the psalm asks God to let the man’s evil bear its own fruit in his house.

May another take his office! When the apostles gathered after the death of Judas, Peter quoted this verse alongside Psalm 69:25, “Let another take his office” (Acts 1:20), and they chose Matthias. Peter heard in this psalm the voice of David’s greater Son, repaid with hatred for his love, and saw the curse fall on the man who betrayed him and never turned back.

Where Christians differ. Two questions. First, whose words are these? Most readers, and the ESV’s wording, take verses 6 to 19 as David’s prayer against the leader of his enemies; others take them as David quoting the curses his enemies hurl at him, with verse 20 answering, let this come back on them instead. Second, may a Christian pray such words? Some say never, since Jesus commands love and prayer for enemies (Matthew 5:44; Romans 12:14). Others note that Peter applies verse 8 to Judas (Acts 1:20), and that David is not taking revenge but leaving it to God (Romans 12:19).

This commentary’s view. This commentary follows the more common reading, while noting that on either reading the curses are handed to God. A Christian may pray for God’s justice against unrepentant evil, while praying first for the enemy’s repentance, knowing that Christ bore the curse for all who turn to him (Galatians 3:13).
verseByVerse.note: On prayers of this kind, see also Psalms 35, 69 and 137.

verseByVerse.quote: May the creditor seize all that he has; may strangers plunder the fruits of his toil! Let there be none to extend kindness to him, nor any to pity his fatherless children! May his posterity be cut off; may his name be blotted out in the second generation! May the iniquity of his fathers be remembered before the LORD, and let not the sin of his mother be blotted out! Let them be before the LORD continually, that he may cut off the memory of them from the earth!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let the man who showed no kindness receive none, and let his name be forgotten while his sins stay remembered before the LORD.

Let there be none to extend kindness to him. Ruin, and no pity: the creditor and strangers take the fruit of his toil. The man who did not remember to show kindness (v. 16) is to receive none.

May his name be blotted out. The deepest curse is to be forgotten: no descendants, no name, no memory. And his sins are to stay before the LORD continually, the exact opposite of what God does for the forgiven: “as far as the east is from the west, so far does he remove our transgressions from us” (Psalm 103:12). David asks that this man receive what all the unrepentant will receive.

Remembered, or remembered no more. Every one of us stands under one of two sentences: sins kept before the LORD continually, or the promise of the new covenant in Christ, “I will remember their sins no more” (Hebrews 8:12).

How should a Christian pray words like these? Not by carrying them out, and not by praying them against a personal enemy: “Bless those who persecute you; bless and do not curse them” (Romans 12:14; see the note on vv. 6–10). But they still teach something true: that God takes wrongs seriously, that the unrepentant enemies of his people face real judgment, and that the right place for your rage at injustice is in God’s hands. Why are such prayers in Scripture at all? Because God would rather his wronged people bring him their fury honestly than nurse it in secret, and because they tell the truth about what unrepented evil deserves. If you have been wronged by someone who preys on the weak, this psalm gives your anger words and sends it to God’s courtroom.

If the wrong is abuse. Seek safety at once and tell those who can protect you, including the police where a crime has been done. Handing vengeance to God never means staying in harm’s way.

verseByVerse.quote: For he did not remember to show kindness, but pursued the poor and needy and the brokenhearted, to put them to death. He loved to curse; let curses come upon him! He did not delight in blessing; may it be far from him! He clothed himself with cursing as his coat; may it soak into his body like water, like oil into his bones! May it be like a garment that he wraps around him, like a belt that he puts on every day! May this be the reward of my accusers from the LORD, of those who speak evil against my life!
verseByVerse.commentary:
The curses have a reason: this man hunted the poor and the brokenhearted to death and loved to curse, so let the curses he chose come back on him.

Pursued the poor and needy. This is not a private quarrel. The man pursued the poor and needy and the brokenhearted, to put them to death. He is a predator of the weak, and the psalm’s anger is the anger of justice on behalf of his victims.

He loved to curse. The principle: what a man loves, he gets. He loved to curse, so let curses come; he did not delight in blessing, so let blessing stay away. Cursing was his coat and his daily belt, and the cursing he chose to wear soaks into him like water and oil (vv. 18–19). The judgment is not arbitrary.

May this be the reward of my accusers from the LORD. The plural returns, and the reward is left to the LORD to give.

Uncertain wording. The ESV notes that its wording in verse 17 follows a small change of vowels; the Hebrew as it stands reads as statements, curses “have come” and blessing “is far”. Either way, the man receives what he loved.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–31 — He Stands at the Right Hand of the Needy
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The accused man turns from his enemy to God, and finds God standing beside him as his defender. He pleads nothing of his own, only God’s name and steadfast love (v. 21), for he is himself poor, frail and worn with fasting, and mocked by those who see him (vv. 22–25). He asks for a rescue so plainly God’s that his enemies will know it (vv. 26–27). “Let them curse, but you will bless!” (v. 28): their curses will turn to their own shame, and he will give thanks in public (vv. 29–30). For the God who seemed silent stands “at the right hand of the needy one”, the defender’s place (v. 31).
verseByVerse.theology: The accuser stood at the wicked man's right hand; God stands at the right hand of the poor.

verseByVerse.quote: But you, O GOD my Lord, deal on my behalf for your name's sake; because your steadfast love is good, deliver me! For I am poor and needy, and my heart is stricken within me. I am gone like a shadow at evening; I am shaken off like a locust. My knees are weak through fasting; my body has become gaunt, with no fat. I am an object of scorn to my accusers; when they see me, they wag their heads.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Turning from the enemy to God, David pleads not his own deserving but God’s name and steadfast love, for he is himself poor, frail and mocked.

Because your steadfast love is good, deliver me! The grounds of the appeal are God’s name and God’s steadfast love, not David’s merit.

O GOD my Lord. The name is unusual. The ESV prints the first word in capitals because it stands for the covenant name of God, joined here to my Lord, the word for a master. He appeals to the God who bound himself by covenant and to the Master he serves, and a servant under attack has a right to call on his master.

For I am poor and needy. The man who prayed those fierce curses is himself fragile: a fading evening shadow, a locust shaken off a sleeve, weak-kneed and thin from fasting. He has been praying and fasting under the attack. He is one of the poor and needy, the very people the wicked man hunted (v. 16).

When they see me, they wag their heads. At the cross, “those who passed by derided him, wagging their heads” (Matthew 27:39). The one who was truly poor and needy, repaid with hatred for his love, was mocked with the same gesture.

verseByVerse.quote: Help me, O LORD my God! Save me according to your steadfast love! Let them know that this is your hand; you, O LORD, have done it! Let them curse, but you will bless! They arise and are put to shame, but your servant will be glad! May my accusers be clothed with dishonor; may they be wrapped in their own shame as in a cloak! With my mouth I will give great thanks to the LORD; I will praise him in the midst of the throng. For he stands at the right hand of the needy one, to save him from those who condemn his soul to death.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let them curse: God’s blessing will have the last word, the accused man will give public thanks, and God stands at the right hand of the needy as his defender.

Let them know that this is your hand. He wants the rescue to be unmistakably God’s, so that his enemies will know who acted.

Let them curse, but you will bless! Here is the heart of the psalm and the key to reading the curses. The enemies’ words have no final power. If God blesses, their cursing is empty noise.

Wrapped in their own shame as in a cloak! The one who wore cursing as a coat (v. 18) is wrapped in shame as a cloak; the one who was cursed opens his mouth in public thanks in the midst of the throng.

He stands at the right hand of the needy one. The last line reverses the whole psalm. In verse 6 an accuser stood at his right hand, the place of the prosecutor. Now God stands at the right hand of the needy one, the place of the defender. The poor man in the dock looks to his right, and the advocate standing there is God.

Father, forgive them. This is the freedom the gospel gives a believer who is slandered. Jesus, cursed and mocked, prayed, “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do” (Luke 23:34). “When he was reviled, he did not revile in return; when he suffered, he did not threaten, but continued entrusting himself to him who judges justly” (1 Peter 2:23). A Christian can let people curse, because God blesses.

For anyone falsely accused. The wicked man has an accuser beside him; you have a Defender beside you. The New Testament gives him a name: “Who is to condemn? Christ Jesus is the one who died … who is at the right hand of God, who indeed is interceding for us” (Romans 8:34).

109.title: Let Them Curse, but You Will Bless
109.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 109 is the middle of three psalms of David near the start of Book Five (108 to 110; see the introduction). Psalm 108 ended in confidence, “With God we shall do valiantly”; here the same king is slandered by people he had loved. The psalm ends with God standing “at the right hand of the needy one” (v. 31), and the very next psalm opens with God seating David’s Lord at his own right hand.

The message. When you are lied about and repaid with hatred for your love, do not answer in kind: give yourself to prayer and hand the case to God. The psalm does not hide how fierce the anger of the wronged can be, but it carries that anger to God’s courtroom instead of acting it out. And it ends in confidence: “Let them curse, but you will bless!” (v. 28). The poor man in the dock has God himself as his defender.
