Why it was said. David was a king who knew slander, betrayal and plots (see the introduction), and the title gives no single occasion. The psalm was handed “to the choirmaster”, so Israel sang it: a people taught that God takes the hunting of the poor seriously (v. 16), and that the wronged may bring him their fury honestly rather than take revenge.

How the chapter makes its case. Lying mouths attack a man who loved them, and he answers with prayer (vv. 1–5). Then come the fiercest curses in the Psalter, on one man: on his trial, office, family and name (vv. 6–15), because he hunted the poor to death and loved to curse (vv. 16–20). David, himself poor and needy, pleads God’s name and steadfast love (vv. 21–25), and ends sure that God’s blessing outweighs every curse (vv. 26–31). At the start an accuser stands at the wicked man’s right hand (v. 6); at the end God stands at the right hand of the needy (v. 31).

Where it leads. By pattern, and by the need it exposes. David, the king repaid with hatred for love, foreshadows his greater Son: Peter applied verse 8 to Judas (Acts 1:20), and those who passed the cross wagged their heads (v. 25; Matthew 27:39). The psalm’s cry for justice is real, and the curse it calls down must fall somewhere: on the unrepentant, or on the one who “redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us” (Galatians 3:13). And the Defender at the right hand has a name: “Christ Jesus … who is at the right hand of God, who indeed is interceding for us” (Romans 8:34).

For us. When you are slandered, you do not have to win the argument: you can give yourself to prayer. Bring your anger at injustice to God rather than act it out, and pray first for your enemy’s repentance, since you too were rescued from the curse. Whoever curses you, if God blesses, the curse is empty.
109.theology: Answering slander with prayer (v. 4) is the believer's alternative to retaliation. The curses (vv. 6-19) are handed to God, not carried out, and they are grounded in the enemy's hunting of the poor (v. 16). God's blessing makes curses empty (v. 28), and the accuser at the wicked man's right hand (v. 6) is answered by God at the right hand of the needy (v. 31).
109.examples: Someone slandered at work, or betrayed by a friend they helped, can learn from this psalm to answer with prayer instead of accusation, to hand their anger to God the Judge, and to remember that God stands at their right hand as their Defender.

keyVerse.quote: Let them curse, but you will bless! They arise and are put to shame, but your servant will be glad!
keyVerse.note: This is the key to reading the whole psalm, curses included. The enemies’ words have no final power: if God blesses, their cursing is empty noise. It is the freedom Christ showed when, reviled, he did not revile in return but entrusted himself to the Judge.

109.reflection:
David answers lies and hatred with prayer: literally, “I, prayer” (v. 4). When you have been misjudged or slandered, what do you usually do instead, and what would it look like to give yourself to prayer?

The curses of verses 6–20 are shocking. Why might God put prayers like these in Scripture, and how does the cross change the way a Christian prays about people who do evil?

Verse 16 gives the reason for the psalm’s anger: the man hunted “the poor and needy and the brokenhearted.” Where do we see the weak preyed on today, and how should God’s anger at it shape our prayers and actions?

An accuser stood at the wicked man’s right hand (v. 6); God stands at the right hand of the needy (v. 31). How does Romans 8:34 make this personal for you?

110.text: A Psalm of David. 1The LORD says to my Lord: "Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool."2The LORD sends forth from Zion your mighty scepter. Rule in the midst of your enemies!3Your people will offer themselves freely on the day of your power, in holy garments; from the womb of the morning, the dew of your youth will be yours.4The LORD has sworn and will not change his mind, "You are a priest forever after the order of Melchizedek."5The Lord is at your right hand; he will shatter kings on the day of his wrath.6He will execute judgment among the nations, filling them with corpses; he will shatter chiefs over the wide earth.7He will drink from the brook by the way; therefore he will lift up his head.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–3 — The LORD Says to My Lord
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God has seated David’s Lord at his right hand, and he reigns now, in the midst of his enemies, with a willing people. David overhears the LORD speaking to someone David calls “my Lord”, a King greater than David himself, and inviting him to sit at God’s right hand until every enemy is his footstool (v. 1). His sceptre goes out from Zion, and he rules before his enemies are gone (v. 2). His people are volunteers, not conscripts: they offer themselves freely on the day of his power, dressed like priests, fresh as the dew at dawn (v. 3).
verseByVerse.theology: David hears God speak to a King greater than David, seated beside God, reigning while his enemies remain.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD says to my Lord: "Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God speaks to David’s Lord, a King greater than David, and seats him at his own right hand to reign until every enemy lies beneath his feet.

The LORD says to my Lord. The LORD, the covenant name of God, says to my Lord: David overhears God speaking to someone David calls my Lord. But who is a king’s lord? In Israel, David was the king; no one on earth was his lord.

David’s son and David’s Lord. Jesus put exactly that question to the teachers in the temple: “If then David calls him Lord, how is he his son?” And “no one was able to answer him a word” (Matthew 22:45–46). The answer they could not give is that the Messiah would be both David’s son and David’s Lord: human, and more than human.

Sit at my right hand. The right hand of a king was the place of highest honour, and of authority to rule for him. And sit is the posture of a finished work. At Pentecost Peter said that “David did not ascend into the heavens”, quoted this verse, and concluded, “God has made him both Lord and Christ, this Jesus whom you crucified” (Acts 2:34–36). Hebrews explains why he sits: “when Christ had offered for all time a single sacrifice for sins, he sat down at the right hand of God” (Hebrews 10:12). The priests in the temple never sat; their work was never done. This one sat down.

Until I make your enemies your footstool. But there is an until. The King is enthroned now, and his enemies are not yet all under his feet: that is the age we live in (1 Corinthians 15:25). He is “waiting from that time until his enemies should be made a footstool” (Hebrews 10:13). At his trial Jesus told the high priest, “you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of Power” (Mark 14:62). The prisoner in the dock was quoting this verse about himself.

Who wrote it? The Hebrew word for “my Lord” is the ordinary word for a master, used of kings and superiors, and some scholars think a court singer wrote the psalm about the king as his lord. But the title credits David, and Jesus’ argument rests on David himself speaking “in the Spirit” (Matthew 22:43). This commentary follows Jesus, while granting that the question is discussed.

How Jewish readers take it. The Talmud (Nedarim 32b) and Rashi read the psalm of Abraham: after his victory over the kings, when he met Melchizedek (Genesis 14), God seated him at his right hand, and the priesthood of verse 4 passed to him. Others read it of David. Yet the Midrash on the Psalms also sets the Messiah at God’s right hand from this verse, so the messianic reading is not only Christian. This commentary reads it as Jesus did (Matthew 22:41–46), and with Hebrews, of the King who is also a priest in Melchizedek’s order (Hebrews 7:17).

Where Christians differ. Is Christ reigning now? Premillennial readers distinguish his sitting at God’s right hand now from a future reign on David’s throne on earth. Others note that Peter ties David’s throne to Christ’s ascension (Acts 2:30–36), and that Paul says “he must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet” (1 Corinthians 15:25): he reigns now, from heaven, until the last enemy, death, is destroyed.

This commentary’s view. That is why this commentary takes the amillennial view. Faithful Christians who hold premillennial or postmillennial views read these texts differently, and all confess the seated King who will come again.
verseByVerse.note: Verse 1 is quoted or echoed in Matt 22:44; Acts 2:34-35; 1 Cor 15:25; Heb 1:13 and 10:12-13, among other places.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD sends forth from Zion your mighty scepter. Rule in the midst of your enemies! Your people will offer themselves freely on the day of your power, in holy garments; from the womb of the morning, the dew of your youth will be yours.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The enthroned King already rules from Zion in the midst of his enemies, and his people come to him as willing volunteers, dressed like priests.

Rule in the midst of your enemies! The King’s rule goes out from Zion, and it is exercised in the midst of your enemies. He does not wait until every enemy has gone before he begins to reign. That is how the church experiences Christ’s kingship: he is Lord, and the world is still hostile. God “seated him at his right hand in the heavenly places, far above all rule and authority” (Ephesians 1:20–21), while the church on earth still suffers.

Your people will offer themselves freely. The King’s army is made of volunteers. No one is conscripted into this kingdom; the willingness is itself his work by his Spirit on the day of your power. And they come in holy garments, dressed not in armour but like priests, as the armies of heaven in Revelation follow the King “arrayed in fine linen, white and pure” (Revelation 19:14).

Uncertain wording. The rest of verse 3 is one of the hardest lines in the Psalms to translate, and the ESV is honest about it: it notes that on the day of your power may mean “on the day you lead your forces”, that some manuscripts read “on the holy mountains” for in holy garments, and that the meaning of the Hebrew in the last line is uncertain. The picture of the womb of the morning and the dew of your youth seems to be fresh strength appearing like dew at dawn: a young army, or the King’s own unfading vigour. It is wise not to build much on a line the translators themselves hold loosely.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: By God’s unchangeable oath the King is also a priest for ever, and the seated King will rise to judge the earth. No king of Israel could be a priest, yet God swears that this one is, not of Aaron’s line but “after the order of Melchizedek”, the king-priest of Salem who blessed Abraham (v. 4). Then the picture turns to battle: with the Lord at his right hand, he will shatter kings and judge the nations on the day of wrath (vv. 5–6). The psalm ends quietly: refreshed from a brook on the way, he lifts up his head in victory (v. 7).
verseByVerse.theology: The King is also a Priest by God's oath, something no king of Israel could be, and he will judge the earth.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD has sworn and will not change his mind, "You are a priest forever after the order of Melchizedek."
verseByVerse.commentary:
By an oath he will never take back, God makes the King a priest as well, a priest for ever of Melchizedek’s order, which no king of Israel could ever be.

The LORD has sworn and will not change his mind. God does not merely speak; he swears, and will not change his mind. And what he swears is that the King is also a priest.

You are a priest forever. In Israel that was impossible. Kings came from Judah; priests came from Levi. The two offices were strictly separate, and when King Uzziah tried to act as a priest he was struck with leprosy (2 Chronicles 26:16–21). Yet God swears that this King is a priest, not of Aaron’s order, but after the order of Melchizedek.

After the order of Melchizedek. Melchizedek appears briefly in Genesis. After Abraham’s victory the king of Salem, “priest of God Most High”, brought out bread and wine and blessed Abraham, who gave him a tenth (Genesis 14:18–20). He was a real king and a priest in one person, in Salem, that is Jerusalem, generations before Levi was born, and God arranged his life to foreshadow Christ (see on Genesis 14).

Hebrews and this verse. Hebrews builds much of its argument here. Christ “did not exalt himself to be made a high priest” but was appointed by God (Hebrews 5:5–6), and unlike the Levitical priests he “was made a priest with an oath” (Hebrews 7:21).

Why this matters. A king rules you; a priest represents you before God. Jesus is both. The one on the throne is the one who offered the sacrifice for your sins and now intercedes for you. And his priesthood is forever: it will never be handed to a successor who does not know you.

Why would anyone need a priest? To many modern people the idea is an affront: surely I can deal with God directly, on my own terms. But that assumes that I am fit to stand before God as I am, and that the only barrier is religious red tape. The Bible’s diagnosis goes deeper. The problem is not that someone is blocking the door, but that we could not survive walking through it. Israel’s whole priesthood existed to say that a holy God is approached only by sacrifice and through a representative. Religious people err the other way, trusting the ritual or the human priest as though the institution could save them. This verse leaves both behind. It promises a priest who is also the King, appointed by oath, who will never retire or be replaced. Through him the door really is open, and we may “draw near to the throne of grace” with confidence (Hebrews 4:16), not because God has become less holy, but because our priest has gone in ahead of us.
verseByVerse.note: Psalm 76:2 uses Salem, Melchizedek's city, as a name for Jerusalem.

verseByVerse.quote: The Lord is at your right hand; he will shatter kings on the day of his wrath. He will execute judgment among the nations, filling them with corpses; he will shatter chiefs over the wide earth. He will drink from the brook by the way; therefore he will lift up his head.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The seated King will rise as Judge: with the Lord beside him he will shatter hostile kings on the day of wrath, and, refreshed on the way, lift up his head in victory.

The Lord is at your right hand. In verse 1 the King sat at God’s right hand; now the King is told, the Lord is at your right hand: God fights beside him. And a day of his wrath is coming, when kings who have set themselves against him will be shattered. The seated King will not sit for ever while his enemies rage.

He will execute judgment among the nations. The language of the battlefield is meant to be terrible. John saw that day: “for the great day of their wrath has come” (Revelation 6:17). The gospel invitation is urgent because the day of wrath is real. There is time now, while he sits, to come to him as priest before he rises as judge.

He will drink from the brook by the way. A quiet, strange image to end with: the warrior-King, in the middle of the campaign, stops to drink from the brook by the way, refreshed on the march, and then will lift up his head, the posture of victory.

Therefore he will lift up his head. Many Christians have heard in it the shape of Christ’s whole life: the King who stooped low and walked the dusty roads like any traveller, who “bowed his head and gave up his spirit” (John 19:30), and who was raised and exalted to the right hand of God (Philippians 2:8–9). The psalm begins with him sitting down and ends with his head lifted high. Everything between is his reign, and the church lives in the until of verse 1, waiting for the day when every enemy is under his feet.

Uncertain wording. In verses 5 to 7 the Hebrew does not make plain at each point who “he” is: the Lord fighting at the King’s side, or the King himself. Most take the one who drinks and lifts his head (v. 7) to be the King. Either way, God and his King act as one. The ESV also notes that chiefs (v. 6) may be read “the head”, which may set the head of the enemy that is shattered against the King’s head that is lifted up.

110.title: Sit at My Right Hand
110.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 110 closes the little group of David’s psalms at the start of Book Five (108 to 110). Psalm 109 ended with God standing “at the right hand of the needy one”; this psalm opens with God seating David’s Lord at his own right hand. Short as it is, it is quoted or echoed in the New Testament more often than almost any other Old Testament passage.

The message. God has enthroned a King greater than David, seated at his right hand and ruling now in the midst of his enemies, with a people who come to him willingly. By an oath he will never take back, God has also made this King a priest for ever, of Melchizedek’s order. One day the seated King will rise to judge the nations. The one who rules his people is also the one who represents them before God, and he will never be replaced.

Why it was said. Israel’s kings were never more than men, and even David’s line would fail and fall into exile (see the introduction). Spoken by David “in the Holy Spirit” (Mark 12:36), this psalm taught Israel to look beyond every king they had to one David himself called Lord, a king who would also be a priest, which the law allowed no king of Israel to be.

How the chapter makes its case. Two oracles, each followed by its result. First, God speaks: sit at my right hand until your enemies are your footstool (v. 1). So the King rules from Zion in the midst of his enemies, and his people offer themselves freely on the day of his power (vv. 2–3). Second, God swears: you are a priest for ever after the order of Melchizedek (v. 4). So, with the Lord at his right hand, the King will shatter hostile kings on the day of wrath, drink from the brook by the way, and lift up his head (vv. 5–7).

Where it leads. By direct promise. This is one of the few psalms the New Testament reads straight of the Messiah. Jesus asked how David’s son could be David’s Lord (Matthew 22:41–46), and at his trial claimed verse 1 for himself (Mark 14:62). Peter preached it at Pentecost of the risen Jesus (Acts 2:34–36), Paul of his present reign (1 Corinthians 15:25), and Hebrews builds its whole account of Christ’s priesthood on verse 4. The King who sat down at God’s right hand sat down because his sacrifice was finished (Hebrews 10:12).

For us. Your King has sat down, so the sacrifice for your sins is complete; and he reigns now, even when the world is hostile, because we live in the “until” of verse 1. Through him, your priest for ever, you may draw near to God with confidence. And since a day of wrath is coming, the time to come to him as priest is now, while he sits, before he rises as Judge.
110.theology: The Messiah is David's son and David's Lord (v. 1). He is seated at God's right hand, his sacrifice finished, reigning now amid his enemies until all are under his feet (vv. 1-2), with a people who offer themselves freely (v. 3). By an unchangeable oath he is also a priest forever after the order of Melchizedek (v. 4), and the seated King will rise as Judge (vv. 5-6).
110.examples: The priests in the temple never sat down; this one did, because his work is finished. A Christian discouraged by the hostility of the world lives in the time of the word until (v. 1): Christ reigns already, and his enemies are not yet under his feet. His King is also his Priest, whose priesthood will never pass to a successor who does not know him.

keyVerse.quote: The LORD says to my Lord: “Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool.”
keyVerse.note: No Old Testament verse is quoted more often in the New. It shows a King who is David’s son and also David’s Lord, seated beside God because his work is finished, reigning now while his enemies remain. The word “until” describes the age the church lives in.

110.reflection:
Jesus asked, “If then David calls him Lord, how is he his son?” (Matthew 22:45). How would you answer his question, and why does the answer matter for who Jesus is?

The priests in the temple never sat down; Christ “sat down at the right hand of God” (Hebrews 10:12). What difference does a finished sacrifice make to the way you approach God when you feel guilty?

Christ rules “in the midst of your enemies” (v. 2), and his enemies are not yet under his feet. Where do you find it hard to believe he is reigning now, and how does the word “until” help?

In Jesus the King is also the Priest (v. 4). Why do we need both, and which do we tend to forget?

111.text: <sup>1</sup>Praise the LORD! I will give thanks to the LORD with my whole heart, in the company of the upright, in the congregation.<sup>2</sup>Great are the works of the LORD, studied by all who delight in them.<sup>3</sup>Full of splendor and majesty is his work, and his righteousness endures forever.<sup>4</sup>He has caused his wondrous works to be remembered; the LORD is gracious and merciful.<sup>5</sup>He provides food for those who fear him; he remembers his covenant forever.<sup>6</sup>He has shown his people the power of his works, in giving them the inheritance of the nations.<sup>7</sup>The works of his hands are faithful and just; all his precepts are trustworthy;<sup>8</sup>they are established forever and ever, to be performed with faithfulness and uprightness.<sup>9</sup>He sent redemption to his people; he has commanded his covenant forever. Holy and awesome is his name!<sup>10</sup>The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom; all those who practice it have a good understanding. His praise endures forever!

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — Studied by All Who Delight in Them
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s works are great enough to study with delight for a lifetime, and behind them stands a gracious and merciful God. The psalm is an alphabet of praise, A to Z, given with the whole heart and in the gathered congregation (v. 1). The works of the LORD are great, “studied by all who delight in them” (v. 2); they are full of splendour and majesty, and his righteousness endures for ever (v. 3). He has built memorials into his people’s life so that his wonders are not forgotten, and the character they reveal is that “the LORD is gracious and merciful” (v. 4).
verseByVerse.theology: An alphabet of praise: God's works are great enough to study for a lifetime.

verseByVerse.quote: Praise the LORD! I will give thanks to the LORD with my whole heart, in the company of the upright, in the congregation. Great are the works of the LORD, studied by all who delight in them. Full of splendor and majesty is his work, and his righteousness endures forever. He has caused his wondrous works to be remembered; the LORD is gracious and merciful.
verseByVerse.commentary:
With his whole heart and among God’s people the psalmist praises the LORD’s works: great enough to study for a lifetime, splendid and lasting, and done by a God who is gracious and merciful.

Twin psalms. This psalm and the next are twins. Both begin Praise the LORD! Both are acrostics: as the ESV notes, each line in Hebrew begins with the next letter of the alphabet, twenty-two lines packed into ten verses, praise from A to Z with nothing left out. And they are designed as a pair: Psalm 111 describes God, and Psalm 112 describes the person who fears God, using many of the same words. Read together, they show a believer growing to resemble the God he worships.

With my whole heart. The praise is given with my whole heart and in the congregation: wholehearted and public. Private devotion and gathered worship belong together.

Studied by all who delight in them. God’s works are not only to be admired but studied: searched out, investigated, pondered, by all who delight in them. Study is a form of delight, and delight drives study. This verse is a charter for every believer who has ever looked through a microscope or a telescope, read history, or traced the providence of God in a single life. In Latin it was carved over the door of the Cavendish Laboratory in Cambridge, where much of modern physics was done.

His righteousness endures forever. Hold that phrase; Psalm 112 will say the same of a human being (112:3).

He has caused his wondrous works to be remembered. God built memorials into Israel’s life, the Passover, the feasts, the stones by the Jordan, so that no generation would forget. The Lord’s Supper does the same for Christians: “Do this in remembrance of me” (Luke 22:19).

The LORD is gracious and merciful. The character behind the works is the one God proclaimed to Moses: “The LORD, the LORD, a God merciful and gracious” (Exodus 34:6). Psalm 112 will use the same words of the upright man (112:4).
verseByVerse.note: Psalms 111 and 112 are a matched pair of acrostics; compare also Psalms 25, 34, 119 and 145.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–10 — Holy and Awesome Is His Name
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The God who feeds and redeems his people is holy, and the first lesson of wisdom is to fear him. He provides food for those who fear him and never forgets his covenant (v. 5). He showed his power by giving a nation of slaves the land of stronger nations (v. 6). His works are faithful and just, and so are his commands, which stand for ever (vv. 7–8). Greatest of all, he sent redemption to his people and bound himself to them by covenant: holy and awesome is his name (v. 9). So the psalm ends where wisdom begins, with the fear of the LORD (v. 10).
verseByVerse.theology: The God who feeds and redeems his people is holy, and the first lesson of wisdom is to fear him.

verseByVerse.quote: He provides food for those who fear him; he remembers his covenant forever. He has shown his people the power of his works, in giving them the inheritance of the nations. The works of his hands are faithful and just; all his precepts are trustworthy; they are established forever and ever, to be performed with faithfulness and uprightness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The God of great works cares for daily needs, keeps his covenant, gave his people the land, and his commands are as faithful as his deeds.

He provides food for those who fear him. Food first: the manna and the quail in the wilderness, and every daily meal since. God’s greatness does not make him distant from ordinary needs, and he keeps providing because he remembers his covenant forever. Jesus, who fed the hungry crowds, said, “I am the bread of life” (John 6:35): the God who feeds those who fear him finally gives himself.

The inheritance of the nations. The gift of the land showed God’s power: a people of slaves given the territory of nations stronger than they. It was also judgment: God had waited centuries, until the sin of Canaan’s peoples was full (Genesis 15:16).

All his precepts are trustworthy. The psalm moves from God’s works to God’s precepts without a break. What God does and what God commands come from the same character: both are faithful, just, trustworthy. A person who trusts God’s works but resents his commands has not seen that the same faithful God stands behind both. And the precepts are established, a word Psalm 112 will use of the believer’s heart (the ESV notes it at 112:8, with a pointer back to this verse).

Uncertain wording. The word for food (v. 5) usually means prey, food torn by a wild beast. Here, as occasionally elsewhere, it seems to mean simply food or provision. The sense is plain: God feeds his people.

verseByVerse.quote: He sent redemption to his people; he has commanded his covenant forever. Holy and awesome is his name! The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom; all those who practice it have a good understanding. His praise endures forever!
verseByVerse.commentary:
The greatest of God’s works is redemption, and it makes his name more awesome, not less; so the wise begin where the psalm ends, with the fear of the LORD.

He sent redemption to his people. The deepest work of all. In Israel’s history that was the exodus and the return from exile. In its fullest sense it is the redemption God sent in his Son: at the birth of John the Baptist, Zechariah blessed the God who “has visited and redeemed his people” (Luke 1:68).

Holy and awesome is his name! Mary, carrying that redemption in her womb, sang words that echo this line: “for he who is mighty has done great things for me, and holy is his name” (Luke 1:49). God’s kindness in redeeming does not make him a God to treat casually. Redemption gives more reason to revere his name, not less.

The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom. The psalm arrives at the motto of the Bible’s wisdom literature (compare Proverbs 9:10). After studying God’s great works, his grace, his faithfulness and his holiness, the wise response is fear: not terror that runs away, but reverent awe that bows down and obeys. Beginning means both the starting point and the first principle. You cannot be wise about anything, money, marriage, work or death, while ignoring the God who made it. And wisdom is not only knowing: all those who practice it have a good understanding. The next psalm begins exactly where this one ends: Blessed is the man who fears the LORD (112:1).

More information, less wisdom. We are the best-informed generation in history, and it is not obvious that we are the wisest. Anyone can look up the dose of a drug or the history of an empire in seconds. What no search engine can tell us is what a life is for, what we should love most, and what to do with all we know. The modern assumption is that wisdom is simply knowledge plus experience, piled up on our own. The psalm says it begins somewhere else: with the fear of the LORD, a right relation to the One who made the facts. Without that beginning, knowledge does not make us wise; it makes us clever, and cleverness is very good at justifying what we already wanted. The religious can make the same mistake, collecting Bible knowledge while the heart stays proud. The New Testament names the beginning more personally: in Christ “are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Colossians 2:3). Wisdom starts not with a better database but with bowing before a person.

111.title: The Fear of the LORD Is the Beginning of Wisdom
111.overview:
Where we are. After the royal Psalm 110, Book Five turns to pure praise: Psalms 111, 112 and 113 all begin “Praise the LORD!” (in Hebrew, Hallelujah). Psalms 111 and 112 are twins, matching alphabet poems: this one describes God, and the next describes the person who fears him, in many of the same words.

The message. The works of the LORD are great, gracious and faithful, from daily bread to the redemption he sent his people, and they are worth a lifetime of delighted study. Behind every work stands one character, gracious and merciful, faithful and just, holy and awesome. The right response to such a God is reverent awe, and that is where all true wisdom begins.

Why it was said. Israel praised God “in the congregation” (v. 1), and this psalm kept the great works of their history before each generation: the manna, the covenant, the gift of the land, the redemption from slavery. God “caused his wondrous works to be remembered” (v. 4), and the psalm is one of the ways he did it. It ends with the motto of Israel’s wisdom books (see the introduction on the kinds of psalms).

How the chapter makes its case. A vow of wholehearted, public thanks (v. 1). God’s works are great and studied by those who delight in them, splendid, lasting and memorable, the works of a gracious and merciful God (vv. 2–4). He feeds those who fear him, remembers his covenant, and gave his people the land (vv. 5–6). His works and his precepts share one faithful character (vv. 7–8). Above all he sent redemption, and his name is holy and awesome (v. 9). So the wise begin with the fear of the LORD (v. 10).

Where it leads. By the character of God revealed in Christ, and by the redemption he promised. “He sent redemption to his people” (v. 9) is fulfilled when God sends his Son: Zechariah blessed the God who “has visited and redeemed his people” (Luke 1:68), and Mary sang, “holy is his name” (Luke 1:49). The God who fed Israel gives himself as “the bread of life” (John 6:35), and in Christ “are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Colossians 2:3).

For us. Look for God’s works with delight, in creation, in history and in your own life, and let the Lord’s Supper keep his greatest work before you. Let his grace deepen your reverence rather than make you casual with him. Whatever you want to be wise about, begin by bowing before him.
111.theology: Psalm 111 describes God, and its twin, Psalm 112, describes the God-fearer in the same words: worshippers grow like the God they worship. God's works invite delighted study (v. 2), and his works and precepts share one faithful character (vv. 7-8). Redemption makes his name more awesome, not less (v. 9), and the fear of the LORD is where wisdom begins (v. 10).
111.examples: The scientist at a microscope, the historian in an archive and the believer tracing God's hand through one ordinary life are all doing what verse 2 commends. The Lord's Supper is one of the memorials God built into his people's calendar so that they would not forget.

keyVerse.quote: The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom; all those who practice it have a good understanding.
keyVerse.note: After nine verses on God’s great, gracious and faithful works, this is the conclusion: a God like this is to be revered. It is the motto of the Bible’s wisdom books, and it leads straight into Psalm 112, which describes the person who fears the LORD.

111.reflection:
“Great are the works of the LORD, studied by all who delight in them” (v. 2). Which of God’s works, in creation, in Scripture or in your own life, would you most like to study more closely, and why?

God “has caused his wondrous works to be remembered” (v. 4). What helps you remember what God has done, and how does the Lord’s Supper serve that purpose?

Verses 7–8 put God’s works and his commands side by side as equally trustworthy. Are there commands of God you find easier to resent than to trust? What does this psalm say to that?

What is the difference between the fear of the LORD and being afraid of God, and why does grace deepen this fear rather than remove it?

112.text: <sup>1</sup>Praise the LORD! Blessed is the man who fears the LORD, who greatly delights in his commandments!<sup>2</sup>His offspring will be mighty in the land; the generation of the upright will be blessed.<sup>3</sup>Wealth and riches are in his house, and his righteousness endures forever.<sup>4</sup>Light dawns in the darkness for the upright; he is gracious, merciful, and righteous.<sup>5</sup>It is well with the man who deals generously and lends; who conducts his affairs with justice.<sup>6</sup>For the righteous will never be moved; he will be remembered forever.<sup>7</sup>He is not afraid of bad news; his heart is firm, trusting in the LORD.<sup>8</sup>His heart is steady; he will not be afraid, until he looks in triumph on his adversaries.<sup>9</sup>He has distributed freely; he has given to the poor; his righteousness endures forever; his horn is exalted in honor.<sup>10</sup>The wicked man sees it and is angry; he gnashes his teeth and melts away; the desire of the wicked will perish!

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Blessed Is the Man Who Fears the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Psalm 111 described God; Psalm 112 describes the person who fears him, and he has begun to look like God. He fears the LORD and delights in his commands (v. 1). His household is blessed, and, in words Psalm 111 used of God, “his righteousness endures forever” (vv. 2–3). He is not spared darkness, but light dawns for him, and like the LORD he is “gracious, merciful, and righteous” (v. 4). His grace shows in his finances: he lends generously and conducts his affairs with justice (v. 5). Such a person will not be moved, and will be remembered for ever (v. 6).
verseByVerse.theology: Psalm 111 described God; Psalm 112 describes the person who fears him, and he has begun to look like God.

verseByVerse.quote: Praise the LORD! Blessed is the man who fears the LORD, who greatly delights in his commandments! His offspring will be mighty in the land; the generation of the upright will be blessed. Wealth and riches are in his house, and his righteousness endures forever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The person who fears the LORD and delights in his commands is truly blessed, and his righteousness, like God’s, endures for ever.

The twin psalm. Psalm 111 ended, The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom. Psalm 112 describes the man who has made that beginning. It is another acrostic, and it uses the language of 111 deliberately: what was said of God there is said of the God-fearer here.

Blessed is the man who fears the LORD. Two things we might keep apart belong together: he fears the LORD and he greatly delights in his commandments. He is the man of the first psalm, whose “delight is in the law of the LORD” (Psalm 1:2). Reverence for God does not make his commands a burden; it makes them a joy.

His offspring will be mighty in the land. Strong children and a prosperous household must be read as the wisdom books read: the normal pattern of God’s world, not a guarantee for every individual. Job feared God and lost everything, and Psalm 73 wrestled with the wicked prospering. The psalm is not a promise that believers will be rich; it is a picture of the goodness that tends to grow around a righteous life.

His righteousness endures forever. The first echo. Psalm 111:3 said of God, his righteousness endures forever; now the same words are used of a man. His righteousness reflects God’s own, and because it is rooted in God it lasts. Wealth passes; this does not.
verseByVerse.note: Like Psalm 1, which it echoes, it opens with a blessing and closes with the end of the wicked.

verseByVerse.quote: Light dawns in the darkness for the upright; he is gracious, merciful, and righteous. It is well with the man who deals generously and lends; who conducts his affairs with justice. For the righteous will never be moved; he will be remembered forever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The upright are not spared darkness, but light dawns for them, and like the God they fear they become gracious, merciful and generous, dealing justly and standing firm.

Light dawns in the darkness for the upright. The upright man is not spared darkness, but in the darkness light dawns: the same promise as Psalm 97:11, where light is “sown for the righteous” and some ancient witnesses read “Light dawns”.

He is gracious, merciful, and righteous. The second echo, and the whole point of the twin psalms. Psalm 111:4 said, the LORD is gracious and merciful. The man who fears God becomes gracious and merciful himself. We become like what we worship: a person who spends his life delighting in a gracious God is slowly made gracious by the Spirit (2 Corinthians 3:18).

The man who deals generously and lends. The grace shows in his finances. He deals generously and lends, not grasping, not exploiting. In Israel a loan was usually help for a neighbour fallen on hard times, and the law forbade charging a poor brother interest (Exodus 22:25; Deuteronomy 15:7–8), so to lend was an act of mercy, not a business deal. And he conducts his affairs with justice. Godliness is not only what happens in the congregation; it is visible in how a man handles money and contracts.

He will be remembered forever. He is stable, and his memory lasts: “The memory of the righteous is a blessing, but the name of the wicked will rot” (Proverbs 10:7).

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew of verse 4 does not say who is gracious, merciful and righteous. The ESV takes it of the upright man; some take it of the LORD himself, the light who dawns for the upright. Either way, the upright reflect him.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A heart fixed on God does not panic at bad news, and an open hand gives to the poor. The God-fearer is not afraid of bad news, because his heart is firm, trusting in the LORD; it is steady, and he will not be afraid until he sees God’s justice done (vv. 7–8). He has distributed freely to the poor, his righteousness endures, and God raises his horn in honour (v. 9). The wicked man watches this steady, generous life with fury; he gnashes his teeth and melts away, and his desire perishes with him (v. 10). As in Psalm 1, the two ways end far apart.
verseByVerse.theology: A heart fixed on God does not panic at the phone call, and an open hand gives to the poor.

verseByVerse.quote: He is not afraid of bad news; his heart is firm, trusting in the LORD. His heart is steady; he will not be afraid, until he looks in triumph on his adversaries.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The God-fearer does not live in dread of bad news, because his heart is fixed and steadied by trust in the LORD.

He is not afraid of bad news. Not that bad news never comes; the verse assumes it will. The phone rings late at night; the letter from the hospital arrives; the manager asks to see you. The God-fearer is not immune to any of it, but he is not ruled by the dread of it.

His heart is firm, trusting in the LORD. His heart is fixed on something bad news cannot touch. Isaiah said the same: “You keep him in perfect peace whose mind is stayed on you, because he trusts in you” (Isaiah 26:3). Fear of bad news is really fear that something will happen outside God’s hand. The heart that trusts God knows nothing can.

His heart is steady. Steady may be read “established”, the ESV notes, pointing back to 111:8, where God’s precepts are established forever. The heart is steady because it rests on what God has established. And the fearlessness lasts until he looks in triumph on his adversaries: not gloating, but seeing God’s justice done. “Perfect love casts out fear” (1 John 4:18).

A test to run on yourself. What is the news you most dread? Put it into this verse: he is not afraid of that, his heart is firm, trusting in the LORD. The fear will not vanish in a moment, but the verse shows where firmness comes from. If dread has become constant and crushing, talk to a pastor or biblical counsellor and see your doctor as well; medicine for anxiety is no failure of faith.

verseByVerse.quote: He has distributed freely; he has given to the poor; his righteousness endures forever; his horn is exalted in honor. The wicked man sees it and is angry; he gnashes his teeth and melts away; the desire of the wicked will perish!
verseByVerse.commentary:
The God-fearer gives freely to the poor and is raised in honour, while the wicked watch with fury and their desires come to nothing.

He has given to the poor. His generosity is not occasional: he has distributed freely; he has given to the poor. And for the second time, his righteousness endures forever (vv. 3, 9).

His horn is exalted in honor. A “horn” is the Old Testament picture of strength and honour; the generous man is raised in standing before God and men (compare 1 Samuel 2:1).

The desire of the wicked will perish! As in Psalm 1, the end is a contrast. The wicked man watches the righteous man’s steady, generous life and is enraged by it. He grinds his teeth and melts away. The righteous man’s righteousness endures for ever; the wicked man’s desire perishes with him.

One man fitted it completely. Side by side, the two psalms show that the fear of the LORD makes a person like God. Only one man has ever fitted Psalm 112 completely: the Son, of whom Isaiah said, “And his delight shall be in the fear of the LORD” (Isaiah 11:3). Those joined to him by faith are counted righteous in him, even where they fall short of this psalm, and are slowly made like him.

Christian giving. Paul quoted verse 9 when he urged the Corinthians to give generously to the poor believers in Jerusalem (2 Corinthians 9:9). Christian giving is not a tax; it is what the God-fearing heart does, and it lasts longer than the money that was given.
verseByVerse.note: Compare 75:10 and 92:10, where God also raises the horn of the righteous.

112.title: He Is Not Afraid of Bad News
112.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 112 is the twin of Psalm 111, another alphabet poem that begins “Praise the LORD!” Psalm 111 ended, “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom”; Psalm 112 begins, “Blessed is the man who fears the LORD”, and describes him in words Psalm 111 used of God himself.

The message. The person who fears the LORD and delights in his commands comes to resemble the God he worships: gracious, merciful and righteous, generous to the poor and just in business. He is not spared darkness or bad news, but his heart is fixed on the LORD, so he is not ruled by dread. His righteousness lasts for ever, while the desire of the wicked comes to nothing.

Why it was said. Like Psalm 1, which it echoes, this is wisdom teaching for Israel’s worshippers, showing what a God-fearing life looks like at home, with money and under pressure (see the introduction). Its blessings describe the normal pattern of God’s world, not a guarantee for every believer, as Job and Psalm 73 make plain.

How the chapter makes its case. The God-fearer is blessed and delights in God’s commands (v. 1); his household flourishes and his righteousness endures (vv. 2–3). Light dawns for him in the dark, and he is gracious, merciful and righteous (v. 4), lending generously and dealing justly, never moved and long remembered (vv. 5–6). He is not afraid of bad news, because his heart is firm and steady in the LORD (vv. 7–8). He gives freely to the poor and is raised in honour (v. 9), while the wicked watch, rage, and melt away (v. 10).

Where it leads. By pattern, and by the need it exposes. Only one man has ever fitted this portrait completely: the Son of whom Isaiah said, “And his delight shall be in the fear of the LORD” (Isaiah 11:3), who gave everything to the poor and did not flinch from the worst news of all, the cross. The rest of us fall short of this psalm. Joined to Christ by faith we are counted righteous in him, and by his Spirit we are slowly made like him; so Paul can quote verse 9 of the generosity grace produces (2 Corinthians 9:9).

For us. The fear of God frees us from the fear of everything else, including the phone call we dread. And grace received should show in grace given: in our lending, our business dealings and our giving to the poor.
112.theology: The God-fearer is described in the terms Psalm 111 used of God (vv. 3, 4, 8, 9): those who fear God come to resemble him. Fear of God and delight in his commands belong together (v. 1). Material blessing is the general pattern, not a guarantee (vv. 2-3), and godliness shows itself in generosity (vv. 5, 9) and in a heart that trusts God when bad news comes (vv. 7-8).
112.examples: The person who dreads the late-night phone call can take this psalm to that fear. Its answer is not that nothing bad will happen but that a heart fixed on God has something no news can take. And a person who spends his life delighting in a gracious God slowly becomes gracious too, in his contracts, loans and gifts.

keyVerse.quote: He is not afraid of bad news; his heart is firm, trusting in the LORD.
keyVerse.note: The verse does not promise that bad news will never come; it assumes it will. It shows where firmness comes from: a heart fixed on the LORD has something no news can take away. The one who fears God need not fear anything else.

112.reflection:
Psalm 112 describes the God-fearer in words Psalm 111 used of God (compare 111:3–4 with 112:3–4). In what ways have you seen someone grow to resemble the God they worship?

How should we read the promises of prosperity in verses 2–3, given Job, Psalm 73 and the cross? What does the psalm promise, and what does it not?

What is the bad news you most dread? What would it mean for your heart to be “firm, trusting in the LORD” (v. 7) about that very thing?

Paul quotes verse 9 to encourage generous giving (2 Corinthians 9:9). How does God’s grace to us shape the way we handle money, lending and giving?

113.text: <sup>1</sup>Praise the LORD! Praise, O servants of the LORD, praise the name of the LORD!<sup>2</sup>Blessed be the name of the LORD from this time forth and forevermore!<sup>3</sup>From the rising of the sun to its setting, the name of the LORD is to be praised!<sup>4</sup>The LORD is high above all nations, and his glory above the heavens!<sup>5</sup>Who is like the LORD our God, who is seated on high,<sup>6</sup>who looks far down on the heavens and the earth?<sup>7</sup>He raises the poor from the dust and lifts the needy from the ash heap,<sup>8</sup>to make them sit with princes, with the princes of his people.<sup>9</sup>He gives the barren woman a home, making her the joyous mother of children. Praise the LORD!

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–3 — From the Rising of the Sun to Its Setting
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The LORD’s name is to be praised by his servants always and everywhere. The psalm opens with a threefold call to praise, addressed to “servants of the LORD”, a people who once served Pharaoh and now serve the God who freed them (v. 1). Then the praise is stretched in two directions. Verse 2 stretches it through time, “from this time forth and forevermore”. Verse 3 stretches it across space, “from the rising of the sun to its setting”. There is no hour of history and no corner of the earth where the LORD’s name does not deserve to be blessed.
verseByVerse.theology: Praise for the name of the LORD in every time and every place.

verseByVerse.quote: Praise the LORD! Praise, O servants of the LORD, praise the name of the LORD! Blessed be the name of the LORD from this time forth and forevermore! From the rising of the sun to its setting, the name of the LORD is to be praised!
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD’s servants are to bless his name at every time and in every place.

Praise, O servants of the LORD. Praise is called for three times over, and the singers are “servants of the LORD”: a people brought out of Egypt, who once served Pharaoh now serve and praise the LORD.

Blessed be the name of the LORD. Three times in three verses comes “the name of the LORD”, his revealed character. Verse 2 stretches its praise through time, “from this time forth and forevermore”; verse 3 across space, “from the rising of the sun to its setting”. No hour and no place is outside it, and Malachi promised that this name “will be great among the nations” (Malachi 1:11).

The Hallel psalms. This psalm opens a group of six (113–118), the Hallel (“praise”), that in later Jewish practice were sung at the great festivals, and especially at Passover. By tradition Psalms 113 and 114 were sung before the Passover meal and 115 to 118 after it. So when the Gospels say of the Last Supper, “And when they had sung a hymn, they went out to the Mount of Olives” (Mark 14:26), these are very probably the words Jesus sang that night.
verseByVerse.note: Psalms 113–118 are called the “Egyptian Hallel” because they celebrate the exodus; they are still sung in synagogues at the great festivals.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–9 — He Raises the Poor from the Dust
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The God who is higher than the heavens stoops lower than anyone else would go. He is high above every nation, and his glory is above the heavens, so that even to see the sky he must look far down (vv. 4–6). That leads to the question “Who is like the LORD our God?” and the answer is the surprise of the psalm. His height does not keep him distant; it is the measure of how far he bends. He lifts the poor from the dust and the needy from the ash heap and seats them with princes, and he gives the barren woman a home and the joy of children (vv. 7–9).
verseByVerse.theology: The God so high that he stoops to see the sky stoops further still, to the rubbish heap, to lift the poor.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD is high above all nations, and his glory above the heavens! Who is like the LORD our God, who is seated on high, who looks far down on the heavens and the earth?
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one is like the LORD: he is so high that he must stoop even to look at the heavens.

The LORD is high above all nations. Now the reason for the praise. God is high above every empire, including the one Israel came out of, and his glory is “above the heavens”: the sky is not his ceiling but beneath his feet.

Who is like the LORD our God? He “looks far down”, not only on the earth but on “the heavens”. To see the stars, he has to stoop. Who is like him? No one.

The God who stoops. Yet this God does not stay aloof: he bends. And it goes further than the psalmist could see. The Son, “though he was in the form of God”, “emptied himself, by taking the form of a servant”, and “humbled himself by becoming obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross” (Philippians 2:6–8). God did not only look down. He came down.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew of verses 5–6 is compressed, roughly “who sits high, who stoops low to see, in the heavens and on the earth”. The ESV has God looking down on both; others translate “who humbles himself to look”, or pair the lines: enthroned in the heavens, looking down on the earth. Either way, the one who sits highest is the one who stoops.

verseByVerse.quote: He raises the poor from the dust and lifts the needy from the ash heap, to make them sit with princes, with the princes of his people. He gives the barren woman a home, making her the joyous mother of children. Praise the LORD!
verseByVerse.commentary:
The high God stoops lowest of all: he lifts the destitute from the rubbish heap to sit with princes, and gives the childless woman a home.

He raises the poor from the dust. He looks not at the palaces but at “the dust” and “the ash heap”, the town rubbish dump outside the walls, where the destitute and diseased sat and begged. There he picks up the poor.

To make them sit with princes. He does not merely feed them there; he seats them “with the princes of his people”. From the dump to the royal table. These are almost exactly the words of Hannah, mother of Samuel, when God answered her prayer (1 Samuel 2:8). And Mary sang the same reversal when she carried the Christ: “he has brought down the mighty from their thrones and exalted those of humble estate; he has filled the hungry with good things” (Luke 1:52–53). That is the gospel: God finds people on the rubbish heap of their sin and shame and seats them at the King’s table.

He gives the barren woman a home. The psalm ends with the most personal reversal. In Israel a woman without children often lived with shame and insecurity. The Bible tells of many, Sarah, Rachel, Hannah and Elizabeth among them, and God gave each a child.

For those who long for a child. This verse needs to be handled tenderly. It describes the kind of thing God does; it is not a promise that every woman who longs for a child will have one, and many faithful women do not. But it tells every woman who carries that sorrow that God sees the one society overlooks, and that his heart is to give her a home: a place, belonging, joy. In Christ, no one in God’s household is without family. The God who stoops to the ash heap has not stopped stooping.

113.title: Who Is Like the LORD Our God?
113.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 113 opens the Hallel (Psalms 113–118), the six psalms of praise that Israel came to sing at its great feasts, and especially at Passover. Like the twin psalms before it, 111 and 112, it begins with “Praise the LORD!”, and it ends with the same cry.

The message. No one is like the LORD. He is so high that even the heavens lie beneath him, and yet his greatness is shown most clearly in how low he stoops: down to the rubbish heap, to lift the poor to a seat among princes, and into the quiet grief of a childless home. Because he is that kind of God, his name deserves praise at every hour and in every place.

Why it was said. Israel had once been the poor in the dust, slaves in Egypt, and this was a song for a people who remembered their rescue (see the introduction on the Passover psalms). The gods of the great empires were thought to favour the strong; Israel’s God notices the overlooked, and his servants sing it.

How the chapter makes its case. The psalm moves from the widest horizon to a single house. First the call: the servants of the LORD are to bless his name through all time and across all the earth (vv. 1–3). Then the reason: the LORD is high above the nations and the heavens, so high that he must stoop even to look at them (vv. 4–6). Then the surprise: he stoops further still, raising the needy from the ash heap to sit with princes and giving the barren woman a home and children (vv. 7–9).

Where it leads. To Christ, by the character of God revealed in him and by a pattern that runs through Scripture. Hannah sang this reversal when God gave her a son (1 Samuel 2:8), and Mary sang it when she carried the Christ (Luke 1:52–53). In the psalm God stoops to look; in Christ he came down, “taking the form of a servant” and going to “death on a cross” (Philippians 2:7–8). Jesus very probably sang this psalm on the night he was betrayed, on his way lower than any ash heap, so that God might raise us up and seat us with him “in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus” (Ephesians 2:6).

For us. No one is beneath God’s notice: not the poor, not the ashamed, not the woman whose sorrow no one else sees. Praise him wherever you are today, and let his stooping shape how you treat the people others overlook.
113.theology: God is incomparably exalted, above the heavens themselves (vv. 4-6), and his greatness is shown in his stooping to the lowest (vv. 7-9). In the psalm God stoops to look; in Christ he came down, when the Son humbled himself to the cross (Phil 2:6-8).
113.examples: Jesus very probably sang this psalm on the night he was betrayed, about to go lower than any ash heap. Anyone who feels overlooked, by society or even by their own family, can sing it as he did: the God who must stoop even to see the stars sees every overlooked person.

keyVerse.quote: Who is like the LORD our God, who is seated on high, who looks far down on the heavens and the earth?
keyVerse.note: This question is the hinge of the psalm. It gathers up the height of verse 4 and opens the surprise of verses 7–9: the God who must stoop even to see the heavens is the God who stoops to the ash heap. In Christ that stoop became a coming down, all the way to the cross.

113.reflection:
The psalm calls for praise “from this time forth and forevermore” and “from the rising of the sun to its setting” (vv. 2–3). Are there times or places in your week where praising God feels out of place? Why might the psalm insist there are none?

God is so high that he must stoop even to look at the heavens (vv. 4–6). How does seeing God’s height make his care for the lowly more wonderful rather than less?

Verses 7–8 echo Hannah (1 Samuel 2:8) and Mary (Luke 1:52–53), and Philippians 2:6–8 shows the Son coming down to the cross. How has God lifted you from the “ash heap”, and what does it mean to be seated “with princes”?

Verse 9 must be handled tenderly with those who long for children and do not have them. How can a church reflect God’s care for people whose sorrows are easily overlooked?

114.text: <sup>1</sup>When Israel went out from Egypt, the house of Jacob from a people of strange language,<sup>2</sup>Judah became his sanctuary, Israel his dominion.<sup>3</sup>The sea looked and fled; Jordan turned back.<sup>4</sup>The mountains skipped like rams, the hills like lambs.<sup>5</sup>What ails you, O sea, that you flee? O Jordan, that you turn back?<sup>6</sup>O mountains, that you skip like rams? O hills, like lambs?<sup>7</sup>Tremble, O earth, at the presence of the Lord, at the presence of the God of Jacob,<sup>8</sup>who turns the rock into a pool of water, the flint into a spring of water.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — When Israel Went Out from Egypt
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When God brought his people out of Egypt, he made them his home, and creation gave way before them. The psalm begins with the exodus, Israel leaving a land whose language was foreign to it (v. 1). In that moment the people themselves became God’s sanctuary and the realm he ruled, though the poet does not yet say whose (v. 2). Then forty years are folded into one picture: the Red Sea at the start of the journey runs away, the Jordan at its end turns back, and the mountains, remembering Sinai’s quaking, leap like rams and lambs (vv. 3–4).
verseByVerse.theology: The exodus told as a poem in which the sea runs away and the mountains dance.

verseByVerse.quote: When Israel went out from Egypt, the house of Jacob from a people of strange language, Judah became his sanctuary, Israel his dominion.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When God brought Israel out of Egypt, he made the people themselves his dwelling place and his kingdom.

A people of strange language. This short, lively retelling of the exodus begins with a detail an Israelite would feel: some four hundred years where the masters spoke a tongue that was not theirs. Coming out was coming home to being understood.

Judah became his sanctuary. There was no tent or temple yet: the people themselves were where God dwelt, and Israel was the territory he ruled. Before God lived in a building, he lived among a people, and he still does: the church is a people in whom God is present (1 Corinthians 3:16). Notice that the psalm does not yet say whose sanctuary this is; it holds back his name until verse 7.

A greater exodus. Luke tells how Moses and Elijah spoke with Jesus on the mountain about “his departure, which he was about to accomplish at Jerusalem” (Luke 9:31). The Greek word is exodus: the greater rescue this Passover song looks toward.

verseByVerse.quote: The sea looked and fled; Jordan turned back. The mountains skipped like rams, the hills like lambs.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the Red Sea, the Jordan and Sinai, the strongest things in creation gave way before God as his people passed.

The sea looked and fled; Jordan turned back. Forty years in one line. At the start, the Red Sea: “the LORD drove the sea back by a strong east wind all night and made the sea dry land” (Exodus 14:21). At the end, the Jordan: “the waters coming down from above stood and rose up in a heap very far away” (Joshua 3:16). The first and last obstacles, both water, got out of the way; the sea, like a person, looked and ran.

The mountains skipped like rams. At Sinai “the whole mountain trembled greatly” (Exodus 19:18). The psalm makes the earthquake almost comic: great mountains leaping like rams, little hills bouncing like lambs, the solid earth behaving like a flock of startled sheep.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–8 — At the Presence of the God of Jacob
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: What made creation run? The presence of the God of Jacob, who gives water to his people. The poet turns to the sea, the river and the mountains and asks them, almost teasingly, what is the matter with them (vv. 5–6). The answer comes with the name the psalm has held back: the earth should tremble at the presence of the Lord, the God of Jacob (v. 7). Yet the psalm ends not in terror but in kindness. The same presence that makes the sea flee turns hard rock into a pool and flint into a spring (v. 8).
verseByVerse.theology: The poet asks creation what frightened it, and the answer is a name held back until the end.

verseByVerse.quote: What ails you, O sea, that you flee? O Jordan, that you turn back? O mountains, that you skip like rams? O hills, like lambs?
verseByVerse.commentary:
The poet asks the sea, the river and the mountains what frightened them, holding back the answer.

What ails you, O sea, that you flee? Now the poet teases creation, speaking to it as if to frightened animals: what is the matter with you? Why are you running, and jumping?

Who then is this? What could make an ocean run and a mountain range jump? When the Sea of Galilee went still at a word from Jesus, his frightened disciples asked the same kind of question: “Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?” (Mark 4:41). The psalm has already given the answer.

verseByVerse.quote: Tremble, O earth, at the presence of the Lord, at the presence of the God of Jacob, who turns the rock into a pool of water, the flint into a spring of water.
verseByVerse.commentary:
It was the presence of the God of Jacob that shook creation, and the same presence brings water out of rock for his people.

At the presence of the God of Jacob. Here is the answer, and for the first time God is named. Until now he has been only “his” (v. 2). Now he is “the Lord”, the Master, who at the Jordan was called “the Lord of all the earth” (Joshua 3:13), and “the God of Jacob”, the God of a family’s promises. It was his presence the sea saw.

Tremble, O earth. If the sea ran and the mountains jumped at his presence, the whole earth should tremble, and so should we. The presence of God is not a mild spiritual atmosphere; it is the thing oceans run from.

Who turns the rock into a pool of water. Yet the psalm ends not with terror but with a gift: the presence that makes the sea flee makes a rock flow. In the desert God told Moses, “you shall strike the rock, and water shall come out of it” (Exodus 17:6), and not a trickle: a pool, a spring, out of flint, a byword for hardness.

The Rock was Christ. Paul says the people “drank from the spiritual Rock that followed them, and the Rock was Christ” (1 Corinthians 10:4). The God whose presence terrifies the sea is the God who became the Rock that was struck so that his people could drink. Tremble at his presence, and come to him thirsty.

114.title: The Sea Looked and Fled
114.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 114 is the second of the Hallel psalms (113–118), and in Jewish tradition it was sung with Psalm 113 before the Passover meal. Psalm 113 praised the God who lifts the poor from the dust; Psalm 114 tells the greatest example Israel knew, the day he lifted a nation of slaves out of Egypt.

The message. When God came to live among his people, creation itself got out of the way. The sea, the river and the mountains could not stand before the presence of the God of Jacob, and that same presence, which makes the earth tremble, brings water out of rock for his thirsty people. So the right response to him is both trembling and trust.

Why it was said. The psalm was sung by generations who had never seen the Red Sea part (see the introduction on the Passover psalms). It told them that the God who did those things was still their God, living among them, and that the obstacles in front of them were no more fixed than the sea had been.

How the chapter makes its case. It is a tiny drama in four short scenes. Israel leaves Egypt and becomes God’s sanctuary and kingdom, though God is not yet named (vv. 1–2). The Red Sea flees, the Jordan turns back, and the mountains skip like startled sheep: forty years of journey in two lines (vv. 3–4). The poet teases creation, asking what is the matter with it (vv. 5–6). Then the answer, and at last the name: it was the presence of the Lord, the God of Jacob, who also turns flint into a spring (vv. 7–8).

Where it leads. To Christ by pattern, a pattern the New Testament itself draws. On the mountain of transfiguration Jesus spoke with Moses and Elijah about “his departure”, in Greek his exodus, which he would accomplish at Jerusalem (Luke 9:31). The God who made a people his sanctuary came to dwell among us in his Son (John 1:14). When Jesus stilled the storm, his disciples asked the psalm’s question, “Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?” (Mark 4:41). And Paul says of the water from the rock, “the Rock was Christ” (1 Corinthians 10:4).

For us. Nothing that stands between God’s people and his purposes is as immovable as it looks; seas and mountains move at his presence. But that presence is not tame. Come to him with reverence, and come to him thirsty, for the Rock was struck so that we might drink.
114.theology: God's sanctuary was first a people, not a building (v. 2). Creation retreats before his presence (vv. 3-6), and his name, held back until verse 7, explains why. The same presence brings water from the rock (v. 8), which Paul identifies with Christ (1 Cor 10:4).
114.examples: The psalm is short enough to learn by heart and lively enough to sing with children: mountains like startled sheep, a sea asked what is the matter with it. Behind the fun is the presence that frightens oceans and the Rock that was struck so that people could drink.

keyVerse.quote: Tremble, O earth, at the presence of the Lord, at the presence of the God of Jacob, who turns the rock into a pool of water, the flint into a spring of water.
keyVerse.note: These verses answer the riddle of the whole psalm: what made the sea flee and the mountains skip was the presence of God himself. They hold together the two things the psalm wants us to feel, awe before a God the earth cannot withstand and trust in a God who gives water from the rock. Paul says that Rock was Christ.

114.reflection:
The psalm says that when Israel came out of Egypt, the people themselves became God’s sanctuary (v. 2). What difference does it make to think of the church as a people in whom God lives rather than a building we go to?

The sea, the Jordan and the mountains all gave way before God’s presence (vv. 3–6). What obstacles in your life or your church seem as immovable as a sea or a mountain? How does this psalm speak to them?

When Jesus calmed the storm, the disciples asked, “Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?” (Mark 4:41). How does Psalm 114 help answer their question?

The psalm calls the earth to tremble and then shows God giving water from the rock (vv. 7–8). Why do we need both awe and trust? Which do you find harder, and what does it mean to come to Christ, the Rock, thirsty?

115.text: <sup>1</sup>Not to us, O LORD, not to us, but to your name give glory, for the sake of your steadfast love and your faithfulness!<sup>2</sup>Why should the nations say, "Where is their God?"<sup>3</sup>Our God is in the heavens; he does all that he pleases.<sup>4</sup>Their idols are silver and gold, the work of human hands.<sup>5</sup>They have mouths, but do not speak; eyes, but do not see.<sup>6</sup>They have ears, but do not hear; noses, but do not smell.<sup>7</sup>They have hands, but do not feel; feet, but do not walk; and they do not make a sound in their throat.<sup>8</sup>Those who make them become like them; so do all who trust in them.<sup>9</sup>O Israel, trust in the LORD! He is their help and their shield.<sup>10</sup>O house of Aaron, trust in the LORD! He is their help and their shield.<sup>11</sup>You who fear the LORD, trust in the LORD! He is their help and their shield.<sup>12</sup>The LORD has remembered us; he will bless us; he will bless the house of Israel; he will bless the house of Aaron;<sup>13</sup>he will bless those who fear the LORD, both the small and the great.<sup>14</sup>May the LORD give you increase, you and your children!<sup>15</sup>May you be blessed by the LORD, who made heaven and earth!<sup>16</sup>The heavens are the LORD's heavens, but the earth he has given to the children of man.<sup>17</sup>The dead do not praise the LORD, nor do any who go down into silence.<sup>18</sup>But we will bless the LORD from this time forth and forevermore. Praise the LORD!

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — Those Who Make Them Become Like Them
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Glory belongs to the living God, not to us, and certainly not to idols that make their worshippers lifeless. The psalm opens by refusing the credit for anything God has done and asking him to glorify his own name for the sake of his love and faithfulness (v. 1). When the nations taunt “Where is their God?”, the answer is that he is in the heavens and does all that he pleases (vv. 2–3). Their gods, by contrast, are silver and gold shaped by human hands, with mouths, eyes, ears, noses, hands and feet that do nothing (vv. 4–7). And the worshipper becomes like the thing worshipped (v. 8).
verseByVerse.theology: The nations taunt Israel, but Israel’s God acts, while their idols can do nothing and make their worshippers as lifeless as themselves.

verseByVerse.quote: Not to us, O LORD, not to us, but to your name give glory, for the sake of your steadfast love and your faithfulness! Why should the nations say, "Where is their God?" Our God is in the heavens; he does all that he pleases.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s people refuse the credit for what he has done, and answer the nations’ taunt: their God is in the heavens, doing all that he pleases.

Not to us, O LORD, not to us. The psalm opens with a refusal, said twice for emphasis. Whatever God has done for his people, the credit belongs to his name, for the sake of his “steadfast love” and “faithfulness”, not their merit.

Where is their God? The taunt of Psalms 42 and 79 comes again (Psalm 42:3; 79:10). The nations can see their gods, but Israel’s God cannot be seen.

Our God is in the heavens. Above everything, not in a shrine; and he “does all that he pleases”. He is not a statue waiting to be carried; he acts, freely and sovereignly. His invisibility is not a weakness but a sign that he is too great to be made into an object.

The image of the invisible God. Yet God has answered the nations’ question with his own image, not one carved by human hands: the Son, who “is the image of the invisible God” (Colossians 1:15) and who said, “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father” (John 14:9). Where is their God? He came among us and spoke, saw, touched and walked, everything the idols could not do.

When God blesses your work. This is a searching prayer for anyone who has seen God bless a church, a ministry or a family: the temptation to take a little of the glory is strong.

The hunger to be recognised. People want to be seen and honoured. The political scientist Francis Fukuyama has argued that this demand for recognition, which Plato called thymos, drives much of modern politics, from nationalism to identity movements. It drives private life too: the follower count, the title on the door, the hope that someone will notice how hard we worked. The hunger is not wicked in itself; Paul speaks of those who “seek for glory and honor” from God (Romans 2:7). The trouble starts when we feed it ourselves, and every success becomes a small throne to defend. The double refusal, “not to us”, sounds like self-erasure, but it is liberation: someone who no longer needs the credit can rejoice in others’ success, take failure without collapsing, and work without the ache of being overlooked. That is possible because the recognition we craved has been given another way. The Father said over his Son, “with you I am well pleased” (Luke 3:22), and everyone who is in Christ is welcomed under those words.

How far does God’s sovereignty reach? Over all things (Ephesians 1:11), including evil, which he governs and overrules for good (Genesis 50:20). Yet he is not the author of sin, and people remain responsible for what they do (Acts 2:23; James 1:13).

verseByVerse.quote: Their idols are silver and gold, the work of human hands. They have mouths, but do not speak; eyes, but do not see. They have ears, but do not hear; noses, but do not smell. They have hands, but do not feel; feet, but do not walk; and they do not make a sound in their throat. Those who make them become like them; so do all who trust in them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Idols, however costly, are lifeless human handiwork, and those who trust them become as lifeless as they are.

The work of human hands. The nations’ gods are expensive, “silver and gold”, and man-made, “the work of human hands”. That second point is fatal: something you make cannot be greater than you.

They have mouths, but do not speak. The psalm walks round the statue inspecting it: mouth, eyes, ears, nose, hands, feet, throat. Seven features, beautifully carved, and not one works. Our God “does all that he pleases” (v. 3); their god cannot do anything at all. Isaiah mocked the man who burns half a log to cook his dinner and carves the other half into a god, then “prays to it and says, ‘Deliver me, for you are my god!’” (Isaiah 44:17).

Those who make them become like them. The devastating conclusion: worshippers become like what they worship, spiritually blind, deaf and dumb. The historian of Kings said the same of Israel: “They went after false idols and became false” (2 Kings 17:15).

Modern idols. It is as true of modern idols. Worship money and you become hard and cold like it. Worship pleasure and you become shallow. Worship yourself and you shrink to your own size. The good news, hinted at in the twin Psalms 111 and 112, runs the other way: worship the living God and by his Spirit you become gracious and merciful like him, “transformed into the same image” as the Lord you behold (2 Corinthians 3:18). “Little children, keep yourselves from idols” (1 John 5:21).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–18 — He Is Their Help and Their Shield
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: All God’s people, small and great, are called to trust the LORD, who remembers and blesses them, and to praise him for ever. Three groups, Israel, the house of Aaron and those who fear the LORD, hear the same call and the same answer: he is their help and their shield (vv. 9–11). The LORD has remembered his people and will bless every group, “both the small and the great”, and their children after them, for he made heaven and earth (vv. 12–15). Heaven is his, the earth he has entrusted to us; the dead are silent, but the living will bless him from now on and for ever (vv. 16–18).
verseByVerse.theology: Three groups called to trust, three times the same answer, and a blessing for small and great alike.

verseByVerse.quote: O Israel, trust in the LORD! He is their help and their shield. O house of Aaron, trust in the LORD! He is their help and their shield. You who fear the LORD, trust in the LORD! He is their help and their shield.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every part of God’s people is called to trust the LORD, and each hears the same promise: he is their help and their shield.

O Israel, trust in the LORD! Three groups, and three times the same call and the same answer. “Israel” is the whole nation; “the house of Aaron” is the priests; and then come “you who fear the LORD” (see below).

He is their help and their shield. The refrain is the point: help for what they cannot do, a shield against what would harm them. The idol’s hands cannot move (v. 7); the LORD’s hand helps. Whatever group you belong to in the church, ordinary member, leader or newcomer, the call is the same and so is the promise.

Uncertain wording. It is not certain who “you who fear the LORD” are. They may be all the faithful together, summing up the first two groups, or foreigners who had come to worship Israel’s God, like the God-fearers of the book of Acts. Either way, no one who fears the LORD is left outside the promise.

Textual note. In verse 9 the ESV notes that many manuscripts read “O house of Israel”.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD has remembered us; he will bless us; he will bless the house of Israel; he will bless the house of Aaron; he will bless those who fear the LORD, both the small and the great. May the LORD give you increase, you and your children! May you be blessed by the LORD, who made heaven and earth!
