verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD has remembered his people and will bless them all, small and great, and their children.

The LORD has remembered us. The idols cannot remember anyone, because they know nothing; the LORD “has remembered us”. And “bless” comes four times in two verses, to the same three groups, and then to “both the small and the great”. John heard that phrase at the end of history, when God rewards “those who fear your name, both small and great” (Revelation 11:18). No one is too insignificant to be blessed, and no one too important to need it.

May the LORD give you increase. The blessing reaches the next generation, and it comes from “the LORD, who made heaven and earth”: not from a god made by human hands, but from the Maker of everything.

verseByVerse.quote: The heavens are the LORD's heavens, but the earth he has given to the children of man. The dead do not praise the LORD, nor do any who go down into silence. But we will bless the LORD from this time forth and forevermore. Praise the LORD!
verseByVerse.commentary:
The dead fall silent, but the people of the living God will bless him for ever.

The earth he has given to the children of man. Heaven belongs to God; the earth he has entrusted to humanity, to be cared for under him, not territory where he is absent. The idol-worshippers had it backwards: they tried to bring gods down to earth in silver and gold, instead of looking up to the God of heaven and serving him on the earth he gave them.

The dead do not praise the LORD. Their praise on earth has ended. Heman asked, “Do the departed rise up to praise you?” (Psalm 88:10). So the living must praise while they have breath: “But we will bless the LORD”, and then the phrase from Psalm 113, “from this time forth and forevermore” (Psalm 113:2). The people who trust the living God will praise him for ever, when every idol has been melted down.

Breaking the silence. The idols were silent (v. 7); the dead “go down into silence” (v. 17); those who trust idols end in the same silence. The people of the living God are the ones who break it.

Does this deny life after death? It speaks of the grave as seen from earth: the dead no longer praise God among the living. Believers who die are with the Lord (Philippians 1:23; Luke 23:43), and Christ, raised from the dead, has broken that silence for all who are his (1 Corinthians 15:20). The psalm’s own answer is its last verse: “we will bless the LORD from this time forth and forevermore”.

115.title: Not to Us, O LORD
115.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 115 is the third of the Hallel psalms (113–118), and in Jewish tradition the first of those sung after the Passover meal. Psalms 113 and 114 praised what God has done; Psalm 115 faces the mockery of the nations, who look at Israel and ask, “Where is their God?”

The message. The glory belongs to God’s name, not to us. Israel’s God cannot be seen, not because he is absent but because he is in the heavens, doing all that he pleases, while the idols of the nations, however costly, cannot do anything at all and make their worshippers as lifeless as themselves. So let all God’s people, great and small, trust him: he remembers them, he blesses them, and the living will praise him for ever.

Why it was said. The psalm answers a time when God’s people looked weak and their neighbours could point to impressive gods of silver and gold while Israel had only an invisible one (see the introduction). Its first words also guard the people against the opposite danger: when God does act, taking the credit for themselves.

How the chapter makes its case. It opens with a prayer that God would glorify his own name and answers the nations’ taunt: our God is in the heavens and does all he pleases (vv. 1–3). Then it walks round an idol and inspects it, mouth, eyes, ears, nose, hands, feet and throat, none of which works, and draws the conclusion that those who make them become like them (vv. 4–8). Three times it calls Israel, the priests and all who fear the LORD to trust him, their help and shield (vv. 9–11), promises that he will bless small and great and their children (vv. 12–15), and ends with the living who bless the LORD for ever while the dead are silent (vv. 16–18).

Where it leads. To Christ by the need it exposes and by the character of God revealed in him. The psalm shows that we become like what we worship, and that every human heart is drawn to gods it can see and handle. God answers the taunt “Where is their God?” not with a statue but with his Son, “the image of the invisible God” (Colossians 1:15), who spoke, saw, touched and walked among us. And the psalm’s grim law runs the other way in the gospel: “beholding the glory of the Lord”, believers “are being transformed into the same image” (2 Corinthians 3:18).

For us. Ask of anything you are tempted to trust, money, success, reputation, whether it can see, hear or help you; and notice what it is making you. Then give the glory away: “Not to us, O LORD, not to us.” The God who remembers small and great is worth trusting.
115.theology: Glory belongs to God's name, not to his people (v. 1). His invisibility is not absence: he is in the heavens and does all that he pleases (v. 3). Idols are man-made and powerless, and worshippers become like what they worship (vv. 4-8). All God's people are called to trust him as help and shield, and he blesses small and great (vv. 9-15).
115.examples: A pastor whose church has grown, or parents whose children have turned out well, can make verse 1 their first prayer: not to us. And anyone who has given their heart to money or success can ask the psalm's question of it: does it see, hear, help? No one is too small to be blessed by the living God, and no one too great to need it.

keyVerse.quote: Not to us, O LORD, not to us, but to your name give glory, for the sake of your steadfast love and your faithfulness!
keyVerse.note: The whole psalm flows from this refusal. Glory belongs to God’s name, not to his people and not to the idols the nations trust, and the grounds are his steadfast love and faithfulness, not anyone’s merit. Someone who has stopped needing the credit is free to trust the living God and to praise him for ever.

115.reflection:
“Not to us, O LORD, not to us” (v. 1). Where are you most tempted to take a little of the glory for what God has done? What would it look like to give it away?

The nations mock, “Where is their God?” (v. 2). How would you answer someone who asks that today, and how does Christ, “the image of the invisible God” (Colossians 1:15), change the answer?

“Those who make them become like them” (v. 8). What modern idols do people around you trust, and what are those idols making them? What are you becoming like?

The blessing reaches “both the small and the great” (v. 13). How should that shape the way a church treats its least noticed members, and the way you think of your own place in it?

116.text: <sup>1</sup>I love the LORD, because he has heard my voice and my pleas for mercy.<sup>2</sup>Because he inclined his ear to me, therefore I will call on him as long as I live.<sup>3</sup>The snares of death encompassed me; the pangs of Sheol laid hold on me; I suffered distress and anguish.<sup>4</sup>Then I called on the name of the LORD: "O LORD, I pray, deliver my soul!"<sup>5</sup>Gracious is the LORD, and righteous; our God is merciful.<sup>6</sup>The LORD preserves the simple; when I was brought low, he saved me.<sup>7</sup>Return, O my soul, to your rest; for the LORD has dealt bountifully with you.<sup>8</sup>For you have delivered my soul from death, my eyes from tears, my feet from stumbling;<sup>9</sup>I will walk before the LORD in the land of the living.<sup>10</sup>I believed, even when I spoke: "I am greatly afflicted";<sup>11</sup>I said in my alarm, "All mankind are liars."<sup>12</sup>What shall I render to the LORD for all his benefits to me?<sup>13</sup>I will lift up the cup of salvation and call on the name of the LORD,<sup>14</sup>I will pay my vows to the LORD in the presence of all his people.<sup>15</sup>Precious in the sight of the LORD is the death of his saints.<sup>16</sup>O LORD, I am your servant; I am your servant, the son of your maidservant. You have loosed my bonds.<sup>17</sup>I will offer to you the sacrifice of thanksgiving and call on the name of the LORD.<sup>18</sup>I will pay my vows to the LORD in the presence of all his people,<sup>19</sup>in the courts of the house of the LORD, in your midst, O Jerusalem. Praise the LORD!

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — I Love the LORD, Because He Has Heard
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Love for God grows out of being heard by him in the worst hour of life. The psalm opens with a simple confession, “I love the LORD”, and gives the reason: he heard my voice and bent down to listen, so I will call on him as long as I live (vv. 1–2). Then the man explains what he was heard from. The snares of death had caught him and the grave had its grip on him, and in that extremity he prayed one short line: “O LORD, I pray, deliver my soul!” (vv. 3–4).
verseByVerse.theology: A man who nearly died begins with the simplest confession in the Psalter: I love the LORD, because he heard me.

verseByVerse.quote: I love the LORD, because he has heard my voice and my pleas for mercy. Because he inclined his ear to me, therefore I will call on him as long as I live.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He loves the LORD because the LORD heard him, and will pray to him all his life.

I love the LORD. Few psalms open so simply (the Hebrew is more abrupt still: “I love, because the LORD has heard”), and the reason is just as simple: not a theory about God, but an experience of him.

He inclined his ear to me. God bent down to listen, the way a parent crouches to hear a small child. And the response is lifelong, “as long as I live”: one answered prayer has made him a praying man for the rest of his days.

How love for God grows. It is not first commanded into existence; it is drawn out by being cared for. “We love because he first loved us” (1 John 4:19). A person who struggles to feel love for God might begin by remembering, specifically, the times God has heard them.

Isn’t loving God for what he gives a little mercenary? The sceptic suspects that believers love God as a child loves a generous uncle, for the presents, and the earnest believer may worry about the same thing. C. S. Lewis took up the question in The Four Loves. He distinguished need-love, which cries out of our emptiness, from gift-love, which gives out of fullness, and argued that our love for God must always be very largely need-love; to pretend otherwise would be to pretend we are not creatures. A drowning man does not love his rescuer less because he needed rescuing. What would be mercenary is loving the gifts and not the Giver, and the psalm guards against that by ending with the man giving himself away: “I am your servant” (v. 16). That is the gospel’s order. We do not climb to a pure love for God by effort; he loves us first, hears us and rescues us, and the love that begins as gratitude for his gifts grows into delight in him.

verseByVerse.quote: The snares of death encompassed me; the pangs of Sheol laid hold on me; I suffered distress and anguish. Then I called on the name of the LORD: "O LORD, I pray, deliver my soul!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Trapped by death, he prayed one short, desperate prayer.

The snares of death encompassed me. “The pangs of Sheol”: the grave reaching up and gripping him. It may have been illness or danger; the psalm says only that it was nearly the end.

O LORD, I pray, deliver my soul! At the worst moment of his life he prayed seven words. No eloquence, no theology: a cry. In real extremity the prayers that matter most are often the shortest, and God heard that one.

The one who went all the way in. Jesus, who very probably sang this psalm the night he was betrayed, went further into death’s snares than this man. He prayed “with loud cries and tears, to him who was able to save him from death, and he was heard” (Hebrews 5:7): not by being spared death but raised from it, “loosing the pangs of death” (Acts 2:24).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–11 — Return, O My Soul, to Your Rest
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The God who rescued him is gracious, so his frightened soul can come home and rest. He describes the LORD as gracious, righteous and merciful, the guardian of simple people with no resources of their own (vv. 5–6). He tells his soul to return to its rest, for God has dealt generously with it (v. 7), and he lists what was rescued: his life from death, his eyes from tears, his feet from stumbling, so that he can walk before the LORD among the living (vv. 8–9). He admits honestly that in his alarm he said bitter things, yet he kept believing all through it (vv. 10–11).
verseByVerse.theology: After the crisis, a man tells his own soul to come home and rest.

verseByVerse.quote: Gracious is the LORD, and righteous; our God is merciful. The LORD preserves the simple; when I was brought low, he saved me. Return, O my soul, to your rest; for the LORD has dealt bountifully with you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The God who saved him is gracious and keeps the helpless, so his frightened soul can come home and rest.

Gracious is the LORD, and righteous. He describes his rescuer: gracious, righteous, merciful, the words God used of himself to Moses (Exodus 34:6). Righteous stands in the middle: God’s mercy never compromises his justice.

The LORD preserves the simple. “The simple” are people without resources, clever plans or influence, and God guards them. The man counts himself among them: “when I was brought low, he saved me”. You do not have to be spiritually impressive to be kept by God.

Return, O my soul, to your rest. He speaks to his own soul, as Psalm 42 does, but gently. The soul has been out in the storm, frightened and running; the danger is over: come home. Jesus offers the same to every weary person: “Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28).

For the anxious. Some believers stay anxious long after God has rescued them, as if the soul has not heard the news. This verse is for them. Tell your soul what God has done, and tell it to rest.

verseByVerse.quote: For you have delivered my soul from death, my eyes from tears, my feet from stumbling; I will walk before the LORD in the land of the living.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Given back his life, joy and footing, he will live in God’s sight.

For you have delivered my soul from death. Three rescues: his soul from death, his eyes from tears, his feet from stumbling. And the result is a walk: “I will walk before the LORD in the land of the living”.

verseByVerse.quote: I believed, even when I spoke: "I am greatly afflicted"; I said in my alarm, "All mankind are liars."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even while he complained of his suffering and spoke rashly in panic, he kept believing.

I believed, even when I spoke. On the ESV’s reading, faith and honest complaint lived together.

Faith speaks. Paul quoted the Greek form of this verse when he described his own suffering ministry: “Since we have the same spirit of faith according to what has been written, ‘I believed, and so I spoke,’ we also believe, and so we also speak” (2 Corinthians 4:13). Faith speaks. It speaks about affliction honestly, and it speaks the gospel boldly, both at once.

All mankind are liars. This was said “in my alarm”. Not a considered doctrine but what a frightened man says when every human support seems to fail; the psalm keeps it in, with the admission. Paul later turned the thought towards God’s faithfulness: “Let God be true though every one were a liar” (Romans 3:4).

Uncertain wording. Verse 10 is difficult to translate, and the ESV notes other possibilities: “I believed, indeed”, or, following the Greek translation, “I believed, therefore”. The ESV has faith holding on through the complaint; the Greek, which Paul quotes, makes faith the reason for speaking.
verseByVerse.note: The Greek translation that Paul quotes begins a new psalm at verse 10.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–19 — I Will Lift Up the Cup of Salvation
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The only way to repay God’s grace is to receive more of it and to give thanks in front of his people. The man asks what he can render to the LORD, and answers by lifting the cup of salvation, calling on God’s name and paying his vows publicly (vv. 12–14). He confesses that the death of God’s saints is precious, weighty, in God’s sight (v. 15). And he ends as a freed man who gladly calls himself God’s servant, offering the sacrifice of thanksgiving in the temple courts in the middle of Jerusalem (vv. 16–19).
verseByVerse.theology: The only way to repay God is to take more from him, and to thank him in front of everyone.

verseByVerse.quote: What shall I render to the LORD for all his benefits to me? I will lift up the cup of salvation and call on the name of the LORD, I will pay my vows to the LORD in the presence of all his people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He cannot repay God, so he thanks him by taking the cup of salvation from his hand and keeping his promises in public.

What shall I render to the LORD? It is the right question, with a surprising answer.

I will lift up the cup of salvation. Nothing he could offer would match what he has received. So he will “lift up the cup of salvation”: he takes more, raising the cup of thanksgiving at the feast and drinking from what God gives. The only way to repay grace is to receive more of it, gladly and publicly.

I will pay my vows to the LORD. In his distress he had made promises to God. Now he will keep them, “in the presence of all his people”, a line so important to him that he repeats it word for word in verse 18. Such vows were normally paid with a sacrifice at the temple, a peace offering eaten as a meal (Leviticus 7:16), so keeping his promise meant telling the story among the crowd.

He drank all of it. If these psalms were sung at Passover, Jesus sang this verse on the night he was betrayed, the night he lifted a cup and said, “This cup is the new covenant in my blood. Do this, as often as you drink it, in remembrance of me” (1 Corinthians 11:25), and then “when they had sung a hymn, they went out to the Mount of Olives” (Matthew 26:30). Every time a Christian lifts the cup at the Lord’s Supper, this verse finds its fullest echo: not paying God back, but receiving the cup of salvation, filled by the one who prayed in Gethsemane that a different cup, the cup of suffering under God’s judgment, might pass from him, and then drank all of it (Mark 14:36).

verseByVerse.quote: Precious in the sight of the LORD is the death of his saints.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The death of God’s people is weighty and costly in his sight.

Precious in the sight of the LORD. This verse has comforted countless grieving believers, and needs to be understood rightly. “Precious” means costly, weighty, of great value. The death of one of God’s people is not a small thing to him. He does not shrug at it or allow it carelessly; he watches it closely, and it matters to him greatly.

The death of his saints. In context the man is thanking God for not letting him die, because God values the lives of his saints too highly to let them go cheaply. And when a believer does die, the verse still holds: that death was seen, weighed and precious in God’s sight. No Christian dies unnoticed or unvalued.

For them it was not the end. The one who makes that true is the Son, who “partook of the same things, that through death he might destroy the one who has the power of death” and “deliver all those who through fear of death were subject to lifelong slavery” (Hebrews 2:14–15). Death is still an enemy, and grief at it is not a lack of faith: “Jesus wept” at the grave of his friend (John 11:35). But if you are grieving someone who died in Christ, their death was precious to God, and for them it was not the end.

verseByVerse.quote: O LORD, I am your servant; I am your servant, the son of your maidservant. You have loosed my bonds. I will offer to you the sacrifice of thanksgiving and call on the name of the LORD. I will pay my vows to the LORD in the presence of all his people, in the courts of the house of the LORD, in your midst, O Jerusalem. Praise the LORD!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Set free, he gladly calls himself God’s servant and gives thanks before all God’s people.

O LORD, I am your servant. He says it twice, and then adds the phrase from Psalm 86, “the son of your maidservant” (Psalm 86:16): a servant born in the household, belonging from birth.

You have loosed my bonds. The paradox: God freed him, and the freed man’s response is to declare himself God’s servant. The chains of death are off, and he binds himself willingly to the one who removed them. That is Christian freedom: not freedom from God, but freedom to serve him.

In the presence of all his people. The psalm ends in public, at the temple, in the crowd. A rescue God performed in secret, at the edge of the grave, becomes a song sung where all his people can hear.

In practice. A Christian rescued from illness, danger or despair can do the same two things. Keep any promise made to God in the dark, gladly and not as payment, since the cup has already been filled for you; and tell what he did where his people can hear, in a testimony, a prayer meeting or a conversation after church.

116.title: What Shall I Render to the LORD?
116.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 116 is the fourth of the Hallel psalms (113–118), sung in Jewish tradition after the Passover meal. Psalm 115 called all God’s people to trust the LORD; Psalm 116 is one voice telling what happened when he did. A man who had been at the edge of death comes to the temple to give thanks in front of everyone.

The message. God heard me when I was dying, and that is why I love him. The rescued man tells his frightened soul to come home and rest, and he asks what he can give back to the LORD. His surprising answer is that he can repay grace only by receiving more of it: lifting the cup of salvation, calling on God’s name, and keeping his promises where all God’s people can see.

Why it was said. The occasion is not named; it may have been illness or danger. But a personal thanksgiving became a song for the whole people at the feasts, so that every worshipper could make it his own, and vows made in distress were paid at the temple with a thank offering shared as a meal (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. It begins with love drawn out by answered prayer: death had him trapped, he cried a single line to God, and God bent down and heard (vv. 1–4). It then describes the God who saved him, gracious, righteous and merciful, and calls his soul to rest; he admits that in his alarm he said rash things, yet he kept believing (vv. 5–11). Finally it asks, “What shall I render to the LORD?” and answers with the cup of salvation, public vows, the confession that the death of God’s saints is precious to him, and the glad service of a man whose bonds have been loosed (vv. 12–19).

Where it leads. To Christ by pattern, and by the setting in which he sang it. If these psalms were sung at Passover, Jesus sang this one on the night he was betrayed, and then walked into the snares of death himself. He prayed “with loud cries and tears, to him who was able to save him from death, and he was heard” (Hebrews 5:7): not by being spared death, but by being raised from it, “loosing the pangs of death” (Acts 2:24). He drank the cup of suffering under God’s judgment so that his people might lift the cup of salvation.

For us. Remember, specifically, the times God has heard you, and let that memory grow into love. When the danger is past, tell your anxious soul to rest. And give thanks where others can hear: not to pay God back, but because the cup has already been filled for you.
116.theology: Love for God grows from answered prayer (vv. 1-2), and faith and honest lament live together (vv. 10-11). The only repayment of grace is to receive more of it and give thanks publicly (vv. 12-14). The death of God's people is weighty in his sight (v. 15), and the freed believer becomes his willing servant (v. 16).
116.examples: A believer who has come through surgery, a car crash or a long depression may find himself still anxious long after the danger has passed. This psalm teaches him to tell his soul to rest, to thank God where others can hear, and to remember that no Christian dies unnoticed.

keyVerse.quote: What shall I render to the LORD for all his benefits to me? I will lift up the cup of salvation and call on the name of the LORD
keyVerse.note: These verses carry the psalm’s surprising logic of grace. The rescued man cannot pay God back, so he gives thanks by receiving more: lifting the cup of salvation and calling on God’s name. Jesus very probably sang them on the night he took the cup of the new covenant, and then drank the cup of judgment so that this cup could be ours.

116.reflection:
“I love the LORD, because he has heard my voice” (v. 1). Can you name specific times God has heard you? How has remembering them, or forgetting them, affected your love for him?

The man prayed a seven-word prayer in his worst moment (v. 4), and later admitted he said rash things in his alarm (v. 11). What does this teach about how honest and how simple our prayers can be?

“Return, O my soul, to your rest” (v. 7). Are there fears that linger in you after God has already brought you through? What would it look like to tell your soul what he has done?

“What shall I render to the LORD?” (v. 12). Why is receiving the cup of salvation, rather than trying to pay God back, the right answer? How does the Lord’s Supper put this into practice, and how might you give thanks “in the presence of all his people”?

117.text: <sup>1</sup>Praise the LORD, all nations! Extol him, all peoples!<sup>2</sup>For great is his steadfast love toward us, and the faithfulness of the LORD endures forever. Praise the LORD!

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The shortest psalm calls the whole world to praise Israel’s God, and it gives one reason: his love for his own people. Verse 1 issues the summons in two parallel lines, “all nations” and “all peoples”, a horizon that includes Israel’s idol-worshipping enemies. Verse 2 supplies the ground with the two great words of God’s covenant name, steadfast love and faithfulness: his love has proved stronger than Israel’s failures, and his faithfulness lasts forever. The nations are not asked to praise a general idea of God but the God who kept his promises to one people, and in Christ they are brought in to share that love. The psalm begins and ends with “Praise the LORD”.
verseByVerse.theology: The shortest psalm has the widest reach: every nation called to praise, because of what God did for one.

verseByVerse.quote: Praise the LORD, all nations! Extol him, all peoples!
verseByVerse.commentary:
God summons every nation and people on earth, even Israel’s enemies, to praise him.

Praise the LORD, all nations! The shortest psalm has one of the widest horizons in the Psalter: “all nations” and “all peoples”, every tribe and language on the face of the earth.

Even the enemy nations. That was a startling thing for an Israelite to sing. The nations were the peoples who worshipped idols and had enslaved and invaded Israel, yet this psalm, sung in the temple, calls them to praise Israel’s God.

Extol him, all peoples! Paul saw exactly what that meant. When he wanted to show the church in Rome, Jews and Gentiles struggling to accept one another, that God had always intended the Gentiles to be among his worshippers, he quoted this verse: “Praise the Lord, all you Gentiles, and let all the peoples extol him” (Romans 15:11). The gospel going to the nations was not a change of plan. It was in the Psalms all along.

A missionary charter. The unreached tribe, the hostile nation, the neighbour from a culture you find strange: God wants to be praised by all of them. That is why the church sends missionaries, and why it prays for the nations.
verseByVerse.note: The shortest psalm, and the shortest chapter in the Bible.

verseByVerse.quote: For great is his steadfast love toward us, and the faithfulness of the LORD endures forever. Praise the LORD!
verseByVerse.commentary:
The nations are to praise God for his prevailing love and lasting faithfulness toward his own people, Israel.

His steadfast love toward us. The reason is surprising: not a general statement about God’s love for everyone, but his steadfast love “toward us”, toward Israel.

Great is his steadfast love. The Hebrew verb is used of a warrior who prevails. This love is not merely large; it is stronger than the unfaithfulness of the people it is set on.

The faithfulness of the LORD endures forever. The two great words come again, steadfast love and faithfulness, the name God proclaimed to Moses: “abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness” (Exodus 34:6). His love is powerful; his faithfulness is permanent. What he has promised, he will do, forever.

How the gospel works. God did not reveal himself in a vague, general way to humanity. He chose Abraham, rescued Israel from Egypt, made promises to David, and finally sent his Son as a Jew from Nazareth. His love toward that one people is the good news that goes to every other people. The nations praise God by looking at what he did for Israel, and in Christ they are brought in to share it.

The whole of redemption. Two verses, and the whole of redemption is in them: a God whose love prevails, whose faithfulness never ends, and who wants every nation on earth to know it.

117.title: Praise the LORD, All Nations
117.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 117 is the fifth of the Hallel psalms (113–118), sung at the great festivals and especially at Passover. It sits between Psalm 116, one man’s thanks for rescue from death, and Psalm 118, the festival procession to the temple gate. It is the shortest psalm and the shortest chapter in the Bible.

The message. Every nation on earth is called to praise Israel’s God. And the reason they should praise him is not some vague goodness spread thinly over everyone, but his strong, faithful love shown to one people. What God did for Israel is good news for the whole world, and the whole world is meant to sing about it.

Why it was said. Israel sang this in the temple, often surrounded and threatened by the very nations it addresses (see the introduction on the Hallel and the pilgrim feasts). The psalm lifted their eyes beyond their own survival: their God was not a tribal deity, and his covenant love with them was meant from the start to draw the nations to worship him, as he had promised Abraham (Genesis 12:3).

How the chapter makes its case. Two lines. First the summons, as wide as it can be: “all nations”, “all peoples” (v. 1). Then the reason, as particular as it can be: “his steadfast love toward us”, a love that prevails, and a faithfulness that never ends (v. 2). The psalm opens and closes with “Praise the LORD”, and everything between is the case for it.

Where it leads. To Christ by promise, and the New Testament draws the line itself. Paul quotes verse 1 to show that the Gentiles praising God was always God’s plan, and he says that Christ came to the Jews “to show God’s truthfulness” and “in order that the Gentiles might glorify God for his mercy” (Romans 15:8–9, 11). In Jesus, the steadfast love and faithfulness God showed Israel became the good news of every nation.

For us. If you are not Jewish and you worship Israel’s God, you are this psalm being answered. That should humble us and make us glad, and it should make us care about the nations still not praising him: praying for them, sending to them, and welcoming the stranger next door.
117.theology: Every nation is summoned to worship Israel's God (v. 1), and the reason they are to praise him is his love toward one people, Israel (v. 2), a love that reaches the nations in Christ.
117.examples: A congregation that prays for a missionary among a people it has never met, or welcomes a neighbour from a culture it finds strange, is singing Psalm 117. The nations praise God for what he did for Israel, and in Christ that love becomes theirs.

keyVerse.quote: For great is his steadfast love toward us, and the faithfulness of the LORD endures forever. Praise the LORD!
keyVerse.note: Verse 1 calls the world to praise; verse 2 gives the reason, and the reason is the heart of the psalm. The nations are to praise God for his prevailing love and endless faithfulness to one people, the love that in Christ reaches them too.

117.reflection:
Psalm 117 calls “all nations” to praise Israel’s God, including nations that had been Israel’s enemies (v. 1). Who are the people or peoples you find hardest to imagine praising God alongside you?

Paul quotes this psalm to show that the Gentiles were always part of God’s plan (Romans 15:11). How does that change the way a church thinks about mission, or about the stranger in its own neighbourhood?

The reason given for the nations’ praise is God’s love “toward us”, toward Israel (v. 2). Why is it good news for the world that God worked through one particular people and one particular Jewish man, Jesus?

God’s steadfast love is “great”, prevailing like a warrior, and his faithfulness “endures forever” (v. 2). Where do you most need to remember that his love is stronger than your unfaithfulness?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — His Steadfast Love Endures Forever
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A festival procession begins with a call to give thanks, and every group of worshippers answers with the same line. The leader calls the people to thank the LORD because he is good and his steadfast love endures forever (v. 1). Then three groups are summoned in turn: Israel as a nation, the house of Aaron who served as priests, and all who fear the LORD, a group wide enough to include believing foreigners (vv. 2–4). Each answers with the same confession. That sentence frames the whole psalm and returns at its end (v. 29): whatever comes between, distress, battle, discipline or rejection, is held inside the steadfast love of God.
verseByVerse.theology: A festival procession begins with a call-and-response that every group of worshippers joins.

verseByVerse.quote: Oh give thanks to the LORD, for he is good; for his steadfast love endures forever! Let Israel say, "His steadfast love endures forever." Let the house of Aaron say, "His steadfast love endures forever." Let those who fear the LORD say, "His steadfast love endures forever."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every group of God’s worshippers is called to confess the one truth that frames the whole psalm: the LORD is good, and his steadfast love endures forever.

The last Hallel psalm. This is the last of the six psalms (113–118) sung at the great festivals, and the one the New Testament quotes most among them. If, as is very likely, these were the “hymn” Jesus and his disciples sang before they “went out to the Mount of Olives” (Matthew 26:30), then this was the last song Jesus sang before his arrest: a song about a rejected stone.

A procession. The psalm is built like a procession. It begins outside, with a call to give thanks, and ends at the gates of the temple and the altar.

Let Israel say. A leader calls, and the crowd answers. The three groups are those of Psalm 115: the nation, the priests (the house of Aaron), and all who fear the LORD (Psalm 115:9–11). The response is the same line each time. Count it through the psalm: “his steadfast love endures forever” five times, and the last verse is the first verse again (v. 29). Everything in between, distress, battle, rejection and rescue, is framed by that one sentence.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–18 — The LORD Is My Strength and My Song
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A king tells how the LORD rescued him when he was surrounded and falling, and he sings Israel’s oldest song of salvation. Out of distress he called, and God set him free, so he need not fear what man can do, and he has learned to take refuge in the LORD rather than in princes (vv. 5–9). All nations swarmed round him like bees, but in the LORD’s name he cut them off; pushed to the point of falling, he was helped, and he sings the song of the Red Sea (vv. 10–14). The camp celebrates the LORD’s right hand; the king will live to tell God’s deeds, for the discipline was severe but stopped short of death (vv. 15–18).
verseByVerse.theology: A king surrounded and pushed to the point of falling sings the song Israel sang on the far side of the Red Sea.

verseByVerse.quote: Out of my distress I called on the LORD; the LORD answered me and set me free. The LORD is on my side; I will not fear. What can man do to me? The LORD is on my side as my helper; I shall look in triumph on those who hate me. It is better to take refuge in the LORD than to trust in man. It is better to take refuge in the LORD than to trust in princes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because the LORD answered him and is on his side, the king need not fear what people can do, and he has learned that refuge in God is better than trust in the powerful.

Out of my distress I called on the LORD. Now a single voice speaks, apparently a king or leader who has come through a terrible crisis. Out of his distress God “set me free”, literally brought him into a broad place.

What can man do to me? Verse 6 is one of the great fear-destroying verses of the Bible. Men can do a great deal; the psalm will describe it. But nothing they do can undo the fact that “the LORD is on my side”. Hebrews gave these words to Christians facing loss and persecution: “So we can confidently say, ‘The Lord is my helper; I will not fear; what can man do to me?’” (Hebrews 13:6).

Living for the verdict of others. What can man do to me? Quite a lot, we feel: withhold approval, laugh at us, leave us out, unfollow us. For many people today other people’s opinion is not one concern among many; it is the scoreboard. We check it many times a day and shape our clothes, our views and even our faith to keep the numbers up. The religious have their own version: being admired for devotion, being thought sound. Both are the same fear, and Scripture calls it a snare (Proverbs 29:25). The psalm does not cure it by telling us to stop caring what anyone thinks, which is impossible and would make us hard. It cures it by giving us someone to fear and love more: “The LORD is on my side”. When the one opinion that finally matters is settled in our favour, the others shrink to their proper size. For the Christian it is settled, because Christ was rejected by men and chosen by God in our place. The stone the builders threw away became the cornerstone (v. 22), and all who are in him are accepted with him.

It is better to take refuge in the LORD. He says it twice, the second time more pointedly: better than trusting not just man but “princes”, the powerful and well-connected who seem able to fix things. A king saying this about princes means it; he has seen how little they can do. In practice, taking refuge in the LORD means bringing the crisis to him in prayer first, before ringing round for the right contact, and then using the help of doctors, lawyers or officials gratefully, without leaning one’s whole weight on them.

verseByVerse.quote: All nations surrounded me; in the name of the LORD I cut them off! They surrounded me, surrounded me on every side; in the name of the LORD I cut them off! They surrounded me like bees; they went out like a fire among thorns; in the name of the LORD I cut them off! I was pushed hard, so that I was falling, but the LORD helped me. The LORD is my strength and my song; he has become my salvation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Surrounded by enemies and pushed to the point of falling, the king was saved by the LORD, and he sings the song Israel sang at the Red Sea.

In the name of the LORD I cut them off! The attack is total: “all nations”, “on every side”, swarming “like bees”. Three times he says he was surrounded, and three times comes the same answer: “in the name of the LORD I cut them off”. The swarm that seemed so terrifying “went out like a fire among thorns”: thorn bushes blaze up fast and fierce and burn out in minutes.

I was pushed hard, so that I was falling. He was actually going down. This is not a man who never stumbled; it is a man who was falling when God caught him.

The LORD is my strength and my song. Here he quotes the oldest song of rescue Israel had. On the far shore of the Red Sea, Moses and Israel sang, “The LORD is my strength and my song, and he has become my salvation” (Exodus 15:2), and Isaiah promised the song would be sung again (Isaiah 12:2). The king’s rescue is a new exodus. God is not only his strength in the fight but his song afterwards: the one who saves becomes the subject of the singing.

What it does not mean. This is a king’s account of defending his people against invasion, not a charter for holy war. The greater King would win his victory not with a sword but by being rejected and crucified (vv. 22–24).

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew of verse 13 speaks to the enemy directly, “You pushed me hard”, as the ESV footnote says; the ESV text smooths it to “I was pushed hard”. The sense is the same either way: he was being driven to a fall.

verseByVerse.quote: Glad songs of salvation are in the tents of the righteous: "The right hand of the LORD does valiantly, the right hand of the LORD exalts, the right hand of the LORD does valiantly!" I shall not die, but I shall live, and recount the deeds of the LORD. The LORD has disciplined me severely, but he has not given me over to death.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The victory belongs to the LORD’s right hand, and the king, disciplined severely but not handed over to death, will live to tell what God has done.

The right hand of the LORD does valiantly. The celebration spreads through the camp, and the song is about God’s right hand, three times, like the three “I cut them off” of verses 10–12. The victory was not the king’s right hand. It was God’s.

I shall not die, but I shall live. He had been sure he was going to die. Now he declares that he will live, and the purpose of his life is to “recount the deeds of the LORD”. A rescued life is a testimony.

The LORD has disciplined me severely. A remarkable admission: the crisis was also God’s discipline. He does not pretend the suffering was mild, nor that it was outside God’s hand. But God set a limit: “he has not given me over to death”. A believer under God’s hard discipline can hold on to that line. The discipline is real, and so is its boundary.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–29 — Blessed Is He Who Comes
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The procession reaches the temple, the rejected stone is set at the head of the corner, and the crowd blesses the one who comes in the LORD’s name. The king asks for the gates of righteousness to be opened and gives thanks inside (vv. 19–21). Then comes the great turn: the stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone, the LORD’s marvellous doing, and the day he made calls for joy (vv. 22–24). The crowd cries “Save us, we pray” and blesses the one who comes, and the procession ends at the altar (vv. 25–27). The psalm closes with personal thanks and its opening line (vv. 28–29). Jesus and the crowds made these words his.
verseByVerse.theology: The procession reaches the temple gate, the rejected stone is set at the head of the corner, and the crowd shouts the words that greeted Jesus.

verseByVerse.quote: Open to me the gates of righteousness, that I may enter through them and give thanks to the LORD. This is the gate of the LORD; the righteous shall enter through it. I thank you that you have answered me and have become my salvation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the temple gate the rescued king asks to enter and give thanks, and learns that the LORD’s gate is for the righteous.

Open to me the gates of righteousness. The procession reaches the temple. The king stands outside and asks for the gates to be opened, so that he can go in and give thanks.

This is the gate of the LORD. A voice from inside, perhaps the gatekeepers, answers: this is the LORD’s gate, and it is for “the righteous”. Who can go in? Jesus gave the answer: “I am the door. If anyone enters by me, he will be saved” (John 10:9). The way in to God is a person, and those who enter through him are counted righteous.

I thank you that you have answered me. Inside, he says it to God directly: you “have become my salvation”, the words of verse 14 again, now as thanks.

verseByVerse.quote: The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone. This is the LORD's doing; it is marvelous in our eyes. This is the day that the LORD has made; let us rejoice and be glad in it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The stone the builders threw away God has made the cornerstone, and the day he did it is a day for joy: fulfilled when the crucified Jesus was raised.

The stone that the builders rejected. This is the most important verse in the psalm. Builders examine stones, reject one as unfit, and that very stone becomes “the cornerstone”, literally (as the ESV notes) “the head of the corner”, the stone that holds two walls together and bears the weight.

He was the stone. In the psalm the stone is the king, despised by the nations and the powerful, pushed until he was falling, and raised by God to the place of honour. But the New Testament sees the verse fulfilled completely in one person. After telling the parable of the tenants who killed the owner’s son, Jesus said to the religious leaders, “Have you never read in the Scriptures: ‘The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone; this was the Lord’s doing, and it is marvelous in our eyes’?” (Matthew 21:42). They were the builders, and he was the stone.

Peter before the council. Weeks later Peter stood before the same council and said it to their faces: “Jesus Christ of Nazareth, whom you crucified, whom God raised from the dead”, “This Jesus is the stone that was rejected by you, the builders, which has become the cornerstone” (Acts 4:10–11). The church is “built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the cornerstone” (Ephesians 2:20). And the same stone divides people: “So the honor is for you who believe, but for those who do not believe, ‘The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone’” (1 Peter 2:7).

This is the day that the LORD has made. It is often quoted as a cheerful verse for any morning, and every day is indeed God’s gift. But in the psalm it means a particular day: the day the rejected stone was made the cornerstone. For Christians that day has a name: the day God raised the one the builders crucified. Every Sunday the church gathers on that day, and the right response is exactly the psalm’s: “rejoice and be glad in it”.

How Jewish readers take it. Jewish readers commonly take the rejected stone as Israel, despised by the empires and raised by God (so Rashi), or as David; the Aramaic Targum makes the stone a youth among the sons of Jesse, passed over and then made king. Both traditions read the verse of someone God vindicates against all expectation. This commentary reads it of Christ because he applied it to himself (Matthew 21:42), probably sang it with his disciples after the Last Supper (Matthew 26:30), and was preached by the apostles as the stone God raised (Acts 4:10–11).

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew phrase “head of the corner” is clear in its point, the most important stone in the building, but not in its exact position. Most take it as the cornerstone at the foundation, which sets the line of two walls; some think of a capstone or keystone at the top. Either way the despised stone ends up holding the building together.
verseByVerse.note: Isaiah 28:16 speaks of a tested, precious cornerstone laid in Zion, and 1 Peter 2:6-7 joins the two texts.

verseByVerse.quote: Save us, we pray, O LORD! O LORD, we pray, give us success! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the LORD! We bless you from the house of the LORD. The LORD is God, and he has made his light to shine upon us. Bind the festal sacrifice with cords, up to the horns of the altar!
verseByVerse.commentary:
The festival crowd cries “Hosanna” and blesses the one who comes in the LORD’s name, words the crowds sang to Jesus as he entered Jerusalem.

Save us, we pray, O LORD! In Hebrew this is the cry that came into the Gospels untranslated: Hosanna.

Blessed is he who comes in the name of the LORD! Here the psalm walks straight into Palm Sunday. When Jesus rode into Jerusalem, “the crowds that went before him and that followed him were shouting, ‘Hosanna to the Son of David! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord! Hosanna in the highest!’” (Matthew 21:9). The festival crowd was singing Psalm 118, and applying it to him.

Rejected, and coming again. Days later the same city rejected him. Jesus had already said what that meant: “you will not see me until you say, ‘Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord!’” (Luke 13:35). The line that welcomed him on the road will one day be said again, when he comes the second time.

He has made his light to shine upon us. This echoes the priestly blessing, “the LORD make his face to shine upon you” (Numbers 6:25). And the procession ends at the altar, where the festival sacrifice is tied to the horns of the altar, the raised points at its corners. The rejected stone, the one who comes in the LORD’s name, the altar and the sacrifice: within a week of hearing this psalm on the road into Jerusalem, Jesus was all of them.

Uncertain wording. The last line of verse 27 is difficult. The word the ESV renders “festal sacrifice” usually means a festival, and the verb can mean to bind or to join. So some translations read it as a call to join the festal procession with branches in hand, up to the altar, the very thing the Palm Sunday crowd did. The ESV’s reading, an animal tied for sacrifice, is also well supported. Both picture worship reaching the altar.
verseByVerse.note: The cry is also recorded in Mark 11:9-10 and John 12:13.

verseByVerse.quote: You are my God, and I will give thanks to you; you are my God; I will extol you. Oh give thanks to the LORD, for he is good; for his steadfast love endures forever!
verseByVerse.commentary:
The psalm narrows to one worshipper’s thanks and ends with its first line: through everything, God’s steadfast love has endured.

You are my God. Twice, “you are my God”. After the crowd, the gates and the altar, the psalm narrows to one worshipper and his God.

His steadfast love endures forever. The psalm ends with its first line. Surrounded, pushed, falling, disciplined, rejected, and at the end of all of it, the same confession as at the start. If Jesus sang these words on the way to Gethsemane, he sang them knowing what the next day held. The steadfast love of God was not disproved by the cross. It was displayed there, and vindicated on the third day, the day the LORD made.

118.title: The Stone the Builders Rejected
118.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 118 is the last of the Hallel psalms (113–118), sung at Passover and the other pilgrim feasts. Psalm 117 called the nations to praise God’s steadfast love; Psalm 118 shows that love at work in one man’s rescue, and it is the Hallel psalm the New Testament quotes most.

The message. God’s steadfast love endures forever, and it is proved in the one he rescues from death and raises to honour. A king, surrounded, pushed until he was falling and disciplined to the edge of death, is saved by the LORD’s right hand; the stone the builders threw away becomes the cornerstone. It is the LORD’s doing, and his people can only give thanks.

Why it was said. The psalm was written for a festival procession, probably celebrating a king’s victory, and it was sung year after year by pilgrims going up to the temple (see the introduction on the Hallel). It taught Israel that its survival among hostile nations rested not on princes but on the LORD, and it kept alive the hope of the one who comes in the LORD’s name.

How the chapter makes its case. A call and response sets the theme: “his steadfast love endures forever” (vv. 1–4). The king tells his story: freed from distress, he will not fear man (vv. 5–9); surrounded by all nations, he was falling until the LORD helped him, and he sings the song of the Red Sea (vv. 10–14); the camp rejoices, and though severely disciplined he will live (vv. 15–18). At the temple gate he asks to enter and gives thanks (vv. 19–21). The rejected stone is made the cornerstone (vv. 22–24), the crowd cries “Save us” and blesses the one who comes (vv. 25–27), and the psalm ends where it began (vv. 28–29).

Where it leads. To Christ by pattern and by promise, as Jesus himself taught. He applied verse 22 to himself: he was the stone the builders rejected (Matthew 21:42). The Palm Sunday crowd greeted him with verses 25–26, “Hosanna… Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord!” (Matthew 21:9). He very probably sang this psalm with his disciples before going out to Gethsemane (Matthew 26:30). Rejected and crucified, he was raised by God and made the cornerstone of his church (Acts 4:10–11), and the day the LORD made is the day of his resurrection.

For us. Because the LORD is on our side in Christ, we need not live for the verdict of others: “What can man do to me?” Take refuge in him rather than in the powerful, accept his discipline as having a limit, and every Lord’s Day rejoice in the day he made, the day the rejected stone was raised.
118.theology: God's steadfast love frames every experience, from first verse to last (vv. 1, 29). Because the LORD is on his side, the believer need not fear what man can do (v. 6), and God's discipline, though severe, has a limit (v. 18). The rejected stone made cornerstone is Christ, rejected by the builders and raised by God (v. 22), and the day that the LORD has made is the day of that vindication (v. 24).
118.examples: A believer who was falling when God caught him can sing this psalm as his own. And every Sunday morning, when the church says This is the day that the LORD has made, it is remembering the day the stone the builders threw away was raised, the stone Jesus sang about on his way to Gethsemane.

keyVerse.quote: The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone.
keyVerse.note: This is the turning point of the psalm: the king pushed to the point of falling is raised by God to the place of honour. Jesus applied the verse to himself, and the apostles preached it of the crucified and risen Christ, making it one of the Old Testament texts the New Testament quotes most.

118.reflection:
The psalm is framed by “his steadfast love endures forever” (vv. 1, 29), with distress, battle and discipline in between. How does knowing the beginning and the end of the story change the way you face the middle?

“The LORD is on my side; I will not fear. What can man do to me?” (v. 6). Whose opinion or approval do you find yourself living for, and how does being accepted in Christ, the rejected stone, set you free?

The king says, “The LORD has disciplined me severely, but he has not given me over to death” (v. 18). How can a believer hold together the reality of God’s hard discipline and its limit?

Jesus applied verse 22 to himself, and the crowds greeted him with verses 25–26. How does seeing Christ as the rejected stone and the one who comes in the LORD’s name deepen the way you celebrate the Lord’s Day (v. 24)?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — Aleph: Blessed Are Those Whose Way Is Blameless
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The psalm opens with a blessing on those who walk in God’s law, and at once the singer sighs that he might keep it. Those who keep God’s testimonies are blessed because they seek God himself with their whole heart (vv. 1–3). God has commanded his precepts to be kept diligently (v. 4), and the singer’s answer is not a boast but a longing: “Oh that my ways may be steadfast” (vv. 5–6). He resolves to praise and to learn (v. 7), and the stanza ends with a vow and a plea in one breath: “I will keep your statutes; do not utterly forsake me!” (v. 8). That is the voice of the whole psalm.
verseByVerse.theology: The psalm opens with a blessing on obedience, and its first prayer admits how far the singer is from it.

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed are those whose way is blameless, who walk in the law of the LORD! Blessed are those who keep his testimonies, who seek him with their whole heart, who also do no wrong, but walk in his ways! You have commanded your precepts to be kept diligently. Oh that my ways may be steadfast in keeping your statutes! Then I shall not be put to shame, having my eyes fixed on all your commandments. I will praise you with an upright heart, when I learn your righteous rules. I will keep your statutes; do not utterly forsake me!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those who walk in God’s word are blessed because it leads them to God himself, and the singer, longing to keep it, knows he must hold on to God to do so.

The longest psalm. This is the longest psalm and the longest chapter in the Bible: 176 verses in twenty-two stanzas. It is an acrostic, as the ESV notes: each stanza takes one letter of the Hebrew alphabet, and every one of its eight verses begins with that letter. It is a love song to the word of God written from A to Z.

Words for God’s word. Almost every verse speaks of God’s word, under a cluster of names: law, testimonies, precepts, statutes, commandments, rules (the ESV notes the sense is “just decrees”), word, promise. They are not a legal code for specialists but everything God has said, looked at from different sides. Even “law” translates torah, which means instruction, the teaching a father gives his child, not only rules.

How should an ordinary reader take in 176 verses? Not at one sitting. The psalm was built to be read a stanza at a time: twenty-two stanzas make about three weeks of short daily readings. Watch three threads that run through every stanza: the word of God, which the singer loves; the trouble he is in, from affliction and from proud men who mock him; and his prayers, which keep asking God to teach him, give him life and hold him up. The psalm circles like a man turning a jewel in the light. Its author is not named; some have thought of David, many place it after the exile, and no one can now be sure.

Blessed are those whose way is blameless. It opens where the whole Psalter opened: “Blessed” (Psalm 1:1). And the law is not a set of rules held at arm’s length: those who keep it “seek him with their whole heart”. The commands lead to a person.

Oh that my ways may be steadfast. At once the tone turns personal and honest. God commands diligence; the singer’s response is a sigh. He is not boasting that he keeps the law. He wishes he did.

Do not utterly forsake me! The first stanza ends with a resolution and a plea in the same breath: “I will keep your statutes; do not utterly forsake me!” This is the voice of the whole psalm: a man who loves God’s word, knows he fails it, and holds on to God to keep him. Anyone who reads Psalm 119 as the boast of a self-righteous man has not listened to it.

Without a false step. Read alongside the New Testament, the psalm points beyond its singer. Only one man has walked this whole road without a false step: Jesus, “one who in every respect has been tempted as we are, yet without sin” (Hebrews 4:15), who met temptation with Scripture stored in his heart and said of the Scriptures, “it is they that bear witness about me” (John 5:39). The blessing of verse 1 belongs fully to him, and it reaches us through him: those joined to him by faith are counted blameless in him, and his Spirit writes the law on their hearts (Jeremiah 31:33).

Which law do Christians walk in? Read through Christ, the law still binds in its moral substance (Romans 13:8–10), while its ceremonies are fulfilled in Christ (Hebrews 10:1) and its civil laws ended with Israel’s nation. All of it remains God’s word for our instruction (2 Timothy 3:16). And how does this love for the law fit with Paul, who says no one is justified by works of the law (Galatians 2:16)? The singer does not treat the law as a ladder to earn God’s favour; he loves it as the word of a God who has already redeemed him, and he keeps asking for mercy (vv. 41, 132, 176). Paul opposes the first use, never the second (Romans 7:12).
verseByVerse.note: The longest psalm and the longest chapter in the Bible: an acrostic of twenty-two stanzas, one for each letter of the Hebrew alphabet, with each verse in a stanza beginning with the same letter (ESV note). Almost every verse names God’s word under some term.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–16 — Beth: I Have Stored Up Your Word in My Heart
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A young life is kept pure by God’s word stored in the heart and by God’s own teaching. The stanza asks the question every young person faces, how to keep one’s way pure, and answers it: by guarding it according to God’s word (v. 9). The singer seeks God wholeheartedly and asks not to wander (v. 10), and he has treasured God’s word inside so that he will not sin (v. 11). He blesses God and asks to be taught (v. 12), declares God’s rules aloud, and delights in them as much as in riches (vv. 13–14). Four daily habits close the stanza: meditate, fix the eyes, delight, and do not forget (vv. 15–16).
verseByVerse.theology: The defence of a young life against sin is Scripture kept in the heart.

verseByVerse.quote: How can a young man keep his way pure? By guarding it according to your word. With my whole heart I seek you; let me not wander from your commandments! I have stored up your word in my heart, that I might not sin against you. Blessed are you, O LORD; teach me your statutes! With my lips I declare all the rules of your mouth. In the way of your testimonies I delight as much as in all riches. I will meditate on your precepts and fix my eyes on your ways. I will delight in your statutes; I will not forget your word.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A young life is kept pure by guarding it with God’s word, treasured in the heart, delighted in daily, and taught by God himself.

How can a young man keep his way pure? It is a question every parent asks, and every honest young person. The pressures are strong and the temptations constant, and the answer is not a set of rules invented for the occasion. It is guarding the way “according to your word”, as a watchman guards a road.

I have stored up your word in my heart. “Stored up” is the word for treasure hidden away for safe keeping. Scripture read once and forgotten cannot help in the moment of temptation; Scripture stored in the heart is there when it is needed. That is the case for memorising the Bible. Jesus met the devil in the wilderness with Scripture he already knew: “Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from the mouth of God” (Matthew 4:4). Paul says, “Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly” (Colossians 3:16), and Jesus told his disciples, “Already you are clean because of the word that I have spoken to you” (John 15:3).

How do I store up God’s word? Slowly, a little at a time, and not to earn anything: it is the word of a God who has already spoken to you in his Son (Hebrews 1:2). Choose one verse a week. Pick one that meets a real fight in your life: anxiety at 2 a.m., lust, a quick temper, a sharp tongue. Put it where you will see it. A card in your pocket, the lock screen of your phone, the bathroom mirror. Say it aloud morning and evening, with the reference. Use it in the moment. When the temptation comes, say the verse under your breath and pray it back to God; that is what it was stored for. Go back over the old ones. Review them once a week, or they slip away. Families can do this at the table, and children often learn faster than their parents. You are not left to do it alone: Jesus promised that the Holy Spirit “will teach you all things and bring to your remembrance all that I have said to you” (John 14:26).

Blessed are you, O LORD. The young man blesses God, asks to be taught, and speaks the word aloud. He enjoys it “as much as in all riches”: the pleasure a person takes in money, he takes in God’s ways.

Four daily habits. Meditate, fix the eyes, delight, do not forget: four habits of a young life kept pure, none spectacular, all daily. And they rest on a prayer, “teach me”, because the God who gave the word is the one who keeps the young man by it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A stranger on earth asks God for life, opened eyes and his word as a guide, while the proud scorn him and princes plot. He asks God to deal generously with him so that he may live and obey (v. 17), and prays one of the great prayers for every Bible reader: “Open my eyes” (v. 18). As a sojourner in a foreign land he needs God’s commandments as a traveller needs a guide, and he longs for them constantly (vv. 19–20). God rebukes the proud who wander, and the singer asks him to roll away their scorn (vv. 21–22). While princes sit plotting, he sits meditating, for God’s testimonies are his counsellors (vv. 23–24).
verseByVerse.theology: A stranger on earth asks for eyes to see the wonders already in front of him.

verseByVerse.quote: Deal bountifully with your servant, that I may live and keep your word. Open my eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of your law.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The singer asks God for life to obey him, and for opened eyes to see the wonders already in his word.

Deal bountifully with your servant. The stanza opens by asking for God’s generosity. The same verb is used when a believer says the LORD “has dealt bountifully with me” (Psalm 13:6; compare 116:7). The purpose is plain: “that I may live and keep your word”. He wants life in order to obey, and asks for both as a gift.

Open my eyes. Verse 18 is one of the most important prayers a Bible reader can pray. The wonders are already in the text; the problem is the reader’s blindness. Knowledge, study and intelligence are not enough to see them: God has to open the eyes. After his resurrection Jesus did exactly that for his disciples: “he opened their minds to understand the Scriptures” (Luke 24:45). Pray this verse before you open your Bible.

parallels.desc: Christ opens minds to Scripture; Heb 11:13

verseByVerse.quote: I am a sojourner on the earth; hide not your commandments from me! My soul is consumed with longing for your rules at all times.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A stranger passing through the world needs God’s commandments as a traveller needs a guide, and the singer longs for them constantly.

I am a sojourner on the earth. A sojourner is a foreigner passing through, without citizenship or property. In a strange country the one thing a traveller cannot do without is a guide. So: “hide not your commandments from me!” And his hunger for God’s word is not occasional; it consumes him “at all times”.

A sojourner like his fathers. Abraham called himself “a sojourner and foreigner” among the Hittites (Genesis 23:4), and David prayed, “we are strangers before you and sojourners, as all our fathers were” (1 Chronicles 29:15). The patriarchs “acknowledged that they were strangers and exiles on the earth” (Hebrews 11:13), and Peter writes to Christians “as sojourners and exiles” (1 Peter 2:11). Whoever belongs to God is not fully at home here, and needs his word all the more.

verseByVerse.quote: You rebuke the insolent, accursed ones, who wander from your commandments. Take away from me scorn and contempt, for I have kept your testimonies.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God rebukes the proud who wander from his word, and the singer asks him to roll away the scorn they heap on him.

You rebuke the insolent, accursed ones. The insolent are the proud, people who treat God and his word with contempt; they appear again and again in the psalm (vv. 51, 69, 78, 85, 122). They are accursed because the law itself pronounced the curse: “Cursed be anyone who does not confirm the words of this law by doing them” (Deuteronomy 27:26). And they wander, the very thing the singer prayed to be kept from: “let me not wander from your commandments!” (v. 10). He sees in them where he too could end.

Take away from me scorn and contempt. The verb probably means “roll away”, as when God said to Israel at Gilgal, “Today I have rolled away the reproach of Egypt from you” (Joshua 5:9). The proud mock him because he keeps God’s testimonies, and he does not answer scorn with scorn. He asks God to lift its weight off him. Believers laughed at for their faith may pray the same, and leave the answer to God.

verseByVerse.quote: Even though princes sit plotting against me, your servant will meditate on your statutes. Your testimonies are my delight; they are my counselors.
verseByVerse.commentary:
While powerful men plot against him, the singer meditates on God’s word and takes it as his counsel.

Even though princes sit plotting against me. The opposition that runs through the whole psalm here takes the form of princes, powerful men sitting in council against him. His response is not to plot back: “your servant will meditate on your statutes”. While they discuss him, he thinks about God’s word.

They are my counselors. The princes have their council; he has his, God’s testimonies. When powerful people are deciding your fate, it matters very much whose counsel you are listening to.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 25–32 — Daleth: My Soul Clings to the Dust
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The stanza moves from a soul lying in the dust to a heart set free and running in God’s ways. It opens face down, with a prayer for life according to God’s word (v. 25). The singer has confessed his ways and been answered, and he asks to understand and to meditate (vv. 26–27). His soul melts with sorrow, and he asks for strength and for the law as a gift of grace (vv. 28–29). He has chosen the way of faithfulness and now clings, with the same verb as verse 25, not to the dust but to God’s testimonies (vv. 30–31). The stanza ends running, because God enlarges his heart (v. 32).
verseByVerse.theology: From lying in the dust to running — and the difference is God's word and an enlarged heart.

verseByVerse.quote: My soul clings to the dust; give me life according to your word! When I told of my ways, you answered me; teach me your statutes! Make me understand the way of your precepts, and I will meditate on your wondrous works. My soul melts away for sorrow; strengthen me according to your word! Put false ways far from me and graciously teach me your law! I have chosen the way of faithfulness; I set your rules before me. I cling to your testimonies, O LORD; let me not be put to shame! I will run in the way of your commandments when you enlarge my heart!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Flattened in the dust and melting with grief, the singer asks God for life and strength through his word, and ends running in God’s ways with a heart God has set free.

My soul clings to the dust. The fourth stanza begins face down: flattened, as low as a person can go, the posture of mourning or defeat. And the prayer is for life “according to your word”. The word is not only information; it gives life: “man does not live by bread alone, but man lives by every word that comes from the mouth of the LORD” (Deuteronomy 8:3).

When I told of my ways, you answered me. He confessed his ways honestly to God, and God answered. Honest confession opens the way to being taught.

My soul melts away for sorrow. His soul drips away like wax with grief: not only in the dust but dissolving. Again the remedy is God’s word, which strengthens, and he prays, “graciously teach me your law!” The law is received as grace.

I cling to your testimonies. His soul clung to the dust in verse 25; now he clings, with the same verb, to God’s testimonies. He has transferred his grip from the dust to the word. And the stanza that began lying down ends running: “I will run in the way of your commandments when you enlarge my heart!” The ESV notes another rendering: “for you set my heart free”. Obedience does not come from a cramped, anxious heart, but from a heart God has made large and free.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Almost every verse in this stanza is a request, because the singer knows he cannot keep God’s word unless God changes him. He asks to be taught, to be given understanding and to be led, so that he may keep God’s law to the end and with his whole heart (vv. 33–35). Then come two searching prayers: that God would incline his heart away from selfish gain, and turn his eyes from worthless things (vv. 36–37). He asks God to confirm his promise, to turn away the reproach he dreads, and, as the stanza began with teaching, to end it with life: “in your righteousness give me life!” (vv. 38–40).
verseByVerse.theology: A stanza made almost entirely of requests: teach, lead, incline, turn, give life.

verseByVerse.quote: Teach me, O LORD, the way of your statutes; and I will keep it to the end. Give me understanding, that I may keep your law and observe it with my whole heart. Lead me in the path of your commandments, for I delight in it. Incline my heart to your testimonies, and not to selfish gain! Turn my eyes from looking at worthless things; and give me life in your ways. Confirm to your servant your promise, that you may be feared. Turn away the reproach that I dread, for your rules are good. Behold, I long for your precepts; in your righteousness give me life!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Knowing he cannot keep God’s word by willpower, the singer asks God to teach him, lead him, turn his heart from greed and his eyes from worthless things, and give him life.

Teach me, O LORD. Almost every verse in this stanza is a request: teach me, give me understanding, lead me, incline my heart, turn my eyes, confirm, turn away, give me life. The singer knows he needs God to do something to him first.

I will keep it to the end. Obedience is not a burden to be endured until release, but a path walked all the way (see the Uncertain wording note below).

Incline my heart. Verses 36 and 37 are two of the most searching prayers in the psalm. The heart leans naturally toward “selfish gain”: money, advantage, getting ahead. Only God can tilt it the other way. And the eyes are drawn to “worthless things”, empty, useless and corrupting. David vowed, “I will not set before my eyes anything that is worthless” (Psalm 101:3); here the same resolve becomes a prayer, because the man knows he cannot keep it alone. For anyone who struggles with what they look at, this is a verse to pray before picking up a phone.

Your rules are good. He does not merely submit to God’s commands; he calls them good. And the last request of the stanza is the same as the first of the previous one: “give me life!”

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew word behind “to the end” in verse 33 (and again in verse 112) can mean “end” or “reward”, and the ESV notes the alternative, “keep it as my reward”. The likely sense is “to the end”, all the way; but either reading makes the same point, that keeping God’s word is not a burden but a road worth walking to its end, and a reward in itself.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 41–48 — Waw: I Shall Walk in a Wide Place
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Everything in this stanza flows from God’s steadfast love: an answer for the mocker, hope, obedience, freedom and bold speech. The singer asks for God’s love and salvation to come to him, so that he may answer the man who taunts him (vv. 41–42). He prays that the word of truth will never be taken from his mouth, and vows to keep God’s law forever (vv. 43–44). Far from narrowing his life, the law sets him walking in open country (v. 45). He will speak of it before kings without shame, because he loves God’s commandments and lifts his hands toward them (vv. 46–48).
verseByVerse.theology: God's commands, far from confining, set a man walking in open country and speaking before kings.

verseByVerse.quote: Let your steadfast love come to me, O LORD, your salvation according to your promise; then shall I have an answer for him who taunts me, for I trust in your word.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everything the singer does with God’s word flows from God’s steadfast love and salvation, which give him an answer for those who mock him.

Let your steadfast love come to me. The stanza begins with God’s steadfast love and salvation. Everything the singer does with the word flows from being loved and saved first. The result is “an answer for him who taunts me”. The word of God is “the sword of the Spirit” (Ephesians 6:17), and the believer who trusts it is not left without a reply.

Every line begins with “and”. Few Hebrew words begin with the letter waw, so in this stanza nearly every line begins with it as the little word “and”. The ESV keeps it at the start of verse 43, “And take not”. The effect is a chain of linked thoughts: love, then an answer, then hope, then obedience, then freedom, then bold speech.

verseByVerse.quote: And take not the word of truth utterly out of my mouth, for my hope is in your rules.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The singer prays that, when he must speak for God, the truth will never be taken wholly from his mouth.

Take not the word of truth utterly out of my mouth. He has just said he needs an answer for the one who taunts him (v. 42). Now he prays that the truth will not be taken from his mouth when he must speak it. “Utterly” is the same word as in verse 8, “do not utterly forsake me”: he knows he may falter and fall silent for a time, but asks that God never leave him with nothing to say. His confidence is not in his own quickness: “my hope is in your rules”, in what God has decided and will do.

verseByVerse.quote: I will keep your law continually, forever and ever, and I shall walk in a wide place, for I have sought your precepts.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Keeping God’s law forever does not narrow life but sets the singer walking in open country.

Continually, forever and ever. Three ways of saying the same thing: he means to keep God’s law without a break and without an end. It is a vow, and the next verse shows its spirit: he expects not a narrower life but a wider one.

I shall walk in a wide place. This verse turns a common assumption upside down. People think of God’s commands as a fence, narrowing life. The psalm says the opposite: “I shall walk in a wide place, for I have sought your precepts.” Open country; room to move. James calls it “the perfect law, the law of liberty” (James 1:25). Sin promises freedom and delivers a cell; God’s word looks like limits and turns out to be open ground.

verseByVerse.quote: I will also speak of your testimonies before kings and shall not be put to shame, for I find my delight in your commandments, which I love. I will lift up my hands toward your commandments, which I love, and I will meditate on your statutes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because he loves God’s commandments, the singer will speak of them before kings without shame and lift his hands to them in worship.

Before kings. The man who walks in a wide place is not intimidated in high places. And the stanza ends with love, said twice: “which I love”. He lifts his hands toward the commandments, the gesture of prayer and worship. This is not legalism. It is love for God expressed as love for what God has said. Jesus put it simply: “If you love me, you will keep my commandments” (John 14:15).

And shall not be put to shame.
