Jesus told his disciples they would be “dragged before governors and kings for my sake, to bear witness before them”, and promised them words when the time came (Matthew 10:18–19). Paul stood before King Agrippa and spoke of Christ without embarrassment (Acts 26). The singer’s boldness comes not from rank or skill but from delight: the man who loves God’s word is not ashamed of it, even in a palace.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 49–56 — Zayin: Your Statutes Have Been My Songs
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In affliction and far from home, God’s promise gives the singer life and God’s statutes become his songs. He asks God to remember the word that gave him hope, for that promise is what keeps him alive in suffering (vv. 49–50). The proud mock him, but he holds to God’s law and takes comfort in how God has acted in the past (vv. 51–52). The wicked who abandon God’s law make him burn with holy anger (v. 53). In the lodgings of his journey God’s statutes are his songs, and at night he remembers God’s name (vv. 54–55). Keeping God’s word is not a burden but a blessing given to him (v. 56).
verseByVerse.theology: In affliction and far from home, God's promises become the songs a traveller sings at night.

verseByVerse.quote: Remember your word to your servant, in which you have made me hope. This is my comfort in my affliction, that your promise gives me life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s promise, which first gave the singer hope, is what keeps him alive in his suffering.

Remember your word to your servant. He asks God to remember, not because God forgets, but because he wants to hold God to his promise. God’s word created his hope in the first place: “in which you have made me hope”. In suffering the promise is his comfort. It does not remove the affliction; it “gives me life” in the middle of it.

This is my comfort in my affliction. In hospital beds and at gravesides, a single promise remembered in the dark keeps a person alive inside.

verseByVerse.quote: The insolent utterly deride me, but I do not turn away from your law. When I think of your rules from of old, I take comfort, O LORD. Hot indignation seizes me because of the wicked, who forsake your law.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Mockery does not move the singer: God’s dealings in the past comfort him, and those who abandon God’s law stir him to holy anger.

The insolent utterly deride me. Mockery does not turn him from God’s law. Remembering what God did long ago comforts him.

Your rules from of old. These are probably God’s judgments in the past as well as his written laws: what he decided and did at the flood, at the exodus, in the wilderness. The proud mock now, but the record shows how God has dealt with pride and how he has kept his people. The God who judged and rescued then is the same God now, and that is comfort.

Hot indignation seizes me. The word is used of a scorching wind (Psalm 11:6): the anger comes over him like a blast of desert heat. It is not personal irritation but grief at God being dishonoured. The same man who burns at those who forsake God’s law also weeps for them (v. 136; see the note on vv. 129–136). Holy anger and sorrow belong together.

verseByVerse.quote: Your statutes have been my songs in the house of my sojourning. I remember your name in the night, O LORD, and keep your law. This blessing has fallen to me, that I have kept your precepts.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Far from home, the singer sings God’s statutes like songs of home and remembers God’s name in the night, counting obedience a blessing.

Your statutes have been my songs. “The house of my sojourning” is wherever a traveller stops for the night, a temporary lodging far from home. There God’s statutes become songs. The commandments are not recited like a legal code; they are sung, the way a homesick traveller sings the songs of home.

I remember your name in the night. God’s name is God as he has made himself known, above all in the words proclaimed to Moses: “The LORD, the LORD, a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness” (Exodus 34:6). In the dark, when fears grow, he calls to mind who God is. And remembering leads to doing: “and keep your law”.

This blessing has fallen to me. Keeping God’s word is not a burden laid on him. It is a blessing that has come to him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 57–64 — Heth: The LORD Is My Portion
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The man whose inheritance is God himself turns quickly to obey, praises at midnight and sees the earth full of God’s love. The LORD is his portion, so he promises to keep God’s words and asks for favour on the ground of God’s promise (vv. 57–58). He takes stock of his ways and turns his feet at once, without delay (vv. 59–60). Though the cords of the wicked bind him, he does not forget God’s law, and rises at midnight to give thanks (vv. 61–62). He is a friend of all who fear God (v. 63). The stanza ends by looking out on an earth full of steadfast love, and asking again to be taught (v. 64).
verseByVerse.theology: A man whose inheritance is God himself obeys without delay and sings at midnight.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD is my portion; I promise to keep your words. I entreat your favor with all my heart; be gracious to me according to your promise. When I think on my ways, I turn my feet to your testimonies; I hasten and do not delay to keep your commandments. Though the cords of the wicked ensnare me, I do not forget your law. At midnight I rise to praise you, because of your righteous rules. I am a companion of all who fear you, of those who keep your precepts. The earth, O LORD, is full of your steadfast love; teach me your statutes!
verseByVerse.commentary:
The man whose inheritance is God himself turns quickly to obey, praises God at midnight, befriends all who fear God, and sees the earth full of God’s love.

The LORD is my portion. This is the language of Psalm 16 (16:5). Other people inherit land; his inheritance is God himself. A man whose whole portion is God wants to keep God’s words. He asks for favour “with all my heart”, and he asks it on the basis of God’s promise, not his own record.

I turn my feet to your testimonies. Here is repentance in two verses. He thinks about the way he is going, takes stock honestly, and turns his feet. Then he acts at once: “I hasten and do not delay”. Delayed obedience is usually disobedience in disguise. But the haste is not anxious striving: a man whose portion is already the LORD runs to the one who has given him everything.

At midnight I rise to praise you. Bound by the cords of the wicked, he does not forget God’s law, and at midnight he gets up to praise. Paul and Silas did exactly that in a prison in Philippi, singing hymns about midnight with their feet in the stocks (Acts 16:25).

I am a companion of all who fear you. Love of God’s word draws a person into friendship with others who love it. And the stanza ends by looking up and out: “The earth, O LORD, is full of your steadfast love”. The man surrounded by the cords of the wicked sees a world full of God’s love, and asks, again, to be taught.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 65–72 — Teth: It Is Good for Me That I Was Afflicted
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Looking back, the singer calls his affliction good, because it brought him back to God’s word. The stanza opens with a verdict over everything that follows: “You have dealt well with your servant” (vv. 65–66). Before he was afflicted, he went astray; now he keeps God’s word (v. 67). At the centre stands what holds it together: God is good and does good (v. 68). The proud smear him with lies, their hearts grown thick and unfeeling, while he delights in God’s law (vv. 69–70). So he can say the hardest sentence of the psalm, “It is good for me that I was afflicted”, and count God’s word richer than all gold (vv. 71–72).
verseByVerse.theology: Looking back, a man calls his suffering good, because it brought him home to God's word.

verseByVerse.quote: You have dealt well with your servant, O LORD, according to your word. Teach me good judgment and knowledge, for I believe in your commandments. Before I was afflicted I went astray, but now I keep your word. You are good and do good; teach me your statutes. The insolent smear me with lies, but with my whole heart I keep your precepts; their heart is unfeeling like fat, but I delight in your law. It is good for me that I was afflicted, that I might learn your statutes. The law of your mouth is better to me than thousands of gold and silver pieces.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Looking back, the singer calls his affliction good, because the good God used it to bring him back from straying to his word.

You have dealt well with your servant. The ninth stanza looks back over suffering, and it begins with a verdict: “You have dealt well with your servant”. Everything that follows must be read in the light of that sentence.

Before I was afflicted I went astray. An honest confession. Prosperity had made him careless: things went well, and he drifted. Then trouble came, and it brought him back: “but now I keep your word.”

You are good and do good. In the middle of that confession stands a statement about God that holds everything together. God did not stop being good when the affliction came. The affliction was one of the good things he did.

Their heart is unfeeling like fat. The proud have hearts thick and padded, unable to feel anything. Comfort without God does that to a heart. Affliction with God does the opposite.

It is good for me that I was afflicted. Verse 71 is one of the hardest and most precious sentences in Scripture. No one says it during the affliction. It is the verdict of a man looking back from the other side, who can see what the pain taught him. Hebrews says the same: discipline “seems painful rather than pleasant, but later it yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness to those who have been trained by it” (Hebrews 12:11). And he gained something: God’s law, “better to me than thousands of gold and silver pieces”. He lost comfort and found treasure.

If you are suffering now. If you are in the middle of affliction, do not force yourself to say this verse yet. But hold on to the possibility that one day you will.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 73–80 — Yodh: In Faithfulness You Have Afflicted Me
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The hands that made the singer have afflicted him in faithfulness, and he asks those same hands for comfort and understanding. He reasons from creation: the God who fashioned him will surely teach him how to live (v. 73). His steadfastness will encourage others who fear God (v. 74). He confesses that God’s rules are righteous and that God afflicted him in faithfulness (v. 75), yet he still asks for comfort from God’s steadfast love and mercy (vv. 76–77). He asks God to shame the liars and to turn God-fearing people to him, and prays that his own heart may be blameless (vv. 78–80).
verseByVerse.theology: The hands that made him are the hands that afflict him — and both are faithful.

verseByVerse.quote: Your hands have made and fashioned me; give me understanding that I may learn your commandments. Those who fear you shall see me and rejoice, because I have hoped in your word. I know, O LORD, that your rules are righteous, and that in faithfulness you have afflicted me. Let your steadfast love comfort me according to your promise to your servant. Let your mercy come to me, that I may live; for your law is my delight. Let the insolent be put to shame, because they have wronged me with falsehood; as for me, I will meditate on your precepts. Let those who fear you turn to me, that they may know your testimonies. May my heart be blameless in your statutes, that I may not be put to shame!
verseByVerse.commentary:
The God whose hands made the singer has afflicted him in faithfulness, and the singer still asks those hands for understanding, comfort and mercy.

Your hands have made and fashioned me. An argument from creation. God made him with his own hands; surely the Maker will teach the thing he made how to live. A craftsman does not build a delicate instrument and refuse to explain how it works.

Those who fear you shall see me and rejoice. His steadiness under trouble will encourage others. A believer who holds on to God’s word through suffering becomes a gift to the church.

In faithfulness you have afflicted me. The hands that fashioned him (v. 73) are the hands that have afflicted him, and he calls it faithfulness. Not cruelty, not carelessness, not a lapse: God afflicted him because God was being faithful to him, to his purpose of making him holy. That is a conclusion only faith can reach, and it is a firm place to stand.

Let your steadfast love comfort me. Knowing the affliction is faithful does not make it painless. He still needs comfort, and he asks for it from God’s steadfast love and mercy. Faith accepts the hard things God sends, and still asks him for tenderness.

Let those who fear you turn to me. He wants to be a help to other believers, and he wants his own heart to be blameless. The man who has suffered well becomes someone others come to.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 81–88 — Kaph: Like a Wineskin in the Smoke
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: This is the darkest stanza of the psalm: the singer is shrivelled like a wineskin in the smoke, nearly finished, and still holding on to God’s word. He faints with longing for God’s salvation, and his eyes strain for the promise: “When will you comfort me?” (vv. 81–82). Dried up and blackened like an old wineskin, he has not forgotten God’s statutes (v. 83). He asks how long he must endure, as the proud dig pits and persecute him with lies (vv. 84–86). They have almost made an end of him, but he has not forsaken God’s precepts, and he ends asking for life so that he may obey (vv. 87–88).
verseByVerse.theology: The lowest point of the psalm: shrivelled, persecuted, almost finished, and still holding on.

verseByVerse.quote: My soul longs for your salvation; I hope in your word. My eyes long for your promise; I ask, "When will you comfort me?" For I have become like a wineskin in the smoke, yet I have not forgotten your statutes. How long must your servant endure? When will you judge those who persecute me? The insolent have dug pitfalls for me; they do not live according to your law. All your commandments are sure; they persecute me with falsehood; help me! They have almost made an end of me on earth, but I have not forsaken your precepts. In your steadfast love give me life, that I may keep the testimonies of your mouth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Worn out with waiting, dried up and nearly destroyed by his persecutors, the singer still holds on to God’s word and asks for life so that he may keep it.

My soul longs for your salvation. This is the darkest stanza in the psalm. The word for “longs” means to faint, to waste away with waiting. His eyes are strained from looking for God’s promise to come true: “When will you comfort me?” Faith asks when, not whether. But it does ask.

Like a wineskin in the smoke. A leather wineskin hung near the fire in a house with no chimney would slowly dry out, blacken, shrivel and crack. That is how he feels: dried up, useless, smoke-stained, ready to split. “Yet I have not forgotten your statutes.” The container is ruined; the contents are kept.

How long must your servant endure? The ESV notes the Hebrew is literally “How many are the days of your servant?”: how long do I have left? He wonders whether he will live long enough to see God act.

The insolent have dug pitfalls for me. Traps dug in his path, and lies. “They have almost made an end of me”. Almost. Then one of the shortest prayers in the psalm: “help me!” Against their lies, “all your commandments are sure”.

In your steadfast love give me life. The stanza that began fainting ends asking for life, not to escape, but to keep God’s word. Even at the bottom, his desire is to obey.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 89–96 — Lamedh: Forever, O LORD, Your Word Is Fixed
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: After the darkest stanza the psalm looks up and finds God’s word fixed forever in heaven, holding up a man who nearly perished. God’s word stands firm in the heavens, and his faithfulness has established the earth, which serves him (vv. 89–91). The singer testifies that delight in God’s law kept him alive in his affliction, and that God’s precepts gave him life (vv. 92–93). His whole appeal is that he belongs to God: “I am yours; save me” (vv. 94–95). He has seen the edge of every human perfection, but God’s commandment has no edge: it is exceedingly broad (v. 96).
verseByVerse.theology: At the centre of the psalm, the word that does not change holds up the man who nearly perished.

verseByVerse.quote: Forever, O LORD, your word is firmly fixed in the heavens. Your faithfulness endures to all generations; you have established the earth, and it stands fast. By your appointment they stand this day, for all things are your servants. If your law had not been my delight, I would have perished in my affliction. I will never forget your precepts, for by them you have given me life. I am yours; save me, for I have sought your precepts. The wicked lie in wait to destroy me, but I consider your testimonies. I have seen a limit to all perfection, but your commandment is exceedingly broad.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s word stands fixed forever in heaven, unlike every limited human perfection, and delight in it kept the singer alive when he was nearly lost.

Your word is firmly fixed in the heavens. After the darkest stanza, the psalm lifts its eyes, and the turn is sudden and complete. On earth he was a shrivelled wineskin; in heaven the word stands like a fixed star. His life is nearly over; God’s word is forever. “The grass withers, the flower fades, but the word of our God will stand forever” (Isaiah 40:8). Jesus said he had not come to abolish the Law and the Prophets “but to fulfill them” (Matthew 5:17).

All things are your servants. Heaven and earth keep standing because God appointed them to. The sun, the sea, the seasons, and the troubles too: nothing in creation is outside his service.

If your law had not been my delight. Verse 92 is his testimony in one sentence: what kept him alive through the affliction of the last stanza was his delight in God’s law, not his strength or his circumstances. Anyone who has come through a long darkness with faith intact can usually point to the passage that held them.

I am yours; save me. That is the whole ground of his appeal: not “I have earned it”, but “I belong to you”. An owner saves his own.

I have seen a limit to all perfection. He has looked at every human achievement, every perfect-seeming thing, and found where it ends. Everything has an edge. But God’s commandment has none: “exceedingly broad”, wider than any life can exhaust. You can read it for eighty years and never reach the boundary.

The tyranny of the perfect. We live surrounded by images of perfection: the flawless kitchen, the toned body, the curated holiday, the career that seems to rise without a stumble. Many people, the young especially, measure themselves against these every day, and researchers have found perfectionism rising steadily among students over recent decades. The trouble is not high standards but the hope underneath them: if I can only get my life flawless, I will finally be acceptable, to others and to myself. The psalmist has already done the experiment. He has found the edge of every perfect-seeming thing, so he stops looking for something unlimited in a limited place. The gospel’s reversal is that the perfection we keep chasing has already been lived, by someone else, on our behalf. Christ kept the commandment that is exceedingly broad, all the way to the end, and God counts his record as ours: “For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God” (2 Corinthians 5:21). A person who knows that can still work with great care. But they no longer need to be flawless in order to be loved.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew word translated “perfection” in verse 96 occurs only here in the Old Testament. It comes from a root meaning to complete or finish, so it probably means everything that seems complete or perfect. The contrast is clear either way: everything else has a limit, and God’s commandment does not.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 97–104 — Mem: Oh How I Love Your Law
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Love for God’s law shows itself in meditation, wisdom, obedience and delight. The stanza begins with an exclamation of love: the law is the singer’s meditation all day (v. 97). That constant meditation makes him wiser than his enemies, his teachers and the elders, because God’s word is always with him and he obeys it (vv. 98–100). He keeps back from every evil way and does not turn aside, because God himself has taught him (vv. 101–102). God’s words are sweeter than honey, and the understanding they give makes him hate every false way (vv. 103–104).
verseByVerse.theology: Love for God's law, tasted like honey, makes an ordinary believer wise.

verseByVerse.quote: Oh how I love your law! It is my meditation all the day. Your commandment makes me wiser than my enemies, for it is ever with me. I have more understanding than all my teachers, for your testimonies are my meditation. I understand more than the aged, for I keep your precepts. I hold back my feet from every evil way, in order to keep your word. I do not turn aside from your rules, for you have taught me. How sweet are your words to my taste, sweeter than honey to my mouth! Through your precepts I get understanding; therefore I hate every false way.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Love for God’s law shows itself in constant meditation, and it makes the singer wise, keeps him from evil and tastes sweeter than honey, because God himself is teaching him.

Oh how I love your law! One of the most famous verses in the psalm is an exclamation of love. Not “how I respect your law”, but how I love it. And love shows itself in attention: “It is my meditation all the day.” God told Joshua, “you shall meditate on it day and night, so that you may be careful to do according to all that is written in it” (Joshua 1:8). What we love, we think about.

What it means to meditate. For many people today meditation means emptying the mind. Biblical meditation is the opposite: filling the mind with what God has said and turning it over until it reaches the heart. The Hebrew word given to Joshua pictures a low murmuring, someone going over the words half aloud, the way you reread a letter from someone you love. Timothy Keller often pointed out that Martin Luther’s advice to his barber, Peter, is still one of the best guides: take a passage and weave it into a garland of four strands, instruction (what is God teaching me here?), thanksgiving (what can I thank him for?), confession (where have I failed?) and prayer (what must I now ask?). That keeps reading from staying in the head. And it is not a technique for getting more out of a book. Jesus said, “The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life” (John 6:63): to meditate on Scripture is to let the living Christ speak to you, and to answer him. Try it with one verse tomorrow morning, and carry it with you through the day.

I have more understanding than all my teachers. Wiser than enemies, than teachers, than “the aged” (the ESV notes “the elders”). This is not arrogance: he is saying where wisdom comes from. A person who meditates on God’s word will understand life better than a brilliant person who does not, because all Scripture is “breathed out by God and profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, and for training in righteousness” (2 Timothy 3:16). And the last reason matters: “for I keep your precepts”. Wisdom grows by obeying, not only by reading. Behind it all stands the true teacher: “for you have taught me”.

Sweeter than honey to my mouth! God’s words are not medicine to be swallowed but honey to be tasted. Jeremiah said, “Your words were found, and I ate them, and your words became to me a joy and the delight of my heart” (Jeremiah 15:16). If the Bible tastes dry to you, pray verse 18 again, “Open my eyes”, and keep eating. Taste grows with feeding.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 105–112 — Nun: A Lamp to My Feet
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s word is a lamp for the next step on a dark and dangerous road, and the singer binds himself to follow it to the end. The stanza opens with the psalm’s best-known verse: a small lamp lighting the path ahead (v. 105). He has sworn to keep God’s rules, though he is severely afflicted and needs God to give him life (vv. 106–107). He offers his praise and asks to be taught (v. 108). His life is in constant danger and the wicked have set traps, yet he does not forget or stray (vv. 109–110). God’s testimonies are his inheritance and joy, and he sets his heart to obey to the end (vv. 111–112).
verseByVerse.theology: The word is light for the next step on a dark road, not a floodlight on the whole journey.

verseByVerse.quote: Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my path. I have sworn an oath and confirmed it, to keep your righteous rules. I am severely afflicted; give me life, O LORD, according to your word! Accept my freewill offerings of praise, O LORD, and teach me your rules. I hold my life in my hand continually, but I do not forget your law. The wicked have laid a snare for me, but I do not stray from your precepts. Your testimonies are my heritage forever, for they are the joy of my heart. I incline my heart to perform your statutes forever, to the end.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s word lights the next step on a dark and dangerous road, and the singer, afflicted and in danger, takes it as his inheritance and binds himself to follow it to the end.

Your word is a lamp to my feet. It is worth noticing exactly what the best-known verse in the psalm says. A lamp in the ancient world was a small clay oil lamp that threw a pool of light a few steps ahead. It did not light up the whole road. It lit the next step.

How God’s word guides. That is how God’s word usually guides. It does not always show the whole shape of your future. It shows you what to do next, the next act of obedience, the next step of trust, and then the next. “The commandment is a lamp and the teaching a light” (Proverbs 6:23), and Peter says we do well to pay attention to it “as to a lamp shining in a dark place, until the day dawns” (2 Peter 1:19). The lamp is for the dark, and the dark will not last forever.

I am severely afflicted. The lamp does not mean the road is easy. He needs light precisely because it is dark.

I hold my life in my hand. A phrase for living in constant danger, as if carrying your life around exposed, liable to be dropped. And still he does not forget and does not stray.

Your testimonies are my heritage forever. His inheritance is God’s word, “the joy of my heart”, and his heart leans toward obeying “forever, to the end” (the ESV notes it may mean “the reward is eternal”; see the note on vv. 33–40).

Why should an ancient book guide a modern life? It is a fair question. We replace our phones every few years; why steer by a lamp lit three thousand years ago? Behind the question sits a quiet assumption that newer is truer. C. S. Lewis, in his introduction to a translation of Athanasius’s On the Incarnation, argued the opposite. Every age has its own blind spots, invisible to the people inside it, and the only way to see ours is to read books written outside it. A book from our own decade can only agree with us; a book from outside every decade can correct us all, the progressive and the traditionalist alike. But the psalm claims more than old wisdom. It calls this word a lamp because God speaks in it, and in the end the light has a face: “I am the light of the world. Whoever follows me will not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life” (John 8:12). The lamp is old. The one who holds it is alive, and he still knows the next step of every road.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 113–120 — Samekh: You Are My Hiding Place
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A single-hearted man hides in God and trembles before him. Against the divided loyalty he hates, the singer sets his undivided love for God’s law (v. 113). God is his hiding place and shield, so he sends away the evildoers who would pull him from obedience to “my God” (vv. 114–115). Twice he asks God to hold him up, so that his hope will not be put to shame (vv. 116–117). God throws away those who stray from his statutes like dross skimmed from metal, and that makes the singer love God’s word more (vv. 118–119). The stanza ends with trembling: the God who shelters him is to be feared (v. 120).
verseByVerse.theology: A single-hearted man hides in God — and trembles before him.

verseByVerse.quote: I hate the double-minded, but I love your law. You are my hiding place and my shield; I hope in your word. Depart from me, you evildoers, that I may keep the commandments of my God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Against divided loyalty the singer sets an undivided love for God’s law, hides in God, and sends away the company that would pull him from obeying “my God”.

I hate the double-minded. The double-minded are the divided, people who try to love God and something else equally, keeping a foot in each world. James says such a man is “unstable in all his ways” (James 1:8). What the singer hates is that divided loyalty, and against it he sets a single love: “I love your law”. The prayer of Psalm 86:11, “unite my heart”, has been answered in him.

My hiding place and my shield. Two pictures of safety: a place to hide from danger, and a shield to hold against it. Both are God himself, and the singer takes shelter in him by hoping in his word.

Depart from me, you evildoers. He sends away the company that would pull him from obedience, “that I may keep the commandments of my God”. Paul warns, “Bad company ruins good morals” (1 Corinthians 15:33). This is the only place in the psalm where the singer calls God “my God”: the commandments are dear to him because the God who gave them is his own.

Uncertain wording. The word translated “the double-minded” occurs only here. It is related to a word for branches or divided opinions, as when Elijah asked Israel, “How long will you go limping between two different opinions?” (1 Kings 18:21). So it probably means people who waver, divided in their loyalty.

verseByVerse.quote: Uphold me according to your promise, that I may live, and let me not be put to shame in my hope! Hold me up, that I may be safe and have regard for your statutes continually!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not trusting his own strength, the singer twice asks God to hold him up so that his hope will not end in shame.

Uphold me according to your promise. “Uphold me”, “Hold me up”: twice. He does not trust his own strength to keep his hope from collapsing. He needs God’s hands under him.

Let me not be put to shame in my hope! To be put to shame is to have trusted and been let down in front of everyone. He has staked everything on God’s promise; if it failed, he would be shown a fool. The New Testament answers the prayer: “hope does not put us to shame, because God’s love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit” (Romans 5:5).

verseByVerse.quote: You spurn all who go astray from your statutes, for their cunning is in vain. All the wicked of the earth you discard like dross, therefore I love your testimonies. My flesh trembles for fear of you, and I am afraid of your judgments.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God throws away the wicked like dross, which makes the singer love God’s word more and tremble before God himself.

You discard like dross. Dross is the scum skimmed off molten metal and thrown away. That is what the wicked are in God’s eyes. Their cunning is “in vain”.

Therefore I love your testimonies. Seeing God throw away the wicked does not make him smug; it makes him love God’s word more. God’s judgments show that his word is not idle talk: what he has said about sin, he does. A word that God backs with action is a word worth loving, and worth fearing, as the next verse says.

My flesh trembles for fear of you. The stanza ends with trembling. The man who hides in God (v. 114) shakes before him. These are not opposites. The God who is our hiding place is the God whose judgments throw the wicked away like dross, and a believer who loves him never loses a holy fear of him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 121–128 — Ayin: It Is Time for the LORD to Act
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When God’s law is openly broken, the singer asks God to act, and his love for God’s commandments grows stronger. He is in the right against his oppressors, and asks God not to abandon him but to stand surety for him (vv. 121–122). His eyes are worn out watching for God’s salvation, and he asks to be dealt with by steadfast love and given understanding as God’s servant (vv. 123–125). Then the cry: “It is time for the LORD to act, for your law has been broken” (v. 126). The world’s contempt does not weaken his love but sharpens it: he loves God’s commandments above fine gold and hates every false way (vv. 127–128).
verseByVerse.theology: When God's law is trampled around him, the believer loves it more, not less.

verseByVerse.quote: I have done what is just and right; do not leave me to my oppressors. Give your servant a pledge of good; let not the insolent oppress me. My eyes long for your salvation and for the fulfillment of your righteous promise. Deal with your servant according to your steadfast love, and teach me your statutes. I am your servant; give me understanding, that I may know your testimonies! It is time for the LORD to act, for your law has been broken. Therefore I love your commandments above gold, above fine gold. Therefore I consider all your precepts to be right; I hate every false way.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When God’s law is openly broken, the singer asks God to stand surety for him and to act, and the world’s contempt only makes him love God’s commandments more.

I have done what is just and right. He appeals to God as a man in the right being mistreated. This is not a claim to be sinless (verse 176 settles that); it is the plea of a man in the right in this quarrel. And he asks for something unusual: “a pledge of good”. A pledge is what a guarantor gives when he stands surety for another person’s debt with his own resources. He asks God to put himself on the line for his servant. That is precisely what God did in Christ, “the guarantor of a better covenant” (Hebrews 7:22).

Deal with your servant. Three times in four verses, “your servant”. And the request is to be dealt with “according to your steadfast love”, not according to what he deserves.

It is time for the LORD to act. A cry every generation of believers has prayed. When God’s law is openly despised, when what he calls good is mocked and what he calls evil is celebrated, the believer may say: it is time for the LORD to act. Not to take matters into his own hands, but to call on God to take them into his.

Therefore I love your commandments. The logic is surprising: “your law has been broken. Therefore I love your commandments”. You might expect the opposite: when everyone ignores God’s word, it is easy to drift with them. The psalm does the reverse. The more the world tramples God’s law, the more precious it becomes to the one who loves it, “above gold, above fine gold”. A culture’s contempt for Scripture can sharpen a believer’s love for it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 129–136 — Pe: The Unfolding of Your Words Gives Light
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s word, opened by God, gives light even to simple people, and the singer longs for it, asks for grace, and weeps for those who ignore it. He keeps God’s testimonies because they are wonderful (v. 129). When God’s words are opened they give light and understanding to the simple (v. 130). He pants for God’s commandments like an animal for water (v. 131). He asks God to turn to him in grace, to keep his steps steady, to break the rule of sin within and the oppression of men without (vv. 132–134), and to make his face shine on him (v. 135). The stanza ends with streams of tears for those who do not keep God’s law (v. 136).
verseByVerse.theology: God's word, unfolded, lets in light — and a man who loves it weeps for those who ignore it.

verseByVerse.quote: Your testimonies are wonderful; therefore my soul keeps them. The unfolding of your words gives light; it imparts understanding to the simple. I open my mouth and pant, because I long for your commandments. Turn to me and be gracious to me, as is your way with those who love your name. Keep steady my steps according to your promise, and let no iniquity get dominion over me. Redeem me from man's oppression, that I may keep your precepts. Make your face shine upon your servant, and teach me your statutes. My eyes shed streams of tears, because people do not keep your law.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s wonderful word, opened by him, gives light even to simple people; the singer pants for it, asks God to rule him by it, and weeps for those who ignore it.

Your testimonies are wonderful. He keeps God’s word not because he is forced to, but because it is wonderful. Obedience flows from wonder.

The unfolding of your words gives light. The word means an opening, like a door swung open or a scroll unrolled, letting light in. And the light is for “the simple”: not the educated elite but ordinary, unsophisticated people. The Bible is not a puzzle for scholars. When God opens it, a plain person can understand it.

I open my mouth and pant. The picture is of an animal gasping for water, mouth open. God said in Psalm 81, “Open your mouth wide, and I will fill it” (Psalm 81:10). Here is a man with his mouth open, panting for God’s word.

Let no iniquity get dominion over me. He fears not only oppressors outside but sin inside, ruling him like a tyrant, and asks God to break its reign.

Make your face shine upon your servant. Verse 135 turns the priestly blessing, “the LORD make his face to shine upon you” (Numbers 6:25), into a personal prayer.

My eyes shed streams of tears. The stanza ends in tears, not for himself but for others, because people do not keep God’s law. Love for Scripture does not make a person proud or harsh toward those who reject it. It makes him weep for them. Jesus wept over Jerusalem (Luke 19:41). Such tears are not worked up; they are the Spirit’s gift, and worth asking for.

Uncertain wording. The word translated “unfolding” in verse 130 is rare, and the older English translations rendered it “entrance” (“the entrance of thy words giveth light”). It comes from the verb “to open”, so it may mean the opening up or explaining of God’s words, or the door by which they come in. Either way, the light comes when God’s words are opened to us.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 137–144 — Tsadhe: Your Law Is True
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God is righteous, so everything he says is righteous and true, and a small, despised believer can stand on it. The stanza is built on the word “righteous”: God himself is righteous, and his rules and testimonies come from his righteous, faithful character (vv. 137–138). The singer burns with zeal because his foes forget God’s words, while he loves God’s well-tested promise (vv. 139–140). He is small and despised, yet he holds to what is righteous forever and true (vv. 141–142). Trouble and anguish have found him, but God’s commandments are his delight, and he asks for understanding that he may live (vv. 143–144).
verseByVerse.theology: Small and despised, the believer rests on a righteousness and a truth that last forever.

verseByVerse.quote: Righteous are you, O LORD, and right are your rules. You have appointed your testimonies in righteousness and in all faithfulness. My zeal consumes me, because my foes forget your words. Your promise is well tried, and your servant loves it. I am small and despised, yet I do not forget your precepts. Your righteousness is righteous forever, and your law is true. Trouble and anguish have found me out, but your commandments are my delight. Your testimonies are righteous forever; give me understanding that I may live.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everything God says flows from his righteous and faithful character, so a small and despised believer, in trouble, can stand on it with delight.

Righteous are you, O LORD. This stanza is built on the word “righteous”. God is righteous, his rules are right, his testimonies were appointed in righteousness. What God says flows from what God is. Paul says the same: “the law is holy, and the commandment is holy and righteous and good” (Romans 7:12).

My zeal consumes me. He is like the man in Psalm 69 who said, “zeal for your house has consumed me” (Psalm 69:9). It burns the psalmist up that people forget God’s words. The disciples remembered that line when Jesus cleared the temple (John 2:17): the zeal of this psalm burned fully in him.

Your promise is well tried. It is refined, like metal tested in the fire and found pure. God’s promises have been through every test for thousands of years and have never failed. That is why his servant loves them.

I am small and despised. He has no status, no influence, no respect, and yet he holds on to something “righteous forever” and “true”. The smallness of the believer does not reduce the size of what he believes. On the night before he died, Jesus prayed for his small, frightened disciples, “Sanctify them in the truth; your word is truth” (John 17:17).

Trouble and anguish have found me out. They have tracked him down like hunters. “But your commandments are my delight.” Trouble and delight in the same verse: that is the Christian life as this psalm describes it, not one instead of the other, but both at once.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 145–152 — Qoph: But You Are Near, O LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In urgent prayer before dawn the singer finds that his enemies are near, but God is nearer. He cries with his whole heart, asking to be answered and saved so that he may obey (vv. 145–146). He rises before dawn to cry for help, and lies awake through the night to meditate on God’s promise (vv. 147–148). He appeals to God’s steadfast love and justice for life (v. 149). The persecutors draw near, but they are far from God’s law; and God is nearer still, and all his commandments are true (vv. 150–151). Long experience has taught him that God’s testimonies are founded forever (v. 152).
verseByVerse.theology: Enemies come near — and God is nearer.

verseByVerse.quote: With my whole heart I cry; answer me, O LORD! I will keep your statutes. I call to you; save me, that I may observe your testimonies.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The singer cries to God with his whole heart to be saved, so that he may obey.

With my whole heart I cry. The nineteenth stanza is a stanza of urgent, repeated prayer: I cry, I call, I cry for help. And every request for rescue is joined to a purpose: “that I may observe your testimonies”. He wants to be saved in order to obey.

verseByVerse.quote: I rise before dawn and cry for help; I hope in your words. My eyes are awake before the watches of the night, that I may meditate on your promise.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before dawn and through the night watches the singer prays and meditates on God’s promise.

I rise before dawn. He is praying before anyone else is awake, and lying awake meditating when others sleep. For the anxious believer who cannot sleep, this is a model: use the wakeful hours to think over God’s promises.

The watches of the night. Israel divided the night into watches, the hours when guards took turns on the walls (Judges 7:19; Lamentations 2:19). His eyes are open before the watch changes. And what he meditates on is a promise, not his trouble.

verseByVerse.quote: Hear my voice according to your steadfast love; O LORD, according to your justice give me life. They draw near who persecute me with evil purpose; they are far from your law. But you are near, O LORD, and all your commandments are true.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Appealing to God’s steadfast love and justice, the singer finds that though his persecutors are near, God is nearer.

According to your justice give me life. He appeals to two things in God: his steadfast love, his faithful covenant kindness, and his justice, the same Hebrew word the ESV elsewhere translates “rules” (as in v. 156). He does not ask God to bend his rules for him; he asks God to act as he is and as he has said. For a believer God’s justice is not only a threat but a ground of appeal, because God has bound himself by promise. John says the same: “he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins” (1 John 1:9).

But you are near, O LORD. Here is the heart of the stanza, built on two words, near and far. The persecutors “draw near”, closing in, but they are “far from your law”. And then: “But you are near, O LORD.” The enemies are close; God is closer. Whatever is approaching you with evil purpose, the LORD is nearer than it is.

verseByVerse.quote: Long have I known from your testimonies that you have founded them forever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A lifetime with God’s word has taught the singer that it stands forever.

Long have I known. Not a new discovery: a lifetime of reading God’s word has taught him that it is founded forever. Experience confirms Scripture.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 153–160 — Resh: Plead My Cause and Redeem Me
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The singer asks God to be his advocate and redeemer, and rests on the sum of God’s word, which is truth. He asks God to look on his affliction and rescue him (v. 153), to plead his cause as a lawyer and redeem him as a kinsman (v. 154). Salvation is far from the wicked, but God’s mercy is great (vv. 155–156). Many persecute him, yet he does not swerve, and the faithless fill him with disgust (vv. 157–158). Three times he asks for life, on the ground of God’s promise, rules and steadfast love (vv. 154, 156, 159). The stanza ends on the whole of God’s word: its sum is truth, and every rule endures (v. 160).
verseByVerse.theology: The afflicted man asks God to be his advocate and redeemer, and rests on the whole of his word.

verseByVerse.quote: Look on my affliction and deliver me, for I do not forget your law. Plead my cause and redeem me; give me life according to your promise!
verseByVerse.commentary:
The singer asks God to see his affliction and to act for him as advocate and redeemer, which is what Christ is for his people.

Look on my affliction. He asks God to look, as God looked on Israel in Egypt: “I have surely seen the affliction of my people” (Exodus 3:7). When God sees the affliction of his people, rescue follows. The reason given, “for I do not forget your law”, is not a claim to have earned help but the mark of one who belongs to God.

Plead my cause and redeem me. Two legal pictures. Plead my cause: be my advocate in court, argue my case. Redeem me: act as the kinsman who buys back a relative from debt or slavery. He asks God to be both his lawyer and his next of kin.

Christ our advocate. That is exactly who Christ is for his people. “We have an advocate with the Father” (1 John 2:1), and he is the kinsman who shared our flesh and blood in order to redeem us (Hebrews 2:14).

verseByVerse.quote: Salvation is far from the wicked, for they do not seek your statutes. Great is your mercy, O LORD; give me life according to your rules.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Salvation is far from those who ignore God’s word, and the singer’s hope rests not on his own goodness but on God’s great mercy.

Salvation is far from the wicked. Salvation is far from those who do not seek God’s word: the near-and-far picture of the last stanza again. And his hope is not his own goodness but this: “Great is your mercy, O LORD”.

verseByVerse.quote: Many are my persecutors and my adversaries, but I do not swerve from your testimonies. I look at the faithless with disgust, because they do not keep your commands. Consider how I love your precepts! Give me life, O LORD, according to your steadfast love.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Surrounded by persecutors, the singer does not swerve; he grieves over the faithless and asks God, who sees his love for his word, to give him life.

Many are my persecutors. Many enemies, and one steady answer: “I do not swerve”. His disgust at the faithless is not contempt for people beneath him. It is the loathing of a man who loves God at seeing God’s word thrown aside, and in the same psalm he weeps for such people (v. 136).

Consider how I love your precepts! This is not a boast to win God’s favour, for the same verse rests on God’s steadfast love. It is the plea of a child who says, “See, I love what you love.” Peter said something like it after his fall: “Lord, you know everything; you know that I love you” (John 21:17).

Give me life. Three times in this stanza he asks God to give him life (vv. 154, 156, 159): according to God’s promise, rules and steadfast love. The life he needs comes from God’s word and God’s character together.

verseByVerse.quote: The sum of your word is truth, and every one of your righteous rules endures forever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s word is true not only in its parts but in its whole, and none of it expires.

The sum of your word is truth. The sum is the whole of it, added up. Not merely that God’s word contains truth, or is mostly true, but that the total is truth. And “every one” of his rules endures. Nothing in it expires. A believer can trust not just the parts of Scripture he likes, but the sum.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew word translated “sum” is literally “head”, which can mean the total of a count, the chief part, or the beginning (older translations had “thy word is true from the beginning”). The ESV’s “sum” fits the parallel with “every one” in the second line: the whole and each part are true.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 161–168 — Sin and Shin: Like One Who Finds Great Spoil
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Awe before God’s word drives out the fear of princes and brings joy, praise and great peace. Princes persecute the singer without cause, but his heart trembles only before God’s words (v. 161). He rejoices in God’s word like a soldier finding great treasure after battle (v. 162). He hates falsehood and loves God’s law, and praises God seven times a day (vv. 163–164). Those who love God’s law have great peace, and nothing can make them stumble (v. 165). He hopes for God’s salvation and keeps his word with deep love, living openly before God (vv. 166–168).
verseByVerse.theology: A man who fears God's words more than princes finds treasure, peace and praise seven times a day.

verseByVerse.quote: Princes persecute me without cause, but my heart stands in awe of your words. I rejoice at your word like one who finds great spoil. I hate and abhor falsehood, but I love your law. Seven times a day I praise you for your righteous rules. Great peace have those who love your law; nothing can make them stumble. I hope for your salvation, O LORD, and I do your commandments. My soul keeps your testimonies; I love them exceedingly. I keep your precepts and testimonies, for all my ways are before you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Awe before God’s word drives out the fear of powerful men and brings joy like a soldier’s treasure, constant praise and great peace.

My heart stands in awe of your words. Powerful men persecute him, and he should be terrified of them. But his heart trembles before something else: God’s words. The fear of God drives out the fear of princes. Whoever fears God’s word most will fear everything else less.

Like one who finds great spoil. The picture is of a soldier after battle stumbling on a great treasure left behind by the enemy: sudden, unexpected, overwhelming joy. Jesus described the kingdom that way: “like treasure hidden in a field, which a man found and covered up. Then in his joy he goes and sells all that he has” (Matthew 13:44). A believer reading Scripture can have that experience again and again: a verse read a hundred times suddenly opens like a chest of gold.

Seven times a day I praise you. Seven is the number of completeness: praise woven through the whole day, not reserved for one hour a week.

Great peace have those who love your law. Not small peace; great peace. And not because nothing bad happens, for this psalm is full of persecution and affliction, but because “nothing can make them stumble”. Their footing is sure, because it rests on the word that is fixed in the heavens.

All my ways are before you. He lives openly before God, hiding nothing. That is not a claim to perfection, as the final stanza will make plain, but a life lived in God’s sight.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The psalm gathers itself into prayer and ends with a lost sheep asking the shepherd to find it. The singer asks that his cry and his plea come before God, for understanding and deliverance according to God’s word (vv. 169–170). His lips and tongue will pour out praise for all God has taught him (vv. 171–172). He asks for God’s hand to help him, longs for God’s salvation, and wants to live so that he may praise (vv. 173–175). Then the astonishing last verse: after 175 verses of love for God’s law, he confesses, “I have gone astray like a lost sheep”, and asks, “seek your servant” (v. 176).
verseByVerse.theology: The longest psalm ends not with a boast of obedience but with a lost sheep asking to be found.

verseByVerse.quote: Let my cry come before you, O LORD; give me understanding according to your word! Let my plea come before you; deliver me according to your word. My lips will pour forth praise, for you teach me your statutes. My tongue will sing of your word, for all your commandments are right. Let your hand be ready to help me, for I have chosen your precepts. I long for your salvation, O LORD, and your law is my delight. Let my soul live and praise you, and let your rules help me. I have gone astray like a lost sheep; seek your servant, for I do not forget your commandments.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The psalm gathers into prayer and praise, and ends with a man who loves God’s word confessing that he has wandered like a lost sheep and asking the Shepherd to seek him.

Let my cry come before you. The last stanza gathers up the whole psalm into prayer: cry, plea, understanding, deliverance, all “according to your word”.

My lips will pour forth praise. Lips and tongue: the word taken in comes out as song. The goal of Bible reading is not only knowledge but worship.

Let my soul live and praise you. A final triple request: help me, save me, let me live. And why does he want to live? To praise God.

I have gone astray like a lost sheep. Here is the last verse of the longest psalm in the Bible, and it is astonishing. After 175 verses of love for God’s law, delight, meditation, obedience, zeal and tears, the singer does not end with a claim to have kept it all. He ends with a confession.

How to read the whole psalm. That changes how the whole psalm should be read. This is not a proud man listing his achievements, but a man who loves God’s word with all his heart and still wanders, and knows it. He does not say “I will find my way back”. He says “seek your servant”. The sheep cannot find the shepherd; the shepherd has to come looking.

Seek your servant. And the shepherd did. Jesus told of a man with a hundred sheep who, losing one, goes “after the one that is lost, until he finds it? And when he has found it, he lays it on his shoulders, rejoicing” (Luke 15:4–5). The psalm that is all about God’s word ends by asking for the Word made flesh (John 1:14), the Good Shepherd who seeks and carries home every lost sheep who cries, “seek your servant”.

119.title: Your Word Is a Lamp to My Feet
119.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 119 stands in Book Five of the Psalter, between the festival praise of the Hallel psalms (113–118) and the pilgrim Songs of Ascents (120–134). It is the longest psalm and the longest chapter in the Bible: an acrostic of twenty-two eight-verse stanzas, one for each letter of the Hebrew alphabet (see the introduction).

The message. God’s word is the life, light and joy of those who belong to him, because in it God himself speaks. The singer loves not rules for their own sake but the God whose word they are, and he keeps asking God to teach him, give him life and hold him up. Yet after 175 verses of love for that word, he ends confessing he has gone astray, and asks to be found.

Why it was said. Its author is unnamed; many place it after the exile, when Israel had no king on David’s throne but did have the word of God (see the introduction). It speaks for believers who are small, despised and afflicted, mocked by the proud and plotted against by princes, and shows that a life rooted in God’s word stands when everything else gives way.

How the chapter makes its case. It circles rather than argues in a line, turning one jewel in the light. A blessing on those who walk in the law meets an honest sigh to keep it (vv. 1–8). The singer asks for a pure life, opened eyes and a heart raised from the dust (vv. 9–40), and finds freedom, songs and a portion in God (vv. 41–64). At its heart he calls his affliction good and faithful (vv. 65–80), shrivels like a wineskin in the smoke (vv. 81–88), and finds God’s word fixed forever in heaven (vv. 89–96). Then he loves the law, walks by its lamp, weeps for those who ignore it and finds God nearer than his enemies (vv. 97–168), before ending as a lost sheep asking to be sought (vv. 169–176).

Where it leads. To Christ in two ways. By the need it exposes: no one but Jesus has walked this whole road without a false step, the blessed man whose way is blameless, who met temptation with Scripture stored in his heart and said of the Scriptures, “it is they that bear witness about me” (John 5:39). And by God’s character revealed in him: the God whose word gives life sent his Word made flesh (John 1:14), and the Good Shepherd answered the psalm’s last prayer by coming “to seek and to save the lost” (Luke 19:10).

For us. Read it a stanza a day and pray “Open my eyes” (v. 18) before you start. Store God’s word in your heart for the moment of temptation, trust it in affliction, and love it because it brings you to Christ. And when you have wandered, do not try to find your own way back: ask the Shepherd to seek you, for he does.
119.theology:
God's word, in all its forms, is the expression of his righteous, faithful character (vv. 137-138), fixed forever (v. 89), true in its sum (v. 160), and life-giving (vv. 25, 50, 93; Deut 8:3).

Love for the law is not legalism, the attempt to earn God’s favour by keeping rules: its commands lead to God himself (v. 2), bring freedom (v. 45), and are kept out of love (vv. 47-48, 97). Understanding requires God to open the eyes (v. 18), and Scripture stored in the heart guards against sin (v. 11).

Affliction is God's faithful teaching (vv. 67, 71, 75). The word guides step by step (v. 105), gives wisdom to the simple (vv. 98-100, 130), and great peace to those who love it (v. 165). The psalm ends not in self-righteousness but in confession and dependence: the lost sheep must be sought (v. 176), as the Good Shepherd does (Luke 15:4-6).
119.examples: Read a stanza a day for three weeks, and pray verse 18 before each one. When temptation comes, the verse you have stored up is the one you will have. And on the days the Bible tastes dry, keep eating: the singer who loved it most still ends by asking the Shepherd to come and find him.

keyVerse.quote: Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my path.
keyVerse.note: This is the psalm’s best-known verse, and it gathers up its whole theme: God’s word is how God guides his people through a dark and dangerous world. It promises light for the next step rather than a map of the whole road, and in the end the light has a face, for Jesus is the light of the world (John 8:12).

119.reflection:
The singer begins with a sigh, “Oh that my ways may be steadfast” (v. 5), and ends confessing, “I have gone astray like a lost sheep; seek your servant” (v. 176). How does that change the way you read his love for God’s law in between?

“I have stored up your word in my heart, that I might not sin against you” (v. 11). What verse could you store up this week for a temptation or fear you actually face, and how will you keep it in front of you?

“It is good for me that I was afflicted” (v. 71) and “in faithfulness you have afflicted me” (v. 75). Can you look back on a hard time and see what God taught you through it? How should we speak about these verses to someone who is suffering now?

The psalm says God’s word gives life, light, freedom and great peace (vv. 25, 45, 105, 165). Which of these do you most need, and how does Christ, the Word made flesh and the Good Shepherd, give it?

120.text: A Song of Ascents. 1In my distress I called to the LORD, and he answered me.2Deliver me, O LORD, from lying lips, from a deceitful tongue.3What shall be given to you, and what more shall be done to you, you deceitful tongue?4A warrior's sharp arrows, with glowing coals of the broom tree!5Woe to me, that I sojourn in Meshech, that I dwell among the tents of Kedar!6Too long have I had my dwelling among those who hate peace.7I am for peace, but when I speak, they are for war!

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — Deliver Me from Lying Lips
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The singer brings a deceitful tongue to God and leaves its punishment with him. He begins by remembering that when he called before, the LORD answered (v. 1), and that memory gives him confidence to ask again, this time for rescue from lying lips (v. 2). Then he turns and addresses the lying tongue directly, asking what more will be done to it (v. 3). The answer is fitting: a tongue that wounds like arrows and burns like fire will meet a warrior’s arrows and the long, fierce heat of broom-wood coals (v. 4). The slandered believer does not shoot back; he hands the arrows to God.
verseByVerse.theology: The first song of the pilgrim road begins with a man surrounded by lies.

verseByVerse.quote: In my distress I called to the LORD, and he answered me. Deliver me, O LORD, from lying lips, from a deceitful tongue.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Remembering that God answered him before, the singer asks the LORD to rescue him from lying lips.

The Songs of Ascents. Fifteen psalms (120–134) now carry the title “A Song of Ascents”, very probably pilgrims’ songs for the road up to Jerusalem, the city “to which the tribes go up” (Psalm 122:4; see the introduction). Others link the title with the fifteen steps of the temple courts, or with the return from exile.

In my distress. The first song of the journey begins not in Jerusalem but far from it, in trouble. Every pilgrimage to God starts with some dissatisfaction with where you are.

He answered me. He begins with a memory: he has prayed before, and God answered. That past answer is the ground for the prayer he now prays.

From lying lips, from a deceitful tongue. The trouble is words: lies, deceit, slander. Anyone lied about at work, at home or in church knows how it wounds and how helpless it makes you feel. You cannot answer every lie. You can bring them to God.
verseByVerse.note: Psalms 120–134 are the “Songs of Ascents,” probably sung by pilgrims going up to Jerusalem for the feasts.

verseByVerse.quote: What shall be given to you, and what more shall be done to you, you deceitful tongue? A warrior's sharp arrows, with glowing coals of the broom tree!
verseByVerse.commentary:
The lying tongue that wounds and burns will itself be answered by God with arrows and fire, so the singer need not answer it himself.

What more shall be done to you? The singer turns to address the deceitful tongue directly. The wording echoes the Hebrew oath, “May God do so to you and more also” (1 Samuel 3:17).

Sharp arrows, with glowing coals. The punishment fits the crime. A lying tongue shoots words like arrows and sets things on fire; God’s judgment answers in kind. The broom tree grows in the desert, and its wood makes charcoal that burns long and very hot. James says the same of the tongue: it is “a fire, a world of unrighteousness”, “setting on fire the entire course of life, and set on fire by hell” (James 3:6).

Leaving it to God. The singer does not shoot back. He leaves the arrows and the coals to God. That is the believer’s freedom when slandered: the lying tongue will be answered, but not necessarily by you. Jesus walked this road before us. “Many bore false witness against him” (Mark 14:56), and “when he was reviled, he did not revile in return”, but “continued entrusting himself to him who judges justly” (1 Peter 2:23).

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew of verses 3–4 is compressed. Most take it as the ESV does: verse 4 names the tongue’s punishment. Others read verse 4 as describing the lying tongue itself, sharp as arrows and hot as coals (compare Psalm 57:4). Either way, a tongue like arrows and fire will meet arrows and fire.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–7 — Among Those Who Hate Peace
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The psalm ends with the ache of living too long among people who want a fight. The singer names two distant peoples, Meshech in the far north and Kedar in the desert, not as an address but as a description of his company: he is a stranger among the hostile (v. 5). He has lived among those who hate peace for far too long (v. 6). He is for peace with all his being, but every time he speaks they reach for war (v. 7). The psalm does not resolve the tension. It leaves the pilgrim weary of where he is, and so ready to set out for the city of peace.
verseByVerse.theology: The journey to God's city begins with the ache of living among people who want a fight.

verseByVerse.quote: Woe to me, that I sojourn in Meshech, that I dwell among the tents of Kedar! Too long have I had my dwelling among those who hate peace. I am for peace, but when I speak, they are for war!
verseByVerse.commentary:
The singer is weary of living so long among people who hate peace: he is for peace, but they are for war.

Meshech and Kedar. Two place names, and they point in opposite directions. Meshech was one of the sons of Japheth (Genesis 10:2), a people of the far north. Kedar was a son of Ishmael (Genesis 25:13), the ancestor of desert tribes to the south and east. No one could live in both places at once. The singer is describing his company, not his address: a foreigner stranded among hostile peoples, for too long.

I am for peace. In Hebrew the first half of verse 7 is almost just “I, peace”. That is who he is. But the moment he speaks, they reach for weapons. Some people cannot be reconciled however gently you speak.

Living at peace with all. Paul’s instruction fits exactly: “If possible, so far as it depends on you, live peaceably with all” (Romans 12:18). “If possible”, because sometimes it is not; “so far as it depends on you”, because your part is to be for peace even when they are for war. We do not manage that by willpower: God has made peace with us in Christ, and his Spirit grows peace in us as his fruit (Galatians 5:22).

What it does not mean. Being for peace does not mean staying silent about wrong or remaining in danger; anyone facing threats or abuse should seek safety and help.

Too long have I had my dwelling. The psalm ends there, unresolved, in Meshech. The pilgrimage begins not with arrival but with longing: a person tired of the tents of Kedar who has started to look toward the city of peace. The next psalm lifts its eyes to the hills.
verseByVerse.note: Meshech lay far to the north and Kedar in the Arabian desert — distant, hostile places.

120.title: I Am for Peace
120.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 120 opens the Songs of Ascents (120–134), fifteen short psalms very probably sung by pilgrims going up to Jerusalem for the pilgrim feasts. It follows the towering Psalm 119, and it begins the journey not in Jerusalem but as far from it as the singer can imagine.

The message. The road to God’s city begins with a cry from a place of lies and hostility. The singer has been lied about and lives among people who want a fight. He does not hit back: he brings the lying tongue to the God who has answered him before, leaves its judgment to God, and goes on being for peace. Weariness with where you are is the first step of pilgrimage.

Why it was said. Israelites living scattered among other peoples, or simply surrounded by deceit at home, would sing this as they set out for the festivals (see the introduction on the Songs of Ascents). It gave words to the ache of belonging to God while living among those who do not, and it turned that ache toward Zion, the city of peace.

How the chapter makes its case. It begins with a memory of answered prayer, which grounds a fresh prayer for rescue from lying lips (vv. 1–2). It then turns to the deceitful tongue itself and declares that God will answer it with arrows and fire (vv. 3–4). Finally it laments a long exile among people who hate peace: “I am for peace, but when I speak, they are for war!” (vv. 5–7). The psalm ends unresolved, still far away; the climb begins in the next psalm.

Where it leads. To Christ by pattern. No one was more lied about than Jesus: “many bore false witness against him” (Mark 14:56). Yet “when he was reviled, he did not revile in return” but “continued entrusting himself to him who judges justly” (1 Peter 2:23), the very path this psalm walks. He is the man of peace whom the world met with war, and by his cross he made the peace we could never make (Ephesians 2:14–17).

For us. When you are lied about, you do not have to answer every lie; you can bring it to God and leave the verdict with him. Be for peace as far as it depends on you, and let your weariness with a hostile world turn your heart toward home.
120.theology:
The Songs of Ascents (120-134) were probably sung on pilgrimage to Jerusalem; this first one begins far from Zion, in distress.

God’s answers to prayer in the past give confidence to pray now (v. 1). Lying tongues are fire and will be judged in kind (vv. 3-4; Jas 3:6), and vengeance is left to God. The believer is to be for peace even when others are for war (v. 7; Rom 12:18).
120.examples: Someone lied about cannot answer every lie, but can hand the arrows and the coals to God. And when you are for peace and they reach for weapons, Paul’s two conditions free you from blaming yourself: if possible, and so far as it depends on you (Rom 12:18).

keyVerse.quote: I am for peace, but when I speak, they are for war!
keyVerse.note: This line gathers up the whole psalm: the singer’s heart is set on peace, and the world around him answers with hostility. That tension is what sets the pilgrim on the road to Jerusalem, the city of peace, and it is the path Christ walked, the man of peace met with war.

120.reflection:
The first Song of Ascents begins far from Jerusalem, in distress (v. 1). Why might dissatisfaction with where we are be a necessary part of turning toward God?

The singer remembers that God answered him before (v. 1). What past answers to prayer can you recall, and how do they help you pray now?

Lies and slander are brought to God, and their judgment is left with him (vv. 2–4). How does Jesus, who “when he was reviled, he did not revile in return” (1 Peter 2:23), help us when we are lied about?

“I am for peace, but when I speak, they are for war!” (v. 7). What does it look like to be for peace “so far as it depends on you” (Romans 12:18) in your family, workplace or church, and where are its limits?

121.text: A Song of Ascents. 1I lift up my eyes to the hills. From where does my help come?2My help comes from the LORD, who made heaven and earth.3He will not let your foot be moved; he who keeps you will not slumber.4Behold, he who keeps Israel will neither slumber nor sleep.5The LORD is your keeper; the LORD is your shade on your right hand.6The sun shall not strike you by day, nor the moon by night.7The LORD will keep you from all evil; he will keep your life.8The LORD will keep your going out and your coming in from this time forth and forevermore.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–2 — I Lift Up My Eyes to the Hills
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Your help comes not from the hills but from the one who made them. The pilgrim raises his eyes to the hills of Judah, with their steep paths and their hilltop shrines, and asks the question every traveller feels: where will help come from (v. 1)? He answers himself with a confession that looks straight past the hills to their Maker: “My help comes from the LORD, who made heaven and earth” (v. 2). Everything on the road ahead was made by the LORD, so nothing he must face is bigger than the one who helps him. The same confession, now on the lips of the whole people, closes Psalm 124.
verseByVerse.theology: A pilgrim looks up at the hills and asks where help will come from — and answers with the Maker of the hills.

verseByVerse.quote: I lift up my eyes to the hills. From where does my help come? My help comes from the LORD, who made heaven and earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The pilgrim looks up at the hard hills ahead and confesses that his help comes not from them but from the LORD who made them.

I lift up my eyes to the hills. The pilgrim is on the road, with the hills of Judah ahead and Jerusalem among them. The hills can be read two ways, and both help. They were dangerous: steep paths, robbers in the rocks, exhausting climbs in the heat. And the hilltops were where the shrines of other gods stood, where people went looking for help that never came (Jeremiah 3:23). Either way, help does not come from the hills themselves.

Who made heaven and earth. The answer looks past the hills to the one who made them. Whatever waits on the hilltops, danger or false gods, was made by the LORD or is nothing at all. The same confession returns in the plural at the end of Psalm 124 (Psalm 124:8).

Why this matters. Every believer’s security starts here: not with the size of the problem ahead, but with the greatness of the God who made heaven and earth. The diagnosis or the court date is a real and steep hill, but he made it, and he helps you climb it.

Uncertain wording. The King James Version read verse 1 as one sentence (“unto the hills, from whence cometh my help”), as if help came from the hills. The ESV and almost all modern translations rightly take the second line as a question: the Hebrew word is the ordinary “from where?”, and verse 2 answers it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 3–8 — He Who Keeps Israel Will Neither Slumber nor Sleep
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The LORD keeps his people completely: every step, every hour, every danger, all of life, for ever. A second voice answers the pilgrim, and the word “keep” rings through every verse, six times in all. The keeper never dozes at his post as human watchmen do (vv. 3–4). He walks at the traveller’s right hand like moving shade, so that neither the sun by day nor the moon by night can harm him (vv. 5–6). Then his keeping widens until it takes in everything: all evil, the whole life, every going out and coming in, from this time forth and for evermore (vv. 7–8). The pilgrim’s safety rests on his keeper’s wakefulness, not his own.
verseByVerse.theology: Six times in six verses: the LORD keeps — awake all night, at every step, for the whole journey of life.

verseByVerse.quote: He will not let your foot be moved; he who keeps you will not slumber. Behold, he who keeps Israel will neither slumber nor sleep.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The one who keeps his people never dozes off, so he will not let their foot slip.

A second voice. Now a different voice answers. Verses 1–2 said “my help”; from here to the end it is “your keeper”, “keep you”. Perhaps a priest blessing the pilgrims, a fellow traveller, or the singer preaching to himself; either way, the promise comes from outside him, a word to hold on to.

He who keeps you will not slumber. On a rocky path one slip could be fatal, and at night someone had to keep watch over the camp. Human watchmen doze off; God does not. When Elijah faced the prophets of Baal, he mocked their god: “perhaps he is asleep and must be awakened” (1 Kings 18:27). The LORD is not like that: “He does not faint or grow weary” (Isaiah 40:28).

The keeper who slept. Once the keeper of Israel did sleep, “asleep on the cushion” in a boat filling with water (Mark 4:38), for he had become truly man. Yet woken, he rebuked the wind. And on the night it mattered most, the disciples slept and Jesus kept watch (Mark 14:37).

Neither slumber nor sleep. That is a verse for the night. When you lie awake in the small hours with everything you cannot control, you need not stay on watch. Someone else is awake. You can sleep because he does not.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD is your keeper; the LORD is your shade on your right hand. The sun shall not strike you by day, nor the moon by night.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD himself guards his people, close beside them like shade, so that no danger of the day or fear of the night can harm them.

The LORD is your keeper. Here is the heart of the psalm. “Keep” is its great word, six times in verses 3–8. A keeper is a guard, a watchman, a shepherd.

Your shade on your right hand. On a road in the Judean summer, shade was life, and the right hand is where a helper or defender stood (Psalm 16:8). God walks beside the traveller like a moving shadow, keeping the sun off him.

The sun shall not strike you by day. The sun could kill with heatstroke; the moon was widely feared in the ancient world as harming those who slept in the open. Every danger of the day, every fear of the night: there is no hour when the keeper is off duty. Scripture’s last picture of the redeemed takes up the words, “the sun shall not strike them”, because the Lamb is their shepherd (Revelation 7:16–17).

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD will keep you from all evil; he will keep your life. The LORD will keep your going out and your coming in from this time forth and forevermore.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD’s keeping covers every evil, the whole person and the whole of life, from now and for ever.

The LORD will keep you from all evil. Not that believers never suffer (the Psalms are full of suffering believers), but that no evil will ever get past God to destroy the life he keeps. “He will keep your life”: your soul, your self. Jesus says of his sheep, “no one will snatch them out of my hand” (John 10:28). Believers “by God’s power are being guarded through faith” (1 Peter 1:5), and Jude praises him “who is able to keep you from stumbling and to present you blameless before the presence of his glory with great joy” (Jude 24).

Your going out and your coming in. A Hebrew way of saying everything: leaving home and coming back, starting a job and finishing it, being born and dying. All of it is kept, and not for a season.

The promise to Jacob. God said the same to Jacob when he set out alone on a long journey, afraid and far from home: “Behold, I am with you and will keep you wherever you go, and will bring you back to this land” (Genesis 28:15). Every believer is on a journey like that. One day you will go out of this world, and the same keeper who watched every step will bring you home.

121.title: The LORD Is Your Keeper
121.overview:
