Where we are. Psalm 121 is the second of the Songs of Ascents (120–134), the songs pilgrims sang on the road up to Jerusalem for the pilgrim feasts. Psalm 120 left the singer weary among strangers, far from the city of peace; now he is on the road, and the hills of Judah rise in front of him.

The message. The God who made the hills keeps the traveller who must climb them. He never dozes at his post, he walks beside his people like shade in the heat, and his keeping covers every danger, every hour and every step of life, to its very end. Your safety does not rest on the size of the road ahead, but on the greatness and the wakefulness of your keeper.

Why it was said. Pilgrims faced real dangers: steep paths, robbers, heat, and nights in the open (see the introduction on the Songs of Ascents). More deeply, Israel was a small people in a dangerous world, always tempted to look for help to the gods of the high places. The psalm sent them up the road with a confession on their lips and a promise in their ears.

How the chapter makes its case. The pilgrim asks where help will come from and answers with the Maker of heaven and earth (vv. 1–2). Then a second voice takes up the word “keep” and will not let it go: the keeper never sleeps (vv. 3–4), he shades his people by day and by night (vv. 5–6), and he keeps their whole life, all its goings out and comings in, for ever (vv. 7–8). “My help” is answered by “your keeper”: the confession meets a promise.

Where it leads. To Christ, in whom the character of the keeper is shown in person. The keeper of Israel became man, and once fell asleep in the stern of a boat; yet woken, he rebuked the wind, for the Maker of heaven and earth was in the boat (Mark 4:38–41). In Gethsemane his friends slept while he kept watch (Mark 14:37), and he could say to his Father, “I kept them in your name” (John 17:12). The good shepherd who says “no one will snatch them out of my hand” (John 10:28) is this psalm’s keeper with a human face.

For us. You do not have to keep yourself, or stay awake for fear of what will happen if you let go. The LORD who made heaven and earth is awake over your going out and your coming in, and in Christ he will keep you to the end and bring you home.
121.theology:
Help comes not from the hills, whether they hold dangers or the shrines of false gods, but from their Maker (vv. 1-2). God is the ever-watchful keeper, unlike idols that sleep (vv. 3-4).

Keeping from all evil means that no evil can destroy the life God keeps, not that suffering never comes (v. 7). The keeping covers the whole course of life and beyond (v. 8), fulfilled in Christ's keeping of his own (John 17:12; 1 Pet 1:5; Jude 24).
121.examples: Your safety is not measured by the size of the problem ahead, but by the greatness of the God who made heaven and earth. And at night, when the worries will not let you sleep, this psalm hands the watch to someone who never dozes off.

keyVerse.quote: The LORD is your keeper; the LORD is your shade on your right hand.
keyVerse.note: “Keep” is the psalm’s great word, and here it becomes almost a name: the LORD is your keeper. The verse stands at the centre of the promise, gathering up the sleepless watch of verses 3–4 and opening into the all-embracing keeping of verses 7–8, and it promises not only protection but presence, the LORD close at your right hand.

121.reflection:
The pilgrim looks at the hills and asks, “From where does my help come?” (v. 1). What are the hills in front of you just now, and where are you tempted to look for help?

The LORD “will neither slumber nor sleep” (v. 4). How might that change the way you face sleepless nights and the things you cannot control?

Jesus slept in the boat yet stilled the storm, and kept watch in Gethsemane while his friends slept (Mark 4:38–41; 14:37). What do these scenes show you about how he keeps his people?

The LORD will keep “your going out and your coming in” (v. 8), yet believers still suffer. How would you explain to a struggling friend what this promise does and does not mean?

122.text: A Song of Ascents. Of David. 1I was glad when they said to me, "Let us go to the house of the LORD!"2Our feet have been standing within your gates, O Jerusalem!3Jerusalem— built as a city that is bound firmly together,4to which the tribes go up, the tribes of the LORD, as was decreed for Israel, to give thanks to the name of the LORD.5There thrones for judgment were set, the thrones of the house of David.6Pray for the peace of Jerusalem! "May they be secure who love you!7Peace be within your walls and security within your towers!"8For my brothers and companions' sake I will say, "Peace be within you!"9For the sake of the house of the LORD our God, I will seek your good.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — Let Us Go to the House of the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Gladness at going to God’s house rests on what God has made his city to be. The pilgrim remembers the invitation, “Let us go to the house of the LORD!”, and the joy it stirred, and now savours standing inside Jerusalem’s gates with his companions (vv. 1–2). Then he looks at the city itself: closely built and firmly joined, a picture of the unity of the tribes who come up to it, as God decreed, to give thanks to his name (vv. 3–4). It is also the seat of justice, where the thrones of David’s house were set (v. 5). Worship, unity and justice belong together in the city of God.
verseByVerse.theology: The pilgrim arrives, remembers the invitation that started the journey, and looks around the city with joy.

verseByVerse.quote: I was glad when they said to me, "Let us go to the house of the LORD!" Our feet have been standing within your gates, O Jerusalem!
verseByVerse.commentary:
The pilgrim remembers the gladness with which he answered the call to go to God’s house, and now savours standing inside Jerusalem with his companions.

I was glad when they said to me. The third Song of Ascents, and the pilgrim has arrived. He looks back to the moment the journey began: someone said, “Let us go”, and he was glad.

Let us go to the house of the LORD! The invitation came from others: worship is not a private hobby, and believers call one another to it (Hebrews 10:24–25). And the response was gladness, not duty.

Our feet have been standing within your gates. After days on the road, “our feet”, plural, stand inside the gates together, and he savours it.

In everyday life. When someone says, “Let’s go to church,” or “Let’s pray together,” what rises in you first: gladness, reluctance, or boredom? Gladness cannot be manufactured. It grows where God has first welcomed us into his house, and it is the Spirit’s work to give it, so the honest response to a cold heart is to ask him for it.

Before the temple was built? The title says “Of David”, yet Solomon built the temple. But Scripture also calls the tent where the ark rested “the house of the LORD” (1 Samuel 1:7), and David “went into the house of the LORD and worshiped” (2 Samuel 12:20), so the psalm needs no later date (see the introduction on the titles).

verseByVerse.quote: Jerusalem— built as a city that is bound firmly together, to which the tribes go up, the tribes of the LORD, as was decreed for Israel, to give thanks to the name of the LORD. There thrones for judgment were set, the thrones of the house of David.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jerusalem is the city where God’s scattered tribes are bound together to thank him, and where David’s house gives justice.

Bound firmly together. The city is compact, its houses and walls closely joined, a picture of unity. That fits its purpose: twelve tribes, scattered and often at odds, gathered in one city to give thanks.

As was decreed for Israel. The pilgrims climbed to Jerusalem because God had told them to come. Three times a year, at the feasts of Unleavened Bread, Weeks and Booths, every man of Israel was to “appear before the LORD your God at the place that he will choose” (Deuteronomy 16:16).

One people in Christ. So God’s people gather still, bound firmly together. Christ “has made us both one and has broken down in his flesh the dividing wall of hostility” (Ephesians 2:14), gathering not twelve tribes only but every nation into one body.

There thrones for judgment were set. Jerusalem was also the seat of justice, where David’s line judged the people. Worship and justice lived in the same city; a place of thanksgiving should also be a place where wrongs are set right. Those thrones stood empty after the exile, but the angel promised Mary of her son, “the Lord God will give to him the throne of his father David”, “and of his kingdom there will be no end” (Luke 1:32–33).

Uncertain wording. Two phrases are hard. “Bound firmly together” renders a compressed Hebrew phrase, roughly “joined to itself together”: most take it of the city’s close-built walls and houses, some of the people it unites, and the two belong together. And the ESV notes that “as was decreed for” may be read “as a testimony for”, since the Hebrew word can mean a statute or a witness. Either way, the tribes go up because God appointed it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–9 — Peace Be Within Your Walls
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Love for God’s city becomes prayer and work for its peace. The pilgrim calls others to pray for Jerusalem’s peace and gives them the words: security for those who love her, peace within her walls and towers (vv. 6–7). The Hebrew rings with the sound of the city’s own name. Then he gives his reasons. For the sake of his brothers and companions he blesses her (v. 8); for the sake of the house of the LORD he will seek her good (v. 9). His love is not vague goodwill. It is love for God’s people and for the God who dwells among them, and it ends in action.
verseByVerse.theology: Standing in the city, the pilgrim prays for its peace — for his brothers' sake, and for God's house.

verseByVerse.quote: Pray for the peace of Jerusalem! "May they be secure who love you! Peace be within your walls and security within your towers!" For my brothers and companions' sake I will say, "Peace be within you!" For the sake of the house of the LORD our God, I will seek your good.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because he loves God’s city, the pilgrim prays for its peace and resolves to seek its good, for the sake of God’s people and God’s house.

Pray for the peace of Jerusalem! The pilgrim turns from looking to praying. “Peace” comes three times in three verses, and the Hebrew words for peace and security echo the sound of the city’s name. Jerusalem was very probably the Salem where Melchizedek had been king (Genesis 14:18; Psalm 76:2), “king of Salem, that is, king of peace” (Hebrews 7:2). The city of peace had to be prayed for, because it so seldom had any.

Peace be within your walls. Peace (shalom) is more than the absence of war: wholeness, everything as it should be. Within the defences he prays for peace, not just strength.

For my brothers and companions’ sake. Two reasons for the prayer. First, his brothers and companions, the people he travelled with: love for the city is love for the people in it. Second, the house of the LORD, where God put his name. And he will not only wish the city well; he will “seek your good”, and work for it.

Christ and Jerusalem. Jesus came to this city and wept over it: “Would that you, even you, had known on this day the things that make for peace!” (Luke 19:42). The earthly Jerusalem rejected its King, but now believers “have come to Mount Zion and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem” (Hebrews 12:22), and “the Jerusalem above is free, and she is our mother” (Galatians 4:26).

Praying it today. So a Christian prays this psalm for the peace of God’s people, the church all over the world. Its peace is first a gift, “For he himself is our peace” (Ephesians 2:14), and Christ “loved the church and gave himself up for her” (Ephesians 5:25), so praying for her is joining in what he already loves.

How do I pray for the peace of the church? Start with your own congregation, and be specific. Pray by name. Your pastor and elders, the family who has stopped coming, the two members who are no longer speaking: name them before God, as the pilgrim prayed for his brothers and companions. Pray before you speak. When a decision or a sermon has annoyed you, take it to God before you take it to the car park; many church quarrels grow from words said first to the wrong person. Pray wider. Choose another congregation in your town and one persecuted church abroad, and pray for them each week. Then seek its good. The psalm moves from “I will say” to “I will seek your good”: turn up, take a turn on a rota, welcome the newcomer, speak well of your leaders.

Where Christians differ. Does praying for the peace of Jerusalem mean supporting the modern state of Israel? Christian Zionists and many dispensationalists hold that the earthly city and nation remain God’s covenant people and land, see the modern state as prophecy fulfilled, and pray this psalm for it directly. Others read the psalm through the New Testament’s heavenly Jerusalem (see above). Faithful Christians differ here, often over how to read Paul’s hope for Israel in Romans 11:25–29, and they can disagree in love.

This commentary’s view. The psalm finds its fulfilment in Christ and his one people, gathered from Jews and Gentiles, and the modern state of Israel is not the fulfilment of the land promises. Christians may still pray for the peace of the present city and all who live there, and should love the Jewish people, praying for Jews and Arabs alike to find the peace that is in Christ.

122.title: Pray for the Peace of Jerusalem
122.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 122, a Song of Ascents “Of David”, is the moment of arrival. Psalm 120 began far away among people who hate peace; Psalm 121 walked the road under the LORD’s keeping; now the pilgrims’ feet stand inside Jerusalem’s gates.

The message. Gladness in God’s house turns into prayer and work for the peace of God’s people. The pilgrim rejoices in the city where the scattered tribes are bound together to thank the LORD and where David’s throne gives justice. Because he loves it, he prays for its peace and seeks its good, for the sake of his brothers and of the house of God. To love God is to love the people among whom he has put his name.

Why it was said. Three times a year the law called every man of Israel to appear before the LORD at the place he would choose (Deuteronomy 16:16; see the introduction on the Songs of Ascents). The tribes were often divided and the city often threatened, and this psalm taught the pilgrims what their gathering meant: unity, thanksgiving, justice, and a peace that had to be prayed for, because Jerusalem, whose very name echoes “peace”, so seldom had any.

How the chapter makes its case. It moves from joy to prayer. The invitation and the arrival (vv. 1–2) lead into a description of the city: compact and united, the goal of the tribes, the place of thanksgiving and of David’s thrones of justice (vv. 3–5). Then the pilgrim calls for prayer for its peace (vv. 6–7) and gives his two reasons: his brothers and companions, and the house of the LORD (vv. 8–9).

Where it leads. To Christ by promise and by pattern. The thrones of the house of David stood empty after the exile, but the angel promised Mary that God would give her son “the throne of his father David” (Luke 1:32). Jesus came to Jerusalem and wept because it did not know “the things that make for peace” (Luke 19:42); then he made peace by the blood of his cross (Colossians 1:20). In him the tribes are gathered into a greater city: believers “have come to Mount Zion and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem” (Hebrews 12:22).

For us. Be glad when someone says, “Let us go to the house of the LORD”, and say it to others. Then love your church as the pilgrim loved Jerusalem: pray for its peace by name, and seek its good with your hands, as one who already has peace with God through Christ.
122.theology:
Worship is a shared joy to which believers invite one another (v. 1). God's city binds a scattered people together in thanksgiving (vv. 3-4), and justice belongs beside worship (v. 5).

Prayer for the city's peace flows from love for fellow believers and for God's house (vv. 6-9). The earthly city did not recognise its King, who came to bring it peace (Luke 19:42); Christians belong to the heavenly Jerusalem (Heb 12:22; Gal 4:26) and pray for the peace and good of the church.
122.examples: Twelve quarrelsome tribes were bound into one city by a shared reason to give thanks; a congregation of very different people is held together the same way. To pray for peace within its walls, for your brothers' sake, is to pray for unity, sound teaching and love, and then to go and seek its good.

keyVerse.quote: I was glad when they said to me, “Let us go to the house of the LORD!”
keyVerse.note: The whole psalm grows from this gladness. Called by others and shared with them, joy in God’s house becomes love for God’s city, and that love becomes prayer and work for its peace (vv. 6–9). It is the heart God gives to all who have been welcomed into his house through Christ.

122.reflection:
“I was glad when they said to me, ‘Let us go to the house of the LORD!’” (v. 1). What helps or hinders your gladness at gathering with God’s people, and whom could you invite this week?

Jerusalem was “bound firmly together”, a place where scattered tribes gathered to give thanks (vv. 3–4). What divides believers in your church, and how does Christ, who “has made us both one” (Ephesians 2:14), answer it?

Jesus wept over Jerusalem because it did not know “the things that make for peace” (Luke 19:42). What does his weeping tell you about his heart for his people?

The pilgrim moves from “I will say” to “I will seek your good” (vv. 8–9). What is one concrete way you could pray for, and work for, the peace of your congregation this month?

123.text: A Song of Ascents. 1To you I lift up my eyes, O you who are enthroned in the heavens!2Behold, as the eyes of servants look to the hand of their master, as the eyes of a maidservant to the hand of her mistress, so our eyes look to the LORD our God, till he has mercy upon us.3Have mercy upon us, O LORD, have mercy upon us, for we have had more than enough of contempt.4Our soul has had more than enough of the scorn of those who are at ease, of the contempt of the proud.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — Till He Has Mercy upon Us
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Despised by the comfortable, God’s people look steadily to the LORD until he shows mercy. One voice lifts its eyes past every earthly power to the LORD enthroned in heaven (v. 1). Then the whole people take up the picture of servants in a great household, eyes fixed on the master’s or mistress’s hand for the smallest sign: so they watch the LORD their God, and keep watching till he has mercy (v. 2). The reason comes in the prayer itself. They have been fed contempt until they are sick of it, the scorn of those at ease and of the proud (vv. 3–4). The psalm ends still waiting, eyes still raised.
verseByVerse.theology: A people worn out by contempt fix their eyes on God's hand and wait for mercy.

verseByVerse.quote: To you I lift up my eyes, O you who are enthroned in the heavens! Behold, as the eyes of servants look to the hand of their master, as the eyes of a maidservant to the hand of her mistress, so our eyes look to the LORD our God, till he has mercy upon us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s people look past every earthly power to the LORD enthroned in heaven, and keep their eyes on him, as servants watch their master’s hand, until he shows mercy.

To you I lift up my eyes. Two psalms ago the pilgrim lifted his eyes “to the hills” (Psalm 121:1). Now he lifts them higher, to the one “enthroned in the heavens”. The first look asked where help might come from; this one goes straight to the throne, above the proud people of verse 4.

As the eyes of servants. The picture comes from any large household of the time. Servants stood quietly at the edge of the room, eyes on the master’s hand. A gesture told them everything: bring the food, clear the table, you may go. And the single voice of verse 1 becomes “our eyes”: the whole people look together.

Till he has mercy upon us. So God’s people look to him: not now and then, but steadily, waiting for his signal. The word “till” matters. They do not look away when the answer does not come at once.

The Canaanite woman. A woman in the Gospels did exactly this. When Jesus seemed to refuse her, she said, “Yes, Lord, yet even the dogs eat the crumbs that fall from their masters’ table” (Matthew 15:27). Her eyes were on the master’s hand, and she would not look away until mercy came. It came. Hebrews gives the same instruction for the whole Christian life: “looking to Jesus, the founder and perfecter of our faith” (Hebrews 12:2).

verseByVerse.quote: Have mercy upon us, O LORD, have mercy upon us, for we have had more than enough of contempt. Our soul has had more than enough of the scorn of those who are at ease, of the contempt of the proud.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sick of the scorn of comfortable and proud people, God’s people do not answer them but cry to the LORD for mercy.

More than enough of contempt. The Hebrew behind “more than enough” pictures being glutted, fed until you cannot take any more. They have eaten contempt until they are sick of it.

Those who are at ease. The scorners are comfortable people, secure and untroubled, looking down on believers who are struggling: the sneer of those who have never felt their need of mercy and cannot imagine why anyone would wait on God for it. The psalm does not name its occasion. Many have heard in it the years after the exile, when the small community rebuilding Jerusalem in Nehemiah’s day was mocked by Sanballat and Tobiah: “they jeered at us and despised us” (Nehemiah 2:19). That setting is probable rather than certain, but it shows the kind of scorn the psalm means.

Have mercy upon us, O LORD. The psalm does not try to win the scorners’ respect. It turns its eyes to the master’s hand and asks, twice, for mercy: the servants claim no rights, only their Lord’s kindness.

The scorned Saviour. Jesus knew this contempt from the inside: “the rulers scoffed at him” (Luke 23:35). Yet “when he was reviled, he did not revile in return … but continued entrusting himself to him who judges justly” (1 Peter 2:23). He bore the scorn so that mercy could reach even those who scorned him.

The same contempt today. Many Christians know this. Not prisons and swords, but the quieter, wearing contempt of a culture that finds faith naive: a colleague who smirks, a relative who treats belief as weakness. It can wear you down more than open hostility. Yet “If you are insulted for the name of Christ, you are blessed, because the Spirit of glory and of God rests upon you” (1 Peter 4:14). The contempt of the comfortable is not the last word; the mercy of the one enthroned in the heavens is. Not every criticism is persecution, though; sometimes our own folly earns it (1 Peter 4:15).

Still waiting. The psalm ends with no answer yet. That is honest. Some seasons of the Christian life are simply this: eyes on the hand, “till he has mercy”.

123.title: Our Eyes Look to the LORD
123.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 123 is the fourth Song of Ascents. Psalm 121 lifted its eyes to the hills, and Psalm 122 rejoiced inside Jerusalem’s gates; now the pilgrims lift their eyes higher still, to the LORD enthroned in heaven, because they are worn out with being despised.

The message. When God’s people are mocked and cannot make it stop, the place for their eyes is God’s hand. Like servants watching their master for the smallest sign, they look steadily to the LORD and keep looking until he shows mercy. They do not answer the scorners or try to win their approval; they ask the King of heaven for mercy, and they wait.

Why it was said. The psalm does not name its occasion, but it fits a small, struggling people looked down on by the comfortable and powerful, as the community that returned from exile was mocked while it rebuilt Jerusalem (Nehemiah 2:19; see the introduction). Pilgrims who sang it on the road gave voice to the weariness of the faithful in a scornful world.

How the chapter makes its case. One voice looks up to the throne of heaven (v. 1). The whole people join in, with the picture of servants watching their master’s hand (v. 2). Then the look becomes urgent prayer, “Have mercy upon us”, twice, because they have swallowed more than enough of the scorn of those at ease (vv. 3–4). The psalm ends without an answer, still watching.

Where it leads. To Christ, by the need it exposes and by pattern. No one was more scorned by the comfortable than Jesus: at the cross “the rulers scoffed at him” (Luke 23:35), and he was “despised and rejected by men” (Isaiah 53:3). He bore that contempt for us, and so the mercy this psalm waits for has a face. The psalm’s posture becomes the whole Christian life: “looking to Jesus, the founder and perfecter of our faith, who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising the shame” (Hebrews 12:2).

For us. When faith makes you look foolish to colleagues, friends or family, you do not need their approval; you need the Lord’s mercy, and in Christ you have it. Keep your eyes on his hand, even when the answer is slow, and do not let contempt set the terms of your life.
123.theology: Dependence on God is steady, attentive watching of his hand, persisting till he shows mercy (v. 2). Believers may have had their fill of contempt from the comfortable and proud (vv. 3-4); the response is not argument but a plea for mercy.
123.examples: A colleague's smirk or a relative's quiet scorn can wear faith down more than open hostility. This psalm does not teach a clever reply; it teaches where to look, and to keep looking when the answer is slow.

keyVerse.quote: so our eyes look to the LORD our God, till he has mercy upon us.
keyVerse.note: The servant picture is the heart of the psalm, and this line applies it: God’s people fix their eyes on him and keep them there. The word “till” turns a glance into patient, persistent waiting, the same posture Hebrews asks of every Christian, “looking to Jesus”.

123.reflection:
The pilgrim lifts his eyes past the hills to the one “enthroned in the heavens” (v. 1). What difference does it make to remember who is on the throne when you feel small or despised?

Servants watched their master’s hand for every signal (v. 2). What would it look like for you to watch the Lord like that this week, in his word and in prayer?

The psalm’s scorners are “those who are at ease” and “the proud” (v. 4). Where do you meet contempt for faith, and where might you be tempted to show that contempt to others?

Jesus was “despised and rejected by men” (Isaiah 53:3). How does his bearing of scorn help you to wait, like this psalm, “till he has mercy”?

124.text: A Song of Ascents. Of David. 1If it had not been the LORD who was on our side— let Israel now say—2if it had not been the LORD who was on our side when people rose up against us,3then they would have swallowed us up alive, when their anger was kindled against us;4then the flood would have swept us away, the torrent would have gone over us;5then over us would have gone the raging waters.6Blessed be the LORD, who has not given us as prey to their teeth!7We have escaped like a bird from the snare of the fowlers; the snare is broken, and we have escaped!8Our help is in the name of the LORD, who made heaven and earth.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — If It Had Not Been the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Without the LORD on their side, Israel would not have survived. A leader calls the congregation to repeat the opening line, “If it had not been the LORD who was on our side”, so that every voice owns the confession (vv. 1–2). Then the psalm traces the road not taken, in three pictures that build like rising water: enemies who would have swallowed them alive in their anger (v. 3), a flash flood sweeping them away (v. 4), raging waters closing over their heads (v. 5). The point is not the size of the danger but the deliverer: they are alive only because God stood with them.
verseByVerse.theology: A people look back at how close they came to being destroyed, and see only one reason they survived.

verseByVerse.quote: If it had not been the LORD who was on our side— let Israel now say— if it had not been the LORD who was on our side when people rose up against us,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel is called to confess together that only the LORD standing on their side kept them alive when enemies rose against them.

Let Israel now say. A leader calls out a line and tells the crowd to say it back.

If it had not been the LORD. The psalm hangs on one word, “if”. Most of us remember our rescues vaguely and forget how close we came; this psalm makes the congregation trace the other road, the one where God was not there.

The LORD who was on our side. Paul asked the same question the other way round: “If God is for us, who can be against us?” (Romans 8:31). The psalm answers from experience; Paul answers from the cross (Romans 8:32).

What it does not mean. God is not a mascot to be claimed for our causes. When Joshua asked the commander of the LORD’s army, “Are you for us, or for our adversaries?”, the answer was, “No; but I am the commander of the army of the LORD” (Joshua 5:13–14). This psalm belongs to the people God has bound to himself by grace.

verseByVerse.quote: then they would have swallowed us up alive, when their anger was kindled against us; then the flood would have swept us away, the torrent would have gone over us; then over us would have gone the raging waters.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Without the LORD, the enemy’s fury would have swallowed them alive and overwhelmed them like a flood.

They would have swallowed us up alive. Three “then”s picture what would have happened. First, the enemy as a monster with an open mouth, or the earth itself opening: Israel remembered the day “the earth opened its mouth and swallowed” Korah and his rebels in the wilderness (Numbers 16:32). Without God, that would have been them.

The torrent would have gone over us. Then a flash flood tearing down a dry valley after a storm, sweeping away anything in its path in minutes. The images build, wave on wave, the way the danger felt.

The waters do not overwhelm. God promised the opposite through Isaiah: “When you pass through the waters, I will be with you; and through the rivers, they shall not overwhelm you” (Isaiah 43:2). The waters come; they do not overwhelm. Paul “despaired of life itself”, yet could say, “He delivered us from such a deadly peril, and he will deliver us” (2 Corinthians 1:8, 10).

Uncertain wording. “Raging waters” renders a Hebrew word found only here, from a root meaning proud or insolent; older translations had “the proud waters”. The picture is of floodwaters swollen and arrogant, bursting every bound; yet even proud waters have a limit God has set (Job 38:11).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–8 — We Have Escaped Like a Bird
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Rescue becomes blessing, and blessing becomes confession. The people bless the LORD who did not give them as prey to their enemies’ teeth (v. 6). Then comes the most vivid picture of all: a small bird caught in a fowler’s trap, until the snare breaks and the bird flies free. The bird did not break it, and could not (v. 7). The psalm ends with the confession that explains everything: “Our help is in the name of the LORD, who made heaven and earth” (v. 8). The God who made the floods and the fowlers is the one on our side.
verseByVerse.theology: The trap broke, the bird flew free, and the credit goes to the Maker of heaven and earth.

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed be the LORD, who has not given us as prey to their teeth! We have escaped like a bird from the snare of the fowlers; the snare is broken, and we have escaped!
verseByVerse.commentary:
The people bless the LORD for a rescue that was entirely his: like a trapped bird, they escaped only because the snare was broken.

As prey to their teeth. A third image: wild beasts with teeth, and God’s people as prey. But God did not hand them over, and the response is not relief alone but worship: “Blessed be the LORD”.

The snare is broken. Then a small bird caught in a fowler’s trap, helpless, waiting for the fowler to come. And then “the snare is broken”. Birds cannot break traps. The snare was broken for the bird, and the bird simply flew.

Christ broke the snare. That is the shape of the gospel. We were caught in sin, guilt and the power of death, and could not free ourselves. Christ broke the snare: through his death he destroyed “the one who has the power of death, that is, the devil”, and set free those held all their lives by the fear of death (Hebrews 2:14–15). Our part was to fly out of the open trap. “We have escaped!”, said twice, as if they can hardly believe it.

verseByVerse.quote: Our help is in the name of the LORD, who made heaven and earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The people’s help rests on the LORD himself, the Maker of everything that threatened them.

Our help is in the name of the LORD. The psalm closes with a confession many churches use to open their worship. Three psalms ago a single pilgrim said “My help” (Psalm 121:2); now the whole congregation says “Our help”. One person’s trust has become a people’s testimony.

Who made heaven and earth. His “name” is who he has shown himself to be, and he made heaven and earth: the flood, the teeth, the fowlers and the traps are all inside his creation. The Maker of everything was on our side, so none of it could win.

In everyday life. Try the exercise of this psalm on your own life. Think of the worst moment you have come through, and ask honestly where you would be if the LORD had not been on your side. Then say the last verse, and mean it.

124.title: The Snare Is Broken
124.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 124, a Song of Ascents “Of David”, follows the scorn of Psalm 123 with a story of rescue. The pilgrims who waited “till he has mercy” now look back on a time when mercy came just in time, and the whole congregation is called to say so.

The message. If the LORD had not been on our side, we would not be here. The psalm makes God’s people trace the road not taken (swallowed alive, swept away, torn by teeth) so that they see how close they came and whose hand saved them. The rescue was entirely his: the snare was broken, and we escaped. So our help rests on his name, the Maker of heaven and earth.

Why it was said. Israel was repeatedly threatened by stronger nations, and a people that survives is tempted to forget how near the end it came, or to credit its own strength (see the introduction). Sung by pilgrims together, the psalm turned a nation’s memory into shared thanksgiving.

How the chapter makes its case. A leader calls the people to say it after him: “If it had not been the LORD who was on our side” (vv. 1–2). Three “then”s picture what would have happened: swallowed alive, swept away by a flood, drowned by raging waters (vv. 3–5). Then the turn to praise: not given as prey, but escaped like a bird from a broken snare (vv. 6–7). Last comes the confession that grounds it all: “Our help is in the name of the LORD, who made heaven and earth” (v. 8).

Where it leads. To Christ, by pattern and by the need it exposes. Israel’s rescues were small pictures of the great rescue. We were caught in a snare we could not break, sin, guilt and death, and Christ broke it: through his death he destroyed “the one who has the power of death, that is, the devil” (Hebrews 2:14). Paul’s question, “If God is for us, who can be against us?” (Romans 8:31), turns this psalm’s memory into a certainty, because God “did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all” (Romans 8:32).

For us. Look back on your life and ask honestly where you would be if the LORD had not been on your side. Then thank him aloud, with others, for rescues you did not engineer, and face what lies ahead knowing that the Maker of heaven and earth is for you in Christ.
124.theology:
To remember a rescue properly, God’s people think through what would have happened without him, so that he alone gets the credit for their survival (vv. 1-5). The waters come, but do not overwhelm those God is with.

Rescue is God's act: the snare is broken for the bird, not by it (v. 7), a picture of the gospel. The personal confession of 121:2 becomes the congregation's (v. 8).
124.examples: Most of us remember our rescues vaguely. This psalm is meant to be said aloud together, a leader calling out the line and the people answering, so that a whole church traces the road it did not have to take and gives the credit where it belongs.

keyVerse.quote: Our help is in the name of the LORD, who made heaven and earth.
keyVerse.note: Every rescue the psalm remembers is gathered into this one confession. The help that saved Israel was not luck or strength but the LORD himself, Maker of the very floods and snares that threatened them. One pilgrim’s “My help” (Psalm 121:2) has become the whole people’s “Our help”, and the church still says it as it gathers.

124.reflection:
The psalm begins, “If it had not been the LORD who was on our side” (v. 1). Looking back, where can you see that you would not have come through without him?

Leader and people say the words together (v. 1). Why does it matter to give thanks aloud with God’s people, and not only privately?

The bird did not break the snare; it simply flew when the snare was broken (v. 7). How does this picture help you understand what Christ has done in rescuing you from sin and death (Hebrews 2:14–15)?

“Our help is in the name of the LORD, who made heaven and earth” (v. 8). What present danger or fear do you need to bring under that confession this week?

125.text: A Song of Ascents. 1Those who trust in the LORD are like Mount Zion, which cannot be moved, but abides forever.2As the mountains surround Jerusalem, so the LORD surrounds his people, from this time forth and forevermore.3For the scepter of wickedness shall not rest on the land allotted to the righteous, lest the righteous stretch out their hands to do wrong.4Do good, O LORD, to those who are good, and to those who are upright in their hearts!5But those who turn aside to their crooked ways the LORD will lead away with evildoers! Peace be upon Israel!

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Those who trust in the LORD are as secure as Zion itself, because the LORD surrounds them. Nearing Jerusalem, the pilgrims are given two pictures from the landscape in front of them. First, Mount Zion: solid rock, unmoved and abiding for ever. That is what trusting people are like, not because they are strong but because of the One they lean on (v. 1). Second, the ring of hills around the city: as they enclose Jerusalem, so the LORD encloses his people, and unlike the hills he will never wear away, “from this time forth and forevermore” (v. 2). Security lies not in the one who trusts but in the One who is trusted.
verseByVerse.theology: Pilgrims see the hills ringing Jerusalem and are told that God surrounds his people like that.

verseByVerse.quote: Those who trust in the LORD are like Mount Zion, which cannot be moved, but abides forever. As the mountains surround Jerusalem, so the LORD surrounds his people, from this time forth and forevermore.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those who trust in the LORD are as secure as Mount Zion, because the LORD himself surrounds them for ever.

Like Mount Zion. The pilgrims are near Jerusalem now, and the psalm uses what they can see: Mount Zion, solid rock, unmoved through every storm and every generation. Not that believers are strong: those who trust are immovable because of the One they trust, and the kingdom they belong to “cannot be shaken” (Hebrews 12:28).

As the mountains surround Jerusalem. Jerusalem sat in a ring of higher ground, the Mount of Olives to the east and ridges on the other sides, like a city held in cupped hands. So the LORD surrounds his people. Elisha’s servant once woke to find an army surrounding their town, and panicked. Elisha prayed, “O LORD, please open his eyes that he may see,” and the young man saw that “the mountain was full of horses and chariots of fire all around Elisha” (2 Kings 6:17). The enemy surrounded the city; God surrounded the enemy.

From this time forth and forevermore. Even mountains are only a picture: “the mountains may depart and the hills be removed, but my steadfast love shall not depart from you” (Isaiah 54:10). God’s surrounding care outlasts the hills that picture it.

Kept by Christ. Jesus promised the same: his sheep will never perish, “and no one will snatch them out of my hand” (John 10:28). You may not feel immovable, but your stability is measured by the One around you, not by how steady you feel.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God sets a limit to the power of the wicked, and calls his people to keep straight while it lasts. The sceptre of wickedness may lie on God’s land for a time, but it will not settle there, because God knows that long oppression tempts even the righteous to do wrong (v. 3). So the psalm prays for good on those who are upright in heart (v. 4), and warns that those who bend to crooked ways will be led away with the evildoers they have joined (v. 5). It closes with a benediction on the people who trust: “Peace be upon Israel!”
verseByVerse.theology: God sets a limit to the rule of the wicked, so that it does not bend the righteous out of shape.

verseByVerse.quote: For the scepter of wickedness shall not rest on the land allotted to the righteous, lest the righteous stretch out their hands to do wrong.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God will not let wicked rule settle on his people for good, because long oppression tempts even the righteous to do wrong.

The scepter of wickedness. Oppression, injustice in power. It may come on God’s people for a time, but it will not “rest” there. The land allotted to the righteous recalls the shares of Canaan given to the tribes by lot under Joshua (Joshua 14:1–2). God will not let a godless power settle for ever on the inheritance he gave.

Lest the righteous stretch out their hands to do wrong. If good people live long enough under bad rule, they begin to compromise: to cut corners, go along, fight dirty, or despair of doing right. Long oppression does not only hurt the righteous; it tempts them. So God, knowing their frailty, will not let the pressure last beyond what they can bear (1 Corinthians 10:13).

The one who never bent. Jesus lived under Herod and Pilate and suffered the greatest injustice ever done, yet never stretched out his hand to wrong: “When he was reviled, he did not revile in return; when he suffered, he did not threaten, but continued entrusting himself to him who judges justly” (1 Peter 2:23). Where we bend, he stood straight for us.

In everyday life. That is a comfort for anyone under a harsh boss, a corrupt system or a hostile culture: God sees the temptation as well as the injustice, and has set its limit. Watch for the slow bend: bitterness, or small dishonesty excused because the other side plays dirty.

verseByVerse.quote: Do good, O LORD, to those who are good, and to those who are upright in their hearts! But those who turn aside to their crooked ways the LORD will lead away with evildoers! Peace be upon Israel!
verseByVerse.commentary:
God is asked to do good to the upright in heart; those who turn aside to crooked ways will share the end of evildoers.

Upright in their hearts. The “good” are defined by their hearts: not the sinless but those who trust (v. 1) and keep walking straight, upheld by the LORD who surrounds them.

Those who turn aside. The temptation of v. 3 has claimed them, and they go the way of the evildoers they joined. Yet anyone who has stepped onto a crooked path may still turn back by confession (1 John 1:9) to the God of steadfast love, whose people are kept by Christ’s righteousness, not their own.

Peace be upon Israel! The same blessing closes Psalm 128 (128:6). Paul ended Galatians with an echo of it: “peace and mercy be upon them, and upon the Israel of God” (Galatians 6:16). Those who trust in the LORD receive this peace.

Where Christians differ: can a true believer turn aside and be finally lost? Arminians read warnings like v. 5 as showing that a genuine believer can fall away; Reformed Christians hold that those God has truly saved will be kept to the end. This commentary’s view: v. 1 says those who trust in the LORD cannot be moved, so v. 5 is the warning that marks out who truly trusts: those who turn aside for good show they never truly belonged (1 John 2:19). The warning is real, and it is one of the means by which God keeps his own (Hebrews 3:14).

125.title: The LORD Surrounds His People
125.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 125 is the sixth of the Songs of Ascents (120–134), sung by pilgrims on the road up to Jerusalem for the pilgrim feasts. Psalm 124 looked back on an escape; now the pilgrims can see Zion and the hills around the city, and the psalm turns from a rescue remembered to a security that lasts.

The message. Those who trust in the LORD are as secure as the mountain they are walking towards, because the LORD himself surrounds them, for ever. That security is no licence to drift: God will not let wicked rule settle on his people for good, lest it bend them, and the psalm draws a line between those who keep straight and those who turn aside. Peace rests on the people who trust.

Why it was said. Israel often knew what it was to see the land God had given ruled by the wicked, whether by foreign powers or by corrupt rulers of its own, and to feel the pull to make peace with it (see the introduction on the Songs of Ascents). This psalm sent the pilgrims up to the feast with both a comfort and a warning.

How the chapter makes its case. Two pictures from the landscape: Mount Zion, which cannot be moved, and the hills around Jerusalem, picturing the LORD around his people (vv. 1–2). Then comes a promise with a reason: the sceptre of wickedness will not rest on the land of the righteous, lest they too reach out to do wrong (v. 3). It ends with a prayer for good on the upright in heart, a warning for those who turn aside, and a benediction on Israel (vv. 4–5).

Where it leads. To Christ, by the character of God shown in him and by the need the psalm exposes. The God who surrounds his people like the hills is the Good Shepherd who says of his sheep, “no one will snatch them out of my hand” (John 10:28), and believers have now “come to Mount Zion and to the city of the living God” (Hebrews 12:22), where he reigns. And the psalm asks who is truly upright in heart and never turns aside under wicked rule. Only Jesus lived under Herod and Pilate without once stretching out his hand to wrong, and his righteousness is given to all who trust him.

For us. Your stability does not depend on how steady you feel, but on the One who surrounds you. Under pressure that seems endless, remember that God has set its limit, and watch for the slow bend in your own heart. If you have turned aside, the way back is open: he keeps his people by Christ’s righteousness, not by their own.
125.theology:
Stability belongs to those who trust, because of the one they trust (v. 1), and God surrounds his people with a love more lasting than mountains (v. 2).

God limits the duration of oppression because prolonged wicked rule tempts the righteous to compromise (v. 3). Those who turn aside share the fate of evildoers, and peace rests on the people of God (v. 5).
125.examples: Under a harsh boss or a hostile culture, the danger is not only being hurt but being bent. This psalm promises both a limit to the pressure and a ring of protection you may not be able to see, as Elisha's servant could not until his eyes were opened.

keyVerse.quote: As the mountains surround Jerusalem, so the LORD surrounds his people, from this time forth and forevermore.
keyVerse.note: The pilgrims could see the picture with their own eyes: a city held in a ring of hills. This verse turns the landscape into a promise and explains why those who trust cannot be moved (v. 1). Their security does not lie in themselves but in the LORD who encloses them, and unlike the hills, he will never wear away.

125.reflection:
The psalm compares those who trust in the LORD to Mount Zion, “which cannot be moved” (v. 1). Why does it locate their firmness in the One they trust rather than in their own strength? How does that help on days when your faith feels weak?

Elisha’s servant saw only the enemy army until his eyes were opened (2 Kings 6:17). What situations make it hardest for you to believe that the LORD surrounds his people (v. 2)?

Verse 3 says long oppression tempts the righteous “to do wrong”. Where have you seen pressure, at work, in a family or in a culture, slowly bend good people? How does Jesus, who never returned evil for evil (1 Peter 2:23), help us stand?

How do the promise of v. 1 and the warning of v. 5 fit together? How would you use them to encourage a friend who has drifted, or one who fears they have lost their faith?

126.text: A Song of Ascents. 1When the LORD restored the fortunes of Zion, we were like those who dream.2Then our mouth was filled with laughter, and our tongue with shouts of joy; then they said among the nations, "The LORD has done great things for them."3The LORD has done great things for us; we are glad.4Restore our fortunes, O LORD, like streams in the Negeb!5Those who sow in tears shall reap with shouts of joy!6He who goes out weeping, bearing the seed for sowing, shall come home with shouts of joy, bringing his sheaves with him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–3 — The LORD Has Done Great Things for Us
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Remembering what God has done is the ground of joy and of witness. The psalm looks back to the day the LORD restored Zion’s fortunes, most likely the return from exile, a rescue so sudden and so large that it felt like a dream (v. 1). Laughter and shouts of joy filled the people’s mouths, and even the nations said, “The LORD has done great things for them” (v. 2). Israel takes up the verdict of the watching world and makes it its own glad confession: “The LORD has done great things for us; we are glad” (v. 3).
verseByVerse.theology: A restoration so great it felt like a dream — and even the nations noticed.

verseByVerse.quote: When the LORD restored the fortunes of Zion, we were like those who dream. Then our mouth was filled with laughter, and our tongue with shouts of joy; then they said among the nations, "The LORD has done great things for them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When God brought his people home, the joy felt like a dream, and even the nations admitted that Israel’s God had done it.

When the LORD restored the fortunes of Zion. A memory of something too good to seem real. The likeliest setting is the return from exile, when “the LORD stirred up the spirit of Cyrus king of Persia” to send the captives home (Ezra 1:1): after some seventy years (Jeremiah 29:10), the gates opened.

Like those who dream. Many believers know the feeling: an answer to prayer so large you keep waking up expecting it to be gone. A prodigal come home, a diagnosis reversed, a marriage restored.

Our mouth was filled with laughter. Not polite happiness but the helpless laughter of relief. And nations who worshipped other gods looked at Israel coming home and said, their God did this. God’s rescue of his people is a testimony to the watching world.

Uncertain wording. The KJV reads “turned again the captivity of Zion”. The Hebrew phrase can mean bringing back captives, but it is also used where no captivity is in view, as when “the LORD restored the fortunes of Job” (Job 42:10), so it most likely means a complete reversal of the people’s lot. The psalm does not name the occasion; some think of an earlier deliverance, but the return from exile fits best.
verseByVerse.note: Probably sung after the return from exile in Babylon.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD has done great things for us; we are glad.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel takes the nations’ verdict on its lips as its own glad confession.

The LORD has done great things for us. The people pick up the nations’ very words (v. 2) and make them their own: the testimony of unbelievers echoed back as the confession of believers.

We are glad. Simple, and enough. Mary sang the same when she carried the Christ: “for he who is mighty has done great things for me, and holy is his name” (Luke 1:49). The great things God did in bringing exiles home were a small foretaste of the great thing he was doing in her.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–6 — Like Streams in the Negeb
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Past mercy becomes the reason to ask for more, and present sorrow becomes seed. The restoration was real but unfinished, so the people pray for God to restore their fortunes again, as suddenly as winter rain fills the dry stream beds of the Negeb (v. 4). The answer comes as a promise from the farmer’s year: those who sow in tears will reap with shouts of joy (v. 5). The man who goes out weeping with his precious seed will come home singing, his arms full of sheaves (v. 6). Tears sown in faith are not wasted; God will raise a harvest from them.
verseByVerse.theology: Remembering past joy, the people ask for it again — and learn that tears sown in faith come up as harvest.

verseByVerse.quote: Restore our fortunes, O LORD, like streams in the Negeb!
verseByVerse.commentary:
The return was real but unfinished, so the people ask God to complete it, suddenly and abundantly, like floodwater in a desert.

Restore our fortunes, O LORD. The restoration of v. 1 was real but not complete: those who came home from Babylon found ruins, drought and hardship (Haggai 1:10–11). So the psalm asks for restoration again, as Psalm 85 does (85:1–7).

Like streams in the Negeb! The Negeb is the dry southern desert of Judah. Most of the year its stream beds are channels of dust and stones, but when the winter rains come, water rushes down them almost overnight, and the desert blooms. They ask not for slow improvement but for a sudden flood of God’s goodness into dry places.

In everyday life. If your life or your church feels like a dry stream bed, past blessing only a memory and nothing but dust now, this is your prayer. God has done it before. Ask him to send the water again.
verseByVerse.note: The Negeb’s dry stream beds fill suddenly with the winter rains.

verseByVerse.quote: Those who sow in tears shall reap with shouts of joy! He who goes out weeping, bearing the seed for sowing, shall come home with shouts of joy, bringing his sheaves with him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Tears sown in faith come up as a harvest of joy: grief carried faithfully before God is seed, not waste.

Those who sow in tears. In hard years seed grain was precious: a farmer sowing his last seed was burying food his family could have eaten. He planted it in hope, often in tears. But it came up.

Bringing his sheaves with him. He goes out with a small bag of seed and comes home with arms full of sheaves: the same road, the same man, the tears turned into harvest. The “shouts of joy” are those of v. 2. What God did once, he will do again.

More than grain. The promise covers the parent praying for years for a wayward child, the teacher who sees no fruit, the missionary in hard soil, and the grieving, who plant their tears in faith. “And let us not grow weary of doing good, for in due season we will reap, if we do not give up” (Galatians 6:9). Faith does not pretend there are no tears; it plants them and waits, kept going not by grit but by the Spirit, who “helps us in our weakness” (Romans 8:26). Jesus said, “Blessed are you who weep now, for you shall laugh” (Luke 6:21), and, “You will be sorrowful, but your sorrow will turn into joy” (John 16:20).

The Sower who went out weeping. Jesus spoke of his own death in the same farming terms: “unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit” (John 12:24). He went out to the cross in sorrow, “with loud cries and tears” (Hebrews 5:7), and his harvest is the people he brings home. The final harvest is coming: “the ransomed of the LORD shall return and come to Zion with singing; everlasting joy shall be upon their heads” (Isaiah 35:10).

Is this a promise that every prayer, for every wayward child, will be answered as we hope? The sure promise is God’s final joy for his people (Isaiah 35:10). We sow in hope, but the harvest is God’s, in his time and in his way.

126.title: Those Who Sow in Tears
126.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 126 is the seventh of the Songs of Ascents (120–134). Psalm 125 promised that the sceptre of wickedness would not rest for ever on God’s people; this psalm remembers a day when God did turn everything round, and then asks him to do it again.

The message. The God who has turned his people’s sorrow into laughter before will do it again, so pray boldly and keep sowing, even through tears. Past mercy is the ground for present prayer, and present grief, carried in faith, is not waste but seed: God will bring a harvest of joy from it.

Why it was said. The likeliest setting is the return from exile in Babylon, when Cyrus let the captives go home (Ezra 1:1–4; see the introduction). The joy was overwhelming, but those who returned found ruins, opposition and failed harvests (Haggai 1:10–11). The psalm held both together: thanks for what God had done, and prayer for what was still lacking.

How the chapter makes its case. It moves from memory to prayer to promise. The people remember a restoration so great it felt like a dream, which even the nations credited to the LORD (vv. 1–3). Because he did it once, they ask him to do it again, as suddenly as winter rain floods the dry stream beds of the Negeb (v. 4). The answer is a promise from the farmer’s year: those who go out weeping with their seed will come home singing with their sheaves (vv. 5–6).

Where it leads. To Christ, by pattern and by promise. The return from Babylon was real but partial; the great restoration it pointed to came when Jesus, who went out to the cross “with loud cries and tears” (Hebrews 5:7), was sown like a grain of wheat in the ground and rose to bear “much fruit” (John 12:24). His resurrection is the first sheaf of the harvest, and the promise of the psalm will be complete when “the ransomed of the LORD shall return and come to Zion with singing” (Isaiah 35:10).

For us. Remember what God has done for you in Christ, and let it make you bold to ask for more. If you are in a season of tears, keep sowing: prayer for a wayward child, faithful work with no fruit yet, grief brought to God week after week. Nothing sown in faith is lost, and the morning of shouts of joy is coming.
126.theology:
God's past restorations are so great they seem like a dream, and they testify to the nations, whose verdict God's people gladly echo (vv. 1-3).

Remembering God’s past kindness is the reason to ask for it again, pictured as a sudden flood in dry places (v. 4; cf. 85:1-7).

Faithful sowing in sorrow leads to joyful harvest (vv. 5-6; 2 Cor 9:6): tears are not wasted but planted, and sorrow will turn into everlasting joy when the ransomed come home.
126.examples: Some seasons are all sowing: years of prayer for someone, faithful work with no visible fruit, grief carried to church week after week. The psalm does not tell you to stop weeping. It tells you that what you plant in faith, God will raise.

keyVerse.quote: Those who sow in tears shall reap with shouts of joy!
keyVerse.note: This verse turns the psalm’s prayer into a promise. It joins the two halves of the psalm, taking up the “shouts of joy” of the remembered restoration (v. 2) and promising them again to people still in tears. It teaches that grief carried in faith is not wasted but sown, and the harvest belongs to God.

126.reflection:
The people say they were “like those who dream” when God restored them (v. 1). When have you seen God do something so good it was hard to believe? How does remembering it help you pray now?

The nations said, “The LORD has done great things for them,” and Israel answered, “The LORD has done great things for us” (vv. 2–3). How does what God does for his people become a witness to those outside? What great things would you name?

The restoration was real but unfinished, so they prayed, “Restore our fortunes, O LORD” (v. 4). Where in your life or your church do you long for God to send water into a dry stream bed?

Jesus described his death as a grain of wheat falling into the ground (John 12:24). How does his going out in tears and coming back in triumph give hope to someone sowing in tears today, without promising that every prayer will be answered as we wish?

127.text: A Song of Ascents. Of Solomon. 1Unless the LORD builds the house, those who build it labor in vain. Unless the LORD watches over the city, the watchman stays awake in vain.2It is in vain that you rise up early and go late to rest, eating the bread of anxious toil; for he gives to his beloved sleep.3Behold, children are a heritage from the LORD, the fruit of the womb a reward.4Like arrows in the hand of a warrior are the children of one's youth.5Blessed is the man who fills his quiver with them! He shall not be put to shame when he speaks with his enemies in the gate.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–2 — He Gives to His Beloved Sleep
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Everything we build, guard and work for stands or falls by the LORD, so work without anxiety and rest in his care. Three times the psalm says “in vain”. Builders labour in vain unless the LORD builds the house, and the watchman stays awake in vain unless the LORD watches over the city (v. 1). Rising early, working late and eating “the bread of anxious toil” is in vain too, not because work is wrong but because anxiety assumes everything depends on us (v. 2). Then comes the turn: “he gives to his beloved sleep.” The God who never sleeps lets his people lie down.
verseByVerse.theology: All human effort without God is wasted — and God gives rest to those he loves.

verseByVerse.quote: Unless the LORD builds the house, those who build it labor in vain. Unless the LORD watches over the city, the watchman stays awake in vain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Without the LORD, all our building and guarding is wasted effort; only what he builds and keeps will stand.

Solomon’s song. The only Song of Ascents that bears Solomon’s name: the man who built the house of God, Israel’s greatest building project, writes that builders labour in vain without the LORD. He proved it himself: when his heart turned to other gods, the LORD tore most of the kingdom from his son (1 Kings 11:9–13).

Unless the LORD builds the house. “House” in the Bible also means a household, a family, a dynasty: God had promised to build David a house of descendants (2 Samuel 7:11). That promise is fulfilled in Christ, who said, “I will build my church” (Matthew 16:18); “we are his house” (Hebrews 3:6). So the verse covers the house, the family inside it, the church, a business, a life. Without God, the work is empty.

Unless the LORD watches over the city. The guard on the wall can do his job perfectly and still fail, if God is not guarding the city. Jesus said the house that stands in the storm belongs to “a wise man who built his house on the rock” (Matthew 7:24).

What it does not mean. Not that the builders should stop building or the watchman go to sleep, but that they should build and watch as people who know the outcome rests with God. “I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth” (1 Corinthians 3:6). “Apart from me you can do nothing” (John 15:5).
verseByVerse.note: One of two psalms credited to Solomon (with Psalm 72).

verseByVerse.quote: It is in vain that you rise up early and go late to rest, eating the bread of anxious toil; for he gives to his beloved sleep.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Anxious overwork achieves nothing; God provides for those he loves, and they can sleep because he never does.

The bread of anxious toil. Up before dawn, working late, eating in a hurry, shoulders tight with worry: food earned by labour that never feels like enough. It is “in vain” not because work is wrong, but because anxious overwork assumes everything depends on you. It does not.

He gives to his beloved sleep. The people God loves can lie down and rest, because he does not. The keeper of Psalm 121 “will neither slumber nor sleep” (121:4); his beloved can.

Jedidiah, the beloved. There may be a quiet signature here. At Solomon’s birth the LORD sent word through Nathan, “So he called his name Jedidiah, because of the LORD” (2 Samuel 12:25), a name that means “beloved of the LORD”. The man called God’s beloved writes that God gives his beloved sleep. The Father’s true Beloved (Matthew 3:17) slept in a boat in a storm (Mark 4:38), so perfectly did he trust; in him we are beloved too.

The seed grows while he sleeps. Jesus told of a farmer who scatters seed, and then “he sleeps and rises night and day, and the seed sprouts and grows; he knows not how” (Mark 4:27). “The blessing of the LORD makes rich, and he adds no sorrow with it” (Proverbs 10:22). If worry keeps you awake, this verse invites you to trust the One who is awake. (Persistent sleeplessness may also need a doctor; seeing one is no failure of faith.)

Uncertain wording. The last line can also be read to mean that he provides for his beloved while they sleep. Both readings rest on the same trust: God’s care does not depend on our staying awake.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 3–5 — Children Are a Heritage from the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Children, like every other blessing, are God’s gift and not our achievement. The house the LORD builds is a household, and the psalm calls children a heritage and a reward from him (v. 3). The children of a man’s youth are like arrows in a warrior’s hand: shaped, aimed and sent into a future he will not see (v. 4). A man with a full quiver is blessed, for his grown children stand with him when he faces opponents in the city gate, where disputes were settled (v. 5). The psalm that began with building ends with a family that God has built.
verseByVerse.theology: The house God builds includes a household, and children are his gift, not a man's achievement.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, children are a heritage from the LORD, the fruit of the womb a reward. Like arrows in the hand of a warrior are the children of one's youth. Blessed is the man who fills his quiver with them! He shall not be put to shame when he speaks with his enemies in the gate.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Children are God’s gift, not our achievement, and a household of them is strength for the future.

Children are a heritage from the LORD. Not a human achievement, a lifestyle choice or a burden, but a gift. This belongs with the first half of the psalm. Parents can do everything right and still find that their children do not turn out as hoped; couples can long for years for children and have none. Children come from God, which frees parents from both pride and despair. For those who long for children and have none, the verse describes God’s gift, not a verdict on anyone’s worth to him. God promised the childless who hold fast to him “a name better than sons and daughters” (Isaiah 56:5).

Like arrows in the hand of a warrior. Arrows are shaped, straightened and aimed, and then released to go where the archer cannot. Children are raised and then sent out into a future their parents will not see.

His enemies in the gate. The city gate was the place of legal disputes and public business. A man with grown children standing with him was not easily pushed around there.

The children God has given. Hebrews hears Christ say of his people, “Behold, I and the children God has given me” (Hebrews 2:13). Every believer is a child given by the Father to the Son, and he will lose none of them (John 6:39).

Psalm 128 answers. Here labour without God is “anxious toil”. In Psalm 128 the one who fears the LORD “shall eat the fruit of the labor of your hands” (128:2). The work is the same; what differs is whether the LORD is at its centre.

Where Christians differ: must Christians have as many children as possible? Roman Catholic teaching forbids artificial contraception, and some Protestants hold that couples should not plan their family at all; most Protestants hold that a couple may plan or space their children. This commentary’s view: the psalm celebrates children as a blessing, and couples should welcome them gladly. But it is wisdom poetry, not a command to maximise births; wise, unselfish planning is not sin, while methods that end a life after conception are another matter.

Uncertain wording. The word for “children” in vv. 3–4 can mean “sons”, and the last line has “they” rather than “he”. It may mean the father, standing with his sons, or the grown sons themselves, defending the family. Either way, the household stands together.

127.title: Unless the LORD Builds the House
127.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 127 stands at the centre of the fifteen Songs of Ascents (120–134), and it is the only one that bears the name of Solomon, the king who built the temple. Psalm 126 ended with sowing and harvest; this psalm turns to the house, the city, the day’s work and the family.

The message. Everything that matters, a house, a city, a livelihood, a family, is finally God’s gift and not our achievement. So work hard, but without anxiety, and go to sleep, because the One who loves you is awake. And receive children as what they are: his heritage, entrusted to you.

Why it was said. Israel’s life rested on building houses, guarding cities and raising families. Pilgrims going up to the feasts left all three behind, trusting God’s promise that “no one shall covet your land, when you go up to appear before the LORD your God three times in the year” (Exodus 34:24; see the introduction on the Songs of Ascents). The psalm reminded them, on the road and at home, who really holds a household together.

How the chapter makes its case. Three times it says “in vain”. Building without the LORD, guarding without the LORD, and anxious overwork are all wasted effort, but he gives his beloved sleep (vv. 1–2). Then it shows what the LORD builds: a household. Children are his heritage, like arrows in a warrior’s hand, and a strength to their father when he faces opponents in the gate (vv. 3–5). The two halves are one lesson: what lasts is what God gives.

Where it leads. To Christ, by covenant promise. “House” recalls God’s promise to build David a house, a royal line, whose son would build a house for God’s name (2 Samuel 7:11–13). Solomon built a temple of stone, but the house the LORD himself builds is Christ’s: “I will build my church” (Matthew 16:18), and “we are his house” (Hebrews 3:6). Even the gift of children finds its fulfilment in him, for the Son of God says of his people, “Behold, I and the children God has given me” (Hebrews 2:13).

For us. Build your work, your home and your church as hard and as well as you can, and then rest, because the outcome was never yours to carry. Receive every child as a gift, and if you long for children and have none, know that God’s love for you is not measured by the size of your household. In Christ you belong to the house that he is building, which cannot fail.
127.theology:
All human building, guarding and working is futile without God (vv. 1-2). Anxious overwork assumes everything depends on us; God gives rest to his beloved (v. 2).

Children are God's gift, not human achievement (v. 3), raised and then sent like arrows (v. 4), and a strength to a household (v. 5). The psalm pairs with 128, where labour under the fear of the LORD bears fruit.
127.examples: A church plant, a business, a marriage: build and watch as hard as you can, then go to bed. The outcome was never yours to carry, and the one who loves you is awake.

keyVerse.quote: Unless the LORD builds the house, those who build it labor in vain. Unless the LORD watches over the city, the watchman stays awake in vain.
keyVerse.note: This verse sets the theme for the whole psalm: what we build and guard stands only if the LORD builds and guards it. Everything that follows, the futility of anxious toil, the gift of sleep and the gift of children, works out this one truth. It is not a call to stop working, but to work as people whose outcome rests in God’s hands.

127.reflection:
Verse 1 names the house and the city. What are you building or guarding at the moment, at work, at home or in church? What would it look like to do it as someone who knows that unless the LORD builds it, the effort is in vain?

Verse 2 describes “the bread of anxious toil”. What drives anxious overwork in your life or culture, and what does it reveal about where we think our security lies? How does “he gives to his beloved sleep” answer it?

Children are called “a heritage from the LORD” (v. 3). How does seeing children as a gift rather than an achievement free parents from both pride and despair? How can a church care well for those who long for children and have none?

Christ says of his people, “Behold, I and the children God has given me” (Hebrews 2:13). What does it mean for you to be part of the house that Christ is building (Hebrews 3:6)?

128.text: A Song of Ascents. 1Blessed is everyone who fears the LORD, who walks in his ways!2You shall eat the fruit of the labor of your hands; you shall be blessed, and it shall be well with you.3Your wife will be like a fruitful vine within your house; your children will be like olive shoots around your table.4Behold, thus shall the man be blessed who fears the LORD.5The LORD bless you from Zion! May you see the prosperity of Jerusalem all the days of your life!6May you see your children's children! Peace be upon Israel!

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — Blessed Is Everyone Who Fears the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The fear of the LORD brings blessing into the ordinary places of life: work and home. The psalm opens with a beatitude for everyone who fears the LORD and shows it by walking in his ways (v. 1). Then it speaks to that person directly: you will eat what your hands have worked for, and it will go well with you (v. 2). The scene moves indoors to the family meal: a wife flourishing like a fruitful vine at the heart of the home, children growing like olive shoots around the table (v. 3). “Behold,” the psalm concludes: this is how the man who fears the LORD is blessed (v. 4).
verseByVerse.theology: The fear of the LORD turns anxious toil into fruitful work and a house into a home.

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed is everyone who fears the LORD, who walks in his ways! You shall eat the fruit of the labor of your hands; you shall be blessed, and it shall be well with you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everyone who fears the LORD is blessed, and his ordinary work bears fruit he lives to enjoy.

Blessed is everyone who fears the LORD. Not only kings, priests or the wealthy, but every person, man or woman, rich or poor. This fear is reverent, trusting awe, not terror, and it shows itself in how a person lives, “who walks in his ways”, as in Psalm 112 (112:1). It is not a fee that buys the blessing. It is the trust of people God has already forgiven: “But with you there is forgiveness, that you may be feared” (Psalm 130:4). Those who have stumbled come back the same way, through forgiveness.

The fruit of the labor of your hands. Now the psalm speaks to “you” directly. Psalm 127 described “the bread of anxious toil” (127:2). Here the same work bears fruit, and the worker gets to eat it. Not the job but the centre has changed: Psalm 127 is work without God, Psalm 128 is work under God.

In everyday life. For anyone whose work feels futile, the answer may not be a different job, but a different relation to God in the same job.

verseByVerse.quote: Your wife will be like a fruitful vine within your house; your children will be like olive shoots around your table. Behold, thus shall the man be blessed who fears the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A flourishing wife and growing children round the table are among God’s good gifts to those who fear him.

Like a fruitful vine. Two pictures from the farm. The wife is a fruitful vine “within your house”, literally in its innermost part: full of life at the heart of the home. The children are olive shoots, young shoots springing up around an olive tree that lives for generations: a small grove, growing.

Around your table. Ordinary domestic happiness is a real blessing from God. The blessing of fearing God is found not only in heaven, but at the kitchen table.

What it does not mean. As with Psalm 112, this is the pattern of God’s world, not a guarantee for every home. Some who fear God are single, widowed or childless; some faithful families face terrible loss. The psalm describes the goodness that tends to grow where God is feared, not a promise that no believer’s table will be empty. And Jesus promised those who leave home and family for his sake a hundredfold now in houses, brothers, sisters, mothers and children (Mark 10:29–30). In his church no one need eat alone.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–6 — May You See Your Children's Children
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The blessing of one household widens to God’s city, the coming generations and all his people. Spoken perhaps by a priest over the pilgrim, the blessing comes “from Zion”, where God dwells, and ties the family’s good to the good of Jerusalem: may you see the city prosper all the days of your life (v. 5). It reaches forward in time to grandchildren, the sign of a household God has built to last, and outward to the whole nation: “Peace be upon Israel!” (v. 6). No home flourishes on its own; its blessing flows from God’s presence among his people and back into their peace.
verseByVerse.theology: The blessing on one household widens to the city of God and reaches the grandchildren.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD bless you from Zion! May you see the prosperity of Jerusalem all the days of your life! May you see your children's children! Peace be upon Israel!
verseByVerse.commentary:
The blessing from Zion widens from one home to God’s city, the grandchildren, and all his people.

The LORD bless you from Zion! Now the blessing is spoken over the pilgrim, perhaps by a priest. It comes from Zion, where God dwells, and ties the man’s private happiness to the good of God’s city. You cannot flourish in a corner while the church withers.

May you see your children’s children! It reaches forward in time too. To see grandchildren was a sign that the family God built was lasting; faith lived at the table is passed down the generations. Isaiah promised the suffering Servant the same reward: “he shall see his offspring” (Isaiah 53:10).

Peace be upon Israel! The last words are those of Psalm 125 (125:5): one God-fearing home’s blessing flows out into peace for all God’s people. Paul closed Galatians with a blessing of “peace and mercy be upon them, and upon the Israel of God” (Galatians 6:16).

Where Christians differ: who is “the Israel of God” in Galatians 6:16? Many take it to mean all who belong to Christ, Jew and Gentile; others read it of Jewish believers or the Jewish people. This commentary’s view: it is all believers, the one people of God, with believing Gentiles grafted into Israel’s olive tree (Romans 11:17): fulfilment, not replacement.
