128.title: Olive Shoots Around Your Table
128.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 128 is the ninth of the Songs of Ascents (120–134) and the companion of Psalm 127. There, work without the LORD was “anxious toil” and children were his gift; here, work under the fear of the LORD bears fruit, and the family gathers round the table. It ends, like Psalm 125, with “Peace be upon Israel!”

The message. The fear of the LORD turns ordinary life, daily work, marriage, meals and children, into a place of God’s blessing. And no home is blessed on its own: the good of one household flows from God’s presence among his people, is bound up with the good of his city, and reaches down the generations.

Why it was said. Pilgrims came up to Jerusalem from farms and villages, and went home again to fields, vines, olive trees and families (see the introduction on the Songs of Ascents). The psalm, perhaps spoken over them as a blessing at Zion, sent them home knowing that the God they had worshipped at the temple was the God of their kitchen tables too.

How the chapter makes its case. It begins with a beatitude for everyone who fears the LORD and walks in his ways, and promises that their work will bear fruit they enjoy (vv. 1–2). It then steps indoors to the family meal: a wife like a fruitful vine, children like olive shoots round the table (vv. 3–4). Finally the blessing widens: from Zion, to the prosperity of Jerusalem, to grandchildren, and to peace on all Israel (vv. 5–6).

Where it leads. To Christ, by the need the psalm exposes and by promise. No one has feared the LORD and walked in his ways perfectly except the One of whom Isaiah said, “his delight shall be in the fear of the LORD” (Isaiah 11:3). His labour was the cross, and its fruit is a family: “he shall see his offspring” (Isaiah 53:10). He gathers them round his table now, and will at last, for “Blessed are those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb” (Revelation 19:9).

For us. Fear the LORD where you are: at work, at home, at the table. Ordinary family life is not a distraction from God’s blessing but one of the places it is tasted. And if your own table is empty, the psalm is not a verdict on you: in Christ you belong to a family, and the church is meant to make room for you at its table.
128.theology:
The fear of the LORD, shown in walking in his ways, brings blessing to every kind of person and turns anxious toil into fruitful labour (vv. 1-2).

Ordinary family life is a real blessing from God, though as a pattern rather than a guarantee (vv. 3-4). Household blessing is tied to the good of God's people and reaches across generations (vv. 5-6).
128.examples: A shared meal with people you love is not a distraction from spiritual things; it is one of the places God's blessing is meant to be tasted. And where someone has no family at the table, the church is meant to make room at its own.

keyVerse.quote: Blessed is everyone who fears the LORD, who walks in his ways!
keyVerse.note: The whole psalm unfolds this opening beatitude. The fear of the LORD, shown in walking his ways, is the root, and fruitful work, a flourishing home and a blessing that reaches the city and the generations are its fruit. “Everyone” opens the blessing to any person who fears him, whatever their station.

128.reflection:
Psalm 127 speaks of “the bread of anxious toil”, while Psalm 128 promises “the fruit of the labor of your hands” (v. 2). What makes the difference between the two? How might fearing the LORD change the way you approach the same work?

The psalm finds God’s blessing at the family table (v. 3). What does it mean to see ordinary meals, marriage and children as places where God’s goodness is tasted? How could your home share that table with others?

The psalm describes a pattern, not a guarantee, and some who fear God are single, childless or bereaved. How can a church make sure such people are part of its family table (Mark 10:29–30)?

The blessing widens from one home to Zion, to grandchildren, and to peace on all Israel (vv. 5–6). How is your household’s good tied to the good of the church, and what are you passing on to the next generation?

129.text: A Song of Ascents. 1"Greatly have they afflicted me from my youth"— let Israel now say—2"Greatly have they afflicted me from my youth, yet they have not prevailed against me.3The plowers plowed upon my back; they made long their furrows."4The LORD is righteous; he has cut the cords of the wicked.5May all who hate Zion be put to shame and turned backward!6Let them be like the grass on the housetops, which withers before it grows up,7with which the reaper does not fill his hand nor the binder of sheaves his arms,8nor do those who pass by say, "The blessing of the LORD be upon you! We bless you in the name of the LORD!"

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — Yet They Have Not Prevailed
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel’s enemies have wounded her deeply from the beginning, but they have never won, because the righteous LORD stops them. Like Psalm 124, the psalm opens as a call and response: a leader sings the line and Israel repeats it, so that the whole people confess their history together (vv. 1–2). The affliction is pictured with shocking honesty as ploughmen cutting long furrows down a man’s back (v. 3). Then the image turns. The LORD is righteous, and he has cut the cords that harnessed the plough to the oxen, so the furrows end in the middle of the field (v. 4). Suffering is real; it is not final.
verseByVerse.theology: Israel looks back over a history of suffering that cut deep, and sees that its enemies never won.

verseByVerse.quote: "Greatly have they afflicted me from my youth"— let Israel now say— "Greatly have they afflicted me from my youth, yet they have not prevailed against me. The plowers plowed upon my back; they made long their furrows."
verseByVerse.commentary:
From the start of its history Israel has been attacked, and the wounds have cut deep, yet no enemy has ever overcome God’s people.

Greatly have they afflicted me from my youth. Another call and response, like Psalm 124: a leader gives the line, “let Israel now say”, and the people sing it back. It sums up the nation’s history: from its youth in Egypt (Hosea 11:1), through wilderness, judges, invasions and exile, Israel has been attacked.

Yet they have not prevailed against me. The repeated line gains an ending: “not prevailed”. Pharaoh, the Philistines, Assyria and Babylon all tried to destroy God’s people, and all are gone. Israel is still singing. So is the church: “We are afflicted in every way, but not crushed; perplexed, but not driven to despair; persecuted, but not forsaken; struck down, but not destroyed” (2 Corinthians 4:8–9).

The plowers plowed upon my back. A shocking image: Israel’s back is a field, and the long furrows are the wounds of a flogging, laid in rows like ploughed ground.

His back was ploughed for them. A Christian cannot read that line without thinking of the Servant who said, “I gave my back to those who strike” (Isaiah 50:6), and of the Roman scourge on the back of Jesus (Matthew 27:26). The sufferings of God’s people were gathered up in the sufferings of their King. His enemies seemed to prevail, yet death could not hold him, and of his church he says, “the gates of hell shall not prevail against it” (Matthew 16:18).

Uncertain wording. The word translated “greatly” can also mean “often”, as the ESV notes. Either way, the attacks were heavy and repeated.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD is righteous; he has cut the cords of the wicked.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The ploughing stopped because the righteous LORD cut the harness: God sets a limit to what the enemies of his people can do.

He has cut the cords of the wicked. Here the image turns. A plough was pulled by oxen harnessed with ropes. Cut the ropes, and the plough stops dead in the middle of the field. The furrows go no further.

The LORD is righteous. The righteous LORD would not let the ploughing go on forever. The oppressors could wound Israel’s back, but they could not finish the field.

In everyday life. There is comfort here for anyone who feels ploughed by a long illness, a persecution, a grief that keeps cutting. The ploughing is real, and the furrows are long. But the righteous God holds a knife over the cords, and he will cut them at the time he chooses. The suffering has a limit, as Psalm 125:3 said. That is not a promise that every trouble ends soon: for some the last cord is cut only when God brings them home, where “He will wipe away every tear from their eyes” (Revelation 21:4). But it is always cut.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–8 — Like Grass on the Housetops
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Those who hate God’s people will come to nothing. The psalm prays that all who hate Zion be shamed and driven back (v. 5), and paints their end from Israel’s farming life. They are like grass on a flat earth roof, quick to sprout after rain and quick to wither, with no root and no harvest (vv. 6–7). No reaper fills his hand with it, and no neighbour passing by calls out the harvest blessing (v. 8). The contrast with the sheaves of Psalm 126 is deliberate: God’s people sow in tears and reap with joy, while their enemies have nothing at all to bring in.
verseByVerse.theology: Those who hate God's people will be like weeds on a roof: quick, shallow, and never harvested.

verseByVerse.quote: May all who hate Zion be put to shame and turned backward! Let them be like the grass on the housetops, which withers before it grows up, with which the reaper does not fill his hand nor the binder of sheaves his arms, nor do those who pass by say, "The blessing of the LORD be upon you! We bless you in the name of the LORD!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those who hate God’s people will come to nothing: like grass on a roof, they spring up fast, wither, and leave no harvest and no blessing.

Put to shame and turned backward! “Turned backward”: their attack reversed, their advance halted.

Like the grass on the housetops. Israelite houses had flat roofs of packed earth. After rain, grass would sprout there, bright green and doomed: with no depth of soil, it withered as soon as the sun came out. No farmer ever harvested his roof. So those who hate Zion may spring up fast, but they have no roots and leave nothing behind.

The blessing of the LORD be upon you! At harvest, passers-by greeted the reapers with a blessing, and the reapers answered. When Boaz came out to his fields, he said to the reapers, “The LORD be with you!” and they answered, “The LORD bless you” (Ruth 2:4). No one blesses a man harvesting his roof. Those who sow in tears come home with sheaves (Psalm 126:6); those who hate Zion have no sheaves, and no blessing, at all.

May a Christian pray this? It asks that God’s enemies fail, not for personal revenge (see the introduction). Christians may pray that opposition to the gospel will fail, while praying for the persecutors themselves (Matthew 5:44). The prayer will be answered in full when Christ returns; until then, Saul the persecutor who became Paul the apostle shows that God may answer it by turning an enemy into a brother.

Uncertain wording. The verb behind “grows up” (v. 6) is uncertain: it may mean “shoots up” or “is pulled up”. Either way the grass comes to nothing.

129.title: The Plowers Plowed upon My Back
129.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 129 is the tenth Song of Ascents. Psalm 128 ended with a blessing, “Peace be upon Israel!”, and now Israel is asked to look back over its whole life as a nation, a life marked less by peace than by persecution.

The message. God’s people have been attacked again and again from the very beginning, and the wounds went deep, but no enemy has ever finished them, because the righteous LORD sets a limit to what the wicked can do. Those who hate his people may spring up quickly, but they wither without fruit and without blessing. So the faithful can look back on long suffering with thanks, and look ahead without fear.

Why it was said. Pilgrims climbing to Jerusalem were a small people in a hostile world, with a long memory of Egypt, invasion and exile (see the introduction). The psalm gave them words to sing that history as a story of God’s faithfulness, not of defeat.

How the chapter makes its case. A leader gives the line and Israel repeats it: afflicted greatly from youth, yet never overcome (vv. 1–2). The suffering is pictured as a back ploughed into long furrows (v. 3). Then the picture turns: the righteous LORD has cut the harness, and the plough stops (v. 4). The psalm ends with a prayer that all who hate Zion fail, like grass on a flat roof that withers before it grows, which no one harvests and no passer-by blesses (vv. 5–8).

Where it leads. To Christ, by pattern. The sufferings of God’s people come to a head in the King who said, “I gave my back to those who strike” (Isaiah 50:6), and whose back was torn by the Roman scourge. In him the people were ploughed to death and yet not overcome, for he rose, and he promises his church that “the gates of hell shall not prevail against it” (Matthew 16:18). The blessing withheld from Zion’s enemies is the blessing he gives to all who come to him.

For us. When the church is pressed, or your own life feels ploughed by long trouble, remember the long view: every power that tried to erase God’s people is gone, and they are still singing. The cords will be cut at God’s time. Meanwhile pray that opposition to the gospel fails, and pray for the opponents themselves.
129.theology:
God's people suffer greatly throughout their history but are not overcome (vv. 1-2), and the ploughed back of verse 3 points forward to Christ, the Servant of Isaiah 50:6, who gave his back to be flogged.

The righteous God sets a limit to oppression by cutting the harness of the wicked (v. 4). Those who hate Zion are rootless and fruitless, without the harvest blessing, in contrast to those who sow in tears (vv. 5-8; 126:6).
129.examples: Every power that set out to erase God's people is now a name in a history book, and the people are still singing. That long view steadies a church under pressure today, and it reminds us to pray for the persecutor as well as against the persecution.

keyVerse.quote: Greatly have they afflicted me from my youth, yet they have not prevailed against me.
keyVerse.note: The whole psalm turns on the word “yet”. Israel does not deny how deep the suffering went, but the last word of its history is that the enemies did not win, because the righteous LORD would not let them. It is the confession of the church in every age, kept by the Lord who promised that the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.

129.reflection:
Israel is told to say its history out loud: “Greatly have they afflicted me … yet they have not prevailed against me” (vv. 1–2). What would it look like to tell the story of your own life, or your church’s, in that shape?

The ploughed back of verse 3 points to Jesus, who said, “I gave my back to those who strike” (Isaiah 50:6). How does knowing that he suffered this way help you when you feel ploughed by trouble?

The LORD “has cut the cords of the wicked” (v. 4). Where do you need to trust that God has set a limit to a trial, even when you cannot yet see the end of it?

The psalm prays that those who hate Zion fail (vv. 5–8), yet Jesus tells us to pray for those who persecute us. How can we pray both prayers honestly? Who might you pray for this week?

130.text: A Song of Ascents. 1Out of the depths I cry to you, O LORD!2O Lord, hear my voice! Let your ears be attentive to the voice of my pleas for mercy!3If you, O LORD, should mark iniquities, O Lord, who could stand?4But with you there is forgiveness, that you may be feared.5I wait for the LORD, my soul waits, and in his word I hope;6my soul waits for the Lord more than watchmen for the morning, more than watchmen for the morning.7O Israel, hope in the LORD! For with the LORD there is steadfast love, and with him is plentiful redemption.8And he will redeem Israel from all his iniquities.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — With You There Is Forgiveness
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: From the bottom of the pit, a sinner finds that God forgives. The psalmist cries “out of the depths”, asking not for justice but for mercy (vv. 1–2). He names what has dragged him down: if the LORD kept a record of iniquities, no one could stand before him, not even the most devout pilgrim (v. 3). Then comes one of the great turns of the Old Testament: “But with you there is forgiveness” (v. 4). And the purpose of forgiveness surprises: not that people may grow careless, but that God may be feared. Grace received produces reverent, grateful awe.
verseByVerse.theology: From the bottom of the pit, a sinner learns that God keeps no record against those he forgives.

verseByVerse.quote: Out of the depths I cry to you, O LORD! O Lord, hear my voice! Let your ears be attentive to the voice of my pleas for mercy!
verseByVerse.commentary:
From the lowest place a person can sink, the psalmist cries to the LORD, asking not for what he deserves but for mercy.

Out of the depths. This much-loved psalm begins at the bottom. “The depths” are the deep waters where a drowning man sinks, overwhelmed, far from help, with the weight of water overhead (compare Jonah 2:2). As verse 3 shows, what has dragged him down is not only trouble, but sin.

I cry to you, O LORD! And from there he cries. No place is so low that a cry from it cannot reach God.

My pleas for mercy! He asks for mercy, not justice: a man who asks for mercy knows he does not deserve it. That is the right way to begin with God, and because of Christ, our great high priest, it may be done boldly: “Let us then with confidence draw near to the throne of grace, that we may receive mercy and find grace to help in time of need” (Hebrews 4:16).
verseByVerse.note: One of the seven penitential psalms (6, 32, 38, 51, 102, 130 and 143), prayers of repentance used in the church since early times.

verseByVerse.quote: If you, O LORD, should mark iniquities, O Lord, who could stand? But with you there is forgiveness, that you may be feared.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If God kept a record of our sins, no one could stand before him; but he forgives, and his forgiveness makes us revere him, not take him lightly.

If you, O LORD, should mark iniquities. Now the real depths appear. If God kept a record of every sin, stored up against us, “who could stand?” No one, not even the most devout pilgrim: every one of us would fall at the judgment. This is the honest heart of true religion: before we can understand grace, we must understand that on our own record we cannot stand before God (Romans 3:20).

But with you there is forgiveness. Here is one of the great turns of the Old Testament. God does not keep that record against those he forgives. Paul quotes David’s word for it: “Blessed are those whose lawless deeds are forgiven, and whose sins are covered; blessed is the man against whom the Lord will not count his sin” (Romans 4:7–8). “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins” (1 John 1:9).

Where the record went. The psalm does not say how a righteous God can leave iniquities unmarked. The gospel does. The record was not torn up and forgotten; it was laid on another: “the LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all” (Isaiah 53:6). God put Christ forward as a sacrifice for sin, “so that he might be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus” (Romans 3:26). That is why John can call God not only faithful but “just” to forgive.

That you may be feared. Then the surprise. You might expect forgiveness to make people careless. The psalm says the opposite: it produces reverent awe. A person who knows what the record would have held does not treat God lightly afterwards; he trembles with gratitude before the God who wiped it out. Here is the order of all obedience: forgiven first, and then fearing, walking and serving. A forgiveness we think cost nothing makes us careless about sin. Real forgiveness makes us worship.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–8 — More Than Watchmen for the Morning
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The forgiven sinner waits for God with sure hope and calls the whole people to share it. His whole self leans towards the LORD, and he hopes in God’s word (v. 5). He waits more than night watchmen long for the dawn, and says it twice, as a tired man does in the last dark hour (v. 6). Then the psalm turns from “my soul” to “O Israel”: hope in the LORD, because with him is steadfast love and plentiful redemption (v. 7). The last promise is complete: he will redeem Israel from all its iniquities, not just their consequences (v. 8).
verseByVerse.theology: A forgiven man waits for God like a night watchman for dawn, and calls the whole nation to hope.

verseByVerse.quote: I wait for the LORD, my soul waits, and in his word I hope; my soul waits for the Lord more than watchmen for the morning, more than watchmen for the morning.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Forgiven, the psalmist waits for the LORD with his whole self, longing for him more than night watchmen long for the dawn, and just as sure that he will come.

My soul waits. His whole self leans towards God, waiting for him to do what he has said.

More than watchmen for the morning. A watchman on the city wall spent the long dark watches of the night staring east, cold and tired, longing for the first grey light that meant his watch was over. And he knew the morning would come. It always does. The psalm says it twice, the way a tired man repeats himself in the last hour before dawn. The psalmist longs for God even more than the watchman longs for morning, and his hope is just as sure.

The waiting church. “The LORD is good to those who wait for him … It is good that one should wait quietly for the salvation of the LORD” (Lamentations 3:25–26). The whole church waits like this now: “we ourselves, who have the firstfruits of the Spirit, groan inwardly as we wait eagerly for adoption as sons, the redemption of our bodies” (Romans 8:23). If you are in the long night, the dawn is coming.

How do I wait for the LORD? Waiting in Scripture is not sitting idle; it is leaning your whole weight towards God while the answer has not yet come. Wait on his word. The psalmist adds, “in his word I hope” (v. 5). When the long illness, the unanswered prayer for a child or the months without work wear you down, take one promise and hold it up to God, morning by morning. Keep your post. The watchman does not leave the wall because the night is long: keep praying, keep turning up with God’s people, keep doing the next ordinary duty. Say how long it feels. Waiting is not pretending; tell him the night is long, as this psalm does by repeating itself. Remember the first morning. The psalmist waits after forgiveness (v. 4), not for it. At the cross God has already done the greatest thing he will ever do for you: “He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all, how will he not also with him graciously give us all things?” (Romans 8:32).

verseByVerse.quote: O Israel, hope in the LORD! For with the LORD there is steadfast love, and with him is plentiful redemption. And he will redeem Israel from all his iniquities.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The forgiven man calls the whole people to hope in the LORD, whose love does not quit and whose redemption is more than enough to free them from every sin.

O Israel, hope in the LORD! Now the psalm turns outward, from “my soul” to “O Israel”. The man forgiven in the depths calls the whole people to hope. That is how testimony works.

Plentiful redemption. The grounds for hope are two: “steadfast love”, God’s covenant love that does not quit, and “plentiful redemption”, setting free at a price. Not scarce, not rationed, not barely enough: plentiful, more than sufficient for every sinner who cries from the depths.

From all his iniquities. The last promise is total. God will redeem his people not merely from the consequences of sin, or from enemies, but from the sins themselves.

The Redeemer went down into the depths. An angel told Joseph the name of the one who would keep that promise: “you shall call his name Jesus, for he will save his people from their sins” (Matthew 1:21). He “gave himself for us to redeem us from all lawlessness” (Titus 2:14), and the price was his own blood (Ephesians 1:7). The psalm that began in the depths ends with a Redeemer who went down into them himself, so that no one who cries from there need stay.

130.title: Out of the Depths
130.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 130 is the eleventh Song of Ascents and one of the best loved of all the psalms. Psalm 129 looked back on enemies who ploughed Israel’s back; now the pilgrim faces a deeper enemy, his own sin, and cries to God from the bottom of the pit.

The message. If God kept a record of our sins, no one could stand before him, but with him there is forgiveness, and that forgiveness makes us fear him rather than take him lightly. So the forgiven sinner waits for God with sure hope, like a watchman for the dawn, and calls all God’s people to hope in a redemption that is plentiful and complete.

Why it was said. Pilgrims went up to Jerusalem to worship at the temple, where sacrifices for sin were offered (see the introduction). This psalm taught them that the deepest trouble of God’s people is not their enemies but their iniquities, and that the God they were going to meet is the God who forgives. The church has long counted it among the seven penitential psalms.

How the chapter makes its case. A single voice cries from the depths for mercy (vv. 1–2). He admits that on his own record he could not stand, and rejoices that God forgives, so that he may be feared (vv. 3–4). Forgiven, he waits for the LORD and hopes in his word, more than watchmen for the morning (vv. 5–6). Then he turns to the whole people: hope in the LORD, whose steadfast love and plentiful redemption will free Israel from all its iniquities (vv. 7–8).

Where it leads. To Christ, by the need it exposes and by promise. The psalm leaves a question it does not answer: how can a righteous God simply not mark iniquities? The answer is the cross, where “the LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all” (Isaiah 53:6). The promise that God “will redeem Israel from all his iniquities” is kept in the one whose name means “the LORD saves”, for “he will save his people from their sins” (Matthew 1:21).

For us. You may pray this psalm from any depth, guilt, grief or a night that will not end. Do not hide your sins from God or minimise them; bring them to the God who forgives, and let his forgiveness make you reverent, not careless. Then wait for him with the watchman’s certainty, and tell others where hope is found.
130.theology:
No one can stand if God marks iniquities, but God forgives, and forgiveness produces reverent fear rather than presumption (vv. 3-4).

The forgiven wait for God with sure hope, like watchmen for dawn (vv. 5-6), and personal experience of grace becomes a call to God's people (v. 7). God's redemption is plentiful and complete, from all iniquities (vv. 7-8), fulfilled in Jesus, who saves his people from their sins.
130.examples: Whatever the pit, sin, grief or a night that will not end, this psalm gives words to pray from the bottom of it, and ends by telling us that the redemption is bigger than the sin.

keyVerse.quote: But with you there is forgiveness, that you may be feared.
keyVerse.note: This is the hinge of the psalm, the turn from “who could stand?” to hope. It tells us that God forgives, and why: not to make us careless but to bring us to reverent, grateful worship. The cross shows how such forgiveness can be just, and the rest of the psalm, the waiting and the hope, stands on this verse.

130.reflection:
The psalm begins “Out of the depths” (v. 1). What kinds of depths have you known, and what difference does it make that prayer can reach God from there?

“If you, O LORD, should mark iniquities, O Lord, who could stand?” (v. 3). Why is it necessary to see this before we can rejoice in forgiveness? How does the cross answer the question the psalm leaves open?

Forgiveness is given “that you may be feared” (v. 4). Why does real forgiveness make us more reverent rather than careless? Where have you seen the opposite?

The watchman knows the morning will come (v. 6). What are you waiting for God to do, and which promise in his word can you hold on to while you wait?

131.text: A Song of Ascents. Of David. 1O LORD, my heart is not lifted up; my eyes are not raised too high; I do not occupy myself with things too great and too marvelous for me.2But I have calmed and quieted my soul, like a weaned child with its mother; like a weaned child is my soul within me.3O Israel, hope in the LORD from this time forth and forevermore.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–3 — I Have Calmed and Quieted My Soul
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A soul at rest in God has laid down its pride and learned to be content with him. In three short verses David first tells the LORD what he has put away: a heart lifted up, eyes raised too high, and a mind busy with things too great and marvellous for him (v. 1). Then he says what has taken their place: he has calmed and quieted his soul until it is like a weaned child with its mother, no longer crying to be fed but content simply to be with her (v. 2). From that quiet, he calls all Israel to hope in the LORD for ever (v. 3).
verseByVerse.theology: One of the shortest of David's pilgrim songs: a proud heart laid down, and a soul resting like a child against its mother.

verseByVerse.quote: O LORD, my heart is not lifted up; my eyes are not raised too high; I do not occupy myself with things too great and too marvelous for me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
David tells the LORD that he has put pride away: he is not reaching for a place, a look or a knowledge that belongs to God alone.

O LORD, my heart is not lifted up. Three verses, and one of the most beautiful pictures of the soul in Scripture. David, a king and a warrior with every reason for ambition, begins by telling God what he is not.

My eyes are not raised too high. Pride starts in the heart that swells with its own importance. It shows in the eyes that look down on people and fix on the next rung of the ladder. And it shows in what a person busies himself with: questions he is not meant to answer, plans that belong to God.

Things too great and too marvelous for me. This is not a refusal to think or work hard, but a refusal to pretend to be God. Why does God allow what he allows? What does tomorrow hold? A proud soul frets and demands answers; a humble soul leaves them with God. “Do not be haughty, but associate with the lowly. Never be wise in your own sight” (Romans 12:16).

The lowly King. The one who was greatest of all said, “I am gentle and lowly in heart” (Matthew 11:29). He who had every right to the highest place “did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped” (Philippians 2:6). David’s humility is a small likeness of the King who would come from his line.

The burden of being unlimited. We tell our children they can be anything they want, and we mean it kindly. There is real good in that: gifts should be used, and nobody should be held down by prejudice. But it lays a weight on us our ancestors did not carry. If I can be anything, then whatever I am not is my own fault, and every ordinary life looks like a failure of nerve. Augustine traced pride to this root: the craving for a height that is not ours, wanting to be our own source and our own goal. David, a king with more scope than any of us, chooses a different freedom, the freedom of a creature who does not have to be God. Some things are too great for him, and that is a relief, not a defeat. The one who really was unlimited took limits on himself: a body, a village, a carpenter’s bench, a cross. “He humbled himself by becoming obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross” (Philippians 2:8). If he did not need to be everything, neither do we. We need only to be his.

verseByVerse.quote: But I have calmed and quieted my soul, like a weaned child with its mother; like a weaned child is my soul within me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
David has stilled his restless soul until it rests in God himself, like a weaned child content simply to be with its mother.

Like a weaned child with its mother. Not a nursing baby, but a weaned child. A baby at the breast cries and demands to be fed; it wants its mother for what she gives. A weaned child, perhaps two or three years old in that culture, has gone through the struggle of giving that up, and can sit quietly in its mother’s lap, not demanding anything, simply content to be with her.

Like a weaned child is my soul within me. So David’s soul, which used to come to God crying, grasping, demanding, has been weaned. Now it rests against him, content with him, not only with what he gives.

I have calmed and quieted my soul. The verbs matter. Weaning is not easy: David has told his restless soul to be still, again and again, until it learned. Yet the lap was there first: the child can rest because the mother holds it, and the soul learns quiet because God has already drawn it close. Paul described the same schooling: “I have learned in whatever situation I am to be content” (Philippians 4:11).

Become like children. Jesus put a child in the middle of his arguing disciples and said, “unless you turn and become like children, you will never enter the kingdom of heaven. Whoever humbles himself like this child is the greatest in the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 18:3–4). If your prayers are all requests and your soul is always restless, this psalm is an invitation to be weaned: to sit with God in his word and in prayer, and want him. That is not achieved by willpower alone; peace is the Spirit’s fruit in us (Galatians 5:22).

How do I quiet my soul? David says “I have calmed and quieted”, which means he did something. Name what you are grasping for. When you lie awake rehearsing the meeting, the test result or what people think of you, ask what you are demanding of God that he has not promised. Hand back what is too great for you. Some questions, why this happened and how it will turn out, are not yours to settle tonight; tell God so in words, and leave them with him. Sit without asking. Spend a few minutes in prayer that is not a list: read a psalm slowly, thank him for who he is, and stay. Stop feeding the noise. Put down the phone that keeps the restlessness stirred up. Get help if it will not lift. If anxiety stays and wears you down, talk to your pastor or a biblical counsellor, and see your doctor as well; that is no failure of faith. And remember why the child can rest: the lap was there first. The Son let go of everything so that we could be held by the Father. In him you are not earning a place on the lap, only learning to rest in it.

Uncertain wording. The word for “weaned child” normally means a child who has been weaned (Hannah kept Samuel at home “until she weaned him”, 1 Samuel 1:23). A few suggest instead a child who has just been fed and is satisfied. The usual meaning fits the psalm best: a child no longer crying for the breast, content with its mother herself.

verseByVerse.quote: O Israel, hope in the LORD from this time forth and forevermore.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The humble, quiet soul is free to hope, and David calls all God’s people to hope in the LORD for the rest of their days.

O Israel, hope in the LORD. From his own quiet soul, David turns to the whole people with the call that closed Psalm 130: “O Israel, hope in the LORD!” (Psalm 130:7). There hope came after forgiveness; here, after pride is laid down.

From this time forth and forevermore. The humble, contented soul is a hopeful one. When you stop occupying yourself with things too great for you, you are free to hope in the one for whom nothing is too great. And this is “forevermore”: not a mood for a quiet afternoon but a way to live for the rest of life, like a child on its mother’s lap, all the way home.

131.title: Like a Weaned Child
131.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 131 is the twelfth Song of Ascents and one of four in the group that bear David’s name. Psalm 130 cried from the depths and ended, “O Israel, hope in the LORD!” This tiny psalm of three verses ends with the same call, but reaches it by a different road: not forgiveness after sin, but quiet after pride.

The message. A soul at rest in God is a humble soul. David has laid down the proud heart, the ambitious eyes and the restless mind that tries to master things only God can know, and has stilled himself until he rests in God the way a weaned child rests with its mother: wanting her, not only what she gives. Such a soul is free to hope in the LORD for ever.

Why it was said. David was a king and a warrior with every reason for ambition and every opportunity for pride. Pilgrims singing his words on the road to Jerusalem learned that the way to God’s house is the way of a child, not of a conqueror (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. David first tells the LORD what he is not: lifted up in heart, lofty in his gaze, or busy with matters too great for him (v. 1). Then he says what he has done: calmed and quieted his soul, until it is like a weaned child with its mother (v. 2). Finally he turns from his own soul to the whole people and calls them to hope in the LORD, now and for ever (v. 3).

Where it leads. To Christ, by pattern and by the character of God revealed in him. The one who truly was great beyond measure said, “I am gentle and lowly in heart” (Matthew 11:29), and “did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped” (Philippians 2:6). He trusted his Father from his mother’s breast to the cross, and he tells us that unless we “turn and become like children” we will never enter the kingdom of heaven (Matthew 18:3). The lowly Son makes a place for us on the Father’s lap.

For us. Many of us live with restless, grasping souls, carrying burdens and questions that were never ours to carry. This psalm invites us to give them back to God, to come to him for himself and not only for his gifts, and to learn, slowly, the quiet of a child who is held.
131.theology:
Humility refuses the pride of heart, eye and ambition that would take God's place, following the lowliness of Christ (v. 1).

Contentment is learned by stilling the soul until it rests in God himself rather than demanding his gifts (v. 2), and such childlikeness is the way into the kingdom. The humble soul becomes a hopeful one and calls God's people to hope (v. 3).
131.examples: Pride shows in the heart, the eyes and what we busy ourselves with. Try one prayer this week that asks for nothing at all, and simply sits with God.

keyVerse.quote: But I have calmed and quieted my soul, like a weaned child with its mother; like a weaned child is my soul within me.
keyVerse.note: This picture is the heart of the psalm. The weaned child no longer comes to its mother only to be fed but rests in her for her own sake, and so the humble soul rests in God himself, not only in his gifts. It is the childlikeness Jesus says marks those who enter the kingdom.

131.reflection:
David says his heart is not lifted up and his eyes are not raised too high (v. 1). Where does pride show itself in your heart, your eyes or the things you busy yourself with?

What “things too great and too marvelous” for you are you tempted to fret over? What would it mean to leave them with God?

A weaned child wants its mother, not only her milk (v. 2). Are your prayers mostly requests? How could you learn to come to God for himself?

Jesus said, “I am gentle and lowly in heart” (Matthew 11:29). How does his humility make it possible for us to rest, and to hope in the LORD “from this time forth and forevermore” (v. 3)?

132.text: A Song of Ascents. 1Remember, O LORD, in David's favor, all the hardships he endured,2how he swore to the LORD and vowed to the Mighty One of Jacob,3"I will not enter my house or get into my bed,4I will not give sleep to my eyes or slumber to my eyelids,5until I find a place for the LORD, a dwelling place for the Mighty One of Jacob."6Behold, we heard of it in Ephrathah; we found it in the fields of Jaar.7"Let us go to his dwelling place; let us worship at his footstool!"8Arise, O LORD, and go to your resting place, you and the ark of your might.9Let your priests be clothed with righteousness, and let your saints shout for joy.10For the sake of your servant David, do not turn away the face of your anointed one.11The LORD swore to David a sure oath from which he will not turn back: "One of the sons of your body I will set on your throne.12If your sons keep my covenant and my testimonies that I shall teach them, their sons also forever shall sit on your throne."13For the LORD has chosen Zion; he has desired it for his dwelling place:14"This is my resting place forever; here I will dwell, for I have desired it.15I will abundantly bless her provisions; I will satisfy her poor with bread.16Her priests I will clothe with salvation, and her saints will shout for joy.17There I will make a horn to sprout for David; I have prepared a lamp for my anointed.18His enemies I will clothe with shame, but on him his crown will shine."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — Remember David and All His Hardships
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A king who would not rest until God had a home, and a people who pray for God to come and rest among them. The pilgrims ask the LORD to remember David’s hardships and his vow: no house, no bed and no sleep until he found a dwelling place for the Mighty One of Jacob (vv. 1–5). They recall how the ark, long forgotten in a country village, was found and brought up, and they call one another to worship at God’s footstool (vv. 6–7). Then they pray, in words Solomon used at the temple’s dedication, that the LORD would arise to his resting place, clothe his priests with righteousness, give his people joy, and not turn away from David’s anointed son (vv. 8–10).
verseByVerse.theology: A king who would not rest until God had a home, and a people who pray for God to come and rest among them.

verseByVerse.quote: Remember, O LORD, in David's favor, all the hardships he endured, how he swore to the LORD and vowed to the Mighty One of Jacob, "I will not enter my house or get into my bed, I will not give sleep to my eyes or slumber to my eyelids, until I find a place for the LORD, a dwelling place for the Mighty One of Jacob."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The people ask God to remember David, the king who vowed not to rest until the LORD had a dwelling place.

Until I find a place for the LORD. Once David was settled in his palace, it troubled him that God’s ark (the gold-covered chest that marked his presence among his people) was still in a tent. He said to Nathan, “See now, I dwell in a house of cedar, but the ark of God dwells in a tent” (2 Samuel 7:2). The psalm puts that restlessness in the form of a vow: no comfortable bed, no sleep, until the “Mighty One of Jacob” (an old title from Genesis 49:24) has a home. The “hardships” David endured (v. 1) probably include the trouble and cost of that work: he later told Solomon, “With great pains I have provided for the house of the LORD” (1 Chronicles 22:14).

I will not give sleep to my eyes. David refused himself something precious. The psalms around this one call sleep God’s gift (Psalm 127:2), from the God who never sleeps (Psalm 121:4). David would not take the gift until God had a resting place. Hold on to that vow. The psalm will end with God answering: “This is my resting place forever” (v. 14).

Our houses of cedar. Any believer who has made life comfortable may ask whether God’s people and worship are neglected while we live in houses of cedar. Yet this zeal is a response, not a way of earning God’s presence: God first chose to dwell with us, and in Christ has made us his house.

May we plead another’s merit before God? The appeal rests on God’s own promise to David, sworn in verse 11, not on David’s goodness. It is answered in David’s greater Son, whose merit is the only ground any of us can plead.

Uncertain wording. “Hardships” comes from a root meaning to be afflicted or bowed down: David’s toil and troubles, as the ESV takes it, or possibly his humbling of himself.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, we heard of it in Ephrathah; we found it in the fields of Jaar. "Let us go to his dwelling place; let us worship at his footstool!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The people remember how the neglected ark was found and brought up, and call one another to worship at God’s footstool.

We heard of it in Ephrathah; we found it in the fields of Jaar. Two place names tell a small story. In Ephrathah, probably the Bethlehem district, David’s home, they heard of the ark, perhaps as an old story. In the fields of Jaar, probably Kiriath-jearim, they found it. After the Philistines returned the ark, “the men of Kiriath-jearim came and took up the ark of the LORD”, and “a long time passed, some twenty years” (1 Samuel 7:1–2). The ark sat almost forgotten for a generation, until David fetched it.

Let us worship at his footstool! David called the temple he planned a house “for the footstool of our God” (1 Chronicles 28:2; compare Psalm 99:5): the place where the King of heaven, so to speak, set his feet on earth.

Uncertain wording. The places are probable, not certain. Ephrathah is Bethlehem in Micah 5:2, though some think it names a wider clan district that included Kiriath-jearim. “Jaar” means “forest”, most likely short for Kiriath-jearim, “town of forests”. And “it” is most likely the ark, though some take it as the dwelling place of verse 5.
verseByVerse.note: Ephrathah is the Bethlehem area; the “fields of Jaar” is probably Kiriath-jearim, where the ark stayed.

verseByVerse.quote: Arise, O LORD, and go to your resting place, you and the ark of your might. Let your priests be clothed with righteousness, and let your saints shout for joy. For the sake of your servant David, do not turn away the face of your anointed one.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The people pray that God will come to his resting place, bless his priests and people, and not refuse David’s anointed king.

Arise, O LORD, and go to your resting place. These verses were prayed again when the temple was finished. Solomon ended his dedication prayer with almost the same words: “And now arise, O LORD God, and go to your resting place, you and the ark of your might” (2 Chronicles 6:41). What David vowed, Solomon completed, and the pilgrims sang both.

Three requests. That God come to his resting place; that the priests be clothed with righteousness and the people rejoice; and that God not turn away the face of his anointed, that is, not send the king of David’s line away with his request refused. The second half of the psalm answers each one.

Your anointed one. The Hebrew word gives us “Messiah”; in Greek it is “Christ”. Every king of David’s line pointed, however faintly, to the Anointed One the Father would never turn away.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–18 — The LORD Swore to David a Sure Oath
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God answers David’s vow with his own oath, and grants every request more fully than it was made. David swore to find a place for the LORD; now the LORD swears that David’s son will sit on his throne, and that his line will rule forever if they keep his covenant (vv. 11–12). The first request is answered: Zion is God’s chosen resting place forever, where he will feed the poor (vv. 13–15). The second is answered and surpassed: priests clothed not only with righteousness but with salvation, and saints who will shout for joy (v. 16). The third is answered with a horn and a lamp for the anointed, his enemies shamed and his crown shining (vv. 17–18).
verseByVerse.theology: David's vow to build God a house is answered by God’s oath to build David a house (a royal line), and every request is granted more fully than it was asked.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD swore to David a sure oath from which he will not turn back: "One of the sons of your body I will set on your throne. If your sons keep my covenant and my testimonies that I shall teach them, their sons also forever shall sit on your throne."
verseByVerse.commentary:
David swore to God; now God swears a far greater oath to David: a son of his will sit on his throne forever.

The LORD swore to David a sure oath. Here is the hinge of the psalm. In verse 2, David swore to the LORD; in verse 11, the LORD swears to David. David vowed to build God a house; God answers with an oath to build David a house, a dynasty (2 Samuel 7:12–16), and his oath is “sure”.

One of the sons of your body. That is always how it goes with God. Whatever we offer him, he answers with something far greater: David offered a building; God promised a King who would reign forever. Peter preached at Pentecost that David, “knowing that God had sworn with an oath to him that he would set one of his descendants on his throne”, spoke of the resurrection of Christ (Acts 2:30).

If your sons keep my covenant. And there is a condition: David’s sons must keep the covenant. Many did not, and the throne was lost to exile, though, as Psalm 89 says, the steadfast love was not removed (Psalm 89:30–33). The condition was finally met by one Son of David who kept the covenant perfectly, and his throne is forever. We fail its terms as David’s sons did; his obedience is counted as ours, and that is why the oath still stands for us.

verseByVerse.quote: For the LORD has chosen Zion; he has desired it for his dwelling place: "This is my resting place forever; here I will dwell, for I have desired it. I will abundantly bless her provisions; I will satisfy her poor with bread. Her priests I will clothe with salvation, and her saints will shout for joy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God chooses Zion as his home forever, with bread for the poor, salvation for the priests and joy for his people.

This is my resting place forever. Now God answers the first request (v. 8): not a temporary stop, like the tent or the village house, but “forever”. And the reason is desire: God wants to dwell among his people.

I will satisfy her poor with bread. Where God dwells there is provision, especially for “the poor”. The God of Zion feeds the hungry. It is fitting that the King who fulfilled this psalm was born in Bethlehem (the name means “house of bread”) and said, “I am the bread of life” (John 6:35).

Her priests I will clothe with salvation. The second request is answered, and more. They asked for priests “clothed with righteousness” (v. 9); God promises “clothed with salvation”, the very word Solomon used (2 Chronicles 6:41), and the saints “will” shout for joy.

After the temple fell. Zion is “my resting place forever”, but the temple fell. Jesus spoke of “the temple of his body” (John 2:21); the church “grows into a holy temple in the Lord” (Ephesians 2:21); and believers “have come to Mount Zion” (Hebrews 12:22). God’s forever home is found in Christ and his people, and at the last “the dwelling place of God is with man” (Revelation 21:3).

Where Christians differ. Dispensationalists look for a rebuilt temple in Jerusalem, since some read the prophets’ temple promises literally for a future Israel.

This commentary’s view. With the New Testament, this commentary reads these promises as fulfilled in Christ, his church and the new Jerusalem, while honouring brothers and sisters who see it otherwise.

verseByVerse.quote: There I will make a horn to sprout for David; I have prepared a lamp for my anointed. His enemies I will clothe with shame, but on him his crown will shine."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God promises David a strong King and an unfailing lamp, whose enemies will be shamed and whose crown will shine.

A horn to sprout for David. The third request (v. 10) is answered with two pictures. A “horn”, the symbol of strength, will “sprout” like a branch from David’s line, and a “lamp”, a light that will not go out, is prepared for the anointed. Through the prophet Ahijah, God promised to leave one tribe to Solomon’s son, “that David my servant may always have a lamp before me in Jerusalem” (1 Kings 11:36).

The horn sprouts in Christ. Zechariah, the father of John the Baptist, praised God because he “has raised up a horn of salvation for us in the house of his servant David” (Luke 1:69). The horn had sprouted.

On him his crown will shine. The clothing theme finishes the psalm: priests clothed with righteousness, then with salvation, and now enemies “clothed with shame”, while the King’s crown shines. At the very end of the Bible that King says, “I am the root and the descendant of David, the bright morning star” (Revelation 22:16). David would not rest until God had a home. God has made his home with his people forever, in the Son of David whose crown will never dim.

Uncertain wording. The verb translated “shine” is related to the Hebrew word for a flower, so it may mean “flourish”, as older translations have it, fitting the sprouting horn of verse 17. Either way the crown is bright and living.

132.title: A Lamp for My Anointed
132.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 132 is the thirteenth and longest Song of Ascents. Psalm 131 showed David’s soul quiet as a weaned child; now the pilgrims, nearing Jerusalem, remember how there came to be a house of God in Zion at all, and what God promised to David’s family there.

The message. David would not rest until the LORD had a dwelling place among his people, and God answered his zeal with something far greater: an oath that David’s son would sit on his throne, and a promise that Zion would be God’s resting place forever. Every request the people make is granted more fully than they ask. God’s people can therefore pray with confidence, because their hope rests not on David’s devotion but on God’s sworn promise.

Why it was said. The psalm recalls David bringing the ark to Jerusalem and Solomon dedicating the temple (2 Samuel 6–7; 2 Chronicles 6). Sung by later pilgrims, perhaps when kings failed or the throne lay empty after the exile (see the introduction), it held God to his oath and kept alive the hope of a coming Anointed King.

How the chapter makes its case. The psalm falls in two halves that mirror each other. In the first, the people ask God to remember David’s vow not to sleep until he found a place for the LORD (vv. 1–5), recall how the neglected ark was found and brought up (vv. 6–7), and pray that God would come to his resting place, clothe his priests and not reject his anointed (vv. 8–10). In the second, the LORD answers with his own oath to David’s line (vv. 11–12), declares Zion his resting place forever with bread for the poor and salvation for the priests (vv. 13–16), and promises a horn and a lamp for his anointed, whose crown will shine (vv. 17–18).

Where it leads. To Christ, by promise and covenant. The oath of verse 11 is the covenant God made with David in 2 Samuel 7, and the New Testament says plainly that it is kept in Jesus: Peter preached that David knew “God had sworn with an oath to him that he would set one of his descendants on his throne” and so spoke of Christ’s resurrection (Acts 2:30). Zechariah praised God for raising “a horn of salvation for us in the house of his servant David” (Luke 1:69). And God’s desire to dwell with his people is fulfilled in the Word who “became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14).

For us. Like David, we may ask whether we can rest comfortably while God’s worship and people are neglected. But more than that, we may rest because God has done what David could not: he has given his Son as the King who kept the covenant, and he has made his home with his people for ever.
132.theology:
Zeal for God's dwelling among his people moved David to vow, and the neglected ark was found and brought to Zion (vv. 1-7).

The people's prayer (vv. 8-10) is answered point by point and more fully (vv. 14, 16, 17). David's vow to build God a house is met by God's sure oath to build David's house (v. 11), conditioned on covenant faithfulness (v. 12) and fulfilled in the one Son who kept it.

God desires to dwell with his people forever, providing for the poor (vv. 13-15). The horn and lamp of David (v. 17) are fulfilled in Christ, the horn of salvation and the root of David.
132.examples: David could not sleep while God's ark sat in a tent; the question for a comfortable church is what neglect of God’s worship it is able to sleep through. But the psalm's deeper surprise is the exchange: offer God a building, and he answers with an everlasting King.

keyVerse.quote: The LORD swore to David a sure oath from which he will not turn back: “One of the sons of your body I will set on your throne.
keyVerse.note: This is the hinge of the psalm, where David’s vow to God is answered by God’s oath to David. Everything after it flows from this promise, and the New Testament says it is kept in Jesus, the Son of David raised from the dead to sit on his throne forever (Acts 2:30).

132.reflection:
David would not rest until God had a dwelling place (vv. 3–5). What are you able to “sleep through” in your own life or church that ought to trouble you more?

David vowed to build God a house, and God answered by swearing to build David a house (v. 11). Where have you seen God answer what you offered him with something far greater?

The oath depended on David’s sons keeping the covenant (v. 12), and many failed. How does Jesus, the Son who kept it, change the way you think about God’s promises to you?

God says of Zion, “This is my resting place forever; here I will dwell” (v. 14). What does it mean for you that God now dwells with his people in Christ, and how should it shape the way we gather to worship?

133.text: A Song of Ascents. Of David. 1Behold, how good and pleasant it is when brothers dwell in unity!2It is like the precious oil on the head, running down on the beard, on the beard of Aaron, running down on the collar of his robes!3It is like the dew of Hermon, which falls on the mountains of Zion! For there the LORD has commanded the blessing, life forevermore.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–3 — Like the Dew of Hermon
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Unity among God’s people is a delight and a gift from above, and it is where the LORD has commanded life. David begins with a cry of wonder at how good and pleasant it is when brothers live together (v. 1). He then gives two pictures, each of something coming down. The holy oil poured on Aaron’s head runs down his beard to the collar of his robes, so unity is holy and flows from the anointed head (v. 2). The heavy dew of Hermon falls on the hills of Zion, so unity is life brought to dry ground (v. 3). There, among his gathered people, the LORD has commanded his blessing, life forevermore.
verseByVerse.theology: The unity of God's people is holy like anointing oil and life-giving like mountain dew, and both come from above.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, how good and pleasant it is when brothers dwell in unity!
verseByVerse.commentary:
It is right and it is a joy when God’s people live together as one family. Looking round at pilgrims gathered from every tribe and town, David invites us to stop and see how good this is.

Behold. Pilgrims came up to Jerusalem from every tribe: northerners and southerners, rich and poor, families with old feuds. For a few days at the festival they camped, ate and worshipped together, and someone looked around and said, “Behold”.

How good and pleasant it is. Good: right, as God intends. Pleasant: delightful to experience. Unity is not merely a duty but a joy. The brothers are fellow members of one covenant family, and to dwell in unity (the ESV notes it may be “dwell together”) is to live side by side, not only to agree in principle.

Jesus prayed for it. The night before he died, he asked “that they may all be one … so that the world may believe that you have sent me” (John 17:21). Anyone who has been through a church split knows how bitter the opposite is; anyone in a congregation that loves across every difference knows this verse is true.

Does this mean unity at all costs? The unity is of brothers who share one Lord and one faith (Ephesians 4:3–6). It is never agreement bought at the price of the gospel (Galatians 1:8). Christians are to keep it, not manufacture it with those who deny the faith.

verseByVerse.quote: It is like the precious oil on the head, running down on the beard, on the beard of Aaron, running down on the collar of his robes!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Unity among God’s people is holy and precious, and like the anointing oil it flows down from the head over the whole body.

Like the precious oil on the head. The first picture is the high priest’s anointing. God told Moses, “You shall anoint Aaron and his sons, and consecrate them, that they may serve me as priests” (Exodus 30:30). The oil was poured on Aaron’s head lavishly and fragrantly, and ran down his beard onto the collar of his robes.

Running down on the beard. The direction matters: “running down”, twice. The oil begins on the head and flows over the whole man. So unity among God’s people does not start at the bottom, with everyone working very hard to get along. It flows down from the head.

A holy unity. The oil was precious and holy, setting Aaron apart for God. Unity among believers is not merely social harmony but a holy thing, fragrant before God.

The greater High Priest. Christians have long seen here the one Aaron pointed to. “Christ” means “Anointed”: God anointed Jesus “with the Holy Spirit and with power” (Acts 10:38), and once exalted, he poured out that Spirit on his people (Acts 2:33). As the oil ran from Aaron’s head to his collar, so the Spirit who rests on Christ the Head flows down to every member of his body. That is why Paul tells believers to be “eager to maintain the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (Ephesians 4:3): not to manufacture it, but to keep what the Spirit has given.

verseByVerse.quote: It is like the dew of Hermon, which falls on the mountains of Zion! For there the LORD has commanded the blessing, life forevermore.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Unity is like life-giving dew brought from far away to dry ground, and it is where God has commanded his blessing of life for ever.

Like the dew of Hermon. The second picture. Mount Hermon is the great snow-topped mountain in the far north, and its heavy dew kept its slopes green through the rainless summer. Zion lies far to the south, and Hermon’s dew does not literally fall there. That is the point of the picture: unity is like the moisture of a far-off mountain brought to dry ground from above, making it live.

A gift from above. Both pictures are of something that comes down, oil from the head and dew from the heights. Unity is a gift before it is a task.

There the LORD has commanded the blessing. “There”: where brothers dwell together in God’s city. “Commanded” is a king’s word: God does not merely allow blessing there, he decrees it. And the blessing is “life forevermore”, a glimpse of the eternal life Christ gives (John 10:10).

Why this matters. Division does not only make a congregation unpleasant; it hinders the blessing. Unity does not only make a congregation happy; it is where God has commanded life. If your church is tense, pray for the oil and the dew, and do what you can to “maintain the unity of the Spirit”.

What this looks like. Keeping unity is mostly small and local. Guard your tongue about other members. When the talk over coffee turns to the elder who annoyed you or the family who left, decline to add to it, and speak to the person rather than about them (Matthew 18:15). Go first. If there is coolness between you and someone in your church, do not wait for them to move; ring them this week. Hold your preferences loosely. The style of music, the time of the service and the colour of the hall are not worth a split; the gospel is. Sit with someone unlike you. The pilgrims camped beside families from other tribes; eat with people outside your own circle. All this is possible because the oil is already on the Head. Christ “has made us both one and has broken down in his flesh the dividing wall of hostility” (Ephesians 2:14). We do not create peace between believers; we stop undoing what he has done, “bearing with one another in love” (Ephesians 4:2).

Uncertain wording. How the dew of Hermon, nearly two hundred kilometres (about 120 miles) north, can fall “on the mountains of Zion” has long puzzled readers. Some take it as a dew as heavy as Hermon’s falling on Zion; others as a picture of north and south, the whole land, joined in one blessing. Either way the sense is clear: life-giving moisture brought from afar to the hills where God’s people meet.
verseByVerse.note: Mount Hermon, in the far north, is famous for heavy dew.

133.title: When Brothers Dwell in Unity
133.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 133 is the fourteenth of the fifteen Songs of Ascents and the last of the four that bear David’s name. Psalm 132 has just carried the ark up to Zion and set the LORD’s promise to David’s house at the centre of the city. Now the pilgrims who have arrived there look around at one another.

The message. When God’s people live together as the family they are, it is both right and a delight, and it is a gift that comes down from above. Like the holy oil running down from Aaron’s head and the dew of a far mountain falling on Zion, such unity flows from God, and it is there, among his gathered people, that he has commanded his blessing of life for ever.

Why it was said. Israel was twelve tribes with long memories of rivalry, north against south, family against family. Three times a year they came up to Jerusalem for the pilgrim feasts and, for a few days, camped, ate and worshipped side by side (see the introduction). David knew how precious and how fragile that was: the tribes had only come to him at Hebron after years of civil war (2 Samuel 5:1).

How the chapter makes its case. One exclamation and two pictures. First the delighted cry: see how good and pleasant brothers living together are (v. 1). Then the anointing oil poured on Aaron’s head, running down his beard to the collar of his robes: unity is holy, and it flows from the head (v. 2). Then the heavy dew of Hermon, falling on the hills of Zion: unity is life brought down to dry ground. And the reason it matters: there the LORD has commanded the blessing, life forevermore (v. 3).

Where it leads. To Christ, by pattern. Aaron was the anointed priest whose anointing flowed down over his whole person; Jesus is the Christ, the Anointed One, on whom the Spirit was poured without measure, and who, exalted, has poured out that same Spirit on his body, the church (Acts 2:33). The unity of his people flows down from him, their Head, and the “life forevermore” commanded on Zion is the eternal life he gives. He prayed the night before he died that his people would be one (John 17:21), and he made them one through his cross (Ephesians 2:14).

For us. Christian unity is not something we manufacture by working hard at getting along; it is something Christ has given and we are to keep. That turns the small acts of peace, speaking to someone rather than about them, going first after a quarrel, sitting with someone unlike you, into ways of guarding the place where God has commanded life.
133.theology:
Unity among God's people is both good and pleasant, the object of Christ's prayer (v. 1; John 17:21).

It is holy, flowing down from the anointed head (v. 2), and it is life brought from above (v. 3). God commands his blessing of eternal life where his people dwell in unity.
133.examples: At the festival, families with old feuds camped side by side and worshipped together. A congregation that does the same across age, class and background is not just pleasant to visit; it is a living answer to Jesus' prayer.

keyVerse.quote: Behold, how good and pleasant it is when brothers dwell in unity!
keyVerse.note: The whole psalm unfolds this cry of delight. Unity among God’s people is good, as he intends, and pleasant, a joy to live in, and the two pictures that follow show where it comes from: down from the anointed Head, as a gift from above.

133.reflection:
David calls unity among God’s people both “good” and “pleasant” (v. 1). When have you tasted that pleasure in a church or a Christian friendship? What made it so?

Both pictures describe something that comes down from above: oil from the head, dew from the heights (vv. 2–3). How does it change our efforts at unity to see it first as a gift from Christ, the Head, rather than something we have to create?

Unity in this psalm is unity of “brothers”, people who share one Lord and one faith. How do we keep it without either splitting over small things or giving away the gospel to avoid conflict?

Is there someone in your church you are cool towards, or a conversation you have been avoiding? What would one step towards peace look like this week?

134.text: A Song of Ascents. 1Come, bless the LORD, all you servants of the LORD, who stand by night in the house of the LORD!2Lift up your hands to the holy place and bless the LORD!3May the LORD bless you from Zion, he who made heaven and earth!

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–3 — May the LORD Bless You from Zion
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The pilgrim songs end at night in the temple, with blessing given to God and blessing given back. The psalm first calls the servants who stand in the house of the LORD by night, the Levites on duty while the crowds sleep, to bless the LORD (v. 1). They are to lift their hands toward the holy place, the posture of open, reaching prayer, and bless him again (v. 2). Then the blessing returns: the LORD, the Maker of heaven and earth, blesses his people from Zion (v. 3). Worship ascends, and grace descends.
verseByVerse.theology: The pilgrim songs end at night in the temple, with blessing given to God and blessing given back.

verseByVerse.quote: Come, bless the LORD, all you servants of the LORD, who stand by night in the house of the LORD!
verseByVerse.commentary:
The servants who keep watch in God’s house at night are called to their real work: to bless the LORD.

The journey’s end. The journey that began far from home, in Meshech and Kedar among liars (120:5), ends inside the house of the LORD, at night.

Who stand by night. When the festival crowds had gone to sleep, the Levites kept watch in the temple. The Chronicler describes singers who “were on duty day and night” (1 Chronicles 9:33). Perhaps departing pilgrims called this out to them; perhaps it was the evening call to the night shift. Either way, the psalm honours those who serve God when no one is watching. To “stand” before the LORD is the language of a servant ready to minister (Deuteronomy 10:8).

Unseen servants today. Every church has them: the ones who stay late to clean, who pray through the night for others, who serve unnoticed long after the crowd has gone home. This psalm is for them, and it tells them their real work: not only guarding the building, but blessing the LORD.

How can a creature bless God? To bless God is to praise him and speak well of him; he gains nothing from it. Our blessing goes up to him as praise, and his blessing comes down to us as grace (v. 3).

verseByVerse.quote: Lift up your hands to the holy place and bless the LORD!
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the dark and the quiet, the night servants are to reach out to God with open hands and praise him.

Lift up your hands to the holy place. Lifted hands were the posture of prayer and praise: empty, open, reaching toward God. The holy place is the sanctuary where his presence dwelt. In the dark and the quiet, the night servants turn toward God and bless him. Lifted hands remain a biblical posture, neither required nor forbidden (1 Timothy 2:8).

Praise at night. There is something especially fitting about praise at night. It is praise without an audience, when you are tired, in the dark. John saw the redeemed in heaven doing what these Levites did: they “serve him day and night in his temple” (Revelation 7:15). The night watch in Jerusalem was a small picture of that endless worship, and Jesus himself kept such watches, spending whole nights in prayer to his Father (Luke 6:12).

verseByVerse.quote: May the LORD bless you from Zion, he who made heaven and earth!
verseByVerse.commentary:
The blessing comes back: the Maker of heaven and earth blesses his people from Zion. Worship has gone up; now grace comes down.

May the LORD bless you from Zion. A voice, perhaps the night servants answering the pilgrims, perhaps a priest, pronounces the LORD’s blessing on “you”. It is the same exchange the priests spoke over Israel: “The LORD bless you and keep you” (Numbers 6:24).

He who made heaven and earth! This last line gathers up phrases from the whole collection of pilgrim songs: “bless you from Zion” from 128:5, and “he who made heaven and earth” from 121:2 and 124:8. The songs that began with a man far from home, crying out in distress, end with a blessing from the Maker of everything, pronounced in his own house.

Our High Priest blesses. The last thing the disciples saw of Jesus was this very act: “lifting up his hands he blessed them. While he blessed them, he parted from them” (Luke 24:50–51). He did not leave with a warning or a frown but with his hands raised in blessing, and he still blesses his people from the heavenly Zion.

The shape of the Christian life. It begins far off from God. It travels up, through trouble, tears and waiting. And it ends in the presence of God, blessing him and being blessed by him, for ever. The next psalm opens with the same call, “O servants of the LORD, who stand in the house of the LORD” (135:1–2), as if the praise, once begun, will not stop.

134.title: Bless the LORD by Night
134.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 134 is the fifteenth and last Song of Ascents. The pilgrims’ journey began far from home among people who hated peace (120:5–7), climbed through danger, waiting and tears, and arrived in Zion; Psalm 133 rejoiced in God’s people gathered there. Now it is night in the house of the LORD.

The message. The highest work of God’s servants is to bless the LORD, even in the dark when no one is watching, and the God they bless blesses them in return. Praise goes up from his house; blessing comes down from the Maker of heaven and earth. The pilgrimage ends not in a place but in that exchange.

Why it was said. When the festival crowds had gone to sleep, Levites kept watch and served in the temple through the night (1 Chronicles 9:33). The psalm honours them, perhaps as departing pilgrims called up to them, and sends the worshippers home under the LORD’s blessing (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. A call and an answer. First the call to the night servants: come, bless the LORD, lift your hands toward the holy place and bless him (vv. 1–2). Then the answering blessing, in words that gather up the whole collection: may the LORD who made heaven and earth bless you from Zion (v. 3).

Where it leads. To Christ, by pattern and fulfilment of the priestly blessing. The priests blessed Israel in the LORD’s name (Numbers 6:24–26); the last thing the disciples saw of Jesus was their great High Priest lifting up his hands and blessing them as he was carried into heaven (Luke 24:50–51). From the heavenly Zion he goes on blessing his people, and in him God has “blessed us … with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places” (Ephesians 1:3). And he is the true night servant, who “all night … continued in prayer to God” (Luke 6:12) and “always lives to make intercession” for us (Hebrews 7:25).

For us. Much faithful service is done at night and out of sight: the one who locks up after the meeting, the parent awake with a sick child, the believer praying for a friend at midnight. This psalm tells them their real work is to bless the LORD, and promises that the blessing of the Maker of heaven and earth rests on them.
134.theology:
The pilgrim songs end inside God's house at night, honouring those who serve unseen. Their chief work is blessing the LORD (vv. 1-2), a foretaste of the day-and-night worship of heaven.

Worship ascends and blessing descends (v. 3): the journey that began far off in distress ends in blessing from the Creator in Zion.
134.examples: The person who locks up after the evening meeting, or prays alone at midnight for a friend, is doing what these Levites did. No one may see it, but the praise goes up, and the blessing comes down.

keyVerse.quote: May the LORD bless you from Zion, he who made heaven and earth!
keyVerse.note: This blessing is where the whole pilgrimage of the Songs of Ascents arrives. Praise has gone up from the night servants, and now blessing comes down from the Maker of everything, in words gathered from earlier songs. It is the blessing the risen Christ pronounced on his disciples as he ascended, and still pronounces on his people.

134.reflection:
The psalm honours those who serve “by night in the house of the LORD” (v. 1). Who are the unseen servants in your church, and how could you thank and encourage them?

Their chief work, the psalm says, is not guarding the building but blessing the LORD. How can ordinary tasks, done out of sight, become a way of blessing God?

Praise goes up and blessing comes down (vv. 2–3). How does it help to know that your worship is answered by God’s blessing, and that the risen Christ blessed his disciples with lifted hands (Luke 24:50–51)?

Looking back over the Songs of Ascents (Psalms 120–134), which one has spoken most to your own journey, and why?

135.text: <sup>1</sup>Praise the LORD! Praise the name of the LORD, give praise, O servants of the LORD,<sup>2</sup>who stand in the house of the LORD, in the courts of the house of our God!<sup>3</sup>Praise the LORD, for the LORD is good; sing to his name, for it is pleasant!<sup>4</sup>For the LORD has chosen Jacob for himself, Israel as his own possession.<sup>5</sup>For I know that the LORD is great, and that our Lord is above all gods.<sup>6</sup>Whatever the LORD pleases, he does, in heaven and on earth, in the seas and all deeps.<sup>7</sup>He it is who makes the clouds rise at the end of the earth, who makes lightnings for the rain and brings forth the wind from his storehouses.<sup>8</sup>He it was who struck down the firstborn of Egypt, both of man and of beast;<sup>9</sup>who in your midst, O Egypt, sent signs and wonders against Pharaoh and all his servants;<sup>10</sup>who struck down many nations and killed mighty kings,<sup>11</sup>Sihon, king of the Amorites, and Og, king of Bashan, and all the kingdoms of Canaan,<sup>12</sup>and gave their land as a heritage, a heritage to his people Israel.<sup>13</sup>Your name, O LORD, endures forever, your renown, O LORD, throughout all ages.<sup>14</sup>For the LORD will vindicate his people and have compassion on his servants.<sup>15</sup>The idols of the nations are silver and gold, the work of human hands.<sup>16</sup>They have mouths, but do not speak; they have eyes, but do not see;<sup>17</sup>they have ears, but do not hear, nor is there any breath in their mouths.<sup>18</sup>Those who make them become like them; so do all who trust in them.<sup>19</sup>O house of Israel, bless the LORD! O house of Aaron, bless the LORD!<sup>20</sup>O house of Levi, bless the LORD! You who fear the LORD, bless the LORD!<sup>21</sup>Blessed be the LORD from Zion, he who dwells in Jerusalem! Praise the LORD!

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — Praise the Name of the LORD
