verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Praise the LORD, because he is good and because he chose a people for himself. The psalm picks up the call of Psalm 134 to the servants who stand in God’s house (vv. 1–2), then gives two reasons. The LORD is good, and singing to his name is pleasant (v. 3). And above all, he chose Jacob for himself, Israel as his treasured possession (v. 4). Praise begins not with what we have done for God but with what he freely decided to do for us.
verseByVerse.theology: The servants in God's house are called to praise, because he chose a people for himself.

verseByVerse.quote: Praise the LORD! Praise the name of the LORD, give praise, O servants of the LORD, who stand in the house of the LORD, in the courts of the house of our God! Praise the LORD, for the LORD is good; sing to his name, for it is pleasant! For the LORD has chosen Jacob for himself, Israel as his own possession.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s servants are called to praise him, because he is good and because he freely chose a people for himself.

O servants of the LORD. The last Song of Ascents ended by calling “servants of the LORD, who stand by night in the house of the LORD” to bless him (134:1). This psalm picks up there, as if the praise keeps going. “Praise the LORD” is hallelu-yah, the word that frames the psalm at both ends.

A psalm woven from Scripture. Much of Psalm 135 is lines from psalms, prophets and law woven into a new song by someone who knew the Bible so well that his praise came out in its words: a good thing for a believer to aim at.

For the LORD is good. Two reasons to praise: God is good, and singing to his name is pleasant. Worship is not a chore. It is delightful.

The LORD has chosen Jacob for himself. The deepest reason is election: God freely chose a people for himself, out of love and not because of anything in them (Deuteronomy 7:7–8). Moses told Israel, “The LORD your God has chosen you to be a people for his treasured possession, out of all the peoples who are on the face of the earth” (Deuteronomy 7:6). Peter says the same of the church: “you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for his own possession, that you may proclaim the excellencies of him who called you” (1 Peter 2:9). And Paul says where that choosing happened: “he chose us in him before the foundation of the world” (Ephesians 1:4). Chosen people praise.

Uncertain wording. In “for it is pleasant”, the Hebrew does not make clear what is pleasant: the name, the singing, or the LORD himself (the ESV notes it may be “for he is beautiful”). All three are true.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–14 — Whatever the LORD Pleases, He Does
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The God who does whatever he pleases has pleased to rescue and keep his people. The psalmist knows that the LORD is above all gods, because nothing in heaven, earth or sea lies outside his will (vv. 5–6). He rules the storm that the nations credited to their gods (v. 7). He struck Egypt’s firstborn and sent signs against Pharaoh (vv. 8–9), overthrew Sihon, Og and the kings of Canaan, and gave their land to Israel (vv. 10–12). So his name endures through every age, and he will vindicate his servants and have compassion on them (vv. 13–14).
verseByVerse.theology: The God who does whatever he pleases in the storm and in history has pleased to keep his people.

verseByVerse.quote: For I know that the LORD is great, and that our Lord is above all gods. Whatever the LORD pleases, he does, in heaven and on earth, in the seas and all deeps. He it is who makes the clouds rise at the end of the earth, who makes lightnings for the rain and brings forth the wind from his storehouses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD is greater than every so-called god, because he is free: whatever he pleases he does, everywhere, even in the storm.

For I know that the LORD is great. “I know”: settled knowledge, not “I hope”. The proof of God’s greatness is his freedom: “Whatever the LORD pleases, he does”, the same confession Psalm 115 made against the powerless idols (115:3). In heaven, on earth, in the sea, in the depths: nowhere is outside his will.

Who makes the clouds rise. Verse 7 is almost word for word from Jeremiah: “he makes the mist rise from the ends of the earth. He makes lightning for the rain, and he brings forth the wind from his storehouses” (Jeremiah 10:13). The neighbouring nations worshipped storm gods such as Baal. The psalm says the storm belongs to the LORD: the clouds, the lightning and the wind come out of his storerooms.

Above all gods. The “gods” are the powers the nations worshipped, which are no gods (vv. 15–18; 1 Corinthians 8:4–6), though demonic powers lie behind idolatry (1 Corinthians 10:20). The LORD alone is God.

The Lord of the storm in a boat. When Jesus rebuked the wind and waves on Galilee, his disciples asked, “What sort of man is this, that even winds and sea obey him?” (Matthew 8:27). This psalm gives the answer: only the one who brings the wind from his storehouses.

Does God then cause evil? His rule includes all things, so nothing happens by fate or chance; yet he is not the author of sin, and those who do evil are responsible (Acts 2:23; James 1:13). The verse is a comfort: no power on earth is beyond his hand.

verseByVerse.quote: He it was who struck down the firstborn of Egypt, both of man and of beast; who in your midst, O Egypt, sent signs and wonders against Pharaoh and all his servants; who struck down many nations and killed mighty kings, Sihon, king of the Amorites, and Og, king of Bashan, and all the kingdoms of Canaan, and gave their land as a heritage, a heritage to his people Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The same God who rules the storm acted in history: he broke Egypt, overthrew the kings who barred the way, and gave his people their land.

Who struck down many nations. From the storm to history. The God who does whatever he pleases in the sky did what he pleased in Egypt, against Pharaoh and all his servants. Sihon and Og, the kings east of the Jordan who blocked Israel’s way, became a standing example of God’s power (136:19–20). The history told at length in Psalms 78 and 105 is compressed into a few lines, ending in the land given as “a heritage”.

Was it just? This was God’s judgment on peoples whose sin had long ripened (Genesis 15:16; Deuteronomy 9:4–5), delayed for centuries and carried out once through Israel. It is no pattern for any later war, nation or church.

verseByVerse.quote: Your name, O LORD, endures forever, your renown, O LORD, throughout all ages. For the LORD will vindicate his people and have compassion on his servants.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The name God revealed to Moses will never be forgotten, and he will do right by his people and have compassion on them.

Your name, O LORD, endures forever. The ESV notes “renown” may be “remembrance”. The line echoes what God said to Moses at the burning bush: “This is my name forever, and thus I am to be remembered throughout all generations” (Exodus 3:15). The name God revealed then has not changed. Empires are forgotten; his name is still remembered.

The LORD will vindicate his people. Verse 14 is from the Song of Moses: “For the LORD will vindicate his people and have compassion on his servants” (Deuteronomy 32:36). He will vindicate them, show them to be in the right, and have compassion. Paul asks who can accuse those God has chosen in Christ, and answers from the cross and the empty tomb: “Who shall bring any charge against God’s elect? It is God who justifies” (Romans 8:33). Their vindication rests not on their record but on their Saviour’s.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–21 — Those Who Make Them Become Like Them
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Lifeless idols make lifeless worshippers, so let all God’s people bless the living God. The idols of the nations are only silver and gold shaped by human hands; they have mouths, eyes and ears that do nothing, and no breath at all (vv. 15–17). Those who make and trust them become like them (v. 18). Against that dead silence the psalm calls every part of God’s people, Israel, the priests, the Levites and all who fear the LORD, to bless him from Zion, and ends where it began: “Praise the LORD!” (vv. 19–21).
verseByVerse.theology: Breathless idols against the living God, and every group of his people called to bless him.

verseByVerse.quote: The idols of the nations are silver and gold, the work of human hands. They have mouths, but do not speak; they have eyes, but do not see; they have ears, but do not hear, nor is there any breath in their mouths. Those who make them become like them; so do all who trust in them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Idols are lifeless, and those who trust them become as lifeless as they are.

Nor is there any breath in their mouths. Silver and gold, but only what human hands had made. The psalm quotes Psalm 115 (115:4–8) with one change: it cuts short the list of noses, hands and feet and adds a single devastating line, that there is no breath in their mouths. The idol is not merely silent; it is not alive. The God of verse 7 brings the wind out of his storehouses; the idol cannot draw one breath.

Those who make them become like them. The same warning as Psalm 115: worshippers become like what they worship, and gods with no breath of life make people with no spiritual life. The cure is not trying harder to be alive but turning to the living God, whose Spirit is the breath of life: “I will put my Spirit within you, and you shall live” (Ezekiel 37:14). The same rule works the other way: those who behold the glory of the Lord “are being transformed into the same image” (2 Corinthians 3:18).

Our idols. Anything we trust for life or worth in God’s place, money, a career, approval, works the same way: it cannot speak, see or save, and it makes us smaller. “Little children, keep yourselves from idols” (1 John 5:21).

verseByVerse.quote: O house of Israel, bless the LORD! O house of Aaron, bless the LORD! O house of Levi, bless the LORD! You who fear the LORD, bless the LORD! Blessed be the LORD from Zion, he who dwells in Jerusalem! Praise the LORD!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every part of God’s people, from priests to ordinary believers, is called to bless the living God who dwells among them.

O house of Levi, bless the LORD! Psalm 115 called three groups to trust the LORD: Israel, the house of Aaron, and those who fear him (115:9–11). This psalm calls four groups to bless him, adding the house of Levi, the Levites who served in the temple, the night servants of the previous psalm. The whole of God’s people, from the priests to the ordinary God-fearer, is summoned to bless the God who chose them.

Blessed be the LORD from Zion. The Songs of Ascents ended with the LORD blessing his people from Zion (134:3); here the people bless the LORD from Zion, and the psalm closes as it opened: “Praise the LORD!” The next psalm will take up a refrain and repeat it twenty-six times.

135.title: Your Name, O LORD, Endures Forever
135.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 135 follows straight on from the Songs of Ascents. Psalm 134 called the “servants of the LORD” standing in his house to bless him; this psalm takes up the same call and turns it into a full hymn of praise, opening and closing with “Praise the LORD!” It is a twin of Psalm 136, which retells the same history with a refrain after every line.

The message. Praise the LORD, because he is good, he chose a people for himself, and he does whatever he pleases, in the sky and in history, for their sake. The idols people trust are lifeless metal that make their worshippers as lifeless as themselves; the living God, whose name endures for ever, will vindicate his people. So let all who belong to him bless him.

Why it was said. Israel lived among nations whose gods of silver and gold were impressive, and after the exile it often lived as a small, unimpressive people under foreign rule (see the introduction). The psalm reminds such a people who chose them, what he has done, and how empty the rivals are.

How the chapter makes its case. It is woven almost entirely from earlier Scripture: law, prophets and psalms. The call to praise rests on God’s goodness and his free choice of Israel (vv. 1–4). His greatness shows in his freedom: he rules storm and sea (vv. 5–7), struck Egypt, overthrew the kings who barred the way, and gave the land to his people (vv. 8–12). So his name endures, and he will do right by his servants (vv. 13–14). Against him stand the idols, breathless and useless, and those who trust them become like them (vv. 15–18). The psalm ends by calling every part of God’s people to bless him (vv. 19–21).

Where it leads. To Christ, by covenant and by the character of God revealed in him. The God who chose Israel “chose us in him before the foundation of the world” (Ephesians 1:4), so that a people from every nation is now “a people for his own possession” (1 Peter 2:9). The God who commands the wind stood up in a boat and “even winds and sea obey him” (Matthew 8:27). The promise that the LORD will vindicate his people is kept at the cross and the empty tomb, where God declared his chosen righteous (Romans 8:33). And against breathless idols stands the risen Christ, who breathed on his disciples and gave them the Spirit of life (John 20:22).

For us. Our idols are seldom silver statues, but money, success and approval are just as unable to speak, see or save, and they shrink those who trust them. The cure is not trying harder to be alive but turning to the living God, who chose us in Christ, and filling our mouths, as this psalmist did, with his word and his praise.
135.theology:
Praise is grounded in God's goodness and his choice of a people for himself (vv. 3-4). His sovereignty extends over creation, storm and history (vv. 5-12).

His name endures as revealed to Moses, and he will vindicate his servants (vv. 13-14). Idols are breathless and make their worshippers like them, while all God's people are called to bless the living God (vv. 15-21).

The psalm is woven from earlier Scripture, praise shaped by a mind full of the Bible; see the fuller treatments at Psalms 78, 105, 115 and 136.
135.examples: A believer who has soaked in Scripture will find, as this psalmist did, that its words become the natural language of praise. And whatever we trust in place of God, money, success or approval, cannot breathe life into us; only the living God can.

keyVerse.quote: Whatever the LORD pleases, he does, in heaven and on earth, in the seas and all deeps.
keyVerse.note: This verse is the hinge of the psalm. Everything before it calls for praise and everything after it gives the evidence: the storm, the exodus, the land and the fall of the idols all show a God who is free to do what he pleases. And what he has pleased to do is to choose and keep a people for himself.

135.reflection:
The psalm’s deepest reason for praise is that “the LORD has chosen Jacob for himself” (v. 4). How does knowing that God chose you in Christ, not because of anything in you, change the way you worship and the way you see yourself?

“Whatever the LORD pleases, he does” (v. 6). Where do you find this truth a comfort, and where do you find it hard?

Verses 15–18 say that idols have mouths but cannot speak, and that those who trust them become like them. What do people around you trust for life and security, and what does it slowly do to them? What about you?

This psalm is woven from earlier Scripture. How could you let the Bible shape the words of your own prayers and praise this week?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–3 — Give Thanks to the God of Gods
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The theme of the whole psalm is set in three calls to give thanks, each answered with the refrain. Thank the LORD, for he is good (v. 1). Thank the God of gods, supreme over every power people worship (v. 2). Thank the Lord of lords, ruler over every ruler (v. 3). And every time the reason is the same: his steadfast love, his loyal covenant love, endures for ever. A leader sings the call; the whole people sing the answer.
verseByVerse.theology: A call to thanks with an answer the congregation will give twenty-six times.

verseByVerse.quote: Give thanks to the LORD, for he is good, for his steadfast love endures forever. Give thanks to the God of gods, for his steadfast love endures forever. Give thanks to the Lord of lords, for his steadfast love endures forever;
verseByVerse.commentary:
Thank the LORD, the God above every god and the Lord above every lord, because his loyal love never ends.

For his steadfast love endures forever. This psalm was made to be sung in two voices. A leader, or a choir, sings the first half of each line, and the whole congregation answers with the second. When the foundation of the second temple was laid, they “sang responsively, praising and giving thanks to the LORD”, in these very words: “For he is good, for his steadfast love endures forever toward Israel” (Ezra 3:11). When fire came down at the dedication of Solomon’s temple, the people bowed to the ground and said the same (2 Chronicles 7:3).

Twenty-six times. The answer comes in every one of the twenty-six verses. Count it; it never misses a line. Nothing in the psalm, creation, rescue, judgment or provision, is left without it.

Give thanks to the LORD. Three calls to thanks, three names. The LORD: the covenant name. The God of gods: supreme over every power people worship. The Lord of lords: ruler over every ruler. “God of gods” does not grant that other gods are real; it says that no power people worship can stand beside him (1 Corinthians 8:4–6).

Steadfast love. Behind all three names is the same reason. The Hebrew word, hesed, has no single English equivalent; older versions said “mercy” or “lovingkindness”. It is loyal covenant love, love that has bound itself by promise and keeps faith when the other party does not deserve it. The God above all gods is not a remote supreme being. He is loyal love that never ends: “The steadfast love of the LORD never ceases; his mercies never come to an end; they are new every morning” (Lamentations 3:22–23).
verseByVerse.note: The refrain “for his steadfast love endures forever” runs through all 26 verses.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–9 — To Him Who Made the Great Lights
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Creation itself is the work of God’s steadfast love. The God who alone does great wonders made the heavens with understanding (vv. 4–5), spread out the dry land above the waters (v. 6), and made the great lights, the sun to rule the day and the moon and stars to rule the night (vv. 7–9). After each act the people answer with the refrain, so that every sunrise and every starry night becomes a line in the same song of covenant love.
verseByVerse.theology: Every sunrise and every starry night is an act of God's steadfast love.

verseByVerse.quote: to him who alone does great wonders, for his steadfast love endures forever; to him who by understanding made the heavens, for his steadfast love endures forever; to him who spread out the earth above the waters, for his steadfast love endures forever; to him who made the great lights, for his steadfast love endures forever; the sun to rule over the day, for his steadfast love endures forever; the moon and stars to rule over the night, for his steadfast love endures forever;
verseByVerse.commentary:
Creation itself, from the heavens to the daily rising of the sun, is an act of God’s steadfast love.

Who by understanding made the heavens. The story begins with creation. God made the heavens with wisdom and design (Proverbs 3:19), spread out the dry land above the waters, and after each act the congregation answers with the refrain. The New Testament adds that the Son was the one through whom all things were made (John 1:3): the wisdom by which the heavens were made has a name.

Who made the great lights. The words come from Genesis: God made “the greater light to rule the day and the lesser light to rule the night” (Genesis 1:16). The psalm puts the refrain after the sun, and again after the moon. Israel’s neighbours worshipped the sun and moon; here they are servants, made and set in their places by love.

In everyday life. Tomorrow morning, when the sun comes up, that is God’s steadfast love. Tonight, when the moon rises, that is his steadfast love. The ordinary, reliable rhythms of day and night, which we barely notice, are daily evidence that God keeps faith with his world. Every sunrise is a line of this psalm.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–22 — To Him Who Divided the Red Sea
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The whole history of rescue, from Egypt to the land, is told one line at a time, each followed by the same answer. God struck down Egypt’s firstborn and brought Israel out with a strong hand (vv. 10–12). He divided the Red Sea, led his people through and overthrew Pharaoh’s army (vv. 13–15). He led them through the wilderness, struck down the kings who stood in their way, Sihon and Og, and gave their land to Israel as a heritage (vv. 16–22). Judgment and rescue alike are love keeping its promise.
verseByVerse.theology: The whole history of rescue, from Egypt to the land, told one line at a time, each followed by the same answer.

verseByVerse.quote: to him who struck down the firstborn of Egypt, for his steadfast love endures forever; and brought Israel out from among them, for his steadfast love endures forever; with a strong hand and an outstretched arm, for his steadfast love endures forever; to him who divided the Red Sea in two, for his steadfast love endures forever; and made Israel pass through the midst of it, for his steadfast love endures forever; but overthrew Pharaoh and his host in the Red Sea, for his steadfast love endures forever;
verseByVerse.commentary:
In rescuing his people from Egypt and the sea, God’s steadfast love broke the power of their oppressor. Judgment on Pharaoh and freedom for Israel were one act of love.

Who struck down the firstborn of Egypt. From creation to redemption, and here the refrain does something that can startle a modern reader. After the firstborn of Egypt are struck down comes “for his steadfast love endures forever”. A line about judgment is answered with a line about love.

Why judgment is love. That is not cruelty. God’s steadfast love is his covenant love for his people, and loving the enslaved meant breaking the power of the slaver, who had himself drowned Israel’s baby sons (Exodus 1:22). The judgment on Egypt was the rescue of Israel. A love that never judged oppressors would not be love for the oppressed.

With a strong hand and an outstretched arm. The phrase echoes Moses’ words in Deuteronomy (4:34; 5:15), the picture of a warrior reaching out to strike and to save.

Overthrew Pharaoh and his host. The sea split, the people walked through, and Pharaoh’s army went under. The ESV notes that “overthrew” is literally “shook off”, the way a man shakes something off his hand. Exodus says “the LORD threw the Egyptians into the midst of the sea” (Exodus 14:27). Three acts: divide, lead through, overthrow. Three times, the same answer.

The greater exodus. When Jesus spoke with Moses and Elijah on the mountain, they talked of “his departure, which he was about to accomplish at Jerusalem” (Luke 9:31); the Greek word is exodos. At the cross he went down into the deep waters of judgment and came through, to lead his people out of a worse slavery than Egypt’s.

verseByVerse.quote: to him who led his people through the wilderness, for his steadfast love endures forever; to him who struck down great kings, for his steadfast love endures forever; and killed mighty kings, for his steadfast love endures forever; Sihon, king of the Amorites, for his steadfast love endures forever; and Og, king of Bashan, for his steadfast love endures forever; and gave their land as a heritage, for his steadfast love endures forever; a heritage to Israel his servant, for his steadfast love endures forever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God led his people all the way, defeated the kings who stood against them, and gave them the land he had promised.

Who led his people through the wilderness. Forty years compressed into one line, and not a word about Israel’s grumbling. This is not forgetfulness; Psalm 106 has already told that side. This psalm is looking only at what God did: he led.

Sihon, king of the Amorites. Sihon and Og appear again, as in the previous psalm (135:11): great kings who stood in the way of God’s people, each named and followed by the refrain.

Gave their land as a heritage. The story of the exodus ends with a gift: the land, a heritage to “Israel his servant”. Everything from the burning bush to the Jordan was love keeping a promise.

How can steadfast love follow “killed mighty kings”? The love is for his covenant people, whom these kings came out to attack (Numbers 21:23, 33). The judgment was on peoples ripe for it after long patience (Genesis 15:16), carried out once, and no pattern for today.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–26 — He Remembered Us in Our Low Estate
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The great history now comes home to “us”, and ends in thanks. The God of creation and exodus remembered his people in their low estate and rescued them from their foes (vv. 23–24). His care reaches beyond Israel to every creature, for he gives food to all flesh (v. 25). So the psalm closes as it opened, with thanks to the God of heaven, whose steadfast love endures for ever (v. 26).
verseByVerse.theology: The great history comes home to us: remembered when we were low, rescued, and fed.

verseByVerse.quote: It is he who remembered us in our low estate, for his steadfast love endures forever; and rescued us from our foes, for his steadfast love endures forever; he who gives food to all flesh, for his steadfast love endures forever. Give thanks to the God of heaven, for his steadfast love endures forever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The same steadfast love that made the world and rescued Israel found us when we were low, set us free, and feeds every living thing, so give thanks.

Who remembered us in our low estate. Now the psalm comes home: for twenty-two verses it has been “him who”; now it is “us”. Perhaps the singers were the returned exiles, poor and humbled. Whoever they were, the great history of creation and exodus has become their own story.

Found at our lowest. Mary sang the same thing when God chose her: “he has looked on the humble estate of his servant” (Luke 1:48). That is where God’s steadfast love finds people: not at their best, but at their lowest. And it found us lowest of all at the cross: “God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us” (Romans 5:8). Every line of this psalm leads there.

He who gives food to all flesh. The psalm widens to the whole living world. Every creature is fed by God. Jesus pointed to the birds that “neither sow nor reap nor gather into barns, and yet your heavenly Father feeds them” (Matthew 6:26). Every meal is a line of this psalm.

Give thanks to the God of heaven. The psalm ends where it began, with thanks. “For from him and through him and to him are all things. To him be glory forever. Amen” (Romans 11:36).

Praying this psalm. Take the events of your own life (your birth, your family, the day you came to Christ, the time God brought you through, this morning’s breakfast) and after each one, say the refrain: “for his steadfast love endures forever.” You will find it fits every line, even the hard ones, because the cross guarantees that nothing in a believer’s story falls outside that love (Romans 8:38–39).

136.title: His Steadfast Love Endures Forever
136.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 136 is the twin of Psalm 135, which ended by calling all Israel to bless the LORD. It retells the same history, from creation through the exodus to the land, but now as a responsive song in which every one of its twenty-six lines is answered with the same refrain. Jewish tradition came to call it the Great Hallel, the great song of praise.

The message. Everything God has done, in making the world, in rescuing his people, in judging their enemies, in remembering them when they were low and in feeding every creature, is the work of one thing: his steadfast love, his loyal covenant love, which never runs out. So give him thanks, and keep giving thanks, for every line of your story has the same answer.

Why it was said. Israel sang this refrain at the great moments of its worship: when the ark came to Jerusalem, at the dedication of Solomon’s temple, and when the foundation of the second temple was laid after the exile (1 Chronicles 16:34; 2 Chronicles 7:3; Ezra 3:11). A people who had known slavery, wilderness and exile needed to say, over and over, that God’s love had not ended (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. A leader sings the first half of each line and the people answer. Three calls to thank the LORD, the God of gods and Lord of lords, set the theme (vv. 1–3). Then creation: the heavens, the earth, the sun, moon and stars (vv. 4–9). Then redemption: the blow on Egypt’s firstborn, the people brought out, the sea divided and Pharaoh overthrown (vv. 10–15), the wilderness journey, the kings defeated and the land given as a heritage (vv. 16–22). Finally the story comes home to “us”, remembered in our low estate, rescued and fed, and the psalm ends where it began, with thanks (vv. 23–26).

Where it leads. To Christ, by pattern and by the character of God revealed in him. The exodus that the psalm celebrates was a picture of a greater one: on the mountain Jesus spoke of “his departure” (literally, his exodus) “which he was about to accomplish at Jerusalem” (Luke 9:31). At the cross God’s steadfast love reached its fullest measure, for there he remembered us in our lowest estate: “while we were still sinners, Christ died for us” (Romans 5:8). And the Word through whom the heavens were made (John 1:3) is the one who rescues us from our foes, sin and death, and feeds us with himself, the bread of life.

For us. The refrain teaches us to read every part of life, sunrise and supper, rescue and loss, as held by a love that has bound itself to us by promise and will not let go. When we cannot feel it, we can still say it, and in Christ it remains true.
136.theology:
God's steadfast love is the ground of every act in creation, redemption, judgment and providence (his daily care for what he has made), confessed after each line, as Israel sang at great moments (Ezra 3:11; 2 Chr 7:3; Jer 33:11).

Creation's ordinary rhythms are expressions of covenant love (vv. 7-9), and God's love for his people includes judgment on their oppressors (vv. 10-20). The history becomes personal: God remembers his people in their low estate and feeds all creatures (vv. 23-25).
136.examples: Said in turns, by a leader and a congregation, the refrain lodges itself in memory until it shapes how you see a sunrise, a deliverance or an ordinary breakfast: each one a line of the same song.

keyVerse.quote: Give thanks to the LORD, for he is good, for his steadfast love endures forever.
keyVerse.note: This verse states the theme the whole psalm repeats. God’s goodness is the reason for thanks, and his steadfast love, his loyal covenant love, is the answer the people give to every line that follows, from creation to the daily meal. It was the song of Israel’s great days of worship, and it is the song of all who know that love in Christ.

136.reflection:
The congregation answers every line of this psalm with the same words, twenty-six times. What does repetition do for us in worship and in memory? Why might God want this truth said so often?

The refrain follows the sunrise and the moonrise (vv. 8–9) as well as the parting of the sea. Which ordinary, daily gifts in your life do you tend to forget are signs of God’s steadfast love?

The refrain also follows the striking down of Egypt’s firstborn (v. 10). How can judgment on oppressors be an expression of love for the oppressed? Where else in Scripture do you see this?

“It is he who remembered us in our low estate” (v. 23). Try writing your own lines of this psalm from your life, each followed by the refrain. Where does the cross of Christ fit in your list?

137.text: <sup>1</sup>By the waters of Babylon, there we sat down and wept, when we remembered Zion.<sup>2</sup>On the willows there we hung up our lyres.<sup>3</sup>For there our captors required of us songs, and our tormentors, mirth, saying, "Sing us one of the songs of Zion!"<sup>4</sup>How shall we sing the LORD's song in a foreign land?<sup>5</sup>If I forget you, O Jerusalem, let my right hand forget its skill!<sup>6</sup>Let my tongue stick to the roof of my mouth, if I do not remember you, if I do not set Jerusalem above my highest joy!<sup>7</sup>Remember, O LORD, against the Edomites the day of Jerusalem, how they said, "Lay it bare, lay it bare, down to its foundations!"<sup>8</sup>O daughter of Babylon, doomed to be destroyed, blessed shall he be who repays you with what you have done to us!<sup>9</sup>Blessed shall he be who takes your little ones and dashes them against the rock!

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — How Shall We Sing the LORD's Song?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Exiles in Babylon refuse to forget Zion or to turn her songs into entertainment for their captors. By the rivers and canals of Babylon the survivors of Jerusalem’s fall sit and weep at the memory of Zion, their lyres hung silent on the trees (vv. 1–2). Their captors, the men who burned the temple, demand a song of Zion for amusement (v. 3). The exiles answer with a question: how can the LORD’s song be sung as a show in a foreign land? (v. 4). Then one voice swears an oath against his own hand and tongue: better never to play or sing again than to forget Jerusalem or rank it below his highest joy (vv. 5–6).
verseByVerse.theology: Exiles refuse to turn the songs of God into entertainment for the people who burned his house.

verseByVerse.quote: By the waters of Babylon, there we sat down and wept, when we remembered Zion. On the willows there we hung up our lyres. For there our captors required of us songs, and our tormentors, mirth, saying, "Sing us one of the songs of Zion!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Exiles weep by Babylon’s rivers for the city they have lost, while their captors mock them with demands for a song of Zion.

By the waters of Babylon. The setting is in the first line. Jerusalem had fallen in 586 BC: Nebuchadnezzar’s commander “burned the house of the LORD and the king’s house and all the houses of Jerusalem”, broke down the walls and carried the people away (2 Kings 25:9–11). Now the survivors sit by the rivers and canals of Babylon, hundreds of miles east, and weep.

When we remembered Zion. Memory is what hurts: the city, the temple, the festivals, the Songs of Ascents sung on the way up, all gone.

On the willows there we hung up our lyres. The harps that once accompanied the temple songs hang on the branches, unplayed. There is a time when the music stops, and the psalm does not pretend otherwise.

Sing us one of the songs of Zion! Then the cruelty: the captors demand entertainment, perhaps mocking a God who could not save his city. They want the worship of the LORD turned into a show for the people who burned his temple.

Tears are allowed. God put this weeping in his hymnbook. Faith does not require a cheerful face among the ruins (compare Lamentations 1:1–3), and Jesus himself wept (John 11:35).

Uncertain wording. The ESV notes that the “willows” may be “poplars”, perhaps the poplars common along Babylon’s watercourses. The picture is the same: silent harps on riverside trees.
verseByVerse.note: Written in or just after the Babylonian exile.

verseByVerse.quote: How shall we sing the LORD's song in a foreign land? If I forget you, O Jerusalem, let my right hand forget its skill! Let my tongue stick to the roof of my mouth, if I do not remember you, if I do not set Jerusalem above my highest joy!
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD’s songs are not entertainment for his enemies, and the singer would rather lose hand and voice than forget Jerusalem or love anything more.

How shall we sing the LORD’s song in a foreign land? The question is not simply “we are too sad to sing”, but how the LORD’s songs of his dwelling and his victories can be performed as amusement for his enemies. Some things are too holy for entertainment. The world often wants the church’s songs without the church’s God; this psalm says no.

Let my right hand forget its skill! The singer takes an oath against himself. The right hand plays the lyre; the tongue sings. If I forget Jerusalem, let me lose the very abilities I would use to sing for Babylon. Better never to make music again than to forget Zion in the land of the captors.

Above my highest joy! The heart of the oath is to set Jerusalem “above my highest joy”, above anything Babylon can offer. The city mattered because the LORD had put his name there; to forget it was to forget him.

Our Jerusalem. For a Christian the city is “the Jerusalem above” (Galatians 4:26) and the God who dwells there. Exiles are tempted to settle and forget. We keep the vow imperfectly, but we are held by one who never forgot us, who has gone to prepare a place for us (John 14:2), and whose Spirit keeps turning our hearts homeward (Romans 8:23).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–9 — Remember, O LORD, Against the Edomites
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Grief turns into a cry for justice, and the psalmist hands that cry to God rather than acting on it. He asks the LORD to remember Edom, Israel’s brother nation, which urged on the destruction of Jerusalem with “Lay it bare, lay it bare” (v. 7). Then he turns to Babylon, already doomed by God’s word, and pronounces blessed whoever repays it with what it has done, even to its children (vv. 8–9). These are the hardest words in the Psalms. They ask for no more than God had announced through his prophets, and they leave the doing of it with God.
verseByVerse.theology: The rawest words in the Psalter: the grief of people who watched atrocity, handed over to God for judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: Remember, O LORD, against the Edomites the day of Jerusalem, how they said, "Lay it bare, lay it bare, down to its foundations!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The psalmist asks the LORD to remember how Edom, Israel’s own kin, cheered Jerusalem’s destruction, and leaves the reckoning with him.

Remember, O LORD, against the Edomites. Grief turns to anger, and the first target is not Babylon but Edom, the descendants of Jacob’s brother Esau. On the day Jerusalem fell, they stood by and cheered: “Lay it bare, lay it bare, down to its foundations!”

The same betrayal in Obadiah. The prophet Obadiah records it: “On the day that you stood aloof, on the day that strangers carried off his wealth … you were like one of them”, and he warns, “do not gloat over the day of your brother in the day of his misfortune” (Obadiah 11–12). Lamentations says the cup of judgment Jerusalem drank will pass to Edom (Lamentations 4:21–22). The wound of a relative cheering your destruction goes very deep. Yet the psalmist does not take revenge. To ask God to “remember” is to lay the case before the Judge and leave it there.
verseByVerse.note: Edom gloated over Jerusalem’s fall.

verseByVerse.quote: O daughter of Babylon, doomed to be destroyed, blessed shall he be who repays you with what you have done to us! Blessed shall he be who takes your little ones and dashes them against the rock!
verseByVerse.commentary:
The psalmist calls blessed whoever repays Babylon’s cruelty in kind, even to its children: a cry for the justice God had already announced, left in God’s hands.

O daughter of Babylon, doomed to be destroyed. Babylon is doomed because God has already pronounced judgment on it, and “blessed”, fortunate, will be whoever carries it out. God had said, “I will repay Babylon and all the inhabitants of Chaldea before your very eyes for all the evil that they have done in Zion” (Jeremiah 51:24).

Does God approve of killing infants? Verse 9 is the most shocking verse in the Psalms, and it must not be skipped or softened. Three things need to be said honestly.

With what you have done to us. First, it is repayment in kind. Ancient armies killed children, and the psalmist had very probably seen it done to Jerusalem’s. He is not inventing a cruelty; he is asking that the cruelty Babylon committed come back on Babylon.

God had announced it. Second, God had already announced this very judgment. Isaiah’s oracle against Babylon said, “Their infants will be dashed in pieces before their eyes” (Isaiah 13:16). The psalmist is praying for what God had said he would do. (Babylon itself fell to Persia in 539 BC almost without a fight; Revelation 18 takes up its name for every proud, cruel power still to fall.)

Leaving vengeance to God. Third, the psalmist does not do it, and does not ask to. He hands the justice to God and to whoever God uses. Christians are commanded, “never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God” (Romans 12:19). This verse is never a licence for violence, but the cry of people who have seen atrocity, spoken to the only one who can judge it.

Where justice and mercy meet. The final answer to Babylon’s crime was the cross, where God’s judgment on sin fell on his Son, and from which mercy is offered even to Babylonians. Jesus wept as he foretold that Jerusalem would be torn down to the ground with its children within it (Luke 19:44), and he went to the cross praying, “Father, forgive them” (Luke 23:34). The cry for justice and the prayer for the enemy belong together, because both were answered in the same place, on a hill outside Jerusalem.

Words for rage. For anyone who has suffered abuse or atrocity, this psalm gives permission to bring the rage to God in words, rather than burying it or acting on it; he can bear it, and he will judge justly. Indignation handed to the Judge is what makes forgiveness possible: if God will put it right, I need not (see the note on Romans 12:19). If you are still in danger, getting safe comes first: tell someone who can help today.

Too angry, or not angry enough? Many modern readers take this verse as proof that religion breeds violence, and it is right to be shaken by it. But those most offended have usually never watched soldiers kill their children. C. S. Lewis, himself troubled by the cursing psalms, warned in Reflections on the Psalms against feeling superior to them: the absence of indignation, he suggested, can be a worse sign than its presence, because it may mean we no longer quite believe that cruelty is wrong. A culture that cannot be angry at atrocity has not become gentle; it has become numb. The psalmist’s anger is the anger of a man who still believes in justice, and he does the one thing that keeps anger from becoming violence: he hands it to God.

Where Christians differ. May a Christian pray this? Some say never, since Jesus commands us to love our enemies and pray for those who persecute us (Matthew 5:44). Others point out that the martyrs in heaven still ask God to avenge their blood (Revelation 6:10), and that heaven is called to rejoice over Babylon’s fall (Revelation 18:20).

This commentary’s view. A Christian may pray for God’s justice against cruelty and unrepentant evil, leaving vengeance to him (Romans 12:19), while praying first for enemies to repent (Matthew 5:44), as Christ prayed for those who crucified him (see the introduction on the psalms that curse).
verseByVerse.note: A cry for justice in the language of war, echoing what Babylon itself had done; it leaves vengeance to God.

137.title: By the Waters of Babylon
137.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 137 is the one psalm set by the waters of Babylon, sung by exiles there or just after. The Songs of Ascents (120 to 134) have climbed to Zion, and Psalms 135 and 136 have praised the LORD whose steadfast love endures for ever; now Jerusalem lies in ruins, the temple is burned, and the songs have fallen silent.

The message. God’s people in a foreign land must not forget Zion, nor let her songs become entertainment for those who mock her God; they are to love God’s city above their highest joy. And when they have suffered atrocity, they are not to avenge themselves but to bring their grief and their cry for justice to the LORD, who has promised to repay.

Why it was said. In 586 BC Babylon destroyed Jerusalem and its temple and carried the people east, while Edom cheered (see the introduction). The exiles faced two temptations: to settle into Babylon and forget, and to be eaten up by bitterness. The psalm gave them words for both grief and rage, and kept their hearts pointed home.

How the chapter makes its case. By Babylon’s waters the exiles weep, hang up their lyres and are mocked with demands for a song of Zion (vv. 1–3). They ask how the LORD’s song can be sung there, and one voice swears an oath against his own hand and tongue never to forget Jerusalem (vv. 4–6). Then grief turns to a cry for justice: he asks the LORD to remember Edom’s treachery (v. 7), and pronounces blessed whoever repays Babylon in kind, as God had announced through his prophets (vv. 8–9).

Where it leads. To Christ, by the need it exposes and by the character of God revealed in him. The psalm cries for justice against atrocity but cannot see how justice and mercy will meet. They meet at the cross, where God’s judgment on sin fell on his own Son, and from which mercy is offered even to Babylonians. Christ also shares the exiles’ tears: he wept over Jerusalem (Luke 19:41–44) and suffered outside its gate to bring his people home to the city that is to come (Hebrews 13:12–14).

For us. Christians are “sojourners and exiles” too (1 Peter 2:11), living in a world that wants our songs without our God. Set the city of God above your highest joy, and refuse to let worship become a show. And when you have been deeply wronged, do not bury the anger or act on it: tell it to God, the just Judge, and leave vengeance to him.
137.theology:
Grief for the loss of God's dwelling is right (vv. 1-2). The LORD's song must not be turned into entertainment for his enemies, and God's city is to be set above every joy (vv. 3-6).

The prayers for judgment (vv. 7-9) are the cry of victims of atrocity, asking for judgment God had already announced (Obad 10-12), repayment in kind, handed to God rather than taken. Heaven rejoices at the final fall of Babylon (Rev 18:20-21), and Jesus, who wept over Jerusalem, bore judgment himself at the cross.
137.examples: There are seasons when the music stops: after a bereavement, a betrayal, a church that fell apart. This psalm lets the harps hang in the trees without shame, and it lets rage at real cruelty be spoken to God rather than buried or acted on.

keyVerse.quote: How shall we sing the LORD’s song in a foreign land?
keyVerse.note: This question is the hinge of the psalm. It refuses to turn the worship of the LORD into amusement for the people who burned his temple, and it opens the oath never to forget Jerusalem. Every believer living as an exile in this world must answer it: we sing, but never for Babylon’s entertainment, and always with our hearts set on the city of God.

137.reflection:
The exiles weep “when we remembered Zion” (v. 1), and God put their tears in his hymnbook. What does that teach us about grief and loss in the Christian life?

Their captors wanted the songs of Zion without the God of Zion (vv. 3–4). Where does our world want the church’s words, music or morals without its Lord, and how should we respond?

The psalmist vows to set Jerusalem “above my highest joy” (v. 6). What competes for that place in your heart, and what would it look like to renew his vow?

Verses 7–9 hand a cry for justice to God instead of taking revenge. How does the cross, where Jesus prayed “Father, forgive them” (Luke 23:34), help us to pray honestly about those who have done terrible wrong?

138.text: Of David. 1I give you thanks, O LORD, with my whole heart; before the gods I sing your praise;2I bow down toward your holy temple and give thanks to your name for your steadfast love and your faithfulness, for you have exalted above all things your name and your word.3On the day I called, you answered me; my strength of soul you increased.4All the kings of the earth shall give you thanks, O LORD, for they have heard the words of your mouth,5and they shall sing of the ways of the LORD, for great is the glory of the LORD.6For though the LORD is high, he regards the lowly, but the haughty he knows from afar.7Though I walk in the midst of trouble, you preserve my life; you stretch out your hand against the wrath of my enemies, and your right hand delivers me.8The LORD will fulfill his purpose for me; your steadfast love, O LORD, endures forever. Do not forsake the work of your hands.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David answers God’s goodness with wholehearted, unembarrassed thanks. He praises the LORD “before the gods”, in full view of every rival claim to worship, and bows toward the place where God promised to meet his people (vv. 1–2). His reasons are the two great covenant words, steadfast love and faithfulness, and the word God has exalted along with his name: God has staked his name on doing what he says. And David has proved it for himself. On the day he called, God answered, not necessarily by removing the trouble, but by making him strong in soul (v. 3).
verseByVerse.theology: Unashamed praise in front of every rival power, for a God who answered and made a weak soul strong.

verseByVerse.quote: I give you thanks, O LORD, with my whole heart; before the gods I sing your praise; I bow down toward your holy temple and give thanks to your name for your steadfast love and your faithfulness, for you have exalted above all things your name and your word.
verseByVerse.commentary:
David thanks the LORD with his whole heart, openly before every rival god, for the steadfast love and faithfulness that stand behind God’s word.

With my whole heart. This psalm opens the last group bearing David’s name (138–145) with wholehearted thanks, sung “before the gods”: in front of every idol and every authority that claimed divine honour. David is not embarrassed to praise the LORD in their presence, and we need not lower our voices either in a world full of other gods (money, status, pleasure, ideologies).

I bow down toward your holy temple. How could David bow toward a temple not yet built? The Hebrew word was also used of the tabernacle (1 Samuel 1:9) and of God’s heavenly dwelling (Psalm 11:4): he bows toward the place where God promised to meet his people.

Your steadfast love and your faithfulness. The two great covenant words appear again, and God has exalted “your name and your word” above everything: he has staked his own name on keeping what he has said, and a believer may lean the whole weight of trust on it.

Uncertain wording. “Before the gods” most likely means before the gods of the nations, in defiance of them; some take it of angels or of earthly rulers. And the end of verse 2 is compressed in Hebrew: the ESV notes it may read “you have exalted your word above all your name”. Either way God’s word stands at the top.

verseByVerse.quote: On the day I called, you answered me; my strength of soul you increased.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God answered David’s prayer by making him strong inside, whether or not the trouble had yet gone.

On the day I called, you answered me. He called; God answered, not necessarily by removing the trouble, but by increasing his “strength of soul”. The ESV notes the Hebrew is vivid: “you made me bold in my soul with strength”.

My strength of soul you increased. Sometimes God answers by changing the circumstances; often by changing the person, giving courage to face what has not yet changed. A believer who prays for the storm to stop and is made brave in it has been answered. Paul was answered the same way: “My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness” (2 Corinthians 12:9).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The God who is high above all stoops to the lowly, and he finishes what he starts. David’s thanks widens into a vision of every king on earth hearing God’s words and singing of his glory (vv. 4–5). The reason sits at the centre: though the LORD is high, he regards the lowly, while the proud are kept at a distance (v. 6). Then the psalm comes home to David’s own road. In the midst of trouble God preserves him and stretches out his hand against his enemies (v. 7). He will fulfil his purpose, because his steadfast love endures for ever, and so David prays, “Do not forsake the work of your hands” (v. 8).
verseByVerse.theology: The high God stoops to the lowly, keeps them alive in trouble, and finishes what he has begun in them.

verseByVerse.quote: All the kings of the earth shall give you thanks, O LORD, for they have heard the words of your mouth, and they shall sing of the ways of the LORD, for great is the glory of the LORD. For though the LORD is high, he regards the lowly, but the haughty he knows from afar.
verseByVerse.commentary:
All the world’s kings will praise the LORD, because the God higher than all comes close to the lowly and keeps the proud at a distance.

All the kings of the earth. From one man’s thanks the psalm leaps to the whole world: the word God has exalted (v. 2) will go out, and kings will hear it and sing “of the ways of the LORD”. That began when the gospel of David’s greater Son went to the nations (compare Revelation 21:24).

He regards the lowly. Here is the heart of the psalm. God is high, above kings and gods, and yet “he regards the lowly”: he looks closely and cares, like the one seated on high who lifts the needy from the ash heap (Psalm 113:5–7).

The haughty he knows from afar. The proud he knows only at a distance; the humble get near. Isaiah heard God say, “I dwell in the high and holy place, and also with him who is of a contrite and lowly spirit” (Isaiah 57:15). And Peter: “God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble” (1 Peter 5:5). Humbling ourselves is not a technique for earning God’s nearness; it is simply where people stand who know they live by grace.

The high God came down. The stooping of verse 6 went further than David could have imagined. The Son of God, “though he was in the form of God”, “humbled himself by becoming obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross” (Philippians 2:6, 8). In Christ the high God became lowly, so that the lowly could be lifted up with him. His mother sang of it: God “has brought down the mighty from their thrones and exalted those of humble estate” (Luke 1:52).

verseByVerse.quote: Though I walk in the midst of trouble, you preserve my life; you stretch out your hand against the wrath of my enemies, and your right hand delivers me. The LORD will fulfill his purpose for me; your steadfast love, O LORD, endures forever. Do not forsake the work of your hands.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God keeps his servant alive in trouble and will finish all he has purposed for him, so David prays that he will never let go of his handiwork.

In the midst of trouble. Not around trouble, not past it, but in the midst of it. Faith is not promised a route that avoids hardship, but God’s company and preservation inside it.

The LORD will fulfill his purpose for me. Here is a verse to lean on: whatever God set out to do in a person’s life, he will finish. Paul said the same to the Philippians: “I am sure of this, that he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion at the day of Jesus Christ” (Philippians 1:6). And the reason is the refrain of Psalm 136: “your steadfast love, O LORD, endures forever”.

Do not forsake the work of your hands. Then, strikingly, a prayer right after the promise. David is sure God will finish, and still asks. Faith does not stop praying because it is confident; it prays because it is confident. And the argument is beautiful: I am the work of your hands, and a craftsman does not abandon a piece he has worked on so long. Believers are his work twice over: “we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus” (Ephesians 2:10). If you feel half-finished, pray this verse. You are his work, and he does not leave his work undone.

138.title: Do Not Forsake the Work of Your Hands
138.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 138 opens the last collection bearing David’s name (138 to 145). After the silent harps of Psalm 137, a voice is singing again, and singing boldly, “before the gods”.

The message. The LORD is high above every rival, yet he has bound himself to his word and his steadfast love, and so he stoops to the lowly, answers those who call, keeps them in the middle of trouble and finishes what he has begun in them. One man’s thanks for answered prayer grows into a vision of all the kings of the earth praising him.

Why it was said. David knew danger and enemies (v. 7), and he knew the promise God had made him of a lasting house and throne (2 Samuel 7; see the introduction). The psalm teaches God’s people that his word can bear the whole weight of their trust, whatever powers and gods stand against them, and that thanks for one answered prayer belongs to a story that will reach the whole world.

How the chapter makes its case. David gives thanks with his whole heart before the gods, bowing toward God’s temple, for God’s steadfast love and faithfulness and the word he has exalted (vv. 1–2), and because God answered his call and made him strong (v. 3). Then the circle widens: all the kings of the earth will hear God’s words and sing of his glory (vv. 4–5), for the high LORD regards the lowly and knows the proud only from afar (v. 6). Finally David comes back to his own road: in the midst of trouble God preserves him and will fulfil his purpose, so David prays that God will not forsake the work of his hands (vv. 7–8).

Where it leads. To Christ, by the character of God revealed in him and by promise. The God who “regards the lowly” came down further than David imagined, when the Son “humbled himself” to death on a cross (Philippians 2:8). The kings who will praise the LORD (v. 4) are the nations now hearing the gospel of David’s greater Son. And David’s confidence that “the LORD will fulfill his purpose for me” becomes Paul’s, that God will complete his good work “at the day of Jesus Christ” (Philippians 1:6).

For us. Thank God with your whole heart, unembarrassed among the gods of our day. Pray in trouble, and count it an answer when God makes you strong in it before he takes it away. And if you feel half-finished, plead the last line: you are the work of his hands, and he does not abandon his work.
138.theology:
God is to be praised openly before every rival power, and he has bound his name to his word (vv. 1-2). He may answer prayer by strengthening the soul rather than removing the trouble (v. 3).

The high God draws near to the lowly and keeps the proud at a distance (v. 6), and in Christ he came down to the lowest place. He preserves his people in the midst of trouble and will complete his purpose for them (vv. 7-8).
138.examples: You may pray for the storm to stop and find instead that you have been made brave in it; that too is an answer. And on the days you feel unfinished, verse 8 gives you a prayer to the God who made you: Do not forsake the work of your hands.

keyVerse.quote: For though the LORD is high, he regards the lowly, but the haughty he knows from afar.
keyVerse.note: This verse holds the psalm together. The God exalted above gods and kings (vv. 1–5) is the same God who bends down to keep one troubled man alive (vv. 7–8), and it tells us who comes near him: not the proud but the humble. In Christ the high God came lower still, to lift the lowly up with him.

138.reflection:
David sings God’s praise “before the gods” (v. 1). What are the gods of our culture, and what would it look like to praise the LORD openly in front of them, at work, among friends or online?

God answered David by increasing his “strength of soul” (v. 3), not necessarily by removing his trouble. Have you known an answer like that? How does it change the way you pray?

“Though the LORD is high, he regards the lowly” (v. 6). How does the coming of Jesus show this most fully, and why does pride keep us at a distance from God?

David is sure that “the LORD will fulfill his purpose for me”, and still prays, “Do not forsake the work of your hands” (v. 8). Where do you feel unfinished, and how could you pray this verse this week?

139.text: To the choirmaster. A Psalm of David. 1O LORD, you have searched me and known me!2You know when I sit down and when I rise up; you discern my thoughts from afar.3You search out my path and my lying down and are acquainted with all my ways.4Even before a word is on my tongue, behold, O LORD, you know it altogether.5You hem me in, behind and before, and lay your hand upon me.6Such knowledge is too wonderful for me; it is high; I cannot attain it.7Where shall I go from your Spirit? Or where shall I flee from your presence?8If I ascend to heaven, you are there! If I make my bed in Sheol, you are there!9If I take the wings of the morning and dwell in the uttermost parts of the sea,10even there your hand shall lead me, and your right hand shall hold me.11If I say, "Surely the darkness shall cover me, and the light about me be night,"12even the darkness is not dark to you; the night is bright as the day, for darkness is as light with you.13For you formed my inward parts; you knitted me together in my mother's womb.14I praise you, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made. Wonderful are your works; my soul knows it very well.15My frame was not hidden from you, when I was being made in secret, intricately woven in the depths of the earth.16Your eyes saw my unformed substance; in your book were written, every one of them, the days that were formed for me, when as yet there was none of them.17How precious to me are your thoughts, O God! How vast is the sum of them!18If I would count them, they are more than the sand. I awake, and I am still with you.19Oh that you would slay the wicked, O God! O men of blood, depart from me!20They speak against you with malicious intent; your enemies take your name in vain.21Do I not hate those who hate you, O LORD? And do I not loathe those who rise up against you?22I hate them with complete hatred; I count them my enemies.23Search me, O God, and know my heart! Try me and know my thoughts!24And see if there be any grievous way in me, and lead me in the way everlasting!

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — You Have Searched Me and Known Me
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God knows David completely, and David finds it too wonderful to grasp. The LORD has searched him and knows him, not merely about him (v. 1). He knows the ordinary movements of the day, sitting and rising, going out and lying down, and he discerns David’s thoughts from far away (vv. 2–3). He knows every word before it reaches the tongue (v. 4). This knowledge does not pin David down like a specimen; it surrounds him, behind and before, with a hand laid on him (v. 5). David cannot take it in: it is too high for him, and the only fitting response is worship (v. 6).
verseByVerse.theology: A man discovers that he is completely known, and finds it too wonderful to understand.

verseByVerse.quote: O LORD, you have searched me and known me! You know when I sit down and when I rise up; you discern my thoughts from afar. You search out my path and my lying down and are acquainted with all my ways. Even before a word is on my tongue, behold, O LORD, you know it altogether.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God knows David through and through: every movement, every thought, every word before it is spoken.

You have searched me and known me! This much-loved psalm begins with a fact: God has searched David, like a man searching a house, and known him. Not known about him; known him.

You discern my thoughts from afar. God knows every ordinary movement of the day, sitting down and rising up, and not only actions but thoughts, and he knows them from afar: no distance hides what goes on inside a person. “Acquainted” is the familiarity of someone you have lived with for years.

Even before a word is on my tongue. Before a word is spoken, God knows it “altogether”, motive included. “No creature is hidden from his sight, but all are naked and exposed to the eyes of him to whom we must give account” (Hebrews 4:13).

Terror or comfort. That can terrify or deeply comfort. Jesus showed this same knowledge on earth: “he himself knew what was in man” (John 2:25). And John writes to troubled believers, “whenever our heart condemns us, God is greater than our heart, and he knows everything” (1 John 3:20). To be completely known and still loved is what every human heart longs for, and the psalm will show that David is both.

Isn’t an all-seeing God the ultimate surveillance? To many modern ears this psalm sounds like Orwell: an eye that never closes, a file with every thought in it. We guard our privacy, with reason, because being watched usually means being managed: companies track our clicks to sell to us, governments track citizens to control them. Jean-Paul Sartre had a character say that hell is other people, partly because another’s gaze turns us into an object. But notice what God’s knowledge does in this psalm. It does not catalogue David; it surrounds him, lays a hand on him and leads him (vv. 5, 10). The difference is not how much is known but who knows, and why. The God who sees every hidden thought did not use what he saw to manage us. He came close enough to be stared at himself, stripped and gazed on by a crowd at a cross, so that people who are fully known could also be fully welcomed. Only a knower like that is safe to be seen by.

verseByVerse.quote: You hem me in, behind and before, and lay your hand upon me. Such knowledge is too wonderful for me; it is high; I cannot attain it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s knowledge surrounds David like a protecting hand, and it is too wonderful for him to grasp.

You hem me in, behind and before. “Hem me in” could sound like a prison, but the picture is protection: God behind, God in front, his hand resting on him, like a child walking between two parents with a hand on the shoulder. The one who knows everything about him has surrounded him.

Such knowledge is too wonderful for me. David tries to take in what it means to be known like this, and cannot: it is too high, beyond his reach. Paul reached the same limit: “Oh, the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and how inscrutable his ways!” (Romans 11:33). The right response to God’s knowledge is not to understand it fully, but to worship.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–12 — Where Shall I Flee from Your Presence?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: There is nowhere David could go to escape God’s presence, and at the end of every road he would find God’s guiding hand. He asks where he could flee from God’s Spirit (v. 7). Not up to heaven or down to Sheol, the realm of the dead (v. 8); not east with the dawn or to the far west across the sea, for even there God’s hand would lead and hold him (vv. 9–10). Not even the dark can hide him, because darkness is as light to God (vv. 11–12). What is a warning to the one who runs from God is a comfort to the one who is afraid of being lost.
verseByVerse.theology: There is nowhere, up, down, east, west or in the dark, where God is not.

verseByVerse.quote: Where shall I go from your Spirit? Or where shall I flee from your presence? If I ascend to heaven, you are there! If I make my bed in Sheol, you are there! If I take the wings of the morning and dwell in the uttermost parts of the sea, even there your hand shall lead me, and your right hand shall hold me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
There is nowhere David could run from God, and wherever he went he would find God’s hand there to lead and hold him.

Where shall I flee from your presence? From knowledge to presence; “your Spirit” and “your presence” stand side by side, for God is present by his Spirit. Jonah tried to get away. He “rose to flee to Tarshish from the presence of the LORD” and paid his fare on a ship (Jonah 1:3). God met him in the storm.

If I ascend to heaven, you are there! Up to the highest heaven, God is there; down to Sheol, the realm of the dead, God is there too. There is no vertical escape. “Do I not fill heaven and earth? declares the LORD” (Jeremiah 23:24).

The wings of the morning. Nor is there a horizontal escape: “the wings of the morning” is the dawn in the east, “the uttermost parts of the sea” the far west. Fly with the sunrise from east to west, and God is there when you land.

Your right hand shall hold me. What God does when David gets there is not arrest but guidance. The person who runs from God finds, at the end of the running, the same hand. Paul told the Athenians that God “is actually not far from each one of us”, for in him “we live and move and have our being” (Acts 17:27–28).

The God who comes after runaways. In Jesus the God from whom no one can flee came looking for those who had fled: “the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost” (Luke 19:10). No one has run so far that his hand cannot reach them.

verseByVerse.quote: If I say, "Surely the darkness shall cover me, and the light about me be night," even the darkness is not dark to you; the night is bright as the day, for darkness is as light with you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even the darkness cannot hide anyone from God: a warning to those who hide in it, a comfort to those lost in it.

Surely the darkness shall cover me. One last hiding place: the dark, where people do what they would never do in daylight, or disappear into despair.

Even the darkness is not dark to you. God does not need light to see; the dark is as clear to him as noon. That is a warning for anyone who thinks the night hides what they do, and a comfort for anyone in the darkness of grief, depression or fear: the darkness that hides everything from you hides nothing from God, including you. He sees you there as clearly as in daylight, and he has sent his light into it: “I am the light of the world” (John 8:12).

If the dark is depression. Tell someone: a pastor or biblical counsellor, and your doctor too, since there may be a physical cause, and medicine is no failure of faith. If you are thinking of ending your life, seek help the same day.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God knows David so completely because God made him, and planned every day of his life before it began. God formed his inward parts and knitted him together in his mother’s womb, and David praises him for being fearfully and wonderfully made (vv. 13–14). His frame was never hidden from God while it was being woven in secret; God’s eyes saw his unformed substance, and all his days were written in God’s book before one of them came (vv. 15–16). Overwhelmed, David calls God’s thoughts precious and more than the sand, and wakes to find God still with him (vv. 17–18).
verseByVerse.theology: Before anyone saw him, God was knitting him together and writing his days in a book.

verseByVerse.quote: For you formed my inward parts; you knitted me together in my mother's womb. I praise you, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made. Wonderful are your works; my soul knows it very well.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God knows David so completely because he made him in the womb, and David praises him for the awe-inspiring work.

You formed my inward parts. Now David explains why God knows him so completely: God made him. The “inward parts” (literally “kidneys”, in the Old Testament the seat of the hidden inner life) are the deepest organs, and God worked them together with bone and sinew as a craftsman knits. Job used the same image: “You clothed me with skin and flesh, and knit me together with bones and sinews” (Job 10:11).

You knitted me together in my mother’s womb. Every human being, before birth, was being made by God. This is why Christians have always held that life in the womb is precious: the unborn child is not a thing but someone God is knitting.

I am fearfully and wonderfully made. That is, made in a way that inspires awe. Many people struggle to say this, disliking their bodies, faces, weaknesses or disabilities. This verse does not say every body is perfect in a fallen world. It says every person was made with awe-inspiring care by God, and that this is a reason to praise him, not to despise ourselves.

The Son in the womb. God has honoured that hidden beginning in the highest way possible: the eternal Son was himself conceived and knit together in a mother’s womb (Luke 1:31, 35). He “had to be made like his brothers in every respect” (Hebrews 2:17), including the months no one sees.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew behind “fearfully and wonderfully made” is unusual; the ESV notes it may mean “fearfully set apart”. Either way the line praises God’s workmanship.
verseByVerse.note: “Inward parts” is literally “kidneys.”

verseByVerse.quote: My frame was not hidden from you, when I was being made in secret, intricately woven in the depths of the earth. Your eyes saw my unformed substance; in your book were written, every one of them, the days that were formed for me, when as yet there was none of them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God watched over David’s hidden beginning and wrote all his days in his book before the first of them came.

Intricately woven in the depths of the earth. “The depths of the earth” is a poetic way of saying hidden, beyond human sight. No one could see a child forming; God could. “Intricately woven” is like fine embroidery.

Your eyes saw my unformed substance. This is most likely the embryo, before it had any recognisable shape. God’s eyes were on it. And before any of David’s days had happened, “every one of them” was written in God’s book. God told Jeremiah, “Before I formed you in the womb I knew you” (Jeremiah 1:5), and Paul says God “chose us in him before the foundation of the world” (Ephesians 1:4).

No day unplanned. So no believer’s life is an accident, and no day of it, including the hard days, is unplanned by God. That is not fatalism (the idea that a blind fate rules us); it is the security of being in the hands of a God who knew you before you were. And notice where Paul says we were chosen: “in him”, in Christ. The one who holds the book of our days is the Lamb whose book of life holds his people’s names (Revelation 21:27).

When the days were few. What about a child lost by miscarriage or stillbirth, whose life ended before anyone but God had seen it? God’s eyes saw that unformed substance too; that child was known, written in his book, and is not forgotten. Scripture does not tell us all we would like to know, but the Westminster Confession and the 1689 London Baptist Confession both speak of elect infants dying in infancy as saved by Christ through the Spirit, and many grieving parents have taken comfort in David’s words about his infant son, “I shall go to him” (2 Samuel 12:23). Grief for such a child is love for a real person, and it may be brought to God without shame.

For a troubled conscience. If you read these verses with an abortion on your conscience, whether you chose it, pressed for it or performed it, the psalm is not here to crush you. The God who sees in the dark (v. 12) has seen it, and he forgives: “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:9). There is no sin the blood of Christ cannot wash away. Bring the grief and the guilt to him, and to a pastor or Christian friend who can walk with you.

Uncertain wording. “Unformed substance” translates a word found only here in the Old Testament, meaning something rolled up or not yet shaped; most take it of the embryo. “The depths of the earth” probably pictures the hidden womb, perhaps echoing man’s forming from the dust (Genesis 2:7).

verseByVerse.quote: How precious to me are your thoughts, O God! How vast is the sum of them! If I would count them, they are more than the sand. I awake, and I am still with you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
David is overwhelmed by God’s countless, precious thoughts toward him, and wakes to find God still with him.

How precious to me are your thoughts, O God! God has been thinking about David since before he was formed, and David, overwhelmed, calls those thoughts precious and uncountable, “more than the sand”.

I awake, and I am still with you. Perhaps he fell asleep counting God’s thoughts, and woke, and God was still there. Every morning a believer wakes into the presence of the God who never left during the night. And one day believers will wake from death itself and find him still with them: “so we will always be with the Lord” (1 Thessalonians 4:17).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–24 — Search Me, O God, and Know My Heart
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A man who loves God cannot be neutral toward those who hate him, but the same man asks God to search his own heart. David suddenly prays that God would slay the wicked, men of blood who speak against God with malice (vv. 19–20). He counts God’s enemies his own and hates them with complete hatred, out of loyalty to God rather than personal spite (vv. 21–22). Then, at once, he turns the searchlight on himself: search me, try me, see if there is any grievous way in me, and lead me in the way everlasting (vv. 23–24). What was a fact in verse 1 has become a prayer.
verseByVerse.theology: Zeal against God's enemies turns at once into a prayer that God would examine his own heart.

verseByVerse.quote: Oh that you would slay the wicked, O God! O men of blood, depart from me! They speak against you with malicious intent; your enemies take your name in vain. Do I not hate those who hate you, O LORD? And do I not loathe those who rise up against you? I hate them with complete hatred; I count them my enemies.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Loving God, David cannot be neutral toward murderous men who defy him, and counts them his own enemies.

Oh that you would slay the wicked, O God! After such tender verses the turn is abrupt, but connected. A man overwhelmed by the goodness of God cannot be neutral toward those who speak against that God “with malicious intent”. The more you love God, the more his enemies’ contempt for him grieves you.

Do I not hate those who hate you, O LORD? This is not personal spite; David does not say they have wronged him. It is loyalty: God’s enemies are his enemies. It is the same instinct as “O you who love the LORD, hate evil!” (Psalm 97:10).

Christ’s zeal and Christ’s mercy. Jesus shared this zeal: his disciples remembered, “Zeal for your house will consume me” (John 2:17). Yet the one who hated evil most perfectly wept over those who rejected him and died for his enemies (Romans 5:10).

How does a Christian hold this? The New Testament keeps both sides. “Abhor what is evil” (Romans 12:9): never make peace with rebellion against God. And “Bless those who persecute you; bless and do not curse them” (Romans 12:14): love the persons and pray for their salvation (see the introduction on the psalms that curse). The hatred of this psalm is directed at settled, bloody opposition to God, and it is immediately followed by something that keeps it from turning into self-righteousness.

Uncertain wording. The ESV notes that “your name” in verse 20 is not in the Hebrew, which reads more literally “your enemies take in vain”; it is supplied because the phrase echoes the third commandment (Exodus 20:7). The sense is clear: they treat God with contempt.
