In verse 14 the word for cattle can also mean chiefs (Genesis 36:15), and the ESV notes that part of the verse is literally with no breaking in or going out: cattle bearing without loss, or a city with no breach in its walls and no captives led into exile. Either way the picture is of a land at peace.

144.title: Blessed Are the People Whose God Is the LORD
144.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 144 follows David’s four prayers under attack (140–143) with a king’s prayer for victory and peace. It stands just before Psalm 145, the last psalm of David, and the run of praise that closes the book.

The message. The God who trains the king’s hands and rescues him is the true strength and blessing of his people. A king who is only a breath asks the God of the storm to come down and rescue him from lying enemies, promises a new song, and prays for the peace that follows victory: flourishing children, full barns, safe streets. But the psalm ends on a blessing greater than all of these: to have the LORD as your God.

Why it was said. Israel’s king fought real wars against nations who broke their treaties and their oaths (see the introduction). The psalm taught king and people that victory comes from God, that even a king is mortal, and that prosperity is a gift to pray for, not the heart of their blessing.

How the chapter makes its case. David blesses the LORD, who trains his hands and is his steadfast love and fortress (vv. 1–2), then marvels that God takes notice of man, a breath and a passing shadow (vv. 3–4). He asks God to come down in storm and fire and rescue him from the many waters and from lying foreigners (vv. 5–8), vows a new song to the God who rescues David his servant, and repeats his plea (vv. 9–11). Then the prayer looks beyond the battle to sons and daughters flourishing, granaries full, flocks and herds increasing and no cry of distress in the streets (vv. 12–14), and ends with a double blessing whose second line outranks the first (v. 15).

Where it leads. By promise and by covenant. God promised David a son whose throne would last for ever (2 Samuel 7:12–16), and Jesus, “the son of David” (Matthew 1:1), won his victory not with trained fingers but by the cross (Colossians 2:15), and was rescued not from death but out of it. The prayer that God would bow the heavens and come down was answered more deeply than David knew, when the Son said, “I have come down from heaven” (John 6:38). And the last line is the covenant’s heart, fulfilled when “God himself will be with them as their God” (Revelation 21:3).

For us. Thank God for every skill you have; he trained your hands. Remember that you are a breath, and marvel that he cares for you. Pray for the families, work and streets of your town. And whatever you have or lose, hold on to the one blessing no enemy can take: the LORD is your God.
144.theology:
Skill and victory are God's gifts (vv. 1-2, 10; 1 Sam 17:45); the psalm reuses Psalm 18, a prayer shaped by Scripture.

God's attention to mortal man is a wonder (vv. 3-4; 8:4; Heb 2:6). The God who came down in storm is asked to come again (vv. 5-8; 18:9; 104:32), and a new rescue calls for a new song (v. 9).

The promise to David his servant (v. 10) is fulfilled in Jesus, the Son of David, who triumphed through the cross (Col 2:15). Peace, prosperity and flourishing families are real blessings to pray for, not guarantees (vv. 12-14), but the supreme blessing is to have the LORD as God (v. 15).
144.examples: Whatever a believer's work, surgery, carpentry or teaching, the skill in the fingers is God's training, and the thanks belong to him. A Christian can pray verses 12 to 14 for a town and its families. But a church that has lost much, or a family whose barns are empty, can still say the last line: blessed are the people whose God is the LORD.

keyVerse.quote: Blessed are the people to whom such blessings fall! Blessed are the people whose God is the LORD!
keyVerse.note: The psalm’s last line weighs every blessing in it. Victory, children, harvests and safe streets are good gifts, but the supreme blessing is the covenant itself, to have the LORD as your God. It is the one blessing no enemy can take, and in Christ it is offered to people of every nation.

144.reflection:
David credits God with training his hands and giving his victories (vv. 1–2, 10). Which of your own skills or successes do you most easily treat as your own, and what would it look like to thank God for them specifically?

Verses 3–4 set God’s care beside human frailty: we are a breath and a passing shadow. How can facing your own mortality make God’s attention to you more wonderful rather than more frightening?

David asks God to bow the heavens and come down (v. 5). How did God answer that prayer in Jesus, in a way David could not have imagined?

Verse 15 sets two blessings side by side. If you lost the blessings of verses 12–14, would you still count yourself blessed? How can a church help its members, and its town, see the difference?

145.text: A Song of Praise. Of David. 1I will extol you, my God and King, and bless your name forever and ever.2Every day I will bless you and praise your name forever and ever.3Great is the LORD, and greatly to be praised, and his greatness is unsearchable.4One generation shall commend your works to another, and shall declare your mighty acts.5On the glorious splendor of your majesty, and on your wondrous works, I will meditate.6They shall speak of the might of your awesome deeds, and I will declare your greatness.7They shall pour forth the fame of your abundant goodness and shall sing aloud of your righteousness.8The LORD is gracious and merciful, slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love.9The LORD is good to all, and his mercy is over all that he has made.10All your works shall give thanks to you, O LORD, and all your saints shall bless you!11They shall speak of the glory of your kingdom and tell of your power,12to make known to the children of man your mighty deeds, and the glorious splendor of your kingdom.13Your kingdom is an everlasting kingdom, and your dominion endures throughout all generations. [The LORD is faithful in all his words and kind in all his works.]14The LORD upholds all who are falling and raises up all who are bowed down.15The eyes of all look to you, and you give them their food in due season.16You open your hand; you satisfy the desire of every living thing.17The LORD is righteous in all his ways and kind in all his works.18The LORD is near to all who call on him, to all who call on him in truth.19He fulfills the desire of those who fear him; he also hears their cry and saves them.20The LORD preserves all who love him, but all the wicked he will destroy.21My mouth will speak the praise of the LORD, and let all flesh bless his holy name forever and ever.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — I Will Extol You, My God and King
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David vows to praise God every day and for ever, because his greatness can never be fully searched out. He opens with a double vow, to extol and bless his God and King daily and endlessly (vv. 1–2), and gives the reason: the LORD is great and his greatness is unsearchable, so praise will never run out of things to say (v. 3). Then the praise spreads outwards. One generation tells the next of God’s mighty acts, while David himself quietly meditates on them, so that private wonder and public celebration feed each other until the people pour out the fame of his goodness and sing of his righteousness (vv. 4–7).
verseByVerse.theology: David's last psalm opens with praise every day and forever, passed from one generation to the next.

verseByVerse.quote: I will extol you, my God and King, and bless your name forever and ever. Every day I will bless you and praise your name forever and ever. Great is the LORD, and greatly to be praised, and his greatness is unsearchable.
verseByVerse.commentary:
David, himself a king, vows daily and endless praise to God his King, whose greatness no one will ever fully search out.

A Song of Praise. The last psalm with David’s name on it is the only one with this title, and David, who sat on Israel’s throne, calls God my God and King. It is an acrostic (as the ESV notes, each verse begins with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet): praise from A to Z. After it come five psalms (146–150) that each begin and end with Praise the LORD! The Psalter is gathering itself into a final crescendo, and David leads it off.

Every day I will bless you. Every day and forever: praise is not only for festivals or good days; it is daily, and it will never end. The daily habit is practice for eternity.

His greatness is unsearchable. No one will ever reach the bottom of it. Isaiah says the same of the Creator: “his understanding is unsearchable” (Isaiah 40:28),. Forever will not be long enough to explore him, which is why praise forever will never grow dull.
verseByVerse.note: The Hebrew behind “Praise the LORD” in Psalms 146 to 150 is hallelu-yah, the source of the word hallelujah.

verseByVerse.quote: One generation shall commend your works to another, and shall declare your mighty acts. On the glorious splendor of your majesty, and on your wondrous works, I will meditate. They shall speak of the might of your awesome deeds, and I will declare your greatness. They shall pour forth the fame of your abundant goodness and shall sing aloud of your righteousness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Praise is handed down the generations, and quiet meditation and loud celebration of God’s works feed each other.

One generation shall commend your works to another. Psalm 78 made this the purpose of Israel’s history: to “tell to the coming generation the glorious deeds of the LORD” (Psalm 78:4). The faith of a family or a church lives on when one generation deliberately tells the next what God has done.

Private and public praise. The lines alternate: I will meditate, they shall speak; I will declare, they shall pour forth. David ponders God’s works quietly; the congregation talks about them loudly. Pour forth is the word for a spring bubbling up: praise that cannot be held in.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–13 — Your Kingdom Is an Everlasting Kingdom
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: At the heart of the psalm stands God’s own description of himself, and from it flows praise from all he has made. The LORD is gracious and merciful, slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love, the name he proclaimed to Moses at Sinai (v. 8), and his goodness and mercy reach over everything he has made (v. 9). So all his works give thanks, and his saints do more: they speak of the glory of his kingdom so that all humanity may know it (vv. 10–12). Unlike every earthly throne, this kingdom is everlasting (v. 13).
verseByVerse.theology: The King whose kingdom lasts forever is gracious, merciful and good to everything he has made.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD is gracious and merciful, slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love. The LORD is good to all, and his mercy is over all that he has made.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the centre of the psalm is God’s own name, gracious, merciful, patient and full of steadfast love, and his goodness covers all he has made.

The LORD is gracious and merciful. This is the name God proclaimed to Moses on the mountain: “a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness” (Exodus 34:6). Few descriptions of God are repeated more often in the Old Testament, and of everything that could be said about the great King, this is what David wants remembered.

The LORD is good to all. Not only to Israel, not only to believers. God “makes his sun rise on the evil and on the good, and sends rain on the just and on the unjust” (Matthew 5:45). His mercy spreads over all that he has made like a canopy, and every meal an unbeliever eats is a gift of his goodness. Theologians call this common grace, the kindness God shows to everyone, believer or not, and it gives everyone a reason to praise him.

The name with a face. Spoken on Sinai, this name was lived among us in the Word made flesh, “full of grace and truth” (John 1:14). Watch Jesus with lepers, prostitutes and slow disciples, and you see what “gracious and merciful, slow to anger” looks like in a human life.

verseByVerse.quote: All your works shall give thanks to you, O LORD, and all your saints shall bless you! They shall speak of the glory of your kingdom and tell of your power, to make known to the children of man your mighty deeds, and the glorious splendor of your kingdom. Your kingdom is an everlasting kingdom, and your dominion endures throughout all generations. [The LORD is faithful in all his words and kind in all his works.]
verseByVerse.commentary:
All creation thanks God, but his people also tell the world of his kingdom, which, unlike every other, will never end.

All your saints shall bless you! All creation gives thanks; the saints, God’s own people, do more: they speak and tell, so that the children of man, everyone, will know. (The ESV notes the Hebrew says “his mighty deeds” and “his kingdom”, as though the saints turn from addressing God to telling others about him.) Praising God and telling others about him belong together.

Your kingdom is an everlasting kingdom. Every earthly kingdom ends; David’s did. This one does not. Nebuchadnezzar, humbled, confessed the same words: “His kingdom is an everlasting kingdom” (Daniel 4:3). At the last trumpet heaven announces, “The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ, and he shall reign forever and ever” (Revelation 11:15).

Textual note. The ESV prints two more lines here in brackets, The LORD is faithful in all his words and kind in all his works, and notes that they are supplied by one Hebrew manuscript and the ancient Greek and Syriac translations (compare the Dead Sea Scroll). In most Hebrew manuscripts the verse for one letter of the alphabet (nun) is missing from this acrostic, and these lines appear to fill the gap. Whether original or not, they say nothing the psalm does not say elsewhere (compare v. 17).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–21 — The LORD Is Near to All Who Call on Him
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The everlasting King uses his power to stoop down: to hold up, feed, draw near and save. He upholds the falling and lifts the bowed down (v. 14); every creature looks to him and he opens his hand to feed it (vv. 15–16). He is righteous and kind in all he does, near to all who call on him in truth, fulfilling the desire of those who fear him and hearing their cry (vv. 17–19). He preserves those who love him and will destroy the wicked (v. 20). David ends where he began, with his own mouth praising, and calls all flesh to join him for ever (v. 21).
verseByVerse.theology: The great King stoops to hold up the falling, feed every creature, and come near to everyone who calls.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD upholds all who are falling and raises up all who are bowed down. The eyes of all look to you, and you give them their food in due season. You open your hand; you satisfy the desire of every living thing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The everlasting King stoops to hold up the falling, lift the bowed down and feed every creature from his open hand.

The LORD upholds all who are falling. The most tender verse in the psalm: the King of eternity reaches down to all who are falling, stumbling, collapsing, going under, and holds them up; all who are bowed down, bent double under grief, shame or burdens, he lifts. If you are falling today, this verse is yours.

The hand that caught Peter. The disciples saw this verse with their own eyes. When Peter began to sink in the waves and cried out, “Jesus immediately reached out his hand and took hold of him” (Matthew 14:31). Peter later wrote, “casting all your anxieties on him, because he cares for you” (1 Peter 5:7).

You open your hand. The picture comes from Psalm 104: every creature looking to God, and God opening his hand (Psalm 104:27–28). You satisfy the desire of every living thing. The great King is also the one who feeds the sparrows (Matthew 6:26).

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD is righteous in all his ways and kind in all his works. The LORD is near to all who call on him, to all who call on him in truth. He fulfills the desire of those who fear him; he also hears their cry and saves them. The LORD preserves all who love him, but all the wicked he will destroy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD is just and kind in all he does, near to all who sincerely call on him and saving those who fear him, but he will destroy the wicked.

Righteous in all his ways and kind in all his works. Justice and love together, in all his ways. Nothing God does is right but unkind, or kind but unjust.

The LORD is near to all who call on him. Here is the promise for anyone who feels far from God. He is near to all who call on him, with no exceptions for background, failure or unworthiness. The one condition is in truth: genuinely, not as a performance. Paul gives the gospel form of the promise: “everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved” (Romans 10:13).

All the wicked he will destroy. The psalm is honest that God’s goodness includes judgment; his kindness is not indifference to evil. He is good to all in this age (v. 9), but that is not the end of the story: the final judgment is real and everlasting (Matthew 25:46; 2 Thessalonians 1:9).

Does God give believers whatever they want? Those who fear him come to desire what he wills, and he fulfils those desires in his time and way. “If we ask anything according to his will he hears us” (1 John 5:14); unanswered prayer is not a broken promise.

verseByVerse.quote: My mouth will speak the praise of the LORD, and let all flesh bless his holy name forever and ever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
David ends with his own mouth praising, and calls all flesh to join him for ever.

My mouth will speak the praise of the LORD. These are David’s last words in the Psalter. He began with I will extol you and ends with my mouth will speak, but in between the circle has grown to include every generation, all creation and all flesh.

Let all flesh bless his holy name. The shepherd boy who became a king, who sinned and was forgiven, who wept in caves and danced before the ark, finishes his psalms with a call for every living creature to praise God for ever. The next five psalms answer that call.

145.title: Great Is the LORD and Greatly to Be Praised
145.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 145 is the last psalm that bears David’s name, and the only one titled “A Song of Praise”. It follows his prayer for rescue and blessing in Psalm 144 and opens the door to the five Hallelujah psalms (146–150) with which the whole book ends in praise.

The message. The God who reigns as King for ever is great beyond anything we will ever search out, and the heart of his greatness is his grace. He is gracious and merciful, good to all he has made, and he stoops to hold up the falling, feed every creature and come near to anyone who calls on him in truth. Such a King deserves praise every day, from every generation and from all flesh.

Why it was said. Israel needed to know what kind of King stood behind the throne of David, a throne that would one day be empty (see the introduction). The psalm teaches the congregation to praise in an orderly, complete way: it is an acrostic, each verse beginning with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet, praise from A to Z.

How the chapter makes its case. David vows daily, endless praise to his unsearchably great King, and pictures each generation telling the next of his works (vv. 1–7). At the centre he gives God’s own name from Sinai, gracious and merciful, slow to anger, abounding in steadfast love, and widens it to all creation; then the saints tell the nations of his everlasting kingdom (vv. 8–13). Next, what the King does with his power: he upholds the falling, opens his hand to feed every living thing, is near to all who call on him, and preserves those who love him, while the wicked will be destroyed (vv. 14–20). Finally David’s own mouth and all flesh bless his holy name for ever (v. 21).

Where it leads. Chiefly by the character of God revealed in Christ, and by the promise of an everlasting kingdom. The name proclaimed to Moses, “merciful and gracious”, took flesh in the Son, “full of grace and truth” (John 1:14). The King who “upholds all who are falling” reached out his hand to sinking Peter, and the everlasting kingdom is the one the angel promised to David’s greater Son: “of his kingdom there will be no end” (Luke 1:33).

For us. Praise is not for good days only; it is a daily habit that rehearses eternity. Tell your children and your church what God has done. And if you are falling, or bowed down, or feel far from God, the word in this psalm is “all”: the LORD is near to all who call on him in truth, and in Christ he has come near to you.
145.theology:
Praise is daily and eternal (vv. 1-2), because God's greatness is unsearchable (v. 3; Isa 40:28), and it is passed down the generations (v. 4; 78:4).

The heart of God's character is the name revealed to Moses (v. 8; Exod 34:6). His goodness extends to all creation (v. 9; Matt 5:45). His kingdom is everlasting (v. 13; Dan 4:3; Rev 11:15).

The eternal King stoops to uphold the falling and feed every creature (vv. 14-16; 1 Pet 5:7), is near to all who call on him in truth (v. 18; Rom 10:13), as Jesus showed when he caught the sinking Peter (Matt 14:31), and preserves those who love him while judging the wicked (v. 20).
145.examples: A family that tells its children at the table what God has done is doing what verse 4 describes. Anyone falling under grief or shame can take verse 14 as spoken to him. And anyone who feels too far gone may notice the word all in verse 18: the LORD is near to all who call on him in truth.

keyVerse.quote: The LORD is gracious and merciful, slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love.
keyVerse.note: This verse stands at the centre of David’s last psalm and gives the reason for all its praise. It is the name God proclaimed to Moses at Sinai (Exodus 34:6), and of all that could be said about the great King, this is what David wants every generation to remember. In Jesus, “full of grace and truth” (John 1:14), that name took flesh.

145.reflection:
David vows to praise God “every day” (v. 2), not only on good days. What would daily praise look like in your life, and what most often crowds it out?

Verse 4 pictures one generation telling the next of God’s works. Who told you? What has God done that you could deliberately tell a child, a newer believer or a younger friend this week?

The centre of the psalm is that the LORD is “gracious and merciful, slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love” (v. 8). Which part of that description do you find hardest to believe about God for yourself, and where do you see it most clearly in Jesus?

“The LORD upholds all who are falling” and “The LORD is near to all who call on him” (vv. 14, 18). How could this psalm shape the way you pray for, and speak to, someone who feels they are falling or far from God?

146.text: <sup>1</sup>Praise the LORD! Praise the LORD, O my soul!<sup>2</sup>I will praise the LORD as long as I live; I will sing praises to my God while I have my being.<sup>3</sup>Put not your trust in princes, in a son of man, in whom there is no salvation.<sup>4</sup>When his breath departs, he returns to the earth; on that very day his plans perish.<sup>5</sup>Blessed is he whose help is the God of Jacob, whose hope is in the LORD his God,<sup>6</sup>who made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that is in them, who keeps faith forever;<sup>7</sup>who executes justice for the oppressed, who gives food to the hungry. The LORD sets the prisoners free;<sup>8</sup>the LORD opens the eyes of the blind. The LORD lifts up those who are bowed down; the LORD loves the righteous.<sup>9</sup>The LORD watches over the sojourners; he upholds the widow and the fatherless, but the way of the wicked he brings to ruin.<sup>10</sup>The LORD will reign forever, your God, O Zion, to all generations. Praise the LORD!

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — As Long as I Live
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Praise God for as long as you live, and do not put your hope in mortal rulers. The psalm opens with the first of the closing hallelujahs and a vow of lifelong praise (vv. 1–2). Then, before the reasons for praise, comes a warning: do not trust princes, the powerful people who seem able to fix things, for they are only sons of men and there is no salvation in them (v. 3). Their breath leaves them, their bodies return to the dust, and on that very day all their plans die with them (v. 4).
verseByVerse.theology: A lifelong vow of praise, and a warning against trusting anyone whose breath can stop.

verseByVerse.quote: Praise the LORD! Praise the LORD, O my soul! I will praise the LORD as long as I live; I will sing praises to my God while I have my being.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The first of the Psalter’s closing hallelujahs is a personal vow to praise the LORD with every breath of life.

Praise the LORD! The Psalter closes with five psalms (146–150), and every one begins and ends with Praise the LORD! (in Hebrew, hallelujah). The book that held so many laments, tears and questions ends in an unbroken wave of praise. This first one begins, like Psalms 103 and 104, by speaking to the soul.

As long as I live. Verse 2 makes the same vow as Psalm 104:33. Not a mood but a lifetime commitment: praise is how the singer means to spend every breath he has, and the next verse will say how few those breaths are.

verseByVerse.quote: Put not your trust in princes, in a son of man, in whom there is no salvation. When his breath departs, he returns to the earth; on that very day his plans perish.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not stake your hope on powerful people: they die, and their plans die with them.

Put not your trust in princes. A warning at the start of the great praise. Princes are the powerful, the people who seem able to fix things, but there is no salvation in them. Psalm 118 said it: “It is better to take refuge in the LORD than to trust in princes” (Psalm 118:9). Jeremiah said it more severely: “Cursed is the man who trusts in man and makes flesh his strength” (Jeremiah 17:5).

On that very day his plans perish. Every prince is a son of man, mortal. One day his breath stops, his body goes back to the earth, and the great programmes and promised reforms people were counting on die with him. That is a word for every generation that hopes in a political leader, a movement, a celebrity or an expert. They may do real good; they cannot be your salvation. Their breath is borrowed.

The Prince whose plans did not perish. Every prince’s breath departs, and Christ’s did too. Then he rose, and “he always lives to make intercession” for his people (Hebrews 7:25). His plans do not perish on any day. That frees you to work hard for good government without needing it to save you.

What this looks like. Trusting princes rarely looks like worship; it looks like what you lean on. Watch your mood at election time. If a result leaves you elated or in despair for weeks, you were hoping in a son of man. Vote and campaign as a citizen, and pray “for kings and all who are in high positions” (1 Timothy 2:2), but not as one whose future hangs on them. Notice whom you go to first. The specialist, the manager who controls your promotion, the expert on the news: listen to them and respect them, and still take the matter to God first. Do not court the powerful. Refuse the small flatteries and silences that keep you in favour with the people who can help you.

Uncertain wording. The word translated plans occurs only here in the Old Testament. It comes from a root meaning to think, so it refers to a person’s thoughts, schemes or intentions; “plans” is the likely sense, and the point is clear either way.
verseByVerse.note: He returns to the earth echoes the sentence on Adam: to dust you shall return (Gen 3:19).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–10 — Blessed Is He Whose Help Is the God of Jacob
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Blessed is the one who trusts the living God, because he made everything, keeps faith for ever and uses his power for the helpless. The God of Jacob is the true help: Creator of heaven, earth and sea, who never breaks his word (vv. 5–6). The psalm then names what he does, a line at a time: justice for the oppressed, food for the hungry, freedom for prisoners, sight for the blind, lifting for the bowed down, love for the righteous, protection for the stranger, the widow and the orphan, and ruin for the wicked (vv. 7–9). Princes die; the LORD reigns for ever (v. 10).
verseByVerse.theology: The God who made everything spends his power on the oppressed, the hungry, the blind and the orphan.

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed is he whose help is the God of Jacob, whose hope is in the LORD his God, who made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that is in them, who keeps faith forever; who executes justice for the oppressed, who gives food to the hungry. The LORD sets the prisoners free;
verseByVerse.commentary:
Truly happy is the one who relies on the God of Jacob, the faithful Creator who takes the side of the oppressed.

Whose help is the God of Jacob. Here is the alternative. Blessed is the person whose help is not a prince but the God of Jacob, the God who stuck with a flawed and scheming man. This God made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that is in them; he is not a son of man whose breath departs. And he keeps faith forever. Princes’ plans perish on the day they die; God’s promises never do.

Who executes justice for the oppressed. What this Creator does with his power is not what princes usually do. He takes the side of the people at the bottom: justice for the oppressed, food to the hungry, freedom for prisoners.

verseByVerse.quote: the LORD opens the eyes of the blind. The LORD lifts up those who are bowed down; the LORD loves the righteous. The LORD watches over the sojourners; he upholds the widow and the fatherless, but the way of the wicked he brings to ruin. The LORD will reign forever, your God, O Zion, to all generations. Praise the LORD!
verseByVerse.commentary:
It is the LORD, again and again, who lifts and protects the helpless and ruins the wicked, and he will reign for ever.

The LORD opens the eyes of the blind. The LORD, again and again: five times from the end of verse 7 to verse 9,, hammering home who does these things. He opens blind eyes. He lifts people bent double under their burdens. He loves the righteous. He watches over foreigners with no one to protect them, and holds up widows and orphans. And the wicked, who prey on all these people, he brings to ruin.

The God of Psalm 146 in Galilee. Read that list and think of Jesus. When John the Baptist, in prison, sent to ask whether Jesus was the promised one, Jesus answered with this kind of list: “the blind receive their sight and the lame walk, lepers are cleansed and the deaf hear, and the dead are raised up, and the poor have good news preached to them” (Matthew 11:5). In the synagogue at Nazareth he said he had come “to proclaim liberty to the captives and recovering of sight to the blind” (Luke 4:18). The God of Psalm 146 walked the roads of Galilee doing Psalm 146.

He upholds the widow and the fatherless. Those he has set free are to do the same, as people who were once the prisoners and the blind. “Religion that is pure and undefiled before God the Father is this: to visit orphans and widows in their affliction” (James 1:27). A church that praises this God and ignores the widow and the stranger has not understood the psalm.

The LORD will reign forever. Princes reign a few years and die: the final reason to trust him instead. Praise the LORD!

146.title: Put Not Your Trust in Princes
146.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 145 ended with David calling “all flesh” to bless God’s holy name for ever. Psalm 146 is the first answer: the first of five closing psalms (146–150) that each begin and end with “Praise the LORD!”, the Hebrew hallelujah.

The message. Do not stake your life on powerful people, who die and take their plans with them. Trust the living God instead: he made everything, he keeps his promises for ever, and he spends his power on the people the powerful overlook, the oppressed, the hungry, the prisoner, the blind, the stranger, the widow and the orphan. He alone will reign for ever, so praise him for as long as you live.

Why it was said. Israel knew the failure of princes all too well: kings who led them into idolatry, foreign rulers who crushed them, and protectors who could not save them from exile (see the introduction). A small, weak people was always tempted to look for safety in the next strong man or the next alliance. This psalm teaches them, and us, where real help is found.

How the chapter makes its case. The singer vows lifelong praise (vv. 1–2), then warns against trusting princes, mortal men whose breath departs and whose plans perish the same day (vv. 3–4). Over against them stands the blessed person whose help is the God of Jacob (v. 5): the Creator of heaven, earth and sea, who keeps faith for ever (v. 6), and who acts, in a rush of short lines each beginning with “the LORD”, for the oppressed, the hungry, the prisoners, the blind, the bowed down, the righteous, the sojourner, the widow and the fatherless, while bringing the way of the wicked to ruin (vv. 7–9). He will reign for ever; praise the LORD (v. 10).

Where it leads. By the character of God revealed in Christ. When John the Baptist asked from prison whether Jesus was the one, Jesus answered with a list very like this psalm’s: the blind see, the poor hear good news (Matthew 11:5). The God of Psalm 146 walked the roads of Galilee doing Psalm 146. And he is the one Prince whose plans did not perish on the day his breath departed, for he rose and reigns for ever.

For us. Respect leaders and pray for them, but do not hope in them; the risen Christ is the only King who cannot die. And a church that sings this psalm should be found where this God is found: beside the widow, the stranger, the prisoner and the hungry.
146.theology:
Praise is a lifelong vow (vv. 1-2; 104:33). Human rulers cannot save, because they are mortal and their plans die with them (vv. 3-4; 118:9; Jer 17:5).

The eternal Creator who keeps faith forever is the true help (vv. 5-6), and he uses his power for the oppressed, hungry, imprisoned, blind, bowed down, foreigner, widow and orphan (vv. 7-9). Jesus did these works as signs of who he was (Matt 11:5; Luke 4:18), and his people are to imitate them (Jas 1:27). His reign is everlasting (v. 10).
146.examples: When a new leader seems to promise everything, verse 3 steadies us: leaders may do real good, but they cannot be anyone's salvation. And a church singing this psalm can ask who in its own town are the hungry, the prisoners, the strangers and the widows.

keyVerse.quote: Blessed is he whose help is the God of Jacob, whose hope is in the LORD his God,
keyVerse.note: This is the hinge of the psalm. After the warning against trusting mortal princes (vv. 3–4), it names the only help that cannot die, and everything after it describes who this God is and what he does. The happy person is not the one with powerful friends but the one whose hope rests on the faithful God of Jacob.

146.reflection:
Verses 3–4 warn against trusting princes. Apart from politicians, who are the “princes” you are most tempted to lean on: an employer, a doctor, an expert, a celebrity, a spouse? How can you respect them without making them your salvation?

The psalm calls God “the God of Jacob” (v. 5), a flawed and scheming man. Why is that name an encouragement to people who know their own failures?

Verses 7–9 list the people God helps: the oppressed, the hungry, prisoners, the blind, the bowed down, sojourners, widows and the fatherless. Jesus did these very works (Matthew 11:5). Who in your town or church fits this list, and what could your group do for them?

“The LORD will reign forever” (v. 10). How does Christ’s resurrection and everlasting reign free us to work hard for good government without being crushed when it fails?

147.text: <sup>1</sup>Praise the LORD! For it is good to sing praises to our God; for it is pleasant, and a song of praise is fitting.<sup>2</sup>The LORD builds up Jerusalem; he gathers the outcasts of Israel.<sup>3</sup>He heals the brokenhearted and binds up their wounds.<sup>4</sup>He determines the number of the stars; he gives to all of them their names.<sup>5</sup>Great is our Lord, and abundant in power; his understanding is beyond measure.<sup>6</sup>The LORD lifts up the humble; he casts the wicked to the ground.<sup>7</sup>Sing to the LORD with thanksgiving; make melody to our God on the lyre!<sup>8</sup>He covers the heavens with clouds; he prepares rain for the earth; he makes grass grow on the hills.<sup>9</sup>He gives to the beasts their food, and to the young ravens that cry.<sup>10</sup>His delight is not in the strength of the horse, nor his pleasure in the legs of a man,<sup>11</sup>but the LORD takes pleasure in those who fear him, in those who hope in his steadfast love.<sup>12</sup>Praise the LORD, O Jerusalem! Praise your God, O Zion!<sup>13</sup>For he strengthens the bars of your gates; he blesses your children within you.<sup>14</sup>He makes peace in your borders; he fills you with the finest of the wheat.<sup>15</sup>He sends out his command to the earth; his word runs swiftly.<sup>16</sup>He gives snow like wool; he scatters frost like ashes.<sup>17</sup>He hurls down his crystals of ice like crumbs; who can stand before his cold?<sup>18</sup>He sends out his word, and melts them; he makes his wind blow and the waters flow.<sup>19</sup>He declares his word to Jacob, his statutes and rules to Israel.<sup>20</sup>He has not dealt thus with any other nation; they do not know his rules. Praise the LORD!

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — He Determines the Number of the Stars
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Praise is right and lovely, because the God who rebuilds cities and heals broken hearts is the same God who numbers the stars. The psalm opens by saying that praise is good, pleasant and fitting (v. 1). Its first reasons are tender: the LORD rebuilds Jerusalem, gathers its scattered outcasts, and binds up the wounds of the brokenhearted (vv. 2–3). Then it looks up: he counts the stars and names every one, for his power is great and his understanding beyond counting (vv. 4–5). He uses that power to lift the humble and bring the wicked down (v. 6).
verseByVerse.theology: The God who counts and names the stars bends down to bandage broken hearts.

verseByVerse.quote: Praise the LORD! For it is good to sing praises to our God; for it is pleasant, and a song of praise is fitting. The LORD builds up Jerusalem; he gathers the outcasts of Israel. He heals the brokenhearted and binds up their wounds.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Praise is right and delightful, for the LORD gathers his scattered people and heals broken hearts.

It is good to sing praises to our God. Three reasons to praise, all about praise itself. It is good, that is, right. It is pleasant, a joy. And it is fitting, the natural response to who God is. Praise is not an unnatural duty; it is what a creature was made for.

The LORD builds up Jerusalem. A city rebuilt, and people who had been scattered and cast out brought home. Very likely the psalm celebrates the return from exile and the rebuilding of Jerusalem’s walls. God is a builder of ruins and a gatherer of outcasts.

He heals the brokenhearted. Then, at once, the most personal kind of healing: God heals the brokenhearted, crushed by grief or betrayal, and binds up their wounds like a nurse wrapping a bandage. He does not only rebuild cities; he tends individual wounds.

He came in person to do it. Isaiah promised an anointed one whom the LORD would send “to bind up the brokenhearted” (Isaiah 61:1). Jesus stood up in the synagogue at Nazareth, read from that passage, and said, “Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing” (Luke 4:21).

Two psalms in the Greek. The Greek Old Testament, the Septuagint, divides this psalm into two, so some older Bibles that follow its numbering count verses 12–20 as a separate psalm; from Psalm 148 the numbers agree again.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew of for it is pleasant is brief and can be read two ways: praise is pleasant, or, as the ESV notes, “for he is beautiful” (or gracious). Both fit, and both are true: praise is a delight because the God we praise is delightful.

verseByVerse.quote: He determines the number of the stars; he gives to all of them their names. Great is our Lord, and abundant in power; his understanding is beyond measure. The LORD lifts up the humble; he casts the wicked to the ground.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The God who names every star stoops to the brokenhearted, and uses his limitless power for the humble.

He determines the number of the stars. Straight after the bandages, the psalm looks up at the night sky, at stars beyond counting. Isaiah said, “Lift up your eyes on high and see: who created these? He who brings out their host by number, calling them all by name” (Isaiah 40:26).

Stars and broken hearts. Put verses 3 and 4 side by side. The one who knows every star by name knows your broken heart, and stoops to bandage it. His greatness does not make him too big to care; it makes his care unlimited. Jesus said, “even the hairs of your head are all numbered” (Matthew 10:30).

His understanding is beyond measure. Literally “without number”, using the same word as the number of the stars in verse 4: his understanding cannot be counted. And he uses his power to lift up the humble (the ESV notes “afflicted”) and bring down the wicked.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–11 — The LORD Takes Pleasure in Those Who Fear Him
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God provides for every creature, and what delights him is not strength but trust. A second call to sing and play to God (v. 7) leads into a chain of provision: clouds, rain, grass on the hills, food for the animals, and even for the squawking young ravens (vv. 8–9). Then comes a contrast. The war horse and the strong legs of a soldier, the things the world admires, give him no pleasure (v. 10). He takes pleasure in those who fear him and hope in his steadfast love (v. 11).
verseByVerse.theology: God feeds the ravens and is not impressed by strength; he delights in those who hope in his love.

verseByVerse.quote: Sing to the LORD with thanksgiving; make melody to our God on the lyre! He covers the heavens with clouds; he prepares rain for the earth; he makes grass grow on the hills. He gives to the beasts their food, and to the young ravens that cry.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God feeds every creature, even the squawking young ravens, so he will surely hear his children’s cry.

The young ravens that cry. A second call to praise brings the whole chain of provision (clouds, rain, grass, food), each link something God does, and a detail easy to miss. Ravens were unclean birds, scavengers, of no value to anyone, and their chicks squawk in the nest. God hears them and feeds them (compare Job 38:41). Jesus made the same point: “your heavenly Father feeds them. Are you not of more value than they?” (Matthew 6:26). If God answers the cry of a raven chick, he will hear yours.

verseByVerse.quote: His delight is not in the strength of the horse, nor his pleasure in the legs of a man, but the LORD takes pleasure in those who fear him, in those who hope in his steadfast love.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Power and speed do not impress God; he delights in those who fear him and rely on his love.

Not in the strength of the horse. The horse was the ancient war machine, all speed and power. The legs of a man are the runner’s, the athlete’s, the soldier’s strength. These are what the world admires, and they do not delight God.

The LORD takes pleasure in those who fear him. He delights in those who fear him, who take him seriously, and in those who have given up relying on their own strength and wait on his love. That is a comfort for anyone who feels weak or unimpressive: the weakest believer who trusts God’s love delights him more than the mightiest army.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–20 — He Declares His Word to Jacob
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jerusalem is to praise the God whose word rules the weather and who has given that word to his people. He secures the city’s gates, blesses its children, gives peace at its borders and fills it with the best wheat (vv. 12–14). His word runs swiftly across the earth: at his command come snow like wool, frost like ash and hail like crumbs, and at another word everything thaws and the waters flow again (vv. 15–18). Above all, he has declared his word, his statutes and rules, to Israel, a privilege no other nation had (vv. 19–20).
verseByVerse.theology: The same word that sends the snow and melts it has been spoken to God's people, a privilege no other nation had.

verseByVerse.quote: Praise the LORD, O Jerusalem! Praise your God, O Zion! For he strengthens the bars of your gates; he blesses your children within you. He makes peace in your borders; he fills you with the finest of the wheat.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jerusalem is to praise the God who has made her safe, blessed and well fed.

Praise the LORD, O Jerusalem! A third call to praise, now to the city. The rebuilt gates are strong, their bars secure, and inside them are children, blessed. If the psalm comes from the years after the exile, as verse 2 suggests, its first singers had watched those bars go in: Nehemiah’s builders set up the gates of Jerusalem with “its doors, its bolts, and its bars” (Nehemiah 3:3).

The finest of the wheat. Peace at the borders, and the best bread: the gift God longed to give his people in Psalm 81 if only they would listen (Psalm 81:16). Here they have it.

verseByVerse.quote: He sends out his command to the earth; his word runs swiftly. He gives snow like wool; he scatters frost like ashes. He hurls down his crystals of ice like crumbs; who can stand before his cold? He sends out his word, and melts them; he makes his wind blow and the waters flow.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s word brings the winter, and another word sends the thaw.

His word runs swiftly. The word of God is pictured as a runner, racing across the earth to carry out his command.

He gives snow like wool. And what the word does: winter. Snow falls like soft white wool; frost lies over the ground like grey ash; hail is thrown down like crumbs. Who can stand before his cold? God speaks, and “to the snow he says, ‘Fall on the earth’” (Job 37:6).

He sends out his word, and melts them. Then, by the same word, thaw. He speaks again, the ice melts, the wind turns warm, and frozen streams flow. The word that brought the winter ends it. For a believer in a frozen season of life, that is a hopeful thing to know: the God who sent the cold can send the word that melts it.

verseByVerse.quote: He declares his word to Jacob, his statutes and rules to Israel. He has not dealt thus with any other nation; they do not know his rules. Praise the LORD!
verseByVerse.commentary:
The word that commands the snow has been spoken to God’s people, the greatest privilege a nation could have.

He declares his word to Jacob. The climax. His statutes and rules (the ESV notes “just decrees”) were a great privilege. Every nation receives snow and rain; only Israel had received God’s revealed word. Moses asked, “what great nation is there, that has statutes and rules so righteous as all this law” (Deuteronomy 4:8). Paul said the chief advantage of the Jews was that they “were entrusted with the oracles of God” (Romans 3:2).

Now to every nation. That word has now gone out beyond Israel. God “in these last days he has spoken to us by his Son” (Hebrews 1:2), and the risen Christ sent his disciples to “make disciples of all nations” (Matthew 28:19). If you have a Bible in your language, you hold the privilege this psalm celebrates: the God who names the stars and melts the ice has spoken to you. Praise the LORD!

147.title: He Heals the Brokenhearted
147.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 147 is the second of the five hallelujah psalms that close the book (146–150). Psalm 146 praised the God who helps the helpless; this psalm adds the rebuilt city, the stars, the weather, and above all the word God has spoken to his people.

The message. The God who counts and names the stars, sends the snow and melts it, is the same God who gathers outcasts and bandages broken hearts. He is not impressed by strength or speed, but delights in people who fear him and hope in his steadfast love. And his greatest gift is that he has spoken: the word that commands the weather has been given, in words, to his people.

Why it was said. The psalm very likely celebrates the return from exile and the rebuilding of Jerusalem’s walls in the days of Nehemiah (see the introduction): a small, battered community, its outcasts gathered home, its gates newly barred. They needed to know that their God was as great as the heavens and as tender as a nurse, and that being entrusted with his word made them rich.

How the chapter makes its case. Three calls to praise each open a stanza. First (vv. 1–6): praise is good and fitting, for the LORD rebuilds Jerusalem, gathers the outcasts and heals the brokenhearted, the same God who numbers the stars, lifting the humble and casting down the wicked. Second (vv. 7–11): sing with thanksgiving to the God who sends rain and feeds even the young ravens, who takes no pleasure in the strength of horse or man but in those who hope in his steadfast love. Third (vv. 12–20): let Jerusalem praise the God who secures her gates, blesses her children and fills her with the finest wheat; whose word runs out to bring snow, frost and hail and then to melt them; and who has declared that word to Israel as to no other nation.

Where it leads. By promise and by the character of God revealed in Christ. Isaiah promised one anointed “to bind up the brokenhearted” (Isaiah 61:1), and Jesus read those words at Nazareth and said they were fulfilled. And the word God once declared to Jacob alone he has now spoken “by his Son” (Hebrews 1:2), the Word made flesh, and sent out to every nation.

For us. Your heart is never too small for the God of the stars, nor your weakness a barrier to his delight; he takes pleasure in those who simply hope in his love. In a frozen season, wait for the word that melts the ice. And if you hold a Bible in your own language, you hold the privilege this psalm celebrates.
147.theology:
The God who numbers and names the stars heals individual broken hearts (vv. 3-4; Isa 40:26; Matt 10:30), and came in person in Christ to do it (Isa 61:1; Luke 4:21). He cares for the least creatures (v. 9; Matt 6:26).

God delights not in human strength but in those who fear him and hope in his love (vv. 10-11). His word governs creation, sending and ending winter (vv. 15-18; Job 37:6).

The supreme gift is God's revealed word, given first to Israel (vv. 19-20; Deut 4:7-8; Rom 3:2) and now sent to all nations (Matt 28:19).
147.examples: Someone sitting in a hospital corridor after bad news can look up at the night sky and remember verses 3 and 4 together. A believer in a long, frozen season of grief need not pretend it is spring; he can wait for the God who sends the word that melts the ice. And anyone who owns a Bible in his own language holds the privilege once given to Israel alone.

keyVerse.quote: He heals the brokenhearted and binds up their wounds.
keyVerse.note: This verse gives the psalm its title and its heart. Set beside verse 4, it shows that the God who numbers and names the stars stoops to bandage individual wounds. Isaiah promised an anointed one sent “to bind up the brokenhearted” (Isaiah 61:1), and Jesus said that promise was fulfilled in him.

147.reflection:
Read verses 3 and 4 together. Why does it matter that the God who heals broken hearts is the same God who numbers the stars? Which truth do you need more right now?

God takes no pleasure in “the strength of the horse” but in “those who hope in his steadfast love” (vv. 10–11). Where are you tempted to think God is more pleased with your strength, usefulness or performance than with your trust?

The word that sends the snow also melts it (vv. 15–18). How might this encourage someone in a long, frozen season of grief, illness or spiritual dryness?

Verses 19–20 call it a unique privilege to have God’s word. How does this psalm challenge the way you treat your Bible, and how could you share that privilege with people who do not yet have it?

148.text: <sup>1</sup>Praise the LORD! Praise the LORD from the heavens; praise him in the heights!<sup>2</sup>Praise him, all his angels; praise him, all his hosts!<sup>3</sup>Praise him, sun and moon, praise him, all you shining stars!<sup>4</sup>Praise him, you highest heavens, and you waters above the heavens!<sup>5</sup>Let them praise the name of the LORD! For he commanded and they were created.<sup>6</sup>And he established them forever and ever; he gave a decree, and it shall not pass away.<sup>7</sup>Praise the LORD from the earth, you great sea creatures and all deeps,<sup>8</sup>fire and hail, snow and mist, stormy wind fulfilling his word!<sup>9</sup>Mountains and all hills, fruit trees and all cedars!<sup>10</sup>Beasts and all livestock, creeping things and flying birds!<sup>11</sup>Kings of the earth and all peoples, princes and all rulers of the earth!<sup>12</sup>Young men and maidens together, old men and children!<sup>13</sup>Let them praise the name of the LORD, for his name alone is exalted; his majesty is above earth and heaven.<sup>14</sup>He has raised up a horn for his people, praise for all his saints, for the people of Israel who are near to him. Praise the LORD!

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Praise the LORD from the Heavens
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Everything in the heavens is to praise the LORD, because he spoke it into being and keeps it in its place. The psalm calls first on the heavens and the heights (v. 1), then on the angels and the armies of heaven (v. 2), then on the sun, moon and shining stars, which the nations worshipped as gods (v. 3), and finally on the highest heavens and the waters above them (v. 4). The reason follows: he commanded and they were created (v. 5), and he established them for ever by a decree that will not pass away (v. 6).
verseByVerse.theology: Angels, stars and the highest heavens are summoned to praise the one who spoke them into being.

verseByVerse.quote: Praise the LORD! Praise the LORD from the heavens; praise him in the heights! Praise him, all his angels; praise him, all his hosts! Praise him, sun and moon, praise him, all you shining stars! Praise him, you highest heavens, and you waters above the heavens!
verseByVerse.commentary:
All heaven, angels, sun, moon, stars and highest skies, is summoned to praise the LORD, and praises him by being what he made it to be.

Praise him, all his angels. The psalm is a roll call of the universe in two choirs, heaven (vv. 1–6) and earth (vv. 7–14). First the angels, the armies of heaven, who already praise. The Levites prayed in Nehemiah’s day, “the host of heaven worships you” (Nehemiah 9:6), and the psalm joins its voice to theirs.

Praise him, sun and moon. Then the sky itself. The sun, which the nations worshipped as a god, is told to worship the LORD. The stars God numbers and names (Psalm 147:4) are summoned too. Nothing in the sky is too high to bow.

How can a star praise? Not with words, but by shining as God made it to shine. Every star in its course is a note in the song.

You waters above the heavens! These recall Genesis 1:7, the waters above the expanse. The psalm speaks poetically of the skies as we see them; its point is that every part of creation, high and low, is called to praise.

Machine or choir? Many of us have absorbed the idea that the universe is a vast machine, matter obeying laws that need no one behind them: the sun rises every morning because it must. G. K. Chesterton turned that round in Orthodoxy. Repetition, he pointed out, need not mean deadness. Children ask for a thing to be done again and again because they are so full of life, and it may be, he suggested, that God says to the sun every morning, “Do it again,” with the delight of a Father who has never grown tired. Psalm 148 sees the world that way. The sun and moon are not gods, as the nations around Israel thought, and not a dead mechanism, as many now assume. They are a choir, singing simply by being what they were made to be. That is why a Christian can do science with full seriousness and still be astonished by a sunrise (see the note on Genesis 1:1). And the gospel tells us the conductor’s name: “all things were created through him and for him” (Colossians 1:16).

verseByVerse.quote: Let them praise the name of the LORD! For he commanded and they were created. And he established them forever and ever; he gave a decree, and it shall not pass away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The heavens exist by God’s command and keep their order by his unbreakable decree.

For he commanded and they were created. The heavenly choir exists because he spoke. A creature praises its Creator simply by acknowledging where it came from.

He gave a decree. And he keeps them there. The laws that govern the sky, the orbits, the seasons, the rising sun, are his decree. The regularity of the universe shows the faithfulness of God.

Uncertain wording. The last line of verse 6 may mean that God’s decree shall not pass away, or, as the ESV notes, “it shall not be transgressed”: the heavenly bodies never overstep the bounds he set. Either way, the order of the heavens rests on God’s word and does not fail.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–14 — Praise the LORD from the Earth
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Everything on earth, from sea monsters to small children, is to praise the name that alone is exalted, and God’s own people most of all. The earthly choir starts in the depths of the sea (v. 7), moves through the weather obeying his word (v. 8), the mountains and trees (v. 9), wild and tame animals, creeping things and birds (v. 10), and reaches humanity: kings and peoples, princes and rulers, young and old, men and women together (vv. 11–12). His name alone is exalted (v. 13), and he has raised up a horn for the people who are near to him (v. 14).
verseByVerse.theology: From the sea monsters to the smallest child, all earth joins the choir, and God's own people most of all.

verseByVerse.quote: Praise the LORD from the earth, you great sea creatures and all deeps, fire and hail, snow and mist, stormy wind fulfilling his word! Mountains and all hills, fruit trees and all cedars! Beasts and all livestock, creeping things and flying birds!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everything God made on earth, from the ocean depths to storm, mountain, tree and animal, is called to praise him.

You great sea creatures and all deeps. The earthly choir starts at the bottom: the depths of the sea and the great sea creatures, the monsters of the deep, the whales, the things sailors feared.

Stormy wind fulfilling his word! Then the weather: lightning, hail, snow, fog and the stormy wind fulfilling his word. The previous psalm showed God’s word sending the snow and melting it (Psalm 147:15–18). Here the storms praise him by obeying.

Mountains and all hills. Then the land: mountains and hills, orchards and forests; wild animals and farm animals; the things that crawl and the things that fly. The list almost follows the order of the creation days in Genesis 1.

verseByVerse.quote: Kings of the earth and all peoples, princes and all rulers of the earth! Young men and maidens together, old men and children!
verseByVerse.commentary:
No human being is exempt from praising God, from the mightiest king to the smallest child.

Kings of the earth and all peoples. Humanity comes last, and it starts with the most powerful: kings, princes, rulers. The mightiest human being is called to bow and praise with the birds and the cattle.

Young men and maidens together. Then everyone else, paired across every difference; no age, sex or rank is left out. A little child singing to God and an old man singing to God are in the same choir as the sun and the angels.

Where the choir is heading. God has given Jesus “the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father” (Philippians 2:9–11). The name of the LORD that this psalm calls everything to praise is the name now given to the risen Christ. When the crowds praised Jesus on the road into Jerusalem and the Pharisees told him to silence them, he said, “if these were silent, the very stones would cry out” (Luke 19:40).

verseByVerse.quote: Let them praise the name of the LORD, for his name alone is exalted; his majesty is above earth and heaven. He has raised up a horn for his people, praise for all his saints, for the people of Israel who are near to him. Praise the LORD!
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s name alone is exalted, and the psalm ends with the people he has made strong and brought near.

His name alone is exalted. The earthly choir ends with the same line as the heavenly one (compare v. 5), and the reason: his name alone is exalted. Not the sun’s, not the king’s. His majesty is above earth and heaven, above both choirs.

He has raised up a horn for his people. The psalm narrows from the whole universe to one people. A horn, like the horn of a wild ox, is a picture of strength: God has given his people strength and a deliverer, the horn he promised to make “sprout for David” (Psalm 132:17). Zechariah sang as Christ was coming that God “has raised up a horn of salvation for us in the house of his servant David” (Luke 1:69).

Who are near to him. The stars praise from far away; God’s people praise from close up. Paul tells Gentile believers, “you who once were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ” (Ephesians 2:13). All creation sings; the redeemed sing nearest.

Uncertain wording. Praise for all his saints is compressed in Hebrew. It may mean that the horn God raised up gives his saints cause to praise, or that he himself is their praise, the one they boast in. Either way, the people near to him have most reason to praise.

148.title: Praise Him, Sun and Moon
148.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 148 is the third of the five hallelujah psalms that close the book (146–150). After Psalm 147’s God of the weather and the word, the circle widens to everything that exists.

The message. Everything God made exists to praise him, from the angels and the stars down to the sea monsters, the hailstorm, the cattle, kings and little children, because he spoke them into being and holds them in place. His name alone is exalted. And of all his creatures, his own people have the closest reason to praise, for he has raised up a horn of strength for them and drawn them near to himself.

Why it was said. Israel lived among nations that worshipped the sun, moon and stars, feared the sea and the storm, and bowed before kings who claimed to be divine (see the introduction). This psalm takes every one of those rivals and puts it in the choir: they are not gods but fellow creatures, summoned to praise the LORD alongside a small and often overlooked people.

How the chapter makes its case. The psalm is a roll call of the universe in two choirs. The heavenly choir (vv. 1–6): angels and hosts, sun, moon and shining stars, the highest heavens and the waters above them, all called to praise the name of the LORD, because he commanded and they were created and he fixed them by a decree that will not pass away. The earthly choir (vv. 7–12): from the sea creatures and the deeps, through storm, mountain, tree and beast, to kings and children. Both choirs end with the same summons, for his name alone is exalted (v. 13), and the psalm closes by narrowing to one people, near to him, for whom he has raised up a horn (v. 14).

Where it leads. By promise, and by the place Christ holds in creation. The “horn” God raised up for his people is the promised strength of David’s line, and Zechariah sang that God had “raised up a horn of salvation for us in the house of his servant David” (Luke 1:69) as Christ was about to be born. The New Testament names the one through whom all things were made and to whom every knee will bow (Philippians 2:10), and shows the redeemed brought near “by the blood of Christ” (Ephesians 2:13).

For us. You live in a choir, not a machine: every sunrise and every storm is praising God, and so may you. No rank exempts anyone and no age excludes anyone. And if you belong to Christ, you sing not from far off, like the stars, but from close up, as one brought near.
148.theology:
All creation, in heaven and on earth, is called to praise its Creator (vv. 1-12; Neh 9:6; Phil 2:9-11); creatures praise by being and doing what God made them for. His word created them and sustains their order (vv. 5-6, 8).

Human rank and age give no exemption (vv. 11-12). God's name alone is exalted (v. 13).

His own people have a unique reason and nearness: the horn of salvation he has raised up (v. 14; 132:17; Luke 1:69), and they are brought near to him (Eph 2:13).
148.examples: On a clear night, a walk under the stars can become worship: each one is doing exactly what it was made for, and so may we. The child in the pew and the old man beside her are singing in the same choir as the angels. And a believer who feels small in a vast universe may remember that the stars praise from far off, but the redeemed from close up.

keyVerse.quote: Let them praise the name of the LORD, for his name alone is exalted; his majesty is above earth and heaven.
keyVerse.note: This verse gathers both choirs, heaven and earth, into one summons and gives the reason for all of it. Sun, kings and sea monsters were all worshipped somewhere, but only the LORD’s name is exalted. The New Testament shows that name given to the risen Jesus, at whose name every knee will bow (Philippians 2:9–11).

148.reflection:
Psalm 148 calls stars, storms, animals and trees to praise God simply by being what he made them to be. How does seeing creation as a choir rather than a machine change the way you look at the sky, the weather or your own daily work?

The nations worshipped the sun, moon and powerful kings; this psalm puts them all in the choir (vv. 3, 11). What do people around you treat as ultimate, and how does this psalm put it in its place?

“Young men and maidens together, old men and children!” (v. 12). How could your church make sure every age and kind of person is included in its praise?

The stars praise from far off, but God’s people are “near to him” (v. 14), brought near by the blood of Christ (Ephesians 2:13). How should that nearness shape the way you pray and sing this week?

149.text: <sup>1</sup>Praise the LORD! Sing to the LORD a new song, his praise in the assembly of the godly!<sup>2</sup>Let Israel be glad in his Maker; let the children of Zion rejoice in their King!<sup>3</sup>Let them praise his name with dancing, making melody to him with tambourine and lyre!<sup>4</sup>For the LORD takes pleasure in his people; he adorns the humble with salvation.<sup>5</sup>Let the godly exult in glory; let them sing for joy on their beds.<sup>6</sup>Let the high praises of God be in their throats and two-edged swords in their hands,<sup>7</sup>to execute vengeance on the nations and punishments on the peoples,<sup>8</sup>to bind their kings with chains and their nobles with fetters of iron,<sup>9</sup>to execute on them the judgment written! This is honor for all his godly ones. Praise the LORD!

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — The LORD Takes Pleasure in His People
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s people praise him with joy because he delights in them. The psalm calls the assembly of the godly to a new song for a new act of God (v. 1), glad in the LORD as both their Maker, who formed them as a people, and their King, who rules and defends them (v. 2). Their joy may be loud and physical, with dancing, tambourine and lyre (v. 3). Then comes the reason under it all: the LORD takes pleasure in his people and adorns the humble with salvation (v. 4). So the joy follows them home, and they sing even on their beds (v. 5).
verseByVerse.theology: God's people dance and sing because their King takes pleasure in them.

verseByVerse.quote: Praise the LORD! Sing to the LORD a new song, his praise in the assembly of the godly! Let Israel be glad in his Maker; let the children of Zion rejoice in their King! Let them praise his name with dancing, making melody to him with tambourine and lyre!
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s gathered people are to sing a new song of glad, whole-hearted praise to the God who made them and rules them as their King.

Sing to the LORD a new song. After Psalm 148 summoned the whole universe, this psalm turns to the assembly of the godly, a word related to God’s steadfast love: the people who have received his covenant love. A new song answers a new act of God (96:1; 98:1), here perhaps the return from exile. And the King leads it himself: Hebrews hears Christ saying, “in the midst of the congregation I will sing your praise” (Hebrews 2:12). The assembly of the godly never sings alone.

Glad in his Maker, rejoicing in their King. The LORD formed Israel as a people and rules them as King, and they are glad in both: not ashamed of the one who made them, nor resentful of the one who rules them.

Praise his name with dancing. Worship in the Psalms is not always solemn. When God saves his people, joy may be loud and physical: Miriam and the women danced with tambourines at the Red Sea (Exodus 15:20), and David “danced before the LORD with all his might” (2 Samuel 6:14).

Where Christians differ: may we dance in worship? The New Testament gives no rule on it. Churches following the normative principle (worship may include whatever Scripture does not forbid) allow dance in public worship; many holding the regulative principle (public worship should include only what Scripture commands) exclude it.

This commentary’s view. Scripture governs the elements of public worship, and liturgical dance is an addition to them; dancing for joy at a wedding or celebration is another matter. What every service requires is joy, reverence and order (1 Corinthians 14:40).

verseByVerse.quote: For the LORD takes pleasure in his people; he adorns the humble with salvation. Let the godly exult in glory; let them sing for joy on their beds.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The reason for all this joy is that the LORD delights in his lowly people and dresses them in salvation, so their joy goes with them even to bed.

The LORD takes pleasure in his people. Here is the ground of the whole psalm. God does not merely tolerate or use his people; he delights in them, not for their record but because they are his own. Zephaniah said the same: “he will rejoice over you with gladness; he will quiet you by his love; he will exult over you with loud singing” (Zephaniah 3:17). God’s people sing to God, and God sings over his people.

He adorns the humble with salvation. Salvation (the word can also mean victory) is pictured as an ornament God puts on the humble, the lowly who know their need. The proud dress themselves; God dresses the lowly in splendour.

In the Beloved. How can a holy God take pleasure in sinners? Only in his Son, of whom he said, “This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3:17). Joined to Christ, we share the delight that rests on him (Ephesians 1:6). If you have ever thought that God merely endures you, read verse 4 again.

Sing for joy on their beds. In many psalms the bed was a place of tears (6:6). Now joy follows the godly home, and they lie awake not with worry but with song.

Uncertain wording. Why the psalm mentions beds is not certain: most think of rest at night, where the assembly’s joy continues in private; some of the couches on which worshippers reclined at festival meals. Either way, joy in God reaches beyond the hour of worship.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–9 — This Is Honor for All His Godly Ones
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Praise and the coming victory of God belong together. The godly hold the high praises of God in their throats and two-edged swords in their hands (v. 6), to carry out on hostile nations, kings and nobles the judgment God has already written (vv. 7–9a). It is God’s sentence, not private revenge, and to share in it is honour for all his godly ones (v. 9b). For the church this is fulfilled in Christ: our sword is the word of God, the final judgment belongs to the King whose sword comes from his mouth, and his saints share in it only as he gives it.
verseByVerse.theology: Praise and judgment belong together; for the church, the sword is the word, and the judgment is Christ's.

verseByVerse.quote: Let the high praises of God be in their throats and two-edged swords in their hands, to execute vengeance on the nations and punishments on the peoples, to bind their kings with chains and their nobles with fetters of iron, to execute on them the judgment written! This is honor for all his godly ones. Praise the LORD!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Praise of God and the sword of his judgment belong together: God gives his people the honour of carrying out the sentence he has already pronounced on those who oppose him. For Christians the sword is the word of God, and the final judgment belongs to Christ.

Two-edged swords in their hands. Worship and warfare in one line: a verse to read with great care. If the psalm comes from after the exile, its first singers knew what it was to praise with a weapon close by; as Nehemiah’s builders rebuilt Jerusalem’s walls, “each labored on the work with one hand and held his weapon with the other” (Nehemiah 4:17).

The judgment written. In its first setting this was Israel as God’s army, carrying out on hostile nations and their kings the sentence God had pronounced. It was not private revenge, and it was not unlimited: it was God’s verdict, written before they acted, carried out under his command. Like the conquest of Canaan, it was a unique judgment in Israel’s history, never a pattern or licence for violence today.

How not to read it. This text has been badly misused to bless wars, crusades and violence done in God’s name. That is a grave mistake, and the New Testament shows how to read it. First, the church’s warfare is not with physical weapons: “the weapons of our warfare are not of the flesh but have divine power to destroy strongholds” (2 Corinthians 10:4). Our sword is “the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Ephesians 6:17), “sharper than any two-edged sword” (Hebrews 4:12). The praises of God and the preaching of his word go out together, and they bring down strongholds of unbelief.

The judgment belongs to Christ. Second, the final judgment of the nations belongs to Christ himself. John saw him: “From his mouth comes a sharp sword with which to strike down the nations” (Revelation 19:15). The sword comes from his mouth: it is his word. And he has already “disarmed the rulers and authorities” (Colossians 2:15), not by shedding his enemies’ blood but by shedding his own. Believers will share in his judgment only as he shares it with them: “the saints will judge the world” (1 Corinthians 6:2). Until then, “never avenge yourselves” (Romans 12:19).

This is honor for all his godly ones. The humble whom God adorned (v. 4) are the ones he honours. Today that honour is to praise God with full throats, to carry his word into a world in rebellion, and to share one day in the victory of the King who takes pleasure in them. Praise the LORD!

Uncertain wording. What was written? Probably the sentence Scripture had already pronounced on nations that set themselves against the LORD and his people, as in the Song of Moses (Deuteronomy 32:41–43) and the prophets’ oracles against the nations; possibly God’s decree recorded before him (compare Isaiah 65:6). Either way, the judgment is God’s, not theirs to invent.

149.title: A New Song in the Assembly of the Godly
149.overview:
Where we are. Psalm 149 is the fourth of the five “Praise the LORD!” psalms that close the book (146–150). Psalm 148 summoned the whole universe to praise and ended with “the people of Israel who are near to him” (148:14). Now the psalm turns to that people.

The message. The LORD delights in his humble people and crowns them with salvation, so they should praise him with whole-hearted, even physical, joy. Their praise is joined to a sure hope: the God they worship will bring every power that opposes him to justice, and his people will share the honour of his victory.

Why it was said. The psalm most likely comes from the years after the return from exile (see the introduction), when Israel was small, poor and surrounded by hostile neighbours and powerful empires. To such a people it says two things: the King of the universe takes pleasure in you, and the nations that despise you will not have the last word.

How the chapter makes its case. It opens with a call to a new song in the assembly, glad in Israel’s Maker and King, with dancing, tambourine and lyre (vv. 1–3). Then comes the reason: the LORD takes pleasure in his people and adorns the humble with salvation, so let them exult, even on their beds (vv. 4–5). The second half joins praise in the throat to a sword in the hand (v. 6): the godly are to carry out the judgment already written against hostile nations and their kings (vv. 7–9a). This, the psalm ends, is honour for all his godly ones (v. 9b).

Where it leads. By promise and by pattern. The King in whom Zion rejoices has come. Over Jesus the Father said, “This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3:17), and in him God takes pleasure in his people, whom he “has blessed… in the Beloved” (Ephesians 1:6). The risen Christ leads his people’s new song (Hebrews 2:12), and the judgment of the nations promised to David’s son (Psalm 2:8–9) is his. But his sword comes from his mouth (Revelation 19:15), and he disarmed the powers of evil by his own cross (Colossians 2:15). So the church shares his victory by the word now, and by his gift at the end (1 Corinthians 6:2).

For us. If you are in Christ, God does not merely put up with you; he takes pleasure in you. Let that make your worship glad and your nights less anxious. And let the hope of Christ’s final victory steady you, while you fight with no weapon but his word and leave vengeance to him.
149.theology:
God's people rejoice in their Maker and King, and God takes pleasure in them, clothing the humble with salvation (vv. 2-4; Zeph 3:17).

For the church the sword of verse 6 is the word of God (2 Cor 10:4; Eph 6:17; Heb 4:12); the final judgment is Christ's (Rev 19:15), shared by the saints only as he grants it (1 Cor 6:2); and personal vengeance is forbidden (Rom 12:19). The text gives no warrant for violence in God's name.
149.examples: A believer who lies awake at night may turn the hours into song, as verse 5 pictures. A Christian who quietly assumes God only puts up with him can sit with verse 4 until he believes it. And when someone quotes verse 6 to bless violence, the answer is the New Testament's: the church's only sword is the word of God.
