keyVerse.quote: For the LORD takes pleasure in his people; he adorns the humble with salvation.
keyVerse.note: Everything in the psalm rests on this verse. The singing, the dancing and even the honour of sharing God’s victory flow not from the people’s greatness but from God’s delight in them, and the ones he crowns are the humble. In Christ, the beloved Son, that delight rests on everyone who trusts him.

149.reflection:
Verse 4 says the LORD takes pleasure in his people. Do you more often think of God as delighting in you or merely putting up with you, and what difference does being joined to his beloved Son make?

The psalm pictures joy that is loud and public (vv. 1–3) and joy that continues on our beds at night (v. 5). Which comes harder to you, and how could praise reach further into your ordinary days and nights?

Verses 6–9 have been used to justify violence in God’s name. How does the New Testament teach us to read them, and what is the “sword” Christians carry today?

How does knowing that the final judgment belongs to Christ free us both from revenge and from despair when evil seems to be winning?

150.text: <sup>1</sup>Praise the LORD! Praise God in his sanctuary; praise him in his mighty heavens!<sup>2</sup>Praise him for his mighty deeds; praise him according to his excellent greatness!<sup>3</sup>Praise him with trumpet sound; praise him with lute and harp!<sup>4</sup>Praise him with tambourine and dance; praise him with strings and pipe!<sup>5</sup>Praise him with sounding cymbals; praise him with loud clashing cymbals!<sup>6</sup>Let everything that has breath praise the LORD! Praise the LORD!

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–2 — Praise God in His Sanctuary
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Psalter’s last word begins with where and why. God is to be praised in his sanctuary, where his people gather, and in his mighty heavens, where the heavenly host worships him: there is no place where praise is out of place (v. 1). He is to be praised for his mighty deeds, every rescue the psalms have sung, from creation and the exodus onwards, and according to his excellent greatness, which has no limit, so praise never reaches its end (v. 2). Every psalm before this has been a record of these two things: what God has done and who God is.
verseByVerse.theology: Where to praise and why: everywhere God is, for everything he has done and is.

verseByVerse.quote: Praise the LORD! Praise God in his sanctuary; praise him in his mighty heavens!
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Psalter’s last psalm is nothing but praise, and it begins by calling for praise everywhere God is: in his sanctuary on earth and in the heavens above.

Praise the LORD! No lament, no request, no enemies, no questions. In six verses the word praise comes thirteen times. The book that has walked through guilt, grief, fear, exile, doubt and joy ends here.

Praise God in his sanctuary. First, where. The sanctuary is God’s holy place, where his people gather; the heavens are the “expanse” (ESV note) God made on the second day. Praise on earth and praise in heaven: the two choirs of Psalm 148, joined. There is no place where praise is out of place, because there is no place where God is not.

Uncertain wording. In his sanctuary can also be read “in his holiness”. Most take it as a place, parallel to his mighty heavens, but whether the earthly temple or God’s heavenly dwelling is meant is uncertain; the psalm may intend both.
verseByVerse.note: Each of the Psalter's five books ends with a doxology, a short burst of praise to God (41:13; 72:19; 89:52; 106:48); this whole psalm is the doxology that closes the fifth book and the Psalter.

verseByVerse.quote: Praise him for his mighty deeds; praise him according to his excellent greatness!
verseByVerse.commentary:
God is to be praised for what he has done and for who he is, and since his greatness has no limit, neither does the praise he deserves.

Praise him for his mighty deeds. Then why. First for what God has done: creation, the exodus, every rescue in every psalm before this one; the whole Psalter has recorded them. The mightiest were still to come: the cross and resurrection of Jesus, “the mighty works of God” proclaimed at Pentecost (Acts 2:11).

According to his excellent greatness. Then for who God is, in the abundance of his greatness. Praise is to match it, so it never reaches its end.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 3–6 — Let Everything That Has Breath
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Then how and who. God is to be praised with every kind of music Israel knew: the trumpet of the priests, the lute and harp of the Levites, the tambourine and dance of the people, strings and pipe, and finally cymbals, the loud and the louder (vv. 3–5). Nothing is too loud, too joyful or too ordinary to offer him. And the last call widens beyond every musician to everything that has breath (v. 6). Breath is God’s gift on loan to every creature, and the book ends by saying what it is for. The final word is the first word: Praise the LORD!
verseByVerse.theology: Every instrument, and then every living thing: the book of Psalms ends in one great shout of praise.

verseByVerse.quote: Praise him with trumpet sound; praise him with lute and harp! Praise him with tambourine and dance; praise him with strings and pipe! Praise him with sounding cymbals; praise him with loud clashing cymbals!
verseByVerse.commentary:
God is to be praised with every kind of music his people have, from the priests’ trumpet to the loudest cymbals: nothing is too joyful or too ordinary to be offered to him.

Praise him with trumpet sound. Now how: with everything. The trumpet was the ram’s horn the priests blew at festivals and coronations; the strings belonged to the Levite musicians; the tambourine and dance to ordinary people, like the women with Miriam at the sea; the pipe to shepherds. The list moves from the priests’ instruments to the people’s, and builds to the cymbals: every kind of music in Israel is enlisted, for nothing is too loud, too joyful or too ordinary to offer to God.

The house filled with glory. When Solomon’s temple was dedicated, “when the song was raised, with trumpets and cymbals and other musical instruments, in praise to the LORD, ‘For he is good, for his steadfast love endures forever,’ the house, the house of the LORD, was filled with a cloud” (2 Chronicles 5:13). God filled the house with his glory while the music played.

What the psalm is not saying. It is not laying down which instruments churches must use. Paul calls Christians to “psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody to the Lord with your heart” (Ephesians 5:19). The heart is the instrument that matters most.

Where Christians differ: instruments in worship. Some Reformed churches sing unaccompanied, holding that instruments and dance belonged to the temple worship, which ended with the temple. Most churches use instruments.

This commentary’s view. The New Testament does not forbid instruments, and they may rightly serve the praise of God’s people, provided the words come first and all is done in order (Colossians 3:16; 1 Corinthians 14:40). Liturgical dance, however, is an addition to public worship (see the note on 149:1–3).

Uncertain wording. Apart from the ram’s horn, these instruments cannot be identified with certainty: lute and harp are stringed instruments of unknown shape, pipe may be a flute or reed pipe, and the two kinds of cymbals may be smaller clear-toned ones and larger loud ones. The sense is plain: every sound Israel could make.

verseByVerse.quote: Let everything that has breath praise the LORD! Praise the LORD!
verseByVerse.commentary:
The last call is to every living, breathing creature: the breath God lends is given to be returned to him as praise.

Let everything that has breath praise the LORD! Finally, who: not only the priests, Israel or the musicians, but everything that breathes. Think of what breath has meant in these psalms: “When you take away their breath, they die and return to their dust” (104:29); “When his breath departs, he returns to the earth” (146:4). Breath is God’s gift, lent to every creature and taken back. Every breath you take is on loan from God, and it was given to be returned as praise.

The end of the Psalter. The book began, “Blessed is the man who walks not in the counsel of the wicked” (1:1): a blessing, and a choice between two ways. It ends with every breathing thing praising the LORD. Between lie tears and trust, sin and forgiveness, exile and homecoming, and the destination of it all is praise.

The destination reached. John saw it reached. “Every creature in heaven and on earth and under the earth and in the sea” was singing, “To him who sits on the throne and to the Lamb be blessing and honor and glory and might forever and ever!” (Revelation 5:13). And he heard “what seemed to be the voice of a great multitude, like the roar of many waters”, crying, “Hallelujah! For the Lord our God the Almighty reigns” (Revelation 19:6). “For from him and through him and to him are all things. To him be glory forever. Amen” (Romans 11:36).

The breath of the Son. Only one man ever gave every breath back to God as praise. Jesus spent his last breath in trust: “Father, into your hands I commit my spirit!” (Luke 23:46). Risen, he breathed on his disciples and gave them the Holy Spirit (John 20:22), so that people who have wasted their breath might be forgiven and learn to praise.

You are included. If you have breath, you are included in this last verse. Praise the LORD!

150.title: Let Everything That Has Breath Praise the LORD
150.overview:
Where we are. This is the last psalm, the doxology that closes Book Five and the whole Psalter, and the fifth of the closing “Praise the LORD!” psalms (146–150). The book has walked through guilt and forgiveness, fear, grief, exile and homecoming, and here it arrives.

The message. Praise is where everything is heading. God is to be praised everywhere, for everything he has done and everything he is, with every sound we can make, by every creature that breathes. The breath God lends was given to be returned to him as praise.

Why it was said. The Psalms were Israel’s songbook through centuries of trouble, and the collection took its final shape after the exile (see the introduction). A people who had learned to pray in lament needed to know where the road ends. The Psalter does not end with a question or a cry, but with nothing except praise.

How the chapter makes its case. Six verses answer four questions. Where? In God’s sanctuary and in his mighty heavens (v. 1). Why? For his mighty deeds and his excellent greatness (v. 2). How? With every instrument Israel had, from the priests’ trumpet to the people’s tambourine and dance, building to the loud clashing cymbals (vv. 3–5). Who? Everything that has breath (v. 6). The word praise sounds thirteen times.

Where it leads. By promise and fulfilment. The psalm’s call is answered when John hears “every creature in heaven and on earth” singing “To him who sits on the throne and to the Lamb” (Revelation 5:13): the praise of God is now the praise of God and the Lamb. God’s mightiest deeds are the cross and the empty tomb. And Jesus is the one man whose every breath was praise to his Father: he gave up his last breath into his Father’s hands (Luke 23:46), and the risen Lord breathed on his disciples and gave them the Spirit (John 20:22), so that people who had wasted their breath might learn to praise.

For us. If you have breath, this psalm is addressed to you. Praise God in public worship and under the open sky, for what he has done in Christ and for who he is. If you cannot yet sing it, you are still on the road that ends here; even a tired breath can be offered back to him.
150.theology: The Psalter ends in pure praise: where (heaven and earth, v. 1), why (God's deeds and greatness, v. 2), how (every kind of music and the whole heart, vv. 3-5; 2 Chr 5:13; Eph 5:19), and who (everything that has breath, v. 6). Breath is God's gift (104:29-30; 146:4), given to be returned in praise. The book that begins with the blessed man's choice of ways (1:1) ends in the song of all creation to God and the Lamb (Rev 5:13; 19:6), for all things are from him, through him and to him (Rom 11:36).
150.examples: Psalm 150 has a word for the person who cannot yet sing it. The Psalter reached this last psalm only by way of its laments; a grieving believer who has more tears than songs is still on the road that ends here. And meanwhile, every breath, even a tired one, is a gift on loan and can be offered back.

keyVerse.quote: Let everything that has breath praise the LORD! Praise the LORD!
keyVerse.note: The last verse of the Psalter says what all the psalms, and all of life, are for. Breath is God’s gift on loan to every creature, and this verse names its purpose: to be returned to him as praise. The whole book, with all its tears, ends here, and so will history, in the praise of God and the Lamb.

150.reflection:
Psalm 150 answers four questions: where, why, how and who should praise God. Which of the four do you most need to hear this week, and why?

Verse 2 calls us to praise God for his mighty deeds. Which of his deeds, in Scripture and in your own life, would you name first, and how does the cross change the list?

The Psalter reaches this psalm only through many laments. How can this help someone who has more tears than songs right now, and how can a church help them on the way?

Every breath is on loan from God (v. 6). What would it look like for your ordinary days, not only Sunday worship, to be returned to him as praise?
